lessons.title: Arizona Real Estate Salesperson Prelicense — Module AZ-13

chunks.heading: Arizona Real Estate Salesperson Prelicense — Module AZ-13
chunks.excerpt:
# Arizona Real Estate Salesperson Prelicense — Module AZ-13

## Arizona documents, disclosures, rescission and public reports

**Course:** Real Estate Salesperson Prelicense · **Instructional hours: 6.0** of 90.0
**Arizona-specific:** ★ **YES** — this module completes the **27-hour Arizona-specific course** that
**A.R.S. § 32-2124(B)** and **A.A.C. R4-28-401(A)(2)** provide **may not be waived.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Arizona prelicensure credit is available.

> ### The last of the 27 hours
>
> **AZ-10 (7) + AZ-11 (7) + AZ-12 (7) + AZ-13 (6) = 27**, and this is the sixth of them.
>
> Modules AZ-10 through AZ-12 covered licensing, duties and supervision. This module covers **the paper**:
> what a licensee must deliver and when, what a contract must say on its face, when a purchaser may cancel
> without cause, and what a compensation-sharing disclosure must contain. **Every deadline in this module is
> counted in days**, and each one is different from the others — that is the reason they are taught
> together.
>
> **A.A.C. R4-28-701, R4-28-802, R4-28-803 and R4-28-804** were read in the **2026 ADRE Law Book** on
> **2026-08-20**. Every quoted passage below is transcribed from that reading.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Compensation sharing: A.A.C. R4-28-701
chunks.excerpt:
1. State when R4-28-701 requires a compensation-sharing disclosure and what it must name.
2. State the delivery duty in R4-28-802(A).
3. State the offer-submission duty in R4-28-802(B), including what does **not** release the licensee from it.
4. State what a broker must retain under R4-28-802(C).
5. State the contract disclosures R4-28-803 requires where a public report is required, and the two
   earnest-money provisions.
6. State the **seventh calendar day** and **tenth calendar day** rescission rules and which transactions
   each applies to.
7. State the six-month inspection right for an uninspected lot or parcel.
8. State how rescission notices are delivered and deemed received.

---

## A. Compensation sharing: A.A.C. R4-28-701

> *"A real estate broker shall **disclose to all the parties in a transaction, in writing at least THREE
> CALENDAR DAYS BEFORE CLOSING, the name of each employing broker who represents a party to the transaction
> and who will receive compensation from the transaction.**"*

Break the sentence into its five requirements:

| Element | The rule |
|---|---|
| **Who discloses** | A **real estate broker** |
| **To whom** | **All the parties** in the transaction |
| **Form** | **In writing** |
| **When** | **At least three calendar days before closing** |
| **Content** | The **name of each employing broker** who **represents a party** and **will receive compensation** from the transaction |

**"Calendar days,"** not business days. The rule says calendar and this module states nothing else.

**"At least three ... before closing"** is a floor, not a target. A disclosure delivered two days before
closing is late, and lateness cannot be cured at the closing table.

chunks.heading: B. Conveyance documents: A.A.C. R4-28-802
chunks.excerpt:
**The content is narrower than licensees assume.** The rule requires **names of employing brokers** meeting
**both** conditions — representing a party **and** receiving compensation. **The rule as read does not
require the amount**, and **this module states no amount requirement**, because none appears in the text
read.

**Where it sits against Module AZ-11.** R4-28-1101(F) requires **prior written consent of all parties**
before a licensee accepts compensation from, or represents, more than one party; R4-28-1101(G) requires
**prior written acknowledgement** for compensation for related goods or services. **R4-28-701 is a third,
separate obligation** with its own deadline. **Satisfying one does not satisfy another**, and a licensee who
treats them as one document has missed two rules.

---

## B. Conveyance documents: A.A.C. R4-28-802

### B.1 Delivery of signed documents — subsection (A)

> **(A)**: *"Upon execution of any transaction document a licensee shall **expeditiously deliver a legible
> copy of the signed document and final agreement to each party signing the document.**"*

Four elements: **upon execution**, **expeditiously**, a **legible copy**, to **each party signing.**

**"Legible"** is in the rule. A copy that cannot be read is not delivery.

**"Each party signing the document."** Not the client only.

**"Expeditiously"** is the same word R4-28-1101(C) uses for performance generally, and the two work
together: a licensee who does not deliver has both failed (A) here and delayed performance under
R4-28-1101(C) — which, recall, reaches delay **through neglect** as well as intentional delay.

### B.2 Submitting offers — subsection (B)

This is the longest operative sentence in the module and the most consequential. Read it whole.

chunks.heading: B.2 Submitting offers — subsection (B)
chunks.excerpt:
> **(B)**: *"During the term of a listing agreement, a licensee shall **promptly submit to the licensee's
> client all offers to purchase or lease** the listed property. **Upon receiving permission from the seller
> or lessor**, the licensee ... **may disclose to all offerors or their agents the existence and terms of
> all additional offers**. The licensee shall submit to the client **all offers made prior to closing and
> IS NOT RELEASED FROM THIS DUTY BY THE CLIENT'S ACCEPTANCE OF AN OFFER** unless the client instructs the
> licensee **in writing** to cease submitting offers or unless otherwise provided in the listing agreement,
> lease, or purchase contract. The licensee **may voluntarily submit offers ... regardless of any
> limitations contained in the listing agreement and may submit offers after the listing agreement is
> terminated.**"*

| The rule says | What follows from it |
|---|---|
| **Promptly submit all offers** during the listing term | No screening by price, terms, or the licensee's view of seriousness |
| Disclosure of the **existence and terms of additional offers** requires **permission from the seller or lessor** | The licensee does not decide this; the client does. Without permission, no disclosure. |
| **All offers made prior to closing**, and **acceptance of an offer does NOT release the duty** | The duty continues **after** the property is under contract |
| Released only by a **written** instruction from the client to cease, **or** as otherwise provided in the listing agreement, lease, or purchase contract | An oral "stop sending them" does **not** release the duty |
| The licensee **may voluntarily** submit offers regardless of limitations in the listing agreement, **and after the listing agreement is terminated** | A permission, not a duty

chunks.heading: B.3 Retention — subsection (C)
chunks.excerpt:
— it survives limitations and termination |

**The sentence licensees get wrong:** *"is not released from this duty by the client's acceptance of an
offer."* Under contract is not the end of the duty. It continues **until closing** unless one of the two
stated releases applies, and the first of them must be **in writing.**

**And note the direction of the last clause.** The rule permits a licensee to submit offers **despite**
listing-agreement limitations and **after** termination. It converts what a licensee might fear is a breach
of the listing agreement into something the rule expressly allows.

### B.3 Retention — subsection (C)

> **(C)**: The broker shall retain **copies of all receipts and disbursements**, **copies of the executed and
> delivered escrow closing statements**, and **any transaction documents signed by parties or any
> disclosures made as part of the transaction** — **in addition to A.R.S. §§ 32-2151.01 and 32-2174.**

Three categories, stated as **additions** to two statutes.

**The rule points to statutes this project did not read.** R4-28-802(C) says its list is *"in addition to"*
**A.R.S. §§ 32-2151.01 and 32-2174**, and **neither statute was read by this project.** **No retention
period appears anywhere in this module** for that reason — the periods live in those statutes, and this
course states nothing it has not read. **Obtaining them is a submission gate**, and it is recorded as one in
`arizona/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

Compare Module AZ-10, which does state a **five-year** school record requirement — that figure comes from
**A.A.C. R4-28-404**, which *was* read. **The distinction between what has been read and what has not is
maintained item by item throughout this course.**

---

## C. Contract disclosures: A.A.C. R4-28-803

chunks.heading: C.1 The public report legend
chunks.excerpt:
### C.1 The public report legend

Where a **public report** is required, the agreement must carry, **in bold or larger print above the
signature portion**:

> ***"THE DEVELOPER SHALL GIVE A PROSPECTIVE PURCHASER A COPY OF THE PUBLIC REPORT AND AN OPPORTUNITY TO
> READ AND REVIEW IT BEFORE THE PROSPECTIVE PURCHASER SIGNS THIS DOCUMENT."***

Three placement requirements travel with the words: **bold or larger print**, **above the signature
portion**, and **in the agreement itself.**

**A boundary this module holds.** **When a public report is required, what one contains, who issues it, and
the subdivision and unsubdivided-land statutes behind it were NOT read by this project.** This module states
**only that R4-28-803 requires this legend where a public report is required** — it states **no rule about
when that is.** A licensee working in subdivided lots, unsubdivided land, or time-shares takes that question
to the designated broker and to the Department.

### C.2 Where the earnest money goes — subsection (C)

> **(C)**: *"The contract **shall indicate where the earnest money or down payment, if any, will be
> deposited** and shall include the **name of the title company, the name of the broker's trust account, or
> other depository.**"*

**The contract must say where the money goes, by name.** Three named possibilities: the **title company**,
the **broker's trust account**, or **other depository.**

### C.3 Money paid directly to the seller — subsection (D)

chunks.heading: D. Rescission: A.A.C. R4-28-804
chunks.excerpt:
> **(D)**: Where money is paid **directly to the seller and not placed in a neutral escrow depository**, the
> document must **conspicuously disclose** it and **the purchaser shall sign or initial the provision**, and
> a bold or large-print warning must appear in the **public report, purchase contract and agreement of
> sale**:
>
> ***"PROSPECTIVE PURCHASERS ARE ADVISED THAT EARNEST MONEY DEPOSITS, DOWN PAYMENTS, AND OTHER ADVANCED
> MONEY WILL NOT BE PLACED IN A NEUTRAL ESCROW. THIS MONEY WILL BE PAID DIRECTLY TO THE SELLER AND MAY BE
> USED BY THE SELLER. THIS MEANS THE PURCHASER ASSUMES A RISK OF LOSING THE MONEY IF THE SELLER IS UNABLE
> OR UNWILLING TO PERFORM UNDER THE TERMS OF THE PURCHASE CONTRACT."***

**Three requirements, all of which must be met:**

1. **Conspicuous disclosure** in the document;
2. The **purchaser signs or initials the provision** — the rule requires the purchaser's own mark on it,
   not merely a signature on the contract as a whole; and
3. The **bold or large-print warning** in the **public report, the purchase contract, and the agreement of
   sale.**

**Read what the warning actually says.** *"May be used by the seller"* and *"assumes a risk of losing the
money."* The Department wrote a warning that names the risk in plain words rather than describing the
arrangement neutrally, and a licensee should not soften it in explanation.

---

## D. Rescission: A.A.C. R4-28-804

**Two different periods, and a licensee must not confuse them.** They are the two figures most likely to be
transposed under examination pressure, so learn them by the transaction type they attach to.

chunks.heading: D.1 The unimproved-lot and unsubdivided-land legend — subsection (A)
chunks.excerpt:
| Transaction | Deadline | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **An unimproved subdivided lot, or any unsubdivided land** | **By midnight of the SEVENTH calendar day** following the day the purchaser or lessee executed the agreement | **R4-28-804(A)** |
| **A time-share interval** | **By midnight of the TENTH calendar day** following the day the purchaser or lessee executed the agreement | **R4-28-804(B)** |

### D.1 The unimproved-lot and unsubdivided-land legend — subsection (A)

The agreement must contain, **in bold or larger print above the signature portion**, substantially:

> ***"HAS THE LEGAL RIGHT TO RESCIND (CANCEL) THIS AGREEMENT WITHOUT CAUSE OR REASON OF ANY KIND ... BY
> MIDNIGHT OF THE SEVENTH CALENDAR DAY FOLLOWING THE DAY THE PURCHASER OR LESSEE EXECUTED THE AGREEMENT. IF
> THE PURCHASER OR LESSEE DOES NOT INSPECT THE LOT OR PARCEL BEFORE THE EXECUTION OF THE AGREEMENT, THE
> PURCHASER OR LESSEE SHALL HAVE SIX MONTHS TO INSPECT ... AND AT THE TIME OF INSPECTION SHALL HAVE THE
> RIGHT TO UNILATERALLY RESCIND THE AGREEMENT."***

Four things in one legend:

1. **"Without cause or reason of any kind."** The purchaser owes no explanation, and the licensee may not
   ask for one as a condition.
2. **"By midnight of the seventh calendar day following the day"** of execution. The count starts the day
   **after** execution, and the deadline is **midnight**, not the close of business.
3. **The six-month inspection right**, which attaches only where the purchaser or lessee **did not inspect
   the lot or parcel before execution.**
4. **At the time of inspection, the right to UNILATERALLY rescind.** A separate right from the seven-day
   right, triggered by a different fact, exercisable at a different time.

chunks.heading: D.2 Time-share intervals — subsection (B)
chunks.excerpt:
**The six-month right is the one that surprises people.** An uninspected lot carries a rescission right that
does not expire with the seventh day. **Both rights are in the same legend and both must be in the
agreement.**

### D.2 Time-share intervals — subsection (B)

> **(B)**: Rescission ***"by midnight of the TENTH calendar day following the day the purchaser or lessee
> executed the agreement."***

**Ten, not seven**, and the same midnight-and-following-day counting.

### D.3 How the opportunity is given and how notice works — subsection (C)

> **(C)**: An opportunity to exercise rescission ***"shall be provided by conspicuously disclosing the
> complete and current name, address, telephone number, and email address of the seller ON THE FACE of all
> agreements and contracts."*** Notices of rescission **must be in writing** and are **deemed delivered and
> received when hand delivered, sent via email, sent by courier service, or certified mail** — and the
> **seller must issue a receipt if hand delivered.**

**Four items of seller contact detail, complete and current, on the FACE of the agreement:** **name**,
**address**, **telephone number**, **email address.** Buried contact details do not satisfy (C) — the rule
says *"conspicuously"* and *"on the face."*

**Notice must be in writing**, and the rule states four methods that are **deemed delivered and received**:

| Method | Deemed delivered and received |
|---|---|
| **Hand delivery** | Yes — **and the seller must issue a receipt** |
| **Email** | Yes, **when sent** |
| **Courier service** | Yes, **when sent** |
| **Certified mail** | Yes, **when sent** |

chunks.heading: E. The whole module as one page of deadlines
chunks.excerpt:
**"When ... sent"** is what makes this rule work for the purchaser: a notice emailed on the seventh day is
deemed received then, whatever happens afterwards. **The only method carrying an extra obligation on the
seller is hand delivery**, which requires a **receipt.**

---

## E. The whole module as one page of deadlines

Every deadline this module states, in one place, each with the rule that states it. **No period in this
table is stated anywhere else in this course, and none of them is a StateCourse figure.**

| Period | Applies to | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Three calendar days before closing** | Written compensation-sharing disclosure to all parties | **R4-28-701** |
| **Expeditiously, upon execution** | Delivery of a legible copy of a signed document to each signing party | **R4-28-802(A)** |
| **Promptly, and until closing** | Submission of all offers to the client | **R4-28-802(B)** |
| **Midnight of the seventh calendar day** after execution | Rescission — unimproved subdivided lot or unsubdivided land | **R4-28-804(A)** |
| **Six months** to inspect, with a right to rescind at inspection | Purchaser or lessee who did **not** inspect the lot or parcel before execution | **R4-28-804(A)** |
| **Midnight of the tenth calendar day** after execution | Rescission — time-share interval | **R4-28-804(B)** |

**And one period this module deliberately does not state:** the **retention period** for transaction
records. **R4-28-802(C)** points to **A.R.S. §§ 32-2151.01 and 32-2174**; **neither was read**; **no number
appears.**

---

## F. Where the 27 hours end

chunks.heading: Module AZ-13 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Modules AZ-10 through AZ-13 are the **27-hour Arizona-specific course** that **A.R.S. § 32-2124(B)** and
**A.A.C. R4-28-401(A)(2)** provide **may not be waived** for a licensee coming from another state. Reading
the four together, the reason is visible:

| Module | What is genuinely Arizona's own |
|---|---|
| **AZ-10** | 90 hours, **proctored in person**, a **ten-year** completion window, **75 percent**, weekly examinations, and **passing is not a licence** |
| **AZ-11** | A **fiduciary** standard where neighbouring states legislated one away; disclosure of **either party's inability to perform**; an affirmative duty to **obtain** information |
| **AZ-12** | A **progressive disciplinary policy** required by rule; **"owner/agent"**; **43,560 square feet**; **artificial intelligence** named as an advertising medium; **no scrolling** |
| **AZ-13** | **Three calendar days**; a duty to submit offers that **survives acceptance**; **seven days**, **ten days**, and **six months** |

**An experienced out-of-state licensee who skipped these 27 hours would carry the wrong rule into an
Arizona transaction in every one of those rows.** That is what the statute's closing sentence protects
against, and it is why this course labels each of the four modules on its first page.

---

## Module AZ-13 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module AZ-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100 percent**
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; **the 75 percent in R4-28-401(A)(1)** applies to the
**proctored, in-person course examination**, which is a separate event.

---

## Instructor source note for Module AZ-13

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module AZ-13
chunks.excerpt:
Drawn entirely from **A.A.C. R4-28-701, R4-28-802, R4-28-803 and R4-28-804**, read in the **2026 ADRE Law
Book** at re.az.gov on **2026-08-20**, and recorded in `arizona/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** **A.R.S. §§ 32-2151.01 and 32-2174**, to which
R4-28-802(C) refers and which hold the **records retention periods**; the **subdivided land, unsubdivided
land and time-share statutes** in A.R.S. Title 32, Chapter 20, including **when a public report is
required** and **what one contains**; Arizona's **residential seller disclosure statutes**; any **Department
form, contract, or approved legend**; and any **disciplinary ground or penalty.**

**No retention period, public report requirement, subdivision threshold, form version, fee, disclosure
exception, or penalty is stated in this module.** The **three calendar days**, the **delivery and offer
duties**, the **retention categories**, the **public report legend**, the **earnest money provisions**, the
**seventh** and **tenth calendar day** rescission periods, the **six-month** inspection right, and the
**notice methods** are all **transcribed from A.A.C. R4-28-701, R4-28-802, R4-28-803 and R4-28-804.**

lessons.title: Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-01

chunks.heading: Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-01
chunks.excerpt:
# Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-01

## Contract law, and drafting a contract to purchase real property

**Course:** Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing · **Instructional hours: 3.0** of 6.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Arizona credit is available.

> ### What this course is, and why it is not part of the 90
>
> **A.R.S. § 32-2124(L)**: *"An applicant for an original real estate salesperson's license, **after
> completing the requirements of subsection B of this section**, shall provide certification to the
> department **at the time of application** evidencing completion of **six hours of instruction in real
> estate contract law and contract writing**. **This instruction shall include participation by the
> applicant in drafting contracts to purchase real property, listing agreements and lease agreements.**"*
>
> Three things follow from that sentence, and this course is built on all three.
>
> **1. It is additional.** *"After completing the requirements of subsection B"* — subsection (B) is the
> **90 hours**. These six are not a segment of them. **Ninety plus six is ninety-six**, and the Arizona
> Salesperson Prelicense course in this project delivers the 90 separately.
>
> **2. It is proved at application.** The certification goes to the Department **at the time of
> application**, not at examination.
>
> **3. It is not a lecture.** The statute requires **participation by the applicant in drafting**, and names
> **three document types**: **contracts to purchase real property**, **listing agreements**, and **lease
> agreements**. **A course that reads contract law aloud for six hours has not satisfied § 32-2124(L).**
> Every hour of this course therefore end

chunks.heading: Learning objectives
chunks.excerpt:
s in the student drafting, and the drafting is the assessed work.

> ### The drafting requirement drives the design of this course
>
> | § 32-2124(L) names | Delivered in | Drafting exercise |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Contracts to purchase real property** | **Module CW-01**, Part D | The student drafts a purchase contract |
> | **Listing agreements** | **Module CW-02**, Part B | The student drafts a listing agreement |
> | **Lease agreements** | **Module CW-02**, Part C | The student drafts a lease agreement |
>
> **All three are required by the statute, and all three are drafted by the student.** A student who
> completes the reading and not the drafting has **not** completed this course, and the course engine does
> not credit them.

## Learning objectives

1. State the elements a contract requires and apply them to a real estate transaction.
2. Distinguish an offer from an invitation to treat, and a counter-offer from an acceptance.
3. State what the statute of frauds requires of a contract for the sale of an interest in land.
4. Distinguish contingencies, conditions and covenants, and draft each correctly.
5. Draft a contract to purchase real property containing the terms Arizona rule requires on its face.
6. State the Arizona rules that govern what a purchase contract must say and when it must be delivered.

---

## A. The elements, applied to real estate

Contract law is general content, and it is delivered here as the working foundation for drafting rather
than as theory.

chunks.heading: A.1 Offer, and what is not an offer
chunks.excerpt:
| Element | What it means in a purchase contract |
|---|---|
| **Offer** | A definite proposal, communicated, showing intent to be bound on stated terms |
| **Acceptance** | Unqualified assent to those exact terms, communicated to the offeror |
| **Consideration** | Something of legal value each way — the price and the promise to convey |
| **Capacity** | Legal ability of each party to contract |
| **Legality of object** | A lawful purpose |
| **Mutual assent** | A genuine meeting of the minds on the same terms |
| **Writing** | Required for an interest in land — see Part C |

### A.1 Offer, and what is not an offer

A **listing** is not an offer to sell; it is an employment agreement between owner and broker. An
**advertisement** is ordinarily an invitation to make an offer. **The buyer's written purchase contract is
usually the first offer in the transaction**, and the salesperson who prepares it is preparing the offer
itself — which is why drafting error at this stage is expensive.

### A.2 Acceptance must be unqualified

Any change to a term is a **counter-offer**. A counter-offer **rejects** the original offer, and the
original cannot then be accepted unless it is renewed. Students draft counter-offers wrongly more often than
they draft offers wrongly, because a counter-offer written as if it were an acceptance leaves the parties
disagreeing about which document controls.

**Communication matters.** An acceptance signed and left in a drawer has not been communicated. Drafting
practice: state in the document **how and by when** acceptance must be communicated.

### A.3 Capacity and legality

chunks.heading: B. Contingencies, conditions and covenants
chunks.excerpt:
Minors, persons adjudicated incompetent, and entities acting outside their authority raise capacity
questions. **Who signs for an entity, a trust or an estate is a legal question**, and this course states no
Arizona rule about it — **no Arizona statute on capacity, entity authority, or trust or probate signature
authority was read by this project.** The drafting instruction is: **identify the parties exactly as they
hold title, and route any doubt to the designated broker and to counsel.**

---

## B. Contingencies, conditions and covenants

Students conflate these three, and the conflation produces contracts that do not do what the parties
intended.

| Term | What it is | Effect if not satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| **Condition precedent** | An event that must occur **before** a duty to perform arises | The duty never arises |
| **Contingency** | A stated event on which a party's obligation depends, usually with a deadline and a stated remedy | The contract operates as the clause provides — commonly cancellation and return of deposit |
| **Covenant** | A **promise** to do or not do something | Breach — the contract stands, and the remedy is for breach |

**The drafting rule that follows:** a contingency clause is not finished until it states **three** things —
**what event**, **by when**, and **what happens if it does not occur.** A clause naming an event without a
deadline, or a deadline without a consequence, is the single most common defect in student drafting, and it
is checked directly in the Part D exercise.

chunks.heading: C. Writing, and the statute of frauds
chunks.excerpt:
**Time.** Whether time is of the essence changes the effect of a missed date. **This course does not state
an Arizona rule on it** — none was read — and the drafting instruction is to **state the parties' intention
expressly in the document rather than leave it to be inferred.**

---

## C. Writing, and the statute of frauds

A contract for the sale of an interest in land must be **in writing** and **signed by the party to be
charged**, identifying the **parties**, the **property**, and the **price or a means of determining it.**

**Arizona's own statute of frauds was NOT read by this project**, and **no Arizona section number, wording,
or exception is stated in this course.** What is stated here is the general common-law requirement, taught
because it drives the drafting standard: **write it down, completely, and have it signed.**

### C.1 What "identify the property" means when drafting

A street address is an identifier, not a legal description. Module AZ-02 of the 90-hour course delivered the
general content on legal descriptions. **The drafting instruction is to use the description that identifies
the property unambiguously, and never to invent or abbreviate one.**

### C.2 Electronic signatures and delivery

Contracts in practice are signed and delivered electronically. **No Arizona electronic transactions statute
was read by this project** and **none is stated here.** What *is* stated, because it was read, is
**A.A.C. R4-28-802(A)**: *"Upon execution of any transaction document a licensee shall **expeditiously
deliver a legible copy of the signed document and final agreement to each party signing the document.**"*
**"Legible"** and **"each party signing"** are drafting-and-delivery requirements, not clerical ones.

---

chunks.heading: D. Drafting exercise — a contract to purchase real property
chunks.excerpt:
## D. Drafting exercise — a contract to purchase real property

**This is the statutory core of the module.** § 32-2124(L) requires **participation by the applicant in
drafting contracts to purchase real property**, and the student drafts one here.

### D.1 What the draft must contain

The student drafts a complete purchase contract for a stated fact pattern. The draft is assessed against a
checklist in two parts: **general drafting requirements**, and **the Arizona rules read by this project.**

**General drafting requirements:**

1. **Parties**, identified exactly as they hold or will hold title.
2. **Property**, unambiguously identified.
3. **Price**, and how it is to be paid.
4. **Earnest money** — amount, and what happens to it in each outcome.
5. **Closing date**, and what occurs on it.
6. **Possession** — when, and by whom.
7. **Each contingency**, stating **event, deadline, and consequence.**
8. **Title and conveyance** — what is to be delivered.
9. **Prorations** — what is prorated and as of when.
10. **Signature and acceptance provisions**, including **how and by when acceptance is communicated.**

**Arizona rules the draft must satisfy — every one transcribed from a rule this project read:**

chunks.heading: D.2 What the exercise assesses
chunks.excerpt:
| Requirement | Rule |
|---|---|
| The contract **indicates where the earnest money or down payment will be deposited**, and **names** the **title company**, the **broker's trust account**, or **other depository** | **A.A.C. R4-28-803(C)** |
| Where money is paid **directly to the seller and not into neutral escrow**: **conspicuous disclosure**, the **purchaser signs or initials the provision**, and the **bold or large-print warning** appears | **A.A.C. R4-28-803(D)** |
| Where a **public report** is required: the legend **in bold or larger print above the signature portion** | **A.A.C. R4-28-803** |
| Where the transaction is an **unimproved subdivided lot or unsubdivided land**: the rescission legend — **midnight of the seventh calendar day**, and the **six-month** inspection right | **A.A.C. R4-28-804(A)** |
| Where the transaction is a **time-share interval**: **midnight of the tenth calendar day** | **A.A.C. R4-28-804(B)** |
| The **seller's complete and current name, address, telephone number and email address**, **conspicuously, on the face** of the agreement, where a rescission right applies | **A.A.C. R4-28-804(C)** |
| Any **conflict** under R4-28-1101(E) disclosed **in writing before the parties enter any binding agreement** | **A.A.C. R4-28-1101(E)** |

### D.2 What the exercise assesses

The student's draft is reviewed against that checklist. **A draft missing any of the ten general items, or
any Arizona item applicable to the stated fact pattern, is returned for correction.** Completion of this
course requires a completed draft, not an attempted one — the statute requires **participation in
drafting**, and a partial draft is not participation in it.

### D.3 The limits of the exercise, stated to the student

chunks.heading: Module CW-01 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**A licensee is not a lawyer.** Module AZ-11 of the 90-hour course covers **A.A.C. R4-28-1101(K)**, which
requires a licensee to **recommend that the client seek appropriate counsel from insurance, legal, tax and
accounting professionals** regarding pre-possession and post-possession risk. **This course teaches drafting
within a licensee's role**, and states **no rule about the boundary between real estate practice and the
unauthorised practice of law in Arizona** — **no Arizona statute, rule or authority on that boundary was
read by this project**, and inventing one would be worse than silence. **That boundary is a question for the
designated broker and for counsel.**

**No form is prescribed here.** **No Department-approved or industry contract form was read by this
project**, and **this course reproduces none.** The student drafts; the brokerage supplies the forms it
requires under **A.A.C. R4-28-1103(A)**, which obliges the designated broker to maintain **written policies
on the use of disclosure forms and contracts.**

---

## Module CW-01 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in the 90-hour course. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards.** **The drafting exercise in Part D is separately
required and separately recorded** — the engagement items do not substitute for it, because **§ 32-2124(L)
requires participation in drafting.**

lessons.title: Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-02

chunks.heading: Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-02
chunks.excerpt:
# Arizona Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing — Module CW-02

## Drafting listing agreements and lease agreements

**Course:** Real Estate Contract Law and Contract Writing · **Instructional hours: 3.0** of 6.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Arizona credit is available.

> ### The two remaining document types the statute names
>
> **A.R.S. § 32-2124(L)** requires that the six hours *"**include participation by the applicant in drafting
> contracts to purchase real property, listing agreements and lease agreements.**"*
>
> Module CW-01 delivered the first. **This module delivers the other two, and the student drafts both.**
> Completion of this course requires **three completed drafts** — one per document type the statute names.
> Two out of three does not satisfy § 32-2124(L), and the course engine does not credit it.

## Learning objectives

1. State what a listing agreement is as a contract, and who the parties to it are.
2. Draft a listing agreement containing the terms a listing must settle.
3. State the Arizona rules that bear on a listing agreement's operation, including the offer-submission
   duty that survives acceptance.
4. State the elements a lease agreement must settle and the estate it creates.
5. Draft a lease agreement.
6. State what this course does **not** state about Arizona landlord-tenant law, and why.

---

## A. Contract review, applied to employment and to tenancy

Both documents in this module are contracts, so Module CW-01's Parts A through C apply in full: offer,
acceptance, consideration, capacity, legality, mutual assent, and writing. What changes is **what the
contract does.**

chunks.heading: B. Drafting exercise — a listing agreement
chunks.excerpt:
| Document | What it is | Parties |
|---|---|---|
| **Purchase contract** (CW-01) | A contract for the **sale of an interest in land** | Buyer and seller |
| **Listing agreement** (this module) | A contract of **employment** — the owner employs the broker | Owner and **broker** |
| **Lease agreement** (this module) | A contract **creating an estate** — a leasehold — and containing covenants | Landlord and tenant |

**The listing is the one students misclassify.** It is **not** an offer to sell and it does **not** convey
anything. It employs a broker. Module AZ-05 of the 90-hour course developed the agency content this rests
on, and **Module AZ-11 delivered A.A.C. R4-28-1101 — the fiduciary duty the listing brings into being.**

**Who the broker party is.** The employment runs to the **broker**, not to the salesperson personally. A
salesperson drafting a listing writes the **employing broker** in as the party. This is the same distinction
**A.A.C. R4-28-502(E)** enforces in advertising, requiring the **employing broker's legal name or a dba on
the licence certificate**, and the same one **R4-28-1103(D)** rests on in making the employing broker
**responsible for the acts of all licensees.**

---

## B. Drafting exercise — a listing agreement

### B.1 What the draft must settle

The student drafts a complete listing agreement for a stated fact pattern. The draft is assessed against:

chunks.heading: B.2 The Arizona rules the drafter must know are operating
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Parties** — the **owner** as they hold title, and the **employing broker**.
2. **Property**, unambiguously identified.
3. **Price and terms** the owner will accept.
4. **The broker's authority** — what the broker is employed to do.
5. **Term** — a **definite beginning and a definite end.**
6. **Compensation** — amount or rate, and **what earns it.**
7. **Cooperation and compensation with other brokers**, if any.
8. **Owner's undertakings** — what the owner will do or refrain from doing.
9. **Any limitation the owner places on the broker's authority**, expressly stated.
10. **Signatures**, with the broker party correctly named.

**Item 5 is checked strictly.** A listing without a stated end date has no stated end date, and no rule read
by this project supplies one. **This course states no maximum listing term for Arizona and no rule that a
listing terminates automatically** — **no Arizona statute or rule on listing duration was read by this
project**, so **none is stated.** The drafting instruction is therefore: **state the term expressly.**

### B.2 The Arizona rules the drafter must know are operating

A listing agreement in Arizona operates against rules the drafter does not get to vary. **Each of these was
read by this project and is transcribed in `arizona/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.**

chunks.heading: B.2 The Arizona rules the drafter must know are operating
chunks.excerpt:
| Rule | What it does to a listing |
|---|---|
| **R4-28-1101(A)** | The listing creates a **fiduciary duty** to the client, and a duty to **deal fairly with all other parties** |
| **R4-28-802(B)** | The licensee must **promptly submit all offers** during the term — and **is not released from that duty by the client's acceptance of an offer**, unless the client instructs **in writing** to cease, **or as otherwise provided in the listing agreement** |
| **R4-28-802(B)**, continued | Disclosure of the **existence and terms of additional offers** requires the **seller's or lessor's permission** |
| **R4-28-802(B)**, continued | A licensee **may voluntarily submit offers regardless of limitations in the listing agreement, and after the listing agreement is terminated** |
| **R4-28-1101(E)** | Conflicts — including that the **licensee is acting as a principal** or that the owner is in the **licensee's or designated broker's immediate family** — must be disclosed **in writing before any binding agreement** |
| **R4-28-1101(F)** | Compensation from, or representation of, **more than one party** requires the **prior written consent of all parties** |
| **R4-28-701** | The **compensation-sharing disclosure** — in writing to **all parties**, at least **three calendar days before closing**, naming each employing broker who represents a party and will receive compensation |
| **R4-28-502(B)** | If the licensee owns the property, the advertisement must disclose the licence and carry **"owner/agent"** |

**Two drafting consequences follow directly, and both are assessed.**

chunks.heading: C. Drafting exercise — a lease agreement
chunks.excerpt:
**First**, R4-28-802(B) names the listing agreement itself as a place where the continuing offer-submission
duty may be *"otherwise provided."* A drafter who intends the duty to end on acceptance must **say so in the
listing**; a drafter who says nothing leaves the duty running **until closing.** Either is permissible; what
is not permissible is not knowing which the document does.

**Second**, the same subsection permits a licensee to submit offers **despite limitations in the listing
agreement** and **after termination.** A limitation drafted into the listing therefore does not do what an
inexperienced drafter may expect it to do.

---

## C. Drafting exercise — a lease agreement

### C.1 What a lease creates

A lease conveys a **leasehold estate** — possession for a term — and simultaneously contains **covenants**
between the parties. Module AZ-01 of the 90-hour course delivered the general content on leasehold estates.
The drafting consequence is that a lease must settle both halves: **the estate** (who has possession, of
what, for how long) and **the promises** (who does what during it).

### C.2 What the draft must settle

chunks.heading: C.3 A boundary this module states plainly
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Parties** — landlord and tenant, identified exactly.
2. **Premises** — what is let, including anything included or excluded.
3. **Term** — beginning and end, and what happens at the end.
4. **Rent** — amount, when due, where and how paid.
5. **Deposits** — amount, purpose, and the conditions of return.
6. **Use** — what the premises may be used for.
7. **Maintenance and repair** — allocated between the parties, item by item.
8. **Utilities and services** — who pays and who arranges.
9. **Assignment and subletting** — permitted, prohibited, or conditional.
10. **Default and remedies** — what constitutes default and what follows.
11. **Access by the landlord** — when, and on what notice.
12. **Signatures.**

### C.3 A boundary this module states plainly

**Arizona's landlord-tenant statutes were NOT read by this project.** Neither residential nor commercial
landlord-tenant law appears in the readings file, and **this course therefore states no Arizona rule on
security deposit limits, deposit return periods, notice periods, entry notice, habitability, late fees,
eviction procedure, retaliation, or any tenant remedy.**

**Nothing in the list at C.2 is an Arizona legal requirement**, and the list does not present itself as
one — it is a **drafting checklist of what a lease must settle**, which is a different thing. **Any figure
or period a student writes into items 3, 5, 10 or 11 must come from the brokerage's forms and from counsel,
not from this course**, and the exercise instruction says so on its face.

**This is a submission gate**, recorded as one in `arizona/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`. A version
of this course that states Arizona landlord-tenant requirements must first read those statutes.

### C.4 One Arizona rule that does apply, and was read

chunks.heading: D. The three drafts, and what completion of this course requires
chunks.excerpt:
**A.A.C. R4-28-802(B)** covers offers **to purchase or lease**, and R4-28-802(A) requires expeditious
delivery of a **legible copy of the signed document and final agreement to each party signing** — leases
included. **A.A.C. R4-28-1101(J)** applies with particular force in leasing: a licensee shall not **permit
or facilitate access to or occupancy in a person's real property without prior written authorization from
the owner.** A salesperson handing over keys is inside that rule.

---

## D. The three drafts, and what completion of this course requires

| Statutory document type | Module | Part | Required for completion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contracts to purchase real property** | **CW-01** | **D** | **Yes** |
| **Listing agreements** | **CW-02** | **B** | **Yes** |
| **Lease agreements** | **CW-02** | **C** | **Yes** |

**All three, because A.R.S. § 32-2124(L) names all three.** The course engine records each draft
separately, and **credit for this course is not issued unless all three are recorded complete.** Reading
without drafting does not satisfy the statute, and this course does not certify it as though it did.

**What the certificate would say, and what it cannot say yet.** **A.R.S. § 32-2135(B)** governs certificates
of course attendance, and **this school and this course are not approved.** **No certificate can issue**,
and **no Arizona credit is available**, until approval is recorded. That status is stated on the first page
of every module of this course for exactly that reason.

---

## Module CW-02 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module CW-02
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items, delivered as in the 90-hour course. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards.** **The drafting exercises in Parts B and C are
separately required and separately recorded**, as Part D of CW-01 is — **§ 32-2124(L) requires
participation in drafting**, and engagement items do not substitute for it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module CW-02

The statutory basis is **A.R.S. § 32-2124(L)**, read at azleg.gov on **2026-08-20**. The Arizona rules in
Parts B and C are **A.A.C. R4-28-701, R4-28-802, R4-28-1101 and R4-28-502**, read in the **2026 ADRE Law
Book** at re.az.gov on the same date. The contract and drafting content is otherwise **general content**,
and is labelled as such.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** **Arizona's residential and commercial
landlord-tenant statutes**, in their entirety; any **Arizona statute or rule on listing agreement
duration**; **Arizona's statute of frauds**; any **Department-approved or industry listing or lease form**;
**A.R.S. § 32-2151 and the trust account statutes** bearing on deposits; and any **Department prescribed
content for the six-hour course**, if one exists.

**No security deposit limit, deposit return period, notice period, entry notice, habitability standard,
late fee, eviction procedure, maximum listing term, form version, or fee is stated in this module.** The
**six hours**, the **three document types**, and the **participation in drafting** requirement are
**transcribed from A.R.S. § 32-2124(L)**; every Arizona rule cited in Parts B and C is **transcribed from
the A.A.C. rule named beside it.**

chunks.heading: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 01
chunks.excerpt:
# Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 01

## The real estate profession and California regulatory structure

**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Assignment time:** 180 instructional minutes
**Regulatory status:** Not approved; no California credit is available.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why real property is treated differently in law from other assets, and identify the consequences that follow from immobility, durability, and uniqueness.
- Describe the Department of Real Estate's jurisdiction and the consumer-protection purpose that shapes it.
- Distinguish the broker's and the salesperson's roles, and explain why the salesperson acts for the broker rather than for the client directly.
- Identify the boundary between real estate practice and the unauthorized practice of law, and apply it to specific questions a consumer asks.
- Rank the sources of California real estate law and determine which controls a given question.
- Identify each participant in a residential transaction, what each is accountable for, and where the accountability gaps occur.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: the asset and the regulator | 55 | Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved |
| Guided reading: license structure and professional scope | 50 | Sections 3-4 viewed |
| Guided reading: sources of law and transaction participants | 45 | Sections 5-6 viewed |
| Applied scenario and decision memorandum | 20 | Written response submitted |
| Lesson assessment | 10 | Five scored items submitted |
| **Total** | **180** | **One of 15 separate lesson assignments** |

## 1. Real property as an economic and legal asset

### 1.1 Why real property gets its own body of law

chunks.heading: 1.2 The economic consequences
chunks.excerpt:
Almost everything in this course follows from three physical characteristics of land, and it is worth establishing them at the start because they explain rules that otherwise look arbitrary.

**Immobility.** Land cannot be moved. Therefore the law that governs a parcel is the law of the place where it sits, disputes about it are heard where it sits, and value depends heavily on what surrounds it — none of which is true of a car or a share of stock.

**Indestructibility.** The land itself endures, though improvements do not. Interests in it can therefore be carved up across time — a life estate now and a remainder afterwards, a lease for ten years, an easement forever — in ways that would be meaningless for a perishable asset.

**Uniqueness.** No two parcels occupy the same location. This is why a buyer who is denied the parcel he contracted for may seek the parcel itself rather than damages, and why valuation is an act of judgment rather than a lookup.

### 1.2 The economic consequences

Three more characteristics shape how the market behaves, and licensees who understand them give better advice than those who do not.

| Characteristic | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Scarcity** | Supply in a desirable location cannot be expanded to meet demand; price responds accordingly |
| **Improvements** | A single improvement — or a single deterioration — changes the value of surrounding parcels |
| **Permanence of investment** | Capital committed to land is committed for a long time, so decisions about it are slow to reverse |
| **Area preference** | Buyers pay for location, meaning access, surroundings, and reputation, not merely coordinates |

chunks.heading: 1.3 The bundle of rights
chunks.excerpt:
**Immobility also produces the market's defining inefficiency.** Real estate markets are local, information about them is imperfect, transactions are infrequent, and each property is different. That combination is precisely why licensed intermediaries exist and why the standard of care asks what a competent professional would have done rather than what the client could have discovered.

### 1.3 The bundle of rights

Ownership of real property is not one right. It is a collection, conventionally described as a bundle:

- The right to **possess** — to occupy and control.
- The right to **use** — subject to law and to private restrictions.
- The right to **transfer** — to sell, gift, or devise.
- The right to **encumber** — to pledge as security or grant lesser interests.
- The right to **exclude** — to keep others out.

Each stick can be separated and dealt with independently. A landlord transfers possession and use while retaining transfer and encumbrance. A borrower encumbers without transferring possession. An easement holder receives a specific use without possession at all.

> **Why this framework earns its place in the first lesson.** Almost every later topic is an operation on the bundle. A lease separates possession. A deed of trust separates a security interest. An easement separates a use. A covenant restricts use. Eminent domain removes the whole bundle. Students who hold this picture find the later material coherent rather than a list.

### 1.4 Real property versus real estate versus land

The terms are used loosely in conversation and precisely in documents.

chunks.heading: 1.5 The market these characteristics produce
chunks.excerpt:
**Land** is the surface, what lies beneath it, and the airspace above it, within legal limits. **Real estate** is land plus permanent improvements. **Real property** is real estate plus the bundle of legal rights in it.

The distinction that matters in practice is between real property and **personal property**, because they transfer differently, are financed differently, and are described differently. Lesson 02 takes that up in detail.

### 1.5 The market these characteristics produce

The legal treatment in Section 1.1 and the economic consequences in Section 1.2 combine to produce a market that behaves unlike almost any other, and the differences explain most of what a licensee spends his time on.

| Characteristic | What follows |
|---|---|
| **Immobility** | **Every market is local**, and there is no national real estate market in any operational sense. Conditions two miles away can differ from conditions here, which is why Lesson 05 of the practice course spends its first section defining a market area. |
| **Fixed short-run supply** | New supply takes years — entitlement, financing, construction. **Demand moves in weeks and supply cannot answer**, which is why prices move sharply rather than smoothly. |
| **Heterogeneity** | No two parcels are identical, so **there is no single price and no ticker.** Value is estimated by comparison, which is a judgment rather than a lookup. |
| **High transaction costs** | Commissions, financing costs, title, escrow, moving, and time. **This suppresses trading**, which means the market has far fewer data points than a liquid market and each one matters more. |
| **Information asymmetry** | The seller knows the property; the buyer does not. **Almost the entire disclosure framework exists to address this one line**, and it is why

chunks.heading: 1.6 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
Lesson 09 of the practice course is as long as it is. |
| **Financing dependence** | Most transactions require credit, so **credit conditions transmit directly into prices** and a change in rates moves the market without anything happening to any property. |
| **Durability** | Buildings last decades, so **most of what will be sold in twenty years already exists**, and its condition, location, and design were determined by decisions made long ago. |
| **Government influence** | Zoning, building standards, taxation, environmental regulation, and public investment shape what may be built, where, and at what cost. |

**Two conclusions a licensee should carry out of this table.**

**The information asymmetry is the licensee's actual job.** Buyers cannot evaluate what they cannot see, and the entire apparatus of disclosure, investigation, and professional duty exists to close a gap the market cannot close by itself. **A licensee who understands his function as closing that gap will make correct decisions in situations no rule covers.**

**Illiquidity is why mistakes are expensive.** In a liquid market an error is corrected by selling. **Here the correction costs a substantial fraction of the asset's value and takes months**, which is why the consumer's decision has to be right the first time, and why the framework insists so heavily that information arrive before decisions rather than after them.

### 1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to name a rule from later in this course and trace it back to immobility, indestructibility, or uniqueness.

## 2. DRE jurisdiction and consumer protection

### 2.1 What the Department does

chunks.heading: 2.2 The purpose behind the structure
chunks.excerpt:
The California Department of Real Estate administers the state's real estate license law. Its functions include examining and licensing applicants, setting and enforcing standards of conduct, investigating complaints, taking disciplinary action against licensees, and approving the education that supports licensure — including the course you are reading.

The Department is led by the Real Estate Commissioner, who is responsible for enforcing the license law and who issues the regulations that implement it.

### 2.2 The purpose behind the structure

The license law exists to protect the public. That single sentence explains features of the system that otherwise look excessive:

- **Why licensing is required at all.** Consumers transact infrequently, in a market with imperfect information, on the largest asset most of them will own.
- **Why the broker is responsible for the salesperson.** The consumer deals with an individual; the accountable party must be one with the resources and the duty to supervise.
- **Why trust fund rules are strict.** The money is not the licensee's, and the harm from mishandling is immediate and often unrecoverable.
- **Why education is required and approved.** Competence cannot be verified transaction by transaction, so it is established in advance.
- **Why advertising is regulated.** A consumer cannot evaluate a claim about a property they have not seen, made by a person whose accountability they cannot trace.

### 2.3 What is licensed activity

chunks.heading: 2.4 Discipline and what triggers it
chunks.excerpt:
Broadly, acting for another, for compensation or the expectation of it, in connection with real property transactions — listing, selling, buying, leasing, soliciting listings or buyers, negotiating loans secured by real property, and collecting rents or managing property for others, among other activities.

Two consequences follow immediately.

**The activity is what matters, not the title.** A person who performs licensed activity without a license does not escape the requirement by calling themselves an assistant, a consultant, or a marketing coordinator.

**Compensation is central.** The expectation of compensation is what converts helping a friend into licensed activity, which is why arrangements to pay unlicensed people for referrals or for tasks that shade into negotiation are a recurring compliance problem.

### 2.4 Discipline and what triggers it

The Department may investigate and may take action against a license. In practice the recurring categories are worth knowing early, because they are the topics this course keeps returning to:

| Category | Typical conduct |
|---|---|
| **Misrepresentation** | Stating as fact something unverified or untrue, or concealing a material fact |
| **Trust fund violations** | Commingling, conversion, shortages, inadequate records |
| **Failure to supervise** | A broker who did not review files, enforce policy, or notice a pattern |
| **Unlicensed activity** | Performing licensed acts, or compensating an unlicensed person for them |
| **Discrimination** | Conduct violating fair housing obligations |
| **Dishonest dealing** | Conduct demonstrating unfitness, including outside a transaction |

chunks.heading: 2.5 The Real Estate Recovery Account
chunks.excerpt:
Note that most of these do not require anyone to have set out to defraud. Careless misrepresentation and inadequate trust fund records are the ordinary cases.

### 2.5 The Real Estate Recovery Account

California maintains an account, funded by license fees, from which a consumer who obtains a judgment against a licensee for fraud, misrepresentation, deceit, or conversion of trust funds may seek payment where the judgment cannot be collected from the licensee.

Two features are worth understanding. It is a **last resort**, available after the consumer has pursued the licensee. And payment from it has consequences for the licensee, whose license is affected until the account is reimbursed.

### 2.6 How a complaint actually proceeds

Section 2.4 lists what triggers discipline. Licensees rarely learn what the process looks like from the inside, and the gap produces two errors: panic at the first contact, and improvisation at the moment improvisation is most costly.

**The general shape**, stated at the level of generality that is accurate:

chunks.heading: 2.6 How a complaint actually proceeds
chunks.excerpt:
1. **A complaint arrives**, from a consumer, another licensee, a lender, a title company, or an agency. **It does not require that anyone lost money**, and it does not require that the complainant be the licensee's own client.
2. **A review determines whether the allegations, if true, would describe a violation.** Many complaints end here — not because the licensee did well, but because the conduct described is not something the Department regulates.
3. **An investigation gathers facts**, which means requests for documents, for a written response, and sometimes an interview.
4. **A determination follows** — no action, an informal resolution, or a formal accusation initiating an administrative proceeding.
5. **An administrative proceeding** carries process rights, and its outcomes range through a range of sanctions up to revocation, with conditions and restrictions available in between.

**What matters most to the licensee happens at step three, and it happens in the first week.**

**The response is prepared with the broker and, where appropriate, counsel.** A licensee who answers a document request personally, quickly, and in his own voice will say something he did not need to say.

**The file is what answers the questions.** Everything in Section 6 of this lesson exists for this moment: dated documents, evidenced delivery, sourced statements, and contemporaneous notes. **The investigation asks what happened and when, and the file answers or it does not.**

**Preservation is immediate and total.** Nothing is deleted, tidied, reorganized, or "cleaned up." **This includes text messages, informal notes, and drafts** — and it includes material that is unflattering.

chunks.heading: 2.8 The statute itself: what makes activity licensed
chunks.excerpt:
**Nothing is created after the fact and presented as contemporaneous.** This is the line the practice course returns to repeatedly, and it is worth stating here in its regulatory form: **a documentation gap produces a finding; a fabricated document produces a different proceeding about a different subject**, and the second one is the one that ends a career.

> **The most useful thing to know about this process in advance** is that it is largely documentary. **The licensee's recollection, sincerity, and explanation carry very little weight against a record that says something else, and they carry almost none against a record that says nothing at all.**

### 2.8 The statute itself: what makes activity licensed

Section 2.3 described licensed activity in functional terms — what the person did, and whether it was for compensation. That description is accurate, but a licensee who has only the description will eventually meet a situation the description does not settle. The statute settles it, and it is short enough to read.

**Business and Professions Code § 10130** creates the prohibition:

> *"It is unlawful for any person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within this state without first obtaining a real estate license from the department, or to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a mortgage loan originator within this state without having obtained a license endorsement."*

chunks.heading: 2.9 The five categories, in the statute's own words
chunks.excerpt:
**Four verbs, and the fourth is the one to notice.** It is unlawful to *engage in the business of*, to *act in the capacity of*, to **advertise as**, and to *assume to act as*. Advertising is listed separately from acting. A person who advertises real estate brokerage services and never takes a single call has violated § 10130 on the face of the section, because the advertising is itself a prohibited act rather than evidence of one.

The section closes by making enforcement somebody's job rather than nobody's: the Commissioner *"may prefer a complaint for violation of this section before any court of competent jurisdiction,"* and *"it is the duty of the district attorney of each county in this state to prosecute all violations of this section in their respective counties."* Unlicensed practice is not merely a licensing matter to be sorted out administratively. It is a crime that a district attorney has a duty to prosecute.

### 2.9 The five categories, in the statute's own words

**Business and Professions Code § 10131** defines the broker by describing the acts:

> *"A real estate broker within the meaning of this part is a person who, **for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, regardless of the form or time of payment**, does or negotiates to do one or more of the following acts for another or others:"*

**Read the qualifying clause before the list.** Three conditions are packed into it, and each is doing work:

chunks.heading: 2.9 The five categories, in the statute's own words
chunks.excerpt:
- **"For a compensation or in expectation of a compensation."** The expectation is enough. A person who performs a listed act hoping to be paid, and is never paid, has still performed it for compensation within the meaning of the section.
- **"Regardless of the form or time of payment."** A referral fee, a reduced rent, a share of a business, a favour returned later — the Legislature closed the form question deliberately. A person who says "I wasn't paid a commission" has answered a question the statute does not ask.
- **"For another or others."** This is the boundary that keeps an owner selling their own property outside the section, and it is why the owner exemption is structural rather than a carve-out: an owner acting for themselves is not acting for another.

The five categories then follow:

> **(a)** *"Sells or offers to sell, buys or offers to buy, solicits prospective sellers or buyers of, solicits or obtains listings of, or negotiates the purchase, sale, or exchange of real property or a business opportunity."*
>
> **(b)** *"Leases or rents or offers to lease or rent, or places for rent, or solicits listings of places for rent, or solicits for prospective tenants, or negotiates the sale, purchase, or exchanges of leases on real property, or on a business opportunity, or **collects rents** from real property, or improvements thereon, or from business opportunities."*
>
> **(c)** *"Assists or offers to assist in filing an application for the purchase or lease of, or in locating or entering upon, lands owned by the state or federal government."*
>
> **(d)** *"Solicits borrowers or lenders for or negotiates loans or collects payments or performs services for borrowers or lenders or note owners in connection with loans secured directly or collaterally by liens on r

chunks.heading: 2.9 The five categories, in the statute's own words
chunks.excerpt:
eal property or on a business opportunity."*
>
> **(e)** *"Sells or offers to sell, buys or offers to buy, or exchanges or offers to exchange a real property sales contract, or a promissory note secured directly or collaterally by a lien on real property or on a business opportunity, and performs services for the holders thereof."*

**Three things in that list surprise people who learned the subject from a summary.**

**Subdivision (b) reaches rent collection.** Collecting rents for an owner, for compensation, is licensed activity in its own right. It appears in the same subdivision as leasing because the Legislature treated the management of tenancies as brokerage, and it is the reason Assignment 15's treatment of property management is a treatment of licensed activity rather than of a related trade.

**Subdivision (d) reaches loan activity, and reaches it broadly.** Soliciting borrowers *or* lenders; negotiating loans; collecting payments; performing services for note owners. This is the statutory foundation of the Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending course, and it is why a licensee who "just refers people to a lender" for a fee should read (d) before deciding the arrangement is outside the section.

**"Offers to" appears in every operative clause.** Offers to sell, offers to buy, offers to lease, offers to assist, offers to exchange. The offer is the act. A transaction that never happens does not retroactively unlicense the conduct that preceded it.

chunks.heading: 2.10 A worked application of § 10131
chunks.excerpt:
**Section 10131 also settles the licence question in the direction people least expect.** Because the section defines the *broker*, and because a salesperson may only act through an employing broker, the answer to "does this activity need a licence" is always found by asking whether it is one of these acts, done for another, for compensation or the expectation of it. The person's title, their business card, their intentions and the outcome of the deal are all outside the test.

### 2.10 A worked application of § 10131

> A software developer builds a website that matches apartment seekers with landlords. Landlords pay a monthly fee to list. The developer never speaks to a tenant, never shows a unit, never signs anything, and never handles money other than the listing fees.
>
> A second person, working from the same website, telephones prospective tenants on behalf of listed landlords, describes the units, arranges viewings, and receives $200 from the landlord for each tenancy that results.

**The first is the harder question, and the answer turns on what "places for rent" and "solicits listings of places for rent" mean in subdivision (b).** A platform that accepts a landlord's listing for a fee is, on the words, soliciting listings of places for rent for compensation. Whether a given website falls inside § 10131 is a question that has been litigated and legislated around, and it is exactly the sort of question a licensee must route to counsel rather than resolve from a course. **What the course can say with confidence is that the question is a real one and that "we are only a website" is not an answer to it.**

chunks.heading: 2.11 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**The second is not a hard question at all.** Soliciting for prospective tenants, negotiating a tenancy, and being paid per result is squarely within subdivision (b), performed for another, for compensation. The $200 is a compensation regardless of its form. The person needs a licence and must act under an employing broker. The website's business model does not change what the second person is doing.

**The professional habit this builds:** when an arrangement feels novel, read § 10131 and ask whether the conduct is on the list, rather than asking whether the arrangement resembles brokerage. The section is a list of acts. Novel business models are made of the same acts.

### 2.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the purpose of the license law and use it to explain why a particular rule takes the form it does.

## 3. Broker and salesperson license relationships

### 3.1 The two licenses

A **broker** may conduct licensed activity independently and may employ salespersons. A **salesperson** may conduct licensed activity **only for and under a responsible broker.**

The requirements for the broker license are higher — more education, an examination, and experience — because the broker carries responsibility for everything done under the license.

### 3.2 The relationship that surprises new licensees

> **The salesperson's client is the broker's client. The salesperson's contract is the broker's contract. The salesperson's compensation comes from the broker.**

A listing agreement is between the seller and the **brokerage**, not the individual. A buyer representation agreement is likewise the brokerage's. The salesperson performs the work; the brokerage is the party.

chunks.heading: 3.3 Supervision is an affirmative duty
chunks.excerpt:
This is not a technicality. It determines who may cancel a listing, who is exposed when something goes wrong, who owns the transaction file, and why assigning a second salesperson to the other side of a transaction does not eliminate a dual agency question — both salespersons act for the same brokerage, which is the agent.

### 3.3 Supervision is an affirmative duty

The responsible broker must exercise reasonable supervision over the activities of the salespersons. In practice supervision means an actual system:

1. **Written policies** covering the conduct the brokerage requires.
2. **File review**, close enough in time to catch a problem before it matures.
3. **Advertising review** before publication.
4. **Trust fund controls**, including reconciliation.
5. **Training**, particularly for new licensees.
6. **An escalation path** a salesperson can actually use.

A policy nobody follows is not supervision, and it is not a defense for anyone — not for the broker who wrote it and not for the salesperson who departed from it.

### 3.4 Independent contractor status does not reduce supervision

Many salespersons are treated as independent contractors for tax purposes. That characterization addresses the tax and compensation relationship. **It does not reduce the broker's supervisory duty or the salesperson's obligation to act under the broker.**

A brokerage that responds to a supervision question with "our agents are independent contractors" has answered a different question.

### 3.5 What a salesperson may not do

chunks.heading: 3.6 A worked supervision failure
chunks.excerpt:
- Act for more than one responsible broker at a time.
- Accept compensation for licensed activity from anyone other than their responsible broker.
- Contract in their own name for licensed activity — the listing, the lease, and the representation agreement belong to the brokerage.
- Continue to act after the relationship with the broker ends.

That third one recurs in property management, where a salesperson signing leases in her own name is a common and serious audit finding.

### 3.6 A worked supervision failure

> **The facts.** A brokerage has one responsible broker and forty-one salespersons across three offices. The broker reviews files "when something comes up." Advertising approval is delegated to an office manager who is a salesperson. Trust deposits are made by whoever is in the office. A salesperson at the second office has been signing listing agreements with a term left blank and filling it in later.
>
> **This surfaces when a seller complains** that his listing "was supposed to be three months" and the copy in the file says six.
>
> **What the review finds.**
>
> **The blank term.** The individual failure, and the one everyone will focus on. It is real: an agreement with a material term left blank and completed afterward is not the agreement the seller signed.
>
> **But the salesperson's conduct is the smallest finding here**, and treating it as the whole problem is how a brokerage repeats it.
>
> **The delegated advertising approval.** Section 3.3 establishes supervision as an affirmative duty and Section 3.5 establishes what a salesperson may not do. **Delegation of a supervisory function to a salesperson does not move the duty**, and a brokerage whose approvals are performed by someone without supervisory authority has a structural defect rather than a

chunks.heading: 3.7 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
staffing arrangement.
>
> **Trust deposits by whoever is present.** A control that depends on availability is not a control. **The accounting duty is the broker's**, and an unassigned task is an unperformed one, which is exactly the failure Lesson 11 of the practice course names.
>
> **File review "when something comes up."** Review that is triggered by problems cannot find problems. **A review at defined points — at listing, at acceptance, at closing — is the only kind that detects a pattern before a complaint does**, and this pattern ran for months.
>
> **Forty-one licensees across three offices under one broker.** Whether that is supervisable is a question about capacity, not about intent. Section 2.4 of Lesson 01 of the practice course raises branch offices and scale for this reason: **a supervision structure that cannot function at the brokerage's actual size is a defect of the structure.**
>
> **The conclusion the file supports.** One salesperson made an error that a functioning review would have caught at the first listing. **The brokerage's exposure is not that error; it is that nothing in the brokerage was built to find it**, and the same absence applies to every other file the brokerage holds.
>
> **What a licensee should take from this.** Lesson 03 of the practice course states that delegation does not transfer responsibility. **The reciprocal is equally true and less often said: a salesperson working inside a brokerage with no functioning supervision is exposed personally**, because when the review arrives there will be no record that anyone checked anything, including his own work.

### 3.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a listing agreement names the brokerage, and what follows from that when a seller wants to cancel.

chunks.heading: 4. Professional scope and unauthorized legal practice
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. Professional scope and unauthorized legal practice

### 4.1 The boundary

A real estate licensee may explain process, complete forms within the scope of the transaction, describe what documents ordinarily do, and give a professional opinion on matters within the license — value, marketing, negotiation strategy.

A licensee may **not** give legal advice: advising on the legal effect of documents, on rights and remedies, on entitlement to money, on how title should be taken, or on whether a party may cancel or refuse to perform.

### 4.2 The reliable test

Not who asked, not how confident the licensee feels, and not how many years they have practiced:

> **Would answering require a legal conclusion?** If yes, refer.

Applied to the questions consumers actually ask:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| "What does this contingency do?" | Explain what the provision does in the transaction — within scope |
| "Can I cancel and get my deposit back?" | Legal conclusion. Refer |
| "Should I take title as joint tenants?" | Legal and tax conclusion. Refer |
| "What does the disclosure timeline look like?" | Process. Within scope |
| "Is the neighbor's fence on my land?" | Boundary claim. Refer, and recommend a survey |
| "What is this house worth?" | Opinion of value. Within scope, as an opinion |
| "Will the city approve my second unit?" | Prediction about a discretionary decision. Refer to the jurisdiction |

### 4.3 Why the boundary protects the licensee

Consumers rely on what licensees tell them. A wrong legal answer, given confidently, becomes the basis of a decision — and the licensee who gave it has both exceeded the license and created liability that no experience defense will meet.

chunks.heading: 4.4 How to refer without appearing unhelpful
chunks.excerpt:
**Experience does not extend the scope of the license.** A licensee with twenty years of practice is no more entitled to advise on the legal effect of a contract than one with two weeks.

### 4.4 How to refer without appearing unhelpful

Referring badly costs the relationship; referring well strengthens it. The components:

> "That one's outside what I can answer — it's a legal question, and if I guessed and got it wrong you'd be making a real decision on my guess. What I can tell you is [the process, the timeline, what the document does in the transaction]. And I'd get you an answer from an attorney before [the date it matters]."

Name the limit, give what you can, and connect the referral to the deadline that makes it urgent.

### 4.5 The questions licensees are actually asked

Section 4.2 supplies the test. This section applies it to the questions that arrive in practice, because the boundary is easy in the abstract and hard at nine in the evening with a client on the phone.

chunks.heading: 4.5 The questions licensees are actually asked
chunks.excerpt:
| The question | Category | The answer |
|---|---|---|
