**Everything in California is subject to reasonable and beneficial use.** No right in the table is a right to waste water, and the scope of every one of them is measured by what use is reasonable — which is why California water rights are less like a quantity and more like a share of a variable resource.

**This course does not read the water statutes or the constitutional provision in their own text.** No quantity, priority date, permitting requirement, adjudication procedure or reporting obligation in this assignment comes from them. **Groundwater in particular is now governed by a substantial statutory scheme of basin management that is outside this course entirely.**

### 5.10 What a licensee must recognise about water and minerals

**The questions that mean "stop and route this."**

**"Does the property have water?"** For a rural parcel this is the most consequential question in the transaction, and it has three separate parts: is there a **legal right** to the water; is there a **physical source** — a well, a district connection; and is the water **potable and adequate**, which is a testing question. A property can have any one without the others.

**"Is the well permitted, and what does it produce?"** A well permit, a well completion report, and a pump test are documents. A seller's recollection is not.

**"Is there a water district, and what does it require?"** A will-serve letter, connection fees, and availability are district questions with district answers.

chunks.heading: 5.10 What a licensee must recognise about water and minerals
chunks.excerpt:
**"Who owns the minerals?"** Mineral rights are frequently severed in California, often long ago, and a severance appears in the title chain rather than on the land. **A severed mineral estate may carry a right of surface access**, which is a materially different thing to own next to a house than a mere royalty interest.

**"What is that pipeline easement?"** Oil, gas and water conveyance easements are common in parts of the state, and their terms — width, access, the right to enter and maintain — are in the recorded instrument, not in the one-line title exception.

**A worked situation.**

> A buyer is purchasing 12 acres with a house and an old orchard. The seller says the property has "riparian rights on the creek and a good well." The preliminary report shows a mineral reservation from 1948 in favour of an oil company, and an exception for "water rights, as reserved in the deed recorded [date]."

**Three problems, and the seller has described none of them.**

**Water rights may have been reserved away.** The exception in the report says a prior deed reserved water rights. **If they were reserved, the buyer is not acquiring them**, and "riparian rights on the creek" describes what the land would have if nobody had reserved them.

**The 1948 mineral reservation is live until it is examined.** The question is not whether oil will be drilled; it is **whether the mineral owner has a right of surface entry**, which is answered by reading the 1948 instrument.

**The well is a separate question from the water right.** A well can be lawful and productive on land whose surface water rights were reserved, or unlawful and unpermitted on land with excellent rights.

chunks.heading: 5.11 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**What the licensee does:** obtain both recorded instruments, give them to the buyer, and say in writing that water and mineral rights are legal questions for counsel and that well adequacy is a testing question for a qualified professional. **What the licensee does not do is repeat the seller's summary**, which is how a licensee ends up having represented that a buyer was acquiring rights they were not.

### 5.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to list the water questions you would ask on a rural listing and explain what a severed mineral interest means for a buyer.

## 6. Fixture disputes in a sale

### 6.1 The professional answer

Everything in Sections 1 through 4 describes how a dispute is **resolved**. This section is about not having one.

> **The professional practice is to make the fixture tests unnecessary by naming the disputable items in the agreement.**

Agreement overrides the tests. A contract that says the chandelier stays and the mounted television goes has answered the question, and no analysis of intention or adaptation is required.

### 6.2 The naming list

In most residential transactions, these are worth addressing expressly:

- Appliances — refrigerator, washer, dryer, freestanding range
- Window coverings — rods and panels separately
- Mounted televisions **and their brackets**
- Chandeliers and distinctive light fixtures
- Above-ground spas and portable water features
- Storage sheds and outbuildings
- Security cameras, doorbells, thermostats, and other smart-home devices
- Water treatment and filtration systems
- Mounted shelving and closet systems
- Potted and container plantings
- Anything the seller has mentioned intending to take
- Anything the buyer has admired aloud

chunks.heading: 6.3 The intake conversation
chunks.excerpt:
The last two are the practical ones. **A seller who says "I'll be taking the dining room fixture, it was my grandmother's" has just told you what to name in the contract.** A licensee who nods and writes nothing has created the dispute.

### 6.3 The intake conversation

The right time is the listing appointment, and the right question is direct:

> "Before we photograph, walk me through anything you're planning to take with you — light fixtures, appliances, anything mounted, anything with sentimental value. I'd rather name it now than have it come up two days before closing."

This costs five minutes and prevents the most common non-financial dispute in residential practice.

### 6.4 Marketing consistency

A second source of disputes is the gap between marketing and contract. If the photographs show the chandelier, the description mentions the built-in wine refrigerator, and the seller intends to take both, the buyer has been shown something he is not getting.

**Photographs are advertising**, and they are held to the truthfulness standard. Where staging includes items that are not conveying — or where the seller intends to remove a photographed fixture — say so in the marketing rather than leaving it for the walkthrough.

### 6.5 When it surfaces at the walkthrough

The final verification confirms that included items are present. Where a named item is missing:

1. **Document it** — photographs and dated notes.
2. **Address it through the contract before closing**, because the ordinary leverage disappears at closing.
3. **Do not instruct escrow to hold funds** — escrow acts only on mutual written instructions.
4. **Do not close and pursue afterward**, which converts a solvable issue into a claim.

### 6.6 The licensee's limits

chunks.heading: 6.7 The habits that eliminate the category
chunks.excerpt:
Where the parties genuinely dispute whether an item was a fixture and the contract is silent, the licensee's role is to state what the contract says, document the positions, and escalate. **Whether a particular item was a fixture is a legal conclusion** the licensee should not deliver, however clear it seems.

The honest position is: "The contract doesn't name it, which means this comes down to how the law classifies it. That's a question for counsel, and here's what I can do in the meantime."

### 6.7 The habits that eliminate the category

Fixture disputes are among the most preventable problems in a transaction, and three habits eliminate nearly all of them.

**One: the seller names what he is taking, before listing.** Section 6.3's intake conversation, asked directly — "is there anything here you intend to take with you?" — and written down. **The chandelier, the appliance, the light fixture, the plant, the mounted equipment.** The best answer is that the seller removes and replaces it before any photograph is taken, so no buyer ever saw it.

**Two: the marketing shows what conveys.** Section 6.4's consistency requirement. **A photograph is a representation**, and a buyer who saw an item in the listing and does not find it at the walkthrough has a grievance whatever the fixture analysis says. Where an item appears in a photograph and is excluded, **the exclusion is stated where the photograph is**, not buried in a document delivered later.

**Three: the uncertain items are named in the agreement.** Not the obvious ones — the uncertain ones. **Section 2.7's shed, television bracket, and wine refrigerator are the items to name**, because the items whose classification is clear do not produce disputes.

chunks.heading: 6.9 A fixture schedule, and how to build one
chunks.excerpt:
**A fourth habit for the buyer's side**, less often stated: **walk the property asking what the buyer assumes is included.** Lesson 08 of the practice course makes the same point about the agreement generally — "if it matters to you and it isn't written down, it isn't part of the deal" — and fixtures are where that sentence earns its keep. **A buyer who assumed the play structure, the workbench, or the water softener conveys should learn now rather than at the walkthrough.**

> **Why this is worth a licensee's time.** The amounts in dispute are usually small and the damage is not. **A transaction that reaches the walkthrough and turns into an argument about a chandelier has lost the goodwill that was carrying every other unresolved item**, and the closing that was on schedule is now a negotiation between people who are angry.

**And the limit, restated.** Section 6.6 applies to all of it. **When a dispute arises anyway, the licensee identifies the issue and declines to declare who is right.** The classification of a contested item is a legal question, and a licensee who announces the answer at the walkthrough has given legal advice under pressure to a party who will rely on it.

### 6.9 A fixture schedule, and how to build one

Sections 6.1 to 6.4 explained why fixture disputes happen and how the contract prevents them. This section is the working method: how a licensee actually walks a property and produces a schedule that survives a closing.

**Walk the property with the list in hand, not from memory.** The recurring items, in the order a walk-through encounters them:

chunks.heading: 6.9 A fixture schedule, and how to build one
chunks.excerpt:
| Location | Items that generate disputes | Usual § 660 answer | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exterior | Satellite dish, mounted address plaque, playground equipment, potted trees, fountain | Bolted or footed items are affixed; pots are not | List anything the seller wants, by name |
| Entry and halls | Mirrors, coat hooks, security keypad, doorbell camera | Screwed items affixed; adhesive items argued | Name the doorbell camera specifically — it is the most common single dispute |
| Kitchen | Range, refrigerator, dishwasher, microwave, wine cooler, pot rack | Built-in affixed; freestanding not | Say which appliances convey, by appliance |
| Living areas | Wall-mounted television and its bracket, speakers, shelving, curtains, rods, blinds | Brackets and rods affixed; the television and the curtains are personal | **Bracket and television are usually separated** — name both |
| Bedrooms | Closet organizers, ceiling fans, wall safes | Screwed and wired items affixed | Wall safes: name the safe and whether it is emptied |
| Garage and utility | Cabinets, workbench, water softener, generator, EV charger, shelving | Bolted items affixed; leased equipment is neither party's to convey | **Ask whether any of it is leased** |
| Systems | Solar array, propane tank, alarm panel, irrigation controller | Usually affixed, but ownership is the question | Leased or financed equipment needs its own line |

**The three questions that resolve most items before the fixture tests are needed.**

chunks.heading: 6.10 Two worked disputes, and what each cost
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Is it attached by cement, plaster, nails, bolts, or screws?** If yes, it is presumptively real property and the seller must ask for it in writing to take it.
2. **Is it leased, financed, or subject to a service contract?** A leased solar array or propane tank is not the seller's to convey, and the transfer of the agreement is a separate transaction that will not happen by itself.
3. **Does the seller want it?** If so, it comes out of the schedule now and not in a phone call the week of closing.

### 6.10 Two worked disputes, and what each cost

> **Dispute one — the mounted television.** The listing photographs show a large television on a living-room wall. The purchase agreement is silent. At final walk-through the television is gone and so is the bracket, leaving four anchor holes and torn drywall.

**The television is personal property.** It rests in a bracket and is not attached by any means § 660 names. **The bracket is a fixture**: it is screwed to the wall, which is imbedded and therefore permanent, and screws are on the statutory list. Removing the bracket removed a fixture, and doing it badly caused damage.

**What the parties will argue about is not the law.** They will argue about the photographs, because the buyer will say the television was shown and therefore included. **The photograph is not the contract**, and a buyer relying on a listing image has relied on marketing rather than on an agreement — which is precisely the failure Assignment 01 Section 6.2 describes. The cost of the dispute exceeded the value of the bracket within the first hour.

chunks.heading: 6.11 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
> **Dispute two — the leased solar array.** A seller's disclosure describes "solar panels — owned." Escrow closes. Two months later the buyer receives an invoice from a solar finance company and discovers a twenty-year lease with an escalating payment and a UCC filing against the property.

**This is a different order of problem, and it is not a fixture dispute at all.** The panels are affixed and would pass with the land if the seller owned them. The seller did not own them. **A licensee cannot verify ownership of a solar array by looking at it**, and the two documents that would have surfaced the lease — the preliminary report, which would show the financing statement, and a direct question in writing to the seller — both existed and were available.

**The habit that prevents it:** treat every solar array, propane tank, water-treatment system, security system and EV charger as **presumptively encumbered until a document says otherwise**, and put the question in writing. A seller who answers "owned" in writing has made a representation; a seller who was never asked has not.

**Both disputes share a shape.** Neither turned on a difficult legal question — § 660 answers both in a sentence. Both turned on a question nobody asked in time. **The fixture law is easy and the fixture schedule is the work.**

### 6.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to run the intake conversation, produce the naming list for a specific property, and state the correct sequence when an item is missing at the walkthrough.

## Key terms

chunks.heading: Key terms
chunks.excerpt:
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Real property** | Land, permanent attachments, and the bundle of legal rights. Transfers by deed, is recorded, and **conveys unless excluded**. |
| **Personal property** | Movable things not permanently attached. Transfers by bill of sale or delivery, and **does not convey unless included**. |
| **Annexation** | Personal property becoming real property by attachment. |
| **Severance** | Real property becoming personal property by detachment — physically, or **on paper** by contract or reservation. |
| **Fixture** | An item that was personal property and became real property through attachment. Conveys unless excluded. |
| **MARIA** | Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of the parties, Intention, Agreement. |
| **Intention** | Generally the most important test. The other tests are largely evidence of it, since intention itself is invisible. |
| **Agreement** | The test that overrides the others. Where the parties named the item, the analysis is never reached. |
| **Adaptability** | Special adaptation to this property — custom storm windows, a key to this lock — pointing toward fixture status even where removal is easy. |
| **Relationship of the parties** | Why "is it a fixture?" is incomplete. Doubt tends to favor the buyer against a seller, the tenant against a landlord, and the lender against a borrower. |
| **Trade fixture** | An item a tenant attaches to leased premises for the tenant's trade or business, generally removable at or before the end of the tenancy, with repair of removal damage. |
| **Accession** | The rule by which trade fixtures not removed in time may become the landlord's property. |
| **Building improvement** | A change to the building itself rather than trade equipment — a new roof, upgraded serv

chunks.heading: Practice problems
chunks.excerpt:
ice. Not a trade fixture. |
| **Natural attachment** | Things growing on the land. |
| **Artificial attachment** | Things people placed — buildings, fences, walls, paving. |
| **Perennial growth** | Trees, shrubs, and growth not requiring annual cultivation. Generally real property, conveying with the land. |
| **Annual crop** | Growth requiring annual planting and cultivation. Generally **personal property**, even while growing, because it represents the season's labor rather than a permanent characteristic of the land. |
| **Riparian rights** | Rights arising from ownership of land bordering a watercourse, to reasonable use. |
| **Appropriative rights** | Rights arising from diversion to beneficial use, under a system of priority. |
| **Littoral rights** | Rights of an owner adjoining a lake or sea rather than a flowing watercourse. |
| **Accretion and avulsion** | Gradual deposit, which generally benefits the owner; and sudden change, which generally does not shift boundaries. |
| **Severed mineral rights** | Subsurface rights sold or reserved separately. Once severed they stay severed, appear as a title exception, and may carry surface access rights. |
| **Lateral and subjacent support** | Support a parcel receives from adjoining land, and from beneath. |
| **Naming the item** | The professional practice that makes the fixture tests unnecessary. |

## Practice problems

### Problem 1

A buyer and seller dispute the refrigerator. The buyer says it was in the house when he saw it and
nobody said it was going. The seller says appliances are obviously hers and she never offered it. The
contract is silent.

**Explain why both are reasoning correctly, and state the professional failure.**

chunks.heading: Problem 2
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** They are applying **opposite defaults, and each default is correct for its own
> category.** Real property conveys unless excluded; personal property does not convey unless included.
> The buyer looked at the house and applied one; the seller looked at her appliance and applied the
> other.
>
> A freestanding refrigerator is usually personal property — which makes it the single most disputed
> item in residential practice, because it is also the item buyers most reliably assume conveys.
>
> **The professional failure is the silent contract.** Neither party did anything unreasonable. The
> licensee had one job in this dispute — to name the item at the listing appointment — and did not do
> it.

### Problem 2

Apply the tests to a wall-mounted television and its bracket, a hardwired chandelier, and a custom
storm window cut to fit one opening.

**State which test does the work in each.**

chunks.heading: Problem 3
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The television and bracket: method of attachment separates them.** The bracket is
> bolted to studs and cannot come off without damage; the set lifts off. They are frequently treated
> differently, which is exactly why both are named in contracts rather than analyzed.
>
> **The chandelier: attachment plus intention.** Hardwired into a ceiling box, it is ordinarily a
> fixture — and it is among the most commonly removed by sellers who assumed otherwise, usually for
> sentimental reasons.
>
> **The storm window: adaptability.** It is easy to remove and worth very little anywhere else, and
> that special adaptation is evidence the annexor meant it to stay. The same reasoning covers a key to
> this lock and shelving built to these alcove dimensions.
>
> **What transfers:** the five tests are not a checklist of equal weight. **Intention is generally the
> most important**, and the others are largely evidence of it — because intention itself is invisible
> and must be inferred.

### Problem 3

The same above-ground spa is argued over in three settings: between a buyer and a seller at closing;
between a landlord and a tenant at the end of a lease; and between a lender and a borrower after
default.

**Does the analysis change?**

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** The item is identical and the outcome may differ, because **"is it a fixture?" is an
> incomplete question. A fixture as between whom?**
>
> **Buyer and seller:** doubt is generally resolved in favor of the buyer — the item stays.
>
> **Landlord and tenant:** doubt tends to favor the tenant, particularly where the item is a trade
> fixture.
>
> **Lender and borrower:** doubt tends to favor the lender, whose security was measured by the property
> as it stood when the loan was made.
>
> The spa itself is genuinely contested on the other tests — adaptation and wiring pull toward fixture,
> portability pulls away — which is why the relationship test carries more weight here than it would
> for a hardwired chandelier.

### Problem 4

A restaurant tenant installed walk-in refrigeration, a commercial hood, a built bar, and a new roof.
The lease is silent on removal. The tenant vacates on the last day of the term, returns three weeks
later for the equipment, and finds the landlord has changed the locks.

**Classify each item and assess the timing.**

chunks.heading: Problem 5
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Trade fixtures:** the refrigeration, the hood, and the bar — equipment the tenant
> attached for the conduct of its business, removable at or before the end of the tenancy with repair
> of the damage removal causes. The hood's removal damage may be substantial, and repairing it is the
> tenant's obligation, not a reason the fixture is not removable.
>
> **Not a trade fixture:** the roof. That is a **building improvement** rather than trade equipment,
> and the distinction runs exactly there.
>
> **The timing is fatal.** Removal happens during the tenancy or within the period the lease or law
> allows. A tenant who vacates and returns three weeks later has usually lost the right, and under
> **accession** the unremoved trade fixtures may become the landlord's property.
>
> **What transfers:** this rule exists because businesses could not operate in leased space if their
> equipment became the landlord's on installation — and inattention converts that protection into a
> gift. A well-drafted lease addressing installation, removal, condition, and restoration makes the
> whole analysis unnecessary.

### Problem 5

A licensee lists a 40-acre parcel with a mature walnut orchard, forty acres of tomatoes planted this
spring, mature landscaping around the house, and solar panels on the roof. The seller mentions he
plans to dig up several ornamental trees before closing.

**Classify each item and identify what must be addressed.**

chunks.heading: Problem 6
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The orchard is real property** — perennial growth not requiring annual cultivation,
> conveying with the land.
>
> **The tomatoes are generally personal property**, even while growing and attached, because an annual
> crop represents the cultivator's labor and investment for the season rather than a permanent
> characteristic of the land. This does **not** pass automatically the way the orchard does, and the
> agreement must address who owns the crop in the ground, who harvests it, and who bears the cost.
>
> **The mature landscaping is real property.** A seller who removes it before closing has removed real
> property — a contract problem, not a matter of taste. Say so now, and name any specific plants he is
> keeping.
>
> **The solar panels require a question, not a classification.** They are frequently subject to a lease
> or financing arrangement that does not convey automatically. A licensee who assumes they convey has
> skipped a question that changes both what the buyer receives and what the buyer owes.

### Problem 6

A buyer is purchasing rural acreage intending to plant an orchard and build a house. The preliminary
report shows a reservation of mineral rights to a third party. The listing agent tells him mineral
reservations are standard in the area and nothing to worry about, and that the well "has always been
fine."

**Assess both statements and list the questions that should have been asked.**

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Both statements are outside the license**, and the mineral one is a legal opinion on
> a document neither of them has read.
>
> A severed mineral interest **stays severed** through subsequent transfers, and the mineral estate may
> carry **surface access rights** that affect the surface owner's use — which matters a great deal to a
> buyer planning an orchard and a house. Whether and how is a legal question. The licensee's role is to
> ensure the buyer sees the exception, obtains the underlying document, and gets it reviewed **before
> his contingency expires.**
>
> **The water questions belong at the listing appointment:** what is the source — municipal, well,
> shared well, mutual water company, district? If a well, what is its documented production and
> quality, and when was it tested? Is any water right appurtenant to the parcel and documented? Is the
> property within a groundwater management area? Are there shared-facility agreements — a shared well,
> a pipeline, an access easement? And is the supply sufficient for **the buyer's intended use**, which
> here includes irrigating an orchard.
>
> **What transfers:** for every topic in this area the response is the same three steps — **recognize,
> ask and obtain, refer.** "It has always been fine" is not a documented answer to any of the six
> questions.

### Problem 7

At the listing appointment a seller mentions that the dining room chandelier was her grandmother's and
she will be taking it. The licensee nods, photographs the room with the chandelier in it, and lists
the property. Two days before closing the buyer's agent asks about it.

**Trace the failures.**

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** Three, and they compound.
>
> **The seller told the licensee exactly what to name in the contract**, and nothing was written.
> "Anything the seller has mentioned intending to take" is at the top of the naming list precisely
> because sellers volunteer it.
>
> **The photograph made it worse.** Photographs are advertising and are held to the truthfulness
> standard. The buyer has been shown something he is not getting — and where staging or photography
> includes items that are not conveying, the marketing should say so rather than leaving it for the
> walkthrough.
>
> **The timing is now the worst possible.** With two days to closing the parties have maximum pressure
> and minimum flexibility, over an item that five minutes at the listing appointment would have
> settled.
>
> **The conversation that prevents it:** *"Before we photograph, walk me through anything you're
> planning to take — light fixtures, appliances, anything mounted, anything with sentimental value.
> I'd rather name it now than have it come up two days before closing."*

### Problem 8

At the final verification the buyer finds a named built-in wine refrigerator has been removed. His
agent proposes instructing escrow to hold $4,000 and closing on schedule; the listing agent says the
item was "obviously personal property anyway."

**State the correct sequence and the licensee's limit.**

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The item was named**, which ends the fixture argument entirely — agreement overrides
> the tests, and the listing agent's classification opinion is both irrelevant and outside the license.
>
> **The sequence:** document the finding with photographs and dated notes; **address it through the
> contract before closing**, because the ordinary leverage to resolve it disappears once the
> transaction closes; do not instruct escrow to hold funds, since escrow acts only on **mutual** written
> instructions; and do not close intending to pursue the seller afterward, which converts a solvable
> issue into a claim.
>
> **Where an item is genuinely disputed and the contract is silent**, the licensee states what the
> contract says, documents both positions, and escalates. Whether a particular item was a fixture is a
> **legal conclusion**, however clear it seems. The honest position: "The contract doesn't name it,
> which means this comes down to how the law classifies it — that's a question for counsel, and here's
> what I can do in the meantime."

## Chapter summary

**The classification decides transfer, recording, description, security interests, taxation, and what
conveys.** Real property transfers by deed and conveys unless excluded; personal property transfers by
bill of sale and does not convey unless included — and those opposite defaults are why ordinary
disputes arise between reasonable people.

**Items move between categories** by annexation and severance, and severance can occur on paper
without anything physically moving.

**Classification is made at a moment in time** — when the deed was delivered, when the lien attached,
when the contract was signed.

chunks.heading: Required applied assignment
chunks.excerpt:
**MARIA lists the tests; intention generally decides them**, with the others serving largely as
evidence of an invisible fact. **Agreement overrides everything.**

**Relationship matters:** doubt tends to favor the buyer against a seller, the tenant against a
landlord, and the lender against a borrower. "Is it a fixture?" is incomplete without "as between
whom?"

**Trade fixtures are the tenant's business equipment**, removable at or before the end of the tenancy
with repair of damage — and lost to accession if left. Building improvements are not trade fixtures,
and a well-drafted lease makes the analysis unnecessary.

**Perennial growth is real property; annual crops are generally personal property**, which must be
addressed expressly in agricultural transactions. Removing mature landscaping before closing removes
real property.

**Solar panels require a question rather than an assumption**, because a lease or financing
arrangement may not convey with the property.

**Water and mineral interests are specialist areas** where the licensee's job is to recognize, ask and
obtain, and refer. Ask the six water questions on rural property, and never characterize a severed
mineral interest as routine.

**Do not resolve fixture disputes — prevent them.** Run the intake conversation, name the disputable
items, keep marketing consistent with what conveys, and at the walkthrough document, address it before
closing, and leave the legal conclusion to counsel.

## Required applied assignment

chunks.heading: Knowledge check and remediation
chunks.excerpt:
Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Classify each item in dispute and state which test drives your analysis, identify how the relationship of the parties affects the outcome, state what the agreement should have said and draft that language, identify anything you would refer to counsel or to a specialist, and state the evidence you would create and retain. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

## Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

## Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

lessons.title: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 03

chunks.heading: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 03

## Estates, ownership, and common interests

**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Assignment time:** 180 instructional minutes
**Regulatory status:** Not approved; no California credit is available.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish freehold from leasehold estates and identify the leasehold types by how each terminates.
- Explain fee simple and life estates, and identify who holds what interest during and after a life estate.
- Distinguish joint tenancy from tenancy in common by their operative differences, and explain what severance does.
- Describe California community property at the level a licensee must recognize, and identify what belongs to counsel.
- Explain how a common interest development is organized and what a buyer must review before the contingency expires.
- Verify authority to convey where title is held in a trust or by an entity.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: estates and their duration | 55 | Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved |
| Guided reading: concurrent ownership and community property | 50 | Sections 3-4 viewed |
| Guided reading: common interest developments, trusts, and entities | 45 | Sections 5-6 viewed |
| Applied scenario and decision memorandum | 20 | Written response submitted |
| Lesson assessment | 10 | Five scored items submitted |
| **Total** | **180** | **One of 15 separate lesson assignments** |

## 1. Freehold and leasehold estates

### 1.1 What an estate is

An **estate** is the nature and extent of a person's interest in land. It answers two questions: what rights does the holder have, and for how long?

The primary division is by **duration**:

chunks.heading: 1.2 The four leasehold estates
chunks.excerpt:
| | Duration | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Freehold estate** | Indefinite — potentially forever, or for a life | An interest in the land itself |
| **Leasehold estate** | A fixed or terminable period | A right of possession, with the owner retaining the reversion |

The practical difference: a freehold holder owns; a leasehold holder possesses. Both are real property interests, and both can be bought, sold, and encumbered.

### 1.2 The four leasehold estates

Leaseholds are classified by **how they end**, which is the useful way to hold them.

| Estate | Duration | How it ends |
|---|---|---|
| **Estate for years** | A definite period stated in the lease | Automatically, at the stated end. **No notice required.** |
| **Periodic estate** | Renews period to period — month to month | By notice from either party, per the required period |
| **Estate at will** | Indefinite, with the consent of both | When either party ends it, subject to statutory notice |
| **Estate at sufferance** | The tenant holds over after the right ends | By the landlord's action; the tenant is a holdover, not a trespasser |

**The name misleads on the first one.** An "estate for years" is defined by having a **definite ending date**, not by lasting years. A six-month lease and a ten-day lease are both estates for years.

### 1.3 The distinctions that matter in practice

**Estate for years versus periodic estate: notice.** An estate for years expires on its stated date without anyone giving notice. A periodic tenancy continues until someone gives the required notice. A licensee who advises a landlord that a fixed-term lease "needs a 30-day notice to end" has described the wrong estate.

chunks.heading: 1.4 The reversion
chunks.excerpt:
**Estate at sufferance is not trespass.** The holdover tenant entered lawfully. That is why the landlord's remedy is a legal process rather than self-help, and why changing the locks is unlawful no matter how clear the tenant's obligation to leave.

**A leasehold survives a sale.** The buyer of a leased property takes subject to the lease on its terms. This is why existing leases and their terms are an intake item, and why "the tenant will be out by closing" needs to be verified against the lease rather than accepted.

### 1.4 The reversion

When a leasehold ends, possession returns to the owner. That future interest is the **reversion**, and it is what the landlord holds during the tenancy.

The landlord's estate is not suspended by the lease. It is a fee simple subject to a leasehold, which is why the landlord can sell, mortgage, and devise it while the tenant is in possession.

### 1.5 Why the estate concept controls everything downstream

A principles course opens with estates because **the estate held determines what can be done with the property**, and every later topic assumes the answer.

chunks.heading: 1.5 Why the estate concept controls everything downstream
chunks.excerpt:
| What the estate determines | Where it surfaces later |
|---|---|
| **What can be conveyed** | A seller cannot convey more than he holds. A life tenant conveying "the property" conveys a life estate measured by his life, and the buyer finds out later. |
| **What can be encumbered** | A lender's security is limited by the estate pledged, which is why a lender's title requirements probe the estate rather than accepting a description. |
| **Who must sign** | Concurrent owners, spouses, trustees, and entity signatories — Sections 3, 4, and 6 of this lesson are all versions of this one question. |
| **What happens at death** | Survivorship, probate, or the terms of an instrument. **The difference between two forms of concurrent ownership is invisible on the property and total in effect.** |
| **What a creditor can reach** | Which affects who is willing to lend and on what terms. |
| **What the occupant may do** | Alter, encumber, lease, or let deteriorate — the life tenant's limits in Section 2.4 are the clearest case. |
| **How long it lasts** | Perpetual, for a life, for a term, or until a condition occurs. |

**Two conclusions.**

**The most consequential fact about a property is frequently invisible.** Two identical houses on the same street can be held under estates with completely different consequences for conveyance, financing, and inheritance, and **nothing about the property reveals it.** The estate is established from documents, which is why the intake practice in Section 6.5 asks for them rather than for a description.

chunks.heading: 1.6 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**"Who owns it?" is the wrong question.** The professional question is **"what interest is held, by whom, and who has authority to convey it?"** — three questions, frequently with three different answers, and a transaction that assumes they collapse into one is the transaction that fails at title clearance.

> **The failure this prevents.** A listing taken from a person who describes himself as the owner, marketed, and put under contract — after which title clearance reveals a co-owner, a life estate, a trust with a successor trustee requirement, or an entity whose authority document says something other than what the signer said. **Every one of those is discoverable at intake with a question and a document**, and every one of them is expensive at day nineteen.

### 1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to name a leasehold estate from a description of how it terminates, and state what happens to a lease when the property is sold.

## 2. Fee simple and life estates

### 2.1 Fee simple absolute

**Fee simple absolute** is the greatest estate the law recognizes: ownership of indefinite duration, freely transferable during life and at death, with the full bundle of rights.

It is the default. A deed conveying property without limiting language conveys a fee simple absolute, and most residential transactions transfer exactly this.

Fee simple is still subject to the four government powers taken up in Lesson 06, and to private restrictions taken up in Lesson 05. "Absolute" describes the estate's duration and transferability, not freedom from regulation.

### 2.2 Defeasible fees

chunks.heading: 2.3 Life estates
chunks.excerpt:
A fee can be granted subject to a condition, so that it may end if the condition is broken. These are called **defeasible** fees, and California practice encounters them mainly in older chains of title and in conveyances to public or charitable uses.

The practical point for a licensee is narrow and important: **a deed containing conditional language is a title matter, not a curiosity.** It goes to title and to counsel, and the buyer needs to understand it before the contingency expires. Whether a condition is enforceable, and what happens if it is broken, is a legal question.

### 2.3 Life estates

A **life estate** is ownership measured by a lifetime rather than by a fixed period.

| Party | Interest |
|---|---|
| **Life tenant** | Owns and possesses for the measuring life |
| **Remainderman** | Takes when the measuring life ends, where the grantor named a third party |
| **Reversion holder** | Takes when the measuring life ends, where the interest returns to the grantor |

A variant worth naming: a life estate **pur autre vie** is measured by the life of someone other than the holder. The holder may die first, in which case the estate passes to the holder's successors until the measuring life ends.

### 2.4 What a life tenant may and may not do

**May:** possess and use the property, receive its income, and transfer whatever interest they hold — which is the life estate, and no more.

**May not:** commit **waste** — conduct that permanently impairs the property to the detriment of the remainderman. Neglecting maintenance, removing valuable timber, or allowing the property to deteriorate can all be waste.

**Must generally:** maintain the property, pay taxes and ordinary carrying charges, and preserve the remainderman's interest.

### 2.5 The transaction problem

chunks.heading: 2.6 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
A life tenant can only sell what they own, and what they own ends when the measuring life ends. A buyer purchasing from a life tenant alone receives an interest that terminates on someone else's death.

> **The professional response:** where title shows a life estate, a conveyance in fee requires the life tenant **and** the remainderman or reversion holder to join. This is an authority question of exactly the kind Lesson 01 described, and it is verified against the instrument, not assumed.

A licensee who takes a listing from a life tenant without identifying the remainderman has taken a listing that cannot deliver a fee.

### 2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to say who must sign to convey a fee where a life estate exists, and explain what waste is.

## 3. Joint tenancy and tenancy in common

### 3.1 Concurrent ownership

Where two or more people own the same property at the same time, they hold it concurrently. California's principal forms are **tenancy in common**, **joint tenancy**, and the community property forms taken up in Section 4.

### 3.2 The operative comparison

| | Tenancy in common | Joint tenancy |
|---|---|---|
| **Shares** | May be unequal | Equal |
| **Right of survivorship** | **No** | **Yes** |
| **On death** | The share passes by will or intestate succession | The interest passes to the surviving joint tenants |
| **Transferable during life** | Yes, freely | Yes — but transfer **severs** the joint tenancy as to that interest |
| **Creation** | The default where two or more take without specifying | Requires express language creating it |
| **Number of owners** | Any number | Two or more |

**The survivorship difference is the whole point**, and it is what makes vesting an estate planning question rather than a form selection.

chunks.heading: 3.3 The four unities
chunks.excerpt:
### 3.3 The four unities

Joint tenancy traditionally requires four unities, conventionally remembered as **PITT**:

- **Possession** — each holds an undivided right to possess the whole.
- **Interest** — equal interests.
- **Time** — the interests vested at the same time.
- **Title** — the interests arose from the same instrument.

Tenancy in common requires only unity of **possession**. That single requirement is why tenants in common may hold unequal shares acquired at different times from different sources.

### 3.4 Severance

A joint tenant who transfers their interest during life **severs** the joint tenancy as to that interest, which becomes a tenancy in common.

> Three joint tenants each hold a one-third interest. One sells to an outsider.
>
> **The buyer holds a one-third interest as a tenant in common.** The remaining two continue as joint tenants **between themselves** as to their two-thirds, with survivorship operating between them and not as to the outsider's third.

Severance is a recurring examination topic and a recurring practical surprise, because the transferring joint tenant has changed the survivorship expectations of people who did not agree to the change.

### 3.5 Partition

Where concurrent owners cannot agree, any of them may generally seek **partition** — a court-supervised division of the property, either physically or by sale with division of the proceeds.

This is a legal remedy, and a licensee's role is to recognize it as the answer to "we can't agree what to do with the house" and refer it. Licensees are frequently asked to take a listing where the co-owners disagree; the authority question must be answered before the listing is signed, not during escrow.

### 3.6 What the licensee actually does

chunks.heading: 3.7 A worked ownership intake
chunks.excerpt:
Vesting has ownership, survivorship, tax, and estate consequences, and **advising which to choose is outside the license.** The licensee's obligations are:

1. **Explain that the choice matters** and that changing it later is neither free nor simple.
2. **Refer to legal and tax counsel before escrow prepares the deed.**
3. **At intake on a listing, confirm how title is held and who must sign** — against the record, not from the seller's description.

> Two unmarried siblings say they want the survivor to take the whole property automatically, **and** each to be able to leave her share to her own children.
>
> Those goals point in different directions. Survivorship and the ability to devise a share are not both satisfied by a single form. Resolving that tension is estate planning, and it belongs to counsel — not to the licensee, and not to escrow's deadline for the deed instruction.

### 3.7 A worked ownership intake

chunks.heading: 3.7 A worked ownership intake
chunks.excerpt:
> **Six listing appointments in one week.** At each, the licensee asks the Section 6.5 questions: **how is title currently held, may I see the document, and who must sign to convey?**
>
> **1. "My wife and I own it."** Two people, married, and the form of ownership is a question with several possible answers — Section 4.2's concepts are engaged, and the answer affects survivorship, creditors, and taxation. **The licensee does not advise on which form is better** and does not assume which one applies. He obtains the vesting from the record.
>
> **2. "It's in my trust."** Section 6.2 governs. **The trustee conveys, and the question is who currently holds that office** — which the trust instrument answers and the seller's description does not. A successor trustee acting after a death or incapacity is a different situation with its own documentary requirements. **The licensee obtains the documentation the title company and counsel will require, and routes the legal questions.**
>
> **3. "My brother and I inherited it."** Two owners, and the form of their concurrent ownership determines what happens if one dies before closing and whether one can act alone. **Both sign.** How the property passed to them — by will, by trust, by operation of law — may also determine whether an administration is required, which is a legal question with a timeline attached to it.
>
> **4. "It's owned by our LLC."** Section 6.3. **The entity conveys, through whoever its governing documents authorize**, and the authority is established from the documents rather than from the person's title on a business card. **A member is not automatically authorized.**
>
> **5. "I have power of attorney for my father."** Section 6.4. **The instrument's scope is what matters** — whether it reaches real property, w

chunks.heading: 3.9 The joint tenancy statute, and the words that create it
chunks.excerpt:
hether it is currently effective, and whether any conditions on it have been satisfied. **This is a legal question and it goes to counsel and the title company early**, because a defect discovered at closing cannot be repaired at closing. **And where the principal's capacity is in question, Lesson 15 of the practice course applies:** speak with the principal directly, document what you observed, and escalate.
>
> **6. "I bought it with my partner but it's really mine — she just helped with the loan."** **Two different claims: what the record says and what the seller believes the arrangement was.** The record controls who must sign. **What the parties intended between themselves is a legal question the licensee does not resolve**, and a listing taken on the seller's characterization is a listing that will fail.
>
> **What the week produced.** Six appointments, six documents requested, two matters routed to counsel before listing. **None of the six sellers described their situation inaccurately on purpose.** Each described it the way people describe ownership in conversation, which is by relationship rather than by interest — and Section 1.5's point is that those are not the same thing.

### 3.9 The joint tenancy statute, and the words that create it

Section 3.1 gave the four unities. Section 3.3 explained survivorship. **Civil Code § 683** is where both come from, and its most important instruction is about drafting rather than about theory:

chunks.heading: 3.9 The joint tenancy statute, and the words that create it
chunks.excerpt:
> *"(a) A joint interest is one owned by two or more persons in equal shares, by a title created by a single will or transfer, **when expressly declared in the will or transfer to be a joint tenancy**, or by transfer from a sole owner to himself and others, or from tenants in common or joint tenants to themselves or some of them, or to themselves or any of them and others, or from spouses, when holding title as community property or otherwise to themselves or to themselves and others or to one of them and to another or others, **when expressly declared in the transfer to be a joint tenancy**, or when granted or devised to executors or trustees as joint tenants."*

**"Expressly declared" appears twice, and it is the operative phrase.** A joint tenancy is not inferred from equal shares, from a shared purchase, from a marriage, or from the parties' evident intention. **It exists because the instrument says the words.** A deed to "Ana Ruiz and Beatriz Ruiz" creates a tenancy in common no matter what the two of them meant; a deed to "Ana Ruiz and Beatriz Ruiz, as joint tenants" creates a joint tenancy.

**This is the single most consequential drafting point in the whole of concurrent ownership**, because the difference between the two is whether the property passes automatically to the survivor or through the decedent's estate — and by the time anyone consults the deed, one of the owners has usually died and cannot say what was intended.

**Two structural points the section also settles.**

chunks.heading: 3.10 What the licensee does and does not do with this
chunks.excerpt:
**"In equal shares."** Joint tenants hold equally by definition. Two joint tenants hold halves; four hold quarters. Unequal shares are not a variant of joint tenancy — they are inconsistent with it, and an instrument purporting to create a joint tenancy in unequal shares creates something else.

**A sole owner may create one directly.** The section expressly allows a transfer *"from a sole owner to himself and others"* and from spouses *"to themselves or to themselves and others."* This abolished a common-law trap: at common law the unities of time and title meant a sole owner could not simply deed themselves into a joint tenancy and had to convey through a third party — the "straw man." § 683 removed the need. **A licensee who encounters a straw-man conveyance in an old chain of title is looking at the fossil of a rule that no longer applies.**

**And one boundary the section draws for itself.** § 683(b): *"Provisions of this section do not apply to a joint account in a financial institution if Part 2 (commencing with Section 5100) of Division 5 of the Probate Code applies to such account."* Bank accounts held jointly are governed by a different statute, and reasoning from real property survivorship to a bank account is reasoning from the wrong code.

### 3.10 What the licensee does and does not do with this

**Do not advise on the form of title.** How co-buyers should take title is a decision with tax, estate, creditor and marital consequences that vary by family, and it is a question for a lawyer, an accountant, or both. Recommending joint tenancy because it "avoids probate" is legal advice, is often wrong, and is squarely inside the boundary Assignment 01 Section 4.2 draws.

chunks.heading: 3.11 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**Do make sure the question is asked, in time.** Escrow will require vesting instructions. A licensee who lets the question arrive for the first time three days before closing has created a situation in which buyers make an estate-planning decision under deadline pressure with nobody qualified in the room. **Raise it at the point of writing the offer**, and route it out.

**Do read the vesting on the preliminary report and notice when it does not match what the client told you.** A seller who says "my sister and I own it together, it passes to me if anything happens" and a preliminary report showing a tenancy in common are describing different things, and the difference matters before the property is listed, not after.

**A worked situation.**

> Two siblings inherit a duplex from their mother, taking title as tenants in common. Some years later they refinance, and the new deed of trust is signed by both. One sibling dies. Her will leaves everything to her husband.

**The surviving sibling does not take the whole property.** A tenancy in common carries no survivorship, so the deceased sibling's undivided one-half passes under her will to her husband, who becomes a co-tenant with his sister-in-law. **The refinance did not change the vesting** — a deed of trust encumbers the title, it does not re-grant it — and nothing in the transaction converted a tenancy in common into a joint tenancy, because nothing expressly declared it.

**What the licensee should have done years earlier:** noticed the vesting when the property was inherited, told the siblings that how they held title was a question with consequences, and sent them to counsel. That is a fifteen-second conversation that would have been worth having.

### 3.11 Checkpoint

chunks.heading: 4. Community property orientation
chunks.excerpt:
You should be able to state the operative differences between the two forms, explain what severance does to a three-party joint tenancy, and say what you would do when a client asks which to choose.

## 4. Community property orientation

### 4.1 What the system is

California is a **community property** state. In outline, property acquired by a married person during marriage is generally community property, and property acquired before marriage or by gift or inheritance during marriage is generally that spouse's separate property.

**This section is an orientation, not a guide.** The rules governing characterization, transmutation, commingled assets, and dissolution are complex, fact-dependent, and squarely legal. What a licensee needs is enough to recognize the issue at intake and to route it correctly.

### 4.2 The three concepts to hold

**Community property.** Generally, property acquired during marriage other than by gift or inheritance. Each spouse generally holds an equal interest.

**Separate property.** Generally, property owned before marriage, or acquired during marriage by gift, devise, or inheritance — together with the rents, issues, and profits of separate property.

**Community property with right of survivorship.** A form California recognizes that combines community property characterization with survivorship. It has both tax and estate consequences, and whether it fits a particular couple is a question for their advisors.

### 4.3 The intake question that matters

The licensee's operative concern is authority to convey.

> **Where community property is involved, both spouses generally must join in a conveyance or encumbrance of real property.**

That single proposition drives the intake practice:

chunks.heading: 4.4 Dissolution and separation
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Ask marital status** as part of confirming authority, in the same neutral way as every other intake question.
2. **Check how title is held** against the record.
3. **Where the record and the answer do not reconcile**, stop and escalate rather than proceeding.
4. **Where a spouse is not on title but may have an interest**, that is a title and legal question — route it to title and to counsel before the listing is signed.

A listing signed by one spouse where the other has an interest is the same category of failure as a listing signed by a beneficiary rather than a trustee: it cannot deliver what it promises, and it surfaces in escrow where the cost is highest.

### 4.4 Dissolution and separation

Where a marriage is being dissolved, authority to convey may be affected by court orders, and the timing of a sale may be constrained. A licensee working on a sale during a dissolution should expect that **counsel is already involved** and should coordinate rather than improvise.

What the licensee must not do is advise either spouse on their rights, characterize property as community or separate, or predict how a court will divide it. Each of those is a legal conclusion.

### 4.5 A note on neutrality

Questions about marital status at intake exist to establish authority to convey. They are asked of every client in the same way, recorded, and used for that purpose. A licensee who asks selectively, or who uses the answer for anything other than the authority analysis, has created a fair housing problem alongside the compliance one.

### 4.7 Community property, and the presumption that does the work

California is a community property state, and the consequences reach every residential transaction where a married person or registered domestic partner is on title.

chunks.heading: 4.7 Community property, and the presumption that does the work
chunks.excerpt:
**The organising presumption.** Property acquired by a married person during marriage, while domiciled in California, is presumed to be **community property**. Property acquired before marriage, or during marriage by gift, bequest, devise or descent, is **separate property**. So are the rents, issues and profits of separate property.

**Both halves of that sentence matter to a licensee.** The presumption means a house bought during a marriage is community property **even if only one spouse is named on the deed**, unless something rebuts the presumption. And a house owned before the marriage does not become community property merely because the couple lived in it for thirty years.

| | Community property | Separate property |
|---|---|---|
| **Typical origin** | Earnings during marriage; anything bought with them | Owned before marriage; gift; inheritance |
| **Management** | Either spouse may manage, **with limits on real property** | The owning spouse |
| **On death** | Decedent's half passes by will or intestacy; **community property with right of survivorship passes to the survivor** | By will or intestacy |
| **Conveying or encumbering real property** | **Both spouses must join** | The owning spouse alone |

**The rule in that last row is the one that stops transactions**, and it is worth stating flatly: **a conveyance or encumbrance of community real property requires the joinder of both spouses.** A listing signed by one spouse, a deed signed by one spouse, a deed of trust signed by one spouse — each is a problem discovered in escrow if not before.

chunks.heading: 4.8 What a licensee does about marital status, and what they must not
chunks.excerpt:
**"Community property with right of survivorship"** is a distinct vesting available to spouses, combining community property character with automatic survivorship. Like joint tenancy under Civil Code § 683, **it must be expressly declared in the instrument.**

### 4.8 What a licensee does about marital status, and what they must not

**Do ask how title is held and whether the owner is married**, as a transactional question at listing. It is not idle: it determines who must sign.

**Do not treat marital status as a screening criterion.** Marital status is a protected characteristic under Government Code § 12955 and Civil Code § 51. Asking a **seller** who must sign the deed is transactional necessity; treating a **buyer or tenant** differently because of their marital status is unlawful. **The question is proper in one direction and prohibited in the other**, and the difference is what the information is used for.

**Do read the vesting on the preliminary report and ask about anything that does not match.** A single person on title who is now married; a married person holding "as his sole and separate property"; an interspousal transfer deed in the chain. **Each is a real question with a real answer**, and each is answered by a title officer or counsel rather than by the licensee.

**Do not advise on characterisation.** Whether a particular asset is community or separate — where separate funds bought a house during marriage, where community earnings paid the mortgage on a separate property, where a spouse signed a deed they now dispute — is a question with a substantial body of law behind it and no reliable shortcut.

**A worked situation.**

chunks.heading: 4.9 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
> A seller lists a house. Title reads: *"Marcos Delgado, a married man, as his sole and separate property."* His wife signed an interspousal transfer deed at purchase eight years ago. The couple has since separated but is not divorced. The listing agreement is signed by Marcos alone. An offer arrives.

**Three separate questions, none of which the licensee resolves.**

**Does the vesting settle it?** The deed says separate property and the wife executed an interspousal transfer. That is substantial, and it is not conclusive — characterisation can be affected by what happened afterwards, including how the mortgage was paid.

**Does the pending separation change who must sign?** A marital dissolution proceeding commonly carries restraining provisions affecting the disposition of property. **A sale during a pending dissolution is a situation where escrow, the title insurer and counsel all have a view**, and none of them is the listing agent.

**Will the title company insure it?** In practical terms this is the question that decides whether the transaction closes, and it is answered by asking them — early, before the property is marketed, not after an offer is accepted.

**What the licensee should have done at listing:** noticed the interspousal transfer deed in the preliminary report, noticed that the seller described himself as separated, and raised both with the broker and with escrow **before spending the seller's money on marketing.** The cost of asking on day one is a phone call. The cost of asking after an accepted offer is a failed escrow and a buyer who has paid for an inspection.

### 4.9 Checkpoint

chunks.heading: 5. Condominiums and common interest developments
chunks.excerpt:
You should be able to state the general rule about joining in a conveyance, and describe what you do when the record and the client's description of title do not match.

## 5. Condominiums and common interest developments

### 5.1 What a common interest development is

A **common interest development** combines individually owned interests with a shared interest in common areas, governed by a set of recorded documents and administered by an association.

The recurring forms:

| Form | What the owner owns |
|---|---|
| **Condominium** | An individual unit — often defined by interior surfaces — plus an undivided interest in the common areas |
| **Planned development** | A separate lot, plus membership in an association owning or managing common areas |
| **Stock cooperative** | Shares in a corporation owning the building, plus a right of occupancy |
| **Community apartment** | An undivided interest in the whole, plus an exclusive right to occupy a unit |

The differences matter for financing, for what is being conveyed, and for how the owner's obligations arise.

### 5.2 The governing documents

Ownership in a common interest development comes with a body of private law the buyer is agreeing to be bound by:

chunks.heading: 5.3 Why this belongs in a principles course
chunks.excerpt:
- **The declaration** — recorded covenants, conditions, and restrictions establishing the scheme and the use restrictions.
- **Bylaws** — how the association operates and is governed.
- **Rules and regulations** — adopted by the association, and easier to change than the declaration.
- **The budget and reserve study** — what the association plans to spend and what it has set aside.
- **Meeting minutes** — where problems appear before they appear anywhere else.
- **Financial statements and assessment history.**
- **Pending or threatened litigation**, including construction defect claims.

### 5.3 Why this belongs in a principles course

Because the documents impose obligations that bind the buyer regardless of zoning and regardless of what the seller told him:

**Use restrictions.** Whether he may rent the unit, and on what terms. Whether he may keep animals. What he may do to the exterior, the patio, or the windows. Whether he may run a business from it.

**Assessments.** The regular assessment, and the association's power to levy **special assessments** — which can be substantial and which a buyer inherits.

**Reserves.** An association with inadequate reserves against known future work has a special assessment in its future, whether or not one has been declared.

**Litigation.** Construction defect litigation affecting the building is a material fact, and it can also affect the availability of financing.

### 5.4 The timing point

The buyer must have the documents **in time to review them within the contingency period** — which means requesting them promptly rather than late.

chunks.heading: 5.5 What a licensee does and does not do
chunks.excerpt:
This is one of the slow items. An association that takes three weeks to produce documents will destroy a fourteen-day review contingency that was ordered on day ten. A licensee who orders the documents at the start has given the buyer a real review; one who orders them late has given him a formality.

### 5.5 What a licensee does and does not do

**Does:** identify that the property is in a common interest development; order or ensure the documents are ordered immediately; confirm the buyer received them; recommend he read the declaration, the budget and reserves, the minutes, and any litigation disclosure; and document the recommendation.

**Does not:** summarize the declaration for the buyer, characterize the reserves as adequate, predict whether a special assessment will be levied, or advise whether litigation is serious. Each of those exceeds the license and invites reliance.

> **A buyer asks: "Are the reserves okay?"**
>
> **Correct:** "That's outside what I can assess, and it's exactly what to have reviewed before your contingency expires — the reserve study and the budget are in the packet, and a CPA or your attorney can tell you what they show. I'll note that we discussed it."
>
> **Incorrect:** "They look fine to me — this association seems well run."

### 5.6 What a buyer in a common interest development is actually buying

Section 5.3 explains why this belongs in a principles course. This section makes the point concrete, because the gap between what a buyer thinks he is buying and what he is buying is wider here than anywhere else in residential real estate.

**The buyer is acquiring four things at once:**

chunks.heading: 5.6 What a buyer in a common interest development is actually buying
chunks.excerpt:
1. **An interest in a unit or a lot**, defined by an instrument rather than by the walls he can see. **What is his, what is common, and what is exclusive-use common area is a documentary question**, and it determines who repairs what.
2. **An undivided interest in common area**, with its condition, its deferred maintenance, and its future costs.
3. **Membership in an association**, with governing documents that bind him and a board that can act.
4. **A share of an ongoing financial obligation** — regular assessments, and special assessments that have not happened yet.

**What the documents answer, and what each one is for:**

| The document | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Declaration and restrictions** | What may and may not be done — rentals, pets, alterations, business use, parking, occupancy |
| **Bylaws and rules** | How the association operates and what it may enforce |
| **Budget and reserve study** | **Whether the association can pay for what is coming** — the single most predictive document in the package |
| **Financial statements** | Present condition, delinquency rates, and whether assessments are being collected |
| **Minutes** | What the board has been discussing, which is frequently where a future special assessment first appears |
| **Insurance information** | What the association covers and, more importantly, what it does not |
| **Litigation disclosures** | Pending matters, which can affect both value and financing availability |

**Three points a licensee should make to every buyer, in writing.**

chunks.heading: 5.8 What a common interest development actually is, statutorily
chunks.excerpt:
**Order the documents on day one.** Section 5.4's timing point. **The buyer's review period is what remains after delivery**, and a package ordered on day six against a seven-day delivery obligation leaves a buyer reading hundreds of pages in a weekend.

**Read the reserve study and the minutes.** Buyers read the pet rules and skip these two. **A thinly funded reserve is a special assessment that has not been announced yet**, and the minutes are where it is visible first.

**Confirm what financing requires.** Some programs impose conditions on the development itself — owner-occupancy ratios, litigation status, budget requirements — and **a buyer can be approved while the development is not.**

> **Section 5.5's limit governs all of it.** The licensee delivers the documents, recommends they be reviewed with counsel, and **does not interpret the restrictions.** Whether a provision permits a particular use is a legal question about a recorded instrument, and it is asked of licensees constantly.

### 5.8 What a common interest development actually is, statutorily

Section 5.1 described condominiums functionally. The statutory frame matters because it determines which documents a buyer is entitled to, and when.

chunks.heading: 5.8 What a common interest development actually is, statutorily
chunks.excerpt:
The **Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act**, Civil Code Part 5 of Division 4 beginning at **§ 4000**, governs residential common interest developments in California. Its existence is confirmed by a section this course has already read for another purpose: **Business and Professions Code § 10153.2(a)(2)(K)** lists, among the courses that qualify an applicant for the broker examination, *"California law that relates to common interest developments, including, but not limited to, topics addressed in the **Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act** (Part 5 (commencing with Section 4000) of Division 4 of the Civil Code) and in the **Commercial and Industrial Common Interest Development Act** (Part 5.3 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 4 of the Civil Code)."*

**Two things follow from that citation, and both are useful to a Principles student.**

**There are two acts, not one.** Residential common interest developments are governed by Davis-Stirling; commercial and industrial ones by a separate act beginning at § 6500. A licensee working a commercial condominium is not working under the residential statute, and the disclosure obligations differ.

**The Legislature treats this as its own subject.** It appears in § 10153.2 as a standalone course option alongside escrows, property management and appraisal. **A licensee who treats a condominium as "a house with a homeowners association" is treating a distinct body of law as a detail**, and the transactions that go wrong are the ones handled that way.

chunks.heading: 5.9 The documents, and the diligence period problem
chunks.excerpt:
**This course does not teach Davis-Stirling.** It is not read here in its own text, and no rule, deadline, fee cap, election procedure, or enforcement mechanism in this assignment comes from it. What a Principles student should carry forward is the shape of the thing: a residential common interest development is a creature of a specific statute; that statute gives buyers rights to specific documents on specific timelines; and the person who knows which documents those are is the escrow holder, the association's manager, or counsel — not the licensee working from memory.

### 5.9 The documents, and the diligence period problem

**What a buyer in a common interest development is buying** is three things at once: a unit, an undivided interest in common area, and **membership in a corporation with the power to assess them**. The third is the one that produces surprises, and the surprises live in documents.

chunks.heading: 5.9 The documents, and the diligence period problem
chunks.excerpt:
| Document | What it answers | Why it is read early |
|---|---|---|
| **Declaration (CC&Rs)** | What the owner may and may not do; what is common area; how assessments are levied | It is recorded and it binds. Restrictions on rentals, pets, vehicles and alterations live here |
| **Bylaws and articles** | How the association is governed; who votes; how directors are elected | A dysfunctional board is a real risk to a buyer's use and resale |
| **Operating rules** | Day-to-day rules the board may adopt without amending the declaration | These change more often than the CC&Rs and are frequently the ones a buyer breaches |
| **Budget and reserve study** | What the association spends and whether it has saved for what is coming | **The single best predictor of a future special assessment** |
| **Assessment and delinquency statement** | What is owed on this unit, and what the association is owed generally | An association with heavy delinquencies is an association that will assess |
| **Minutes** | What the board is actually worried about | Litigation, construction defects and insurance problems appear here before they appear anywhere else |
| **Insurance summary** | What the association's policy covers and what the owner must insure | Determines what a buyer's own policy has to do |

**The structural problem is timing.** These documents come from the association, the association is often managed by a third party, and production takes days that the contract's diligence period does not always allow. **A buyer who receives a reserve study on the last afternoon of the contingency period has not had a diligence period.**

chunks.heading: 5.10 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**What a licensee does about it, concretely:** order the documents the day the offer is accepted rather than the day the contingency clock starts; tell the buyer in writing when they were ordered; and when they arrive late, **advise the buyer in writing that an extension of the contingency is available and that proceeding without reading them is the buyer's decision.** The licensee does not interpret the documents — reserve adequacy and litigation exposure are questions for an accountant and a lawyer — but the licensee is responsible for the documents arriving in time to be read by whoever should read them.

**A worked failure.**

> A buyer closes on a condominium in a 96-unit development. Four months later the association levies a $14,200 special assessment per unit to replace failed plumbing risers. The minutes for the preceding two years discuss the risers at eleven separate meetings, and the reserve study describes the component as "past useful life, unfunded."

**Nothing was concealed.** Every fact was in documents the buyer was entitled to and did receive — three days before closing, in a 340-page bundle, unread. **The failure was not disclosure. It was sequencing**, and sequencing is inside a licensee's control in a way that a board's spending decisions are not.

### 5.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to name what a buyer must review, explain why the documents must be ordered early, and answer a reserves question correctly.

## 6. Trust and entity ownership basics

### 6.1 Why this section exists

Because the most common and most expensive intake failure in residential practice is **unverified authority to convey**, and trusts and entities are where it happens.

chunks.heading: 6.2 Trust ownership
chunks.excerpt:
The failure has a consistent shape: someone with an obvious connection to the property — the occupant, the person paying the taxes, a beneficiary, an officer — signs a listing they have no authority to sign. It surfaces in escrow, where unwinding costs the most.

### 6.2 Trust ownership

Where title is held in a trust, the **trustee** holds legal title and may convey **only within the authority the trust document grants.**

| Party | Role |
|---|---|
| **Trustor / settlor** | Created the trust and transferred property into it |
| **Trustee** | Holds legal title and administers the trust; **signs** |
| **Beneficiary** | Holds the beneficial interest; **does not sign** |

What must be verified at intake:

1. **Who the current trustee is** — trustees change, and the person who was trustee three years ago may not be.
2. **That the trust authorizes sale of real property.**
3. **What the trust requires of the trustee in doing so** — some require consents or notices.
4. **That title is actually held in the trust**, against the record.

Occupancy, payment of taxes, and beneficial interest are each evidence of connection to the property, and **none establishes authority to sell it.**

### 6.3 Entity ownership
