chunks.heading: Practice problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Subordination agreement** | A lienholder's agreement to take a lower position than it would otherwise hold. A significant decision for counsel, not a formality. |
| **Preliminary report** | A report of record title stating the terms on which a policy would issue. Not a guarantee, not the policy, not a survey. |
| **Exception** | An item the policy **will not insure against**. The buyer bears that risk unless otherwise addressed. |
| **Exclusion** | A category the policy form does not cover at all — governmental regulation, eminent domain, matters created by the insured. |
| **Requirement** | Something the insurer needs before issuing. The items with deadlines attached. |

## Practice problems

### Problem 1

Classify each on both axes and state one practical consequence of the classification: (a) a deed of
trust; (b) a property tax lien; (c) a judgment lien; (d) a mechanic's lien.

**Answer.**

chunks.heading: Problem 2
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** (a) **Voluntary and specific.** Created by the owner's agreement and attached to this
> property. Consequence: it can be sold subject to, or paid from proceeds at closing — which is why the
> payoff demand, including accrued interest, is obtained rather than assumed from the balance.
>
> (b) **Involuntary and specific.** Consequence: it generally takes **priority regardless of when it
> attached**, which is the principal exception to first-in-time and exists because the taxing power
> does not depend on the order private parties recorded.
>
> (c) **Involuntary and general.** Consequence: it reaches **every parcel the debtor owns in the
> county**, including property acquired later while the lien is effective — which is why a buyer with an
> outstanding judgment discovers it attaching to the property he is buying, and why a judgment against
> a similarly named person must be resolved through title rather than assumed away.
>
> (d) **Involuntary and specific.** Consequence: its priority is **measured from commencement of the
> work**, so it can outrank an instrument recorded before the lien **if that instrument attached after
> the work commenced** — and not one already attached and of record when the work began (Civil Code
> § 8450(a)).

### Problem 2

A seller renovated the kitchen and rebuilt the deck last spring. He is in an unresolved dispute with
the general contractor over the final $18,000, and says two subcontractors he never met have been
calling. The preliminary report is clean.

**What is the exposure, and what does the licensee do?**

chunks.heading: Problem 3
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **A clean report is a snapshot, not a forecast.** Mechanic's lien exposure is exactly
> what a current report can fail to show.
>
> **Two features make this dangerous.** Priority is **measured from commencement of the work**, so a lien
> recorded next month can outrank a deed of trust recorded before the lien **if that deed of trust
> attached after last spring's work commenced** — though not one already attached and of record before
> the work began (Civil Code § 8450(a)). That is why lenders care about recent construction. And lien rights arise **from work, not from a contract with the owner**: the
> subcontractors and suppliers the seller never dealt with can have rights of their own.
>
> **What the licensee does:** ask the intake question — *has any work been done recently, by whom, and
> is everyone paid?* — route it to escrow, title, and counsel immediately, and ensure it is addressed
> before the contingency expires.
>
> **What the licensee does not do:** advise whether a lien would be valid or timely, or reassure the
> buyer that the dispute is between the seller and his contractor. The statutory scheme's notices and
> deadlines are legal questions.

### Problem 3

A preliminary report shows a ten-foot utility easement along the rear property line. The buyer is
purchasing the lot specifically to build a workshop at the rear. The agent tells him easements are
routine, offers to ask title to remove it, and says the workshop should be fine.

**Assess all three responses.**

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** All three are wrong, and the third is the one the buyer will rely on.
>
> **"Routine" is not an analysis.** Most properties have easements; this one may prevent exactly the
> structure the buyer is buying the property to build.
>
> **Title cannot "remove" an exception**, and asking misunderstands what an exception is: **an item the
> policy will not insure against.** It is not a blemish the insurer chose to note.
>
> **Predicting the effect on his plans is outside the license**, and it is a legal and land-use question
> at once.
>
> **What the licensee does:** obtain the underlying recorded document — width, location, permitted use,
> maintenance obligations — ensure the buyer reviews it, and route the effect on his plans to counsel
> and to the jurisdiction **before the contingency expires.** The exception names the easement; only the
> document says where it runs.

### Problem 4

A neighbor has parked in the seller's driveway for eleven years with permission. The seller says he
can revoke it any time. The buyer's agent says eleven years means the neighbor now has an easement.
Separately, an old access road across the property has not been used in twenty years, and the seller
says it is therefore gone.

**Assess each statement.**

chunks.heading: Problem 5
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** Three statements, and all three are conclusions a licensee must not deliver.
>
> **The permission is, in the ordinary case, a license** — revocable permission creating no interest in
> the land and not running with it. So far the seller's description is the usual one.
>
> **But "eleven years" raises a prescriptive claim**, which is a legal doctrine with requirements
> neither agent can evaluate — and permission itself bears on the analysis. Neither "it's just a
> license" nor "he has an easement now" is a statement a licensee can make.
>
> **Non-use alone generally does not terminate an easement.** Easements end by express release, merger,
> expiration of a stated term, abandonment where the requirements are met, or impossibility of purpose
> — not by twenty years of nobody driving on it.
>
> **What transfers:** "we've always let them" and "nobody has used it in years" are both sentences a
> licensee **routes** rather than resolves. Disclose the facts, obtain the documents, and refer.

### Problem 5

A buyer wants to add a second dwelling unit. The city's zoning permits it. The recorded CC&Rs prohibit
more than one dwelling per lot. The agent tells him he is "zoned for it, so you're fine," and adds that
the restriction is probably unenforceable because nobody has enforced it in years.

**Correct both.**

chunks.heading: Problem 6
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Zoning permission answers half the question.** Private restrictions and zoning come
> from different sources, are enforced by different parties, and are changed by different procedures —
> and **neither overrides the other.** In practice the **more restrictive governs**: zoning permitting a
> duplex does not authorize one where the recorded restrictions prohibit it. The buyer must satisfy
> both.
>
> **The enforceability opinion is a legal conclusion the licensee cannot give**, and it is the kind a
> buyer will spend money relying on. Restrictions are enforced by those entitled to enforce them —
> other owners in the scheme, or the association — and non-enforcement history is a legal argument, not
> a fact the licensee can assert.
>
> **The correct answer:** *"There are two separate questions — what the city allows and what the
> recorded restrictions allow, and you have to satisfy both. Here are the CC&Rs; the use article starts
> on page eleven. The city's planning counter answers the zoning half. Get both answers before your
> contingency expires, and I'll note that we discussed it."*

### Problem 6

A buyer notices a well-worn path crossing the rear of the lot and an occupant in the guest house who
is not the seller. The seller says the occupant is "just a friend staying temporarily" and there is
nothing recorded about the path.

**What kind of notice is in play, and what should happen?**

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Inquiry notice** — the one that surprises people, because nothing was recorded.
>
> The recording system answers who has notice of what. **Actual notice** is knowing in fact.
> **Constructive notice** is what the law charges a person with because a document was recorded — a
> recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so everyone is treated as knowing it. **Inquiry
> notice** arises from facts that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate.
>
> An occupant who is not the record owner and a worn path across the lot are the textbook facts. The
> buyer may be charged with **what a reasonable investigation would have revealed**, recorded or not —
> which could include an unrecorded lease, a claimed prescriptive right, or an occupancy the seller
> cannot terminate on schedule.
>
> **What should happen:** the facts are disclosed and investigated rather than explained away. Ask for
> any written agreement with the occupant, route the path to a survey and to counsel, and do not accept
> "just a friend" as a description of a possessory interest.

### Problem 7

A seller carrying financing on a parcel is asked to sign a subordination agreement so a construction
lender can record in first position. His agent tells him it is standard and to go ahead. Separately,
the buyer declines an owner's title policy because "the lender is getting a title policy anyway."

**Assess both.**

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Subordination is a significant decision, not a formality.** The seller is agreeing to
> take a **lower position than he would otherwise hold**, behind a construction loan — and priority
> determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A junior
> lienholder wiped out by a senior foreclosure has lost its security whatever the merits of the debt.
> Whether to sign belongs to **counsel**, and "it's standard" is the single most expensive sentence a
> licensee can say about it.
>
> **The owner's and lender's policies insure different interests.** The lender's policy insures the
> lender's lien and its priority — **not the buyer's ownership.** A buyer who declines an owner's policy
> has not economized on a duplicate; he has left his own interest uninsured.
>
> Worth adding while the subject is open: **extended coverage** may address matters a standard policy
> excepts, including some survey matters, typically requiring a survey or other evidence. Whether to
> obtain it is the buyer's decision, made informed.

### Problem 8

A preliminary report received on day twelve of a fourteen-day review shows: recorded CC&Rs; an
unreleased deed of trust the seller says was paid in 2016; a judgment against a person with a name
similar to the seller's; a lis pendens; and a requirement for a corporate resolution.

**Handle each, and state what went wrong before any of it.**

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The timing failure came first**, and it is the one that made everything else harder.
> The preliminary report and its underlying documents belong at the **front** of the queue with the
> association documents and hazard-area insurance quotes. An exception discovered on day twelve — an
> unreleased lien needing a document from a lender that may no longer exist — leaves a formality where
> a review should have been.
>
> **The CC&Rs:** obtain and review; they bind the buyer regardless of zoning.
>
> **The unreleased deed of trust:** a recorded **reconveyance** must be obtained. Payment of the debt
> does not clear the record; a document does, and the seller's recollection is not that document.
>
> **The similar-name judgment:** route to title for resolution. Do not assume it is or is not the
> seller — a judgment lien is general and reaches everything the debtor owns in the county.
>
> **The lis pendens:** recognize it as a serious cloud. It is not itself a lien, but it gives notice
> that pending litigation may affect anyone acquiring an interest, which in practice stops
> transactions. Route to counsel immediately.
>
> **The resolution:** this is a **requirement**, not an exception — something the insurer needs before
> issuing, and therefore the item with a deadline attached. Distinguish the three throughout:
> **exceptions** are risks not insured, **exclusions** are categories outside the policy, and
> **requirements** must be satisfied before closing.

## Chapter summary

**An encumbrance affects title or use.** Liens secure debts; easements, restrictions, and encroachments
govern what may be done.

**Classify liens on two axes** — voluntary or involuntary, general or specific — and read the practical
consequence off the classification.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
**A lien does not prevent a sale**; it is ordinarily paid from proceeds, which is why payoff figures
exceed principal balances.

**Payment does not clear the record.** A recorded reconveyance does.

**Property tax liens generally take priority regardless of timing, and mechanic's lien priority may
relate back** — the two exceptions that defeat the first-recorded intuition. Recent construction is an
intake question.

**An easement is a non-possessory right that runs with the land.** The servient parcel serves the
dominant one; appurtenant easements pass with the dominant parcel automatically. Non-use generally does
not terminate one, and long permitted use is a doctrine to route rather than resolve.

**A license is revocable, creates no interest, and does not run with the land** — but "we've always let
them" belongs to counsel.

**Zoning and recorded restrictions are independent, and the more restrictive governs.** "Zoned for it,
so you're fine" answers half the question, and enforceability is never the licensee's call.

**Encroachments are disclosed, surveyed, and referred — never characterized.**

**Recording answers who has notice.** Constructive notice comes from the record; **inquiry notice**
comes from facts on the ground that would prompt investigation.

**Priority determines who is paid first and whose interest survives foreclosure**, which is why
subordination is a decision for counsel rather than a standard formality.

**An exception is a risk the policy will not insure against.** Read exceptions, obtain the underlying
documents, distinguish exceptions from exclusions and requirements, and never treat an item as routine,
ask for its removal, or predict its effect.

**Order the report early.** Late discovery converts a review into a formality.

chunks.heading: Required applied assignment
chunks.excerpt:
## Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Classify each encumbrance on both axes, state how each arose and what would remove it, identify the priority questions and any exception to first-in-time that applies, distinguish the exceptions from the exclusions and requirements on the report given, state what you would obtain and in what order and by what deadline, identify what you would route to title, to a surveyor, and to counsel, and state what you would decline to characterize and why. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

## Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

## Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

lessons.title: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 06

chunks.heading: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 06
chunks.excerpt:
# Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 06

## Government powers, land use, and environmental controls

**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Assignment time:** 180 instructional minutes
**Regulatory status:** Not approved; no California credit is available.

## Learning objectives

- Identify the four government powers over private property and distinguish them by what each takes and what compensation each requires.
- Explain how a general plan, zoning, and the entitlement process relate, and identify what each answers.
- Describe subdivision and building controls and explain what a permit record does and does not establish.
- Identify the environmental hazards a California residential transaction commonly raises and state the licensee's role for each.
- Explain natural hazard disclosure and water-related requirements at the level a licensee must handle them.
- Build a land-use due diligence sequence that puts slow items first.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: government powers and the planning framework | 55 | Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved |
| Guided reading: subdivision, building controls, and environmental hazards | 50 | Sections 3-4 viewed |
| Guided reading: natural hazard context and due diligence | 45 | Sections 5-6 viewed |
| Applied scenario and decision memorandum | 20 | Written response submitted |
| Lesson assessment | 10 | Five scored items submitted |
| **Total** | **180** | **One of 15 separate lesson assignments** |

## 1. Taxation, eminent domain, police power, and escheat

### 1.1 Fee simple absolute is not absolute against government

chunks.heading: 1.2 Police power
chunks.excerpt:
Lesson 03 established that fee simple absolute is the greatest estate the law recognizes. It is nonetheless subject to four government powers, conventionally remembered as **PETE**:

| Power | What it does | Compensation |
|---|---|---|
| **P** — Police power | Regulates use for public health, safety, morals, and general welfare | **None** |
| **E** — Eminent domain | Takes property for public use | **Just compensation required** |
| **T** — Taxation | Levies on property to fund government | None; it is a charge, not a taking |
| **E** — Escheat | Property passes to the state where an owner dies with no heirs and no will | None |

**The compensation column is the distinction that matters.** Regulation under the police power reduces what an owner may do without paying him; eminent domain takes and pays.

### 1.2 Police power

The broadest of the four, and the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision regulation, environmental controls, health and safety requirements, and rent regulation where a jurisdiction has adopted it.

The power is exercised by state and local government. Its exercise must serve a legitimate public purpose and must not be arbitrary — but within those limits it can substantially reduce what an owner may do, and the owner is not compensated.

> A parcel zoned for commercial use is rezoned residential, and its market value falls by half. **That is regulation, not a taking**, in the ordinary case. The owner has not lost the property; he has lost uses.

chunks.heading: 1.3 Eminent domain
chunks.excerpt:
Where regulation goes so far as to deprive an owner of substantially all economically beneficial use, the question of a **regulatory taking** arises. Whether a particular regulation crosses that line is a legal question of real complexity, and a licensee's role is to recognize the concept, never to advise that a client has a claim.

### 1.3 Eminent domain

The power to take private property for public use upon payment of just compensation. The process is called **condemnation**.

Two situations a licensee should be able to name:

**Partial taking.** Where only part of a parcel is taken, compensation may address both the part taken and **severance damages** to what remains — for example, where the remainder is left an unusable shape or loses its access.

**Inverse condemnation.** Where government action effectively takes or damages property without a formal proceeding, and the owner brings the claim rather than the government.

**A pending or threatened condemnation is a material fact.** It affects value, marketability, and the buyer's plans, and it is disclosed. Whether the owner has a claim, what compensation is due, and how to respond are legal questions for counsel.

### 1.4 Taxation

Property taxation is taken up in Lesson 13. For present purposes:

- Property taxes become a **lien on the property**, generally with priority over other liens regardless of when they attached.
- **Special assessments** fund improvements benefiting particular property, and a buyer inherits the remaining obligation.
- Unpaid property taxes can ultimately lead to sale of the property under the applicable process.

### 1.5 Escheat

chunks.heading: 1.6 What a licensee actually does with this section
chunks.excerpt:
Where a person dies owning property with no will and no heirs who take under the law of intestate succession, the property passes to the state. It is uncommon in residential practice and appears mainly as a concept and occasionally in a chain of title.

### 1.6 What a licensee actually does with this section

Three things:

1. **Recognize which power is operating.** A rezoning is police power; a road widening that takes twelve feet of frontage is eminent domain.
2. **Treat pending government action as a material fact** — a proposed rezoning, an announced project, a pending condemnation.
3. **Refer the legal questions.** Whether compensation is owed, whether a regulation has gone too far, and what a taking is worth are all outside the license.

### 1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the four powers, state which requires compensation, and distinguish regulation from a taking on a set of facts.

## 2. Zoning and general plans

### 2.1 The planning hierarchy

California land use is organized in layers, and each answers a different question.

| Layer | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **General plan** | What does this jurisdiction intend this area to become? |
| **Specific plan** | How will that intent be implemented in this particular area? |
| **Zoning ordinance** | What uses and development standards apply to this parcel **now**? |
| **Entitlements and permits** | What has this particular parcel actually been approved for? |

**The general plan is the long-range policy document**, and California requires local general plans to address specified elements — land use, circulation, housing, conservation, open space, noise, and safety among them. **Zoning is generally required to be consistent with the general plan.**

chunks.heading: 2.2 What a zoning ordinance controls
chunks.excerpt:
For a licensee the operative point is that the general plan describes intent while zoning controls today, and a buyer asking "will this area change?" is asking a general plan question, answered by the jurisdiction rather than by the licensee.

### 2.2 What a zoning ordinance controls

**Use** — what may occur on the parcel: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, mixed, and the subcategories within each.

**Development standards** — the physical envelope: setbacks from each property line, maximum height, lot coverage, floor area ratio, minimum lot size, parking requirements, and open space.

Both halves matter. A parcel zoned to permit a second unit may still be unable to accommodate one within the setbacks, the height limit, and the parking requirement. **Permitted use and physical feasibility are different questions**, and clients routinely conflate them.

### 2.3 The relief mechanisms

Where a proposal does not fit the ordinance, three mechanisms are commonly available, and they are frequently confused.

| Mechanism | What it addresses |
|---|---|
| **Variance** | Relief from a **development standard** — a setback, a height limit — usually requiring a hardship arising from the property itself |
| **Conditional use permit** | Permission for a **use** the ordinance allows in that zone subject to review and conditions |
| **Rezoning** | A change to the ordinance itself, moving the parcel to a different zone |

> **The distinction to hold:** a variance addresses the envelope; a conditional use permit addresses the use; a rezoning changes the rule.

chunks.heading: 2.4 Nonconforming use
chunks.excerpt:
All three are **discretionary**. Nobody is entitled to one, and a licensee who tells a buyer a variance "won't be a problem" has predicted a discretionary decision — which Lesson 13 of the Practice course identifies as a prediction stated as certainty.

### 2.4 Nonconforming use

A **legal nonconforming use** is one that was lawful when established and no longer conforms because the ordinance changed. It is commonly permitted to continue — often described as being "grandfathered."

Three limits that surprise owners:

- **Expansion is generally restricted.** The right is usually to continue, not to enlarge.
- **Discontinuance can end it.** Many ordinances terminate the right after a period of abandonment.
- **Destruction can end it.** Rebuilding after substantial destruction may not be permitted.

**And a use that was never lawful is not a nonconforming use.** It is an unpermitted use, which is a different and worse problem — and "it's been like that for thirty years" does not convert one into the other.

### 2.5 Recorded restrictions again

From Lesson 05, restated because it belongs here too: **zoning and recorded private restrictions are independent, and the more restrictive generally governs in practice.** Zoning permitting a use does not authorize it where the CC&Rs prohibit it. A buyer must satisfy both.

### 2.6 What a licensee may say

**May:** identify the current zoning designation with its source; explain that zoning governs use and development standards; explain that variances, conditional use permits, and rezonings exist and are discretionary; direct the buyer to the planning counter; and confirm that the buyer investigated before his contingency expired.

chunks.heading: 2.7 A worked land-use inquiry
chunks.excerpt:
**May not:** state that a use is permitted; predict that an application will be approved; interpret setback or height provisions for the buyer's project; or characterize an existing condition as legally nonconforming.

> **A buyer asks: "Can I build a second unit here?"**
>
> **Correct:** "That's two questions — what the zoning allows and whether the lot can physically fit it within setbacks, height, and parking, plus whatever the recorded restrictions say. The city's planning counter answers the first two, and I'll get you the CC&Rs for the third. Let's get both before your contingency expires, and I'll note we discussed it."
>
> **Incorrect:** "The zoning allows it, so you're fine."

### 2.7 A worked land-use inquiry

> **A buyer under contract on a residence tells the licensee he intends to convert the detached garage into a rental unit, run a small contracting business from the property, and add a second story.**
>
> **Three plans, and each is governed by more than one system.**
>
> **The public side — Section 2.2's ordinance.** Whether the zone permits an accessory dwelling unit, what standards apply to it, whether a home occupation is permitted and on what conditions, and what height, setback, and coverage limits apply to a second story. **Each has an answer, and the answers come from the jurisdiction rather than from the licensee.**
>
> **The relief mechanisms — Section 2.3.** Where the ordinance does not permit something as of right, a variance or a conditional use permit may exist as a path. **They are processes with standards, timelines, hearings, and no guaranteed outcome**, and "you can just get a variance" is one of the more damaging sentences a licensee can say.
>
> **The private side — Section 2.5 and Lesson 05, Section 4.2.** Recorded restrictions can pr

chunks.heading: 2.7 A worked land-use inquiry
chunks.excerpt:
ohibit what zoning permits. **A property in a development whose declaration forbids rentals or business use is a property where the zoning answer is irrelevant to the buyer's plan.**
>
> **The building side — Section 3.2.** Permits, plans, and inspections, and a conversion of existing space carries its own requirements. **Section 3.3's unpermitted-work problem is what this becomes if the buyer proceeds without them.**
>
> **The practical sequence the licensee recommends, in writing:**
>
> 1. **Ask the jurisdiction** — planning for use and standards, building for permit requirements — **before removing contingencies.**
> 2. **Obtain and read the recorded restrictions**, and route their interpretation to counsel.
> 3. **Confirm with a design or construction professional** what the existing structure will actually support.
> 4. **Confirm insurance and financing implications** where a use changes.
>
> **What the licensee says, and what he does not.**
>
> **He says:** these are three separate questions with four sources of answers, here is where each answer comes from, and here is the deadline by which you need them.
>
> **He does not say:** "ADUs are allowed everywhere now," "nobody enforces the home-occupation rules," "you can add a second story, the neighbor did," or **any version of what the ordinance permits.** Section 2.6 states the boundary, and the neighbor's second story is the least reliable evidence available — it may have been permitted under a different ordinance, granted relief, or built without permission.
>
> > **The recurring error this prevents.** A buyer removes his contingencies on the strength of a licensee's encouragement, closes, and discovers that the conversion he bought the property for requires a discretionary approval he will not get. **The inform

chunks.heading: 2.8 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
ation was available on day two, from a phone call to a public counter, and the licensee's contribution was to say who to call.**

### 2.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish a variance from a conditional use permit, explain the limits on a nonconforming use, and answer a buildability question correctly.

## 3. Subdivision and building controls

### 3.1 The two subdivision statutes, revisited

From Lesson 04, because it is the land use half that matters here:

**The Subdivision Map Act** governs the **creation** of parcels — the tentative and final map process, the conditions a local agency may impose, dedications, and required improvements. It answers whether a parcel may lawfully be created and sold.

**The Subdivided Lands Law** is the DRE-administered consumer protection statute governing the **sale** of subdivided interests, including the public report requirement before certain subdivided property may be offered.

The recurring practice point: **a separate tax bill is not evidence of a lawful split.** Where a parcel's creation is in question, it goes to the local agency, to title, and to counsel — before it is marketed as a separate building site, because marketing it as one is a factual claim about entitlement.

### 3.2 Building codes and permits

Building codes set minimum standards for construction, and work generally requires a **permit** and **inspections** culminating in a final approval.

What a permit record establishes and does not:

chunks.heading: 3.3 Unpermitted work
chunks.excerpt:
| Establishes | Does not establish |
|---|---|
| That a permit was issued for described work | That the work was completed |
| That inspections were performed, where finaled | That the work was done well |
| The scope as permitted | That subsequent work was permitted |
| A date | That current condition matches the permit |

**A permit that was issued but never finaled is a real problem** — an open permit can complicate a sale, and the obligation to close it out generally follows the property.

### 3.3 Unpermitted work

This is among the most common problems in California residential transactions, and licensees mishandle it in both directions.

**The facts to establish:** what work was done, when, whether a permit was issued, whether it was finaled, and whether the work is habitable and safe as built.

**What the licensee does:**

1. **Disclose what is known**, including what the seller said and what the licensee observed.
2. **Recommend permit research** at the jurisdiction — which is a public record and is where the answer actually lives.
3. **Do not include unpermitted area in advertised square footage** without disclosing its status.
4. **Recommend the buyer investigate what legalization would require**, since the cost can be substantial and sometimes the work cannot be legalized at all.
5. **Document the recommendation and the buyer's response.**

**What the licensee does not do:** state that the work is legal because it looks fine, characterize the risk as low, predict what the city would require, or advise the seller to say nothing because "everyone does it."

chunks.heading: 3.4 Certificates and clearances
chunks.excerpt:
> **The asymmetry worth teaching:** unpermitted work does not automatically make a property unsaleable, and it does automatically make it a disclosure item. Licensees fail on both sides — some conceal it, some describe it as a disaster. The professional response is to make it visible and investigable.

### 3.4 Certificates and clearances

Depending on the jurisdiction and the property type, a transfer may trigger local requirements — retrofit obligations for smoke and carbon monoxide devices and water conservation fixtures, occupancy or resale inspections, sewer lateral requirements, or point-of-sale reports.

**These are local and they vary.** A licensee working across city lines who assumes uniformity will eventually miss one, and a missed point-of-sale requirement can delay a closing.

### 3.5 Accessibility in new construction

Certain multifamily housing is subject to accessible design and construction requirements, and California standards can exceed the federal baseline. A licensee marketing new construction should not represent that a property meets accessibility requirements without confirming it, and should direct specific questions to the developer, the architect, or the jurisdiction.

### 3.7 Two subdivision statutes, and why California has both

Section 3.1 described subdivision approval as a local process. It is that, and it is also a state one, and the two run on different definitions. A licensee who knows only "five or more parcels" has half of it.

chunks.heading: 3.7 Two subdivision statutes, and why California has both
chunks.excerpt:
**The Subdivision Map Act — Government Code § 66410 and following.** The Act names itself in a single sentence: *"This division may be cited as the Subdivision Map Act."* It is the **local land-division statute**: it governs how land is divided, what maps are filed, and what conditions a city or county may impose.

Its definition, at **Government Code § 66424**, is deliberately broad:

> *"…any unimproved land, or any portion thereof, shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll as a unit or as contiguous units, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future. **Property shall be considered as contiguous units, even if it is separated by roads, streets, utility easement, or railroad rights-of-way.** 'Subdivision' includes a **condominium project** …, a **community apartment project** …, or the **conversion of five or more existing dwelling units to a stock cooperative**…"*

**The Subdivided Lands Act — Business and Professions Code § 11000 and following.** This is the **consumer-protection statute**, administered by the Department of Real Estate, and it is why a public report exists. Its definition is narrower and counts differently:

> *"'Subdivided lands' and 'subdivision' refer to improved or unimproved land or lands, wherever situated within California, divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale or lease or financing, whether immediate or future, into **five or more lots or parcels**."*

**The two acts do not overlap neatly, and that is the point.**

chunks.heading: 3.8 The 160-acre carve-out and the exclusions
chunks.excerpt:
| | Subdivision Map Act | Subdivided Lands Act |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | Gov. Code § 66410 et seq. | B&P Code § 11000 et seq. |
| **Administered by** | Cities and counties | The Department of Real Estate |
| **Purpose** | How land may be divided; maps, conditions, dedications | Whether the offering may be sold to the public; disclosure |
| **Trigger** | Division of land into parcels, including two | **Five or more** lots or parcels |
| **Output** | Tentative and final maps; parcel maps | **Public report** |

**Three consequences worth carrying.**

**A two-lot split is a subdivision for map purposes and not for public-report purposes.** The owner deals with the county and files a parcel map; no DRE public report is involved. **A licensee who tells such an owner they need a public report is wrong, and one who tells a five-lot subdivider they do not is wrong more expensively.**

**"Contiguous even if separated by roads" closes an obvious avoidance route.** An owner cannot escape the Map Act by pointing at the street between their two holdings.

**A condominium project is a subdivision.** § 66424 says so expressly. Converting an apartment building to condominiums is a land division in the eyes of the Map Act even though no soil is moved, and converting five or more units to a stock cooperative is too. **The most common "subdivision" a residential licensee will ever touch involves no vacant land at all.**

### 3.8 The 160-acre carve-out and the exclusions

§ 11000 carries exclusions that show what the Legislature was aiming at.

chunks.heading: 3.9 What this means for a residential licensee, concretely
chunks.excerpt:
**The 160-acre parcels.** Land *"sold by lots or parcels of not less than 160 acres which are designated by lot or parcel description by government surveys and appear as such on the current assessment roll"* is not subdivided land — **unless** it is divided for sale for oil and gas purposes, in which case it is. The consumer-protection concern was never large agricultural parcels described by government survey; it was the sale of small parcels to buyers who cannot inspect what they are buying. **But oil and gas is carved back in**, because that is a pattern the Legislature had specific reason to reach.

**Ordinary leasing is out.** The chapter *"does not apply to the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment building, industrial building, commercial building, or mobilehome park."* Renting an office suite is not subdividing.

**With two exceptions that are back in.** Mobile home park leases *"for a term in excess of five years … as a mandatory requirement and prerequisite to tenancy"* are subject to the chapter. And leasing apartments in a **community apartment project** is subject to it. Both are situations where a "lease" is functionally the sale of a long-term interest to a consumer.

**And the two acts are told not to disturb each other.** § 11000(b): *"Nothing in this section shall in any way modify or affect any of the provisions of Section 66424 of the Government Code."* The Legislature knew the definitions differ and said so.

### 3.9 What this means for a residential licensee, concretely

Most licensees will never subdivide anything. They will, regularly, meet the consequences.

chunks.heading: 3.10 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**A buyer purchasing in a new development is entitled to a public report.** Where the Subdivided Lands Act applies, the subdivider may not sell or lease before the Department has issued one, and the buyer receives and acknowledges it. **A licensee representing a buyer in a new tract who has not seen the public report has not seen the central disclosure document of the transaction.**

**A seller who "split off the back lot" years ago may have created a problem.** A division that did not follow the Map Act may have produced a parcel that is not legally separate, which surfaces when a buyer's lender asks for a legal description and a title insurer declines to insure. **The question to ask is not "is it a separate parcel" but "what map created it, and when."**

**A condominium conversion is a subdivision.** A client proposing to convert a four-plex is proposing a land division under § 66424 and should be sent to counsel and to the city before, not after, they market units.

**None of these is a question a licensee answers.** Each is a question a licensee must be able to *recognise*, early enough that the person who does answer it can be brought in while the answer still matters.

### 3.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what a permit record establishes, handle unpermitted work correctly, and explain why local transfer requirements need to be checked jurisdiction by jurisdiction.

## 4. Environmental hazards and disclosure

### 4.1 The licensee's role, stated once for all of them

For every hazard in this section the role is the same three steps:

1. **Disclose what is known**, including the licensee's own observations.
2. **Recommend appropriate investigation** by a qualified professional, matched to the property.
3. **Do not evaluate.**

chunks.heading: 4.2 Age-triggered: lead-based paint
chunks.excerpt:
A licensee who tells a buyer that visible growth "is just surface mold, it'll clean off" has made an assessment they are not qualified to make, on which the buyer may rely.

### 4.2 Age-triggered: lead-based paint

For target housing built **before 1978**, the federal lead-based paint requirements apply. They are triggered by the **age of the housing**, not by whether children will occupy it, and licensees routinely misstate them in both directions.

| The obligation is | The obligation is not |
|---|---|
| Disclose **known** lead-based paint and hazards | Test the property |
| Provide **available records and reports** | Create records that do not exist |
| Provide the required **pamphlet** | Certify the property is free of lead |
| Give the buyer an **opportunity to conduct an assessment** | Remediate before transfer |

### 4.3 The other common hazards

**Asbestos.** Present in older construction in insulation, flooring, roofing, and other materials. Generally of most concern when disturbed. Evaluation and abatement are specialist work.

**Radon.** A naturally occurring soil gas that can accumulate indoors. Testing is inexpensive relative to the transaction and is the only way to know.

**Mold.** Requires moisture, which means the underlying question is usually where the water is coming from. A licensee should disclose visible growth and moisture evidence as **observations** and recommend evaluation — never characterize the type or the risk.

**Methamphetamine contamination.** Where a property was used for manufacture, remediation obligations and notice requirements can apply. A licensee learning of a history routes it immediately.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Proximity and off-site conditions
chunks.excerpt:
**Underground storage tanks.** Common on older and rural property. Leaking tanks create soil and groundwater contamination questions and potentially substantial liability.

**Soil and groundwater contamination.** Arising from prior industrial or agricultural use, adjacent operations, or historic fill. On any property with an industrial or agricultural history, the question belongs at intake.

**Formaldehyde, PCBs, and other building-material issues**, which appear in particular construction eras and product types.

### 4.4 Proximity and off-site conditions

Some conditions are not on the property at all: a neighboring industrial use, an agricultural operation with spraying or odor, a rail corridor, a flight path, a former landfill, a high-voltage corridor.

These raise the same discipline. **Disclose what is known, point the buyer to objective sources, and do not characterize.** Whether an odor from an adjacent dairy is tolerable is the buyer's judgment to make with accurate information — not the licensee's to make for him.

### 4.5 The environmental site assessment, in outline

For commercial and some other transactions, environmental due diligence is conducted through a phased assessment: a **Phase I** records and site reconnaissance review to identify recognized environmental conditions, followed where warranted by a **Phase II** involving sampling.

A licensee should know the terms, know that these are specialist reports, and know that they take time — which puts them at the front of the due diligence queue rather than the back.

### 4.7 The natural hazard zones, and what disclosure of them means

chunks.heading: 4.7 The natural hazard zones, and what disclosure of them means
chunks.excerpt:
Section 4.3 listed the hazard disclosures. This section is the working knowledge: which zones exist, what each says about the property, and what it obliges a buyer to do.

| Zone | What it means | Practical consequence for a buyer |
|---|---|---|
| **Special flood hazard area** | Mapped by FEMA as subject to inundation in a base flood | A federally regulated lender **will require flood insurance**. Premiums vary by an order of magnitude between zones |
| **Area of potential flooding** | Downstream of a dam, subject to inundation if the dam failed | Rarely insurable as such; a disclosure item rather than a lending condition |
| **Very high fire hazard severity zone** | Mapped by the state or a local agency | **Insurance availability, not price, is the issue.** Carriers have withdrawn from these areas |
| **Wildland area / state responsibility area** | Fire protection is the state's rather than a local district's | Defensible-space obligations; a fire prevention fee history |
| **Earthquake fault zone** | Alquist-Priolo mapped surface fault trace | Restricts construction across the trace; affects the feasibility of an addition |
| **Seismic hazard zone** | Mapped liquefaction or landslide susceptibility | May require a geotechnical report before permits issue |

**This course does not read the mapping statutes in their own text.** No deadline, exemption, form requirement, or fee in this assignment is taken from them. What a Principles student needs is the shape: **six zones, each mapped by a public agency, each disclosed on a natural hazard disclosure statement, and each meaning something different to a buyer.**

chunks.heading: 4.8 Disclosure is not investigation, and the line between them
chunks.excerpt:
**The distinction that decides transactions is insurance.** A flood zone is a **price** problem — coverage exists and costs money. A very high fire hazard severity zone is increasingly an **availability** problem, and a buyer who cannot obtain a policy cannot obtain a loan. **A licensee should tell a buyer to get an insurance quote in the first days of the contingency period**, not the last, because in some markets the quote takes longer than the contingency.

### 4.8 Disclosure is not investigation, and the line between them

**What the disclosure does.** It reports what the public maps show. The maps are the source; the report is a transcription.

**What it does not do.** It does not say whether *this house* will flood, burn or shift. It does not survey the site. A property just outside a mapped zone may face nearly the same physical risk as one just inside, because the line on the map is a regulatory boundary and not a change in the ground.

**Three failures that follow from confusing the two.**

**Treating "not in a zone" as "no risk."** The most common. A buyer who reads *"not in a special flood hazard area"* and concludes the property does not flood has read a statement about a map.

**Treating "in a zone" as a defect to be argued about.** A property in a mapped zone is not defective; it is located where it is located. The transaction question is insurability and cost, and both are answerable with a phone call.

**Treating the report as the end of diligence.** The natural hazard report is one input. The others — an inspection, an insurance quote, a geotechnical opinion where the seismic map warrants one, and the seller's own knowledge of past flooding or fire — are separate, and no one of them substitutes for another.

**A worked situation.**

chunks.heading: 4.9 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
> A buyer is in contract on a hillside property. The natural hazard disclosure reports: not in a flood zone; **in a very high fire hazard severity zone**; **in a seismic hazard zone (landslide)**; not in an earthquake fault zone. The buyer's agent forwards the report on day 4 of a 17-day contingency period with the note "standard disclosures attached."

**Two items on that report should have generated action rather than a forward.**

**The fire zone means the buyer must confirm insurance is available before removing contingencies**, and in some California markets that has meant weeks and a surplus-lines policy at several times the expected premium. A buyer who removes contingencies without a bound quote has removed the only exit.

**The landslide designation means a geotechnical question exists**, and if the buyer intends any addition or grading, the designation will meet them again at the permit counter. That is a question for a geotechnical engineer inside the contingency period.

**What "standard disclosures attached" communicated instead** was that the report was routine and required no thought. **The licensee's obligation was not to interpret the hazards** — they are not qualified to — **but to say which items have consequences and which professionals answer them**, in writing, on day 4.

### 4.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the lead-based paint obligations correctly in both directions, and give the correct response to a buyer asking whether visible mold is serious.

## 5. Water conservation and natural-hazard context

### 5.1 Natural hazard disclosure

chunks.heading: 5.2 Why it matters more than buyers assume
chunks.excerpt:
California requires disclosure of whether a property lies within certain mapped hazard zones — flood, fire, seismic, and related designations. The disclosure is commonly prepared by a third-party report provider.

What it does and does not do:

- **Does:** tell the buyer the property is within a mapped zone, so he can investigate what that means for insurance, construction requirements, and risk.
- **Does not:** certify the property is safe, predict whether an event will occur, or substitute for the buyer's own investigation.

**It applies based on mapping, not on the property's event history.** A property that has never flooded in the seller's twenty years of ownership is disclosed as within a flood zone if it is mapped in one, and a buyer's view that the mapping is outdated changes nothing about the obligation.

### 5.2 Why it matters more than buyers assume

Hazard zone status drives consequences buyers regularly discover late:

**Insurance availability and cost.** In some California areas this is now the determining factor in whether a transaction closes at all.

**Construction and improvement requirements**, which can materially affect renovation plans.

**Financing**, where lenders require particular coverage.

**Disclosure obligations the buyer inherits** as a future seller.

> **The single most preventable failure in this area:** insurance quotes obtained at the end of the contingency period rather than at the beginning. A buyer who learns in week one that coverage will cost far more than assumed can act. A buyer who learns it two days before closing generally cannot.

### 5.3 Seismic context

chunks.heading: 5.4 Fire hazard severity
chunks.excerpt:
California's seismic mapping includes zones related to fault rupture and to seismic hazards such as liquefaction and landslide. Older residential construction may present retrofit questions — foundation bolting, cripple wall bracing, chimney condition.

The licensee's role is the familiar one: disclose what is known and what is mapped, recommend evaluation by a qualified professional, and route the engineering questions.

### 5.4 Fire hazard severity

Mapped fire hazard severity zones carry consequences including defensible space obligations, construction and material requirements in some areas, and — most acutely in current California practice — insurance availability.

A licensee listing or selling in a mapped fire area should treat insurance as a **first-week item**, not an administrative closing task.

### 5.5 Water: supply, rights, and conservation

Three distinct topics that clients merge.

**Supply.** Where does the water come from — municipal, district, mutual water company, private well, shared well? For rural property this is the question that determines whether the property is usable as intended.

**Rights.** Riparian, appropriative, and groundwater rights are the specialist area from Lesson 02. Recognize, ask, refer.

**Conservation requirements.** California transactions increasingly involve water conservation obligations, including fixture requirements that can be triggered at transfer, and local restrictions on landscaping and use.

**Groundwater management** adds a layer on rural and agricultural property: a parcel within a managed basin may face pumping constraints that affect what can be grown or built.

### 5.6 The rural intake questions

For rural, agricultural, or unimproved property, at the listing appointment:

chunks.heading: 5.8 Due diligence on land use, in the order it should be done
chunks.excerpt:
1. What is the water source, and is it documented?
2. If a well: production, quality, and date of the last test?
3. Is any water right appurtenant to the parcel, and is it documented?
4. Is the property within a groundwater management area?
5. Are there shared-facility agreements — a shared well, a pipeline, an access easement?
6. Is the supply sufficient for the buyer's intended use?
7. What is the septic situation, and when was it last inspected?
8. Is access legal and documented, or is it by long-standing custom?

That last question closes the loop with Lesson 05: a rural parcel reached by a road nobody has a recorded right to use has an access problem the buyer will discover after closing.

### 5.8 Due diligence on land use, in the order it should be done

Sections 5.1 to 5.4 covered the controls. This section is the sequence a licensee should be able to run for any buyer whose plans depend on what the land may be used for.

**Step one — the zoning designation and the general plan designation, which are two different things.** Zoning is the current regulation; the general plan is the long-range policy the zoning is supposed to implement. **They can disagree**, and where they do, a property's future is contested rather than settled. Both come from the planning department and both are usually online.

**Step two — the permitted uses in that zone, read rather than assumed.** A zone's name conveys almost nothing. What matters is the schedule of uses: permitted by right, permitted with a conditional use permit, and prohibited. **A buyer who wants to run a business from a house is asking a question this schedule answers.**

chunks.heading: 5.9 The three answers a licensee must never give
chunks.excerpt:
**Step three — the development standards.** Setbacks, height, lot coverage, floor-area ratio, parking. **These decide whether the addition a buyer intends is possible**, and they are the reason a large lot does not necessarily mean a large house.

**Step four — the overlays.** Historic districts, hillside ordinances, coastal zones, airport influence areas, specific plans. **An overlay sits on top of the base zoning and frequently governs.** A property can be in a permissive base zone and a restrictive overlay.

**Step five — the permit history.** What has been permitted on this parcel, and what has been finalled. Assignment 15 Section 5.12 explains why unpermitted work matters; the permit history is where it becomes visible.

**Step six — anything pending nearby.** A proposed project on an adjacent parcel is a matter of public record and can change the property a buyer is buying.

**All six are free or nearly free, and all six are answered by the planning and building departments to anyone who asks.** The obstacle is not access. It is that nobody asks until a problem has already arrived.

### 5.9 The three answers a licensee must never give

**"You can build that."** Whether a proposed structure may be built is a determination made by a jurisdiction on an application, against standards, overlays and a permit history the licensee has not read in full. **A licensee who says it can be built has given a client a reason not to check.**

chunks.heading: 5.9 The three answers a licensee must never give
chunks.excerpt:
**"That's grandfathered."** Legal non-conforming status is a specific legal condition — a use lawfully established before a regulation changed, continued without the interruptions or expansions that forfeit it. **It is not a synonym for "old."** Whether a use qualifies, and what would end it, is a question for the jurisdiction and for counsel.

**"You can get a variance."** A variance is discretionary relief granted on findings a body must make. It is not obtainable on request, and a buyer who purchases in reliance on obtaining one has bought a property on a condition nobody promised.

**What to say instead, in each case:** *"That's a question for the planning department, and it's worth getting the answer in writing before your contingency period ends. I can give you their number, and here is what I would ask them."*

**A worked situation.**

> A buyer is purchasing a corner lot with an older house, intending to add a 900-square-foot second unit for a parent. The listing describes the property as "great ADU potential — huge lot!" The buyer's agent forwards a zoning printout showing the base zone permits two units.

**The printout answers one of six questions.** It does not address the corner-lot setbacks, which on corner parcels are frequently more restrictive on the street side; the lot coverage and floor-area ratio, which decide whether 900 square feet fits after the existing house; any overlay; the permit history of the existing structure; or whether the parcel's utilities and sewer capacity support a second unit.

**And "great ADU potential" in the listing is a representation** somebody made about a use nobody had confirmed. **The licensee who repeats it to a buyer has adopted it.**

chunks.heading: 5.10 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**What the buyer's agent should have done on day one:** telephoned the planning department, described the parcel and the intended addition, asked what would be required, and **sent the buyer the answer in writing** — including the parts that were "you'd need to apply and find out."

### 5.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why hazard disclosure applies on mapping rather than history, and list the rural intake questions.

## 6. Public and private land-use due diligence

### 6.1 The two halves

Every land use question has a public half and a private half, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other.

| Public | Private |
|---|---|
| General plan and zoning | Recorded CC&Rs and restrictions |
| Permits and building code | Association rules and architectural approval |
| Subdivision and parcel legality | Easements burdening the parcel |
| Environmental and hazard requirements | Private agreements — shared wells, access, maintenance |
| Local transfer requirements | Leases and occupancy agreements |

**A buyer must clear both columns.** The most common failure is checking the public half, receiving a "yes," and treating the question as answered.

### 6.2 The sequence

Order the work by **how long it takes**, not by how important it seems. The slow items are the ones that fail transactions.

**Week one:**
- Order the preliminary report and the underlying documents.
- Order association documents where applicable.
- Obtain insurance quotes where the property is in a mapped hazard area.
- Begin permit research at the jurisdiction.
- Order the natural hazard report.

chunks.heading: 6.3 The questions that identify the work
chunks.excerpt:
**Week two:**
- General and specialist inspections, matched to the property.
- Zoning and entitlement questions at the planning counter.
- Survey where a boundary trigger is present.
- Environmental assessment where the property's history calls for one.

**Ongoing:**
- Track every item against the contingency deadline in writing.
- Confirm receipt of each report and the buyer's review.
- Escalate anything that will not arrive in time, while there is still time to act.

### 6.3 The questions that identify the work

A short intake interrogation identifies most of what a particular property needs:

- **What does the buyer intend to do with it** beyond live in it?
- **What is the property's history** — industrial, agricultural, prior uses, prior construction?
- **What is visibly present** — additions, conversions, outbuildings, slopes, retaining walls, wells, tanks, solar?
- **What is adjacent** — commercial, agricultural, rail, flight path, corridor?
- **What is mapped** — fire, flood, seismic?
- **What is recorded** — easements, restrictions, association?

Notice that the buyer's **intent** is the first question. A buyer who plans to build, subdivide, run a business, or keep animals needs due diligence a buyer who plans to move in does not.

### 6.4 What defensible due diligence looks like in the file

- The buyer's stated intentions, recorded at intake.
- Each investigation recommended, with the date.
- Each report ordered, with the date ordered and the date received.
- The buyer's confirmation that he received and reviewed each.
- Recommendations to consult the jurisdiction, a specialist, or counsel — with the buyer's response.
- Anything that could not be obtained in time, and what was done about it.

chunks.heading: 6.5 The recurring failure
chunks.excerpt:
**The last item is the one licensees omit.** A report that never arrived, with no record of the escalation, looks in hindsight exactly like a report nobody ordered.

### 6.5 The recurring failure

Not that a licensee gave wrong land use advice. That a licensee **gave land use advice at all** — and the confident answer arrived faster than the correct referral would have.

The questions in this lesson are answered by the planning counter, the building department, the recorded documents, the specialist, and counsel. The licensee's professional contribution is knowing which question goes where, and getting it there while the buyer can still act on the answer.

### 6.6 The due diligence failure, restated for a new licensee

Section 6.5 names the recurring failure. Stated as a working rule, it is this: **the buyer's plan was never tested against the property's actual constraints, and nobody noticed until after closing.**

**The pattern is always the same:**

1. The buyer says what he intends to do with the property.
2. Everyone finds it reasonable, because it usually is.
3. **Nobody asks the jurisdiction, and nobody reads the recorded restrictions.**
4. Contingencies are removed on the strength of the plan being reasonable.
5. The plan turns out to require an approval, a permit, or a use the restrictions forbid.

**Step three is the whole failure**, and it costs a phone call and a document request.

**The three questions that prevent it**, asked as soon as a buyer states an intention:

- **"Have you confirmed with the city or county that this is permitted here?"**
- **"Have we read what the recorded restrictions say about it?"**
- **"Do we know what permits this needs and what the existing structure will support?"**

chunks.heading: 6.7 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**The licensee answers none of them.** He asks them, in writing, with a date, before the contingency deadline — and records the answer.

> **Why this belongs at the end of a government-powers lesson.** Every concept in Sections 1 through 5 — police power, zoning, subdivision control, building regulation, environmental and hazard frameworks — **operates on a property whether or not anyone looked.** The lesson's purpose is not to make a licensee an expert in any of them. **It is to make him the participant who asks, on day two, whether anyone has checked.**

### 6.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to build a due diligence sequence for a specific property, justify the ordering by lead time, and state what the file must show.

## Key terms

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **PETE** | Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat — the four government powers over private property. |
| **Police power** | Regulation of use for public health, safety, morals, and general welfare. **No compensation.** The source of zoning, building codes, and environmental controls. |
| **Eminent domain** | The power to take private property for public use upon **just compensation**. The process is condemnation. |
| **Severance damages** | Compensation for harm to the remainder where only part of a parcel is taken. |
| **Inverse condemnation** | A claim brought by an owner where government action effectively took or damaged property without a formal proceeding. |
| **Regulatory taking** | The question arising where regulation deprives an owner of substantially all economically beneficial use. A legal question — recognize, never advise. |
| **Escheat** | Property passing to the state where an owner dies with no will and no heirs. |
| **General plan** | The long-range local policy document, a

| **Zoning ordinance** | What uses and development standards apply to a parcel now. |
| **Development standards** | The physical envelope — setbacks, height, coverage, floor area ratio, minimum lot size, parking, open space. |
| **Permitted use versus physical feasibility** | Different questions. A parcel may permit a second unit that cannot fit within the setbacks, height, and parking. |
| **Variance** | Discretionary relief from a **development standard**, usually requiring hardship arising from the property itself. |
| **Conditional use permit** | Discretionary permission for a **use** the ordinance allows in that zone subject to review and conditions. |

| **Legal nonconforming use** | A use lawful when established that no longer conforms. Generally may continue but not expand, and may be lost by discontinuance or destruction. |
