## Practice problems

### Problem 1

A city rezones a commercially zoned parcel to residential and the owner's market value falls by half.
Separately, the city takes twelve feet of frontage from an adjacent parcel for a road widening,
leaving the remainder without its former driveway access. A licensee tells the first owner he has "a
taking claim worth half his value."

**Identify the power in each and assess the advice.**

chunks.heading: Problem 2
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The rezoning is police power** — regulation of use for public health, safety, and
> general welfare, and **no compensation is owed** in the ordinary case. The owner has not lost the
> property; he has lost uses. Regulation reducing value substantially is still regulation.
>
> **The road widening is eminent domain**, exercised through condemnation, requiring **just
> compensation.** Because only part was taken and the remainder lost its access, compensation may
> address both the part taken and **severance damages** to what remains.
>
> **The advice is wrong and outside the license.** Whether regulation goes so far as to deprive an
> owner of substantially all economically beneficial use — a **regulatory taking** — is a legal question
> of real complexity, and telling a client he has a claim worth a specific amount is both a legal
> conclusion and a valuation of it.
>
> **What the licensee actually does:** recognize which power is operating, treat pending government
> action as a **material fact** to disclose, and refer the legal questions.

### Problem 2

A buyer asks whether he can build a second unit. Zoning permits second units in the district. The lot
is 40 feet wide with 5-foot side setbacks, a 25-foot height limit, and a two-space parking
requirement. The CC&Rs prohibit more than one dwelling per lot. His agent says "the zoning allows it,
so you're fine."

**Identify everything the answer missed.**

chunks.heading: Problem 3
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Three separate questions, and the agent answered one of them.**
>
> **Permitted use is not physical feasibility.** Zoning controls both use and the **development
> standards** — setbacks, height, coverage, parking, open space. A 40-foot lot with 5-foot side
> setbacks leaves 30 feet of buildable width, and the parking requirement has to land somewhere. The
> zoning may permit a unit the lot cannot hold.
>
> **The CC&Rs prohibit it**, and private restrictions and zoning are independent. **The more restrictive
> generally governs** — zoning permission does not authorize what the recorded restrictions forbid, and
> the buyer must satisfy both.
>
> **The correct answer:** *"That's two questions on the public side — what the zoning allows and whether
> the lot can physically fit it within setbacks, height, and parking — plus whatever the recorded
> restrictions say. The city's planning counter answers the first two; I'll get you the CC&Rs for the
> third. Let's have both before your contingency expires, and I'll note we discussed it."*

### Problem 3

Three owners want to do things the ordinance does not currently allow: one wants to build within the
required rear setback because of an unusual lot shape; one wants to operate a childcare facility in a
residential zone where the ordinance lists it as subject to review; one wants his industrial parcel
treated as commercial. A licensee tells each that the approval "won't be a problem."

**Name the correct mechanism for each and assess the reassurance.**

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **A variance** for the setback — relief from a **development standard**, usually
> requiring a hardship arising from the property itself, which an unusual lot shape may supply.
>
> **A conditional use permit** for the childcare facility — permission for a **use** the ordinance
> already allows in that zone subject to review and conditions.
>
> **A rezoning** for the industrial parcel — a change to the ordinance itself, moving the parcel to a
> different zone.
>
> **The distinction to hold:** a variance addresses the envelope, a conditional use permit addresses the
> use, a rezoning changes the rule.
>
> **All three are discretionary, and nobody is entitled to one.** "Won't be a problem" predicts a
> discretionary decision — a prediction stated as certainty, on which a buyer may commit hundreds of
> thousands of dollars.

### Problem 4

A converted garage has been used as a bedroom for thirty years. The seller says it is grandfathered.
Permit records show a permit issued in 1994 for a garage conversion, never finaled. The listing
advertises 2,340 square feet including the converted space.

**Assess each element.**

chunks.heading: Problem 5
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **"Grandfathered" is being used for the wrong concept.** A **legal nonconforming use**
> was lawful when established and no longer conforms because the ordinance changed. **A use that was
> never lawful is not a nonconforming use** — it is unpermitted, which is a different and worse
> problem, and thirty years does not convert one into the other.
>
> **The open permit is a real problem, not a technicality.** A permit issued but never finaled can
> complicate the sale, and the obligation to close it out generally follows the property to the buyer.
> Note also what the record does establish and does not: it shows a permit was issued for described
> work and gives a date. It does **not** establish that the work was completed, done well, or that
> current condition matches the permit.
>
> **The square footage is a misrepresentation as stated.** Unpermitted area is not included in
> advertised living area without disclosing its status.
>
> **What the licensee does:** disclose what is known including the seller's statement and the licensee's
> observations; recommend permit research at the jurisdiction, which is public record; recommend the
> buyer investigate what legalization would require, since the cost can be substantial and some work
> cannot be legalized at all; and document. **What the licensee does not do:** say it is legal because
> it looks fine, characterize the risk, predict what the city will require, or advise the seller to stay
> quiet.

### Problem 5

chunks.heading: Problem 6
chunks.excerpt:
A 1962 house is being sold to a buyer with no children. There is visible dark growth under a bathroom
window and a rusted vent pipe in the rear yard the seller says served "an old oil tank, probably still
down there." The agent tells the buyer lead rules do not apply without children, that the growth is
"just surface mold," and that old tanks are common in the neighborhood.

**Correct all three.**

> **Solution.** **Lead-based paint obligations are triggered by the age of the housing**, not by whether
> children will occupy it — pre-1978 target housing is covered. And the obligation is misstated in the
> other direction too: **disclose what is known**, provide available records and reports, provide the
> required **pamphlet**, and give the buyer an **opportunity to conduct an assessment.** It does not
> require testing, creating records that do not exist, certifying the property lead-free, or
> remediating.
>
> **"Just surface mold" is an assessment the licensee is not qualified to make**, on which the buyer may
> rely. Mold requires moisture, so the underlying question is where the water is coming from. Disclose
> the **observation** — visible growth and its location — and recommend evaluation.
>
> **An underground storage tank is not made harmless by being common.** Leaking tanks create soil and
> groundwater contamination questions and potentially substantial liability. Disclose what the seller
> said, recommend specialist investigation, and route it.
>
> **The rule covering all three:** disclose what is known including your own observations, recommend
> appropriate investigation by a qualified professional, and **do not evaluate.**

### Problem 6

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
A property has never flooded in the seller's twenty-two years but sits in a mapped flood zone and a
mapped fire hazard severity zone. The buyer says the flood mapping is "obviously outdated." The
licensee plans to have the buyer get insurance quotes after the inspection contingency closes.

**Correct the buyer and assess the plan.**

> **Solution.** **The disclosure applies on mapping, not on event history.** A property that never
> flooded is disclosed as within a flood zone if it is mapped in one, and the buyer's view of the
> mapping's currency changes nothing. The disclosure tells him he is in a mapped zone so he can
> investigate what that means; it does **not** certify safety, predict an event, or substitute for his
> own investigation.
>
> **The insurance plan is the single most preventable failure in this area.** Hazard zone status drives
> insurance availability and cost — in some California areas now the determining factor in whether a
> transaction closes at all — along with construction requirements, financing conditions, and the
> disclosure obligations the buyer inherits as a future seller.
>
> **Insurance is a first-week item in a mapped fire or flood area, not an administrative closing task.**
> A buyer who learns in week one that coverage will cost far more than assumed can act; one who learns
> it two days before closing generally cannot.

### Problem 7

A buyer is purchasing 20 rural acres to plant an orchard and build a house. The property has a well, a
septic system, and is reached by a gravel road across a neighbor's land that the seller says "everyone
has always used."

**List the questions and identify the most serious issue.**

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The access is the most serious issue**, and it is the one dressed up to sound
> harmless. "Everyone has always used it" describes a **custom, not a right.** A rural parcel reached
> by a road nobody has a recorded right to use has an access problem the buyer discovers after closing —
> and long permitted use raises a prescriptive question that is a legal doctrine to route, not a
> conclusion to assert.
>
> **The rural intake questions:** What is the water source, and is it documented? For the well —
> production, quality, and the date of the last test? Is any water right appurtenant to the parcel and
> documented? Is the property within a **groundwater management area**, where pumping constraints could
> affect what can be grown? Are there shared-facility agreements — shared well, pipeline, access
> easement? Is the supply sufficient for **the buyer's intended use**, which here means irrigating an
> orchard rather than serving a household? What is the septic situation and when was it last inspected?
> And is access legal and documented, or by custom?
>
> **What transfers:** the buyer's **intent** is the first due diligence question. A buyer planning to
> plant and build needs investigation a buyer planning to move in does not.

### Problem 8

A buyer intends to build. On day eleven of a fourteen-day contingency, the association documents have
not arrived, the permit research has not started, no survey was ordered despite a fence that appears
to cross the rear line, and the preliminary report was received that morning. The agent's file
contains a list of properties shown and the executed contract.

**Diagnose the sequencing and state what the file should have shown.**

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Everything slow was started last.** Order due diligence by **lead time**, not by
> apparent importance — the slow items are the ones that fail transactions.
>
> **Week one** should have carried: the preliminary report and its underlying documents; association
> documents; insurance quotes if the property is in a mapped hazard area; permit research at the
> jurisdiction; and the natural hazard report. **Week two:** inspections matched to the property;
> zoning and entitlement questions at the planning counter, which this buyer needs because he intends
> to build; the survey, triggered here by a fence apparently crossing a line; and environmental
> assessment if the property's history called for one.
>
> **And the two halves were never separated.** Public — general plan and zoning, permits, parcel
> legality, hazard requirements, local transfer requirements. Private — CC&Rs, association rules and
> architectural approval, easements burdening the parcel, private agreements, leases. **A buyer must
> clear both columns**, and the common failure is getting a "yes" from the public half and treating the
> question as answered.
>
> **What the file should show:** the buyer's stated intentions recorded at intake; each investigation
> recommended with its date; each report ordered with the date ordered and received; the buyer's
> confirmation of receipt and review; recommendations to consult the jurisdiction, a specialist, or
> counsel with the buyer's responses; and **anything that could not be obtained in time and what was
> done about it.** That last item is the one licensees omit — and a report that never arrived, with no
> record of the escalation, looks in hindsight exactly like a report nobody ordered.

## Chapter summary

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
**Four government powers limit fee simple absolute**, and the compensation column separates them:
police power regulates without paying, eminent domain takes and pays, taxation charges, escheat
collects where there are no heirs.

**Regulation that reduces value is not a taking** in the ordinary case. Whether it has gone far enough
to become one is a legal question to recognize and refer, never to advise on.

**Pending government action is a material fact** — proposed rezonings, announced projects, threatened
condemnation.

**The general plan states intent; zoning controls today; entitlements record what a parcel has actually
been approved for.** Zoning governs use **and** development standards, and permitted use is not the
same question as physical feasibility.

**Variance for the envelope, conditional use permit for the use, rezoning to change the rule** — all
discretionary, and none is a formality.

**A nonconforming use may continue but generally not expand, and may be lost.** A use that was never
lawful is not nonconforming, and time does not cure it.

**Zoning and recorded restrictions are independent, and the more restrictive governs.**

**A permit record establishes issuance and a date** — not completion, quality, or current condition. An
open permit follows the property.

**Unpermitted work is a disclosure item, not automatically a disaster.** Disclose, recommend permit
research and a legalization inquiry, keep it out of advertised square footage without disclosure, and
never characterize the risk.

**Local transfer requirements vary by jurisdiction** and must be checked rather than assumed.

chunks.heading: Required applied assignment
chunks.excerpt:
**For every environmental hazard the role is the same:** disclose what is known including your own
observations, recommend appropriate investigation, and do not evaluate. Lead-based paint is triggered
by housing age, not by children.

**Natural hazard disclosure applies on mapping, not event history**, and its most consequential
downstream effect is insurance — a first-week item in mapped areas, never a closing task.

**Water is three questions**: supply, rights, and conservation. On rural property, ask all eight intake
questions — and treat "everyone has always used that road" as an access problem, not an answer.

**Every land use question has a public half and a private half**, and clearing one does not clear the
other.

**Sequence due diligence by lead time**, document what was recommended, ordered, received, and
reviewed — and document what did not arrive and what you did about it.

**The recurring failure is not wrong land use advice. It is land use advice at all.**

## Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify which government power is operating on each fact given, separate the public land use questions from the private restriction questions and state who answers each, build a due diligence sequence ordered by lead time with the reason for the ordering, identify every hazard or condition requiring disclosure and state what you would disclose and what you would decline to characterize, identify what you would refer to the jurisdiction, to a specialist, and to counsel, and state the evidence you would create and retain including for anything that could not be obtained in time. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

## Knowledge check and remediation

chunks.heading: Assignment completion
chunks.excerpt:
Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

## Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

lessons.title: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 07

chunks.heading: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 07
chunks.excerpt:
# Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 07

## Agency and brokerage relationships

**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Assignment time:** 180 instructional minutes
**Regulatory status:** Not approved; no California credit is available.

## Learning objectives

- Identify the three ways agency is created and explain why conduct is the route that surprises licensees.
- State each fiduciary duty and identify the conduct that breaches it, including breaches involving no dishonesty.
- Distinguish what is owed to a principal from what is owed to everyone, and locate the boundary between confidentiality and disclosure.
- Apply California's disclose-elect-confirm sequence and state when each step must occur.
- Explain the broker's supervisory duty and the salesperson's authority, and why the brokerage is the agent.
- Disclose compensation conflicts in time to matter, and distinguish the power to terminate an agency from the right to do so without consequence.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: creation of agency and fiduciary duties | 55 | Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved |
| Guided reading: representation forms and the disclosure sequence | 50 | Sections 3-4 viewed |
| Guided reading: supervision, compensation conflicts, and termination | 45 | Sections 5-6 viewed |
| Applied scenario and decision memorandum | 20 | Written response submitted |
| Lesson assessment | 10 | Five scored items submitted |
| **Total** | **180** | **One of 15 separate lesson assignments** |

## 1. Creation of agency

### 1.1 What agency is

**Agency** is the relationship in which one person is authorized to act on behalf of another in dealings with third parties.

chunks.heading: 1.2 The three ways agency arises
chunks.excerpt:
| Party | Role |
|---|---|
| **Principal** | The person represented. Also called the client |
| **Agent** | The person authorized to act for the principal |
| **Third party** | A participant who is not the agent's principal. In residential practice, the other side |

In California residential practice, **the broker is the agent** and the salesperson acts for the broker. Section 5 develops why that matters.

### 1.2 The three ways agency arises

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Express agreement** | A listing agreement, representation agreement, or other engagement — written or oral |
| **Conduct (implication)** | The licensee acted as an agent and the consumer reasonably relied |
| **Ratification** | The principal accepts the benefit of acts performed on their behalf, adopting them after the fact |

**Conduct is the route that surprises licensees**, and it is the reason the agency disclosure belongs early rather than at the offer.

> A homeowner and a licensee have talked for five weeks. He has advised her on pricing, recommended repairs, and told her what he thinks buyers will accept. Nothing is signed and he has not been paid. He now represents a buyer making an offer on her home and says no agency existed.
>
> **He may be wrong.** Agency can arise from conduct, and five weeks of advice she reasonably relied on looks like the conduct of an agent. Payment is not what creates duties, and the absence of a signed agreement does not prevent the relationship.
>
> The consequence is not merely that he cannot claim a commission. He may have owed her fiduciary duties throughout, and representing the buyer without disclosure and consent breaches duties actually owed.

### 1.3 What does not create agency

chunks.heading: 1.4 Scope of authority
chunks.excerpt:
**Payment does not.** A buyer's agent compensated from the seller's side still represents the buyer. Who pays and who is represented are separate questions, and this must be explained to clients rather than assumed.

**A signed form alone does not, where conduct contradicts it.** A form naming one relationship while the licensee behaves as the other party's advisor creates exactly the contradiction that later gets litigated.

### 1.4 Scope of authority

Agency comes with a scope, and a licensee should know its limits.

**Actual authority** is what the principal has granted, expressly or by implication from what the engagement requires.

**Apparent authority** arises where the principal's conduct leads a third party reasonably to believe the agent has authority the agent does not in fact have. It can bind the principal, which is why loose statements about what a licensee may commit to are dangerous.

**What a residential licensee ordinarily may not do without specific authority:** accept an offer on the client's behalf, sign documents for the client, or bind the client to terms.

### 1.5 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the three ways agency arises and explain why the disclosure belongs before the relationship has been operating.

## 2. Fiduciary duties

### 2.1 What a fiduciary duty is

A **fiduciary** owes the highest duties the law imposes in a commercial relationship: to act in the principal's interest rather than the fiduciary's own.

The conventional list, with the memory device **OLD CAR**:

chunks.heading: 2.2 Obedience and its limit
chunks.excerpt:
| Duty | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **O** — Obedience | Follow the principal's instructions — **lawful instructions only** |
| **L** — Loyalty | Place the principal's interests ahead of the agent's own |
| **D** — Disclosure | Disclose material facts known to the agent |
| **C** — Confidentiality | Protect the principal's confidential information |
| **A** — Accounting | Account for all funds and property belonging to the principal |
| **R** — Reasonable care and diligence | Perform with the skill of a competent licensee |

### 2.2 Obedience and its limit

Obedience extends to **lawful** instructions and no further. An instruction to conceal a material defect, to refuse to show property to a category of buyer, or to misrepresent competing offers is not an instruction to be followed.

> A principal instructs her agent not to show the property to a category of buyers. The agent believes refusing will cost her the listing.
>
> **Required:** refuse the instruction, explain that it would be unlawful discrimination, escalate to the broker, and address whether the listing can continue.
>
> **Three failures:** following it while documenting that it came from the client — documentation does not transfer responsibility for the act; following it informally by scheduling around those buyers — which achieves the same exclusion; and withdrawing quietly without explanation — which leaves the client free to repeat the instruction with the next licensee.

### 2.3 Loyalty

Loyalty means surfacing conflicts rather than silently resolving them in the agent's favor. The recurring breaches:

chunks.heading: 2.4 Disclosure, and the confidentiality boundary
chunks.excerpt:
- Acting as an undisclosed principal — buying the client's property, or having an interest in the buyer.
- Accepting an undisclosed benefit from a third party.
- Steering the client toward an outcome that pays the agent more.
- Representing a competing interest without disclosure and consent.

### 2.4 Disclosure, and the confidentiality boundary

This is the most consequential line in agency practice, and it falls in the same place every time.

> **Confidentiality protects the principal's negotiating position. It never authorizes concealing a material fact about the property.**

| Protected as confidential | Must be disclosed |
|---|---|
| The seller's lowest acceptable price | A known material defect |
| The buyer's maximum | The condition of the property |
| The client's motivation and timeline | Facts affecting value or desirability |
| The client's financial position | The licensee's own observations |

> A seller's agent learns the foundation was underpinned after movement six years ago. The seller says the work was done properly, produces no records, and instructs the agent not to mention it because "it's fixed."
>
> **Disclosure controls.** The instruction cannot be followed. Confidentiality protects the negotiating position, not concealment of a material physical condition — and the adequacy of a repair with no records is exactly what a buyer would want to evaluate. Careful silence while avoiding an affirmative false statement is still concealment.

### 2.5 Reasonable care and diligence

The duty breached most often, and the one that requires no dishonesty at all.

chunks.heading: 2.6 What is owed to non-clients
chunks.excerpt:
A licensee who repeats an unverified square footage figure, misses a contingency deadline, fails to deliver a disclosure, or does not perform the visual inspection has breached this duty without lying to anyone. **Most claims against licensees are negligence claims.**

### 2.6 What is owed to non-clients

Non-clients are not unprotected. Every licensee owes **honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts** to everyone in the transaction — the other party, their agent, lenders, escrow, appraisers.

> **"I don't represent them" answers the wrong question.** It correctly identifies whose interests the licensee advances. It says nothing about whether the licensee may mislead them.

The distinction is whose interests you advance, not whether you owe anything.

### 2.7 Which duty was breached

Section 2.1 through 2.6 state the duties. **The skill a principles course is trying to build is recognizing which duty a given failure breaches**, because the answer determines the analysis, the remedy, and frequently whether the conduct is negligence or something worse.

chunks.heading: 2.7 Which duty was breached
chunks.excerpt:
| The conduct | The duty breached |
|---|---|
| Failing to present a competing offer to the seller | **Disclosure** |
| Telling a buyer's agent the lowest price the seller would take | **Confidentiality** |
| Buying the client's property through a relative without saying so | **Loyalty** |
| Missing a contingency deadline | **Reasonable care** |
| Following an instruction not to show the property to a category of buyers | **The obedience limit** — the instruction was unlawful, and following it is the licensee's own violation |
| Depositing an earnest money check into an operating account | **Accounting** |
| Recommending a vendor who pays a fee, without disclosing it | **Loyalty**, and the conflict framework |
| Preparing a pricing analysis from three comparables in a market with twenty | **Reasonable care** |
| Concealing a known material defect at the seller's instruction | **Honesty to non-clients**, and the obedience limit |
| Substituting the licensee's judgment on price for the seller's | **Obedience** — the decision was the principal's |
| Telling a buyer client "the seller will take 700" without knowing | **Reasonable care**, and it is a misrepresentation |
| Continuing to use a former client's confidential information | **Confidentiality**, which survives termination — Section 6.8 |

**Two observations worth carrying.**

**Reasonable care is the most frequently breached and the least dramatic.** Section 2.5 notes it can be breached without dishonesty, and most rows on any real list of claims are careless rather than dishonest. **A licensee who does careful work is protected from most of this table without ever facing an ethical dilemma.**

chunks.heading: 2.9 The fiduciary duties, one at a time
chunks.excerpt:
**Several rows breach two duties at once**, and the second is usually the more serious. Concealing a defect at the seller's instruction breaches honesty to the buyer **and** describes the licensee performing an unlawful instruction. Recommending an undisclosed paid referral breaches loyalty **and** engages a separate framework with its own consequences.

> **The diagnostic question that resolves most cases:** whose interest was subordinated, and to what? **If the answer is "the principal's, to the licensee's," it is loyalty. If it is "the principal's, to nobody's — it was just done badly," it is care.** If it is "a non-client's, to the principal's," it is the honesty duty in Section 2.6, and that duty does not bend to fiduciary loyalty.

### 2.9 The fiduciary duties, one at a time

Section 2.1 named the duties. They are worth taking individually, because each fails in its own characteristic way and the failures look nothing alike.

**Loyalty.** The client's interests come before the agent's. **The characteristic failure is not betrayal; it is a conflict nobody disclosed** — the agent who wants the deal to close because of the commission, and lets that shape the advice about whether to accept.

**Obedience.** Follow the client's lawful instructions. **The limits are in the word "lawful."** An instruction to conceal a material defect, to exclude a protected class, or to alter a date is not an instruction to be followed, and Government Code § 12955(g) reaches the licensee who carries out the second of those.

**Disclosure.** Tell the client everything relevant to the transaction. **The failure is almost always omission under pressure** — the agent who does not pass on a weak second offer because they think the first is better.

chunks.heading: 2.10 Where the duties collide, and how to think about it
chunks.excerpt:
**Confidentiality.** Do not reveal the client's financial position, motivation or bargaining position. **The failure is conversational**, at an open house or between agents, and it usually happens without anyone noticing.

**Accounting.** Account for all funds and documents. **The failure is administrative** and it is what § 10145 exists to prevent.

**Reasonable care and diligence.** Competent work, or referral to someone competent. **The failure is the licensee working outside their knowledge rather than saying so.**

**Notice what the list does not contain.** It does not contain a duty to get the best price, to guarantee an outcome, or to have an opinion about matters requiring another profession. **A licensee who believes their duty is to deliver a result rather than to perform competently and loyally will eventually breach one of the six trying to deliver it.**

### 2.10 Where the duties collide, and how to think about it

The duties are stated as though they are independent. In practice two pairs pull against each other, and being able to name the tension is most of the answer.

**Confidentiality against disclosure to the other party.** The seller's agent learns from the seller that the foundation was repaired after a slide. Confidentiality protects the client; the § 2079.16 duty to disclose material facts to the buyer does not stop at the client's edge.

**The resolution is one-directional and it is not close.** The duty to disclose facts materially affecting the value or desirability of the property runs to both parties. **A material defect learned in confidence is still a material defect**, and confidentiality protects the client's *bargaining position*, not the property's condition.

chunks.heading: 2.11 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**Obedience against loyalty.** A client instructs the agent to do something legal that the agent believes is against the client's interest — refusing a strong offer over a small repair, for instance.

**The resolution here is the opposite: the client decides.** Loyalty does not mean substituting the agent's judgment. **It means giving the client the information and the recommendation, in writing, and then following the instruction.**

**A worked collision.**

> A seller tells their agent, in confidence, that they are three months behind on the mortgage and must close quickly. An offer arrives $30,000 below list with a 21-day close. A second offer arrives at full price with a 45-day close and a loan contingency.

**What is confidential:** the arrears, the urgency, the motivation. **None of it goes to any buyer or buyer's agent**, and mentioning "my seller needs a fast close" is a disclosure of bargaining position that costs the client money.

**What is owed to the client:** both offers, promptly, with an analysis — the $30,000 difference against the risk that the 45-day offer does not fund, and what the seller's own timeline can absorb.

**What the agent must not do:** decide. **The seller's financial situation is exactly why the seller, not the agent, must weigh the trade-off**, and an agent who presents only the fast offer because they know about the arrears has substituted their judgment on the client's most consequential decision.

### 2.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the six duties, state the confidentiality-disclosure boundary, and explain why a careless licensee can breach a fiduciary duty without any dishonesty.

## 3. Seller, buyer, and dual agency

### 3.1 The representation forms

chunks.heading: 3.2 Dual agency requires informed written consent from both
chunks.excerpt:
| Form | The brokerage represents |
|---|---|
| **Seller's agent** | The seller only |
| **Buyer's agent** | The buyer only |
| **Dual agent** | Both parties in the same transaction |

A brokerage becomes a dual agent when it represents both sides — including where **two different salespersons** of the same brokerage represent the two parties, because the brokerage is the agent.

### 3.2 Dual agency requires informed written consent from both

Not one. Not implied. Not obtained afterwards.

**Informed** means each party understands what dual agency means and what it limits. **Written** means documented. **From both** means each party consents on their own behalf. And the consent must **precede** the brokerage acting on both sides rather than follow it.

### 3.3 What dual agency does and does not permit

The single most misunderstood point in agency, and the source of real breaches:

> **Consent to dual agency permits the brokerage to represent both parties. It does not convert either party's confidential negotiating position into shared information.**

> Both parties sign a dual agency consent. During negotiation the seller privately tells the broker the lowest number he would take. The buyer asks the broker directly what the seller will accept.
>
> **The broker may say nothing about the seller's floor** without the seller's permission.
>
> Two wrong answers worth naming: *both are clients so both are entitled to what the broker knows* — being a client entitles a party to loyalty about their own interests, not to the other client's confidences; and *disclosing both sides' limits keeps it balanced* — that does not cure the breach, it commits it twice.
>
> A vague answer conveying the same information is still a disclosure. The form of words does not matter.

chunks.heading: 3.4 What a dual agent can still do
chunks.excerpt:
### 3.4 What a dual agent can still do

Dual agency is not paralysis. The brokerage can still deliver information, prepare documents, coordinate the transaction, disclose material facts, and advise each party on matters not involving the other's confidences.

What it cannot do is advocate one party's negotiating position against the other's, or move confidential information across.

### 3.5 The structural tension

A dual agent owes loyalty to two parties whose interests on price are directly opposed. That tension is why consent must be informed — the party is agreeing to a relationship in which the agent cannot advocate for them the way a single-side agent would.

A licensee explaining dual agency badly — "it just means we handle both sides, it's more efficient" — has obtained a signature rather than consent.

### 3.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what dual agency requires, what consent does and does not permit, and why assigning a second salesperson does not avoid it.

## 4. California agency disclosure

### 4.1 The three steps

California's agency disclosure operates in three steps that occur at **three different times**:

| Step | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Disclose** | Provide the statutory disclosure describing the relationship options and the duties in each |
| **Elect** | The relationship is chosen |
| **Confirm** | The relationship actually elected is recorded, in or with the purchase agreement |

### 4.2 The timing

| Role | When the disclosure must be provided |
|---|---|
| **Seller's agent** | **Before the listing agreement is signed** |
| **Buyer's agent** | **As soon as practicable before the buyer signs an offer** |
| **Agent presenting an offer to the seller** | **Before or at the time the offer is presented** |

chunks.heading: 4.3 Why late delivery is not cured by delivery
chunks.excerpt:
**Every one of these is the same principle: the disclosure precedes the decision it informs.**

A student who holds that principle can resolve unfamiliar timing questions without memorizing a table. Apply it and the answers fall out: the seller should know whose interests the presenting agent serves **while evaluating the offer**, not afterward.

### 4.3 Why late delivery is not cured by delivery

> A buyer's agent presents an offer. The agency disclosure reaches the listing side the following week, after acceptance, and is signed and dated then.
>
> **The file now contains a signed disclosure and is still defective.** The document exists; the protection it was meant to give does not, because the seller made the decision without it.

This is the shape of every timing defect in the course. The remedy for a late disclosure is not a later signature.

### 4.4 The confirmation

The agency confirmation records which relationship was actually elected. Two failure modes appear in file audits:

**A confirmation contradicting the earlier disclosure** — naming the brokerage as buyer's agent while the listing file shows seller's agent, with no dual agency consent anywhere. That is not a documentation problem. It describes the brokerage acting on both sides without either party's consent, and it is the most serious finding in a typical residential audit.

**A confirmation left blank or unchecked**, which leaves the file unable to show what relationship existed.

### 4.5 The disclosure is not the agreement

A recurring confusion: the agency disclosure describes the relationship options and the duties; the listing or representation agreement creates the engagement and its terms. They are different documents doing different work, and providing one does not accomplish the other.

chunks.heading: 4.6 The dates, and what they prove
chunks.excerpt:
**The agency disclosure is required regardless of whether a representation agreement is signed.** A licensee who requires a signed representation agreement before showing property is stating a brokerage policy, which is legitimate — but the disclosure obligation does not depend on it.

### 4.6 The dates, and what they prove

The three steps in Section 4.1 exist as a sequence, and **their dates are what a file audit examines** — not their presence.

**The chain, with what each date has to precede:**

| Step | Its date must precede |
|---|---|
| **Disclosure to the seller** | The listing agreement. The seller must know what the relationship is before he commits to it. |
| **Disclosure to the buyer** | The advice. Section 4.2's timing runs from the outset of the working relationship, not from the offer. |
| **Disclosure to the other party** | The presentation of the offer. |
| **Election** | Recorded in the agreement itself. |
| **Consent to dual agency**, where applicable | **The brokerage acting on both sides.** Consent dated after the conduct is a record of the problem. |
| **Confirmation** | Nothing — it is the last link, and its job is to be **consistent with the four above.** |

**Three defects a file audit finds, in descending order of seriousness:**

**1. A confirmation that contradicts the file.** A purchase agreement confirming the brokerage as buyer's agent while the listing file shows it as seller's agent, with no consent anywhere, **describes an undisclosed dual agency** — a breach of duties actually owed rather than a documentation failure.

**2. A disclosure dated after the agreement.** The document exists and the protection it was designed to give never operated.

chunks.heading: 4.8 The disclosure form is a statute, printed
chunks.excerpt:
**3. A signature with no evidence of delivery.** Section 4.3 establishes that late delivery is not cured by delivery. **A file that cannot show when a disclosure reached the party cannot show that it was timely**, and the burden of that ambiguity does not fall on the consumer.

**Why the buyer side fails more often than the listing side.** A listing agreement forces the paperwork; **nothing forces it on the buyer side.** A licensee can work with a buyer for six weeks, give advice throughout, and produce a disclosure on the day the offer is written — and the file will contain a properly executed document that proves nothing about the six weeks.

> **The one habit that closes all three defects:** date everything at the moment it happens, evidence delivery rather than relying on signature, and **read the chain forward as a sequence** rather than checking off documents as a set. If the dates do not run in order, something happened out of order — and that is worth knowing while the transaction can still respond to it.

### 4.8 The disclosure form is a statute, printed

Section 4.1 called the agency disclosure a required form. It is more particular than that: **Civil Code § 2079.16 sets out the words**, and the form a licensee hands a client is that section reproduced. Reading it is reading the law.

chunks.heading: 4.9 The three relationships, in the statute's words
chunks.excerpt:
> *"The disclosure form required by Section 2079.14 shall have Sections 2079.13 to 2079.24, inclusive, excluding this section, **printed on the back**, and on the front of the disclosure form the following shall appear:*
>
> ***DISCLOSURE REGARDING REAL ESTATE AGENCY RELATIONSHIP** (As required by the Civil Code)*
>
> *When you enter into a discussion with a real estate agent regarding a real estate transaction, you should from the outset understand what type of agency relationship or representation you wish to have with the agent in the transaction."*

**The structure tells you what the Legislature was worried about.** The front of the form is plain-language explanation for a consumer. The back is the statute itself — §§ 2079.13 through 2079.24 — printed in full so that the consumer holds the law rather than a summary of it. **A licensee who prints only the front has produced a form the statute does not describe.**

### 4.9 The three relationships, in the statute's words

**The seller's agent.** *"A Seller's agent under a listing agreement with the Seller acts as the agent for the Seller only."* The obligations then split into two groups, and the split is the heart of California agency:

> **To the Seller:** *"A fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty in dealings with the Seller."*
>
> **To the Buyer and the Seller:** *"(a) Diligent exercise of reasonable skill and care in performance of the agent's duties. (b) A duty of honest and fair dealing and good faith. (c) A duty to disclose all facts known to the agent materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that are not known to, or within the diligent attention and observation of, the parties."*

chunks.heading: 4.10 Dual agency, and the list the statute makes
chunks.excerpt:
**Subdivision (c) is the one that surprises new licensees.** A seller's agent owes a duty of disclosure **to the buyer** — a party they do not represent. The fiduciary duty runs one way; the disclosure duty runs both. **A seller's agent who conceals a known material defect from a buyer has breached a duty owed to that buyer**, and the fact that the buyer was not their client is not a defence.

**The buyer's agent** carries the mirror image: fiduciary duty to the buyer, and the same three both-party duties. The section adds a point about payment that resolves a persistent confusion: *"the agent is not the Seller's agent, even if by agreement the agent may receive compensation for services rendered, either in full or in part from the Seller."* **Who pays does not determine whom the agent represents.**

**And the confidentiality boundary is stated in both:** *"An agent is not obligated to reveal to either party any confidential information obtained from the other party that does not involve the affirmative duties set forth above."* Confidentiality yields to the disclosure duty, not the other way round. A material defect learned in confidence is still a material defect.

### 4.10 Dual agency, and the list the statute makes

> *"A real estate agent, either acting directly or through one or more salespersons and broker associates, **can legally be the agent of both the Seller and the Buyer in a transaction, but only with the knowledge and consent of both**."*

**Two features of that sentence do a great deal of work.**

chunks.heading: 4.11 A worked confirmation problem
chunks.excerpt:
**"Acting directly or through one or more salespersons."** Dual agency is a *brokerage* status, not a personal one. Where one salesperson lists and a different salesperson in the same brokerage represents the buyer, **the brokerage is a dual agent** even though no individual is on both sides. This is the single most commonly missed instance of dual agency, and it happens in ordinary offices every week.

**"Only with the knowledge and consent of both."** Knowledge and consent, from both, before acting. Undisclosed dual agency is not a paperwork failure — it is acting without the authority the statute requires.

**What a dual agent may not disclose.** The statute enumerates it rather than leaving it to judgment:

> *"a dual agent may not, without the express permission of the respective party, disclose to the other party confidential information, including, but not limited to, facts relating to either the Buyer's or Seller's **financial position, motivations, bargaining position, or other personal information that may impact price**, including the **Seller's willingness to accept a price less than the listing price** or the **Buyer's willingness to pay a price greater than the price offered**."*

**Those last two examples are the whole difficulty of dual agency in one clause.** The dual agent knows the seller would take less and the buyer would pay more, owes each of them utmost loyalty, and may tell neither. The duties do not conflict on paper — the statute resolves the conflict by prohibiting the disclosure — but **the agent is left holding information that would help each client and cannot be used for either.**

### 4.11 A worked confirmation problem

chunks.heading: 4.12 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
> A brokerage lists a property. A salesperson at the same brokerage brings a buyer. The listing agent gives the seller a disclosure form at listing; the buyer's salesperson gives the buyer one at first showing. The purchase agreement's confirmation section names the listing salesperson as "Seller's Agent" and the buyer's salesperson as "Buyer's Agent." No dual agency consent is signed by anyone.

**The disclosures were given and the confirmation is wrong.** § 2079.16 says an agent *"acting directly or through one or more salespersons"* can be the agent of both. Here one brokerage is on both sides. **The brokerage is a dual agent**, and the confirmation must say so for the brokerage even while identifying each salesperson's role.

**What the file will look like to a reviewer later:** two properly delivered disclosure forms, a confirmation that describes a single agency on each side, and a brokerage that in fact acted for both parties without the knowledge and consent the statute requires. **The documents make it look correct, which is worse than an obvious gap**, and it is precisely the pattern Assignment 07 Section 6.3 warns about — the file that reads well and does not describe what happened.

**The fix is procedural and takes a minute:** when the offer comes from inside the house, the dual agency consent is prepared at the same time as the offer, not looked for afterwards.

### 4.12 Checkpoint

You should be able to state when each disclosure is due, explain why a signature after the decision does not cure lateness, and identify what an audit finding of a contradictory confirmation means.

## 5. Broker supervision and salesperson authority

### 5.1 The brokerage is the agent

Stated in Lesson 01 and applied here:

chunks.heading: 5.2 The supervisory duty
chunks.excerpt:
> **The salesperson's client is the broker's client. The listing is the brokerage's contract. The salesperson's compensation comes from the broker.**

What follows:

- **Cancellation of a listing is a broker-level decision** governed by the agreement, not the individual salesperson's to grant.
- **The transaction file belongs to the brokerage**, whoever created the documents.
- **A second salesperson on the other side does not avoid dual agency**, because the brokerage is the agent.
- **A salesperson may not contract in her own name** for licensed activity.

### 5.2 The supervisory duty

The responsible broker must exercise reasonable supervision. Discharged by a system:

1. **Written policies** covering the conduct required.
2. **File review**, close enough in time to catch problems before they mature.
3. **Advertising review** before publication.
4. **Trust fund controls**, including reconciliation.
5. **Training**, particularly for new licensees.
6. **An escalation path** a salesperson can actually use.

**A policy nobody follows is not supervision**, and it is not a defense for anyone — not for the broker who wrote it and not for the salesperson who departed from it.

**Independent contractor status does not reduce any of this.** It characterizes the tax and compensation relationship and answers a different question.

### 5.3 Supervision from the receiving end

Licensees encounter supervision failures from below, and the correct responses are worth stating:

chunks.heading: 5.4 Delegation and unlicensed assistants
chunks.excerpt:
| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| A manager tells you to conceal an error | **Escalate to the responsible broker.** The instruction does not protect you |
| Office practice deviates from the written policy | Raise it; a policy nobody follows protects no one |
| You are asked to handle work beyond your competence with no support | Say so in writing and ask for supervision or reassignment |

**Following an improper instruction and documenting that it came from someone else does not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.**

### 5.4 Delegation and unlicensed assistants

Unlicensed assistants may perform administrative work. They may not perform licensed activity — soliciting, negotiating, showing property, or discussing terms — and they may not be compensated for referrals.

The boundary is not the job title. It is the activity.

### 5.5 Vicarious responsibility

The broker answers for the salesperson's conduct in the course of the agency, which is why the supervisory system exists and why brokerages care about advertising approval, file review, and policy compliance in ways that can feel bureaucratic to a new licensee.

The principal may also bear responsibility for the agent's conduct within the scope of the agency, which is one reason a seller cannot instruct an agent into unlawful conduct and stand clear of it.

### 5.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a listing is not the salesperson's to cancel, describe what real supervision consists of, and state the correct response to an improper instruction from a manager.

## 6. Compensation, conflicts, and termination

### 6.1 Compensation is negotiable

chunks.heading: 6.2 Source of payment does not determine representation
chunks.excerpt:
**Brokerage compensation is set independently by each brokerage and negotiated with the client.** It is not standard, not customary, and not set by any association or listing service.

Describing a rate as standard is both factually wrong and an antitrust exposure. The correct sentence:

> "Compensation is negotiable between you and our brokerage. There is no standard rate, and no rate set by any association or listing service. Here is what our brokerage charges and what it covers."

### 6.2 Source of payment does not determine representation

Restated because clients and licensees both get it wrong: **a buyer's agent compensated from the seller's side still represents the buyer.** The arrangement must be explained rather than assumed, along with what happens if the seller's side offers less than the agreed compensation or offers none.

### 6.3 Conflicts of interest

Any interest that could reasonably influence the licensee's advice:

- A referral fee or thing of value from a service provider.
- An ownership or financial interest — including a relative's — in a recommended provider.
- A bonus contingent on a sale or a price threshold.
- The licensee's own interest, or a relative's, in a property.
- Representation of another party with a competing interest.
- A personal relationship a client would want to know about.

### 6.4 Disclosure must arrive in time to matter

> **Disclose before the client relies on the advice the conflict affects.**

chunks.heading: 6.5 The referral fee prohibition is different
chunks.excerpt:
| Inadequate approach | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "The client is free to choose someone else" | The client cannot weigh a recommendation without knowing what the recommender receives |
| "I'll disclose if they ask" | The client does not know to ask |
| "I won't let it influence me" | A private intention is not something the client can evaluate |
| "I'll disclose after acceptance" | Information after the decision has no value |
| "The fee comes from the seller, not the buyer's pocket" | Who pays does not change that the advice carries an interest |

### 6.5 The referral fee prohibition is different

A conflict is ordinarily **managed by disclosure**. One category is not:

> **A licensee may not give or accept a fee, kickback, or thing of value for the referral of settlement service business, and may not split a fee where no services were performed. Disclosure does not cure it.**

This reaches arrangements that feel like ordinary business courtesy — an escrow company paying per file, a lender covering marketing costs in exchange for referrals, a warranty company paying per policy.

Where the brokerage has an **ownership interest** in a provider it refers to, that is an **affiliated business arrangement** carrying its own disclosure and conditions.

### 6.6 The licensee as principal

Where a licensee buys or sells for their own account, or for a relative or an entity they have an interest in, the licensee's status must be disclosed. A licensee purchasing from a client, or holding an interest in a buyer of a client's property, occupies the highest-risk position in the business, and it requires disclosure, the client's informed consent, and the broker's involvement.

### 6.7 Termination of agency

Agency ends by:

chunks.heading: 6.8 What survives termination
chunks.excerpt:
| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Completion** | The purpose is accomplished |
| **Expiration** | The stated term ends |
| **Mutual agreement** | Both parties agree |
| **Revocation** | The principal ends it |
| **Renunciation** | The agent ends it |
| **Operation of law** | Death or incapacity of a party, destruction of the property, or similar events |

**The power to terminate and the right to terminate without consequence are different.** A principal generally has the power to revoke, and exercising it may still breach the agreement and expose the principal to a claim. A licensee who tells a seller "you can cancel any time" has described the power and omitted the consequence — and has given a legal opinion about the agreement's terms.

### 6.8 What survives termination

**Confidentiality generally survives.** A licensee may not use or disclose a former principal's confidential information afterwards — including for a new client, and including after the property is relisted elsewhere.

> A listing expires unsold. Six months later the same licensee represents a buyer interested in the property, now listed with another brokerage. He knows the former seller's lowest acceptable price. **He may not use it.**
>
> A duty that evaporated when the engagement ended would not be worth having. This is why the obligation is described as surviving rather than lapsing.

**Compensation provisions may also survive**, including a protection clause applying to buyers identified during the term.

### 6.9 A worked agency audit

chunks.heading: 6.9 A worked agency audit
chunks.excerpt:
> **A brokerage reviews one closed file.** It contains:
>
> - **(a)** A listing agreement dated March 4. An agency disclosure signed by the seller dated March 7.
> - **(b)** A buyer working with the same brokerage since February, with no disclosure in the buyer file until April 19 — the date of the purchase agreement.
> - **(c)** A purchase agreement confirming the brokerage as **both** the listing and the selling brokerage.
> - **(d)** **No dual agency consent from either party.**
> - **(e)** An email dated April 12 from the buyer's salesperson to the buyer: "I talked to our listing side — I think they'd take 690."
> - **(f)** A referral fee received from a home warranty company, disclosed nowhere in the file.
> - **(g)** A commission disbursement showing the brokerage paid from both sides.
>
> **The findings, ranked.**
>
> **1. (c) and (d) together: an undisclosed dual agency.** Section 3.2 requires informed written consent from **both** parties, and there is none. **This is a breach of duties actually owed rather than a documentation failure**, and it is the finding that changes the character of the whole file.
>
> **2. (e) The confidential information moved between sides.** Section 3.3 states what dual agency does not permit, and this is the clearest possible violation of it: **the seller's negotiating position, communicated by the brokerage to the party negotiating against the seller.** It also proves item 1 was operating in fact rather than only on paper.
>
> **3. (f) The undisclosed referral fee.** Section 6.3 and Section 6.4. **Money received in connection with a recommendation the client relied on, with no disclosure at any point.** Unlike the timing failures below, this involves value moving without the client's knowledge.
>
> **4. (b) The disclosure that arri

chunks.heading: 6.10 The agency questions a licensee answers, and the ones he does not
chunks.excerpt:
ved at the offer.** Ten weeks of a working relationship, and the disclosure is dated the day of the purchase agreement. Section 4.3: **late delivery is not cured by delivery.** The document exists; nothing it was designed to accomplish occurred.
>
> **5. (a) The disclosure after the listing agreement.** Three days late, and the seller committed before being informed.
>
> **6. (g) The two-sided payment.** Section 6.2 establishes that source of payment does not determine representation, so **this is not itself a violation.** It is listed because it is the item an examiner uses to find item 1 — the disbursement is what makes the dual agency visible in thirty seconds.
>
> **What the brokerage does.** Records every finding with its date; preserves the file including item (e); escalates to counsel, because items 1, 2, and 3 are not internal training matters; determines what obligation exists to the parties, which is a legal question; and **changes the procedures that produced items (a), (b), and (d)** — because a brokerage whose buyer files have no disclosure step and whose system does not detect that both sides are its own will produce this file again.
>
> **What the brokerage does not do.** Produce a consent now, re-date item (b), or add a referral disclosure to the file today. **A documented gap is a compliance problem. A manufactured document is a different proceeding**, and every one of these findings is survivable in a way that fabrication is not.

### 6.10 The agency questions a licensee answers, and the ones he does not

This lesson has drawn several boundaries. Collecting them makes the working rule visible.

**What a licensee explains, and should be able to explain well:**

chunks.heading: 6.10 The agency questions a licensee answers, and the ones he does not
chunks.excerpt:
- **What the three disclosure steps are and when each happens.** Section 4.1 and Section 4.2.
- **What representation means** — that the brokerage owes the client fiduciary duties and owes everyone honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts.
- **That the brokerage, not the individual, is the agent.** Section 5.1, which surprises consumers and licensees alike.
- **That who pays does not determine who is represented.** Section 6.2, and consumers regularly assume the opposite.
- **What dual agency is, what it requires, and what it costs the parties** — specifically that no one will advocate against the other side on price. Sections 3.2 through 3.5.
- **That compensation is negotiable.** Section 6.1.
- **What conflicts exist in this transaction**, disclosed before the client acts. Section 6.4.

**What routes to counsel:**

- Whether a particular agency relationship arose on particular facts.
- The legal effect of a defective or late disclosure.
- Whether a duty was breached and what follows.
- What a representation agreement's provisions mean for the client's obligations.
- Whether the client can terminate, and what termination costs. Section 6.7 describes the mechanisms; **the application is legal.**

**What routes to the broker:**

- Any dual agency, at the moment it becomes foreseeable rather than at the offer.
- Any request to release a client from an agreement.
- Any instruction the licensee believes is unlawful. Section 2.2's limit.
- Any conduct by another licensee that engages a duty — including confidential information volunteered by the other side.
- Any compensation arrangement that varies from the brokerage's standard.

chunks.heading: 6.12 Compensation does not determine agency, and three consequences
chunks.excerpt:
> **The organizing principle across all three lists.** A licensee explains **how the framework works**; counsel says **what it means for these facts**; the broker decides **what the brokerage does.** Almost every agency question a consumer asks fits one of those three, and a licensee who can sort them in the moment will handle correctly a great many situations he has never seen.

**And the one question that appears in all three lists at once**, which is why it is the hardest: *"Whose side are you on?"* **The explanation is the licensee's, the legal characterization is counsel's, and if the honest answer is uncomfortable, that discomfort is information the broker needs before the transaction goes further.**

### 6.12 Compensation does not determine agency, and three consequences

Section 6.1 explained how compensation is negotiated. The point that matters legally is the one **Civil Code § 2079.16** makes in passing, in the buyer's agent paragraph: an agent acting for a buyer *"is not the Seller's agent, **even if by agreement the agent may receive compensation for services rendered, either in full or in part from the Seller**."*

**Three consequences follow, and each answers a question clients actually ask.**

**"If the seller pays you, don't you work for the seller?"** No. Agency arises from the agreement to represent, not from the source of payment. This is worth being able to answer cleanly, because a buyer who suspects divided loyalty and is given a vague answer will keep suspecting it.

chunks.heading: 6.13 Termination, and the date that must be on the form
chunks.excerpt:
**A commission dispute is not an agency dispute.** A broker who is not paid has a contract claim. That claim does not retroactively change whom they represented or what duties they owed, and a broker who begins arguing that they "really represented" someone else in order to reach a fee has created a far larger problem than the fee.

**Compensation must be disclosed in full — the statute makes it a discipline ground.** **Business and Professions Code § 10176(g)** reaches *"the claiming or taking by a licensee of any secret or undisclosed amount of compensation, commission, or profit or **the failure of a licensee to reveal to the buyer or seller** contracting with the licensee **the full amount** of the licensee's compensation."* **A referral fee from a lender, a home warranty company or a service provider is compensation**, and the obligation is to reveal the full amount before or at the time the client commits.

### 6.13 Termination, and the date that must be on the form

Agency ends. How it ends determines what survives it.

| How it ends | What happens | What survives |
|---|---|---|
| **Expiration** | The stated term runs out | Confidentiality; any protection period the agreement provides |
| **Completion** | The purpose is accomplished | Confidentiality; obligations under the closed transaction |
| **Mutual agreement** | Both parties release | Whatever the release says — get it in writing |
| **Revocation by the principal** | The client withdraws the authority | The agent may have a claim for compensation; the authority is gone either way |
| **Renunciation by the agent** | The agent withdraws | Potential liability for abandoning a client mid-transaction |
| **Operation of law** | Death, incapacity, destruction of the property, bankruptcy | Immediate |

chunks.heading: 6.14 A worked termination problem
chunks.excerpt:
**Two duties outlive the agency and are regularly forgotten.**

**Confidentiality does not expire with the listing.** Information about a former client's finances, motivations or circumstances remains confidential. A licensee who mentions at an open house that the previous seller "had to move fast because of the divorce" has breached a duty to a person who is no longer a client.

**Accounting survives.** Funds held, documents held, and records of the transaction remain the licensee's obligation after the relationship ends.

**And the termination date is a statutory requirement, not a form convention.** **§ 10176(f)** makes it a ground for discipline to claim or receive a fee *"under any exclusive agreement authorizing a licensee to perform any acts set forth in Section 10131 for compensation … **where the agreement does not contain a definite, specified date of final and complete termination**."*

**Read that carefully, because the offence is not signing the open-ended agreement — it is claiming a fee under one.** A broker holding an exclusive listing with no termination date has an instrument they cannot safely be paid on. **"Definite, specified date of final and complete termination"** admits no substitutes: not "90 days from acceptance", not "until sold", not "until cancelled". A date.

### 6.14 A worked termination problem

> A broker takes a 90-day exclusive right to sell. On day 62 the seller says by telephone, "I've changed my mind, take it off the market." The broker withdraws the listing from the multiple listing service. On day 81 the seller sells privately to a buyer the broker introduced on day 40, at a price the broker had negotiated to within $5,000.

chunks.heading: 6.15 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**Three separate questions sit inside those facts, and a licensee should be able to see all three without answering any of them.**

**Did the agency terminate?** A principal generally has the *power* to revoke, which is not the same as the *right* to revoke without consequence. Whether an oral instruction revoked this agreement, and with what effect, is a contract question.

**Does the agreement have a protection period?** Most exclusive listings provide that a sale within a stated period after termination, to a buyer the broker procured and identified in writing, still earns a commission. **Whether the broker identified this buyer in writing, and when, is likely to decide the whole matter** — and it is a purely clerical act that either was or was not done on day 40.

**Was the termination date definite?** If the agreement said "90 days" without a date, § 10176(f) is in play against the broker's own claim.

**What the licensee should have done on day 62**, in order: confirm the cancellation in writing; **deliver the written list of protected buyers immediately**; and consult the broker about the fee position before doing anything else. **All three take under an hour on day 62 and are unavailable on day 81.**

### 6.15 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the negotiability sentence correctly, explain why the referral fee prohibition is not cured by disclosure, and say what survives the end of an agency.

chunks.excerpt:

| **Principal / client** | The party represented. |
| **Agent** | The party authorized to act for the principal. In California residential practice, **the broker**. |
| **Third party** | A participant who is not the agent's principal. Owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts. |
| **Agency by conduct** | Agency arising because the licensee acted as an agent and the consumer reasonably relied. The route that surprises licensees. |
| **Ratification** | Agency created when a principal accepts the benefit of acts performed on their behalf. |

| **Apparent authority** | Authority a third party reasonably believes the agent has because of the principal's conduct. Can bind the principal. |
| **OLD CAR** | Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care — the fiduciary duties. |
| **Obedience** | Following the principal's instructions — **lawful instructions only**. |
| **Loyalty** | Placing the principal's interests ahead of the agent's own, and surfacing conflicts rather than silently resolving them. |
| **The confidentiality boundary** | Confidentiality protects the **negotiating position**. It never authorizes concealing a material fact about the property. |
| **Reasonable care and diligence** | The duty breached most often, and breachable by carelessness alone with no dishonesty. |
| **What is owed to everyone** | Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts. "I don't represent them" answers a different question. |

| **What consent permits** | Representation of both parties. **Not** the movement of either party's confidential position to the other, and a vague answer conveying it is still a disclosure. |
| **Disclose, elect, confirm** | California's three-step agency disclosure, occurring at three different times. |
| **The timing principle** | The disclosure precedes the decision it informs — before the listing is signed, before the buyer signs an offer, and before or when the offer is presented. |

| **Source of payment** | Does not determine representation. A buyer's agent paid from the seller's side still represents the buyer. |
| **Conflict of interest** | Any interest that could reasonably influence the licensee's advice. Managed by disclosure that arrives **before** the client relies on the advice. |
