## Practice problems

### Problem 1

A homeowner and a licensee have talked for five weeks. He advised her on pricing, recommended
repairs, and told her what buyers would accept. Nothing is signed and he has not been paid. He now
represents a buyer offering on her home and says no agency existed with her.

**Is he right, and what is the consequence?**

> **Solution.** **He may well be wrong.** Agency can arise **from conduct**, and five weeks of advice
> she reasonably relied on looks like the conduct of an agent. **Payment is not what creates duties**,
> and the absence of a signed agreement does not prevent the relationship.
>
> **The consequence is not merely that he cannot claim a commission.** He may have owed her fiduciary
> duties throughout, and representing the buyer without disclosure and consent breaches duties actually
> owed.
>
> **What transfers:** this is precisely why the agency disclosure belongs early rather than at the
> offer. The relationship may already exist while the consumer is unaware of it — and the licensee
> frequently is too.

### Problem 2

chunks.heading: Problem 3
chunks.excerpt:
A seller's agent learns the foundation was underpinned after movement six years ago. The seller says
the work was done properly, produces no records, and instructs the agent not to mention it because
"it's fixed." Separately, the seller tells her the lowest price he will accept, and the buyer's agent
asks her directly what the seller will take.

**Which instruction binds her, and what may she say about the price?**

> **Solution.** **The two facts fall on opposite sides of the same line, and the line is always in the
> same place.**
>
> **The foundation must be disclosed.** Confidentiality protects the seller's **negotiating position**,
> not concealment of a material physical condition — and the adequacy of a repair with no records is
> exactly what a buyer would want to evaluate. Obedience extends to **lawful** instructions only, so
> this one cannot be followed. She tells the seller it must be disclosed and why, involves the broker,
> and does not follow the instruction. Careful silence while avoiding an affirmative false statement is
> still concealment.
>
> **The lowest price is confidential** and stays confidential. She may say nothing about it without the
> seller's permission.
>
> **What transfers:** the confidentiality-disclosure boundary is the most consequential line in agency
> practice, and it resolves the majority of agency questions.

### Problem 3

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
A brokerage lists a home. A buyer the same brokerage has been working with wants to offer. Both parties
sign a dual agency consent. During negotiation the seller privately tells the broker his floor. The
buyer asks directly what the seller will accept. The broker considers three answers: telling him,
since both are clients; disclosing both sides' limits to keep it balanced; and giving a vague answer
that gets the point across.

**Assess each.**

> **Solution.** **All three breach the duty**, and the third is the one licensees think is safe.
>
> **Consent to dual agency permits the brokerage to represent both parties. It does not convert either
> party's confidential negotiating position into shared information.**
>
> *Both are clients so both are entitled to what I know* — being a client entitles a party to loyalty
> about their **own** interests, not to the other client's confidences.
>
> *Disclosing both sides' limits keeps it balanced* — that does not cure the breach, it commits it
> twice.
>
> *A vague answer* conveying the same information **is still a disclosure.** The form of words does not
> matter.
>
> **What the broker may say:** nothing about the seller's floor without the seller's permission. Dual
> agency is not paralysis — the brokerage can still deliver information, prepare documents, coordinate,
> disclose material facts, and advise each party on matters not involving the other's confidences. What
> it cannot do is advocate one negotiating position against the other or move confidences across.

### Problem 4

chunks.heading: Problem 5
chunks.excerpt:
A buyer's agent presents an offer. The agency disclosure reaches the listing side the following week,
after acceptance, and is signed and dated then. The file also contains a confirmation naming the
brokerage as buyer's agent, while the listing file shows it as seller's agent, and there is no dual
agency consent anywhere.

**Rank the two findings and state the correct response.**

> **Solution.** **The contradiction is the more serious, and it is different in kind.** It describes the
> brokerage **acting on both sides without either party's informed written consent** — a breach of
> duties actually owed, not a documentation failure. In an ordinary residential file audit this is the
> most serious finding available.
>
> **The late disclosure is second.** It must be provided **before or at the time the offer is
> presented**, so the seller knows whose interests the presenting agent serves **while evaluating it**.
> The file now contains a signed disclosure and is still defective: the document exists, the protection
> it was meant to give does not, because the seller decided without it. **A later signature does not
> cure lateness.**
>
> **The correct response:** record both findings, escalate to the broker, and obtain anything that
> legitimately exists. **What must not happen** is creating the consent that was never obtained or
> re-dating the disclosure. A documented gap is survivable; a manufactured document is falsification.

### Problem 5

chunks.heading: Problem 6
chunks.excerpt:
A seller wants to cancel her listing two weeks in. The salesperson who took it says he is willing to
release her. Separately, the brokerage's manager tells him to leave a square footage error
uncorrected because escrow closes in four days, and an unlicensed assistant has been calling
expired listings to solicit business, paid $300 per listing obtained.

**Assess all three.**

> **Solution.** **The listing is not his to release.** It is the **brokerage's contract** with the
> seller, and cancellation is a broker-level decision governed by the agreement's terms. The same
> principle determines who owns the file and why a second salesperson would not cure dual agency.
>
> **The manager's instruction must be escalated above him.** A licensee told to conceal a known error
> escalates to the **responsible broker** — the instruction does not protect her, and following an
> improper instruction while documenting that it came from someone else **does not transfer
> responsibility for the act. It documents that she knew.**
>
> **The assistant is performing licensed activity and being compensated for it.** Soliciting listings
> is licensed activity, and the boundary is **the activity, not the job title.** Unlicensed assistants
> may perform administrative work; they may not solicit, negotiate, show property, discuss terms, or be
> compensated for referrals.
>
> **What ties them together:** reasonable supervision is a system — policies, file review, advertising
> review, trust fund controls, training, and a usable escalation path. Two of these three failures are
> supervision failures at the manager level.

### Problem 6

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
A seller asks why the listing states a negotiated compensation figure rather than "the standard rate."
The licensee's brokerage also receives $300 per file from its preferred escrow company, and the
licensee's brother owns the home warranty provider she recommends. She plans to mention both after
the offer is accepted, noting that clients are always free to use someone else.

**Answer the seller and assess the two arrangements.**

> **Solution.** **The answer to the seller:** *"Compensation is negotiable between you and our
> brokerage. There is no standard rate, and no rate set by any association or listing service. Here is
> what our brokerage charges and what it covers."* Describing a rate as standard or customary is both
> factually wrong and an antitrust exposure.
>
> **The $300 per file is prohibited, not merely undisclosed.** A licensee may not give or accept a fee,
> kickback, or thing of value for referring settlement service business, or split a fee where no
> services were performed — and **disclosure does not cure it.** This is what makes it different from
> an ordinary conflict, and its resemblance to routine business courtesy is exactly why it catches
> people.
>
> **The brother's company is a conflict requiring disclosure before the client relies on the advice it
> affects.** Both of her justifications fail: "free to choose someone else" ignores that a client cannot
> weigh a recommendation without knowing what the recommender receives, and disclosure after acceptance
> arrives after the decision it should have informed.

### Problem 7

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
A listing expires unsold. Six months later the same licensee represents a buyer interested in the
property, now listed with another brokerage. He knows the former seller's lowest acceptable price and
that she needed to close by a certain date.

**May he use either fact?**

> **Solution.** **No, to both.** **Confidentiality generally survives the end of the agency.** He may
> not use or disclose a former principal's confidential information afterwards — including for a new
> client, and including after the property is relisted elsewhere.
>
> Her floor and her timeline are both negotiating-position information, protected for the same reason.
>
> **Why the rule takes this shape:** a duty that evaporated when the engagement ended would not be worth
> having. That is why the obligation is described as **surviving** rather than lapsing.
>
> Worth noting alongside it: **compensation provisions may also survive**, including a protection clause
> applying to buyers identified to the seller during the term.

### Problem 8

A seller under an exclusive listing tells her agent she is unhappy and wants out. The agent says
"you can cancel any time — just let me know." A week later the brokerage sends her an invoice for
marketing costs and asserts a compensation claim.

**What was wrong with the agent's statement?**

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **He conflated the power to terminate with the right to terminate without
> consequence.**
>
> A principal generally has the **power** to revoke an agency. Exercising it may nonetheless **breach
> the agreement** and expose the principal to a claim — which is exactly what happened here.
>
> **And the statement was a legal opinion about the agreement's terms**, given confidently by someone
> not entitled to give it, on which she acted.
>
> **What he should have done:** state that the decision is a broker-level one governed by the
> agreement's cancellation and compensation terms, escalate to the broker, and — a useful first step —
> find out what she actually wants. "I want to cancel" often means "nothing is happening and no one is
> telling me why," which is a communication problem with a different fix.
>
> Agency ends by completion, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, renunciation, or operation of
> law. **None of those routes automatically extinguishes what the agreement says about compensation.**

## Chapter summary

**Agency arises by express agreement, by conduct, or by ratification.** Conduct is the route that
surprises licensees, and it is why the disclosure belongs early.

**Payment does not create or determine agency.** A buyer's agent paid from the seller's side still
represents the buyer.

**Six fiduciary duties — OLD CAR — run to the principal.** Obedience covers lawful instructions only,
and reasonable care is the duty most often breached, by carelessness alone.

**Confidentiality protects the negotiating position and never authorizes concealing a material fact.**
That single boundary resolves most agency questions.

chunks.heading: Required applied assignment
chunks.excerpt:
**Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts run to everyone.** "I don't represent them"
answers a different question.

**A brokerage is a dual agent when it represents both sides**, including through two salespersons, and
it requires informed written consent from both, **before** it acts on both sides.

**Consent permits representation, not disclosure.** Neither party's confidences cross, disclosing both
does not balance it, and a vague answer conveying the information is still a disclosure.

**Disclose, elect, confirm — at three different times**, each preceding the decision it informs. A
signature after the decision does not cure a late disclosure, and a confirmation contradicting the
disclosure with no consent is the most serious ordinary audit finding.

**The brokerage is the agent and the party.** The listing is not the salesperson's to cancel, the file
is the brokerage's, and a salesperson may not contract in her own name.

**Supervision is a system, not a manual**, and independent contractor status does not reduce it.
Documenting an improper instruction does not transfer responsibility — it documents that you knew.

**Compensation is negotiable and never standard.** Say the sentence correctly.

**Conflicts are managed by disclosure that arrives before reliance** — with one exception: paying or
accepting anything of value for a settlement service referral is prohibited outright, and disclosure
does not cure it.

**Agency ends six ways, and the power to terminate is not the right to do so without consequence.**
Confidentiality, and often compensation provisions, survive the ending.

## Required applied assignment

chunks.heading: Knowledge check and remediation
chunks.excerpt:
Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify how any agency relationship arose and with whom, state which fiduciary duties are engaged and by what conduct, locate any confidentiality-versus-disclosure question and resolve it, state what disclosure was required and by when and whether the timing was satisfied, identify any conflict and when it had to be disclosed, state what you would decline to do and why, identify what you would escalate to the broker and what you would refer to counsel, and state the evidence you would create and retain. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

## Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

## Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

lessons.title: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 08

chunks.heading: Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 08
chunks.excerpt:
# Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 08

## Contracts and transaction formation

**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Assignment time:** 180 instructional minutes
**Regulatory status:** Not approved; no California credit is available.

## Learning objectives

- Identify the elements required to form a contract and classify contracts by the standard categories.
- Apply the offer, acceptance, and counteroffer rules to determine whether a contract exists and on whose terms.
- Explain consideration, capacity, and legality, and identify what makes a contract void, voidable, or unenforceable.
- State what the Statute of Frauds requires in real estate and identify the recurring exceptions.
- Explain what a contingency does inside a formed contract and how performance obligations are discharged.
- Distinguish the remedies available for breach and explain what a licensee may say about them.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: contract elements and formation | 55 | Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved |
| Guided reading: consideration, capacity, legality, and the Statute of Frauds | 50 | Sections 3-4 viewed |
| Guided reading: contingencies, performance, and remedies | 45 | Sections 5-6 viewed |
| Applied scenario and decision memorandum | 20 | Written response submitted |
| Lesson assessment | 10 | Five scored items submitted |
| **Total** | **180** | **One of 15 separate lesson assignments** |

## 1. Contract elements

### 1.1 The four elements

A contract is an agreement the law will enforce. Four elements are required:

chunks.heading: 1.2 The classifications
chunks.excerpt:
| Element | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **Mutual assent** | An offer and an acceptance — a meeting of the minds on the same terms |
| **Consideration** | Something of value exchanged, or a legally recognized substitute |
| **Capacity** | Parties legally able to contract |
| **Lawful object** | A purpose the law permits |

Where any is missing, the analysis in Section 3 determines whether what exists is void, voidable, or unenforceable — three different outcomes that students routinely merge.

### 1.2 The classifications

Contracts are described along several axes, and the vocabulary appears throughout the transaction.

| Axis | Types |
|---|---|
| **Formation** | **Express** — stated in words. **Implied** — inferred from conduct |
| **Obligation** | **Bilateral** — a promise for a promise. **Unilateral** — a promise for an act |
| **Performance** | **Executory** — something remains to be done. **Executed** — fully performed |
| **Enforceability** | Valid, void, voidable, unenforceable |

### 1.3 Bilateral and unilateral, in practice

**A residential purchase agreement is bilateral.** The buyer promises to buy; the seller promises to sell. Both are bound on formation.

**An open listing or a reward is unilateral.** The offeror promises to pay if someone performs an act; nobody is bound to perform.

**An exclusive right to sell listing is bilateral** — the brokerage promises to market and the seller promises to pay on the terms agreed.

The distinction matters because in a unilateral contract there is no breach by failing to act. Nobody promised to.

### 1.4 Executory and executed

**A purchase agreement is executory** from acceptance until closing. Both parties still owe performance.

**It becomes executed at closing**, when both have fully performed.

chunks.heading: 1.5 What a licensee's role in contracts actually is
chunks.excerpt:
The vocabulary trips students because "executed" also colloquially means "signed." In contract classification it means **fully performed**, and a signed but unperformed agreement is executory.

### 1.5 What a licensee's role in contracts actually is

A licensee prepares transaction documents within the scope of the transaction and explains what provisions do in the transaction.

A licensee does **not** advise on legal effect, on rights and remedies, on whether a party may cancel or refuse to perform, or on entitlement to money. The test from Lesson 01 governs: **would answering require a legal conclusion?**

This lesson teaches contract principles so a licensee can recognize what is happening and route it — not so the licensee can advise on it.

### 1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the four elements, classify a purchase agreement on all four axes, and state what "executed" means in classification.

## 2. Offer, acceptance, and counteroffer

### 2.1 The three formation rules

Three rules resolve most questions in practice:

1. **An offer is a proposal that, if accepted without change, forms a contract.**
2. **An acceptance must match the offer.** Any change to a material term is not an acceptance.
3. **Acceptance must be communicated** to the offeror in the manner the offer or the law contemplates.

**The third rule is the one that gets skipped.** A signed acceptance sitting in a drawer, or in a signing platform nobody delivered, has not been communicated — and no contract has formed.

### 2.2 What makes an offer an offer

An offer must show present intent to be bound, be reasonably definite in its terms, and be communicated to the offeree.

chunks.heading: 2.3 The counteroffer
chunks.excerpt:
Statements that are **not** offers: an invitation to negotiate, an advertisement in the ordinary case, a listing, or a statement of what someone might accept. A listing invites offers; it is not one.

### 2.3 The counteroffer

The single most misunderstood formation rule, and it is worth stating in full:

> **A counteroffer rejects the original offer and substitutes a new one. The original can no longer be accepted unless it is renewed.**

Two consequences licensees regularly get wrong:

- It is **not** an "acceptance with modifications" forming a contract on the counterofferor's terms.
- It does **not** suspend the original offer, leaving it available if the counteroffer is rejected. **The original is gone.**

And it works in both directions. **A party who signs a counteroffer but writes a change on it before returning it has made a further counteroffer**, however small the change. Signing does not convert a modification into an acceptance.

### 2.4 Revocation, rejection, lapse, and death

An offer can end without ever being accepted:

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Revocation** | The offeror withdraws it **before acceptance** — generally permitted even where the offer states a deadline, unless supported by consideration as an option |
| **Rejection** | The offeree declines; a counteroffer is a rejection |
| **Lapse** | The stated time expires, or a reasonable time passes where none is stated |
| **Death or incapacity** | Of either party, before acceptance, generally terminates the offer |

**The revocation rule surprises people in both directions.** A buyer's offer stated to be open until Friday can be withdrawn Wednesday, and a buyer relying on the deadline should know that. A seller intending to accept should not assume the offer will still be there.

chunks.heading: 2.5 The option
chunks.excerpt:
### 2.5 The option

An **option** is a contract in which the optionor gives the optionee the right to buy on stated terms within a stated time, supported by consideration.

The difference from an ordinary offer is precisely that consideration makes it **irrevocable** for the period. That is what the optionee paid for.

An option is generally unilateral in the sense that the optionee is not obligated to exercise it — but the option contract itself binds the optionor.

### 2.6 Electronic signature and delivery

Electronic signature is ordinary in California residential practice. Two points matter:

**Delivery still has to happen and still has to be evidenced.** An executed document in a signing platform that no one delivered has not been delivered, and the platform's audit trail is frequently the best evidence of when it was.

**The contract's own notice provisions govern** what constitutes delivery for a communication carrying legal effect. Delivery by a method the contract does not authorize may not count.

### 2.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to trace a sequence of signed documents and say at which point, if any, a contract formed and on whose terms.

## 3. Consideration, capacity, and legality

### 3.1 Consideration

**Consideration** is what each party gives in exchange — a benefit conferred or a detriment incurred. It is what distinguishes a contract from a gift promise.

Points that recur:

**Adequacy is generally not examined.** Courts do not ordinarily weigh whether the price was a good deal. Gross inadequacy may be evidence of something else — fraud, duress, or incapacity — but by itself it is not a defect.

chunks.heading: 3.2 Capacity
chunks.excerpt:
**Past consideration is generally not consideration.** A promise to pay for something already done, with nothing new exchanged, is generally not enforceable as a contract.

**Forbearance can be consideration.** Agreeing not to do something you have a right to do can support a promise.

### 3.2 Capacity

Parties must be legally able to contract. The recurring categories:

| Category | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Minors** | Contracts of a minor are generally **voidable by the minor** |
| **Mental incapacity** | Depending on the circumstances, a contract may be voidable, or void where a guardianship or conservatorship applies |
| **Entities** | Capacity depends on existence and on internal authorization |

**A licensee's practical concern is authority, not diagnosis.** A licensee does not assess mental capacity. Where a party's capacity is genuinely in question, the licensee's role is to stop, escalate to the broker, and route it to counsel — never to proceed on the theory that the person seemed fine, and never to characterize a person's capacity in the file.

### 3.3 Lawful object

A contract for an unlawful purpose is not enforceable, and a contract can be unlawful in part.

Two forms recur in real estate:

**Contracts to accomplish an unlawful act** — an agreement to conceal a material defect, or to discriminate in the sale or rental of housing.

**Provisions the law will not enforce** — a lease clause purporting to waive the habitability obligation, or a restriction that discriminates on a protected basis. The provision fails whether or not both parties agreed to it.

### 3.4 Void, voidable, and unenforceable

Three outcomes students merge, with three different consequences.

chunks.heading: 3.5 Defects in assent
chunks.excerpt:
| | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Void** | No contract exists and never did. Nobody can enforce it | An agreement for an unlawful purpose |
| **Voidable** | A valid contract that one party may **elect** to avoid | A minor's contract; one induced by fraud or duress |
| **Unenforceable** | A contract the court will not enforce, though it may have other effects | An oral agreement within the Statute of Frauds |

**The critical distinction is between void and voidable.** A voidable contract is valid and binding until the party entitled to avoid it does so — and that party may instead choose to affirm it. A void agreement was never a contract at all.

### 3.5 Defects in assent

Even where the four elements appear present, assent can be defective:

**Fraud** — a knowing misstatement or concealment of a material fact, intended to be relied on and relied on.

**Misrepresentation** — including negligent misrepresentation, made without reasonable basis or care. Most claims against licensees are here rather than in fraud.

**Duress and undue influence** — coercion, or improper pressure exploiting a relationship of trust or a party's weakness.

**Mistake** — mutual mistake about a material fact may affect a contract; a unilateral mistake generally does not, with exceptions.

**Whether any of these applies is a legal conclusion.** A licensee who recognizes the pattern escalates and refers; a licensee who tells a client "you were defrauded, you can get out of this" has practiced law and may be wrong.

### 3.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish void from voidable and state the practical difference, and explain what a licensee does when capacity is in question.

## 4. Statute of Frauds

### 4.1 The requirement

chunks.heading: 4.2 What "in writing" requires
chunks.excerpt:
The **Statute of Frauds** requires certain contracts to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged in order to be enforceable.

In real estate the categories that matter:

- **Contracts for the sale of real property or an interest in it.**
- **Leases exceeding one year.**
- **Agreements to pay compensation for services in connection with the sale or purchase of real property** — the reason a listing agreement's compensation provision is written.
- **Agreements not to be performed within one year.**

### 4.2 What "in writing" requires

The writing must generally identify the parties, describe the property, state the price or the method of determining it, and reflect the essential terms — signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought.

**It need not be a single elegant document** in every case; the essential point is a signed writing containing the essential terms. But a transaction assembled from fragments is a transaction in trouble, which is why practice uses a complete written agreement.

### 4.3 The consequence of non-compliance

An oral agreement within the statute is **unenforceable**, not void. That distinction has consequences: the agreement may have other effects, a party may perform voluntarily, and doctrines exist under which a court may enforce despite the absence of a writing.

**Part performance** is the recurring one: where a buyer has taken possession, paid, and made improvements in reliance, a court may enforce an oral agreement. **Estoppel** doctrines may operate similarly where one party relied to their detriment.

These are legal doctrines with requirements. A licensee should know they exist — so as not to tell a client that an oral agreement is worthless — and should route the question rather than answering it.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Why this matters to a licensee daily
chunks.excerpt:
### 4.4 Why this matters to a licensee daily

Because the practical rule that flows from it is one licensees violate constantly:

> **Every agreement affecting the transaction goes in a signed writing.**

An extension of the closing date, a change to what conveys, an agreed repair, a price adjustment — each is a **change to a term of the contract**, made by written amendment signed by both parties and delivered to escrow.

**What does not change a contract:** an email between the agents, a verbal agreement between the parties, an instruction to escrow alone, or a shared understanding that a short extension "won't matter."

> The parties agree during escrow to move closing by a week. The agents confirm by email. Escrow is told. No amendment is signed.
>
> If the transaction later fails, **the parties are litigating on a contract whose closing date is the original one**, with an email chain between non-parties as the evidence of a change.

### 4.5 Oral agreements that are enforceable

Not everything must be written. Many agreements are enforceable orally, including agreements outside the statute's categories and short leases. The professional practice of writing everything down is a **risk practice**, not a legal requirement in every case — and it is worth doing precisely because the boundary is not obvious in the moment.

### 4.7 The statute of frauds, and the sentence that matters

Section 4.1 said that contracts for the sale of real property must be in writing. **Civil Code § 1624** is where that comes from, and the operative subdivision is worth reading exactly because its structure is unusual: it is a list of contracts that are *invalid* unless written.

chunks.heading: 4.7 The statute of frauds, and the sentence that matters
chunks.excerpt:
> *"(a) The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent:"*

**Three phrases carry the whole doctrine.**

**"Or some note or memorandum thereof."** The statute does not require a contract; it requires a writing sufficient to evidence one. A signed memorandum recording the essential terms can satisfy it even where no formal agreement was ever drawn.

**"Subscribed by the party to be charged."** Only the party being sued needs to have signed. A writing signed by the seller and not the buyer can be enforced *against the seller*. **This asymmetry is the most frequently misremembered feature of the statute** — licensees commonly believe both signatures are required for any enforceability, and the section says otherwise.

**"Or by the party's agent."** An agent may subscribe — which raises the immediate question of the agent's own authority, and the statute answers it in the same breath for real property: an agent's authority to sign a contract for the sale of real property must itself be in writing. **A licensee has no authority to sign a purchase agreement for a client from an oral instruction**, however clear that instruction was.

**Among the contracts listed** are agreements that by their terms cannot be performed within a year; agreements for the sale of real property, or of an interest in it; leases for longer than a year; and — the one that pays licensees' wages — an agreement **authorising or employing an agent or broker to purchase or sell real estate for compensation or a commission**.

chunks.heading: 4.8 What "invalid" means, and what it does not
chunks.excerpt:
**That last one deserves its own sentence.** A listing agreement is inside the statute of frauds. **An oral listing is not an enforceable listing**, and a broker who works on a handshake and then sues for a commission is suing on a contract the Civil Code declares invalid.

### 4.8 What "invalid" means, and what it does not

**It does not mean nothing happened.** A contract inside the statute and not in writing is generally unenforceable rather than void in every sense; performance already rendered, restitution, and doctrines that operate outside the statute may still matter. **This is exactly where a licensee stops and counsel starts.**

**It does mean the writing is the thing to produce.** In any dispute about whether there is a deal, the first question is what writing exists and who signed it. A licensee's practical contribution is to make sure that a writing exists and is signed at the moment agreement is reached, rather than to reason about doctrine afterwards.

**Electronic signatures are writings.** California's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act treats a record or signature in electronic form as satisfying a writing requirement where the parties have agreed to transact electronically. **This course does not read that act in its own text**, and no rule about its scope, its exclusions, or its consent requirements is taken from it here. What matters at Principles level is that "in writing" has not meant "on paper" for a long time, and that the licensee's obligation is to obtain and preserve the record either way.

### 4.9 Three worked problems

chunks.heading: 4.9 Three worked problems
chunks.excerpt:
> **One.** A seller and buyer agree terms by telephone. The buyer's agent emails the seller's agent a summary of the terms; the seller's agent replies "Confirmed, my seller agrees." Two days later the seller accepts a higher offer.

**The question is whether a note or memorandum subscribed by the party to be charged exists.** The party to be charged is the seller. The writing is an email from the seller's *agent*, and an agent's authority to bind a seller to a sale of real property must itself be in writing. **A buyer in this position has a genuine dispute and not an obvious win**, and the resolution is a lawyer's, not a licensee's. What the licensee should take from it: **the reply email is not the contract, and treating it as one leads a client into a fight.**

> **Two.** A broker takes a listing orally, markets the property for six weeks, produces the buyer, and the property sells. The seller declines to pay a commission.

**The agreement employing a broker to sell real estate for a commission is inside § 1624.** An oral listing is not an enforceable listing. The broker has done the work and has no written contract. **This is the least sympathetic and most avoidable loss in the business**, and it is prevented by a signature at the beginning rather than an argument at the end.

> **Three.** A tenant and landlord orally agree to a three-year lease at a fixed rent. The tenant moves in and pays for four months. The landlord then demands a higher rent.

chunks.heading: 4.10 The practical rule this reduces to
chunks.excerpt:
**A lease for longer than a year is inside the statute.** An oral three-year lease is not enforceable as a three-year lease. What the tenancy *is* instead — and what the four months of accepted rent established — is a question with a real answer that is outside this course. **The licensee's role is to have papered the lease**, and, having failed to, to route the parties to counsel rather than to advise either of them about what they now have.

### 4.10 The practical rule this reduces to

**Get it in writing at the moment of agreement, signed by everyone, and keep the record.**

That single sentence disposes of § 1624 in practice. Every worked problem above is a problem only because somebody deferred a signature — by a phone call, by an email, by a handshake — and the deferral is always for the same reason, which is that asking for a signature feels like doubting the other person's word.

**It is not doubting their word. It is the statute's requirement**, and a licensee who explains it that way — *"the Civil Code requires this in writing; it protects both of you"* — will almost never meet resistance.

### 4.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to state which real estate agreements must be written, explain why an oral agreement is unenforceable rather than void, and state what actually amends a contract.

## 5. Contingencies and performance

### 5.1 What a contingency is

A **contingency** conditions a party's obligation on a defined event or approval, **inside a contract that has already been formed.**

Three things it is not:

- It does not delay formation. **The contract exists.**
- It is not a general right to cancel for any reason.
- It does not transfer the underlying responsibility to the other party.

### 5.2 The common residential contingencies

chunks.heading: 5.3 How removal actually works
chunks.excerpt:
| Contingency | What it protects |
|---|---|
| **Investigation / inspection** | The buyer's ability to evaluate condition |
| **Loan** | The buyer's ability to obtain the financing described |
| **Appraisal** | The buyer's exposure if value does not support the price |
| **Sale of buyer's property** | The buyer's dependence on another closing |
| **Review of documents** | Time to review disclosures, reports, association documents |
| **Title review** | The buyer's ability to evaluate title exceptions |

### 5.3 How removal actually works

The single most misunderstood mechanic in California residential practice:

> **Under the standard California residential purchase agreement form, contingencies remain in effect until the buyer removes them in writing. They do not expire automatically when the date passes.**

Consequences:

- A buyer who lets the date pass without delivering a removal has **not** removed the contingency.
- A seller cannot treat the transaction as firm merely because the date passed.
- The seller's route is to deliver **the notice the contract requires**, giving the buyer a defined period to act, after which the seller may cancel per the contract.

**The habit is more durable than the rule: read the contract's own removal mechanism.** Different forms and negotiated terms can operate differently, and the contract in front of you governs.

### 5.4 Time and performance

Nearly every obligation carries a date or a period, and those are **terms of the contract** rather than administrative targets.

chunks.heading: 5.5 Discharge of obligations
chunks.excerpt:
Contracts define how time is counted, and the definitions vary: calendar days versus business days, whether the triggering day counts, when a period ending on a weekend or holiday rolls, and what time of day a deadline falls. **Read the definitions in the contract in front of you.** A licensee who assumes and is wrong by one day has cost a client a right.

### 5.5 Discharge of obligations

A contractual obligation can end several ways:

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Performance** | The obligation is carried out |
| **Substantial performance** | Performance falling short in a minor respect may discharge the obligation, subject to an allowance |
| **Agreement** | The parties release, rescind, or substitute — including **novation**, where a new party or contract is substituted with consent |
| **Impossibility** | Performance becomes objectively impossible |
| **Operation of law** | Including the running of limitations periods |
| **Breach by the other party** | Which may excuse further performance |

**Assignment and novation are worth distinguishing.** Assignment transfers rights, and the assignor may remain liable. Novation substitutes a party with all parties' consent and generally releases the original. A seller who "let the buyer assign" and assumes he is released has assumed a novation he did not obtain.

### 5.6 Waiver

A party may waive a contract right — a contingency, a condition, a requirement. Two points the client must understand:

chunks.heading: 5.8 Contingencies as a sequence, not a list
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Waiving the contingency removes the contractual path to act**, not the ability to investigate. A buyer may still inspect; he simply has no contractual route to respond to what he finds.
2. **The exposure is concrete.** Where an appraisal contingency is waived and the appraisal is low, the buyer's options narrow to bringing funds, renegotiating without leverage, or defaulting with his deposit exposed.

**The licensee's obligation is to put that in writing before the buyer decides, then follow the decision.** Both failure modes are wrong: refusing to write what the client instructs overstates the licensee's role; writing it without comment abandons the advisory duty.

### 5.8 Contingencies as a sequence, not a list

Section 5.2 named the common contingencies. What makes them work — or fail — is that they run on a clock, in an order, and each one's removal forecloses a route out.

| Contingency | What it protects | What must happen inside it |
|---|---|---|
| **Inspection / investigation** | The buyer's ability to discover condition | Inspections ordered, performed, read; specialists engaged; a request for repairs if any |
| **Appraisal** | The buyer against paying above the lender's supported value | Appraisal ordered by the lender, performed, delivered |
| **Loan** | The buyer against being obliged to buy without financing | Application complete, underwriting cleared, conditions satisfied |
| **Title** | The buyer against unacceptable exceptions | Preliminary report read, exception documents obtained and reviewed |
| **Sale of buyer's property** | The buyer whose funds are in another house | That property in contract and progressing |
| **Common interest documents** | The buyer buying into an association | Documents received and read, budget and minutes included |

chunks.heading: 5.9 Removing a contingency, and what it costs
chunks.excerpt:
**The dependency that trips people.** The appraisal usually cannot be ordered until the loan application is in and the lender orders it; the loan cannot clear until the appraisal is back; **and the appraisal contingency and the loan contingency often expire on the same day.** A buyer who applies late has compressed two dependent processes into the tail of one period.

**The sequencing rule that prevents most of it:** **order everything on day one.** Inspections, the association documents, the insurance quote, the title exception instruments. Nothing about a contingency period requires waiting to see whether the inspection goes well before ordering the documents.

### 5.9 Removing a contingency, and what it costs

**Removal is a decision, not an expiry.** In the California residential form the buyer removes contingencies actively, in writing; a passive lapse is not the same thing and the seller's remedy for a buyer who has not removed is to serve notice.

**What removal costs the buyer:** the deposit. Once contingencies are removed, a buyer who does not close is exposed to the liquidated damages clause Assignment 08 Section 6.13 describes. **Removing the loan contingency before the loan is actually approved is putting the deposit behind an underwriter's decision the buyer does not control.**

**Three removals that are commonly made too early, and the question each one should be asked with.**

**The inspection contingency, before specialists have reported.** A general inspector who recommends a roofer, a structural engineer and a sewer camera has not completed the investigation — they have identified who must. **Removing before those reports arrive removes the contingency on the basis of the report that said more information was needed.**

chunks.heading: 5.10 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**The loan contingency, on a pre-approval.** A pre-approval is an underwriting opinion on stated facts. **A loan is approved when the lender says the loan is approved**, in writing, with conditions cleared.

**The appraisal contingency, before the appraisal is read.** A verbal "it came in at value" is a statement about a document nobody has seen.

**A worked timeline.**

> 17-day inspection contingency, 21-day loan and appraisal. Day 1 acceptance. The buyer schedules the general inspection for day 9, because that is when the inspector is available.

**Day 9 has already lost the transaction its margin.** A general inspection on day 9 produces a report on day 10 or 11; specialist referrals are scheduled for days 13 to 16; their reports arrive on day 17 or later. **The contingency expires with the specialist reports unread.**

**What day 1 should have looked like:** general inspection booked for day 2 or 3 with two inspectors called; association documents ordered; insurance quote requested; title exception instruments requested; loan application submitted the same day. **The buyer's options at day 17 are entirely determined by what was ordered on day 1**, and the licensee is the only person in the transaction whose job that is.

### 5.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain what a contingency does inside a formed contract, state how removal works under the standard form, and distinguish assignment from novation.

## 6. Breach, rescission, and remedies

### 6.1 What breach is

A **breach** is a failure to perform a contractual obligation without a legal excuse. A **material breach** goes to the essence of the bargain and may excuse the other party's further performance; a minor breach generally does not.

chunks.heading: 6.2 The remedies
chunks.excerpt:
Whether a given failure is material is a legal question, and it is one clients ask licensees constantly.

### 6.2 The remedies

| Remedy | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Damages** | Money compensating the injured party |
| **Specific performance** | A court order requiring the actual performance promised |
| **Rescission** | Unwinding the contract and restoring the parties to their prior positions |
| **Liquidated damages** | An amount the parties agreed in advance would be the recovery on default |
| **Reformation** | Correcting a writing to reflect what the parties actually agreed |

### 6.3 Specific performance and why real estate is different

**Specific performance is available for real property in a way it is not for most goods**, and the reason traces to Lesson 01: **uniqueness.** No two parcels occupy the same location, so damages may not make a buyer whole — only the parcel will.

This is the clearest example in the course of a legal rule flowing directly from a physical characteristic of land.

### 6.4 Liquidated damages

Where the parties agree in advance that a specified amount — commonly the deposit, subject to limits — will be the seller's recovery on the buyer's default, that is a **liquidated damages** provision.

Three points:

- **It must be properly agreed**, which typically requires specific formalities.
- **Its enforceability is constrained by law.** It is not a penalty the seller may simply impose.
- **It generally limits the recovery** rather than adding to it.

### 6.5 Rescission

Rescission unwinds the contract, and it typically requires **restoration** — each party giving back what they received. It is available on grounds including fraud, mistake, duress, undue influence, and failure of consideration, and it is sometimes available by agreement.

chunks.heading: 6.6 What the licensee must not do
chunks.excerpt:
A licensee should recognize that rescission is a remedy with requirements, not a synonym for cancellation. **Cancelling under a contract's own contingency provision is not rescission**; it is performing the contract according to its terms.

### 6.6 What the licensee must not do

This section produces more improper legal advice than any other in the course, because the questions arrive in emotional moments.

**Must not:**

- Tell a party whether they may cancel, rescind, or refuse to perform.
- Tell a party whether they are entitled to the deposit.
- Characterize a breach as material or minor.
- Predict what a court would do.
- Advise a party to stop performing.
- Instruct escrow on a party's behalf, or attempt to resolve a dispute between the parties.

**Must:**

- Explain the mechanism — that escrow acts only on mutual written instructions, that the contract has a cancellation procedure, that the deposit is held pending resolution.
- Follow the contract's procedures for any notice the licensee's client wishes to give.
- Document communications and their dates.
- Escalate to the broker and recommend counsel, before any deadline passes.

> **A buyer whose loan is denied asks whether he gets his deposit back.**
>
> **Correct:** "That's a legal question and I can't answer it. What I can tell you is the mechanism: the contract has a cancellation procedure with a written notice requirement, escrow can only act on instructions both parties sign, and if you disagree the deposit stays put until it's resolved. Let's get the notice right and get you an answer from an attorney before the date runs."

### 6.7 Cancellation is a procedure

chunks.heading: 6.8 What actually prevents disputes
chunks.excerpt:
Cancellation is accomplished by exercising a right the contract provides, following the procedure the contract specifies. It is **not** accomplished by announcing an intention, by ceasing to perform, or by instructing escrow.

What forfeits a contingency's protection: notifying the other agent verbally, instructing escrow unilaterally to return the deposit, or simply ceasing to perform and letting the other party cancel for non-performance — which is a materially worse position.

### 6.8 What actually prevents disputes

Most transaction disputes are not about substance. They are about **whether something was delivered, to whom, and when** — which is why the practices that prevent them are documentary:

1. Build the deadline calendar from the contract and share it in writing.
2. Deliver notices by the authorized method and keep the evidence.
3. Confirm materially important conversations in writing.
4. Amend in writing, signed, and deliver to escrow.
5. Correct errors immediately, in writing, to everyone who received the original.
6. Keep superseded drafts, so the sequence of versions shows how terms changed.
7. Audit the file at closing while memories are fresh.

### 6.9 The contract questions a licensee must route

This lesson describes contract law because a licensee works with contracts daily. **It does not qualify him to answer questions about them**, and the boundary is harder here than anywhere else in the course, because the questions arrive constantly and they sound like transaction questions.

chunks.heading: 6.9 The contract questions a licensee must route
chunks.excerpt:
| The question | Why it routes |
|---|---|
| "Is this contract still enforceable?" | **Enforceability is the legal conclusion**, and it depends on facts and law rather than on the document's appearance |
| "Did they breach?" | A legal characterization with consequences attached to it |
| "Can I cancel and get my deposit back?" | Two legal questions — the right to cancel and the disposition of the deposit |
| "What are my damages?" | Section 6.1's territory, and none of it is the licensee's |
| "Does the liquidated damages clause apply here?" | Section 6.4 explains the concept; **whether it operates on these facts is counsel's** |
| "Can I sue for specific performance?" | Section 6.3 explains why the remedy exists; **whether to pursue it is legal advice** |
| "Is this counteroffer still open?" | Formation and revocation, applied to facts — the practice course's worked formation problem shows how quickly this gets hard |
| "Was that email an acceptance?" | Same |
| "Can I add a clause saying they'll pay if the appraisal is low?" | **Drafting a provision that alters rights.** Section 4.1 of Lesson 01 |
| "They signed but wrote a note in the margin — what does that do?" | Formation, again, and the answer is genuinely uncertain |
| "Do I have to disclose that the last deal fell through?" | A disclosure question with a legal answer |

**What the licensee can do with every one of these**, and it is substantial:

chunks.heading: 6.10 What actually goes wrong in formation
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Explain what the document provides for procedurally** — what step comes next, what the deadline is, what the form requires.
2. **Identify that a legal question exists**, which is a service most clients cannot perform for themselves.
3. **Recommend counsel in writing, with a date**, before the deadline that makes the answer moot.
4. **Preserve the facts** — the dates, the communications, the sequence — so that counsel is answering from a record rather than from recollection.
5. **Escalate to the broker**, who decides what the brokerage does.

> **The distinction that makes this workable.** "Your contingency period ends Friday at 5" is a fact about the document. **"Your contingency protects you if you cancel Friday" is a legal opinion about your rights**, and the two sentences are one word apart.

**And the reason the boundary is protective rather than restrictive.** Section 4.3 of Lesson 01 makes the general point; here it is specific. **A licensee who answers a contract question and is wrong has caused a loss he is answerable for**, on a subject where he had no authority to speak and where the client had a right to a qualified answer. **The referral costs nothing and transfers the question to the person who can answer it.**

### 6.10 What actually goes wrong in formation

The elements in Section 1 and the mechanics in Section 2 describe how a contract forms. **Real transactions fail formation in a small number of recognizable ways**, and each is prevented by a habit rather than by knowledge.

chunks.heading: 6.10 What actually goes wrong in formation
chunks.excerpt:
| The failure | What happened | The habit that prevents it |
|---|---|---|
| **Acceptance not communicated** | A signature exists; nothing shows it reached the offeror before expiration | Transmit and confirm receipt the moment a document is signed |
| **Signed after expiration** | The offer lapsed before the signature | Calendar every expiration, on both sides |
| **A counteroffer treated as an acceptance** | A term was changed; the original offer is terminated and a new one exists | Read what was returned rather than assuming it came back the way it went out |
| **Two documents both signed** | An offer and a counteroffer both executed, in an unclear order | One live document at a time, and the sequence dated |
| **A term left blank** | Filled in later, by someone, off the page | Never transmit an incomplete document, and never complete one after signature |
| **An oral agreement to change a term** | Section 4's problem, and the operative document still says the original | Same-day written amendment, without exception |
| **Delivery to the wrong person** | Sent to a party rather than through the agreed channel, or to an address never consented to | Use the transmission method the agreement specifies, and evidence it |
| **Signature by someone without authority** | A co-owner, a trustee, an entity signatory, or an attorney-in-fact whose authority was assumed | Lesson 03's intake questions, asked before the offer |
| **A margin note** | An annotation on a signed page that may or may not be a change of terms | Anything that changes a term goes in an amendment, not in a margin |

**Two of these deserve emphasis because they recur most.**

chunks.heading: 6.11 What a licensee actually does with contract law
chunks.excerpt:
**Communication of acceptance.** Formation turns on it, and licensees consistently treat the signature as the event. **A signed acceptance in an outbox has not formed a contract**, and the practice course's worked formation problem shows how quickly that fact becomes consequential when circumstances change in the intervening hour.

**The incomplete document.** A blank in a material term is not a formality. **The document the party signed is not the document in the file**, and no explanation of good intent survives that fact.

> **What a licensee should take from this section.** Section 6.9 establishes that the legal questions route to counsel. **This table is not legal analysis — it is a list of operational habits**, and every one of them is performed by the licensee rather than by anyone else in the transaction. **The contract questions belong to counsel; the reasons counsel gets called usually belong to the file.**

### 6.11 What a licensee actually does with contract law

This lesson is the longest legal treatment in the course, and its practical yield is smaller and more specific than students expect.

**It does not qualify a licensee to advise on contracts.** Section 6.9 lists what routes.

**What it does is make four things possible.**

**One: recognizing that a legal question exists.** A client asks something that sounds procedural and is not. **A licensee who has studied formation, capacity, the Statute of Frauds, and remedies will notice** — and noticing is the whole service, because a client who does not know he needs counsel will not call one.

chunks.heading: 6.13 Damages, specific performance, and liquidated damages compared
chunks.excerpt:
**Two: performing the operational work correctly.** Section 6.10's table is entirely operational: transmitting, confirming, calendaring, refusing to send an incomplete document, reducing agreements to writing the same day. **None of that requires legal judgment and all of it prevents legal problems.**

**Three: preserving the facts an answer will depend on.** When a contract question does arise, its answer turns on dates, sequence, what was communicated, and what each party received. **A licensee who has kept that record has given counsel something to work with; one who has not has given counsel four recollections.**

**Four: explaining the document's own terms without characterizing their effect.** "Your contingency period ends Friday at five, and here is what the agreement says the removal has to look like" is a service. **"You're protected until Friday" is an opinion about rights.** The two sentences are close, and the distance between them is the entire boundary.

**The three habits that carry most of the value:**

1. **Everything material in writing, the same day.**
2. **Every deadline in a system**, counted from the event the agreement names rather than from the day everyone remembers.
3. **Every transmission evidenced**, because formation and performance both turn on communication rather than on signature.

> **The test of whether this lesson worked.** Not whether a student can recite the elements — **but whether, handed a real situation, he can say which parts are his to handle, which parts are counsel's, and what the file needs to show either way.** Those three judgments are what the lesson was for, and they are what a first year in practice will ask for repeatedly.

### 6.13 Damages, specific performance, and liquidated damages compared

chunks.heading: 6.13 Damages, specific performance, and liquidated damages compared
chunks.excerpt:
Section 6.4 named the remedies. This section sets them against each other, because a client's real question is always "what do I actually get."

| Remedy | What it gives | When it is realistic |
|---|---|---|
| **Compensatory damages** | Money to put the injured party where performance would have | Whenever loss can be proved. The usual remedy |
| **Specific performance** | A court order to convey the property | **Real property only, in practice** — because each parcel is treated as unique, money is presumed inadequate |
| **Liquidated damages** | The agreed sum, without proving actual loss | Where the clause was properly formed and initialled |
| **Rescission and restitution** | Unwinding; each party returns what they received | Fraud, mutual mistake, failure of consideration |

**Specific performance is the remedy that distinguishes real property.** A buyer of a car who is refused delivery buys another car and sues for the difference. A buyer of a particular house cannot, because there is no other identical house. **The uniqueness of land is not sentiment; it is the doctrinal reason the remedy exists.**

**Liquidated damages solve a problem that money damages create.** A seller whose buyer defaults must otherwise prove what the breach cost — carrying costs, a lower resale price, time on market — which is expensive and uncertain. A liquidated damages clause fixes the number in advance. In California residential purchase agreements the clause is separately initialled, and **that separate initialling is not a formality**: it is the parties' evidence that they agreed to the substitution rather than absorbing it in the boilerplate.

chunks.heading: 6.14 A worked breach, four ways
chunks.excerpt:
**What a licensee must not do with any of this.** Tell a client what they will recover. **Every row in that table is a legal conclusion**, and each depends on facts a licensee has not verified and doctrines a licensee has not studied.

### 6.14 A worked breach, four ways

> A buyer and seller sign a purchase agreement at $880,000 with a $26,400 deposit and an initialled liquidated damages clause. The buyer removes all contingencies. Two weeks before closing, the buyer's circumstances change and the buyer refuses to close. The seller relists and sells four months later for $845,000, having carried the property at $4,200 a month.

**If the seller pursues actual damages.** The measurable loss is roughly $35,000 in price plus about $16,800 in carrying costs — call it **$51,800** — less anything the seller saved. The seller must **prove** each element, and the buyer will contest the resale price, the marketing, and whether the carrying costs were avoidable.

**If the seller relies on liquidated damages.** The seller takes the **$26,400** deposit and proves nothing. That is roughly half the arguable loss, and it is available immediately and without litigation.

**Which is better is not obvious**, and it is exactly the sort of judgment that belongs to the seller with counsel's advice. The licensee's contribution is to make sure the seller understands there is a choice, and to say nothing about which way it should go.

**If the buyer sues for return of the deposit**, arguing the clause is unenforceable — the analysis turns on how the clause was formed and on statutory limits applicable to residential purchases. **A licensee has no view on this.**

chunks.heading: 6.15 Checkpoint
chunks.excerpt:
**If the seller had wanted the buyer to complete**, specific performance would in principle be available to a seller as well as to a buyer, though it is far less commonly pursued: a seller usually wants money and another buyer, not a decree compelling a reluctant purchaser to take a house.

**The single most useful thing a licensee can do in this scenario happens before any of it** — making sure the liquidated damages clause was properly initialled at signing. A clause not initialled is a remedy the seller does not have, and discovering that at the moment of breach is discovering it too late.

### 6.15 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the remedies, explain why specific performance is available for real property, and give the correct answer to a client asking about a deposit.

## Key terms

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **The four elements** | Mutual assent, consideration, capacity, and lawful object. |
| **Express / implied** | Stated in words, or inferred from conduct. |
| **Bilateral / unilateral** | A promise for a promise, or a promise for an act. A purchase agreement is bilateral; an open listing is unilateral. |
| **Executory / executed** | Something remains to be done, or fully performed. **"Executed" in classification means performed, not signed.** |
| **Offer** | A proposal showing present intent to be bound, reasonably definite, and communicated. A listing invites offers; it is not one. |
| **Mirror-image acceptance** | An acceptance must match the offer; any change to a material term is not an acceptance. |
| **Communication of acceptance** | The rule most often skipped. A signed acceptance nobody delivered has not been communicated. |
| **Counteroffer** | A **rejection** of the original offer and the substitution of a new one. The original is g

| **Revocation** | Withdrawal before acceptance, generally permitted even where the offer states a deadline. |
| **Option** | A contract making an offer **irrevocable** for a period, supported by consideration. |
| **Consideration** | Value exchanged. Adequacy is generally not examined; past consideration generally is not consideration; forbearance can be. |
| **Capacity** | The legal ability to contract. A licensee's concern is **authority, not diagnosis** — where capacity is in question, stop, escalate, and refer. |
| **Lawful object** | A purpose the law permits. Provisions the law will not enforce fail whether or not both parties agreed. |
| **Void** | No contract exists and never did. |
| **Voidable** | A valid contract one party may **elect** to avoid — and may instead affirm. |
| **Unenforceable** | A contract a court will not enforce, though it may have other effects. |
| **Fraud / negligent misrepresentation** | A knowing misstatement intended to be relied on; or a statement made without reasonable basis or care. Most claims against licensees are the second. |
| **Statute of Frauds** | The requirement that certain contracts be in writing and signed by the party to be charged — including sales of real property, leases over one year, and compensation agreements. |
| **Part performance** | A doctrine under which a court may enforce an oral agreement where a party took possession, paid, and improved in reliance. |
| **Written amendment** | The only thing that changes a contract term. Agent emails, verbal agreements, and escrow instructions alone change nothing. |
| **Contingency** | A condition on a party's obligation **inside a formed contract** — not a delay of formation, not a gen

| **Written removal** | How contingencies end under the standard California form. A passed date removes nothing; the seller's route is the contractual notice. |
| **Assignment** | Transfer of contract rights, with the assignor frequently remaining liable. |
| **Novation** | Substitution of a party or contract with all parties' consent, generally releasing the original. |
| **Waiver** | Giving up a contract right. Removes the contractual path to act, not the ability to investigate. |
| **Material breach** | A failure going to the essence of the bargain, which may excuse further performance. Whether a breach is material is a **legal question**. |
| **Specific performance** | A court order requiring the promised performance. Available for real property because of **uniqueness**. |
