| **The four questions** | What is my capacity, what has already started running, does the consumer have what this decision requires, and what will the file show. |

## Practice problems

### Problem 1

On a Tuesday a consumer emails an originator: "We're buying 418 Cedar Lane, asking 640,000, we'd put
20 percent down, I make about 175,000 and my wife makes 90,000, my social is on the attached form."
The originator replies that he will "start looking at options." He pulls credit Wednesday. He sends the
Loan Estimate the following Friday, nine days later, dating the application to the Thursday before it
because that is when the borrower signed the brokerage's intake form.

**When did the application arise, what does the file now show, and what will an examiner compare?**

> **Solution.** **The application arose Tuesday.** All six items were in the originator's hands in the
> email: name, income, Social Security number, property address, an estimate of value — the asking price
> in a purchase context — and the loan amount sought, derivable from price and stated down payment.
>
> **The signature is irrelevant.** The trigger does not wait for a form, a portal submission, or the
> originator's readiness. The intake form documents an application that had already existed for eight
> days.
>
> **What the file now shows:** an application date that is nine days later than the facts support, and a
> Loan Estimate whose timing is measured from the wrong event.
>
> **What the examiner compares:** the earliest email in the file, the credit report pull date, and the
> stated application date. **The credit pull is the one that closes it** — a permissible purpose to pull
> the report existed by virtue of an application the file says had not yet

chunks.heading: Problem 2
chunks.excerpt:
occurred. The file
> contradicts itself, and the contradiction was produced by the brokerage.
>
> **The correct handling on Tuesday:** record the application date as Tuesday, start the Loan Estimate
> clock and the California disclosure statement clock from it, and treat the intake form as what it is —
> a document collected during an application already in progress.

### Problem 2

An originator presents three products to a borrower over the phone, carefully and accurately: a
thirty-year fixed, a seven-year adjustable, and the same fixed with two points. He explains the
adjustment mechanics and the worst-case payment on the adjustable. The borrower selects the fixed. The
file contains the disclosures for the fixed and nothing else. Two years later the borrower complains
that the adjustable was never explained and that he would have chosen it.

**What is the brokerage's position, and what would have changed it?**

chunks.heading: Problem 3
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The brokerage's position is that it cannot prove a presentation that in fact occurred**
> — which, for every practical purpose, is the same position as not having made it.
>
> The originator's recollection is honest and probably accurate. It is also unverifiable, it is the
> recollection of the interested party, and it is two years old. The complaint is answered by the file
> or it is not answered.
>
> **What would have changed it:** a one-page comparison sheet, dated, listing all three options on a
> common basis — same loan amount, same assumed closing date, same horizon for the total-cost figure —
> with rate, payment, **worst-case payment**, and total cost for each, retained in the file whether or
> not the borrower kept his copy.
>
> **Two additional notes.** First, the sheet is retained even where the borrower declines it, because
> the file's purpose is not to serve the borrower's convenience. Second, the complaint here is about a
> product the borrower did **not** select, which is why the comparison must include **the option the
> originator expected to be declined.** The options a file omits are the ones later disputes are about.

### Problem 3

Underwriting conditions a loan on an explanation for an 18,400 deposit. The borrower is traveling and
hard to reach. The processor drafts a letter on brokerage letterhead explaining that the deposit was
proceeds from the sale of a vehicle, emails it to the borrower, who replies "yes that's right, go
ahead," and the processor signs the borrower's name with his permission and transmits it. The
underwriter clears the condition.

**Identify every defect and state the correct handling.**

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **Three defects, escalating.**
>
> **1. The brokerage authored the borrower's account of a material fact.** The lender receives the letter
> as the borrower's own statement about the source of his funds. It is the processor's statement. This is
> the line in Section 2.5 and Lesson 14 placed it on the fraud side, not the documentation side.
>
> **2. The condition was not cleared with source evidence.** The condition asks where the money came
> from. A narrative — from anyone — is not the answer. **The bill of sale, the buyer's payment
> instrument, and the deposit record** are the answer, and the borrower's own written explanation
> accompanies them rather than replacing them.
>
> **3. Signing the borrower's name.** Verbal permission by email does not make the brokerage the
> borrower's signatory on a document a lender relies on. The document now bears a signature the borrower
> did not make, on a statement he did not write, about a fact the lender is relying on. **That is three
> separate misrepresentations in one page.**
>
> **The correct handling:** send the borrower the condition in the underwriter's words, ask him for the
> source documents and his own explanation in his own words with his own signature, and tell the lender
> the condition is pending while the borrower travels. **A delayed closing is a scheduling problem. This
> letter is not.**
>
> **And if it has already been transmitted:** escalate to the responsible broker in writing, with facts
> rather than a characterization. The remedy is a corrected submission with the real evidence, made
> visibly — **not the quiet substitution of a better letter.**

### Problem 4

chunks.heading: Problem 4
chunks.excerpt:
An appraisal returns at 605,000 against a 640,000 contract. The originator's manager tells him to call
the appraiser, mention that "the contract is at 640 and everyone is expecting it to work," and send
over three sales the manager selected. The manager adds: "And next time use Whitfield — his numbers
come in."

**Assess each instruction.**

> **Solution.** **All three are improper, and the third is the worst.**
>
> **Mentioning the contract price as an expectation is a target.** The rule is **information, never a
> target.** The contract itself is information and the appraiser typically already has it. "Everyone is
> expecting it to work" communicates the number the file needs, which is coercion regardless of the
> polite phrasing.
>
> **Manager-selected comparables are a target in disguise.** Supplying sales the appraiser may not have
> is legitimate when the sales are supplied because they are relevant. Supplying three chosen because
> they support a number is the same instruction with an extra step. The correct form is a
> **reconsideration through the prescribed channel**, with the data submitted as data and the appraiser
> free to reject it.
>
> **Selecting appraisers by favorable history builds coercion into the ordering pattern**, which Lesson
> 14 identified specifically. It is worse than a single improper call because it is systemic, it affects
> every future file, and it is discoverable in the brokerage's own ordering records.
>
> **"My manager told me to" does not transfer responsibility**, and Lesson 14 established that
> documenting an improper instruction does not either — **it documents that you knew.**
>
> **The correct response:** decline all three, put the reconsideration through the prescribed channel
> with data rather than a target, and escalate th

chunks.heading: Problem 5
chunks.excerpt:
e appraiser-selection instruction, because it describes
> a practice rather than a single transaction.

### Problem 5

Two days before closing the originator issues a revised Loan Estimate increasing two fees, citing
"changed circumstances." The file contains no document identifying what changed. At closing, the
Closing Disclosure shows broker compensation of 8,900. The brokerage ledger shows 9,400 received — the
difference being a lender rebate recorded by accounting but not reflected on the disclosure. The
brokerage also holds a 214 overage in trust from the transaction that no one has been able to allocate.

**Rank these findings and state the remedy for each.**

> **Solution.** **Ranked:**
>
> **1. The compensation discrepancy (500).** The brokerage's own records contradict its own disclosure
> on the one subject the consumer has no independent way to verify. This is the fact pattern of the most
> common enforcement matter in mortgage brokerage, and it is found by comparing two documents the
> brokerage produced itself. **The amount is not the point.**
>
> **2. The unsupported revision.** "Changed circumstances" is **a category with contents, not a phrase.**
> A revision with no traceable reason is a tolerance violation, and its timing — two days before closing,
> when the borrower is least able to walk away — is what makes it least likely to be read as an
> oversight.
>
> **3. The trust overage (214).** Small, on the books, and **not the brokerage's money.** It does not
> become income through the passage of time or the difficulty of identifying its owner.
>
> **The remedies.** For the compensation: determine which figure is correct, and where the consumer was
> under-disclosed, cure on the terms the framework requires and document what was cured, how much, and
> w

chunks.heading: Problem 6
chunks.excerpt:
hen. For the revision: if a valid changed circumstance actually existed, the contemporaneous document
> proving it either exists somewhere or does not — **and if it does not, the fees revert to the prior
> baseline and the excess is cured.** For the overage: research the source, correct the trust ledger now,
> and follow the framework for funds whose owner cannot be identified.
>
> **What must not happen:** adjusting the ledger to match the disclosure, or writing a
> changed-circumstance memorandum today and filing it as though it were written then. **The first is
> falsifying an accounting record; the second is manufacturing a document.**

### Problem 6

A borrower's file is denied for insufficient documented income. The originator, who has spent six weeks
on it, tells the borrower to "hang on" while he moves the file to a second lender with a different
program. He does not send an adverse action notice. He codes the first submission as "withdrawn by
applicant." The second lender approves.

**Assess.**

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The coding is the violation, and it is not a clerical one.**
>
> **The applicant did not withdraw.** He was denied. Coding it as a withdrawal removes the file from the
> denial data, removes the adverse action notice he was owed, and — where this practice is applied more
> readily to some applicants than others — produces **exactly the pattern Lesson 14 described as
> invisible discouragement**, because it converts denials into events that appear in no denial record.
>
> **Moving the file to a second lender is legitimate**, and often the right service to the borrower. It
> does not change what happened at the first lender.
>
> **The adverse action obligation attached at the first denial** and is not extinguished by a later
> approval elsewhere. Where a creditor denied, the notice is owed with either the specific reasons or the
> right to obtain them, the ECOA notice, and the **FCRA content** if a consumer report was used.
>
> **The correct handling:** code the first submission as denied, issue the notice, tell the borrower
> plainly that the first lender declined and why, and place the second submission in the file as its own
> event with its own dates. **The borrower ends up in the same house either way. The difference is
> whether the brokerage's data is true.**
>
> **The originator's motive here is worth naming:** he was not concealing a denial from the borrower — he
> was avoiding an awkward conversation and a data point. That is how the great majority of
> miscoded dispositions happen, and it is why the control has to be procedural rather than a matter of
> good intentions.

### Problem 7

chunks.heading: Problem 7
chunks.excerpt:
An originator's file for a borrower with limited English proficiency contains: marketing in English
only, a nephew who did most of the talking and is not on the loan, an adjustable product where the
initial payment was discussed and the worst case was not, a signed acknowledgment of every disclosure,
and a note reading "borrower confirms he understands all terms."

**What is present here, and what does the acknowledgment establish?**

> **Solution.** **Several distinct problems, and the note establishes almost nothing.**
>
> **The acknowledgment establishes delivery, not understanding.** A signature proves the document was
> presented. "He signed it" answers a different question than "was it explained," and a self-serving note
> that the borrower confirmed understanding is the brokerage's own statement about the borrower's mental
> state. **The presentation is proved by what the file shows was explained, with what numbers.**
>
> **The worst case was not shown**, which Lesson 09 identified as the least noticed misleading
> comparison. On an adjustable product the initial payment is the number guaranteed to be true for the
> shortest time, and a presentation built on it is incomplete regardless of accuracy.
>
> **The third party controlling the conversation is a signal requiring attention**, not an assumption.
> It may be an ordinary family arrangement. It may be the pattern Lesson 14 described. **The response is
> to establish direct communication with the borrower** — through a competent interpreter where needed —
> and to record that it occurred.
>
> **Language access is a live California issue.** California's protected characteristics include primary
> language, and California has statutory frameworks addressing the language in which certain
> negotiations were conduc

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
ted and what must be provided as a result. **Do not improvise here** — this is
> a question routed to the responsible broker and, where the answer is unclear, to counsel.
>
> **What must not be done:** treat the nephew's fluency as satisfying the brokerage's obligation, treat
> the signature as the record of the explanation, or apply heightened scrutiny to the borrower because of
> his language. **The scrutiny goes to the pattern of third-party control, never to the characteristic.**

### Problem 8

You are the responsible broker. A post-closing audit of one originator's last twenty files finds: four
Loan Estimates dated after the earliest email identifying all six items, six files with no California
mortgage loan disclosure statement, two condition letters written on brokerage letterhead in the
originator's phrasing, three product comparisons referenced in emails but absent from the files, and
one compensation figure that does not match the ledger.

**State what you do, in order, and what you do not do.**

chunks.heading: Problem 8
chunks.excerpt:
> **Solution.** **The ranking first, because the response differs by category.**
>
> **The two authored condition letters are different in kind** from everything else on the list. Every
> other item is a documentation or procedure failure. Those two are documents offered to lenders as
> borrowers' own statements about material facts. **They are escalated as such** — to counsel, and on
> counsel's direction to the lenders — and they are the reason this audit does not end at a training
> memo.
>
> **The compensation mismatch is next**, for the reasons in Problem 5.
>
> **The six missing California disclosures are a procedure failure, not an originator failure** — six of
> twenty means the process does not produce the document, and no amount of counseling one originator
> fixes a process.
>
> **The four late Loan Estimates are the same conclusion:** the brokerage's application-date rule is
> being applied by judgment. It is replaced by the rule in Section 2.7 — **the date the sixth item
> arrived** — enforced by a system check against the credit pull date.
>
> **The three missing comparisons are a retention failure**, remedied by making the comparison sheet a
> required file document rather than an optional courtesy.
>
> **What you do, in order:** record every finding with its file and date; preserve everything, including
> emails and drafts; escalate the authored letters to counsel; cure the compensation discrepancy on the
> framework's terms; change the three processes that produced the recurring items; retrain and
> re-examine this originator's files going back further, because twenty files is a sample; and document
> the audit itself, because **the audit is the evidence that the brokerage supervises.**
>
> **What you do not do:** back-date anything, produce the six Cal

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
ifornia disclosures today with
> application-era dates, reconstruct the three comparison sheets and file them as originals, adjust the
> ledger, or handle the authored letters by asking the borrowers to sign replacements that say the same
> thing. **The gaps are survivable. The repairs would not be.**
>
> **And one thing you must do that is easy to skip:** consider whether the pattern of missing California
> disclosures falls disproportionately on any group of applicants. A procedure failure that is uniform is
> a procedure failure. **The same failure distributed unevenly is a fair lending finding**, and the only
> way to know which one you have is to look.

## Chapter summary

**A mortgage file is one chronology**, and the frameworks attach to moments in it without announcing
that they have. **Almost every serious defect is a timing defect** — the right act, after the moment at
which it protected anyone.

**The first conversation settles capacity, authority, scope, and compensation**, usually silently, and
the failure is that nothing is written down. A dated intake note is the only evidence that will exist.

**Facts and estimates are statable; assurances are not** — and confidence does not convert one into the
other.

**An application exists when the six items are in hand.** It does not wait for a signature, a form, or
the originator's readiness, and **the application date is the date the sixth item arrived, whatever else
the file says.** The credit pull date is what exposes a later one.

**Disposition coding is substantive.** A denial coded as a withdrawal removes the applicant from the
denial data and from the notice he was owed, and "he stopped answering" is incomplete or denied, not
withdrawn.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary
chunks.excerpt:
**The originator requests, receives, reviews, and transmits. He never creates** — and drafting the
borrower's explanation in the borrower's voice is authorship, not assistance.

**Where the file contradicts itself on a material point, escalate rather than resolve it yourself.**

**Two disclosure systems run at once**, overlapping in subject and not in law. **The Loan Estimate does
not satisfy the California mortgage loan disclosure statement**, and delivery is evidenced for both.

**Present every option on a common basis with the worst case for each**, including the option you expect
to be declined — because the options a file omits are what later disputes are about. **Explain every
feature with its number.**

**"Changed circumstances" is a category with contents.** A revision whose reason cannot be traced to a
contemporaneous document is a tolerance violation with a label on it.

**Every condition is cleared with evidence obtained from its source, in the form the source produces
it.** A condition that cannot be met is information, and routing around it is where a compliance problem
becomes something else.

**Supply the appraiser information, never a target** — and selecting appraisers by favorable history
builds coercion into the ordering pattern.

**Disclosed compensation and received compensation must agree exactly**, paid by the disclosed party,
across the disclosures, the ledger, and the settlement statement.

**Trust overages are not income and advance fees are not renamed out of the framework.**

**The standard for the closed file is reconstructability:** could someone who was not present determine
what happened, when, on what basis, and who decided.

chunks.heading: Required applied assignment
chunks.excerpt:
**A documented gap is survivable. A manufactured document is not** — and a late document that says what
it is and when it was made is honest, while the same content filed as contemporaneous is falsification.

**Four questions answer situations this course did not cover:** what is my capacity, what has already
started running, does the consumer have what this decision requires, and what will the file show.

## Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Place every event in the scenario on the origination chronology and state which obligations attached at each point, determine the application date the facts support and identify the evidence that establishes it, identify every disclosure owed under both the federal and California frameworks with its timing and the delivery evidence you would retain, rebuild the product presentation on a common basis with the worst case for each option, assess each underwriting condition and state whether it was cleared with source evidence or with a document the brokerage produced, reconcile disclosed compensation against compensation received and identify who paid it, rank every defect you find by seriousness with your reasoning for the ranking, and state for each defect whether the remedy is a document you may create today, a cure the framework prescribes, a process change, or an escalation you must make instead. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

## Knowledge check and remediation

chunks.heading: Assignment completion
chunks.excerpt:
Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

## Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

chunks.heading: Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
# Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 01

## Real property: characteristics, definitions, ownership, restrictions and transfer

**Course:** Real Estate Law and Practice (48 classroom hours) · **Instructional hours: 10.0** of 48.0
**Commission outline topic:** **I — Real Property Characteristics, Definitions, Ownership, Restrictions &
Transfer**, allocated **10 hours** by the Commission's own outline
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Colorado qualifying education hours are available.

> ### This course is written to the Commission's own outline
>
> **C.R.S. § 12-10-203(4)(a)(I)** requires *"**forty-eight hours** of classroom instruction or equivalent
> correspondent hours in **real estate law and real estate practice**."* **4 CCR 725-1, Rule 2.1.A.2.a**
> states the same figure: *"Real Estate Law and Real Estate Practice: **48 hours**."*
>
> The **Colorado Real Estate Commission approved a course outline for it on April 1, 1998**, and that
> outline — obtained from dre.colorado.gov and read in full on 2026-08-20 — states the **course objective**,
> the **five major topics**, and **the hours allocated to each.** This course delivers those five topics as
> five modules at exactly the Commission's hours:
>
> | Module | Commission topic | Hours |
> |---|---|---|
> | **01** | I. Real Property — characteristics, definitions, ownership, restrictions & transfer | **10** |
> | 02 | II. Valuation and Appraisal | 7 |
> | 03 | III. Contracts, Agency & Federal Requirements | 12 |
> | 04 | IV. Real Estate Finance & Settlement | 12 |
> | 05 | V. Property Management, Leases, Rents | 7 |
> | | **TOTAL** | **48** |
>
> **The Commission's stated objective for this course:** *"To protect the public by introducing the stu

chunks.heading: Learning objectives
chunks.excerpt:
dent
> to the practice of real estate through the study of a common body of knowledge, including key terms and
> concepts in real estate as well as **related federal laws practiced in a majority of states on a national
> level**."*
>
> **Read that last clause.** This is the **national** course of the six. Colorado's own statutes, rules and
> forms are the subject of the **Contracts and Regulations** course, and this course points forward to it
> rather than duplicating it.
>
> *"**Testing is required** to establish individual's satisfactory completion of the statutory
> requirements."* — the Commission's outline. The in-module items here are **not** that examination.

## Learning objectives

1. Distinguish real from personal property, and state why the distinction decides what a deed conveys.
2. State the methods of legal description and why a street address is not one.
3. Name the estates in real property and distinguish freehold from non-freehold.
4. Distinguish the forms of co-ownership and severalty, and state what legal capacity means.
5. Distinguish public land use control from private, and state the priority principle for liens.
6. Distinguish easements, encroachments, and covenants, conditions and restrictions.
7. State the voluntary and involuntary means of transferring title the Commission's outline names.
8. Distinguish the types of deed by what the grantor warrants, and name the assurances of title.

---

## A. Definitions, description and ways to hold title

### A.1 Elements of real and personal property

chunks.heading: A.2 Water rights — named by the Commission's outline
chunks.excerpt:
**Real property** is land, everything permanently attached to it, and the rights that go with it.
**Personal property** is movable. The line decides which instrument conveys what: a **deed** conveys real
property, a **bill of sale** conveys personal property, and a purchase contract that names the disputed
items settles the argument before anyone has it.

**Fixtures** sit on the line. The tests ordinarily applied are the **method of attachment**, the
**adaptation** of the item to the property, the **intention** of the party who installed it, and **any
agreement between the parties.** The last of the four is the only one a broker controls, and it is the one
to use.

### A.2 Water rights — named by the Commission's outline

The Commission's outline names **water rights** under this topic, and again under **Topic V of the
Contracts and Regulations course.** That is deliberate: water is a distinct estate in the western states
and it does not necessarily travel with the land.

> **A boundary this module holds.** **No Colorado water law statute was read by this project**, and **this
> course states no Colorado rule on the appropriation, adjudication, transfer, or conveyance of water
> rights.** What is stated is the fact the outline requires a student to know: **water rights may be owned,
> conveyed and encumbered separately from the land**, so a broker who assumes a well or a ditch right
> passes with the parcel has assumed something that may not be true. **That question goes to counsel and to
> a water engineer**, and Rule 6.2's four routes — decline, obtain the knowledge, obtain assistance, or
> co-list — are the broker's own options.

### A.3 Methods of legal description

Three systems:

chunks.heading: A.4 Estates in real property
chunks.excerpt:
| System | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Metes and bounds** | A perimeter traced by courses and distances from a point of beginning, returning to it |
| **Rectangular (government) survey** | Townships six miles square, each divided into **36 sections** of **640 acres**, numbered 1 to 36 beginning in the northeast corner in a serpentine pattern |
| **Lot and block** | A lot within a block within a **recorded plat**, referenced to the plat's recording data |

**An acre is 43,560 square feet.** A section is 640 acres; a quarter section is 160; a quarter-quarter is
40. Quarter descriptions are read **right to left**: *the northeast quarter of the southwest quarter of
Section 14* is 40 acres.

**A street address and a tax parcel number are identifiers, not legal descriptions.** They exist for
administration and mail. A conveyance needs the description that identifies the parcel unambiguously, and a
broker completing a Commission-approved form uses the description the record supplies rather than one they
compose.

**The Contracts and Regulations course carries this forward.** Its Topic V names **land descriptions,
surveys and Improvement Location Certificates** — the Colorado-specific practice — and this module supplies
the general framework beneath it.

### A.4 Estates in real property

chunks.heading: A.5 Forms, rights, interests and obligations of ownership
chunks.excerpt:
| Estate | Duration | Family |
|---|---|---|
| **Fee simple absolute** | Potentially infinite, no conditions | Freehold |
| **Defeasible fee** | Potentially infinite, but may end on a stated condition or use ceasing | Freehold |
| **Life estate** | Measured by a life, then to a remainderman or reverting to the grantor | Freehold |
| **Estate for years** | A fixed term with a stated end | Leasehold (non-freehold) |
| **Periodic tenancy** | Period to period, renewing until notice | Leasehold |
| **Tenancy at will** | At the will of either party | Leasehold |
| **Tenancy at sufferance** | A holdover after a lawful tenancy ends | Leasehold |

**Freehold means ownership of indefinite duration; non-freehold means possession for a term.** A life
tenant can convey no more than they hold, which is why a purchaser dealing with a life tenant alone
receives an interest that ends when the measuring life does.

**Module 05 of this course develops the leasehold estates** under the Commission's Topic V.

### A.5 Forms, rights, interests and obligations of ownership

The Commission's outline names five sub-items, and each is here.

**a. Joint ownership.** Two or more owners holding concurrently, each with an **undivided** interest — a
right to possession of the whole rather than to a physical portion. The principal forms are:

| Form | Survivorship | Interests |
|---|---|---|
| **Tenancy in common** | **No** — the decedent's share passes to their estate | May be unequal |
| **Joint tenancy** | **Yes** — the decedent's interest passes to the survivors outside probate | Ordinarily equal |

chunks.heading: A.5 Forms, rights, interests and obligations of ownership
chunks.excerpt:
**How co-owners describe themselves to each other creates nothing.** The **recorded instrument** determines
the form, and whether survivorship exists is a question of what the deed says and of the law that governs
it.

> **A boundary this module holds.** **No Colorado statute on joint tenancy, survivorship, community
> property, intestacy or probate was read by this project**, and **this course states no Colorado rule on
> how a joint tenancy is created, severed, or terminated, and none on what happens to a decedent's
> interest.** A client's question about survivorship is a legal question. **§ 12-10-403(4) and Rule 7.1
> require a broker to advise the parties that standard forms have important legal consequences and that
> they should consult legal counsel before signing**, and a survivorship question is squarely inside that.

**b. Severalty ownership.** Ownership by **one** person or entity alone. The word does not mean "several"
in the ordinary sense — it means severed from anyone else's interest.

**c. Legal capacity.** The legal ability of a person or entity to contract and to convey. Minors, persons
adjudicated incompetent, and entities acting outside their authority raise capacity questions.

**d. Individuals.** An individual conveys in their own name, as they hold title.

**e. Corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships.** **Who may sign for an entity is a question
of the entity's own governing documents and of the statute under which it exists.** A broker identifies
the owner **exactly as they hold title** and routes every authority question — corporate resolution,
operating agreement, partnership authority, trustee's power — **to counsel.** **No Colorado entity statute
was read by this project and none is stated here.**

chunks.heading: B. Land use controls and restrictions
chunks.excerpt:
**Note where Colorado's own rules touch this.** **Rule 5.10.D and 5.10.E** turn on whether a broker's
ownership in an entity or property held in partnership, joint venture or syndication exceeds the **20
percent threshold in § 12-10-201(6)(b)(VII)** — a figure this build states because Chapter 5 was read.
Module 02 of the Trust Accounts and Record Keeping course covers it.

---

## B. Land use controls and restrictions

### B.1 Public controls

> The **police power** is the government's power to regulate for public health, safety, morals and general
> welfare — **without compensating the owner.** **Eminent domain** is the power to take private property
> for public use **on payment of just compensation.** The absence or presence of compensation is what
> distinguishes them.

**a. Zoning.** Districts, permitted uses, dimensional standards, and the mechanisms that bend them —
**variance** (relief from a dimensional standard on hardship), **special or conditional use permit** (a use
allowed subject to conditions), **rezoning** (a change to the map), and **nonconforming use** (a use lawful
when established that no longer conforms, ordinarily permitted to continue subject to limits on expansion
and on resumption after abandonment).

**The limits on a nonconforming use are what matter to a buyer.** A use that cannot be expanded, rebuilt
after destruction, or resumed after a period of abandonment is worth less than a buyer may assume, and
**every one of those limits is in the local ordinance.** **No Colorado zoning or land use statute and no
local ordinance was read by this project.** The answer for any parcel comes from the jurisdiction that
zoned it.

chunks.heading: B.2 Private controls
chunks.excerpt:
**b. Taxation.** The Commission's outline names **capital gains, income tax and property tax** under this
head. General property taxes are an **ad valorem** lien on the parcel, ordinarily taking priority over
other liens. Capital gains and income tax consequences of a sale belong to the client's **accountant** —
**§§ 12-10-404(1)(c)(V), 12-10-405(1)(c)(V) and 12-10-407(2)(b)(II) each require the broker to advise the
party to obtain expert advice as to material matters beyond the broker's expertise**, and tax is the
clearest example.

**No Colorado property tax statute, rate, exemption, assessment ratio or deadline was read by this
project, and none is stated in this course.** The Contracts and Regulations course's Topic V names
**general property taxes and special districts**; Module 05 of that course routes them to the Colorado
sources.

**c. Police power.** Named above, and the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision regulation and
environmental controls alike.

### B.2 Private controls

**a. Covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs).** Private restrictions recorded against the land,
ordinarily enforced by other owners bound by the same scheme or by an association — **not** by a government
body. Where a private restriction and public zoning conflict, **the more restrictive governs the owner's
practical options**, because the owner must satisfy both.

**Colorado has a statute on common interest communities — the Colorado Common Interest Ownership Act,
article 33.3 of title 38 — which the Contracts and Regulations outline names under its Topic I.** **CCIOA
was NOT read by this project, and no module states any of its requirements.**

**b. Types and priority of liens.**

chunks.heading: B.2 Private controls
chunks.excerpt:
| Distinction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Voluntary** vs **involuntary** | Created by the owner's act (a deed of trust) vs imposed by law (a judgment, a tax lien, a mechanics' lien) |
| **General** vs **specific** | Attaching to all of a debtor's property vs to identified property |

**Priority.** The general principle is **first in time, first in right** as established by **recording** —
with statutory exceptions that ordinarily include **property tax liens** and, in many states, **mechanics'
liens relating back to an earlier date.** **Colorado's mechanics' lien statute was NOT read by this
project**, and **this course states no Colorado priority rule, relation-back date, filing deadline or
notice requirement.** The Contracts and Regulations outline names **deeds of trust, foreclosure, general
property taxes, special districts and other liens** under its Topic V, and that is where a Colorado answer
belongs.

**Every lien is an encumbrance; not every encumbrance is a lien.** An easement, a restrictive covenant and
an encroachment are encumbrances securing no debt.

**c. Easements.**

| Kind | Benefits | Passes with the land? |
|---|---|---|
| **Easement appurtenant** | A **dominant parcel**, burdening a **servient parcel** | **Yes** — with the dominant estate, whether or not the deed mentions it |
| **Easement in gross** | A **person or entity**, as a utility easement does | Not with a parcel |

Easements may arise by **express grant or reservation**, by **implication**, by **necessity**, or by
**prescription**. **Colorado's own law on prescription and on easement creation was NOT read**, and no
period, standard or element is stated here.

chunks.heading: C. Transfer and alienation of title
chunks.excerpt:
**d. Encroachments.** An unauthorised physical intrusion of an improvement onto adjoining land. **A records
search will not surface one; a survey will.** It is the classic defect that lives outside the recorded
record, which is why a fence, shed or driveway in an unexpected place is a question a broker raises rather
than assumes away. The Contracts and Regulations outline names the **Improvement Location Certificate**
under its Topic V.

**e. Recording and priorities.** Recording gives **constructive notice to the world** and establishes
priority against later claimants. **It does not pass title between grantor and grantee** — delivery and
acceptance do. An unrecorded deed is good between the parties and dangerous against everyone else.

**Constructive notice** is notice the law imputes because a fact is recorded or would be revealed by
inspection, whether or not the person knows it. **Actual notice** is what the person in fact knows.
**Possession is the third source**: a person in visible possession puts a purchaser on **inquiry**, which
is why an unrecorded interest held by an occupant is not the safe assumption a buyer may think.

**Colorado's recording statutes were NOT read by this project.** Which class of recording act Colorado
follows, and what its priority rules provide, are **not stated in this course.**

---

## C. Transfer and alienation of title

### C.1 Voluntary transfer

By **deed** during life; by **will** at death; by **dedication** of land to public use; by **gift**.

### C.2 Involuntary transfer — the Commission's own list

The outline names seven, and each is here:

chunks.heading: C.3 Deeds, warranties and defects in title
chunks.excerpt:
| Means | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Dedication** | Transfer of private land to public use, which may be statutory or by common law |
| **Adverse possession** | Title acquired by possession that is, in general terms, actual, open and notorious, hostile, exclusive and continuous for a statutory period |
| **Sheriff's sale** | A judicial sale of property to satisfy a judgment |
| **Foreclosure** | Enforcement of a security interest against the property |
| **Condemnation** | The proceeding by which the power of eminent domain is exercised |
| **Escheat** | Property passing to the state where an owner dies with no will and no heirs |
| **Eminent domain** | The power itself — a taking for public use on payment of just compensation |

> **A boundary this module holds, and it is a large one.** **Colorado's adverse possession statute, its
> foreclosure statutes and public trustee process, its condemnation procedure, its escheat provisions and
> its intestacy statutes were NONE of them read by this project.** **No period, no element, no notice
> requirement, no redemption right and no procedure is stated anywhere in this course.** Every one of these
> is a court proceeding or a statutory process, and a client facing one needs counsel, not a broker.
>
> Colorado's **public trustee** system is distinctive among the states, and this course does not describe it
> because the statute establishing it was not read.

### C.3 Deeds, warranties and defects in title

**a. Types**, distinguished by **what the grantor warrants** rather than by the size of the estate
conveyed:

chunks.heading: C.4 Assurances of title
chunks.excerpt:
| Deed | What the grantor warrants |
|---|---|
| **General warranty** | Against defects arising **at any time**, including before the grantor owned |
| **Special warranty** | Against defects arising **during the grantor's own ownership** only |
| **Bargain and sale** | Ordinarily implies the grantor holds title, with limited or no express warranty |
| **Quitclaim** | **Nothing.** It conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any |

**A quitclaim and a general warranty deed can convey an identical estate.** What differs is the promise
about it, and that promise is the bargain. A buyer paying market value and receiving no warranty has taken
a risk they may not have understood.

**b. Characteristics and elements.** A competent grantor and an identifiable grantee; **words of
conveyance**; an adequate **description**; the **grantor's signature**; and **delivery to and acceptance by
the grantee.** **Delivery and acceptance are the elements students forget**, and they decide when title
actually passed. A signed deed in a drawer has conveyed nothing.

**c. Warranties.** The covenants traditionally associated with a general warranty deed — seisin, right to
convey, against encumbrances, quiet enjoyment, warranty, and further assurance.

**A broker does not select the form of deed.** The choice determines what the grantor warrants and what
the grantee receives, which is a legal question. **Rule 6.2.B** gives the broker four routes and the first
is to **decline**; **§ 12-10-403(4)** and **Rule 7.1** require the broker to advise the parties that the
forms have important legal consequences and that they should consult counsel before signing.

### C.4 Assurances of title

chunks.heading: Module 01 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
| Assurance | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Abstract and opinion** | A summary of the record with an attorney's opinion of title based on it |
| **Title insurance** | A policy indemnifying against covered defects **existing as of the policy date**, subject to the policy's **exceptions and exclusions** |
| **Torrens registration** | A registration system used in some jurisdictions |

**The exceptions schedule is where a title policy's substance lives.** A policy does not insure against
what it excepts, does not insure against events after the policy date, and does not insure the physical
condition of the property. Reading the commitment is a task for the buyer, the title company and counsel —
and **Rule 6.2** tells a broker what to do when the reading is beyond them.

**Note one Colorado rule that touches title work and WAS read.** **Rule 6.20** requires a broker and
brokerage firm to **retain transaction files for four years** from the consummation date or from the
expiration of a listing contract that does not consummate — but expressly does **not** require a broker to
obtain and retain **existing public records, title commitments, loan applications, lender required
disclosures, or related affirmations from independent third-party closing entities after the closing
date.**

---

## Module 01 engagement check

Eleven items — one applied, five engagement, five remediation. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and
the **100 percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**. The Commission's outline requires that
*"**testing is required** to establish individual's satisfactory completion of the statutory
requirements"*, and **these items are not that test.**

---

## Instructor source note for Module 01

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
Written to the **Colorado Real Estate Commission's Real Estate Law and Practice (48 Classroom Hours)
qualifying education outline, approved April 1, 1998**, Topic I, obtained from dre.colorado.gov and read on
2026-08-20. The hour figure is the Commission's. The Colorado rules cited — **Rule 6.2**, **Rule 6.20**,
**Rule 7.1**, **Rule 5.10.D and E**, **§ 12-10-203(4)(a)(I)**, **§ 12-10-403(4)** and the expert-advice
duties in **§§ 12-10-404, 12-10-405 and 12-10-407** — are transcribed from **C.R.S. Title 12 Article 10**
and **4 CCR 725-1**, read the same day and recorded in `colorado/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** Colorado's **water law**; its **joint tenancy,
survivorship, community property, intestacy and probate** statutes; its **entity statutes**; its **zoning,
land use, subdivision and local ordinances**; its **property tax** statutes; the **Colorado Common Interest
Ownership Act**; its **mechanics' lien**, **recording**, **adverse possession**, **foreclosure and public
trustee**, **condemnation** and **escheat** statutes; and **C.R.S. § 38-35.5-101** on psychologically
impacted property.

**No Colorado period, element, deadline, notice requirement, redemption right, priority rule, tax rate,
exemption or procedure is stated in this module.** The **four-year** transaction file retention period, the
**20 percent** entity ownership threshold, the four routes in **Rule 6.2.B**, and the **48 hours** are
transcribed from the rules and statutes named above.

lessons.title: Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 02

chunks.heading: Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
# Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 02

## Valuation and appraisal

**Course:** Real Estate Law and Practice (48 classroom hours) · **Instructional hours: 7.0** of 48.0
**Commission outline topic:** **II — Valuation and Appraisal**, allocated **7 hours**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Colorado qualifying education hours are available.

> ### What the Commission's outline puts in this topic
>
> | Sub-topic | Delivered in |
> |---|---|
> | **A.** Principles, types and estimates of property value | Part A |
> | **B.** Influences on property value | Part B |
> | **C.** Approaches to property valuation — **1. Cost, 2. Income, 3. Market data** | Part C |
> | **D.** Investment analysis — **1. Gross rent multiplier, 2. Principles of capitalization, 3. Neighborhood** | Part D |
>
> Seven hours, and the Commission names the three approaches and the three investment-analysis items
> explicitly. **They are delivered here in the Commission's own order.**
>
> **One Colorado rule governs what a broker may call their own valuation work, and it was read in full.**
> **Rule 6.12** prescribes **the exact words** a broker must put on a CMA or BPO prepared for any purpose
> other than an anticipated sale or purchase. Part E carries it.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Principles, types and estimates of value
chunks.excerpt:
1. Distinguish value, price and cost, and state the elements value is ordinarily said to require.
2. State the principal economic principles that bear on value, including substitution.
3. Name the four categories of influence on value the appraisal literature ordinarily uses.
4. State each of the three approaches to value, what it measures, and where it is most reliable.
5. Apply the sales comparison approach, adjusting in the correct direction.
6. Calculate a gross rent multiplier and apply it; calculate value from net operating income and a rate.
7. State Rule 6.12's required notice **verbatim** and say when it must appear.
8. State what Rule 6.12 provides about CMAs or BPOs used to obtain financing.

---

## A. Principles, types and estimates of value

### A.1 Value, price and cost are three different numbers

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Market value** | An estimate of what a property **should** bring under stated conditions, between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither under compulsion, each reasonably informed, with the property exposed for a reasonable time |
| **Price** | What was **actually paid** in a particular transaction, which may have been affected by circumstances peculiar to those parties |
| **Cost** | What it took, or would take, **to build or improve** |

None of the three need equal the others, and a client who uses them interchangeably will misread every
figure a broker gives them.

**Other types of value the literature names:** investment value (to a particular investor), insurable
value, assessed value (for property taxation), going concern value, and liquidation value. **Assessed value
is not market value**, and a Colorado assessor's figure is produced under statutes **this project did not
read.**

### A.2 The elements of value

chunks.heading: A.3 The economic principles
chunks.excerpt:
Value is ordinarily said to require four elements together — **demand**, **utility**, **scarcity**, and
**transferability**. Remove any one and there is no market value: a thing everyone wants but nobody may
transfer has none, and a thing freely transferable that nobody wants has none either.

### A.3 The economic principles

| Principle | What it says |
|---|---|
| **Substitution** | A buyer will pay no more than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute |
| **Supply and demand** | Value moves with the relation between available properties and buyers for them |
| **Highest and best use** | The legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive use |
| **Conformity** | Value is supported where a property conforms reasonably to those around it |
| **Progression and regression** | A lesser property benefits from better neighbours; a better property is dragged by lesser ones |
| **Contribution** | An improvement adds what it contributes to value, not what it cost |
| **Anticipation** | Value reflects the expectation of future benefits |
| **Change** | No condition is permanent; every estimate has a date |
| **Increasing and diminishing returns** | Added investment increases value up to a point, and beyond it does not |
| **Plottage** | Combining parcels under one ownership may produce more value than the sum |
| **Externalities** | Influences outside the property affect it |

**Substitution is the one that matters most in daily practice**, because it is why recent sales of
comparable properties indicate value at all — and why a "comparable" that is not genuinely comparable is
worse than none.

**Contribution is the one clients most often get wrong.** The question is never what a renovation cost; it
is what it contributes.

chunks.heading: B. Influences on property value
chunks.excerpt:
---

## B. Influences on property value

Four categories, and a broker who can name them can explain almost any client question about why a figure
moved:

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Physical and environmental** | Size, shape, topography, soils, view, exposure, condition, hazards, climate |
| **Economic** | Employment, income levels, interest rates, rents, vacancy, construction costs, tax burden |
| **Governmental and legal** | Zoning, building codes, land use plans, taxation, public services, environmental regulation |
| **Social** | Population change, household composition, and the pattern of demand for property types |

**Location is not a category; it is the intersection of all four at a point.** That is why the same
structure is worth different sums a mile apart, and it is why the Commission's outline puts
**neighborhood** into the investment analysis sub-topic at D.3 rather than treating it as a physical
attribute.

**A fair housing boundary that runs through this whole topic.** A broker may discuss **the property and
the physical, economic, governmental and legal characteristics of an area** using sources a client can
check. A broker may **not** characterise an area by the protected characteristics of the people in it,
whatever the client asks and however accurate the characterisation would be. Module 03 of this course
delivers the federal fair housing content under the Commission's Topic III.F.1; the discipline belongs
here too, because valuation conversations are where the question usually arises.

---

## C. The three approaches to value

The Commission's outline names them in this order: **Cost**, **Income**, **Market data.**

### C.1 The cost approach

chunks.heading: C.1 The cost approach
chunks.excerpt:
**Estimated cost to reproduce or replace the improvements, less accrued depreciation, plus the site value
as if vacant.**

**Reproduction cost** is the cost of an exact replica, including its obsolete features. **Replacement
cost** is the cost of a structure of equal utility using current materials and standards. Replacement cost
is the more common basis.

**Accrued depreciation** — loss in value from any cause — comes in three forms, and distinguishing them is
the substance of the approach:

| Form | What it is | Ordinarily curable? |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical deterioration** | Wear, tear, and the action of the elements | Often, at least in part |
| **Functional obsolescence** | A defect in the structure itself — poor layout, obsolete systems, a superadequacy | Sometimes |
| **External (economic) obsolescence** | Loss caused by something **outside** the property — the neighbourhood, the market, a nuisance nearby | **No** — the cause is not on the site |

**Where it is most reliable:** **new construction** (little depreciation to estimate) and **special-purpose
properties** (too few comparable sales for the market data approach, and no income stream).

**Where it is weakest:** older buildings, where estimating accrued depreciation in all three forms becomes
the largest and least certain part of the calculation.

chunks.heading: C.2 The income approach
chunks.excerpt:
**Note the vocabulary trap.** Depreciation in the **appraisal** sense — loss in value from any cause — and
depreciation in the **tax** sense — a deduction taken by an owner of investment property under a schedule —
are different concepts sharing a word. **A broker does not use one to explain the other**, and the tax
question belongs to the client's accountant. **§ 12-10-404(1)(c)(V)**, **§ 12-10-405(1)(c)(V)** and
**§ 12-10-407(2)(b)(II)** each require the broker to advise the party to obtain expert advice on material
matters beyond the broker's expertise.

### C.2 The income approach

**Value is the present worth of the future income the property will produce.**

The direct capitalisation form is a single relationship, rearranged three ways:

> **Value = Net Operating Income ÷ Capitalisation Rate**
> **Net Operating Income = Value × Rate**
> **Rate = Net Operating Income ÷ Value**

**Building net operating income, in order:**

| Step | Line |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Potential gross income** — full occupancy, full collection |
| 2 | less **vacancy and collection loss** |
| 3 | plus **other income** |
| 4 | = **Effective gross income** |
| 5 | less **operating expenses** |
| 6 | = **Net operating income** |
| 7 | less **debt service** → cash flow before tax |

**Debt service comes off AFTER net operating income, not before it.** That is what makes NOI a measure of
the **property** rather than of a particular owner's financing, and it is why two buyers with different
loans can value the same building identically at the property level.

**Operating expenses** include fixed expenses, variable expenses, and reserves for replacement. They do
**not** include debt service, depreciation, or capital improvements.

chunks.heading: C.3 The market data (sales comparison) approach
chunks.excerpt:
**A higher capitalisation rate produces a lower value at the same income.** The rate carries the market's
view of risk: riskier income, higher rate, lower value.

### C.3 The market data (sales comparison) approach

**Comparable properties that have sold are adjusted to the subject.** It rests directly on **substitution**.

**The rule that decides every adjustment:** **adjust the COMPARABLE, never the subject.**

| If the comparable is | Adjust its sale price |
|---|---|
| **Superior** to the subject | **Downward** — it sold for more than the subject would |
| **Inferior** to the subject | **Upward** — it sold for less than the subject would |

Getting the direction backwards is the single most common error in student work, and the way to keep it
straight is to say the sentence: *the comparable had a better kitchen, so it sold for more than my subject
would have; take that difference off.*

**Elements ordinarily adjusted for:** property rights conveyed; financing terms; conditions of sale;
market conditions (time); location; physical characteristics; and use.

**Where it is most reliable:** residential property in an active market with genuine comparables — which is
most of what a Colorado broker does.

### C.4 Reconciliation

An appraiser **reconciles** the indications the approaches give — weighing each by the reliability of its
data and its applicability to the assignment — and does **not average them.** An average would give equal
weight to the least reliable indication.

---

## D. Investment analysis

### D.1 Gross rent multiplier

> **GRM = Sale Price ÷ Gross Rent** for the same period, and then
> **Indicated Value = Subject's Gross Rent × GRM**

chunks.heading: D.2 Principles of capitalization
chunks.excerpt:
**A screening tool, not the income approach.** It uses **gross** rent, so it takes no account of operating
expenses, vacancy, or the differences between two properties' operating positions. Two buildings with the
same gross rent and very different expense loads produce the same GRM indication and are not worth the
same.

**Use the same period throughout.** A multiplier built on monthly rent and applied to annual rent is out by
a factor of twelve, and that is the usual student error.

### D.2 Principles of capitalization

Direct capitalisation is stated at C.2 above. Three further ideas the Commission's outline reaches:

**The rate can be derived from the market.** If comparable sales show what investors paid for given
incomes, dividing NOI by price for each gives a rate the market itself is using.

**The overall rate covers return ON and return OF capital.** An investor requires both a return on the
money invested and its eventual recovery.

**Cash-on-cash return is a different measure from the capitalisation rate.** Cash flow before tax divided
by cash invested measures the **equity position**; the capitalisation rate measures **the property.** A
client who conflates them will misjudge leverage in both directions.

### D.3 Neighborhood

The outline puts **neighborhood** inside investment analysis, and the reason is that an income property's
future depends on the area's trajectory more than on its own condition. The analysis looks at the stage of
the neighbourhood's life cycle, the direction of rents and vacancy, the pattern of new construction, the
condition of public services and infrastructure, and access.

chunks.heading: E. What a Colorado broker may call their own valuation work — Rule 6.12
chunks.excerpt:
**The fair housing discipline from Part B applies here without qualification.** Neighbourhood analysis in
an investment context is analysis of **economic and physical** conditions, and every prospect is given the
same information and the same sources.

---

## E. What a Colorado broker may call their own valuation work — Rule 6.12

This is the one part of this module that states a **Colorado** requirement, and it was read in full.

> **4 CCR 725-1, Rule 6.12 — Notice Required on Competitive Market Analysis (CMA) or Broker's Price Opinion
> (BPO) for Purposes Other Than Marketing**
>
> *"When a Broker prepares a CMA or BPO **for any reason other than the anticipated sale or purchase of the
> property**, the Broker **must include a notice stating**:*
>
> ***'This evaluation was prepared by a licensed real estate broker and is not an appraisal. This evaluation
> cannot be used for the purposes of obtaining financing.'***
>
> *"Pursuant to section 12-10-602(9)(b)(II), C.R.S, **Brokers are prohibited from completing CMAs or BPOs
> that are used for the purpose of obtaining financing.** Preparation of CMAs or BPOs for reasons other than
> anticipated sale, purchase, or lease **is not considered Real Estate Brokerage Services.** As such, any
> compensation received for such preparation **is not required to be paid to the Broker's Brokerage Firm
> unless stated otherwise in Brokerage Firm's Office Policy Manual.**"*

**Four separate things in one rule:**

chunks.heading: Module 02 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
1. **The trigger.** Any CMA or BPO prepared for a reason **other than an anticipated sale or purchase.**
2. **The notice.** The rule prescribes **the words**, and this module states them exactly as the rule does.
3. **The prohibition.** A broker **may not** complete a CMA or BPO **used to obtain financing.** That is
   not a disclosure requirement — it is a prohibition, and the rule cites § 12-10-602(9)(b)(II) for it.
4. **The compensation consequence.** Because such preparation is **not Real Estate Brokerage Services**,
   compensation for it **need not** go to the brokerage firm — **unless the firm's office policy manual
   says otherwise.** A broker checks the manual before assuming.

**A CMA is not an appraisal, and the rule makes a broker say so in writing in the situations it covers.**
The general point stands everywhere: describing a CMA as an appraisal describes it as something it is not,
and **Rule 6.2** requires a broker to possess the necessary experience, training and knowledge — or to
decline, obtain them, obtain assistance, or co-list.

**§ 12-10-602 itself was NOT read by this project.** This module states only what **Rule 6.12** says about
it, in the rule's own words, and states **no Colorado appraisal licensing requirement, exemption, standard
or penalty.**

**Rule 6.11's square footage requirements bear on valuation work too**, and Module 03 of the Practical
Applications course delivers them; they are transcribed in
`colorado/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md` § 5.3.

---

## Module 02 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items — one applied, five engagement, five remediation. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and
the **100 percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**. The Commission's outline requires that
*"**testing is required** to establish individual's satisfactory completion of the statutory
requirements"*, and **these items are not that test.**

---

## Instructor source note for Module 02

Written to the **Commission's Real Estate Law and Practice qualifying education outline, approved April 1,
1998**, Topic II and its sub-topics A through D, in the outline's own order. The hour figure is the
Commission's. **Rule 6.12** is transcribed from **4 CCR 725-1**, read on 2026-08-20; **Rule 6.2** and the
expert-advice duties in **§§ 12-10-404(1)(c)(V), 12-10-405(1)(c)(V) and 12-10-407(2)(b)(II)** likewise.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** **C.R.S. § 12-10-602** and Colorado's **appraiser
licensing statutes and rules**; **USPAP**; Colorado's **property tax and assessment statutes**; the
**Colorado Fair Housing Act** and the **federal Fair Housing Act**; and any **Commission position
statement** on valuation, CMAs or BPOs.

**No appraisal licensing requirement, exemption, standard, assessment ratio, tax rate, capitalisation rate,
multiplier, adjustment percentage or penalty is stated in this module**, and every figure used in a
calculation is supplied inside the calculation as a given. **Rule 6.12's notice is quoted verbatim** and is
the only prescribed wording in this module.

lessons.title: Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 03

chunks.heading: Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Colorado Real Estate Law and Practice — Module 03

## Contracts, agency relationships with buyers and sellers, and federal requirements

**Course:** Real Estate Law and Practice (48 classroom hours) · **Instructional hours: 12.0** of 48.0
**Commission outline topic:** **III — Contracts, Agency Relationships with Buyer & Sellers, and Federal
Requirements**, allocated **12 hours**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Colorado qualifying education hours are available.

> ### What this module is, and what it deliberately is not
>
> The Commission's outline for this course states its objective as *"...a common body of knowledge ... as
> well as **related federal laws practiced in a majority of states on a national level**."* **This is the
> national agency and contract module.**
>
> **Colorado's own brokerage relationship law is a different course.** The **Contracts and Regulations**
> course carries **Topic II, Colorado Statutory Relationships**, allocated four hours, and it delivers
> **§§ 12-10-402 through 12-10-411** section by section. **This module supplies the general framework that
> Colorado's statute then displaces in specific and important ways**, and it says so at each point rather
> than letting a student carry a general rule into a Colorado transaction.
>
> **Three places where Colorado departs from the general account, flagged here and delivered there:**
>
> | General rule taught here | Colorado's own rule |
> |---|---|
> | Agency arises from the relationship, often by default | **§ 12-10-403(2): a broker is a TRANSACTION-BROKER unless single agency is established through a WRITTEN agreement** |
> | Dual agency is permitted with informed consent | **§ 12-10-406: "A broker shall not establish dual agenc

chunks.heading: Learning objectives
chunks.excerpt:
y with any seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant."** |
> | An agent's acts bind the principal and the firm | **§ 12-10-403(6)(b): the relationship does NOT extend to the employing broker or to the firm** — though § 12-10-408(2)(e)(II) preserves supervision and vicarious liability |
>
> The outline's sub-topics **A** through **F** are delivered in the Commission's own order.

## Learning objectives

1. State the elements of an enforceable contract and the terminology the outline names.
2. Distinguish listing agreements and buyer agency agreements as employment contracts.
3. State what a purchase contract must settle and how a contingency clause is completed.
4. State the general fiduciary duties, and state where Colorado's statute replaces them.
5. State a broker's obligation on property conditions and disclosures.
6. State the protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act and identify steering and blockbusting.
7. Name the other federal requirements the Commission's outline lists and say what each governs.
8. State the firm/licensee relationship concepts the outline names.

---

## A. Contract elements, types and terminology

### A.1 The elements

| Element | In a real estate transaction |
|---|---|
| **Offer** | A definite proposal, communicated, showing intent to be bound on stated terms |
| **Acceptance** | Unqualified assent to those exact terms, communicated to the offeror |
| **Consideration** | Something of legal value each way |
| **Capacity** | Legal ability of each party to contract |
| **Legality of object** | A lawful purpose |
| **Mutual assent** | A genuine meeting of the minds |
| **Writing** | Required for a contract for the sale of an interest in land |

chunks.heading: A.2 Terminology the outline expects
chunks.excerpt:
**A counter-offer rejects the original offer.** The original cannot then be accepted unless renewed, and
the counter operates as a new offer. A document drafted to look like an acceptance while changing a term
leaves the parties disagreeing about which paper controls — the most common drafting failure a new broker
produces.

**Acceptance must be communicated.** One signed and left in a drawer has not been. Say in the document
**how and by when** acceptance must be communicated.

### A.2 Terminology the outline expects

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Bilateral / unilateral** | Promise for a promise / promise for an act |
| **Express / implied** | Stated in words / inferred from conduct |
| **Executed / executory** | Fully performed / still to be performed |
| **Valid / void / voidable / unenforceable** | Fully effective / no effect from the outset / effective until avoided by the party with that power / valid but not enforceable in court |
| **Novation** | Substitution of a new party or contract, **releasing** the original |
| **Assignment** | Transfer of rights, which does **not** by itself release the assignor |
| **Contingency** | An obligation made dependent on a stated event |
| **Condition precedent** | An event that must occur **before** a duty arises |
| **Covenant** | A promise; failure to perform is a **breach** |
| **Liquidated damages** | An agreed sum stated in the contract |
| **Specific performance** | A remedy compelling performance rather than paying damages |

**Assignment and novation are different, and the difference is whether the original party is still
liable.** That is a legal question and it goes to counsel.

### A.3 The statute of frauds, in general terms

chunks.heading: A.4 Completing a contingency
chunks.excerpt:
A contract for the sale of an interest in land must ordinarily be **in writing** and **signed by the party
to be charged**, identifying the **parties**, the **property**, and the **price or a means of determining
it**.

**Colorado's own statute of frauds was NOT read by this project**, and **no Colorado section number,
wording or exception is stated in this course.** The **Contracts and Regulations** outline names the
Statute of Frauds under its Topic I.B.4, and that is where a Colorado answer belongs.

### A.4 Completing a contingency

A contingency clause is not finished until it states **three** things:

1. **What event**;
2. **By when**; and
3. **What happens if the event does not occur.**

An event with no deadline, or a deadline with no consequence, has settled nothing. This is the drafting
discipline the **Contracts and Regulations** course then applies to **Commission-approved forms**, whose
Topic IV requires students to complete one of each of four families of sales contracts and one of each of
the related forms.

---

## B. Agency and employment contracts: listing and buyer agency agreements

### B.1 What they are

A **listing agreement** is a contract of **employment**: an owner employs a broker. It **conveys nothing**
and it is **not an offer to sell.** A **buyer agency agreement** is the same instrument facing the other
way.

**What either must settle:** the parties, identified as they hold or will hold title; the property or the
search criteria; price and terms; the broker's authority; a **definite term with a beginning and an end**;
compensation and what earns it; cooperation and compensation with other brokers; the party's own
undertakings; any express limitation on authority; and signatures.

### B.2 The general families

chunks.heading: B.3 The Colorado duration rule, flagged here
chunks.excerpt:
| Listing type | What the owner gives up |
|---|---|
| **Open listing** | Nothing exclusive — the owner may sell themselves or engage others, and pays only the broker who produces |
| **Exclusive agency** | Exclusivity against other brokers, but the owner may still sell themselves without compensation |
| **Exclusive right to sell** | Full exclusivity — compensation is earned however the sale comes about during the term |

> **In Colorado these are Commission-promulgated forms, and the Contracts course requires the student to
> complete them.** The Contracts and Regulations outline's Topic III.A names **six families**: Exclusive
> Right-to-Sell, Exclusive Agency Listing, Open Listing, Exclusive Right-to-Buy, Exclusive Right-to-Lease
> Listing, and Exclusive Tenant Contracts — and requires *"a minimum of one of each of the 6 families."*
>
> **No Commission-approved form was obtained by this project**, and **no module of this build reproduces
> one or states its contents.** That is recorded as the build's largest submission gate.

### B.3 The Colorado duration rule, flagged here

The general law lets the parties fix the term. **Colorado adds a backstop that runs whether or not anyone
remembers it:**

> **§ 12-10-409(1)(b)**: if the agreement is not performed or completed for any reason, the relationship
> ends at the **earlier** of any agreed expiration date, any termination or relinquishment by the parties,
> or **one year after the date of the engagement.**

Delivered in full by the **Contracts and Regulations** course, Topic II.H.

---

## C. Purchase and sales contracts and contingencies

chunks.heading: D. General agency relationships and fiduciary responsibilities
chunks.excerpt:
**What a purchase contract must settle:** parties; property; price and how paid; earnest money and its
disposition in each outcome; closing date; possession; each contingency with **event, deadline and
consequence**; title and conveyance; prorations; and signature and acceptance provisions.

**The common contingencies:** financing; inspection; appraisal; title review; sale of the buyer's existing
property; survey; and, in common interest communities, review of association documents.

> **Two Colorado rules govern this in practice, and both were read.**
>
> **§ 12-10-403(4)(c)** and **Rule 7.1.A**: *"**A Broker must use a Commission-Approved Form when such form
> exists and is appropriate for the transaction.**"* A broker in Colorado is not drafting a purchase
> contract from scratch; they are completing the Commission's.
>
> **§ 12-10-403(4)(c)**, closing sentence: the broker *"**shall advise the parties that the forms have
> important legal consequences and that the parties should consult legal counsel before signing the
> forms.**"*
>
> Both are delivered by the **Contracts and Regulations** course, whose Topic IV allocates sixteen hours to
> the sales contracts and related forms.

**Earnest money in Colorado is governed by rules this project read**, and a student meets them in the
**Record Keeping and Trust Accounts** course: **Rule 5.12** requires a broker receiving earnest money to
deliver it to the earnest money holder **and obtain a dated and signed receipt**; **Rule 5.7.B** fixes
deposit **no later than three business days** following receipt or mutual execution, whichever is later.

---

## D. General agency relationships and fiduciary responsibilities

### D.1 The general account

At common law an agent owes a principal:

chunks.heading: D.2 Where Colorado departs, stated plainly
chunks.excerpt:
| Duty | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **Loyalty** | To put the principal's interest ahead of the agent's own |
| **Obedience** | To follow **lawful** instructions |
| **Disclosure** | To tell the principal what is material |
| **Confidentiality** | To keep the principal's confidences |
| **Reasonable care and skill** | To perform competently |
| **Accounting** | To account for money and property |

**Agency may arise** by express agreement, by implication from conduct, by ratification, or by estoppel.
**Actual authority** is what the principal conferred; **apparent authority** is what a third party
reasonably believes because of **the principal's own conduct.**

**A client is the party to whom agency duties are owed; a customer is a party the broker deals with but
does not represent.**

### D.2 Where Colorado departs, stated plainly

This is the point of putting the general account in a national course, and a student who leaves this module
carrying only the general account into a Colorado transaction will be wrong three times over.

**First — the default.** **§ 12-10-403(2)**: *"**A broker shall be considered a transaction-broker unless a
single agency relationship is established through a written agreement** between the broker and the party or
parties to be represented by the broker."* Agency in Colorado is **opt-in and in writing.** A broker who
signs nothing is a **transaction-broker**, and **§ 12-10-407(1)** says a transaction-broker *"**is not an
agent for either party.**"*

chunks.heading: E. Property conditions and disclosures
chunks.excerpt:
**Second — dual agency.** **§ 12-10-406** in its entirety: *"**A broker shall not establish dual agency
with any seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant.**"* No consent cures it, because the statute offers no consent
mechanism. **Rule 6.7** then states the three lawful ways a broker or team may work with both consumers:
transaction-broker for both; transaction-broker for one and the other as a **customer**; or single agent
for one and the other as a **customer.**

**Third — who the relationship binds.** **§ 12-10-403(6)(b)**: the relationship with a **designated broker**
*"**shall not extend to the employing broker nor to any other broker** ... **and shall not extend to the
firm.**"* And immediately, **§ 12-10-408(2)(e)(II)**: *"**Nothing ... shall be construed to limit the
employing broker's or firm's responsibility to supervise licensees** ... **nor to shield the broker or firm
from vicarious liability.**"* **Two different things**, and a module that merges them misstates both.

**Fourth, and it is not a departure but an addition — Colorado's single agent is a LIMITED agent.**
**§§ 12-10-404(1) and 12-10-405(1)** each open: *"A broker engaged by a [party] ... **is a limited agent**
with the following duties and obligations"* — and then list them, closing with the requirement to promote
the party's interests *"**with the utmost good faith, loyalty, and fidelity.**"* **The Contracts and
Regulations course delivers both lists in full.**

---

## E. Property conditions and disclosures

**The general standard a broker works to:** disclose what you know that is material; do not misrepresent;
do not conceal; and route every question of condition to a professional qualified to answer it.

**Colorado's own standard was read and it uses a specific phrase — "actually known".**

chunks.heading: E. Property conditions and disclosures
chunks.excerpt:
