lessons.title: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 02

chunks.heading: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
# Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 02

## Hours 8–14 · Agency relationships

**Commission topic covered:** Agency Relationships (13%, 390 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Maine sales agent credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- State the § 13282 presumption and explain what it takes to displace it.
- Distinguish a transaction broker from a seller agent, buyer agent, subagent and disclosed dual
  agent, and say what each owes.
- Recite the seven duties in § 13272 and the specific obligations in §§ 13273 and 13274.
- Explain why knowledge is not imputed within a Maine agency, and where the statute says so.
- Complete the relationship analysis for a multi-party transaction and identify the documents each
  step requires.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Minutes | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 8 | 30–60 | Brokerage versus transaction brokerage; the presumption | Section completed |
| 9 | 0–60 | The seven duties; vicarious liability and imputed knowledge | Section completed |
| 10 | 0–60 | Written client agreements and their required components | Section completed |
| 11 | 0–60 | Seller agency, buyer agency, subagency, and disclosed dual agency | Section completed |
| 12 | 0–60 | Appointed agents, company policy, and supervision | Section completed |
| 13 | 0–60 | The relationship disclosure form and documentation | Section completed |
| 14 | 0–60 | Termination, surviving duties, conflicts, and integrated scenarios | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **390** | | Quiz 1 follows Hour 15 |

---

## Hour 08, second half — The presumption, and what displaces it

### 8.4 § 13282, read exactly

chunks.heading: 8.5 The five relationships
chunks.excerpt:
> Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, a real estate brokerage agency providing real
> estate brokerage services is **presumed to be acting as a transaction broker** unless the real
> estate brokerage agency has agreed, **in a written brokerage agreement**, to represent one or more
> parties to the real estate transaction as the real estate brokerage agency's clients.
> **Client representation may not be created orally or by implication** or be assumed by a real
> estate brokerage agency or any party to a real estate transaction.

Four consequences, each of which a sales agent will meet in the first month.

**Nobody is a client until there is a written brokerage agreement.** Not after a long conversation.
Not after three showings. Not because the consumer thinks so.

**Nothing a licensee does creates representation by implication.** Helpfulness does not create
agency in Maine. This protects the licensee as much as the consumer, and it is the reason the
relationship disclosure form exists.

**The default has real content.** A transaction broker is not nothing: § 13283 2 imposes six
duties. But it is not agency, and the seven duties in § 13272 do not attach.

**The consumer must be told which they have.** § 13279 requires the agency to provide buyers and
sellers of residential real property a meaningful, written relationship disclosure form in a timely
manner, as the Commission's rules define and mandate.

### 8.5 The five relationships

**Transaction broker — § 13283.** Represents nobody as a client, is not bound by § 13272, and owes
the six duties in § 13283 2.

**Seller agent — § 13273.** Represents the seller as a client.

**Buyer agent — § 13274.** Represents the buyer as a client.

chunks.heading: Hour 09 — The seven duties, and what is not imputed
chunks.excerpt:
**Subagent.** § 13272 names the subagent as one of the forms an agency may take. A subagent works
through another agency's client relationship.

**Disclosed dual agent — § 13275.** Represents both clients in the same transaction, only with the
informed written consent of all parties.

To which add the **appointed agent** under § 13278 — not a fifth relationship but a way of
allocating an agency's client relationships among its licensees.

---

## Hour 09 — The seven duties, and what is not imputed

### 9.1 § 13272, verbatim

> A real estate brokerage agency that provides services through a brokerage agreement for a client
> is bound by the duties of **loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care,
> diligence and accounting** as set forth in this chapter.

Seven duties, and unlike Virginia — where § 54.1-2144 abrogates the common law of agency to the
extent inconsistent — Maine keeps them. A student who has read national agency material will find it
useful here, provided they check every proposition against §§ 13273 and 13274, which are where the
duties acquire their Maine content.

chunks.heading: 9.2 The seller agent's specific obligations — § 13273 1
chunks.excerpt:
**Loyalty.** The client's interests come before the licensee's and before anyone else's.
**Obedience.** Lawful instructions are followed. Unlawful ones are not, and § 13273 1 E makes
compliance with fair housing and civil rights law a duty in its own right, so a client instruction
cannot authorise a violation.
**Disclosure.** § 13273 1 B (3) — material facts of actual knowledge **or which the agent, acting
reasonably, should have known**.
**Confidentiality.** § 13273 1 F — information provided during the relationship that might have a
negative impact on the client's real estate activity, subject to four exceptions.
**Reasonable care.** § 13273 1 C — reasonable skill and care.
**Diligence.** Pursuing the client's objective actively, not passively.
**Accounting.** § 13273 1 B (5) — timely accounting for all money and property in which the client
has or may have an interest.

### 9.2 The seller agent's specific obligations — § 13273 1

**A.** Perform the terms of the brokerage agreement.

chunks.heading: 9.2 The seller agent's specific obligations — § 13273 1
chunks.excerpt:
**B.** Promote the seller's interests by:
 **(1)** seeking a sale at the price and terms stated in the agreement or acceptable to the seller —
 with the express carve-out that **the seller agent is not obligated to seek additional offers while
 the property is subject to a contract of sale unless the brokerage agreement so provides**;
 **(2) presenting in a timely manner all offers to and from the seller, even when the property is
 subject to a contract of sale**;
 **(3) disclosing material facts of actual knowledge or which the agent, acting in a reasonable
 manner, should have known**, except as directed in § 13280;
 **(4) advising the seller to obtain expert advice on material matters beyond the seller agent's
 expertise**; and
 **(5)** accounting in a timely manner for all money and property received in which the seller has
 or may have an interest.

**C.** Exercise reasonable skill and care.
**D.** Comply with the brokerage licence laws and the Commission's rules.
**E.** Comply with applicable federal, state and local law, **including fair housing and civil rights
law**.
**F.** Preserve confidential information provided by the seller that might have a negative impact on
the seller's real estate activity, unless **(1)** the seller consents, **(2)** disclosure is required
by law, **(3)** the information is or becomes public otherwise than through the agent, or **(4)**
disclosure is necessary to defend the agent against an accusation of wrongful conduct before a
court, the Commission, or a professional committee.

**§ 13274** carries the same architecture for a buyer agent.

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are broader than the equivalents in several other states.

chunks.heading: 9.3 Vicarious liability, and the two places Maine says knowledge is not imputed
chunks.excerpt:
**B (3) is a constructive-knowledge standard.** "Should have known" means a Maine seller agent
cannot rely on not having asked. Where a reasonable agent in the circumstances would have known a
material fact, the duty attaches.

**B (4) is an affirmative duty to send the client elsewhere.** The statute requires the agent to
advise the client to get expert advice on material matters beyond the agent's expertise. That is not
a defensive habit; it is a statutory obligation, and it is the answer to almost every question a
sales agent is not qualified to answer.

### 9.3 Vicarious liability, and the two places Maine says knowledge is not imputed

A licensee's acts within the scope of the agency relationship can expose the agency; the designated
broker's supervision duty under § 13179 is the mechanism that manages that exposure. But Maine
limits the doctrine in a specific and examinable way.

**§ 13275 3** — in a disclosed dual agency, each client, the agency and its affiliated licensees are
considered to possess **only actual knowledge and information**, and **there is no imputation of
knowledge or information by operation of law** among or between them.

**§ 13278 3** — the same rule where agents have been appointed.

So in a Maine agency operating with appointed agents, what the seller's appointed agent knows is not
attributed to the buyer's appointed agent, nor to the buyer, nor to the agency at large. A course
teaching that knowledge is imputed within a firm is teaching the opposite of the statute — and it is
what makes appointed agency workable at all.

---

## Hour 10 — Written client agreements

### 10.1 § 13177-A, applied

Module 01 stated the five required components. This hour uses them.

chunks.heading: 10.2 The two protections
chunks.excerpt:
**A. The signature of the client to be charged.** The party who will owe the fee signs. Where a
property is jointly owned, everyone whose signature is needed to convey should be on the agreement.

**B. The terms and conditions of the brokerage services to be provided.** What the agency will
actually do. A client who later says "I did not know you would not do that" is describing a defect
in this component.

**C. The method or amount of compensation to be paid.** Stated, not implied, and negotiable.

**D. The date upon which the agreement will expire.** Maine requires an end date. There is no
open-ended Maine listing, and no default period fills a gap — the statute requires the date to be
in the agreement.

**E. A statement that the agreement creates an agency-client relationship.** This is the component
that connects § 13177-A to § 13282. Without a written brokerage agreement the presumption is
transaction brokerage; element E is the agreement saying, in terms, that representation exists.

### 10.2 The two protections

> A brokerage agreement may not be enforced against any client who **in good faith subsequently
> engages the services of another real estate brokerage agency following the expiration date** of
> the first brokerage agreement.

> Any brokerage agreement provision extending a real estate brokerage agency's right to a fee
> following expiration **may not extend that right beyond 6 months.**

A protection period, holdover clause, or fee tail is permitted — capped at six months from
expiration — and it cannot be used against a client who has in good faith engaged another agency
after the expiration date.

### 10.3 Before the agreement: policy and consent

chunks.heading: 10.4 What the agreement does not do
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 13278 4** requires the Commission's rules to include a requirement that clients be **informed of
the agency's appointed agent policy and give written consent to that policy in advance of entering
into a brokerage agreement.** § 13277 requires the agency to have a **written policy**.

So the order in a Maine agency is: the relationship disclosure form under § 13279 in a timely
manner; the appointed agent policy explained and consented to in writing; and then the brokerage
agreement satisfying § 13177-A. Doing them out of order is how an agency ends up with a signed
agreement and an uninformed client.

### 10.4 What the agreement does not do

It does not make the licensee a lawyer. It does not permit the licensee to draft bespoke legal
terms. And it does not convert the client's obligations into the licensee's: the client still signs
their own contracts, gives their own instructions, and makes their own decisions.

---

## Hour 11 — Seller agency, buyer agency, subagency, and disclosed dual agency

### 11.1 Seller agency

The agency has a written brokerage agreement with the seller. § 13273 governs. The seller is the
client; the buyer, unless separately represented, is a **customer**.

To the buyer as customer the seller agent owes honesty, no knowingly false information, and — under
the same principle that runs through the chapter — disclosure of material defects in the physical
condition of the property that the agent knows about. The agent does **not** owe the buyer loyalty,
confidentiality, or advocacy, and saying so plainly at the outset prevents most complaints.

### 11.2 Buyer agency

chunks.heading: 11.3 Subagency
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 13274** carries the § 13273 architecture to the buyer side: perform the agreement; promote the
buyer's interests; disclose material facts; exercise reasonable skill and care; comply with the
brokerage laws, the Commission's rules, and fair housing law; and preserve confidential information
on the same four exceptions.

The seller is then the customer, and the same boundary applies in reverse.

### 11.3 Subagency

**§ 13272** names the subagent. A subagent is an agency that works through another agency's client
relationship, owing the client's duties without a direct agreement with the client. Subagency has
largely fallen out of use in practice, and where it is offered it must be accepted or declined
deliberately rather than by default.

### 11.4 Disclosed dual agency — § 13275

Permitted **only with the informed written consent of all parties**, on the five statements Module
01 listed, and subject to the four categories of information a disclosed dual agent may **never**
disclose:

1. the willingness or ability of the seller to accept less than the asking price;
2. the willingness or ability of the buyer to pay more than has been offered;
3. confidential negotiating strategy not disclosed in the sales offer as terms of the sale;
4. the motivation of the seller for selling and the motivation of the buyer for buying.

**§ 13275 4** provides that the dual agent's duty to the selling client is the same as § 13273's and
to the buying client the same as § 13274's, subject to the section's exceptions.

chunks.heading: 11.5 Choosing
chunks.excerpt:
The practical consequence, and it must be explained to clients before consent rather than after: a
disclosed dual agent **cannot advocate on price or terms for either side**, because advocating for
one is acting against the other. What the dual agent can do is facilitate — carry offers, explain
process, keep the transaction moving — and the four protected categories are what stops the
arrangement from being a trap for whichever client speaks first.

### 11.5 Choosing

For a consumer the choice is real, and § 13275 1 D requires the consent agreement to say so: the
client **may choose to consent or not consent**. A client who declines dual agency in an agency that
has both sides may be offered appointed agents under § 13278, or may take their business elsewhere.
A licensee who presents consent as a formality has defeated the section.

---

## Hour 12 — Appointed agents, company policy, and supervision

### 12.1 § 13278, worked

**Subsection 1.** The agency, **through the designated broker**, may **appoint in writing to the
client** those affiliated licensees who will act as **appointed agents** of that client, **to the
exclusion of all other affiliated licensees** in the agency.

**Subsection 2.** The agency and the designated broker are **not dual agents solely because of an
appointment** — **except** that any affiliated licensee who **personally represents both the seller
and the buyer as clients** in a particular transaction **is** a dual agent and must comply with
§ 13275.

**Subsection 3.** No imputation of knowledge or information among the clients, the agency, and the
appointed agents. Each possesses only actual knowledge and information.

chunks.heading: 12.2 Why subsection 2 matters
chunks.excerpt:
**Subsection 4.** The Commission's rules define the methods of appointment and the roles of the
agency and designated broker, and must require that clients be **informed of the appointed agent
policy and give written consent to it in advance of entering into a brokerage agreement.**

### 12.2 Why subsection 2 matters

In several states a designated or appointed arrangement makes the supervising broker a dual agent —
Virginia's § 54.1-2139.1 A says so expressly. **Maine says the opposite.** The agency and the
designated broker are not dual agents merely because appointments were made.

That is a different architecture, and a licensee moving between the two states must not carry one
into the other. The exception is narrow and personal: an individual licensee who represents both
clients in the same transaction is a dual agent no matter what the agency's structure is.

### 12.3 Company policy — § 13277

The agency must have a **written policy**. For a sales agent, the policy answers the questions the
statute leaves to the agency: whether the agency practises appointed agency at all; whether and when
it will act as a disclosed dual agent; how relationship disclosure forms are delivered and recorded;
how deposits are handled; what advertising must contain; and what must be escalated to the designated
broker.

A sales agent who has not read their agency's written policy cannot answer a client's first question
about how the agency works.

### 12.4 Supervision — § 13179

chunks.heading: Hour 13 — The relationship disclosure form and documentation
chunks.excerpt:
Supervision is the designated broker's duty. What it means for a sales agent in practice: the
designated broker reviews agreements and documents; the designated broker is responsible for the
agency's records under § 13184 and its trust accounts under § 13178; and the designated broker is
the escalation point for anything unusual.

The instinct to solve a problem quietly before anyone notices is the instinct that turns a small
error into a disciplinary matter.

---

## Hour 13 — The relationship disclosure form and documentation

### 13.1 § 13279

> A real estate brokerage agency shall provide **in a timely manner** to buyers and sellers of
> residential real property **a meaningful, written real estate brokerage relationship disclosure
> form as defined and mandated by rules adopted by the commission.** For purposes of this section,
> "residential real property" means real estate consisting of **not less than one nor more than 4
> residential dwelling units.**

Four things to hold.

**It is mandatory** for residential property of one to four dwelling units.

**Its content and its timing are set by the Commission's rules** under § 13280 — so it is used as
published, and this course states no timing rule of its own.

**It is a disclosure, not an agreement.** Giving it creates nothing. Under § 13282 representation
requires a written brokerage agreement, and cannot arise by implication.

**Its purpose is to prevent the misunderstanding in Module 01's engagement check** — the consumer who
believes, reasonably but wrongly, that the helpful licensee is their agent.

### 13.2 Documentation as a practice

What belongs in the file, and when:

chunks.heading: 13.3 Why the record wins
chunks.excerpt:
**At first substantive contact:** the relationship disclosure form, delivered and recorded.
**Before the brokerage agreement:** the appointed agent policy, explained and consented to in
writing where the agency practises appointed agency.
**At engagement:** the written brokerage agreement satisfying § 13177-A, signed by the client to be
charged, with the expiration date and the statement that it creates an agency-client relationship.
**Where the agency will be on both sides:** the § 13275 disclosed dual agency consent, or the
§ 13278 written appointments — never neither.
**Throughout:** every offer and counteroffer with date and time and evidence of presentation, since
§ 13273 1 B (2) requires all offers to be presented in a timely manner **even when the property is
under contract**; the property disclosure statement under 33 M.R.S. § 173; and a note of every
material conversation.
**On termination:** the record of how and when it ended, because § 13281 measures the surviving
duties from that point.

### 13.3 Why the record wins

Every complaint in brokerage is a dispute about what was said, when, and to whom. A file that
answers those three questions contemporaneously answers the complaint. A file assembled afterwards
answers nothing and suggests that nothing was kept.

---

## Hour 14 — Termination, surviving duties, conflicts, and integration

### 14.1 § 13281 — duration

**Subsection 1.** The relationships commence on the **effective date of the brokerage agreement**
and continue until **performance, completion, termination or expiration** of that agreement.

**Subsection 2.** After termination, expiration, completion or performance, the agency and the
affiliated licensee **owe no further duty or obligation except**:

chunks.heading: 14.2 Conflicts
chunks.excerpt:
**A.** **Accounting** in a timely manner for all money and property related to, and received during,
the relationship; and

**B.** For seller agents, buyer agents, subagents and disclosed dual agents, **treating as
confidential** information provided by the client during the relationship that **could have a
negative impact on the client's real estate activity** — unless **(1)** the client grants **written**
consent, **(2)** disclosure is required by law, **(3)** the information is or becomes public
otherwise than through the agency or licensee, or **(4)** disclosure is necessary to defend against
an action of wrongful conduct before a court, the Commission, or a professional committee.

Two features worth noticing. The surviving confidentiality duty requires **written** consent to
release, where the in-relationship duty under § 13273 1 F (1) says only "grants consent". And the
list is exhaustive: **no other duty survives**, which is a protection for the licensee as much as an
obligation.

### 14.2 Conflicts

**§ 13251-A** — a broker or associate broker may not knowingly provide or offer an **appraisal or
opinion of market value** on real estate in a transaction where the broker, or **any other licensee
licensed with the agency**, is to receive a fee on that transaction.

**Self-interest.** A licensee buying or selling for their own account, for family, or through an
entity they hold an interest in, must disclose the position.

**Two clients whose interests conflict.** § 13275 if the same licensee represents both; § 13278 if
the agency allocates them to different appointed agents; and a decision, made before the conflict
arises rather than during it, about which the agency will do.

chunks.heading: 14.3 Integrated scenario
chunks.excerpt:
**A former client.** § 13281 2 B is the section, and the duty does not expire with the agreement.

### 14.3 Integrated scenario

*A Maine agency has a written brokerage agreement with a seller, signed 3 March, expiring 3
September, with a 90-day protection period. On 12 August a buyer who has been working with the same
agency for six weeks — no written agreement — decides to offer. The agency practises appointed
agency and has a written policy. During the negotiation the buyer tells their licensee they would go
$15,000 higher. The seller has told the listing licensee they will take $20,000 less.*

Work it through:

**The buyer is not a client.** § 13282 — no written brokerage agreement, and representation cannot
arise by implication from six weeks of showings. The agency is a **transaction broker** as to the
buyer, owing the § 13283 2 duties and bound by the § 13283 3 prohibitions.

**The seller is a client**, under a § 13177-A agreement that is still within its term.

**So this is not dual agency**, and appointed agency is not needed for the buyer's side, because the
buyer has no client relationship to allocate. The agency should have provided the buyer the § 13279
relationship disclosure form long before now, and should offer the buyer the choice of a written
brokerage agreement or of proceeding as a customer — clearly, and before the offer.

chunks.heading: Module 02 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**The buyer's statement that they would go higher.** As a transaction broker the agency owes the
buyer no confidentiality — § 13283 1 says a transaction broker is not bound by the § 13272 duties.
But the agency **does** owe the seller, as its client, disclosure of material facts under
§ 13273 1 B (3). That is exactly why the buyer must be told, before they speak, that the agency is
not representing them — and why the relationship disclosure form is mandatory.

**The seller's statement that they will take less.** Confidential under § 13273 1 F, and it stays
confidential after the agreement ends under § 13281 2 B.

**The protection period.** Permitted, and capped at six months from expiration by § 13177-A, and
unenforceable against a client who in good faith engages another agency after the expiration date.

### Module 02 engagement check

**Question.** An agency has written brokerage agreements with both the seller and the buyer in the
same transaction. The designated broker appoints Licensee A to the seller and Licensee B to the
buyer, in writing, and both clients consented in writing to the agency's appointed agent policy
before signing their agreements. The buyer asks Licensee B whether the seller would take less;
Licensee A knows the seller would. What is each person's status, and what may be said?

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — agency worked through
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** This is **appointed agency under § 13278**. Under **§ 13278 2** the agency and
the **designated broker are not dual agents solely because of the appointment** — which is the
opposite of the rule in some other states — and neither A nor B is a dual agent, because neither
personally represents both clients. Under **§ 13278 3** each client, the agency and the appointed
agents possess **only actual knowledge and information**, with **no imputation of knowledge by
operation of law**, so what A knows is not attributed to B or to B's client.

Licensee A owes the seller **confidentiality** under § 13273 1 F as to information that might have a
negative impact on the seller's real estate activity, and the seller's willingness to take less is
squarely that. So **A may not tell B**, and B — who genuinely does not know — tells the buyer that
they do not know and cannot obtain it. Had the same licensee represented both, § 13278 2's exception
would make them a **disclosed dual agent** under § 13275, and the willingness of the seller to accept
less than the asking price is the **first** of the four categories a disclosed dual agent may never
disclose.

---

## Extended treatment — agency worked through

### E2.1 The four relationships, side by side

chunks.heading: E2.2 Duties illustrated, one at a time
chunks.excerpt:
| | Transaction broker | Seller agent | Buyer agent | Disclosed dual agent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Source | § 13283 (default under § 13282) | § 13273 | § 13274 | § 13275 |
| Requires | Nothing; it is the presumption | Written brokerage agreement | Written brokerage agreement | Written agreement plus **informed written consent of all parties** |
| Bound by the § 13272 duties | **No** — § 13283 1 | Yes | Yes | Yes, as limited by § 13275 |
| Disclosure standard | **Actual notice or knowledge** of material defects in physical condition, to a buyer | **Actual knowledge or should have known**, of material facts, to the client | Same architecture as § 13273 | Both, as limited |
| Must advise client to get expert advice | No such duty | **Yes** — § 13273 1 B (4) | Yes | Yes |
| May investigate for a party | **No** — § 13283 3 A | Yes, within competence | Yes, within competence | Yes, as limited |
| May verify others' statements | **No** — § 13283 3 B | — | — | — |
| May promote a party's interests | **No** — § 13283 3 C | Yes, for the client | Yes, for the client | **Neither** — the duties are limited |
| Four protected categories | n/a | n/a | n/a | **§ 13275 1 C** |

The table is the module in one page, and the column that surprises people is the first. A transaction
broker is the **default**, owes real duties, and is **prohibited** from doing three things a consumer
will assume they are doing.

### E2.2 Duties illustrated, one at a time

**Loyalty.** A listing agent learns the buyer's agent is a friend and would like to help the deal
close. Loyalty means the seller's interest governs, and any personal interest is disclosed.

chunks.heading: E2.3 What is owed to a customer
chunks.excerpt:
**Obedience.** A seller instructs the agent not to present offers below a figure. That instruction
**cannot be followed**: § 13273 1 B (2) requires all offers to be presented in a timely manner even
when the property is under contract. Obedience is to **lawful** instructions.

**Disclosure.** The agent learns from a neighbour that the road association has voted a $9,000 per lot
assessment. Actual knowledge of a material fact concerning the transaction; § 13273 1 B (3) requires
it be disclosed to the client — and the "should have known" limb means the agent cannot avoid the
duty by declining to ask an obvious question.

**Confidentiality.** The seller says they are relocating for a job in six weeks. That could have a
negative impact on the seller's real estate activity, so § 13273 1 F protects it — and § 13281 2 B
keeps protecting it after the agreement ends.

**Reasonable care.** The agent computes a net-proceeds estimate and omits the mortgage prepayment
penalty. § 13273 1 C is engaged, and the fix is to state assumptions and to say what has not been
verified.

**Diligence.** A listing sits unmarketed for five weeks. § 13272 lists diligence as a duty, and
§ 13273 1 A requires performance of the agreement's terms.

**Accounting.** A deposit is held by the agency for four months and never reconciled against the
client's file. § 13273 1 B (5) and § 13178.

### E2.3 What is owed to a customer

A **customer** is a party to the transaction whom the agency does not represent. What is owed:

**Honesty**, and **no knowingly false information** — § 13283 2 E for a transaction broker, and the
same principle throughout the chapter.

**Disclosure of material defects in the physical condition** of the property that are actually known.

chunks.heading: E2.4 The conversation that prevents the complaint
chunks.excerpt:
**Fair housing compliance**, which runs to everyone.

**Ministerial acts** as agreed — opening a door, providing a form, transmitting a document.

What is **not** owed: loyalty, confidentiality, advocacy, or advice. And saying so plainly, early, in
writing, and with the § 13279 form, prevents most complaints in Maine brokerage.

### E2.4 The conversation that prevents the complaint

A Maine licensee meeting a consumer for the first time has one job before anything else: make the
relationship visible.

*"Before we go any further — I want to be clear about who I work for. Right now I'm not representing
you. In Maine that's the default, and it's called transaction brokerage. Here's the Commission's
disclosure form that explains it. What it means practically is that I'll be honest with you, I'll
tell you about any material defect in the property's condition that I actually know about, and I'll
handle the paperwork — but I won't be advising you on price or strategy, I can't investigate the
property for you, and I can't verify what the seller tells you. If you'd like me to represent you,
that takes a written agreement, and I'd be glad to explain what that would change."*

That paragraph is the whole of §§ 13279, 13282, 13283 2 and 13283 3 in language a consumer can act
on. A licensee who says it in the first ten minutes will rarely have the argument later.

### E2.5 Termination scenarios

**Expiration.** The agreement's stated date arrives — and § 13177-A requires every Maine agreement to
have one. The relationship ends; § 13281 2's two duties survive; and a protection period, if any,
runs but cannot extend beyond **six months** and cannot be enforced against a client who in good
faith engaged another agency after expiration.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
**Mutual release.** Both sides agree in writing. Record who released what, and whether any protection
period survives.

**Client termination.** A client may end the relationship; whether they owe a fee is a contract
question. A licensee who argues about it rather than referring it to the designated broker has made a
service problem into a dispute.

**Agency withdrawal.** An agency may withdraw, and must where continuing would require a violation —
a client instructing a fair housing breach being the clearest case.

**Completion.** Performance completes it, and § 13281 1 says so.

**Death or incapacity of the client**, which raises questions of authority and of the estate that go
to counsel.

In every case: the record of **how and when it ended** is what the surviving duties are measured
from, and it belongs in the file.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 02

Every Maine statement in this module rests on text read directly from `legislature.maine.gov` on
2026-08-20 and recorded in `maine/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`. Quoted verbatim or in
substance: **§ 13177-A**, **§ 13251-A**, **§ 13272**, **§ 13273 1 A–F**, **§ 13274**, **§ 13275 1–4**,
**§ 13277**, **§ 13278 1–4**, **§ 13279**, **§ 13281 1–2**, **§ 13282**, **§ 13283 1–3**, and
**§ 13179** and **§ 13280** by title.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
**Two contrasts are drawn deliberately and are the point of the module.** Maine did **not** abrogate
the agency duties — § 13272 keeps loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care,
diligence and accounting — where Virginia's § 54.1-2144 abrogates the common law of agency to the
extent inconsistent. And **§ 13278 2 provides that the agency and designated broker are not dual
agents solely because of an appointment**, where Virginia's § 54.1-2139.1 A makes the supervising
broker a dual agent. A licensee moving between the two frameworks must not carry one into the other,
and Hour 12.2 says so.

**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** the **content and timing rules for the
relationship disclosure form**, which § 13280 delegates to the Commission's rules; the requirements
of **§ 13277 (written policy)**, **§ 13178 (trust accounts)** and **§ 13179 (supervision)**; and the
**methods of appointment** § 13278 4 delegates to the Commission. Each is cited by title, and the
hour routes the licensee to the current rules rather than stating a requirement it has not read.

**§ 13274 is cited as carrying the § 13273 architecture to the buyer side.** Its subsection lettering
was not read item by item, and no buyer-agent duty is quoted here as verbatim text.

chunks.heading: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 03

## Hours 15–22 · Product knowledge I: property, ownership, and interests

**Commission topic covered:** Product Knowledge (28%, 840 instructional minutes) — this module
carries 435 of them; Module 04 carries the remaining 405.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Maine sales agent credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Apply a fixture test and explain which factor controls.
- Read a metes-and-bounds description well enough to spot an ambiguity, and say what a Maine
  mortgage inspection is and is not.
- Classify freehold and leasehold estates and diagram present and future interests.
- Distinguish joint tenancy, tenancy in common, condominium and cooperative ownership.
- Identify the questions a Maine landlord-tenant matter raises and where the answers live.
- Distinguish private land-use control from public land-use control and say who enforces each.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 15 — Real property, personal property, and fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Minutes | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 15 | 0–15 | Real and personal property; fixtures | Section completed |
| 16 | 0–60 | Legal descriptions, survey systems, mortgage inspections | Section completed |
| 17 | 0–60 | Freehold estates, future interests, bundle of rights | Section completed |
| 18 | 0–60 | Concurrent ownership; condominium and cooperative | Section completed |
| 19 | 0–60 | Leasehold estates, lease types, sale and foreclosure effects | Section completed |
| 20 | 0–60 | Maine landlord-tenant fundamentals | Section completed |
| 21 | 0–60 | Private land-use controls, covenants, associations | Section completed |
| 22 | 0–60 | Zoning, permits, variances, nonconforming use, codes | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **435** | | Quiz 1 is delivered in Hour 15, minutes 15–60 |

---

## Hour 15 — Real property, personal property, and fixtures

### 15.1 The three words

**Land** is the surface, the space above, and the ground beneath, to the extent the law recognises
rights in each. **Real estate** is land plus everything permanently attached by nature or by people.
**Real property** is real estate plus the legal interests a person may hold in it — and it is what
is actually bought and sold.

The traditional image is the **bundle of rights**: possession, use, exclusion, encumbrance,
transfer, and the right to do nothing. The sticks separate. A seller who conveys the surface and
reserves timber rights has sold real property and kept real property.

### 15.2 Fixtures

A **fixture** was personal property and became real property by attachment. Once a fixture, it
passes with the deed unless the contract says otherwise.

The test, in the common mnemonic **MARIA**:

chunks.heading: 15.3 The Maine practice point
chunks.excerpt:
**Method of annexation** — how it is attached, and what removal would do. Bolted, wired, plumbed, or
built in points to a fixture; so does damage on removal.

**Adaptation** — has it been fitted to this particular property? Custom-cut storm windows, a
built-in bookcase sized to an alcove, and the key to the front door are adapted, and adaptation
makes a fixture even where the physical attachment is slight.

**Relationship of the parties** — the same item is treated differently between landlord and tenant
than between seller and buyer, and doubt is generally resolved in favour of the weaker position.

**Intention**, judged objectively, which the courts treat as controlling. The first two are evidence
of it.

**Agreement**, which is decisive when it exists.

**Trade fixtures** are installed by a *tenant* for the tenant's trade or business, remain the
tenant's personal property, and must be removed before the term ends — after which they generally
pass to the landlord by **accession**. **Severance** runs the other way: standing timber is real
estate, cut timber is personal property.

### 15.3 The Maine practice point

Most fixture disputes are contracts that failed to say. At listing, walk the property and record
what conveys and what does not — light fittings, mounted televisions and brackets, appliances,
window treatments, generators, water-treatment equipment, sheds, above-ground pools, and anything
the seller intends to take.

Two Maine items recur: **heating equipment**, including free-standing stoves, propane tanks that are
frequently **leased from the dealer rather than owned**, and buried oil tanks; and **water-treatment
systems**, which on a private well are often the only reason the water is usable and are sometimes
rented.

chunks.heading: Hour 16 — Legal descriptions, survey systems, and mortgage inspections
chunks.excerpt:
A leased propane tank is not the seller's to convey. Discovering that at the walk-through is a
failure of the listing conversation, not of the contract.

---

## Hour 16 — Legal descriptions, survey systems, and mortgage inspections

### 16.1 Why an address is not a description

A street address identifies a mailbox. A **legal description** identifies a unique parcel in a way a
surveyor could reproduce on the ground. Deeds, mortgages, plans, and judgments use legal
descriptions; contracts should.

### 16.2 Metes and bounds

Maine is a **metes and bounds** state. A description begins at a **point of beginning**, proceeds by
**calls** of bearing and distance, and must **close** back at the point of beginning.

A call reads, for example, *N 42° 15′ 00″ E, 318.6 feet to an iron pin*. Bearings are read as a
deviation from north or south toward east or west; sixty minutes to a degree, sixty seconds to a
minute.

**Monuments** are the physical markers a call references — an iron pin, a drill hole in a ledge, a
stone wall, a large tree, the centreline of a road, the thread of a stream. The rule of construction
is that **monuments control over courses and distances**, because a monument is what a person on the
ground can find.

Maine descriptions carry the specific difficulties of a long-settled, heavily wooded, coastal state:
calls referencing stone walls and trees that are two centuries old; adjoining-owner references to
families long gone; **shoreline boundaries that move**; and descriptions carried forward unchanged
through generations of deeds while the physical world changed around them.

### 16.3 Recorded plans

chunks.heading: 16.4 The rectangular survey system, and why Maine does not use it
chunks.excerpt:
A **lot and block** or recorded-plan description references a plan recorded at the Registry of
Deeds: *Lot 7 as shown on a plan entitled "…", recorded in the ___ County Registry of Deeds in Plan
Book __, Page __.* The plan itself carries the metes and bounds, the easements, and the surveyor's
certification.

**A lot does not exist until the plan is recorded.** Selling from an unrecorded sketch is selling
something with no legal description.

### 16.4 The rectangular survey system, and why Maine does not use it

The government survey system of principal meridians, base lines, townships six miles square and
sections of 640 acres governs most land west and north of the original states. **Maine is not a
public land survey state.** A student should know the arithmetic for a national licensing
examination — a quarter of a quarter section is 40 acres — but should not expect it in a Maine deed.

Maine's unorganised territory is described by **township and range** in its own historical system
(T5 R7 BKP WKR and the like), which is a Maine convention and not the federal rectangular system.

### 16.5 Survey, and the Maine "mortgage inspection"

A **boundary survey** is a licensed surveyor's determination of where the lines are on the ground,
and it is the only thing that answers a boundary question.

A **mortgage loan inspection**, sometimes called a mortgage inspection plan, is something else
entirely: a limited drawing prepared for a lender to show, approximately, that the improvements sit
within the apparent boundaries and outside easements. It is **not a boundary survey**, it is
**usually stamped to say so**, and it does not establish a line.

chunks.heading: Hour 17 — Freehold estates and future interests
chunks.excerpt:
The distinction matters because buyers and licensees routinely treat the mortgage inspection as
though it were a survey. It is not, and a licensee who lets a buyer believe it is has caused the
problem that surfaces when the neighbour builds a garage.

When to recommend a survey: irregular parcels; older metes-and-bounds descriptions; visible fences,
walls or structures near a line; planned construction; unimproved land; waterfront; any mention of a
boundary dispute; and any right of way whose location is not obvious.

---

## Hour 17 — Freehold estates and future interests

### 17.1 Estates

An **estate** is the degree, quantity, nature and extent of a person's interest in land. The primary
division is **freehold** — of indefinite duration, involving ownership — and **leasehold** — of
fixed or determinable duration, involving possession.

### 17.2 Fee simple

**Fee simple absolute** is the largest estate: potentially infinite, freely transferable in life and
at death, subject only to the four government powers and to private restrictions the owner or a
predecessor accepted. A conveyance is presumed to convey a fee simple absolute unless the deed says
otherwise.

**Defeasible fees** may end on a stated event.

A **fee simple determinable** ends **automatically**, and the grantor keeps a **possibility of
reverter**. The language is durational — "so long as", "while", "until".

A **fee simple subject to a condition subsequent** gives the grantor a **right of re-entry** that
must be exercised. The language is conditional — "but if", "provided that", "on condition that".

Both are title matters and appear in the record. They belong to the title examiner and to counsel.

### 17.3 Life estates

chunks.heading: 17.4 The government powers
chunks.excerpt:
A **life estate** is measured by a life. The **life tenant** has full use and possession, may lease
or convey what they have, and takes the income — but may not convey more than they own and may not
commit **waste**, meaning they must not damage the property or let it deteriorate and must
ordinarily pay taxes and interest on existing debt.

When the measuring life ends: a **reversion** if the property returns to the grantor or their heirs;
a **remainder** if it passes to a named third party.

A **life estate pur autre vie** is measured by someone else's life and is the one life estate that
can be inherited — if the holder dies while the measuring life continues, the balance passes to the
holder's heirs.

Life estates are common in Maine estate planning, and their practical effect on a sale is that
**everyone with an interest must sign**: the life tenant and the remaindermen. A licensee taking a
listing from a life tenant alone has taken a listing that cannot close.

### 17.4 The government powers

Every public limitation traces to one of four — **police power** (regulation for health, safety and
welfare, without compensation: zoning, codes, shoreland regulation, subdivision control),
**eminent domain** (taking for public use with just compensation, executed by condemnation),
**taxation**, and **escheat** (property passing to the State where an owner dies with no will and no
heirs).

---

## Hour 18 — Concurrent ownership, condominium, and cooperative

### 18.1 Severalty and co-ownership

**Severalty** is ownership by one person or one entity alone.

chunks.heading: 18.2 Trusts and entities
chunks.excerpt:
**Tenancy in common** is the default when two or more take title without specifying otherwise. Each
holds an **undivided fractional interest** — undivided meaning each may possess the whole, not a
marked-off part. Shares need not be equal. There is **no survivorship**: a deceased owner's share
passes to their heirs or devisees. Any co-tenant may transfer their share, and any may seek
**partition**.

**Joint tenancy** adds the **right of survivorship**: the deceased joint tenant's interest passes to
the survivors outside probate. The common-law unities are **time, title, interest and possession**.
Survivorship must be expressed; it is not presumed. A joint tenant who conveys their interest
destroys the joint tenancy as to that share, and the transferee holds as a tenant in common.

**Maine is not a community property state.** A student who has met that term in national material
should know it does not describe Maine title. Maine's protection for a surviving spouse operates
through Title 18-C, the Probate Code, and it is a legal question — the practical brokerage
consequence is that **a spouse may have an interest that must be released at closing**, and that is
determined by the closing attorney and the title examiner, not by the licensee.

### 18.2 Trusts and entities

Property may be held by a corporation, a partnership, a limited liability company, or a **trust**.
In a trust the trustee holds legal title and the beneficiary takes the benefit, and **the trustee
signs**. Whether the signatory has authority is evidenced by organisational documents, trust
instruments and certificates, and it is verified by the closing attorney.

### 18.3 Condominium

chunks.heading: 18.4 Cooperative
chunks.excerpt:
A condominium divides a project into individually owned **units** and **common elements** owned in
undivided shares by all unit owners, with **limited common elements** — a deck, an assigned parking
space, a storage bay — serving fewer than all units. The instruments are the **declaration**, the
**bylaws**, the recorded **plats and plans**, and the **rules**.

Maine's condominium regime sits in **Title 33**, and this course states no requirement from it,
because the chapter has not been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee must do is
obtain the governing documents, the budget, the reserve position, the minutes, the assessment
history, any pending or discussed special assessment, and the association's rules on leasing, pets
and alterations — before the offer, not after.

### 18.4 Cooperative

In a cooperative a **corporation owns the real property**; the resident owns **shares** and holds a
**proprietary lease**. The resident therefore owns **personal property**, not real property. There
is no deed, financing is a share loan rather than a mortgage, and the board typically has approval
rights over a transfer — subject always to fair housing law.

### 18.5 Assessments, reserves, and the special assessment risk

Regular assessments fund the budget; **special assessments** fund what the budget did not. The
second is the largest financial risk in common-interest ownership, and it is discovered by reading
the **reserve study and two years of minutes** — where a roof, a seawall, a private road or a septic
replacement is discussed long before it is levied. In coastal and lakefront Maine, shared shoreline
structures and private road maintenance are the recurring examples.

---

## Hour 19 — Leasehold estates and leases

### 19.1 The four leasehold estates

chunks.heading: 19.2 A lease is two things at once
chunks.excerpt:
**Estate for years** — a fixed term with a definite beginning and end. It expires without notice.
The name misleads: a two-week lease is an estate for years.

**Periodic estate** — renews automatically for successive periods until one party gives notice.
Month-to-month tenancies are the common case.

**Estate at will** — possession with consent, no fixed period, terminable by either party, subject
to statutory notice.

**Estate at sufferance** — a tenant who entered lawfully and stayed past the term without consent.
It is distinguished from trespass only by the lawful entry, and removing such a tenant is a legal
process rather than a self-help matter.

### 19.2 A lease is two things at once

A lease is a **conveyance** — it transfers a leasehold estate and the right of exclusive possession
— and a **contract** — it creates mutual promises. The first explains why a tenant may exclude even
the landlord except as the lease and the law allow; the second explains how breach is analysed.

Essential terms: parties; premises; term; rent, its amount, due date and method; the security
deposit; utilities; permitted use and occupancy; maintenance on each side; the landlord's right of
entry and the notice required; rules on pets, smoking, parking and alterations; assignment and
subletting; default and remedies; renewal or termination; and required disclosures.

### 19.3 Assignment and sublease

**Assignment** transfers the tenant's **entire** remaining interest; **sublease** transfers less
than all of it, and the original tenant becomes a landlord to the subtenant while remaining a tenant
to the landlord.

In neither case is the original tenant automatically released. Release requires the landlord's
agreement, which is a **novation**.

chunks.heading: 19.4 What a sale or a foreclosure does to a lease
chunks.excerpt:
### 19.4 What a sale or a foreclosure does to a lease

**A sale does not end a lease.** The buyer takes subject to the tenancy, and the tenant's rights run
against the new owner. Security deposits and prepaid rent must be transferred and accounted for, and
this is a term of the purchase contract that must be written rather than assumed.

**Foreclosure** is more complicated: whether a lease survives depends on whether it predates the
mortgage and on the statutory protections available to residential tenants. That is a legal question
with real consequences for occupied property, and it goes to counsel — not to a licensee's
assumption.

A licensee listing occupied property must, at intake: obtain every lease; confirm the deposits held
and where; confirm rent paid through what date; and confirm whether any tenancy is oral, because an
oral tenancy is still a tenancy.

---

## Hour 20 — Maine landlord-tenant fundamentals

### 20.1 Where the law is

Maine's residential landlord-tenant law is principally in **14 M.R.S.**, and it covers security
deposits, the landlord's obligations as to fitness and habitability, access, notice and termination,
the process for recovering possession, and prohibited conduct.

**This course states no Maine security deposit maximum, no return deadline, no notice period, and no
entry notice**, because **14 M.R.S. has not been read from primary text for this project**. Those
figures are exactly the ones a course gets wrong by carrying them from another state or from an
out-of-date summary, and exactly the ones on which a landlord loses a case.

### 20.2 The method, which is the examinable skill

chunks.heading: 20.3 What is certain, whatever the figures
chunks.excerpt:
**One — classify the tenancy.** Residential or commercial? A dwelling unit, a mobile home park lot,
or a seasonal rental? Within the statute's scope or excluded?

**Two — go to the statute**, at `legislature.maine.gov`, in its current text. Read the operative
section **and the sections around it**.

**Three — read the lease**, which may give the tenant more than the statute requires but not less
where the statute sets a floor.

**Four — refer.** Whether a notice was validly given, whether a breach is material, and what remedy
is available are legal conclusions.

### 20.3 What is certain, whatever the figures

**Self-help is unlawful.** Changing locks, removing possessions, or shutting off utilities to force
a tenant out is prohibited, and a licensee who advises a landlord client to do any of it has advised
a violation — against the duty in § 13273 1 E to comply with applicable law, and against § 13273 1 D
to comply with the Commission's rules.

**Deposits are the tenant's money held in trust.** Where an agency holds them, they are trust funds
under § 13178 and the designated broker is responsible for them.

**Habitability obligations run to the condition of the premises**, and the record of what was
reported and what was done is the whole of the defence in a dispute.

**Fair housing applies to leasing exactly as it applies to sale**, and screening is where discretion
— and therefore risk — lives. Written, objective, uniform criteria applied identically to every
applicant is the only defensible practice.

### 20.4 Maine-specific practicalities

chunks.heading: Hour 21 — Private land-use controls
chunks.excerpt:
Several conditions recur in Maine tenancies and belong in a licensee's intake list: **heating fuel
responsibility** and who fills the tank; **snow removal and winter road maintenance**;
**wood and pellet stoves** and their insurance implications; **seasonal and short-term rentals**,
which many municipalities now regulate separately; **lead-based paint** in a housing stock that is
substantially pre-1978, which triggers the federal disclosure and, for rentals, federal renovation
rules; and **radon**, which Maine addresses in the rental context by statute.

Each is a question to be raised and routed, and the statutory detail must be read rather than
recalled.

---

## Hour 21 — Private land-use controls

### 21.1 Encumbrances that affect use

An **encumbrance** is a claim or right held by someone other than the owner that affects title or
limits use. Those affecting **use** are easements, restrictive covenants and encroachments; those
affecting **title as security for money** are liens, and they belong to Hour 25.

### 21.2 Easements

An **easement** is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a stated purpose, and it is an
interest in land.

An **easement appurtenant** benefits a parcel: the benefited parcel is the **dominant tenement**, the
burdened one the **servient tenement**, and it **runs with the land** — it passes automatically to
the next owner. Shared driveways, access to a back lot, and drainage are the everyday cases.

An **easement in gross** benefits a person or entity rather than a parcel. Utility easements are the
common example.

chunks.heading: 21.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall
chunks.excerpt:
**Creation:** by express grant or reservation in a deed; by **implication**, where a use was
apparent, continuous and necessary when a parcel was divided; by **necessity**, the landlocked-parcel
case, requiring common ownership at severance; by **prescription**, from open, notorious, continuous
and adverse use for the statutory period; and by **condemnation**.

**Termination:** by merger, release, abandonment shown by conduct rather than mere non-use, the end
of the necessity, or the easement's own terms.

**This course states no Maine prescriptive period and no adverse possession period**, because those
provisions of **14 M.R.S.** have not been read from primary text for this project. They are legal
determinations in any event.

Maine adds two access questions that arise constantly: **rights of way to water**, which may be
deeded, prescriptive, or merely tolerated; and **private roads**, where the existence, terms and
enforceability of a **road maintenance agreement** decide whether a buyer can reach their house in
February. Both are title and legal questions and both must be answered in writing before closing.

### 21.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall

A **licence** is revocable personal permission and is not an interest in land — the neighbour who
has "always" crossed the corner usually has one, unless the use has ripened into a prescriptive
easement, which is a legal determination on facts nobody in the conversation has established.

An **encroachment** is an unauthorised physical intrusion across a line. It is found by **survey**,
not by looking, and long-standing encroachments can mature into rights.

A **party wall** is a shared wall on a boundary, each owner typically owning to the centre with an
easement of support in the other half.

chunks.heading: 21.4 Restrictive covenants and associations
chunks.excerpt:
### 21.4 Restrictive covenants and associations

**Restrictive covenants** are private limits on use, recorded so they bind successors. They regulate
setbacks, minimum sizes, materials, outbuildings, signage, tree cutting, and short-term rental.

Three points:

**They can be stricter than zoning**, and where zoning permits and a covenant forbids, the owner is
bound by both and must satisfy the stricter.

**They are enforced privately** — by an association or a neighbour — not by the municipality.

**Discriminatory covenants are void and must not be honoured.** Historic racial covenants remain
physically present in Maine chains of title. They are unenforceable, and repeating them as though
they operated is itself a fair housing problem — Hour 51 returns to it.

Associations — condominium associations, road associations, lake associations, homeowners
associations — hold the enforcement power and the assessment power. A buyer needs the documents, the
budget, the reserve position, the minutes, and the assessment history.

---

## Hour 22 — Public land-use control: zoning, permits, and codes

### 22.1 The structure

Maine delegates land-use regulation to **municipalities** under **30-A M.R.S.**, and municipal
practice varies widely. In the **unorganised territory** the **Land Use Planning Commission** stands
in the municipality's place. Hour 23 takes the Maine statutes in detail; this hour builds the
national framework the Maine provisions attach to.

chunks.heading: 22.2 The relief mechanisms, distinguished
chunks.excerpt:
A **comprehensive plan** is the municipality's long-range policy statement. **Zoning** is the
ordinance that implements it and has legal force, dividing the municipality into districts and
prescribing for each the permitted **uses** and the **bulk** controls — minimum lot size, frontage,
setbacks, height, lot coverage, and often signage and parking.

### 22.2 The relief mechanisms, distinguished

A **variance** relieves a **dimensional** requirement where strict application causes an undue
hardship arising from the property itself — shape, topography, soils. It is granted by the board of
appeals. **A variance does not authorise a use the district forbids**, and self-created hardship and
mere financial disadvantage are not grounds. Maine's undue-hardship standard is set by statute and
is applied strictly; it is a legal question and this course states no element of it.

A **conditional use permit** or **special exception** authorises a use the ordinance lists as
permissible **subject to review and conditions**. It is the ordinance operating as written, not an
exception to it.

A **nonconforming use** or **nonconforming structure** was lawful when established and became
non-compliant on a later ordinance change. It may generally continue, typically may not be expanded,
and may be lost on abandonment or destruction.

**In Maine the nonconforming-structure question is unusually important**, because a very large part
of the shorefront housing stock is nonconforming as to setback from the water. What may be done to
such a structure — expanded, replaced, moved, rebuilt after fire — is governed by the municipality's
shoreland zoning ordinance and by state minimum standards, and the answer differs between
municipalities.

chunks.heading: 22.3 Permits and codes
chunks.excerpt:
A **rezoning** is an amendment to the ordinance itself and is a legislative act of the municipal
legislative body.

### 22.3 Permits and codes

Construction is governed by building and life-safety codes and administered by the **code
enforcement officer**. Maine's statewide code, the **Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code**,
applies as adopted, and its applicability varies with municipal size and adoption — a fact that
surprises people who assume a single statewide rule. **Plumbing and subsurface wastewater** are
permitted through the local plumbing inspector, and **septic system design** is done by a licensed
site evaluator.

The **certificate of occupancy**, where the municipality issues one, is the document saying the
building may lawfully be occupied.

### 22.4 The licensee's boundary

Every question in this hour is answered by a public official and recorded in a public office. The
licensee's job is to know that the question exists, to know **who** answers it — the code
enforcement officer, the planning board, the assessor, the plumbing inspector, the Department of
Environmental Protection, the Land Use Planning Commission, the Department of Transportation — and
to send the client there **in writing**.

Under **§ 13273 1 B (4)** the seller agent must **advise the client to obtain expert advice on
material matters beyond the agent's expertise**, and under **§ 13283 3 A and B** a transaction broker
may not conduct an investigation or analysis for a party's benefit, nor verify the accuracy or
completeness of statements made by anyone. Both point the same way: raise the question, name the
office, and put it in writing.

### Module 03 engagement check

chunks.heading: Module 03 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**Question.** A buyer is under contract on a lakefront camp built in 1962, twenty feet from the
water. They tell you they intend to demolish it and build a larger year-round house on the same
footprint, and ask whether that will be "fine since it's already there". They also mention that the
neighbour's driveway crosses the corner of the lot and that a mortgage inspection plan from the
seller's refinance "shows everything is okay". Respond.

**Expected answer.** Neither question is mine to answer, and both must be routed in writing.

**The structure is almost certainly a nonconforming structure** as to shoreland setback. What may be
done to it — expanded, replaced, demolished and rebuilt, moved — is governed by the municipality's
**shoreland zoning ordinance** and state minimum standards, differs between municipalities, and is
answered by the **code enforcement officer in writing** before the contingency period ends. "It's
already there" is not an answer, and a demolition frequently ends the nonconforming status the buyer
is relying on. A larger year-round house also raises **subsurface wastewater** capacity, which the
local plumbing inspector and a licensed site evaluator answer.

**The driveway is a boundary and title question.** It may be a recorded easement appurtenant running
with the land, a prescriptive easement, a revocable licence, or an encroachment — and which it is
decides whether the buyer can stop it. That is for the title examiner, a surveyor, and counsel.

**The mortgage inspection plan is not a survey.** It is a limited drawing prepared for a lender, it
is usually stamped to say it may not be used to establish boundaries, and it does not answer the
driveway question. I would recommend a **boundary survey** and confirm that recommendation in
writing.

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — product knowledge developed
chunks.excerpt:
Under **§ 13273 1 B (4)** — if the buyer is my client — I am required to advise them to obtain expert
advice on material matters beyond my expertise; as a **transaction broker** under § 13283 3 I am
barred from conducting the investigation or verifying anyone's statements. Either way the answer is
the same: name the offices, get it in writing, and do not opine.

## Extended treatment — product knowledge developed

### E3.1 Estates and interests, in one table

| Interest | Duration | Holder's power | What the grantor keeps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fee simple absolute | Potentially infinite | Full, subject to PETE and private restrictions | Nothing |
| Fee simple determinable | Until the stated event, **automatically** | Full while it lasts | **Possibility of reverter** |
| Fee simple subject to condition subsequent | Until the grantor **acts** on the condition | Full until re-entry | **Right of re-entry** |
| Life estate | The measuring life | Use, possession, income; **no waste**; cannot convey more than held | **Reversion** (or a third party holds a **remainder**) |
| Life estate pur autre vie | Another's life | Same, and **inheritable** while the measuring life continues | Same |
| Estate for years | Fixed term | Exclusive possession | Reversion |
| Periodic estate | Renews until notice | Exclusive possession | Reversion |
| Estate at will | No fixed period | Exclusive possession | Reversion |
| Estate at sufferance | None — holdover | Bare possession | Right to recover possession |

### E3.2 Co-ownership consequences, worked

*Three siblings inherit a camp. The deed says "to A, B and C".*

chunks.heading: E3.3 Leases: the terms that actually get argued about
chunks.excerpt:
No survivorship language, so they hold as **tenants in common** in equal undivided thirds. Each may
possess the whole. Each may sell or mortgage their third without the others' consent — and a
purchaser of one third becomes a co-tenant with the other two, which is how camps end up owned by
strangers. On a sibling's death, that third passes under their will or by intestate succession rather
than to the survivors. Any of them may seek **partition**, and where physical division is impractical
— which it is for a camp — partition means a court-ordered **sale**.

*The same deed reading "to A, B and C as joint tenants with right of survivorship".*

Survivorship operates: on a death the interest passes to the survivors outside probate. But if A
conveys their interest to X, the joint tenancy is severed as to that third: X holds a third as a
**tenant in common**, while B and C remain joint tenants as between themselves.

**The listing consequence.** A licensee taking a listing on inherited or jointly held Maine property
must establish, at intake, **exactly who is on title, in what form, and who must sign to convey**.
Life estates with remaindermen, tenancies in common among a dispersed family, and unprobated estates
are all common in Maine, and each is discovered at listing or at closing — and closing is expensive.

### E3.3 Leases: the terms that actually get argued about

**Rent and escalation** — the amount, the due date, the grace period if any, the late fee, and any
increase mechanism.

**Utilities** — and in Maine specifically **heating fuel**: who fills the tank, at what level it is
delivered and returned, and who pays for the fuel in it at the start and end of the term.

chunks.heading: E3.4 Private land-use control, worked into a Maine transaction
chunks.excerpt:
**Snow removal and maintenance** — allocated expressly, because "reasonable" means different things
in December.

**Access** — the landlord's right of entry and the notice required, which is statutory and must be
read from **14 M.R.S.** rather than assumed.

**Alterations**, including satellite dishes, garden beds, and — increasingly — vehicle charging.

**Pets**, and the separate question of **assistance animals**, which are not pets and which Module 09
covers.

**Subletting and assignment**, usually restricted, and the rule from Hour 19.3 that consent is not a
release.

**Use and occupancy limits**, and any **short-term rental** prohibition, which matters in Maine
tourist markets and which many municipalities now regulate separately.

**Termination and holdover**, and what happens to a security deposit.

### E3.4 Private land-use control, worked into a Maine transaction

*A buyer is under contract on a lot in a 1978 subdivision. The recorded declaration restricts
buildings to a single family dwelling of at least 1,200 square feet, prohibits mobile homes, requires
approval of plans by an architectural committee that has not met since 2004, and grants each lot
owner a right of way over "the roadway as shown on the plan".*

The questions this raises, and where each goes:

**Does the declaration still bind?** Recorded covenants generally run with the land, and Maine's
**Marketable Title Act** in 33 M.R.S. can extinguish certain ancient interests after a statutory
period — which this course does not state and which is a legal question for counsel.

chunks.heading: E3.5 Public land-use control: the questions a Maine licensee asks first
chunks.excerpt:
**Who enforces it?** Privately — by a lot owner or an association. Not the municipality. An
architectural committee that has not met may be defunct, dormant, or revivable, and which of those it
is decides whether the buyer's plans need approval.

**Is the roadway a right of way, a private way, or a town way?** Registry of Deeds for the recorded
plan and any maintenance agreement; the municipal road commissioner for the road's status; and
counsel for what the grant actually conveys. Whether the road is **plowed** is a separate and equally
important question.

**Does the covenant conflict with zoning?** If zoning permits an accessory dwelling and the covenant
forbids one, the owner is bound by both and must satisfy the stricter.

**Is there anything in the declaration that is void?** Any discriminatory covenant is unenforceable
and must not be honoured.

### E3.5 Public land-use control: the questions a Maine licensee asks first

For any Maine property, before marketing:

chunks.heading: E3.6 Zoning relief compared
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Is the property in an organised municipality or in LUPC jurisdiction?**
2. **Does the municipality have zoning at all?** Several do not, and that is a fact a buyer needs.
3. **What district is it in, and what are the dimensional requirements?** Code enforcement officer.
4. **Is any part of it in the shoreland zone?** If so, which sub-district?
5. **Is any structure nonconforming?** As to what — setback, height, lot coverage, lot size?
6. **Are there open permits or violations?**
7. **Was every structure permitted?** An unpermitted addition is a title, insurance and financing
   problem as well as a code one.
8. **Is there a subsurface wastewater permit on file, and for how many bedrooms?**
9. **Is the lot a lawfully created lot?** Subdivision status, and whether the plan is recorded.
10. **Is the access a public way, a private way, or a discontinued way?**

Ten questions, ten offices, and none of them answered by the licensee. A licensee who has this list
and uses it is doing the job; one who improvises answers is creating liability.

### E3.6 Zoning relief compared

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
| | Variance | Conditional use permit | Nonconforming use | Rezoning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relieves | A **dimensional** requirement | Nothing — it is the ordinance operating | Nothing — it predates the change | The ordinance itself |
| Granted by | Board of appeals | Planning board or board of appeals | No one; it exists | Municipal legislative body |
| Requires | **Undue hardship** arising from the property | Satisfying stated criteria and conditions | Lawful establishment before the change | A legislative decision |
| Does **not** authorise | **A prohibited use** | An unlisted use | Expansion, generally | — |
| Lost by | — | Breach of conditions | **Abandonment or destruction**, often | Amendment |

Maine's undue-hardship standard is statutory and is applied strictly; this course states no element
of it, and the board of appeals and counsel answer it.

requirements of **Title 33** governing condominiums; the elements of Maine's **undue hardship**
variance standard; and the applicability rules of the **Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code**.
Hour 20.1 and Hour 21.2 each say so in terms, and Hour 20.2 teaches the navigation instead of a
number — its engagement value is the method, not a figure to memorise.

**Maine-specific practice content** — mortgage inspection plans, leased propane tanks, private road
maintenance agreements, shoreland nonconforming structures, rights of way to water, and the
unorganised territory's township-and-range convention — is stated as practice, not as a statement of
any statute or ordinance, and each is routed to the office that answers it.

**Municipal variation is stated as variation.** Maine land-use regulation is delegated to
municipalities under 30-A M.R.S. and administered by the Land Use Planning Commission in the
unorganised territory; the hour gives the general structure and directs every specific question to
the municipality.

lessons.title: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 04

chunks.heading: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
# Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 04

## Hours 23–29 · Product knowledge II: Maine land use, environment, transfer, and construction

**Commission topic covered:** Product Knowledge (28%, 840 instructional minutes) — this module
carries the remaining 405, and includes Case Study 1.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Maine sales agent credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Name the Maine land-use regimes a property may sit under and say which office administers each.
- Identify the environmental conditions a Maine transaction commonly raises and route each.
- Explain Maine's current-use tax classifications and the withdrawal risk they carry.
- Distinguish voluntary from involuntary transfer and read a chain of title for gaps and clouds.
- Name the information source that answers each Maine due-diligence question.
- Describe residential construction well enough to report a condition accurately without diagnosing
  it.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 23 — Maine land-use statutes
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Minutes | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 23 | 0–60 | Maine land-use statutes: subdivision, shoreland, LUPC, minimum lot size | Section completed |
| 24 | 0–60 | Environmental issues in Maine transactions | Section completed |
| 25 | 0–60 | Taxation, exemptions, current use; voluntary and involuntary transfer | Section completed |
| 26 | 0–60 | Recording, deeds, covenants, and title defects | Section completed |
| 27 | 0–60 | Registry, municipal, DEP/LUPC/DOT and service-provider sources | Section completed |
| 28 | 0–60 | House styles, construction components, condition vocabulary | Section completed |
| 29 | 0–45 | Case Study 1 — rural and waterfront property investigation and disclosure | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **405** | | Hour 29, minutes 45–60, begins Module 05 |

---

## Hour 23 — Maine land-use statutes

### 23.1 Who regulates what

**Organised municipalities** regulate land use under authority delegated by **30-A M.R.S.**, through
a comprehensive plan, a zoning ordinance, a subdivision ordinance, a shoreland zoning ordinance, and
building and plumbing administration. Practice varies substantially between municipalities, and
several Maine towns have no zoning at all — which is itself a fact a buyer needs to know.

The **Land Use Planning Commission** is the planning and zoning authority for Maine's **unorganised
and deorganised areas**, plantations, and townships — roughly half the state's land area. Where the
LUPC has jurisdiction, it performs the functions a municipality would.

The **Department of Environmental Protection** administers the state environmental permitting
regimes that sit above municipal control.

### 23.2 Subdivision

Maine regulates subdivision at two levels.

chunks.heading: 23.3 Shoreland zoning
chunks.excerpt:
**Municipal subdivision review** under 30-A M.R.S. applies where land is divided into the statutory
number of lots within a defined period. The review runs through the planning board against criteria
in the statute and the local ordinance, and it ends in a **recorded plan**.

**State-level review** applies to larger developments through the DEP's site location of development
programme and the stormwater and natural resources protection permitting regimes.

**This course states no lot count, no acreage threshold, and no time period**, because the
subdivision provisions of **30-A M.R.S.** and the DEP's thresholds have not been read from primary
text for this project. The reason to be careful here is specific: **an unlawful subdivision is a
title and marketability problem**, and a licensee who tells a seller that dividing a lot "should be
fine" has stated a conclusion with real consequences.

The one rule that carries: **a lot does not exist until a plan creating it is recorded**, and where
subdivision review applies, it must have been completed first.

### 23.3 Shoreland zoning
