Maine requires municipalities to adopt **shoreland zoning** meeting state minimum guidelines, and
the LUPC administers equivalent standards in its jurisdiction. Shoreland zoning applies within a
defined distance of the normal high-water line of great ponds, rivers, and coastal wetlands, and
within a distance of the upland edge of freshwater wetlands.

What it controls, in outline: **setbacks** from the water; **lot size and frontage**; **vegetative
buffers and tree cutting**, which is the provision owners breach most often and least knowingly;
**expansion, replacement and relocation of nonconforming structures**; **new construction and land
disturbance**; and **subsurface wastewater**.

chunks.heading: 23.4 Minimum lot size and wastewater
chunks.excerpt:
The practical consequences for brokerage are large. A very substantial part of Maine's waterfront
housing stock is **nonconforming** as to setback. Whether such a structure may be expanded, replaced
after a fire, or demolished and rebuilt is answered by the municipality's ordinance and the state
minimum standards — and the answer differs between municipalities. **Clearing a view** frequently
requires a permit and can produce enforcement and civil penalties. And a buyer's plan for a
property, if it depends on any of this, must be confirmed **in writing with the code enforcement
officer** before the contingency period ends.

**This course states no setback distance, no shoreland zone width, and no buffer standard.** Those
are in the state minimum guidelines and in each municipality's ordinance, neither of which has been
read from primary text for this project.

### 23.4 Minimum lot size and wastewater

Minimum lot size in Maine is driven as much by **subsurface wastewater disposal** as by zoning. A
lot must have soils capable of supporting a septic system sized to the proposed use, established by
a **site evaluation** performed by a licensed site evaluator and permitted through the local
plumbing inspector. A physically attractive lot with unsuitable soils is not a buildable lot.

Where public sewer is available, the question becomes capacity and connection permission — and
"available" is not the same as "permitted".

### 23.5 Other regimes a property may sit under

chunks.heading: Hour 24 — Environmental issues in Maine transactions
chunks.excerpt:
**Natural resources protection** for work in, on or adjacent to protected natural resources.
**Stormwater** permitting for disturbed area above thresholds. **Erosion control**. **Flood hazard**
regulation through municipal ordinances tied to the federal mapping. **Historic district** review
where adopted. **Right-to-farm** and forestry provisions that limit nuisance claims against existing
agricultural and forestry operations. And **road access**, where a driveway or entrance onto a state
or state-aid highway needs a **Department of Transportation entrance permit**.

Each is named here so a licensee recognises the question. None is answered here.

---

## Hour 24 — Environmental issues in Maine transactions

### 24.1 Lead-based paint

Federal law applies in Maine and is not optional. For **target housing** — most residential housing
built **before 1978** — a seller or landlord must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards,
provide available records and reports, give the EPA-approved pamphlet, include the prescribed
warning and acknowledgments in the contract or lease, and, **for sales, give the purchaser a
ten-day opportunity to conduct a risk assessment or inspection** unless the parties agree in writing
to a different period.

**Maine's housing stock is substantially pre-1978**, so this is a routine requirement rather than an
occasional one. **33 M.R.S. § 173(4)(B)** also brings lead-based paint for pre-1978 homes into the
Maine property disclosure statement expressly.

chunks.heading: 24.2 Radon
chunks.excerpt:
Maine additionally regulates lead in rental housing and in renovation work, and the federal
Renovation, Repair and Painting rule requires certified firms for disturbing painted surfaces in
target housing. A licensee's role is to ensure the sale-side requirements are met and the
acknowledgment retained, and to route the rest.

### 24.2 Radon

Radon is common in Maine soils and Maine well water, and it appears in the **§ 173(4)(C)** disclosure
list. It is measured by testing, and mitigation is a defined trade. Maine has legislated on radon in
rental housing; that provision has not been read from primary text for this project and no
requirement from it is stated here.

For a buyer the professional advice is straightforward: **test, in both air and — on a private well —
water**, within the inspection period.

### 24.3 Arsenic and other private-well contaminants

Naturally occurring **arsenic** in bedrock is a well-documented Maine groundwater issue, alongside
**uranium**, **radon in water**, **manganese**, **fluoride**, **nitrates**, and **bacteria**. Water
from a private well is not tested by any public authority; it is tested because someone paid for it.

**§ 173(1)** requires the seller to disclose, for a private supply, the type, location, any
malfunctions, **the date of the most recent water test**, and **whether the seller has experienced a
problem such as an unsatisfactory water test or a test with notations.** A blank in that field is
information, and it is a question for the buyer's investigation rather than an answer.

### 24.4 Subsurface wastewater and shoreland septic

chunks.heading: 24.5 Heating oil and underground tanks
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 173(3)** requires detailed septic disclosure — type, tank size and type and location,
malfunctions, installation dates for tank and leach field, most recent servicing and the contractor —
and, **for systems within shoreland zones, the disclosures required by 30-A M.R.S. § 4216.**

The recurring problems: systems older than their design life; systems whose permits cannot be found;
systems sized for a two-bedroom camp being bought by a family who intend four bedrooms; and
**cesspools and other non-conforming systems**, which frequently cannot be replaced in the same
location under current setbacks.

### 24.5 Heating oil and underground tanks

**§ 173(4)(D)** brings **underground oil storage tanks as required under 38 M.R.S. § 563(6)** into
the disclosure statement.

Buried tanks are a Maine legacy issue. An abandoned tank that was never properly removed or closed
is an environmental liability that attaches to the property, and above-ground tanks have their own
age, condition, and insurance consequences. **The heating disclosure under § 173(2-A)** — type, age,
servicing company, most recent service call, **annual fuel consumption**, malfunctions within two
years, and **most recent chimney and vent inspection** — is one of the most informative sections of
the whole statement, and annual fuel consumption is the line a buyer should read first.

### 24.6 Asbestos, mould, PFAS, and wetlands

**Asbestos** — § 173(4)(A) — in insulation, flooring, siding and pipe wrap in older housing.

**Mould** — a condition question, assessed by a qualified assessor. A licensee never characterises a
stain.

chunks.heading: 24.7 The rule that governs all of it
chunks.excerpt:
**PFAS** — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances have become a significant Maine issue, particularly
where **licensed sludge or septage was historically spread on farmland**. The State has an
investigation and testing programme, and affected properties may have well contamination and
restrictions on agricultural use. This is a live and developing area, it is a question for the
Maine Department of Environmental Protection and the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and
Forestry, and **a licensee must not characterise a property's PFAS status**. Where a property has
been farmed, or is near land that has been, the question belongs in the buyer's investigation list.

**Wetlands and flood plains** — presence, mapping, and the permitting consequences of any proposed
work. Both are answered by mapping, by the DEP or LUPC, and by the municipality.

### 24.7 The rule that governs all of it

The licensee is not the person who determines an environmental condition. The licensee is the person
who **knows the question exists, discloses what is actually known, and routes the question to the
person who answers it** — under § 13273 1 B (4) for a client, and within the § 13283 3 prohibitions
for a transaction broker.

---

## Hour 25 — Taxation, exemptions, current use, and transfer

### 25.1 Property tax

Maine property tax is levied by the **municipality** on assessed value, at a rate set annually. It
is administered by the municipal **assessor**, and Maine Revenue Services administers the
unorganised territory and the state-level programmes.

chunks.heading: 25.2 Exemptions
chunks.excerpt:
**Assessed value is not market value**, and a licensee must never present it as evidence of value.
Maine assessors work to a **certified ratio**, and the relationship between assessment and market is
itself a stated figure in the municipality's commitment.

### 25.2 Exemptions

Maine's exemption programmes — the **homestead exemption**, the **veteran exemption**, the
**blind exemption**, and the property tax relief programmes the Legislature adjusts periodically —
are applied for by the owner and are administered by the assessor.

**This course states no exemption amount and no eligibility rule.** Both change, they are set in
**36 M.R.S.**, and the applicant's own circumstances decide. A licensee tells a client the programmes
exist and directs them to the assessor and to Maine Revenue Services.

### 25.3 Current-use classification — the Maine trap

Maine's current-use programmes — **Tree Growth**, **Farmland**, **Open Space**, and **Working
Waterfront** — value enrolled land at its current use rather than its market value, which
substantially reduces the tax.

The consequence a buyer must understand before closing: **withdrawal from the programme triggers a
penalty**, and for Tree Growth in particular that penalty can be very large. Whether the buyer
intends to continue the classification, whether the land qualifies under their intended use, and who
bears any withdrawal penalty are **contract terms**, not afterthoughts.

chunks.heading: 25.4 Transfer tax and liens
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no penalty formula and no eligibility acreage.** They are in **36 M.R.S.** and
have not been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee must do is: identify from the
assessor's records whether the land is enrolled; disclose it; and get the buyer to the assessor,
Maine Revenue Services, a forester where Tree Growth is involved, and counsel — in writing, before
the contingency period ends.

### 25.4 Transfer tax and liens

Maine imposes a **real estate transfer tax** on conveyances, collected at the Registry of Deeds on a
declaration of value, and conventionally shared between the parties. **This course states no rate**;
it is in 36 M.R.S. and the closing agent computes it.

**Property tax liens** attach for unpaid taxes and are enforced by the municipality through a
statutory lien and foreclosure process on its own timetable. Unpaid taxes are discovered from the
assessor and the tax collector, and they are paid at closing.

**Other liens** — mortgages, judgment liens, mechanics' liens for labour and materials, state tax
liens, and municipal sewer and water liens — are found by the title examination and cleared at
closing.

### 25.5 Voluntary and involuntary transfer

**Voluntary:** by **deed**, in life; by **will**, at death, to a devisee; by **gift**.

**Involuntary:** by **intestate succession** under Title 18-C where there is no will; by
**foreclosure**; by **tax lien foreclosure**; by **eminent domain**; by **adverse possession**; by
**escheat**; and by **partition**.

chunks.heading: Hour 26 — Recording, deeds, covenants, and title defects
chunks.excerpt:
Each appears in a chain of title as something other than an ordinary deed, and each carries its own
questions about authority — did the personal representative have power to sell, was the foreclosure
completed properly, was the tax lien matured. Those are the title examiner's and counsel's
questions, and they are why a Maine closing runs through an attorney.

---

## Hour 26 — Recording, deeds, covenants, and title defects

### 26.1 The Registry of Deeds

Maine records land instruments in the **county Registry of Deeds**. Recording gives **constructive
notice to the world**, which is what allows a stranger to a transaction to discover what interests
exist in a parcel without asking anyone.

**Recording does not transfer title.** Title passes on **delivery and acceptance** of the deed.
Recording protects the grantee against later claims, which is why it is done immediately.

### 26.2 The deed

A valid deed requires a **competent grantor**; an **identifiable grantee**; a recital of
**consideration**; **words of conveyance**; an adequate **legal description**; the **grantor's
signature**; and **delivery and acceptance**. **Acknowledgment** before a notary or other authorised
officer is what makes it recordable.

**The grantee does not sign a deed.**

Maine deed types by what the grantor promises:

**Warranty deed** — warrants title against all defects, whenever arising. The norm in Maine
residential resale.

**Quitclaim deed with covenant** — a Maine form that warrants against defects arising **during the
grantor's ownership**, and which functions as a limited or special warranty deed. **This is a Maine
usage that misleads people from other states**, where "quitclaim" means no warranty at all.

chunks.heading: 26.3 Chain of title, gaps, clouds
chunks.excerpt:
**Release deed**, sometimes called a quitclaim without covenant — conveys whatever the grantor has
and warrants nothing. A curative instrument.

**Fiduciary deeds** — personal representative's, trustee's, guardian's, and deeds from a
municipality after tax foreclosure — each carrying the authority under which the signer acts.

**In Maine the deed is prepared by an attorney.** Selecting between deed forms is legal advice, and a
licensee asked "which deed?" has one correct answer: your attorney or the closing agent, and here is
how to reach them.

### 26.3 Chain of title, gaps, clouds

A **chain of title** is the succession of recorded owners. A searcher works backward from the current
owner and then forward again, checking each ownership period for liens and adverse instruments.

A **gap** is a break — a conveyance out from someone who never appears as a grantee, often an
unrecorded deed, an unrecorded probate, or a name change. A **cloud** is a recorded instrument or
claim casting doubt without necessarily defeating title.

**Marketable title** is title a reasonable, well-informed purchaser would accept — not perfect title,
but title free from reasonable doubt and the threat of litigation.

Maine has a **Marketable Title Act** in **33 M.R.S.** which extinguishes certain ancient interests
after a statutory period. **This course states no period from it**, because it has not been read from
primary text for this project.

### 26.4 Title insurance

Title insurance is **backward-looking indemnity** against defects existing at the policy date and not
excepted. One premium, paid at closing.

chunks.heading: 26.5 Covenants in the record
chunks.excerpt:
An **owner's policy** insures the buyer for the purchase price; a **lender's policy** insures the
lender for the loan amount, declining as it is repaid. **A lender's policy does not protect the
buyer**, and a buyer who pays for one and declines the other has bought protection for someone else.

A **commitment** carries **Schedule A** facts, **Schedule B-I requirements** — actions that must be
completed before the policy issues — and **Schedule B-II exceptions** — risks the insurer declines,
commonly including rights of parties in possession and **matters an accurate survey would show**.
**Exclusions** are printed categories, including zoning and eminent domain.

**Title insurance covers no physical condition of the property.** Buyers conflate the two constantly.

### 26.5 Covenants in the record

Restrictive covenants, easements, and reservations discovered in the chain bind successors whether
or not anyone mentioned them at the showing. Maine specifics that recur: **rights of way to water**;
**private road maintenance obligations**; **timber and mineral reservations**; **conservation
easements**, which are common in Maine and permanently limit development; and **historic
discriminatory covenants**, which are void, must not be honoured, and must not be repeated as though
they operated.

---

## Hour 27 — Where the answers live

### 27.1 The Registry of Deeds

Deeds, mortgages and discharges, easements, restrictive covenants, recorded plans, foreclosure
documents, and lis pendens. Indexed by grantor and grantee. This is where **what is recorded** is
found — and only that.

### 27.2 The municipal office

chunks.heading: 27.3 State agencies
chunks.excerpt:
**Code enforcement officer** — zoning district and requirements, permits issued, shoreland status,
nonconforming status, open violations, and the certificate of occupancy where one issues. The single
most useful office in a Maine transaction.

**Assessor** — assessed value, the certified ratio, tax status, acreage and mapping, exemptions, and
**current-use classification** including Tree Growth, Farmland and Open Space.

**Tax collector** — what is owed and whether any lien has matured.

**Plumbing inspector** — subsurface wastewater permits, the septic design on file, and internal
plumbing permits.

**Town clerk and planning board** — ordinances, comprehensive plan, subdivision approvals, board of
appeals decisions, and minutes.

**Road commissioner or public works** — whether a road is public, private, or a discontinued way, and
whether it is plowed in winter. This question decides more Maine purchases than people expect.

### 27.3 State agencies

**Department of Environmental Protection** — natural resources protection, stormwater, site location
of development, PFAS programmes, underground tanks, and shoreland guidance.

**Land Use Planning Commission** — the planning and zoning authority in the unorganised territory.

**Department of Transportation** — entrance permits and road status on state and state-aid highways.

**Maine Revenue Services** — transfer tax, current-use programmes, and the unorganised territory.

**Department of Health and Human Services** — drinking water programmes and testing guidance.

### 27.4 Service providers and private records

chunks.heading: 27.5 What the licensee does with all of it
chunks.excerpt:
Well drillers for well logs and yield; septic contractors for pumping and service history; fuel
dealers for delivery history, which corroborates the § 173(2-A) annual consumption figure; chimney
sweeps for inspection records; and utilities for availability and capacity.

### 27.5 What the licensee does with all of it

Not answer. **Route, and record the routing.** A licensee's investigation prompt list for a Maine
property should name, for each question, the office that answers it and the document that records
the answer. A buyer who is handed that list, in writing, has been served properly whether the
licensee is their agent or a transaction broker.

---

## Hour 28 — Construction, condition, and the vocabulary to describe it

### 28.1 Why the vocabulary matters

Not to inspect. To **describe accurately, recognise a question, and route it**. A licensee who calls
a truss a rafter, a service panel a meter, or a leach field a septic tank will be misunderstood by
the professionals they are trying to involve.

### 28.2 Maine house types

Older Maine housing has recognisable forms: the **Cape**; the **Colonial** and its saltbox and
gambrel variants; the **New Englander** or upright-and-wing; the **connected farmstead** — the
"big house, little house, back house, barn" arrangement, which raises specific fire-separation and
insurance questions; the **camp**, often seasonal, uninsulated, and on posts or piers rather than a
foundation; the **ranch** and **raised ranch**; and the **contemporary** and **post-and-beam** forms.

The seasonal camp is the type most often misdescribed. **A camp is not automatically a year-round
dwelling**, and converting one raises foundation, insulation, water supply, wastewater, access and
code questions all at once.

### 28.3 Components

chunks.heading: 28.4 Condition vocabulary, and the boundary
chunks.excerpt:
**Site** — grading and drainage away from the structure, the driveway, and utility connections. Poor
site drainage is behind a large share of residential water problems.

**Foundation** — full basement, crawl space, slab, or posts and piers; footings below the local
**frost depth**, which in Maine is deep; foundation material, which in older housing is frequently
fieldstone or brick rather than poured concrete; damp-proofing and perimeter drainage.

**Framing** — sills, which in older Maine housing are the component most often rotted at the
foundation line; floor joists; stud walls; headers; and roof **rafters** or engineered **trusses**,
which must never be cut or modified.

**Envelope** — sheathing, weather barrier, **flashing** at every penetration and intersection,
cladding, windows and doors, roof covering and underlayment, and **ice-and-water membrane at the
eaves**, which matters in a climate that produces ice dams. Flashing is where roofs and walls
actually leak, and it is invisible from the ground.

**Insulation and ventilation** — R-values, air sealing, attic and crawl-space ventilation, and vapour
control appropriate to a cold climate.

**Systems** — electrical service and panel, branch circuits, grounding, and ground-fault and
arc-fault protection; plumbing supply material, drain-waste-vent, water heater with its relief valve
and discharge, and shutoffs; heating, including oil, propane, natural gas where available, wood,
pellet and heat pumps, with the flue or venting and the age of each component; and the ventilation
terminations, which must exit the building rather than the attic.

### 28.4 Condition vocabulary, and the boundary

chunks.heading: Hour 29 (0–45) — Case Study 1: rural and waterfront property investigation
chunks.excerpt:
**Physical deterioration** is wear and age. **Functional obsolescence** is a defect in the design or
utility of the improvement — one bathroom for four bedrooms, a bedroom reachable only through
another. **External obsolescence** is loss caused by something outside the property and is always
incurable from inside the boundary.

The licensee's sentence, in every case: *I can see it, I have written it down, and here is who can
tell you what it is.* "It's just settling", "that stain is old", and "the system has plenty of life
left" are opinions outside the licence, they are frequently wrong, and a wrong one is a
misrepresentation.

---

## Hour 29 (0–45) — Case Study 1: rural and waterfront property investigation

### 29.1 The facts

*A 1958 camp on 3.2 acres with 210 feet of frontage on a great pond, reached by a private gravel
road shared with four other camps. The seller has owned it since 1994. The listing says "year-round
potential". The property has a dug well and a septic system the seller believes was installed "in
the eighties". The land is enrolled in Tree Growth. The seller's disclosure statement leaves the
water test date blank and states the heating source as a propane wall furnace, age unknown, with an
annual consumption figure of 210 gallons. There is a small bunkhouse near the water. The neighbour's
boat is stored on the corner of the lot each winter.*

### 29.2 The deliverable

The student produces, for a buyer, an investigation prompt list. Each line must name **the question,
the office or professional who answers it, and the document that would record the answer** — and the
student must separately identify **what the licensee must disclose**, and under which section,
depending on whether the licensee is a seller agent or a transaction broker.

chunks.heading: 29.3 The lines the case is designed to produce
chunks.excerpt:
### 29.3 The lines the case is designed to produce

**"Year-round potential"** is a marketing claim about a 1958 camp, and it is the most dangerous
sentence in the listing. Year-round use raises **insulation, foundation and frost depth, water supply
in winter, wastewater capacity, road maintenance and plowing, and code** — every one of which is
answered by someone other than the licensee. A licensee who wrote that line must be able to say what
it was based on.

**The private road.** Public, private, or a discontinued way? Is there a recorded **road maintenance
agreement**, and does it bind successors? Who plows, and who pays? Registry of Deeds and the
municipal road commissioner.

**The dug well.** Dug wells are shallow and are the most vulnerable Maine supply type. The blank
water test date is information: **§ 173(1)** required the seller to state the date of the most recent
test and whether they had experienced an unsatisfactory test or one with notations. The buyer tests
for bacteria, nitrates, **arsenic**, uranium, and **radon in water**.

**The septic system.** "Believes, in the eighties" is not a record. The **plumbing inspector** holds
the permit and design if one exists, and the design tells the buyer how many bedrooms the system is
sized for. **§ 173(3)** required the seller to state the tank type, size and location, the leach
field location, installation dates, and the most recent servicing and contractor, and — because this
is a shoreland property — the disclosures required by **30-A M.R.S. § 4216**.

**The bunkhouse near the water.** Shoreland setback, whether it was permitted, and whether it is a
**nonconforming structure** — and whether it may be replaced or expanded. **Code enforcement officer,
in writing.**

chunks.heading: Module 04 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**Tree Growth.** Enrolled land, so the buyer must understand the **withdrawal penalty** before
closing, whether their intended use qualifies, and who bears any penalty. Assessor, Maine Revenue
Services, a licensed forester, and counsel — and it is a **contract term**.

**The propane furnace with age unknown and 210 gallons a year.** 210 gallons is a low consumption
figure and is consistent with seasonal use rather than year-round occupancy, which bears directly on
the "year-round potential" claim. **§ 173(2-A)** also required the servicing company, the most recent
service call, and the most recent chimney and vent inspection. And the **propane tank is very often
leased from the dealer**, in which case it is not the seller's to convey.

**The neighbour's boat.** A licence, a prescriptive claim, or an encroachment — and the difference
decides whether the buyer can stop it. Survey, title examination, counsel.

**1958 construction.** Pre-1978, so **target housing**: the federal lead-based paint disclosure, the
pamphlet, the records, the contract acknowledgments, and the **ten-day** assessment opportunity —
plus **§ 173(4)(B)** in the Maine statement.

### Module 04 engagement check

**Question.** From the case study, the buyer asks you two things: "Can I take down the trees between
the camp and the water so we get the view?" and "The listing says year-round potential — so I can
live there in winter, right?" Answer both as a Maine licensee.

**Expected answer.** Neither is mine to answer, and answering either would be the mistake this module
exists to prevent.

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — Maine conditions and the record
chunks.excerpt:
**The trees** sit in the **shoreland zone**, where vegetative buffer and tree-cutting standards apply
under the municipality's shoreland zoning ordinance and the state minimum guidelines. Clearing
frequently requires a permit and unpermitted clearing carries enforcement and civil penalties. The
question goes to the **code enforcement officer, in writing**, before the contingency period ends.

**"Year-round potential" is a marketing claim, not a determination.** Whether the camp can lawfully
and practically be occupied year-round depends on insulation and heating, the foundation and frost
depth, winter water supply, **wastewater capacity — the septic design on file at the plumbing
inspector tells the buyer how many bedrooms it is sized for** — road maintenance and winter plowing,
and code. The stated **210 gallons of annual propane** is itself evidence pointing toward seasonal
rather than year-round use, and I would say so as an observation and route it.

If the buyer is my **client**, **§ 13273 1 B (4)** requires me to **advise them to obtain expert
advice on material matters beyond my expertise**, which both of these plainly are. If I am a
**transaction broker**, **§ 13283 3 A** bars me from conducting an investigation or analysis for
their benefit and **§ 13283 3 B** from verifying the accuracy or completeness of the seller's
statements — including "year-round potential". Either way: name the office, put it in writing, and do
not opine.

---

## Extended treatment — Maine conditions and the record

### E4.1 The Maine due-diligence matrix

For a typical Maine residential property, the question, the office, and the document:

chunks.heading: E4.2 Reading a Maine property card
chunks.excerpt:
| Question | Who answers | Document that records it |
|---|---|---|
| Zoning district and dimensional requirements | Code enforcement officer | Written zoning determination |
| Shoreland zone and sub-district | Code enforcement officer | Ordinance and official map |
| Nonconforming status of a structure | Code enforcement officer | Written determination |
| Permits issued; open violations | Code enforcement officer | Permit file |
| Subsurface wastewater permit and bedroom count | Local plumbing inspector | HHE-200 design on file |
| Water quality on a private well | Certified laboratory | Test report |
| Radon in air and water | Certified tester | Test report |
| Lot lawfully created; subdivision status | Planning board; Registry | Recorded plan; approval file |
| Access: public, private or discontinued way | Road commissioner; Registry | Town records; recorded plan |
| Road maintenance obligation | Registry; road association | Recorded agreement |
| Assessed value; current-use classification | Assessor | Property card; classification file |
| Taxes owed; liens | Tax collector | Tax status letter |
| Recorded easements, covenants, reservations | Title abstractor | Title commitment |
| Flood zone | FEMA mapping; municipality | Flood map determination |
| Underground oil storage tank | DEP; seller; fuel dealer | Registration; removal records |
| Entrance permit on a state highway | Maine DOT | Permit |
| Conservation easement | Registry; holder | Recorded easement |

A licensee who hands a buyer this matrix, populated with what is known and blank where it is not, has
served them properly whether they are a client or a customer — and has done it without giving a
single answer that was not theirs to give.

### E4.2 Reading a Maine property card

chunks.heading: E4.3 The chain of title, read
chunks.excerpt:
The municipal assessor's property card is the most under-used document in Maine brokerage. It
typically carries: the owner of record and the deed reference; the map and lot; acreage; assessed
land and building values and the year of the last revaluation; a sketch with dimensions; a
description of the improvements including year built, living area, bedroom and bath count, heating
type, and outbuildings; and — critically — any **exemption or current-use classification**.

Three uses:

**Corroboration.** The card's living area, bedroom count and year built can be checked against the
listing. A discrepancy is a question, not a fact — assessors' records contain errors — but it is a
question a licensee should have asked before advertising the number.

**Discovery.** A current-use classification, an exemption, or an outbuilding on the sketch that is
not on the ground each tells the licensee something.

**Boundaries the card does not answer.** Assessors' maps are for taxation and are **not survey
grade**. They must never be used to describe a boundary.

### E4.3 The chain of title, read

A title abstractor works backward from the current owner and forward again. What a licensee should be
able to recognise when the commitment arrives:

**A gap.** A conveyance out from someone who never appears as a grantee. In Maine the usual causes are
an **unprobated estate**, a deed never recorded, or a name change on marriage.

**An unprobated estate.** Extremely common on inherited camps and family land. Title cannot be
conveyed until the estate is administered, and the time that takes is measured in months.

**An unreleased mortgage.** Payment does not clear the record; a **discharge** does.

chunks.heading: E4.4 Construction conditions a Maine licensee reports accurately
chunks.excerpt:
**A reservation.** Timber, mineral, or a right of way reserved by a predecessor, which binds the
current owner whether or not anyone mentioned it.

**A conservation easement.** Common in Maine, permanent, and it limits development in ways a buyer
must understand before closing.

**A tax-acquired chain.** Title through a municipal tax foreclosure raises its own questions about
whether the process was completed correctly, and it is why title insurers examine those chains
closely.

None of these is the licensee's to resolve. All of them are the licensee's to **notice, escalate, and
diary**, because each takes time and each is discovered when the commitment arrives — which is why
title is ordered early.

### E4.4 Construction conditions a Maine licensee reports accurately

Described, never diagnosed:

**Sill and foundation.** Rot at the sill plate where it meets the foundation; a fieldstone or brick
foundation with mortar loss; a crawl space with standing water; a camp on posts or piers with no
frost protection.

**Roof and ice.** Ice damming at the eaves and the staining that follows it inside; a roof with
multiple layers; missing or improvised flashing at a chimney or valley.

**Heating.** An aged boiler or furnace; a buried or above-ground tank; a wood stove without
documented clearances; a chimney with no recent inspection; a heat pump as the sole heat source in a
climate that will test it.

**Water.** A dug well; a spring; a shared well with no recorded agreement; a pressure tank that
short-cycles; treatment equipment whose purpose nobody can explain.

**Wastewater.** A tank with no permit on file; a leach field with lush green growth or standing
water; a cesspool; a system in the shoreland zone that could not be replaced where it sits.

chunks.heading: E4.5 Case Study 1 debrief — what the file must show
chunks.excerpt:
**Insects and structure.** Carpenter ant frass; powder-post beetle damage; a beam that has been
sistered without documentation.

For every one of them the sentence is the same: **I can see it, I have written it down, and here is
who can tell you what it is.**

### E4.5 Case Study 1 debrief — what the file must show

The case is graded not on conclusions but on the **file**. At the end of it, the student's
documentation must show:

The **§ 173 disclosure statement** as furnished, with every blank identified.
The **investigation prompt list**, with an office named against every line.
**Written** communication to the buyer of each item, with the contingency deadline stated.
The **licensee's own disclosures**, and the section they were made under — § 13273 1 B (3) to a
client, or § 13283 2 B to a buyer as a transaction broker.
The **referrals**, with the person or office and the date.
And the **absence of any characterisation** by the licensee of the condition, the legality, or the
outcome of any of it.

A file that shows all six is a file that answers a complaint. A file that shows a licensee's opinion
about the septic system is a file that creates one.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 04

Maine statements rest on text read directly from `legislature.maine.gov` on 2026-08-20 and recorded
in `maine/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **33 M.R.S. § 173(1), (2-A), (3) and (4)** with
**§ 172** named as the exemption section, including the express cross-references in § 173 to
**30-A M.R.S. § 4216** for shoreland septic disclosures and **38 M.R.S. § 563(6)** for underground
oil storage tanks; and **32 M.R.S. §§ 13273 1 B (4) and 13283 3 A and B**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** every threshold in the **30-A M.R.S.**
subdivision provisions and the DEP's site location thresholds; every **shoreland zoning** setback,
zone width, buffer standard and nonconforming-structure rule, which sit in the state minimum
guidelines and in each municipality's ordinance; every figure in **36 M.R.S.** — exemption amounts,
current-use eligibility and **withdrawal penalties**, and the **transfer tax rate**; the period in
Maine's **Marketable Title Act** in 33 M.R.S.; Maine's **radon in rental housing** provisions; and
the **condominium** provisions of Title 33. Each is named where a curriculum hour reaches it, and the
hour routes the question rather than answering it.

**PFAS is stated as a live and developing programme**, not as a settled rule, and the hour instructs
the licensee not to characterise a property's PFAS status. That is a deliberate limit: the State's
investigation and testing programme is active, the science and the response are both moving, and a
licensee's characterisation would be a representation about a matter they cannot support.

**The Maine "quitclaim deed with covenant" is flagged in Hour 26.2 deliberately.** It functions as a
limited warranty deed, which is not what "quitclaim" means in most other states, and it is a
recurring source of confusion for licensees and buyers arriving from elsewhere.

Construction content in Hour 28 is general residential construction practice and is not a statement
of the **Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code** or of any municipal code. Frost depth, code
applicability, and permit requirements are set locally and are routed to the code enforcement
officer.

lessons.title: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 05

chunks.heading: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 05
chunks.excerpt:
# Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 05

## Hours 29–34 · Property valuation and appraisal

**Commission topic covered:** Property Valuation and Appraisal (9%, 270 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Maine sales agent credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Distinguish value, price and cost, and state the conditions in the definition of market value.
- Apply the principles of value to a property change and identify highest and best use.
- Adjust comparable sales in the correct direction and reconcile to a supported range.
- Compute value by direct capitalization and by gross rent and gross income multipliers.
- Compute value by the cost approach and classify depreciation by type.
- State what § 13251-A prohibits and how it constrains a Maine licensee's valuation work.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Minutes | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 29 | 45–60 | Types of value and the scope of sales-agent activity | Section completed |
| 30 | 0–60 | Principles of value, highest and best use, substitution | Section completed |
| 31 | 0–60 | The market-data approach and comparable adjustments | Section completed |
| 32 | 0–60 | The income approach: cap rate, GRM, GIM | Section completed |
| 33 | 0–60 | The cost approach and the three depreciations | Section completed |
| 34 | 0–15 | Integrated three-approach review; the appraisal-law boundary | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **270** | | Quiz 2 is delivered in Hour 34, minutes 15–60 |

---

## Hour 29 (45–60) — Types of value, and where a sales agent stands

### 29.4 Value, price, and cost

chunks.heading: 29.5 The § 13251-A boundary, stated before the methods
chunks.excerpt:
**Value** is an opinion of what a property should bring under stated conditions. **Price** is what
was actually paid in a particular transaction, which may reflect unusual motivation or terms.
**Cost** is what it takes to create the improvements, which may be more or less than what they add
to value.

**Market value** is the classic definition, and its conditions do the work: the most probable price
in a competitive and open market, under conditions requisite to a fair sale, with buyer and seller
each acting prudently and knowledgeably, **neither under duress**, allowing a reasonable exposure
time, with payment in cash or its equivalent and terms typical of the market.

Strip out any one of those conditions — a distressed seller, a sale between family members, no market
exposure, seller financing at an off-market rate — and the observed price is not evidence of market
value without adjustment. That is the screen applied when comparables are selected.

Other values a licensee will meet: **assessed value**, set by the municipal assessor for taxation
and worked to a **certified ratio**; **insurable value**, which is a replacement cost concept and
excludes land; **investment value**, which is value to a particular investor with particular
objectives; and **liquidation value**, which assumes an inadequate exposure period.

### 29.5 The § 13251-A boundary, stated before the methods

Before learning the methods, a Maine sales agent must know the limit on using them:

chunks.heading: Hour 30 — Principles of value and highest and best use
chunks.excerpt:
> A real estate broker or associate broker **may not knowingly provide or offer an appraisal or
> opinion of market value**, as set forth in section 14004, on real estate in a transaction **where
> the broker or associate broker, or any other licensee licensed with the agency, is to receive a
> fee on that transaction.**

The prohibition reaches the **whole agency**, not the individual. Hour 34 returns to it with the
methods in hand.

---

## Hour 30 — Principles of value and highest and best use

### 30.1 The principles

**Supply and demand.** Value moves with the relationship between them, and real estate's supply is
slow to respond, so a demand change shows up first as price.

**Substitution.** A buyer will pay no more than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable
substitute. This is the foundation of all three approaches: sales comparison, cost and income each
ask what a substitute would cost.

**Anticipation.** Value reflects expected future benefits, not past cost.

**Contribution.** A component adds value equal to what it contributes to the whole — measured in the
market — which is frequently far less than it cost. This is the principle a seller most often needs
explained.

**Conformity, progression and regression.** Value is maximised where a property conforms reasonably
to its surroundings; a lesser property gains from better neighbours and a superior property is
dragged toward the level of lesser ones.

**Increasing and diminishing returns.** Additional investment adds value up to a point and then does
not.

**Competition.** Excess profit invites competition, which erodes it.

**Change.** No condition is permanent, which is why every value opinion has an effective date.

chunks.heading: 30.2 Highest and best use
chunks.excerpt:
**Plottage** is the increment from combining adjacent parcels under one ownership; **assemblage** is
the act of combining them.

**Externalities.** Influences outside the property affect its value — the closed mill, the new
bypass, the neighbouring quarry.

### 30.2 Highest and best use

The reasonably probable use that is **legally permissible, physically possible, financially
feasible, and maximally productive** — all four tests, in that order.

Land is valued at its highest and best use **as though vacant**, which is why an obsolete building on
a well-located lot may sell for land value.

In Maine the **legally permissible** test carries unusual weight, because a parcel's use can be
constrained simultaneously by municipal zoning, shoreland zoning, subdivision status, subsurface
wastewater capacity, a conservation easement, a current-use classification, and private covenants.
A "highest and best use" conclusion that has not checked those is a guess.

### 30.3 The four forces

**Physical and environmental** — location, topography, soils, water, climate, improvements.
**Economic** — employment, income, credit, rents, construction costs.
**Governmental** — zoning, codes, taxation, public services.
**Social** — population, household formation, tastes.

Maine adds a seasonal dimension that a national text will not: in many markets the buyer pool, the
exposure period, and the achievable price all move with the season, and a sale in February is not
evidence of the same market as a sale in July.

---

## Hour 31 — The market data approach

### 31.1 The rule

**Adjust the comparable, never the subject.** The subject is the unknown; the comparables are the
evidence. Every adjustment answers: *what would this comparable have sold for if it had been like the
subject?*

chunks.heading: 31.2 Selecting comparables
chunks.excerpt:
**Comparable superior to the subject → adjust the comparable DOWN.**
**Comparable inferior to the subject → adjust the comparable UP.**

The memory hook: **comparable better, subtract**.

### 31.2 Selecting comparables

**Closed sales are evidence. Active listings are not** — an active listing is an unaccepted offer.
Pending sales are better evidence than actives, and **expired and withdrawn** listings are useful in
one specific way: they show prices the market **refused**, which brackets the top of the range.

Screen for **arm's-length conditions**: unrelated parties, adequate exposure, no unusual pressure,
market terms.

Then compare on: **real property rights conveyed**; **financing terms** including seller
concessions; **conditions of sale**; **expenditures made immediately after purchase**; **market
conditions**, which is the time adjustment; **location**; **physical characteristics**; and
**economic characteristics, use and non-realty components** — the boat, the furniture, the tractor
that were included in the price.

In Maine, **water frontage** is frequently the dominant variable and is measured in feet of frontage
as well as by quality of frontage — sand versus ledge, western versus eastern exposure, depth at the
shore, and whether the frontage is on a great pond, a river, or tidal water. **Seasonal versus
year-round** is a second dominant variable, and **acreage with or without development potential** a
third.

### 31.3 A worked grid

*Subject: 1,750 sq ft year-round house, 3 bed, 2 bath, detached garage, 150 feet of frontage on a
great pond.*

chunks.heading: 31.4 Reconciling
chunks.excerpt:
| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sale price | $498,000 | $455,000 | $529,000 |
| Sold | 3 months ago | 7 months ago | 1 month ago |
| Market conditions +0.5%/month | +$7,470 | +$15,925 | +$2,645 |
| Frontage | 150 ft | 110 ft (−40) | 190 ft (+40) |
| Frontage adj. at $1,200/ft | $0 | +$48,000 | −$48,000 |
| Living area | 1,800 (+50) | 1,700 (−50) | 1,750 (same) |
| Area adj. at $95/sq ft | −$4,750 | +$4,750 | $0 |
| Garage | detached | none | detached |
| Garage adj. | $0 | +$18,000 | $0 |
| **Net adjustment** | **+$2,720** | **+$86,675** | **−$45,355** |
| **Adjusted price** | **$500,720** | **$541,675** | **$483,645** |

Note the directions. Comp A is **larger** — superior — so the area adjustment is negative. Comp B is
**inferior** on frontage, area and garage, so all three adjustments are positive. Comp C has **more
frontage** — superior — so that adjustment is negative.

### 31.4 Reconciling

The indicated range is **$483,645 to $541,675**, and reconciliation is judgment rather than
averaging. It weighs each comparable by reliability: how few adjustments it needed, how large the
**gross adjustment** was, how recent the sale, how close the location.

Comp B needed **$86,675** of gross adjustment on a $455,000 sale — nearly a fifth of the price — and
is therefore the weakest evidence, however tidy its arithmetic looks. Comps A and C are the stronger
indications, and a defensible conclusion sits between them, weighted toward A.

**Gross adjustment measures comparability; net adjustment does not.** A comparable whose large
adjustments happen to offset is not a good comparable; it is a lucky one.

---

## Hour 32 — The income approach

### 32.1 The statement

chunks.heading: 32.2 Direct capitalization
chunks.excerpt:
**Potential Gross Income** — all income at full occupancy at market rent, plus other income.
**less Vacancy and Collection Loss**, supported by market evidence.
**= Effective Gross Income.**
**less Operating Expenses** — fixed, variable, and **replacement reserves**.
**= Net Operating Income.**

Three items are **excluded** from operating expenses, and the exclusion is the most examinable point
in the hour:

**Debt service.** NOI measures the property's own performance independent of how any owner financed
it. Including the mortgage payment would give the same building a different NOI for every buyer.

**Depreciation.** An accounting and tax entry, not a cash expense.

**Capital expenditures.** A new roof is capital; the **replacement reserve** that spreads its
anticipated cost **is** an operating expense, but the outlay itself is not.

### 32.2 Direct capitalization

**Value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate**, written **V = I ÷ R**, with **I = V × R** and **R = I ÷ V**.

*Worked:* an 8-unit building at $1,350 per month plus $3,600 other annual income.
PGI = 8 × 1,350 × 12 + 3,600 = 129,600 + 3,600 = **$133,200**.
Vacancy and collection loss 6% = 7,992. **EGI = $125,208.**
Operating expenses $47,500, including a $4,000 replacement reserve.
**NOI = 125,208 − 47,500 = $77,708.**
At a market rate of 7.25%: **V = 77,708 ÷ 0.0725 = $1,071,834**, say $1,072,000.

Two consequences a licensee must be able to state. **The rate is derived from the market**, by
dividing comparable properties' NOI by their sale prices — it is not chosen. And **a higher rate
gives a lower value at the same NOI**: at 8.25% the same building indicates $941,915, about $130,000
less for one percentage point. So a market in which rates rise is a market in which values fall even
if rents do not change.

chunks.heading: 32.3 Multipliers
chunks.excerpt:
### 32.3 Multipliers

**Gross rent multiplier** relates sale price to **monthly** gross rent; **gross income multiplier**
relates it to **annual** gross income.

**GRM = sale price ÷ monthly gross rent**, then **value = GRM × the subject's monthly gross rent**.

*Worked:* comparable GRMs of 12.8, 13.4 and 13.1; the subject's monthly gross rent is $10,800. At
13.1: **value = 13.1 × 10,800 = $141,480**.

**What the multiplier omits is the point.** It uses **gross** rent, so it ignores vacancy and every
operating expense. Two buildings with identical gross rents and different expense structures look
identical to a GRM and are not. It is a screening tool for small residential income property, not a
valuation method for anything serious.

### 32.4 The Maine seasonal-rental complication

A great many Maine income properties are **seasonal**: a coastal cottage let by the week in summer, a
ski-area condominium let in winter. Applying an annual-rent model to them produces nonsense.

The honest treatment states the **season length**, the **achieved occupancy within the season**, the
**rate by week or night**, and the **costs the model must carry that a long-term rental does not** —
cleaning and turnover, management commission, booking platform fees, furnishings replacement,
utilities carried year-round, insurance rated for short-term use, and any municipal short-term rental
registration or restriction. Many Maine municipalities now regulate short-term rentals, and whether a
property may lawfully be let that way is a question for the municipality before it is a question for
the arithmetic.

---

## Hour 33 — The cost approach and depreciation

### 33.1 The formula

**Value = land value + cost new of the improvements − accrued depreciation.**

chunks.heading: 33.2 The three depreciations
chunks.excerpt:
**Land value** is estimated separately, normally by sales comparison of vacant sites — which in Maine
means comparing frontage, acreage, soils and wastewater capacity, access, and development status
rather than simply acreage.

**Cost new** is either **reproduction cost** — an exact replica including its obsolete features — or
**replacement cost** — a substitute of equivalent utility built with current materials and methods.
Replacement cost is used more often, because nobody would rebuild the obsolete features.

### 33.2 The three depreciations

**Physical deterioration** — wear, tear and age. **Curable** where the cost to fix is recovered in
value; **incurable** where it is not.

**Functional obsolescence** — a defect in the design or utility of the improvement itself: one
bathroom for four bedrooms, a bedroom reached only through another, a kitchen that cannot fit a
dishwasher, a camp layout in a year-round market. Curable or incurable.

**External obsolescence** — loss caused by something **outside** the property: a closed employer, a
new road, a changed neighbourhood, a quarry. **Always incurable**, because the owner cannot fix it
from inside the boundary.

*Worked:* land value $185,000; replacement cost new $340,000; physical deterioration $61,000;
functional obsolescence $14,000; external obsolescence $9,000.
185,000 + 340,000 − 61,000 − 14,000 − 9,000 = **$441,000**.

### 33.3 When the cost approach is reliable

Most reliable for **new construction** and for **special-purpose property** with few comparable
sales. Least reliable for old improvements, where the depreciation estimate carries most of the
answer.

chunks.heading: Hour 34 (0–15) — Integration, and the appraisal-law boundary
chunks.excerpt:
In Maine it has one common and useful application: a **seasonal camp** in a market where the buyer
is plainly paying for the land and the frontage. Where the cost approach indicates that the
improvements contribute little, that is itself the answer — and it is often the honest explanation a
seller needs.

---

## Hour 34 (0–15) — Integration, and the appraisal-law boundary

### 34.1 Reconciling three approaches

The three approaches answer the same question by different evidence, and reconciliation weights them
by the assignment and the property:

**Residential, owner-occupied** — the **market data approach** governs; the cost approach supports;
the income approach is largely irrelevant.
**Income property** — the **income approach** governs; market data supports.
**New construction and special purpose** — the **cost approach** carries more weight.

Reconciliation is **not averaging**, and a reconciled figure with no stated reasoning is a number
without evidence.

### 34.2 The boundary — § 13251-A and Title 32, chapter 124

Maine licenses appraisers separately, under **Title 32, chapter 124**, and § 13251-A refers to
**§ 14004** in that chapter for what constitutes an appraisal or opinion of market value.

Then it prohibits, in terms:

> A real estate broker or associate broker **may not knowingly provide or offer an appraisal or
> opinion of market value** … on real estate in a transaction **where the broker or associate broker,
> or any other licensee licensed with the agency, is to receive a fee on that transaction.**

Three features of that sentence a Maine licensee must hold:

chunks.heading: Module 05 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**It reaches the agency, not just the individual.** If any licensee in the agency is to be paid a fee
on the transaction, no broker or associate broker in that agency may provide an appraisal or opinion
of market value on it.

**It applies to "an appraisal or opinion of market value" as § 14004 sets that out.** The scope of
that phrase is a legal question, and it is exactly why a licensee should not improvise near this
line.

**It does not prohibit brokerage.** Presenting market evidence to a client for the purpose of setting
a listing price or an offer price is ordinary brokerage work and is what §§ 13273 and 13274 expect a
Maine agent to do. What § 13251-A prohibits is providing or offering **an appraisal or opinion of
market value** into a transaction the agency is being paid on.

The practical rule for a sales agent: **present the evidence, describe the range it supports, never
style the work as an appraisal or an opinion of market value, never sign anything so titled, and
take any question near the line to the designated broker.** Where an appraisal is what is actually
needed, a licensed appraiser does it.

### Module 05 engagement check

**Question.** A seller under a listing agreement with your agency asks you to "give me a written
opinion of market value for my divorce lawyer" on the property you have listed. What do you do, and
why?

**Expected answer.** I decline, and I say why in writing.

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — valuation topics the Commission's competencies require
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 13251-A** provides that a broker or associate broker may not knowingly provide or offer **an
appraisal or opinion of market value**, as set forth in § 14004, on real estate in a transaction
**where the broker or associate broker, or any other licensee licensed with the agency, is to receive
a fee on that transaction.** The agency holds the listing and will be paid on the sale, so the
prohibition applies — and it reaches **any** licensee in the agency, not just me.

What the client actually needs is an **appraisal by a licensed appraiser**, licensed under Title 32,
chapter 124, who can be engaged independently and whose work is intended for exactly this use. I
refer them there.

What I may still do is what I was engaged to do: present **market evidence** — closed comparable
sales, screened for arm's-length conditions, adjusted toward the subject, reconciled to a range with
my reasoning stated — for the purpose of setting a listing price. I must not style that work as an
opinion of market value, and I must not sign anything so titled. If the client presses, the question
goes to my **designated broker**, and under **§ 13273 1 B (4)** I am in any event required to advise
the client to obtain expert advice on a material matter beyond my expertise.

---

## Extended treatment — valuation topics the Commission's competencies require

### E5.1 The appraisal process, in sequence

A student should be able to reproduce the sequence, because it is examinable and because it explains
why an appraisal cannot simply be reused for a different purpose.

chunks.heading: E5.2 Deriving a capitalization rate
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Define the problem** — the client, the intended user, the intended use, the type of value, the
   effective date, the property rights being appraised, and any assumptions or limiting conditions.
2. **Determine the scope of work** — how much investigation the assignment requires.
3. **Collect data** — general data about the market and the area; specific data about the subject and
   the comparables.
4. **Analyse highest and best use** — as vacant and as improved.
5. **Estimate land value** separately, which the cost approach requires.
6. **Apply the approaches** — sales comparison, cost, income.
7. **Reconcile** into an opinion or a range.
8. **Report** in the form the assignment requires.

Change the intended use — a mortgage loan, a divorce, an estate, a tax appeal, a relocation — and the
scope of work and sometimes the type of value change with it. That is why an appraisal prepared for
one purpose is not evidence for another, and it is part of why § 13251-A treats an appraisal or
opinion of market value as a distinct product rather than as an incident of brokerage.

### E5.2 Deriving a capitalization rate

Hour 32 said the rate is derived rather than chosen. Three derivations a licensee should recognise:

**Market extraction.** Divide each comparable sale's NOI by its sale price and reconcile the results.
This is the most defensible method and it requires reliable NOI figures for the comparables, which is
the hard part.

*Worked:* three sales — NOI $84,000 at $1,150,000 gives 7.30%; NOI $61,500 at $860,000 gives 7.15%;
NOI $128,000 at $1,700,000 gives 7.53%. Reconciled, the market indicates roughly **7.3%**, and a
subject with a weaker tenant profile or deferred maintenance would carry a higher rate.

chunks.heading: E5.3 The reserve line, and how a pro forma is manipulated
chunks.excerpt:
**Band of investment.** Weight the mortgage constant and the equity dividend rate by their shares of
the capital stack.

*Worked:* 70% debt at a mortgage constant of 0.0812 and 30% equity at a required dividend rate of
6.0%. (0.70 × 0.0812) + (0.30 × 0.060) = 0.05684 + 0.018 = **0.0748**, or **7.48%**.

**Built-up.** A safe rate plus increments for risk, illiquidity and management burden. It is the
least precise and the most argued about.

The point for a sales agent is not to produce a rate. It is to know that a rate quoted without a
derivation is an assertion, and that a seller's pro forma showing a "6% cap" is describing an asking
price rather than a market.

### E5.3 The reserve line, and how a pro forma is manipulated

The most common way an income statement is dressed is by **omitting the replacement reserve**. Leave
it out and NOI rises; capitalise the inflated NOI and value rises with it.

*Worked:* a building with a genuine NOI of $77,708 including a $4,000 reserve. Remove the reserve and
NOI appears to be $81,708. At 7.25% that is $1,127,007 rather than $1,071,834 — **$55,000 of apparent
value created by deleting one line**.

The second most common is presenting **market rent** as though it were **contract rent**. A building
with below-market leases is worth what its leases produce until they roll, and the difference is a
timing and risk question rather than a free upgrade.

The third, in Maine, is annualising a **seasonal** rental at its peak weekly rate. A cottage that
achieves $3,200 a week for ten weeks does not produce $166,400 a year.

### E5.4 A comparative market analysis, assembled

The method, which a Maine sales agent uses weekly and which must stay inside § 13251-A:

chunks.heading: E5.5 The three approaches compared, in one table
chunks.excerpt:
**Define the market area** by what actually changes buyer behaviour — the water body, the school
administrative unit, the town line that changes the mil rate, the road that is or is not plowed. A
ZIP code is a mail-delivery convenience, not a market area.

**Pull closed sales** within a defensible period — usually six to twelve months in a Maine market
where sales volume is thin, extended further only where the data requires it and the extension is
stated.

**Screen for arm's-length conditions.** Family sales, estate sales, foreclosure sales, and sales with
unusual seller financing are excluded or adjusted, and the exclusion is written down.

**Adjust toward the subject**, in the direction Hour 31 gave, and record every adjustment's basis.

**Reconcile to a range**, weighting by gross adjustment, recency and location — not by averaging.

**Disclose the limits** — how many sales, how old, what could not be verified, and what the analysis
did not consider.

**And describe the work accurately.** It is market evidence presented in the course of brokerage. It
is not an appraisal, it is not an opinion of market value as § 13251-A uses that phrase, and it must
not be titled as either.

### E5.5 The three approaches compared, in one table

chunks.heading: E5.6 Common valuation errors, and the correction
chunks.excerpt:
| | Sales comparison | Cost | Income |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asks | What did substitutes sell for? | What would it cost to replace, less depreciation, plus land? | What income does it produce, and what is that worth? |
| Needs | Comparable closed sales | Reliable cost data and a land value | Reliable income and expense data and a market rate |
| Best for | Residential, owner-occupied | New construction; special purpose | Income property |
| Weakest when | Few or no comparables | Old improvements, where depreciation carries the answer | Owner-occupied property with no income |
| Maine complication | Thin sales volume; frontage and seasonality dominate | Seasonal building window; remote-site cost premiums | Seasonal rentals; municipal short-term rental rules |

### E5.6 Common valuation errors, and the correction

**Averaging the three approaches.** Reconciliation weights; it does not average.

**Using assessed value as evidence of market value.** It is an administrative figure produced on an
assessment cycle and worked to a certified ratio.

**Adjusting the subject.** Adjust the comparable, always.

**Treating a net adjustment as a measure of comparability.** Gross adjustment measures it.

**Using list prices as comparables.** They are unaccepted offers.

**Ignoring seasonality in a Maine market.** A February sale and a July sale are not evidence of the
same market, and the adjustment for market conditions has to carry it.

**Quoting a cap rate with no derivation.**

**Calling any of it an opinion of market value in a transaction the agency is paid on.** § 13251-A.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 05

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 05
chunks.excerpt:
Maine statements rest on text read directly from `legislature.maine.gov` on 2026-08-20 and recorded
in `maine/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **32 M.R.S. § 13251-A**, quoted verbatim, and
**§ 13273 1 B (4)**. **§ 14004** is cited because § 13251-A cites it; **Title 32, chapter 124 has not
been read for this project**, and this course states no appraiser qualification, standard, or
definition from it.

**The scope of "appraisal or opinion of market value" is deliberately left as a legal question.**
Hour 34.2 states what § 13251-A prohibits, states that presenting market evidence in the course of
brokerage is what §§ 13273 and 13274 expect, and routes anything near the line to the designated
broker. Drawing that line precisely would require reading § 14004 and the Commission's guidance, and
neither has been read here.

**Appraisal method is taught because the Commission's outline requires it** — Property Valuation and
Appraisal is 9 percent of the course — and because a Maine licensee uses the method to present market
evidence. It is not taught as appraisal practice, and Maine licenses appraisers under a separate
chapter.

All arithmetic is worked in full so a reviewer can verify each figure. **The prices, rates,
adjustment amounts, capitalization rates and multipliers are illustrative teaching figures and are
not market data for any Maine market.** The $1,200 per foot of frontage in Hour 31.3 in particular is
a teaching number; real frontage adjustments vary enormously by water body, exposure, and shoreline
character, and are derived from paired sales.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 05
chunks.excerpt:
**The seasonal-rental treatment in Hour 32.4 is stated as analytical practice**, and the observation
that many Maine municipalities now regulate short-term rentals is stated as a question for the
municipality. No municipal registration requirement or restriction is stated here.

lessons.title: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 06

chunks.heading: Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 06
chunks.excerpt:
# Maine Sales Agent Course — Module 06

## Hours 35–39 · Financing the transaction

**Commission topic covered:** Financing the Transaction (9%, 270 instructional minutes) — all 270 of them, ending at Hour 39 minute 30, where Module 07 begins.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Maine sales agent credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Describe the primary and secondary mortgage markets and name the participants.
- Distinguish the note from the mortgage, name the clauses that decide outcomes, and say why a Maine
  mortgage is not a deed of trust.
- Match a borrower or property scenario to a programme category without representing eligibility.
- Compute loan-to-value, points, interest, a payment from a factor, and qualifying ratios.
- Identify the consumer-protection statutes that bear on a residential loan and the signs of
  predatory lending and mortgage fraud.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Minutes | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 35 | 0–60 | Sources of funds; primary and secondary markets; participants | Section completed |
| 36 | 0–60 | Notes, mortgages, clauses, contract for deed, deed of trust compared | Section completed |
| 37 | 0–60 | Conventional, FHA, VA, MaineHousing, Rural Development, construction, seller financing | Section completed |
| 38 | 0–60 | Repayment structures, points, qualification ratios, credit | Section completed |
| 39 | 0–30 | Lender requirements; predatory lending and mortgage fraud | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **270** | | Hour 39, minutes 30–60, begins Module 07 |

---

## Hour 35 — Sources of funds and the market structure

### 35.1 The primary market

chunks.heading: 35.2 The secondary market
chunks.excerpt:
The **primary mortgage market** is where loans are originated: banks, savings institutions, **credit
unions**, mortgage bankers, and mortgage brokers. In Maine, credit unions and community banks
originate a substantial share of residential lending, and small local institutions are more likely to
hold loans in **portfolio** rather than sell them.

That matters practically. A **portfolio lender** sets its own underwriting standards and may lend on
property a secondary-market lender will not — a seasonal camp, an unconventional water supply, an
island property, a large acreage parcel, a property with no comparable sales. When a buyer's property
is unusual, the answer is often a local portfolio lender, and a licensee who knows that serves their
client without ever advising on credit.

### 35.2 The secondary market

The **secondary mortgage market** is where originated loans are sold. **Fannie Mae** and **Freddie
Mac** purchase conforming conventional loans; **Ginnie Mae** guarantees securities backed by
government loans. Selling loans returns capital to the originator so it can lend again, and it is why
underwriting guidelines exist at all: a loan that does not meet the purchaser's criteria cannot be
sold.

**MaineHousing** — the Maine State Housing Authority — operates first-time homebuyer and other
programmes through participating lenders. Its programmes have their own eligibility criteria and
change; a licensee names the programme and refers the buyer to a participating lender.

### 35.3 The participants

chunks.heading: Hour 36 — Notes, mortgages, and the Maine instrument
chunks.excerpt:
**Loan originator**, licensed under the federal SAFE Act framework and state law. **Processor**.
**Underwriter**. **Appraiser**. **Title and closing agent** — in Maine, frequently an attorney.
**Mortgage insurer** for conventional loans with a small down payment. **Servicer**, who collects
payments after closing and who is very often not the originator.

A licensee's role among them is coordination and deadline management, and nothing else. The licensee
does not complete the application, does not advise on credit, and does not receive anything of value
for a referral — which is Hour 39's RESPA point.

---

## Hour 36 — Notes, mortgages, and the Maine instrument

### 36.1 Two documents, two jobs

Every secured loan has two instruments, and confusing them is the most common error in this half of
the course.

**The promissory note** is the **debt** — the borrower's personal promise to repay, with the rate,
the payment, the term, late charges, prepayment terms, default and acceleration. It is a negotiable
instrument and it can be sold, which is what happens on the secondary market. **It is not recorded.**

**The mortgage** is the **collateral** — it pledges the real property as security for the note and
creates the lien. **It is recorded**, at the Registry of Deeds.

Pay off the note and the mortgage must be **discharged** of record. A recorded but undischarged
mortgage is one of the most common clouds a Maine title examination reveals.

### 36.2 Maine uses a mortgage, not a deed of trust

A **mortgage** has **two parties**: the **mortgagor**, who is the borrower and who gives the
mortgage, and the **mortgagee**, who is the lender.

A **deed of trust** has three — borrower, trustee, and lender — and the trustee conducts a sale on
default under a power of sale.

chunks.heading: 36.3 The clauses that decide outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
**Maine is a mortgage state**, and residential foreclosure in Maine is **judicial**: the lender
brings an action in court. A student who has learned "grantor, trustee, beneficiary" from a national
text, or from this project's Virginia course, must translate.

The practical consequences are real. Judicial foreclosure is slower, it produces a court record, and
Maine imposes procedural requirements on residential foreclosure — including notice requirements and
a **mediation programme** for owner-occupied residential property. **This course states no notice
period, no redemption period, and no mediation rule**, because those provisions of **14 M.R.S.** have
not been read from primary text for this project. A licensee meeting a distressed property routes the
borrower to counsel and to a **HUD-approved housing counselling agency**, and says nothing about
timing.

### 36.3 The clauses that decide outcomes

**Acceleration** — on default the lender may declare the whole balance due. Without it a lender could
sue only for missed payments, and every foreclosure begins here.

**Alienation, or due-on-sale** — the lender may accelerate if the property is transferred without
consent. This is what makes most modern loans **non-assumable**, and why "taking over payments" is
usually not available.

**Prepayment** — whether the borrower may pay early and on what terms.

**Defeasance** — on full payment the mortgage is defeated and must be **discharged**.

**Subordination** — an agreement to take a lower lien position than recording order would give.
Refinancing a first mortgage while a home equity line remains requires it, or the equity line would
advance to first position.

chunks.heading: 36.4 Contract for deed and other structures
chunks.excerpt:
**Escrow or impound** — the lender collects taxes and insurance monthly and pays them when due,
protecting its own collateral against a tax lien or an uninsured loss.

### 36.4 Contract for deed and other structures

A **contract for deed** — also called an installment land contract or bond for a deed — leaves legal
title with the seller until payment is complete while the buyer takes possession and equitable title.
Maine regulates these arrangements, and this course states no requirement from that regime because it
has not been read from primary text for this project. A licensee who meets one routes it to counsel
before anything is signed.

**Assumption** — the buyer takes over the existing loan and becomes personally liable; the seller is
released **only** by a written release from the lender. **Subject to** — the buyer takes title with
the loan in place but assumes no personal liability, the seller stays liable, and the due-on-sale
clause is very likely triggered.

**Seller financing** — the seller takes back a note secured by a mortgage. Federal rules constrain
seller financing of owner-occupied residential property, and every version of it is a legal and tax
structure. The licensee's role is to say so.

---

## Hour 37 — Programme categories

### 37.1 The one rule for this hour

**Programme guidelines change, sometimes several times a year, and eligibility depends on facts the
licensee does not have.** A licensee describes **categories**; a lender determines **eligibility**.

Telling a buyer "you'll qualify" is a representation the licensee cannot support, and under
§ 13273 1 C the duty is to exercise reasonable skill and care.

### 37.2 Conventional

chunks.heading: 37.3 FHA
chunks.excerpt:
Not insured or guaranteed by a government agency. **Conforming** loans meet the purchase criteria of
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, including a maximum loan amount that is set annually and varies by
county; **non-conforming** loans do not, and **jumbo** loans exceed the limit.

**Private mortgage insurance** is generally required where the down payment is under 20 percent, and
it protects **the lender**, not the borrower — the most persistent consumer misunderstanding in
residential lending. Federal law provides for cancellation and automatic termination of borrower-paid
PMI on the basis of the loan's amortisation; the thresholds are the lender's and the statute's to
state.

### 37.3 FHA

The **Federal Housing Administration** **insures** loans made by approved lenders; it does not lend.
Characteristic features: a low minimum down payment; more flexible credit and ratio criteria;
**mortgage insurance premiums**, upfront and annual; **maximum loan amounts that vary by county**;
and a requirement that the property meet **minimum property standards** and be appraised by an
FHA-approved appraiser. FHA loans are for **owner-occupants**.

The Maine consequence worth naming: an FHA appraisal serves the insurer's interest in the property's
condition as well as its value, and older Maine housing — with knob-and-tube wiring, peeling paint on
a pre-1978 house, an unpermitted septic system, or a failing sill — may need repair before the loan
can close. That is a real scheduling consequence for a seller.

### 37.4 VA

chunks.heading: 37.5 Rural Development
chunks.excerpt:
The **Department of Veterans Affairs** **guarantees** a portion of a loan made by an approved lender
to an eligible veteran, service member, or surviving spouse. No down payment in many cases; no monthly
mortgage insurance; a **funding fee** that varies and is waived in defined circumstances; entitlement
established by a **certificate of eligibility**; a VA appraisal producing a notice of value; and
**occupancy** requirements.

A licensee never tells a veteran whether they are eligible, how much entitlement they have, or
whether the funding fee is waived.

### 37.5 Rural Development

The **US Department of Agriculture** operates rural housing programmes, guaranteeing loans made by
approved lenders and, in some programmes, lending directly. No down payment; **geographic
eligibility** limited to designated rural areas defined by USDA maps that change; **household income
limits** by area and household size; owner-occupancy; and guarantee and annual fees.

**A very large part of Maine is within designated rural areas**, which makes this programme far more
relevant here than in most states — and makes the two eligibility gates, **the property's location**
and **the household's income**, worth checking early. Both are checked against USDA's own tools, and
both change.

### 37.6 MaineHousing and construction lending

**MaineHousing** operates first-time homebuyer programmes through participating lenders, with their
own eligibility criteria, purchase price limits and income limits, all of which change. Name the
programme; refer to a participating lender.

chunks.heading: Hour 38 — The arithmetic
chunks.excerpt:
**Construction lending** is short-term, disbursed in **draws** against inspected progress, with
