Michigan requires attendance at 100 percent of a prelicensure course and, for distance learning, hours attended equal to hours approved (R 339.22152). These four clock hours are the civil rights and equal opportunity in housing instruction required by MCL 339.2504, and no part of that requirement is satisfied by any other module of this course.

lessons.title: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 08

chunks.heading: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 08
chunks.excerpt:
# Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 08

## Real estate finance and settlement law

**Course version:** 1.0-submission-draft
**Module time:** 4 clock hours (240 instructional minutes)
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Michigan prelicensure credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Distinguish the promissory note from the mortgage and explain what each does.
- Identify the loan types a Michigan buyer uses and the property consequences of each.
- Explain amortisation, points, loan-to-value, and the ratios a lender applies, and compute each.
- Describe Michigan foreclosure, including foreclosure by advertisement and the redemption period, well enough to know what to ask and what not to state.
- Apply the federal settlement and lending rules — RESPA, TILA and the integrated disclosures, ECOA — to a licensee's conduct.
- Recognise predatory and fraudulent lending patterns and state what a licensee does on encountering one.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: the instruments and the loan types | 75 | Sections 1-2 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: the arithmetic and Michigan foreclosure | 70 | Sections 3-4 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: federal settlement and lending law | 65 | Sections 5-6 recorded as viewed |
| Applied exercise: financing memorandum + confirmation | 20 | Written response and applied-confirmation result recorded |
| Scored engagement check | 10 | Five items submitted |
| **Total** | **240** | **One of ten modules of instruction** |

## 1. The instruments

### 1.1 Note and mortgage are two documents

chunks.heading: 1.2 The clauses that matter
chunks.excerpt:
The **promissory note** is the promise to repay: amount, rate, term, payment, default terms. It is the debt.

The **mortgage** is the security instrument: it pledges the property as collateral and gives the lender the right to foreclose. It is recorded; the note is not.

Students conflate them constantly, and the distinction decides real questions. A note can exist without a mortgage — an unsecured loan. A mortgage without a note secures nothing. When a loan is sold, the note is what is transferred, and the mortgage follows it.

Michigan is a **lien theory** state: the borrower holds title and the lender holds a lien. The lender does not own the property during the loan.

### 1.2 The clauses that matter

**Acceleration** — on default, the whole balance becomes due. Without it a lender could only sue for missed payments.

**Due-on-sale** — the balance becomes due if the property is transferred. This is why a buyer generally cannot simply take over a seller's mortgage, and why "assumable" is a specific feature rather than a default.

**Prepayment** — whether early payoff carries a penalty.

**Escrow** — the lender collects taxes and insurance monthly and pays them. Ubiquitous in Michigan residential lending, and the reason property tax delinquency on a mortgaged property is unusual.

**Subordination** — an agreement that one lien will rank behind another. This is how a first mortgage is refinanced without a second lien moving into first position.

### 1.3 Discharge and satisfaction

When the note is paid, the lender must record a **discharge**. An undischarged mortgage remains an exception on the title commitment even though the debt is gone — module 03 — and obtaining a discharge from a lender that has since been acquired is a recurring source of delay.

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 1.1
chunks.excerpt:
#### Checkpoint 1.1

A buyer asks whether he can "take over" the seller's 3.1 percent mortgage rather than borrowing at current rates. What does the licensee say?

*Answer:* That most mortgages contain a due-on-sale clause making the balance payable on transfer, that assumability is a specific feature of some government-backed loans and not a general right, and that whether this particular loan may be assumed is answered by the lender and the loan documents. The licensee gets the note and the mortgage to the lender or to counsel and does not read them for the buyer.

## 2. Loan types

### 2.1 Conventional

Not insured or guaranteed by a government agency. Conforming loans meet the limits and standards of the secondary-market purchasers; non-conforming and jumbo loans do not.

**Private mortgage insurance** is generally required where the loan-to-value exceeds 80 percent, and under federal law it is cancellable in defined circumstances as the balance falls.

### 2.2 FHA

Insured by the Federal Housing Administration, with a lower down payment and more flexible credit. Two consequences for property rather than borrower:

**Property standards.** FHA appraisals identify condition issues that must be corrected before closing — peeling paint on pre-1978 housing, missing handrails, roof condition, non-functioning systems.

**Mortgage insurance premiums**, upfront and annual, which change the payment materially.

A listing agent whose seller accepts an FHA offer should expect condition items and should raise them with the seller before the appraisal rather than after.

### 2.3 VA

chunks.heading: 2.4 Rural development, MSHDA, and land contract
chunks.excerpt:
Guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans and service members. Frequently no down payment, no monthly mortgage insurance, and a funding fee. VA appraisals carry their own minimum property requirements.

A licensee must never treat a VA buyer's offer as weaker for being VA. Beyond the commercial error, refusing or disadvantaging offers by loan type can operate against protected classes.

### 2.4 Rural development, MSHDA, and land contract

**USDA rural development** loans serve eligible rural areas with income limits — much of Michigan outside the metropolitan areas qualifies geographically.

**MSHDA** — the Michigan State Housing Development Authority — administers down-payment assistance and first-time buyer programmes with their own eligibility rules and property requirements.

**Land contract**, from module 02, remains a genuine Michigan financing route and carries the same warning: recognise, refer, never draft.

### 2.5 Structures

**Fixed rate** — rate constant for the term.

**Adjustable rate** — an index plus a margin, adjusting on a schedule, with caps per adjustment and over the life. A licensee should be able to explain that structure in a sentence and should send every specific question to the lender.

**Balloon** — payments computed on a long amortisation with the balance due early. Common in land contracts and seller financing, and the source of the failure when the balloon arrives and refinancing is unavailable.

#### Checkpoint 2.1

A seller receives two offers: $305,000 cash with no contingencies, and $312,000 FHA. What should the licensee explain?

chunks.heading: 3. The arithmetic
chunks.excerpt:
*Answer:* The difference in net and in risk — the FHA offer is higher but carries an appraisal and property-condition requirements the cash offer does not, and a longer timeline. The licensee lays out both and lets the seller decide. What the licensee must not do is characterise the FHA buyer as less desirable in a way that becomes a pattern of disadvantaging a loan type.

## 3. The arithmetic

### 3.1 Loan-to-value

LTV = loan amount ÷ lesser of price or appraised value.

A $240,000 loan on a $300,000 property is 80 percent. If the appraisal comes in at $290,000, the same loan is 82.8 percent of value and the lender will reduce the loan, not raise the value.

### 3.2 Down payment

A 20 percent down payment on $285,000 is $57,000, leaving a $228,000 loan. Students should be able to move between the three numbers in either direction.

### 3.3 Points and interest

One **point** is one percent of the loan amount, paid at closing. Two points on a $228,000 loan is $4,560. Discount points buy a lower rate; origination points are a fee.

Simple interest for one period: principal × rate. A $228,000 loan at 6.5 percent accrues $14,820 in the first year, about $1,235 in the first month. In an amortising loan the early payments are mostly interest, which is why a borrower's balance falls slowly at first.

### 3.4 Amortisation

An amortised loan's constant payment covers accruing interest first and applies the remainder to principal. As principal falls, the interest portion falls and the principal portion grows.

Worked, on $228,000 at 6.5 percent with a monthly payment of $1,441.16:

- Month 1 interest: 228,000 × 0.065 ÷ 12 = $1,235.00. Principal: $206.16. Balance: $227,793.84.
- Month 2 interest: 227,793.84 × 0.065 ÷ 12 = $1,233.88. Principal: $207.28. Balance: $227,586.56.

chunks.heading: 3.5 Qualifying ratios
chunks.excerpt:
Two payments in, the borrower has repaid $413.44 of $228,000. A licensee who can show that to a client explains more about mortgage debt in thirty seconds than a brochure does.

### 3.5 Qualifying ratios

**Housing ratio** — housing expense ÷ gross monthly income. Housing expense is principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and association dues where applicable.

**Total debt ratio** — housing expense plus other monthly obligations ÷ gross monthly income.

A borrower with $7,500 gross monthly income and a proposed housing expense of $2,100 has a 28 percent housing ratio. With $600 of other obligations, the total debt ratio is 36 percent.

**The licensee does not qualify buyers.** Lenders do. Understanding the ratios lets a licensee ask useful questions and recognise when a buyer's plan is unrealistic; it does not license a licensee to tell a buyer what they can afford.

#### Checkpoint 3.1

A buyer earning $6,000 gross monthly wants a house with a $1,900 housing expense and has a $520 car payment. Compute both ratios and comment.

*Answer:* Housing ratio 1,900 ÷ 6,000 = 31.7 percent. Total debt ratio 2,420 ÷ 6,000 = 40.3 percent. Both are above conventional guideline figures, which does not mean the buyer will be declined — programmes and compensating factors vary. The comment a licensee should make is that these are questions for the lender, and that the buyer should have a written pre-approval before shopping at this price.

## 4. Michigan foreclosure

### 4.1 Two routes

Michigan permits **foreclosure by advertisement** — a non-judicial process where the mortgage contains a power of sale — and **judicial foreclosure**, brought as a court action. Foreclosure by advertisement is the ordinary residential route and involves published notice, posting, and a sheriff's sale.

chunks.heading: 4.2 Redemption
chunks.excerpt:
### 4.2 Redemption

After the sheriff's sale, Michigan provides a **redemption period** during which the borrower may redeem the property by paying the sale amount with interest and costs. The length depends on the circumstances, including the property type and how much of the original loan has been repaid, and it can be shortened where the property is abandoned.

**A licensee must not state the length of a redemption period from memory.** It is a fact with large consequences for a buyer's ability to take possession and for what the buyer is actually acquiring, and it comes from the title company and counsel in writing.

### 4.3 What a buyer of foreclosed property is buying

During redemption, the purchaser at the sale holds a sheriff's deed subject to the right of redemption. Occupancy, condition, access, and even the ability to inspect may be restricted. Title questions are more common than in an ordinary sale.

The licensee's role is to make sure the buyer knows they are in a different kind of transaction, to get the title company involved early, and to refuse to predict outcomes.

### 4.4 Short sales and deeds in lieu

A **short sale** is a sale for less than the balance, requiring the lender's approval. Timelines are long and uncertain, approval is not guaranteed by any lender statement short of a written approval, and whether the borrower remains liable for the shortfall is a legal and tax question the licensee must not answer.

A **deed in lieu** conveys the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure, and whether it extinguishes the debt is likewise a legal question.

### 4.5 Tax foreclosure

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 4.1
chunks.excerpt:
Separate from mortgage foreclosure, Michigan counties foreclose for delinquent property taxes on a statutory schedule that ends in the loss of the property. It moves faster than most owners expect, and a licensee who sees delinquency should treat it as urgent — module 04.

#### Checkpoint 4.1

A buyer wants to make an offer on a property that went to sheriff's sale five weeks ago. What does the licensee establish first, and from whom?

*Answer:* Whether a redemption period is running and when it ends, from the title company and counsel, in writing. Until that is answered the buyer does not know what they would be purchasing or when they could occupy. The licensee should not state the period from memory and should not let the buyer proceed on an assumption.

## 5. Federal settlement and lending law

### 5.1 RESPA

The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, implemented by **Regulation X**, governs federally related mortgage loans on residential property. Three parts touch a licensee directly.

**Section 8 prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees.** Giving or accepting anything of value for the referral of settlement service business is prohibited. This reaches payments from title companies, lenders, inspectors, warranty companies, and anyone else in the settlement chain. It also reaches arrangements dressed as marketing agreements where the payment is really for referrals.

**Affiliated business arrangements** are permitted where the relationship is disclosed in writing, the consumer is told they are not required to use the affiliate, and no fee is paid for the referral itself.

**Section 9 prohibits a seller from requiring the buyer to use a particular title insurer** as a condition of sale.

chunks.heading: 5.2 TILA and the integrated disclosures
chunks.excerpt:
Combined with R 339.22137 from module 05, the working rule is: any value flowing to a licensee from a settlement service provider is presumptively a problem, and is disclosed and examined before it flows.

### 5.2 TILA and the integrated disclosures

The Truth in Lending Act, implemented by **Regulation Z**, requires disclosure of the cost of credit, expressed as the **annual percentage rate**, which includes finance charges and not merely the note rate.

The integrated disclosures apply to most closed-end consumer mortgages:

**The Loan Estimate** must be delivered within three business days of application.

**The Closing Disclosure** must be received by the borrower at least **three business days before consummation**. Certain changes — an APR increase beyond tolerance, a change in loan product, the addition of a prepayment penalty — restart the three-day period.

**Why a licensee cares:** the three-day rule is a hard constraint on closing dates. A change late in a transaction can move the closing, and a licensee who promises a date without accounting for it has promised something the timeline may not allow.

**Advertising triggers.** Stating certain credit terms in an advertisement — a down payment amount, a payment amount, a term, a rate — triggers required additional disclosures. The safe practice for a real estate licensee is not to advertise financing terms at all.

### 5.3 ECOA and Regulation B

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in credit on the basis of race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public assistance income, or the good-faith exercise of consumer-protection rights.

chunks.heading: 5.4 Other federal rules a licensee meets
chunks.excerpt:
Note that **marital status, age, and public assistance income** appear here and not in the federal Fair Housing Act. The licensee's fair-housing obligations in module 07 and the lending rules overlap without being identical.

### 5.4 Other federal rules a licensee meets

**The Home Mortgage Disclosure Act**, which produces the lending data used to identify redlining.

**The Fair Credit Reporting Act**, governing credit information — relevant where a licensee handles a rental application.

**Anti-money-laundering reporting** in certain non-financed transactions in defined areas, which title companies administer.

#### Checkpoint 5.1

A title company offers a licensee $150 per closing, described as a "marketing co-op fee", with no marketing services identified. Evaluate.

*Answer:* This is a referral payment with a label on it, and RESPA section 8 prohibits it. A genuine marketing agreement requires actual services at fair market value, documented, and unrelated to the volume of referrals. The licensee declines, tells their broker, and does not accept an arrangement whose only variable is how many closings they send.

## 6. Predatory lending and fraud

### 6.1 Patterns to recognise

**Equity stripping** — a loan the borrower cannot repay, made on the strength of the equity rather than the income.

**Loan flipping** — repeated refinancing that generates fees and erodes equity.

**Steering to higher-cost products** where the borrower qualifies for better.

**Balloon structures** presented as ordinary payments, where the balloon arrives without a refinancing plan.

**Fee packing** — inflated or duplicated charges buried in the closing costs.

**Undisclosed adjustable terms** — a payment that rises sharply after a teaser period the borrower did not understand.

chunks.heading: 6.2 Mortgage fraud, and how licensees get drawn into it
chunks.excerpt:
### 6.2 Mortgage fraud, and how licensees get drawn into it

Two families of fraud, and the second one catches honest people.

**Fraud for profit** — the organised kind: straw buyers, inflated appraisals, fictitious sellers, silent second mortgages concealed from the primary lender.

**Fraud for housing** — a buyer who wants a house misstating income, occupancy intention, or the source of the down payment.

The licensee's exposure arises through documents. A purchase agreement with a "seller concession" that does not appear on the closing statement, a side agreement for cash back after closing, a second document with a different price, an occupancy declaration everyone knows is false — a licensee who participates in any of these has participated in mortgage fraud, and the intent to help does not change that.

### 6.3 What a licensee does

**Refuse to sign or transmit a document you know to be inaccurate.**

**Refuse to prepare a second version of an agreement for the lender.**

**Escalate to the broker immediately** — this is not a judgment to make alone.

**Document what you were asked and what you did.**

**Withdraw** where the client persists.

There is no version of this where going along is the smaller risk.

### 6.4 The honest sentence

Most of what this module asks of a licensee reduces to one habit: describe accurately, refer specifics to the lender, and never let a document say something you know is untrue. A licensee who does that will occasionally be the reason a transaction slows down, and will never be the reason one becomes a criminal matter.

#### Checkpoint 6.1

A buyer asks the licensee to write the purchase agreement at $315,000 with a $15,000 "repair credit" instead of $300,000, so he can finance the down payment. What is the answer?

chunks.heading: Key terms
chunks.excerpt:
*Answer:* No, and the reason must be said plainly: the structure misstates the price to the lender, which is mortgage fraud, and the licensee would be participating by preparing it. The licensee refuses, tells the buyer why, informs the broker, and documents it. A repair credit supported by an actual repair, disclosed to the lender and appearing on the closing statement, is a different thing entirely — and the difference is disclosure.

## Key terms

**Acceleration clause** — makes the entire balance due on default.

**Annual percentage rate** — the cost of credit expressed as a yearly rate, including finance charges beyond the note rate.

**Due-on-sale clause** — makes the balance due on transfer of the property.

**Lien theory** — the doctrine, followed in Michigan, under which the borrower holds title and the lender holds a lien.

**Loan-to-value** — loan amount as a percentage of the lesser of price or appraised value.

**Point** — one percent of the loan amount, paid at closing.

**Redemption period** — the period after a sheriff's sale during which the borrower may redeem; length varies and must be verified.

**Short sale** — a sale for less than the mortgage balance, requiring lender approval.

## Practice problems

**Problem 1.** A property sells for $268,000 with 15 percent down. Compute the down payment, loan amount, and LTV.

*Working:* Down payment 268,000 × 0.15 = $40,200. Loan 268,000 − 40,200 = $227,800. LTV = 227,800 ÷ 268,000 = 85 percent, which is above 80 and so will ordinarily carry mortgage insurance.

**Problem 2.** The buyer pays 1.5 discount points on that loan. What is the cost?

*Working:* 227,800 × 0.015 = $3,417.

**Problem 3.** First-month interest on the same loan at 6.75 percent.

*Working:* 227,800 × 0.0675 ÷ 12 = $1,281.38.

chunks.heading: Module summary
chunks.excerpt:
**Problem 4.** A lender issues a revised Closing Disclosure two days before a Friday closing, increasing the APR beyond tolerance. What happens to the date?

*Working:* The three-business-day period restarts, so the closing moves. The licensee's job is to have told all parties that this could happen and to manage the possession and moving arrangements that depend on the date — not to argue with the lender about a federal timing rule.

**Problem 5.** A seller offers to pay the buyer's agent a bonus directly if the transaction closes by month end. Analyse.

*Working:* Compensation to a salesperson flows through the broker, from module 01. A direct payment is improper on that ground alone. Whether the bonus must also be disclosed to the lender and appear on the closing statement is a settlement question, and undisclosed payments in a financed transaction raise RESPA and fraud issues. Route it through the broker and disclose it.

**Problem 6.** A buyer says she will occupy the property as her residence, and mentions to the licensee that she actually intends to rent it out immediately.

*Working:* The occupancy declaration in the loan file will be false, and the licensee now knows it. The licensee cannot transmit or facilitate the false declaration, must tell the buyer that investment financing is a different product, and should escalate. Saying nothing because "it's the lender's problem" is participation.

## Module summary

**The note is the debt and the mortgage is the security.** Michigan is a lien theory state.

**Due-on-sale is why assumption is a feature, not a right.** Acceleration is why default reaches the whole balance.

chunks.heading: Required applied exercise
chunks.excerpt:
**Loan type changes the property**, not only the borrower — FHA and VA property standards, MSHDA and USDA eligibility, and the land contract's separate legal world.

**LTV, points, and the qualifying ratios are arithmetic a licensee should do in their head** — and qualification is still the lender's job.

**Michigan foreclosure has two routes and a redemption period whose length must be verified, never recalled.**

**RESPA prohibits paying or accepting anything of value for a referral**, and a marketing agreement with no services is a referral fee with a label.

**The Closing Disclosure's three-business-day rule constrains closing dates**, and certain changes restart it.

**ECOA protects marital status, age, and public assistance income** — classes the federal Fair Housing Act does not reach.

**Never transmit a document you know to be inaccurate.** The intent to help a buyer does not convert a false statement to a lender into anything other than fraud.

## Required applied exercise

Prepare a one-page financing review memorandum for the transaction supplied with this module. Compute the loan amount, LTV, points, first-month interest, and both qualifying ratios; identify the loan type and every property consequence it carries; identify each federal timing rule that constrains the closing date; identify any payment, credit, or side arrangement that raises a RESPA or fraud question and state what you would do about it; and state what you would refer to the lender and what to counsel. The approved instructor scores it under the common 10-point applied-memo rubric; 8/10 with no zero on legal accuracy or professional boundaries is satisfactory, and a needs-revision result receives feedback and must be resubmitted.

## Knowledge check and remediation

chunks.heading: Module completion
chunks.excerpt:
After submitting the memo, complete the one-item applied confirmation check at 100 percent, then the five-item engagement check at 80 percent. A missed confirmation returns you to the relevant instruction. An unsuccessful engagement attempt opens remediation with an alternate explanation, a second worked scenario, and a separately authored five-item set. The module cannot complete until the memo is satisfactory, the confirmation is correct, and the student reaches the StateCourse 80 percent threshold on any remediation set — R 339.22157(2)(f).

## Module completion

Completion requires all six instructional sections, the applied exercise, the engagement check, and any triggered remediation. Michigan requires attendance at 100 percent of a prelicensure course and, for distance learning, hours attended equal to hours approved (R 339.22152).

lessons.title: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 09

chunks.heading: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 09
chunks.excerpt:
# Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 09

## Valuation, appraisal, and real estate mathematics

**Course version:** 1.0-submission-draft
**Module time:** 4 clock hours (240 instructional minutes)
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Michigan prelicensure credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Distinguish market value, price, and cost, and explain why the three differ.
- Apply the four elements of value and the principles that explain market behaviour.
- Perform a sales comparison analysis, selecting comparables and adjusting in the correct direction.
- Explain the cost and income approaches and when each is the appropriate one.
- State the boundary between a licensee's market analysis and an appraisal, and act on it.
- Compute area, commission, proration, and investment measures accurately.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: value, its elements, and its principles | 75 | Sections 1-2 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: the three approaches to value | 70 | Sections 3-4 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: the market analysis boundary and applied mathematics | 65 | Sections 5-6 recorded as viewed |
| Applied exercise: market-analysis memorandum + confirmation | 20 | Written response and applied-confirmation result recorded |
| Scored engagement check | 10 | Five items submitted |
| **Total** | **240** | **One of ten modules of instruction** |

## 1. Value

### 1.1 Three different numbers

chunks.heading: 1.2 The four elements of value
chunks.excerpt:
**Market value** is the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive and open market, with buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably, neither under undue duress, and with a reasonable exposure time.

**Price** is what was actually paid. It can differ from market value for many reasons — a distressed seller, a related-party transaction, an unusually motivated buyer.

**Cost** is what it took to build or improve. Cost does not equal value, and the gap between them is where owners' expectations most often sit. A $45,000 pool rarely adds $45,000, and in some markets adds very little.

Every one of those sentences is a conversation a licensee will have with a seller.

### 1.2 The four elements of value

Value requires all four; the absence of any one destroys it.

**Demand** — someone must want it, with the means to act.
**Utility** — it must satisfy a use.
**Scarcity** — supply must be limited relative to demand.
**Transferability** — the interest must be capable of being conveyed.

The mnemonic DUST is worth carrying, mainly because it explains failures. Land with a defective title has no transferability, so it has no market value however desirable it is.

### 1.3 The principles

**Substitution.** A buyer will pay no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. This is the foundation of the sales comparison approach.

**Highest and best use.** Value is measured by the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. A house on a corner zoned commercial may be worth more as a site than as a house.

**Conformity.** Value is maximised where a property conforms reasonably to its surroundings.

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 1.1
chunks.excerpt:
**Progression and regression.** A modest house among expensive ones benefits; an expensive house among modest ones is dragged down. This is why over-improvement is a real financial risk and why a licensee should be candid with a seller who has spent heavily.

**Contribution.** An improvement adds what it contributes to value, not what it cost.

**Supply and demand**, **change**, **anticipation**, and **externalities** complete the ordinary set.

#### Checkpoint 1.1

A seller has spent $80,000 finishing a basement and adding a sunroom, and wants the price raised by $80,000. What principles apply?

*Answer:* Contribution — improvements add what they contribute, which is measured in the market, not what they cost. Regression, if the improvements have pushed the house above its neighbourhood. The licensee's job is to show the seller comparable sales with and without similar features and let the data carry the conversation, rather than arguing about the number.

## 2. The sales comparison approach

### 2.1 The method

Find recent sales of similar properties, adjust them for their differences from the subject, and reconcile the adjusted figures into an indication of value.

It is the primary approach for residential property because substitution is how residential buyers actually behave.

### 2.2 Choosing comparables

Recent, nearby, and similar. In practice: closed sales within six months where the market allows, in the same neighbourhood or a genuinely comparable one, of similar age, size, style, and condition, sold in ordinary arm's-length conditions.

Three sales is the working minimum. Sales that are not arm's length — between relatives, foreclosure sales, estate sales — are used only with care and only where the market consists of them.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Adjusting, and the direction that confuses everyone
chunks.excerpt:
### 2.3 Adjusting, and the direction that confuses everyone

**Adjust the comparable, never the subject.** The subject is what you are trying to value; you do not know its value yet.

**If the comparable is better than the subject, subtract.** If the comparable is worse, add.

Say the subject has two bathrooms and the comparable has three, and the market shows a bathroom contributing $9,000. The comparable is superior, so its sale price is adjusted **downward** by $9,000 to indicate what it would have sold for with two.

Students reverse this constantly. The sentence to memorise: **CBS — comparable better, subtract.**

### 2.4 A worked analysis

Subject: 1,780 square feet, three bedrooms, two baths, attached two-car garage, no basement finish, built 1996.

| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sale price | $312,000 | $298,500 | $324,000 |
| Square feet | 1,820 | 1,700 | 1,780 |
| Baths | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| Garage | 2-car | 1-car | 2-car |
| Finished basement | No | No | Yes |
| Adjustments | | | |
| Size at $55/sq ft | −2,200 | +4,400 | 0 |
| Bath at $9,000 | 0 | 0 | −9,000 |
| Garage at $8,000 | 0 | +8,000 | 0 |
| Basement at $14,000 | 0 | 0 | −14,000 |
| **Adjusted** | **$309,800** | **$310,900** | **$301,000** |

Reconciliation is judgment, not arithmetic. The three adjusted figures cluster between $301,000 and $310,900. Comp C required the largest gross adjustment, which makes it the least reliable indicator. A defensible indication is roughly $308,000 to $310,000, weighted toward A and B.

**Never average.** An average treats a poorly matched comparable as equal to a good one, and reconciliation exists precisely to avoid that.

### 2.5 Where adjustment values come from

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 2.1
chunks.excerpt:
From the market — paired sales showing what buyers actually paid for the difference — not from cost and not from an owner's estimate. A licensee who cannot support an adjustment should be conservative with it and should say in the analysis where it came from.

#### Checkpoint 2.1

A comparable sold for $284,000 and has one fewer bedroom than the subject, with the market indicating $12,000 per bedroom in this range. What is the adjusted figure?

*Answer:* $296,000. The comparable is inferior — fewer bedrooms — so the adjustment is upward. If it had one more bedroom the adjustment would be downward to $272,000.

## 3. The cost approach

### 3.1 The method

Estimate the value of the land as though vacant; add the cost to construct the improvements new; subtract accrued depreciation.

Land value plus depreciated improvement cost equals the value indication.

### 3.2 Reproduction and replacement

**Reproduction cost** builds an exact replica, including obsolete features. **Replacement cost** builds a structure of equivalent utility using current materials and methods. Replacement is the ordinary basis; reproduction matters for historic property.

### 3.3 Depreciation

**Physical deterioration** — wear, age, deferred maintenance. Curable where the cost to fix is recovered in value; incurable where it is not.

**Functional obsolescence** — a defect in the structure itself. A three-bedroom house with one bathroom; a bedroom reachable only through another; a floor plan the market has rejected. Curable or incurable.

**External obsolescence** — caused by something outside the property. A new arterial road, a closed employer, an adjacent industrial use. **Always incurable**, because the owner cannot fix what is off their land.

### 3.4 When the cost approach is the right one

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 3.1
chunks.excerpt:
New construction, where depreciation is minimal. Special-purpose property — a church, a school, a fire station — with no meaningful sales market. Insurance valuation. And as a check on the other approaches.

It is weakest for older residential property, where depreciation estimates dominate the answer and are themselves estimates.

#### Checkpoint 3.1

A house backs onto a parcel where a distribution centre has just been approved. Which kind of depreciation, and can it be cured?

*Answer:* External obsolescence, and no. The cause is off the property and outside the owner's control, which is what makes external obsolescence incurable by definition. It is a genuine value effect and a material fact for disclosure once known.

## 4. The income approach

### 4.1 Direct capitalisation

For income property, value is derived from the income it produces.

**Value = Net Operating Income ÷ Capitalisation Rate.**

Net operating income is effective gross income less operating expenses. It does **not** subtract debt service, depreciation, or income taxes — a point students get wrong.

Worked: a small building with $86,000 potential gross income, 6 percent vacancy and collection loss, and $31,500 of operating expenses.

- Effective gross income: 86,000 − (86,000 × 0.06) = 86,000 − 5,160 = $80,840.
- Net operating income: 80,840 − 31,500 = $49,340.
- At an 8.25 percent capitalisation rate: 49,340 ÷ 0.0825 = **$598,061**.

Rearranged: cap rate = NOI ÷ value; NOI = value × cap rate. A student should be able to solve for any of the three.

### 4.2 The gross rent multiplier

A rough residential tool. GRM = sale price ÷ gross monthly rent. Derived from comparable sales and applied to the subject's rent.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Reconciliation
chunks.excerpt:
If comparables show a GRM of 138 and the subject rents for $1,850 monthly, the indication is 138 × 1,850 = $255,300. Its weakness is that it ignores expenses entirely, which is why it is a screen and not a valuation.

### 4.3 Reconciliation

An appraiser weights the approaches according to the property and the data, and reconciles to a single conclusion. Residential work weights sales comparison heavily; income property weights the income approach; special-purpose property leans on cost.

#### Checkpoint 4.1

An owner reports NOI of $52,000 but has subtracted his mortgage payments to get there. What must be corrected?

*Answer:* Debt service is not an operating expense and must be added back. Two owners of identical buildings with different loans would otherwise show different NOIs for the same property, which is precisely what the definition excludes. Correct the figure before capitalising it.

## 5. Market analysis and the appraisal boundary

### 5.1 What a licensee may do

From module 01: providing or offering to provide a market analysis is licensed real estate activity in Michigan. A licensee may prepare a comparative market analysis for a client and may be paid for it.

### 5.2 What a licensee may not do

Prepare an appraisal, describe a market analysis as an appraisal, use appraisal terminology to dress one up, or accept an engagement that calls for an appraisal — a federally related transaction, a lending decision requiring one, a court proceeding requiring an appraiser's opinion.

Appraisal is separately licensed and separately regulated in Michigan, and the appraiser works to the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.

### 5.3 Preparing a defensible market analysis

chunks.heading: 5.4 Pricing conversations
chunks.excerpt:
**Label it accurately** — a comparative market analysis, prepared by a real estate licensee, not an appraisal.

**Show the comparables and the adjustments**, so the client can see the reasoning rather than being handed a number.

**State the source of every figure** — closed sales data, the source of adjustment values, the assessor's record where used.

**Give a range and explain the reconciliation.** A single number implies a precision the method does not have.

**Date it**, because a market analysis is a statement about a moment.

**Disclose your interest.** A market analysis prepared in the hope of a listing is honest work with an obvious incentive, and saying so costs nothing.

### 5.4 Pricing conversations

A seller's number and the market's number differ often. Three things help.

**Lead with the data, not the conclusion.** The comparables carry more weight than the licensee's opinion.

**Separate cost from value** — module 09, section 1.1 — because the seller is usually thinking about what they spent.

**Be explicit about the consequences of overpricing:** longer time on market, a stale listing, and often a lower final price than an accurate one would have produced. That is a professional judgment supported by market behaviour, and it is the advice the seller is paying for.

What a licensee must not do is inflate an analysis to win a listing. It is a misrepresentation, it damages the client, and it produces the price reduction conversation six weeks later from a worse position.

#### Checkpoint 5.1

A lender asks a licensee for "a quick valuation" for a home-equity decision, offering a fee. May the licensee accept?

chunks.heading: 6. Applied mathematics
chunks.excerpt:
*Answer:* No. A valuation for a lender's credit decision is appraisal work, separately licensed, and describing a market analysis as adequate for it would misrepresent both the product and the licensee's authority. The correct response is to decline and refer the lender to a licensed appraiser.

## 6. Applied mathematics

### 6.1 Area

**Rectangle:** length × width. **Triangle:** ½ × base × height. **Composite shapes:** divide into rectangles and triangles and sum.

An acre is **43,560 square feet**. A parcel 250 by 300 feet is 75,000 square feet, or 75,000 ÷ 43,560 = **1.72 acres**.

A section is 640 acres — module 03 — and description fractions divide from there.

### 6.2 Commission

A commission of 6 percent on $327,500 is $19,650. Split evenly between listing and selling brokerages, each receives $9,825. If the salesperson's agreement with their broker is 65 percent, the salesperson receives 9,825 × 0.65 = **$6,386.25**.

Working backwards: a salesperson who received $5,400 on a 60 percent split from a brokerage side of a 3 percent share had a brokerage side of 5,400 ÷ 0.60 = $9,000, on a sale price of 9,000 ÷ 0.03 = **$300,000**.

### 6.3 Proration

Prorations divide a shared expense at closing between seller and buyer. The two conventions are a 360-day banker's year with 30-day months, and a 365-day calendar year. **The contract states which.**

Michigan tax prorations carry a local complication: whether taxes are treated as paid in advance or in arrears is a matter of local custom that differs across the state, and the purchase agreement should say. A licensee must not assume the convention from another county.

Worked, on the 365-day method: annual tax of $3,650 on a closing of 12 September, with the day of closing charged to the buyer.

chunks.heading: 6.4 Investment measures
chunks.excerpt:
- Daily rate: 3,650 ÷ 365 = $10.00.
- Seller's days, 1 January to 11 September: 254.
- Seller's share: 254 × 10.00 = **$2,540**. Buyer's share: $1,110.

Whether that appears as a credit or a charge depends on whether the bill has been paid, which is why the closing statement in module 10 is read line by line.

### 6.4 Investment measures

**Return on investment** = annual net income ÷ investment. $18,600 on $240,000 is 7.75 percent.

**Cash-on-cash return** = annual pre-tax cash flow ÷ cash invested. On $62,000 invested with $5,890 cash flow, 9.5 percent.

**Equity** = market value less liens. A $340,000 property with a $214,000 mortgage carries $126,000 of equity.

**Appreciation.** A property bought at $265,000 and worth $312,000 has appreciated 47,000 ÷ 265,000 = **17.7 percent**.

### 6.5 Percentages, and the direction of the base

The most common arithmetic error in this field is dividing by the wrong number. A property that sold for 4 percent below its $325,000 list price sold for 325,000 × 0.96 = $312,000. But a property that sold for $312,000 after a reduction *from* $325,000 fell by 13,000 ÷ 325,000 = 4 percent — and if someone then says the buyer "paid 4 percent more" than $312,000, that is 312,000 × 1.04 = $324,480, which is not $325,000.

Always identify the base before computing the percentage.

#### Checkpoint 6.1

A parcel measures 400 feet along the road and 550 feet deep, with a triangular addition 400 feet wide at the base and 120 feet deep. How many acres?

*Answer:* Rectangle 400 × 550 = 220,000 square feet. Triangle ½ × 400 × 120 = 24,000. Total 244,000 ÷ 43,560 = **5.60 acres**.

## Key terms

**Capitalisation rate** — the rate converting net operating income into value.

chunks.heading: Practice problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Comparative market analysis** — a licensee's opinion of probable selling price, drawn from market data; not an appraisal.

**External obsolescence** — loss in value from a cause outside the property; always incurable.

**Gross rent multiplier** — sale price divided by gross rent; a screening tool.

**Highest and best use** — the legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive use.

**Net operating income** — effective gross income less operating expenses, before debt service and taxes.

**Reconciliation** — the weighted judgment producing a single value conclusion from several indications.

**Regression** — the drag exerted on a superior property by inferior surroundings.

## Practice problems

**Problem 1.** A comparable sold at $349,000. It has a three-car garage where the subject has two, worth $10,000 in this market, and 120 fewer square feet at $60 per foot. Adjust it.

*Working:* Garage superior: −$10,000. Size inferior: +$7,200. Adjusted: 349,000 − 10,000 + 7,200 = **$346,200**.

**Problem 2.** A building produces $124,000 potential gross income with 8 percent vacancy and $46,800 of operating expenses. At a 7.5 percent cap rate, what is the indicated value?

*Working:* EGI = 124,000 − 9,920 = $114,080. NOI = 114,080 − 46,800 = $67,280. Value = 67,280 ÷ 0.075 = **$897,067**.

**Problem 3.** A house sells for $289,000 at 5.5 percent commission, split 50/50 between brokerages, with the listing salesperson on a 70 percent split. What does the salesperson receive?

*Working:* Total 289,000 × 0.055 = $15,895. Listing brokerage 15,895 ÷ 2 = $7,947.50. Salesperson 7,947.50 × 0.70 = **$5,563.25**.

chunks.heading: Module summary
chunks.excerpt:
**Problem 4.** Annual taxes of $4,745 on a 30 June closing, 365-day method, seller pays through the day before closing, taxes paid in advance by the seller. Who owes whom?

*Working:* Daily 4,745 ÷ 365 = $13.00. Seller's days 1 January to 29 June = 180. Seller's share 180 × 13.00 = $2,340. The seller has paid the whole year, so the buyer reimburses 4,745 − 2,340 = **$2,405** as a credit to the seller.

**Problem 5.** An investor pays $410,000, puts $95,000 down, and clears $8,075 after debt service in year one. Compute cash-on-cash return.

*Working:* 8,075 ÷ 95,000 = **8.5 percent**.

**Problem 6.** A seller insists on listing at $389,000 when the analysis supports $352,000 to $358,000. What does the licensee do?

*Working:* Present the data, state the professional opinion in writing including the expected consequences, and let the seller decide — it is their property. If the licensee takes the listing, the file should contain the analysis and the recommendation, so that the later price-reduction conversation begins from a record rather than an argument. What the licensee must not do is adopt the seller's number as though the analysis supported it.

## Module summary

**Market value, price, and cost are three different numbers**, and the gap between cost and value is where seller expectations live.

**Value needs demand, utility, scarcity, and transferability** — all four.

**Substitution drives residential valuation**, which is why sales comparison is the primary approach.

**Adjust the comparable, never the subject; comparable better, subtract.**

**Reconcile, do not average.** The comparable requiring the largest adjustment is the least reliable.

**Depreciation is physical, functional, or external**, and external is always incurable.

chunks.heading: Required applied exercise
chunks.excerpt:
**NOI excludes debt service.** Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate, and the relation solves in any direction.

**A market analysis is licensed work; an appraisal is not the licensee's to give.** Label it accurately, show the reasoning, state sources, give a range, and date it.

**Identify the base before computing any percentage.**

## Required applied exercise

Prepare a comparative market analysis memorandum for the subject property supplied with this module. Select and justify at least three comparables; show every adjustment with its direction and its source; reconcile to a supported range rather than averaging; state the assumptions and the date; identify what the analysis is not and what would require an appraiser; and draft the pricing recommendation you would give the seller in writing. The approved instructor scores it under the common 10-point applied-memo rubric; 8/10 with no zero on legal accuracy or professional boundaries is satisfactory, and a needs-revision result receives feedback and must be resubmitted.

## Knowledge check and remediation

After submitting the memo, complete the one-item applied confirmation check at 100 percent, then the five-item engagement check at 80 percent. A missed confirmation returns you to the relevant instruction. An unsuccessful engagement attempt opens remediation with an alternate explanation, a second worked scenario, and a separately authored five-item set. The module cannot complete until the memo is satisfactory, the confirmation is correct, and the student reaches the StateCourse 80 percent threshold on any remediation set — R 339.22157(2)(f).

## Module completion

chunks.heading: Module completion
chunks.excerpt: Completion requires all six instructional sections, the applied exercise, the engagement check, and any triggered remediation. Michigan requires attendance at 100 percent of a prelicensure course and, for distance learning, hours attended equal to hours approved (R 339.22152).

lessons.title: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 10

chunks.heading: Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 10
chunks.excerpt:
# Principles of Real Estate - Michigan Salesperson Prelicensure — Module 10

## Closing, trust accounts, and professional practice

**Course version:** 1.0-submission-draft
**Module time:** 4 clock hours (240 instructional minutes)
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Michigan prelicensure credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Describe what happens at a Michigan closing, who does what, and what the licensee is responsible for before it.
- Read a settlement statement line by line and identify what each entry does to each party's bottom line.
- Apply Michigan's trust and escrow account rules, including what must never happen to client money.
- Apply the broker's obligation when a transaction fails and the parties dispute a deposit.
- Identify the professional-practice obligations that survive a closing — records, supervision, advertising, and continuing education.
- State what a new licensee should establish in their first weeks to avoid the failures this course has described.

## Timed sequence

| Activity | Minutes | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Guided reading: the closing and the settlement statement | 75 | Sections 1-2 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: trust accounts and disputed deposits | 70 | Sections 3-4 recorded as viewed |
| Guided reading: professional practice and the first year | 65 | Sections 5-6 recorded as viewed |
| Applied exercise: closing-file memorandum + confirmation | 20 | Written response and applied-confirmation result recorded |
| Scored engagement check | 10 | Five items submitted |
| **Total** | **240** | **One of ten modules of instruction** |

## 1. Closing

### 1.1 What a closing is

chunks.heading: 1.2 The licensee's work happens before
chunks.excerpt:
Closing is the performance of the purchase agreement: the price is paid, the deed is delivered, the mortgage is executed and recorded, liens are paid and released, and possession passes according to the contract.

In Michigan the closing is customarily conducted by a **title company**, which acts as the settlement agent, disburses the funds, and records the instruments. Lawyers are involved in some transactions and not others.

### 1.2 The licensee's work happens before

Almost everything a licensee does for a closing is done in the weeks before it. By closing day the licensee's job is largely to have made the day uneventful.

The pre-closing checklist that matters:

- Every contingency satisfied, waived in writing, or extended in writing.
- Title commitment reviewed, Schedule B-I requirements assigned to whoever must satisfy them, Schedule B-II exceptions delivered to the client.
- Payoffs ordered. Discharges of old mortgages identified and chased.
- Seller's sworn statement and unconditional lien waivers obtained where work was done — module 04.
- Association documents, dues status, and any pending assessment confirmed.
- Municipal requirements — point-of-sale inspection, certificate of occupancy, well and septic — identified and satisfied.
- Utilities arranged for transfer, and final readings scheduled.
- Insurance bound for the buyer, effective on closing.
- The final walkthrough scheduled close to closing, not days before.
- Closing Disclosure timing confirmed with the lender — module 08.
- The parties told what identification and what funds they must bring, and in what form.

### 1.3 The walkthrough

The buyer's opportunity to confirm that the property is in the agreed condition, that agreed repairs were done, and that included items are present.

chunks.heading: 1.4 Possession
chunks.excerpt:
It is not a re-inspection and not a renegotiation, though it becomes one when something is wrong. The licensee's role is to be present, to document with dated photographs, and to raise problems immediately rather than at the closing table where the pressure to overlook is greatest.

### 1.4 Possession

Closing and possession are different events. Where they differ, the occupancy agreement from module 06 governs — the daily rate, the escrow, the condition required, and the remedy if the seller does not leave.

A licensee should treat "the seller will be out by the weekend" as an unwritten agreement that has not been made.

#### Checkpoint 1.1

At the walkthrough the agreed furnace repair has not been done and the seller's contractor cannot come for two weeks. What are the options?

*Answer:* Delay closing; hold funds in escrow at the title company against the repair with a written agreement on amount, scope, and deadline; or the buyer accepts a credit and takes the work on. All three are contract amendments requiring signatures. What must not happen is a verbal promise at the table and a closing on the strength of it.

## 2. The settlement statement

### 2.1 What it is

The settlement statement — for most consumer mortgages, the Closing Disclosure — shows every dollar moving in the transaction: what the buyer pays and finances, what the seller receives, and every charge against each.

A licensee should be able to read one and explain any line to a client, and should review it **before** closing day so that errors are corrected while there is time.

### 2.2 Debits and credits

**Debit** — a charge against a party. **Credit** — an amount in their favour.

chunks.heading: 2.3 A worked statement
chunks.excerpt:
The purchase price is a debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller. Earnest money already paid is a credit to the buyer. The loan amount is a credit to the buyer. Payoff of the seller's mortgage is a debit to the seller. Commission is a debit to the seller, or to whoever the agreement charges.

Prorations run both ways depending on what has been paid — module 09, section 6.3.

### 2.3 A worked statement

Price $310,000; earnest money $5,000 held by the title company; buyer's loan $248,000; seller's mortgage payoff $186,420; total commission 5.5 percent; seller pays state and county transfer tax of $2,635; taxes of $4,380 paid in advance by the seller with closing on 1 October, 365-day method; buyer's closing costs $4,150; seller's other closing costs $1,180.

**Buyer:**
- Debit — purchase price: $310,000
- Credit — earnest money: $5,000
- Credit — loan: $248,000
- Debit — closing costs: $4,150
- Debit — tax proration, 92 days at $12.00: $1,104
- **Cash to close: 310,000 + 4,150 + 1,104 − 5,000 − 248,000 = $62,254**

**Seller:**
- Credit — purchase price: $310,000
- Debit — mortgage payoff: $186,420
- Debit — commission at 5.5 percent: $17,050
- Debit — transfer tax: $2,635
- Debit — other costs: $1,180
- Credit — tax proration: $1,104
- **Net proceeds: 310,000 + 1,104 − 186,420 − 17,050 − 2,635 − 1,180 = $103,819**

The tax proration appears on both sides in opposite directions, which is the structure students most often mis-handle: the seller prepaid the year, so the buyer reimburses the seller for the 92 days from 1 October to 31 December.

### 2.4 Reviewing it

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 2.1
chunks.excerpt:
Check the price, the credits, the commission, the payoff, the prorations, and the names and capacities of the parties. A settlement statement with a seller named differently from the deed is a problem discovered too late — module 03.

#### Checkpoint 2.1

A seller's statement shows a $1,900 charge for a repair credit the parties agreed to, but the purchase agreement was never amended. What is the issue?

*Answer:* The statement reflects an agreement that does not exist in writing. Either the amendment gets signed before closing or the charge does not belong on the statement. And where the transaction is financed, an undisclosed credit raises the lender-disclosure problem from module 08 — the credit must be visible to the lender, not arranged around it.

## 3. Trust and escrow accounts

### 3.1 Whose money it is

Money a broker receives belonging to someone else — earnest money, security deposits, rent collected for owners, funds held for repairs — is **not the broker's money**. It is held in trust, and the rules exist because the temptation is obvious and the harm is severe.

R 339.22134 governs trust and escrow accounts for Michigan brokers.

### 3.2 The rules

**Deposit promptly** in a designated trust or escrow account, separate from the broker's operating funds.

**Never commingle.** The broker's money does not go into the trust account, beyond any minimum the bank requires to keep it open, and trust money never goes into the operating account.

**Never convert.** Using client money for any purpose other than the one it was received for is conversion, and it is the fastest route from a licence to a criminal matter.

**Keep records** identifying whose money is in the account, for what, and when it moved. A ledger per transaction and a reconciliation of the whole.

chunks.heading: 3.3 Property management
chunks.excerpt:
**Disburse only as authorised** — by the contract, by the parties' written agreement, or by a court.

**A salesperson does not hold trust money.** Funds received go to the broker promptly for deposit. This is module 01's chain of authority in its most consequential form.

### 3.3 Property management

Property management magnifies every one of these. Rent collected belongs to owners. Security deposits are held under Michigan's security deposit statute, with its own requirements about where deposits are held, the notice a tenant receives, and the timeline for accounting after a tenancy ends.

A property manager's trust accounting is not a variation on brokerage trust accounting; it is the same discipline applied to more money moving more often.

### 3.4 Reconciliation

The trust account is reconciled regularly against the individual ledgers, and the total of the ledgers must equal the account balance. A discrepancy is investigated immediately, not at month end.

This is the control that catches errors before they become shortfalls, and the absence of it is what turns a mistake into a pattern.

#### Checkpoint 3.1

A broker's operating account is short for payroll and the trust account holds $60,000 of earnest money. The broker intends to move $8,000 and replace it Friday. Evaluate.

*Answer:* This is conversion, and the intention to repay does not change it. Trust money may be disbursed only for its own purpose and only as authorised. The fact that the money would be back before anyone noticed is a description of concealment, not a defence. A licensee who is asked to participate refuses and escalates outside the brokerage if necessary.

## 4. When a transaction fails

### 4.1 The disputed deposit

chunks.heading: 4.2 What the licensee does
chunks.excerpt:
A transaction collapses and both parties claim the earnest money. This is common, and it is the situation where a broker's obligations are most misunderstood.

**The broker does not decide who is right.** The broker holds the funds until the parties agree in writing, or a court orders their disposition, or the applicable procedure for resolving the dispute is followed. Releasing to one party because their argument seems better exposes the broker to the other.

### 4.2 What the licensee does

Get the facts in writing from both sides. Escalate to the broker immediately. Tell each party that the licensee cannot adjudicate the dispute and cannot advise them on their rights. Route both parties to counsel. Document every step and every communication.

The licensee's instinct here is to solve it, and that instinct is the problem. A licensee who tells one party they are entitled to the money has given legal advice and taken a side.

### 4.3 The other failures

**Financing falls through.** Whether the contingency was live, whether it was properly exercised, and by when, decides the outcome. The file's dates answer it.

**A party refuses to close.** Remedies from module 06 — damages, specific performance, forfeiture — are legal questions.

**A death or incapacity** during a transaction raises authority questions that stop everything until an estate or a fiduciary is in place.

**A title defect surfaces late.** Whether the seller can cure and by when, and what the buyer may do, comes from the contract and from counsel.

### 4.4 What survives the failure

Confidentiality survives. The obligation to account for money survives. The record survives, and it is the only thing that will speak for the licensee if the failure becomes a complaint.

#### Checkpoint 4.1

chunks.heading: 5. Professional practice
chunks.excerpt:
A buyer terminates two days after the inspection deadline and demands the deposit. The seller refuses. The buyer's agent believes the buyer is right. What does the agent do?

*Answer:* Nothing that resolves it. The agent escalates to their broker, tells the buyer that the deposit's disposition is not the agent's to decide and that the question is a legal one, refers them to counsel, and documents the timeline — particularly the deadline and the date of the termination notice, which is what the dispute will turn on. Believing the buyer is right is not authority to act on it.

## 5. Professional practice

### 5.1 Records

For the brokerage, the transaction file is the evidence: the agreements, the disclosures, the amendments, the correspondence, the settlement statement, the notes of what was said and when. For a school, R 339.22154 requires a permanent record of each student.

The habit from module 01 stands: an action without a record is, in a dispute, an action that may not have happened.

### 5.2 Supervision

The broker's supervisory duty is affirmative — module 01. A new licensee should expect their broker to review files, approve advertising, and be available for the escalations this course keeps recommending. A brokerage where none of that happens is a brokerage where the new licensee will be alone with problems they are not equipped for.

### 5.3 Advertising, again

Michigan requires advertising to identify the brokerage. Every factual claim is a representation. Fair-housing rules apply to words, images, and targeting — module 07. Online material outlives its deletion.

### 5.4 Continuing education

chunks.heading: 5.5 Discipline
chunks.excerpt:
Michigan licensees complete continuing education on the renewal cycle, and R 339.22161 governs it. Two points a new licensee should know: prelicensure credit does not substitute for continuing education, and continuing education does not substitute for prelicensure credit — MCL 339.2504 says so expressly in both directions.

### 5.5 Discipline

Section 602 of the Occupational Code supplies penalties. R 339.22155 adds education-specific grounds. Conduct that leads to discipline is, almost always, conduct this course has already named: misrepresentation, failure to disclose, mishandling trust money, discrimination, unlicensed activity, and advertising that misleads.

### 5.6 Ethics beyond the rules

The rules set a floor. Most of what makes a licensee trustworthy sits above it: telling a client something they do not want to hear, declining a listing at a price you cannot support, saying "I don't know" and then finding out, refusing a transaction that would work only if a document said something untrue.

None of that is enforceable and all of it is what a client is actually buying.

#### Checkpoint 5.1

A broker's office has no file review, no advertising approval, and tells new licensees to "ask if you need anything." Is that supervision?

*Answer:* No. Supervision is an affirmative duty discharged by a system, not by availability. The broker is accountable for the licensees' conduct whether or not they look at it. For a new licensee choosing a brokerage, the presence of real file review is one of the few reliable indicators of what their first year will be like.

## 6. The first year

### 6.1 What to establish in the first month

**A file standard.** One folder per transaction, every document dated, every conversation that matters recorded the same day.

chunks.heading: 6.2 The failures this course has described
chunks.excerpt:
**A diary.** Every deadline from every contract, entered when the contract is signed, with a reminder before it — module 06.

**Scripts.** The agency disclosure sentence, the neighbourhood-question answer from module 07, the referral sentence from module 01. Written down and rehearsed, because they are needed under pressure.

**A referral list.** Inspectors, lenders, title companies, surveyors, lawyers — more than one of each, with any financial relationship disclosed.

**A relationship with your broker.** Know how to reach them, and use it early rather than late.

### 6.2 The failures this course has described

Every one of them is preventable, and they recur:

- Practising law by answering a question that needed a lawyer.
- Repeating a figure — square footage, acreage, taxes, school district — without its source.
- Quoting the seller's tax bill as the buyer's future tax, without the uncapping warning from module 04.
- Missing a contingency deadline.
- Letting an agency disclosure happen after the buyer has explained their maximum.
- Steering while trying to be helpful.
- Holding a cheque instead of getting it to the broker.
- Preparing a document that says something untrue to a lender.
- Advertising without identifying the brokerage.
- Having no record of what was said.

### 6.3 What competence looks like

A competent licensee is not one who knows every rule. It is one who notices when a question has left their authority, routes it to the right person, meets the deadline, and writes it down.

That is the whole discipline, and it is available to a licensee on their first day.

### 6.4 After this course

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 6.1
chunks.excerpt:
Completing this course satisfies, if the Department approves it, the education requirement in MCL 339.2504. It does not make anyone a licensee: the examination, the application, and association with a broker follow.

**Nothing in this course is legal advice, and completing it does not create Michigan credit while the course is unapproved.**

#### Checkpoint 6.1

A new licensee's first client asks a question the licensee cannot answer, in front of the client's spouse, and the licensee feels the pressure to say something. What is the right response?

*Answer:* "I don't know, and I'm not going to guess on something this important. Let me find out and come back to you today." It costs nothing, it is more impressive than a confident wrong answer, and it is the sentence that separates the licensees who last from the ones who appear in complaints.

## Key terms

**Commingling** — mixing trust funds with the broker's own money; prohibited.

**Conversion** — using trust money for a purpose other than the one it was received for.

**Credit** — an amount in a party's favour on a settlement statement.

**Debit** — a charge against a party on a settlement statement.

**Reconciliation** — matching the trust account balance against the individual transaction ledgers.

**Settlement agent** — the party conducting the closing, in Michigan customarily a title company.

**Walkthrough** — the buyer's pre-closing confirmation of condition and included items.

## Practice problems

**Problem 1.** Price $268,500, earnest money $3,000, loan $214,800, buyer's closing costs $3,890, tax proration debiting the buyer $940. Compute cash to close.

*Working:* 268,500 + 3,890 + 940 − 3,000 − 214,800 = **$55,530**.

chunks.heading: Practice problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Problem 2.** Same transaction: seller's payoff $151,200, commission 6 percent, transfer tax $2,283, other seller costs $960, tax proration crediting the seller $940. Compute net proceeds.

*Working:* Commission 268,500 × 0.06 = $16,110. Net = 268,500 + 940 − 151,200 − 16,110 − 2,283 − 960 = **$98,887**.

**Problem 3.** A salesperson receives a $4,000 earnest money cheque on a Saturday. The office is closed until Tuesday. What should happen?

*Working:* The cheque goes to the broker for deposit as promptly as the broker's procedure allows, and the salesperson should know that procedure before they need it. A salesperson holding client funds over a weekend is a problem waiting for a complaint; if the brokerage has no weekend procedure, that is a question to ask in week one, not week forty.

**Problem 4.** Both parties instruct the broker in writing to release the deposit to the buyer. May the broker?

*Working:* Yes. Written agreement of both parties is one of the authorised bases for disbursement. What the broker may not do is release on one party's instruction, or on the broker's own view of who is right.

**Problem 5.** A seller asks the licensee to delay recording the deed until January for tax reasons.

*Working:* Recording timing affects notice and priority — module 03 — and the tax consequence is a legal and accounting question. The licensee does not control recording, does not advise on the tax effect, and should route the request to the title company and to the seller's accountant or lawyer. Agreeing to it as a favour is advice the licensee is not licensed to give.

**Problem 6.** Six weeks after closing, a buyer calls to say the basement flooded and the seller must have known. What does the licensee do?

chunks.heading: Module summary
chunks.excerpt:
*Working:* Take the facts in writing, do not speculate about what the seller knew, do not offer a view on the buyer's remedy, notify the broker, preserve the file including the seller's disclosure statement and every communication, and refer the buyer to counsel. This is exactly the moment the record from module 06 either protects the licensee or does not exist.

## Module summary

**Closing is the performance of the contract**, conducted in Michigan customarily by a title company — and the licensee's work is done in the weeks before it.

**Read the settlement statement before closing day.** Debits charge, credits favour, and prorations appear on both sides in opposite directions.

**Trust money is never the broker's.** Deposit promptly, never commingle, never convert, record, reconcile, and disburse only as authorised. A salesperson does not hold it.

**A disputed deposit is not the broker's to decide.** Hold, escalate, refer, document.

**Records, supervision, advertising, and continuing education are the practice obligations that outlast any transaction.**

**Every failure this course describes is preventable**, and the prevention is the same each time: notice the limit, route it, meet the deadline, write it down.

## Required applied exercise

chunks.heading: Knowledge check and remediation
chunks.excerpt:
Prepare a one-page closing file review memorandum for the transaction supplied with this module. Build the buyer's cash to close and the seller's net proceeds line by line; identify every entry that does not match the agreement; list every pre-closing item that remains outstanding and who must satisfy it; identify any trust-money handling issue; and state what you would raise with your broker before closing day. The approved instructor scores it under the common 10-point applied-memo rubric; 8/10 with no zero on legal accuracy or professional boundaries is satisfactory, and a needs-revision result receives feedback and must be resubmitted.

## Knowledge check and remediation

After submitting the memo, complete the one-item applied confirmation check at 100 percent, then the five-item engagement check at 80 percent. A missed confirmation returns you to the relevant instruction. An unsuccessful engagement attempt opens remediation with an alternate explanation, a second worked scenario, and a separately authored five-item set. The module cannot complete until the memo is satisfactory, the confirmation is correct, and the student reaches the StateCourse 80 percent threshold on any remediation set — R 339.22157(2)(f).

## Module completion

Completion requires all six instructional sections, the applied exercise, the engagement check, and any triggered remediation. Michigan requires attendance at 100 percent of a prelicensure course and, for distance learning, hours attended equal to hours approved (R 339.22152). Completing this module completes the course only when the other nine are complete; and no completion creates a licence, an application, or Michigan credit while this course is unapproved.

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-01

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-01
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-01

## Hours 1–5 · Real property, ownership, and the real estate business

**Clock hours:** 5. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour Salesperson Pre-Examination Course to be developed from the detailed content outline
supplied by the professional testing service contracted to administer the examination. This project
has not read that outline.** The module structure and hour allocation below are therefore
StateCourse's, and the course must be reconciled against the outline before submission.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module a student can:

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
1. Distinguish land, real estate and real property, and explain why the distinction decides what a
   licensee is actually marketing.
2. Apply the fixture test to a disputed item and state what a licensee does about it at listing.
3. Name the physical and economic characteristics of land and use each to explain a market behaviour.
4. Describe the four government powers over private property and identify which one is operating in
   a given fact pattern.
5. Describe the structure of the real estate business in Missouri — the licence categories, the
   designated broker, the affiliated licensee — and state where a salesperson's authority comes from.
6. Explain why supply responds slowly to demand in real estate and what that does to prices.
7. Identify the six-month education window in § 339.040.6, RSMo, and explain why it matters to the
   student personally.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Land, real estate, real property; the bundle of rights | 50 min |
| 2 | Fixtures, trade fixtures, severance; what a licensee does | 50 min |
| 3 | Characteristics of land; how markets behave | 50 min |
| 4 | Government powers; private property in a regulated system | 50 min |
| 5 | The Missouri real estate business and the path to a licence | 50 min |

Each hour carries up to 10 minutes of recess under 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2). The engagement check at the
end of this module is delivered within the module's assessment allowance; **20 CSR 2250-7.070(2)
permits supervised examination time to be regarded as hours of instruction**, and this course does
not rely on that permission to reach its hour count — the fifty minutes above are teaching.

---

## Hour 1 — Land, real estate, and real property

### 1.1 Three words that are not synonyms

chunks.heading: 1.2 The bundle of rights
chunks.excerpt:
Ordinary speech treats *land*, *real estate* and *real property* as one thing. The law does not, and
a licensee who cannot separate them will make errors in listing, in advertising and in contract.

**Land** is the surface of the earth, the space above it, and the subsurface beneath it — extending
in principle downward toward the centre of the earth and upward into the air, subject to everything
the law has since done to those extremes. Air rights are real and severable; a developer may buy the
right to build above a rail corridor without buying the corridor. Subsurface rights are likewise
severable, and mineral, oil and gas rights may belong to someone who has never seen the surface.

**Real estate** is land plus everything permanently attached to it, whether by nature or by human
effort — trees, water, buildings, fences, in-ground pools, the wiring inside the walls.

**Real property** is real estate plus **the bundle of legal rights** that attach to it. This is the
term that matters most, because it is the only one that describes what is actually being sold. When
a buyer purchases a house they are not purchasing bricks. They are purchasing a set of enforceable
rights against the rest of the world.

### 1.2 The bundle of rights

The traditional bundle contains five rights, and the metaphor is a bundle of sticks precisely because
sticks can be removed one at a time:

- **Possession** — the right to occupy and hold.
- **Use or enjoyment** — the right to use the property in any lawful manner.
- **Exclusion** — the right to keep others out.
- **Disposition** — the right to transfer the interest, by sale, gift, will or otherwise.
- **Encumbrance** — the right to use the property as security, or to grant lesser interests in it.

chunks.heading: 1.3 Personal property, and the line between
chunks.excerpt:
Every stick can be sold, leased, mortgaged, granted or reserved separately. A landowner may convey
the surface and reserve the minerals. A landowner may grant an easement — a slice of the use and
possession sticks — while keeping everything else. A tenant holds possession, use and exclusion for a
term while the landlord holds disposition. A mortgage lender holds a stick that becomes decisive only
if the borrower defaults.

**Why this is the first hour of the course.** Almost every listing dispute a new salesperson meets is
a dispute about which sticks were in the bundle. The seller thought the mineral rights came with the
farm. The buyer thought the boat slip was included. The neighbour thought the driveway easement had
lapsed. None of these is a question about the physical property; all of them are questions about the
