bundle, and the licensee's job is to notice at listing that a stick is missing and get it written
down before anyone photographs the house.

### 1.3 Personal property, and the line between

**Personal property** — *chattels*, in the older vocabulary — is everything that is not real property.
It is movable. It transfers by **bill of sale**, not by deed. It is not conveyed by a contract for
real estate unless the contract says so.

The line matters commercially because it decides what a buyer gets. A refrigerator is personal
property; a built-in oven is usually real estate. A potted tree is personal property; a planted tree
is real estate. Standing timber is real estate; the moment it is cut it becomes personal property, a
transformation called **severance**. The reverse is **annexation** — personal property attached to
land so as to become part of it, which is where the next hour begins.

### 1.4 The licensee's discipline

chunks.heading: Hour 2 — Fixtures, trade fixtures, and the licensee's job
chunks.excerpt:
The professional habit that follows from Hour 1 is simple and is worth adopting before anything else
in the course: **write down what conveys.** At the listing appointment, walk the property with the
seller and settle every item that could be argued about — appliances, window treatments, mounted
televisions, light fixtures, playsets, storage sheds, propane tanks, water treatment equipment. Put
the included and excluded lists in the contract. This costs twenty minutes at listing and saves a
transaction later.

---

## Hour 2 — Fixtures, trade fixtures, and the licensee's job

### 2.1 What a fixture is

A **fixture** is personal property that has been attached to real estate in such a way that it has
become part of it. Once an item is a fixture it conveys with the real estate unless it is expressly
excluded, and the buyer is entitled to find it there at closing.

Whether an item has become a fixture is decided by **the intention of the party who attached it,
judged objectively** — not by what that party privately meant, but by what the circumstances show.
Courts read intention through three kinds of evidence, and the standard mnemonic is **MARIA**, of
which the durable core is:

chunks.heading: 2.2 Trade fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
- **Method of annexation.** How firmly is it attached, and what damage would removal do? A chandelier
  wired into a ceiling box is more firmly annexed than a lamp plugged into a wall.
- **Adaptation to the real estate.** Was the item made or fitted for this particular property? Custom
  storm windows cut for these openings are adapted; a stack of generic screens in the garage is not.
- **Relationship of the parties.** A tenant is treated differently from an owner, and a seller
  differently from a buyer, because the expectations differ.
- **Intention**, read from the above and from any **agreement** the parties made — which is why a
  written agreement settles the question and the absence of one leaves it to be argued.

### 2.2 Trade fixtures

A **trade fixture** is an item a tenant attaches to leased premises for the conduct of their business:
a walk-in cooler in a restaurant, a hydraulic lift in a garage, shelving fitted to a shop floor.

Trade fixtures are the great exception. **They remain the tenant's personal property and may be
removed before the end of the term**, with the tenant responsible for repairing damage caused by
removal. But the right expires with the term. Property left behind after the lease ends generally
becomes the landlord's by **accession** — a departing business that abandons its equipment has
usually made a gift of it.

### 2.3 Where this goes wrong in practice

Three patterns account for most fixture disputes, and all three are preventable at listing:

chunks.heading: 2.4 The Missouri frame
chunks.excerpt:
**The item everyone assumes.** The seller's grandmother's dining room chandelier. It is wired in, it
is a fixture, and it conveys unless excluded. The correct handling is not to note it in the file and
hope: it is to have the seller **remove it and replace it with a fixture that will convey, before the
photographs are taken.** A buyer who fell in love with a photograph of a room has a reasonable
expectation, and a licensee who let that photograph be taken created the problem.

**The item that is not the seller's to convey.** Leased equipment — propane tanks, water softeners,
solar arrays, security systems, some HVAC. It is physically attached and looks like a fixture, and
the seller does not own it. A buyer cannot discover this by looking at it. The licensee's job is to
ask at listing whether any equipment on the property is leased, and to get the answer written down.

**The item installed by a tenant.** On a property with a business tenant, some of what is bolted down
belongs to the tenant and is going with them. That has to be established before a buyer bids on a
building partly furnished with equipment that will leave.

### 2.4 The Missouri frame

Missouri's brokerage relationships statute puts real weight behind this housekeeping. Under
§ 339.730.1(2), RSMo, a seller's agent owes the client the duty **to exercise reasonable skill and
care**. Under § 339.730.1(3)(c) the agent must disclose to the client **all adverse material facts
actually known or that should have been known**. And under § 339.730.3 the agent owes even a
**customer** — a party with no brokerage relationship — the duty to disclose all adverse material
facts actually known or that should have been known.

chunks.heading: Hour 3 — The characteristics of land, and why markets behave as they do
chunks.excerpt:
An **adverse material fact** is defined at § 339.710(1) as *a fact related to the property not
reasonably ascertainable or known to a party which negatively affects the value of the property*, and
the statute's own list includes **material defects in the title to the property**. A leased water
heater that the buyer will inherit a payment obligation for, or an item the seller intends to remove
that the buyer believes conveys, sits close to that line. The safe practice is not to litigate
whether a particular item crosses the statutory threshold. It is to write everything down.

---

## Hour 3 — The characteristics of land, and why markets behave as they do

### 3.1 The physical characteristics

Three, and each explains something about the business:

**Immobility.** A parcel cannot be moved. Demand in Kansas City cannot be satisfied by supply in
Springfield. This is the single most important fact about real estate markets and the reason they are
local: a national statistic about house prices describes no actual market anyone can buy in.
Immobility is also why *location* dominates value and why the same building is worth different
amounts on different streets.

**Indestructibility, or durability.** Land endures. Improvements depreciate, but the land beneath
them does not disappear. This is why land is treated as a long-term investment, why lenders will
write thirty-year loans against it, and why the overwhelming majority of the housing stock in any
Missouri market was built in the past rather than this year.

chunks.heading: 3.2 The economic characteristics
chunks.excerpt:
**Uniqueness, or heterogeneity, or non-homogeneity.** No two parcels are identical; even two
identical houses sit on different ground. This is the legal foundation of **specific performance** as
a remedy in real estate contracts — because damages cannot buy the injured party an equivalent
parcel, courts will order the actual transfer.

### 3.2 The economic characteristics

Four:

**Scarcity.** Land is finite. Not scarce everywhere — Missouri has a great deal of it — but scarce
where people want to be, which is what drives price.

**Improvements.** What is built on and around a parcel changes its value, and improvements to
neighbouring property affect it too. A new interchange, a new school, a new plant.

**Permanence of investment.** Capital sunk into land and improvements — grading, utilities,
foundations, streets — is fixed and long-lived. It cannot be recovered and redeployed elsewhere. This
is why development decisions are slow and why they are hard to reverse.

**Area preference, or *situs*.** People's preference for a particular area, for reasons that are
partly rational and partly not. Situs is the economic expression of immobility, and it is what an
appraiser is measuring when they adjust for location.

### 3.3 Supply, demand, and the lag

Real estate supply is **inelastic in the short run**. Bringing new housing to market takes years:
entitlement, financing, platting, infrastructure, construction. In Missouri the construction season
is further compressed by winter. So when demand rises — a large employer expands, a rate cut brings
buyers off the fence, a demographic wave reaches first-purchase age — supply cannot respond, and the
adjustment happens entirely in **price and in time on market**.

chunks.heading: Hour 4 — Government powers and the limits of private ownership
chunks.excerpt:
That lag is the structural reason real estate cycles. By the time the supply response arrives, the
demand condition that caused it may have passed, which produces the familiar overshoot in both
directions.

**Factors that move demand:** population and household formation, employment and income, interest
rates and credit availability, consumer confidence, and the price of the alternative — rent.

**Factors that move supply:** the availability of land, construction cost including labour and
materials, the cost and availability of construction finance, the entitlement and permitting
environment, and the existing stock coming to market.

**What a licensee may and may not say about this.** Naming these factors and citing recorded data is
providing information. Predicting where prices will go is not — nobody can, and a licensee who states
a forecast as fact has made a representation they cannot support. Under § 339.730.1(2) that is a
reasonable-skill-and-care problem, and under 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)3 the school itself is forbidden
to permit anyone associated with it **to provide any misleading information to the public**.

---

## Hour 4 — Government powers and the limits of private ownership

### 4.1 Four powers, and the mnemonic

Private ownership in the United States has always been ownership **subject to** government authority.
Four powers are traditionally named, and **PETE** holds them:

chunks.heading: 4.2 Where the line between police power and taking runs
chunks.excerpt:
**Police power.** The power to regulate for public health, safety, morals and general welfare —
zoning, building codes, subdivision regulation, environmental controls, licensing. It is exercised
**without compensation**, which is the whole point: a landowner whose property is downzoned and loses
value is generally not entitled to be paid, because the government has regulated rather than taken.

**Eminent domain.** The power to take private property for public use, exercised through the process
called **condemnation**, and requiring **just compensation** under the Fifth Amendment and the
Missouri Constitution. A partial taking — a strip for a road widening — compensates for the strip and
for damage to the remainder.

**Taxation.** The power to raise revenue by charging against property. The real estate tax lien is
the ordinary case, and it customarily takes priority over other liens regardless of recording order.

**Escheat.** The power by which property reverts to the state when an owner dies leaving no heirs and
no will. It exists so that land never becomes ownerless.

### 4.2 Where the line between police power and taking runs

This is a constitutional question, not a licensee's question, and the correct professional response
is to name it and route it. But a licensee should be able to recognise the shape of the argument: a
regulation that goes too far may be a **regulatory taking** requiring compensation, and where that
line falls has occupied the courts for a century. A client who believes a zoning decision has taken
their property needs a lawyer, not a salesperson.

### 4.3 Private limits: the other half

chunks.heading: 4.4 What a licensee does with all of this
chunks.excerpt:
Government is not the only limit. **Private land-use controls** — restrictive covenants, conditions
and restrictions recorded against a subdivision, enforced by the association or by the benefited
owners — operate alongside zoning and are entirely independent of it.

**The more restrictive controls.** A use the city permits may be forbidden by the deed. Buyers
routinely assume that a municipal approval settles the question, and it does not. The covenants are
read before an offer is written, not after a detached garage has been ordered.

### 4.4 What a licensee does with all of this

Identify the question, tell the client it must be answered by whoever answers it, and see that it is
answered before the client's contingencies expire. That last clause is where a licensee actually adds
value. Whether a home occupation is permitted is the municipality's determination; getting the
buyer's question in front of the municipality in week one rather than week four is the licensee's
contribution, and § 339.730.1(3)(d) — the duty to **advise the client to obtain expert advice as to
material matters** beyond the licensee's expertise — is the statutory expression of it.

---

## Hour 5 — The Missouri real estate business

### 5.1 The structure of a Missouri brokerage

Missouri's vocabulary is set by statute and it is worth learning exactly, because the examination
uses it and because the duties attach to the defined terms rather than to ordinary speech.

chunks.heading: 5.2 Where a salesperson's income comes from
chunks.excerpt:
A **designated broker** is, under § 339.710(12), RSMo, an individual licensed as a broker operating
under the definition of real estate broker in § 339.010, or an individual licensed as a broker who is
appointed by a partnership, association, limited liability company, professional corporation or
corporation to be **responsible for the acts of** that entity. Every brokerage entity must appoint
one.

An **affiliated licensee** is, under § 339.710(2), **any broker or salesperson who works under the
supervision of a designated broker.** That is the salesperson's position: a salesperson does not
practise on their own account. Authority flows from the designated broker.

The practical consequence appears immediately in § 339.780.1: **all written agreements for brokerage
services are entered into by the designated broker** on behalf of the broker and the affiliated
licensees — unless the designated broker has authorised affiliated licensees **in writing** to enter
into them. A salesperson signing a listing agreement is doing so on the broker's behalf, under the
broker's written authority, and needs to know that authority exists.

**Every designated broker with affiliated licensees must adopt a written policy** identifying and
describing the relationships the broker and the affiliated licensees may engage in with any seller,
landlord, buyer or tenant — § 339.760. Read your firm's policy on your first day. It tells you which
brokerage relationships you are permitted to offer, and it is not the same at every firm.

### 5.2 Where a salesperson's income comes from

**Compensation is negotiable.** It is not set by any board, association, rule or custom, and any
suggestion that a rate is standard is a serious problem in itself.

chunks.heading: 5.3 The specialties
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.800, RSMo, governs how it moves, and three of its subsections matter to a new licensee:

- **.1** The designated broker's compensation may be paid by the seller, the landlord, the buyer, the
  tenant, or a third party, or shared between designated brokers.
- **.2** **Payment of compensation by itself shall not establish an agency relationship or transaction
  brokerage relationship** between the party who paid and the broker. This is the single most
  misunderstood sentence in Missouri brokerage law. Who pays does not decide whom you represent. The
  written agreement decides.
- **.5** A designated broker may be compensated by more than one party **with the knowledge of all
  the parties at or before the time of entering into a written contract** to buy, sell or lease.

And **.6**: nothing in the section relieves the licensee of the requirement to obtain a written
agreement for brokerage services or another written agreement addressing compensation.

Note also that a salesperson is compensated **by their designated broker**, not by the parties. Money
does not flow from a seller to a salesperson.

### 5.3 The specialties

The business is wider than residential sale. Residential brokerage; commercial brokerage — and note
that § 339.710(7) defines **commercial real estate** as real estate other than one-to-four
residential units or property classified agricultural and horticultural under § 137.016, with
single-family units sold unit-by-unit excluded; farm and land brokerage, which is substantial in
Missouri; property management; appraisal, which is a separately licensed profession and not something
a salesperson does; leasing; auction; development; and the mortgage, title and inspection businesses
that surround every transaction.

chunks.heading: 5.4 The path to a Missouri salesperson licence, and one date that catches people
chunks.excerpt:
**Competence in the specialty is not optional.** 20 CSR 2250-7.060 makes a school responsible for
hiring only instructors with practical experience or formal training in the subject taught, and the
same principle governs a licensee: taking on a property type, a market or a transaction structure
you do not understand is a professional failure before it is a bad outcome. The statutory expression
is § 339.730.1(2), reasonable skill and care.

### 5.4 The path to a Missouri salesperson licence, and one date that catches people

The sequence is: complete the **48-hour Salesperson Pre-Examination Course**; complete the **24-hour
Missouri Real Estate Practice Course**; pass the examination administered by the Commission's
contracted testing service; and apply, with the required certificates, while associated with a
licensed broker.

**And then the fact almost nobody is told in time.** Section 339.040.6, RSMo, requires each
application for a salesperson licence to include a certificate from an accredited school that the
applicant **"has, within six months prior to the date of application, successfully completed the
prescribed salesperson curriculum."**

**Six months.** Finish the education, then let eight months pass before applying, and the education
no longer supports the application. Students lose entire courses to this. Plan the application around
it from the day you enrol. (The Commission may waive all or part of the educational requirement on
proof of other educational background or experience acceptable to it — but that is a discretionary
waiver to be applied for, not a fallback to be relied on.)

chunks.heading: 5.5 Two things this school may never say to you
chunks.excerpt:
Applicants must be at least eighteen — § 339.040.3. And 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(D) requires this school
to advise every student, **before contractual obligation**, that **certain criminal convictions may
prevent a student from receiving or retaining a real estate licence**. That notice is given at
enrolment and repeated here. If it may apply to you, get the question answered before you pay for
education, not after you have finished it.

### 5.5 Two things this school may never say to you

Both are rules on the school rather than on the student, and knowing them helps you evaluate every
provider you will ever meet:

- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)4** — no school shall permit anyone associated with it **to make any
  warranties or guarantees that a student will pass the real estate licence examination** by taking
  its courses. A provider advertising a guaranteed pass is telling you something about itself.
- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)2** — no school shall advertise or imply that it is **recommended,
  endorsed or approved by the Commission**, though an accredited school may state which courses the
  Commission has approved it to teach. There is a real difference between "the Commission approved
  this course" and "the Commission endorses this school," and only the first can ever be true.

**And the status of this course today.** It is a version 1.0 submission draft. It is **not approved**,
no Missouri pre-license credit is available for it, and under 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)6 no course may
even be announced or advertised for credit until the Commission has approved it in writing.

### Module MO-01 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module MO-01
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items: one applied scenario, five engagement items and five remediation items. The applied
item must be answered correctly; the engagement and remediation sets are passed at 80 percent. Both
thresholds are **StateCourse standards** — 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment and no
in-module passing score. The 75 percent standard that does come from the rule applies to the **final
examination** under 20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E), and it is a real Commission figure.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-01

Every Missouri citation in this module was read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and is recorded in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: §§ 339.040, 339.710, 339.730, 339.760, 339.780,
339.800, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.010, 2250-7.060 and 2250-7.070.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the testing service's detailed content
outline; § 339.010's enumeration of the activities requiring a licence; § 339.100 and § 339.105; any
Commission-prescribed form; and 20 CSR 2250 chapters 1 through 5 and 8. Where this module reaches one
of those, it names the question and routes it.

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-02

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-02
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-02

## Hours 6–11 · Interests in real estate, forms of ownership, and legal descriptions

**Clock hours:** 6. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Classify an estate in land by duration and by possession, and identify a defeasible fee from its
   granting language.
2. Distinguish a life estate from a fee, name the future interests that follow it, and explain waste.
3. Distinguish easement appurtenant, easement in gross, licence and encroachment, and say how each
   arises and how each ends.
4. Compare the forms of concurrent ownership and state what happens at a death under each.
5. Explain what a condominium owner owns and how it differs from a cooperative and a time-share.
6. Read a rectangular-survey description, compute the acreage it describes, and recognise a
   metes-and-bounds description and a lot-and-block description.
7. State why a licensee never supplies a legal description from memory, a tax record or a prior
   listing.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 6 — Freehold estates
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 6 | Freehold estates: fee simple and its defeasible forms | 50 min |
| 7 | Life estates, future interests, and waste | 50 min |
| 8 | Encumbrances I: easements, licences, encroachments | 50 min |
| 9 | Encumbrances II: liens, deed restrictions, and priority | 50 min |
| 10 | Concurrent ownership, marital interests, and common-interest ownership | 50 min |
| 11 | Legal descriptions and land measurement | 50 min |

---

## Hour 6 — Freehold estates

### 6.1 The classification

An **estate** is the degree, quantity, nature and extent of a person's interest in land. Estates
divide first into **freehold** — of indefinite duration, involving ownership — and **leasehold** — of
determinable duration, involving possession without ownership. Leaseholds are Module MO-06's
business; freeholds are this hour's.

**Fee simple absolute** is the greatest interest known to the law: perpetual duration, freely
transferable during life and at death, subject only to the four government powers and to whatever
private encumbrances burden it. It is what most Missouri residential transactions convey, and it is
what a buyer assumes they are getting unless told otherwise.

### 6.2 Defeasible fees

A **defeasible fee** is a fee that may end on the happening of a stated event. Two forms, and the
difference is in what happens when the event occurs:

**Fee simple determinable.** Created by durational language — *so long as*, *while*, *during*,
*until*. The estate **ends automatically** when the condition fails, and the grantor holds a
**possibility of reverter**. "To the School District so long as the land is used for a school."

chunks.heading: 6.3 What the examination tests, and what practice tests
chunks.excerpt:
**Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.** Created by conditional language — *provided that*,
*on condition that*, *but if*. The estate **does not end automatically**; the grantor holds a **right
of re-entry** and must act to reclaim. "To the School District, provided that if the land ceases to
be used for a school the grantor may re-enter."

The distinction is drafted by counsel and litigated by counsel. What a licensee must do is
**recognise the language in a title commitment and route it**. A defeasible fee is a genuine
limitation on what a buyer is acquiring and it will not announce itself in the listing.

### 6.3 What the examination tests, and what practice tests

The examination will give you granting language and ask which estate it creates. Practice asks
something narrower and more useful: **did you read the exceptions in the title commitment, and did
you ask about anything you did not understand?** Most licensees will never meet a defeasible fee.
The ones who do will meet it in Schedule B.

---

## Hour 7 — Life estates, future interests, and waste

### 7.1 The life estate

A **life estate** is a freehold estate measured by a lifetime. Its holder — the **life tenant** — has
the right to possess, use and take the profits of the property for the duration of the measuring life,
and no right at all after it.

Measured by whose life? Usually the life tenant's. Where it is measured by the life of some **other**
person it is an estate **pur autre vie** — "for the life of another." An estate pur autre vie can
outlive its holder, in which case it passes to the holder's estate until the measuring life ends.

### 7.2 What follows

When the measuring life ends the estate must go somewhere, and there are exactly two possibilities:

chunks.heading: 7.3 Waste
chunks.excerpt:
- back to the **grantor** or the grantor's successors, which is a **reversion**; or
- to a named **third party**, which is a **remainder**, and that party is the **remainderman**.

Both are **future interests** — presently existing property rights whose enjoyment is postponed. A
remainderman owns something today, which is why a life tenant cannot sell the fee.

### 7.3 Waste

A life tenant must not commit **waste** — must not damage or diminish the property to the injury of
the remainderman. The life tenant is generally responsible for ordinary maintenance, taxes and
interest on encumbrances; permanent structural changes and destruction are waste.

**The practical consequence for a licensee is severe and immediate.** *A life tenant cannot convey a
fee simple.* If the seller holds a life estate, a sale of the fee requires the remainderman to join
in the conveyance. A licensee who takes a listing without establishing who must sign has built a
transaction on a defect that will surface at the closing table, and § 339.730.1(2) — reasonable skill
and care — is what makes establishing it part of the job. The determination is the title company's
and counsel's; the noticing is the licensee's.

### 7.4 The bundle, revisited

Note what the life estate does to Hour 1's bundle. The life tenant holds possession, use and
exclusion. The remainderman holds a form of disposition. Neither holds the whole thing, and neither
can convey what the other has. This is the clearest illustration in the course of why the bundle
metaphor is not decoration.

---

## Hour 8 — Encumbrances I: easements, licences, encroachments

### 8.1 What an encumbrance is

chunks.heading: 8.2 Easements
chunks.excerpt:
An **encumbrance** is any claim, right or interest held by someone other than the owner that
diminishes the value or restricts the use of the property, without preventing the owner from
transferring it. Encumbrances divide into those that **affect use** — easements, deed restrictions,
encroachments — and those that **affect title as security for a debt** — liens, which are Hour 9.

### 8.2 Easements

An **easement** is a right to use another's land for a particular purpose. Two kinds, and the
difference decides whether the right survives a sale:

**Easement appurtenant.** Benefits a **parcel** rather than a person. It has a **dominant tenement**
— the parcel benefited — and a **servient tenement** — the parcel burdened. It **runs with the land**,
passing automatically to each new owner of the dominant tenement. A driveway easement across a
neighbour's lot is the standard example. This is the kind that matters most in residential practice
because it transfers whether or not anyone mentions it.

**Easement in gross.** Benefits a **person or entity** rather than a parcel. There is a servient
tenement but no dominant one. Utility easements are the everyday case, and commercial easements in
gross are generally assignable.

**How easements are created:** by express grant or reservation in a deed; by implication, where prior
use and necessity are evident at severance; by **necessity**, most commonly for a landlocked parcel;
and by **prescription**, through long open use in the manner of adverse possession.

**How they end:** by merger — the two tenements coming into one ownership; by release from the
dominant owner; by abandonment shown by conduct rather than mere non-use; by expiration of a stated
term; or by the end of the necessity that created an easement by necessity.

chunks.heading: 8.3 Licence
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no Missouri prescriptive period**, because the relevant Missouri statute has not
been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee carries is the recognition: a
long-standing use of someone else's land — a drive, a path, a mowed strip, a dock — is routed to
counsel and a surveyor, not resolved on the tailgate.

### 8.3 Licence

A **licence** is mere permission to enter land for a particular purpose. It is personal, **revocable
at will**, and does not run with the land. Permission to fish in a pond is a licence; a recorded
right of access is an easement. The two look identical on the ground and are entirely different in
law, which is why the question is answered from the records rather than from what the neighbours say.

### 8.4 Encroachment

An **encroachment** is an unauthorised physical intrusion of an improvement onto adjoining land — a
fence, a shed, an eave, a driveway. It is not a permission of any kind; it is a trespass that has been
built.

Encroachments are discovered by **survey**, and this is the reason a survey matters. A title
commitment will typically **except** survey matters and encroachments unless a survey is furnished
and the exception removed. A buyer who declines a survey has accepted that risk, and should be told
so in those words. Left long enough, an encroachment can mature into a prescriptive easement or an
adverse possession claim, which converts a fixable problem into a legal one.

---

## Hour 9 — Encumbrances II: liens, restrictions, and priority

### 9.1 Liens

A **lien** is a charge against property that secures a debt or obligation. It affects title; it does
not by itself dispossess the owner. Every lien is classified twice:

chunks.heading: 9.2 Priority
chunks.excerpt:
- **Voluntary** — the owner created it, as with a mortgage — or **involuntary** — the law or a court
  imposed it, as with a tax lien or a judgment.
- **General** — attaching to the debtor's property generally, as a judgment lien does — or
  **specific** — attaching to one identified parcel, as a mortgage, mechanic's lien or property tax
  lien does.

A judgment lien is the one that surprises people, because it can surface against a parcel nobody
associated with the debt.

### 9.2 Priority

The general rule is **first in time, first in right**, measured by recording. The standard exception
is the **real estate tax lien**, which customarily takes priority over earlier recorded liens
regardless of order. Priority may also be rearranged by contract through a **subordination
agreement**, which is why the **title commitment** rather than a list of recording dates is the
operative document in any real transaction.

### 9.3 Mechanic's and materialman's liens

A lien claimed by someone who furnished labour or materials for improvement of the property. Its
danger is structural: in many states the lien's priority may **relate back to a date earlier than the
filing** — the commencement of work or the first furnishing of materials — so a claim not yet in the
records can outrank an interest that is.

**This course states no Missouri filing period, notice requirement or priority date**, because
Missouri's mechanic's lien chapter has not been read from primary text for this project. What a
licensee carries is the **warning sign and the routing**: recent or ongoing construction, a
renovation finished in the past several months, an unpaid or disputed contractor. Raise it at
listing, route it to the title company and counsel, and do not let it be discovered a week before
closing.

chunks.heading: 9.4 Deed restrictions and covenants
chunks.excerpt:
### 9.4 Deed restrictions and covenants

Private limits recorded against the land, most commonly as a declaration of covenants, conditions and
restrictions governing a subdivision. They **run with the land** and are enforceable by the
association or by benefited owners.

They are **entirely separate from zoning**, and the **more restrictive controls**. A city may permit
a use the covenants forbid, and the covenants win. A buyer who intends to run a business, park a
recreational vehicle, keep animals, build an outbuilding or install a fence needs the covenants read
**before** the offer is written.

Note also that a restriction that discriminates on a protected basis is unenforceable and void
regardless of what the record says — a subject Module MO-08 takes up in full.

---

## Hour 10 — Concurrent ownership and common-interest ownership

### 10.1 Forms of concurrent ownership

**Tenancy in common.** Two or more owners hold **undivided** interests, which may be **unequal**.
Each interest is freely transferable during life and **passes by will or intestacy at death**. This is
the default in most circumstances where a deed does not say otherwise.

**Joint tenancy.** Equal undivided interests with the **right of survivorship** — the great
distinction. On a joint tenant's death their interest passes to the surviving joint tenants and does
not go through the estate. It traditionally requires four unities: time, title, interest and
possession.

**Tenancy by the entirety.** A form available to married couples in Missouri, carrying survivorship
and creditor characteristics that differ from joint tenancy.

chunks.heading: 10.2 Partition
chunks.excerpt:
**How a licensee handles this.** Which form a deed creates, and which form a particular buyer should
take, is a **legal and tax question for counsel and the buyer's tax adviser**. A licensee who advises
a buying couple on how to take title has practised law. The licensee's contribution is to raise the
question early enough that it is decided deliberately rather than by whatever the title company's
default happened to be.

**Missouri marital property.** Missouri's marital-property regime and the rules governing which
spouse must join in a conveyance were **not read from primary text for this project, and this course
states no rule from them.** The practice consequence is the one that matters: **do not assume from
the name on the deed who must sign.** Route it to counsel and the closing agent, and raise it at
listing rather than at the closing table.

### 10.2 Partition

Any co-owner may generally seek **partition** — a court division of the property in kind, or a sale
and division of proceeds. It is the remedy when co-owners cannot agree, and it is a lawsuit.

### 10.3 Condominium, cooperative, time-share

**Condominium.** The owner holds the **unit in fee**, plus an **undivided interest in the common
elements**. Governance is by a declaration, bylaws and an owners' association, funded by assessments.
Each unit is separately assessed, separately taxed, separately financed and separately transferred.

chunks.heading: Hour 11 — Legal descriptions and land measurement
chunks.excerpt:
**Cooperative.** The owner holds **shares in a corporation** and a **proprietary lease** of a unit.
The corporation owns the real estate; the resident owns personal property. This changes financing —
share loans, not mortgages — changes transfer, because the board usually must approve a purchaser,
and changes the risk, because the corporation's blanket mortgage and the other shareholders'
delinquencies affect everyone.

**Time-share.** An interval interest, in one of several legal forms, carrying its own consumer
protection rules and a resale market that bears no resemblance to the sale market.

**The questions a licensee must ask about any common-interest property**, and get answered in
writing before the buyer's contingencies expire: what is the assessment and what does it cover; what
reserves does the association hold; is there a special assessment pending or a deferred maintenance
problem that implies one; is there litigation; what do the rules restrict — pets, rentals, vehicles,
occupancy; and will the buyer's intended lender lend on this project at all, which for condominiums
is a live question and not a formality.

---

## Hour 11 — Legal descriptions and land measurement

### 11.1 Three methods, and one non-method

**Metes and bounds.** Describes a boundary by courses and distances from a **point of beginning**,
running around the perimeter through calls that reference bearings, distances and monuments, and
**closing back to the point of beginning**. A description that does not close does not describe a
parcel. This is the method for irregular parcels and for older land.

chunks.heading: 11.2 Reading a rectangular description
chunks.excerpt:
**Rectangular survey, or government survey.** A grid built from **principal meridians** running north
and south and **base lines** running east and west. **Townships** are laid out in horizontal tiers and
vertical **ranges**; each township is six miles square and is divided into **36 sections**, each one
mile square and containing **640 acres**. Sections are numbered 1 through 36, beginning in the
north-east corner and running **boustrophedonically** — right to left, then left to right, back and
forth — so that section 36 lands in the south-east corner.

**Lot and block, or recorded plat.** References a lot and block on a subdivision plat recorded in the
county records. This is the everyday description for platted urban and suburban land, and it is the
one most Missouri residential licensees see.

**And the non-method: a street address is never a legal description.** Neither is a tax parcel
identification number. Both are conveniences for finding a property, not descriptions of it.

### 11.2 Reading a rectangular description

Read it **backwards**, dividing as you go, because the description narrows from the largest unit to
the smallest.

*The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 14.*

Start with the section: **640 acres**. The SW 1/4 of it: 640 ÷ 4 = **160 acres**. The NE 1/4 of that:
160 ÷ 4 = **40 acres**.

*The S 1/2 of the NW 1/4 of the SE 1/4.* 640 ÷ 4 = 160; ÷ 4 = 40; ÷ 2 = **20 acres**.

Each division by a quarter divides by four. Each division by a half divides by two. Work from the
right-hand end of the description toward the left and the arithmetic is trivial; work from the left
and it is confusing.

### 11.3 The measurements worth memorising

chunks.heading: 11.4 The licensee's rule about descriptions
chunks.excerpt:
| Unit | Equivalent |
|---|---|
| 1 acre | **43,560 square feet** |
| 1 section | 1 square mile, **640 acres** |
| 1 township | 6 miles square, **36 sections**, 23,040 acres |
| 1 mile | 5,280 feet |
| 1 square mile | 640 acres |

**A worked problem.** A rectangular lot is 150 feet by 290.4 feet. Its area is 150 × 290.4 = 43,560
square feet — **exactly one acre**. Recognising 43,560 on sight saves time on the examination and in
practice.

**Another.** A parcel described as the W 1/2 of the NE 1/4 of Section 8 is 640 ÷ 4 ÷ 2 = **80 acres**.
At $6,200 an acre it is worth 80 × 6,200 = **$496,000**.

### 11.4 The licensee's rule about descriptions

**Never supply a legal description from memory, from a tax record, from a prior listing or from the
seller's recollection.** The legal description comes from the **deed** or from the **title company**,
and it is copied exactly, character for character.

The same discipline covers acreage. The assessment roll is an assessment record, not a survey.
Repeating its figure as fact in a listing is a representation about a measurement nobody verified,
and where acreage matters to the buyer's decision the source of the figure matters too. Route
acreage, boundaries and anything touching a water line to a **surveyor**.

### Module MO-02 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-02

Missouri citations in this module — §§ 339.710 and 339.730, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060 and
2250-7.070 — were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module MO-02
chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Missouri's mechanic's lien chapter, its
adverse possession and prescription periods, its marital property regime, its condominium and
subdivision chapters, and its recording statutes. Where this module reaches one of those it names the
question and routes it, and no period, threshold or figure from any of them appears.

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-03

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-03
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-03

## Hours 12–17 · Agency and the Missouri brokerage relationships

**Clock hours:** 6. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. State the common-law agency vocabulary and explain how Missouri's statute departs from it.
2. Recite the six duties a limited agent owes a client under § 339.730.1 and § 339.740.1, RSMo.
3. State exactly what is owed to a **customer**, and explain why that one sentence decides most
   Missouri complaints.
4. Define adverse material fact from § 339.710(1) and identify one in a fact pattern, including the
   item that is not about the property at all.
5. Distinguish dual agent, transaction broker and designated agent, and name the five items neither a
   dual agent nor a transaction broker may disclose.
6. State when a written agreement is required under § 339.780 and what each kind must contain.
7. Explain what survives termination under § 339.790.2 and what does not.
8. Identify a ministerial act and explain why the category exists.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 12 — Common-law agency and Missouri's statutory replacement
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 12 | Common-law agency, and how Missouri replaced it | 50 min |
| 13 | The limited agent's six duties; client and customer | 50 min |
| 14 | Adverse material facts and confidential information | 50 min |
| 15 | Dual agency and transaction brokerage | 50 min |
| 16 | Designated agency, subagency, and the firm's written policy | 50 min |
| 17 | Written agreements, disclosure, termination, compensation | 50 min |

---

## Hour 12 — Common-law agency and Missouri's statutory replacement

### 12.1 The common-law vocabulary

Agency is the relationship in which one person, the **agent**, acts on behalf of another, the
**principal**, in dealings with third parties. Common law traditionally described the agent's duties
to the principal with the mnemonic **OLD CAR**: Obedience to lawful instructions, Loyalty, Disclosure,
Confidentiality, Accounting, and Reasonable care.

Common law also classified agents by scope. A **universal agent** may act in all matters. A
**general agent** may act in a continuing series of transactions — a property manager is the standard
example. A **special agent** is authorised for one transaction with limited authority — which is what
a listing broker traditionally was.

And it classified authority as **express** (stated), **implied** (reasonably necessary to carry out
express authority), or **apparent** (created by the principal's conduct leading a third party
reasonably to believe authority exists, whether or not it does). Apparent authority is the dangerous
one, because it can bind a principal to something they never authorised.

### 12.2 Why Missouri's statute matters more than the common law

chunks.heading: 12.3 The two words the statute turns on
chunks.excerpt:
You should learn the common-law vocabulary because examinations test it and because it is the frame
the statute sits inside. But **in Missouri the operative law is the statute**, and it does not simply
codify the common law — it displaces it in specific and important ways.

Sections 339.710 through 339.860, RSMo — the Missouri brokerage relationships provisions — create a
category the common law did not have: the **limited agent**. Section 339.710(18) defines a limited
agent as *a licensee whose duties and obligations to a client are those set forth in sections 339.730
to 339.750.*

That definition is the whole point. A Missouri limited agent's duties are **the ones the statute
lists** — not the general fiduciary obligations a court might otherwise imply. The statute is a
closed list, and a licensee who knows the list knows their duties.

### 12.3 The two words the statute turns on

**Client** — § 339.710(6) — *a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant who has entered into a brokerage
relationship with a licensee.*

**Customer** — § 339.710(10) — *an actual or potential seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant in a real
estate transaction in which a licensee is involved but who has not entered into a brokerage
relationship with the licensee.*

Everything in Missouri agency law follows from which of these two words describes the person in front
of you, and the difference is created by **a written agreement**, not by helpfulness, rapport, time
spent, or who is paying. Section 339.800.2 says so explicitly: *payment of compensation by itself
shall not establish an agency relationship or transaction brokerage relationship.*

### 12.4 Ministerial acts

chunks.heading: Hour 13 — The limited agent's duties, and the customer sentence
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.710(19) defines **ministerial acts** as *those acts that a licensee may perform for a
person or entity that are informative in nature and do not rise to the level which requires the
creation of a brokerage relationship.* The statute's own examples:

- responding to telephone inquiries from consumers about the availability and pricing of brokerage
  services;
- responding to telephone inquiries about the price or location of property;
- attending an open house and responding to questions about the property from a consumer;
- setting an appointment to view property;
- responding to questions of consumers walking into a licensee's office.

The category exists so that ordinary courtesy does not accidentally create a representation. You may
answer the phone. You may hold an open house. You may set a showing. None of that makes anyone your
client — and equally, none of it suspends the disclosure duty you owe every customer.

---

## Hour 13 — The limited agent's duties, and the customer sentence

### 13.1 Six duties, and they are the same on both sides

Section 339.730.1 sets out what a **seller's or landlord's agent** owes the client. Section 339.740.1
sets out what a **buyer's or tenant's agent** owes the client. They are the same six, mirrored:

chunks.heading: 13.1 Six duties, and they are the same on both sides
chunks.excerpt:
1. **To perform the terms of the written agreement** made with the client.
2. **To exercise reasonable skill and care** for the client.
3. **To promote the interests of the client with the utmost good faith, loyalty, and fidelity**,
   including four specified things:
   - **(a)** seeking a price and terms acceptable to the client — with an express carve-out that the
     licensee is **not obligated to seek additional offers** while the property is already subject to
     a contract for sale, or a lease or letter of intent to lease;
   - **(b)** **presenting all written offers to and from the client in a timely manner regardless of
     whether the property is subject to a contract** for sale or lease;
   - **(c)** **disclosing to the client all adverse material facts actually known or that should have
     been known** by the licensee;
   - **(d)** **advising the client to obtain expert advice** as to material matters about which the
     licensee knows but the specifics of which are beyond the licensee's expertise.
4. **To account in a timely manner for all money and property received.**
5. **To comply** with §§ 339.710–339.860, with § 339.100.2, and with the rules under them.
6. **To comply with applicable federal, state and local laws, rules, regulations and ordinances,
   including fair housing and civil rights statutes and regulations.**

**Read (3)(a) and (3)(b) together, because they are a matched pair and they are commonly misread.**
Once a property is under contract you need not go looking for more offers — but if a written offer
arrives anyway, **you must still present it.** The obligation to present is not suspended by the
existence of a contract. Sellers ask about this constantly and licensees get it wrong constantly.

chunks.heading: 13.2 What is owed to a customer
chunks.excerpt:
**And (3)(d) is the sentence that keeps a licensee inside their licence.** The duty is not to answer
the legal, tax, engineering or environmental question. It is to *know that the question exists and
tell the client to get it answered by someone qualified.* That is the whole of what is required, and
doing more than it is how licensees end up practising law.

### 13.2 What is owed to a customer

Section 339.730.3 — and § 339.740.3 in the mirror — is the most consequential sentence in Missouri
brokerage law:

> A licensee acting as a seller's or landlord's agent **owes no duty or obligation to a customer,
> except that a licensee shall disclose to any customer all adverse material facts actually known or
> that should have been known** by the licensee.

**No duty — except one, and it is a real one.** The same subsection continues: the agent **owes no
duty to conduct an independent inspection** or discover adverse material facts for the customer, and
**owes no duty to independently verify** the accuracy or completeness of any statement made by the
client or by any independent inspector.

Section 339.740.3 adds the buyer-side analogue: a buyer's agent **owes no duty to conduct an
independent investigation of the client's financial condition for the benefit of the customer.**

So the structure is: everything to the client, and to the customer honesty about adverse material
facts. That is not a small residue. A licensee cannot conceal a known defect from the other side and
then say the buyer was not their client. That defence does not exist in Missouri.

### 13.3 What an agent may do without breaching anything

Sections 339.730.4 and 339.740.4 protect ordinary practice explicitly:

chunks.heading: Hour 14 — Adverse material facts and confidential information
chunks.excerpt:
- A **seller's or landlord's agent may show alternative properties** not owned by the client to
  prospective buyers, and **may list competing properties**, without breach.
- A **buyer's or tenant's agent may show properties the client is interested in to other prospective
  buyers**, and may assist competing buyers in attempting to purchase the same property, without
  breach.

These provisions exist because otherwise every listing would be a conflict with every other listing.

---

## Hour 14 — Adverse material facts and confidential information

### 14.1 The definition, read exactly

Section 339.710(1) defines an **adverse material fact** as:

> a fact related to the property not reasonably ascertainable or known to a party which negatively
> affects the value of the property.

Three elements, and each does work. It must be **related to the property**. It must be **not
reasonably ascertainable or known** to the party — a fact the buyer can see for themselves is not
concealed by not mentioning it. And it must **negatively affect value**.

The statute then lists what such facts *may* include:

- **(a)** environmental hazards affecting the property;
- **(b)** physical condition of the property which adversely affects value;
- **(c)** material defects in the property;
- **(d)** material defects in the **title** to the property;
- **(e)** **material limitation of the party's ability to perform under the terms of the contract.**

### 14.2 Item (e), which is not about the property at all

chunks.heading: 14.3 The two standards, and the difference between them
chunks.excerpt:
Read (e) again. *Material limitation of the party's ability to perform under the terms of the
contract.* That is not a defect in a house. It is a fact about a **party** — a buyer whose financing
has collapsed, a seller who cannot deliver clear title, a party who has told you they cannot close.

New licensees skip this item because the other four are about buildings. It belongs on the list
because a party's inability to perform destroys value in a transaction as surely as a cracked
foundation does, and because a licensee usually learns it before anyone else.

### 14.3 The two standards, and the difference between them

Missouri uses **two different disclosure standards** depending on the relationship, and the difference
is precise:

- A **limited agent** under §§ 339.730.1(3)(c), 339.730.3, 339.740 discloses adverse material facts
  **actually known or that should have been known.**
- A **transaction broker** under § 339.755(2)(d) discloses adverse material facts **of which the
  licensee has actual notice or knowledge.**

"Should have been known" is an objective standard and it makes wilful ignorance unavailable. A
licensee who arranges not to learn something has not escaped the duty. "Actual notice or knowledge"
is narrower.

The examination tests this distinction. Practice tests something simpler: **disclose it.** The
professional method is not to litigate which standard applies to a fact you already know. It is to
put it in writing, to everyone, and move on.

### 14.4 Confidential information

chunks.heading: Hour 15 — Dual agency and transaction brokerage
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.710(9) defines **confidential information** as information obtained from the client and
designated confidential by the client; information made confidential by §§ 339.710–339.860 or any
other statute or regulation; or written instructions from the client — **unless** the information is
or becomes public by the client's own words or conduct, or from a source other than the licensee.

Section 339.730.2 and § 339.740.2 forbid disclosure of confidential information about the client
**unless** disclosure is required by statute, rule or regulation; **or failure to disclose would
constitute a misrepresentation**; or disclosure is necessary to defend the licensee against an action
of wrongful conduct in an administrative or judicial proceeding or before a professional committee.
And: **no cause of action arises against the licensee for making any required or permitted
disclosure.**

**That middle exception is where confidentiality and adverse-material-fact disclosure meet.** A
client may not make a fact confidential by asking. If withholding it would make what you have said a
misrepresentation, or if the law requires disclosure, it goes out. A seller who tells you in
confidence that the basement floods has not sealed your mouth; they have told you an adverse material
fact, and § 339.730.3 requires you to disclose it to any customer.

---

## Hour 15 — Dual agency and transaction brokerage

### 15.1 Dual agency

A **dual agent** represents both sides of the same transaction. Section 339.750.1: a licensee may act
as a dual agent **only with the consent of all parties**, and consent **is presumed by a written
agreement pursuant to § 339.780.**

chunks.heading: 15.2 The five items — memorise them
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.750.2: a dual agent is a **limited agent for both** the seller and buyer, or landlord and
tenant, with the duties of §§ 339.730 and 339.740 except as the section provides.

The structural problem is obvious and the statute does not pretend otherwise: two clients with
opposed interests cannot both receive undivided loyalty. So the statute narrows what a dual agent may
say.

### 15.2 The five items — memorise them

Section 339.750.4 lists five things a dual agent **shall not disclose without the consent of the
client to whom the information pertains**:

1. That a **buyer or tenant is willing to pay more** than the purchase price or lease rate offered.
2. That a **seller or landlord is willing to accept less** than the asking price or lease rate.
3. **What the motivating factors are** for any client buying, selling or leasing the property.
4. That a client **will agree to financing terms other than those offered**.
5. **The terms of any prior offers or counter offers** made by any party.

Section 339.750.3 supplies the other half: **outside those five items and outside confidential
information, a dual agent MAY disclose to one client information gained from the other if it is
material to the transaction.** Dual agency is not a vow of silence; it is a specific list of things
that stay in.

And § 339.750.6: **in a dual agency relationship there is no imputation of knowledge or information**
between the client and the dual agent, or among persons within an entity engaged as a dual agent.

### 15.3 Transaction brokerage

chunks.heading: 15.3 Transaction brokerage
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.755.1 permits a licensee to serve any party **without an agency or fiduciary relationship
to anyone**. Such a licensee is a **transaction broker**, and § 339.710's definition describes them
as **neutral, serving neither as an advocate nor advisor for either party.**

The § 339.755.2 duties:

- perform the terms of any **written or oral** agreement with any party — note that this is the one
  place the statute contemplates an oral agreement;
- exercise **reasonable skill, care and diligence**, including presenting all written offers and
  counteroffers timely; **informing the parties** regarding the transaction and **suggesting they
  obtain expert advice** on material matters beyond the broker's expertise; accounting timely for
  money and property; **disclosing to each party any adverse material facts of which the licensee has
  actual notice or knowledge**; and **assisting the parties in complying with the terms and
  conditions of any contract**.

Section 339.755.3 carries **the same five non-disclosure items** as dual agency, phrased as requiring
the **informed consent** of the party who disclosed them, plus confidential information about the
other party unless disclosure is required by law or failure to disclose would constitute fraud or
dishonest dealing.

Sections 339.755.4 and .5: a transaction broker **has no duty to conduct an independent inspection or
investigation for adverse material facts**, and **no duty to investigate the buyer's financial
condition.**

Section 339.755.7: **each party and the transaction broker possess only actual knowledge and
information. There is no imputation of knowledge or information by operation of law.**

chunks.heading: 15.4 Choosing between them
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.755.13: a licensee may **without liability withdraw** from representing a client who has
not consented to a conversion to transaction brokerage — and that withdrawal does not prejudice the
licensee's ability to continue representing the other client, or to represent the refusing client in
a different transaction.

### 15.4 Choosing between them

This is a **firm policy question before it is a transaction question.** Section 339.760 requires every
designated broker with affiliated licensees to adopt a written policy identifying and describing the
relationships the broker and the affiliated licensees may engage in. Some Missouri firms offer dual
agency; some route in-house situations to transaction brokerage; some appoint designated agents. **You
practise your firm's policy, not your preference**, and you read it before your first appointment.

---

## Hour 16 — Designated agency, subagency, and the firm

### 16.1 Designated agency

Section 339.820.1: a designated broker entering a limited agency agreement with a client — for a
listing or to represent a person in buying, selling, exchanging, renting or leasing — **may appoint in
writing affiliated licensees as designated agents to the exclusion of all other affiliated
licensees.** The same mechanism applies to designated transaction brokers under a transaction
brokerage agreement.

This solves the in-house problem. Without it, one firm listing a property and also working with the
buyer would be a dual agency for the entire firm. With it, one licensee is appointed to the seller and
another to the buyer, each with full limited-agent duties, and the firm is not thereby a dual agent.

chunks.heading: 16.2 Subagency
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.820.2 draws the boundary precisely: a designated broker **is not** a dual agent or
transaction broker **solely because** of making an appointment — **but any licensee who personally
represents both the seller and buyer in a particular transaction IS** a dual agent or transaction
broker and must comply accordingly.

So: the firm is protected by the appointment; the individual is not, if the individual is on both
sides. If both sides of your transaction are yours personally, you are a dual agent or a transaction
broker, and the appointment does not change that.

There is also a default rule worth knowing. Where an appointment has been made under § 339.820.1, an
affiliated licensee assisting a party **without a written agreement is presumed to be a transaction
broker** to the exclusion of all other affiliated licensees, unless a different status has been
disclosed to or established with that party.

Section 339.830.1: designated agents and designated transaction brokers **have the same duties and
responsibilities to the client and customer under §§ 339.730 to 339.755 as the designated broker**,
except as § 339.820 provides. Section 339.830.2: all licensees have **the same protections from
vicarious liability** as their designated broker.

### 16.2 Subagency

A **subagent** is a designated broker working for the client through the client's designated broker.
Section 339.730.5 permits a seller or landlord to agree in writing that other designated brokers may
be retained and compensated as subagents, and any such subagent is **a limited agent with the same
obligations** under §§ 339.730.1 to .4. Section 339.740.5 mirrors it for the buyer side.

chunks.heading: Hour 17 — Written agreements, disclosure, termination
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.780.5 sets out how a subagency is entered: by written agreement with the client's
designated broker; or, where a designated broker has made a **unilateral offer of subagency**, by the
act of the second broker **disclosing to the customer that they are a subagent of the client**; or,
where a § 339.820 appointment has been made, by an excluded affiliated licensee disclosing the same.

Subagency has become uncommon in residential practice as buyer representation has become normal.
Know what it is, know that it makes the subagent the **seller's** agent while working with a buyer,
and know that the buyer must be told.

---

## Hour 17 — Written agreements, disclosure, termination

### 17.1 Section 339.780: what must be in writing, and when

Section 339.780.1: **all written agreements for brokerage services are entered into by the designated
broker** on behalf of the broker and the affiliated licensees — except that the designated broker may
**authorise affiliated licensees in writing** to enter into them.

Then, **before engaging in any of the activities enumerated in § 339.010**:

chunks.heading: 17.1 Section 339.780: what must be in writing, and when
chunks.excerpt:
- **.2 Seller or landlord limited agency** — a written agency agreement including the § 339.730
  duties, **the terms of compensation**, and **whether an offer of subagency may be made** to any
  other designated broker.
- **.3 Single agency for a buyer or tenant** — a written agency agreement including the § 339.740
  duties and the terms of compensation. Note the carve-out: this applies **except for ministerial
  acts** as defined in § 339.710.
- **.4 Dual agency** — a written agreement **with both** seller and buyer (or landlord and tenant)
  permitting the broker to serve as dual agent, including the § 339.750 duties and terms of
  compensation.
- **.5 Subagency** — a written agreement with the client's designated broker, or the two disclosure
  routes described above.
- **.6 Transaction brokerage** — a designated broker who **expects to receive compensation from the
  party assisted** enters a written transaction brokerage agreement including the § 339.755 duties
  and terms of compensation.

**And § 339.780.7 — the minimum service standard for exclusive agreements.** Every exclusive brokerage
agreement must specify that the broker will provide at minimum:

1. **accepting delivery of and presenting** to the client or customer offers and counteroffers;
2. **assisting** the client or customer in developing, communicating, negotiating and presenting
   offers, counteroffers and notices **until a lease or purchase agreement is signed and all
   contingencies are satisfied or waived**;
3. **answering** the client's or customer's questions relating to offers, counteroffers, notices and
   contingencies.

That is a floor, not a ceiling — § 339.780.8 preserves the public's freedom to contract for more.

chunks.heading: 17.2 Section 339.770: the Broker Disclosure Form
chunks.excerpt:
**Section 339.780 was amended in 2025**, effective 28 August 2025. It is read here in its current
text as of 2026-08-20 and is re-read before submission, because a recently amended section is the one
most likely to move again.

### 17.2 Section 339.770: the Broker Disclosure Form

In a **residential** real estate transaction, **at the earliest practicable opportunity during or
following the first substantial contact** with a seller, landlord, buyer or tenant **who has not
entered into a written agreement for services**, the licensee **shall provide that person with a
written copy of the current broker disclosure form prescribed by the Commission** — § 339.770.1.

Three conditions, all of which must be present: residential; first substantial contact; no existing
written agreement. Section 339.770.2 supplies the exception — where the person **has already** entered
into a written agreement with a designated broker, **no other licensee** is required to make the
disclosure.

And § 339.770.3: **disclosures made in accordance with §§ 339.710 to 339.860 are sufficient as a
matter of law** to disclose brokerage relationships to the public.

**The form itself is a Commission-prescribed form and has NOT been read for this project. This course
does not reproduce it, state its fields, or describe its layout.** What you carry out of this hour is
the statutory trigger and the routing: use the **current** form, obtained from the Commission, and
check that it is current rather than assuming the copy in your firm's drawer still is.

chunks.heading: 17.3 Termination, and what survives it
chunks.excerpt:
*What is "first substantial contact"?* The statute does not define it, and this course will not invent
a definition. The safe practice is the early one: give the form at the point the conversation stops
being ministerial and starts being about this person's transaction.

### 17.3 Termination, and what survives it

Section 339.790.1: the relationships **commence on the effective date of the broker's agreement** and
continue until **performance, completion, termination or expiration** of that agreement.

Section 339.790.2: after that point the broker and affiliated licensee **owe no further duty or
obligation, except**:

1. **accounting in a timely manner** for all money and property related to and received during the
   relationship; and
2. **treating as confidential** information provided by the client during the relationship **that may
   reasonably be expected to have a negative impact on the client's real estate activity** — unless
   the client gives written consent, disclosure is required by law, the information became public
   through the client or a source other than the brokerage, or disclosure is necessary to defend
   against an action of wrongful conduct.

**Confidentiality outlives the relationship. The rest of it does not.** A licensee who learned a
seller's divorce was forcing the sale does not become free to mention it when the listing expires.

### 17.4 A working method

Before every first appointment, four questions, answered in this order:

chunks.heading: Module MO-03 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
1. **What does my firm's § 339.760 written policy permit me to be here?**
2. **Is this residential, is this first substantial contact, and does this person already have a
   written agreement?** If the answer is residential / yes / no, the current Commission broker
   disclosure form goes in their hands.
3. **What relationship are we entering, and what written agreement does § 339.780 require for it?**
4. **What do I already know about this property or these parties that is an adverse material fact
   under § 339.710(1)?** Whatever it is, it goes in writing to everyone entitled to it.

Do those four things every time and most of Missouri agency law takes care of itself.

### Module MO-03 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-03

Every section cited in this module — §§ 339.710, 339.730, 339.740, 339.750, 339.755, 339.760,
339.770, 339.780, 339.790, 339.800, 339.820 and 339.830, RSMo — was read from primary text on
2026-08-20 and is transcribed in `missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the Commission-prescribed broker disclosure
