§ 339.100.2 beyond its cross-reference; and § 339.105. Where this module reaches one of those it names
the question and routes it.

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-04

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-04
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-04

## Hours 18–23 · Contracts

**Clock hours:** 6. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Name the elements of a valid contract and identify which one is missing from a defective fact
   pattern.
2. Distinguish valid, void, voidable and unenforceable, and executory from executed.
3. Explain the statute of frauds as it applies to real estate and name what it requires.
4. Trace an offer through acceptance, counter-offer, revocation and lapse, and state the effect of
   each.
5. Distinguish a contingency from a general right to cancel, and explain how contingencies actually
   fail.
6. Distinguish assignment from novation and state who remains liable under each.
7. Name the remedies for breach and explain why specific performance is available in real estate.
8. State the boundary between completing a form and practising law, and route accordingly.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 18 — Elements and classifications
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 18 | Elements of a contract; classifications | 50 min |
| 19 | The statute of frauds; offer, acceptance, counter-offer | 50 min |
| 20 | The purchase contract: what each provision does | 50 min |
| 21 | Contingencies, deadlines, and how transactions actually fail | 50 min |
| 22 | Assignment, novation, discharge, breach, remedies | 50 min |
| 23 | Other real estate contracts; the licensee's drafting boundary | 50 min |

---

## Hour 18 — Elements and classifications

### 18.1 The elements of a valid contract

A contract is a legally enforceable agreement to do or refrain from doing a legal act. Five elements,
and for real estate a sixth:

1. **Offer and acceptance** — mutual assent, sometimes called a meeting of the minds. There must be a
   definite offer and an unqualified acceptance of it.
2. **Consideration** — something of legal value exchanged. In a purchase contract the consideration is
   the mutual promises: the buyer promises to pay, the seller promises to convey. Earnest money is not
   the consideration; it is evidence of good faith and a fund for damages.
3. **Legal capacity** — parties competent to contract. Minors, persons adjudicated incompetent, and
   persons acting under an inadequate power of attorney all raise capacity questions, and every one of
   them is a question for counsel and the title company rather than for a licensee.
4. **Lawful object** — a legal purpose. A contract to do something illegal is void.
5. **Genuine assent** — agreement not produced by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake, duress or undue
   influence.
6. **A writing** — for a conveyance of an interest in real estate, under the statute of frauds.

chunks.heading: 18.2 Classifications
chunks.excerpt:
**Genuine assent is where a licensee most often supplies the defect.** A misrepresentation — even an
innocent one, even a repeated one, even one the licensee believed — can undermine the assent the
contract depends on. That is why Module MO-08's treatment of avoiding misrepresentation is not a
professional courtesy topic but a contract-formation topic.

### 18.2 Classifications

**By validity.** *Valid* — meets all elements and is enforceable. *Void* — never had legal effect at
all; there is nothing to enforce and nothing to disaffirm. *Voidable* — valid and enforceable **unless
and until** a party with the power to disaffirm elects to do so. *Unenforceable* — has the elements
but cannot be enforced in court, typically because it is not in writing or a limitation period has
run.

The examination tests void against voidable relentlessly. The distinction: a void contract is a
nullity; a voidable contract is real and binding on at least one party until the other one gets out
of it.

**By performance.** *Executory* — something remains to be done. A signed purchase contract before
closing is executory. *Executed* — fully performed by all parties. Note that "executed" in this sense
means *completed*, not *signed*, which is a genuine trap because the word is used both ways in
ordinary practice.

**By the shape of the promise.** *Bilateral* — a promise for a promise; both sides are bound. A
purchase contract is bilateral. *Unilateral* — a promise for an act; only the offeror is bound until
someone performs. An open listing is the classic example: the seller promises to pay whoever produces
a buyer, and nobody is obliged to try.

**By formation.** *Express* — stated in words. *Implied* — inferred from conduct.

---

## Hour 19 — The statute of frauds, and the life of an offer

chunks.heading: 19.1 The statute of frauds
chunks.excerpt:
### 19.1 The statute of frauds

The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be **in writing and signed by the party to be
charged** in order to be enforceable. Contracts for the sale of an interest in real estate are within
it, as are leases beyond a stated duration.

Two consequences worth stating plainly. First, **an oral real estate contract is not void — it is
unenforceable**, which is a different thing and produces different arguments. Second, the writing must
contain the essential terms: the parties, the property described adequately, the price, and the
signature of the party against whom enforcement is sought.

**This course states no Missouri lease-duration threshold** for the writing requirement, because
Missouri's statute of frauds has not been read from primary text for this project. The practice rule
does not depend on the threshold: **get it in writing.**

### 19.2 Offer

An **offer** is a definite proposal, communicated to the offeree, showing an intention to be bound on
acceptance. An advertisement is generally not an offer; it is an invitation to make one — which is why
a listing at a price is not a promise to sell at that price.

An offer ends in one of five ways:

- **Acceptance** — it becomes a contract.
- **Rejection** by the offeree.
- **Counter-offer**, which is a rejection plus a new offer.
- **Revocation** by the offeror **before acceptance is communicated**.
- **Lapse** — the time stated in the offer expires, or a reasonable time passes where none is stated.

Death or incapacity of a party before acceptance also terminates an offer.

### 19.3 Acceptance

chunks.heading: 19.4 Counter-offers
chunks.excerpt:
Acceptance must be **unqualified** — the mirror image of the offer — and it must be **communicated in
the manner the offer requires.** Signature and delivery are different events and may fall on different
days. **The formation date anchors provisions that expressly measure time from formation or the
effective date; it is not the trigger for every contractual deadline.** Other provisions may use
receipt of a document, delivery of a notice, a specified event, or a fixed calendar date.

The practical discipline: when acceptance is delivered, **record the date in the place the contract
provides and build a deadline calendar using each provision's own trigger.** Check calendar versus
business days, the counting convention, cut-off time, permitted delivery method, designated recipient,
and any amendment. Record the receipt evidence when a period begins on receipt. Do not replace a
clause-specific trigger with the signature or formation date. Ask the designated broker and, where
interpretation is required, counsel about ambiguous terms before a deadline passes.

### 19.4 Counter-offers

A **counter-offer rejects the original offer and substitutes a new one.** The original is dead and can
no longer simply be accepted.

This creates a real problem for a seller with several offers, because countering all of them destroys
all of them. The standard solution is a **multiple counter-proposal** instrument that reserves the
seller's right to accept only one — and whether such an instrument is available to you depends on the
forms your firm uses. What a licensee must never do is invent language to solve this. See Hour 23.

### 19.5 Amendments and notices

Distinguish three instruments that are routinely confused:

chunks.heading: Hour 20 — The purchase contract, provision by provision
chunks.excerpt:
- An **offer** or **counter-offer** proposes terms before there is a contract.
- An **amendment** changes a contract that already exists, and requires the agreement of all parties.
- A **notice** exercises a right the contract already gives — removing a contingency, giving notice of
  a defect, giving notice of an inability to obtain financing. A notice is **unilateral**: it does not
  need the other party's agreement, but it does need to be given in the manner and by the deadline the
  contract specifies.

Using the wrong one is a common and expensive error. A buyer who "amends" when they should have given
notice has asked permission for something they were entitled to do.

---

## Hour 20 — The purchase contract, provision by provision

### 20.1 What the contract must settle

Whatever form your firm uses, a residential purchase contract has to answer the same questions, and a
licensee should be able to find each of them:

chunks.heading: 20.2 Earnest money
chunks.excerpt:
- **Parties and property.** Full names of every party who must sign; the legal description copied from
  the deed or supplied by the title company, not from a tax record.
- **Price and how it will be paid** — cash, financing, or a combination, and the terms of the
  financing the buyer will seek.
- **Earnest money** — the amount, who holds it, when it is deposited, and what happens to it in each
  of the ways the contract can end.
- **Included and excluded items** — the fixture discipline from Module MO-01, reduced to two lists.
- **Contingencies** — each with its own condition, deadline, method of notice, and stated effect if
  the condition fails.
- **Title evidence** — what will be furnished, by whom, by when, and what happens if the buyer objects.
- **Closing date and possession.** These are not the same date and the contract must say so if they
  differ. Possession before closing, or after, needs its own written agreement.
- **Prorations** — taxes, assessments, rents, fuel, association dues, and the basis on which each is
  divided.
- **Risk of loss** before closing.
- **Default and remedies** — what each party may do if the other fails to perform.
- **Signatures and the date of acceptance.**

### 20.2 Earnest money

Earnest money is **not** the consideration for the contract and it is **not** a fee. It is a deposit
evidencing the buyer's good faith, held in trust, and applied to the purchase price at closing.

Three things a licensee must know cold:

**It is trust money the moment it is received.** It goes to the firm for handling under the firm's
trust account procedures. It is never held uncashed in a drawer as a favour to a buyer, and it never
touches an operating account.

chunks.heading: 20.3 Risk of loss, possession, and the gap between contract and closing
chunks.excerpt:
**Its disposition on a dispute is not the licensee's decision.** What happens to disputed earnest
money is decided by what the contract provides and by the parties or a court. A licensee who releases
disputed funds to keep a client happy has committed a licence problem regardless of who turns out to
have been right about the contract.

**This course states no Missouri deposit deadline or trust-account requirement**, because 20 CSR 2250
chapters 1 through 5 and 8, and § 339.105, RSMo, have not been read from primary text for this
project. The operative deadlines come from those chapters and from your firm's policy, and both are
read before you accept your first cheque.

### 20.3 Risk of loss, possession, and the gap between contract and closing

Between formation and closing the buyer holds **equitable title** — a recognised interest in the
property — while the seller retains legal title. The contract allocates the risk of casualty loss in
that interval, and it should be read rather than assumed.

Possession before closing is a bad idea executed badly more often than it is a bad idea. If it must
happen it needs a separate written agreement addressing rent, insurance, utilities, damage,
maintenance, and what happens if the sale does not close. A buyer already living in the house who
cannot close is a problem with no good solution.

---

## Hour 21 — Contingencies and how transactions actually fail

### 21.1 What a contingency is

A **contingency** is a condition that must be satisfied or waived before a party is obliged to
perform. It is not a general right to change one's mind. A buyer who has found a house they like
better has not triggered the inspection contingency.

Every contingency has four parts, and all four must be read:

chunks.heading: 21.2 The common contingencies
chunks.excerpt:
1. **The condition** — what must happen.
2. **The deadline** — by when.
3. **The method of notice** — how the party tells the other side, in what form, delivered how.
4. **The effect of silence** — what happens if the deadline passes with no notice given. Sometimes the
   contingency is waived; sometimes the contract terminates. **It depends entirely on the form**, and
   assuming is how transactions die.

### 21.2 The common contingencies

**Financing.** The buyer's obligation is conditioned on obtaining a loan of a stated type and amount
on stated terms. A pre-approval is not a commitment — this is why the contingency exists, and a buyer
who has been allowed to think otherwise will not understand why anyone is worried.

**Inspection.** The buyer may inspect within a period and then, depending on the form, object,
request repairs, or terminate. Note what an inspection contingency is *not*: a warranty of condition,
a price renegotiation clause, or a way out for a buyer who has changed their mind — though in practice
it is used as the last of these constantly.

**Appraisal.** The property must appraise at or above a stated value for the lender's purposes. A low
appraisal does not lower the price by itself; it creates a gap someone must close.

**Sale of the buyer's existing home.** The most fragile contingency in residential practice, because
it makes this transaction depend on another one nobody in this room controls.

**Title.** The buyer may examine title evidence and object to defects within a period.

**Survey.** Where the buyer wants boundaries, encroachments and easements established, and it is the
only way to remove the survey exception from the title policy.

### 21.3 How contingencies actually fail

chunks.heading: Hour 22 — Assignment, discharge, breach, remedies
chunks.excerpt:
Not through the condition. Through **inattention.** The overwhelming majority of contingency failures
in residential practice are a deadline that passed while everyone assumed the contingency was still
open, or a notice given in the wrong form, or a notice given to the wrong person.

The method that prevents this is unglamorous and it works:

1. On the day of acceptance, **write every deadline in the file and in your calendar**, computed from
   the date of acceptance.
2. Work backwards from each deadline to the date the underlying work must **start** — an inspection
   deadline is useless if the inspector is booked out ten days.
3. **Confirm every notice in the form the contract requires**, and keep proof of delivery.
4. When a deadline is at risk, raise it with the client **before** it passes, in writing.

This is what § 339.730.1(2) — reasonable skill and care — actually looks like in daily practice. It is
almost entirely calendar work.

---

## Hour 22 — Assignment, discharge, breach, remedies

### 22.1 Assignment and novation

**Assignment** transfers rights under a contract to another party. Unless the contract prohibits it or
the duties are personal, contract rights are generally assignable — but **the original party
ordinarily remains liable** for performance.

**Novation** substitutes a new party for an original one **and releases the original**. It requires
the consent of all parties.

The practical difference is who can be sued when performance fails. A buyer who assigns a purchase
contract and believes they have walked away usually has not. Only a novation does that, and a novation
is a document the parties actually sign.

### 22.2 Discharge

chunks.heading: 22.3 Breach and remedies
chunks.excerpt:
A contract can be discharged by **performance** — the ordinary case; by **agreement** — mutual
rescission, novation, or accord and satisfaction; by **operation of law** — bankruptcy, expiration of
a limitation period, destruction of the subject matter, impossibility; and by **breach**.

### 22.3 Breach and remedies

A **breach** is a failure to perform without legal excuse. The remedies:

- **Compensatory damages** — money to put the injured party where performance would have.
- **Liquidated damages** — an amount the parties fixed in advance. In residential practice earnest
  money is frequently the agreed liquidated damages for a buyer's default, which is one reason the
  amount matters.
- **Specific performance** — a court order compelling the actual transfer. **Available in real estate
  because each parcel is unique**, so money may not make the injured party whole. This is Module
  MO-02's uniqueness characteristic doing legal work.
- **Rescission** — unwinding the contract and restoring the parties to their prior positions.
- **Reformation** — correcting a writing to reflect what the parties actually agreed.

**None of these is a licensee's to advise on.** A client asking what they can do about a breach is
asking a legal question, and § 339.730.1(3)(d) requires the licensee to tell them to get expert
advice. What a licensee contributes is an accurate factual record of what happened and when.

---

## Hour 23 — Other real estate contracts, and the drafting boundary

### 23.1 The other contracts a salesperson meets

chunks.heading: 23.2 The boundary: completing a form is not drafting one
chunks.excerpt:
**Listing agreements** — the contract between the seller and the firm. Exclusive right to sell: the
firm is owed a commission on a sale during the term regardless of who procures the buyer, including
the seller. Exclusive agency: the seller may sell themselves without owing a commission. Open listing:
only the procuring broker is paid, and the seller may give it to many firms. In Missouri each of these
is a written agreement required by § 339.780.2 and entered into by the designated broker.

**Buyer agency agreements** — § 339.780.3, required before any of the § 339.010 activities except
ministerial acts, and containing the § 339.740 duties and the terms of compensation.

**Transaction brokerage agreements** — § 339.780.6, required where the transaction broker expects
compensation from the party assisted.

**Options** — a unilateral contract in which the optionor gives the optionee the right, but not the
obligation, to buy on stated terms within a period, for consideration. The optionee is not bound.

**Land contracts, or contracts for deed** — the buyer takes possession and equitable title while the
seller retains legal title until the payments are complete. Structurally, this is the arrangement in
which the buyer has the least protection, and the consequences of default are a legal question with
real stakes. A licensee explains the structure and routes the decision to counsel. **This course
states no Missouri rule governing land contracts**, because the relevant chapter has not been read
from primary text for this project.

**Leases** — a conveyance of a possessory interest and a contract of covenants at once.

### 23.2 The boundary: completing a form is not drafting one

This is the most important professional line in the module, and it is not a technicality.

chunks.heading: 23.3 A working method for the contract stage
chunks.excerpt:
**Inside the licence:** completing forms the firm supplies by filling in the facts of the transaction;
selecting among the approved provisions the forms offer; explaining what a provision means in the
ordinary sense; and advising the client to obtain expert advice, as § 339.730.1(3)(d) requires.

**Outside the licence:** composing new legal language to solve a client's specific legal problem;
advising which form of ownership to take title in; opining on the legal effect of a provision;
drafting an addendum to address something the forms do not cover.

When the forms do not fit, the answer is not to write something. The answer is: **counsel drafts it
and it is attached.** A licensee who composes a clause has practised law, and — separately — has
usually produced a clause that does not do what the client wanted.

### 23.3 A working method for the contract stage

1. **Read the whole form before you use it the first time**, not the first time a client asks about a
   provision.
2. **Fill nothing in from memory.** Legal description from the deed or the title company. Names from
   identification. Figures from the documents.
3. **Date the acceptance correctly and calendar every deadline the same day.**
4. **Where a term does not fit, say so and route it** rather than improvising.
5. **Confirm in writing.** Every material conversation about the contract ends with an email that says
   what was decided.

### Module MO-04 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

339.755, 339.780 and 339.800, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060 and 2250-7.070 — were read from primary

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-05

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-05
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-05

## Hours 24–29 · Real estate finance and real estate mathematics

**Clock hours:** 6. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Describe what underwriting examines and compute a housing ratio and a total debt ratio.
2. Distinguish the note from the security instrument and name the clauses that decide outcomes.
3. Describe the categories of loan programme without recommending one, and route pricing to the lender.
4. Explain the secondary market and what a borrower actually feels from it.
5. Compute loan-to-value, down payment, points, simple interest, commission, area and proration.
6. Read an amortisation schedule and explain why early payments are mostly interest.
7. Compute a buyer's cash to close and a seller's net, and state what makes each an estimate.
8. State the boundary between explaining a structure and quoting a payment.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 24 — Buyer qualification
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 24 | Buyer qualification and underwriting | 50 min |
| 25 | The note, the security instrument, and the clauses | 50 min |
| 26 | Programme categories; default and alternatives | 50 min |
| 27 | The secondary market and servicing | 50 min |
| 28 | Mathematics I: percentages, LTV, points, interest, area | 50 min |
| 29 | Mathematics II: amortisation, proration, cash to close, seller's net | 50 min |

---

## Hour 24 — Buyer qualification

### 24.1 What underwriting examines

Four things, traditionally the four Cs:

**Capacity** — can the borrower repay from income? Measured by the ratios below.
**Credit** — has the borrower repaid before? Measured by score and by the record behind it.
**Capital** — what does the borrower have for down payment, closing costs and reserves, and where did
it come from? Sourcing and seasoning of funds are real underwriting steps and they surprise buyers who
were gifted money at the last minute.
**Collateral** — is the property worth enough and is it acceptable security? This is where the
appraisal enters.

### 24.2 The ratios

**Housing ratio** — the proposed monthly housing payment divided by gross monthly income. The housing
payment is not the loan payment: it is **PITI** — principal, interest, taxes and insurance — plus
mortgage insurance and any association dues.

**Total debt ratio** — housing payment plus all other recurring monthly obligations, divided by gross
monthly income. Car payments, student loans, minimum credit card payments, court-ordered support.

*Worked.* Gross monthly income $6,400. Proposed PITI $1,536. Car payment $410, student loan $220,
credit card minimums $95.

chunks.heading: 24.3 Pre-qualification, pre-approval, and commitment
chunks.excerpt:
Housing ratio: 1,536 ÷ 6,400 = **24%**.
Total obligations: 1,536 + 410 + 220 + 95 = 2,261. Total debt ratio: 2,261 ÷ 6,400 = **35.3%**.

**The thresholds are the lender's and the loan programme's, not the licensee's.** They differ by
programme, they move, and they are subject to compensating factors and to automated underwriting
decisions no licensee sees. A licensee who states a qualifying ratio as though it were a rule has
stated a lender's underwriting standard as law.

### 24.3 Pre-qualification, pre-approval, and commitment

**Pre-qualification** is an estimate from information the borrower stated. **Pre-approval** follows
verification and underwriting. **Neither is a loan commitment.**

That gap is the reason the financing contingency exists, and a buyer who believes a pre-approval is a
promise will not understand why the contingency matters or why anyone is anxious in week three. Say it
plainly at the beginning: *this is what the lender expects today, based on what has been verified; the
commitment comes later, and the contingency protects you until it does.*

### 24.4 What a licensee says about financing, and what they must not

**Do:** explain what the categories are and how they differ structurally; explain what the ratios
measure; explain the difference between pre-qualification, pre-approval and commitment; insist the
buyer speak to a lender early; explain what a rate lock is and that it expires.

**Do not:** recommend a programme as cheapest; compute a payment and give it to the buyer as their
payment; quote a rate; predict what rates will do; or characterise what a lender will approve.

chunks.heading: Hour 25 — The note, the security instrument, and the clauses
chunks.excerpt:
Two Missouri provisions bear directly. Section 339.740.1(3)(d), RSMo, requires the buyer's agent to
**advise the client to obtain expert advice** on material matters beyond the licensee's expertise —
loan pricing is squarely that. And § 339.740.1(2) — reasonable skill and care — is what makes getting
the buyer to a lender **early** part of the job rather than a nicety.

---

## Hour 25 — The note, the security instrument, and the clauses

### 25.1 Two documents, two jobs

The **promissory note** is the borrower's promise to repay. It is the debt. It states the amount, the
rate, the term, the payment and the consequences of default.

The **security instrument** pledges the property as security for that promise. It creates the lien.
Without it the lender has a promise and no property; without the note the lender has a lien securing
nothing.

Two forms are used across the United States. A **mortgage** is a two-party instrument — mortgagor
(borrower) and mortgagee (lender) — typically enforced by **judicial** foreclosure. A **deed of
trust** is a three-party instrument — trustor (borrower), beneficiary (lender), and a **trustee** who
holds power of sale — typically enforced **non-judicially**, without a lawsuit.

**Missouri practice uses the deed of trust**, and Missouri foreclosure is predominantly a **trustee's
sale under the power of sale** rather than a court proceeding. **This course states no Missouri
foreclosure timetable, notice requirement or redemption right**, because Missouri's foreclosure
chapter has not been read from primary text for this project. The structural fact — a trustee holding
a power of sale, exercised without a lawsuit — is what a licensee carries, and every question about
timing, notice, deficiency or redemption is routed to counsel.

chunks.heading: 25.2 The clauses that decide outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
### 25.2 The clauses that decide outcomes

**Acceleration.** On default, the lender may declare the entire balance immediately due. Without it,
default would mean suing for each missed payment.

**Alienation, or due-on-sale.** On transfer of the property, the lender may call the balance due. This
is why "taking subject to" an existing loan is not a workaround a licensee should be arranging, and
why **assumption** requires the lender's consent.

**Prepayment.** Whether the borrower may repay early and on what terms.

**Escrow, or impound.** The lender collects taxes and insurance monthly and pays them when due. This
is why the housing payment is PITI rather than principal and interest, and why an escrow analysis can
change a payment after closing without the rate having moved — which buyers experience as a surprise
and should be warned about.

**Subordination.** An agreement that a lien will take a lower priority than it otherwise would.

**Release, or partial release.** Releasing part of the security as principal is repaid, used in
subdivision and land development lending.

### 25.3 Assumption, subject to, release

**Assumption** — the buyer takes over the existing loan. With the lender's consent and a written
release, the seller is off the obligation. **Without** a release, the seller remains liable even
though they no longer own the property.

**Taking subject to** — the buyer makes the payments but does not assume the obligation. The seller
remains fully liable, and the alienation clause is generally triggered by the transfer. This is a
structure a licensee explains and routes to counsel; it is not one a licensee arranges.

### 25.4 Alternatives to foreclosure

chunks.heading: Hour 26 — Programme categories, and what a licensee may say
chunks.excerpt:
**Reinstatement** — curing the default and restoring the loan. **Forbearance or modification** —
agreements with the lender to change the terms. **Deed in lieu of foreclosure** — conveying the
property to the lender voluntarily; it does not automatically eliminate junior liens. **Short sale** —
the lender agrees to accept less than the balance, which is a lender approval process with a timetable
of its own and a set of tax and credit consequences the seller must take to their accountant and
counsel.

A licensee working a distressed file identifies the questions and routes them. The seller's tax
position, deficiency exposure and credit consequences are all outside the licence.

---

## Hour 26 — Programme categories, and what a licensee may say

### 26.1 The categories

**Conventional** — not insured or guaranteed by a government agency. Where the down payment is below
a threshold the lender requires **private mortgage insurance**, which protects the lender rather than
the borrower and which can generally be removed once equity conditions are met.

**FHA-insured** — insured by the Federal Housing Administration, with lower down payment requirements
and mortgage insurance premiums that follow their own rules, and property condition standards the
appraisal applies.

**VA-guaranteed** — guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans and service
members, with no down payment in the ordinary case and a funding fee in place of monthly mortgage
insurance.

**USDA rural development** — for eligible properties in eligible areas and eligible borrowers.

chunks.heading: 26.2 Fixed, adjustable, and the shapes in between
chunks.excerpt:
**State and local programmes** — down payment assistance, first-time buyer programmes, bond
programmes. Missouri has such programmes; **this course states no eligibility criterion, income limit
or purchase price limit for any of them**, because none was read from primary source for this project.
They are routed to the administering agency and to the lender.

**Seller financing** — including the land contract structure discussed in Module MO-04.

### 26.2 Fixed, adjustable, and the shapes in between

**Fixed rate** — the rate does not change for the life of the loan.
**Adjustable rate** — the rate adjusts on a schedule, tied to an index plus a margin, with caps on the
periodic adjustment and on the lifetime rate. A buyer considering one needs to understand the **worst
case**, not the initial rate, and the worst case is computable from the caps.
**Interest-only, balloon, and graduated payment** structures exist and each carries a risk profile a
buyer must understand before signing.

### 26.3 The rule that governs this hour

A licensee **explains structures** and **routes pricing.** The comparison of two programmes for a
particular borrower depends on the rate, the term, the mortgage insurance treatment, the fees, the
tax position and how long the borrower will hold the property — and the licensee controls none of
those and knows some of them not at all. Naming the categories is education. Recommending one is
advice the licensee is not licensed to give.

---

## Hour 27 — The secondary market and servicing

### 27.1 Primary and secondary

The **primary market** is where loans are made — the lender and the borrower. The **secondary market**
is where loans are bought and sold after origination.

chunks.heading: 27.2 What it causes
chunks.excerpt:
It exists because it returns capital to originators, who can then lend again. Without it, a lender's
capacity would be limited to its deposits and its own balance sheet, and thirty-year fixed-rate
lending at scale would not exist.

### 27.2 What it causes

**Standardisation.** Because originators write loans intending to sell them, they write to the
purchaser's guidelines. This is why underwriting looks broadly similar across lenders, why the
documentation requirements feel identical, and why an unusual property or an unusual borrower is
harder to finance than the numbers alone suggest.

**Servicing transfer.** The right to collect payments is itself an asset and is bought and sold. A
borrower may make their first payment to one company and their second to another they never chose.
Tell buyers this will probably happen and that it does not change their loan terms, because otherwise
the notice arrives looking like a scam.

**Rate transmission.** Mortgage rates track the yields investors demand on mortgage-backed securities
more closely than they track any single policy rate — which is why mortgage rates sometimes move
opposite to the direction a news story implies. That is also why a licensee does not forecast them.

---

## Hour 28 — Mathematics I

### 28.1 The one method that solves most problems

Most real estate arithmetic is a single relationship:

> **Part = Whole × Rate**

Rearranged: Rate = Part ÷ Whole. Whole = Part ÷ Rate. Identify which two of the three you have, and
the problem is one operation. Nearly every commission, interest, appreciation, ratio and profit
problem on any examination is this relationship wearing a costume.

### 28.2 Loan-to-value and down payment

**LTV = loan amount ÷ the LESSER of price or appraised value.**

chunks.heading: 28.3 Points and interest
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked.* Price $284,000, appraised $284,000, 10 percent down.
Down payment: 284,000 × 0.10 = **$28,400**. Loan: **$255,600**. LTV: 255,600 ÷ 284,000 = **90%**.

*Worked, with a low appraisal.* Same price, appraisal comes in at $272,000. The lender lends 90
percent **of the lesser figure**: 272,000 × 0.90 = $244,800. The buyer now needs 284,000 − 244,800 =
**$39,200** in cash, not $28,400. The $12,000 appraisal gap became a $10,800 cash problem, and this is
exactly what an appraisal contingency exists to handle.

### 28.3 Points and interest

**A point is one percent of the LOAN AMOUNT**, not of the price. Get that wrong and every points
problem is wrong.

*Worked.* 1.5 points on a $255,600 loan: 255,600 × 0.015 = **$3,834**.

**Simple annual interest = principal × rate.** Monthly interest = that ÷ 12.

*Worked.* $255,600 at 6.25%: annual 255,600 × 0.0625 = $15,975. Monthly: 15,975 ÷ 12 = **$1,331.25**.

### 28.4 Commission

*Worked.* Sale price $284,000, total commission 6 percent, split evenly between two firms, and the
listing salesperson's agreement with their designated broker is 60/40 in the salesperson's favour.

Total: 284,000 × 0.06 = **$17,040**.
Listing firm: 17,040 ÷ 2 = **$8,520**.
Listing salesperson: 8,520 × 0.60 = **$5,112**. Firm retains $3,408.

**Commission rates are negotiable and are never set by any board, association or rule.** And note
where the money goes: from the closing to the **designated broker**, and from the broker to the
salesperson. A salesperson is not paid by a seller.

### 28.5 Area

Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × height. Irregular shapes: divide into rectangles and
triangles, compute each, add.

**1 acre = 43,560 square feet. 1 section = 640 acres. 1 mile = 5,280 feet.**

chunks.heading: Hour 29 — Mathematics II
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked.* A lot 88 feet wide and 165 feet deep. 88 × 165 = 14,520 sq ft. As a fraction of an acre:
14,520 ÷ 43,560 = **1/3 acre**.

*Worked.* A house measures 46 ft by 28 ft with an attached 24 ft by 22 ft addition. 46 × 28 = 1,288;
24 × 22 = 528. Total **1,816 sq ft**. At a construction cost of $148 per square foot: 1,816 × 148 =
**$268,768**.

---

## Hour 29 — Mathematics II

### 29.1 Amortisation, and why early payments are mostly interest

An amortising payment is constant; its **composition** changes every month. Each month, interest is
computed on the **current** balance; whatever is left of the payment reduces principal; the balance
falls; so next month's interest is slightly smaller and next month's principal portion slightly
larger.

*Worked, first three months.* $255,600 at 6.25%, monthly payment $1,573.71.

| Month | Interest | Principal | Ending balance |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 255,600 × .0625 ÷ 12 = **1,331.25** | 242.46 | 255,357.54 |
| 2 | 255,357.54 × .0625 ÷ 12 = **1,329.99** | 243.72 | 255,113.82 |
| 3 | 255,113.82 × .0625 ÷ 12 = **1,328.72** | 244.99 | 254,868.83 |

Three payments of $1,573.71 — $4,721.13 — reduced the balance by **$731.17**. That is not a defect;
it is what amortisation is. A buyer who understands it will not be shocked by their first-year
statement, and a licensee who explains it has done something genuinely useful.

### 29.2 Proration

Proration divides a shared expense between seller and buyer at closing. Three questions must be
answered before any arithmetic:

1. **What is the annual amount?**
2. **What basis** — a 365-day year, or a 360-day banker's year with 30-day months?
3. **Who gets the day of closing**, and is the item **paid in advance** or **in arrears**?

chunks.heading: 29.3 Cash to close
chunks.excerpt:
**The convention comes from the contract, not from habit.** Getting the basis or the closing-day
convention wrong produces a number that is close enough to look right and is wrong.

*Worked, taxes paid in arrears, 365-day basis, closing day to the buyer.* Annual tax $3,284.00.
Closing 19 September.

Daily: 3,284.00 ÷ 365 = **$8.9973**.
Seller's days, 1 January through 18 September: 31+28+31+30+31+30+31+31+18 = **261 days**.
261 × 8.9973 = **$2,348.29**, a **credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller** — because the buyer
will pay the whole bill when it comes due.

*Worked, an item paid in advance.* Association dues of $360 paid annually on 1 January, closing 19
September, 365-day basis. The **seller** has already paid through 31 December. Days remaining to the
buyer, 19 September through 31 December: 12+31+30+31 = 104. 360 ÷ 365 = 0.9863 daily. 104 × 0.9863 =
**$102.56**, a **credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer.**

The direction is the part people get wrong. Ask: **who has had the use, and who has paid?** Whoever
paid for time they will not have gets a credit.

### 29.3 Cash to close

Purchase price, **plus** closing costs and prepaid items, **minus** the loan amount, **minus** the
earnest money already deposited, **plus or minus** the net of the prorations.

*Worked.* Price $284,000. Loan $255,600. Earnest money $3,000. Buyer's closing costs and prepaids
$6,850. Tax proration credit to buyer $2,348.29.

284,000 + 6,850 = 290,850.
290,850 − 255,600 − 3,000 − 2,348.29 = **$29,901.71**.

### 29.4 Seller's net

Sale price, **minus** the payoff of existing loans, **minus** commission, **minus** the seller's
closing costs, **minus** any credits to the buyer, **plus** any credits to the seller.

chunks.heading: 29.5 What makes every one of these an estimate
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked.* Price $284,000. Loan payoff $196,400. Commission 6 percent = $17,040. Seller's closing costs
$2,240. Tax proration debit to seller $2,348.29.

284,000 − 196,400 − 17,040 − 2,240 − 2,348.29 = **$65,971.71**.

### 29.5 What makes every one of these an estimate

Payoff figures include per-diem interest and are quoted to a date. Closing costs are the closing
agent's and the lender's figures, not the licensee's. Prorations depend on a tax bill that may not yet
have issued. Any of these can move between the estimate and the settlement statement.

**So label it.** A net sheet is an estimate, it says so on its face, it shows its assumptions, and the
figures come from the closing agent, the lender and the payoff statement. A licensee who hands a
seller a confident net figure that turns out to be $3,000 optimistic has created a problem that no
apology fixes.

### Module MO-05 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-06
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-06

## Hours 30–34 · Valuation, market analysis, leases, and property management

**Clock hours:** 5. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Distinguish value, price and cost, and explain why an owner's improvement cost is not value.
2. Name the principles of value and apply substitution, contribution, conformity and anticipation.
3. Apply the four tests of highest and best use in the correct order.
4. Build a comparison grid with adjustments in the correct direction and reconcile to a range.
5. Describe the cost and income approaches and say when each governs.
6. State the boundary between a licensee's market analysis and an appraisal.
7. Classify a leasehold estate and identify what notice, if any, ends it.
8. Describe a property manager's functions and compute net operating income.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 30 | Value, price, cost; the principles; the four forces | 50 min |
| 31 | Highest and best use; the sales comparison approach | 50 min |
| 32 | The cost approach and the income approach | 50 min |
| 33 | The appraisal process; the licensee's boundary | 50 min |
| 34 | Leaseholds and property management | 50 min |

---

chunks.heading: Hour 30 — Value, price, cost, and the principles
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 30 — Value, price, cost, and the principles

### 30.1 Three words

**Value** is the worth of a property to a typical buyer under stated conditions — most often **market
value**, the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive and open market under
conditions requisite to a fair sale, with buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably and
neither under undue duress.

**Price** is what was actually paid in a particular transaction. It is a historical fact and it may
have been influenced by a motivated seller, an uninformed buyer, an unusual concession or a
relationship between the parties.

**Cost** is what it took to produce the improvements.

**Cost does not become value.** An owner who spent $92,000 on a pool, a sunroom and a kitchen is
frequently astonished by the appraisal, and the explanation is Hour 30's most important principle:
the **principle of contribution** says an improvement adds what it adds to the value of the whole, not
what it cost.

### 30.2 The principles of value

**Supply and demand.** Value rises when demand exceeds supply and falls when it does not.

**Substitution.** A buyer will pay no more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally
desirable substitute. This is the foundation of all three approaches to value.

**Contribution.** As above. Measured by the change in the value of the whole, not by cost.

**Conformity.** Value is maximised where a property conforms reasonably to those around it. The
corollaries are **progression** — a modest house gains from better neighbours — and **regression** —
an over-improved house loses to worse ones. The most over-built house on the street is the standard
case of regression, and it is also the standard listing where the owner cannot understand the price.

chunks.heading: 30.3 The four forces
chunks.excerpt:
**Anticipation.** Value reflects the expectation of future benefits, which is why a rumoured highway
interchange moves prices before it is built.

**Change.** Nothing is static. Markets, neighbourhoods and buildings all move through phases.

**Increasing and diminishing returns.** Additional investment increases value up to a point, after
which it does not.

**Plottage** — assembling adjacent parcels under one ownership to produce a value greater than the
sum of the parts, the increment being **assemblage** value. **Externalities** — influences from
outside the property.

### 30.3 The four forces

**Social** — demographics, household composition, preferences. **Economic** — employment, income,
rates, credit. **Governmental** — zoning, codes, taxation, public investment. **Environmental** —
physical characteristics, topography, transport, location.

---

## Hour 31 — Highest and best use, and the sales comparison approach

### 31.1 Highest and best use

The use that is:

1. **Legally permissible**,
2. **Physically possible**,
3. **Financially feasible**, and
4. **Maximally productive**.

**All four, and in that order.** A use that is not legally permissible never reaches the profitability
question. This is also where a licensee stops: whether a use is permissible is a determination for the
municipality, not an opinion for a listing presentation.

### 31.2 The sales comparison approach

The most reliable approach for owner-occupied residential property, because that is how the market
actually behaves — buyers compare.

**The rule that governs every grid: adjust the COMPARABLE, never the subject.** The subject is what is
being valued and has no price yet; there is nothing on it to adjust.

chunks.heading: 31.3 Selecting comparables
chunks.excerpt:
- Comparable **superior** to the subject → adjust the comparable **DOWN**.
- Comparable **inferior** to the subject → adjust the comparable **UP**.

Getting the direction wrong moves the answer twice as far as leaving the adjustment out, and it is the
single most common grid error.

### 31.3 Selecting comparables

Recent closed sales, similar in physical characteristics, in the same market area, and arm's-length.
Not listings, which are asking prices. Not pending sales, whose prices are not yet known. Not
distressed sales unless the subject is itself distressed. The fewer and larger the adjustments, the
weaker the comparable.

### 31.4 A worked grid

*Subject: 1,720 sq ft ranch, 3 bed, 2 bath, attached 2-car garage, unfinished basement, 0.31 acre.*

| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sale price | $268,000 | $242,500 | $291,000 |
| Sold | 2 months ago | 7 months ago | 1 month ago |
| Market conditions +0.3%/month | +$1,608 | +$5,093 | +$873 |
| Living area | 1,790 (+70) | 1,610 (−110) | 1,880 (+160) |
| Area adj. at $62/sq ft | −$4,340 | +$6,820 | −$9,920 |
| Bathrooms | 2 | 1.5 (−0.5) | 3 (+1) |
| Bath adj. at $6,500 each | $0 | +$3,250 | −$6,500 |
| Garage | attached 2-car | attached 1-car | attached 2-car |
| Garage adj. | $0 | +$8,000 | $0 |
| Basement | unfinished | unfinished | finished |
| Basement adj. | $0 | $0 | −$14,000 |
| **Net adjustment** | **−$2,732** | **+$23,163** | **−$29,547** |
| **Adjusted price** | **$265,268** | **$265,663** | **$261,453** |

**Check every direction.** Comp A is larger — superior — so the area adjustment is negative. Comp B is
inferior on area, baths and garage, so all three are positive. Comp C is superior on area, baths and
basement, so all three are negative.

### 31.5 Reconciling

chunks.heading: Hour 32 — The cost approach and the income approach
chunks.excerpt:
The three adjusted figures are $265,268, $265,663 and $261,453. **Reconciliation is judgment, not an
average.** Comp A required the smallest adjustments and sold most recently after Comp C; it deserves
the most weight. Comp B required $23,163 of gross adjustment and deserves the least. A defensible
conclusion is a **range of roughly $262,000 to $266,000**, with the weight of the evidence in the
upper half.

Note that the arithmetic average — $264,128 — is inside that range and tells you nothing about which
evidence was strongest. That is why reconciliation is not averaging.

---

## Hour 32 — The cost approach and the income approach

### 32.1 The cost approach

**Land value + (reproduction or replacement cost of the improvements − accrued depreciation) = value.**

**Reproduction cost** is the cost to build an exact replica. **Replacement cost** is the cost to build
a structure of equal utility using current materials and methods, and it is the more common basis.

**Accrued depreciation** has three sources:

- **Physical deterioration** — wear, age, deferred maintenance. Curable or incurable.
- **Functional obsolescence** — a defect in the design itself. A bedroom reachable only through
  another bedroom; a single bathroom in a four-bedroom house; a 1970s floor plan the market has moved
  past. Curable or incurable.
- **External obsolescence** — caused by something **outside** the property boundaries. A new highway,
  a closed employer, a declining area. **Always incurable**, because the owner cannot fix it.

chunks.heading: 32.2 The income approach
chunks.excerpt:
The cost approach governs **new construction** and **special-purpose property** where comparables are
thin — a church, a school, a fire station. It is weakest on older buildings, because estimating
accrued depreciation on a seventy-year-old house is largely guesswork.

### 32.2 The income approach

For income-producing property.

**Potential gross income** — the income at full occupancy.
**Less vacancy and collection loss** → **effective gross income**.
**Less operating expenses** → **net operating income**.
**Net operating income ÷ capitalisation rate = value.**

*Worked.* An eight-unit building. Potential gross income $96,000. Vacancy and collection loss 6
percent = $5,760. Effective gross income **$90,240**. Operating expenses $38,300. **NOI = $51,940.**
At a capitalisation rate of 7.5 percent: 51,940 ÷ 0.075 = **$692,533**.

**Debt service and depreciation are NOT operating expenses.** They sit below the NOI line. This is why
two identical buildings with different financing have the same NOI and different cash flow, and it is
why NOI is the figure a buyer compares.

**The gross rent multiplier** is a cruder tool: sale price ÷ gross rent. It is quick and it ignores
expenses entirely, so it is a screening device, not a valuation.

### 32.3 How an income pro forma is dressed

Three things to check on any pro forma handed to a buyer, because all three inflate value directly:

**Is there a reserve line?** The roof, the mechanicals and the parking will need replacing. A pro
forma with no replacement reserve understates expenses, overstates NOI, and therefore overstates value
— by the reserve amount divided by the cap rate, which is a large number.

**Is the vacancy assumption real?** A pro forma showing 2 percent vacancy in a market running at 8
percent is a wish.

chunks.heading: Hour 33 — The appraisal process and the licensee's boundary
chunks.excerpt:
**Are the rents actual or projected?** "Market rents after renovation" is not income; it is a plan.

---

## Hour 33 — The appraisal process and the licensee's boundary

### 33.1 The process

1. Define the problem — the property, the interest, the purpose, the date and the definition of value.
2. Determine the scope of work.
3. Collect and analyse data — general market data and specific property data.
4. Analyse highest and best use.
5. Estimate land value.
6. Apply the approaches that are applicable.
7. **Reconcile** into a final opinion.
8. Report.

### 33.2 The boundary, stated plainly

**An appraisal is an opinion of value produced by a licensed or certified appraiser under that
person's own licence and under their professional standards.** A salesperson is not an appraiser and
does not perform appraisals.

**A licensee's market analysis** is the licensee's presentation of market evidence supporting a
pricing decision. It uses the same comparison logic. It is not an appraisal, it must not be labelled
or described as one, and it must not be presented in a way that lets a client believe it is one.

The professional method:

- **Present it in writing**, with the comparables and the adjustments shown.
- **Present a range**, not a single figure.
- **Say plainly that the price is the seller's decision.**
- **Label it for what it is.**

### 33.3 Why this boundary is a Missouri problem and not just an etiquette problem

chunks.heading: 33.4 The three things a seller will show you, and what to say about each
chunks.excerpt:
Two provisions. Section 339.730.1(2), RSMo, requires reasonable skill and care — and confirming a
valuation the licensee did not derive is not care. Section 339.730.1(3)(d) requires the licensee to
**advise the client to obtain expert advice** as to material matters beyond the licensee's expertise —
and a valuation question the licensee cannot support is exactly that.

And the school-side rule reinforces it: 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)3 forbids a school to permit anyone
associated with it **to provide any misleading information to the public**.

### 33.4 The three things a seller will show you, and what to say about each

**An automated online valuation.** It is a model's output from public and listing data. It has not
been inside the house and cannot see condition. It is evidence to weigh, not a valuation. Do not adopt
it and do not dismiss it — put your own analysis beside it.

**An old appraisal.** A 2019 appraisal is a 2019 opinion, produced for a purpose that may not be this
one, on a property that may have changed.

**A neighbour's number.** Ask what it is based on. Usually it is a list price, which is an asking
price and not evidence of anything.

---

## Hour 34 — Leaseholds and property management

### 34.1 The four leasehold estates

**Estate for years.** A definite beginning and a definite end. **It terminates on its own terms and
requires no notice.**

**Periodic tenancy, or estate from period to period.** Renews automatically — month to month, year to
year — until proper notice is given by either party.

**Tenancy at will.** Possession with the landlord's consent for an indefinite period, terminable by
either party.

**Tenancy at sufferance.** A holdover — the tenant remains after the right to possess has ended. It is
not a tenancy the landlord agreed to.

chunks.heading: 34.2 A lease is two things at once
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no Missouri notice period for any of these**, because Missouri's landlord-tenant
chapter has not been read from primary text for this project. Which estate exists is what a licensee
must be able to identify; what notice ends it is routed to counsel and to the lease.

### 34.2 A lease is two things at once

A **conveyance** of a possessory interest for a term, and a **contract** of covenants between the
parties. That is why a lease dispute can be framed either as a breach of contract or as an
interference with possession, and why the **covenant of quiet enjoyment** matters as much as any
written clause.

**Assignment** transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest. **Sublease** transfers less than all
of it, leaving the original tenant as a landlord to the subtenant. In both cases the original tenant
generally **remains liable** unless expressly released — which tenants routinely assume they are not.

Lease types by rent structure: **gross**, where the landlord pays operating expenses; **net**, in its
several degrees, where the tenant pays some or all of them; **percentage**, common in retail, where
rent includes a share of sales; and **ground**, a long-term lease of land on which the tenant builds.

### 34.3 Property management

The manager is the **owner's agent**, and every duty in Module MO-03 attaches — while every fair
housing obligation runs to applicants and tenants at the same time.

**Functions:** marketing and leasing; tenant screening applied identically to every applicant;
collections; maintenance, both routine and capital; budgeting and reporting; regulatory compliance;
and risk management.

chunks.heading: Module MO-06 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**The management agreement** must settle the scope of authority, the compensation, the term, the
reporting and accounting obligations, the owner's approval thresholds for expenditure, and the
handling of trust funds. It is a written agreement, and an unwritten scope of authority is how a
manager ends up having spent an owner's money on something the owner did not authorise.

**Trust accounting is where property managers lose licences**, and almost never for theft — for
sloppiness that looks identical on an audit. Security deposits and prepaid rent are **other people's
money**. They never touch an operating account, whatever the owner suggests and whatever spreadsheet
sits behind the arrangement. **This course states no Missouri trust account requirement**, because
§ 339.105 and the relevant 20 CSR 2250 chapters have not been read from primary text for this project;
the rule is read directly before any manager touches a deposit.

*Worked.* Effective gross income $184,000, operating expenses $71,000. **NOI = $113,000.** Debt
service of $76,400 is not subtracted here — it is below the line, and $113,000 − $76,400 = $36,600 is
**before-tax cash flow**, a different figure answering a different question.

### Module MO-06 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-06

Missouri citations in this module — §§ 339.730 and 339.740, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.010
and 2250-7.070 — were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module MO-06
chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Missouri's landlord-tenant chapter and
every notice period, security deposit rule and remedy in it; § 339.105 and the trust-account rules in
20 CSR 2250; and Missouri's appraiser licensing chapter. The worked figures are arithmetic
illustrations using invented amounts and are not Missouri market or legal figures.

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-07
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-07

## Hours 35–39 · Title, transfer of title, and closing

**Clock hours:** 5. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Name the requirements of a valid deed and explain why recording is not one of them.
2. Distinguish the deed types by the covenants each gives and say when each is used.
3. Explain the three kinds of notice and why possession must be checked as well as the records.
4. Describe voluntary and involuntary alienation, including probate and adverse possession.
5. Read a title commitment's structure and say what requirements and exceptions each do.
6. State what an owner's policy covers and what it excepts.
7. Describe what happens at a closing, who does what, and what the licensee's role actually is.
8. Explain what RESPA and TRID require and what the licensee's part in them is.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 35 | Deeds: requirements and types | 50 min |
| 36 | Recording, notice, and the chain of title | 50 min |
| 37 | Involuntary alienation; probate and estate sales | 50 min |
| 38 | Title evidence, commitments, and title insurance | 50 min |
| 39 | The closing: process, documents, and federal disclosure | 50 min |

---

## Hour 35 — Deeds

chunks.heading: 35.1 What makes a deed valid
chunks.excerpt:
### 35.1 What makes a deed valid

A **deed** is the instrument that conveys an interest in real estate. To be valid it requires:

- a **grantor** with legal capacity;
- a **grantee** identified with certainty;
- **words of conveyance** — the granting clause;
- an **adequate legal description**;
- the **grantor's signature**, and in practice acknowledgement before a notary so that it may be
  recorded;
- **delivery** by the grantor and **acceptance** by the grantee.

**Title passes at delivery and acceptance.** Recording is not a requirement of validity. An unrecorded
but delivered deed is valid **between the parties** — and can still lose to a later interest taken and
recorded by someone without notice of it, which is the entire point of Hour 36.

Note also what is **not** required: the grantee's signature, and consideration in any particular
amount. Deeds routinely recite nominal consideration.

### 35.2 Deed types, by what the grantor promises

**General warranty deed.** The broadest covenants. The grantor warrants title against defects arising
at **any** time, including before the grantor owned the property. The traditional covenants are
seisin, right to convey, against encumbrances, quiet enjoyment, further assurance and warranty
forever. This is the ordinary residential sale deed.

**Special or limited warranty deed.** The grantor warrants only against defects arising **during the
grantor's own ownership.** Common where the grantor is an entity, a lender or a fiduciary that cannot
speak to what happened before it held title.

chunks.heading: Hour 36 — Recording, notice, and the chain
chunks.excerpt:
**Quit claim deed.** Conveys whatever interest the grantor has — **if any** — and warrants nothing. It
is a **clearing** instrument, used to remove a cloud, correct a name, release a possible interest or
transfer between related parties. It is not a sale instrument, and a buyer offered one in an
arm's-length purchase should ask why.

**Deeds by fiduciaries** — personal representative's deed, trustee's deed, sheriff's deed, guardian's
deed. Each carries the authority of the proceeding behind it and warrants little or nothing. **The
authority is the question**, and it is a legal one.

**Which deed is used in a particular transaction is a legal decision for counsel and the closing
agent.** A licensee who tells a client which deed to take or give has practised law.

---

## Hour 36 — Recording, notice, and the chain

### 36.1 What recording does

Recording an instrument in the county records gives **constructive notice to the world** of the
recorded interest, protecting its holder against later takers. It does **not** transfer title and it
does **not** validate an invalid instrument.

The practical rule is short: **record immediately.** The entire risk lives in the interval between
delivery and recording.

### 36.2 Three kinds of notice

**Actual notice** — the party in fact knows.

**Constructive notice from the records** — the party is charged with knowing what a proper search of
the public records would reveal, whether or not they searched.

**Inquiry notice, or notice from possession** — the party is charged with what a reasonable inspection
of the property would reveal, and with following up on what that inspection would make a reasonable
person ask about.

chunks.heading: 36.3 The chain of title, and clouds
chunks.excerpt:
**The possession problem is the classic trap and it is a real one.** Someone living in the house, a
tenant with an unrecorded lease, a neighbour openly using a strip of the yard — each is a fact a
purchaser is expected to have noticed. Title is checked in the records **and** on the ground.

### 36.3 The chain of title, and clouds

The **chain of title** is the successive record of conveyances from an accepted starting point to the
present owner. A **cloud** is anything in it — a gap, an unreleased mortgage, a missing signature, a
name discrepancy, an estate that never went through probate — that raises a doubt about the title.

Clouds are resolved **before closing**, not explained away at it. The instruments used are typically a
quit claim deed, a corrective deed, an affidavit, a release, or in a hard case a **suit to quiet
title**.

**Evidence of title** is the proof of title's condition. In current Missouri practice that is
predominantly a **title insurance commitment and policy**; historically it was an abstract of title
with an attorney's opinion. Which form a transaction uses is settled in the purchase contract, which
is one more reason the contract is read before it is signed.

---

## Hour 37 — Involuntary alienation, probate, and estate sales

### 37.1 Voluntary and involuntary

**Voluntary alienation** is transfer by the owner's act — sale, gift, dedication, or transfer at death
by will.

**Involuntary alienation** happens without the owner's consent:

chunks.heading: 37.2 Adverse possession
chunks.excerpt:
- **Escheat** — to the state where an owner dies with no heirs and no will.
- **Eminent domain** — through condemnation, with just compensation.
- **Foreclosure** — enforcement of a lien.
- **Tax sale** — enforcement of the tax lien.
- **Adverse possession** — a court's determination that long possession has ripened into title.
- **Natural processes** — accretion, erosion, avulsion and reliction, which move boundaries along
  watercourses.

### 37.2 Adverse possession

Possession that is **actual, open and notorious, hostile** to the true owner's interest, **exclusive**,
and **continuous for the statutory period** may ripen into title. **Tacking** allows successive
possessors in privity to add their periods together.

Adverse possession is **established by a court**, not asserted by a party. **This course states no
Missouri statutory period**, because the relevant Missouri statute has not been read from primary text
for this project.

What a licensee carries out of this is the recognition, and it is worth stating as a practice rule: a
**fence, drive, dock, garden or building in the wrong place, in place for a long time**, is routed to
counsel and a surveyor. It is never resolved by asking the neighbours what they think.

### 37.3 Transfer at death, and estate sales

**Testate** — the owner died leaving a valid will; real property passes by **devise** to a
**devisee**. **Intestate** — no valid will; property passes to heirs under the state's descent and
distribution statute.

**Probate** is the court proceeding that proves the will, appoints a personal representative, settles
claims and authorises distribution.

**What a licensee must know about an estate sale:**

chunks.heading: Hour 38 — Title evidence and title insurance
chunks.excerpt:
- **Authority to convey comes from the probate proceeding and the personal representative's
  appointment.** It is a legal determination and it is established before a listing is taken, not
  discovered at closing.
- **Probate timing can control the closing date.** Building a closing date around a probate step
  nobody has confirmed is the avoidable error in estate work, and it is the one that happens most.
- The deed will typically be a fiduciary's deed warranting little, and the buyer should understand
  that.

**This course states no Missouri probate rule, procedure or timetable**, because Missouri's probate
chapter has not been read from primary text for this project.

---

## Hour 38 — Title evidence and title insurance

### 38.1 The commitment

A **title commitment** is the title company's conditional promise to insure. Read its structure:

**Schedule A** — the facts. The proposed insured, the amount, the estate or interest, the current
record owner, the legal description.

**Schedule B-I — Requirements.** What must be done before the policy issues: payoff and release of
existing liens, corrective instruments, evidence of authority, satisfaction of judgments, resolution
of probate.

**Schedule B-II — Exceptions.** What the policy will **not** cover. This is where the policy's actual
scope is decided and it is the part a buyer is least likely to read. The standard exceptions commonly
include **rights of parties in possession**, **survey matters and encroachments** absent a survey,
easements not shown by the records, mineral rights, and taxes not yet due and payable.

**A commitment is not a coverage summary.** A licensee who tells a buyer "the title policy will take
care of it" has characterised another party's contract they have not read and cannot bind.

chunks.heading: 38.2 What title insurance covers
chunks.excerpt:
### 38.2 What title insurance covers

An **owner's policy** insures against loss from covered title defects existing **at the date of
policy** — forged instruments, undisclosed heirs, incompetent grantors, recording errors, defective
deeds, undisclosed liens. Coverage is retrospective: it insures the past, not future events.

A **lender's policy** insures the lender's lien position in the amount of the loan and decreases as
the loan is repaid. **A lender's policy does not protect the buyer**, and buyers regularly believe
that it does. Say so.

**What is excepted:** everything in Schedule B-II, plus defects created, assumed or agreed to by the
insured, and defects known to the insured and not disclosed to the company.

**The survey exception is the practical one.** Encroachments, boundary discrepancies and matters a
survey would disclose are typically excepted **unless a survey is furnished and the exception
removed**. A buyer who declines a survey has accepted that risk and should be told so in exactly those
words.

### 38.3 The licensee's part

Get the commitment into the buyer's hands **early**. Tell them to read Schedules B-I and B-II. Route
every question to the title company and counsel. Watch the objection deadline in the contract, because
it will pass while everyone assumes the title work is "in progress."

---

## Hour 39 — The closing

### 39.1 What actually happens

Closing is the simultaneous exchange in which the buyer's funds and the seller's deed change hands and
the instruments are recorded. In Missouri practice it is customarily conducted by a **title company or
closing agent**, and it may be conducted with the parties present or in escrow.

**The steps, in order:**

chunks.heading: 39.2 Who does what
chunks.excerpt:
1. Title examination and clearing of Schedule B-I requirements.
2. The lender's underwriting, appraisal, and clear-to-close.
3. Preparation of the settlement statement and the closing documents.
4. The buyer's **final walkthrough** — not an inspection, but a confirmation that the property is in
   the agreed condition, that agreed repairs were made, and that the included items are still there.
5. Signing, funding, disbursement.
6. **Recording** of the deed and the security instrument.

### 39.2 Who does what

**The closing agent** prepares the settlement statement, handles the funds, records the instruments
and issues the policy. **The lender** funds and sets its own conditions. **Counsel** advises on legal
questions and drafts anything that needs drafting. **The licensee** does none of those things.

**What the licensee actually does at closing** is narrower and useful: makes sure everyone has what
they need before the day; reviews the settlement statement **against the contract** for the items the
contract allocated — the prorations, the credits, the agreed repairs, the commission — and raises any
discrepancy **before** signing; attends; and does not answer questions that belong to the closing
agent, the lender or counsel.

### 39.3 Prorations and credits at settlement

A **credit** to a party is money in their favour; a **debit** is money against them. Items customarily
prorated include real estate taxes, association dues, rents and security deposits on a leased
property, and fuel on a tank.

The **contract** decides the basis and the closing-day convention, and Module MO-05 Hour 29 supplies
the arithmetic. What matters here is the check: does the settlement statement do what the contract
said?

### 39.4 RESPA and TRID

chunks.heading: 39.4 RESPA and TRID
chunks.excerpt:
**RESPA** — the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act — governs settlement services on most federally
related residential mortgage loans. Two prohibitions matter directly to a licensee:

- **Section 8 prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees** for the referral of settlement service business.
  A payment, a thing of value, or a fee for a service not actually performed, in exchange for
  referrals, is prohibited. This is not a technicality; it is the provision that ends careers.
- **Section 9 prohibits a seller from requiring the buyer to use a particular title company** as a
  condition of sale.

RESPA also requires disclosure of **affiliated business arrangements** — where the licensee or the
firm has an ownership interest in a settlement service provider they refer business to. The interest
is disclosed, in writing, and the consumer is told they are not required to use the affiliate.

**TRID** — the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule — requires the **Loan Estimate**, delivered
within three business days of application, and the **Closing Disclosure**, which the consumer must
receive at least **three business days before consummation**. Certain changes restart that three-day
period.

**The licensee's part in TRID is to protect the timeline.** Late-breaking changes — a repair credit
agreed two days before closing, a change in the loan amount — can trigger a redisclosure and move the
closing date. Getting changes decided early, and telling the lender promptly, is a real service and
costs nothing.

chunks.heading: Module MO-07 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no dollar threshold, fee tolerance or exemption under RESPA or TRID**, because
neither the statute nor Regulation X nor Regulation Z was read from primary text for this project. The
prohibitions and the three-day rule above are stated at the level of principle; every specific is
routed to the lender, the closing agent and counsel.

### Module MO-07 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-07

Missouri citations in this module — §§ 339.730 and 339.740, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060 and
2250-7.070 — were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Missouri's recording statutes, adverse
possession period, probate chapter, foreclosure chapter and transfer-tax treatment; RESPA, Regulation
X, TILA and Regulation Z in their own text; and every Commission-prescribed form. Where this module
reaches one of those it names the question and routes it.
