chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-08
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-08

## Hours 40–44 · Fair housing, federal law, land use, and environmental concerns

**Clock hours:** 5. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Name the seven federal protected classes and describe the acts the Fair Housing Act prohibits.
2. Recognise steering, blockbusting and redlining in ordinary language, including when unintended.
3. Distinguish reasonable accommodation from reasonable modification and apply each.
4. Describe the advertising rule and audit a listing description against it.
5. Describe the ADA's application to places of public accommodation in a real estate context.
6. Identify the government and private controls on land use and route each correctly.
7. Recognise the common environmental concerns and state the disclosure obligation that attaches to
   pre-1978 housing.
8. State the licensee's boundary on every subject in this module.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 40 — The Fair Housing Act
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 40 | The Fair Housing Act: classes, acts, exemptions, enforcement | 50 min |
| 41 | Steering, blockbusting, redlining; disability; advertising | 50 min |
| 42 | Other federal law: ECOA, ADA, antitrust, Do Not Call, CAN-SPAM | 50 min |
| 43 | Land use control: zoning, subdivision, private covenants | 50 min |
| 44 | Environmental concerns and the disclosure obligations | 50 min |

---

## Hour 40 — The Fair Housing Act

### 40.1 The seven protected classes

Under the federal Fair Housing Act, as amended:

**Race. Colour. Religion. National origin. Sex. Familial status. Disability.**

Race and colour came first, in the Civil Rights Act of 1866, which prohibits **all** racial
discrimination in the sale or rental of property and has **no exemptions at all**. Religion, colour
and national origin were added by Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968; sex in 1974; and
familial status and disability — the statute's term is *handicap* — by the Fair Housing Amendments Act
of 1988.

**Familial status** means households with children under eighteen, and includes pregnant persons and
those in the process of securing custody. The principal exemption is qualified **housing for older
persons**.

chunks.heading: 40.2 What the Act prohibits
chunks.excerpt:
**These seven are the federal floor.** State and local law may protect additional classes, and a
Missouri licensee's actual obligations are the sum of federal, Missouri and any applicable local
ordinance. **This course states no Missouri or local protected class**, because the Missouri Human
Rights Act and municipal ordinances were not read from primary text for this project. **Read them.**
The classes protected in Kansas City, in St. Louis and under state law are not necessarily the same
seven, and a licensee who works from the federal list alone will eventually be wrong.

### 40.2 What the Act prohibits

- Refusing to sell, rent or negotiate, or otherwise making housing unavailable, because of a protected
  characteristic.
- Discriminating in the terms, conditions, privileges, services or facilities.
- **Advertising** that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination.
- Representing that housing is unavailable when it is available.
- **Blockbusting** — inducing sale or rental for profit by representations about the entry of persons
  of a protected class.
- **Steering** — directing prospects toward or away from areas on the basis of a protected
  characteristic.
- **Redlining** — discrimination in lending or insurance on the basis of the composition of an area.
- Denying access to a multiple listing service or other facility on a protected basis.
- **Coercing, intimidating, threatening or interfering** with a person exercising a fair housing
  right — or **retaliating** against someone who has asserted one or assisted another to.

### 40.3 Narrow exemptions are not blanket permission to discriminate

chunks.heading: 40.4 Enforcement
chunks.excerpt:
[42 USC 3603(b)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-section3603&num=0&edition=prelim)
contains separate, narrow exceptions. The single-family owner exception in subsection (b)(1) has
multiple conditions, including restrictions on using broker or agent sales/rental services. Subsection
(b)(2) separately addresses qualifying owner-occupied dwellings with living quarters for no more than
four families. Its text does not repeat the broker-use condition from subsection (b)(1).

**Do not teach that broker involvement automatically eliminates every exemption, or that an exemption
authorizes discrimination generally.** Section 3603(b) preserves the prohibition on discriminatory
advertising in 3604(c); other federal civil-rights protections, applicable state and local law, and
the licensee's professional duties still require separate analysis. Do not implement a discriminatory
owner instruction on the strength of an assumed exception. Escalate any claimed exemption to the
designated broker and qualified counsel.

### 40.4 Enforcement

A complaint may be filed with HUD, generally within one year of the alleged act, or a civil action may
be brought in federal court within two years. Remedies include actual and punitive damages, injunctive
relief, civil penalties and attorney's fees. The Department of Justice may bring a pattern-or-practice
action.

And a Missouri licensee faces a second track: § 339.730.1(6) and § 339.740.1(6), RSMo, make compliance
with **fair housing and civil rights statutes and regulations** a statutory duty of the limited agent
— so a fair housing violation is also a licence-law violation.

---

## Hour 41 — The practices, disability, and advertising

### 41.1 Steering, in ordinary conversation

chunks.heading: 41.2 The client's discriminatory instruction
chunks.excerpt:
Steering rarely announces itself. It usually arrives as a helpful remark:

> "You'd probably be more comfortable over on the east side."
> "That neighbourhood is really more for young families."
> "Let me show you where people like you tend to buy."
> "I'd stay north of the river if I were you — better element."

Every one of those is steering, and none of them names a protected class. Steering is also committed
by **omission** — by simply not showing or not mentioning areas that meet the buyer's stated criteria.

**The method that prevents it** is to answer with **data the buyer can verify** and to describe
**property**, never people:

- The buyer asks about schools → give them the district's published data and the state's report, and
  tell them to visit. Do not characterise a school as good or bad, because "good schools" functions as
  a proxy in practice.
- The buyer asks about crime → route them to the police department's published statistics.
- The buyer asks "what kind of people live there" → *"I can't characterise the people in an area, and
  I wouldn't be much good at it. Tell me what you need in a property and I'll search on that."*
- The buyer names their own protected characteristic and asks you to search on it → the answer is
  still no, gently and clearly. A buyer's own request does not create an exemption.

### 41.2 The client's discriminatory instruction

A seller says: *don't show it to anyone who would change the character of the street.* A landlord
says: *no children on the second floor.*

**Refuse. Say plainly that you cannot follow the instruction. Withdraw from the representation if it
stands.**

chunks.heading: 41.3 Disability: accommodation and modification
chunks.excerpt:
Three things that are **not** compliance: following the instruction while noting your objection in the
file; applying it "informally"; or asking the client to put it in writing. A written discriminatory
instruction is evidence **against** the licensee, not authority for them.

### 41.3 Disability: accommodation and modification

**Reasonable accommodation** — a change in a **rule, policy, practice or service** necessary to give a
person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. Waiving a no-pets rule for an
assistance animal; a reserved accessible parking space; permitting a rent payment date that matches a
benefit deposit. Generally at the **housing provider's** expense.

**Reasonable modification** — a **physical change** to the premises. A grab bar, a ramp, a widened
doorway, a lowered counter. Generally at the **requesting person's** expense, and the provider may
require restoration of the interior at the end of the tenancy in appropriate cases.

**Rule-change versus physical-change is the whole distinction**, and it is tested constantly and
confused constantly.

**Assistance animals are not pets.** Pet rules, pet rent and pet deposits do not apply to them, and
the questions that may be asked about them are narrowly limited.

**Design and construction.** Covered multifamily dwellings built for first occupancy after March 1991
must meet the Act's accessibility requirements. A licensee marketing new multifamily should know the
requirement exists and route the compliance question to the developer and counsel.

**What may not be asked:** whether a prospect has a disability, the nature or severity of one, or to
see medical records.

### 41.4 Advertising

**Describe the property. Never the buyer, the tenant, or the neighbours.**

chunks.heading: Hour 42 — Other federal law
chunks.excerpt:
Problem phrases and why:

| Phrase | Problem |
|---|---|
| "Perfect for a young professional couple" | age, familial status, marital status |
| "Great family neighbourhood" | familial status |
| "Walk to St. Anne's" | religion |
| "Adult building" | familial status |
| "Must be able to climb stairs" | disability |
| "Exclusive area" | historically coded, and describes people |
| "Bachelor pad" | sex, familial status |
| "Safe neighbourhood" | frequently a proxy, and a claim you cannot support |

Acceptable in the same breath: "two bedrooms," "third floor, no lift," "0.4 miles from the Route 9
bus," "1,720 square feet," "attached two-car garage."

**Auditing an advertisement, line by line.** For every sentence ask three questions: **Who is
speaking?** — the firm must be identifiable, not disguised as a private party. **What is claimed?** —
and can it be supported by something written down. **Who is described?** — if the answer is a person
rather than a building, rewrite it.

And note the school-side rule that governs this course's own advertising: 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)5
requires every advertisement of an approved course to state **the number of hours of education credit
and the correct title of the course as stated in the Commission's approval letter**, and (L)6 forbids
advertising a course at all until it is approved in writing.

---

## Hour 42 — Other federal law

### 42.1 ECOA

The **Equal Credit Opportunity Act** prohibits discrimination in **credit** on the basis of race,
colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (provided the applicant can contract), or
because income derives from a public assistance programme, or because the applicant has exercised a
right under the Consumer Credit Protection Act.

chunks.heading: 42.2 The ADA
chunks.excerpt:
Note two classes ECOA covers that the Fair Housing Act does not: **marital status** and **age**. And
note that a rejected applicant is entitled to notice of the reasons.

### 42.2 The ADA

The **Americans with Disabilities Act** governs **places of public accommodation** and commercial
facilities — Title III — and employment — Title I. In a real estate context this reaches offices,
retail, restaurants and other commercial premises, requiring the removal of architectural barriers
where readily achievable.

**A real estate office is itself a place of public accommodation.** So is an open house held in a
commercial property.

The ADA and the Fair Housing Act cover different ground and are frequently confused. FHA is about
**housing**; ADA Title III is about **public accommodations**. Some property is both.

### 42.3 Antitrust

Four practices, and every one of them is a felony exposure rather than a licence problem:

**Price fixing** — any agreement or understanding among competing firms about commission rates or
fees. Commission is negotiable between the firm and its client, and **any** conversation with a
competitor about what "we" charge is a conversation to leave.

**Market allocation** — agreeing with competitors to divide territories, property types or customer
groups.

**Group boycott** — agreeing with competitors to refuse to deal with a particular broker or business
model.

**Tying** — conditioning the sale of one product or service on the purchase of another.

**The practical rule:** never discuss your firm's commission structure with a competitor, in any
setting, however casual. Do not attend the conversation. Leave it, and be seen to leave it.

### 42.4 Telephone, text and email marketing

chunks.heading: Hour 43 — Land use control
chunks.excerpt:
The **Telephone Consumer Protection Act** and the **National Do Not Call Registry** govern
telemarketing calls, and the rules on autodialled calls and text messages are stricter than most
licensees assume. Firms must maintain an internal do-not-call list and honour requests. **CAN-SPAM**
governs commercial email, requiring accurate headers and subject lines, a physical postal address and
a working opt-out that is honoured promptly.

**This course states no do-not-call registration period, exemption or penalty amount**, because
neither the TCPA nor the FCC rules nor CAN-SPAM was read from primary text for this project. Prospecting
practice is set by the firm's policy, written with counsel, and followed.

---

## Hour 43 — Land use control

### 43.1 Public controls

**The comprehensive plan** is the municipality's long-range policy document. Zoning is meant to
implement it.

**Zoning** divides a jurisdiction into districts and regulates **use** and **dimension** — setbacks,
height, lot coverage, density. The instruments a licensee will hear named:

- **Variance** — permission to depart from a **dimensional** requirement because of a hardship arising
  from the property itself. Granted by a board of adjustment or appeals on its own standards.
- **Conditional or special use permit** — a use the ordinance contemplates subject to review and
  conditions.
- **Rezoning** — a legislative change to the district or the map.
- **Legal nonconforming use** — a use that lawfully predates the current ordinance and is allowed to
  continue **subject to limits** on expansion, on resumption after abandonment, and on rebuilding
  after destruction. Those limits are the point, and a buyer who assumes the use is permanent and
  unrestricted may find they cannot rebuild after a fire.

chunks.heading: 43.2 Subdivision regulation
chunks.excerpt:
**Building codes** set minimum construction standards, enforced through permits and inspections. They
are separate from zoning, and a code-compliant building is **not** a defect-free building. A permit
history records what was applied for, not what was built; unpermitted work is a routine finding and is
routed to the municipality.

### 43.2 Subdivision regulation

Governs the division of land into lots and the standards for the plat, streets, utilities and
dedications. It is a municipal and county process, and a licensee working raw land routes plat
questions to the municipality, the county and a surveyor **before anything is marketed**.

**This course states no Missouri platting requirement**, because Missouri's subdivision chapter has not
been read from primary text for this project.

### 43.3 Private controls

**Restrictive covenants** recorded against the land, enforced by an association or by benefited owners.
As Module MO-02 Hour 9 established: they are **separate from zoning** and **the more restrictive
controls**.

And the necessary qualification: **a covenant that discriminates on a protected basis is unenforceable
and void.** Racially restrictive covenants appear in the older records of essentially every American
city, Missouri's included. They have no legal effect. A licensee who encounters one does not repeat
it, does not describe the neighbourhood by reference to it, and routes the question of removing it from
the record to counsel.

### 43.4 The licensee's boundary, stated once for the whole hour

chunks.heading: Hour 44 — Environmental concerns
chunks.excerpt:
**Identify the question, tell the client which authority answers it, and see that it is answered
before their contingencies run.** Never state what a municipality will permit. Never assume a current
use is permitted merely because it exists. Section 339.730.1(3)(d), RSMo — the duty to advise the
client to obtain expert advice on material matters beyond the licensee's expertise — is the statutory
expression of all of it.

---

## Hour 44 — Environmental concerns

### 44.1 The list, and the rule that governs all of it

The concerns a residential licensee will meet: **lead-based paint; radon; asbestos; mould; underground
storage tanks; methamphetamine contamination; well and septic systems; wetlands and floodplain;
formaldehyde; groundwater and soil contamination; and, in some Missouri markets, mine subsidence and
sinkholes.**

**One rule governs every item on that list: recognise, disclose, route.** Recognise the issue. Disclose
what you know or should know, under § 339.730.1(3)(c) and § 339.730.3, RSMo. Route the determination to
a qualified professional or the responsible agency. **A licensee assesses no environmental condition.**

### 44.2 Lead-based paint — the one with a federal obligation on the licensee

For **target housing built before 1978**, the federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act
and its implementing rule require, in a sale:

chunks.heading: 44.3 The others, briefly, with the routing
chunks.excerpt:
- delivery of the EPA-approved **pamphlet**;
- **disclosure** of any known lead-based paint and hazards and delivery of any available records and
  reports;
- a **ten-day opportunity** for the purchaser to conduct a risk assessment or inspection, which the
  parties may agree in writing to change;
- an **attachment or disclosure form** signed by the parties and by the **agent**; and
- **record retention** of the completed disclosure.

**The agent's signature is on that form.** This is one of the very few places where a licensee is not a
bystander to someone else's disclosure obligation but a participant with an obligation of their own,
including an affirmative duty to ensure compliance.

**1978 is the line, and it is a line about the housing rather than about the paint.** A pre-1978 house
triggers the requirement whether or not anyone believes there is lead in it.

### 44.3 The others, briefly, with the routing

**Radon.** Missouri has areas of elevated radon potential. Testing is by a qualified tester; mitigation
by a qualified contractor. A licensee neither tests nor interprets a result.

**Asbestos.** Common in pre-1980 construction — insulation, floor tile, siding, pipe wrap. Intact
material is often best left undisturbed; disturbance is the risk. Renovation plans on an older house
are a routing trigger.

**Mould.** Route to a qualified professional. The underlying question is almost always a moisture
source, and a licensee who opines on health effects has strayed a long way outside the licence.

**Underground storage tanks.** Heating oil tanks on older properties and agricultural tanks on rural
land. Route to a qualified consultant and the responsible state agency.

chunks.heading: 44.4 Missouri's disclosure position, stated carefully
chunks.excerpt:
**Methamphetamine contamination.** A serious and specific issue in parts of Missouri. Route to the
responsible agency and a qualified remediation professional; a known history is disclosed.

**Well and septic.** On rural Missouri property these decide habitability and financeability. Route to
the county health authority and a qualified inspector.

**Wetlands and floodplain.** An inventory map is an inventory, not a determination. Route to the
responsible agency and a consultant. **Flood insurance is a separate policy** — the standard homeowners
policy excludes flood, and a buyer in or near a mapped zone needs to be told to get a quote **early**,
because it can change what they can afford.

**Mine subsidence and sinkholes.** Real in parts of Missouri. Route to the responsible state agency, a
qualified engineer and the insurer.

### 44.4 Missouri's disclosure position, stated carefully

**This course states no Missouri seller disclosure requirement**, because whatever governs Missouri
residential seller disclosure practice was not read from primary text for this project.

What this course does state, because it **was** read, is the statutory duty: under § 339.730.1(3)(c) a
licensee discloses to the **client** all adverse material facts actually known or that should have been
known; under § 339.730.3 and § 339.740.3 a licensee discloses to any **customer** all adverse material
facts actually known or that should have been known; and under § 339.755(2)(d) a transaction broker
discloses to each party those of which the licensee has actual notice or knowledge. Under
§ 339.710(1)(a) **environmental hazards affecting the property** are on the statute's own list of
adverse material facts.

chunks.heading: Module MO-08 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
That duty is enough to decide almost every environmental question a licensee will face. **If you know
it, and it affects value, and the other side cannot reasonably discover it — disclose it, in writing.**

### Module MO-08 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment.

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-08

Missouri citations in this module — §§ 339.710, 339.730, 339.740 and 339.755, RSMo, and 20 CSR
2250-6.060, 2250-7.010 and 2250-7.070 — were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the Fair Housing Act, ECOA, the ADA, the
Sherman Act, the TCPA, CAN-SPAM and the federal lead-based paint rule in their own text; the Missouri
Human Rights Act and every municipal fair housing ordinance; Missouri's subdivision, environmental and
seller-disclosure provisions. The federal material above is stated at the level of principle, from the
general body of pre-license knowledge, and the course must be reconciled against the testing service's
detailed content outline before submission.

lessons.title: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-09

chunks.heading: Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-09
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Salesperson Pre-Examination Course — Module MO-09

## Hours 45–48 · Missouri licence law, the Commission, and professional conduct

**Clock hours:** 4. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Content basis:** a StateCourse organisation for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) requires
the 48-hour course to be developed from the testing service's detailed content outline, which this
project has not read.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Describe the Missouri Real Estate Commission's place in the regulatory structure and the sources of
   Missouri real estate law.
2. State the licensing requirements of § 339.040, RSMo, including the six-month education window.
3. Describe the education a Missouri salesperson must complete and how the two courses differ.
4. Describe how a complaint proceeds and what a licensee does when one arrives.
5. State the trust fund principle and route every specific to the operative chapter.
6. Explain what this school may and may not say about itself, and why that tells you how to evaluate
   any provider.
7. State what a Missouri salesperson carries out of 48 hours, and what they do not.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 45 | The regulatory structure and the sources of law | 50 min |
| 46 | Licensing: qualification, education, examination, application | 50 min |
| 47 | Conduct, complaints, discipline, and trust funds | 50 min |
| 48 | The school rules, and what you carry forward | 50 min |

---

chunks.heading: Hour 45 — The regulatory structure and the sources of Missouri law
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 45 — The regulatory structure and the sources of Missouri law

### 45.1 Where the rules come from

Four layers, and knowing which one you are reading is the beginning of research competence:

**Statute** — **Chapter 339, RSMo**, enacted by the General Assembly. This is the top of the
hierarchy. Sections 339.010 through 339.180 govern licensing and practice; §§ 339.710 through 339.860
are the brokerage relationships provisions Module MO-03 covered in detail.

**Regulation** — **Title 20, Division 2250** of the Code of State Regulations, promulgated by the
Missouri Real Estate Commission under the authority §§ 339.045, 339.090 and 339.120 give it. Chapter 6
is educational requirements; Chapter 7 is schools. A regulation cannot exceed the statute that
authorises it.

**Commission forms, letters and determinations** — the broker disclosure form, the certificate of
course completion, course approval letters. **These are operative documents**, and using a superseded
version of a prescribed form is a real problem.

**Case law** — the courts' interpretation of all of the above.

**Where to find them.** The statutes at the Revisor of Statutes; the regulations in the Code of State
Regulations published by the Secretary of State; the forms and approved-provider lists on the
Commission's own pages. **Read the section, not a summary of it.** A summary — including this course —
is a navigation aid. The operative text is the operative text.

### 45.2 The Commission

The Missouri Real Estate Commission sits within the Department of Commerce and Insurance, Division
2250. It licenses brokers and salespersons, accredits schools, approves courses, investigates
complaints, and brings disciplinary proceedings.

chunks.heading: Hour 46 — Licensing
chunks.excerpt:
**Note where a disciplinary case actually goes.** Under 20 CSR 2250-7.090(5) the Commission **causes a
complaint to be filed with the Administrative Hearing Commission** — a separate body — when it believes
there is a probability that a school or a person acting on its behalf has committed one of the listed
acts. Missouri splits the accusing function from the adjudicating function, which is worth
understanding: the Commission does not simply decide cases it brings.

---

## Hour 46 — Licensing

### 46.1 The qualification requirements

Section 339.040, RSMo, read on 2026-08-20 in its text effective 28 August 2020:

- **.1** Licences are granted only to persons who present satisfactory proof to the Commission that
  they are **competent to transact the business** in such a manner as to safeguard the interest of the
  public.
- **.2** The Commission holds oral or written examinations at such times and places as it may
  determine.
- **.3** Each applicant is **at least eighteen** and pays the examination fee.
- **.6** Each application for a salesperson licence includes **a certificate from a school accredited
  under § 339.045 that the applicant has, within six months prior to the date of application,
  successfully completed the prescribed salesperson curriculum** — with a Commission discretion to
  waive all or part on proof of other educational background or experience acceptable to it.

### 46.2 The six-month window, again

It was stated in Module MO-01 Hour 5 and it is stated again here because it is the single provision
students most often learn about too late.

**Six months from successful completion of the education to the date of application.** Not to the date
of the examination. Not to the date you decide to look for a broker. To the **date of application**.

chunks.heading: 46.3 The education
chunks.excerpt:
Plan the sequence backwards: finish the education, sit the examination promptly, secure a broker
association, and apply — all inside six months. Students who finish the education and then spend a
year deciding have to do the education again.

### 46.3 The education

Two courses, and they are different in kind:

**The 48-hour Salesperson Pre-Examination Course** — this course. Its content, under 20 CSR
2250-6.060(1), is developed from **the detailed content outline supplied by the professional testing
service** contracted to administer the examination, based on that service's most recent job analysis.
Its purpose is the body of knowledge the examination tests.

**The 24-hour Missouri Real Estate Practice Course** — the MREP. Its content, under 20 CSR
2250-6.060(2), is **sixteen topics the Commission itself lists**, and they are overwhelmingly about
Missouri practice: the broker disclosure form, listing, buyer representation, dual agency and
transaction brokerage, termination, compensation, cooperating with other licensees, obligations to
clients and customers, pricing, the appraiser's role, financing, closing costs, contracts, earnest
money, avoiding misrepresentation, and types of construction.

**Section 339.040.8 is a different thing entirely and must not be confused with either.** It requires
every active licensee to be able to show **twelve hours** of approved instruction in the preceding two
years. That is **continuing education**, after licensure, and it has nothing to do with the pre-licence
requirement.

### 46.4 What this school must tell you before you are contractually obligated

chunks.heading: Hour 47 — Conduct, complaints, and trust funds
chunks.excerpt:
**20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(D)**: the school shall advise all students, **prior to contractual obligation**,
that **certain criminal convictions may prevent the student from receiving or retaining a real estate
licence.**

That notice is given at enrolment and it is repeated here because it is the one that costs the most
when it arrives late. If it may apply to you, get the question answered **before** you pay for
education, not after you have finished it.

**20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(E)**: the school shall enter into a **contract** with each student, identifying
the tuition, the refund policy for dismissal or voluntary or hardship withdrawal, any additional fee
for supplies or materials, **the standard for issuance of a certificate of satisfactory completion**,
and other material matters. Read that contract. It is where the completion standard you will be held
to is written down.

---

## Hour 47 — Conduct, complaints, and trust funds

### 47.1 The conduct standard, restated

Module MO-03 set out the statutory duties in full. Restated here as the working standard a licensee
carries into practice:

chunks.heading: 47.2 What happens when a complaint arrives
chunks.excerpt:
- **Honesty and reasonable skill and care**, to the client, always — § 339.730.1(2).
- **Adverse material facts disclosed in writing**, to clients and to customers alike —
  §§ 339.730.1(3)(c), 339.730.3, 339.740.3, 339.755(2)(d).
- **Confidentiality maintained**, including after the relationship ends — §§ 339.730.2, 339.790.2.
- **Accounting in a timely manner** for all money and property received — § 339.730.1(4).
- **Written agreements** for every brokerage relationship — § 339.780.
- **The broker disclosure form** at first substantial contact in a residential transaction —
  § 339.770.1.
- **Expert advice recommended** on every material matter outside the licence — § 339.730.1(3)(d).
- **Fair housing and civil rights compliance** as a statutory licence duty — § 339.730.1(6).

**This course states no ground for discipline from § 339.100**, because that section was not read from
primary text for this project. What it states is that the section exists, that it is the operative list
of grounds for disciplining a licensee, and that it is read directly by every licensee before they
practise — not summarised from a course.

### 47.2 What happens when a complaint arrives

The Commission may investigate on its own motion or on a written complaint. For schools,
20 CSR 2250-7.090 sets out the mechanism explicitly — investigatory hearings, visits with or without
prior notice, surveys of participants and instructors — and the same investigative posture applies to
licensees under the statute.

**What a licensee does when a complaint arrives:**

chunks.heading: 47.3 Trust funds
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Tell your designated broker immediately.** Not eventually.
2. **Preserve everything.** Every file, email, text message and note. Altering or destroying a record
   after a complaint converts a defensible matter into an indefensible one.
3. **Get counsel.** Before responding.
4. **Respond within the time given.** Ignoring a regulator's letter is its own violation.

And the reason your files matter: **you write every file as though someone else will read it, because
someone may.** That is not defensiveness. It is the ordinary standard of a regulated profession.

### 47.3 Trust funds

The principle, and it does not bend:

**Money that belongs to someone else — earnest money, security deposits, rents collected for an owner
— is trust money from the moment it comes into your hands.** It goes to the firm for handling under the
firm's trust account procedures. It never touches an operating account. It is never held uncashed in a
drawer as a favour. It is never released on a party's request when its disposition is disputed.

Section 339.730.1(4) puts the statutory duty plainly: **to account in a timely manner for all money and
property received.**

**This course states no Missouri trust account requirement, threshold, deadline or exception**, because
§ 339.105 and the relevant chapters of 20 CSR 2250 were not read from primary text for this project.
**Read them, and read your firm's policy, before you accept your first cheque.** Trust account failures
are the fastest route out of this profession, and they are almost never theft — they are convenience,
helpfulness and sloppiness, which look identical on an audit.

### 47.4 Errors, omissions, and the honest response

chunks.heading: Hour 48 — The school rules, and what you carry forward
chunks.excerpt:
Every licensee will eventually make a mistake — a missed deadline, a figure transposed, a disclosure
that went out late. The professional response is the same every time: **tell your broker, tell the
affected party, correct it in writing, and document what happened.**

The alternative — quietly fixing it and hoping — converts an error into a concealment, and concealment
is what turns a survivable problem into a licence problem.

---

## Hour 48 — The school rules, and what you carry forward

### 48.1 What this school may never do, and why you should know

These are rules **on the school**, not on you. Knowing them lets you evaluate every education provider
you will ever deal with:

- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)4** — no school shall permit anyone associated with it to make **any
  warranties or guarantees that a student will pass the real estate licence examination** by taking
  its courses. A provider advertising a guaranteed pass is telling you something about itself.
- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)2** — no school shall advertise or imply that it is **recommended, endorsed
  or approved by the Commission**, though an accredited school may state which courses the Commission
  has approved it to teach. "The Commission approved this course" can be true; "the Commission endorses
  this school" cannot.
- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)3** — no school shall permit anyone associated with it to **provide any
  misleading information to the public or prospective students.**
- **20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)6** — **no course shall be announced or advertised until it is approved by
  the Commission, in writing, for credit.**
- **20 CSR 2250-7.090(5)(K)** — a school may face a complaint for **awarding credit to any student who
  has either not taken the course or who has failed to satisfactorily co

chunks.heading: 48.2 What Missouri measures about this course
chunks.excerpt:
mplete it.**

That last one is why this course's completion tracking is what it is. Credit is awarded by the school's
record of what you actually completed, and by nothing else — not by a payment, not by a request, not by
a plausible explanation.

### 48.2 What Missouri measures about this course

**20 CSR 2250-7.080(4)** requires that by **31 July and 31 January** a distance provider report
statistical information on **completion times** for the preceding period. And: **if the statistics
indicate that at least fifty percent of students took less time to complete the course than the course
submission identified**, the school has **ten days** either to withdraw the course or to file an amended
outline.

Read that as a student and it means something reassuring: **Missouri checks whether the hours are
real.** A provider whose 48-hour course is completed in eleven hours by half its students is required to
withdraw it or fix it. That provision is the strongest anti-inflation rule this project has read in any
state, and it is the reason the hour figures in this course are the hours the material actually takes.

### 48.3 The final examination

**20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(B)** requires, for a distance-delivered pre-examination course, **two final
examination forms — a primary and an alternate — of at least fifty multiple-choice items each, with no
duplication of items between them**, together with a key showing correct responses. The examinations
must reflect sound test development practices and must **measure knowledge of the subject matter of the
entire course as set out in the learning objectives.**

chunks.heading: 48.4 What you carry out of 48 hours — and what you do not
chunks.excerpt:
**20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E)** sets the passing standard: within **ten days** following administration of
the final examination, the school delivers **to the student who achieves a score of at least
seventy-five percent (75%)** a certificate of course completion on a Commission-prescribed form.

**That 75 percent is the Commission's figure**, from the rule, and it is the standard for the final
examination in this course. Distinguish it from the 80 percent in-module engagement threshold and the
100 percent applied threshold, which are **StateCourse standards** the rule does not prescribe.

**20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(D)** requires the school to state **the methods it will use to assure
examinations are maintained securely**, and **7.080(3)** requires a **course introduction statement**
setting out the dates during which the course is approved, the terms and conditions of the final
examination, and **a list of the specific learning objectives referenced in the final examination.**

### 48.4 What you carry out of 48 hours — and what you do not

**What you carry:**

- A working knowledge of property, interests, contracts, finance, valuation, title and closing.
- The Missouri brokerage relationships framework — client and customer, the six duties, adverse
  material facts, the five things a dual agent may not say, the written agreement requirements, the
  broker disclosure form trigger.
- The federal fair housing framework and the practices it forbids, including the ones nobody intends.
- The arithmetic.
- **And, most durably: a reliable sense of which questions are yours and which are routed** — to your
  designated broker, to counsel, to the lender, to the title company, to the municipality, to a
  qualified professional, to the Commission.

**What you do not carry:**

chunks.heading: 48.5 The status of this course, stated one last time
chunks.excerpt:
- The right to give legal, tax, engineering, environmental or appraisal advice.
- The specifics of anything this course could not read from primary text. Every one of those gaps is
  named in `missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`, and each must be read in current text before
  it is relied on. The list is not short and it is honest.
- A licence. This course is one requirement among several.

### 48.5 The status of this course, stated one last time

This is a **version 1.0 submission draft**. It is **not approved**. **No Missouri pre-license credit is
available for it.** Under 20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)6 it cannot even be advertised for credit until the
Commission approves it in writing, and under 20 CSR 2250-6.060(1) it cannot properly be submitted until
it has been reconciled against the testing service's detailed content outline, which this project has
not read.

Those are not disclaimers. They are the actual state of this document, and a school that would not tell
you them is not a school to buy education from.

### Module MO-09 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MO-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the 75 percent final examination standard is the
Commission's, from 20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E).

---

## Instructor source note for Module MO-09

Every Missouri citation in this module — §§ 339.040, 339.710, 339.730, 339.740, 339.755, 339.770,
339.780 and 339.790, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.010, 2250-7.060, 2250-7.070, 2250-7.080 and
2250-7.090 — was read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and is transcribed in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** § 339.100 and its grounds for discipline;

chapters 1 through 5 and 8; every Commission-prescribed form; and the testing service's detailed

lessons.title: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-01

chunks.heading: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-01
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-01

## Hours 1–4 · The Broker Disclosure Form and the obligations of agents to clients and customers

**Commission topics covered:** 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(A) Broker Disclosure Form · (H) Obligations of
Agents to Clients and Customers
**Clock hours:** 4. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** and no more than 10 minutes of recess — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review. **20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) lists
sixteen topics the MREP course must address and allocates no hours among them.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## What this course is, and how it differs from the 48-hour course

The 48-hour Salesperson Pre-Examination Course is built, under 20 CSR 2250-6.060(1), from the
**testing service's** detailed content outline. It teaches the body of knowledge the licensing
examination tests.

**This course is different in kind.** Under 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) the Commission itself lists **sixteen
topics** the Missouri Real Estate Practice Course *must address*, and reading that list tells you what
it is for. Broker disclosure form. Listing a property. Buyer representation. Dual agent or transaction
broker. Termination of brokerage relationships. Compensation. Cooperating with other licensees.
Obligations of agents to clients and customers. Pricing property. Role of the appraiser. Types of
financing. Estimating closing costs. Contracts. Earnest money. Avoiding misrepresentation. Types of
construction.

chunks.heading: Learning objectives
chunks.excerpt:
Fourteen of the sixteen are about **what a Missouri licensee actually does in a transaction**, and
eight of them are about **brokerage relationships specifically**. The Commission is not asking for more
theory. It is asking that a person about to be licensed in Missouri knows how Missouri transactions
work and where the licensee's obligations sit.

**The topics are the Commission's; the hour allocation and the grouping into six modules are
StateCourse's**, and every module in this course says so.

## Learning objectives

1. State the three conditions that trigger the § 339.770.1 broker disclosure obligation and the one
   exception in § 339.770.2.
2. Describe what the broker disclosure form is for and route its content correctly.
3. Distinguish client from customer using the § 339.710 definitions.
4. Recite the six duties owed to a client under §§ 339.730.1 and 339.740.1.
5. State exactly what is owed to a customer and what is not.
6. Identify an adverse material fact under § 339.710(1), including the item that is not about the
   property.
7. Apply the confidentiality rule and its three exceptions.
8. Describe a firm's § 339.760 written policy and explain why you read it before your first
   appointment.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | First substantial contact and the § 339.770 disclosure trigger | 50 min |
| 2 | Client and customer: the definitions that decide everything | 50 min |
| 3 | The six duties to a client, read one at a time | 50 min |
| 4 | The customer sentence; adverse material facts; confidentiality | 50 min |

---

## Hour 1 — The Broker Disclosure Form — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(A)

### 1.1 The statutory trigger, read exactly

Section 339.770.1, RSMo:

chunks.heading: 1.2 The exception
chunks.excerpt:
> In a residential real estate transaction, at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following
> the first substantial contact by the designated broker or the affiliated licensees with a seller,
> landlord, buyer, or tenant who has not entered into a written agreement for services as described in
> subdivision (5) of section 339.710, the licensee shall provide that person with a written copy of the
> current broker disclosure form which has been prescribed by the commission.

**Three conditions, and all three must be present:**

1. **Residential** real estate transaction. Commercial is outside this section. Note that § 339.710(7)
   defines commercial real estate as real estate **other than** one-to-four residential units or
   agricultural and horticultural property under § 137.016, and expressly excludes single-family units
   including condominiums and townhouses sold unit-by-unit.
2. **First substantial contact** — at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following it.
3. **The person has not entered into a written agreement for services.**

### 1.2 The exception

Section 339.770.2: where the person **has already** entered into a written agreement for services with
a designated broker, **no other licensee is required to make the disclosure.**

That is a narrow exception and it is easy to misapply. It applies where the person already has a
written agreement — not where they have merely been working with someone, not where they say they have
an agent, not where you assume they must.

### 1.3 What "first substantial contact" means, and what this course will not do

**The statute does not define it, and this course will not invent a definition.**

chunks.heading: 1.4 What is on the form, and where you get it
chunks.excerpt:
What the course can say is where the safe practice lies. Ministerial acts under § 339.710(19) — a
telephone inquiry about price or location, a question at an open house, setting a showing appointment —
are informative in nature and expressly do not rise to the level requiring a brokerage relationship. So
they are not, in themselves, substantial contact.

But the moment a conversation stops being about the availability of information and starts being about
**this person's transaction** — their needs, their finances, their motivation, what they should offer,
what they should do — you are past the point. **Give the form early.** Nobody has ever been disciplined
for giving the broker disclosure form too soon.

### 1.4 What is on the form, and where you get it

**This course does not reproduce the broker disclosure form, state its fields, or describe its layout,
because the Commission-prescribed form was not read from primary text for this project.**

What the statute requires is a written copy of **the current** form **prescribed by the Commission**.
Two operative words:

- **Current.** Forms are revised. The copy in your firm's drawer, or the PDF someone emailed you in
  your first week, may be superseded. Get it from the Commission and check that what you are handing
  out is what the Commission currently prescribes.
- **Prescribed by the Commission.** Not your firm's version of it, not a summary, not a form you have
  redesigned to look nicer.

And § 339.770.3 supplies the payoff for doing it right: **disclosures made in accordance with
§§ 339.710 to 339.860 are sufficient as a matter of law** to disclose brokerage relationships to the
public.

### 1.5 What the form is not

chunks.heading: 1.6 A practice routine
chunks.excerpt:
**It is not an agency agreement.** Giving someone the broker disclosure form does not make them your
client, and receiving it does not commit them to anything. It is a **disclosure** — it tells a consumer
what the relationships are so that they can decide which one they want.

**It is not a substitute for the written agreement.** Section 339.780 requires a written agreement
before you act in any brokerage capacity. The disclosure form and the written agreement are two
different documents doing two different jobs, and a licensee who has done the first and not the second
has not complied with § 339.780.

### 1.6 A practice routine

Before every first appointment with a person you have not worked with:

1. Is this **residential**?
2. Is this **first substantial contact** — or past it?
3. Do they **already have a written agreement** with a designated broker?

Residential, yes, no → **the current Commission broker disclosure form goes into their hands, in
writing, and the fact that you gave it goes into your file with the date.**

---

## Hour 2 — Client and customer — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(H)

### 2.1 Two definitions that decide everything downstream

**Client** — § 339.710(6), RSMo: *a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant who has entered into a brokerage
relationship with a licensee pursuant to sections 339.710 to 339.860.*

**Customer** — § 339.710(10): *an actual or potential seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant in a real
estate transaction in which a licensee is involved but who has not entered into a brokerage
relationship with the licensee.*

The difference is created by **entering into a brokerage relationship** — which, under § 339.780,
means a **written agreement** in every case except ministerial acts.

### 2.2 What does NOT create a client

chunks.heading: 2.3 Ministerial acts, and why the category exists
chunks.excerpt:
This is where new licensees go wrong, and it is worth listing:

- **Not rapport.** You may have spent nine Saturdays with someone.
- **Not time.** You may have shown them thirty houses.
- **Not helpfulness.** You may have answered every question they ever had.
- **Not who pays.** Section 339.800.2 is explicit: *payment of compensation by itself shall not
  establish an agency relationship or transaction brokerage relationship between the party who paid the
  compensation and the designated broker or any affiliated licensee.*

**A written agreement creates a client. Nothing else does.**

The corollary is a hazard: a licensee who behaves like a buyer's agent for weeks without a written
agreement has created a person who **believes** they are a client, is legally a customer, and will be
furious when the difference surfaces. That is a complaint waiting to happen, and it is entirely
avoidable.

### 2.3 Ministerial acts, and why the category exists

Section 339.710(19) defines **ministerial acts** as acts *informative in nature* that *do not rise to
the level which requires the creation of a brokerage relationship*. The statute's own examples:

- responding to telephone inquiries about the availability and pricing of brokerage services;
- responding to telephone inquiries about the price or location of property;
- attending an open house and responding to questions about the property from a consumer;
- setting an appointment to view property;
- responding to questions of consumers walking into a licensee's office.

The category exists so that ordinary courtesy does not accidentally create a representation. Answer the
phone. Hold the open house. Set the showing.

chunks.heading: 2.4 Read your firm's written policy first
chunks.excerpt:
**But note what ministerial acts do NOT suspend:** the duty every licensee owes every **customer** to
disclose adverse material facts. That duty does not wait for an agreement, and Hour 4 takes it up.

### 2.4 Read your firm's written policy first

Section 339.760: **every designated broker who has affiliated licensees shall adopt a written policy
which identifies and describes the relationships in which the designated broker and affiliated
licensees may engage** with any seller, landlord, buyer or tenant.

This is not paperwork. It tells you **which brokerage relationships you are permitted to offer**, and it
is not the same at every Missouri firm. Some offer dual agency; some route every in-house situation to
transaction brokerage; some appoint designated agents under § 339.820. You practise your firm's policy,
not your preference, and you read it on your first day rather than on the day it matters.

---

## Hour 3 — The six duties to a client

### 3.1 The list

Section 339.730.1 for a seller's or landlord's agent; § 339.740.1 for a buyer's or tenant's agent. They
are the same six, mirrored:

**1. To perform the terms of the written agreement made with the client.**

Which presupposes there is one, and that you have read it. The agreement is the first source of your
obligations and it can add to the statutory floor — § 339.780.8 expressly preserves the public's
freedom to contract for more.

**2. To exercise reasonable skill and care for the client.**

The most-cited duty and the least specific. In daily practice it is mostly unglamorous competence:
calendaring deadlines the day the contract is accepted, confirming things in writing, checking that
what you repeated is what the document says, raising a problem before it becomes one.

chunks.heading: 3.2 (3)(a) and (3)(b) read together
chunks.excerpt:
**3. To promote the interests of the client with the utmost good faith, loyalty, and fidelity**,
including four specified things:

- **(a) Seeking a price and terms acceptable to the client** — with the express carve-out that the
  licensee is **not obligated to seek additional offers** while the property is already subject to a
  contract for sale, or a lease or letter of intent to lease.
- **(b) Presenting all written offers to and from the client in a timely manner regardless of whether
  the property is subject to a contract** for sale or lease.
- **(c) Disclosing to the client all adverse material facts actually known or that should have been
  known** by the licensee.
- **(d) Advising the client to obtain expert advice** as to material matters about which the licensee
  knows but the specifics of which are beyond the licensee's expertise.

**4. To account in a timely manner for all money and property received.**

**5. To comply** with §§ 339.710–339.860, § 339.100.2, and the rules under them.

**6. To comply with applicable federal, state and local laws, rules, regulations and ordinances,
including fair housing and civil rights statutes and regulations.**

### 3.2 (3)(a) and (3)(b) read together

These two are a matched pair and they are misread constantly. Once a property is under contract you
**need not go looking for more offers** — that is (a)'s carve-out. But if a written offer arrives
anyway, **you must still present it** — that is (b), and its "regardless of whether the property is
subject to a contract" clause leaves no room.

chunks.heading: 3.3 (3)(d) is the sentence that keeps you inside your licence
chunks.excerpt:
Sellers ask about this constantly. The accurate answer is: *I am not required to market for further
offers while we are under contract, but if one arrives in writing I am required to bring it to you, and
what you do with it is a legal question about your existing contract that you should take to counsel.*

### 3.3 (3)(d) is the sentence that keeps you inside your licence

The duty is **not** to answer the legal, tax, engineering, environmental or appraisal question. It is to
**know the question exists and tell the client to get it answered by someone qualified.**

That is the entire obligation, and doing more than it is how licensees end up practising law. It is also
a genuine service: the client who is told in week one that they need a lawyer to look at the easement is
far better served than the client who is reassured in week one and finds out in week five.

### 3.4 Duty 6 is not decoration

Section 339.730.1(6) makes compliance with **fair housing and civil rights statutes and regulations** a
statutory duty of the limited agent under Missouri licence law. A fair housing violation by a Missouri
licensee is therefore **both** a fair housing matter **and** a licence-law matter, prosecuted on two
separate tracks by two separate authorities, neither of which waits for the other.

---

## Hour 4 — The customer sentence, adverse material facts, confidentiality

### 4.1 What is owed to a customer

Section 339.730.3 — and § 339.740.3 in the mirror — is the most consequential sentence in Missouri
brokerage law and it should be known by heart:

chunks.heading: 4.2 Adverse material fact — the definition, read exactly
chunks.excerpt:
> A licensee acting as a seller's or landlord's agent **owes no duty or obligation to a customer, except
> that a licensee shall disclose to any customer all adverse material facts actually known or that
> should have been known** by the licensee.

The same subsection continues: the agent **owes no duty to conduct an independent inspection** or to
discover adverse material facts for the benefit of the customer, and **owes no duty to independently
verify** the accuracy or completeness of any statement made by the client or by any independent
inspector.

Section 339.740.3 adds the buyer-side analogue: a buyer's agent **owes no duty to conduct an independent
investigation of the client's financial condition for the benefit of the customer.**

**So the structure is: everything to the client; to the customer, honesty about adverse material facts.**

That residue is not small. **A licensee cannot conceal a known defect from the other side and then say
the buyer was not their client.** That defence does not exist in Missouri, and a licensee who tries it
has usually made their situation worse.

### 4.2 Adverse material fact — the definition, read exactly

Section 339.710(1): *a fact related to the property not reasonably ascertainable or known to a party
which negatively affects the value of the property.*

Three elements, each doing work. **Related to the property.** **Not reasonably ascertainable or known**
to the party — a fact a buyer can see for themselves is not concealed by not mentioning it. **Negatively
affects value.**

The statute's own list of what such facts **may** include:

chunks.heading: 4.3 Item (e), which is not about the property at all
chunks.excerpt:
- **(a)** environmental hazards affecting the property;
- **(b)** physical condition of the property which adversely affects value;
- **(c)** material defects in the property;
- **(d)** material defects in the **title** to the property;
- **(e)** **material limitation of the party's ability to perform under the terms of the contract.**

### 4.3 Item (e), which is not about the property at all

**(e) is about a PARTY, not a building.** A buyer whose financing has collapsed. A seller who cannot
deliver clear title. A party who has told you they cannot close.

Licensees skip it because the other four are about houses. It belongs on the list because a party's
inability to perform destroys value in a transaction as surely as a failed foundation does — and because
the licensee is usually the first person to find out.

### 4.4 The two standards

Missouri applies **two different disclosure standards** depending on the relationship:

- A **limited agent** — §§ 339.730.1(3)(c), 339.730.3, 339.740 — discloses adverse material facts
  **actually known or that should have been known.**
- A **transaction broker** — § 339.755(2)(d) — discloses those **of which the licensee has actual notice
  or knowledge.**

"Should have been known" is objective and makes **wilful ignorance unavailable**. A licensee who
arranges not to learn something has not escaped the duty.

**The professional method is not to litigate which standard covers a fact you already know. It is to put
it in writing, to everyone entitled to it, and move on.**

### 4.5 Confidentiality, and where it stops

chunks.heading: 4.6 What survives the end of the relationship
chunks.excerpt:
**Confidential information** — § 339.710(9) — is information obtained from the client and designated
confidential by the client; information made confidential by §§ 339.710–339.860 or any other statute or
regulation; or written instructions from the client. **Unless** it is or becomes public by the client's
own words or conduct, or from a source other than the licensee.

Sections 339.730.2 and 339.740.2 forbid disclosing it **unless**:

1. disclosure is **required by statute, rule or regulation**;
2. **failure to disclose would constitute a misrepresentation**; or
3. disclosure is necessary to **defend the licensee** against an action of wrongful conduct in an
   administrative or judicial proceeding or before a professional committee.

And: **no cause of action arises against the licensee for making any required or permitted disclosure.**

**Exception 2 is where confidentiality meets adverse-material-fact disclosure, and it decides the hard
cases.** A client cannot make a fact confidential simply by asking. A seller who tells you in confidence
that the basement floods has not sealed your mouth — they have told you an adverse material fact, and
§ 339.730.3 requires you to disclose it to any customer.

The right response in the room is to say so at the time: *I have to tell you that this is something I'll
need to disclose. Let's talk about how we handle it.* Sellers accept that far better than they accept
finding out afterwards.

### 4.6 What survives the end of the relationship

Section 339.790.1: the relationships **commence on the effective date of the broker's agreement** and
continue until performance, completion, termination or expiration.

chunks.heading: Module MREP-01 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.790.2: after that, **no further duty except** (1) accounting in a timely manner for money
and property received during the relationship, and (2) **treating as confidential information provided
by the client during the relationship that may reasonably be expected to have a negative impact on the
client's real estate activity** — unless written consent, disclosure required by law, the information
became public otherwise than through the brokerage, or disclosure is needed to defend against an action
of wrongful conduct.

**Confidentiality outlives the relationship; the rest does not.** A licensee who learned that a divorce
was forcing a sale does not become free to mention it when the listing expires.

### Module MREP-01 engagement check

Eleven items: one applied scenario, five engagement items and five remediation items. The applied item
must be answered correctly; the engagement and remediation sets are passed at 80 percent. **Both are
StateCourse standards** — 20 CSR 2250 prescribes no in-module assessment and no in-module passing score.
The **75 percent** standard that does come from the rule applies to the **final examination**, under
20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E).

---

## Instructor source note for Module MREP-01

Every section cited — §§ 339.710, 339.730, 339.740, 339.755, 339.760, 339.770, 339.780, 339.790 and
339.800, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.070 and 2250-7.080 — was read from primary text on
2026-08-20 and is transcribed in `missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module: the Commission-prescribed broker disclosure
form.** Its content, fields and layout are not described. What is taught is the statutory trigger and
the routing.
