chunks.heading: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-02
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-02

## Hours 5–9 · Listing a property and buyer representation

**Commission topics covered:** 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(B) Listing a Property — 1. Types of seller agency
agreements, 2. Elements of seller agency agreements · (C) Buyer Representation — 1. Types of buyer
agency agreements, 2. Elements of buyer agency agreements
**Clock hours:** 5. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review; 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) allocates no
hours among its sixteen topics.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Distinguish exclusive right to sell, exclusive agency and open listing by who is owed a commission.
2. Name the elements every seller agency agreement must settle, including the two § 339.780.2 requires.
3. Explain who enters a listing agreement in Missouri and under whose authority.
4. Distinguish exclusive and non-exclusive buyer agency and explain the ministerial-acts carve-out.
5. Name the elements every buyer agency agreement must settle.
6. State the § 339.780.7 minimum services an exclusive agreement must specify.
7. Take a listing appointment through the sequence a Missouri licensee must actually follow.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 5 | Types of seller agency agreements | 50 min |
| 6 | Elements of a seller agency agreement | 50 min |
| 7 | The listing appointment, in sequence | 50 min |
| 8 | Types of buyer agency agreements | 50 min |
| 9 | Elements of a buyer agency agreement; the minimum services | 50 min |

---

chunks.heading: Hour 5 — Types of seller agency agreements — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(B)1
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 5 — Types of seller agency agreements — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(B)1

### 5.1 Three types, distinguished by one question

The question is: **in what circumstances is the firm owed a commission?**

**Exclusive right to sell.** The firm is owed on a sale during the term **regardless of who procures
the buyer — including the seller.** This is the ordinary residential listing, and the reason it is
ordinary is that it removes the firm's incentive problem: the firm can spend money marketing without
worrying that the seller's cousin will appear and eliminate the fee.

**Exclusive agency.** The firm is the only firm authorised, **but the seller reserves the right to sell
to a buyer they find themselves without owing a commission.** This produces an obvious dispute: who
found the buyer? The answer needs to be settled in the agreement, in writing, before it becomes an
argument — usually by naming the reserved prospects.

**Open listing.** A **non-exclusive** authorisation. The seller may give it to any number of firms and
**only the firm that procures the buyer is paid.** The seller may also sell themselves and owe nothing.
It is a unilateral contract: the seller promises to pay whoever performs, and nobody is obliged to try.

### 5.2 Net listings

A **net listing** is an arrangement in which the seller receives a fixed net amount and the firm keeps
everything above it.

The structural problem is that the licensee is **paid more the worse the seller does on price** — the
exact inversion of the § 339.730.1(3) duty to promote the client's interests with the utmost good
faith, loyalty and fidelity, which includes **seeking a price and terms acceptable to the client**.

chunks.heading: 5.3 Who enters the agreement
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no Missouri rule permitting or prohibiting net listings**, because 20 CSR 2250
chapters 1 through 5 and 8 and § 339.100, RSMo, were not read from primary text for this project.
Whatever the chapters say, the professional position does not depend on it: this is not an arrangement
a licensee treats as an ordinary fee structure, and any proposal for one goes to the designated broker
before it goes anywhere else.

### 5.3 Who enters the agreement

Section 339.780.1: **all written agreements for brokerage services shall be entered into by the
designated broker** on behalf of that broker and the affiliated licensees — **except that the designated
broker may authorise affiliated licensees in writing** to enter into the written agreements on the
broker's behalf.

So a salesperson taking a listing is signing **on the designated broker's behalf, under the broker's
written authority.** Know that the authority exists and know its scope. The listing is the firm's
contract with the seller, not yours.

### 5.4 Termination, and what a seller can and cannot do

A listing ends by **expiry**, by **performance**, by **mutual agreement**, or by **operation of law** —
destruction of the property, death or incapacity of a party in some circumstances.

**And the distinction that a licensee must state accurately:** a seller has the **power** to revoke the
agency at any time, but that is not the same as a **right** to do so without liability. Whether the firm
has a claim is a legal question between the seller and the firm, and it goes to the designated broker
and counsel. A licensee who tells a seller "you can cancel whenever you like, no consequences" has given
legal advice, and probably wrong legal advice.

chunks.heading: Hour 6 — Elements of a seller agency agreement — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(B)2
chunks.excerpt:
Protection or override clauses — providing for a commission where a buyer introduced during the term
purchases after it — may survive termination on their own terms, and their terms are read rather than
assumed.

---

## Hour 6 — Elements of a seller agency agreement — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(B)2

### 6.1 What § 339.780.2 requires

Read it exactly. Before engaging in any of the activities enumerated in § 339.010, a designated broker
intending to establish a limited agency relationship with a seller or landlord **shall enter into a
written agency agreement with the party to be represented**, and:

> The agreement shall include a licensee's duties and responsibilities specified in section 339.730 and
> the terms of compensation and shall specify whether an offer of subagency may be made to any other
> designated broker.

**Three mandatory contents:**

1. **The § 339.730 duties and responsibilities.** They go in the agreement, not merely in the licensee's
   head. A seller reading their listing agreement is entitled to see what they are owed.
2. **The terms of compensation.**
3. **Whether an offer of subagency may be made** to any other designated broker. This one is
   specifically named, and it is the one most likely to be overlooked.

### 6.2 The commercial elements

Beyond the statutory minimum, every listing must settle:

chunks.heading: 6.3 Pricing, and the boundary
chunks.excerpt:
- **The parties.** Every person who must sign to convey. Missouri's marital property rules and the
  possibility of a life estate, a trust or an estate all mean this is not answered by looking at the
  deed. **Route it to counsel and the title company at listing**, not at closing.
- **The property**, with a legal description taken from the deed or the title company — never from a tax
  record, a prior listing or memory.
- **The price**, which is the seller's decision.
- **The term**, with a definite end date.
- **The compensation and how it is earned** — the event that triggers it.
- **Included and excluded items**, in two written lists.
- **Authorisations**: marketing, photography, lockbox, sign, showings, internet display and any opt-outs.
- **Any reserved prospects**, if the type is exclusive agency.
- **The seller's disclosure obligations**, and the licensee's own separate obligation to disclose adverse
  material facts to clients and customers alike.

### 6.3 Pricing, and the boundary

The comparative market analysis is presented **in writing**, with the comparables and the adjustments
shown, as **evidence supporting a range**. The price is the seller's decision.

**It is not an appraisal**, it is not labelled or described as one, and it is not presented in a way that
lets a client believe it is one. That boundary is a § 339.730.1(3)(d) matter — the duty to advise the
client to obtain expert advice as to material matters beyond the licensee's expertise — and Module
MREP-04 takes it up in full.

Taking a listing you know is unsupportably priced is a competence problem before it is a marketing
problem. The professional response is to put the evidence in front of the seller in writing, let them
decide, and record what you presented.

---

chunks.heading: Hour 7 — The listing appointment, in sequence
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 7 — The listing appointment, in sequence

### 7.1 The sequence

This hour is the practical assembly of everything in Module MREP-01 and Hours 5 and 6.

**Before you arrive:**
- Check your firm's § 339.760 written policy for what relationships you may offer.
- Pull the tax record, the plat, the prior sales and the comparables.
- Have the **current Commission broker disclosure form** with you.

**On arrival, in order:**

1. **The broker disclosure form**, if the three § 339.770.1 conditions are met — residential, first
   substantial contact, no existing written agreement. Give it, note that you gave it, and date the note.
2. **Explain the relationship options** your firm permits, and what each means.
3. **Walk the property.** Settle the included and excluded items as you go. Ask specifically about leased
   equipment, tenant-installed items, recent construction and any unpaid or disputed contractor.
4. **Ask the ownership questions.** Who is on the deed; is anyone deceased; is there a trust, an estate,
   a life estate, a divorce; is there a tenant. Route every complication to counsel and the title company
   rather than resolving it in the driveway.
5. **Present the pricing evidence in writing**, as a range, with the adjustments shown.
6. **Complete the agreement** — all three § 339.780.2 mandatory contents, plus the commercial elements.
7. **Explain the seller's disclosure obligations** and your own separate duty to disclose adverse
   material facts to everyone entitled to them.
8. **Confirm in writing** what was decided, the same day.

### 7.2 The four questions worth asking that most licensees do not

chunks.heading: 7.3 What goes in the file
chunks.excerpt:
- **"Is any equipment on the property leased or financed?"** Propane tank, water treatment, solar,
  security, sometimes HVAC. A buyer cannot discover this by looking, and a licensee who did not ask has
  a "should have known" problem under § 339.730.1(3)(c).
- **"Has any work been done in the last year, and is everyone paid?"** Recent construction plus a payment
  dispute is a construction lien risk, and lien priority may run from a date earlier than any filing.
  **This course states no Missouri mechanic's lien period**, because that chapter was not read from
  primary text for this project — route it to the title company and counsel, at listing.
- **"Is there anything about this property a buyer would want to know and could not find out by
  looking?"** This is the adverse material fact question in plain language, and it works.
- **"Who else has to sign?"** Asked at listing, this is a five-minute conversation. Asked at closing, it
  is a postponement.

### 7.3 What goes in the file

Everything. The date the disclosure form was given. The pricing evidence you actually presented. The
included and excluded lists. Every material conversation, confirmed by email the same day.

You write every file as though someone else will read it, because someone may — 20 CSR 2250-7.090 gives
the Commission investigatory powers over schools and the statute gives it comparable powers over
licensees, and a file that records what happened is the only defence that has ever worked.

---

## Hour 8 — Types of buyer agency agreements — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(C)1

### 8.1 The types

chunks.heading: 8.2 The ministerial acts carve-out, and why it matters here more than anywhere
chunks.excerpt:
**Exclusive buyer agency.** The buyer agrees to work with one firm for a term and in a defined area or
property type. The firm is owed compensation on a purchase within the term regardless of who found the
property, on the terms the agreement states.

**Non-exclusive buyer agency.** The buyer may work with more than one firm; compensation follows only
where this firm's work produced the transaction. It is workable and it is fragile, and the fragility
falls on the licensee.

**Designated agency.** Under § 339.820.1 a designated broker entering a limited agency agreement may
**appoint in writing affiliated licensees as designated agents to the exclusion of all other affiliated
licensees** — which is how a Missouri firm represents both a seller and a buyer in the same transaction
without the whole firm becoming a dual agent. Module MREP-03 takes this up in detail.

**Transaction brokerage** is not buyer agency at all. A transaction broker under § 339.755 assists
without an agency or fiduciary relationship and is **neutral, serving neither as advocate nor advisor**.
It is a different product and the buyer must understand which one they are getting.

### 8.2 The ministerial acts carve-out, and why it matters here more than anywhere

Section 339.780.3: before engaging in any of the § 339.010 activities, **except ministerial acts as
defined in § 339.710**, a designated broker acting as a single agent for a buyer or tenant **shall enter
into a written agency agreement** with the buyer or tenant.

**Ministerial acts do not require an agreement.** You may answer the phone about price and location, hold
an open house and answer questions, and set a showing appointment.

chunks.heading: Hour 9 — Elements of a buyer agency agreement — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(C)2
chunks.excerpt:
**But that carve-out ends where the ministerial acts do.** The hazard in buyer work is drift: a licensee
who shows twenty houses, discusses the buyer's finances, advises on what to offer and negotiates on their
behalf, all without an agreement, has been acting as an agent without one — and has created a person who
believes they are a client, is legally a customer, and will be extremely unhappy when the difference
surfaces.

**Have the conversation early.** Explain the relationship options, explain what each means, and get the
agreement signed before the work becomes representation.

---

## Hour 9 — Elements of a buyer agency agreement — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(C)2

### 9.1 What § 339.780.3 requires

> The agreement shall include a licensee's duties and responsibilities specified in section 339.740 and
> the terms of compensation.

**Two mandatory contents:** the § 339.740 duties, and the terms of compensation. Note that the seller-side
requirement in § 339.780.2 has a third item — whether an offer of subagency may be made — and the
buyer-side requirement does not.

### 9.2 The commercial elements

chunks.heading: 9.3 Compensation: the sentence that must be said out loud
chunks.excerpt:
- **The parties** and the **term**.
- **The scope** — geographic area, property type, price range. A buyer agency agreement covering "any
  real estate anywhere" is a different commitment from one covering a defined search, and the buyer should
  understand which they signed.
- **Compensation: how much, from whom, and what happens if the seller's side pays some or all of it.**
  This is the element most likely to produce a dispute and it must be settled explicitly, in numbers.
- **Whether the agreement is exclusive**, and what happens if the buyer purchases through another firm.
- **Dual agency or designated agency consent**, if the firm's policy contemplates it and the buyer agrees
  in advance — noting that under § 339.750.1 dual agency requires the consent of **all** parties and
  consent is presumed by a written agreement under § 339.780.
- **Any protection period** after termination.

### 9.3 Compensation: the sentence that must be said out loud

Section 339.800.2: **payment of compensation by itself shall not establish an agency relationship or
transaction brokerage relationship** between the party who paid and the designated broker or any
affiliated licensee.

**Who pays does not decide whom you represent.** The written agreement decides.

This has to be said to buyers explicitly, because the intuition runs the other way. A buyer whose agent
is compensated through the transaction may assume they are therefore not really represented, or the
reverse. Section 339.800.1 permits compensation from the seller, the landlord, the buyer, the tenant, a
third party, or by sharing between designated brokers — and **none of those choices changes the agency.**

chunks.heading: 9.4 The § 339.780.7 minimum services
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.800.5 adds that a designated broker may be compensated by more than one party **with the
knowledge of all the parties at or before the time of entering into a written contract** to buy, sell or
lease. At or before — not afterwards.

And § 339.800.6: none of this relieves the licensee of the requirement to obtain a written agreement for
brokerage services or another written agreement addressing compensation.

### 9.4 The § 339.780.7 minimum services

Every **exclusive** brokerage agreement — on either side — must specify that the broker, through the
broker or one or more affiliated licensees, will provide **at a minimum**:

1. **Accepting delivery of and presenting** to the client or customer offers and counteroffers to buy,
   sell or lease.
2. **Assisting** the client or customer in developing, communicating, negotiating and presenting offers,
   counteroffers and notices that relate to them — **until a lease or purchase agreement is signed and
   all contingencies are satisfied or waived.**
3. **Answering** the client's or customer's questions relating to the offers, counteroffers, notices and
   contingencies.

Note the reach of item 2: **through contingency satisfaction, not to contract signature.** A firm that
regards its work as done when the contract is signed has not provided the statutory minimum.

Section 339.780.8 preserves the freedom to contract for **more**: nothing in the section prohibits the
public from entering into written contracts containing duties, obligations or responsibilities in
addition to those specified.

**Section 339.780 was amended in 2025, effective 28 August 2025.** It is read here in its current text as
of 2026-08-20 and is re-read before submission.

chunks.heading: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-03
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-03

## Hours 10–13 · Dual agency, transaction brokerage, termination, compensation, and cooperation

**Commission topics covered:** 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(D) Acting as a Dual Agent or Transaction Broker ·
(E) Termination of Brokerage Relationships · (F) Compensation · (G) Cooperating with Other Licensees
**Clock hours:** 4. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review; 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) allocates no
hours among its sixteen topics.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. State how dual agency is created and recite the five items a dual agent may not disclose.
2. State what a dual agent MAY disclose, and why dual agency is not a vow of silence.
3. Describe the transaction broker's duties and the two ways they differ from a limited agent's.
4. Explain designated agency under § 339.820 and where its protection stops.
5. State when a brokerage relationship commences and exactly what survives its end.
6. Apply § 339.800 to a compensation question, including who may pay and what payment does not create.
7. Describe cooperation and subagency and state what a cooperating licensee owes each party.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 10 | Dual agency: creation, the five items, and no imputation | 50 min |
| 11 | Transaction brokerage: neutrality and its consequences | 50 min |
| 12 | Designated agency, subagency, and cooperating with other licensees | 50 min |
| 13 | Termination and compensation | 50 min |

---

chunks.heading: Hour 10 — Acting as a dual agent — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(D)
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 10 — Acting as a dual agent — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(D)

### 10.1 Creation

Section 339.750.1, RSMo: **a licensee may act as a dual agent only with the consent of all parties to
the transaction. Consent shall be presumed by a written agreement pursuant to section 339.780.**

Section 339.780.4: before engaging in any of the § 339.010 activities, a designated broker intending to
act as a dual agent **shall enter into a written agreement with the seller and buyer** (or landlord and
tenant) permitting the broker to serve as a dual agent, and the agreement **shall include the § 339.750
duties and responsibilities and the terms of compensation**.

So dual agency is created **by written agreement with both sides, in advance**. It is not created by
circumstance, and a licensee who finds themselves on both sides without one has a problem rather than a
relationship.

### 10.2 What a dual agent is

Section 339.750.2: a dual agent is **a limited agent for both** the seller and buyer, or landlord and
tenant, **and shall have the duties and obligations required by §§ 339.730 and 339.740** unless the
section provides otherwise.

Both sets of duties. To both parties. Simultaneously. The statute does not pretend that undivided
loyalty is possible in that position — it narrows what a dual agent may say instead.

### 10.3 The five items — § 339.750.4

**Shall not be disclosed by a dual agent without the consent of the client to whom the information
pertains:**

chunks.heading: 10.4 What a dual agent MAY disclose
chunks.excerpt:
1. That a **buyer or tenant is willing to pay more** than the purchase price or lease rate offered for
   the property.
2. That a **seller or landlord is willing to accept less** than the asking price or lease rate.
3. **What the motivating factors are** for any client buying, selling or leasing the property.
4. That a client **will agree to financing terms other than those offered.**
5. **The terms of any prior offers or counter offers** made by any party.

Learn these five. They are examinable and they are the practical content of dual agency.

Notice what they have in common: each is a piece of **negotiating advantage**. What stays in is the
information one side could use against the other in the negotiation. Everything else about the
transaction is on a different footing.

### 10.4 What a dual agent MAY disclose

Section 339.750.3: **except as provided in subsections 4 and 5, a dual agent may disclose any
information to one client that the licensee gains from the other client if the information is material
to the transaction** — unless it is confidential information as defined in § 339.710.

**Dual agency is not a vow of silence.** It is a specific list of five things that stay in, plus
confidential information. A material fact about the property does not become unmentionable because the
licensee is a dual agent — and in fact the adverse material fact duties under §§ 339.730 and 339.740
continue to apply on both sides.

chunks.heading: 10.5 No imputation
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.750.5: a dual agent shall not disclose to one client any **confidential information** about
the other unless disclosure is required by statute, rule or regulation, or **failure to disclose would
constitute a misrepresentation**, or disclosure is necessary to defend against an action of wrongful
conduct. **No cause of action arises for making any required or permitted disclosure, and a dual agent
does not terminate the dual agency by making one.**

### 10.5 No imputation

Section 339.750.6: **in a dual agency relationship there shall be no imputation of knowledge or
information between the client and the dual agent or among persons within an entity engaged as a dual
agent.**

Under general agency law, what the agent knows is imputed to the principal. Section 339.750.6 switches
that off for dual agency — otherwise every dual agency would immediately impute each side's confidences
to the other and the arrangement would be impossible.

---

## Hour 11 — Acting as a transaction broker — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(D)

### 11.1 What a transaction broker is

Section 339.755.1: **a real estate licensee may provide real estate service to any party in a
prospective transaction without an agency or fiduciary relationship to one or more parties. Such
licensee shall be called a transaction broker.**

Section 339.710's definition adds the character of the role: a transaction broker **assists the parties
without an agency or fiduciary relationship to either party and is, therefore, neutral, serving neither
as an advocate or advisor for either party to the transaction.**

chunks.heading: 11.2 The duties — § 339.755.2
chunks.excerpt:
**Neutral. Not an advocate. Not an advisor.** That is the difference from limited agency, and it must be
explained to a consumer in those terms — because a consumer who thinks they have an advocate and has a
neutral facilitator has been misled about the most important feature of the arrangement.

### 11.2 The duties — § 339.755.2

1. **Perform the terms of any written or oral agreement** made with any party. Note that this is the one
   place in the Missouri scheme where the statute contemplates an **oral** agreement — though
   § 339.780.6 requires a **written** transaction brokerage agreement where the broker **expects to
   receive compensation from the party assisted.**
2. **Exercise reasonable skill, care and diligence**, including:
   - **(a)** presenting all written offers and counteroffers in a timely manner regardless of whether
     the property is subject to a contract, lease or letter of intent, unless the agreement provides
     otherwise;
   - **(b)** **informing the parties regarding the transaction and suggesting that they obtain expert
     advice** as to material matters beyond the broker's expertise;
   - **(c)** **accounting in a timely manner** for all money and property received;
   - **(d)** **disclosing to each party any adverse material facts of which the licensee has actual
     notice or knowledge**;
   - **(e)** **assisting the parties in complying with the terms and conditions of any contract.**

### 11.3 The two differences that matter

chunks.heading: 11.4 The five items again
chunks.excerpt:
**First: the disclosure standard.** A limited agent discloses adverse material facts **actually known or
that should have been known** — §§ 339.730.1(3)(c), 339.730.3, 339.740. A transaction broker discloses
those **of which the licensee has actual notice or knowledge** — § 339.755(2)(d). The transaction
broker's standard is narrower.

**Second: no imputation, and only actual knowledge.** Section 339.755.7: **each party and the transaction
broker, including all persons within an entity engaged as the transaction broker, are considered to
possess only actual knowledge and information. There is no imputation of knowledge or information by
operation of law.**

And §§ 339.755.4 and .5: a transaction broker has **no duty to conduct an independent inspection or
investigation for adverse material facts**, and **no duty to conduct an independent investigation of the
buyer's financial condition.**

### 11.4 The five items again

Section 339.755.3 carries the **same five non-disclosure items** as dual agency, phrased as requiring
**the informed consent of the party or parties disclosing such information to the broker**, and adds
**any confidential information about the other party** unless disclosure is required by law or failure
to disclose would constitute **fraud or dishonest dealing**.

### 11.5 What a transaction broker may do, and the withdrawal right

Section 339.755.6: without breaching any obligation, a transaction broker may show alternative
properties, list competing properties, show properties to other prospective buyers, and **serve as a
single agent, subagent, designated agent, limited agent or disclosed dual agent for the same or
different parties in OTHER transactions.**

chunks.heading: Hour 12 — Designated agency, subagency, and cooperating with other licensees
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.755.8: a transaction broker may **cooperate with other brokers, and such cooperation does
not establish an agency or subagency relationship.**

Section 339.755.12: a licensee who refuses transaction broker status and wants to continue an agency
relationship with both parties **has the right to become a designated agent or a dual agent** as
§§ 339.730 to 339.860 provide.

Section 339.755.13: **a licensee may without liability withdraw from representing a client who has not
consented to a conversion to transaction brokerage.** The withdrawal does not prejudice the licensee's
ability to continue representing the other client in the transaction, or to represent the refusing
client in a different transaction.

Section 339.755.10: none of this alters the **broker's responsibility for the conduct and actions of a
licensee operating under the broker's licence.**

---

## Hour 12 — Designated agency, subagency, and cooperating with other licensees

### 12.1 Designated agency — § 339.820

**The in-house problem.** One firm has the listing. A buyer working with the same firm wants to make an
offer. Without a mechanism, the firm is on both sides and every licensee in it is caught.

**The mechanism** — § 339.820.1: a designated broker entering a limited agency agreement with a client
**may appoint in writing affiliated licensees as designated agents to the exclusion of all other
affiliated licensees.** The same applies to designated transaction brokers under a transaction brokerage
agreement.

chunks.heading: 12.2 Subagency
chunks.excerpt:
One licensee is appointed to the seller; another to the buyer. Each owes the full duties. Section
339.830.1: designated agents and designated transaction brokers have **the same duties and
responsibilities to the client and customer under §§ 339.730 to 339.755 as the designated broker**,
except as § 339.820 provides.

**Where the protection stops** — § 339.820.2: a designated broker is **not** a dual agent or transaction
broker **solely because** of making an appointment — **but any licensee who personally represents both
the seller and buyer in a particular transaction IS a dual agent or a transaction broker** and must
comply accordingly.

**Read that twice.** The firm is protected by the appointment. **You are not, if both sides are yours
personally.** A licensee who has the listing and is also working with the buyer is a dual agent or a
transaction broker, and the appointment does not change it.

**The default rule** — § 339.820.1, final sentence: where an appointment has been made, **an affiliated
licensee assisting a party without a written agreement is presumed to be a transaction broker** to the
exclusion of all other affiliated licensees, unless a different status has been disclosed to or
established with that party.

Section 339.830.2: all licensees have **the same protections from vicarious liability** as their
designated broker.

### 12.2 Subagency

A **subagent** is a designated broker working for the client through the client's designated broker.

Section 339.730.5: a seller or landlord may **agree in writing** that other designated brokers may be
retained and compensated as subagents, and any such subagent is **a limited agent with the obligations
and responsibilities of §§ 339.730.1 to .4.** Section 339.740.5 mirrors it on the buyer side.

chunks.heading: 12.3 Cooperating with other licensees — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(G)
chunks.excerpt:
Section 339.780.5 sets out the three routes in: a written agreement with the client's designated broker;
or, where the client's broker has made a **unilateral offer of subagency**, by the second broker's act
of **disclosing to the customer that they are a subagent of the client**; or, where a § 339.820
appointment has been made, by an excluded affiliated licensee disclosing the same.

**The consequence for the person in front of you.** A subagent working with a buyer is **the seller's
agent.** The buyer is a **customer** — owed adverse material fact disclosure and nothing more. The buyer
must be told, and the disclosure route in § 339.780.5 makes telling them the very act that creates the
subagency.

### 12.3 Cooperating with other licensees — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(G)

**Cooperation is not agency.** Two firms working the same transaction from opposite sides are
cooperating; neither becomes the other's agent, and neither owes the other's client the duties owed to
a client. Section 339.755.8 says so expressly for transaction brokers, and the same principle governs
generally: **the relationship is created by the written agreement, not by the cooperation.**

**What a cooperating licensee owes the other side's client:** the customer duty — **disclosure of all
adverse material facts actually known or that should have been known** (or, for a transaction broker,
of which the licensee has actual notice or knowledge).

**The professional standards of cooperation**, which are not statutory but are what makes the business
work:

chunks.heading: Hour 13 — Termination and compensation
chunks.excerpt:
- **Present offers promptly** and accurately, and confirm receipt.
- **Communicate deadlines** and changes in writing.
- **Do not go around the other licensee to their client.** If a client contacts you directly, tell the
  other licensee.
- **Do not disparage** the other side's client or licensee to your own client. It is unprofessional and
  it can be defamatory.
- **Settle compensation in writing, in advance.** Cooperative compensation arrangements are agreements
  and they are documented like any other.

---

## Hour 13 — Termination and compensation

### 13.1 Termination of brokerage relationships — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(E)

**When it starts.** Section 339.790.1: the relationships **commence on the effective date of the real
estate broker's agreement and continue until performance, completion, termination or expiration of that
agreement.**

**How it ends.** By **performance** — the transaction closes. By **expiration** — the term runs out. By
**termination** — the parties end it. By **operation of law** — destruction of the property, death or
incapacity in some circumstances, bankruptcy.

**Power versus right, again.** A client has the **power** to revoke the agency at any time. Whether they
have the **right** to do so without liability is a question about the contract, and it goes to the
designated broker and counsel. A licensee who answers it has given legal advice.

### 13.2 What survives — § 339.790.2

After termination, expiration, completion or performance, the broker and the affiliated licensee **owe
no further duty or obligation, EXCEPT the duties of:**

chunks.heading: 13.3 Compensation — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(F) and § 339.800
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Accounting in a timely manner for all money and property related to, and received during, the
   relationship**; and
2. **Treating as confidential information provided by the client during the course of the relationship
   that may reasonably be expected to have a negative impact on the client's real estate activity** —
   unless:
   - **(a)** the client to whom the information pertains grants **written consent**;
   - **(b)** disclosure is **required by law**;
   - **(c)** the information **is or becomes public** by the client's words or conduct or from a source
     other than the brokerage or the affiliated licensee; or
   - **(d)** disclosure is **necessary to defend** the designated broker or an affiliated licensee
     against an action of wrongful conduct in an administrative or judicial proceeding or before a
     professional committee.

**Two things survive; everything else stops.** The confidentiality obligation is the one licensees most
often forget, and the one whose breach is most obvious after the fact.

A concrete case: a listing expires. Six months later you are working with a buyer interested in that
same house, now listed with another firm. You know the former seller's motivation, their bottom line and
their divorce. **All of that is still confidential.** Section 339.790.2(2) does not expire with the
listing.

### 13.3 Compensation — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(F) and § 339.800

**§ 339.800.1** — compensation may be paid by the **seller, the landlord, the buyer, the tenant, or a
third party**, or by **sharing between designated brokers.**

chunks.heading: 13.4 Three things a licensee must know about their own pay
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 339.800.2** — **payment of compensation by itself shall not establish an agency relationship or
transaction brokerage relationship** between the party who paid and the designated broker or any
affiliated licensee. **Who pays does not decide whom you represent.**

**§ 339.800.3 and .4** — a seller or landlord may agree that the designated broker may **share** the
compensation with another designated broker; a buyer or tenant may agree the same.

**§ 339.800.5** — a designated broker may be compensated by **more than one party** for services in a
transaction **with the knowledge of all the parties at or before the time of entering into a written
contract** to buy, sell or lease. **At or before** — disclosure after the fact does not satisfy it.

**§ 339.800.6** — nothing in the section relieves the licensee of the requirement to obtain a **written
agreement** for brokerage services or another written agreement addressing compensation.

### 13.4 Three things a licensee must know about their own pay

**Commission is negotiable.** It is not set by any board, association, multiple listing service or rule,
and any suggestion that a rate is standard or customary is an antitrust exposure, not a shorthand.

**A salesperson is paid by their designated broker.** Money moves from the closing to the broker and from
the broker to the affiliated licensee. A salesperson does not accept compensation directly from a party.

**Every compensation arrangement is in writing, in advance.** Between the firm and the client. Between
cooperating firms. Between the firm and the affiliated licensee. Section 339.800.6 requires the first
two, and the third is what stops a disagreement about a split from becoming a dispute about the file.

### Module MREP-03 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module MREP-03
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items, delivered as in Module MREP-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the 75 percent final examination standard is the
Commission's, from 20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E).

---

## Instructor source note for Module MREP-03

Sections 339.710, 339.730, 339.740, 339.750, 339.755, 339.780, 339.790, 339.800, 339.820 and 339.830,
RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.070 and 2250-7.080 were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are
transcribed in `missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** § 339.010; § 339.100 and its grounds for
discipline; 20 CSR 2250 chapters 1 through 5 and 8; and the Sherman Act and federal antitrust law in
their own text. The antitrust material in 13.4 is stated at the level of principle from the general body
of pre-license knowledge.

lessons.title: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-04

chunks.heading: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-04
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-04

## Hours 14–17 · Pricing property, the role of the appraiser, and types of construction

**Commission topics covered:** 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(I) Pricing Property · (J) Role of the Appraiser ·
(P) Types of Construction
**Clock hours:** 4. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review; 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) allocates no
hours among its sixteen topics.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Build a comparative market analysis with the adjustments in the correct direction and reconcile to a
   range rather than an average.
2. Select and reject comparables on stated grounds.
3. State the boundary between a licensee's market analysis and an appraisal, and describe how each is
   labelled.
4. Describe the appraiser's role, who engages the appraiser and why, and what happens on a low appraisal.
5. Identify the principal construction types and components a residential licensee meets, and describe
   each accurately without assessing condition.
6. Recognise construction-related conditions that must be disclosed or routed.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 14 | Pricing property: the analysis and the boundary | 50 min |
| 15 | A worked comparative market analysis, and reconciliation | 50 min |
| 16 | The role of the appraiser; the low appraisal | 50 min |
| 17 | Types of construction | 50 min |

---

## Hour 14 — Pricing property — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(I)

### 14.1 What the licensee is actually producing

chunks.heading: 14.2 Selecting comparables
chunks.excerpt:
A **comparative market analysis** is the licensee's presentation of market evidence supporting a pricing
decision. It is not an opinion of value produced under an appraiser's licence and it must never be
labelled, described or presented as one.

Four rules govern every CMA you will ever produce:

1. **Present it in writing**, with the comparables and the adjustments shown. A CMA delivered orally
   leaves no record of what was actually presented, which harms the client and, when a dispute arrives,
   the licensee.
2. **Present a range**, not a single figure. The market is not that precise and pretending it is
   overstates what the evidence supports.
3. **Say plainly that the price is the seller's decision.**
4. **Label it for what it is.**

### 14.2 Selecting comparables

**Use:** recent **closed** sales; similar in size, age, style, condition and location; in the same
market area and ideally the same submarket; arm's-length transactions between unrelated parties.

**Do not use, or use only with explanation:** current **listings**, which are asking prices and prove
only what someone hoped for; **pending** sales, whose prices are not yet known; **distressed** sales,
unless the subject is itself distressed; sales between family members or otherwise not arm's-length.

**The quality test:** the fewer and smaller the adjustments a comparable needs, the better it is. A
comparable requiring $60,000 of gross adjustment is telling you it is not really comparable.

### 14.3 The adjustment rule

**Adjust the COMPARABLE, never the subject.** The subject is what is being valued; it has no price yet
and there is nothing on it to adjust.

chunks.heading: 14.4 What may and may not be said about price
chunks.excerpt:
- Comparable **superior** to the subject → adjust the comparable **DOWN**.
- Comparable **inferior** to the subject → adjust the comparable **UP**.

Getting the direction wrong moves the answer **twice** as far as leaving the adjustment out. It is the
single most common error in the work and it is worth checking every line before you present.

### 14.4 What may and may not be said about price

**May:** *Here are five closed sales, here are the adjustments and why, here is the range they support,
and here is what I would expect at each price within it. The decision is yours.*

**May not:** confirm a figure the licensee did not derive — an automated online valuation, a neighbour's
number, an old appraisal; state a future value; guarantee a sale price or a time on market; or describe
the analysis as an appraisal.

Two Missouri provisions bear directly. **Section 339.730.1(2), RSMo** — reasonable skill and care — and
confirming a valuation you did not derive is not care. **Section 339.730.1(3)(d)** — the duty to advise
the client to obtain expert advice as to material matters beyond the licensee's expertise — which a
valuation the licensee cannot support squarely is.

And the school-side rule that describes the same principle from the other direction:
20 CSR 2250-7.010(1)(L)3 forbids a school to permit anyone associated with it to **provide any
misleading information to the public.**

### 14.5 The seller who arrives with a number

Three sources, and the accurate response to each:

**An automated online valuation.** A model's output from public and listing data. It has never been
inside the house and cannot see condition, finish or the neighbour's junkyard. Evidence to weigh, not a
valuation. Do not adopt it; do not dismiss it; put your own analysis beside it.

chunks.heading: Hour 15 — A worked comparative market analysis
chunks.excerpt:
**An old appraisal.** A 2019 appraisal is a 2019 opinion, produced for a purpose that may not be this
one, on a property that may since have changed.

**A neighbour's figure.** Ask what it is based on. It is almost always somebody's **list price**, which
is an asking price and is evidence of nothing but hope.

---

## Hour 15 — A worked comparative market analysis

### 15.1 The subject

*1,940 sq ft two-storey, 4 bed, 2.5 bath, attached 2-car garage, unfinished basement, 0.28 acre, built
2004, no recent updates.*

### 15.2 The grid

| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C | Comp D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sale price | $348,000 | $312,000 | $379,500 | $335,000 |
| Sold | 2 months ago | 6 months ago | 1 month ago | 9 months ago |
| Market conditions +0.35%/mo | +$2,436 | +$6,552 | +$1,328 | +$10,553 |
| Living area | 2,010 (+70) | 1,830 (−110) | 2,120 (+180) | 1,905 (−35) |
| Area adj. at $58/sq ft | −$4,060 | +$6,380 | −$10,440 | +$2,030 |
| Bathrooms | 2.5 | 2 (−0.5) | 3.5 (+1) | 2.5 |
| Bath adj. at $7,000 each | $0 | +$3,500 | −$7,000 | $0 |
| Basement | unfinished | unfinished | finished | unfinished |
| Basement adj. | $0 | $0 | −$16,000 | $0 |
| Kitchen | original | original | renovated | renovated |
| Kitchen adj. | $0 | $0 | −$22,000 | −$22,000 |
| **Gross adjustment** | **$6,496** | **$16,432** | **$56,768** | **$34,583** |
| **Net adjustment** | **−$1,624** | **+$16,432** | **−$54,112** | **−$9,417** |
| **Adjusted price** | **$346,376** | **$328,432** | **$325,388** | **$325,583** |

### 15.3 Checking the directions

Do this every time, line by line:

chunks.heading: 15.4 Reconciling — and why it is not averaging
chunks.excerpt:
- **Comp A** is larger — superior — so the area adjustment is **negative**. Correct.
- **Comp B** is smaller and has fewer baths — inferior on both — so both adjustments are **positive**.
  Correct.
- **Comp C** is larger, has more baths, has a finished basement and a renovated kitchen — superior on all
  four — so all four are **negative**. Correct.
- **Comp D** is slightly smaller — inferior — so **positive**; and has a renovated kitchen — superior —
  so **negative**. Correct.

**Market conditions are positive on every comparable** because the market has risen since each sale;
each would sell for more today. Time adjustments are applied before the physical adjustments.

### 15.4 Reconciling — and why it is not averaging

The four adjusted figures: **$346,376 · $328,432 · $325,388 · $325,583.**

The arithmetic mean is $331,445. **That number tells you nothing about which evidence was strongest**,
which is why reconciliation is judgment rather than averaging.

Weigh them:

- **Comp C** required **$56,768 of gross adjustment** — the most by a wide margin — and needed
  adjusting on four separate characteristics. Least reliable.
- **Comp D** sold **nine months ago** and required $34,583 gross. Second least reliable.
- **Comp B** sold six months ago and required $16,432. Moderate.
- **Comp A** sold **two months ago** and required only **$6,496 gross**. **Most reliable by a distance.**

**A defensible conclusion:** the weight of the evidence supports roughly **$332,000 to $345,000**, with
Comp A arguing for the upper part of that range and the three heavily adjusted comparables clustering
near $326,000 in a way that deserves attention rather than dismissal.

chunks.heading: Hour 16 — The role of the appraiser — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(J)
chunks.excerpt:
**And the honest thing to tell the seller:** three of four comparables land within $3,000 of each other
around $326,000 while the single most reliable one lands at $346,000, and the difference is largely the
kitchen. That is worth a sentence in the presentation, because it tells the seller something real about
their choices: renovate, price into the cluster, or price at the top and expect the market to test it.

**A CMA that hides the disagreement between its own comparables is not evidence. It is decoration.**

---

## Hour 16 — The role of the appraiser — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(J)

### 16.1 What an appraiser is

An **appraiser** is separately licensed or certified and works under their own professional standards.
An appraisal is an **opinion of value** produced under that licence, for a stated purpose, as of a
stated date, for a stated interest in a property.

**A real estate salesperson is not an appraiser and does not perform appraisals.** The two roles are
distinct in licence, in standards, in liability and in what the product may be used for.

**This course states no Missouri appraiser licensing requirement**, because Missouri's appraiser
licensing chapter was not read from primary text for this project.

### 16.2 Who engages the appraiser, and why it matters

In a financed purchase the appraisal is ordered **by or for the lender**, to establish that the
collateral supports the loan. The **appraiser's client is the lender**, not the buyer — even where the
buyer pays for the report, which they usually do.

chunks.heading: 16.3 The three approaches, briefly
chunks.excerpt:
The consequence is one buyers regularly misunderstand: **an appraisal is not an inspection and is not a
condition report for the buyer's benefit.** It looks at condition only so far as condition affects value
for the lender's purpose. A buyer who declines an inspection because "the appraiser will look at it" has
made a serious mistake, and the licensee should say so plainly.

### 16.3 The three approaches, briefly

**Sales comparison** — the dominant approach for owner-occupied residential property, because that is
how the market behaves. Its logic is the same as the CMA's in Hour 15, applied under professional
standards.

**Cost** — land value plus the reproduction or replacement cost of the improvements less accrued
depreciation. Governs new construction and special-purpose property where comparables are thin.

**Income** — net operating income divided by a capitalisation rate. Governs income-producing property.

**Reconciliation** into a final opinion is judgment about which evidence is strongest. Again: not an
average.

### 16.4 The low appraisal

The single most common appraisal event in residential practice, and one a licensee must be able to
handle calmly.

**What has happened:** the lender will lend on the **lesser of price or appraised value**, so a gap has
opened between the contract price and what the lender will finance. The buyer must now cover the
difference in cash, or the price must move, or the parties must find another route, or the contract
must end according to whatever the appraisal contingency says.

**What the licensee does:**

chunks.heading: Hour 17 — Types of construction — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(P)
chunks.excerpt:
- **Read the appraisal contingency** and its deadline before saying anything to anyone.
- **Review the report for factual errors** — wrong square footage, wrong bedroom count, a comparable
  that is not comparable, a missed permit. Factual errors are the legitimate basis for a
  reconsideration of value, and they are submitted **through the lender**, not by telephoning the
  appraiser.
- **Present the options to the client** neutrally, and route the decision.
- **Do not attempt to influence the appraiser.** Pressure on an appraiser to reach a number is
  misconduct, and in a federally related transaction it engages appraiser independence rules directly.

**What a licensee may properly do** is provide the appraiser with **factual information** — a list of
improvements with dates and costs, a survey, a plat, the seller's disclosure, comparable sales the
licensee believes relevant. Providing facts is legitimate. Providing a target is not.

---

## Hour 17 — Types of construction — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(P)

### 17.1 Why this topic is on the Commission's list

Because a licensee describes buildings for a living, and a description that is wrong is a
misrepresentation whether or not it was intended to be. This hour is vocabulary and it exists so that
you can say accurate things about a house and recognise when a question is beyond you.

**The rule for the whole hour: describe, do not assess.** A licensee identifies what something is. A
qualified professional says whether it is sound.

### 17.2 Foundations and structure

**Foundation types:** full basement — common in much of Missouri; crawl space; slab on grade; pier and
beam. Materials: poured concrete, concrete block, stone in older buildings, brick.

chunks.heading: 17.3 Roofing, cladding, and openings
chunks.excerpt:
**Framing:** platform framing, the modern standard, where each storey is built on a platform; balloon
framing, found in older houses, where studs run continuously from sill to roof; post and beam; and
structural masonry, where the walls carry the load.

**Conditions to route, never to assess:** foundation cracking or displacement; water in a basement or
crawl space; sagging floors; doors and windows out of square. Every one of those goes to a qualified
inspector or engineer, and any of them that you know about goes into the disclosure.

### 17.3 Roofing, cladding, and openings

**Roof coverings:** asphalt shingle in its several grades; wood shake; metal; tile; slate; and
membrane systems on low-slope roofs. Each has a different expected service life, and **a licensee does
not state the remaining life of a roof.**

**Roof shapes:** gable, hip, gambrel, mansard, shed, flat.

**Cladding:** brick veneer, stone, wood siding, vinyl, fibre cement, stucco, and synthetic stucco —
which has a claim history significant enough that a property clad in it is routed to a specialist
inspector as a matter of course.

**Windows:** single, double or triple glazed; wood, vinyl, aluminium or clad. **Aluminium wiring**,
**single-pane windows**, and **original 1970s systems** are all facts a buyer would want to know.

### 17.4 Systems

**Heating and cooling:** forced air furnace with split-system air conditioning; heat pump; boiler with
radiators or in-floor tubing; mini-split. Fuel: natural gas, propane, electric, oil.

**Electrical:** the service size in amps; the panel type; copper or **aluminium** branch wiring;
**knob-and-tube** in older houses. Certain panel brands have known histories and some insurers decline
them, which is a fact with a direct financial consequence for a buyer.

chunks.heading: 17.5 Measurement and description
chunks.excerpt:
**Plumbing:** copper, PEX, CPVC, galvanised steel — which corrodes internally and reduces flow — and
**cast iron or clay drains**, common in older Missouri housing stock and a source of expensive
surprises. Water supply: municipal or **private well**. Waste: municipal sewer or **septic**.

**On rural Missouri property, well and septic decide habitability and financeability.** They are routed
to the county health authority and a qualified inspector, early, because a failed septic can stop a
loan.

### 17.5 Measurement and description

**Square footage** is measured to a standard, and different standards produce different numbers.
Finished basement space is generally reported separately from above-grade living area, and combining
them inflates the figure in a way that a buyer, an appraiser and a lender will each treat as an error.

**Where the figure comes from matters.** A tax record is an assessment record, not a measurement. A
prior listing is somebody else's figure and may have been wrong then. **Say where the number came from,
or measure it.**

**Age** comes from the record and is stated as such. **"Updated," "renovated" and "new"** are claims:
say what was done and when, and where you know, say who did it and whether it was permitted.

### 17.6 The disclosure connection

Everything in this hour connects back to § 339.710(1), RSMo. **Physical condition of the property which
adversely affects value** and **material defects in the property** are on the statute's own list of
adverse material facts — and under §§ 339.730.1(3)(c), 339.730.3 and 339.740.3 they are disclosed to
clients and customers alike, actually known **or that should have been known.**

chunks.heading: Module MREP-04 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
"Should have been known" is why this vocabulary matters. A licensee who cannot recognise that a stain
running down a basement wall is worth asking about has a harder time explaining that they did not know.

### Module MREP-04 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module MREP-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the 75 percent final examination standard is the
Commission's, from 20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E).

---

## Instructor source note for Module MREP-04

Sections 339.710, 339.730 and 339.740, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.010, 2250-7.070 and
2250-7.080 were read from primary text on 2026-08-20 and are transcribed in
`missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Missouri's appraiser licensing chapter;
federal appraiser independence rules in their own text; and any building code. The worked grid uses
invented figures as an arithmetic illustration and is not Missouri market data. No expected service
life, cost figure or condition standard in Hour 17 is represented as coming from a code or a standard;
each is general construction vocabulary, and every condition question is routed.

lessons.title: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-05

chunks.heading: Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-05
chunks.excerpt:
# Missouri Real Estate Practice Course — Module MREP-05

## Hours 18–21 · Types of financing and estimating closing costs

**Commission topics covered:** 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(K) Types of Financing · (L) Estimating Closing Costs
**Clock hours:** 4. A Missouri clock hour is **60 minutes containing at least 50 minutes of actual
instruction** — 20 CSR 2250-7.070(2).
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review; 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2) allocates no
hours among its sixteen topics.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Missouri pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Describe each category of financing structurally, without recommending one.
2. Explain what a Missouri deed of trust is and what follows from a trustee's power of sale.
3. Distinguish pre-qualification, pre-approval and commitment, and explain the financing contingency.
4. Build a buyer's estimated cost sheet and a seller's estimated net sheet.
5. Prorate a shared expense correctly, in the right direction, on a stated basis.
6. State what makes every one of those figures an estimate and label it accordingly.
7. State the licensee's boundary on financing advice.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 18 | Types of financing: the categories and the structures | 50 min |
| 19 | Missouri instruments; qualification; the financing contingency | 50 min |
| 20 | Estimating closing costs: the buyer's side | 50 min |
| 21 | Prorations and the seller's net | 50 min |

---

## Hour 18 — Types of financing — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(K)

### 18.1 The categories

chunks.heading: 18.2 Rate and payment structures
chunks.excerpt:
**Conventional.** Not insured or guaranteed by a government agency. Below a threshold down payment the
lender requires **private mortgage insurance**, which **protects the lender, not the borrower**, and
which can generally be removed once equity conditions are met. Buyers consistently believe PMI protects
them; it does not, and telling them so is a genuine service.

**FHA-insured.** Insured by the Federal Housing Administration. Lower down payment requirements, mortgage
insurance premiums on their own terms, and property condition standards applied through the appraisal —
which can affect whether a particular house qualifies at all.

**VA-guaranteed.** For eligible veterans and service members. Typically no down payment, a funding fee in
place of monthly mortgage insurance, and its own appraisal and property requirements.

**USDA rural development.** For eligible properties in eligible areas with eligible borrowers. Relevant
across much of Missouri.

**State and local assistance programmes** — down payment assistance, first-time buyer and bond
programmes. **This course states no eligibility criterion, income limit or purchase price limit for any
Missouri programme**, because none was read from primary source for this project. They are routed to the
administering agency and to the lender.

**Seller financing**, including the **land contract or contract for deed** structure, in which the buyer
takes possession and equitable title while the seller retains legal title until the payments are
complete. This is the arrangement in which a buyer has the **least** protection, and the consequences of
default are a legal question with real stakes. **A licensee explains the structure and routes the
decision to counsel.**

### 18.2 Rate and payment structures

chunks.heading: 18.3 The rule that governs this hour
chunks.excerpt:
**Fixed rate** — the rate does not change for the life of the loan.

**Adjustable rate** — a rate tied to an index plus a margin, adjusting on a schedule, with **caps** on
the periodic adjustment and on the lifetime rate. A buyer considering one needs the **worst case**, not
the teaser: the lifetime cap tells you the highest rate possible, and it is computable.

**Interest-only, balloon and graduated payment** structures each carry a risk profile the buyer must
understand before signing. A balloon is a date on which a large sum becomes due, and a buyer who has not
diarised it has a problem waiting.

### 18.3 The rule that governs this hour

**A licensee explains structures and routes pricing.**

Which programme is cheapest for a particular borrower depends on the rate, the term, the mortgage
insurance treatment, the fees, the borrower's tax position and how long they will hold the property. A
licensee controls none of those and knows some of them not at all.

Naming the categories is education. **Recommending one is advice the licensee is not licensed to give**,
and § 339.740.1(3)(d), RSMo — advising the client to obtain expert advice on material matters beyond the
licensee's expertise — is the statutory instruction to route it.

---

## Hour 19 — Missouri instruments, qualification, and the contingency

### 19.1 Note and deed of trust

The **promissory note** is the borrower's promise to repay — the debt. The **security instrument**
pledges the property as security for it — the lien.

chunks.heading: 19.2 The clauses that decide outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
**Missouri practice uses a deed of trust**, a three-party instrument: **trustor** (borrower),
**beneficiary** (lender), and a **trustee** who holds a **power of sale**. On default the trustee may
conduct a sale **without a lawsuit** — a non-judicial process, in contrast to the judicial foreclosure
used in mortgage states.

**This course states no Missouri foreclosure timetable, notice requirement, redemption right or
deficiency rule**, because Missouri's foreclosure chapter was not read from primary text for this
project. The structural fact — a trustee holding a power of sale, exercised without a court — is what a
licensee carries. Every question about timing, notice, redemption or deficiency is routed to counsel,
and a licensee working a distressed file routes the seller's tax and credit consequences to their
accountant.

### 19.2 The clauses that decide outcomes

**Acceleration** — on default the whole balance becomes due. **Alienation, or due-on-sale** — on
transfer the lender may call the balance, which is why "taking subject to" is not a workaround a
licensee arranges and why **assumption requires lender consent**. **Prepayment** — whether early
repayment is permitted and on what terms. **Escrow or impound** — the lender collects taxes and
insurance monthly, which is why the payment is **PITI** and why an escrow analysis can change a payment
after closing without the rate having moved. Warn buyers about that last one; it arrives as a shock
otherwise.

**Assumption with a written release** takes the seller off the obligation. **Assumption without one**
does not — the seller remains liable for a loan on a house they no longer own.

### 19.3 Qualification, in one page

chunks.heading: 19.4 Pre-qualification, pre-approval, commitment — and the contingency
chunks.excerpt:
**The four Cs:** capacity (income against obligations), credit (the record of repayment), capital (funds
for down payment, costs and reserves — and their **sourcing and seasoning**, which surprises buyers
gifted money at the last minute), and collateral (the property, through the appraisal).

**The ratios:** the **housing ratio** is the proposed **PITI** plus mortgage insurance and association
dues, divided by gross monthly income. The **total debt ratio** adds every other recurring obligation.

*Worked.* Gross monthly income $7,100. PITI $1,704. Car $395, student loan $260, card minimums $110.
Housing ratio 1,704 ÷ 7,100 = **24.0%**. Total obligations $2,469 ÷ 7,100 = **34.8%**.

**The thresholds are the lender's and the programme's, not the licensee's**, they differ by programme,
they move, and they yield to compensating factors and automated underwriting decisions no licensee sees.
A licensee who quotes a qualifying ratio as a rule has stated an underwriting standard as law.

### 19.4 Pre-qualification, pre-approval, commitment — and the contingency

**Pre-qualification** is an estimate from stated information. **Pre-approval** follows verification and
underwriting. **Neither is a loan commitment.**

**That gap is the entire reason the financing contingency exists.** A buyer who believes a pre-approval
is a promise will not understand why the contingency matters, will resent the seller's anxiety about it,
and will be blindsided if underwriting turns. Say it at the beginning, plainly.

chunks.heading: Hour 20 — Estimating closing costs: the buyer's side — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(L)
chunks.excerpt:
**The contingency itself** has four parts and all four must be read: the **condition** — a loan of a
stated type and amount on stated terms; the **deadline**; the **method of notice**; and **the effect of
silence** if the deadline passes with no notice. That last one differs by form, and assuming is how
transactions die.

**The licensee's actual job here is calendar work.** On the day of acceptance, write every financing
deadline in the file and in the calendar. Work backwards to the date the application must be complete.
Confirm each step in writing. Raise a slipping date with the client **before** it passes.

---

## Hour 20 — Estimating closing costs: the buyer's side — 20 CSR 2250-6.060(2)(L)

### 20.1 What a buyer pays, by category

**Loan costs.** Origination and underwriting fees; discount points if any; appraisal; credit report;
flood determination; any lender-required inspections.

**Title and settlement.** Lender's title policy and the owner's policy if the buyer is paying for it;
settlement or closing fee; recording fees; and a survey if obtained.

**Prepaid items and escrow deposits.** Prepaid interest from closing to the end of the month; the first
year's hazard insurance premium; and the initial deposit into the tax and insurance escrow.

**Prorations.** The buyer's share of items paid in advance by the seller; and a **credit** to the buyer
for items paid in arrears that the buyer will pay later.

### 20.2 A worked buyer's estimate

*Purchase price $318,000. Loan $286,200 (90 percent). Earnest money $4,000 already deposited. Closing 14
October. Taxes paid in arrears, annual $3,720, 365-day basis, closing day to the buyer.*

chunks.heading: 20.3 Who quotes what
chunks.excerpt:
| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Purchase price | $318,000.00 |
| Loan origination, 0.75% of loan | 2,146.50 |
| Appraisal | 675.00 |
| Credit report and flood determination | 145.00 |
| Lender's title policy | 495.00 |
| Owner's title policy | 1,190.00 |
| Settlement fee | 550.00 |
| Recording | 118.00 |
| Prepaid interest, 17 days at $47.70 | 810.90 |
| Hazard insurance, first year | 1,620.00 |
| Escrow deposit, taxes and insurance | 1,445.00 |
| **Subtotal** | **$327,195.40** |
| Less loan amount | (286,200.00) |
| Less earnest money | (4,000.00) |
| Less tax proration credit to buyer | (2,914.85) |
| **Estimated cash to close** | **$34,080.55** |

**The tax proration, worked.** $3,720 ÷ 365 = **$10.1918** a day. The seller's days run 1 January
through 13 October, because the closing day goes to the buyer: 31+28+31+30+31+30+31+31+30+13 = **286
days**. 286 × 10.1918 = **$2,914.85**.

**Count the days rather than estimating them.** "About nine and a half months" produces a figure that
looks right and is wrong by a hundred dollars or more, and it will be wrong on the settlement statement
too if nobody recomputes it. Add the month lengths, remember February, and check whether the year is a
leap year before dividing by 365.

It is a **credit to the buyer** because the buyer will pay the whole tax bill when it issues, including
the part covering the seller's period of ownership.

### 20.3 Who quotes what

The figures above come from **the lender** (loan costs, prepaid interest, escrow) and **the closing agent
or title company** (title, settlement, recording, prorations). **They do not come from the licensee.**

A licensee assembles the estimate from those sources and labels it as what it is.

---

## Hour 21 — Prorations and the seller's net

### 21.1 Proration, properly

chunks.heading: 21.2 The seller's estimated net
chunks.excerpt:
Three questions before any arithmetic:

1. **What is the annual amount?**
2. **What basis** — 365-day year, or 360-day banker's year with 30-day months?
3. **Who gets the day of closing**, and is the item paid **in advance** or **in arrears**?

**The convention comes from the contract, not from habit.** Getting the basis or the closing-day
convention wrong produces a number close enough to look right and wrong enough to matter.

**Direction.** Ask: **who has had the use, and who has paid?** Whoever paid for time they will not have
gets a **credit**.

*Paid in arrears — taxes.* The seller has had the use and has not paid. The buyer will pay the whole
bill. **Credit the buyer, debit the seller.**

*Paid in advance — annual association dues.* The seller has paid for time the buyer will have. **Credit
the seller, debit the buyer.**

*Worked, in advance.* Association dues $540 paid annually on 1 January. Closing 14 October, 365-day
basis, closing day to the buyer. Daily 540 ÷ 365 = $1.4795. Days from 14 October through 31 December:
18+30+31 = **79**. 79 × 1.4795 = **$116.88**, a **credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer.**

### 21.2 The seller's estimated net

*Sale price $318,000. First deed of trust payoff $214,600. Second lien $18,200. Commission 6 percent.
Seller's title and settlement costs $1,860. Agreed repair credit to buyer $1,500. Tax proration debit to
seller $2,914.85. Association dues credit to seller $116.88.*

chunks.heading: 21.3 What makes every one of these an estimate — and why the label matters
chunks.excerpt:
| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Sale price | $318,000.00 |
| Less first deed of trust payoff | (214,600.00) |
| Less second lien payoff | (18,200.00) |
| Less commission, 6% | (19,080.00) |
| Less seller's title and settlement costs | (1,860.00) |
| Less repair credit to buyer | (1,500.00) |
| Less tax proration | (2,914.85) |
| Plus association dues proration | 116.88 |
| **Estimated seller's net** | **$59,962.03** |

### 21.3 What makes every one of these an estimate — and why the label matters

**Payoff figures include per-diem interest and are quoted only to a stated date.** A closing that slips
three days changes the payoff.

**Closing costs are the closing agent's and the lender's figures**, not the licensee's, and they move.

**Prorations depend on a tax bill that may not yet have issued**, in which case the parties are
estimating from the prior year — and the contract should say what happens if the actual bill differs.

**Repair credits, seller concessions and late changes all move the total**, and under **TRID** a change
close to closing can trigger a redisclosure and a new three-business-day waiting period before
consummation. Getting changes decided **early** and telling the lender promptly is a real service.

**So label it.** A net sheet is an **estimate**; it says so on its face; it shows its assumptions and its
sources; and the figures come from the closing agent, the lender and the payoff statement.

**A licensee who hands a seller a confident net figure that turns out to be $3,000 optimistic has
created a problem no apology fixes** — and, depending on how it was presented, a misrepresentation
question under § 339.730.1(2) and Module MREP-06's topic (O).

### Module MREP-05 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module MREP-05
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items, delivered as in Module MREP-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the 75 percent final examination standard is the
Commission's, from 20 CSR 2250-7.080(1)(E).

Sections 339.730 and 339.740, RSMo, and 20 CSR 2250-6.060, 2250-7.070 and 2250-7.080 were read from
primary text on 2026-08-20 and are transcribed in `missouri/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Missouri's foreclosure chapter; Missouri's
property tax chapter and every rate, cycle and exemption in it; Missouri's transfer-tax treatment; RESPA,
Regulation X, TILA and Regulation Z in their own text; and the eligibility rules of every state and local
