lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-03

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-03
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-03

## Section III · Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions & Property Use

**Commission Syllabus section:** III — Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions & Property Use
**Instructional Level:** **1** unless otherwise noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and
instructors are **REQUIRED to comply**.* Several subtopics carry their own Levels and are marked below —
**Fixtures is Level 3**, and Property Ownership and Interests, Encumbrances, Legal Descriptions, Zoning
concepts, Subdivision regulation and Private controls are **Level 2**.
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 9 items.**
**Recommended allocation:** **5.0 instructional hours**, matching the Commission's recommended 1.0
hour for Basic Real Estate Concepts plus 4.0 for Property Characteristics, Description & Use. This
allocation is a plan, not proof of self-paced seat time; measured text/media time is reported separately.
**Course version:** 1.1 development draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Basic Real Estate Concepts *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
1. Define land, real estate, real property and personal property. *(Level 1)*
2. Name the three physical and four economic characteristics of land. *(Level 1)*
3. Distinguish severance from annexation and state how personal property transfers. *(Level 2)*
4. **Apply the Total Circumstances Test to a disputed item and predict how a court would rule.**
   *(Level 3)*
5. Distinguish fructus naturales from fructus industriales. *(Level 1)*
6. Distinguish an appurtenant easement from an easement in gross, and both from a licence. *(Level 2)*
7. State how easements are created, recorded and terminated. *(Level 2)*
8. Distinguish an encroachment from an easement and state how each is detected. *(Level 2)*
9. Describe the methods of legal description and identify which is primary in North Carolina. *(Level 2)*
10. State the broker's boundary on survey questions.
11. Name the four governmental powers and describe zoning administration in North Carolina.
12. Define the zoning concepts the Syllabus lists and apply them to examples. *(Level 2)*
13. Explain how restrictive covenants operate and which controls where they conflict with zoning. *(Level 2)*

---

## A. Basic Real Estate Concepts *(Level 1)*

### A.1 Terminology

**Land.** The surface, the space above and the subsurface beneath.

**Real estate.** Land plus everything permanently attached to it.

**Real property.** Real estate plus the bundle of legal rights attaching to it.

**Personal property** — *chattel* or *personalty*. Everything that is not real property.

chunks.heading: A.2 Physical characteristics of land
chunks.excerpt:
**Instructor Note, from the Syllabus:** *"The terms real property, real estate and land are often used
interchangeably."* They are used interchangeably in ordinary speech and they are not the same thing,
which is why the definitions are learned rather than assumed.

### A.2 Physical characteristics of land

**Immobility.** **Indestructibility.** **Uniqueness** — non-homogeneity.

### A.3 Economic characteristics of land

**Scarcity.** **Location** — *situs* or area preference. **Improvements** — modifications.
**Permanence of investment** — fixity.

*(Note that the Commission's list differs slightly from the four-item lists used elsewhere: it names
**location** among the economic characteristics and pairs **improvements** with **permanence of
investment**. Learn the Commission's list, because the examination is built on the Syllabus.)*

### A.4 The scope of the real estate business, and the real estate market

Residential and commercial brokerage; property management; appraisal; development; financing; and the
title, closing and inspection businesses surrounding every transaction. The market for real estate is
**local**, because land is immobile, and **slow to respond**, because supply cannot be created quickly.

---

## B. Property Ownership and Interests *(Level 2 except as noted)*

### B.1 The concept of property

**Real property.** **Personal property** — *chattel* or *personalty*:

- **movable items**;
- **severance versus annexation/attachment** — the two events that move an item across the line; and
- **transferred by Bill of Sale**, not by deed.

### B.2 Fruits of the soil *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

chunks.heading: B.3 Fixtures *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Fructus naturales** — naturally occurring growth, treated as real property.
**Fructus industriales**, or **emblements** — annually cultivated crops produced by human labour,
treated as personal property.

### B.3 Fixtures *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

**This is the highest Instructional Level in the section, and the Commission attaches a Required
Activity to it.**

#### The Total Circumstances Test

Used **in court when contract terms are silent about an item**. Written contract terms should clarify
the intent of the contract parties — which is the practical lesson: **the test exists because somebody
failed to write it down.**

**Four test criteria for determining whether an item is a fixture:**

1. **Intent of the annexor.**
2. **Relationship of the annexor to the property.**
3. **Method of annexation.**
4. **Adaptation to the real estate.**

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"All 4 criteria must be present to indicate that an item is a
fixture. Most standard listing agreements and sales contracts include a list of common items that will
be considered fixtures for the transaction unless otherwise addressed in the document."*

**Read the first sentence carefully.** The Commission states the test as **conjunctive — all four must
be present.** That is stricter than the "weigh the factors" formulation used in some materials, and it
is the formulation this course teaches because it is the Commission's.

chunks.heading: Trade fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Use pictures to help students recognize items
> that might cause confusion in a transaction. Have students apply the Total Circumstances Test to
> predict how a judge might rule if the issue went to court."*
>
> **This activity must be completed.** It is a course completion condition, not an enrichment exercise.
> Work each of the following through all four criteria and state the predicted ruling with reasons:
> a wired-in dining room chandelier the seller intends to take; a mounted television and its bracket;
> a portable dishwasher connected to the sink; custom storm windows cut for these openings; a swing set
> anchored in concrete; an above-ground pool; a tenant's walk-in cooler; a propane tank on a lease.

![Eight fixture-dispute illustrations for the Total Circumstances Test](/media/nc-fixture-decision-lab.svg)

**Student activity.** For every pictured item, record four separate observations — intent, relationship,
method of annexation and adaptation — before predicting the result. A label such as “bolted” or “tenant”
does not decide the question by itself. The prediction must use **all four** Commission criteria, and the
transaction documents should expressly settle what conveys whenever the parties can do so.

#### Trade fixtures

Items a **tenant** attaches for the conduct of their **business**. They remain the tenant's personal
property and must be removed before the term ends, with the tenant repairing removal damage. Note how
the Total Circumstances Test handles them: criterion 2, **the relationship of the annexor to the
property**, is what distinguishes a tenant's installation from an owner's.

### B.4 Improvements *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

chunks.heading: B.5 Encumbrances to real property *(Level 2 except as noted)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Improvements to the land** — grading, utilities, streets. **Improvements on the land** — buildings.

**Instructor Note:** *"Depending on context, Improved Land or Improved Lot may have dual meanings."*
And: **"On the National exam section, an improvement is an appurtenance."**

### B.5 Encumbrances to real property *(Level 2 except as noted)*

The Syllabus lists six and cross-references three of them forward:

- **Liens** — discussed in Section VI, Module NC-06.
- **Special assessments** — Section VI.
- **Lis pendens**, notice of pending litigation — Section VI.
- **Restrictive (protective) covenants** — CC&Rs, discussed later in this section at D.2.
- **Easements** — here.
- **Encroachments** — here.

#### Easements

**Terminology:** the **dominant estate or tenement** is benefited; the **servient estate or tenement**
is burdened.

**General categories:**

- **Appurtenant easement** — benefits a parcel; has both a dominant and a servient tenement; runs with
  the land.
- **Easement in gross** — benefits a person or entity. The Syllabus distinguishes **personal versus
  commercial** easements in gross.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Distinguish from a **licence**, which is a **personal, revocable,
non-assignable right, but NOT an encumbrance.**"*

That last clause is the tested point: a licence is not an encumbrance at all.

**Creation of easements:** **express**; **implied**; **arising by operation of law**.

**Recordation.** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"An easement must be **recorded to be binding
against a purchaser of the servient estate**."*

**Termination of easements**, and **party walls (cross easements)**.

#### Encroachments

chunks.heading: C. Understanding Legal Descriptions *(Level 2 except as noted)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Examples.** **Usually detected by an up-to-date survey.** And the tested point:
**"Not discoverable by title search."**

That is why an encroachment and a recorded easement are found by two entirely different investigations,
and why a buyer who orders title work but no survey has looked for only one of them.

---

## C. Understanding Legal Descriptions *(Level 2 except as noted)*

### C.1 Adequacy of description, and the methods

**Metes and bounds** — **"Primary method in original 13 colonies, including NC."**

- **Point-of-beginning (POB).**
- **Outside boundaries are described through a series of calls.**
- Descriptions include **monuments**, **distance (metes)** and **course or direction (bounds)**.

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide a deed and a survey that illustrate
> description by metes and bounds."*

The following StateCourse exhibit is a **fictional teaching facsimile**, not a recorded deed, title
instrument or licensed survey. It shows how deed calls correspond to a plotted boundary, but it does
not yet close the Commission activity: a rights-safe deed and survey acceptable for regulatory review
remain an open course-material dependency.

![Fictional deed calls beside a matching metes-and-bounds plot](/media/nc-metes-bounds-training-exhibit.svg)

**Government (rectangular) survey system** *(Level 1 — this subtopic)* — **"Primary method for states
other than the original 13 colonies."** Division into squares based on the intersection of **prime
meridian lines** running north/south and **base lines** running east/west; **townships**; **sections**.

chunks.heading: C.2 Property survey, and the broker's boundary
chunks.excerpt:
**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Although this method is **not used in NC**, basic principles are
subject to testing on the **National** section of the exam; **no calculations are tested on the
exam**."*

**That note is worth reading twice.** North Carolina does not use the rectangular survey, students are
examined on its principles, and **no rectangular-survey calculations appear on the examination.**

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide a visual illustration of an
> accompanying government survey description."*

![Government rectangular survey hierarchy from township to quarter-quarter section](/media/nc-government-survey-grid.svg)

**Reading the illustration.** Begin with the township created by principal meridian and base-line
references, locate the numbered section, then subdivide the section into quarters and quarter-quarters.
The diagram teaches the hierarchy only. Consistent with the Commission note, the activity requires no
acreage calculation.

**Reference to recorded plat (lot and block).**

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide a copy of an approved subdivision
> plat map."*

**Reference to publicly recorded documents.** **Informal reference** — e.g., a street address, which is
never an adequate legal description.

### C.2 Property survey, and the broker's boundary

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide a copy of a residential property
> survey. Ideally the survey will show setbacks for buildings, utility easements, and possibly an
> encroachment from an adjacent parcel."*

**Instructor Note, transcribed — and this is the single most important sentence in the section for
daily practice:**

chunks.heading: D. Land Use Controls
chunks.excerpt:
> *"A broker should **never offer an opinion** about accuracy of the parcel boundaries, whether
> improvements are properly located on the tract, where easements are located on the property, or
> similar matters; **refer such queries to a licensed surveyor or civil engineer**."*

**Never. Not "be careful" — never.**

And the consequence for the buyer, transcribed: **"Title defects that would have been discovered by a
property survey are frequently not covered by title insurance, if a survey was not performed as part of
the transaction."** With the Commission's own advice attached: **"A buyer should be strongly encouraged
to order an updated survey as part of their due diligence process."**

---

## D. Land Use Controls

### D.1 Public controls

**Governmental powers — PETE:**

- **Police power** — for protection of the public; **includes zoning and environmental laws.**
- **Escheat.**
- **Taxation.**
- **Eminent domain.**

#### Zoning

**Administered primarily by the city or county planning department.** **Local boards of adjustment
generally handle requests for variances or special use permits.** And **extra-territorial jurisdictions
(ETJ)** — a North Carolina feature a licensee must know exists: a municipality may exercise zoning
authority beyond its corporate limits.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"There is **no uniformity of zoning codes**; codes and their meanings
can **vary widely throughout the state**."*

So a licensee who learned "R-3" in one county knows nothing about "R-3" in the next one.

#### Zoning concepts *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide examples of each of the following
> zoning concepts."*

chunks.heading: Required zoning examples
chunks.excerpt:
**Nonconforming use** — with the Commission's own warning attached: *"Buyer should **never assume a
nonconforming use can continue** after transfer of ownership or destruction of improvements."*

**Illegal use. Zoning amendments. Variance. Special-use permit** (or conditional-use permit).
**Overlay district. Historic preservation zoning. Aesthetic zoning. Spot zoning. Cluster zoning.
Buffer zone.**

#### Required zoning examples

These examples identify the concepts; they do **not** state that any particular North Carolina ordinance
allows the result. The current city or county ordinance and the responsible planning office control.

| Concept | Illustrative example |
|---|---|
| Nonconforming use | A neighborhood grocery lawfully operating before the area was rezoned residential continues only to the extent the current ordinance permits. |
| Illegal use | A warehouse begins operating in a residential district after the restriction already applies and without required approval. |
| Zoning amendment | A local government changes a corridor from an industrial classification to a mixed-use classification through its legislative process. |
| Variance | An unusually shaped lot owner asks the board of adjustment for relief from a dimensional setback requirement. |
| Special-use or conditional-use permit | A daycare is a listed conditional use and may operate only after the designated board applies the ordinance's conditions. |
| Overlay district | A flood-hazard overlay adds requirements to property that retains its underlying residential classification. |
| Historic preservation zoning | Exterior work in a designated historic district is reviewed under preservation standards in addition to base zoning. |
| Aesthetic zoning | A sign or facade is reviewed against locally adopted

chunks.heading: Urban and regional use planning
chunks.excerpt:
appearance standards. |
| Spot zoning | One small parcel receives materially different treatment from surrounding parcels; whether that action is lawful is a legal and fact-specific question. |
| Cluster zoning | Homes are grouped more closely on one part of a tract while another part remains common open space, as the ordinance permits. |
| Buffer zone | A required landscaped strip separates a commercial use from adjoining residences. |

#### Urban and regional use planning

**Instructor Note:** these exist *"to assure orderly and systematic development of land use."*

#### Subdivision statutes and regulations *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*

**Typical subdivision approval procedures**, in North Carolina and elsewhere: a **preliminary planning
phase**; a **review and approval phase usually by multiple municipal departments**; and a **final
subdivision plat approved and recorded.**

#### Regulation of special land types

**Flood zones. Wetlands.**

#### Highway access restrictions

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Ability to access an existing public highway or street that abuts
the property **is a material fact**; access may be restricted or forbidden by state or local
municipality."*

#### Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act — 15 USC 1701 et seq.

Purpose; land registration requirement; application; exemptions. **This course states no threshold,
lot count or exemption from the Act, because it was not read from primary text for this project.**

#### Government land ownership

**Instructor Note:** *"Public ownership controls land for the benefit and use of the entire population,
such as national/state/municipal parks, road system, and preservation of natural resources."*

### D.2 Privately-imposed land use controls *(Level 2 except as noted)*

chunks.heading: Required Activities in this section — all six must be completed
chunks.excerpt:
**Restrictive/protective covenants.** Set forth **in a deed or in a separately recorded declaration of
covenants**; also called **covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs)**.

**Typical matters addressed.** **Covenants run with the land (appurtenant) and are binding on all
subsequent owners.** **Enforcement.**

**Instructor Note, transcribed — the tested point:** *"When covenants differ from zoning regulations on
a particular matter, **the more restrictive of the two will control**."*

---

## Required Activities in this section — all six must be completed

1. Total Circumstances Test with pictures, predicting a judge's ruling. *(B.3 — delivered above)*
2. A deed and a survey illustrating metes and bounds. *(C.1 — teaching facsimile prepared; authentic
   rights-safe source still outstanding)*
3. A visual illustration of a government survey description. *(C.1 — delivered above)*
4. An approved subdivision plat map. *(C.1 — outstanding)*
5. A residential property survey showing setbacks, utility easements and ideally an encroachment.
   *(C.2 — outstanding)*
6. Examples of each listed zoning concept. *(D.1 — delivered above)*

## Module NC-03 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-03

Drawn from **Section III** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Every Instructor Note and Required Activity above is **transcribed from
the Syllabus.**

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-03
chunks.excerpt:
The provisions of **NCGS Chapter 93A** and **21 NCAC Chapter 58** used in Modules NC-01 and NC-02 were
read from current official text. No additional provision from them supplies the property-law rules in
this module. **Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the **Interstate Land Sales Full
Disclosure Act**; North Carolina's subdivision, easement and survey statutes; and any municipal zoning
ordinance. No lot threshold, exemption, setback standard, plat requirement or prescriptive period is
stated. Where this module reaches one of those, it names the question and routes it — and on boundaries,
improvements and easement locations the routing is the Commission's own: **to a licensed surveyor or
civil engineer.**

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-04

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-04
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-04

## Section IV · Property Taxes & Insurance

**Commission Syllabus section:** IV — Property Taxes & Insurance
**Instructional Level:** **2** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* At Level 2 the instructor reviews and discusses the topic **in moderate
depth** sufficient to illustrate facts, principles and procedures **and their relevance to brokerage
practice**. **Tax Calculations, Excise Tax Calculations, the Broker's Responsibility on insurance, and
Taxation of Capital Gain are Level 3**; the insurance definitions, package insurance, coinsurance and
most of Federal Income Taxation are **Level 1**.
**Licence examination weight:** **State Exam Category — 4 items.**
**Recommended allocation:** **4.0 instructional hours**, matching the Commission's recommended
emphasis for Taxation & Insurance. This allocation is a plan, not proof of self-paced seat time;
measured text/media time is reported separately.
**Course version:** 1.1 development draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Ad Valorem Property Tax
chunks.excerpt:
1. Define ad valorem and compute a North Carolina property tax from a rate per $100. *(Level 3)*
2. Convert between a North Carolina rate per $100 and a mill rate, and compute from either. *(Level 3)*
3. State how North Carolina assesses real property and how often it reappraises. *(Level 2)*
4. Recite the North Carolina property tax timetable and explain the two-lien situation it can produce.
5. State the priority of a North Carolina real property tax lien.
6. Compute North Carolina excise tax and state who pays it. *(Level 3)*
7. Define the basic insurance terms and describe HO-3, HO-4 and HO-6 coverage. *(Level 1)*
8. Explain what flood insurance is, who administers it, and what a 100-year flood plain means.
9. **State the broker's five insurance responsibilities.** *(Level 3)*
10. Describe the common income tax deductions for owners of personal residences. *(Level 1)*
11. State the rules for taxation of capital gain on the sale of a principal residence. *(Level 3)*
12. State the licensee's boundary on tax advice.

---

## A. Ad Valorem Property Tax

### A.1 Ad valorem

**Ad valorem** — according to value. Real property tax is charged as a proportion of the property's
value rather than as a flat amount.

### A.2 Tax rate and calculations

**North Carolina county and municipal property-tax rates are adopted annually by their governing
boards.** G.S. 159-13 requires the budget ordinance that levies the tax to be adopted not later than
July 1. A parcel inside municipal limits is generally subject to the applicable county levy and the
applicable city or town levy; the live assessor and adopted budget ordinances supply the actual rates.

chunks.heading: A.3 Tax calculations *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"A property located within a city or town limit in NC will be
**subject to both county and city/town taxes**."*

That is a real trap for a licensee quoting a tax figure from a county record on a property inside a
municipality: the county rate is not the whole bill.

**The North Carolina tax rate is expressed as $xxx per $100 of assessed value.**

**Other states express the rate as a mill rate.** From the Syllabus: *"A mill is 1/10th of a cent; a
mill rate is described as mills per dollar of assessed value. [Example: A NC tax rate of $1.50 per $100
(which is $0.015 per dollar) is the same as a mill rate of 15 mills per dollar.]"*

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Either of the above tax rates may be cited in **National** exam
section items and **students must be able to perform calculations using either rate**."*

### A.3 Tax calculations *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

**North Carolina, rate per $100.**

> Tax = (assessed value ÷ 100) × rate per $100

*Worked.* Assessed value **$284,000**; county rate **$0.6150** per $100; city rate **$0.4425** per $100.

County: (284,000 ÷ 100) × 0.6150 = 2,840 × 0.6150 = **$1,746.60**
City: 2,840 × 0.4425 = **$1,256.70**
**Total annual tax = $3,003.30**

*(The rates above are invented for arithmetic. They are not North Carolina rates for any jurisdiction.)*

**Mill rate.**

> Tax = assessed value × (mills ÷ 1,000)

*Worked.* Assessed value **$284,000**, rate **15 mills**. 284,000 × 0.015 = **$4,260.**

**Check the equivalence the Syllabus states:** $1.50 per $100 is $0.015 per dollar is 15 mills. So
2,840 × 1.50 = $4,260 by the North Carolina method and 284,000 × 0.015 = $4,260 by the mill method.
**The same tax, computed two ways.**

chunks.heading: A.4 Property subject to taxation — G.S. 105-274
chunks.excerpt:
**Converting.** Rate per $100 × 10 = mills. Mills ÷ 10 = rate per $100. ($1.50 × 10 = 15 mills.)

### A.4 Property subject to taxation — G.S. 105-274

The current statute starts with the general rule that property within North Carolina is subject to
taxation **unless** a statewide statute or the Constitution excludes or exempts it. That final clause is
part of the rule: a broker must not turn the general rule into “there are no exemptions.” Eligibility
for a specific exclusion, exemption or use-value program goes to the assessor or a qualified adviser.

### A.5 Appraisal and assessment

**The NC Machinery Act regulates property taxation in North Carolina.**

- **Assessed value of real property for property taxation purposes in NC must be, with few exceptions,
  its market value or "…its true value in money" at the time of assessment.**
- **State authority to tax is delegated to local municipalities** — county, city, town.
- **Octennial baseline: each county must reappraise real property every 8 years.**
- **The cycle can be advanced.** G.S. 105-286 requires advancement for a county with population of at
  least 75,000 when the statute's sales-assessment ratio trigger is crossed, and permits a county to
  adopt an earlier or more frequent cycle.

> **Current-law correction:** an older syllabus statement that a fourth-year horizontal reappraisal is
> possible is no longer current. The General Assembly repealed subsections 105-286(b) and (c) effective
> July 1, 2009. Do not teach a fourth-year horizontal adjustment as current law. The present statute's
> mandatory- and optional-advancement rules control, and the syllabus conflict must be flagged for the
> Commission reviewer.

chunks.heading: A.6 The North Carolina property tax timetable
chunks.excerpt:
**In other states**, the assessed value for taxation may be **less than market value** — such as 50
percent of market value.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"National exam section items might mention an assessed value that is
less than market value and **these items should be answered based on the given information rather than
on NC practice**. Also, the term *true market value* should be assumed to mean *market value*."*

**That is examination guidance from the Commission and it is worth carrying into the examination room:
on a National item, use the assessed value the item gives you; do not substitute North Carolina's
market-value rule.**

### A.6 The North Carolina property tax timetable

Five dates, transcribed:

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **January 1** | **The tax lien attaches to the property.** |
| **January 31** | **Ordinary listing period ends.** G.S. 105-307 permits specified general and individual extensions. |
| **July 1** | **Latest date for the governing board to adopt the budget ordinance that levies property taxes.** |
| **September 1** | **The annual tax bill is due and payable.** |
| **January 5 of the next year** | **Last day to pay at face amount; interest applies to payment on or after January 6.** |

**Instructor Note on 1 January, transcribed:** *"Real property tax liens attach to the property on the
1st day of the listing period, **even though the tax is not due until later in the year**."*

**Instructor Note on the overlap, transcribed:** *"If the previous year's taxes are not paid by December
31, it is possible on **January 1–5 for property to have tax liens for two successive years that are
both current**."*

chunks.heading: A.7 Special priority of real property tax liens — G.S. 105-356
chunks.excerpt:
**Read the second note carefully — it is exactly the kind of point the state examination tests.** In
that five-day window, two years' liens exist simultaneously and neither is delinquent, because the prior
year's still has until 5 January and the new year's attached on 1 January.

**And the practical consequence for a closing in that window:** a closing on 3 January must deal with
two current tax liens, and the licensee's job is to notice that and get it in front of the closing
attorney early.

### A.7 Special priority of real property tax liens — G.S. 105-356

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Real property tax liens are **superior to all other liens, charges,
assessments, rights and claims regardless of when acquired**."*

**Regardless of when acquired.** First in time, first in right does not apply to them.

---

## B. NC Excise Tax — G.S. 105-228.30

### B.1 Key concepts

- **G.S. 105-228.30 requires the transferor to pay the tax to the register of deeds before recording
  the conveyance.**
- **Formerly called revenue stamps or deed transfer tax.**

### B.2 The rate

**$1.00 on each $500 (or fractional part) of the consideration or value of the interest conveyed.**

### B.3 Calculations *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Excise tax **always rounds up to a full dollar amount** in NC;
**there are no cents**."*

> Excise tax = **round UP** (sales price ÷ 500) × $1.00

*Worked.* Sales price **$284,000.** 284,000 ÷ 500 = **568** exactly. 568 × $1.00 = **$568.00.**

*Worked, with a remainder.* Sales price **$287,300.** 287,300 ÷ 500 = **574.6**. The rule is **or
portion thereof**, so round **up** to **575**. 575 × $1.00 = **$575.00.**

*Worked again.* Sales price **$310,100.** 310,100 ÷ 500 = 620.2 → **621** → **$621.00.**

chunks.heading: Required four-scenario practice
chunks.excerpt:
**Never round down and never carry cents.** A price $1 above a multiple of $500 adds a whole dollar of
excise tax.

#### Required four-scenario practice

Use the statutory base stated in each problem. City/county location and financing facts may be
irrelevant to the State excise-tax calculation, which is exactly why the Commission requires varied
facts.

| Scenario | Given consideration or value | Other facts | Excise tax |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Inside city limits | $284,000 | Municipal property-tax rate also supplied | $568 |
| County only | $310,000 | No municipal property-tax rate | $620 |
| Odd amount | $287,300 | No other adjustment | $575 |
| Concession and financing | $400,000 | $10,000 seller credit; $320,000 loan; instrument still states $400,000 consideration/value | $800 |

The final scenario does not establish how an unstated or disputed concession affects taxable
consideration. If the instrument, closing instructions and transaction figures do not establish the
statutory base consistently, the broker sends the question to the closing attorney and register of
deeds rather than inventing a number.

### B.4 Local transfer tax

**Possible in some North Carolina counties.** **This course states no county, rate or applicability**,
because no such provision was read from primary text for this project. **Route it to the closing
attorney and the county.**

---

## C. Homeowner's (Hazard) Property Insurance Basics *(Level 1 — these subtopics)*

### C.1 Definitions

**Insurance. Insured. Insurer. Premium. Condition. Endorsement (rider). Exclusion. Property (casualty)
insurance. Liability insurance.**

Those nine are italicised terms in the Syllabus, which means — from its own legend — **students should
know the definitions.**

### C.2 Package insurance

chunks.heading: C.3 Coinsurance clause
chunks.excerpt:
**A combination of property and liability coverage** — for example **HO-3** — and its typical coverage.

### C.3 Coinsurance clause

A provision requiring the insured to carry coverage of at least a stated proportion of value, failing
which a loss is only partly paid.

### C.4 Specialized policies

- **HO-3** — homeowner's coverage.
- **HO-4** — renter's coverage.
- **HO-6** — condominium coverage.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Buyer should make sure insurance is **appropriate for property type
and use**."*

A buyer who buys a condominium and insures it as a house, or who rents out a property insured as an
owner-occupied residence, has coverage that may not respond.

---

## D. Flood Insurance

- **Flood coverage is generally obtained separately; a broker must never promise coverage from the
  label of a homeowner policy. Read the actual policy with the insurer.**
- **The National Flood Insurance Program is administered by FEMA and delivered through private
  insurance companies.**
- Its **purpose**, and **designated or special FEMA flood hazard zones**.

**Instructor Note, transcribed — and it is a genuinely common misunderstanding:**

> *"The **100-year flood plain** refers to a flood having a **1% chance of equalling or exceeding the
> map elevation any given year**, not a flood that occurs only every 100 years."*

Say that to a buyer in those words. A property in a 100-year flood plain does not flood once a century;
it carries a one percent annual probability, which over a thirty-year loan is a materially different
proposition.

---

## E. Insurance Issues

### E.1 Insurability

- **High insurance claim history.**
- **Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (C.L.U.E.)** — the claims database insurers consult.

chunks.heading: E.2 Residential sales transaction concerns
chunks.excerpt:
**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Consumers are entitled to a **free copy of their C.L.U.E. report**
per the **Fair Credit Reporting Act**."* The CFPB's current company listing makes the operational rule
more precise: LexisNexis C.L.U.E. provides one free report every 12 months on request.

The consequence a buyer needs: **a property's claims history can affect whether and at what price it can
be insured**, independently of its condition today — and insurability is a financing question, because a
lender will not close without a bound policy.

### E.2 Residential sales transaction concerns

**Unoccupied Building Exclusion.** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Definition of unoccupied varies
widely; **read policy for specific parameters** for a particular property."*

**Early or late possession by the parties** — which changes who is occupying and therefore whether the
exclusion bites.

**Keep insurance in place until recordation/closing; refer to the "Risk of Loss" provision in the sales
contract.**

### E.3 Broker's responsibility *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

**This is the Level 3 subtopic of the whole insurance topic, and it is a list of five affirmative
duties. Transcribed:**

chunks.heading: F. Federal Income Taxation of Home Ownership *(Level 1 except as noted)*
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Advise the seller client about the importance of having and maintaining appropriate insurance
   coverage throughout the listing and the transfer of title/closing.**
2. **A listing agent should advise an absentee seller to verify continued insurance coverage of the
   unoccupied listed property.**
3. **Be alert for red flags** — for example, nearby water sources possibly requiring flood insurance.
4. **Disclose the location of any part of the property in a FEMA special flood zone as a material
   fact.**
5. **A buyer client should be advised to check availability and cost of insurance as part of buyer due
   diligence.**

**Item 4 is a disclosure duty, not a courtesy.** Any part of the property in a FEMA special flood zone
is **a material fact that must be disclosed.**

**Item 2 pairs with the unoccupied building exclusion at E.2**, and together they describe a real and
common failure: a vacant listing whose owner has moved away, whose policy has quietly stopped
responding, and whose agent never raised it.

---

## F. Federal Income Taxation of Home Ownership *(Level 1 except as noted)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed — read it before the substance:**

> *"Licensees should **never attempt to provide tax advice** to clients or customers unless they possess
> special knowledge and expertise in the tax field that qualifies them to provide such advice. **The
> limited instruction provided in this course in no way qualifies the student to provide tax advice**
> and is merely intended to enable agents to **recognize situations where a consumer might benefit from
> professional tax advice** so that the agent might then **refer the consumer to a qualified tax
> accountant or attorney**."*

chunks.heading: F.1 Potential federal income-tax deductions for owners of personal residences
chunks.excerpt:
**That is the purpose of everything in Part F: recognition and referral. Nothing else.**

### F.1 Potential federal income-tax deductions for owners of personal residences

The syllabus identifies real property taxes, mortgage interest and some points as concepts students
must recognize. It does **not** make them automatically deductible. Itemization, acquisition date,
debt purpose, dollar limits, property use and current federal law all matter. A broker identifies a
possible tax question and refers it; the broker does not calculate or promise a deduction.

### F.2 Taxation of capital gain on sale of a principal residence *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Concepts are testable, but **there are no math calculations on this
topic**."*

**Eligible property**, and the definitions:

- **Basis** and **adjusted basis.**
- **Capital improvement** — with the Commission's note: *"**Maintenance is not a capital
  improvement.**"*
- **Amount realized.**
- **Gain** and **loss.**

**Current 26 U.S.C. §121 recognition rules:**

- The general maximum exclusion is **$250,000**; qualifying spouses filing jointly may receive a
  **$500,000** maximum under the joint-return requirements.
- During the five-year period ending on the sale, the taxpayer generally must have **owned and used**
  the property as a principal residence for periods aggregating at least two years.
- The general exclusion is unavailable when the taxpayer used the exclusion for another sale during
  the two-year period ending on the current sale.

chunks.heading: F.3 Special tax treatment for some residential transactions
chunks.excerpt:
Those are recognition rules, not a tax opinion. Section 121 contains additional joint-return rules,
partial-exclusion provisions, nonqualified-use treatment and other exceptions. Every taxpayer's
eligibility and amount go to a qualified tax accountant or attorney.

### F.3 Special tax treatment for some residential transactions

Each at **basic concept** level only:

- **Installment sales** — or **contract for deed** in North Carolina.
- **Like-Kind or 1031 Tax-Deferred Exchange.**
- **Vacation homes** — the basic rule for owner use.
- **Office in home.**

**Recognise these situations and refer them.** A seller who mentions a 1031 exchange has a timetable
that will control the transaction, and the licensee's contribution is to get them to their tax adviser
**before** an offer is accepted rather than after.

---

## Required Activities in this section

**The Syllabus prescribes no Required Activity for Section IV.** The Level 3 subtopics — tax
calculations, excise tax calculations, the broker's insurance responsibilities and capital gain — carry
Level 3's own requirement that students **complete practical work assignments** applying the material.
**The worked calculations above and this module's applied item are that work.**

## Module NC-04 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-04

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-04
chunks.excerpt:
Drawn from **Section IV** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Reconciled on 2026-09-07 against current official G.S. 105-274,
105-283 through 105-287, 105-307, 105-355, 105-356, 105-360, 105-228.30 and 159-13; current 26 U.S.C.
§121; FEMA's one-percent-annual-chance definition; and the CFPB's C.L.U.E. listing. The current statute
supersedes the syllabus's obsolete fourth-year-horizontal-adjustment sentence.

**Not read, and therefore not stated as a rule in this module:** the full federal mortgage-interest,
property-tax, points, installment-sale, home-office or §1031 provisions; the text of the Fair Credit
Reporting Act and National Flood Insurance Act; any insurance policy form; and any county's local
transfer tax. **Every county or municipal rate used in a worked calculation is invented for arithmetic
and is not a North Carolina rate for any jurisdiction.** No local exemption, deduction limit, insurance
coverage term or local transfer-tax rate is stated.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-05

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-05
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-05

## Section V · Property Disclosures & Environmental Issues

**Commission Syllabus section:** V — Property Disclosures & Environmental Issues
**Instructional Level:** **1** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* **Part A, Disclosure of Property Conditions by Real Estate Brokers, is
Level 3** — the highest level the Commission assigns, and the practical heart of the section. **Lead is
Level 2.**
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 8 items.**
**Instructional hours:** **4.0**, allocated within the Commission's recommended 6.0 hours for the
Property Disclosures subject area; the balance sits in Module NC-15 with the North Carolina disclosure
statutes.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. **State the broker's verification and recognition responsibilities on land use, and apply them to a
   red-flag fact pattern.** *(Level 3)*
2. State the rule about environmental hazards and material facts. *(Level 3)*
3. Explain owner liability for cleanup of hazardous waste caused by a previous owner. *(Level 3)*
4. State the broker's duty on underground storage tanks. *(Level 3)*
5. Explain what the presence of a radon mitigation system requires of a broker. *(Level 3)*
6. State the effect of an "as is" sale on a broker's disclosure responsibilities. *(Level 3)*
7. Describe lead-based paint law and the broker's own legal duty under it. *(Level 2)*
8. Describe asbestos, radon, toxic mould and the miscellaneous hazards. *(Level 1)*
9. Describe CERCLA, the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act. *(Level 1)*

---

chunks.heading: A. Disclosure of Property Conditions by Real Estate Brokers *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
## A. Disclosure of Property Conditions by Real Estate Brokers *(Level 3)*

### A.1 Responsibilities for verification of land use and recognition of potential land use problems

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Recognizing and taking appropriate action with regard to potential
problems with **zoning and restrictive covenants** is particularly important."*

**When a property is or might be subject to zoning and/or covenants, the broker must advise the
consumer that:**

1. **Ordinances or covenants could affect the consumer's use and enjoyment of the property**;
2. **property owners may be subject to owners' association dues and assessments**; and
3. **careful review of any covenants and owners' association governing documents is recommended prior
   to signing any offer.**

**Read item 3.** *Prior to signing any offer.* Not during due diligence, not before closing —
**before the offer is signed.**

**And the broker must:**

- **Avoid any misrepresentation about a property's zoning or permitted land uses.**
- **Recognize "red flag" situations.**
- **Recognize patent signs of flooding on a property, or when a property's location may make it
  susceptible to flooding.**
- **Disclose planned major highway or public transportation changes in the area as a material fact.**

**That last one is broader than new licensees expect.** A planned highway or transit change **in the
area** — not on the property — is a **material fact** that must be disclosed.

Note also how it pairs with Module NC-03: **the ability to access an abutting public highway or street
is itself a material fact**, and access may be restricted or forbidden by the state or the
municipality.

### A.2 Environmental hazards are material facts

**Transcribed:**

chunks.heading: A.3 Liability for cleanup
chunks.excerpt:
> *"The presence on a property of **any of the environmental hazards covered in this Section is a
> material fact that must be disclosed to all transactional parties**."*

**All of them. To all transactional parties.** Not only to a client, and not only on request.

That Syllabus instruction now has a current-law anchor. **G.S. 93A-6(a)(1)** makes willful or negligent
misrepresentation or omission of a material fact a disciplinary ground. For residential property
subject to Chapter 47E, **21 NCAC 58A .0114(c)** separately requires a broker representing an owner or
purchaser to disclose to the purchaser material facts the broker knows or reasonably should know. The
owner's disclosure statement does **not** replace the broker's duty. The rule defines a material fact by
whether a reasonable person would recognize it as relevant to the purchase decision and whether
suppression could reasonably change that decision.

Keep the two layers separate: the **broker's independent license-law duty** and the **owner's statutory
disclosure statement** are not the same duty and do not always have the same coverage or options.

### A.3 Liability for cleanup

**Transcribed:** *"**Owner of a property with hazardous waste may be liable for cleanup, even if caused
by a previous owner.**"*

That is the principle behind CERCLA at Part B.2, and it is why an environmental site assessment exists
as a buyer's due diligence step rather than a formality.

### A.4 Underground storage tanks

**Transcribed, and this is a duty rather than a suggestion:**

> *"Any broker who **knows of any current or abandoned USTs** on the property **must disclose to all
> prospective purchasers or tenants**."*

chunks.heading: A.5 The radon mitigation system
chunks.excerpt:
> *"**Buyer agent should strongly encourage buyer to hire an expert** to inspect any tanks and conduct
> a **soil contamination test**."*

**Current or abandoned.** An abandoned tank is still a disclosure obligation, and an abandoned tank is
precisely the one nobody has thought about for thirty years.

### A.5 The radon mitigation system

**Transcribed, and it is the most quietly demanding sentence in the section:**

> *"The **mere presence of a radon mitigation system** in a property **elevates the broker's
> responsibility to discover and disclose the reason behind that presence**."*

**Not merely to disclose the system — to DISCOVER the reason for it.** A pipe and a fan on the side of
a house is a fact that raises a question, and the Commission places the obligation to pursue that
question on the broker.

The practical method: ask the seller, in writing; ask for the test results that prompted the
installation and the post-mitigation results if any; and disclose what is learned — and disclose that
the reason could not be established if it cannot be.

### A.6 The "as is" sale

**Transcribed:**

> *"**Broker's disclosure responsibilities under Real Estate License Law not affected by "as is"
> status.**"*

**"As is" changes the seller's repair obligations. It changes nothing about yours.** A licensee who
believes an "as is" listing relieves them of disclosing a known material fact has misunderstood whose
obligation it is.

---

## B. Environmental Issues in Real Estate

### B.1 Lead *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*

chunks.heading: B.1 Lead *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Review the **Lead-Based Paint or Lead-Based
> Paint Hazard Addendum, NCAR Form 2A9-T**."*
>
> **This activity must be completed.** **This project has not obtained NCAR Form 2A9-T, and no document
> in this build reproduces, describes or paraphrases it.** Obtaining the current form and conducting
> this review is a **submission gate** for this module.

**Current federal framework.** Congress enacted the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act
in 1992. The disclosure regulation did **not** take effect in 1992: 40 CFR 745.102 phased it in during
1996. The rule applies to covered sales and leases of **target housing**, generally housing constructed
before 1978. The definition excludes zero-bedroom dwellings and housing for older persons or persons
with disabilities unless a child under six resides or is expected to reside there. Section 745.101 also
excludes foreclosure sales, qualifying lead-free leases, short leases of 100 days or less with no renewal
or extension, and specified renewals with no new information. Apply the exact rule to the transaction;
do not turn “pre-1978” into an absolute without checking the exclusions.

chunks.heading: B.1 Lead *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
Before the purchaser or lessee is obligated under a covered contract, the seller or lessor must provide
the EPA-approved pamphlet, disclose known lead-based paint and known hazards, and provide available
records and reports. A covered purchaser must receive a **10-day opportunity** for a risk assessment or
inspection unless the parties agree in writing to a different period; the purchaser may waive the
opportunity in writing. The sales contract and covered lease carry the required warning,
acknowledgments, certifications, signatures and dates. Sellers and their agents retain the completed
sales attachment for at least **three years from completion of the sale**; lessors and their agents retain
the lease disclosure record for at least **three years from commencement of the lease term**.

The regulation expressly says the disclosure rule creates **no positive obligation to test or reduce**
lead. It requires disclosure of what is known, available records, the required pamphlet and opportunity,
not a promise that a building is lead-free.

**And the broker's own duty, transcribed — this is the tested point:**

> *"**Brokers have legal duty to ensure compliance with the lead paint disclosure requirements**
> — informing seller/lessor of their obligations under these rules; **either ensure that seller/lessor
> has performed all activities required by the rules OR broker must personally ensure compliance**."*

chunks.heading: B.2 Asbestos *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Read that.** Current 40 CFR 745.115 confirms the same structure: a seller's or lessor's agent must
inform the principal of the obligations and either ensure the principal performs every required activity
or personally ensure compliance. If the agent performs that notice duty, the agent is not liable for a
seller's or lessor's lead information that was not disclosed to the agent. That protection does not excuse
the other compliance steps.

**North Carolina work rules are a separate system.** Chapter 130A, Article 19A requires certification
for specified inspection, risk-assessment and abatement work in target housing and child-occupied
facilities, and a permit for abatement. G.S. 130A-453.02(b) also says the Article does **not** itself
require inspection, risk assessment or abatement in every situation. Current G.S. 130A-22(b3), not the
older figure in the Syllabus, allows up to **$5,000 for each day a covered Article 19A violation
continues** and excludes a person not required to be certified. Do not quote the Syllabus's stale $750
state or $32,500 federal figures as current law.

### B.2 Asbestos *(Level 1)*

- **Friable** — the operative concept.
- **Serious health risk** for various respiratory diseases and for **lung and stomach cancer**.
- **Response choices can include management in place, repair, encapsulation or removal**, depending on
  condition, disturbance and governing requirements.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"The **mere presence of asbestos is not a health hazard unless it is
friable**."*

chunks.heading: B.3 Radon *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
Current EPA guidance is more precise: material in good condition and left undisturbed is **unlikely** to
present a health risk; risk arises when damage or disturbance releases fibers that can be inhaled.
Renovation, demolition, sanding, cutting or other disturbance can change the risk. A broker does not
sample or decide the response. Route the consumer to a trained asbestos professional.

North Carolina uses **accreditation**, not the blanket phrase “state-licensed asbestos abatement
contractor.” The DHHS Asbestos Hazard Management Program accredits people performing covered
inspection, design and removal work and issues permits for regulated removal projects. Coverage,
thresholds, residence exceptions and county-specific rules are fact-dependent, so do not promise that
every residential job needs the same permit or personnel.

### B.3 Radon *(Level 1)*

- **A health risk as one of the leading causes of lung cancer.**
- The Syllabus treats the actionable-level condition as a material fact. Current EPA guidance says to
  fix a home at **4 pCi/L or more** and to consider fixing between **2 and below 4 pCi/L** because there
  is no known safe exposure level.

The exact unit is **picocuries per liter of air (pCi/L)**. Do not say “over 4.0”; EPA's recommendation
includes a result of exactly 4.0. A broker reports the result, date and source and routes testing and
mitigation questions to a qualified radon professional.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Do-it-yourself radon tests are available; **professional testing is
generally more accurate**."*

**Remediation through a mitigation system that uses ventilation** — which connects back to A.5: a
mitigation system on a house means somebody once had a result worth mitigating.

### B.4 Toxic mould *(Level 1)*

chunks.heading: B.5 Miscellaneous potential issues *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
Characteristics and where found; **allergic reaction, respiratory and sinus problems**; **potential
homeowner's insurance issues**; remediation.

The insurance point matters commercially: a mould claim history can affect insurability, which
Module NC-04 established is a financing question.

### B.5 Miscellaneous potential issues *(Level 1)*

**Groundwater contamination. Underground storage tanks. Waste disposal sites. Brownfields.**

### B.6 The Environmental Protection Agency *(Level 1)*

**CERCLA** — the **Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act**:

- **also known as the Superfund**;
- supports investigation and cleanup of hazardous-substance sites and can impose strict, retroactive,
  and in some circumstances joint-and-several liability on responsible parties, including a current owner
  or operator;
- also contains landowner protections for qualifying bona fide prospective purchasers, contiguous
  property owners and innocent landowners. Protection is not automatic. EPA identifies **All Appropriate
  Inquiries before acquisition** and continuing obligations as elements of the applicable defenses.

A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment may be used to perform All Appropriate Inquiries under current
EPA-recognized standards. It is not a guarantee that no contamination exists and it is not a broker's
inspection. Whether a Phase II investigation is warranted is an environmental professional's conclusion.

**The Clean Air Act:**

- **establishes and enforces air quality standards**;
- includes separate programs for ozone-depleting substances and refrigerants. Do not infer an appliance
  owner's exact duty without checking the current equipment, substance and service rule.

**The Clean Water Act:**

chunks.heading: The rule that governs the whole section
chunks.excerpt:
- **regulates pollutant discharges into water**;
- **sets water quality standards**;
- can regulate discharges of dredged or fill material to jurisdictional waters, including some wetlands.
  Whether a feature is jurisdictional and whether a permit or exception applies are legal and technical
  questions, not conclusions a broker should make from appearance alone.

---

## The rule that governs the whole section

**Recognise, disclose, route.** The Commission's own text places three affirmative obligations on the
broker in this section — **discover the reason for a radon mitigation system**, **disclose known current
or abandoned USTs**, and **ensure lead disclosure compliance personally if the seller has not** — and
beyond those, **a licensee assesses no environmental condition.**

For an underground tank, separate the broker's disclosure duty from tank regulation. NC DEQ applies
different rules to regulated commercial systems and some non-regulated farm or residential systems;
ownership-change, release and closure obligations depend on the system and facts. Disclose what is
known and route status, records, testing and cleanup to DEQ and qualified professionals.

Testing is by a qualified tester. Remediation is by a qualified contractor, and for asbestos by a
**state-licensed abatement contractor**. Interpretation of a result is not a licensee's work, and
neither is reassurance about one.

---

## Required Activities in this section

**One, and it is a submission gate:** review of the **Lead-Based Paint or Lead-Based Paint Hazard
Addendum, NCAR Form 2A9-T**, which this project has not obtained.

chunks.heading: Module NC-05 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Part A's **Level 3** assignment separately requires students to **complete practical work assignments**
applying the disclosure responsibilities to common fact situations. This module's applied item and the
red-flag material at A.1 and A.5 are that work.

## Module NC-05 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-05

Drawn from **Section V** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20, and reconciled on 2026-09-07 to G.S. 93A-6(a)(1), current 21 NCAC 58A
.0114(c), 42 U.S.C. §4852d, 40 CFR part 745 subpart F, HUD/EPA lead guidance, G.S. Chapter 130A
Article 19A and §130A-22(b3), and current EPA, NC DHHS and NC DEQ guidance for radon, asbestos,
CERCLA, All Appropriate Inquiries, air, water and underground tanks.

**Still not obtained:** **NCAR Form 2A9-T** — the Commission's specific Required Activity and a
submission gate. This module does not reproduce or imply review of that proprietary form. The official

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-06

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-06
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-06

## Section VI · Forms of Ownership, Transfer & Recording of Title

**Commission Syllabus section:** VI — Forms of Ownership, Transfer & Recording of Title
**Instructional Level:** **2** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* **Freehold estates, landlord/tenant definitions, the bundle of rights,
cooperative ownership, trusts, the doctrine of prior appropriation, support rights, writ of attachment
and methods of transferring title are Level 1.** **Leasehold estates are Level 2.** **Percentage leases
are Level 3.**
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 8 items.**
**Instructional hours:** **6.0**, matching the Commission's recommended emphasis for Property Ownership
Types and Transfers.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Estates in Real Property
chunks.excerpt:
1. Classify freehold estates and identify a defeasible fee from its granting language. *(Level 1)*
2. Explain a life estate, estovers, and the remainder/reversion distinction.
3. Recite the five rights in the bundle. *(Level 1)*
4. Classify the four leasehold estates by **how each ends**. *(Level 2)*
5. Distinguish privity of estate from privity of contract. *(Level 1)*
6. Compute rent under a percentage lease. *(Level 3)*
7. Distinguish severalty, tenancy in common, joint tenancy and tenancy by the entirety — and state the
   **North Carolina** rule on survivorship.
8. Distinguish condominium, cooperative and time share ownership.
9. Describe appurtenant rights, including water rights and boundary shifts.
10. Classify liens as specific or general and state the lien priority rules and their exceptions.
11. Describe special assessments and lis pendens.
12. Name the methods of transferring title. *(Level 1)*
13. State the essential elements of a valid deed and explain why recordation is not one of them.
14. Distinguish general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, bargain-and-sale, and special-purpose
    deeds by the warranties and authority actually shown in the instrument.

---

## A. Estates in Real Property

### A.1 Freehold estates *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

**Freehold estates last for an indeterminable period of time.**

**Estates of inheritance** — the owner can determine who inherits:

chunks.heading: A.2 The bundle of legal rights *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
- **Fee Simple Estate (Fee Simple Absolute).**
- **Defeasible Fee (Qualified) Estates:**
  - **Fee Simple Determinable** — the Syllabus also calls it *Fee Simple to a Condition Precedent*.
  - **Fee Simple Conditional** — *Fee Simple to a Condition Subsequent*.
- **Estate for Life of Another (pur autre vie)** — **Instructor Note:** *"Based on life of named third
  party, the measuring life."*

**Estates not of inheritance — life estates:**

- **Estate for Tenant's Own Life (Conventional Life Estate)**, with:
  - the **life tenant** — their **rights and restrictions**, and **estovers**, the life tenant's right
    to take timber for necessary repairs and fuel; and
  - the **remainderman**.
- **Marital life estates.**
- **Remainder versus reversionary interest** — to a third party, or back to the grantor.
- **Homestead.**

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide real world examples of each type of
> estate. Make note that **the difference between the different leasehold estates is how they end**."*

### A.2 The bundle of legal rights *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

The Commission states five, and states them in its own words:

- **Right to possession** — to occupy.
- **Right to control** — of the property and legal profits.
- **Right of enjoyment** — to use in any legal manner **without interference from others claiming a
  superior title**.
- **Right of exclusion** — to restrict access.
- **Right of disposition** — to transfer ownership or interests, **including the right to
  encumber/mortgage**.

### A.3 Estates in landlord/tenant *(Level 1 except as noted)*

**Definitions:** **landlord (lessor)**; **tenant (lessee)**; **lease**; **privity of estate**;
**privity of contract**.

chunks.heading: A.4 Leasehold (nonfreehold) estates *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
The last two are worth separating now, because assignment and sublease at A.5 turn on them: **privity of
estate** is the relationship arising from the interest in the land; **privity of contract** is the
relationship arising from the promises.

### A.4 Leasehold (nonfreehold) estates *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*

**And the Required Activity above tells you the organising principle: the difference between them is
HOW THEY END.**

- **Tenancy (or estate) for years.** Definite beginning, definite end. **Ends on its own terms — no
  notice required.**
- **Tenancy (or estate) from period to period.** **Instructor Note:** *"Also known as periodic
  tenancies, week-to-week, month-to-month."* **Ends by proper notice.**
- **Tenancy (or estate) at will.** **Ends at the will of either party.**
- **Tenancy (or estate) at sufferance.** **Instructor Note:** *"**Unlike trespassing, this estate began
  legally.**"* A holdover — possession that started lawfully and outlived its right.

**North Carolina periodic-tenancy notice rule.** Current G.S. 42-14 sets the statutory minimum notice
to quit at **one month before the end of the current rental year** for a year-to-year tenancy,
**seven days** for month-to-month, and **two days** for week-to-week. Rental of only a manufactured-home
space has a separate **60-day** minimum before the end of the current rental period. These are default
statutory rules for the tenancies the section names; the lease, another applicable statute, and counsel
still control a particular termination or eviction.

### A.5 Leases

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Explain real world use of each type of
> lease."*

**Types of leases:**

chunks.heading: A.5 Leases
chunks.excerpt:
- **Fixed rental (flat or gross) lease.**
- **Percentage lease** *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*.
- **Other lease types** *(Level 1)*: **net lease**; **graduated (step-up) lease**; **index lease**;
  **full service lease**; **ground lease**.

**Percentage lease — Level 3, so worked:**

A percentage lease charges a base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's sales above a **breakpoint**.

*Worked.* Base rent **$3,600 per month**. Percentage rent **5% of gross sales over a natural breakpoint**
of **$864,000 per year**. Annual sales are **$1,180,000**.

Base rent: 3,600 × 12 = **$43,200**.
Sales above the breakpoint: 1,180,000 − 864,000 = **$316,000**.
Percentage rent: 316,000 × 0.05 = **$15,800**.
**Total annual rent = 43,200 + 15,800 = $59,000.**

*(Check the natural breakpoint: base rent ÷ percentage = 43,200 ÷ 0.05 = $864,000. A "natural"
breakpoint is the sales figure at which the percentage rent alone would equal the base rent.)*

**Essential lease provisions.** **Instructor Note:** *"Same as for any contract."*

**Other common provisions — the tenant's use of the premises. Instructor Note, transcribed:**

> *"Lessee may make **any legal use** of the property **unless there are use restrictions in the
> lease**. Tenant has **Implied Covenant of Quiet Enjoyment**; **lessor has no right to enter premises
> during lease term unless granted in the lease**."*

The last clause is the Syllabus's general lease instruction, not a complete North Carolina entry code.
Do not convert it into an absolute answer for emergencies, repairs, court process, or another statute.
For an actual property, read the lease and current law and obtain legal advice where the right of entry
is disputed.

chunks.heading: B. Ownership, Interests, and Rights in Real Property
chunks.excerpt:
**Assignments and subleases:** **assignment**; **sublease**; **assignee versus assignor**;
**novation**; **renewal and termination**. And two stated rules:

- **"Lessee has no implied right to renew the lease."**
- **"Automatic renewal clause can be included in the lease terms."**

---

## B. Ownership, Interests, and Rights in Real Property

### B.1 Severalty (sole) ownership

**Instructor Note:** *"Sole owner can be an individual person **or a single business entity**."*

Note that "severalty" means sole ownership, despite sounding like the opposite — a reliable examination
item.

### B.2 Concurrent (joint) ownership

**Tenancy in common:**

- **Undivided fractional interest; may be unequal.**
- **Unity of possession.**
- **A co-owner may dispose of their individual interest without the permission of the co-tenants.**
- **Upon death, the undivided interest passes to the heirs; NO right of survivorship.**

**Joint tenancy:**

chunks.heading: B.2 Concurrent (joint) ownership
chunks.excerpt:
- **Tenancy in common is the default** when a conveyance leaves two or more people owning property.
- Under current G.S. 41-71, the instrument creates a **joint tenancy with right of survivorship** when
  it expresses that intent. The statute recognizes several phrases, including “joint tenants,” “joint
  tenancy,” and “with right of survivorship,” unless the instrument provides otherwise.
- Under G.S. 41-72, interests are **equal unless the instrument provides otherwise**. North Carolina
  therefore permits an expressly stated unequal percentage; the old “four equal unities” mnemonic is
  not a safe statement of current North Carolina law.
- G.S. 41-73 lists collective and unilateral termination events, including specified conveyances or
  instruments and a partition petition. A unilateral self-conveyance that expresses termination must
  be recorded before the joint tenant's death.

**North Carolina's transaction point:** survivorship is not supplied merely because multiple people
take title. The conveyance must create it under G.S. 41-71. The statute, amended in 2025, now states
which wording expresses that intent; the broker still routes drafting and title advice to the closing
attorney.

**Which is emphatically not a licensee's judgment to make.** How a buyer takes title is a legal and tax
question for counsel. **What a licensee must do is know that the question exists, raise it early, and
route it** — and never assure a buying couple that "joint tenancy means the survivor gets it."

**Tenancy by the entirety:**

chunks.heading: B.3 Common interest community (hybrid) ownership
chunks.excerpt:
- **Available to two people legally married to each other.**
- Under G.S. 41-56, a conveyance to spouses creates the estate **unless the conveyance expresses a
  contrary intention**.
- **Instructor Note:** *"Other types of ownership **do not automatically convert** to tenancy by the
  entirety if property owners marry each other later."* Current G.S. 41-82(c) confirms that result for
  cotenants who later marry unless a separate instrument changes the estate.
- **Equal undivided interest.**
- **Survivorship while the estate remains in place.** At death, G.S. 41-64 gives the survivor title and
  leaves no descendable share in the deceased spouse, subject to the statute's slayer exception.
- **Neither spouse may unilaterally sell, lease, mortgage, transfer, convey, or encumber the estate.**
  G.S. 41-58 generally requires the written joinder of the other spouse, subject to its listed statutory
  exceptions.
- **It can be terminated.** G.S. 41-63 lists joint sale, voluntary partition, specified involuntary
  transfers, conveyance from one spouse to the other, absolute divorce, and forfeiture; death is treated
  separately in G.S. 41-64. “Cannot be waived” must not be taught as though spouses can never end it.

**The practical consequences:** a will cannot transfer the deceased spouse's former share while the
estate survives to death, and one spouse ordinarily cannot convey or encumber the estate alone. A
broker verifies title and signatories with the closing attorney rather than drafting an ownership result.

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide an assessment to determine if student
> can **differentiate between these types of hybrid ownership**."*

### B.3 Common interest community (hybrid) ownership

chunks.heading: B.3 Common interest community (hybrid) ownership
chunks.excerpt:
**General concepts.** Managed by owner associations — an **HOA** or **POA** — which **enforce rules
regarding operation and use**, **maintain, repair and clean common areas**, **maintain insurance**, and
take on **additional responsibilities by agreement**. **Governed by covenants and general statutes.**
**May be residential, commercial, industrial or mixed-use.**

**Condominium ownership:**

- **Governed in North Carolina by Chapter 47C** for condominiums created under that Act, with older or
  specially situated projects requiring document and counsel review.
- A unit is real estate whose boundaries are fixed by the declaration. “Title to airspace” is a useful
  classroom picture, but it is not a substitute for those recorded boundaries.
- The unit owner also owns the unit's allocated undivided interest in the common elements. Chapter 47C
  generally prevents partition of the common elements while the condominium exists and recognizes
  limited common elements allocated for fewer than all units.
- For a sale requiring a **public offering statement** under G.S. 47C-4-102(c), G.S. 47C-4-108 gives
  the purchaser an absolute **seven-calendar-day** cancellation period following execution and bars
  conveyance during that period. This is not correctly summarized as “every new condo.”
- For an ordinary resale not requiring a public offering statement and not exempt under
  G.S. 47C-4-101(b), G.S. 47C-4-109 requires the unit owner to provide, before conveyance, a statement
  of monthly common expenses and other owner fees. That section supplies **no statutory cancellation
  right**; any contractual right must be read from the actual contract.
- **Instructor Note:** *"Nationally, a **townhouse is generally a multi-story condo**."*

**Cooperative ownership** *(Level 1)*:

chunks.heading: B.4 Trusts *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
- **Title to land and building held by a corporation.**
- **The tenant purchases corporate stock shares — personal property** — with a **proprietary lease**
  and **no individual deed for units**.

**Time share ownership:**

- **Instructor Note:** *"Also called vacation lease, prepaid hotel reservation, club membership,
  limited partnership, vacation bond."*
- **Allows multiple parties to buy an interest in the same real estate.**
- **The interest may be leasehold or deeded ownership.**
- **Buyers receive the right to occupy for a specific time period.**

**Townhouse is a physical description, not an ownership form.** A townhouse may be a condominium,
planned community, or another structure. Chapter 47C or 47F applies from the recorded legal regime and
statutory coverage, not from the building's appearance. *(North Carolina's current Timeshare Act and
Rules 58B .0400-.0600 are applied in Module NC-15.)*

### B.4 Trusts *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed, and it is a direction rather than a description:**

> *"**Legal advice is strongly recommended before broker handles a transaction involving property owned
> by a trust.**"*

A **fiduciary arrangement**: a **third party trustee holds assets on behalf of a beneficiary**; the
**trust agreement sets the parameters of the trustee's authority**; it **may allow assets to pass
outside of probate**.

**And the operative practice rule, transcribed:** *"**Brokers should deal with the trustee vs. the
beneficiary** regarding disposition of real estate."*

### B.5 Appurtenant rights (appurtenances)

**Subsurface rights. Air rights.**

chunks.heading: B.6 Liens
chunks.excerpt:
**Water rights:** **riparian rights**; **littoral rights**; **foreshore**; **boundary shifts due to
accretion, reliction, erosion, or avulsion**; and the **Doctrine of Prior Appropriation** *(Level 1)*.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**Water rights cannot be retained when the property title is
transferred.**"*

**Support rights** *(Level 1)*: **the right to lateral support** and **the right to subjacent support**.

**The benefit of any appurtenant easement**, and **the benefit of any protective (restrictive)
covenants** — both of which run to the new owner.

### B.6 Liens

**Specific liens** — attaching to an identified parcel:

- **Mortgages (deeds of trust).**
- **Real estate tax and assessment liens.**
- **Mechanics' liens (materialman's lien).**

**General liens** — attaching to the debtor's property generally:

- **Judgment liens.**
- **Personal property tax liens.**
- **State tax liens.**
- **Federal tax liens.**

**Lien priority:**

- The general rule is **order of recordation**.
- **Exceptions to the "pure race system":**
  - **Real property and special assessment liens hold superior priority.**
  - **A perfected claim of lien on real property relates back to the claimant's first furnishing of
    labor or materials at the site** under G.S. 44A-10 and -11.
  - **Voluntary subordination of a superior lien.**

chunks.heading: B.7 Special assessments
chunks.excerpt:
The relation-back point matters, but it does **not** mean every contractor automatically has an
enforceable first-day lien. The statutory service, filing, and enforcement steps still control.
G.S. 44A-12 permits filing no later than **120 days after the claimant's last furnishing**, and
G.S. 44A-13 sets a separate **180-day** outside limit to commence enforcement. Recent or ongoing
construction is therefore a listing and closing question routed to the closing attorney.

**Writ of attachment** *(Level 1)*.

### B.7 Special assessments

**Examples. Levied by local municipalities. Special priority** — see the priority exceptions above.

### B.8 Lis pendens

**Instructor Note:** *"This is **notice of an active lawsuit that may affect title**."*

---

## C. Methods of Transferring Title *(Level 1)*

1. **By descent.** **Instructor Note:** *"When owner dies with no will (intestate), state laws
   regarding **Intestate Succession** will rule **[NCGS Chapter 29]**."*
2. **By will (testate).** **Instructor Note:** *"Remember that **a will cannot override the survivorship
   clause in a deed**."*
3. **By voluntary alienation (by deed).**
4. **By involuntary alienation:** **lien foreclosure sale**; **adverse possession**; **escheat**;
   **eminent domain**.

**The note on wills matters and it connects to B.2.** Tenancy by the entirety's survivorship **overrides
