a will**, and a survivorship clause in a deed is not defeated by a testamentary gift.

chunks.heading: D. Deeds
chunks.excerpt:
Current Chapter 29 supplies the intestate succession framework. It distinguishes the surviving
spouse's share under G.S. 29-14 from the shares of other heirs under G.S. 29-15 and applies a 120-hour
survival rule through G.S. 29-13. A broker identifies intestacy and routes the actual heir and share
determination to the estate attorney. Foreclosure procedure is outside this module.

---

## D. Deeds

### D.1 Grantor and grantee

The **grantor** conveys; the **grantee** receives.

### D.2 Essential elements of a valid deed

The Commission's list, transcribed:

- **Named parties (grantor/grantee).**
- **Words of conveyance (granting clause).**
- **Accurate legal description of the property.**
- **Legal capacity of the grantor.**
- **Signature of the grantor(s).**
- **Delivery to and voluntary acceptance of the deed by the grantee** — usually by recordation.
- **The deed must be in writing.**

**Instructor Note, transcribed:**

> *"**Recordation of the deed is not a legal essential element**; but the standard sales contracts in
> many states like North Carolina **require recordation of the deed to complete closing**. Non-essential
> elements frequently included in a deed are **date, acknowledgement, amount of consideration,
> witnesses, seal, and signature of grantee**."*

**Both halves matter.** Recordation is not an element of validity — **and North Carolina's standard
sales contracts require it to complete closing anyway.** So a licensee should never say "recording
doesn't matter"; it does not go to validity and it does go to whether the transaction has closed.

chunks.heading: D.3 Deed types — the missing required-activity instruction
chunks.excerpt:
Note too what is **not** essential: **the grantee's signature**, **consideration in any stated amount**,
**a seal**, **witnesses**, and **acknowledgement** — though acknowledgement is what makes an instrument
recordable in practice.

### D.3 Deed types — the missing required-activity instruction

The deed type changes the grantor's promises; recording does not upgrade those promises:

| Deed | What the student must distinguish |
|---|---|
| **General warranty deed** | The grantor conveys the described estate with title covenants reaching beyond the grantor's own period of ownership. It offers the broadest ordinary deed warranty, but still does not replace a title search or policy. |
| **Special warranty deed** | The grantor limits title covenants to claims arising by, through, or under that grantor. It does not warrant the entire earlier chain of title. |
| **Quitclaim deed** | Conveys whatever present interest, if any, the grantor has, without promising that the grantor owns the property or that title is clear. It does not release a mortgage debt or make a concealed “subject-to” transaction safe. |
| **Bargain-and-sale deed** | Indicates a conveyance for value but, without express warranties, does not supply the broad covenants of a general warranty deed. Read the instrument instead of deciding from its caption. |
| **Special-purpose deed** | Trustee's, executor's, administrator's, guardian's, commissioner's, and similar deeds depend on the signer’s legal authority and the governing proceeding. Refer authority and drafting questions to the attorney. |

chunks.heading: Required Activities in this section — all three must be completed
chunks.excerpt:
**Required deed-classification exercise.** For each instrument, identify (1) who signs and under what
authority, (2) the estate described, (3) the warranties actually stated, (4) whether delivery and
acceptance occurred, and (5) whether it has been recorded for third-party priority. A recorded
quitclaim deed is still a quitclaim deed; a general warranty deed does not become valid against a
prior protected interest merely because its caption says “general warranty.”

---

## Required Activities in this section — all three must be completed

1. **Real world examples of each type of estate**, noting that **leasehold estates differ in how they
   end**. *(A.1)*
2. **Explain the real world use of each type of lease.** *(A.5)*
3. **An assessment determining whether the student can differentiate the deed types.** *(D.3)*

## Module NC-06 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-06

Drawn from **Section VI** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Every Instructor Note and Required Activity above is **transcribed from
the Syllabus** — including the statement that the joint tenancy right of survivorship is *"Automatic in
states other than NC"*, the entirety and deed notes, the mechanic's-lien priority concept, the water
rights note, the trust routing, and the deed recordation note. Where that shorthand conflicts with or
overstates current statutory text, the current statute is taught and the conflict is identified.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-06
chunks.excerpt:
**Current primary text read on September 7, 2026:** Chapter 41 Articles 5-7 (tenancy by the entirety,
joint tenancy, tenancy in common); G.S. 42-14 (periodic-tenancy notice); Chapter 44A §§44A-10 through
-13 (claim relation-back, perfection, filing and enforcement); Chapter 47C Article 4 (condominium
purchaser protection); G.S. 47-18 (recording priority); and Chapter 29 Articles 1-2 (intestacy).
**Still not read for this module:** the current Timeshare Act, Chapter 47F in full, foreclosure law,
special-purpose deed statutes, and local instruments. The percentage-lease figures are invented for
arithmetic and are not market data.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-07

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-07
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-07

## Section VII · Real Estate Contracts & Agency

**Commission Syllabus section:** VII — Real Estate Contracts & Agency
**Instructional Level:** **3** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* At Level 3 the instructor treats the topic **in substantial depth** and
**requires students to complete practical work assignments** applying it to common fact situations.
**Basic contract concepts and terminology, special contract forms, preemptive rights, brokerage
employment relationships and implied agency are Level 1**; **reality of consent, other contract
concepts, and the importance of the sales contract are Level 2.**
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 16 items — tied for the heaviest section in
the entire examination.**
**Instructional hours:** **6.0**, allocated within the Commission's recommended emphasis for Agency
(13.0) and Contracts and Closing (18.0).
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Basic Contract Concepts, Terminology & Classifications *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
1. Classify contracts by formation, obligation, performance and validity. *(Level 1)*
2. Apply the four essential elements to a defective fact pattern. *(Level 3)*
3. Apply the Mailbox Rule correctly, and state its two limits.
4. State what is and is not the consideration in a sales contract and in a lease.
5. Classify capacity defects as **void** or **voidable**. *(Level 3)*
6. Distinguish mistake, fraud, duress and undue influence. *(Level 2)*
7. Name the ways a contract is terminated or discharged, and distinguish that from termination of an
   offer. *(Level 2)*
8. State the assignor's continuing liability.
9. Name the remedies for breach.
10. State the rules for submitting concurrent offers.
11. Explain why brokers must not draft, and which documents require an attorney. *(Level 1)*
12. **State that facilitator/transaction brokerage is not allowed in North Carolina.**
13. Recite the six agent's duties to a principal. *(Level 3)*
14. Explain the automatic subagency consequence of firm agency.
15. Name the ways an agency terminates and the three exceptions to duties ending.

---

## A. Basic Contract Concepts, Terminology & Classifications *(Level 1)*

**Contract. Express/implied. Bilateral/unilateral. Executed/executory. Valid. Void. Voidable.
Addenda. Amendments. Contingency.**

Ten italicised terms in the Syllabus — which under its own legend means **students should know the
definitions.** Note that the Commission lists **addenda**, **amendments** and **contingency** as basic
terminology rather than as advanced concepts, and it distinguishes them: an **addendum** is added to a
contract, an **amendment** changes one, and a **contingency** is a condition.

---

## B. Essential Elements of a Contract *(Level 3)*

### B.1 Mutual assent

chunks.heading: B.2 Communication of offer and acceptance
chunks.excerpt:
Also known as **meeting of the minds**, mutual agreement, or offer and acceptance.

**The offer.** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Pay careful attention to terminology. **There is a
huge difference between an offer and a contract.**"*

**Offeror versus offeree.** **Instructor Note:** *"Typically, the buyer is the initial offeror and the
seller is the initial offeree; **but sellers can initiate offers.**"*

**Acceptance.** **Instructor Note, transcribed — and this one reaches into every day of practice:**
*"**Communication to the agent is the same as communication to the principal.**"*

So an acceptance delivered to you is delivered to your client. You cannot hold it and treat the
transaction as still open.

### B.2 Communication of offer and acceptance

- **Oral communication.**
- **Personal delivery.**
- **Mail** — traditional or special mail such as USPS, FedEx, UPS — and the **Mailbox Rule.**

**Instructor Note on the Mailbox Rule, transcribed:** *"**Time of actual receipt by offeror is
irrelevant.** This Rule **only applies to communicating ACCEPTANCE of an offer; not termination of an
offer or contract.**"*

**Two limits in one sentence.** Acceptance is effective on dispatch, so receipt does not matter — **and
the rule does not apply to a revocation, a rejection or a termination**, each of which is effective only
on receipt.

- **Electronic methods** — email, text or fax **unless prohibited by the terms of the offer**, and
  **effective upon receipt by the offeror's communication equipment or computer.**

chunks.heading: B.3 Counteroffer
chunks.excerpt:
**Current North Carolina UETA check.** G.S. 66-325 defines when an electronic record is sent and
received. Unless the parties reasonably agree otherwise, receipt occurs when a processable record
enters the recipient's designated or used information-processing system from which it can be
retrieved. An individual need not yet know of the receipt, subject to the statute's additional
consumer-transaction readability protection. That rule identifies electronic delivery; other law and
the offer still determine whether that delivery creates acceptance. The Syllabus contrasts this with
its common-law Mailbox Rule: a qualifying mailed acceptance is effective on dispatch.

### B.3 Counteroffer

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Once an offeree makes a counteroffer, they **cannot change their
mind later and 'accept' the original offer**."*

### B.4 Termination of offer

Distinguish carefully from termination of a **contract** at D.2 — the Commission flags the distinction
in a Required Activity below.

### B.5 Consideration

**Instructor Note, transcribed — and this is a reliably tested point:**

> *"**The sales price is the consideration in a sales contract, NOT the earnest money deposit or the
> due diligence fee. Rent is the consideration in a lease, NOT the tenant security deposit.**"*

### B.6 Legal capacity of the parties — void or voidable?

The Commission's four cases, each with its consequence:

| Party | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Minors** — persons under legal age, **18 in NC** | **voidable** |
| **Persons declared mentally incompetent by a court of law** | **VOID** |
| **Persons mentally incompetent in fact** | **voidable** |
| **Persons intoxicated or under drug influence who temporarily do not understand what they are doing** | **voidable** |

chunks.heading: B.7 Lawful objective of the contract
chunks.excerpt:
**Only one of the four is void, and it is the one where a court has already adjudicated the
incompetence.** Everything else in the capacity list is voidable. That single distinction is worth
memorising exactly as the Commission states it. Current G.S. 48A-2 independently confirms the age
line: a North Carolina minor is a person who has not reached 18. The void/voidable classifications in
this section remain the Commission's prescribed national-contract instruction, not a broker's license
to adjudicate a person's capacity.

### B.7 Lawful objective of the contract

---

## C. Requirement for Voluntary Reality of Consent *(Level 2)*

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide real world examples of each of the
> following ways that real estate contracts may be declared **void or voidable**."*

### C.1 Mistake

**Mistake of fact.** A contract **may be voidable if the mistake of fact:**

- **involves a material term or aspect;**
- **is mutual; and**
- **is not the result of fraud or negligence.**

**All three.** And the corollary the Commission states: **"Unilateral mistakes of fact do not release
parties from their obligations."**

**Mistake of law.**

### C.2 Fraud

Its **elements**; and **voidable by the deceived party — not automatic.**

### C.3 Duress

Examples; **voidable by the injured party.**

### C.4 Undue influence

Examples; **voidable by the injured party.**

**Notice the prescribed classification across C.1 to C.4:** each fact pattern may make the agreement
voidable at the election of the affected party rather than automatically void. A court-adjudicated
incompetent is the distinct void case in the capacity table.

### C.5 Required Activity evidence — void and voidable fact-pattern lab

chunks.heading: D. Other Contract Concepts *(Level 2)*
chunks.excerpt:
For each row, the student must identify the defect, classify the result under the Syllabus, name the
party who may avoid a voidable agreement, and state which fact still needs legal confirmation.

| Scenario | Prescribed classification and analysis |
|---|---|
| A 17-year-old signs as buyer | **Voidable**, not automatically void; minority is the capacity issue. |
| A seller previously adjudicated incompetent signs personally despite the existing court order | **Void** under the Syllabus capacity table; route authority and guardianship issues to counsel. |
| A party who has not been adjudicated cannot understand the transaction because of a mental condition | Potentially **voidable**; capacity is fact- and evidence-dependent. |
| A heavily intoxicated party cannot understand the agreement | Potentially **voidable** by that party; ordinary regret is not incapacity. |
| Both parties reasonably use the wrong parcel number for the material parcel they intended to sell | Potentially **voidable for mutual material mistake**; a unilateral careless assumption is different. |
| A seller intentionally lies that a failed septic permit was approved to induce the buyer to sign | Potentially **voidable by the deceived buyer for fraud**, with other remedies possible. |
| A person signs only because another threatens immediate unlawful harm | Potentially **voidable by the injured party for duress**. |
| A caregiver exploits a vulnerable owner's dependence to obtain a below-market sale | Potentially **voidable by the influenced party for undue influence**. |

These examples teach issue recognition. The broker preserves evidence, makes required disclosures, and
routes rescission, enforceability and capacity conclusions to counsel.

---

## D. Other Contract Concepts *(Level 2)*

chunks.heading: D.1 Uniform Electronic Transaction Act (UETA)
chunks.excerpt:
### D.1 Uniform Electronic Transaction Act (UETA)

- G.S. 66-315 says UETA does **not require** electronic records or signatures and applies only when
  each party has agreed to transact electronically; agreement may be shown by context and conduct.
- G.S. 66-317 says a record, signature, or contract may not be denied effect **solely** because it is
  electronic, and a compliant electronic record/signature can satisfy another law's writing/signature
  requirement. Other applicable law still decides the legal consequence.
- G.S. 66-325 supplies the send/receipt mechanics summarized in B.2. “Electronic” is not a shortcut
  around assent, capacity, lawful purpose, the agreed method, or another substantive rule.

### D.2 Termination or discharge of contracts

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide real world examples of each of the
> following ways that real estate contracts are **terminated**. Be sure to highlight that **termination
> of a CONTRACT is different from termination of an OFFER**."*

- **Full and complete performance.**
- **Material breach of contract.**
- **Subsequent agreement of the parties** due to dispute or negotiation: **release**; **novation**;
  **subsequent modifying agreement**; **accord and satisfaction**; **cancellation**.
- **Impossibility of performance.** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Generally refers to
  **impossibility of the thing to be done, not the inability of the promisor to do it**. For example,
  **if a party dies after contract formation but prior to closing, the contract is binding upon the
  heirs and/or the estate** of contract parties."*
- **Operation of law.**

chunks.heading: D.2.a Required Activity evidence — contract termination versus offer termination
chunks.excerpt:
**That Instructor Note is a frequent misunderstanding and worth saying to clients plainly: a death
between contract and closing does not cancel the contract.**

### D.2.a Required Activity evidence — contract termination versus offer termination

| Event | Contract result |
|---|---|
| Buyer pays, seller conveys, and both complete every promised obligation | Discharge by **full performance**. |
| One party materially refuses a required performance | Potential discharge/remedies for **material breach**, subject to the agreement and counsel. |
| Both sides sign a release ending their remaining obligations | Discharge by **subsequent mutual agreement/release**. |
| All affected parties agree to substitute a new obligor and release the original one | **Novation**; unlike assignment, the agreed release matters. |
| The parties sign a valid amendment changing a remaining obligation | The **subsequent modifying agreement** controls the changed obligation. |
| A disputed payment is accepted under an agreed settlement of the claim | Potential **accord and satisfaction**. |
| Both parties agree to cancel before completion | **Cancellation by agreement**, subject to its terms. |
| The specific subject property is destroyed before performance and the governing law excuses it | Potential **impossibility of the thing to be done**; a promisor's financial inability is different. |
| A controlling court order or law makes performance unavailable | Potential discharge by **operation of law**. |

chunks.heading: D.3 Assignment of contracts
chunks.excerpt:
An **offer** is different because no contract yet exists. A rejection or counteroffer can terminate the
offer; a revocation ordinarily must reach the offeree; an offer may lapse at its stated time; and the
Syllabus's Mailbox Rule concerns a qualifying mailed **acceptance**, not termination of an offer or
contract. Students must not use a contract remedy label to explain why an unaccepted offer ended.

### D.3 Assignment of contracts

**Assignor versus assignee.** And the rule, transcribed: *"**Unless released by the other party to the
contract, the assignor will remain secondarily liable** for performance of contract terms."*

### D.4 Time being of the essence

### D.5 Remedies for breach of contract

- **Money damages:** **compensatory**; **consequential**; **liquidated**.
- **Rescission.**
- **Specific performance.**

---

## E. Basic Sales Contract Concepts

### E.1 The importance of the sales contract *(Level 2)*

- It **sets forth the parameters of the legally binding agreement** between buyer and seller.
- **Standardized forms give uniformity to transactions and reduce brokers' temptation to draft.**
- **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Brokers are expected to **know when it is appropriate to use a
  particular contract form** and to **recognize situations where sellers and buyers should be referred
  to an attorney** to have a suitable contract drafted."*

### E.2 Contract creation, and the prohibition on drafting

**Instructor Note, transcribed, followed by the current North Carolina boundary:**

> *"**Brokers are prohibited from drafting legal documents for others; this is seen as illegal practice
> of law in most states.** Consumers should be encouraged to seek legal assistance if standard forms do
> not fit their needs."*

chunks.heading: E.3 Submitting offers — five stated rules
chunks.excerpt:
- G.S. 84-2.1 defines preparation of deeds, mortgages and legal advice as practicing law. Its narrow
  broker exception permits a Chapter 93A licensee, while acting as agent and following Commission
  rules, to **select or complete a preprinted form**. It does not permit the broker to prepare a custom
  contract or deed for another person. G.S. 93A-6(a)(11) makes unauthorized legal service a disciplinary
  ground.
- **North Carolina Statute of Frauds, G.S. 22-2:** a contract to sell or convey land or an interest in
  it is void unless the contract or a memorandum is in writing and signed by the party to be charged or
  an authorized signer. The same section reaches mineral leases of any duration and other land leases
  exceeding three years from formation.
- **Offer and acceptance** by traditional methods and by **electronic means** — e-mail, DocuSign.

### E.3 Submitting offers — five stated rules

Transcribed, because each is examinable and each is a daily practice rule:

1. **Concurrent offers must be presented AT THE SAME TIME; no particular order of presentation is
   required.**
2. **This applies to ALL brokers in the transaction regardless of who they represent or how they will
   be compensated.**
3. **The listing broker generally has NO AUTHORITY to accept or reject an offer on behalf of the
   seller-client.**
4. **Only 1 contract signed by all parties is required to be binding.**
5. **The buyer acquires EQUITABLE TITLE once under contract.**

### E.4 Handling offer modifications and counteroffers

- **Any change to an offer rejects the original offer; potentially creates a counteroffer.**
- **Numerous term changes should prompt use of a new offer form** completed with the current terms
  under consideration.

### E.5 Earnest money as liquidated damages

chunks.heading: E.6 Furnishing copies of offers and contracts
chunks.excerpt:
### E.6 Furnishing copies of offers and contracts

### E.7 Handling contract disputes and modifications

- **Seek legal advice BEFORE breaching contract terms.**
- **Negotiate an amendment to the contract.**

---

## F. Special Contract Forms *(Level 1)*

> **Important Note — transcribed from the Syllabus:** *"Buyers and sellers **should be referred to an
> attorney for preparation of any of the following documents. Drafting of such documents by a broker
> constitutes the unlawful practice of law.**"*

### F.1 Installment land contract — contract for deed, or land contract

- **A sales contract AND an owner-financing document.**
- **The seller (vendor) retains legal title until the entire purchase price is paid.**
- **The buyer (vendee) receives equitable title and possession.**
- **No standard contract form; consult an attorney.** **Instructor Note: "Do not use a standard sales
  contract."**
- Advantages and disadvantages to both seller and buyer.

### F.2 Option to purchase real estate

chunks.heading: F.3 Agreements for preemptive rights *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
- **No standard option form; consult an attorney.** **"Do not use a standard sales contract."**
- **Optionor** and **optionee**.
- **Two types of consideration should be definitely and separately stated:** the **option fee**,
  **generally non-refundable**, and the **purchase price**.
- Because an option concerns an interest in land, G.S. 22-2 requires the signed writing or memorandum.
  **Recording is not a Statute-of-Frauds formation requirement.** Whether and how to record an option
  to protect it against later interests is a separate title/priority question for the attorney.
- **Time being of the essence in regard to the date to exercise the option.**
- Residential leases may include an option to purchase. **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"No standard
  form exists for a residential lease with option to purchase, and **a broker must not suggest that
  landlords/tenants attempt to tie together lease and offer to purchase forms**. A broker should direct
  the parties to enlist an attorney to draft this special type of agreement."*

### F.3 Agreements for preemptive rights *(Level 1)*

**Right of first refusal.** **Right of first opportunity to purchase.**

---

## G. Overview of Laws and Regulations Governing Brokerage Relationships

### G.1 The three sources

**Common Law of Agency. Contract law. Individual state laws and regulations.**

### G.2 Basic agency terms — and one that does not exist here

**Agency. Principal/client. Agent. Subagent. Third party. Customer.**

**Facilitator/transactional broker** — and the Commission states two things about it:

- **"Disclosure of material facts is normally required."**
- **"NOT ALLOWED IN NORTH CAROLINA."**

chunks.heading: G.3 The fiduciary role
chunks.excerpt:
**Learn the concept, because it is on the National examination. Never practise it, because North
Carolina does not permit it.** North Carolina is an agency state: a broker working with a party is
either their agent or is dealing with them as a customer. There is no neutral middle status.

Current Commission guidance confirms the boundary: there is no default representation and no status
in which a person performs brokerage services for neither party. Representation requires the
consumer's express consent. A broker may deal with an unrepresented person as a customer, but that is
not authority to provide the customer brokerage services as a neutral transaction broker.

*(This is the direct opposite of Oklahoma, where the statute abolished agency and made the neutral
broker the norm. A licensee moving between states cannot carry either assumption across.)*

### G.3 The fiduciary role

**A fiduciary — e.g., an agent — is bound to act primarily for the benefit of the principal — e.g., the
client — BEFORE ANY SELF-INTEREST.**

### G.4 Classifications of agency relationships

**Universal agent. General agent. Special agent.**

### G.5 Creation of real estate agency relationships

**By agency contracts/agreements**, between brokers/firms and transaction parties:

- **Listing contract**
- **Buyer Agency contract**
- **Dual Agency contract**
- **Property Management contract**
- **Tenant Representation contract**

**Between brokers and brokerage companies** *(Level 1)*: **in-house brokerage employment contracts**;
**cooperation agreements between brokers/firms**.

**By conduct of the parties — implied agency** *(Level 1)*: for example, cooperation between firms
**based on brokers' actual conduct and custom rather than an explicit agreement.**

chunks.heading: G.6 Scope of an agent's authority
chunks.excerpt:
### G.6 Scope of an agent's authority

**Express authority. Implied authority. Apparent authority.**

### G.7 Real estate agency relationships

**The consumer employs a sole practitioner broker** — the agency agreement is between the sole
proprietor's company and the consumer.

**The consumer employs a brokerage company/firm** — and the Commission states three consequences that
follow, transcribed:

- **The agency agreement is between the consumer and the FIRM, not with the individual affiliated
  agents.**
- **A broker affiliated with a firm is an agent of the firm under the law of agency.**
- **ALL brokers affiliated with the firm AUTOMATICALLY become subagents of any principal-client of the
  firm.**

**That third consequence is the structural fact behind everything in Module NC-08.** When your firm
takes a listing, **you** become a subagent of that seller automatically — whether or not you have met
them, whether or not you work in that office. It is why in-house sales raise dual agency, and why the
Commission calls careless conduct here **"illegal undisclosed dual agency."**

**Agency relationships in sales:**

chunks.heading: G.7 Real estate agency relationships
chunks.excerpt:
- **Single agency — seller agency only.** The company only represents owners; all affiliated brokers
  represent all seller-clients **as seller subagents**; all potential buyers are shown the company's
  listings **as unrepresented third parties (customers)**.
- **Single agency — buyer agency only.** The company **has no listings**; all affiliated brokers
  represent all buyer-clients **as buyer subagents**; brokers show only properties listed with
  cooperating companies or unrepresented sellers (FSBOs).
- **Cross sale or co-brokered transaction.** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**Beware of illegal
  undisclosed dual agency through careless actions of brokers.**"* Concepts: **exclusive agency**;
  **seller subagency**; **the listing company can refuse to offer subagency to the other company**;
  **switching from seller subagent to buyer agent**.
- **Both seller and buyer agency with dual agency for "in-house" sales.** **Intentional, disclosed dual
  agency**; **unintentional, undisclosed dual agency prohibited**; **dual agency with designated
  agents.**

**Agency relationships in rentals:**

- **Created by a property management agreement.**
- **The management firm/broker is the agent and the landlord is the principal.**
- **Any licensed employees of the management firm/broker are subagents of the landlord.**
- **Residential prospective tenants are usually customers.**
- **Commercial tenants may or may not be represented; any representation agreement should be in writing
  prior to an offer to rent.**

chunks.heading: G.8 The agent's duties to the principal *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
Do not extend the in-firm rule into a false outside-firm default. Commission guidance states that a
broker from another firm is **not automatically** the seller's subagent: seller subagency requires the
seller's written authorization, disclosure to the buyer, and the broker's actual compliance with the
agency rules. Without express authorization to represent the buyer or seller, the outside broker may
not simply provide brokerage services while calling the role “neutral.”

### G.8 The agent's duties to the principal *(Level 3)*

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Use real world examples to illustrate each
> duty."*

The Commission's six:

1. **Obedience.**
2. **Loyalty** — including **avoidance of self-dealing by the agent**, and **written client consent to
   represent adverse interests** such as dual agency.
3. **Disclosure of information**, and the Commission states its scope expansively: **"to include the
   agent's AFFIRMATIVE DUTY TO DISCOVER and disclose all transactional information including, but not
   limited to, material facts."** **Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**Personal information about a
   third party** known to an agent **that might influence the agent's principal** in the transaction
   **must be disclosed to the principal.**"*
4. **Confidentiality.**
5. **Accounting for and safeguarding of goods and funds handled, plus retention of transactional
   records.** **Instructor Note:** *"**No commingling of trust monies with company or personal
   funds.**"*
6. **Skill, care and diligence.**

chunks.heading: G.8.a Required Activity evidence — six agency-duty scenarios
chunks.excerpt:
**Duty 3 is the one that separates North Carolina from a passive-disclosure state.** It is an
**affirmative duty to make reasonable, objective inquiry into material transaction facts** — not merely
to pass on what you happen to learn. It is not authority to collect or use protected-class information,
invade privacy, or turn a customer's confidential remark into discriminatory advice.

### G.8.a Required Activity evidence — six agency-duty scenarios

| Duty | Real-world application |
|---|---|
| **Obedience** | The seller directs a lawful showing window; the agent follows it. A direction to conceal a material defect is unlawful and must be refused. |
| **Loyalty** | Before acquiring the client's property or taking an adverse role, the agent discloses the conflict and obtains the legally required consent or declines. |
| **Disclosure** | The agent verifies and promptly communicates a discovered encroachment or financing fact material to the principal's decision. |
| **Confidentiality** | The buyer's maximum price is not volunteered to the seller; a superseding duty to disclose a material fact is analyzed separately. |
| **Accounting/safeguarding** | Earnest money is handled only under the governing trust-account instructions, never deposited into the broker's operating account. |
| **Skill, care and diligence** | The agent tracks deadlines, uses the correct authorized form, investigates visible warning signs, and refers legal or technical conclusions. |

### G.9 Termination of the agency relationship

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide examples of **terminations and
> exceptions**."*

**Agency terminates by:**

chunks.heading: G.9.a Required Activity evidence — termination and surviving-duty lab
chunks.excerpt:
- **the purpose having been accomplished;**
- **expiration of the term;**
- **mutual agreement to terminate;**
- **breach by a party;**
- **destruction or condemnation of the property;**
- **death or incapacity of either party;**
- **operation of law.**

**Duty generally ends when the agency ends — with three exceptions:**

1. **an express promise or implied obligation;**
2. **a pending transaction at the termination date of the agency agreement;**
3. **self-dealing.**

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**Duty of confidentiality may be expected to continue as long as the
agent has no duty to disclose to a new client.**"*

### G.9.a Required Activity evidence — termination and surviving-duty lab

| Event | Agency analysis |
|---|---|
| The listed property closes | The purpose is **accomplished**; record and pending-obligation duties still follow their own rules. |
| The definite listing term ends without renewal | The agency **expires**. |
| Client and firm sign a termination agreement | The agency ends by **mutual agreement**, subject to surviving terms. |
| A party materially breaches the agency agreement | The relationship may end for **breach** and may leave a damages question. |
| The property is destroyed or condemned | The subject may be unavailable; apply **destruction/condemnation** and the agreement. |
| Principal or agent dies or loses capacity | The Syllabus identifies **death or incapacity** as a termination event; entity and pending-transaction facts still require counsel. |
| A legal prohibition or court order ends the authority | Termination by **operation of law**. |

chunks.heading: G.10 Liabilities and consequences of an agent's breach *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
Three after-termination tests follow. First, an **express promise or implied obligation** may survive.
Second, a **pending transaction** may preserve performance and compensation questions after the agency
term. Third, **self-dealing** does not become permissible because the relationship ended. Confidential
information also remains protected unless a superseding duty requires disclosure.

### G.10 Liabilities and consequences of an agent's breach *(Level 3)*

- **Disciplinary action by the regulatory agency against the agent.**
- **Civil liability of the agent.**
- **Criminal liability of the agent.**
- **Civil liability of the PRINCIPAL for the agent's misconduct — tort.**

**The fourth is the one clients do not expect**, and it is a reason to be careful with what you say on a
principal's behalf: their exposure can follow from your conduct.

---

## Required Activities in this section — all four delivered in this draft

1. **Real world examples of each way a contract may be declared void or voidable.** *(C.5)*
2. **Real world examples of each way a contract is terminated**, highlighting that **termination of a
   contract differs from termination of an offer.** *(D.2.a)*
3. **Real world examples illustrating each of the six agent's duties.** *(G.8.a)*
4. **Examples of agency terminations and of the exceptions to duties ending.** *(G.9.a)*

## Module NC-07 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-07

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-07
chunks.excerpt:
Drawn from **Section VII** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Every Instructor Note, Important Note and Required Activity above is
**transcribed from the Syllabus** — including the Mailbox Rule limits, the consideration note, the
void/voidable capacity table, the concurrent-offer rules, the automatic-subagency consequence, the
affirmative duty to discover, and the statement that **facilitator/transactional brokerage is not
allowed in North Carolina.**

**Current primary text read on 2026-09-07:** G.S. **22-2** (land-sale and lease writing rule), Chapter
66 Article 40 §§ **66-315, -317 and -325** (electronic consent, recognition and receipt), G.S.
**84-2.1** and **93A-6(a)(11)** (practice-of-law boundary), and G.S. **48A-2** (minor under 18). Current
Commission agency guidance was also read for express representation, no neutral transaction-broker
role, and the in-firm/outside-firm subagency distinction.

**Still not read in current controlling text for this module:** the complete **21 NCAC 58A .0104** PDF
and the full current **North Carolina Real Estate Manual**. **NC REALTORS® Offer to Purchase and
Contract Standard Form 2-T** and every other standard form remain unobtained; no provision, deadline or
contingency structure of any form is reproduced, described or paraphrased. Section XI, Contracts &
Closing in NC, records that separate submission gate.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-08

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-08
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-08

## Section VIII · Agency in NC

**Commission Syllabus section:** VIII — Agency in NC
**Instructional Level:** **3** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* **Part A, the overview of laws and regulations, is Level 1**; **Additional
Agency Disclosure Requirements is Level 2**; **Working in Property Management is Level 2 except the
property management fee, which is Level 3**; and the **typical property management duties are Level 1.**
**Licence examination weight:** **State Exam Category — 16 items — tied with Section VII for the
heaviest section in the entire examination, and the heaviest of the 60 state items.**
**Instructional hours:** **7.0**, the largest single allocation in this course, drawn from the
Commission's recommended 13.0 hours for the Agency subject area.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Overview of NC Laws and Regulations Governing Brokerage Relationships *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
1. State the two primary purposes of agency disclosure. *(Level 3)*
2. State when the WWREA Disclosure must be provided, by what method, and within what time.
3. Explain what the **review** component of the disclosure requires and what does not satisfy it.
4. State the retention period for the disclosure form and when it applies.
5. Describe the additional disclosure requirements. *(Level 2)*
6. Explain intentional disclosed dual agency and why unintentional undisclosed dual agency is
   prohibited. *(Level 3)*
7. **Explain designated dual agency and apply its seven major provisions to a fact pattern.** *(Level 3)*
8. Recite the eight agent's duties to a principal under North Carolina License Law and rules.
9. State the agent's duty to third persons and contrast it with the duty to a principal. *(Level 3)*
10. State the four requirements for a written agency agreement and the one exception.
11. Work a listing appointment through the Commission's prelisting and listing sequence.
12. Work a buyer engagement through the Commission's sequence, including oral buyer agency limits.
13. Describe property management agency and the contract's typical provisions. *(Level 2)*

---

## A. Overview of NC Laws and Regulations Governing Brokerage Relationships *(Level 1)*

The three sources the Commission names:

1. **NC Real Estate License Law** — **NCGS 93A**.
2. **NC Real Estate Commission rules** — **Chapter 58A, Title 21 NCAC**.
3. **Disclosure of Agency Relationships in Residential and Commercial Sales** — **NCGS 93A-6(a)(4) and
   (6); Commission Rule 58A .0104(c)–(i), (m), (o) and (p)**.

chunks.heading: B. Agency Disclosure *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
This module is now reconciled to the current General Assembly text of **G.S. 93A-6** and to the
official OAH indexed text of **21 NCAC 58A .0104, .0106, .0108, and .0109**. The Commission's syllabus
still controls prescribed scope and instructional level. The current OAH PDF bytes and the current
WWREA disclosure form still require local capture and page-level review before filing; an indexed rule
is not represented as a byte-verified submission exhibit.

---

## B. Agency Disclosure *(Level 3)*

### B.1 The two primary purposes

Transcribed from the Syllabus:

1. **"To ensure that the consumer understands AS SOON AS POSSIBLE that there is NO CONFIDENTIALITY
   between the broker and the consumer until an agency relationship is established."**
2. **"To introduce the consumer to available agency options."**

**Purpose 1 is the one consumers get wrong and licensees let them.** Before there is an agency
relationship, the consumer does not receive **agency confidentiality from that broker**. A prospective
buyer who tells the seller's agent the maximum they would pay cannot assume the statement will be kept
from the seller. That is why the broker should pause the conversation before seeking or receiving
confidential transaction information. This is an agency rule; it is not a claim that every other
privacy or data-protection duty disappears.

### B.2 The Working with Real Estate Agents (WWREA) Disclosure — Commission Rule 58A .0104(c)

**Scope:**

> **"Applies to ALL residential AND commercial sales transactions; NOT REQUIRED for property management
> or lease transactions."**

**Timing — provide at First Substantial Contact:**

chunks.heading: B.2a Required Activity evidence — first-substantial-contact lab
chunks.excerpt:
- **In person:** **provide and review the WWREA IMMEDIATELY at first substantial contact.**
- **By phone or electronic means** — email, social media and the like: **at the earliest opportunity
  after first substantial contact, NO LATER THAN 3 DAYS AFTER**, transmitting a copy of the WWREA to
  the consumer.

**Then, in both cases:**

- **Review the agency options at the earliest practicable opportunity after receipt by the consumer.**
- **Determine whether the broker will act as an agent of the buyer or the seller in the transaction.**

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Provide examples of **when first substantial
> contact occurs** in various situations, including, but not limited to, contact **in-person, by phone,
> by electronic means such as email or social media, and at open houses.**"*
>
> **This activity must be completed.** Work each of those four settings and state, with reasons, the
> point at which first substantial contact occurred and what the broker was then required to do.

### B.2a Required Activity evidence — first-substantial-contact lab

Classify the trigger, then state the broker's next action. The test is the **substance** of the contact:
the consumer or broker begins to act as though agency exists and the consumer begins to disclose
personal or confidential information. A greeting or request for public property information alone is
not automatically first substantial contact.

chunks.heading: B.2a Required Activity evidence — first-substantial-contact lab
chunks.excerpt:
| Setting | Trigger analysis | Required response |
|---|---|---|
| In-person open house at the firm's listing | The visitor starts to disclose a maximum price and financing limit. This is first substantial contact because confidential bargaining information is beginning to flow to a broker whose firm represents the seller. | Interrupt before more is disclosed; provide the WWREA, add the broker's name and license number, review it, and determine whether the broker will act for buyer or seller. |
| Telephone inquiry | A seller moves from asking about services to explaining the private reason a fast sale is needed. First substantial contact has occurred. | If providing the publication during the call is impractical, explain agency immediately, transmit it at the earliest opportunity and no later than three days after the contact, then review it at the earliest practicable opportunity. |
| Email or social-media message | A buyer sends only a property address and asks for the showing time: no agency-like conduct or confidential information yet. The follow-up message gives a ceiling price and asks the broker to negotiate: first substantial contact occurs then. | Do not treat all electronic contact as an automatic three-day exception. If it is impractical to provide the publication at the trigger, transmit it at the earliest opportunity and within three days, and complete the review at the earliest practicable opportunity. |
| Office consultation | Before asking about urgency, price limits, motivation, or other confidential facts, the broker explains that agency disclosure must be reviewed first. | Provide and review the WWREA before asking the confidential question; identify the agency options the firm actually offers. |

chunks.heading: B.2a Required Activity evidence — first-substantial-contact lab
chunks.excerpt:
**Evidence check:** for each row, the learner records (1) the exact trigger sentence, (2) whom the firm
currently represents, (3) whether immediate delivery was practical, (4) the delivery deadline, and
(5) when the review occurred. A mere email attachment or signature link earns no completion credit.

**Mandatory review of the disclosure form — and what does NOT satisfy it. Transcribed:**

> **"Inclusion of the WWREA Disclosure form in a broker's email signature or sending by an electronic
> signature program ALONE DOES NOT COMPLY with the review component of disclosure requirements."**

**Read that twice, because it is exactly how a modern brokerage would try to automate the obligation
away.** Attaching the form to every outgoing email is not compliance. Sending it through a signature
platform is not compliance. **The rule requires a review**, and a review is something a broker does
with a consumer.

**Completion and retention — Commission Rule 58A .0108:**

> **"Completion and retention of the disclosure form for 3 years (EVEN IF AGENCY IS NOT REACHED)."**

**Even if agency is not reached.** The consumer who received the form and then went elsewhere still
generates a record you keep for three years.

**And the companion piece:** the Commission's **Questions & Answers on: Working with Real Estate
Agents** — *"a companion piece for the WWREA Disclosure that brokers should strongly consider giving
consumers to provide more detail on agency options."*

chunks.heading: B.2b Required Activity evidence — WWREA form and companion Q&A
chunks.excerpt:
Current NCREC guidance confirms that the WWREA disclosure is a one-page, double-sided document with a
seller side and a buyer side. The broker marks the relationship types the **firm offers**; the
consumer's signature acknowledges receipt and does not itself create agency. If a consumer refuses to
sign, the broker still provides the disclosure and documents the refusal. The Commission's public
**Questions & Answers on: Working With Real Estate Agents** page is a companion explanation, not a
replacement for the required review.

### B.2b Required Activity evidence — WWREA form and companion Q&A

The current official pair is retained and page-reviewed: the two-page **REC 4.27 Working With Real
Estate Agents Disclosure** (1/1/2022) and the complete two-page/six-panel **REC 3.45 Questions and
Answers on: Working With Real Estate Agents** brochure (1/3/2022). NCREC also publishes a text-only
version of the Q&A, retained here to confirm multi-column reading order. These are separate documents
with separate jobs: the form is reviewed at first substantial contact; the Q&A supplies consumer
explanation and does not replace that review or create an agency contract.

**Learner review record:**

chunks.heading: B.3 Additional agency disclosure requirements *(Level 2)*
chunks.excerpt:
| Evidence to locate | Correct classification |
|---|---|
| Warning not to disclose confidential information before representation is established | Consumer-protection purpose of the disclosure review |
| Relationship types marked on the form | Relationships the firm offers, not the consumer's final selection and not an agency contract |
| Consumer signature | Evidence of receipt; refusal is documented after the broker still provides and reviews the form |
| Seller agency and buyer agency diagrams | Each client has a different brokerage firm and receives undivided representation from that firm |
| Dual agency diagram | One firm represents both sides with written authority; divided loyalty and confidential-information limits must be understood |
| Designated dual agency diagram | Different affiliated agents are designated to the opposing clients while the firm remains dual agent |
| Unrepresented buyer or seller discussion | Assistance is not representation; the broker's loyalty remains with the client and material-fact duties still apply |
| Termination discussion | The Commission does not cancel private agency contracts; the agreement and legal advice control disputed termination rights |

**Completion prompt:** explain to a prospective buyer, in plain language, why signing REC 4.27 does
not hire a broker; identify when a separate written buyer-agency agreement becomes mandatory; then
compare the confidentiality boundary in buyer agency, seller subagency, dual agency and designated
dual agency. Completion requires all three distinctions. A learner who merely opens the PDFs has not
completed the activity.

### B.3 Additional agency disclosure requirements *(Level 2)*

Five, with the Commission's citations:

chunks.heading: C. Dual Agency *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
- **Disclosure of agency status by a seller agent or subagent to a prospective buyer** — Rule 58A
  .0104(e).
- **Disclosure of agency status by a buyer agent to the seller or seller agent** — Rule 58A .0104(f).
  **Instructor Note:** *"The Standard 2-T Offer to Purchase and Contract provides a place for agency
  disclosure and license numbers in the signature area."*
- **Disclosure of and consent to proposed dual and designated (dual) agency** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(4) and
  (6); Rule 58A .0104(d), (i)–(n).
- **Broker with an ownership interest in a listing** — Rule 58A .0104(o).
- **Disclosure in auction sales situations** — Rule 58A .0104(g)–(h).

---

## C. Dual Agency *(Level 3)*

### C.1 Dual agency basics

- **The inherent potential conflict of interest centres around the agent's common law duty to disclose
  all material facts to their principal.** Two principals with opposed interests cannot both receive
  that.
- **Intentional, disclosed dual agency requires authority from BOTH principals.** Rule .0104(d)
  requires written authority when the relationship is formed, except that a buyer or tenant who may
  lawfully begin without a written agreement must reduce dual-agency authority to writing no later
  than the time one represented party makes an offer.
- **Unintentional, undisclosed dual agency is PROHIBITED.**

**Recall from Module NC-07 why undisclosed dual agency happens by accident:** an agency agreement is
with the firm, and affiliated brokers acting for that firm carry the firm's representation. If that
same firm then undertakes to represent a buyer for its seller-client's property, the **firm** represents
both sides and is a dual agent. This in-firm rule does not turn a broker from another firm into an
automatic seller subagent.

chunks.heading: C.2 Limiting the dual agent's duties by contract
chunks.excerpt:
### C.2 Limiting the dual agent's duties by contract

- **Limiting disclosure of certain information to principals.**
- **Limiting the dual agent's ability to advocate where the principals' interests conflict.**
- **"Effectually eliminates agent's role as an advocate for either client."**

That last phrase is what a consumer must understand before consenting: **in dual agency, nobody is
advocating for you.**

### C.3 Designated dual agency — Commission Rule 58A .0104(i)–(n)

**The basic concept:**

- **An optional approach when the brokerage company is a dual agent.**
- **One or more agents of the company are designated to represent ONLY the interests of the seller.**
- **One or more agents of the company are designated to represent ONLY the interests of the buyer.**
- **The company and all non-designated agents of the company REMAIN AS DUAL AGENTS.**

**Major rule provisions:**

- **Prior express approval required.**
- **Confidential information of a designated client may NOT be shared with the designated agent of the
  other party.**
- **The identity of all designated agents must be disclosed.**

**Key concepts — and these seven are the examinable heart of the section:**

chunks.heading: C.4 Individual broker dual agent — Commission Rule 58A .0104(n)
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Dual agency is NOT eliminated; it is merely a form of dual agency.**
2. **Only possible for in-house dual agency sales situations.**
3. **Prior express approval by both clients is required; written authority is due at formation unless
   the narrow buyer/tenant timing exception in Rule .0104(d) applies, and never later than the first
   offer by a represented party.**
4. **Individual designated dual agents act only as agent for the principal for whom they are
   designated**, similar to an exclusive listing agent or buyer agent.
5. **A comprehensive written company policy on the practice of designated dual agency is recommended.**
6. **A broker may NOT be appointed as a designated dual agent for one party if that broker has ALREADY
   RECEIVED CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION about the other party.**
7. **A broker-in-charge (BIC) must NOT serve as a designated dual agent in a transaction OPPOSITE AN
   AFFILIATED PROVISIONAL BROKER** — Rule 58A .0104(j).

**Instructor Note:** *"Multiple agents can be designated to represent a principal, such as including
the licensed personal assistant of a designated dual agent."*

**Provision 6 is the trap.** A licensee who took a call from the buyer weeks earlier, and learned what
they would pay, cannot then be designated for the seller. **Provision 7 is the one that catches
offices:** your BIC cannot be designated against you, because the supervisory relationship makes the
separation unreal.

### C.4 Individual broker dual agent — Commission Rule 58A .0104(n)

A single broker, not a firm:

chunks.heading: D. Agent's Duties
chunks.excerpt:
- **Can represent a prospective buyer who wishes to buy a property listed with that broker, with the
  permission of both clients.**
- **The broker CANNOT share a client's information without their permission that pertains to:**
  - **willingness to agree to a price, terms or any conditions of sale other than those offered;**
  - **motivation for engaging in the transaction, unless disclosure is required by statute or rule;
    and**
  - **any information the client has identified as confidential, unless disclosure is required by
    statute or rule.**

**Three protected categories, each with the "unless required by statute or rule" carve-out on the last
two.** A client cannot make a material fact confidential merely by labelling it so.

---

## D. Agent's Duties

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"**Compare and contrast duties owed to clients
> vs. third parties.** It is critical that licensees understand the difference in the standard for
> determining what information must be disclosed to a principal/client versus what must be disclosed
> to a third party/customer (such as a lender)."*

### D.1 Duties to the principal under NC License Law and Commission rules — eight

Transcribed, with the Commission's citations:

**a.** **The duty to avoid any wilful or negligent misrepresentation of a material fact to the
principal, and to disclose to the principal all material facts about which the agent has knowledge or
should reasonably have acquired knowledge** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(1) and (3).

**b.** **The duty to avoid making any false promises to the principal** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(2) and (3).

**c.** **The duty to avoid any undisclosed conflict of interest** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(4); Rule 58A
.0104(d)–(f), (i) and (j).

chunks.heading: D.2 Duties to third persons — NCGS 93A-6(a) and case law *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
**d.** **The duty to properly account for funds held in trust for the principal** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(7),
(12) and (14).

**e.** **The duty to act competently in the performance of services required by the agency
relationship** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(8); various rules.

**f.** **The duty to avoid improper conduct and to be honest in all dealings with the principal — as
well as in dealings with other parties** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(10).

**g.** **The duty to deliver a copy of any written agency and transactional documents to the client
WITHIN 3 DAYS of the broker's receipt of the executed document** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(13); Rule 58A .0106.

**h.** **The duty to disclose any commissions, referral fees, kickbacks and similar payments from third
parties** — Rule 58A .0109.

**Duty (g) is a hard deadline and it is the one most often missed in ordinary practice: three days from
your receipt of the executed document.**

### D.2 Duties to third persons — NCGS 93A-6(a) and case law *(Level 3)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed, and it is the Commission telling you where to put the emphasis:**

> *"Emphasis should be on a proper understanding of **misrepresentation and omission**, and especially
> the **AFFIRMATIVE DUTY TO DISCOVER AND DISCLOSE MATERIAL FACTS TO ALL PARTIES to the contract,
> REGARDLESS OF AGENCY RELATIONSHIPS.**"*

The duty itself:

> **"Duty to avoid any wilful or negligent misrepresentation of a material fact to a third party and to
> disclose to the third party all material facts RELATING TO THE PROPERTY about which the broker has
> knowledge or should reasonably have acquired knowledge"** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(1) and (3) and case law.

**Now compare D.1(a) and D.2, which is what the Required Activity asks you to do:**

chunks.heading: D.3 Required Activity evidence — client/customer duty lab
chunks.excerpt:
| | To the **principal/client** | To a **third party/customer** |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | **all material facts** about which the agent has or should have knowledge | **all material facts RELATING TO THE PROPERTY** about which the broker has or should have knowledge |
| Standard | knowledge, or should reasonably have acquired knowledge | knowledge, or should reasonably have acquired knowledge |
| Affirmative duty to discover | yes | **yes** |

**The standard is the same; the SCOPE differs.** To a client, everything material to the transaction —
including, per Module NC-07, **personal information about a third party that might influence your
principal**. To a customer, everything material **relating to the property**.

**And the affirmative duty to DISCOVER runs to everyone.** North Carolina does not permit a broker to
be a passive conduit for whatever the seller happened to mention.

### D.3 Required Activity evidence — client/customer duty lab

For each fact, first identify the broker's principal; then decide who must receive the information.

chunks.heading: E. General Requirements for Agency Contracts — NCGS 93A-13; Rule 58A .0104(a)
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Roof leak in the listed property.** It is a property-related material fact. The listing broker
   must advise the seller-client and disclose it to prospective buyers; a direction to conceal it is
   not a lawful instruction.
2. **Buyer privately says they would pay $25,000 more.** The buyer's agent protects that bargaining
   information and uses it for the buyer's benefit. A seller's agent receiving the same statement does
   not owe buyer-agency confidentiality and must advance the seller-client's interests without making
   a misrepresentation.
3. **Seller's urgent relocation motive.** It may be material to the seller-client's negotiating
   position but is not a physical property fact owed to an unrepresented buyer merely because the
   buyer asks.
4. **False occupancy statement proposed for the lender.** Honesty is owed in dealings with all parties.
   The broker must not submit or assist a false statement even if the client requests it.

**Completion record:** the learner submits a four-row matrix naming the client, customer, property
fact, confidential fact, required disclosure, prohibited disclosure, and controlling duty for each
scenario. The instructor checks the reasoning, not merely the final label.

---

## E. General Requirements for Agency Contracts — NCGS 93A-13; Rule 58A .0104(a)

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Prior to entering an agency agreement with a prospective client, the
broker should **ask if they already have an agency agreement with another broker**. If 'yes,' the broker
should **wait for that existing agency agreement to be terminated or expire**."*

### E.1 The writing requirement

chunks.heading: E.2 Requirements for a written agency agreement — rule text reconciled
chunks.excerpt:
> **"Agency contracts with PROPERTY OWNERS must be in writing FROM THE OUTSET of the relationship."**
>
> **Instructor Note: "Oral listing agreements and property management agreements are UNLAWFUL in NC."**

### E.2 Requirements for a written agency agreement — rule text reconciled

**a.** **Cover a definite period of time and terminate without prior notice when that period expires.**
The landlord-procurement/rent-collection agreement described in Rule .0104(a) may allow automatic
renewal if the landlord may terminate with notice at the end of a contract period or renewal.
**b.** **Contain the anti-discriminatory language prescribed by rule in a clear, conspicuous manner** —
Rule 58A .0104(b).
**c.** **Be signed by all parties.**
**d.** **Include the broker's licence number.** Any early-termination penalty must be clear and
conspicuous.

**Buyer/tenant timing rule:** the agreement must be express and written and signed no later than the
time one party makes an offer. But if the agreement binds the buyer/tenant for a period or restricts
the right to work with other agents or without an agent, it must be written and signed **from
formation**. A broker may not continue representation after the rule requires a writing.

**Note precisely where the exception runs.** Owner-side agreements — listings and property management —
must be written from the outset. A buyer/tenant relationship may begin expressly without a writing
only while it neither binds the consumer for a period nor restricts the consumer's freedom to work
with others, and it must be written no later than the offer deadline.

---

## F. Listing Practices (Working with Sellers)

### F.1 Prelisting activities

Advise the seller to gather:

chunks.heading: F.2 The prelisting/listing meeting
chunks.excerpt:
- **a copy of the seller's deed;**
- **a copy of the survey, if available;**
- **a copy of the protective covenants and HOA information, including dues and assessments;**
- **the balance due on the seller's mortgage(s) and the status of the mortgage(s).**

### F.2 The prelisting/listing meeting

**Agency disclosure first:**

- **Caution the seller about sharing confidential information PRIOR to signing a listing contract** —
  which is purpose 1 of the WWREA disclosure, applied.
- **Advise the seller of the company's proposed brokerage fee and services.**
- **Determine the agency relationship with the seller.**

**Inspect the property and prepare the listing data sheet:**

- **Explain the listing agent's obligation to disclose material facts to ALL prospective buyers.**
- **Note all significant features and defects.**
- **Identify personal property to be transferred and fixtures NOT to be conveyed.**
- **Suggest needed repairs, improvements, staging.**
- **Determine square footage and acreage.**
- **Make sure listing data is accurate and complete.**

**And four further inquiries the Commission specifies:**

- **Inquire about construction/alteration/repair to uncover possible mechanics' lien claims and the
  need for permits.** *(Module NC-06: a properly perfected claim may relate back to first furnishing;
  a notice to the lien agent is not itself perfection.)*
- **Inquire about septic system capacity/permit, if the property has an onsite septic system.**
- **Discuss the marketing plan.**
- **Review documents and information obtained from the seller.**
- **Verify and properly report building square footage.**

chunks.heading: F.3 Determine an appropriate listing price
chunks.excerpt:
*(The Commission's **Residential Square Footage Guidelines** is a required resource for that last item.
**This project has not obtained it and states no measurement standard from it.**)*

### F.3 Determine an appropriate listing price

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"**Assign math practice problems; students
> traditionally have difficulty with this on the license exam.**"*

- **Perform a Comparative Market Analysis (CMA).**
- **Calculate the sale price needed to net "X" amount to the seller**, or estimate net to seller at
  various sale prices.
- **Calculate net profit/loss to the seller on the sale.**
- **Review with the seller all factors that should be considered.**

*Worked — net to seller.* A seller must net **$92,000** after paying a **hypothetical negotiated 6%**
brokerage fee, a loan
payoff of **$186,400**, and other seller costs of **$3,150**.

Required before the fee: 92,000 + 186,400 + 3,150 = **$281,550**.
That is **94%** of the sale price, since the fee takes 6%.
Sale price = 281,550 ÷ 0.94 = **$299,521.28**, so **$299,600** rounded to a workable listing figure.

*Check:* 299,600 × 0.06 = 17,976 fee. 299,600 − 17,976 − 186,400 − 3,150 = **$92,074.** ✓

**Divide by (1 − rate). Do not multiply by (1 + rate)** — that is the error the Commission is warning
about, and it gets the answer wrong every time.

#### F.3a Required Activity evidence — calculation set

The percentages below are invented for practice. They are **not customary, recommended, or set by the
Commission, an MLS, or an association**; actual brokerage compensation is negotiated.

chunks.heading: F.4 Complete the listing contract form
chunks.excerpt:
1. A property sells for **$410,000**. Hypothetical negotiated brokerage compensation is **5%**, the
   payoff is **$248,600**, and other seller debits are **$4,900**. Calculate net proceeds.
2. A seller needs **$135,000** after a **4.5%** hypothetical negotiated fee, a **$276,500** payoff, and
   **$6,250** in other debits. Calculate the minimum price before rounding.
3. The owner bought for **$318,000**, paid **$6,400** buyer-side acquisition costs, later paid
   **$21,500** for improvements, and nets **$382,750** at resale. Calculate arithmetic gain for this
   exercise; do not label it taxable gain.
4. A proposed **$525,000** price produces a hypothetical **$21,000** brokerage charge, a **$301,250**
   payoff, and **$8,875** other seller debits. What is the net and what percentage of price is the
   brokerage charge?

**Answer key:** (1) $136,000. (2) ($135,000 + $276,500 + $6,250) ÷ 0.955 = **$437,434.55**. (3)
$382,750 − $318,000 − $6,400 − $21,500 = **$36,850**. (4) net **$193,875**; brokerage charge **4%**.
Each submission must show the setup and a reverse check.

### F.4 Complete the listing contract form

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**Listing price must be determined BEFORE seller signs listing
contract.**"*

#### F.4a Required Activity evidence — distinguish the three listing types

chunks.heading: F.5 Comply with the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, if applicable
chunks.excerpt:
| Listing type | Exclusivity | When the listing firm ordinarily earns under the described structure |
|---|---|---|
| Exclusive right to sell | One listing firm has the right for the stated term. | A sale during the term ordinarily triggers the agreed compensation regardless of who locates the buyer, subject to the actual contract. |
| Exclusive agency | One listing firm is engaged, but the contract preserves the owner's stated right to sell without owing that firm. | The firm ordinarily earns when it or another broker is the procuring cause; the owner-sale exception depends on the agreement. |
| Open listing | The owner may engage multiple firms and may also sell directly. | The broker who is the procuring cause ordinarily earns the agreed compensation; an owner-direct sale may produce none. |

**Scenario check:** Seller signs an exclusive-agency agreement with Firm A, then personally locates and
contracts with the buyer without broker procurement. The learner must explain why the result differs
from an exclusive-right-to-sell agreement and why the actual signed wording controls. Then change the
facts so Firm B produced the buyer under an open listing and identify the procuring-cause issue.

### F.5 Comply with the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, if applicable

Module NC-05, including the broker's own compliance duty.

### F.6 Market the listed property per the contract and customary marketing practices

## G. Working with Buyers

### G.1 Provide and review the WWREA; explain agency options; create the relationship

**Working with buyers as a SELLER SUBAGENT**, or **as a BUYER AGENT**.

**Buyer-agency writing decision:**

chunks.heading: G.2 The remaining steps
chunks.excerpt:
1. The representation must be **express**; consumer silence does not create it.
2. If it binds the buyer for a period or restricts the buyer's right to work with another agent or
   without an agent, it must be written and signed **when formed**.
3. Otherwise, it may begin without a writing, but every required term should be agreed rather than
   assumed.
4. It must be reduced to a signed writing no later than the time either party makes an offer.
5. The broker may not continue representation after the rule requires the signed writing.

Then: **exclusive versus nonexclusive written agreement**; **the option of limiting the duration of an
exclusive agreement**; **the option of limiting an exclusive agreement to specific properties.**

**Working with an unrepresented seller (FSBO) as a buyer agent — three steps:**

1. **Provide and review the WWREA Disclosure.**
2. If compensation or cooperation is sought from the seller, **obtain the appropriate written
   compensation/cooperation agreement**; do not convert it into a seller-agency agreement.
3. **Refrain from actions that might be interpreted as the broker representing the seller.**

**Step 3 is where undisclosed dual agency is created by accident.** A buyer agent who advises the FSBO
seller on price or legal terms, drafts custom language, or otherwise undertakes to advance the seller's
interests may create a representation conflict and may also cross the legal-practice boundary. A
written fee agreement alone does not make the seller a client.

### G.2 The remaining steps

chunks.heading: H. Working in Property Management *(Level 2 except as noted)*
chunks.excerpt:
2. **Prequalify the buyer.** **Instructor Note:** *"Preferable approach is to have buyer prequalified by
   a mortgage loan officer."*
3. **Select properties for showing.**
4. **Schedule properties for showing** — **disclose agency status to the listing agent, or to the seller
   if a FSBO**, and **obtain a cooperation agreement with the listing company if needed**. **Instructor
   Note:** *"In the Buyer Agency Agreement, the brokerage company promises to **first seek compensation
   from the listing firm or the seller before looking to the buyer client** for payment."*
5. **Show properties.**
6. **Discover and disclose material facts to the buyer.**
7. **Obtain or verify information for the buyer** — property disclosure statements, HOA information,
   protective covenants, other information requested.
8. **Perform a CMA** to assist the buyer in determining an appropriate offer price.
9. **Assist the buyer with preparation of offers; present and negotiate offers.**
10. **Assist the buyer with preparations for closing.**

## H. Working in Property Management *(Level 2 except as noted)*

### H.1 The relationship

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"**In NC, there is NO SEPARATE real estate license for 'property
managers'.**"*

- **The authority of the broker (agent) is established by the property management contract.**
- **Duties of the broker to the property owner (principal) and to third persons (tenants and
  prospective tenants).**
- **Property management fee** *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*.

chunks.heading: H.1a Required Activity evidence — tenant-screening decision matrix
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"**Discuss factors that may/may not be
> considered due to Fair Housing Act criteria (e.g., credit reports, criminal records).**"*
>
> **This activity must be completed**, and Module NC-09 supplies the fair housing framework it applies.

#### H.1a Required Activity evidence — tenant-screening decision matrix

The manager applies the owner's **written, legitimate, transaction-relevant criteria consistently**
and routes disability/accommodation and criminal-record edge cases to the BIC or counsel. A third-party
screening product does not transfer the housing provider's fair-housing responsibility.

| Proposed factor | May be considered? | Required safeguard |
|---|---|---|
| Verified income or ability to pay | Generally yes | Use the same documented standard for similarly situated applicants; account for lawful income sources and accommodation/program rules. |
| Credit history | Generally yes | Use accurate, relevant information consistently; follow consumer-report notice/dispute duties and do not use it as a proxy for a protected class. |
| Prior rental-payment or lease-performance history | Generally yes | Verify comparable facts and apply the same look-back and evidence standard. Do not count disability-related facts without considering a required reasonable accommodation. |
| Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability | No | Never rank, steer, discourage, vary terms, or deny because of a protected characteristic. |
| Presence of children | No as a disqualifier | Apply lawful occupancy standards without treating familial status less favorably. |
| Disability or nature/severity of disability | Not as a screening factor | Ask only for information permitted to evaluate a requested ac

chunks.heading: H.2 Typical provisions of property management contracts
chunks.excerpt:
commodation when the need is not obvious; keep the inquiry limited. |
| Arrest alone or a blanket exclusion for any criminal history | High-risk; do not use as an automatic rule | Criminal history is not itself a federal protected class, but a broad or inconsistently applied policy can create fair-housing liability. Use current counsel-approved criteria tied to a legitimate safety/property interest and current law. |

**Scenarios:** (1) Two applicants have the same verified income and credit profile; the manager demands
extra proof only from the applicant with children — prohibited unequal treatment. (2) A neutral credit
standard flags an error; the manager follows the consumer-report dispute/adverse-action process rather
than improvising. (3) A disability-related rental-history issue accompanies an accommodation request;
the manager pauses the ordinary screen and uses the established accommodation workflow. (4) A blanket
“any arrest ever” denial is rejected and escalated for current legal review.

### H.2 Typical provisions of property management contracts

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Per Commission Rule 58A .0104(a), **all property management
agreements must be in writing from inception of the relationship**."*

- **Property description.**
- **Contract period** — Rule 58A .0104(a) — which **may allow automatic renewal**, and under which the
  **landlord may terminate with notice at the end of any contract period or renewal period.**
- **The agent's management fee.**
- **The agent's authority.**
- **The responsibilities of agent and owner.**

### H.3 Typical property management duties *(Level 1)*

chunks.heading: Required artifacts and activities in this section
chunks.excerpt:
**Preparing a management plan** — establishing a rental schedule, preparing an operating budget;
**marketing the property**; **qualifying and selecting tenants**; **executing leases for the owner**;
**collecting rents and security deposits**; **handling collected monies according to laws/rules**;
**maintaining the property**; **preparing/enforcing rules and regulations**; **maintaining property
insurance**; **maintaining accurate records.**

*(North Carolina's Tenant Security Deposit Act and Vacation Rental Act are Section XIV's business and
are taken up in Module NC-14, where the gap in this project's reading is recorded.)*

The current WWREA disclosure and companion Q&A must be available to the student and reviewer. The
