lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-09

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-09
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-09

## Section IX · Real Estate Practice

**Commission Syllabus section:** IX — Real Estate Practice
**Instructional Level:** **2** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* **Fair Housing is Level 3.** **Typical property management duties, the
design and construction requirement, fair housing enforcement and penalties, the ADA, and the whole of
Risk Management are Level 1.**
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 14 items**, the second-heaviest national
section.
**Instructional hours:** **4.0**, incorporating the Commission's recommended 1.5 hours for Fair
Housing/Anti-discrimination.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. State the three limits on broker responsibility and apply the rule on soliciting another firm's
   active clients.
2. Distinguish the listing contract types, including limited service and protection agreements.
3. Name the eleven typical full service listing contract provisions.
4. Name the ways a brokerage agreement terminates.
5. Describe the types of brokerage compensation and state the position on net listings.
6. **Recite the seven federal protected classes and the prohibited practices.** *(Level 3)*
7. **Distinguish blockbusting, steering and redlining and give examples of each.** *(Level 3)*
8. State the fair housing enforcement routes and their filing periods. *(Level 1)*
9. State what the Civil Rights Act of 1866 covers and how it is enforced.
10. Describe the ADA's application to a real estate office. *(Level 1)*
11. Apply the Do Not Call rules to expired listings and FSBOs. *(L

chunks.heading: A. Broker Responsibility
chunks.excerpt:
evel 1)*
12. Explain vicarious liability and antitrust exposure. *(Level 1)*
13. Distinguish fraud from misrepresentation and describe E&O and general liability cover. *(Level 1)*

---

## A. Broker Responsibility

### A.1 Practise within the scope of your experience

### A.2 Avoid the unauthorized practice of law

Module NC-10 sets out the North Carolina prohibition in full. The principle here: **completing
preprinted forms is permitted; drafting is not.**

### A.3 Soliciting the active clients of other firms

- **May constitute tortious interference with contractual relations.**
- **Violates the Code of Ethics (Article 16) of the National Association of REALTORS®**, which governs
  members of that Association.

**And the Commission's rule for the situation that actually arises, transcribed:**

> If a seller **whose property is currently listed with another company** initiates a conversation with
> a broker about the broker becoming their new listing agent, the broker:
>
> - **"May discuss the terms of the possible listing agreement that would begin AFTER the current
>   listing ends"**; but
> - **"Should NOT suggest that the seller terminate the current listing agreement early."**

**The seller may raise it; you may discuss a future listing; you may not encourage them to break the
present one.**

---

## B. Creating Brokerage Agreements

### B.1 Seller — the listing agreement

**General concepts:** it **usually creates special agency**; it **must usually be in writing** — and in
North Carolina, per Module NC-08, **agency contracts with property owners must be in writing from the
outset and oral listings are unlawful**; and the **agency contract is owned by the brokerage company**,
not by the individual broker.

**Types of listing contracts:**

chunks.heading: B.2 Typical full service listing contract provisions — eleven
chunks.excerpt:
**Full service listing contracts:**

- **Open or nonexclusive listing.**
- **Exclusive agency listing.**
- **Exclusive right to sell listing.**

**Limited service listing contracts:**

- **Brokerage compensation is frequently a fixed or flat fee** rather than a percentage of gross sales
  price.
- **"May limit services, but generally should NOT limit legal duties dictated by statute or state
  regulations."**
- **Instructor Note:** *"Consultation with a real estate attorney is recommended prior to creating such
  an agreement."*

**That distinction — services may be limited, statutory duties may not — is the whole of limited
service brokerage in one line.**

**Protection agreements:**

- **An agreement between a buyer agent and a seller for a single transaction**, usually when dealing
  with a **For Sale By Owner (FSBO)** situation.
- **The agent should provide and review the Working with Real Estate Agents Disclosure with the
  seller.**

**Multiple or Cooperative Listing Services (MLS).** **Instructor Note:** *"Mandatory training on MLS use
is standard among the various MLS organizations."*

### B.2 Typical full service listing contract provisions — eleven

**Term of agreement. Property description**, including fixtures and personal property. **Listing price
and terms of sale. Broker/firm's compensation. Cooperation with and compensation to other brokerages.
The brokerage company's duties. Marketing. Earnest money. Seller's representations and duties.
Dual/designated agency authorization. Names and signatures of parties.**

chunks.heading: B.3 Buyer — the buyer representation agreement
chunks.excerpt:
*(Recall Module NC-08 E.2: a North Carolina written agency agreement must additionally have a **definite
expiration date**, the **prescribed anti-discriminatory language** in a clear conspicuous manner,
**signatures of all parties**, and the **listing broker's individual licence number.**)*

### B.3 Buyer — the buyer representation agreement

**Nonexclusive buyer agency** and **exclusive buyer agency**, and their typical provisions.

### B.4 Landlord — the property management agreement

**Instructor Note:** *"Per Commission Rule 58A .0104(a), **all property management agreements must be in
writing from inception of the relationship**."*

Typical provisions: **property description; contract period; agent's management fee; agent's authority;
responsibilities of agent and owner.**

**Typical property management duties** *(Level 1)*: establishing a rental schedule; preparing an
operating budget; marketing the property; qualifying and selecting tenants; executing leases for the
owner; collecting rents and security deposits; **handling collected monies according to laws/rules**;
maintaining the property; preparing and enforcing rules and regulations; maintaining property
insurance; maintaining accurate records; **preparing income/expense reports and accounting to the
owner**; **performing the landlord's legal duties**; **instituting legal actions such as tenant
eviction**; and **complying with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing laws.**

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Discuss factors that may/may not be considered
> due to **Fair Housing Act criteria (e.g., credit reports, criminal records)**."*

### B.4a Required Activity evidence — neutral tenant-screening matrix

chunks.heading: B.4a Required Activity evidence — neutral tenant-screening matrix
chunks.excerpt:
Apply the same written screening standard to every applicant. A criterion is not made lawful merely by
omitting a protected class from the application, and it is not made unlawful merely because it is not
listed in the Fair Housing Act. The decision turns on **what criterion is used, why it is used, whether
it is applied consistently, and whether disability accommodation or another governing law changes the
analysis.**

| Proposed factor | Federal fair-housing classification | Required broker response |
|---|---|---|
| race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status or disability | protected statutory basis | never use to refuse, rank, steer, alter terms, or decide availability |
| credit history or documented ability to meet rent | not itself one of the seven statutory bases | use only a written, transaction-related standard applied consistently; comply separately with consumer-reporting law |
| conviction record | not itself a statutory protected class | do not treat withdrawn HUD criminal-record guidance as current law; apply the owner's lawful written standard consistently and never as a pretext for protected-class discrimination |
| arrest without a disposition or an inaccurate vendor match | not an automatic fair-housing answer | pause the decision, verify the record and governing policy, and obtain BIC/counsel review rather than improvise a rule |
| source of income | not a federal Fair Housing Act class | check North Carolina, local and housing-program law before using it; do not convert it into a proxy for a protected class |
| disability-related request to change a rule, policy, practice or service | possible reasonable accommodation | route through the accommodation process; do not treat the request itself as a negative screening factor |
| an as

chunks.heading: B.5 Termination of agency agreements
chunks.excerpt:
sistance animal under a no-pets policy | possible reasonable accommodation | evaluate under the accommodation rules, not the pet rules; a pet deposit or fee is not charged merely because the animal is present |

**Current-source warning.** HUD withdrew its 2022 criminal-record guidance on September 17, 2025 and
states on its current fair-housing page that earlier guidance discouraging criminal background checks
is no longer its enforcement policy. This course therefore does **not** teach the withdrawn guidance as
binding. The statutory prohibition on intentional discrimination because of a protected class still
controls every screening decision.

### B.5 Termination of agency agreements

**Expiration. Completion/full performance. Termination by law. Destruction of property or death of
principal. Mutual agreement. Breach of contract.**

### B.6 Broker/firm's compensation

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"Discuss various ways brokerage fees are
> determined."*

**Types:** **percentage of gross sale price; fixed or flat fee; fee for services for named services;
protection period; net listing.**

**Instructor Note on net listings, transcribed:** *"Use of net listing arrangements is **either illegal
or strongly discouraged in most states** due to the great potential for abuse and fraud based on
inherent conflict of interest."*

**Co-listing by more than one broker/company.**

### B.6a Required Activity evidence — compensation-method lab

The numbers below are hypothetical arithmetic inputs, not customary rates. For each method, identify
what the parties must negotiate and where a conflict can arise.

chunks.heading: C. Fair Housing *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
| Method | Worked example | Compliance point |
|---|---|---|
| percentage of sale price | At a hypothetical negotiated 2.4 percent on $410,000, the fee is $9,840. | The parties negotiate the percentage; never describe it as standard or customary. |
| fixed fee | The agreement states $4,500 for the defined package of services. | State the included services and do not contract away statutory or regulatory duties. |
| fee for named service | Photography is $600 and contract coordination is $1,200. | Identify each service and charge rather than implying full service. |
| protection-period fee | A protected buyer identified during the listing closes after expiration. | The written agreement controls the defined period, identified prospects and fee trigger. |
| net listing | The seller is promised a stated net and the broker keeps the excess. | The structure creates an acute conflict and abuse risk; do not use it without current BIC and legal approval. |
| co-listing | Two firms agree how a negotiated fee will be divided. | Division does not authorize competitors to set market-wide prices or exchange future pricing plans. |

---

## C. Fair Housing *(Level 3)*

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"**Provide examples of each type of
> discrimination.**"*
>
> **This activity must be completed.** Work each prohibited practice below and produce a concrete
> example — including at least one that a licensee could commit without intending to.

### C.1 The Federal Fair Housing Act — Title VIII of the 1968 Civil Rights Act

**Purpose: equal opportunity in housing.**

**Protected classes — the Commission's own list and its own order:**

chunks.heading: C.2 Prohibited practices in the sale or rental of housing
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Familial status**
2. **Race**
3. **Sex**
4. **Handicapping condition/disability**
5. **Color**
6. **Religion**
7. **National Origin**

### C.2 Prohibited practices in the sale or rental of housing

- **Blockbusting (or panic peddling).**
- **Steering (or channeling).**
- **Refusing to sell, rent, or negotiate based on membership or PERCEIVED membership in a protected
  class.**
- **Representing that a dwelling is not available for sale or lease when it is.**
- **Discriminatory practices in terms, conditions, or privileges; in the FINANCING of housing** —
  e.g. **redlining** and related practices — **and in ADVERTISING.**

**Instructor Note on advertising, transcribed:** *"**Includes any Internet or social media posting.**"*

**Note "perceived membership".** A refusal based on what a licensee **assumed** about someone is a
violation whether or not the assumption was correct.

**And the practical discipline, which the Required Activity should surface:** steering is most often
committed by helpful-sounding remarks — *"you'd be more comfortable over there," "that's really more of
a family neighbourhood"* — and by **omission**, simply not showing or mentioning areas that meet the
buyer's own stated criteria. **Never characterise who lives anywhere.** Current HUD guidance does not
require silence about school quality or crime information: a broker may provide reliable information
when it is supplied **equally and consistently** and the broker is not intentionally steering because
of a protected characteristic.

### C.2a Required Activity evidence — discrimination examples

chunks.heading: C.2a Required Activity evidence — discrimination examples
chunks.excerpt:
Classify each fact pattern before reading the answer. Intent is not required for the learner to spot
the dangerous act; the exercise is designed to prevent the act before a court or agency must classify
the evidence.

| Type | Concrete example | Correct action |
|---|---|---|
| refusal to sell, rent or negotiate | a landlord rejects an otherwise qualified applicant after learning the applicant is Muslim | stop the decision; religion may not be used |
| false availability | a broker tells a Black prospect “nothing is open” while offering the same unit to a White tester | provide truthful, equal availability information |
| unequal terms or services | families with children are charged a higher deposit than otherwise identical households | use the same lawful written terms |
| discriminatory advertising | a social post says “ideal for Christians” or “no children” | remove the preference; internet and social advertising are covered |
| steering/channeling | a broker omits qualifying homes in one area because of the buyer's race | show options based on the buyer's stated property criteria, not a protected class |
| blockbusting/panic peddling | a broker solicits listings by claiming that families of a named national origin are moving in and values will fall | do not induce a sale through protected-class representations |
| redlining/financing discrimination | a lender changes price or availability because the collateral is in a predominantly Black neighborhood | apply lawful underwriting without protected-class geography as the reason |
| disability accommodation | a housing provider rejects a necessary exception to a no-pets rule without evaluating an assistance-animal request | evaluate the requested policy change and the statute's defenses |
| disability modification | a

chunks.heading: C.2b Current HUD neighborhood-information lab
chunks.excerpt:
landlord categorically refuses a tenant-paid grab bar needed for use of the unit | evaluate and permit a reasonable modification subject to lawful conditions |
| design and construction | an elevator building first occupied after March 13, 1991 has inaccessible common areas and doorways | covered multifamily design requirements reach all units in that elevator building |
| retaliation or interference | a manager threatens a tenant for filing a fair-housing complaint | do not coerce, threaten, intimidate or interfere with protected activity |

### C.2b Current HUD neighborhood-information lab

HUD's April 24, 2026 letter says the Fair Housing Act does not itself prohibit a real-estate
professional from sharing neighborhood crime-rate or school-quality information. It also states that
unlawful steering requires intentional discrimination based on a protected characteristic. Apply that
distinction:

1. A buyer asks for the school district's published performance data. Provide the same reliable source
   and explanation you would provide every similarly situated buyer.
2. A buyer asks for “the right kind of people.” Decline to classify residents or neighborhoods by
   protected characteristics.
3. A broker sends crime data only to buyers of one race to discourage them from an area. The data does
   not cure the intentionally discriminatory use; stop the steering.
4. A brokerage elects a written policy of linking every consumer to the same official school and crime
   sources. Apply it consistently and keep the source/date in the file.

### C.3 Exemptions

The exemptions are narrow and must be read separately from the advertising prohibition:

chunks.heading: C.4 Design and construction of multi-family housing *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
- Under 42 U.S.C. §3603(b)(1), a qualifying private owner of no more than three single-family houses
  may fall outside specified §3604 prohibitions only if the detailed ownership/transaction conditions
  are met, **no real-estate broker or agent is used**, and no discriminatory advertisement is used.
- Under §3603(b)(2), rooms or units in a dwelling for no more than four independent families may fall
  within an exemption when the owner actually occupies one unit. Section 3604(c)'s advertising rule is
  not part of that exemption.
- Section 3607 contains narrow noncommercial religious-organization and private-club rules and the
  housing-for-older-persons provisions. The latter limits familial-status coverage; it is not a general
  license to discriminate on another protected basis.
- Section 1982's race-based equal-property right does not inherit these Fair Housing Act exemptions.
- North Carolina or local law may be more restrictive. Module NC-15 applies that separate state layer.

### C.4 Design and construction of multi-family housing *(Level 1)*

The Syllabus shorthand says all buildings with four or more residential units constructed after March
13, 1991. The current statute is more precise: the requirement concerns **covered multifamily dwellings
designed and constructed for first occupancy after March 13, 1991**. It reaches **all units in a
building with four or more units and one or more elevators**, but only **ground-floor units** in another
building with four or more units. Public/common areas, routes, doors and adaptive-design features carry
the requirements in 42 U.S.C. §3604(f)(3)(C) and (f)(7).

### C.5 Enforcement and penalties *(Level 1)*

chunks.heading: C.6 The Federal Civil Rights Act of 1866
chunks.excerpt:
- **Conciliation** — an attempt to resolve the complaint through **informal negotiations**.
- **HUD administrative complaint:** file with the **Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity
  (FHEO)** no later than **one year after the alleged discriminatory practice occurred or terminated**.
- **Private civil action:** file in an appropriate state or federal court no later than **two years
  after occurrence or termination**; time while a qualifying administrative proceeding is pending is
  excluded from that calculation.
- **Section 3617** makes coercion, intimidation, threats or interference with protected fair-housing
  activity unlawful. Do not turn that civil prohibition into an automatic criminal-penalty statement:
  the separate criminal statute, 42 U.S.C. §3631, requires its own elements, including force or threat
  of force and specified intent.

**One year administratively; two years by private suit.** Both figures are the Commission's.

### C.6 The Federal Civil Rights Act of 1866

- **42 U.S.C. §1982 protects the same right as White citizens to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold
  and convey real and personal property.** The Commission teaches this as the 1866 Act's race rule with
  no Fair Housing Act exemptions.
- Enforce the right through civil litigation. This course does not repeat the Syllabus's unsupported
  “federal court only” shortcut; forum, parties and remedies are legal questions.

### C.7 The Americans with Disabilities Act *(Level 1)*

chunks.heading: D. Risk Management *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Title III addresses places of public accommodation and commercial facilities.** A customer-facing
real-estate or rental office is a sales/rental or service establishment and is covered; an isolated
employees-only administrative office may be only a commercial facility. Obligations include equal
access to services, effective communication, accessible new construction/alterations, and removal of
existing architectural barriers where readily achievable. Do not treat the ADA and the Fair Housing
Act as interchangeable: the office and customer service are the ADA problem; the dwelling transaction
and reasonable accommodation/modification are the Fair Housing Act problem.

---

## D. Risk Management *(Level 1)*

### D.1 Supervision

The basic agency relationships are as Module NC-07 sets out. The client engages the **firm**, and an
affiliated broker may act within that firm's express representation. That is not the same as saying
that every affiliated broker automatically becomes a common-law subagent, and it does not create
outside-firm seller subagency. An outside firm needs the seller's written authorization and the
required disclosure. The Commission adds one further rule here:

> **"When an affiliated broker leaves the brokerage, they CANNOT take the contracts/clients with
> them."**

Because the agency contract is **owned by the brokerage company**, not by the individual.

**Responsibilities of the employing broker — firm or BIC:**

- **Supervising all actions of affiliated licensees and employees.**
- **Providing training for affiliated licensees.**

### D.1a Required Activity evidence — client versus third-party duties

chunks.heading: D.2 Do Not Call laws and rules
chunks.excerpt:
| Situation | Client duty | Duty to customer or other third party |
|---|---|---|
| seller wants a known roof leak concealed | obedience reaches only lawful instructions; loyalty does not permit concealment | disclose the material fact honestly and fairly |
| buyer asks for negotiating advice | provide loyal advocacy, lawful obedience, confidentiality, accounting, disclosure, skill and care | do not misrepresent the buyer's position to the seller |
| unrepresented buyer asks whom the listing broker represents | protect seller confidences | disclose agency status and deal honestly; do not imply representation of the buyer |
| competing offer exists | follow the seller's lawful disclosure instruction and protect confidential strategy | do not invent, exaggerate or reveal offer information without authority |

The evidence rule is simple: **client status adds fiduciary/agency duties; customer status never removes
honesty, fairness and material-fact disclosure.**

### D.2 Do Not Call laws and rules

chunks.heading: D.2 Do Not Call laws and rules
chunks.excerpt:
- **The National Do Not Call Registry is maintained by the Federal Trade Commission.** A live sales
  call to a listed number requires an applicable basis such as the seller's own established business
  relationship or the consumer's clear written permission; an entity-specific do-not-call request
  overrides an established relationship.
- The established-business-relationship periods in the FTC rule are **18 months after a qualifying
  transaction** and **three months after the consumer's inquiry or application**. The relationship is
  with the seller, not every competitor or affiliate.
- A compliance process uses Registry data downloaded no more than **31 days** before the call, written
  procedures, training, an entity-specific suppression list, monitoring and records. The ordinary FTC
  calling window is **8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time** absent prior consent otherwise.
- Do not collapse live calls, prerecorded calls and texts into one rule. Prerecorded sales calls and
  automated calls/texts have separate written-consent and opt-out requirements under the TSR/TCPA;
  an established relationship does not by itself authorize a prerecorded sales call.

**The two North Carolina practice traps the Commission spells out:**

- **Calls to homeowners with EXPIRED listings with another broker/company are prohibited — "the
  'established business relationship' exemption only applies to the expired listing broker."** So the
  broker whose listing expired may call; **you may not.**
- **Calls to solicit a listing from a FSBO on the Registry are prohibited.** **But the Instructor Note
  adds the exception:** *"**Broker MAY call a registered FSBO on behalf of a prospective buyer-client
  who is interested in buying the FSBO property.**"*

chunks.heading: D.2a Do Not Call decision drill
chunks.excerpt:
**No exception survives the consumer's entity-specific request not to be called.** Penalty amounts and
FCC consent rules can change; verify them at the campaign date rather than encoding an old syllabus
figure.

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"Brokers should stay up-to-date on any restrictions on **electronic
communication (e.g., email, texts, social media)** that might affect their solicitation of business in
that manner. **Mass electronic newsletters or 'just listed/sold' emails would be subject to such
restrictions.**"*

### D.2a Do Not Call decision drill

1. You did not hold the expired listing. The seller's prior relationship with the former listing firm
   is not your relationship. If the number is registered and there is no other valid basis, do not call.
2. An FSBO number is registered and your purpose is to solicit the listing. Do not call.
3. A buyer-client asks you to contact that FSBO about the identified property. The Commission treats
   the property inquiry differently from listing solicitation; identify the buyer purpose and do not
   turn the call into a listing pitch.
4. A past client tells your firm “do not call again.” Stop live and automated solicitation even if an
   18-month transaction period otherwise remains.
5. Before any campaign, document the call type, consent or exception, Registry scrub date, local time,
   caller identity and opt-out handling. Escalate automated calls, texts and mass electronic campaigns
   for current TCPA/FCC review.

### D.3 Vicarious liability

chunks.heading: D.4 The Sherman Antitrust Act
chunks.excerpt:
- **Liability for another's actions because of the relationship between the parties.**
- A firm and BIC have regulatory supervision responsibilities for affiliated brokers. Civil vicarious
  liability is a separate, fact-specific agency question: scope of work, control and the act at issue
  matter. Do not tell a student that every act by every affiliate automatically creates civil liability.
- A genuine subagency relationship can create responsibility through agency principles; Module NC-07
  explains why outside-firm seller subagency is not automatic in North Carolina.

### D.4 The Sherman Antitrust Act

Section 1 prohibits agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Agreements among competitors to fix
prices, allocate customers or markets, or rig bids are criminal violations; group boycotts and trade-
association restraints may also violate the Act. Current DOJ enforcement specifically treats real-
estate brokerage competition and commission rules as antitrust issues.

**And the Commission's own instruction, transcribed:**

> **"NEVER imply or state that the quoted fee is 'customary' or 'the going rate' for the industry or a
> local area."**
>
> **Instructor Note:** *"Brokers should **only discuss their company's fee** and **not answer questions
> about how this fee compares to fees of other companies**."*

**That is a stricter practice rule than "don't collude."** It forbids characterising your own fee as
customary, and it forbids answering a comparison question at all.

### D.5 Fraud and misrepresentation

chunks.heading: D.6 Types of liability insurance
chunks.excerpt:
- **The employing broker must discourage all fraud/misrepresentation by affiliates.**
- **Fraud requires intentional deception; negligent misrepresentation is a different theory.** Do not
  teach “negligent fraud” as though intent and negligence were interchangeable.
- North Carolina licensing discipline separately reaches willful **or negligent** material
  misrepresentation or omission under G.S. 93A-6(a)(1). That regulatory wording does not redefine the
  elements of common-law fraud.

### D.6 Types of liability insurance

- **Errors and Omissions (E&O)** — **"covers most mistakes made in listing and selling activities."**
- **General liability** — **"covers the risk assumed when the public enters the brokerage building."**

The Syllabus warns that criminal acts, fraud, civil-rights violations and antitrust conduct may fall
outside coverage. Treat that as a prompt to read the actual policy, not as a universal coverage ruling:
definitions, exclusions, defense obligations and endorsements vary. Intentional misconduct cannot be
made safe by assuming E&O will defend it.

---

## Required Activities in this section — all four must be completed

1. **Discuss factors that may or may not be considered due to Fair Housing Act criteria**, e.g. credit
   reports and criminal records. Evidence: B.4a.
2. **Discuss the various ways brokerage fees are determined.** Evidence: B.6a.
3. **Provide examples of each type of discrimination.** Evidence: C.2a and C.2b.
4. **Compare and contrast duties owed to clients versus third parties.** Evidence: D.1a.

## Module NC-09 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-09
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-09

Drawn from **Section IX** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Every Instructor Note, Required Activity and numbered list above is
**transcribed from the Syllabus** — including the seven protected classes in the Commission's own order,
the March 13 1991 design and construction date, the one-year and two-year filing periods, the Do Not
Call rules on expired listings and FSBOs, the antitrust instruction never to call a fee customary, and
the insurance exclusions.

Current primary-text reconciliation read 42 U.S.C. §§3603-3607, 3610, 3613, 3617 and 1982; current HUD
fair-housing, disability and April 2026 neighborhood-information material; HUD's September 2025
withdrawal notice; ADA Title III; the FTC's current TSR/Do Not Call compliance guide; current DOJ
antitrust guidance; G.S. 93A-6; and Commission Rules 58A .0104, .0105 and .0109. Those sources control
the corrections above.

**Source limitation — still not fully reconciled in its own text:** the TCPA and all current FCC implementing provisions;
the common-law elements and remedies for tortious interference,
fraud, negligent misrepresentation and vicarious liability; insurance policy forms; and the NAR Code
of Ethics, which governs Association members rather than licensees generally. No variable penalty or
damages figure is presented as current. North Carolina's separate anti-discrimination provisions are
reconciled in Module NC-15.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-10

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-10
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-10

## Section X · Brokerage Practices in NC

**Commission Syllabus section:** X — Brokerage Practices in NC
**Instructional Level:** **2** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* **The broker's land-use verification responsibilities, Delivery of
Instruments, Misrepresentation/Omission of Material Facts, and Improper Brokerage Commissions are
Level 3.** **Land Use Controls generally and Trust Account Basics are Level 1.**
**Licence examination weight:** **State Exam Category — 12 items**, the second-heaviest state section.
**Instructional hours:** **4.0**, allocated within the Commission's recommended emphasis for Property
Disclosures and Contracts and Closing.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

> **Important Note on trust accounts, transcribed from the Syllabus:** *"Cover **basics** of trust
> accounts and handling of trust money. **Detailed accounting/recordkeeping procedures for brokerage
> trust accounts are NOT TESTED on the license examination.** Instructors and students are **strongly
> urged to use the coverage of this topic in the Comments section of the LLCR.**"*
>
> **This project has not obtained the current LLCR PDF.** Part A.6 therefore limits detailed accounting
> instruction to a submission gate, but it now states the current text of Rules 58A .0116-.0118 and
> G.S. 93A-6(g) for the basic deposit, custody, dispute and account rules. The rule text is controlling;
> the missing LLCR Comments cannot be simulated.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Selected Regulated Practices
chunks.excerpt:
1. State North Carolina's statutory authority for zoning and describe the broker's land-use
   responsibilities. *(Level 3)*
2. State the North Carolina rule on environmental hazards as material facts.
3. Describe the NC Leaking Petroleum Underground Storage Tank Cleanup Act at the level the Syllabus
   states it.
4. **Apply the 3-day delivery rule for offers, including its five qualifications.** *(Level 3)*
5. State the trust money definition, deposit rule, exceptions and basic account requirements. *(Level 1)*
6. **Classify a fact as material or not material under North Carolina's declared categories.** *(Level 3)*
7. **State the five items North Carolina has declared material or not material.** *(Level 3)*
8. Explain the affirmative duty to discover and why disclaimers do not work.
9. State the prohibition on drafting and what a broker may lawfully do with a form.
10. **Apply the improper brokerage commission rules.** *(Level 3)*
11. **Separate multiple-offer guidance from Rule .0115's prohibition on revealing an offeror's terms.**
12. State the broker's settlement statement obligation.

---

## A. Selected Regulated Practices

### A.1 Land use controls *(Level 1 except as noted)*

**Current NC statutory authority for governmental zoning — Chapter 160D:**

- **The General Assembly has police power per the state constitution.**
- **A local government may adopt zoning regulations under G.S. 160D-702**, subject to the current
  Chapter's procedures, limits and the local ordinance actually governing the property.

chunks.heading: The broker's responsibilities for verification of land use *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
**Currency correction.** The Syllabus still names former county/city enabling provisions in Chapters
153A and 160A. G.S. 160D-111(c) now directs references to repealed or superseded parts of those former
provisions to the most nearly corresponding part of Chapter 160D. A broker verifies the current local
zoning map, ordinance and development approval; the broker does not decide legal validity or vested
rights.

**Highway access restrictions.** **Instructor Note:** *"Ability to access an existing public highway or
street that abuts the property **is a material fact**; access may be restricted or forbidden by state or
local municipality."*

**Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act — 15 USC 1701 et seq.:** purpose; land registration
requirement; application; exemptions.

#### The broker's responsibilities for verification of land use *(Level 3)*

**Instructor Note, transcribed — and this is the section's clearest statement of the North Carolina
standard:**

> *"Under the NC Real Estate License Law, a licensee has **a duty to avoid any misrepresentation
> regarding permitted land use, to recognize potential land use problems, and AN AFFIRMATIVE DUTY TO
> DISCOVER AND DISCLOSE any such problems.** Licensee is **NOT expected to conduct a title search for
> covenants or interpret covenants** as to what activities are permissible; **advising clients to have
> an attorney perform such actions would be appropriate.**"*

**Both halves matter.** There is an affirmative duty to **discover** land use problems — and there is
**no** duty to search title for covenants or to interpret them, and doing the latter would be advising
on the law. **Discover the problem; route the interpretation.**

chunks.heading: A.1a Level 3 evidence — land-use verification lab
chunks.excerpt:
The five specific requirements repeat Module NC-05 A.1 and are stated in both sections because the
Commission states them in both:

- advise that **ordinances or covenants could affect use and enjoyment**;
- advise that owners **may be subject to owners' association dues and assessments**;
- advise that **careful review of covenants and association governing documents is recommended PRIOR TO
  SIGNING ANY OFFER**;
- **avoid any misrepresentation about zoning or permitted land uses**;
- **recognize "red flag" situations**, **recognize patent signs of flooding**, and **disclose planned
  major highway or public transportation changes in the area as a material fact.**

#### A.1a Level 3 evidence — land-use verification lab

For a listing advertised as suitable for a duplex and short-term rental, the broker records: the
current local zoning map and ordinance source; the parcel's district; whether each proposed use is
permitted, conditional or prohibited; known development approvals; access/flood/transit red flags;
and every unresolved question routed to the local authority or counsel. The broker reports source and
date, never promises that a use is “grandfathered,” and does not interpret private covenants.

### A.2 Environmental issues

**The North Carolina formulation, transcribed — note that it is worded more strictly than Section V's:**

> *"The presence on a property of any of the environmental hazards **that is KNOWN OR SHOULD HAVE BEEN
> KNOWN by a North Carolina broker** is a material fact in North Carolina that **must be disclosed to
> all transactional parties.**"*

**NC Leaking Petroleum Underground Storage Tank Cleanup Act — NCGS 143-215.94A-.94E:**

chunks.heading: A.3 Delivery of instruments *(Level 3)* — NCGS 93A-6(a)(13) and (14); Rule 58A .0106
chunks.excerpt:
- G.S. 143-215.94A separately defines the **tank owner**, **operator**, **facility** and **landowner**;
  ownership of the land does not automatically answer who owns or operates the tank.
- When a petroleum release is determined, G.S. 143-215.94E(a) directs the tank owner or operator to
  notify the Department, collect/remove the release and restore the affected area. Current-fact and
  fund-eligibility rules are more specific than the slogan “the present landowner always pays.”
- Current law contains a landowner protection where the person owns the tank only by owning the land,
  did not know or have reason to know it was there, and did not receive the land through a transfer to
  avoid liability. Where the owner/operator cannot be identified or fails to act, G.S. 143-215.94E(b1)
  separately permits the current landowner to undertake work and seek specified fund treatment.
- **Broker responsibilities:**
  - A broker discloses a known or reasonably discoverable release, contamination, abandoned tank or
    other material tank condition. Mere historical tank presence is not converted here into an
    automatic legal-liability conclusion.
  - **The buyer agent should strongly encourage the buyer to hire an expert to inspect the tank and
    conduct a soil contamination test.**

The broker identifies red flags, recommends qualified inspection/DEQ review and discloses the material
facts; counsel and DEQ determine statutory responsibility, cleanup and fund eligibility.

### A.3 Delivery of instruments *(Level 3)* — NCGS 93A-6(a)(13) and (14); Rule 58A .0106

**a. Assist with delivery of completed RPOADS disclosure statements.** *(Module NC-15 now contains the
current Chapter 47E workflow and retained, page-reviewed REC 4.22 and REC 4.25 forms.)*

chunks.heading: A.3a Level 3 evidence — offer presentation and delivery clock
chunks.excerpt:
**b. Submit offers — and this is the rule to know cold:**

> **"Brokers must present ALL offers (including multiple offers and back-up offers) to the offeree (or
> their agent) IMMEDIATELY but in no case LATER THAN 3 DAYS from the broker's receipt of the executed
> offer."** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(13); Rule 58A .0106(a)

**Five qualifications, all transcribed:**

1. **"EVEN IF PROPERTY ALREADY UNDER CONTRACT."**
2. **"Broker CANNOT 'HOLD' offer while negotiating compensation agreement."**
3. **"Concurrent offers must be presented at the same time; no particular order of presentation is
   required."**
4. **"ORAL presentation of the offer terms to the offeree DOES NOT NEGATE the requirement for the broker
   to deliver the offer within 3 days."**
5. **"Applies to ALL brokers in the transaction regardless of who they represent or how they will be
   compensated."**

**Qualification 2 is the one that catches new licensees**, and it is worth stating plainly: **you may
not sit on an offer while you work out what you will be paid.** Qualification 4 closes the other obvious
escape: telling the seller about it over the phone does not satisfy the three-day delivery requirement.

**c. Furnish copies of offers and contracts** — Rule 58A .0106(a).

**d. The broker's responsibilities relating to settlement statements** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(14). See B.6.

#### A.3a Level 3 evidence — offer presentation and delivery clock

chunks.heading: A.4 Advertising — Commission Rule 58A .0105
chunks.excerpt:
At 10:00 a.m. Monday the listing broker receives one signed offer; at noon a second signed offer; the
seller is already under contract. The broker promptly sends both to the seller together rather than
ranking or holding either, records the receipt/presentation times, and delivers each executed offer
document to the proper customer/client no later than three days after receipt. An oral summary does not
replace document delivery. Compensation negotiations do not stop either clock.

### A.4 Advertising — Commission Rule 58A .0105

- A broker needs the BIC's consent to advertise brokerage services or another's real estate and names
  the affiliated firm or sole proprietorship in the advertisement.
- Advertising another's property requires the owner's or authorized agent's written consent.
- A blind ad is prohibited: the advertisement identifies that it is by a broker or firm and is not
  limited to contact information that makes it appear to be the principal's own offer.

### A.5 Record retention — Commission Rule 58A .0108

Transaction records are retained **three years from the later of transaction conclusion or disbursement
of all broker-held funds**. If agency ends before the transaction concludes, the trigger is the later of
agency termination or disbursement. The listed records include contracts, offers, leases, agency and
disclosure documents, trust records, closing statements, advertising and supporting square-footage
work. An affiliated broker provides covered transaction documents to the firm within three days of
receipt. This is not “three years from closing” in every case.

### A.6 Handling trust funds *(Level 2 except as noted)*

#### Definition of trust money — NCGS 93A-6(a)(12); Rule 58A .0116(a)

chunks.heading: Trust account basics *(Level 1)*
chunks.excerpt:
> **"Trust money: Money belonging to others received by a broker who is acting as an agent in a real
> estate transaction."**
>
> **"Includes money received as an escrow agent or temporary custodian of funds belonging to others."**
>
> **"Most common examples: earnest money deposits, down payments, tenant security deposits, and
> rents."**

#### Trust account basics *(Level 1)*

The Commission lists ten points with their citations. Stated here as the Syllabus states them, with the
citations preserved so a student can read the source:

1. **Basic required features** — NCGS 93A-6(g); Rule 58A .0117(b) and (f).
2. **Proper designation of the trust account and FDIC insurance** — Rule 58A .0117(b).
3. **When a trust account is required** — Rule 58A .0116(a): trust money held in a fiduciary capacity
   is deposited in a qualifying trust or escrow account unless a stated exception applies.
4. **Property owners' association account separation** — Rule 58A .0118(a): a dedicated account for
   one association, not commingled with another association's or person's funds, plus statements at
   least every 90 days.
5. **COMMINGLING OF FUNDS PROHIBITED** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(12).
6. **A limited, separately ledgered company-funds exception for bank service charges** — Rule 58A
   .0117(c)(4)(B). It is not permission to operate from client money or mix ordinary business funds.
7. **Requirements for an interest-bearing trust account** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(12); Rule 58A .0116(c).
8. **THE BROKER-IN-CHARGE IS RESPONSIBLE FOR THE TRUST ACCOUNT** — Rule 58A .0110(g)(4). **Instructor
   Note:** *"BIC remains responsible for trust monies and records **even if others are allowed to assist**
   with maintenance of the trust account."*
9. **Disbursement of earnest money to the settlement agent** — Rule 58

chunks.heading: Handling of trust money
chunks.excerpt:
A .0116(e).
10. **Handling disputed trust funds** — NCGS 93A-12; Rule 58A .0116(d).

#### Handling of trust money

**The basic deposit rule:** unless a paragraph (b) exception applies, Rule 58A .0116(a) requires trust
money to be deposited no later than **three banking days after receipt**. The current exceptions are:

- a **Provisional Broker delivers it upon receipt to the affiliated broker**;
- a **Limited Nonresident Commercial Broker delivers it to the affiliated resident NC broker** under
  Rule 58A .1808;
- **non-currency earnest money or tenant security deposits received with a pending offer** are
  deposited no later than three days after acceptance, whose date is stated in the agreement;
- **a check or other negotiable instrument payable to the seller for an option or due diligence fee**
  is delivered or returned under buyer instructions and cannot be retained more than three business
  days after contract acceptance;
- **a check or other negotiable instrument payable to a third party escrow agent in a sales transaction
  for trust monies.**

Before an interest-bearing deposit, all interested parties give written authorization that conspicuously
states how and to whom interest is disbursed. A disputed non-residential-security deposit stays in trust
until written release or court order, subject to Rule .0116(d)'s abandoned-claim route; alternatively,
G.S. 93A-12 permits clerk-of-court deposit after its notice and 90-day waiting procedure. Earnest money
may transfer to the settlement agent no more than 10 days before anticipated settlement; another
pre-settlement use requires written party consent. Rule .0116(g) separately prohibits conversion or
misapplication and requires safeguarding.

chunks.heading: B. Prohibited Practices
chunks.excerpt:
G.S. 93A-6(g) requires a demand deposit account in a federally insured depository institution lawfully
doing business in North Carolina that makes the records available to the Commission. Rule .0117
requires identifying records and monthly reconciliation. The current LLCR Comments and its detailed
ledger examples remain missing; they must be obtained and reviewed before submission, and this lesson
does not invent or reproduce them.

**Three things a provisional broker must nevertheless carry into their first week:**

- **Trust money is other people's money from the moment it reaches you.**
- **Commingling is prohibited by statute** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(12).
- **Your BIC is responsible for the trust account**, and remains responsible even where others assist —
  so **deliver trust money to the firm and follow the firm's procedure exactly.**

---

## B. Prohibited Practices

> **Required Activity — prescribed by the Commission:** *"**Compare and contrast duties owed to clients
> vs. third parties.** It is critical that licensees understand the difference in the standard for
> determining what information must be disclosed to a principal/client versus what must be disclosed to
> a third party/customer (such as a lender)."*
>
### B.0a Required Activity evidence — client versus third-party disclosure

chunks.heading: B.1 Misrepresentation and omission of material facts *(Level 3)*
chunks.excerpt:
| Information | Duty to the client | Duty to a third party/customer |
|---|---|---|
| property defect the broker knows or reasonably should know | disclose promptly; advise investigation/remedy options within competence | volunteer the material fact regardless of whom the broker represents |
| client's motivation or confidential negotiating limit | use for the client's benefit; do not disclose without authority unless law requires | do not disclose merely because it may help the customer |
| buyer's known inability to complete after financing collapses | advise the buyer-client candidly and route legal consequences to counsel | disclose the material ability-to-complete fact; do not help submit a misleading offer |
| lender or settlement-agent document the broker knows is inaccurate | tell the client and correct/route the error | deal honestly; do not transmit or remain silent about a known material falsehood |

The fiduciary layer owed to a client is broader, but the duty not to misrepresent and to disclose
material facts reaches transaction parties. Confidentiality does not authorize concealment of a fact
that law requires the broker to disclose.

### B.1 Misrepresentation and omission of material facts *(Level 3)*

**The disciplinary rule** — NCGS 93A-6(a)(1) permits discipline for any willful or negligent
misrepresentation or omission of material fact; subsection (a)(3) separately reaches a course of
misrepresentation or false promises. Rule 58A .0114(c) preserves the broker's independent duty for
covered residential property even when the owner uses a disclosure statement.

**Concepts: misrepresentation; omission; puffing; material facts.**

#### The four categories of material fact

Transcribed:

chunks.heading: Items declared MATERIAL in North Carolina
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Facts about the property itself.**
2. **Facts relating directly to the property.**
3. **Facts relating directly to the ABILITY OF THE PARTIES TO COMPLETE THE TRANSACTION.**
4. **Facts known to be of SPECIFIC IMPORTANCE TO A PARTY.**

**Category 3 is not about the building at all** — it reaches a buyer whose financing has collapsed or a
seller who cannot deliver title. **Category 4 is client-specific:** information identified as important
may create a fiduciary investigation/advice duty even where it is not a fact that must be volunteered to
every third party. Do not relabel confidential motivation as a universally disclosable material fact.

#### Items declared MATERIAL in North Carolina

Transcribed, and these three are examinable:

- **EIFS / synthetic stucco exterior siding — EVEN IF FULLY REPLACED.**
- **A known history of polybutylene leakage or probable defect — including a repaired history.**
- **A current or former "meth" house.**

**Read the remediation clauses.** Remediation does not erase known history. Current September 2025
Commission guidance also draws the other boundary: the **mere presence** of polybutylene piping is not
itself a material fact. A known leak, evidence of damage, probable defect, or relevant neighboring-unit
failure changes the analysis; a buyer broker should consider the client's insurer restrictions.

#### B.1a Level 3 evidence — material-fact classification lab

chunks.heading: Items declared NOT MATERIAL in North Carolina
chunks.excerpt:
For each case, record category, known/should-have-known evidence, investigation step, recipient and
written disclosure: fully replaced EIFS; polybutylene present with no failure evidence; a documented
prior polybutylene leak; a radon result received after the first contract terminated; a buyer whose
loan approval was withdrawn; seller motivation; a nearby registered offender; and a direct question
about a prior occupant's death. The correct result cannot be produced by the shortcut “physical equals
material, stigma equals immaterial.”

#### Items declared NOT MATERIAL in North Carolina

Transcribed:

- **Reputation as a haunted property.**
- **Death or illness of a previous or current occupant.**

**Both of these are North Carolina positions and they differ from other states.** They also do not
license a licensee to lie: not material means **no duty to volunteer**, not permission to deny a direct
question falsely.

#### Discover and disclose

Four rules, transcribed:

1. **"Affirmative duty to discover and VOLUNTEER material facts to ALL parties to the transaction,
   REGARDLESS OF WHOM THE BROKER REPRESENTS."**
2. **"Broker cannot avoid responsibility for communicating incorrect and/or incomplete information BY
   ISSUING DISCLAIMERS."**
3. **"Broker has a duty to INVESTIGATE 'red flags' or questionable information."**
4. **"Broker's disclosure responsibilities under Real Estate License Law are NOT AFFECTED BY THE
   DOCTRINE OF CAVEAT EMPTOR; broker must still volunteer material facts to all transactional
   parties."**

**Rule 2 disposes of the "information deemed reliable but not guaranteed" footer as a defence.** Rule 4
disposes of "buyer beware." **Rule 3 is the affirmative one: a red flag creates a duty to investigate,
not merely to mention.**

chunks.heading: B.2 Discriminatory practices
chunks.excerpt:
### B.2 Discriminatory practices

Three current North Carolina controls operate together:

- **G.S. 93A-6(a)(10)** permits discipline for conduct the statute characterizes as improper,
  fraudulent or dishonest dealing.
- **Rule 58A .0120(d)** bars a broker from conducting brokerage or promoting broker status in a manner
  that discriminates because of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status or
  disability.
- **Rule 58A .1601** treats a licensee's violation of the North Carolina State Fair Housing Act as
  improper conduct under G.S. 93A-6(a)(10).

Module NC-09 supplies the current federal framework. Module NC-15 supplies the separate current North
Carolina State Fair Housing Act analysis; its definitions, exemptions and procedures are not presumed
identical to federal law.

### B.3 Unauthorized practice of law — NCGS 93A-4(e); 93A-6(a)(11); Rule 58A .0111

G.S. 93A-4(e) grants no authority to practice law, and G.S. 93A-6(a)(11) makes unauthorized practice a
disciplinary ground. G.S. 84-2.1 and Rule 58A .0111 draw the operational boundary:

chunks.heading: B.4 Improper brokerage commissions *(Level 3)* — Rule 58A .0109
chunks.excerpt:
- Acting as agent in the transaction, a broker may select and complete a compliant **preprinted**
  offer, option, sales-contract or lease form when a party authorizes or directs completion.
- The broker may store, complete and print the allowed preprinted forms electronically but may not
  alter the preprinted form before presenting it to the parties.
- If the parties propose a deletion or change, the form is marked to show it. Rule .0111 does not let
  the broker independently invent, rewrite or recommend legal language; unique language goes to an
  attorney.
- A broker may make nonbinding notes, memoranda and correspondence that record negotiations.
- Preparing a custom contract, deed, deed of trust or other legal instrument for another, or advising
  what a legal document means, crosses the boundary.

The safe question is not simply “am I filling a blank?” It is whether the broker is completing an
authorized preprinted transaction form under the rule or independently creating or interpreting legal
rights.

### B.4 Improper brokerage commissions *(Level 3)* — Rule 58A .0109

**a. Affiliated brokers.** Rule 58A .0120(b) permits direct payment of a commission or referral fee
only by the broker's **current BIC** or the person who **served as BIC at the time of the transaction**.
That rule applies to affiliated provisional and nonprovisional brokers; “the supervising BIC” alone is
an incomplete statement because the current-BIC alternative also matters.

**b. Ordinary referral or commission to a broker licensed only in another state.** The Commission's
Syllabus and official compensation guidance state the ordinary condition:

chunks.heading: B.4a Level 3 evidence — compensation routing lab
chunks.excerpt:
- **the out-of-state (foreign) broker holds an ACTIVE real estate licence in the state from which they
  are conducting the brokerage activity**, such as placing a referral; **and**
- **the foreign broker DOES NOT ENTER NC at any time during the transaction to engage in any brokerage
  activity related to the transaction.**

Do not confuse that ordinary out-of-state referral with a **Limited Nonresident Commercial Broker**.
G.S. 93A-9(b) creates a separate North Carolina limited-license route for commercial transactions with
resident-broker affiliation and supervision; Rule .1808 requires that limited licensee to deliver all
trust money to the affiliated resident broker. A referral fact pattern does not silently create that
license.

**c. Payment is prohibited to a broker with an expired or inactive licence, unless:**

- **the licence was on active status when the brokerage activity was performed**; and
- **the broker stopped all brokerage activity when the licence expired or became inactive.**

**Instructor Note, transcribed:** *"If the licences of the firm and the individual broker were on active
status **throughout the period during which brokerage services were rendered**, then the firm may be
paid and the firm may in turn pay the individual broker, **even if their licence is not active at the
time of payment**. **Payment is FORFEITED if EITHER of the licences were not active at ANY time that
brokerage services were being performed.**"*

*(Module NC-02 B.6 states the same rule. It appears in two sections of the Syllabus because it is
tested from both.)*

#### B.4a Level 3 evidence — compensation routing lab

chunks.heading: B.5 Disclosure of offers prohibited — Commission Rule 58A .0115
chunks.excerpt:
Classify each proposed payment before anyone promises it: a buyer rebate stated in the agency
agreement; a title-company gift card; direct payment from a closing attorney to an affiliated broker;
payment by the broker's former BIC for that BIC's transaction; a referral to an active Virginia broker
who never enters North Carolina; a Virginia broker who conducts a North Carolina showing; and work
performed partly while the North Carolina license was inactive. Record the license/affiliation status,
who may pay whom, required principal disclosure or consent, and the source that controls. Do not treat
“paid after closing” as a cure for unlicensed activity.

### B.5 Disclosure of offers prohibited — Commission Rule 58A .0115

Keep the authority layers separate:

- **Rule 58A .0115 itself** prohibits disclosing the **price or other material terms** in one party's
  offer to a competing party without the **express authority of the offering party**. That is the
  enforceable “do not shop the offer” rule.
- Current Commission multiple-offer guidance says the **existence of multiple offers is not a material
  fact** and need not be volunteered. A listing broker may disclose their existence with the seller's
  consent and, once doing so, should share that information fairly, equally and honestly.
- Seller consent to announce that multiple offers exist is **not** the competing offeror's authority to
  reveal price, escalation terms, due diligence fee, closing date or another material term.
- A broker must not answer a direct question falsely. Follow the seller's disclosure direction while
  responding honestly; if not authorized to reveal the existence of offers, do not invent “no.”

chunks.heading: B.6 Failure to deliver settlement statements to a client — NCGS 93A-6(a)(14)
chunks.excerpt:
The practical test has two gates: **seller authority for the existence message; offering-party express
authority for the offer's price or other material terms.**

### B.6 Failure to deliver settlement statements to a client — NCGS 93A-6(a)(14)

- **A broker may be subject to disciplinary action for failing to deliver a detailed and accurate
  settlement statement to their client at closing.**
- **A broker MAY rely on the settlement agent who prepared the statement for its delivery — BUT the
  broker MUST REVIEW THE STATEMENT FOR ACCURACY and NOTIFY ALL PARTIES TO THE CLOSING OF ANY ERRORS.**

**The review is the broker's, and it is not discretionary.** The settlement agent prepares and delivers;
**you check it and you speak up.**

### B.7 Commingling

Covered at A.6 above: **prohibited by NCGS 93A-6(a)(12)**, with the single limited exception at Rule 58A
.0117(c)(4)(B) permitting funds to cover bank service charges on the trust account.

---

## Required Activities in this section

**One:** **compare and contrast duties owed to clients versus third parties** — the same activity the
Commission prescribes in Section VIII. *(B)*

The **Level 3** subtopics — land-use verification, delivery of instruments, material facts, and improper
brokerage commissions — separately carry Level 3's requirement that students **complete practical work
assignments** applying the material to common fact situations.

## Module NC-10 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.
