## Instructor source note for Module NC-12

Drawn from **Section XII** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20. Every Instructor Note, Required Activity, percentage and structural
statement above is **transcribed from the Syllabus.**

Current-law reconciliation additionally uses **G.S. Chapter 45, Article 2A**; **G.S. 45-21.27,
45-21.29A, 45-21.36, 45-21.38 and 45-21.38A**; **G.S. 105-360**; **Regulation Z §§ 1026.19, .24 and .42**;
**Regulation X §§ 1024.14 and .15**; **Regulations B and V**; current official HUD, VA, USDA, FHFA and
Ginnie Mae program pages; and the official CFPB and ALTA form repositories. The Dodd-Frank Act and the
complete agency seller/servicer and underwriting handbooks were not read in full and are not used to
state a live eligibility result.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-12
chunks.excerpt:
The 1% point charge, the 1/8-percent yield **rule of thumb**, the 28/36, 31/43 and 43 percent classroom
ratios and seller-owns-settlement-date convention remain identified as Syllabus/examination inputs. The
stale labels for a statutory redemption period, an August tax due date, reversed Regulations B/V, an
automatic revised-LE waiting period and Ginnie Mae as a GSE are expressly corrected rather than repeated
as current law.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-13

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-13
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-13

## Section XIII · Property Valuation & Appraisal

**Commission Syllabus section:** XIII — Property Valuation & Appraisal
**Instructional Level:** **1** except as noted. *Assigned by the Commission; providers and instructors
are **REQUIRED to comply**.* The Commission raises **Basic Economic Principles of Value to Level 2**,
raises the whole of **Approaches to Value (Part D) to Level 2**, and raises the **Sales Comparison
Approach to Level 3** — the highest level it assigns anywhere in this section. It drops two depreciation
methods, **market abstraction** and **breakdown**, back to **Level 1**.
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 11 items.** *This is the second-heaviest
national category in the course.*
**Instructional hours:** **6.0**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

> ### Why the Sales Comparison Approach is Level 3
>
> The Commission states the reason in its own note, transcribed:
>
> *"Because the theory and methodology involved in this appraisal approach **mirrors that used when a
> broker performs a BPO/CMA on a residential property**, students **should practice its use**, with a
> focus on **estimating the probable sales price of residential properties**."*
>
> A North Carolina broker license, by itself, does not authorize appraisal practice. A broker may
> estimate probable selling or leasing price through a lawful CMA/BPO; a person who also holds an
> Appraisal Board credential may separately act in that credentialed capacity. The analytical overlap
> explains the Level 3 treatment, but it does not erase the statutory boundary.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: A. Introduction
chunks.excerpt:
1. Distinguish an appraisal, a CMA and a BPO, and state who regulates appraisers.
2. Distinguish value, cost and price, and list the four elements of value.
3. State the forces and factors that influence value.
4. **Apply the basic economic principles of value to a described property.** *(Level 2)*
5. State the eight steps of the valuation process in order.
6. **Estimate probable sales price by the Sales Comparison Approach, adjusting comparables correctly.** *(Level 3)*
7. **Apply the Cost Approach, including land value, cost estimation and depreciation.** *(Level 2)*
8. **Apply the Direct Capitalization and GRM income methods.** *(Level 2)*
9. **Reconcile the three approaches and explain why weighting beats averaging.** *(Level 2)*

---

## A. Introduction

### A.1 Key definitions

Three terms the Commission separates, and current North Carolina statutes make the boundary concrete:

- **Real estate appraisal.** G.S. 93E-1-4 defines it as an analysis, opinion or conclusion about the
  value of identified real estate or an interest in it, performed for compensation or other valuable
  consideration. G.S. 93E-1-2.1 generally requires the Appraisal Board credential.
- **Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) / Broker Price Opinion (BPO).** G.S. 93E-1-4 and 93A-82 define
  these as a licensed broker's estimate of a parcel's probable **selling or leasing price**, supported
  by property, market, neighbourhood and comparable information; an automated valuation model is not a
  CMA/BPO.

chunks.heading: A.2 Purpose
chunks.excerpt:
The Syllabus also says: **"On the National exam section, BPOs are performed specifically for lenders."**
Treat that as an examination convention, **not as a complete North Carolina practice rule**. Article 6
of Chapter 93A permits a qualified broker to prepare a CMA/BPO for several listed parties and purposes.
It also says the opinion cannot be the primary basis for determining value for mortgage-loan origination
and cannot be called a valuation or appraisal. A fee opinion carries additional writing, content,
license-status and disclaimer requirements under G.S. 93A-83.

The safe distinction is the product and authority used. A **broker license alone** supports a lawful
CMA/BPO estimating probable selling or leasing price. It does not authorize the broker to hold the work
out as an appraisal. A registered trainee may participate in appraisal work under the immediate personal
direction of a certified appraiser, with the report reviewed and signed as G.S. 93E-1-3(a) requires.

### A.2 Purpose

The Commission asks for the **purpose** of appraisal as its own subtopic.

### A.3 Regulation of appraisers

**Federal framework.** The Syllabus's phrase that FIRREA “created” The Appraisal Foundation is historical
shorthand and is not literally correct. The Foundation was established by appraisal organizations in
1987. Congress enacted FIRREA in 1989 and authorized the Foundation as the source of appraisal standards
and appraiser qualifications within the federal/state regulatory system.

chunks.heading: B. Basic valuation concepts
chunks.excerpt:
**Standards and qualifications.** The Foundation's Appraisal Standards Board develops **USPAP**; its
Appraiser Qualifications Board develops minimum qualification criteria. **USPAP is a body of ethical and
performance standards, not an appraisal form.** The Foundation identifies the 2024 USPAP edition as the
current edition with no scheduled end date as of this module's 2026-09-07 control date. This broker
prelicensing module does not attempt to teach or reproduce the copyrighted USPAP text.

**State regulator.** Chapter 93E creates the **North Carolina Appraisal Board**, which administers state
appraiser credentials and rules. That is a different body from the **North Carolina Real Estate
Commission**, which licenses brokers and regulates a broker's CMA/BPO activity under Article 6 of
Chapter 93A. Direct a complaint according to the capacity and conduct involved; do not assume every
pricing dispute belongs to one agency merely because a broker or appraiser participated.

**Report form.** The **Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR)** is the appraisal reporting product
used in the form activity below. It is separate from USPAP. During the current GSE transition, a legacy
Fannie Mae Form 1004/Freddie Mac Form 70 and the new data-driven UAD 3.6 URAR may both be encountered.

---

## B. Basic valuation concepts

### B.1 Definitions

**Appraisal. Value. Cost. Price / market price. Market value.**

These five are listed separately because they are five different things, and confusing them is the most
common valuation error a new broker makes.

- **Cost** is what was spent to create it.
- **Price** is what someone actually paid.
- **Market value** is what it should bring under defined market conditions.

chunks.heading: B.2 Assessment for tax purposes
chunks.excerpt:
A house can cost $400,000 to build, be priced at $360,000, and have a market value of $375,000, all at
the same moment, with no contradiction. The Commission returns to this in D.1 when it warns that a
feature adjustment is made at **market value**, *"which will probably be less than actual cost."*

### B.2 Assessment for tax purposes

Listed as its own subtopic. Assessed value is a fourth figure, set for taxation, and it need not equal
market value.

### B.3 The four elements of value

- **Demand**
- **Utility**
- **Scarcity**
- **Transferability**

All four must be present. A thing everyone wants, that is useful and rare, has no market value if it
cannot be transferred.

### B.4 Forces and factors influencing property value

- **Social trends**
- **Economic forces**
- **Government controls and regulations**
- **Environmental conditions**

**Required Activity, transcribed: "Provide examples of how each affects value."** Delivered in this
module's worked material, and the examples are drawn from concepts already taught in this course —
Module NC-03's zoning and land-use controls for government controls, Module NC-05's environmental
material for environmental conditions — so students see the connection rather than a fresh list.

chunks.heading: B.5 Basic economic principles of value *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
| Force or factor | Worked example | What the broker may conclude |
|---|---|---|
| **Social trend** | More local buyers seek a home office after work patterns change. | Otherwise similar homes with a functional extra room may command more demand; verify this in current market evidence rather than assuming a fixed adjustment. |
| **Economic force** | Major local employment contracts while mortgage rates rise. | Purchasing power and demand may fall, lengthening marketing time; the effect and effective date must be supported by current data. |
| **Government control or regulation** | A parcel is rezoned from residential to mixed use. | Legally permissible uses change, so highest and best use and market participants may change; zoning alone does not prove value increased. |
| **Environmental condition** | A property borders a noisy industrial use or lies in a mapped flood-hazard area. | Marketability, insurance or buyer demand may be affected; disclose known material facts and use competent data rather than guessing a dollar loss. |

### B.5 Basic economic principles of value *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*

**Required Activity, transcribed: "Provide an example of each principle."** Nine principles, each with an
example, and four of them carry the Commission's own notes:

chunks.heading: B.5 Basic economic principles of value *(Level 2 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
| Principle | Worked example | Commission boundary to remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Anticipation** | Buyers pay today for the expected benefit of a planned transit stop, after discounting approval and completion risk. | Value reflects expected future benefits, not a guaranteed future event. |
| **Change** | A stable residential corridor becomes a redevelopment area over several years. | Physical, economic, social and governmental conditions do not stay fixed. |
| **Competition** | Strong demand for one apartment type attracts new projects until added supply pressures rents. | Profit invites competing supply. |
| **Conformity** | A modest house in a neighbourhood of similar homes usually fits buyer expectations better than an overbuilt house on the same street. | Maximum value tends to occur where use and quality are reasonably compatible. |
| **Contribution** | A $60,000 kitchen adds $30,000 in supported market reaction. | The principle concerns increasing or diminishing return, **not cost**. |
| **Highest and Best Use** | A legally rezoned corner parcel may support a use different from its current house, but only after legal, physical, financial and productivity analysis. | There is **one** highest and best use at a time, and it can change. |
| **Plottage** | Two adjoining lots are worth $110,000 and $120,000 separately but $250,000 as one usable site. | Assemblage is the merger process; the $20,000 value increment is plottage. |
| **Substitution** | A buyer will not pay $420,000 for a house when an equally desirable substitute is available for $400,000. | This is the basis of the Sales Comparison Approach. |
| **Supply and Demand** | Ten similar listings and two active buyers indicate different negotiating pressure from two listings and ten buyers. | The market may be

chunks.heading: C. The valuation process — eight steps, in order
chunks.excerpt:
described as buyer- or seller-favoured, but the evidence and market date control. |

Four of those notes deserve a sentence each.

**Contribution** is the principle a broker uses every time a seller asks whether to renovate before
listing. The question is never what the work costs. It is what the finished feature adds to what the
property will bring — and the Commission's note says so directly. A $60,000 kitchen that adds $30,000 of
value contributed $30,000.

**Highest and best use** is stated with a precision worth keeping: **one** at a time, and it **changes**.
A single-family house on a corner that has been rezoned commercial may have a highest and best use that
is no longer a house.

**Plottage and assemblage** are a pair, and the Commission defines both in one sentence. **Assemblage is
the process**; **plottage is the resulting increment of value.** Merging is the verb; the extra value is
the noun.

**Substitution** is the load-bearing principle of Part D. A buyer will pay no more for this property than
for an equally desirable substitute. Everything the Sales Comparison Approach does is an attempt to find
that substitute and measure the difference.

---

## C. The valuation process — eight steps, in order

1. **Define the problem (task)**
2. **Determine appropriate scope of work**
3. **Collect, record, and verify data**
4. **Analyze data to determine highest and best use**
5. **Estimate value of land**
6. **Apply approaches to value**
7. **Reconcile approaches and estimate final value**
8. **Complete appraisal report**

chunks.heading: D. Approaches to value *(Level 2 except as noted)*
chunks.excerpt:
Note where **highest and best use** sits — step 4, before any approach is applied. The Commission's note
in B.5 called it *"a major factor for the appraisal process,"* and this is why: it is determined before
the valuation methods run, and it conditions them.

Note also that **land is valued separately at step 5**, before the approaches. That reappears in the Cost
Approach, where land is estimated separately and **never depreciated.**

---

## D. Approaches to value *(Level 2 except as noted)*

### D.1 Sales Comparison (Market Data) Approach *(Level 3 — this subtopic)*

#### D.1.a General information

- **Subject property** — the one being valued.
- **Comparable property (Comp)** — one recently sold.
- *"Estimates value by comparing subject property with recently sold similar or comparable properties;
  **based on substitution principle**."*
- *"**Most reliable and most commonly used approach for single-family properties** or any property that
  has an active market with recent comparable sales available."*

#### D.1.b Procedures

**Data collection and analysis**, then **selection of comparables**:

> *"Need **3-4 comps of the same property type** (e.g., residential, single-family detached, townhome,
> condo, etc.)"*
>
> *"As similar as possible to subject —* **Location; Physical characteristics and condition; Terms and
> condition of sale; Date of sale.**"
>
> ***"Cannot use currently listed or under contract property as a comp."***

chunks.heading: D.1.b Procedures
chunks.excerpt:
Those are the Commission's classroom rules for selecting **closed-sale comparables**. Do not enlarge
them into a claim that listings and pending sales are useless. The current UAD 3.6 URAR separately
reports active-listing and pending-sale market metrics, subject listing history, and may identify
additional properties analyzed but not used in the sales grid. A listing is not a closed sale; it can
still inform supply, competition, marketing time or trend analysis. The finished appraisal must explain
the data actually relied upon.

The Syllabus's “3-4” figure is also a course exercise baseline, not a universal form limit. Fannie Mae's
official completed SF5 sample displays five settled-sale comparables after a reconsideration of value,
and identifies another settled sale as analyzed but not used. The defensible rule is **enough relevant,
verified market evidence for credible results**, with the course exercise using the prescribed 3-4
closed-sale baseline unless the activity says otherwise.

**Adjustments to sale prices of comparables.** The single most important rule in this section, in the
Commission's own words:

> ***"Make adjustments to sale prices of the comps; never adjust the subject property."***

Say it as a sentence students can repeat: **you adjust the comps, not the subject.** The subject is the
unknown. Adjusting it would be adjusting the answer.

Which direction? The Commission names the two cases — **superior comparable** and **inferior comparable**
— and the Required Activity requires them to be worked:

> **Required Activity, transcribed: "Provide examples of how adjustments are made to the sales prices of
> superior and inferior comps."**

chunks.heading: D.1.c Required Activity evidence — superior and inferior adjustment lab
chunks.excerpt:
The logic follows from *"never adjust the subject."* You are making each comp into the subject on paper.
If the comp is **superior** — it has something the subject lacks — you **subtract** from the comp's sale
price, because the subject would not have brought that extra. If the comp is **inferior**, you **add**.
Superior down, inferior up.

Then two limits on the adjustment amounts:

> *"**No standard for adjustment amounts** — Value assigned for a feature adjustment is **market value,
> which will probably be less than actual cost.** — **Paired sales analysis.**"*
>
> *"**No adjustment needed for minor differences.**"*

**Paired sales analysis** is the method for deriving an adjustment honestly: find two sales alike in
everything but the one feature, and the difference between them is what the market paid for that feature.
It is the answer to *"no standard for adjustment amounts"* — the market supplies the number, the
appraiser does not invent it. And it is a direct application of **contribution** from B.5, which the
Commission said is measured by return and not by cost.

#### D.1.c Required Activity evidence — superior and inferior adjustment lab

Assume verified paired-market evidence supports a **$15,000** garage adjustment and a **$10,000**
condition adjustment. The subject has a garage and average condition.

| Closed sale | Sale price | Difference from subject | Adjustment to comp | Adjusted indication |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Comp A | $405,000 | No garage; otherwise similar | **+$15,000** because comp is inferior | **$420,000** |
| Comp B | $438,000 | Garage plus superior condition | **−$10,000** because comp is superior in condition | **$428,000** |
| Comp C | $421,000 | Garage; average condition; most similar | $0 | **$421,000** |

chunks.heading: D.2 Cost Approach
chunks.excerpt:
The subject is never adjusted. Comp A moves up to the subject's garage feature; Comp B moves down to the
subject's condition. The adjusted range is **$420,000-$428,000**. Comp C deserves the greatest weight
because it required no adjustment, but “no adjustment” does not mechanically make it perfect; verify
location, sale terms, date, data quality and every remaining difference. A supportable CMA would explain
why the probable-price range is concentrated near the best evidence rather than report a blind average.

**Reconciliation and determination of the value estimate:**

> *"Adjusted sales prices of comps should provide a **tight range of value**."*
> *"**Single indication of value should not be obtained by simple averaging** of the adjusted sales
> prices of comps."*
> *"**Weighted averaging.**"*

Averaging treats a comp that needed $2,000 of adjustment and a comp that needed $40,000 of adjustment as
equally good evidence. They may not be equally persuasive. Similarity, data quality and market support
all affect weight; gross or net adjustment size is not an automatic ranking formula. If the adjusted
figures do **not** form a tight range, recheck selection, verification and adjustment support rather than
average the disagreement away.

### D.2 Cost Approach

#### D.2.a General information

> *"Involves **separate estimates of value for the building and the land** that are combined for a value
> estimate for the entire improved property; **also based on the principle of substitution.**"*
>
> *"**Best approach for unique, non-income producing properties or special use properties** (e.g., houses
> of worship, schools, public buildings) **or newly constructed buildings that do not have comparable
> sales data available.**"*

chunks.heading: D.2.b Estimate of land (lot) value
chunks.excerpt:
The reason is limited comparable-sale evidence. A church, school or public building may have few useful
sales. New construction may have more supportable current-cost data and limited accrued depreciation,
but neither cost nor depreciation is automatically “precise.” The scope, data and property determine how
much weight the approach deserves.

#### D.2.b Estimate of land (lot) value

- *"Estimate using **the sales comparison method**."*
- ***"Land is never depreciated."***

Both halves matter. The Cost Approach does not escape the Sales Comparison Approach — it uses it for the
land component. And land never depreciates, which is why the two components must be estimated separately
before being added back together.

#### D.2.c Estimating building costs

- **Reproduction cost** — *"Frequently used to incorporate inherent value of historical property."*
- **Replacement cost** — by the **quantity survey method**, the **unit-in-place method**, or the
  **square foot method.**

**Reproduction** rebuilds it as it was, with the same materials and design. **Replacement** builds
something of equal utility using current materials and methods. On a Victorian with plaster mouldings,
reproduction and replacement are very different numbers, and the Commission's note says why reproduction
is chosen there. The three replacement methods run from most detailed to least: **quantity survey**
prices every material and labour item; **unit-in-place** prices installed components; **square foot**
applies a rate to area.

#### D.2.d Estimating depreciation

**Definitions:** **depreciation; effective age; economic life.**

**Effective age** is not chronological age. A 40-year-old house maintained impeccably may have an
effective age of 15. It is the age the condition suggests.

chunks.heading: D.2.e Steps in formulating the opinion of value
chunks.excerpt:
The Commission's warning, transcribed:

> ***"This is not the same concept as depreciation for tax purposes."***

Appraisal depreciation is loss in value from any cause. Tax depreciation is a cost-recovery schedule set
by tax law. The two share a word and nothing else.

**Depreciation methods:**

- **Age/life (straight-line) method** *(Level 2 — the section default)*
- **Market abstraction method** *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*
- **Breakdown method** *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*, which the Commission subdivides:
  - **Physical deterioration** — **curable and incurable**
  - **Functional obsolescence** — **curable and incurable**
  - **Economic (external or locational) obsolescence** — ***incurable only***

That last line is the Commission's examinable classification: **economic/external/locational
obsolescence — incurable only.** The classroom reason is structural rather than a repair-budget choice.
Physical deterioration and functional obsolescence arise in the property and may be classified curable
or incurable. External obsolescence arises beyond the property — for example, a neighbouring industrial
use or highway realignment — so the property owner cannot cure the external cause.

#### D.2.e Steps in formulating the opinion of value

1. **Estimate the value of the building and other improvements:**
   - **Estimate the current replacement or reproduction cost of the improvements**
   - **Estimate the depreciation accrued over the life of the improvement**
   - **Deduct the depreciation from the current cost estimate of the improvements**
2. **Estimate the value of the land as if vacant**
3. **Add the depreciated cost of improvements to the estimated land value** to determine the value
   estimate for the entire property

chunks.heading: D.3 Income approaches — Direct Capitalization and GRM only
chunks.excerpt:
*As if vacant* — note the phrase. The land is valued as though nothing stood on it, because whatever
stands on it has already been counted in step 1.

### D.3 Income approaches — Direct Capitalization and GRM only

The Commission limits this part explicitly to **two methods.**

#### D.3.a General information

- *"Based on **present worth of rights to future income**."*
- *"Approach used for **income-producing or investment properties**."*
- **Capitalization (CAP) rate**, with the Commission's note:

> *"The CAP rate **measures the risk** of an investment; **the higher the CAP rate, the higher the risk.**
> **The CAP rate and the market value are inversely related; as one goes up, the other comes down.**"*

Both halves of that note are examinable and students routinely keep only the first. Hold the inverse
relationship: at a fixed income, a **higher** cap rate produces a **lower** value. That falls straight out
of the formula below — the cap rate is the divisor. For the Syllabus exercise, “higher rate, higher risk”
is the required shorthand; in live valuation a market-derived cap rate reflects the market's required
return and multiple property, income, growth, liquidity and risk considerations. It is not a standalone
risk score.

#### D.3.b Direct capitalization method

- *"Converts the estimate of projected future income into an estimate of current market value."*
- *"Used for **most income-producing property other than 1-4 unit residential properties**."*

**The formula, in the Commission's own sequence:**

chunks.heading: D.3.c Gross rent multiplier (GRM) method
chunks.excerpt:
> **Determine net operating income (NOI) estimate**
> - *Estimate **potential annual gross income***
> - *Deduct an allowance for **vacancy and rental loss** to reach **effective gross income***
> - *Deduct **annual operating expenses***
> - ***NOI = Gross income – losses – expenses***
>
> **Note:** ***"Mortgage payments of principal and interest are not operating expenses, and are not
> included in calculations."***
>
> **Derive capitalization rate** *from local market experts or by Market Abstraction Method*
>
> ***Value = Net operating income (NOI) ÷ CAP rate***

The debt-service exclusion is the classic examination trap and it has a reason. NOI describes **the
property's** earning power. Two buyers could purchase the same building with completely different
financing — one all cash, one heavily leveraged — and the building's NOI is identical either way. Debt
service belongs to the buyer, not to the property, so it never enters the calculation.

#### D.3.c Gross rent multiplier (GRM) method

- *"Relates the sales price to the property's expected rental income."*
- *"Used for **1-4 unit residential income-producing properties**."*

**The Commission's sequence, transcribed:**

> *"Obtain sales price and gross income (rent) data on recently-sold comparable properties"*
> ***"Derive GRM for each comparable: GRM = sales price ÷ income"***
> *"Reconcile data to determine appropriate GRM"*
> *"Derive estimate of subject property's value: **Value = Rental income ÷ GRM**"*
>
> **Note:** *"GRM can use **either monthly or yearly** rental income data, but **be sure to be consistent
> throughout calculations.**"*

chunks.heading: D.3.c Gross rent multiplier (GRM) method
chunks.excerpt:
> **Instructor note — a discrepancy in the source, stated openly.**
>
> The two formula lines above are transcribed exactly as they appear in the Syllabus text obtained by
> this project. **They are not algebraically consistent with one another.** If **GRM = sales price ÷
> income**, then solving that same relation for the subject gives **Value = rental income × GRM**, not
> divided by it.
>
> This module **teaches the form that follows from the Commission's own definition of GRM** —
> **Value = rental income × GRM** — because the Commission states that definition first and the second
> line cannot be reconciled with it. A worked check makes the point: comps selling at $240,000 on $2,000
> monthly rent give a GRM of **120**; a subject renting for $2,100 monthly is then worth
> **$2,100 × 120 = $252,000**, which is a sensible figure. Dividing would give $17.50.
>
> **This discrepancy is flagged for the Commission's reviewer as an item to confirm against the current
> official Syllabus PDF before this course is submitted.** It is possible the source text obtained here
> carries an extraction or typographical artefact. **No item in this module's bank turns on the divide
> form**, and the engagement items state the relationship in words — *the multiplier converts rent into
> value, and value is the larger number* — so that a student is never graded on the ambiguity.
>
> **Section XVI settles the practical consequence.** In its Required Activity for the income approach the
> Commission states, in its own words: ***"There will be no calculations using a GRM."*** GRM is therefore
> examinable as a **concept** — what it relates, and which property class it serves — and **no computation
> using it is required anywhere in this course.** See Module NC-16.

chunks.heading: D.4 Reconciliation of the three approaches
chunks.excerpt:
The consistency warning in the Commission's note is worth its own line: a GRM derived from **monthly**
rent must be applied to **monthly** rent. Mixing monthly and annual figures produces an answer wrong by a
factor of twelve, and it is a favourite examination distractor.

**Two methods, two property classes.** Direct capitalization for **most income property other than 1–4
unit residential**; GRM for **1–4 unit residential income property.** The Commission draws that line
itself, and it is examinable.

### D.4 Reconciliation of the three approaches

> *"**Weighted consideration is preferable to averaging** of the approaches; **greater weight given to the
> approach that is best for that particular type of property.**"*

The same principle as D.1's weighting, one level up. For a single-family house, sales comparison often
carries the weight when current comparable evidence is strong. For a special-use property, cost may be
more informative. For an income-producing property, income evidence may be central. This is not a
property-type lookup table: the appraiser explains which approaches were necessary for credible results
and why the available evidence supports the final opinion. A simple arithmetic average conceals that
judgment.

> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"Show students on the appraisers' Uniform Residential Appraisal
> Report (URAR) form **where the appraiser reconciles the approaches used in the appraisal to arrive at a
> single opinion of value**."*

#### D.4.a Required Activity evidence — completed URAR walkthrough

chunks.heading: D.4.a Required Activity evidence — completed URAR walkthrough
chunks.excerpt:
The course uses Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's official **Single Family Scenario 5 (SF5)**. Fannie Mae
identifies SF5 as the most representative straightforward sample. The retained teaching copy contains
the publisher's scenario cover plus all 19 pages of the completed, data-driven UAD 3.6 URAR. It is an
illustrative fictional scenario, not an appraisal of North Carolina property and not a StateCourse
representation that every entry independently satisfies every law or professional standard.

Open `fannie-uad36-sf5-completed-sample.pdf` with the student and complete this guided review:

1. **PDF page 2 / report page 1 — Summary.** Locate the $350,000 Opinion of Market Value, the “As Is”
   condition, effective date, assignment reason, property-valuation method and appraiser identity. The
   summary is the destination, not the explanation.
2. **PDF pages 9-10 / report pages 8-9 — Market.** Locate active-listing and pending-sale counts,
   marketing time, price trend, subject listing information and prior-transfer analysis. This proves why
   a nonclosed property can inform market analysis without becoming a closed-sale comp in the grid.
3. **PDF pages 11-14 / report pages 10-13 — Sales Comparison Approach.** Trace five settled-sale
   comparables. Read every adjustment as an adjustment to the **comparable**, not the subject. On report
   page 11, the first three adjusted prices are $348,000, $350,000 and $353,500 and receive “Less”
   weight. On report page 13, comparables 4 and 5 adjust to $360,000 and $359,500 and receive “Most”
   weight. The report still states an indicated Sales Comparison value of $350,000; therefore a weight
   label is evidence to analyze, not an instruction to calculate a weighted average from disclosed
   percentages.
4. **PDF page 14 / report p

chunks.heading: D.4.b 2026 transition — do not teach one form as the only live format
chunks.excerpt:
age 13 — Reconciliation within the approach.** Read the narrative beneath
   the additional-comparable grid and identify the settled sale analyzed but not used. The report
   explains why data was considered, included or excluded.
5. **PDF page 16 / report page 15 — Reconciliation across approaches.** Locate the `Reconciliation`
   block. It records $350,000 for the Sales Comparison Approach and says the Income and Cost approaches
   were “Not Necessary for Credible Results.” Immediately below, `Appraisal Summary` carries the single
   $350,000 Opinion of Market Value. This is the exact form location and movement the Required Activity
   asks students to find.
6. **PDF page 17 / report page 16 — Revision history.** The borrower-initiated reconsideration of value
   added two reliable sales to the grid, left another as analyzed-not-used, and changed the opinion.
   Reconciliation is therefore an explained conclusion that can change with credible evidence, not a
   hidden average.

#### D.4.b 2026 transition — do not teach one form as the only live format

The retained blank **legacy Form 1004** places its approach indications and final opinion in the lower
`RECONCILIATION` portion of page 2. The new UAD 3.6 URAR uses a dynamic report and no longer depends on
legacy form numbers. The official transition timeline reviewed on **2026-09-07** says:

- through **November 1, 2026**, broad production permits UAD 2.6 or UAD 3.6 submissions;
- beginning **November 2, 2026**, all new UCDP submissions must use UAD 3.6;
- qualifying revisions to UAD 2.6 reports submitted by November 1 remain allowed during the pipeline
  period, which ends **May 3, 2027**.

chunks.heading: Required Activities in this section — all five are now delivered
chunks.excerpt:
At delivery, recheck the official Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac timeline. A date-sensitive transition rule is
not frozen forever by this course file.

---

## Required Activities in this section — all five are now delivered

1. **Provide examples of how each force and factor affects value** (B.4). **Delivered.**
2. **Provide an example of each economic principle of value** (B.5). **Delivered** — all nine.
3. **Provide examples of how adjustments are made to the sales prices of superior and inferior comps**
   (D.1). **Delivered** — worked both directions, with a numeric range and paired-sales boundary.
4. **Use a sample appraisal completed on a Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR) form for
   illustration** (D.1). **Delivered** — official GSE UAD 3.6 SF5 completed sample, all 20 retained pages
   visually reviewed against extracted text.
5. **Show students on the URAR form where the appraiser reconciles the approaches** (D.4).
   **Delivered** — guided report-page/PDF-page map to the within-approach and across-approach
   reconciliation blocks and single opinion of value.

Evidence is retained at
`north-carolina/regulatory/captures/2026-09-07/module-13-appraisal/`. The 302-page official combined
publisher artifact is preserved; the 20-page SF5 teaching derivative consists only of source PDF pages
271-290. Hashes, extracted text, 28 individual page renders and visual-review observations are recorded
in `page-reviews.json`.

## Module NC-13 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the Syllabus quotes it.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-13
chunks.excerpt:
Given the **11-item national examination weight** — the second heaviest in the course — this module's
items are weighted toward the Level 3 subtopic: separating closed-sale comps from other market data, the
direction of an adjustment, the prohibition on adjusting the subject, and reasoned weighting rather
than simple averaging. The Level 2 items cover depreciation categories, the Syllabus classification of
external obsolescence, the exclusion of debt service from NOI, and the property class each income method
serves.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-13

The course outline, levels, examination weight, required activities and quoted classroom propositions
come from **Section XIII** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026. Current-law and current-form boundaries were reconciled on **2026-09-07** against **G.S.
93E-1-2.1, 93E-1-3 and 93E-1-4; G.S. 93A-82 and 93A-83; The Appraisal Foundation's current USPAP and
history pages; the Fannie Mae UAD 3.6 resource/timeline pages; the official completed SF5 sample; and
legacy Fannie Mae Form 1004**.

**Source limitation.** The full copyrighted 2024 USPAP publication was not reproduced or used to teach
individual Standards Rules; the official Foundation overview supplies only the limited current-edition,
standards/qualifications and FIRREA-history facts stated here. The complete North Carolina Appraisal
Board rulebook was not used to state appraiser education, experience, scope or fee requirements. Those

assignment will display identical fields or pages.

lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-14

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-14
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-14

## Section XIV · NC Landlord & Tenant Concepts

**Commission Syllabus section:** XIV — NC Landlord & Tenant Concepts
**Instructional Level:** **2** throughout; students must apply each rule to a situation.
**Licence examination weight:** **State Exam Category — 3 items.**
**Instructional hours:** **2.5**
**Course version:** 1.1 current-law correction draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

This module was reconciled on **2026-09-07** against the current official North Carolina General
Assembly text of Chapter 42, Articles 2A, 3, 4A, 5, 6 and 7; Chapter 42A; and the current indexed text
of Commission Rules 58A .0104, .0116, and .0117. The Commission Syllabus controls topic coverage and
instructional level. The statutes and rules control the legal details.

> **Broker boundary.** These rules let a broker recognize the issue, preserve money and documents,
> follow the authorized procedure, and recommend legal counsel. They do not authorize a broker to
> decide a disputed legal right, draft a custom lease or eviction notice, or predict a court result.

## Learning objectives *(all Level 2)*

By the end of this module, the student can:

chunks.heading: A. Residential Rental Agreements Act — Chapter 42, Article 5
A.2 Mutual obligations and nonwaiver
chunks.excerpt:
For Article 5, **“landlord” includes an owner, rental management company, rental agency, or another
person with actual or apparent authority as an agent to perform the Act's duties**. In the Commission
Syllabus's words, a broker managing the rental property **is defined as “the landlord” under the Act**.
That does not erase the owner's duties or make the broker personally liable in every owner-tenant
dispute. G.S. 42-44(c1), for example, prevents personal liability solely because a managing broker or
firm failed to identify the owner in the rental agreement. It does mean that a managing broker cannot
dismiss a statutory operational duty as “only the owner's problem.”

### A.2 Mutual obligations and nonwaiver

G.S. 42-41 makes the tenant's duties to pay rent and comply with G.S. 42-43 **mutually dependent** with
the landlord's G.S. 42-42(a) duties. That mutuality does not create a self-help remedy for either side.
The tenant may not stop paying merely because the landlord breached, and the landlord may not remove
the tenant without the statutory process.

**Waiver of Act is prohibited.** G.S. 42-42(b) says a tenant's explicit or implicit acceptance of
noncompliant premises does not release the landlord. The parties may later make a separate written,
adequately supported agreement for the tenant to perform specified work, but not to evade the Act.
A lease clause stating “tenant accepts the unit as is and waives all repair rights” therefore does not
cancel the landlord's statutory duties.

### A.3 Landlord duties under G.S. 42-42

The landlord must, among other things:

chunks.heading: A.4 Tenant duties under G.S. 42-43
chunks.excerpt:
- comply with current applicable building and housing codes to the extent those codes apply;
- make repairs and do what is necessary to put and keep the premises **fit and habitable**;
- keep common areas safe;
- maintain and promptly repair supplied or required electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating,
  ventilation, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances after the tenant gives written
  notice, except in emergencies;
- provide and maintain the smoke alarms and qualifying carbon-monoxide alarms required by the statute;
  and
- repair or remedy an **imminently dangerous condition** within a reasonable time based on severity
  after actual knowledge or notice.

The statute's dangerous-condition list includes unsafe wiring, floors, steps, ceilings, roofs,
chimneys or flues; lack of potable water, exterior-door locks, specified ground-level window locks,
qualifying heat, an operable toilet, or an operable bath or shower; structural rat-entry defects; and
specified standing-water, sewage, flooding, mosquito, or mold conditions. The broker's response is not
to promise a universal number of hours. It is to document notice, triage an emergency, notify the
owner, arrange authorized work, preserve communications, and escalate a disputed legal issue.

### A.4 Tenant duties under G.S. 42-43

chunks.heading: A.5 Remedies, rent withholding, and constructive eviction
chunks.excerpt:
The tenant must keep the occupied area as clean and safe as conditions permit; dispose of waste safely;
keep plumbing fixtures reasonably clean; comply with applicable tenant code obligations; avoid
deliberate or negligent damage; avoid disabling required alarms; and notify the landlord in writing
when an alarm needs replacement or repair. The tenant is responsible for damage in the tenant's
exclusive control except ordinary wear, acts of the landlord or agent, defective supplied products or
authorized repairs, acts of noninvitee third parties, and natural forces. Except in emergencies, the
landlord must give written notice of a tenant breach of these statutory duties.

**Application.** A tenant reports a failed heating system in writing during winter. The manager records
the report, determines whether emergency action is required, promptly communicates and arranges an
authorized repair. The manager does not answer by pointing to an “as-is” clause. If evidence instead
shows the tenant deliberately destroyed the equipment, the repair duty and the allocation of actual
cost are separate questions; document both and do not use either as permission for self-help eviction.

### A.5 Remedies, rent withholding, and constructive eviction

Rights and duties under Chapter 42 may be enforced by civil action. The Commission Syllabus also
teaches damages, recovery of some rent paid while premises were uninhabitable, and the common-law
doctrine of constructive eviction. The critical statutory limit is G.S. 42-44(c): a tenant is
**prohibited from unilaterally withholding the rent** before a court determines a right to do so.

chunks.heading: A.6 Negligence concepts assigned by the Syllabus
chunks.excerpt:
Constructive eviction is not a licence to remain in possession rent-free. It generally concerns
substantial interference attributable to the landlord that makes continued occupancy untenable and a
tenant's decision to vacate. The Commission directs that a tenant obtain legal advice before vacating
and stopping future rent because a court may need to determine whether the doctrine actually ended the
rent obligation. A broker should never guarantee that a fact pattern meets the doctrine.

Use this decision sequence:

1. **Document** the condition, notice, lease terms, repair history, and who controls the affected area.
2. **Do not tell the tenant to withhold rent.** Explain the statutory no-unilateral-withholding rule.
3. **Do not give the owner self-help advice.** Use the statutory court route if possession is sought.
4. **Arrange authorized repair and mitigation** consistent with agency authority and safety.
5. **Refer disputed remedies to counsel.** A broker can identify the issue, not adjudicate it.

### A.6 Negligence concepts assigned by the Syllabus

chunks.heading: B. Recovering possession: court process, not self-help
chunks.excerpt:
The Commission asks students to apply these general principles: a landlord may be liable for injury
caused by a lack of maintenance in a common area under the landlord's control, and may be liable for
criminal acts of third persons when the landlord had reason to know of a threat and failed to take
reasonable precautions. A landlord is generally not liable for injury inside a unit under the tenant's
exclusive occupancy. These are **general common-law teaching principles**, not a promise of the result
in a particular case. Control, notice, foreseeability, conduct, causation, contract terms, and current
case law matter. Preserve facts and refer an injury or threat question to counsel and appropriate
emergency authorities.

---

## B. Recovering possession: court process, not self-help

### B.1 Article 2A prohibits self-help and distraint

G.S. 42-25.6 permits a residential tenant to be evicted, dispossessed, or otherwise actually or
constructively removed **only** through Article 3 or Article 7 procedure. Therefore **self-help
eviction is prohibited in NC**. Changing locks, disabling utilities, removing doors, or physically
excluding a tenant without the lawful writ is not a substitute for a court case.

G.S. 42-25.7 prohibits **distress and distraint**. A landlord does not gain a general right to seize a
tenant's personal property as leverage for rent. G.S. 42-25.9 and G.S. 42-36.2 contain narrow rules for
abandoned property and property remaining after execution of a writ. The safe operational rule is:
do not touch, withhold, sell, or discard the property unless the precise statute and procedural facts
have been verified. Unauthorized removal or interference can create actual-damages liability.

### B.2 Ordinary summary ejectment — Article 3

chunks.heading: B.3 Criminal-activity proceedings — Article 7
chunks.excerpt:
Article 3 provides the ordinary **summary ejectment** route. G.S. 42-26 identifies grounds including a
tenant holding over after expiration, an act or omission that ends the estate under the lease, and
specified rent-arrearage circumstances. A landlord seeking possession files a complaint. The clerk
issues a summons with an appearance date no more than seven days after issuance, excluding weekends
and legal holidays. Service and hearing follow the statute; a magistrate decides whether the plaintiff
proved entitlement to possession.

That overview is not a universal notice checklist. Lease terms, subsidized housing, federally protected
tenancies, bankruptcy, fair housing, domestic-violence protections, and the precise ground may add or
change requirements. A broker should use the current court form and counsel-approved process, never
construct a custom eviction timeline from memory.

### B.3 Criminal-activity proceedings — Article 7

Article 7 creates a civil route for drug trafficking and other defined criminal activity that threatens
health, safety, or peaceful enjoyment. It permits complete, partial, and conditional relief, but it
also contains defenses and exemptions. A criminal conviction is not always a prerequisite, and an
isolated-incident argument is not by itself a complete defense. The Syllabus correctly warns that
**expedited eviction for criminal activity may be possible, but legal advice is recommended first**.
The manager documents facts, contacts law enforcement when appropriate, protects threatened people,
and obtains counsel instead of treating an accusation as automatic authority to remove a household.

### B.4 Retaliatory eviction — Article 4A

chunks.heading: B.4 Retaliatory eviction — Article 4A
chunks.excerpt:
Protected activity includes a good-faith repair complaint to the landlord or agent, a good-faith
health-or-safety complaint to government, a formal government complaint, a good-faith attempt to
exercise lease or legal rights, and good-faith involvement with a tenants' rights organization. In a
G.S. 42-26 summary-ejectment action, the tenant may raise retaliation as an affirmative defense and
present evidence that the filing was substantially a response to protected activity occurring within
the prior **12 months**.

The 12-month period is not an immunity from every lawful eviction. G.S. 42-37.1(c) allows the landlord
to prevail on specified grounds, including a rent or substantial-covenant breach that is the actual
reason for eviction; holdover after a definite term when the tenant had no renewal option; a condition
primarily caused by the tenant or household; qualifying work requiring complete displacement; a
good-faith notice to quit given before the protected act; or specified good-faith recovery at the end
of the term for owner occupancy, major work, or at least six months' withdrawal from rental use.

The Syllabus note that there is no requirement to renew an expired lease must be read through those
statutory conditions. It is not permission to disguise retaliation as nonrenewal. A manager should
build a dated file showing the protected activity, decision date, actual business reason, lease status,
and counsel review. If the court finds retaliation, it denies ejectment, although rent and other proper
relief may still be awarded. The statutory rights cannot be waived.

chunks.heading: C. Tenant Security Deposit Act — Chapter 42, Article 6
chunks.excerpt:
**Application.** A tenant complained to code enforcement six weeks ago. The owner now asks the manager
to “get rid of the complainer.” That language and timing create a retaliation issue. The manager does
not send a notice merely because the lease is nearing expiration. The manager records the instruction,
checks whether a genuine statutory ground exists, refuses unlawful conduct, and sends the owner to
counsel. By contrast, documented nonpayment may support an action when nonpayment is the real reason,
but only the court process may recover possession.

---

## C. Tenant Security Deposit Act — Chapter 42, Article 6

### C.1 Who is covered and how the money is held

Article 6 applies to persons and entities in the business of renting or managing residential dwelling
units, excluding single rooms, on a weekly, monthly, or annual basis. Its duties are not limited to
licensed brokers.

G.S. 42-50 gives an owner-landlord two basic custody options:

1. deposit the security deposit in a trust account with a licensed and federally insured depository
   institution or a trust institution authorized to do business in North Carolina; or
2. furnish a bond in the amount of the deposit from an insurance company licensed in North Carolina.

An out-of-state trust account may be used only when the landlord gives the tenant an adequate bond in
the deposit amount. Within **30 days after the lease term begins**, the landlord or agent must notify
the tenant of the name and address of the institution holding the deposit or the insurer furnishing
the bond.

chunks.heading: C.2 Maximum security deposits
chunks.excerpt:
The Commission adds a narrower custody rule for its licensees. A broker working as property manager
does **not** have the bond option and must handle the money under the Commission trust-account rules.
Rule 58A .0116 uses a three-banking-day deposit baseline for received trust money, subject to the
rule's stated exceptions; Rule .0117 governs accounting and monthly reconciliation. Do not confuse the
owner's statutory bond option with a broker's trust-money obligations.

### C.2 Maximum security deposits

G.S. 42-51(b) sets the maximum by the tenancy period:

| Tenancy | Maximum tenant security deposit |
|---|---:|
| week to week | **two weeks' rent** |
| month to month | **one and one-half months' rent** |
| term greater than month to month | **two months' rent** |

The comparison is based on the rental term, not merely how the tenant happens to pay. For a true
twelve-month lease at $1,800 per month, the maximum is **$3,600**. For a month-to-month tenancy at the
same rent, it is **$2,700**. For a week-to-week tenancy at $450 per week, it is **$900**.

### C.3 Permitted uses

The security deposit may be applied only to the uses listed in G.S. 42-51, including possible unpaid
rent and specified utility costs; damage including damage to required alarms; actual damage from
failure to complete the rental period subject to statutory exceptions; qualifying unpaid bills that
become liens; reasonable re-rental costs after breach, including qualifying broker fees; removal and
storage costs after summary ejectment; court costs; and fees authorized by G.S. 42-46.

chunks.heading: C.4 Accounting and transfer
chunks.excerpt:
The deposit is not a penalty fund. A landlord may not deduct for **ordinary wear and tear** or retain
more than actual damage. Every proposed deduction should be tied to a statutory category and supported
by dated condition evidence, invoices or reasonable estimates, and the ledger.

### C.4 Accounting and transfer

After termination and delivery of possession, the landlord must mail or deliver a written itemization
of damage and the remaining balance within **30 days**. If the claim cannot yet be determined, provide
an interim accounting within 30 days and a final accounting within **60 days**. If the tenant's address
is unknown, after 30 days the landlord may apply permitted deductions and must hold the balance for the
tenant for at least **six months**.

When the landlord's interest ends by sale, assignment, death, receivership, or otherwise, G.S. 42-54
requires action within **30 days**: transfer the remaining deposit after lawful deductions to the
successor and notify the tenant by mail of the transfer and successor's name and address, or return the
remaining deposit to the tenant.

Willful noncompliance with deposit, bond, or notice requirements voids the landlord's right to retain
the deposit. A tenant may sue for accounting, the balance, resulting damages, and potentially attorney
fees on a judicial finding of willful noncompliance.

### C.5 Pet fees and assistance animals

chunks.heading: D. Vacation Rental Act — Chapter 42A
chunks.excerpt:
G.S. 42-53 permits a **reasonable, nonrefundable fee for pets**. The statute calls it a fee, not an
automatic damage forfeiture. The Commission's exam note says a **service animal is not a pet** and a
pet deposit cannot be charged for it. In housing, the federal Fair Housing Act also reaches qualifying
assistance animals beyond the ADA's narrower public-accommodation service-animal definition.

Do not label an assistance-animal charge a “pet fee” to evade that rule. A housing provider may apply
ordinary, nondiscriminatory security-deposit rules and may seek compensation for actual damage under
applicable law, but may not impose a pet fee or pet deposit because of the assistance animal. Process
reasonable-accommodation requests under the fair-housing workflow taught in Modules NC-09 and NC-15.

---

## D. Vacation Rental Act — Chapter 42A

### D.1 Coverage and written agreement

A **vacation rental** is residential property rented for vacation, leisure, or recreation for fewer
than **90 days** by a person who has a permanent residence to which the person intends to return.
Chapter 42A does not apply to hotels and similar Chapter 72 lodging, business or employment travel,
renters with no other primary residence, or nominal-consideration rentals.

chunks.heading: D.2 Advance funds and security deposits
chunks.excerpt:
Every covered vacation rental requires a written vacation rental agreement. It becomes accepted by
the tenant's signature, payment after receipt of the agreement, or taking possession after receipt.
The agreement must carry the statutory conspicuous notice and describe the handling of funds,
permitted fees, transfer rights, expedited eviction, evacuation rights, and the other obligations
listed in G.S. 42A-11. A broker's nonconforming or missing agreement can be an unfair trade practice and
can bar that broker from using the expedited-eviction procedure.

### D.2 Advance funds and security deposits

Advance payments other than a security deposit must be placed in a qualifying trust account no later
than **three banking days after receipt**. Before occupancy, no more than **50% of total rent** may be
disbursed, apart from expressly authorized third-party charges for tenant benefits and permitted fees.
The balance stays in trust until tenancy begins, a material breach supports actual damages, the funds
are refunded, or a statutory transfer occurs. Taxes and security deposits are not disbursed before
termination or material breach except as a refund.

The agreement identifies the depository institution and the tenant may reasonably request a
pre-occupancy accounting. Vacation-rental security deposits are generally subject to Article 6, but
**posting a bond is not an option**, even for an unlicensed landlord. The deposit must be applied,
accounted for, or refunded within **45 days after the tenancy concludes**. Automatic forfeiture of all
or part of the deposit for breach is prohibited; only actual damages and other lawful deductions may
be applied.

### D.3 Sale or other transfer of the property

chunks.heading: D.4 Expedited eviction for stays of 30 days or less
chunks.excerpt:
For a voluntary transfer, the new owner takes subject to a vacation rental agreement that ends no
later than **180 days after the new owner's interest is recorded**. A later-ending agreement is
enforceable against the new owner only if the new owner agrees in writing, although the tenant has the
statutory refund right.

Before contracting to sell, the owner discloses the booked rental periods to the buyer. No later than
**10 days after transfer**, the former owner gives the buyer the tenants' names and addresses and
copies or permitted standard-form extracts of each agreement, subject to the Act's management-agent
exception. No later than **20 days after transfer**, the buyer or agent gives each tenant written
notice of the transfer, recording date, occupancy right, and refund right, subject to the Act's
continuing-agent exception. Within **30 days**, advance rent and remaining fees go to the successor for
agreements being honored, or back to the tenant for a later-ending agreement not accepted by the
successor. Security deposits follow G.S. 42A-18.

### D.4 Expedited eviction for stays of 30 days or less

The special expedited proceeding is available only for a covered vacation rental of **30 days or
less** and only on the listed grounds: holdover; a material breach that terminates the tenancy under
the agreement; failure to pay required rent; or possession obtained by fraud or misrepresentation.
Only possession is decided; other disputes belong in a separate civil action.

chunks.heading: D.5 Habitability and broker responsibilities
chunks.excerpt:
Before filing, the landlord or broker gives at least **four hours' notice to quit**, orally or in
writing. If reasonable personal efforts fail, written notice may be posted on the front door. The
complaint and summons are then filed and served as the statute provides. The magistrate hearing occurs
not sooner than **12 hours** and not later than **48 hours** after service. The plaintiff must prove the
30-day-or-less term, a conforming accepted agreement, a statutory ground, and the notice. Abuse of the
procedure without a good-faith belief in statutory grounds can be both an unfair trade practice and a
Class 1 misdemeanor.

### D.5 Habitability and broker responsibilities

The vacation-rental landlord must comply with applicable codes; keep the property fit and habitable;
keep common areas safe; maintain supplied systems and major appliances after written notice; and meet
the smoke- and carbon-monoxide-alarm rules. The duties cannot be waived.

If at the start of occupancy the property cannot be supplied in fit and habitable condition, the
landlord or broker must provide a reasonably comparable substitute in that condition or refund **all
payments**, subject to the separate evacuation rule. A managing broker follows the written agency
agreement, markets lawfully, notifies the owner of necessary repairs and follows authorized repair
directions, and verifies required alarms and recurring battery duties.

### D.6 Mandatory evacuation

chunks.heading: E. Property management agreements and money controls
chunks.excerpt:
When State or local authorities order a mandatory evacuation covering the property, the tenant must
comply. The default rule is a prorated refund of rent, taxes, and other occupancy-condition payments
for nights the tenant cannot occupy. The tenant is not entitled to that statutory refund when, before
possession, the tenant refused qualifying insurance offered by the landlord or broker, or purchased
such offered insurance. The agreement must explain these rights and obligations.

---

## E. Property management agreements and money controls

Rule 58A .0104(a) requires an agreement to provide brokerage services for a property owner to be
**express and in writing from formation of the agency relationship**. The narrow pre-offer window for
an unwritten agreement applies to a buyer or tenant, not to an owner-landlord. Therefore a property
manager does not begin leasing, advertising, collecting money, or arranging tenancy first and “paper
the file later.”

The written agreement identifies the parties, authority, compensation and services; the broker then
acts within that authority. Money belonging to others is separately controlled by Rules .0116 and
.0117 and the applicable statute. A property-management agreement cannot convert trust money into the
broker's operating money, waive habitability, create an unauthorized deposit penalty, or authorize
self-help eviction.

### Integrated property-manager file check

Before accepting a management assignment, verify and document:

chunks.heading: Application lab — one file, six decisions
Required Activities in this section
chunks.excerpt:
1. Property-management authority for the owner must be express and written **from formation**; the
   broker should not have begun performance on an oral owner agreement.
2. The facts fit a Chapter 42A vacation rental: residential, leisure purpose, fewer than 90 days, and
   a tenant with another permanent residence.
3. Advance rent belongs in the qualifying trust account within three banking days. Before occupancy,
   ordinary rent disbursement is capped at 50%, subject to the statute's express exceptions.
4. A reservation ending within 180 days after recording ordinarily binds the voluntary transferee.
   The seller and buyer then perform the 10-, 20-, and 30-day disclosure, notice, and fund-transfer
   steps as applicable; cancellation is not automatic.
5. Automatic security-deposit forfeiture is prohibited. Actual lawful deductions require evidence and
   accounting.
6. At occupancy, provide the property fit and habitable, substitute a reasonably comparable property,
   or refund all payments. Document and escalate; do not improvise a waiver.

---

## A. Ownership of real property in NC

### A.1 Joint tenancy in NC

> **Note:** *"Though **used infrequently in NC**, joint tenancy is **widely used in many other states and
> is also tested on the National exam section**."*

That note is an examination instruction. The student must learn **two** versions: the general rule the
national section tests, and the North Carolina rule the state section tests. Module NC-06 introduced this;
here it is completed.

- **Current G.S. 41-71:** tenancy in common is the default; a joint tenancy with right of survivorship
  exists when the instrument expresses that intent. The statute now recognizes phrases including
  “joint tenants,” “joint tenancy,” and “with right of survivorship” unless the instrument provides
  otherwise.
- **Current G.S. 41-72:** interests are equal unless the instrument provides otherwise; expressly
  unequal ownership shares are permitted.
- **Current G.S. 41-73:** specified collective or unilateral conveyances and instruments, and a
  partition petition, may terminate survivorship. A unilateral self-conveyance must express the intent
  and be recorded before the joint tenant's death.

Two North Carolina departures from the common form, and both are examinable:

The Syllabus's four-unities mnemonic is useful history, but **equal interests are not a safe statement
of current North Carolina law**. Survivorship is not supplied merely because two people own together;
the conveyance must create it under G.S. 41-71. An attorney drafts the instrument. A broker identifies
the objective and routes it, rather than inventing language or promising the legal result.

chunks.heading: A.2 Tenancy by the entirety
chunks.excerpt:
Note also who does the drafting: **an attorney.** This is the drafting prohibition from Module NC-09
appearing in the ownership context. A broker does not supply survivorship language.

### A.2 Tenancy by the entirety

- **Available to two people legally married to each other.**
  - Under **G.S. 41-56**, a conveyance to spouses creates the estate unless the conveyance expresses a
    contrary intention.
  - *"Buyer should **consult with a real estate attorney** to explore what ownership type is desired."*
  - ***"Other types of ownership do not automatically convert to tenancy by the entirety if property
    owners marry each other later."***
- **Equal undivided interest.**
- **At death while the estate remains in place**, G.S. 41-64 gives title to the survivor and leaves no
  descendable share in the deceased spouse, subject to the slayer exception.
- Under G.S. 41-58, neither spouse generally may unilaterally sell, lease, mortgage, transfer, convey,
  or encumber the estate; written joinder is required subject to the statute's listed exceptions.
- G.S. 41-63 expressly lists ways to end the estate, including joint sale, voluntary partition,
  specified involuntary transfers, conveyance from one spouse to the other, and absolute divorce.
  Therefore “cannot be waived” must not be presented as “can never be terminated.”

Set this against A.1 and the contrast is the examinable structure:

chunks.heading: A.3 NC common interest community (hybrid) ownership
chunks.excerpt:
| | **Joint tenancy in NC** | **Tenancy by the entirety in NC** |
|---|---|---|
| Who may hold it | Anyone | **Legally married couples only** |
| Interests | **May be unequal** if stated in title | **Equal undivided interest** |
| Right of survivorship | Must be created by the instrument under G.S. 41-71 | Operates automatically at death while the estate remains in place |
| Default for married buyers | No | ***Yes, if married at the time of purchase*** |

**A will does not displace the survivorship result while the entireties estate remains in place.** The
deceased spouse then has no descendable share. The estate can nevertheless end during life through
the events G.S. 41-63 lists. And the **conversion rule** runs one way only: buying as tenants in common
and marrying afterwards does **not** convert the ownership.

Module NC-12's spousal signature rule connects here. Because a spouse **cannot convey a half interest**,
both spouses must sign the deed of trust even where only one signed the note.

### A.3 NC common interest community (hybrid) ownership

#### A.3.a Condominium ownership

Governed by **horizontal property acts, such as the North Carolina Condominium Act of 1986 [NCGS Chapter
47C]**, under which the Commission lists:

chunks.heading: A.3.b Townhouse ownership
chunks.excerpt:
- **Application**
- **Developer's disclosure requirements**
- **Public offering statement**
- **G.S. 47C-4-108:** for a sale in which G.S. 47C-4-102(c) requires delivery of a public offering
  statement, the purchaser receives an absolute seven-calendar-day cancellation period after contract
  execution and conveyance may not occur during it.
- **G.S. 47C-4-109:** an ordinary nonexempt resale not requiring a public offering statement carries a
  pre-conveyance statement of monthly common expenses and other owner fees, but that section supplies
  no statutory cancellation right.

Ownership structure:

- *"Individual unit owner holds **fee simple 'title to airspace'** for unit."*
- *"Individual unit owners own an **undivided share of common elements** with other unit owners"* —
  including *"land and common areas, such as hallways, elevators, recreational facilities, etc."*
  - ***"Own as tenants in common without right of partition."***
  - *"Periodic fees/assessments charged to unit owners."*
  - *"Possible **exclusive use of limited common elements**."*

The seven-day rule turns on the seller and public-offering-statement requirement, not simply whether a
unit feels “new.” An ordinary resale gets the statutory fee statement but no cancellation right from
§47C-4-109; the actual contract may separately create one. **Common elements are not freely partitioned
while the condominium exists**, because doing so would dismantle the legal regime.

#### A.3.b Townhouse ownership

chunks.heading: A.4 Manufactured (factory built) housing *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
- *"Includes **individual ownership of land**, at least the land upon which the unit sits."*
- *"Usually attached by **party walls**."*
- Common elements *"**owned by the HOA**"*, maintenance funded by periodic fees/assessments.
- *"Most townhouse developments are subject to the **NC Planned Community Act [NCGS Chapter 47F]**."*

**Townhouse is a physical description, not a legal ownership form.** Some townhouse projects are
condominiums; others are planned communities. The declaration, plat, deed, and statutory coverage —
not the building's appearance — determine whether Chapter 47C, Chapter 47F, or another regime applies.

### A.4 Manufactured (factory built) housing *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

**Manufactured housing (mobile home)** *[NCGS 143-143.9(6)]*:

- *"Built to **federal HUD standards**; **red HUD certification label**."*
- *"**Titled and regulated by NC Dept. of Motor Vehicles (DMV)**."*
- *"**Permanent non-removable steel chassis**."*
- ***"Personal property until converted to real property"*** *[NCGS 47-20.6 and 105-273(13)]* by all three of:
  - *"Attaching to permanent foundation on land owned by owner of home;"*
  - *"Removing wheels, axle, and moving hitch; and"*
  - *"Filing **affidavit of conversion to cancel DMV title**"*

**Modular housing** *[NCGS 105-164.3(143) and 143-139.1]*:

- *"Built to **state building code**."*
- *"**State inspection label with serial number**."*
- *"Assembled by builder on-site."*
- ***"Becomes real property as soon as assembled on building site."***

chunks.heading: A.5 Adverse possession
chunks.excerpt:
The pair is examinable as a contrast. **Federal HUD standard, red label, DMV title, chassis, and three
steps to become realty** — manufactured. **State building code, state inspection label, real property on
assembly** — modular. And the practical consequence for a broker: a manufactured home that has **not**
been converted is **personal property**, so it is not conveyed by the deed.

### A.5 Adverse possession

- **General requirements**
- **Statutory time periods for continuous adverse possession:**
  - ***"20 years for regular adverse possession in NC"***
  - ***"7 years if under color of title in NC"***

Both figures are the Commission's, transcribed. **Color of title** — a defective instrument that appears
to convey — cuts the period from twenty years to seven.

### A.6 NC agricultural fixtures

- **Definition**
- *"Per common law, **became part of the real property and could not be removed at the end of the
  lease**."*
- *"**Modern trend is to treat as trade fixtures.**"*
- *"**Lease terms should address right of removal.**"*

Module NC-03 taught fixtures and trade fixtures. This is the North Carolina agricultural wrinkle, and the
practical instruction is the last line: **put it in the lease.** Where a doctrine is in transition, the
document settles it.

### A.7 The UCC and fixtures

The Syllabus cites former **G.S. 25-9-313**. Current Article 9 places the fixture rule in **G.S.
25-9-334**. A security interest may exist and continue in goods that become fixtures, but Article 9
does not create a security interest in ordinary building materials incorporated into an improvement.

chunks.heading: B. NC Connor Act — NCGS 47-18
chunks.excerpt:
The general rule subordinates a fixture security interest to a conflicting interest of an owner or
encumbrancer of the related real property. Statutory exceptions include a properly perfected purchase-
money security interest supported by a **fixture filing before or within 20 days after the goods become
fixtures**, subject to the section's debtor, interest and priority conditions. Manufactured-home title
conversion and competing interests also require the specific rules in **G.S. 47-20.6**. A broker flags
the fixture and financing issue; the closing attorney resolves filing, perfection and priority.

## B. NC Connor Act — NCGS 47-18

> 1. *"Requires **all conveyances of interest in real property be recorded to be effective against claims
>    by third parties**."*
> 2. ***"A pure race statute."***
>    **Note:** *"**Failure to record does not affect the validity of the document between the parties to
>    the instrument.**"*
> 3. *"Documents required to be recorded **in the county where the property is located**."*

**Pure race** is the phrase to understand, not memorise. Under a pure race statute, **the first to record
wins** — full stop. Not the first to record in good faith. Not the first to record without notice of the
earlier deed. **First to record.** A second buyer who knew perfectly well about the first sale and raced
to the register of deeds still takes the property as against the world.

And the Commission's note draws the boundary of that harshness precisely: the unrecorded deed is still
**valid between the parties who signed it.** It fails against **third parties**, which is the only place
the race matters.

chunks.heading: C. Marketable Title Act / Torrens System *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*
chunks.excerpt:
This is the reason Module NC-05's recording material exists, and the reason C.2 in Module NC-11 flagged
uncancelled deeds of trust. In a pure race state, the register of deeds is not a convenience — it is
where ownership is decided.

---

## C. Marketable Title Act / Torrens System *(Level 1 — this subtopic)*

**Marketable Title Act — Chapter 47B.** A person with an unbroken **30-year chain of record title** and
no instrument in that chain denying the interest has marketable record title, subject to Chapter 47B's
substantial exceptions. Older conflicting interests may be extinguished, but the Act does not erase
interests preserved by the chain, possession, mineral and railroad provisions, qualifying easements,
federal rights, mortgages and deeds of trust, registered land, and specified condominium or planned-
community declarations and covenants. A claimant may preserve an otherwise vulnerable interest by
recording the statutory notice in the proper county during the applicable 30-year period; the notice
generally preserves it for another 30 years.

**Torrens system — Chapter 43.** Registered-land title is established through an **in rem Superior Court
proceeding**. Court-appointed title examiners are licensed North Carolina attorneys, and the decree and
certificate establish the registered ownership subject to the statutory system. Land registered before
April 16, 1931 may be removed from the system through the procedure in G.S. 43-56; removal does not
erase existing liens. Neither system is a broker do-it-yourself title opinion. Send chain, exception,
notice and registered-land questions to the closing/title attorney.
