lessons.title: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-16

chunks.heading: North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-16
chunks.excerpt:
# North Carolina Broker Prelicensing Course — Module NC-16

## Section XVI · Real Estate Math Calculations

**Commission Syllabus section:** XVI — Real Estate Math Calculations
**Instructional Level:** **3** for the entire section — **analysis and evaluation**, the highest level the
Commission assigns anywhere in this course, and the only section assigned Level 3 throughout. *Assigned
by the Commission; providers and instructors are **REQUIRED to comply**.*
**Licence examination weight:** **National Exam Category — 7 items.**
**Instructional hours:** **0.0 as a standalone block — this section is delivered inside the other fifteen
modules.** See the Commission's instruction below.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No North Carolina prelicensing credit is available.

> ### The Commission's instruction on how mathematics must be taught — transcribed in full
>
> *"**Instruction on relevant mathematical functions is to be provided under the appropriate subject areas
> rather than as a separate arithmetic course section.** To assist instructors, however, **all required
> real estate mathematics instruction is listed in Section XVI of the Outline.** **Consideration was given
> to the amount of mathematics involved in each subject area when establishing the recommended number of
> instructional hours for subject areas.** This **integrated approach is recommended because it helps
> assure that students understand how various mathematical functions relate to the various areas of real
> estate practice.** **Instruction in basic mathematics concepts such as decimals, fractions, percentages,
> multiplication, division, etc. is not included in this course syllabus.** Students **deficient in basic
> math skills should be provide

chunks.heading: What that instruction means for this course, stated plainly
chunks.excerpt:
d special assistance outside of class or directed to take a math refresher
> course.**"*

### What that instruction means for this course, stated plainly

**Section XVI carries no instructional hours of its own, and it is not a module a student sits through in
sequence.** Three consequences follow, and all three are the Commission's, not this project's:

1. **The mathematics is taught where the subject lives.** Excise tax with property taxes; discount points
   with financing; adjustments with the sales comparison approach; prorations with settlement.
2. **The hours are already allocated.** The Commission states it took the mathematics into account when it
   set the recommended hours for each subject area. Adding separate hours for Section XVI would
   **double-count them** against the 72.0 instructional hours the Commission's own table produces.
3. **Basic arithmetic is out of scope.** Decimals, fractions, percentages, multiplication and division are
   **not part of this course**, and a student who cannot do them is to be **helped outside class or sent to
   a refresher course.** An instructor who spends course time on long division is spending prelicensing
   hours on something the Commission has excluded.

**This module is therefore the course's mathematics register**, not a lesson. It exists so that an
instructor, a reviewer and the Commission can see **every required calculation in one place**, together
with **the module in which it is actually delivered.** Its engagement items are the course's integrated
mathematics practice, drawn across all fifteen subject modules.

## Learning objectives *(all Level 3, all delivered in the modules named)*

chunks.heading: Where each required calculation is delivered
chunks.excerpt:
The student can **perform, and evaluate the result of**, every calculation listed in Parts A through G
below, in the context of the transaction that produces it.

---

## Where each required calculation is delivered

| Syllabus item | Calculation | Delivered in |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Brokerage commissions — sales and property management | **NC-09**, **NC-14** |
| **B.1** | Profit/loss (appreciation/depreciation) on sale, including percentages | **NC-04** |
| **B.2** | Return on investment (NOI) | **NC-13** |
| **B.3** | Tax implications on investment | **NC-04** |
| **C.1–C.4** | Acreage/square footage conversion; areas; square yards; cost per unit | **NC-03**, **NC-15** |
| **D.1–D.8** | All finance calculations | **NC-12** |
| **E.1** | Estimating net to seller; sale price needed to net $X | **NC-09**, **NC-11** |
| **E.2** | Excise tax on property transfers | **NC-04** |
| **E.3** | Individual settlement statement entries, including prorations | **NC-12** |
| **E.4** | Bottom-line settlement figures | **NC-12** |
| **F.1–F.2** | Property management income, expenses, vacancy and rental calculations | **NC-14** |
| **G.1** | Assessed value and ad valorem property taxes | **NC-04** |
| **G.2–G.4** | Sales comparison / CMA, cost approach, income capitalization | **NC-13** |

---

## A. Brokerage commissions — sales and property management transactions

Commission calculations on both sales transactions and property management transactions. Delivered with
the compensation material in Module NC-09 and with property management contracts in Module NC-14.

chunks.heading: B. Investment calculations
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Calculate various sales commissions and property management fees
> based on typical ways they are determined.**"*
>
> **Delivered.** *(Source note: this Required Activity is printed at a page boundary in the Syllabus,
> adjacent to a second activity concerning mechanics' lien priority. The fee calculation activity is
> carried here because Part A is its subject; the lien timeline is carried in Module NC-15 with the same
> note.)*
>
> Note the Commission's phrase — ***"typical ways they are determined."*** Module NC-09 records the
> Commission's own Required Activity to *"discuss various ways brokerage fees are determined,"* and
> Modules NC-08 and NC-09 record that **compensation is negotiable and is never set by the Commission, by
> any association, or by any course.** **No commission rate, split, management fee percentage or minimum
> is stated anywhere in this build.** Every practice problem supplies its own rate inside the problem, as
> a given.

## B. Investment calculations

1. **Profit/loss (appreciation/depreciation) on sale of real estate, including percentages.**
2. **Return on investment (NOI).**
3. **Tax implications on investment.**

*(B.2 uses the NOI derivation taught in Module NC-13 — potential gross income, less vacancy and rental
loss, less operating expenses, and **debt service excluded.**)*

chunks.heading: C. Area and related calculations
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Calculate excise tax for multiple properties: include scenarios
> for property that is located inside city/town limits, located only in the county, have odd purchase
> prices, or include seller concessions or financing information.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-04**, where the current statutory rate, payer, base and four scenarios are
> taught from G.S. 105-228.30.
>
> Four scenario types are prescribed and all four must appear: **inside city/town limits**; **county
> only**; **odd purchase prices**; and **seller concessions or financing information.** The last two are
> there to defeat pattern-matching — a student who has only ever seen round numbers, and who has never had
> to decide whether a concession changes the taxable figure, has not learned the calculation.
>
> G.S. 105-228.30 was read from current official text on 2026-09-07. It requires the transferor to pay
> the register of deeds before recording, at $1 for each $500 or fractional part of the consideration or
> value conveyed. Module NC-04 supplies all four prescribed scenario types.

## C. Area and related calculations

1. **Conversion of acreage to square footage and vice-versa.**
2. **Square footage of variously-shaped buildings and parcels of land with straight line sides, including
   irregular shaped parcels/buildings.** The Commission names the formulas required: *"squares,
   rectangles, **trapezoids** and **right triangles**."*
3. **Square yards.**
4. **Cost/price per square foot / acre / front foot.**

**Trapezoids and right triangles are named explicitly**, which means an irregular parcel must be
decomposed rather than estimated. That is exactly the Level 3 demand: break the shape into shapes you can
compute, compute each, and add.

chunks.heading: D. Finance calculations — all delivered in Module NC-12
chunks.excerpt:
*(Module NC-15 applies the complete retained **2026 NCREC Residential Square Footage Guidelines**,
including current exterior/interior measurement, above/below-grade, heat, finish, access, ceiling and
record-retention criteria.)*

## D. Finance calculations — all delivered in Module NC-12

1. **Simple interest** — *"How to compute monthly interest, and amount of interest paid over life of a
   fixed-rate loan."*
2. **Monthly principal and interest payment** — *"using factors, if given the loan amount, interest rate,
   term and factor."*
3. **Mortgage debt reduction** — *"How to compute principal balance after one monthly payment, given
   previous principal balance, monthly P & I payment and interest rate, **with and without using
   amortization tables**."*
4. **Loan origination fees and discount points.**
5. **Loan value** — *"applying loan-to-value ratios."*
6. **Basic buyer qualification using given income and debt ratios.**
7. **Equity, including percentages.**
8. **Yield** — *"on mortgage loans involving discount points using **'rule of thumb' value**."*

Four of these deserve a note.

**D.2 says "using factors."** The student is **given** the factor. This is not an amortisation-formula
exercise; it is a use-the-table-correctly exercise, and the examinable skill is knowing what the factor
is per and multiplying accordingly.

**D.3 requires both methods** — with and without an amortisation table. The manual method is the one that
proves understanding: interest for the month is computed on the **previous** balance, the remainder of the
payment reduces principal, and the new balance follows.

chunks.heading: E. Settlement and closing costs
chunks.excerpt:
**D.6 says "using given income and debt ratios."** The ratios are supplied in the problem. Module NC-12
transcribes the Commission's own figures — **28/36 conventional, 31/43 FHA, 43 VA** — and the rule that
**a buyer must qualify on both ratios** inside that Syllabus model, which is where most calculation errors
occur. Those figures do not announce live loan eligibility; a real creditor applies current program and
underwriting rules.

**D.8's "rule of thumb"** is the relationship Module NC-12 transcribes from the Syllabus: **1 point = 1/8
percent yield for the investor.** It is an examination shortcut, not a guaranteed market-price result.

## E. Settlement and closing costs

1. **Estimating net to seller after brokerage fee and other closing expenses are paid** — *"when setting
   listing price or considering an offer."* The Commission adds: *"**Includes sale price needed to net $X
   to seller.**"*
2. **Excise tax on property transfers.**
3. **Calculation of individual amounts to be entered on the settlement statement when the licensee has the
   data necessary** — *"e.g., prorations (real estate taxes, rent, HOA dues); interim interest; escrow
   deposits; etc."*
4. **Calculation of bottom-line figures given all relevant needed information:** *"Total settlement charges
   to buyer-borrower and seller; net due seller (cash to seller); cash from buyer-borrower."*

**E.1's second half is the harder problem and it is stated separately for that reason.** Computing a
seller's net from a known price is arithmetic. Computing **the price needed to produce a required net** is
algebra, because the commission is a percentage *of the unknown*. A student who solves it by subtracting
the commission from the desired net has made the classic error.

chunks.heading: E. Settlement and closing costs
chunks.excerpt:
**E.3 and E.4 sit exactly where Module NC-12's Part J note draws the line.** The Commission states there
that a licence candidate **will not be asked to complete a settlement statement**, but **will be asked to
perform calculations for individual entries and to know how they appear — debit or credit, and to whom.**
E.4's bottom-line figures are computed from given data, not built up from a blank form.

> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Explain and demonstrate proration math calculations for handling
> annual homeowners' association dues, monthly rent, and annual real estate taxes. Tax problems should
> include closing dates early and late in the calendar year and when the seller has and has not already
> paid the annual tax bill. Students must be given multiple practice problems on various proration
> scenarios.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-12.**
>
> The prescription is specific and every element is required: **three prorated items** (HOA dues, rent,
> taxes); **closing dates early and late in the year**; **the tax bill both paid and unpaid**; and
> **multiple practice problems**, not one. That is four variables, and the Commission wants them crossed.
>
> Module NC-12 records the three rules that govern every one of these problems, all transcribed from the
> Syllabus: **both the 365-day and the 360-day/30-day methods must be taught**; the **360-day/30-day
> method is the one used on the end-of-course examination and the licence examination**; and **in North
> Carolina the seller "owns" the date of settlement.** Also: **always a double entry.**

chunks.heading: F. Property management calculations — delivered in Module NC-14
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Perform multiple math calculations to determine annual property
> tax liability. Include property tax situations that do and do not require calculation of both county and
> city taxes.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-04.**
>
> The county-only versus county-and-city distinction is the same one the excise tax activity prescribes,
> and it reflects a real North Carolina fact: a property inside municipal limits is taxed by **two**
> jurisdictions, and a student who computes only one has under-stated the liability. **No North Carolina
> tax rate, city rate or county rate is stated anywhere in this build**; every problem supplies its rates
> as givens.

## F. Property management calculations — delivered in Module NC-14

1. **Income and expenses.**
2. **Tenancy/vacancy rates and rental calculations.**

## G. Property valuation (appraisal) calculations — delivered in Module NC-13

**1. Assessed value and ad valorem property taxes.** The Commission states the requirement precisely:

> *"amount of real property tax using a given tax rate and assessed value; **students should be able to
> perform calculations using either a tax rate in dollars per $100 of assessed value [NC method] or a mill
> rate [National method]**"*

**Both methods, and the Commission labels which is which.** **Dollars per $100 of assessed value is the
North Carolina method**; the **mill rate is the national method.** The state section of the licence
examination and the national section will not ask the same way, and a student who knows only one will lose
items on the other. *(Also delivered in Module NC-04, where property taxes are taught.)*

**2. Sales comparison approach and comparative market analysis.**

chunks.heading: G. Property valuation (appraisal) calculations — delivered in Module NC-13
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Have students to prepare a CMA that includes superior and
> inferior comps to arrive at a range for probable sales price.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-13.** Note the deliverable: **a range**, not a single number — which matches
> the Syllabus's statement that adjusted comp prices *"should provide a tight range of value"* and its
> prohibition on **simple averaging.** And note that **both directions of adjustment must appear**:
> superior comps adjusted **down**, inferior comps adjusted **up**, and **never the subject.**

**3. Cost approach.**

> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Provide examples of estimating replacement cost using the square
> foot method. Have students determine a single estimate of value of at least one property by the cost
> approach using the replacement cost method with the square foot method and age/life depreciation for
> estimating the value of the building.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-13.**
>
> The Commission specifies the exact combination to be worked: **replacement cost** (not reproduction),
> by the **square foot method** (not quantity survey or unit-in-place), with **age/life depreciation**
> (not market abstraction or breakdown) — and it wants **a single estimate of value for at least one whole
> property**, which means the land component must be estimated separately and added back, and **land is
> never depreciated.**

**4. Income capitalization approach.**

chunks.heading: Required Activities in this section — all six are delivered in the modules named
chunks.excerpt:
> **Required Activity, transcribed:** *"**Provide an example of estimating value using the Direct
> Capitalization Formula. Have students determine a single estimate of value of at least one property by
> the direct capitalization approach. Provide the CAP rate. There will be no calculations using a GRM.**"*
>
> **Delivered in Module NC-13.**
>
> Three instructions, all binding. **The CAP rate is provided** — students do not derive it. **At least one
> whole-property estimate** must be produced by direct capitalization: **Value = NOI ÷ CAP rate**, with
> **debt service excluded from NOI.** And — stated by the Commission in its own words —
> ***"There will be no calculations using a GRM."***
>
> That last sentence also resolves the formula discrepancy flagged in Module NC-13. The Syllabus's two GRM
> lines are not algebraically consistent with each other, and **the Commission excludes GRM from the
> required calculations entirely.** GRM remains examinable as a **concept** — what it relates, and which
> property class it serves — and **no item in this course requires a GRM computation.**

---

## Required Activities in this section — all six are delivered in the modules named

chunks.heading: Module NC-16 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Calculate various sales commissions and property management fees** → **NC-09**, **NC-14.** **Delivered.**
2. **Calculate excise tax for multiple properties**, across the four prescribed scenario types →
   **NC-04. Delivered from current G.S. 105-228.30.**
3. **Explain and demonstrate proration math** for HOA dues, rent and taxes, across early/late closing dates
   and paid/unpaid tax bills, with multiple practice problems → **NC-12.** **Delivered.**
4. **Perform multiple annual property tax calculations**, with and without city taxes → **NC-04.**
   **Delivered.**
5. **Have students prepare a CMA** with superior and inferior comps, producing a range → **NC-13.**
   **Delivered.**
6. **Estimate replacement cost by the square foot method**, and produce a whole-property value by the cost
   approach with age/life depreciation → **NC-13.** **Delivered.**
7. **Provide an example using the Direct Capitalization Formula**, CAP rate given, **no GRM calculations**
   → **NC-13.** **Delivered.**

*(Seven Required Activities are printed across Section XVI; the numbering above follows the Syllabus's
order of appearance.)*

## Module NC-16 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module NC-01, and **every one of them is a calculation.** This is the
course's integrated mathematics assessment: items are drawn across Parts A through G and each is set in
the transaction context that produces it, because the Commission's stated reason for the integrated
approach is that it *"helps assure that students understand how various mathematical functions relate to
the various areas of real estate practice."*

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-16
chunks.excerpt:
The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**;
the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the Commission's, under Commission Rule 58H .0207 as the
Syllabus quotes it.

**Every variable local property-tax rate, factor, CAP rate, commission rate and amortisation figure used
in an item is supplied inside the item as a given.** North Carolina's statutory excise-tax rate is taught
from current G.S. 105-228.30. **No item requires a
GRM calculation**, because the Commission states there will be none. **No item asks a student to complete
a settlement statement**, because the Commission states the licence examination will not.

---

## Instructor source note for Module NC-16

Drawn from **Section XVI** of the Commission's Prelicensing Course Syllabus, March 2024 Edition amended
May 2026, read on 2026-08-20, together with the Syllabus's front-matter instruction **"Real Estate
Mathematics Instruction,"** transcribed in full at the head of this module. Every Required Activity and
every statement of what is or is not required is **transcribed from the Syllabus.**

G.S. 105-228.30 and the property-tax statutes used in Module NC-04 were read from current official text
on 2026-09-07. **Not read in its own text, and therefore not the source of any figure in this module:**
the **NCREC Residential Square Footage Guidelines** and any **amortisation factor table**. Chapter 93A
and the controlling Chapter 58 rules used in Modules NC-01 and NC-02 were read; later topic-level
reconciliation remains incomplete.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module NC-16
chunks.excerpt:
This module's function is to record, in one place, every calculation the
Commission requires, the module in which each is delivered, and the constraints the Commission places on
how each is to be taught and examined — so that a reviewer can verify coverage of Section XVI without
searching fifteen modules, and so that **the zero standalone hours assigned to this section are visibly
the Commission's own instruction rather than an omission.**

lessons.title: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-01

chunks.heading: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-01
chunks.excerpt:
# Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-01

## Hours 1–5 · Real estate economics, marketing, and the nature of real estate

**Commission areas of study covered:** 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(A) Real Estate Economics and Marketing ·
(B) Nature of Real Estate
**Clock hours:** 5. Under 605:10-5-1(i)(5) **not more than one clock hour may be registered within any
one sixty-minute period and no more than ten minutes of each hour may be used for breaks** — so an
Oklahoma clock hour carries at least fifty minutes of instruction.
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review. **605:10-3-1(a)(1) lists
twenty-two areas of study and allocates no hours among them.**
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is available.

> **The information presented in this course should not be used as a substitute for competent legal
> advice.** — required by 605:10-5-3(i)(6), and meant literally throughout.

## Overview

*(605:10-5-3(i)(2) requires an overview statement for each course. This is Module OK-01's.)*

This module establishes what real estate is as a legal object and how the market for it behaves. It
begins with the vocabulary — land, real estate, real property, the bundle of rights — because every
later module depends on it, and ends with the economics that decide why a property is worth what it
is worth in a particular Oklahoma market in a particular year. It also sets out what this course is
and where it sits: **the Basic Course of Real Estate is Part I of a two-part series**, and 90 hours
does not complete a student's education.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
*(605:10-5-3(i)(1) requires suitable learning objectives. Three or more per clock hour are provided
throughout this course.)*

1. Distinguish land, real estate and real property and explain what a licensee is actually marketing.
2. Name the five rights in the bundle and identify which one a given transaction transfers.
3. Apply the fixture test to a disputed item and state what a licensee does about it at listing.
4. Name the physical and economic characteristics of land and use each to explain a market behaviour.
5. Distinguish personal property from real property and name the two events that convert one to the other.
6. Explain why real estate supply is inelastic in the short run and what that does to price.
7. Name the demand and supply factors that move a local Oklahoma market.
8. State what a licensee may say about market direction and what they may not.
9. Describe the structure of the Oklahoma licensing path, including the three-year education clock.
10. Explain why this course is Part I of II and what Part II is.
11. State the three different passing percentages Oklahoma rules use and which examination each governs.
12. Identify the pre-enrolment notices 605:10-5-1(m) requires and why they matter before payment.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Land, real estate, real property; the bundle of rights | ≥50 min |
| 2 | Fixtures, trade fixtures, severance; the licensee's discipline | ≥50 min |
| 3 | Physical and economic characteristics of land | ≥50 min |
| 4 | Real estate economics: supply, demand, cycles, and Oklahoma's drivers | ≥50 min |
| 5 | Marketing fundamentals, and the Oklahoma licensing path | ≥50 min |

---

## Hour 1 — Land, real estate, and real property

### 1.1 Three words that are not synonyms

chunks.heading: 1.2 The bundle of rights
chunks.excerpt:
**Land** is the surface of the earth, the space above it, and the subsurface beneath it. Air rights are
severable and real; a developer may buy the right to build above a corridor without buying the
corridor. **Subsurface rights are severable too, and in Oklahoma that is not a footnote.** Mineral,
oil and gas rights are routinely severed from surface ownership across the state, and a great deal of
Oklahoma land is sold by an owner who does not own what is under it.

**Real estate** is land plus everything permanently attached, by nature or by human effort — trees,
water, buildings, fences, in-ground pools, the wiring inside the walls.

**Real property** is real estate plus **the bundle of legal rights** attaching to it. This is the term
that matters, because it is the only one that describes what is actually sold. A buyer is not
purchasing bricks; they are purchasing a set of enforceable rights against the rest of the world.

### 1.2 The bundle of rights

Five rights, and the metaphor is a bundle of sticks precisely because sticks come out one at a time:

- **Possession** — to occupy and hold.
- **Use or enjoyment** — to use the property in any lawful manner.
- **Exclusion** — to keep others out.
- **Disposition** — to transfer the interest, by sale, gift, will or otherwise.
- **Encumbrance** — to pledge it as security, or to grant lesser interests in it.

Every stick may be sold, leased, mortgaged, granted or reserved separately. A tenant holds possession,
use and exclusion for a term while the landlord keeps disposition. A lender holds a stick that becomes
decisive only on default. **An Oklahoma seller may convey the surface and reserve the minerals** — and
that is the single most common bundle question a new Oklahoma licensee will meet.

chunks.heading: 1.3 The mineral question, stated once and correctly
chunks.excerpt:
### 1.3 The mineral question, stated once and correctly

Because it comes up immediately and because getting it wrong is expensive:

- **Surface and mineral estates can be, and frequently are, separately owned in Oklahoma.**
- A deed conveys what it says it conveys. **Whether minerals are included is a title question**, and it
  is answered by the title examination and by counsel, not by a licensee, not by the seller's belief,
  and not by what the last listing said.
- **A licensee never states what mineral interest a property carries.** The correct professional
  handling is to raise the question at listing, get it into the title work early, and tell a buyer to
  have it answered by counsel before their contingencies expire.

**This course states no Oklahoma rule of mineral title**, because Oklahoma's oil and gas and title
provisions were not read from primary text for this project. What a licensee carries is the
recognition and the routing, which is enough to keep them out of trouble and to serve the client.

### 1.4 Personal property, and the line between

**Personal property** — *chattels* — is everything that is not real property. It is movable, transfers
by **bill of sale**, and is not conveyed by a real estate contract unless the contract says so.

Two events cross the line. **Annexation** turns personal property into real property by attaching it —
the subject of Hour 2. **Severance** turns real property into personal property by detaching it:
standing timber is real estate, cut timber is personal property; growing crops are generally real
estate, harvested crops are personal property.

---

## Hour 2 — Fixtures, trade fixtures, and what a licensee actually does

### 2.1 The test

chunks.heading: 2.2 Trade fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
A **fixture** is personal property attached to real estate so as to have become part of it. Once it is
a fixture it conveys unless expressly excluded, and the buyer is entitled to find it there at closing.

Whether an item has become a fixture is decided by **the intention of the party who attached it, judged
objectively** — not by what that party privately meant, but by what the circumstances show. Courts read
intention through:

- **Method of annexation.** How firmly attached, and what damage would removal do?
- **Adaptation to the real estate.** Was it made or fitted for this particular property? Custom storm
  windows cut for these openings are adapted; generic screens stacked in the garage are not.
- **Relationship of the parties.** Tenant and owner are treated differently, because expectations differ.
- **Agreement.** A written agreement settles the question, which is why the absence of one leaves it to
  be argued.

### 2.2 Trade fixtures

A **trade fixture** is an item a tenant attaches for the conduct of their business — a walk-in cooler,
a hydraulic lift, shelving fitted to a shop floor. **60 O.S. 334** allows a tenant, during the term,
to remove qualifying items affixed for trade, manufacture, ornament or domestic use if removal can
occur without injury to the premises and the item has not become an integral part of them. An
agreement permitting removal or an owner's permission can also matter. Do not assume every attached
business item is removable or that leaving it behind automatically proves a gift. Review the lease,
attachment, damage and timing; refer disputed ownership or removal rights to counsel.

### 2.3 Three patterns, all preventable at listing

chunks.heading: 2.4 The discipline
chunks.excerpt:
**The item everyone assumes.** The seller's grandmother's chandelier, wired in. It is a fixture and it
conveys unless excluded. The correct handling is not to note it and hope — it is to have the seller
**remove and replace it before the photographs are taken.** A buyer who fell in love with a photograph
has a reasonable expectation, and the licensee who allowed that photograph created the problem.

**The item that is not the seller's to convey.** Leased or financed equipment — propane tanks, water
treatment, solar arrays, security systems, sometimes HVAC. It looks like a fixture and the seller does
not own it, and a buyer cannot discover that by looking.

**The item installed by a tenant.** On a property with a business tenant, some of what is bolted down
is going with them, and a buyer bidding on a partly equipped building needs to know which.

### 2.4 The discipline

**Write down what conveys.** At the listing appointment walk the property with the seller and settle
every arguable item — appliances, window treatments, mounted televisions, light fixtures, playsets,
sheds, tanks, treatment equipment. Two written lists: included and excluded. Twenty minutes at
listing; a saved transaction later.

Ask one question explicitly, every time: **"Is any equipment on this property leased or financed?"**

---

## Hour 3 — The characteristics of land

### 3.1 Physical characteristics

**Immobility.** A parcel cannot be moved, so demand in Tulsa cannot be met by supply in Lawton. This is
why real estate markets are local and why a national statistic describes no market anyone can actually
buy in. It is also why *location* dominates value.

chunks.heading: 3.2 Economic characteristics
chunks.excerpt:
**Indestructibility, or durability.** Land endures. Improvements depreciate; the land beneath them does
not disappear. This is why lenders write thirty-year loans against it and why the overwhelming majority
of any Oklahoma market's housing stock was built in the past rather than this year.

**Uniqueness, or non-homogeneity.** No two parcels are identical; even two identical houses sit on
different ground. This is the legal foundation of **specific performance** as a remedy in real estate
contracts, because damages cannot buy an equivalent parcel.

### 3.2 Economic characteristics

**Scarcity.** Land is finite — not scarce everywhere, and Oklahoma has a great deal of it, but scarce
where people want to be, which is what drives price.

**Improvements.** What is built on and around a parcel changes its value, and improvements to
neighbouring property affect it too — a new interchange, a new school, a new plant.

**Permanence of investment.** Capital sunk into grading, utilities, foundations and streets is fixed
and long-lived. It cannot be recovered and redeployed, which is why development decisions are slow and
hard to reverse.

**Area preference, or *situs*.** People's preference for a particular area, partly rational and partly
not. Situs is the economic expression of immobility and it is what an appraiser measures when adjusting
for location.

---

## Hour 4 — Real estate economics — 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(A)

### 4.1 Supply is inelastic in the short run

chunks.heading: 4.2 What moves demand
chunks.excerpt:
Bringing new housing to market takes years: land assembly, entitlement, financing, platting,
infrastructure, construction. So when demand rises — an employer expands, a rate cut brings buyers off
the fence, a demographic wave reaches first-purchase age — **supply cannot respond, and the adjustment
happens entirely in price and in time on market.**

That lag is the structural reason real estate cycles, and it is why the cycle overshoots in both
directions: by the time the supply response arrives, the demand condition that caused it may have
passed.

### 4.2 What moves demand

Population and household formation; **employment and income**; interest rates and credit availability;
consumer confidence; and the price of the alternative, which is rent.

**In Oklahoma, one demand factor deserves separate naming: the energy sector.** Employment, income and
in-migration in several Oklahoma markets move with oil and gas activity, and a commodity price
movement can change a local housing market within a quarter — faster than employment data reports it
and far faster than supply can respond. A licensee working such a market should understand that they
are working a market with a cycle inside the cycle.

### 4.3 What moves supply

Availability of land; construction cost, including labour and materials; the cost and availability of
construction finance; the entitlement and permitting environment; and the existing stock coming to
market.

### 4.4 The market cycle

chunks.heading: 4.5 What may and may not be said
chunks.excerpt:
**Recovery** — absorption of existing supply, falling vacancy, prices flat then rising. **Expansion** —
demand exceeds supply, prices rise, new construction starts. **Hypersupply** — completions overtake
absorption, vacancy rises, price growth slows. **Recession** — supply exceeds demand, vacancy high,
prices flat or falling, construction stops.

A licensee should be able to say where a local market appears to sit and what evidence says so. A
licensee should **not** predict when it will move.

### 4.5 What may and may not be said

**May:** name the factors; cite recorded data with its source; describe what closed sales show; say
what inventory and days on market are doing.

**May not:** state where prices will go. **Nobody can**, and a licensee who states a forecast as fact
has made a representation they cannot support. Oklahoma's rules put the same principle on the school
itself — 605:10-5-1(d) forbids advertising a course as approved before approval and forbids claiming
Commission endorsement — and the professional standard for a licensee is no lower.

---

## Hour 5 — Marketing fundamentals and the Oklahoma licensing path

### 5.1 What marketing a property actually is

Not advertising. **Marketing is the sequence: price the property from evidence, prepare it, present it
accurately, expose it to the market that will buy it, and manage the response.** Advertising is one
step and it is not the one that decides outcomes.

Two rules govern every piece of it, and both come back in Module OK-13 on Fair Housing:

chunks.heading: 5.2 The Oklahoma path to a licence
chunks.excerpt:
- **Describe the property, never the people.** Never the buyer, never the tenant, never the neighbours.
- **Attribute or verify. Never assert.** Every figure in a listing came from somewhere. Square footage
  from a tax record is an assessment record and not a measurement; acreage from a prior listing is
  somebody else's figure. *"The county record shows 1,940 square feet; if the exact figure matters to
  you, have it measured"* identifies a source. Under 59 O.S. 858-515.1, permitted third-party area
  sources must be identified; independent verification is not required. This does not guarantee area
  accuracy or create blanket protection for unrelated false statements. See the assessment supplement.

### 5.2 The Oklahoma path to a licence

**Ninety clock hours.** 59 O.S. § 858-302(A): a person eighteen or older who submits evidence of
successful completion of **ninety clock hours** of basic real estate instruction in a
Commission-approved course of study may apply to take the examination for a **provisional sales
associate** licence.

**And the three-year clock.** The same subsection: *"The education required in this subsection shall
only be valid for a period of three (3) years from the date the school certified successful completion
of the course; thereafter, the applicant shall be required to successfully complete an additional
ninety (90) clock hours."*

**Three years, measured from the date the SCHOOL CERTIFIED completion** — not from the day you finish
the last module and not from your application date. Plan around it from the day you enrol.

chunks.heading: 5.3 Part I of II — and why that matters to you
chunks.excerpt:
**Then the state examination.** 605:10-3-5(f): **a score of seventy percent (70%) or more is a passing
grade on the provisional sales associate/sales associate examination.** Passing results are valid for
**one year** — 605:10-3-5(g) — and an approved application is valid for **one year** — 605:10-3-3(a)(1).

### 5.3 Part I of II — and why that matters to you

**605:10-5-3(j)** requires each entity to promote the Basic Course of Real Estate as **Part I of a two
part series**, with the **Provisional Postlicense Course of Real Estate as Part II.**

So: ninety hours qualifies you to sit the examination and to hold a **provisional** sales associate
licence. Section 858-302 then requires **further postlicense education after the provisional licence
issues** before a full sales associate licence can be obtained.

**A student who believes ninety hours is the whole of their education has been misled.** This course
says so here, in Hour 5, rather than in a footnote at Hour 90.

### 5.4 Three percentages, three examinations — do not confuse them

Oklahoma's rules use three different passing scores and they belong to three different things:

| Percentage | Examination | Rule |
|---:|---|---|
| **75%** | **this course's** end-of-course final examination | 605:10-5-3(f) |
| **70%** | the **state licensing** examination, provisional sales associate / sales associate | 605:10-3-5(f) |
| **80%** | an **instructor** applicant's qualifying examination | 605:10-5-1(f) |

A document that says "the passing score is 70 percent" without naming the examination has misstated
the regulator. **This course's final examination is passed at 75 percent**, and 605:10-5-3(f) permits
an entity to allow a student who fails to take another examination **without repeating instruction.**

chunks.heading: 5.5 What Oklahoma requires you to be told before you pay
chunks.excerpt:
### 5.5 What Oklahoma requires you to be told before you pay

**605:10-5-1(m)** requires every entity to post or provide a notice, easily observed by anyone desiring
to enrol, containing at least this language:

> "Applicants convicted of felony crimes referenced in Title 59 Section 858-301.1 or 858-4000.1 may be
> ineligible to obtain an Oklahoma Real Estate License for a predetermined number of years. For
> clarification, please contact the Commission and/or review the cited section of law as referenced
> herein. **The Commission will allow the applicant to seek preapproval prior to enrolling in a
> pre-license course.**"

and a statement that applicants who are **not permanent U.S. citizens** should review their eligibility
on the Commission's website **prior to enrolling** in pre-license education.

**Read the emphasised sentence.** Oklahoma expressly offers **preapproval before enrolment**. If the
felony provisions may apply to you, use it — before you pay for ninety hours, not after you finish
them. **This course states no offence, period or eligibility rule from §§ 858-301.1 or 858-4000.1**,
because those sections were not read from primary text for this project. The notice routes you to the
Commission and to the sections themselves, and so does this course.

### 5.6 The status of this course

**This is a version 1.0 submission draft. It is not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is
available for it.** Under 605:10-5-1(d) no person or entity may advertise a course as approved before
the Commission approves it, and may not advertise that it is endorsed, recommended or accredited by
the Commission.

### Module OK-01 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module OK-01
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items: one applied scenario, five engagement items and five remediation items. The applied item
must be answered correctly; the engagement and remediation sets are passed at 80 percent. **Both
thresholds are StateCourse standards** — 605:10-5-3 prescribes no in-module assessment and no in-module
score. **The 75 percent that IS prescribed applies to the end-of-course final examination**, under
605:10-5-3(f), and 605:10-5-3(g) requires this school to publish its grading standards and give them to
you in writing at the beginning of the course.

---

## Instructor source note for Module OK-01

Every Oklahoma citation in this module — 59 O.S. § 858-302, and 605:10-3-1, 605:10-3-3, 605:10-3-5,
605:10-5-1 and 605:10-5-3 — was read on 2026-08-20 from the Commission's *Oklahoma Real Estate License
Code and Rules* effective 1 November 2025, and is recorded in
`oklahoma/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the Oklahoma Broker Relationships Act
(59 O.S. §§ 858-351 to 858-363); the Oklahoma Real Estate Contract Form Committee's promulgated forms;
§§ 858-301.1 and 858-4000.1; Oklahoma's oil, gas and mineral title provisions; and the OREC syllabus
referenced at 605:10-5-1(a)(3). Where this module reaches one of those it names the question and routes
it.

lessons.title: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-02

chunks.heading: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-02
chunks.excerpt:
# Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-02

## Hours 6–11 · Rights and interests in real estate, and legal descriptions

**Commission areas of study covered:** 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(C) Rights and Interest in Real Estate ·
(D) Legal Descriptions
**Clock hours:** 6 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review;
605:10-3-1(a)(1) allocates no hours among its twenty-two areas of study.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is available.

> **The information presented in this course should not be used as a substitute for competent legal
> advice.** — 605:10-5-3(i)(6).

## Overview

The interests a person may hold in Oklahoma land, and the three ways those interests are described in
writing. This module covers freehold estates and their defeasible forms, life estates and the future
interests that follow them, encumbrances of both kinds, the forms of concurrent and common-interest
ownership, and the rectangular survey system — which matters more in Oklahoma than in most states,
because most Oklahoma land outside the platted towns is described by it.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
1. Classify an estate in land by duration and identify a defeasible fee from its granting language.
2. Distinguish a life estate from a fee, name the future interests that follow it, and explain waste.
3. State why a life tenant cannot convey a fee and what a licensee does about it at listing.
4. Distinguish easement appurtenant, easement in gross, licence and encroachment.
5. Name the four government powers and identify which is operating in a fact pattern.
6. Compare the forms of concurrent ownership and state what happens at a death under each.
7. Explain what a condominium owner owns and how that differs from a cooperative.
8. Read a rectangular-survey description and compute the acreage it describes.
9. Recognise a metes-and-bounds description and a lot-and-block description.
10. State why a licensee never supplies a legal description from memory or a tax record.
11. Identify a severed mineral estate as a title question and route it.
12. Compute area problems in square feet and acres.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 6 | Government powers; freehold estates and defeasible fees | ≥50 min |
| 7 | Life estates, future interests, waste | ≥50 min |
| 8 | Encumbrances I: easements, licences, encroachments | ≥50 min |
| 9 | Encumbrances II: liens, restrictions, priority | ≥50 min |
| 10 | Concurrent ownership and common-interest ownership | ≥50 min |
| 11 | Legal descriptions and land measurement | ≥50 min |

---

## Hour 6 — Government powers and freehold estates

### 6.1 Four powers — PETE

chunks.heading: 6.2 Estates
chunks.excerpt:
**Police power.** Regulation for public health, safety, morals and general welfare — zoning, building
codes, subdivision regulation, environmental controls, licensing. Exercised **without compensation**,
which is the point: an owner whose property is downzoned and loses value is generally not entitled to
be paid, because the government has regulated rather than taken.

**Eminent domain.** The power to take private property for public use, exercised through
**condemnation** and requiring **just compensation**. A partial taking compensates for the part taken
and for damage to the remainder.

**Taxation.** The power to charge against property. The real estate tax lien customarily takes priority
over other liens regardless of recording order.

**Escheat.** Reversion to the state when an owner dies leaving no heirs and no will, so that land never
becomes ownerless.

### 6.2 Estates

An **estate** is the degree, quantity, nature and extent of a person's interest in land. **Freehold**
estates are of indefinite duration and involve ownership; **leasehold** estates are of determinable
duration and involve possession without ownership — Module OK-16's business.

**Fee simple absolute** is the greatest interest the law knows: perpetual, freely transferable in life
and at death, subject only to the four powers and to whatever encumbrances burden it.

### 6.3 Defeasible fees

**Fee simple determinable.** Created by durational language — *so long as, while, during, until*. The
estate **ends automatically** on the stated event and the grantor holds a **possibility of reverter**.

chunks.heading: Hour 7 — Life estates, future interests, waste
chunks.excerpt:
**Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.** Created by conditional language — *provided that, on
condition that, but if*. The estate **does not end automatically**; the grantor holds a **right of
re-entry** and must act.

These are drafted and litigated by counsel. **A licensee's job is to recognise the language in a title
commitment and route it**, because a defeasible fee is a genuine limitation on what a buyer is
acquiring and it will not announce itself in the listing.

---

## Hour 7 — Life estates, future interests, waste

### 7.1 The life estate

A freehold estate measured by a lifetime. The **life tenant** may possess, use and take the profits for
the measuring life, and has no right at all after it.

Usually measured by the life tenant's own life. Where measured by another's it is an estate **pur autre
vie** — "for the life of another" — and it can outlive its holder, passing to their estate until the
measuring life ends.

### 7.2 What follows

- Back to the **grantor** or the grantor's successors: a **reversion**.
- To a named **third party**: a **remainder**, and that party is the **remainderman**.

Both are **future interests** — presently existing property rights whose enjoyment is postponed. **A
remainderman owns something today**, which is precisely why a life tenant cannot sell the fee.

### 7.3 Waste

A life tenant must not commit **waste** — must not damage or diminish the property to the injury of the
remainderman. The life tenant is generally responsible for ordinary maintenance, taxes and interest on
encumbrances; permanent structural changes and destruction are waste.

chunks.heading: Hour 8 — Encumbrances I: easements, licences, encroachments
chunks.excerpt:
**The practical consequence is immediate and severe: a life tenant cannot convey a fee simple.** A sale
of the fee requires the remainderman to join. A licensee who takes a listing without establishing who
must sign has built a transaction on a defect that surfaces at the closing table.

The determination is the title company's and counsel's. **The noticing is the licensee's**, and it
happens at the listing appointment, in the form of one question: *"Who else has to sign?"*

---

## Hour 8 — Encumbrances I: easements, licences, encroachments

### 8.1 Easements

An **easement** is a right to use another's land for a particular purpose.

**Easement appurtenant.** Benefits a **parcel**. It has a **dominant tenement** — benefited — and a
**servient tenement** — burdened — and it **runs with the land**, passing automatically to each new
owner of the dominant tenement. This is the kind that matters most in residential practice, because it
transfers whether or not anyone mentions it.

**Easement in gross.** Benefits a **person or entity** rather than a parcel. There is a servient
tenement but no dominant one. Utility easements are the standard case, and commercial easements in
gross are generally assignable.

**In Oklahoma the utility and pipeline easement deserves particular attention.** Gathering lines,
transmission lines and access easements cross a great deal of Oklahoma land, and they carry rights of
access, of surface use and sometimes of future construction that a buyer will not expect from looking
at the ground. Every one of them is a title-work question routed to the title company and counsel.

chunks.heading: 8.2 Licence and encroachment
chunks.excerpt:
**Creation:** by express grant or reservation in a deed; by implication from prior use and necessity at
severance; by **necessity**, most commonly for a landlocked parcel; and by **prescription**, through
long open use.

**Termination:** merger, release, abandonment shown by conduct rather than mere non-use, expiration of
a stated term, or the end of the necessity that created an easement by necessity.

**This course states no Oklahoma prescriptive period**, because Oklahoma's limitations provisions were
not read from primary text for this project. A long-standing use of someone else's land — a drive, a
path, a mowed strip, a gate — is routed to counsel and a surveyor.

### 8.2 Licence and encroachment

A **licence** is mere permission to enter for a purpose. It is personal, **revocable at will**, and does
not run with the land. Permission to hunt on a section is a licence; a recorded right of access is an
easement. They look identical on the ground and are entirely different in law, which is why the
question is answered from the records.

An **encroachment** is an unauthorised physical intrusion of an improvement onto adjoining land — a
fence, a shed, an eave, a drive. It is not permission of any kind; it is a trespass that has been
built.

**Encroachments are discovered by survey.** A title commitment will typically **except survey matters
and encroachments unless a survey is furnished and the exception removed.** A buyer who declines a
survey has accepted that risk and should be told so in those words. Left long enough, an encroachment
can mature into a prescriptive easement or an adverse possession claim, which converts a fixable
problem into a lawsuit.

---

## Hour 9 — Encumbrances II: liens, restrictions, priority

### 9.1 Liens

chunks.heading: 9.2 Priority
chunks.excerpt:
A **lien** is a charge against property securing a debt or obligation. It affects title; it does not by
itself dispossess. Every lien is classified twice:

- **Voluntary** (the owner created it — a mortgage) or **involuntary** (the law or a court imposed it —
  a tax lien, a judgment).
- **General** (attaching to the debtor's property generally — a judgment) or **specific** (attaching to
  one identified parcel — a mortgage, a mechanic's lien, a property tax lien).

The judgment lien is the one that surprises people, because it can surface against a parcel nobody
associated with the debt.

### 9.2 Priority

**First in time, first in right**, measured by recording — with the **real estate tax lien** as the
standard exception, customarily taking priority regardless of order. Priority may also be rearranged by
contract through a **subordination agreement**, which is why the **title commitment** rather than a list
of recording dates is the operative document.

### 9.3 Mechanic's and materialman's liens

Claimed by someone who furnished labour or materials for improvement of the property. Its danger is
structural: in many states a mechanic's lien's priority may **relate back to a date earlier than the
filing** — commencement of work, or first furnishing of materials — so a claim not yet in the records
can outrank one that is.

chunks.heading: 9.4 Deed restrictions and covenants
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no Oklahoma filing period, notice requirement or priority date**, because
Oklahoma's mechanic's lien provisions were not read from primary text for this project. What a licensee
carries is the **warning sign and the routing**: recent or ongoing construction, a renovation finished
in the past several months, an unpaid or disputed contractor. Raise it at listing; route it to the
title company and counsel; do not let it be found a week before closing.

### 9.4 Deed restrictions and covenants

Private limits recorded against the land, commonly as a declaration of covenants, conditions and
restrictions governing a subdivision. They **run with the land** and are enforceable by the association
or by benefited owners.

**They are separate from zoning and the more restrictive controls.** A city may permit a use the
covenants forbid, and the covenants win. Buyers routinely assume municipal approval settles it. It does
not, and the covenants are read **before** the offer is written.

A restriction discriminating on a protected basis is **void and unenforceable** whatever the record
says — Module OK-13.

---

## Hour 10 — Concurrent and common-interest ownership

### 10.1 Concurrent ownership

**Tenancy in common.** Undivided interests, which may be **unequal**, each freely transferable in life
and **passing by will or intestacy at death**.

**Joint tenancy.** Equal undivided interests with the **right of survivorship** — on a joint tenant's
death the interest passes to the survivors and does not go through the estate. Traditionally requires
four unities: time, title, interest and possession.

**Tenancy by the entirety**, where a jurisdiction recognises it for married couples, carries
survivorship and its own creditor characteristics.

chunks.heading: 10.2 Common-interest ownership
chunks.excerpt:
**Which form a deed creates, and which a particular buyer should take, is a legal and tax question for
counsel and the buyer's tax adviser.** A licensee who advises a buying couple on how to take title has
practised law. **This course states no Oklahoma rule of concurrent ownership or marital property**,
because those provisions were not read from primary text for this project. The licensee's contribution
is to raise the question early enough that it is decided deliberately rather than by whatever default
the closing agent used.

**Partition.** Any co-owner may generally seek a court division in kind, or a sale and division of
proceeds. It is the remedy when co-owners cannot agree, and it is a lawsuit.

### 10.2 Common-interest ownership

**Condominium.** The owner holds the **unit in fee** plus an **undivided interest in the common
elements**, governed by a declaration, bylaws and an association funded by assessments. Each unit is
separately assessed, taxed, financed and transferred.

**Cooperative.** The owner holds **shares in a corporation** and a **proprietary lease**. The
corporation owns the real estate; the resident owns personal property. That changes financing — share
loans, not mortgages — changes transfer, because a board usually approves purchasers, and changes the
risk, because the corporation's blanket mortgage and other shareholders' delinquencies affect everyone.

**Time-share.** An interval interest with its own consumer rules and a resale market bearing no
resemblance to the sale market.

chunks.heading: Hour 11 — Legal descriptions and land measurement — 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(D)
chunks.excerpt:
**Questions to get answered in writing before a buyer's contingencies expire:** the assessment and what
it covers; the reserves; any pending or implied special assessment; litigation; restrictions on pets,
rentals, vehicles and occupancy; and whether the buyer's lender will lend on this project at all —
which for condominiums is a live question and not a formality.

---

## Hour 11 — Legal descriptions and land measurement — 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(D)

### 11.1 Three methods, and one non-method

**Metes and bounds.** Courses and distances from a **point of beginning**, running the perimeter and
**closing back to it**. A description that does not close does not describe a parcel.

**Rectangular survey, or government survey.** A grid built from **principal meridians** running north
and south and **base lines** running east and west. **Most of Oklahoma uses the Indian Meridian and
Indian Base Line; the Panhandle uses the Cimarron Meridian and Cimarron Base Line.** Identify the
applicable survey system from the actual description rather than assuming one statewide origin. **Townships** run
in horizontal tiers and vertical **ranges**; each township is six miles square and holds **36
sections**, each one mile square and **640 acres**. Sections are numbered 1 through 36 beginning in the
north-east corner and running back and forth, so section 36 lands in the south-east corner.

**Lot and block, or recorded plat.** References a lot and block on a recorded subdivision plat. The
everyday description for platted urban and suburban land.

**And the non-method: a street address is never a legal description.** Neither is a tax parcel number.
Both find a property; neither describes one.

### 11.2 Reading a rectangular description

chunks.heading: 11.3 The measurements
chunks.excerpt:
Read it **backwards**, dividing as you go, because the description narrows from largest to smallest.

*The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 14.* Section = **640**; SW quarter = 640 ÷ 4 = **160**; NE quarter
of that = 160 ÷ 4 = **40 acres**.

*The S 1/2 of the NW 1/4 of the SE 1/4.* 640 ÷ 4 = 160; ÷ 4 = 40; ÷ 2 = **20 acres**.

*The W 1/2 of the NE 1/4 of Section 8.* 640 ÷ 4 ÷ 2 = **80 acres**. At $4,900 an acre: 80 × 4,900 =
**$392,000**.

Each quarter divides by four; each half divides by two. Work right to left and the arithmetic is
trivial.

### 11.3 The measurements

| Unit | Equivalent |
|---|---|
| 1 acre | **43,560 square feet** |
| 1 section | 1 square mile, **640 acres** |
| 1 township | 6 miles square, **36 sections**, 23,040 acres |
| 1 mile | 5,280 feet |

*Worked.* A lot 150 feet by 290.4 feet is 150 × 290.4 = 43,560 square feet — **exactly one acre**.
Recognising 43,560 on sight saves time on the examination and in practice.

*Worked.* A lot 88 feet by 165 feet is 14,520 square feet; 14,520 ÷ 43,560 = **one third of an acre**.

### 11.4 The rule about descriptions

**Never supply a legal description from memory, from a tax record, from a prior listing or from the
seller's recollection.** It comes from the **deed** or from the **title company**, and it is copied
exactly, character for character.

chunks.heading: Module OK-02 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Distinguish a legal description from an attributed size figure. Under **59 O.S. 858-515.1**, a licensee
is not required to provide an area figure. If the licensee supplies one from a permitted third-party
source, including tax-assessor records, the source must be identified. The statute does not impose an
independent duty to investigate or verify that figure. An assessor figure is not thereby a boundary
survey. Recommend a qualified surveyor where exact acreage or boundaries matter; do not claim that
source attribution guarantees accuracy or immunizes unrelated misrepresentations.

**And in Oklahoma, add one more:** a legal description of the surface says nothing about who owns the
minerals. That is a separate title question and it is routed with the rest of the title work.

### Module OK-02 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module OK-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, from 605:10-5-3(f).

---

## Instructor source note for Module OK-02

Commission's Code and Rules effective 1 November 2025 and are recorded in

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module OK-02
chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Oklahoma's limitations, mechanic's lien,
concurrent ownership, marital property, condominium and subdivision provisions; its oil, gas and

The same repair reviewed 59 O.S. 858-515.1 in the November 2025 OREC Code and Rules and corrected the

The source supplement and final-exam source manifest record this later review separately.
