chunks.heading: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-06
chunks.excerpt:
# Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-06

## Hours 30–35 · Service contracts and marketing activities

**Commission areas of study covered:** 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(G) Service Contracts · (J) Marketing Activities
**Clock hours:** 6 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review;
605:10-3-1(a)(1) allocates no hours among its twenty-two areas of study.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is available.

> **The information presented in this course should not be used as a substitute for competent legal
> advice.** — 605:10-5-3(i)(6).

## Overview

The agreements under which a broker provides brokerage services, and what a licensee does with a
property once one is signed. In Oklahoma the first half of that is governed by §§ 858-355.1, 858-356 and
858-363, and the second half by a set of advertising provisions in § 858-312 that a new licensee should
read before their first listing rather than after their first complaint.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
1. Describe the types of listing arrangement by who is owed compensation and when.
2. State who enters a brokerage agreement in Oklahoma and in whose name.
3. State the three § 858-355.1 disclosure requirements and the § 858-356 confirmation requirement.
4. Apply § 858-353(A)(7)'s one-year cap and sixty-day default to a compensation agreement.
5. Describe the § 858-355.1(E) limited-service disclosure and what it must contain.
6. Take a listing appointment through the sequence an Oklahoma licensee must follow.
7. Identify the § 858-312 grounds that govern advertising and marketing.
8. Audit an advertisement for the licensee-status disclosure § 858-312(20) requires.
9. Explain what § 858-312(12) permits and forbids about prizes, gifts and inducements.
10. Explain why § 858-312(10) forbids guaranteeing future profits.
11. Describe the marketing sequence and the licensee's role at each step.
12. State the rule that prevents most marketing misrepresentation.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 30 | Types of listing arrangement | ≥50 min |
| 31 | Elements of a brokerage agreement in Oklahoma | ≥50 min |
| 32 | The listing appointment, in sequence | ≥50 min |
| 33 | Buyer service agreements and limited service | ≥50 min |
| 34 | Marketing activities: the sequence and the standards | ≥50 min |
| 35 | Advertising and the § 858-312 grounds | ≥50 min |

---

## Hour 30 — Types of listing arrangement

### 30.1 Distinguished by one question

**In what circumstances is the broker owed compensation?**

chunks.heading: 30.2 Net arrangements
chunks.excerpt:
**Exclusive right to sell.** The broker is owed on a sale during the term **regardless of who procures
the buyer, including the owner.** The ordinary residential arrangement, and ordinary because it removes
the broker's incentive problem: the firm can spend on marketing without worrying that the owner's cousin
will appear and eliminate the fee.

**Exclusive agency.** The broker is the only one authorised, **but the owner reserves the right to sell
to a buyer they find themselves** without owing compensation. Which produces the obvious dispute — who
found the buyer? — and the answer belongs in the agreement, in writing, usually by naming the reserved
prospects.

**Open.** Non-exclusive. The owner may authorise any number of brokers and **only the one who procures
the buyer is compensated.** The owner may also sell themselves and owe nothing.

*(The words "listing" and "agency" survive in ordinary usage. Remember Module OK-03: § 858-360(B) means
there is no agency relationship underneath them. What exists is a **brokerage agreement** under which a
**broker** provides **brokerage services** to a **party**.)*

### 30.2 Net arrangements

A **net** arrangement is one in which the owner receives a fixed net amount and the broker keeps whatever
is above it.

chunks.heading: 30.3 Termination
chunks.excerpt:
The potential conflict is that **the broker receives the increase above a fixed seller net**, so the
owner may not appreciate how much market value is being allocated to the broker. The owner's stated
net does not fall merely because the sale price rises; the previous inverse-price description was wrong.
Under § 858-353(A)(1) a broker owes **honesty and reasonable skill and care to all parties**, and under
§ 858-353(A)(7) compensation must be disclosed in writing before the contract's effective date — an
arrangement whose amount is unknown until the sale price is known makes that disclosure difficult to
make meaningfully.

**This course states no Oklahoma rule permitting or prohibiting net arrangements**, because 605:10-3-1
and the broker-relationships sections do not address them and no other provision on the point was read
from primary text for this project. The professional position does not depend on it: any such proposal
goes to your broker before it goes anywhere else.

### 30.3 Termination

An arrangement ends by **expiry**, by **performance**, by **mutual agreement**, or by **operation of
law** — destruction of the property, death or incapacity in some circumstances.

**And § 858-353(A)(7)(b) supplies an Oklahoma-specific termination rule that catches people:** the time
frame for which a compensation agreement is valid **may not exceed one (1) year**, and **if no time frame
is specified it defaults to sixty (60) days.** An undated compensation agreement does not run until
someone cancels it. It expires in sixty days by statute.

Whether a party who ends an arrangement early owes anything is a question about the contract, and it goes
to your broker and counsel. A licensee who says "you can cancel any time, no consequences" has given
legal advice.

---

chunks.heading: Hour 31 — Elements of an Oklahoma brokerage agreement
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 31 — Elements of an Oklahoma brokerage agreement

### 31.1 Who enters it — § 858-363

> Associates **shall not enter into a brokerage agreement with a party in the associate's name** and
> shall only be allowed to enter into the agreement **in the name of the broker.** A real estate broker
> **may authorize associates to provide brokerage services in the name of the real estate broker**, which
> may include the execution of written agreements.

**Every brokerage agreement is in the broker's name.** You sign under your broker's authorisation, and
you should know the scope of yours before your first appointment.

### 31.2 What must be in it — § 858-355.1(A)

> **All brokerage agreements shall incorporate as material terms the duties and responsibilities set
> forth in Section 858-353.**

Not summarised. **Incorporated as material terms.**

### 31.3 The compensation terms — § 858-353(A)(7)

- **In writing.**
- **Communicated before the effective date of the contract** for sale or lease.
- **Covering compensation and fees assessed on each transaction** to the represented party.
- **With a stated time frame not exceeding one year** — and remember the sixty-day default.

### 31.4 The commercial elements

Beyond the statutory minimum, every agreement must settle:

chunks.heading: 31.5 The disclosures that accompany it — §§ 858-355.1(C) and 858-356
chunks.excerpt:
- **The parties.** Everyone who must sign to convey — which Module OK-05 established is not answered by
  looking at the deed. Route it to counsel and the title company **at the appointment.**
- **The property**, with a legal description from the deed or the title company — never from a tax
  record, a prior listing or memory. **And in Oklahoma, whether minerals are included.**
- **The price**, which is the owner's decision.
- **The term**, with a definite end date, within the one-year compensation cap.
- **How compensation is earned** — the event that triggers it.
- **Included and excluded items**, in two written lists — Module OK-01 Hour 2.
- **Authorisations**: marketing, photography, lockbox, sign, showings, internet display, and any opt-outs.
- **Any reserved prospects**, on an exclusive-agency arrangement.
- **The owner's disclosure obligations** under the Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act, and the
  broker's own § 858-353(A)(5) duty.

### 31.5 The disclosures that accompany it — §§ 858-355.1(C) and 858-356

**Describe and disclose the § 858-353 duties in writing, prior to the party signing a contract** to sell,
purchase, lease, option or exchange. Then the disclosure is **confirmed by each party in writing in a
separate provision, incorporated in or attached to the contract.** Where the broker did not prepare the
contract, **the broker documents compliance.**

Do it at the appointment. Nobody has ever been disciplined for disclosing too early.

---

## Hour 32 — The listing appointment, in sequence

**Before you arrive:** confirm your authority under § 858-363; pull the tax record, the plat, the prior
sales and the comparables; and have the written § 858-353 duties disclosure with you.

**On arrival, in order:**

chunks.heading: 32.1 The four questions most licensees do not ask
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Describe and disclose the § 858-353 duties in writing** — § 858-355.1(C). Note that you did, with
   the date.
2. **Explain what your firm can do**, including whether it will provide full or limited services —
   § 858-355.1(E).
3. **Walk the property.** Settle included and excluded items as you go. Ask specifically about **leased or
   financed equipment**, tenant-installed items, recent construction, and any unpaid or disputed
   contractor.
4. **Ask the ownership questions.** Who is on the deed; is anyone deceased; is there a trust, an estate, a
   life estate, a divorce; is there a tenant; **and who owns the minerals.** Route every complication to
   counsel and the title company rather than resolving it in the driveway.
5. **Present the pricing evidence in writing**, as a range, with adjustments shown — Module OK-07.
6. **Complete the agreement**, in the broker's name, incorporating the § 858-353 duties, with compensation
   disclosed in writing and a term inside the one-year cap.
7. **Explain the owner's disclosure obligations** under the Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act
   and your own § 858-353(A)(5) duty.
8. **Confirm in writing** what was decided, the same day.

### 32.1 The four questions most licensees do not ask

- **"Is any equipment on this property leased or financed?"** A buyer cannot discover it by looking.
- **"Has any work been done in the last year, and is everyone paid?"** Recent construction plus a payment
  dispute is a lien risk, routed to the title company at listing.
- **"Who owns the minerals?"** In Oklahoma, asked every time, routed every time.
- **"Who else has to sign?"** Five minutes now; a postponement later.

---

## Hour 33 — Buyer service agreements and limited service

### 33.1 Working with a buyer

chunks.heading: 33.2 The § 858-353(B) duties, in buyer practice
chunks.excerpt:
The same statutory structure applies. A broker **may provide brokerage services to one or both parties**
— § 858-355.1(B) — the § 858-353(A) duties run to **all parties** regardless, and the § 858-353(B) duties
run to the party the broker is serving.

**Serving both parties is not dual agency**, because Oklahoma has none. It requires **written notice to
both parties that the firm is doing so, prior to the parties signing a contract** — § 858-355.1(D) — and
the full duty set applies to both.

### 33.2 The § 858-353(B) duties, in buyer practice

**(B)(1)** — **inform the party in writing, when an offer is made, that they will be expected to pay
certain costs, brokerage service costs and the approximate amount.** This is a statutory duty with a
trigger and a form, and Module OK-08 is where the arithmetic lives.

**(B)(2)** — **keep the party informed regarding the transaction.** Most complaints are about silence
rather than fraud, and this is the subsection they are made under.

### 33.3 Limited service — § 858-355.1(E)

> If a broker intends to provide **fewer brokerage services than those required to complete a
> transaction**, the broker shall provide **written disclosure** to the party for whom the broker is
> providing brokerage services. Such disclosure shall include **a description of those steps in the
> transaction for which the broker will not provide brokerage services**, and also state that **the
> broker assisting the other party in the transaction is not required to provide assistance with these
> steps in any manner.**

Three requirements, and all three must be met:

chunks.heading: Hour 34 — Marketing activities — 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(J)
chunks.excerpt:
1. **In writing.**
2. **A description of the specific steps** not covered. Not "limited services" as a label — a description.
3. **An express statement that the other side's broker need not pick them up.**

The third exists because the predictable harm of limited service is a party who assumes somebody will
handle the gap. The statute requires them to be told, in writing, that nobody will.

**And note the limit of what (E) permits.** It permits fewer **services**. It does not permit fewer
**duties** — § 858-353(A) and (B) are mandatory and unwaivable.

---

## Hour 34 — Marketing activities — 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(J)

### 34.1 What marketing actually is

Not advertising. **The sequence: price from evidence, prepare, present accurately, expose to the market
that will buy it, and manage the response.** Advertising is one step and it is not the one that decides
outcomes.

**Price from evidence** — Module OK-07. **Prepare** — condition, access, information assembled before the
first showing rather than after the first question. **Present accurately** — photographs that show the
property as it is; a description whose every factual claim has a source. **Expose** — the multiple
listing service where the firm participates, digital syndication, signage with the owner's consent,
open houses, direct outreach. **Manage the response** — showing feedback, offer handling under
§ 858-353(A)(2), and keeping the party informed under § 858-353(B)(2).

### 34.2 The two rules that govern all of it

**Describe the property, never the people.** Never the buyer, never the tenant, never the neighbours.
Module OK-13 takes fair housing up in full; the discipline starts here.

chunks.heading: 34.3 Showings and feedback
chunks.excerpt:
**Attribute or verify. Never assert.** Every figure in a listing came from somewhere. Square footage from
a county record is an assessment record and not a measurement. Acreage from a prior listing is somebody
else's figure. School assignment changes. Zoning is the municipality's determination. Flood zone is a
determination, not a glance at a map.

*"The county record shows 1,940 square feet; if the exact figure matters to you, have it measured."*
That sentence identifies the source. Section 858-515.1 permits specified third-party area sources,
including tax-assessor records, with source identification and without independent verification. Its
limited protection is not a guarantee of accuracy or immunity for every marketing statement. Honesty
and reasonable care under 858-353(A)(1) still matter. This clarification was source-reviewed 2026-09-06.

### 34.3 Showings and feedback

Showings happen with the owner's authorisation and on the owner's terms, and what may be said about the
owner's position is limited by § 858-353(A)(4): **willingness to accept less, willingness to accept
different financing terms, motivating factors, and anything specifically designated confidential** stay
in. Everything else about the transaction is on a different footing — but knowing where the line is is
not the same as broadcasting up to it.

---

## Hour 35 — Advertising and the § 858-312 grounds

### 35.1 The provisions to read before your first listing

**§ 858-312(20)** — it is a ground for suspension or revocation to advertise **to buy, sell, rent, or
exchange any real estate without disclosing in writing that the licensee is a real estate licensee.**

chunks.heading: 35.1 The provisions to read before your first listing
chunks.excerpt:
**Every advertisement discloses licensee status, in writing.** Including one placed to buy. Including a
personal purchase. The **blind advertisement** — one that hides that a licensee is involved — is the
classic failure and it is a named ground here.

**§ 858-312(11)** — advertising or offering real estate for sale, rent or lease, or **placing a sign on
any real estate**, **without the consent of the owner or the owner's authorised representative.** Consent
for the sign is part of the authorisations settled in the agreement — Hour 31.

**§ 858-312(2)** — **substantial misrepresentations or false promises in the conduct of business, or
through real estate licensees, or advertising, which are intended to influence, persuade, or induce
others.** Advertising is named expressly.

**§ 858-312(10)** — **guaranteeing, or authorising or permitting any licensee to guarantee, future
profits which may result from the resale of real estate.**

Read (10) carefully, because it forbids something licensees say casually. *"You'll make money on this."*
*"This will be worth $X in five years."* *"You can't lose."* **Guaranteeing future profits from resale is
a named ground for suspension or revocation**, and nobody can support such a statement anyway.

**§ 858-312(12)** — prizes, money, gifts and inducements. This one has a permission inside it and both
halves matter:

> Using prizes, money, gifts or other valuable consideration **as an inducement to secure customers or
> clients to purchase specific property**; however, licensees **may use prizes, money, gifts or other
> valuable consideration for marketing purposes provided they are not contingent or limited to
> individuals making an offer or purchasing a specific property.**

chunks.heading: 35.2 The school-side parallel, worth knowing
chunks.excerpt:
**Forbidden:** an inducement tied to buying a **specific property**. **Permitted:** general marketing use
— a giveaway at an open house, a promotional item — **provided it is not contingent on, or limited to,
people who make an offer or purchase that property.**

**§ 858-312(28)** — soliciting, selling or offering for sale real property **by means of a deceptive
practice.**

**§ 858-312(21)** — paying any part of a fee, commission or other valuable consideration **to any person
not licensed.** Referral arrangements with unlicensed persons are a licence problem.

**§ 858-312(14)** — paying compensation to any person **performing the services of a real estate licensee
who has not first secured a licence.**

### 35.2 The school-side parallel, worth knowing

605:10-5-1(d) forbids an education entity to advertise a course as approved **before approval**, and to
advertise that it is **endorsed, recommended or accredited by the Commission** — though it may say a
course has been approved. The distinction between "approved this course" and "endorses this school" is
the same distinction a licensee must keep between what is verified and what is claimed.

**And this course, accordingly: it is a version 1.0 submission draft, it is not approved, and no Oklahoma
pre-license credit is available for it.**

### 35.3 Auditing an advertisement, line by line

Three questions for every sentence:

1. **Who is speaking?** Is licensee status disclosed in writing — § 858-312(20)?
2. **What is claimed?** Can every factual claim be supported by something written down, and is any of it
   a guarantee of future profit — § 858-312(10) — or a misrepresentation — § 858-312(2)?
3. **Who is described?** If the answer is a person rather than a building, rewrite it.

### Module OK-06 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module OK-06
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items, delivered as in Module OK-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, from 605:10-5-3(f).

---

## Instructor source note for Module OK-06

Oklahoma citations in this module — 59 O.S. §§ 858-312, 858-353, 858-355.1, 858-356, 858-360 and 858-363,
and 605:10-3-1, 605:10-5-1 and 605:10-5-3 — were read on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`oklahoma/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** the Residential Property Condition Disclosure

lessons.title: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-07

chunks.heading: Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-07
chunks.excerpt:
# Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-07

## Hours 36–41 · Value and appraisal

**Commission area of study covered:** 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(I) Value and Appraisal
**Clock hours:** 6 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review;
605:10-3-1(a)(1) allocates no hours among its twenty-two areas of study.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is available.

> **The information presented in this course should not be used as a substitute for competent legal
> advice.** — 605:10-5-3(i)(6).

## Overview

What value is, how it is estimated, and where a licensee's competence ends and an appraiser's begins.
The module works through the principles of value, the four tests of highest and best use, and all three
approaches, with a fully worked comparison grid. It closes on the boundary, which in Oklahoma carries a
specific licence consequence: § 858-312(13) makes contingent appraisal compensation and undisclosed
interest a ground for suspension or revocation.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
1. Distinguish value, price and cost and explain why an owner's improvement cost is not value.
2. Name the principles of value and apply substitution, contribution, conformity and anticipation.
3. Apply the four tests of highest and best use in the correct order.
4. Select and reject comparables on stated grounds.
5. Build a comparison grid with adjustments in the correct direction.
6. Reconcile to a range by weighting evidence rather than averaging.
7. Describe the cost approach and compute a value from it.
8. Describe the income approach and compute net operating income and value.
9. State the boundary between a licensee's market analysis and an appraisal.
10. State what § 858-312(13) forbids about appraisal compensation and interest.
11. Handle a low appraisal correctly, including what may and may not be sent to an appraiser.
12. Respond accurately to an automated valuation, an old appraisal and a neighbour's figure.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 36 | Value, price, cost; the principles; the four forces | ≥50 min |
| 37 | Highest and best use; selecting comparables | ≥50 min |
| 38 | The sales comparison approach: a worked grid | ≥50 min |
| 39 | Reconciliation, and what a range actually says | ≥50 min |
| 40 | The cost approach and the income approach | ≥50 min |
| 41 | The appraisal process, the boundary, and § 858-312(13) | ≥50 min |

---

## Hour 36 — Value, price, cost, and the principles

### 36.1 Three words

**Value** is worth to a typical buyer under stated conditions — most often **market value**: the most
probable price a property should bring in a competitive and open market under conditions requisite to a
fair sale, buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably, neither under undue duress.

chunks.heading: 36.2 The principles
chunks.excerpt:
**Price** is what was actually paid in a particular transaction. A historical fact, possibly influenced
by a motivated seller, an uninformed buyer, an unusual concession, or a relationship between the parties.

**Cost** is what it took to produce the improvements.

**Cost does not become value.** The owner who spent $92,000 on a pool, a shop building and a kitchen is
frequently astonished by the appraisal, and the explanation is the **principle of contribution**: an
improvement adds what it adds **to the value of the whole**, not what it cost.

### 36.2 The principles

**Supply and demand.** Value rises when demand exceeds supply.

**Substitution.** A buyer will pay no more than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute.
**This is the foundation of all three approaches.**

**Contribution.** As above, and measured by the change in the value of the whole.

**Conformity.** Value is maximised where a property conforms reasonably to those around it. Corollaries:
**progression** — a modest house gains from better neighbours; **regression** — an over-improved house
loses to worse ones. The most over-built house on the street is the standard regression case and the
standard listing where the owner cannot understand the price.

**Anticipation.** Value reflects expected future benefits, which is why a rumoured interchange moves
prices before it is built.

**Change.** Nothing is static.

**Increasing and diminishing returns.** Additional investment adds value up to a point, then does not.

**Plottage** — assembling adjacent parcels to produce a whole worth more than the sum of the parts, the
increment being **assemblage** value. **Externalities** — influences from outside the property.

### 36.3 The four forces

chunks.heading: Hour 37 — Highest and best use, and selecting comparables
chunks.excerpt:
**Social** — demographics, household composition, preferences. **Economic** — employment, income, rates,
credit. **Governmental** — zoning, codes, taxation, public investment. **Environmental** — physical
characteristics, topography, transport, location.

**In several Oklahoma markets the economic force carries a distinct component** — energy sector
employment and income, which can move a local market faster than any other single factor. Naming it is
analysis. Predicting it is not, and Module OK-01 Hour 4 explains why.

---

## Hour 37 — Highest and best use, and selecting comparables

### 37.1 Highest and best use

The use that is:

1. **Legally permissible**,
2. **Physically possible**,
3. **Financially feasible**, and
4. **Maximally productive**.

**All four, in that order.** A use that is not legally permissible never reaches the profitability
question — which is also where a licensee stops, because whether a use is permissible is the
municipality's determination.

Note that highest and best use is analysed **as though vacant** and **as improved**, and the two can
differ. Where the value as vacant exceeds the value as improved, the improvement has become a
**demolition candidate** — which happens in changing commercial corridors and occasionally on a large
residential lot.

### 37.2 Selecting comparables

**Use:** recent **closed** sales; similar in size, age, style, condition and location; in the same market
area and ideally the same submarket; **arm's-length** transactions between unrelated parties.

chunks.heading: Hour 38 — The sales comparison approach: a worked grid
chunks.excerpt:
**Do not use, or use only with explanation:** current **listings** — asking prices, which prove only what
someone hoped for; **pending** sales, whose prices are not yet known; **distressed** sales, unless the
subject is itself distressed; and sales between family members or otherwise not arm's-length.

**The quality test:** the **fewer and smaller** the adjustments a comparable needs, the better it is. A
comparable requiring $60,000 of gross adjustment is telling you it is not really comparable.

**And an Oklahoma-specific selection question:** does the comparable convey the same mineral interest as
the subject? A surface-only sale and a sale conveying minerals are not comparable without an adjustment
nobody in this room is qualified to make. Where the question arises, it is named in the analysis and
routed — not silently ignored.

---

## Hour 38 — The sales comparison approach: a worked grid

### 38.1 The rule that governs every grid

**Adjust the COMPARABLE, never the subject.** The subject is what is being valued; it has no price yet
and there is nothing on it to adjust.

- Comparable **superior** to the subject → adjust it **DOWN**.
- Comparable **inferior** to the subject → adjust it **UP**.

Getting the direction wrong moves the answer **twice** as far as leaving the adjustment out. **Check
every line before you present.**

### 38.2 The subject

*1,940 sq ft two-storey, 4 bed, 2.5 bath, attached 2-car garage, unfinished storm shelter, 0.28 acre,
built 2004, original kitchen.*

### 38.3 The grid

chunks.heading: 38.4 Check the directions, line by line
chunks.excerpt:
| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C | Comp D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sale price | $268,000 | $241,000 | $294,500 | $259,000 |
| Sold | 2 months ago | 6 months ago | 1 month ago | 9 months ago |
| Market conditions +0.35%/mo | +$1,876 | +$5,061 | +$1,031 | +$8,159 |
| Living area | 2,010 (+70) | 1,830 (−110) | 2,120 (+180) | 1,905 (−35) |
| Area adj. at $54/sq ft | −$3,780 | +$5,940 | −$9,720 | +$1,890 |
| Bathrooms | 2.5 | 2 (−0.5) | 3.5 (+1) | 2.5 |
| Bath adj. at $6,500 each | $0 | +$3,250 | −$6,500 | $0 |
| Storm shelter | unfinished | none | finished safe room | unfinished |
| Shelter adj. | $0 | +$4,500 | −$5,500 | $0 |
| Kitchen | original | original | renovated | renovated |
| Kitchen adj. | $0 | $0 | −$19,000 | −$19,000 |
| **Gross adjustment** | **$5,656** | **$18,751** | **$41,751** | **$29,049** |
| **Net adjustment** | **−$1,904** | **+$18,751** | **−$39,689** | **−$8,951** |
| **Adjusted price** | **$266,096** | **$259,751** | **$254,811** | **$250,049** |

### 38.4 Check the directions, line by line

- **Comp A** is larger — superior — so the area adjustment is **negative**. Correct.
- **Comp B** is smaller, has fewer baths and no shelter — inferior on all three — so all three are
  **positive**. Correct.
- **Comp C** is larger, has more baths, a finished safe room and a renovated kitchen — superior on all
  four — so all four are **negative**. Correct.
- **Comp D** is slightly smaller — inferior, so **positive** — and has a renovated kitchen — superior, so
  **negative**. Correct.

**Market conditions are positive on every comparable**, because the market has risen since each sale and
each would sell for more today. Time adjustments are applied before the physical adjustments.

chunks.heading: Hour 39 — Reconciliation
chunks.excerpt:
*(The storm shelter line is Oklahoma-specific and real: an in-ground shelter or an engineered safe room
is a recognised feature in this market. The dollar amounts in this grid are illustrative and are not
Oklahoma market data.)*

---

## Hour 39 — Reconciliation

### 39.1 Reconciliation is not averaging

The four adjusted figures: **$266,096 · $259,751 · $254,811 · $250,049.**

The arithmetic mean is **$257,677.** That number tells you **nothing about which evidence was
strongest**, which is exactly why reconciliation is judgment.

### 39.2 Weighting the evidence

- **Comp A** — sold **2 months ago**, needed only **$5,656 gross**. **Most reliable by a distance.**
- **Comp B** — 6 months, $18,751 gross. Moderate.
- **Comp D** — **9 months**, $29,049 gross. Weak on both counts.
- **Comp C** — **$41,751 gross**, adjusted on four separate characteristics. **Least reliable.**

**A defensible conclusion:** the weight of the evidence supports roughly **$256,000 to $266,000**, with
Comp A arguing for the upper part of the range.

### 39.3 And say what the grid actually shows

The three heavily adjusted comparables cluster between $250,000 and $260,000 while the single most
reliable one lands at $266,000 — and the largest single adjustment in the whole grid is the **kitchen**.

**Tell the seller that.** It is a real fact about their choices: renovate, price into the cluster, or
price at the top of the range and expect the market to test it.

**A market analysis that hides the disagreement between its own comparables is not evidence. It is
decoration.**

### 39.4 The four rules for presenting one

chunks.heading: Hour 40 — The cost approach and the income approach
chunks.excerpt:
1. **In writing**, with the comparables and the adjustments shown.
2. **As a range**, not a single figure.
3. **The price is the owner's decision.**
4. **Labelled for what it is** — a licensee's market analysis, not an appraisal.

---

## Hour 40 — The cost approach and the income approach

### 40.1 The cost approach

**Land value + (reproduction or replacement cost of improvements − accrued depreciation) = value.**

**Reproduction cost** builds an exact replica. **Replacement cost** builds a structure of equal utility
with current materials and methods, and is the more common basis.

**Accrued depreciation** has three sources:

- **Physical deterioration** — wear, age, deferred maintenance. Curable or incurable.
- **Functional obsolescence** — a defect in the design itself. A bedroom reachable only through another
  bedroom; one bathroom in a four-bedroom house. Curable or incurable.
- **External obsolescence** — caused by something **outside** the boundaries. A new highway, a closed
  plant, a declining area. **Always incurable**, because the owner cannot fix it.

*Worked.* Land value $42,000. Replacement cost of a 1,940 sq ft house at $158/sq ft = **$306,520**.
Accrued depreciation: physical $52,000, functional $14,000, external $0. Value = 42,000 + (306,520 −
66,000) = **$282,520.**

The cost approach **governs new construction and special-purpose property** where comparables are thin —
a church, a school, a fire station, a grain facility. It is **weakest on older buildings**, because
estimating accrued depreciation on a seventy-year-old house is largely judgment.

### 40.2 The income approach

chunks.heading: 40.3 Three checks on any pro forma
chunks.excerpt:
**Potential gross income**, less **vacancy and collection loss** → **effective gross income**, less
**operating expenses** → **net operating income**. Then **NOI ÷ capitalisation rate = value.**

*Worked.* A twelve-unit building. Potential gross income $129,600. Vacancy and collection loss 7% =
$9,072. **Effective gross income $120,528.** Operating expenses $51,800. **NOI = $68,728.** At a
capitalisation rate of 8.0%: 68,728 ÷ 0.08 = **$859,100.**

**Debt service and depreciation are NOT operating expenses.** They sit below the NOI line. Two identical
buildings with different financing have the **same NOI** and different cash flow, which is why NOI is the
figure a buyer compares.

**The gross rent multiplier** — sale price ÷ gross rent — is a screening device, not a valuation. It
ignores expenses entirely.

### 40.3 Three checks on any pro forma

1. **Is there a replacement reserve line?** Roof, mechanicals, parking. No reserve understates expenses,
   overstates NOI, and overstates value **by the reserve divided by the cap rate** — a large number.
2. **Is the vacancy assumption real?** 2 percent in a market running at 8 is a wish.
3. **Are the rents actual or projected?** "Market rents after renovation" is a plan, not income.

---

## Hour 41 — The appraisal process and the boundary

### 41.1 The process

Define the problem — property, interest, purpose, date, definition of value. Determine the scope of
work. Collect and analyse general and specific data. Analyse highest and best use. Estimate land value.
Apply the applicable approaches. **Reconcile.** Report.

### 41.2 The boundary

chunks.heading: 41.3 § 858-312(13) — read it before you accept any valuation work
chunks.excerpt:
**An appraisal is an opinion of value produced by a licensed or certified appraiser under that person's
own licence and professional standards. A salesperson is not an appraiser and does not perform
appraisals.**

**A licensee's market analysis** uses the same comparison logic and is **not** an appraisal. It must not
be labelled or described as one, and must not be presented so that a client can believe it is one.

**This course states no Oklahoma appraiser licensing requirement**, because Oklahoma's appraiser
licensing provisions were not read from primary text for this project. What **was** read is the licence
consequence in the next paragraph.

### 41.3 § 858-312(13) — read it before you accept any valuation work

It is a ground for suspension or revocation to:

> **Accept employment or compensation for appraising real estate contingent upon the reporting of a
> predetermined value**, or **issue any appraisal report on real estate in which the licensee has an
> interest unless the licensee's interest is disclosed in the report.** **All appraisals shall be in
> compliance with the Oklahoma real estate appraisal law**, and the person performing the appraisal or
> report **shall disclose in writing to the employer whether the person performing the appraisal or
> report is licensed or certified by the Oklahoma Real Estate Appraiser Board.**

Four separate obligations:

1. **No compensation contingent on reaching a predetermined value.** Ever.
2. **Disclose your interest** in the property in any appraisal report you issue.
3. **Comply with the Oklahoma real estate appraisal law.**
4. **Disclose in writing to whoever engaged you whether you are licensed or certified by the Oklahoma
   Real Estate Appraiser Board.**

chunks.heading: 41.4 The low appraisal
chunks.excerpt:
**That fourth one applies to a real estate licensee producing a valuation-type report.** If you are asked
for a "broker price opinion," a "valuation report," or anything a reader might treat as an appraisal, the
disclosure obligation in (13) is live.

### 41.4 The low appraisal

The most common appraisal event in residential practice.

**What happened:** the lender lends on the **lesser of price or appraised value**, so a gap has opened.
The buyer covers it in cash, or the price moves, or another route is found, or the contract ends
according to whatever the appraisal contingency says.

**What the licensee does:**

- **Read the appraisal contingency and its deadline first**, before saying anything to anyone.
- **Review the report for factual errors** — wrong square footage, wrong bedroom count, a comparable that
  is not comparable, a missed permit, a mineral conveyance difference. Factual errors are the legitimate
  basis for a **reconsideration of value**, submitted **through the lender.**
- **Present the options neutrally** and route the decision to the party.
- **Do not attempt to influence the appraiser.** Pressure on an appraiser to reach a number is misconduct,
  it engages appraiser independence rules in a federally related transaction, and § 858-312(13) shows
  what Oklahoma thinks of predetermined values.

**What you may properly provide:** **factual information** — a list of improvements with dates and costs,
a survey, a plat, the seller's disclosure, comparable sales you believe relevant. **Facts, yes. A target,
no.**

### 41.5 The three figures a seller will show you

chunks.heading: Module OK-07 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**An automated online valuation.** A model's output from public and listing data. It has never been inside
the house and cannot see condition or finish. **Evidence to weigh, not a valuation.** Do not adopt it; do
not dismiss it; put your own written analysis beside it.

**An old appraisal.** A 2019 appraisal is a 2019 opinion, for a purpose that may not be this one, on a
property that may since have changed.

**A neighbour's figure.** Ask what it is based on. It is almost always somebody's **list price**, which is
an asking price and evidence of nothing.

**And under no circumstances confirm in writing a figure you did not derive.** That is not honesty and
reasonable skill and care under § 858-353(A)(1), and it is how a licensee ends up defending a number they
never computed.

### Module OK-07 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module OK-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, from 605:10-5-3(f).

chunks.excerpt:
# Oklahoma Basic Course of Real Estate, Part I of II — Module OK-08

## Hours 42–46 · Estimating transaction expenses

**Commission area of study covered:** 605:10-3-1(a)(1)(H) Estimating Transaction Expenses
**Clock hours:** 5 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Commission review;
605:10-3-1(a)(1) allocates no hours among its twenty-two areas of study.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Oklahoma pre-license credit is available.

> **The information presented in this course should not be used as a substitute for competent legal
> advice.** — 605:10-5-3(i)(6).

## Overview

This module exists because Oklahoma made it a **statutory duty**. Section 858-353(B)(1) requires a broker
to **inform the party in writing, when an offer is made, that the party will be expected to pay certain
costs, brokerage service costs and the approximate amount of the costs.** That is a duty with a trigger,
a form and a content requirement, and this module supplies the arithmetic to discharge it.

It covers the categories of cost on each side, proration in both directions, cash to close, seller's net,
and — most importantly — what makes every one of these figures an estimate and how to label it.

## Learning objectives

chunks.heading: Timed sequence
chunks.excerpt:
1. State the § 858-353(B)(1) duty and identify its trigger, form and required content.
2. Name the categories of cost a buyer pays and identify who quotes each.
3. Name the categories of cost a seller pays.
4. Distinguish a debit from a credit and identify which party receives each.
5. Prorate an item paid in arrears, in the correct direction, on a stated basis.
6. Prorate an item paid in advance, in the correct direction.
7. Count proration days correctly rather than estimating months.
8. Compute a buyer's estimated cash to close.
9. Compute a seller's estimated net proceeds.
10. Explain the four reasons every such figure is an estimate.
11. State how a cost sheet must be labelled and where its figures come from.
12. Relate an incorrect net sheet to § 858-312(2) and § 858-353(A)(1).

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Instruction |
|---|---|---:|
| 42 | The § 858-353(B)(1) duty; categories of cost | ≥50 min |
| 43 | Proration: the method, both directions | ≥50 min |
| 44 | The buyer's estimated cost sheet, worked | ≥50 min |
| 45 | The seller's estimated net, worked | ≥50 min |
| 46 | Why it is an estimate, and how to label it | ≥50 min |

---

## Hour 42 — The duty, and the categories

### 42.1 The statutory duty

**§ 858-353(B)** — owed **only to a party for whom the broker is providing brokerage services**, and
**mandatory and unwaivable**:

> 1. **Inform the party in writing when an offer is made that the party will be expected to pay certain
>    costs, brokerage service costs and approximate amount of the costs.**

**Trigger:** when an offer is made. **Form:** writing. **Content:** the costs the party will be expected
to pay, **including brokerage service costs**, and **their approximate amount.**

chunks.heading: 42.2 What a buyer pays
chunks.excerpt:
Note the word **approximate**. The statute does not require a guaranteed figure and could not sensibly do
so. What it requires is a written estimate, made at the right moment, that a party can actually rely on
as an estimate — which is why Hour 46's labelling discipline is part of discharging the duty rather than
an add-on to it.

**And note "brokerage service costs" specifically.** Compensation is named. Section 858-353(A)(7)
independently requires compensation and fees to be disclosed **in writing before the effective date of
the contract**, with a term capped at one year and defaulting to sixty days if unstated. The two
provisions overlap and both must be satisfied.

### 42.2 What a buyer pays

**Loan costs.** Origination and underwriting fees; discount points if any; appraisal; credit report;
flood determination; any lender-required inspections.

**Title and settlement.** Lender's title policy; owner's policy if the buyer pays for it; abstracting or
title examination where used; closing or settlement fee; recording fees; survey if obtained.

**Prepaid items and escrow deposits.** Prepaid interest from closing to month end; the first year's
hazard insurance premium; the initial deposit into the tax and insurance escrow.

**Prorations.** The buyer's share of anything the seller paid in advance; and a **credit** for anything
paid in arrears that the buyer will pay later.

**Inspections** the buyer elects — general, termite, roof, septic, well, structural.

### 42.3 What a seller pays

chunks.heading: 42.4 Who quotes what — and it is not the licensee
chunks.excerpt:
Payoff of existing loans, **including per-diem interest to the payoff date**; brokerage service
compensation; the seller's share of closing or settlement fees; abstracting or the owner's title policy
where the seller pays; recording of releases; agreed repair or closing-cost credits to the buyer;
prorated items; and any liens or judgments that must be cleared.

### 42.4 Who quotes what — and it is not the licensee

**The lender** quotes loan costs, prepaid interest and escrow deposits. **The closing agent or title
company** quotes title, settlement, recording and the prorations. **The lender's payoff department**
quotes the payoff, to a stated date.

**A licensee assembles the estimate from those sources and labels it.** A licensee does not invent any
line on it.

---

## Hour 43 — Proration

### 43.1 Three questions before any arithmetic

1. **What is the annual amount?**
2. **What basis?** A 365-day year, or a 360-day banker's year with 30-day months.
3. **Who gets the day of closing**, and is the item paid **in advance** or **in arrears**?

**The convention comes from the contract, not from habit.** Getting the basis or the closing-day
convention wrong produces a number close enough to look right and wrong enough to matter.

### 43.2 The direction

Ask one question: **who has had the use, and who has paid?** **Whoever paid for time they will not have
gets a credit.**

**Paid in arrears — property taxes.** The seller has had the use and has not paid. The buyer will pay the
whole bill. → **Credit the buyer, debit the seller.**

**Paid in advance — annual association dues, an annual insurance premium being assumed.** The seller has
paid for time the buyer will have. → **Credit the seller, debit the buyer.**

### 43.3 Count the days

chunks.heading: 43.4 Debits and credits
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked, in arrears.* Annual tax **$2,840**, closing **17 October**, 365-day basis, closing day to the
buyer.

Daily: 2,840 ÷ 365 = **$7.7808.**
Seller's days, 1 January through 16 October: 31+28+31+30+31+30+31+31+30+16 = **289 days.**
289 × 7.7808 = **$2,248.65** — a **credit to the buyer, debit to the seller.**

**Add the month lengths. Do not estimate "about ten months."** "About" produces a figure wrong by a
hundred dollars or more, and it will be wrong on the settlement statement too if nobody recomputes it.
And check whether the year is a leap year before dividing by 365.

*Worked, in advance.* Association dues **$480** paid annually on 1 January, same closing, same basis.

Daily: 480 ÷ 365 = **$1.3151.**
Buyer's days, 17 October through 31 December: 15+30+31 = **76 days.**
76 × 1.3151 = **$99.95** — a **credit to the seller, debit to the buyer.**

### 43.4 Debits and credits

A **credit** to a party is money in their favour. A **debit** is money against them.

The buyer's credits reduce cash to close. The seller's debits reduce net proceeds. Every prorated item
appears **twice** — as a credit to one party and a debit to the other — and the two must match.

---

## Hour 44 — The buyer's estimated cost sheet

*Purchase price $268,000. Loan $241,200 (90 percent). Earnest money $3,000 already deposited. Closing 17
October. Taxes paid in arrears, annual $2,840, 365-day basis, closing day to the buyer.*

chunks.heading: Hour 45 — The seller's estimated net
chunks.excerpt:
| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Purchase price | $268,000.00 |
| Loan origination, 0.75% of loan | 1,809.00 |
| Appraisal | 650.00 |
| Credit report and flood determination | 135.00 |
| Lender's title policy | 465.00 |
| Owner's title policy | 1,040.00 |
| Closing fee | 425.00 |
| Recording | 96.00 |
| Prepaid interest, 15 days at $41.86 | 627.90 |
| Hazard insurance, first year | 1,780.00 |
| Escrow deposit, taxes and insurance | 1,215.00 |
| **Subtotal** | **$276,242.90** |
| Less loan amount | (241,200.00) |
| Less earnest money | (3,000.00) |
| Less tax proration credit to buyer | (2,248.65) |
| **Estimated cash to close** | **$29,794.25** |

**Check the arithmetic yourself.** 268,000 + 1,809 + 650 + 135 + 465 + 1,040 + 425 + 96 + 627.90 + 1,780
+ 1,215 = **276,242.90.** Then 276,242.90 − 241,200 − 3,000 − 2,248.65 = **$29,794.25.**

**And note what the buyer actually needs to hear**, beyond the total: that the earnest money is not an
additional cost but a credit against it; that the tax proration is a credit because they will pay the
whole bill in due course; and that the escrow deposit is their own money going into an account, not a
fee.

---

## Hour 45 — The seller's estimated net

*Same transaction. First mortgage payoff $186,400 quoted good through 15 October. Brokerage service
compensation 6 percent. Seller's closing costs $1,540. Agreed repair credit to buyer $1,200. Tax
proration debit to seller $2,248.65.*

| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Sale price | $268,000.00 |
| Less first mortgage payoff | (186,400.00) |
| Less brokerage service compensation, 6% | (16,080.00) |
| Less seller's closing costs | (1,540.00) |
| Less repair credit to buyer | (1,200.00) |
| Less tax proration | (2,248.65) |
| **Estimated seller's net** | **$60,531.35** |

chunks.heading: 45.1 The payoff date, which is not a detail
chunks.excerpt:
268,000 − 186,400 − 16,080 − 1,540 − 1,200 − 2,248.65 = **$60,531.35.**

### 45.1 The payoff date, which is not a detail

**The payoff was quoted good through 15 October and the closing is 17 October.** Payoffs carry per-diem
interest. Two extra days at, say, $30.50 a day is another $61 — small here, and not small on a larger
loan or a longer slip.

**Always check the payoff's good-through date against the closing date**, and tell the seller in writing
that the figure moves if the closing moves. That is § 858-353(B)(2) — keeping the party informed — doing
real work.

### 45.2 Compensation, stated correctly

**Compensation is negotiable.** It is set by agreement between the broker and the party, not by any
board, association, listing service, custom or rule.

**§ 858-359(B)** provides that a broker receiving a fee **based on a selling price or lease cost** does
not thereby breach a duty. **§ 858-359(D)** provides that nothing requires or prohibits charging a
separate fee for each duty or service, and nothing requires a broker or owner of record to offer
compensation to any real estate professional.

**And § 858-312(4):** an **associate** may accept compensation **only from the broker with whom the
associate is associated.** Money moves from the closing to the broker, and from the broker to you.

---

## Hour 46 — Why it is an estimate, and how to label it

### 46.1 Four reasons every figure moves

chunks.heading: 46.2 So label it
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Payoffs carry per-diem interest and are quoted only to a stated date.**
2. **Closing costs are the closing agent's and the lender's figures**, and they change as underwriting
   settles.
3. **Prorations may rest on a tax bill that has not yet issued**, in which case the parties estimate from
   the prior year — and the contract should say what happens if the actual bill differs.
4. **Late changes move the total** — a repair credit agreed two days before closing, a change in the loan
   amount, a concession. Under **TRID** a change close to closing can trigger a redisclosure and a new
   three-business-day waiting period before consummation.

**That fourth point makes early decision-making a real service.** Getting changes settled early and
telling the lender promptly costs nothing and saves closing dates.

### 46.2 So label it

A cost sheet or net sheet:

- **says "estimate" on its face**;
- **shows its assumptions** — the basis, the closing-day convention, the payoff's good-through date, the
  tax year used;
- **names its sources** — lender, closing agent, payoff statement;
- **is delivered in writing**, which is what § 858-353(B)(1) requires anyway; and
- **is updated when a figure changes**, which is what § 858-353(B)(2) requires.

### 46.3 What happens when it is wrong

**A licensee who hands a seller a confident net figure that turns out $3,000 optimistic has created a
problem no apology fixes.** And depending on how it was presented, it is more than a customer-service
problem:

chunks.heading: 46.4 The one-page routine
chunks.excerpt:
- **§ 858-353(A)(1)** — honesty and reasonable skill and care to all parties.
- **§ 858-312(2)** — **substantial misrepresentations or false promises in the conduct of business**,
  intended to influence, persuade or induce. A net figure presented as certain, relied on in deciding to
  accept an offer, is exactly the shape of that ground.

The prevention is not caution about producing estimates. **It is producing them from the right sources,
labelling them honestly, and updating them.**

### 46.4 The one-page routine

At every offer, for the party you serve:

1. **Assemble** the figures from the lender, the closing agent and the payoff statement.
2. **Compute** the prorations by counting days on the contract's basis.
3. **Write** it, labelled as an estimate, with assumptions and sources shown.
4. **Deliver** it in writing — § 858-353(B)(1).
5. **Update** it when anything moves — § 858-353(B)(2).

Do that every time and the statutory duty is discharged and the client is genuinely served, which in this
instance are the same thing.

### Module OK-08 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module OK-01. The 80 percent engagement threshold and the 100 percent
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; the **75 percent** end-of-course standard is the
Commission's, from 605:10-5-3(f).

---

## Instructor source note for Module OK-08

Oklahoma citations in this module — 59 O.S. §§ 858-312, 858-353 and 858-359, and 605:10-3-1 and
605:10-5-3 — were read on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`oklahoma/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module OK-08
chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this module:** Oklahoma's property tax chapter and every
rate, cycle, exemption and payment date in it; Oklahoma's documentary stamp or transfer tax treatment;
RESPA, Regulation X, TILA and Regulation Z in their own text; and the Oklahoma Real Estate Contract Form
Committee's promulgated forms. **Every dollar figure in this module is an invented arithmetic
illustration and is not Oklahoma tax, fee or market data.** The TRID three-business-day rule is stated at
the level of principle from the general body of pre-license knowledge and every specific is routed to the
lender and the closing agent.
