chunks.heading: Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-03
chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-03

## Legal descriptions, land use control and environmental considerations

**Course:** Real Estate Fundamentals · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 30.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Read the three legal description methods and know which Pennsylvania uses.
2. Distinguish a legal description from an address, a tax parcel number and a plat reference.
3. Identify the four government powers that limit private ownership.
4. Distinguish zoning, variances, special exceptions and nonconforming uses.
5. State the § 35.333(a)(6) zoning-classification requirement and the consequence of omitting it.
6. Identify the environmental conditions a licensee must route rather than opine on.

---

## A. Legal descriptions

An **address** identifies a mailbox. A **tax parcel number** identifies an assessment record. **Neither
describes land**, and neither belongs in a deed as the description.

### A.1 Metes and bounds

**Pennsylvania is a metes and bounds Commonwealth.** A metes and bounds description begins at a **point
of beginning**, runs a sequence of **courses** (directions) and **distances**, calls **monuments** —
natural or artificial markers — and **returns to the point of beginning.**

Two working facts follow:

chunks.heading: A.2 Rectangular (government) survey
chunks.excerpt:
- **A description that does not close describes no parcel.** If the courses and distances do not return
  to the point of beginning, something is wrong, and it is a surveyor's problem, not a licensee's.
- **Monuments generally control over distances** where they conflict, because a called monument is
  physical evidence of what the parties actually meant. That is a rule of construction applied by courts,
  and it is named here so a licensee knows a conflict is resolvable — by a surveyor and counsel, not by
  the licensee.

**A fence is not a boundary.** It is evidence of where somebody once thought the boundary was. Where a
fence, a hedge, a driveway or a shed sits near a line, the answer is a **current survey**.

### A.2 Rectangular (government) survey

Townships, ranges, sections and quarter-sections, referenced to principal meridians and base lines. **A
section is one square mile and contains 640 acres.** Pennsylvania is not a public-land-survey state, but
this system is examinable and appears in national content.

### A.3 Reference to a recorded plat (lot and block)

Common in subdivisions: *Lot 14, Block C, of the [named] Plan of Lots, as recorded in Plan Book __, Page
__.* The recorded plat supplies the metes and bounds by reference. **The plat is only as good as its
recording**, which is why a subdivision lot's description points to a book and page.

### A.4 What a licensee actually does with a description

Read it against a **survey** and against the **deed**. Confirm the description in a listing matches the
description in the seller's deed. If the seller says the property "includes the strip behind the garage"
and the deed does not describe it, you have found a question — and § 35.292(a)(8) tells you what to do
with it.

---

chunks.heading: B. Government powers over private property
chunks.excerpt:
## B. Government powers over private property

Four, and they are superior to any private right:

- **Police power** — regulation for public health, safety, morals and general welfare. Zoning, building
  codes, subdivision regulation and environmental rules all rest here. **No compensation is paid**,
  because nothing is taken.
- **Eminent domain** — the power to take private property for public use, **with just compensation.**
  The proceeding is **condemnation**.
- **Taxation** — the power to levy against real property to fund government.
- **Escheat** — property reverts to the state when an owner dies with no heirs and no will.

**PETE** is the usual mnemonic. What matters underneath it is the compensation line: **police power
regulates without paying; eminent domain takes and pays.** A regulation so severe that it destroys all
economic use may be argued to be a taking — and that argument is a lawyer's, not a licensee's.

---

## C. Zoning and land use

### C.1 The instruments

- **Comprehensive plan** — the municipality's long-range policy document.
- **Zoning ordinance** — the enforceable rule: **use districts** (residential, commercial, industrial,
  agricultural, mixed), plus **bulk and dimensional controls** — setbacks, height, lot coverage, minimum
  lot area, frontage.
- **Subdivision and land development ordinance** — governs dividing land and developing it.
- **Building codes** — govern construction, with permits and a **certificate of occupancy**.

**Pennsylvania's Municipalities Planning Code and every local ordinance were not read for this project.
This course states no setback, height limit, lot size, use category, permit fee or approval deadline.**

### C.2 The four relief mechanisms — and how they differ

chunks.heading: C.3 The rule that puts zoning into every Pennsylvania agreement of sale
chunks.excerpt:
| Mechanism | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Variance** | Permission to depart from a **dimensional or use** requirement, granted on application, generally on a showing of hardship not created by the owner. |
| **Special exception / conditional use** | A use the ordinance **already contemplates** in that district, allowed once stated conditions are met. |
| **Nonconforming use** | A use that **lawfully predates** the ordinance. Its permitted scope, expansion limits and conditions of continuation are set by the ordinance itself. |
| **Rezoning** | Amendment of the ordinance itself — a legislative act, not an adjudication. |

Students merge the first three constantly. Hold the difference: a **variance** asks for an exception to
the rule; a **special exception** asks for something the rule already allows on conditions; a
**nonconforming use** asks for nothing because it was there first.

**"Grandfathered" is not a legal term and it is not a broker's conclusion.** When an owner uses it, what
they mean is a legal nonconforming use, whose scope is defined by an ordinance the licensee has not read.
Say what is known — *the owner states the use predates the current zoning* — and route the rest.

### C.3 The rule that puts zoning into every Pennsylvania agreement of sale

**§ 35.333(a)(6)** requires an agreement of sale to contain:

chunks.heading: C.4 § 35.333(a)(10) — the highway occupancy permit statement
chunks.excerpt:
> *"**The zoning classification of the property**, except if the property (or each parcel thereof, if
> subdividable) is **zoned solely or primarily to permit single-family dwellings**, together with a
> statement that **the failure of the agreement of sale to contain the zoning classification of the
> property shall render the agreement voidable at the option of the buyer** and, if voided, **deposits
> tendered by the buyer shall be returned to the buyer without a requirement of court action**."*

Three things to take from it.

**First, the exception is narrow.** It covers property zoned **solely or primarily** for **single-family
dwellings** — and *"each parcel thereof, if subdividable."* A duplex, a mixed-use building, a commercial
parcel, farmland, and a subdividable tract all need the classification stated.

**Second, the consequence runs against the seller.** The agreement becomes **voidable at the buyer's
option** — the buyer chooses. A seller cannot use the omission to escape.

**Third, the deposit comes back without litigation.** *"Without a requirement of court action"* means the
broker holding the deposit does not need an order. That is unusual, and it is why this requirement gets
its own paragraph in the companion course's module on agreements of sale.

### C.4 § 35.333(a)(10) — the highway occupancy permit statement

> *"A statement that **access to a public road may require issuance of a highway occupancy permit from
> the Department of Transportation**."*

Required in every agreement of sale. Its practical importance is largest on unimproved land, where a
buyer may discover after closing that the driveway they planned needs a permit they cannot get.
**This course states no permit standard, fee or process**, because PennDOT's regulations were not read.

chunks.heading: D. Environmental considerations
chunks.excerpt:
---

## D. Environmental considerations

A licensee is neither an inspector nor an environmental professional. § 35.292(b) says so directly:

> *"**A licensee is not required to conduct an independent inspection of the property.**"*

What a licensee **is** required to do is **§ 35.292(a)(8)** — advise the consumer to seek expert advice
beyond the licensee's expertise — and, under **§ 35.292(a)(4)**, to **comply with 68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73,
the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law**, which the companion course covers.

### D.1 Conditions to recognise and route

- **Lead-based paint** — the federal disclosure obligation attaches to **target housing**, generally
  pre-1978 dwellings, and reaches **known** lead-based paint and known hazards. Painting over it does not
  remove it. **The federal regulation was not read for this project; no notice period or record retention
  requirement is stated here.**
- **Radon** — a soil gas, measured by testing. An old test result is not a current reading. Pennsylvania
  has geology that makes this a live question in much of the Commonwealth; the answer is a **current
  test**, not a licensee's reassurance.
- **Asbestos**, **mould**, **underground storage tanks**, **wetlands**, **on-lot septic suitability**,
  **well water quality**, and **abandoned mine subsidence** — each investigated by a different specialist
  or agency.
- **Mine subsidence** deserves a specific note in Pennsylvania. Where a property sits above former deep
  mining, subsidence risk and any available protection are questions for the Commonwealth's own programme
  and for an insurer. **This project read no Pennsylvania mining or subsidence statute or programme
  document, and states nothing about coverage, eligibility or cost.**

chunks.heading: D.2 The habit that carries a licensee through all of it
chunks.excerpt:
### D.2 The habit that carries a licensee through all of it

Separate three things and say which is which, every time:

1. **What you know** — you saw it, measured it, or hold the document.
2. **What you were told** — attribute it to whoever told you.
3. **What you are guessing** — say nothing, and route it.

Every disclosure failure in either of these courses traces back to one of the three being presented as
another.

---

## Module PA-F-03 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-F-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

---

## Instructor source note for Module PA-F-03

**49 Pa. Code Chapter 35** was read on 2026-08-20 and is the source of **§ 35.292(a)(4), (a)(8) and
(b)** and of **§ 35.333(a)(6) and (a)(10)**, transcribed above.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this build:** the **Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning
Code** and every **local zoning, subdivision and building ordinance**; **PennDOT's highway occupancy
permit regulations**; **68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73**; Pennsylvania's **mining, subsidence, wetlands, septic
and well** statutes and programmes; **federal lead-based paint regulations**; and **EPA** guidance of any
kind.

**No setback, height limit, lot size, permit fee, approval deadline, radon action level, testing
protocol, remediation standard or insurance term is stated in this module.**

chunks.heading: Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-04
chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-04

## Transfer of title, deeds and recording

**Course:** Real Estate Fundamentals · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 30.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Distinguish voluntary from involuntary transfer.
2. State the essential elements of a valid deed.
3. Distinguish the deed types by the covenants each carries.
4. Explain what recording does and does not accomplish.
5. Distinguish an abstract, a title opinion and title insurance, and distinguish owner's from lender's
   coverage.
6. Identify what happens at settlement in Pennsylvania and who does it.

---

## A. Voluntary transfer

**By deed**, during life. **By will**, at death — the maker is the **testator**, the gift of real property
a **devise**, its recipient a **devisee**. **By dedication**, where an owner gives land to public use.

## B. Involuntary transfer

chunks.heading: C. The deed
chunks.excerpt:
- **Intestate succession** — no will; the Commonwealth's statute directs distribution. **Pennsylvania's
  intestacy statute was not read for this project; no share, priority or spousal allowance is stated.**
- **Escheat** — no heirs and no will.
- **Eminent domain** — condemnation with just compensation.
- **Foreclosure** — sale to satisfy a lien. **Pennsylvania's foreclosure procedure was not read for this
  project; no notice period, redemption right or deficiency rule is stated.**
- **Tax sale** — for unpaid property taxes, under a statute this project did not read.
- **Adverse possession** — title by long possession that is, in the usual formulation, **open, notorious,
  continuous, exclusive, hostile and under a claim of right for the statutory period.**
  **Pennsylvania's statutory period was not read for this project and is not stated here.** That the
  doctrine exists is the licensee's cue: a long-standing fence, a neighbour's driveway, a shed across a
  line — all are questions for a surveyor and counsel.
- **Accretion, erosion, avulsion and reliction** — the slow or sudden work of water on a boundary.

---

## C. The deed

### C.1 Essential elements

- **Grantor** with legal capacity, and **grantee** identified with certainty.
- **Words of conveyance** — the granting clause.
- **Consideration** recited.
- **Legal description** of the property.
- **Signature of the grantor.** *(The grantee does not sign a deed.)*
- **Delivery and acceptance** — a deed takes effect on delivery, not on signing.

**Acknowledgement before a notary is required for recording**, and recording is what makes the
conveyance effective against third parties. A deed that is valid between grantor and grantee but never
recorded is a problem waiting for a subsequent purchaser.

chunks.heading: C.2 The clauses
chunks.excerpt:
### C.2 The clauses

**Premises** (parties, consideration, description and granting clause); **habendum** (*to have and to
hold* — defining the estate conveyed); **reddendum** (reservations); **covenants**; **exceptions and
reservations**; **execution and acknowledgement.**

### C.3 Deed types, ranked by what the grantee gets

| Deed | What it warrants |
|---|---|
| **General warranty deed** | The fullest covenants, reaching back through the **entire chain of title** — not merely the grantor's own period of ownership. |
| **Special (limited) warranty deed** | Covenants only against defects **arising during the grantor's ownership**. |
| **Bargain and sale deed** | Implies the grantor holds title, with covenants varying by form. |
| **Quitclaim deed** | Conveys whatever interest the grantor has — **possibly none** — with **no warranty at all**. |

The usual covenants of a general warranty deed: **seisin**, **right to convey**, **against
encumbrances**, **quiet enjoyment**, **further assurance**, and **warranty forever.**

**A quitclaim deed is not a lesser-quality conveyance of good title. It is a conveyance of whatever the
grantor happens to hold, warranting nothing** — which is exactly why it is the right instrument for
clearing a cloud and the wrong one for a purchase. Recording does not improve it: **a recorded quitclaim
deed is still a quitclaim deed.**

**Special-purpose deeds** — executor's, administrator's, sheriff's, trustee's, and a **deed in lieu of
foreclosure** — are named here so a licensee recognises them in a chain of title. Each raises questions
of authority that belong to a title examiner and counsel.

---

## D. Recording

### D.1 What recording does

chunks.heading: D.2 What recording does not do
chunks.excerpt:
Recording in the office of the **recorder of deeds for the county where the property lies** gives
**constructive notice** to the world. Everyone is treated as knowing what the record contains, whether
they looked or not.

**Actual notice** is what a person in fact knows. **Constructive notice** is what the record imputes.
**Inquiry notice** is what a person would have learned had they investigated a fact that should have
prompted investigation — someone else in possession, for example.

### D.2 What recording does not do

**Recording does not validate an invalid instrument.** A forged deed is void whether recorded or not.
**Recording does not improve the estate conveyed** — see the quitclaim note above. **Recording does not
establish that the grantor had good title**; it establishes only that the instrument is of record.

### D.3 Priority

**Pennsylvania's recording statute was not read for this project.** This course therefore **states no
Pennsylvania recording priority rule and no recording deadline.** What the licensee needs to know is the
practical consequence, which is universal: **an unrecorded interest is an exposure**, and prompt recording
is how a purchaser protects the thing they just bought.

**Related, and read:** § 35.321(c) provides that where a broker receives money under an **installment
land purchase agreement**, the transaction is considered consummated for escrow purposes *"when the buyer
has been afforded the opportunity, by means of the **seller's written acknowledgement on or affixed to the
agreement, to record the agreement**, unless the agreement specifies otherwise."* Even the escrow rule
turns on the buyer's ability to record.

---

## E. Evidence of title

chunks.heading: E.1 Title insurance
chunks.excerpt:
- **Chain of title** — the successive conveyances from some root to the present owner.
- **Abstract of title** — a condensed history of everything of record affecting the title.
- **Title search and examination** — the work of running the chain and reading what it discloses.
- **Cloud on title** — an outstanding claim or apparent defect: an uncancelled mortgage, a gap in the
  chain, an unreleased judgment, an heir who never joined in a deed.
- **Marketable title** — title a reasonable buyer would accept, free of reasonable doubt.
- **Quiet title action** — a lawsuit to resolve a cloud.

### E.1 Title insurance

An indemnity policy against loss from covered title defects, **paid for once**, covering **defects
existing at the policy date** — not future events.

**Two policies, and they protect different people:**

- **Lender's (mortgagee's) policy** — protects the **lender**, in the amount of the loan, decreasing as
  the loan is paid. It is almost always required by the lender, and the **buyer usually pays for it.**
- **Owner's policy** — protects the **owner**, in the amount of the purchase price.

**A buyer who pays for a lender's policy has bought the lender protection, not themselves.** That is the
single most useful thing a licensee can explain to a first-time buyer at the settlement table, and it
takes one sentence.

Every policy has **exceptions** — matters it does not cover, listed in Schedule B, often including
matters a **survey** would disclose. **This course states no policy term, exception, endorsement or
premium rate**, because no title policy form and no Pennsylvania rate manual was read for this project.
Coverage questions go to the title company and to counsel.

---

## F. Settlement in Pennsylvania

chunks.heading: F.1 What the licensee owes before it — § 35.334
chunks.excerpt:
**Settlement** is where the documents are signed, the funds are exchanged, and the deed and mortgage are
delivered for recording.

### F.1 What the licensee owes before it — § 35.334

> **(a)** *"**Before an agreement of sale is executed**, the brokers involved in the transaction shall
> provide **each party** with a **written estimate of reasonably foreseeable expenses** associated with
> the sale that the party may be expected to pay"* — including **the broker's commission; the mortgage
> payments and financing costs; taxes and assessments; and settlement expenses.**
>
> **(b)** *"The estimates ... shall be **as accurate as may be reasonably expected of a person having
> knowledge of, and experience in, real estate sales**."*

Note the timing: **before the agreement is executed**, not before settlement. And note the standard in
(b) — it is not "best efforts," it is the accuracy expected of someone who knows the business. The rule
then prints an **exemplary Statement of Estimated Costs to Buyer at Settlement**, whose line items name
the costs a Pennsylvania buyer actually meets: **title search and insurance; conveyancing or preparation
of papers; recording fees for the deed and the mortgage; the mortgagee's charges including appraisal fee,
credit report, and origination and placement fees; mortgage service charge; fire insurance; local realty
transfer tax; and Pennsylvania realty transfer tax.**

**This course states no realty transfer tax rate, state or local**, because Pennsylvania's realty
transfer tax statutes and every local transfer tax ordinance were **not read for this project.** Every
practice problem supplies the rate as a given inside the problem.

### F.2 Prorations

chunks.heading: F.3 Who conducts settlement
chunks.excerpt:
Items paid in advance or in arrears are **prorated** between seller and buyer as of settlement — real
estate taxes, municipal charges, homeowner association dues, rents and security deposits on tenanted
property, and fuel remaining in a tank.

**A proration is always a double entry**: whatever is credited to one party is debited to the other. A
prorated item that appears once has been done wrong.

**Which party owns the day of settlement, and whether a 360-day or 365-day convention is used, are matters
of contract and local practice. This course states neither as a Pennsylvania rule**, because 49 Pa. Code
Chapter 35 states neither. Practice problems specify the convention inside the problem.

### F.3 Who conducts settlement

In Pennsylvania settlement is commonly conducted by a **title company** or an **attorney**. **The licensee
does not conduct settlement, does not prepare the deed, and does not give an opinion on the state of the
title.** § 35.292(a)(11) does say a licensee shall *"**provide assistance with document preparation**"* —
and (a)(12) says advise about compliance *"**without rendering legal advice**."* Assistance with the
forms of the transaction is inside the job. Drafting a conveyance is not.

---

## Module PA-F-04 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-F-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

---

## Instructor source note for Module PA-F-04

**49 Pa. Code Chapter 35** was read on 2026-08-20 and is the source of **§ 35.292(a)(11) and (a)(12)**,
**§ 35.321(c)** and **§ 35.334**, transcribed above.

chunks.excerpt:

**intestacy statute**, its **foreclosure and tax sale procedures**, its **adverse possession period**, its
**realty transfer tax statutes** and every **local transfer tax ordinance**; any **title insurance policy
form or rate manual**; and the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act**.

**No recording deadline, priority rule, statutory period, intestate share, redemption right, transfer tax

chunks.heading: Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-05
chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-05

## Contracts — general principles

**Course:** Real Estate Fundamentals · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 30.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

> **Where this module sits.** This is the general contract law a licensee needs before the
> Pennsylvania-specific document rules in the companion course make sense. **§ 35.281, § 35.331,
> § 35.332, § 35.333 and § 35.334** are covered in *Real Estate Practice*; what follows is the framework
> they operate inside.

## Learning objectives

1. State the essential elements of a valid contract.
2. Distinguish void, voidable, unenforceable and valid.
3. Apply offer, acceptance, counteroffer and the mirror image rule.
4. Identify the defects in reality of consent.
5. State what the Statute of Frauds requires of a real estate contract.
6. Distinguish the remedies for breach, and explain why specific performance is available in real estate.
7. State the boundary § 35.292(a)(11) and (12) draw around a licensee and a contract.

---

## A. Essential elements

- **Competent parties** — legal capacity to contract.
- **Mutual assent** — offer and acceptance, a meeting of the minds.
- **Consideration** — something of legal value exchanged.
- **Lawful object** — a purpose the law permits.
- **A writing**, where the Statute of Frauds requires one — which it does for contracts conveying an
  interest in real property.

**Recording and notarisation are not elements of a contract.** They belong to the conveyance and to the
recording statute. A contract can be entirely valid, fully enforceable and never recorded.

### A.1 Four states a contract can be in

chunks.heading: A.2 Classifications worth holding
chunks.excerpt:
| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Valid** | Meets all elements; enforceable by either party. |
| **Void** | Never had legal effect at all. |
| **Voidable** | Valid **until the party with the power to avoid it elects to do so**. |
| **Unenforceable** | Valid in substance, but a court will not enforce it — most commonly for want of a writing. |

The practical difference between void and voidable is **who holds the power.** A contract with a minor is
voidable **at the minor's election** — the adult party cannot escape it. A contract induced by fraud is
voidable **at the defrauded party's election** — the party who lied cannot use their own fraud to get out.

### A.2 Classifications worth holding

**Bilateral** (a promise for a promise — most agreements of sale) versus **unilateral** (a promise for an
act — most option contracts on their face). **Express** versus **implied**. **Executory** (still being
performed) versus **executed** (fully performed).

An agreement of sale is **executory** from signing until settlement. That period — with duties running,
deadlines falling and money in escrow — is where a licensee does most of their work.

---

## B. Offer and acceptance

An **offer** is a manifestation of willingness to be bound on stated terms. It may be **revoked** by the
offeror **at any time before acceptance**, unless consideration was given to hold it open — which is what
an **option** is.

An offer **terminates** by: **revocation**; **rejection**; **lapse of a stated or reasonable time**;
**death or incapacity of either party**; **destruction of the subject matter**; or **counteroffer**.

### B.1 The mirror image rule, and why the last item on that list matters most

chunks.heading: B.2 Which brings in a duty the licensee owes regardless of side
chunks.excerpt:
Acceptance must be **unqualified** and must **mirror** the offer. A purported acceptance that **changes
any term is a counteroffer** — and a counteroffer **rejects and terminates the original offer**, putting
the roles the other way round: the former offeree is now the offeror.

Work it through, because a licensee sees this weekly. A buyer offers Monday. The seller signs Tuesday but
strikes the settlement date and writes a new one. That is **not an acceptance.** The buyer's offer is
**gone** — it cannot be revived by the buyer changing their mind on Wednesday and signing the original.
What exists is the seller's counteroffer, which the buyer is free to accept, reject or counter.

**Acceptance must also be communicated.** A signed agreement sitting in a drawer has accepted nothing.

### B.2 Which brings in a duty the licensee owes regardless of side

**§ 35.292(a)(3)** — owed to **all** consumers and **not waivable**:

> *"**Present, in a reasonably practicable period of time, all offers, counteroffers, notices and
> communications to and from the parties in writing**, unless the property is subject to an existing
> contract and the seller/landlord has agreed in a written waiver."*

**All** offers. Not the ones the licensee thinks are worth presenting. The single exception is narrow and
has two conditions together: the property must already be **under contract**, **and** the seller must have
agreed **in a written waiver.**

---

## C. Reality of consent

Assent must be real. It is defective where there is:

chunks.heading: D. The Statute of Frauds
chunks.excerpt:
- **Fraud** — an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact, relied upon, causing harm.
- **Misrepresentation** — a false statement of material fact, which may be innocent or negligent.
- **Duress** — assent compelled by unlawful pressure.
- **Undue influence** — improper pressure from a position of trust or dominance.
- **Mistake** — mutual mistake of material fact may permit rescission; unilateral mistake usually does
  not.

In each case the contract is **voidable at the election of the injured party.**

**Puffing** is opinion a reasonable person would not take as fact — *"a charming home."* **Misrepresentation
is a false statement of fact** — *"2,400 square feet"*, *"the roof is five years old"*, *"the basement has
never taken water."* The line moves toward misrepresentation as the statement gets **more specific and more
verifiable**, and a licensee who wants to stay on the safe side keeps to what they can document.

**§ 35.282** is the Pennsylvania rule on this and its title is the whole point: **Misleading advice,
assurances and representations.**

---

## D. The Statute of Frauds

Certain contracts must be **in writing** and **signed by the party to be charged** to be enforceable —
including **contracts for the sale of an interest in real property.** The consequence of failing is
**unenforceability**, not invalidity.

**Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds was not read for this project.** This course therefore **states no
Pennsylvania lease-term threshold and no Pennsylvania exception** to it.

**What was read is the licensing rule that reaches further**, and it is broader than the Statute of
Frauds in an important way. **§ 35.281(a):**

chunks.heading: D.1 The parol evidence rule
chunks.excerpt:
> *"**All contracts, commitments and agreements** between a broker, or a licensee employed by the broker,
> and a principal or a consumer **who is required to pay a fee, commission or other valuable consideration
> shall be in writing** and contain the information specified in § 35.331."*

A listing agreement and a buyer agency agreement are **employment agreements**, not contracts to convey —
so the Statute of Frauds may or may not reach them. **§ 35.281 reaches them regardless**, and it does so
as a condition of the licence. A licensee who asks "does the Statute of Frauds require this in writing?"
has asked the wrong question. The right question is what the Commission's rule requires, and the answer is
**in writing, with the § 35.331 contents.**

### D.1 The parol evidence rule

Where a written contract is a complete expression of the parties' agreement, evidence of **prior or
contemporaneous oral agreements offered to vary its terms** is barred. Combined with the writing
requirements above, the working rule for a licensee is simple: **every change goes on paper, signed.**

---

## E. Performance, breach and remedies

A contract discharges by **performance**, by **mutual agreement**, by **operation of law**, or by
**breach**.

**Assignment** transfers rights and **generally leaves the assignor liable**. **Novation** substitutes a
new party and **releases** the original — which is why it requires **all** parties' agreement. Confusing
the two is how a seller discovers, after an assignment they approved, that they are still on the hook.

### E.1 Remedies for breach

chunks.heading: E.2 Where the deposit sits while any of this happens
chunks.excerpt:
- **Damages** — compensation for loss.
- **Liquidated damages** — a sum the parties fixed in advance. In real estate this is commonly the
  earnest money deposit, where the agreement so provides.
- **Rescission** — unwinding the contract and restoring the parties.
- **Specific performance** — a court order compelling performance of the contract itself.

**Specific performance is available in real estate because each parcel is unique**, so damages are often
an inadequate remedy. That is the legal consequence of the physical characteristic taught in Module
PA-F-02: no two parcels are the same, so money cannot buy a substitute.

### E.2 Where the deposit sits while any of this happens

**§ 35.327**, and it is worth reading before any dispute arises:

> *"If a dispute arises between the parties to a real estate transaction over entitlement to money that is
> being held in escrow by a broker, **the broker shall retain the money in escrow until the dispute is
> resolved**. If resolution of the dispute appears remote without legal action, the broker may, **following
> 30 days' notice to the parties, petition the county court having jurisdiction in the matter to interplead
> the rival claimants**."*

**The broker does not decide who wins.** The broker holds. The escrow module in the companion course
develops this fully; it appears here because the moment a contract breaks is the moment a licensee is
asked to release money, and the answer is always the same.

---

## F. Where a licensee stands in relation to a contract

Two sentences from § 35.292(a), read together, define the whole of it:

chunks.heading: Module PA-F-05 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
> **(11)** ***"Provide assistance with document preparation."***
> **(12)** ***"Advise the consumer about compliance with laws pertaining to real estate transactions
> without rendering legal advice."***

**Assistance with document preparation is inside the job.** Completing the blanks on a form, assembling
the addenda a transaction needs, making sure the required contents are present — all of that is what a
licensee is for, and (11) says so affirmatively.

**Composing contract language is not.** Drafting a clause to protect a buyer against a survey problem,
writing a custom contingency, or advising what a provision will mean if litigated — those are the practice
of law, and (12)'s closing words say so.

The reliable test is not the length of what you write. It is whether you are **filling in a form** or
**inventing a term.** When you are inventing a term, the answer is an attorney, and § 35.292(a)(8) makes
sending them there a duty rather than a courtesy.

---

## Module PA-F-05 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-F-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

---

## Instructor source note for Module PA-F-05

**49 Pa. Code Chapter 35** was read on 2026-08-20 and is the source of **§ 35.281(a)**, **§ 35.282**,
**§ 35.292(a)(3), (8), (11) and (12)** and **§ 35.327**, transcribed above. Every other principle in this
module is **general contract law**, taught as framework.

**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this build:** **Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds**;
Pennsylvania's contract, agency and remedies case law; and the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration
Act**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module PA-F-05
chunks.excerpt:
**No Pennsylvania lease-term threshold, limitations period, statutory exception, liquidated damages cap or
deposit-forfeiture rule is stated in this module.**

chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Fundamentals — Module PA-F-06

## Real estate finance and valuation fundamentals

**Course:** Real Estate Fundamentals · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 30.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. Define the basic finance vocabulary and compute with it.
2. Distinguish the note from the security instrument, and the parties to each.
3. Distinguish the loan categories and the repayment types.
4. Distinguish the primary from the secondary mortgage market.
5. Distinguish value, cost, price and assessed value, and list the elements of value.
6. Apply the three approaches to value.
7. State the § 35.340 requirement that governs every comparative market analysis a licensee produces.

---

## A. Finance vocabulary

**Principal and interest. Amortization. Debt service. PITI. Equity. Loan-to-value ratio. Points. Yield.**

**PITI** is the four-part housing payment — principal, interest, taxes, insurance — and it is the figure
qualifying ratios are computed against, not principal and interest alone.

**Equity** is value less what is owed. **Loan-to-value** is the loan divided by the value the lender
recognises — and lenders customarily recognise **the lower of the contract price and the appraised
value.** That single convention is why an appraisal below contract price is a problem for the buyer: the
lender lends against the lower figure and the difference must come from somewhere.

**A discount point is one percent of the loan amount**, paid at closing, and it buys the lender yield. A
useful rule of thumb in national content is that a point moves yield by about **one-eighth of one
percent** — an approximation, not a formula.

chunks.heading: B. The note and the security instrument
chunks.excerpt:
**Worked example.** A $280,000 loan with 2 points: 280,000 × 0.02 = **$5,600** paid at closing. If the
same borrower's monthly payment covers interest of 280,000 × 0.065 ÷ 12 = **$1,516.67** in the first
month, and the payment is $1,770, then **$253.33** reduces principal that month and the new balance is
**$279,746.67.** Interest is always computed on the **previous** balance; only the remainder touches
principal.

---

## B. The note and the security instrument

They are two documents doing two jobs.

**The promissory note** is the borrower's **promise to repay**. It is a contract, and everything in Module
PA-F-05 applies to it. Its special provisions include the **acceleration clause** (on default the whole
balance falls due at once), the **prepayment penalty clause**, and the **due-on-sale (alienation) clause**
(the balance falls due if the property is sold).

**The mortgage** is the instrument that **pledges the property** as security. **Hypothecation** is the
concept that ties them: the borrower pledges the property **while keeping possession of it.** Nothing
about a mortgage loan moves the borrower out.

**Pennsylvania is a mortgage state**, using a two-party mortgage — **mortgagor** (borrower) and
**mortgagee** (lender) — rather than the three-party deed of trust used elsewhere. **Pennsylvania's
mortgage and foreclosure statutes were not read for this project**, and **this course states no
Pennsylvania foreclosure procedure, notice period, redemption right or deficiency rule.**

**The due-on-sale clause is why assumption is rare.** Where the lender may call the loan on transfer, a
buyer taking over a seller's existing financing is the exception rather than the routine.

---

## C. Loan categories and types

### C.1 By programme

chunks.heading: C.2 By repayment
chunks.excerpt:
- **Conventional** — not government insured or guaranteed. **Conforming** loans meet secondary-market
  purchase standards; **nonconforming** loans do not, and are priced accordingly. **Private mortgage
  insurance (PMI)** typically appears where the loan-to-value is high.
- **FHA-insured** — FHA does not build housing and does not lend; it **insures approved lenders against
  loss**. Borrowers pay a **mortgage insurance premium (MIP)**.
- **VA-guaranteed** — the VA **guarantees** approved lenders against loss for eligible veterans; a
  **funding fee** applies; the defining feature is the possibility of **no down payment**.
- **USDA Rural Development** — direct and guaranteed loans in eligible areas.

**This course states no loan limit, down payment percentage, MIP or funding fee rate, or eligibility
threshold**, because no agency handbook or programme guide was read for this project. Those figures change
and they come from the lender.

### C.2 By repayment

**Fixed-rate level payment (fully amortized)** — the most common residential plan. **Adjustable rate
(ARM)** — with a **periodic cap**, a **lifetime cap**, and an **index**; note that a cap on the
**payment** is not a cap on the **interest**, and a payment cap can produce **negative amortization** as
the shortfall is added to principal. **Interest-only / term.** **Balloon (partially amortized).**
**Buydown**, where a lump sum paid at closing reduces the rate temporarily or permanently and may be paid
by buyer, seller or a third party. **Construction**, **blanket**, **package**, **open-end** and **bridge**
loans serve particular purposes.

### C.3 Primary and secondary markets

chunks.heading: C.4 Federal consumer protection, in outline
chunks.excerpt:
The **primary market** is where a loan is **made** — banks, savings institutions, credit unions, mortgage
banking companies and mortgage brokers. The **secondary market** is where a loan already made is
**bought** — **Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae** — through **loan pooling** and **mortgage-backed
securities.**

The link between them is conforming standards: a lender writes to those standards **so the loan can be
sold**, and selling it returns capital to lend again.

### C.4 Federal consumer protection, in outline

**TILA / Regulation Z** governs disclosure of credit terms and advertising of consumer credit; **RESPA /
Regulation X** governs settlement services and prohibits kickbacks and referral fees among settlement
service providers; the **TRID** rule consolidated the two sets of disclosures into the **Loan Estimate**
and the **Closing Disclosure**.

**None of these regulations was read for this project.** **This course states no disclosure deadline, no
tolerance category, no trigger term list and no penalty.** What a licensee should carry away is the shape:
**advertising credit terms pulls in mandatory disclosures**, and **the safest advertising practice is to
publish no numbers other than the price.** For any live deadline, the lender is the source.

---

## D. Valuation

### D.1 Five different figures

**Value** is worth. **Cost** is what was spent to create it. **Price** is what someone actually paid.
**Market value** is what a property should bring under defined market conditions. **Assessed value** is
what a taxing authority places on it, and it need not equal market value.

A house can cost $400,000 to build, be priced at $360,000, have a market value of $375,000 and be assessed
at $290,000, all at once, with no contradiction.

chunks.heading: D.2 The four elements of value
chunks.excerpt:
### D.2 The four elements of value

**Demand, utility, scarcity, transferability.** All four must be present. A thing everyone wants, that is
useful and rare, has no market value if it cannot be transferred.

### D.3 Principles

**Substitution** — a buyer will pay no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute; it is the
basis of the sales comparison approach. **Contribution** — an improvement adds what it **returns**, not
what it **cost**. **Highest and best use** — one at a time, and it changes. **Conformity.**
**Anticipation.** **Supply and demand.** **Plottage**, the increment of value from merging adjacent
parcels, produced by the process of **assemblage**.

### D.4 The three approaches

**Sales comparison.** Compare closed sales of similar properties. Two rules govern it: **adjust the
comparables, never the subject**, and a **currently listed or pending property is not a comparable** — a
listing is what a seller hopes for and a pending has not yet survived appraisal or financing. **Superior
comparables adjust down; inferior comparables adjust up.** Reconcile by **weighted consideration**, giving
most weight to the comparable that needed least adjustment — not by simple averaging, which treats a
$2,000 adjustment and a $40,000 adjustment as equally good evidence.

**Cost.** Estimate the **land** separately by sales comparison (**land is never depreciated**), estimate
**replacement or reproduction cost** of the improvements, subtract **accrued depreciation**, and add the
two. Depreciation is **physical deterioration**, **functional obsolescence**, or **external (economic)
obsolescence** — and **external obsolescence is incurable**, because its cause lies outside the boundary
line and the owner does not own it.

chunks.heading: E. The Pennsylvania rule that governs every CMA you will ever produce
chunks.excerpt:
**Income.** **Direct capitalization: Value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate.** **Net operating income excludes
debt service**, because NOI describes the **property's** earning power and debt service belongs to the
buyer. The cap rate measures risk, and it is inversely related to value: at the same income, a higher cap
rate gives a lower value.

**Worked example.** Potential gross income $190,000, vacancy and collection loss 6 percent, operating
expenses $64,000, annual debt service $71,000, market cap rate 7.5 percent.
Effective gross income = 190,000 × 0.94 = **$178,600.** NOI = 178,600 − 64,000 = **$114,600.**
Value = 114,600 ÷ 0.075 = **$1,528,000.** *(114,600 − 71,000 = $43,600 is before-tax cash flow — a
different figure answering a different question.)*

---

## E. The Pennsylvania rule that governs every CMA you will ever produce

**§ 35.340 — Comparative market analysis:**

> *"A comparative market analysis shall contain the following statement **printed conspicuously and
> without change on the first page**:*
>
> ***"This analysis has not been performed in accordance with the Uniform Standards of Professional
> Appraisal Practice which requires valuers to act as unbiased, disinterested third parties with
> impartiality, objectivity and independence and without accommodation of personal interest. It is not to
> be construed as an appraisal and may not be used as such for any purpose."***

Four requirements in one short rule: **the statement**, **conspicuously**, **without change**, and **on the
first page**. Not paraphrased, not in a footer, not on page three.

chunks.heading: Module PA-F-06 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**A licensee is not an appraiser.** A CMA is a licensee's opinion of probable sales price, produced for a
consumer making a pricing or offering decision. An appraisal is an appraiser's opinion produced under
professional standards. § 35.340 exists so that nobody downstream can mistake one for the other.

**And a broker price opinion is a third thing.** New **Subchapter J (§§ 35.501–35.503)**, added December 26,
2025, effective December 27, 2025, requires the **same USPAP disclaimer** on a BPO, restricts BPOs to four
permitted uses, prohibits them in a list of situations including **mortgage loan origination**, requires a
salesperson to have held an **active licence for the 3 years immediately preceding** the BPO's effective
date, and requires **Commission-approved education**. The companion course covers it in full. It appears
here so that a student learning valuation learns, at the same moment, that **Pennsylvania regulates what
you may call your opinion and what it may be used for.**

---

## Module PA-F-06 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-F-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

**Every rate, factor, cap rate and tax rate used in any item is supplied inside the item as a given**, and
no item requires a student to recall a Pennsylvania statutory rate.

---

## Instructor source note for Module PA-F-06

**49 Pa. Code Chapter 35** was read on 2026-08-20 and is the source of **§ 35.340** and of the
**Subchapter J** provisions summarised above, transcribed from the rule.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module PA-F-06
chunks.excerpt:
**Not read, and therefore stated nowhere in this build:** **TILA and Regulation Z**; **RESPA and
Regulation X**; the **TRID** rule; **FHA, VA and USDA** programme handbooks; **Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and
Ginnie Mae** guides; **USPAP**; any **Pennsylvania appraiser** statute or board rule; **Pennsylvania's
mortgage and foreclosure statutes**; and the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act**.

**No loan limit, insurance premium rate, funding fee, qualifying ratio, disclosure deadline, tolerance
figure, foreclosure period or appraiser requirement is stated in this module.**

**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

> **§ 35.292 is the spine of Pennsylvania practice.** Every relationship section that follows —
> §§ 35.312 to 35.316 — opens with the same phrase: *"**In addition to the duties required in § 35.292**
> ..."* The relationship duties are **additions**. The twelve duties below are owed to **everyone**,
> **whatever the relationship**, and **cannot be waived.** A student who learns nothing else from this
> course should learn this section.

## Learning objectives

1. Recite the twelve duties § 35.292(a) owes to all consumers and state that they may not be waived.
2. Apply the presentation duty in § 35.292(a)(3) and identify its single narrow exception.
3. Apply § 35.292(a)(8) — the duty to route.
4. Apply the boundary between (a)(11) and (a)(12).
5. State the three limits in § 35.292(b), (c) and (d), and what they do not excuse.
6. Distinguish a duty owed to all consumers from a duty owed only to a principal.

---

## A. The twelve, transcribed

chunks.heading: A.1 Read the opening words first
chunks.excerpt:
> **§ 35.292(a)** *"The following duties are **owed to all consumers of real estate services and may not
> be waived**:*
>
> **(1)** *"Exercise **reasonable professional skill and care**."*
> **(2)** *"**Deal honestly and in good faith.**"*
> **(3)** *"**Present, in a reasonably practicable period of time, all offers, counteroffers, notices and
> communications to and from the parties in writing**, unless the property is subject to an existing
> contract and the seller/landlord has agreed in a written waiver."*
> **(4)** *"Comply with **68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73** (relating to Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law)."*
> **(5)** *"**Account for escrow and deposit funds** as required by section 604(a)(5) of the act and
> §§ 35.321—35.328."*
> **(6)** *"**Provide consumers with the information in section 608 of the act at the initial
> interview.**"*
> **(7)** *"**Disclose, in a reasonably practicable period of time, all conflicts of interest and
> financial interests** as required in § 35.283."*
> **(8)** *"**Advise the consumer to seek expert advice on matters about the transaction that are beyond
> the licensee's expertise.**"*
> **(9)** *"Ensure that all services are provided in a **reasonable, professional and competent
> manner**."*
> **(10)** *"**Keep the consumer informed about the transaction and the tasks to be completed.**"*
> **(11)** *"**Provide assistance with document preparation.**"*
> **(12)** *"**Advise the consumer about compliance with laws pertaining to real estate transactions
> without rendering legal advice.**"*

### A.1 Read the opening words first

chunks.heading: B. Duty (3) — the presentation duty, and its exception
chunks.excerpt:
**"Owed to all consumers of real estate services."** Not to clients. Not to principals. To **consumers** —
which reaches the buyer your seller-client is negotiating against, the tenant your landlord-client is
screening, and the person who walks into an open house and never signs anything.

**"And may not be waived."** No agreement, no signature, no disclosure form and no instruction from a
client removes any of the twelve. A licensee who is asked to set one aside has been asked to do something
the rule forecloses, and the answer does not depend on how the request is phrased.

---

## B. Duty (3) — the presentation duty, and its exception

> *"Present, in a **reasonably practicable period of time**, **all** offers, counteroffers, notices and
> communications to and from the parties **in writing** ..."*

Four things it reaches: **offers, counteroffers, notices and communications.** In **both directions** —
*"to and from the parties."* **In writing.** And **all** of them.

**"All" is the word that does the work.** A licensee does not filter offers by their own judgement of
merit. An offer the licensee thinks is insulting still goes to the seller. An offer from a buyer the
licensee doubts still goes. The seller decides what to do with it; the licensee decides nothing.

**The exception has two conditions and they operate together:**

1. **the property is subject to an existing contract**, **and**
2. **the seller/landlord has agreed in a written waiver.**

Either alone is not enough. A property under contract whose seller signed no waiver still gets every
offer presented.

**"Reasonably practicable" is not "when convenient."** It is measured against what the situation allows —
an offer with a short expiry demands faster handling than one open for a week.

---

chunks.heading: C. Duty (8) — the duty to route
chunks.excerpt:
## C. Duty (8) — the duty to route

> *"**Advise the consumer to seek expert advice on matters about the transaction that are beyond the
> licensee's expertise.**"*

This is a **duty**, not a courtesy. It is owed to everyone and cannot be waived. And it is the reason the
routing language throughout both of these courses is not evasion — it is the rule.

Three consequences worth stating.

**It is affirmative.** The licensee must **advise** the consumer to seek advice. Staying silent while a
consumer walks into a question outside your competence is not neutrality; it is a failure of (8).

**It defines competence honestly.** Nobody expects a licensee to know Pennsylvania's mine subsidence
programme, or whether a defeasible fee has been triggered, or what a title exception means. What the rule
expects is that you **know you do not know**, and say so.

**It pairs with (9).** *"Ensure that all services are provided in a reasonable, professional and competent
manner."* Duty (9) requires competence in what you do; duty (8) requires you to hand off what you cannot.
Together they say: **be good at your job, and know where your job ends.**

---

## D. Duties (11) and (12) — the narrowest line in the chapter

> **(11)** *"Provide assistance with document preparation."*
> **(12)** *"Advise the consumer about compliance with laws pertaining to real estate transactions
> **without rendering legal advice**."*

Most states draw the practice-of-law line by prohibition alone. **Pennsylvania draws it by stating the
affirmative duty first.** You are **required** to assist with document preparation. You are **required** to
advise about compliance with laws. And in the same sentence, you may not render legal advice.

**Inside the line — assistance and compliance advice:**

chunks.heading: E. The three limits — § 35.292(b), (c) and (d)
chunks.excerpt:
- Completing the blanks on a form.
- Telling a seller a property disclosure statement is required under the Seller Disclosure Law.
- Telling a buyer that an agreement of sale must contain the zoning classification, and that its omission
  makes the agreement voidable at the buyer's option.
- Telling either party that a written agreement must contain the § 35.331 notifications.
- Assembling the addenda a transaction needs.

**Outside the line — legal advice:**

- Composing a clause.
- Construing what a provision will mean if litigated.
- Advising whether a party has a claim, a defence, or a right to terminate.
- Telling a co-owner what their interest is worth in a partition.

**The test is not length.** It is whether you are **completing a form** or **inventing a term**, and
whether you are **stating what the law requires** or **predicting what a court would do.**

---

## E. The three limits — § 35.292(b), (c) and (d)

> **(b)** *"A licensee is **not required to conduct an independent inspection of the property**."*
> **(c)** *"A licensee is **not required to independently verify the accuracy or completeness of any
> representation made by the consumer** to a transaction **which the licensee reasonably believes to be
> accurate and reliable**."*
> **(d)** *"A licensee is **not liable for the acts of a consumer** unless the consumer is acting at the
> **express direction of the licensee** or as a result of a **representation by a licensee reasonably
> relied on by the consumer**."*

These are real protections and they are narrower than they first read.

chunks.heading: F. Duties owed to all consumers versus duties owed to a principal
chunks.excerpt:
**(b) does not excuse ignoring what you see.** You need not inspect. You may not conceal. A licensee who
notices a stain spreading across a ceiling has not conducted an inspection — they have acquired
information, and duty (2) governs what happens next.

**(c) turns on the words "reasonably believes."** The shelter protects a licensee who relied on a
consumer's statement they had reason to trust. It does **not** protect reliance on a statement that
contradicted what the licensee could see, or that the licensee had reason to doubt. A seller who says the
roof is five years old on a house with visible curling shingles has made a statement the licensee no
longer reasonably believes.

**(d)'s two exceptions are the interesting part.** A licensee **is** answerable for a consumer acting at
the licensee's **express direction**, and for a consumer acting on a **licensee's representation the
consumer reasonably relied on.** Telling a seller "don't mention the basement, nobody asks" is express
direction. Telling a buyer "the survey is fine, you don't need one" is a representation.

---

## F. Duties owed to all consumers versus duties owed to a principal

The structure of Chapter 35 is worth seeing whole, because the rest of this course is built on it.

chunks.heading: G. Two of the twelve point forward
chunks.excerpt:
| | Owed to whom |
|---|---|
| **The twelve § 35.292(a) duties** | **All consumers.** Not waivable. |
| **Loyalty** (§§ 35.312(a)(1), 35.313(a)(1), 35.315(e)(1)) | Only the **principal**. |
| **Confidentiality** (§§ 35.312(a)(2), 35.313(a)(2), 35.314(b)(3), 35.311(d)) | Only the **principal** — and with a stated **material defect** exception for a seller's agent and a dual agent. |
| **Continuous and good faith effort** to find a buyer or a property | Only the **principal**. |
| **Limited confidentiality** — three listed items (§ 35.316(2)) | The consumer a **transaction licensee** works with. |

**Loyalty is the dividing line.** A licensee owes honesty and good faith to everyone; a licensee owes
**loyalty** to the principal alone. That is what an agency relationship adds — and it is why the next
module, on the five permitted relationships, is the heaviest in this course.

---

## G. Two of the twelve point forward

**(4) — comply with 68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73, the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law.** Module PA-P-07 takes
this up with **§ 35.284a** and **§ 35.335a**. **The Seller Disclosure Law itself was not read for this
project**, and nothing in this build states any of its provisions.

**(6) — provide consumers with the information in section 608 of the act at the initial interview.**
Module PA-P-03 takes this up with **§ 35.284** and the four disclosure summaries in **§§ 35.336 to
35.339**. **Section 608 of the Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act was not read for this project.**
What was read is § 35.284's timing rules and the fact that the rule prints each summary in full; **their
text is reproduced nowhere in this build.**

---

## Module PA-P-01 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module PA-P-01
chunks.excerpt:
Eleven items — one applied scenario, five engagement items and five remediation items. The **80 percent**
engagement threshold and the **100 percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**; what
§ 35.358(b)(2) prescribes is that the **course** be **graded by proctored examination.**

## Instructor source note for Module PA-P-01

Drawn from **49 Pa. Code Chapter 35**, read on 2026-08-20, current through **56 Pa.B. 3438 (June 6,
2026)** — specifically **§§ 35.283, 35.284, 35.284a, 35.292, 35.311, 35.312, 35.313, 35.314, 35.315,
35.316, 35.321—35.328 and 35.335a.**

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act,

lessons.title: Pennsylvania Real Estate Practice — Module PA-P-02

chunks.heading: Pennsylvania Real Estate Practice — Module PA-P-02
chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Practice — Module PA-P-02

## Permitted relationships — §§ 35.311 to 35.316

**Course:** Real Estate Practice · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 45.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

> **Pennsylvania recognises FIVE named relationships, and one of them is not an agency at all.** They are
> creatures of rule and statute, not of common law, and each is defined by the duties it **adds** to
> § 35.292. Get the five straight and most of Pennsylvania practice follows.

## Learning objectives

1. Name the five permitted relationships and state what each adds to § 35.292.
2. State the two things a broker may not do with an agency relationship without written consent.
3. State the five exceptions to the confidentiality duty in § 35.311(d).
4. Distinguish the seller's agent's confidentiality duty from the buyer's agent's.
5. Explain why compensation does not determine representation.
6. Apply designated agency, including what it makes the employing broker.
7. State exactly what a transaction licensee may not disclose — and what that list does not include.

---

## A. § 35.311 — Generally

chunks.heading: A.1 Three things to take from § 35.311
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"A licensee and a consumer may enter into the relationship specified in **sections 606.2—606.4
> and 606.6 of the act**."*
> **(b)** *"**A broker may not extend or delegate the broker's agency relationship without the written
> consent of the principal.**"*
> **(c)** *"**Compensation paid by a broker to another broker** who assists in the marketing and sale/lease
> of a consumer's property **does not create an agency relationship** between the consumer and that other
> broker."*
> **(d)** *A licensee in an agency relationship **may not knowingly, during or following the termination of
> an agency relationship, reveal or use confidential information of the principal**, except where one or
> more of the following apply:*
> **(1)** *"The principal **consented** to the disclosure."*
> **(2)** *"The information is disclosed to **another licensee or third party acting solely on behalf of
> the principal**."*
> **(3)** *"The information is **required to be disclosed under subpoena or court order**."*
> **(4)** *"The disclosure is **necessary to prevent the principal from committing a crime**."*
> **(5)** *"The information is used by the licensee to **defend in a legal proceeding against an accusation
> of wrongdoing**."*

### A.1 Three things to take from § 35.311

**Subsection (b) is why subagency needs paper.** A broker cannot hand the agency relationship to someone
else — cannot extend it, cannot delegate it — without the **principal's written consent.** § 35.312(c)
says the same thing from the other side for subagents specifically.

chunks.heading: B. § 35.312 — Seller's agent
chunks.excerpt:
**Subsection (c) severs compensation from representation, and it is the most misunderstood sentence in the
chapter.** Paying a cooperating broker does not make that broker the payer's agent, or the payer's client's
agent. Money moves one way; representation is decided another way — by **agreement**, in writing. § 35.313(c)
says the converse plainly: *"**A buyer's agent represents the interests of the buyer/tenant even if paid by
the seller/landlord.**"*

**Subsection (d) makes confidentiality outlive the relationship.** *"During **or following the termination
of** an agency relationship."* A licensee who learned a seller's bottom line does not become free to mention
it when the listing expires.

**And its five exceptions are worth reading as a group**, because they show what the duty is for and what it
is not. Confidentiality protects a principal's bargaining position and private information. It does **not**
shield a **crime the principal is about to commit** — (4) — and it does not require a licensee to stay silent
while being **accused of wrongdoing** — (5). Neither exception is an invitation; both are narrow.

---

## B. § 35.312 — Seller's agent

chunks.heading: B.1 The material defect exception — the most important seven words in the section
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"In addition to the duties required in § 35.292, a seller's agent owes the additional duties
> of:*
> **(1)** *"**Loyalty** to the seller/landlord **by acting in the seller's/landlord's best interest**."*
> **(2)** *"**Confidentiality, except that a licensee has a duty to reveal known material defects about
> the property.**"*
> **(3)** *"Making a **continuous and good faith effort to find a buyer/tenant** for the property except
> when the property is subject to an existing agreement of sale/lease."*
> **(4)** *"**Disclosure to other parties in the transaction that the licensee has been engaged as a
> seller's agent.**"*

And four operating rules:

> **(b)** *"A licensee **does not breach a duty** to a seller/landlord by **showing alternative properties**
> to a prospective buyer/tenant **or listing competing properties**."*
> **(c)** *"A seller's agent **may compensate other brokers as subagents if the seller/landlord agrees in
> writing**. **Subagents have the same duties and obligations to the seller/landlord as the seller's
> agent.**"*
> **(d)** *"A seller's agent may also compensate **a buyer's agent and a transaction licensee who do not
> have the same duties and obligations** to the seller/landlord as the seller's agent."*
> **(e)** *"Upon entering into a written agreement with the seller/landlord, **each licensee employed by the
> broker will act as a seller's agent** unless a licensee has been named ... a designated agent."*

### B.1 The material defect exception — the most important seven words in the section

> *"**Confidentiality, except that a licensee has a duty to reveal known material defects about the
> property.**"*

chunks.heading: B.2 Subsection (c) and (d) side by side
chunks.excerpt:
**Loyalty to the seller does not buy the seller silence about a known material defect.** The exception is
written into the confidentiality duty itself, so there is no tension to resolve: confidentiality never
covered it.

A seller who instructs a licensee to keep quiet about a known defect has asked for something § 35.312(a)(2)
forecloses, and duty (2) of § 35.292 — deal honestly and in good faith — is owed to the buyer anyway.

### B.2 Subsection (c) and (d) side by side

Read together they say something precise about the Pennsylvania market:

- **A subagent has the same duties to the seller as the seller's agent** — which is why creating one takes
  the **seller's written agreement.**
- **A buyer's agent and a transaction licensee do not** — and a seller's agent may compensate them anyway.

**So a cheque from the listing broker tells you nothing about whose side anyone is on.** That is § 35.311(c)
made concrete.

### B.3 Subsection (e) — the firm-wide default

Sign a listing and **every licensee in the firm is a seller's agent** for that property, unless designated
agency has been used. A buyer who walks into that firm and starts talking is talking to the seller's agents.

---

## C. § 35.313 — Buyer's agent

chunks.heading: C.1 A difference students miss
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *Additional duties: **loyalty** to the buyer/tenant; **confidentiality**; **a continuous and good
> faith effort to find a property**, except where the buyer is subject to an existing contract; and
> **disclosure to other parties that the licensee has been engaged as a buyer's agent.***
> **(b)** *"A licensee does not breach a duty to a buyer/tenant by **showing a property the buyer/tenant is
> interested in to other buyer/tenants**."*
> **(c)** ***"A buyer's agent represents the interests of the buyer/tenant even if paid by the
> seller/landlord."***
> **(d)** *Upon a written agreement with the buyer/tenant, **each licensee employed by the broker acts as a
> buyer's agent** unless designated.*

### C.1 A difference students miss

Compare § 35.312(a)(2) with § 35.313(a)(2):

| | Confidentiality duty as stated |
|---|---|
| **Seller's agent** | *"Confidentiality, **except that a licensee has a duty to reveal known material defects about the property**."* |
| **Buyer's agent** | *"**Confidentiality.**"* |
| **Dual agent** | *"Confidentiality, **except that a licensee is required to disclose known material defects about the property**."* |

**The material defect exception appears in the seller's agent and dual agent duties. It is not written into
the buyer's agent duty** — and the structural reason is plain: the defects in question are defects **about
the property**, and it is the seller's side that ordinarily knows them.

This is a difference in the **text of the rules**, stated here as such. A licensee facing a live question
about what they must reveal reads the rule that applies to their own relationship, and where anything turns
on it, § 35.292(a)(8) says what to do.

---

## D. § 35.314 — Dual agent

chunks.heading: D.1 What is missing from the dual agent's list, and why
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"A licensee **may act as a dual agent if both parties consent in writing**."*
>
> **(b)** *Additional duties:*
> **(1)** *"**Taking no action that is adverse or detrimental to either party's interest in the
> transaction.**"*
> **(2)** *"Unless otherwise agreed in writing, making a **continuous and good faith effort** to find a
> buyer/tenant for the property **and** a property for the buyer/tenant, except where either is subject to
> an existing contract."*
> **(3)** *"**Confidentiality, except that a licensee is required to disclose known material defects about
> the property.**"*
>
> **(c)** and **(d)** — a dual agent does not breach a duty by **showing properties not owned by the
> seller** to the buyer, by **listing competing properties**, or by **showing the buyer's property of
> interest to other buyers.**

### D.1 What is missing from the dual agent's list, and why

**Loyalty does not appear.** § 35.312 and § 35.313 both name loyalty first; § 35.314 does not name it at
all. In its place stands **(b)(1)** — *"taking no action that is adverse or detrimental to either party's
interest."*

That substitution is the whole concept. **A dual agent cannot advocate for one side against the other**, so
the rule does not ask for loyalty it could not deliver. What it asks for is **neutrality with teeth**: not
merely refraining from favouring one side, but taking **no action adverse or detrimental to either.**

**Written consent from both parties is the entry condition**, and it is a condition, not a formality. A
dual agency without both written consents is not a permitted relationship.

---

## E. § 35.315 — Designated agent

chunks.heading: E. § 35.315 — Designated agent
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"A broker, **with the written consent of the principal**, may **designate one or more licensees to
> act exclusively as the agent of the seller/landlord**, and designate one or more licensees to act
> **exclusively** as the agent of the buyer/tenant **in the same transaction**."*
>
> **(b)** *"**Designation may take place at any time.**"* If it happens after an initial designation or after
> a written agreement, the broker shall **obtain the principal's written consent to the newly designated
> licensee** and, where applicable, **the principal's agreement to renounce any previous agency relationship
> with the other licensees employed by the broker.**
>
> **(c)** *"Regardless of when the designation takes place, the broker and the designated agents shall use
> **reasonable care to ensure that confidential information is not disclosed or used**."*
>
> **(d)** ***"The licensees employed by the broker who are not designated have no agency relationship with
> either party in the transaction."***
>
> **(e)** *Each designated agent owes, in addition to § 35.292:* **loyalty to their own principal**; a
> **continuous and good faith effort**; ***"Disclose to the principal prior to writing or presenting an offer
> to purchase that the other party to the transaction is represented by a designated agent also employed by
> the broker"***; and ***"Confirm that the broker is a dual agent in the transaction."***
>
> **(f)** *The employing broker, **as a dual agent**, additionally owes:* ***"Taking reasonable care to
> protect any confidential information that has been disclosed to the designated licensees"*** and
> ***"Taking responsibility to direct and supervise the business activities of the designated licensees
> while taking no action that is adverse or detrimental to e

chunks.heading: E.1 The structural fact that makes designated agency work
chunks.excerpt:
ither party's interest."***

### E.1 The structural fact that makes designated agency work

**When designation happens, the broker becomes a dual agent.** The rule says so twice — in (e)(4), where
each designated agent must *"confirm that the broker is a dual agent in the transaction,"* and in (f), which
imposes dual agency duties on the employing broker by name.

So designated agency is not an escape from dual agency. It is **dual agency at the broker level with
exclusive representation at the licensee level.** The broker takes on the neutrality duty; the two
designated licensees each keep loyalty to their own principal.

**And (d) is the clean-up rule that makes it coherent.** Everyone else in the firm has **no agency
relationship with either party.** Compare § 35.312(e) and § 35.313(d), where the whole firm takes the
relationship — designation switches that default off for the undesignated.

### E.2 The disclosure in (e)(3) has a deadline attached to an event

> *"Disclose to the principal **prior to writing or presenting an offer to purchase** that the other party
> to the transaction is represented by a designated agent also employed by the broker."*

**Before writing or presenting the offer** — not at settlement, not when asked. The principal is entitled to
know the shape of the transaction before they commit to a number.

---

## F. § 35.316 — Transaction licensee — **not an agent**

chunks.heading: F.1 The fifth relationship, and the one students get wrong
chunks.excerpt:
> *"In addition to the duties required in § 35.292, a transaction licensee shall **advise the consumer** that
> the licensee:*
>
> **(1)** ***"Is not acting as an agent or advocate for the consumer and should not be provided with
> confidential information."***
>
> **(2)** *"Owes the additional duty of **limited confidentiality** in that the following information may not
> be disclosed:*
> **(i)** *"The **seller/landlord will accept a price less than the asking/listing price**."*
> **(ii)** *"The **buyer/tenant will pay a price greater than the price submitted in a written offer**."*
> **(iii)** *"The **seller/landlord or buyer/tenant will agree to financing terms other than those
> offered**."*

### F.1 The fifth relationship, and the one students get wrong

A **transaction licensee provides services without being anyone's agent.** § 35.292's twelve duties still
apply in full — honesty, good faith, presentation of all offers, routing, competence, all of it. What is
absent is **loyalty**, **advocacy**, and general **confidentiality**.

**Note the affirmative duty in (1).** The transaction licensee must **advise the consumer** of the
arrangement — including, in the rule's own words, that the consumer *"should not be provided with
confidential information."* That is a warning the rule requires the licensee to give.

### F.2 "Limited confidentiality" is a list, not a standard

**Three items. That is the whole of it.** Price flexibility on the seller's side, price flexibility on the
buyer's side, and financing flexibility on either side.

chunks.heading: G. The five, in one table
chunks.excerpt:
**What is not on the list is not protected.** A consumer's motivation for moving, their timeline, their
personal circumstances, their other properties — none of those appear in § 35.316(2), which is precisely
why (1) tells the licensee to warn the consumer not to share confidential information in the first place.

---

## G. The five, in one table

| Relationship | Loyalty? | Confidentiality | Key condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Seller's agent** | **Yes**, to seller/landlord | Yes — **except known material defects about the property** | Written agreement; firm-wide default under (e) |
| **Buyer's agent** | **Yes**, to buyer/tenant | Yes | Written agreement; **represents the buyer even if paid by the seller** |
| **Dual agent** | **Not named** — replaced by *no action adverse or detrimental to either* | Yes — **except known material defects about the property** | **Both parties consent in writing** |
| **Designated agent** | **Yes**, each to their own principal | **Reasonable care that confidential information is not disclosed or used** | **Written consent of the principal**; the **broker becomes a dual agent**; undesignated licensees have **no** relationship |
| **Transaction licensee** | **No — not an agent or advocate** | **Limited** — three listed items only | Must **advise the consumer** of the arrangement |

**All five sit on top of § 35.292.** None of them subtracts anything from it.

---

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-P-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100
percent** applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act,
63 P.S. §§ 455.101—455.902**, including **§§ 455.606.2—455.606.4 and 455.606f**, which § 35.311(a) cites as
the source of the permitted relationships. Those citations are **the regulation's, reproduced so a reader
knows where to go.**

**No statutory duty, penalty, disclosure deadline or agency provision from RELRA is stated in this
module.** Where a reader needs the statute, it is named and routed to.
