chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Practice — Module PA-P-08

## Advertising, solicitation and prohibited practices — §§ 35.282, 35.283, 35.288, 35.301 to 35.308

**Course:** Real Estate Practice · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 45.0
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. State the authority requirement before advertising any property.
2. Apply the harassment and panic-selling rules.
3. State the two disclosure obligations a licensee has when selling or leasing their own real estate.
4. State what must appear in an advertisement by a salesperson or associate broker, and in what size.
5. State the five items required in a prize, contest or gift advertisement.
6. State the three restrictions on claims about sales volume, market position and number of offices.
7. Apply § 35.283 and § 35.282 to a conflict of interest and to a misleading assurance.

---

## A. § 35.301 — you may not advertise property you were not authorised to advertise

> **(a)** *"A licensee **may not advertise the sale or lease of real estate, or otherwise solicit prospective
> buyers or tenants** for the real estate, **without the authority of the seller or lessor or of the agent of
> the seller or lessor**."*

**Authority first.** Not a phone call afterwards, not an assumption that the owner will be pleased. A licensee
who posts an expired listing, or a property they have heard is coming to market, has advertised without
authority.

chunks.heading: B. § 35.302 — Harassment
chunks.excerpt:
**(b)** applies the same principle to a rental listing referral agent: no publishing a rental property where
*"the lessor or property manager **expressly states that the property is not to be included** in lists prepared
by rental listing referral agents."*

---

## B. § 35.302 — Harassment

> *"A licensee, **whether acting on behalf of a prospective buyer or not**, may not solicit — **by personal
> contact, telephone, mail or advertising** — the sale or other disposition of real estate **with such
> frequency as to amount to clear harassment of the owner** or other person who controls the sale or
> disposition."*

**Note "whether acting on behalf of a prospective buyer or not."** Having a real buyer with a real need is no
defence. The rule is about **frequency**, and it names **four channels**: personal contact, telephone, mail and
advertising.

Prospecting is lawful and normal. Prospecting the same owner until it amounts to **clear harassment** is not,
and a licensee who has been told to stop and has not stopped is on the wrong side of the line.

---

## C. § 35.303 — Panic selling

> **(a)** *"The Commission will regard an **attempt by a licensee to bring about panic selling in order to
> profit from it** as **bad faith** under section 604(a)(20) of the act. For purposes of this section, **'panic
> selling' is frequent efforts to sell residential real estate in a particular neighborhood because of fear of
> declining real estate values when the fear is not based on facts relating to the intrinsic value of the real
> estate itself**."*
> **(b)** *"**Proof of systematic solicitation of sales listings may be considered sufficient, but not
> conclusive, evidence** of an attempt to bring about panic selling."*

### C.1 Read the definition's last clause

chunks.heading: D. § 35.288 and § 35.304 — selling your own property
chunks.excerpt:
> *"... when the fear is **not based on facts relating to the intrinsic value of the real estate itself**."*

That clause is what separates panic selling from ordinary market commentary. A licensee may tell an owner that
a nearby plant is closing and that comparable sales have softened — those are **facts relating to the intrinsic
value**. What the rule prohibits is generating fear from something else, and profiting from the listings that
fear produces.

**In practice the "something else" is usually who is moving into the neighbourhood**, which is why this rule
sits beside federal and state fair housing law. **This course states no provision of the federal Fair Housing
Act or of any Pennsylvania anti-discrimination statute**, because neither was read for this project; the rule
transcribed above is the Commission's own, and it is enough to answer the practice question.

**And subsection (b) tells a licensee what evidence looks like.** **Systematic solicitation of listings** in a
neighbourhood **may be sufficient** — not conclusive, but sufficient — proof of the attempt. A licensee whose
entire prospecting strategy is one street, at one moment, in one direction, has created the record.

---

## D. § 35.288 and § 35.304 — selling your own property

**Two separate obligations, at two different moments.**

chunks.heading: E. § 35.305 — the business name and the equal-size rule
chunks.excerpt:
> **§ 35.288(b):** *"A broker or salesperson who is selling or leasing his own real estate shall **disclose his
> licensed status to a prospective buyer or lessee before the buyer or lessee enters into an agreement of sale
> or lease**."*
>
> **§ 35.304:** *"A licensee who sells or leases his own real estate **shall disclose that he is a real estate
> licensee in advertisements for the property**. **This requirement does not apply if the property is listed
> with a real estate company.**"*

**§ 35.288(b) is disclosure to the person**, before they sign. **§ 35.304 is disclosure in the advertisement**,
to everyone who sees it.

**Only § 35.304 has the listed-with-a-company exception**, and the reason is structural: an advertisement placed
by a brokerage already carries the brokerage's name under § 35.305, so the reader knows a licensee is involved.
An advertisement placed by the owner privately carries nothing.

**§ 35.288(a)** states the general principle these sit under: *"A broker or salesperson who sells or leases his
own real estate **shall comply with the requirements of the act and this chapter**."* Selling your own house
does not put you outside the rules.

---

## E. § 35.305 — the business name and the equal-size rule

chunks.heading: E.1 The equal-size rule is not decorative
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"Brokerage companies ... shall advertise or otherwise hold themselves out to the public **only under
> the business name designated on their license**."*
> **(b)** *"Licensees who wish to use and advertise a **nickname** for their first names shall **include the
> nickname on their licensure applications or biennial renewal applications**."*
> **(c)** *"An advertisement by an **associate broker, salesperson**, cemetery associate broker or cemetery
> salesperson **shall contain the business name and telephone number of the employing broker**. **The names and
> telephone numbers shall be of equal size.**"*

### E.1 The equal-size rule is not decorative

**"The names and telephone numbers shall be of equal size."** A salesperson's name in 48 point over the
employing broker's in 8 point violates the rule even though both appear.

**Pennsylvania courts have enforced this closely.** The regulation's own annotations record cases where
advertisements carried the employing broker's name **and a telephone number the broker owned**, but where that
number **connected directly to the salesperson** and **directory assistance gave a different number for the
broker** — held not to satisfy the rule. The purpose the courts identified is worth carrying: the requirement
**advances employee supervision** and **prevents the public from mistakenly believing the salesperson is
self-employed.**

**So the test is functional, not cosmetic.** A number that reaches the salesperson is not the employing broker's
telephone number, however it was purchased.

**And (b) means a nickname is not a free choice.** "Bill" for William must be on the licensure or renewal
application before it goes in an advertisement.

---

## F. § 35.306 — prizes, contests, gifts and free lots

chunks.heading: F. § 35.306 — prizes, contests, gifts and free lots
chunks.excerpt:
An advertisement employing **lotteries or contests**, or offering **prizes, certificates, gifts or free lots**,
shall contain **five** things:

> **(1)** *"A **description** of each prize, certificate, gift or lot offered."*
> **(2)** *"The **prerequisites for receiving** each ... offered."*
> **(3)** *"**Limitation on the number** of prizes ... offered."*
> **(4)** *"The **fair market value** of each ... **If the advertisement is in a print medium, the statement of
> fair market value shall be in the same size type as the description**."*
> **(5)** *"The **odds of winning or receiving** each ... **If the advertisement is in a print medium, the
> statement of odds shall be the same size type as the description, and shall appear immediately adjacent to
> the description**."*

**The rule defines fair market value itself:** *"the price or value that a prospective buyer would expect to pay,
or be charged for, if he were to acquire a **similar item of like quality and quantity in a retail outlet that
offers the item for sale to the general public**."*

**(b)** requires records: the **number and description** of each item distributed; **the name and address of each
person who received one**; and **the name and address of each person who responded but did not receive one.**

**(c)** names four things the Commission **will regard as deceptive conduct** under section 604(a)(18) of the
act: **failure to comply with (a) or (b)**; **failure to disclose the possibility that a particular item may not
be distributed**; **advertising the availability of an item when it is not available**; and **giving a misleading
description.**

chunks.heading: G. § 35.307 — claims about volume, market and offices
chunks.excerpt:
**The two type-size requirements in (4) and (5) are the operative ones**, because the whole abuse the rule
addresses is a headline prize in large type with the value and the odds in small type below.

---

## G. § 35.307 — claims about volume, market and offices

> **(a)** *"An advertisement by a broker about **'sales volume' or 'production' shall refer only to closed
> transactions**. ... a **'closed transaction' is either a listing sold or a sale made after a fully executed
> deed is delivered**."*
> **(b)** *"An advertisement by a broker about his production or position in the **'market' shall identify the
> municipality that the market comprises**."*
> **(c)** *"An advertisement by a broker about the **number of offices** that he operates **shall refer only to
> those offices that have been issued branch office licenses by the Commission**."*

Three claims, three limits, and each closes a specific gap.

**(a) closes the pipeline gap.** Pending sales are not volume. The rule defines a closed transaction precisely:
**a listing sold, or a sale made after a fully executed deed is delivered.**

**(b) closes the moving-boundary gap.** "Number one in the region" means nothing until the region is named, and
the rule requires a **municipality** — a definite unit, not a marketing area the advertiser drew.

**(c) closes the office-count gap.** Only offices that hold **branch office licences from the Commission** may
be counted. A desk in a shared workspace is not an office for this purpose.

---

## H. Two general rules that catch what the specific ones miss

### H.1 § 35.282 — Misleading advice, assurances and representations

chunks.heading: H.2 § 35.283 — Disclosure of interest
chunks.excerpt:
The section's **title** is the substance. A licensee's assurances are regulated, not merely their formal
advertisements. *"It'll appraise, don't worry."* *"That contingency protects you."* *"The township always
approves those."* Each is an **assurance**, and each is the kind of statement this section exists for.

Module PA-F-05 gave the test: **puffing** is opinion nobody would reasonably rely on; **misrepresentation** is a
false statement of fact; and the line moves toward misrepresentation as the statement becomes **more specific and
more verifiable.**

### H.2 § 35.283 — Disclosure of interest

Read with **§ 35.292(a)(7)**, one of the twelve unwaivable duties:

> *"**Disclose, in a reasonably practicable period of time, all conflicts of interest and financial interests**
> as required in § 35.283."*

And with **§ 35.331(a)(6)**, which requires every written agreement to carry *"notification of the licensee's
**continuing duty** to disclose in a reasonably practicable period of time **any conflict of interest**."*

**Continuing.** The duty does not discharge at signing. An interest that arises in week six is disclosed in week
six.

### H.3 § 35.308 — relationships with education providers

A real estate company, franchise or network **may** promote or advertise its association with a real estate
education provider or an accredited college — but *"**an association, affiliation or connection which includes an
ownership interest shall be disclosed in all promotions, endorsements or advertisements**."*

The rule then defines ownership interest broadly: *"proprietary or beneficial interests through which the real
estate company ... **earns or has the potential to earn income, or which produces a direct or indirect economic
benefit**."*

chunks.heading: I. The advertising checklist
chunks.excerpt:
**"Potential to earn"** and **"indirect economic benefit"** are wide words, and they are chosen so that a
recommendation that looks disinterested cannot quietly be a revenue stream.

---

## I. The advertising checklist

Before anything goes out:

1. **Do I have authority** to advertise this property? *(§ 35.301)*
2. **Does it carry the employing broker's business name and telephone number, in equal size?** *(§ 35.305(c))*
3. **Is the company name the one on the licence?** Is any nickname on file? *(§ 35.305(a), (b))*
4. **If I own it** — does the advertisement say I am a licensee? *(§ 35.304)*
5. **If it makes a volume, market or office claim** — closed transactions only, municipality named, licensed
   branch offices only? *(§ 35.307)*
6. **If it offers a prize or gift** — description, prerequisites, limits, **fair market value in the same size
   type**, and **odds in the same size type immediately adjacent**? *(§ 35.306)*
7. **Does it contain any assurance I could not stand behind?** *(§ 35.282)*
8. **Does it disclose any interest I hold?** *(§ 35.283, § 35.292(a)(7))*
9. **If it advertises credit terms** — Module PA-F-06's note applies: **Regulation Z was not read for this
   project**, and the safest practice is to publish **no numbers other than the price.** For anything more, ask
   the lender.

---

## Module PA-P-08 engagement check

Eleven items, delivered as in Module PA-P-01. The **80 percent** engagement threshold and the **100 percent**
applied threshold are **StateCourse standards**.

---

## Instructor source note for Module PA-P-08

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module PA-P-08
chunks.excerpt:
Drawn from **49 Pa. Code §§ 35.282, 35.283, 35.288, 35.292, 35.301 to 35.308 and 35.331**, read on 2026-08-20,
current through **56 Pa.B. 3438 (June 6, 2026)**. Every prohibition, required disclosure, type-size rule and
quoted definition above is **transcribed from that text**, including the courts' stated purpose for the
equal-size rule, which appears in the regulation's own annotations.

**Not read, and therefore the source of nothing here:** the **Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act**,
including **§§ 455.604(a)(18) and (a)(20)**, which §§ 35.303 and 35.306 cite; the **federal Fair Housing Act**;
any **Pennsylvania anti-discrimination statute**; **TILA and Regulation Z**; and the **Telephone Consumer
Protection Act** and any do-not-call rule.

**No statutory penalty, protected class list, credit advertising trigger term, or calling restriction is stated
in this module.**

chunks.excerpt:
# Pennsylvania Real Estate Practice — Module PA-P-09

## Valuation products, property management, records and risk management

**Course:** Real Estate Practice · **Instructional hours: 5.0** of 45.0 — the final module of the course
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Pennsylvania prelicensing credit is available.

## Learning objectives

1. State what § 35.340 requires on every comparative market analysis.
2. State what a broker price opinion must contain, who may prepare one, and who must sign it.
3. State the four permitted uses of a BPO and the seven situations in which one may not be used.
4. State the BPO education requirements.
5. State what a salesperson may and may not do in property management.
6. State the retention periods in § 35.286 and § 35.328.
7. State the reporting obligations in § 35.290 and the continuing education requirement in § 35.384.

---

## A. Three different opinions of value, and Pennsylvania regulates all three

| | Who produces it | What Pennsylvania requires |
|---|---|---|
| **Appraisal** | A licensed or certified **appraiser**, under professional standards | Governed by appraiser licensing law, **not read for this project** |
| **Comparative market analysis (CMA)** | A **licensee** | **§ 35.340** — the USPAP disclaimer, **conspicuously and without change, on the first page** |
| **Broker price opinion (BPO)** | A **broker, associate broker or qualified salesperson** | **Subchapter J, §§ 35.501—35.503** — content, signature, permitted uses, and education |

### A.1 § 35.340 — the CMA disclaimer

chunks.heading: B. Broker price opinions — Subchapter J
chunks.excerpt:
> *"A comparative market analysis shall contain the following statement **printed conspicuously and without
> change on the first page**:*
>
> ***"This analysis has not been performed in accordance with the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal
> Practice which requires valuers to act as unbiased, disinterested third parties with impartiality,
> objectivity and independence and without accommodation of personal interest. It is not to be construed as an
> appraisal and may not be used as such for any purpose."***

**Four requirements: the statement, conspicuously, without change, on the first page.** Not paraphrased, not
in a footer, not on page three. A CMA that omits it does not comply, however good the analysis inside it is.

---

## B. Broker price opinions — Subchapter J

**Subchapter J was added December 26, 2025, effective December 27, 2025, at 55 Pa.B. 8747.** It is recent, and
it is current law.

### B.1 § 35.501 — what a BPO must contain, and who may make one

**The same USPAP disclaimer § 35.340 requires on a CMA** must appear on a BPO, *"displayed conspicuously and
without change."*

A BPO must be **signed manually or electronically by the person who prepared it** and contain **nine** items:

chunks.heading: B.1 § 35.501 — what a BPO must contain, and who may make one
chunks.excerpt:
> **(1)** *"An identification of the **intended users and intended uses** of the broker price opinion, if
> known."*
> **(2)** *"A brief **description of the subject property**."*
> **(3)** *"A brief **description of the property interest to be priced**."*
> **(4)** *"The **basis for the conclusion as to the price**, including applicable **market data, cost data or
> capitalization computation**."*
> **(5)** *"**Each assumption or limiting condition.**"*
> **(6)** *"**Each existing or contemplated interest of the licensee** who prepared the broker price
> opinion."*
> **(7)** *"The **effective date** of the broker price opinion."*
> **(8)** *"The **date that the document is signed**."*
> **(9)** *"The **real estate license number of the preparer** and, if applicable, **the reviewing broker or
> associate broker**."*

**Note (7) and (8) are two different dates**, and the rule wants both. The **effective date** is the date as of
which the opinion speaks; the **signature date** is when it was signed. They are often not the same day.

**Note (6) — each existing or contemplated interest.** *Contemplated.* A licensee thinking about making an offer
on the property discloses that.

**Compensation — § 35.501(c):** *"A **fee or valuable consideration** for a broker price opinion, if any, **shall
be paid directly to the employing broker**."* Not to the salesperson.

**Who may prepare one — § 35.501(d):**

> *"**A salesperson may not prepare a broker price opinion unless the salesperson has held an active license for
> the 3 years immediately preceding the effective date of the broker price opinion** and has satisfied the
> educational requirements in § 35.503."*

chunks.heading: B.2 § 35.502 — the four permitted uses
chunks.excerpt:
**Three years of active licensure, measured to the BPO's effective date** — and the education as well. **Both
conditions.**

**And § 35.501(e):** a BPO prepared by a salesperson *"**shall be signed by the salesperson and reviewed and
signed by the employing broker or a designated associate broker**."*

**So a salesperson's BPO carries two signatures**, and the second one is a review, not a formality.

### B.2 § 35.502 — the four permitted uses

> **(a)** *A BPO **may be prepared ... only for use in conjunction with** any of the following:*
> **(1)** *"A property **owned by a lender after an unsuccessful sale at a foreclosure auction**."*
> **(2)** *"A **modification of a first or junior mortgage or equity line of credit**."*
> **(3)** *"A **short sale** of a property."*
> **(4)** *"An **evaluation or monitoring of a portfolio of properties**."*

**"Only."** Four uses, and the list is closed.

### B.3 § 35.502(b) — where a BPO may NOT be used

> **(1)** *"**As the basis to determine the value of a parcel of real property for a mortgage loan
> origination**, including a first or junior mortgage, refinancing or equity line of credit."*
> **(2)** *In connection with:* **an eminent domain proceeding**; **a Federal, State or local tax appeal**; **a
> bankruptcy or insolvency proceeding**; **an action or proceeding involving divorce or equitable distribution
> of property**; ***"any other action or proceeding before a court of record"***; **the distribution of a
> decedent's estate.**

### B.4 Reading (a)(2) against (b)(1) — the distinction that matters

**A loan MODIFICATION is a permitted use. A loan ORIGINATION is prohibited.**

chunks.heading: B.5 § 35.503 — the education
chunks.excerpt:
Both involve a lender and a mortgage, and a licensee who does not hold the distinction will get it wrong. The
line is whether **new credit is being extended on the strength of the value.** Modifying an existing loan
adjusts terms on a debt that already exists; originating one puts new money out against the property. **The
prohibition names refinancing and equity lines of credit expressly**, so a licensee cannot reason their way
around it.

**And (b)(2)'s catch-all is very wide:** *"any other action or proceeding **before a court of record**."*
Litigation of any kind takes a BPO off the table. Divorce, estate distribution, tax appeals and bankruptcy are
named because they are where the requests actually come from.

### B.5 § 35.503 — the education

- **Initial education before preparing one.** A **Commission-approved initial education course** in the
  preparation of BPOs.
- **Initial education before signing one.** A broker or associate broker **may not sign** a salesperson's BPO
  unless they too have completed it.
- **Continuing education.** *"at least **3 hours** of Commission-approved continuing education in broker price
  opinion topics **during the current or immediately preceding 2-year license period**."*
- **Records.** The licensee **shall retain the transcript or certificate of instruction** for all required BPO
  courses and **provide a copy to the Commission upon request.**

**Four broker prelicensure courses are Commission-approved for the initial requirement:** *"valuation of
residential property; valuation of income-producing property; basic appraisal principles; basic appraisal
procedures."*

chunks.heading: C. Property management — § 35.287 and § 35.321(b)
chunks.excerpt:
**Other courses qualify** if **3 or more hours** in length and covering four stated topic areas — valuation
definitions including **BPO, CMA and AVM**; the **permitted and non-permitted uses**; the **qualifications and
limitations** on preparation, signature and fees; and the **basics of preparation**, including sources,
analysis, and **liability issues arising from broker price opinions.**

---

## C. Property management — § 35.287 and § 35.321(b)

> **§ 35.287:** *"A salesperson **may assist in property management if the salesperson's work is supervised and
> controlled by the employing broker**. The salesperson **may not independently negotiate the terms of a lease
> nor execute a lease on behalf of the lessor**."*

**Two prohibitions, both containing a word that carries the meaning.**

**"Independently negotiate."** A salesperson may participate in a negotiation the broker supervises and
controls. What they may not do is negotiate terms **on their own authority.**

**"Execute a lease on behalf of the lessor."** Signing for the owner is the broker's, not the salesperson's.

**And the money — § 35.321(b):** rents are **not** escrow, but they are **not the broker's** either. They go
into a **rental management account separate from both the escrow account and the general business account.**
**Security deposits are different again**: they **are** escrow, and under **§ 35.321(e)** the duty to pay over
**arises when the tenancy ends.**

**Three accounts.** Escrow, rental management, general business. Module PA-P-06 has the detail.

**Pennsylvania's Landlord and Tenant Act was not read for this project.** **No security deposit limit, notice
period, eviction procedure or lessor interest entitlement is stated anywhere in this build.**

---

chunks.heading: D. Records — the periods, in one place
chunks.excerpt:
## D. Records — the periods, in one place

| Record | Period | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Records pertaining to a real estate transaction | **3 years following consummation** | § 35.286(a) |
| Acknowledgement of the § 35.336 consumer notice **where there is no transaction** | **6 months** | § 35.286(a)(1) |
| Acknowledgement of the § 35.338 time-share notice | **6 months** | § 35.286(a)(2) |
| Acknowledgement of the § 35.336 / § 35.337 lease notices | **6 months** | § 35.286(a)(3) |
| Written disclosure establishing a **subagent or transaction licensee** relationship | **6 months** | § 35.286(a)(4) |
| **Escrow records** — three names and three dates | Kept and **produced on written request or office inspection** | § 35.328 |
| Education provider **continuing education** records | **4 years** | § 35.360(e)(1) |
| Education provider **all other** records | **10 years** | § 35.360(e)(2) |
| A licensee's own **BPO course transcripts** | Retained; **copy to the Commission on request** | § 35.503(d) |

**Production is not optional.** § 35.286(b) and § 35.328 both require production **upon written request** or
**pursuant to an office inspection under § 35.246**, and § 35.325(d) requires the broker to hand the Commission
**a letter authorising the bank to release the escrow account's records.**

---

## E. Reporting and continuing obligations

### E.1 § 35.290 — what you must tell the Commission

chunks.heading: E.2 § 35.291 — posting a suspension
chunks.excerpt:
> **(a)** *"A licensee shall notify the Commission of being **convicted of, or pleading guilty or nolo
> contendere to, a felony or misdemeanor, within 30 days of the verdict or plea**."*
> **(b)** *"A licensee shall notify the Commission of **disciplinary action taken against him by the real estate
> licensing authority of another jurisdiction within 30 days of receiving notice** of the disciplinary
> action."*

**Both 30 days.** Both self-reporting. **(a)'s trigger is the verdict or the plea** — not the sentence, not the
end of appeals — and a **nolo contendere** plea counts.

### E.2 § 35.291 — posting a suspension

A **broker** whose licence is suspended **returns the licence** and **posts the Commission's notice prominently
on or near the public entrance** of the main office and every branch. *"Failure to post the notice constitutes
grounds for further disciplinary action."*

### E.3 § 35.384 — continuing education, once you are licensed

> **(a)** *"a licensee shall complete **14 hours of continuing education** in acceptable courses in a **minimum
> of 2-hour increments**."*
> **(b)** *"during the **first biennial period** that continuing education is required, a **new licensee shall
> complete the Commission-developed 14-hour required course for new licensees** in satisfaction of the
> continuing education requirement."*

**A new licensee does not choose their first 14 hours.** The Commission has developed the course and it is
required.

chunks.heading: F. Risk management — the whole of both courses in one page
chunks.excerpt:
The rule then lists **25 acceptable subjects** — from real estate ethics and laws affecting real estate through
agency relationships, landlord-tenant law, environmental issues, antitrust, and use of technology in delivering
real estate services — and, in **(d)**, what is **not** acceptable: *"mechanical office and business skills; for
example, typing, speed writing, preparation of advertising copy, development of sales promotional devices, word
processing, calculator and computer operation and office management and related internal operations procedures
**that do not have a bearing on the public interest**."*

**The test in (d) is the public interest.** Courses that make you a better salesperson are not thereby
continuing education; courses that make you a safer one are.

---

## F. Risk management — the whole of both courses in one page

Nine habits, each traceable to a rule you have now read.

chunks.heading: G. What these courses did not read, restated at the end
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Disclose the relationship at the initial interview**, in the right form, and **note a refusal to sign.**
   *(§ 35.284)*
2. **Put it in writing** — every commitment where compensation may be owed, with all eight § 35.331 contents.
   *(§ 35.281, § 35.331)*
3. **Present every offer**, in writing, in a reasonably practicable time. *(§ 35.292(a)(3))*
4. **Deposit money belonging to another by the end of the next business day**, into an account that is insured,
   names you as trustee, allows withdrawal without notice, and is used exclusively for escrow. *(§ 35.324,
   § 35.325)*
5. **Never mix and never use.** *(§ 35.326)*
6. **On a dispute, hold.** *(§ 35.327)*
7. **Reveal known material defects** — the exception written inside the confidentiality duty itself.
   *(§ 35.312(a)(2), § 35.314(b)(3))*
8. **Route what is beyond you**, because it is a duty and not a courtesy. *(§ 35.292(a)(8))*
9. **Keep the record** — three years, six months, or the escrow record's three names and three dates.
   *(§ 35.286, § 35.328)*

**And the one that holds the rest together — § 35.292(a)(2): deal honestly and in good faith.** Owed to
everyone. Not waivable. Every violation in these two courses is, underneath, a failure of that sentence.

---

## G. What these courses did not read, restated at the end

**Obtained and read in full:** 49 Pa. Code Chapter 35, current through **56 Pa.B. 3438 (June 6, 2026)**.

chunks.heading: Module PA-P-09 engagement check

**Not obtained.** Nothing in this build states a rule, figure, deadline, form provision, fee or penalty from

Chapter 73, the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law**; the **Commission's content outlines** for *Real Estate
Fundamentals* and *Real Estate Practice*; the **verbatim text of the §§ 35.336—35.339 consumer disclosure
summaries**; the **itemised disclosures in § 35.335a**; the **Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Act**;
**Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax statutes** and local transfer tax ordinances; the **Municipalities

examination content outline or candidate handbook**; **USPAP**; and **TILA, RESPA, TRID, ECOA, FCRA, the federal
Fair Housing Act and the federal lead-based paint regulations.**

**A course that names its gaps has told you something useful, not withheld something.** That list is your map to
where the answers live.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 01

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 01

## TREC Topic: Introduction to Modern Real Estate Practice

**Prescribed time: 100 minutes.** This module carries the four units the Commission's PRINS1-1 course
approval form places under *Introduction to Modern Real Estate Practice*, whose scope note is
*"Licensing as a broker and salesperson."*

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: identify the fields of work
that make up the Texas real estate business and the licence, if any, each requires; explain what the
Texas Real Estate Commission is, who sits on it, and where its authority to regulate education comes
from; describe the economic characteristics that make real estate markets local, slow-moving and
imperfect; state which activities require a Texas licence, in the statute's own terms; and name the
persons and transactions The Real Estate License Act does not reach.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a section of the Texas Occupations Code that was
read for this course.** Where a statement is practice rather than law — how brokerages are commonly
organised, what a typical day looks like — the module says so, and no section is cited for it.

## Unit: Real Estate - A Business of Many Opportunities

The phrase "real estate business" suggests one occupation: the agent who lists and sells houses. The
business is in fact a cluster of occupations organised around a single asset class, and a student
entering it should be able to see the whole cluster before choosing a place in it — partly because the
choice matters, and partly because the licence you are studying for reaches some of these occupations
and not others.

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - A Business of Many Opportunities
chunks.excerpt:
**Brokerage** is the core licensed activity: bringing parties to a real property transaction together
for compensation. Texas defines it not by the job title but by a list of acts. Occupations Code
§ 1101.002(1) defines a **broker** as a person who, *for a commission or other valuable consideration
or with the expectation of receiving one*, performs *for another person* any of twelve acts — among
them selling, exchanging, purchasing or leasing real estate; offering to do any of those; negotiating
or attempting to negotiate a listing, sale, exchange, purchase or lease; listing real estate for sale;
auctioning it; dealing in options on it; aiding in locating or obtaining real estate for purchase or
lease; procuring a prospect or procuring property to effect a sale, exchange or lease; and controlling
the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a single-family residential unit.

Three features of that definition organise everything else in this course.

**First, the definition runs on compensation.** Every act on the list becomes brokerage only when done
for consideration or the expectation of it. A neighbour who helps you find a house as a favour is not
acting as a broker; the same help for a fee is squarely inside § 1101.002(1).

**Second, the definition runs on acting *for another person*.** An owner selling the owner's own
property is not performing an act "for another," which is why owners can sell their own real estate
without a licence and why several of the statutory exemptions you will meet later in this module are
structural rather than special favours.

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - A Business of Many Opportunities
chunks.excerpt:
**Third, the list is longer than the popular image of the job.** Notice item (x): *controlling the
acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a single-family residential real property unit*.
Residential property management — collecting rent on a house for an owner, for a fee — is brokerage in
Texas. Notice also that § 1101.002(1)(B) sweeps in a person *employed by or for an owner to sell any
portion of the owner's real estate*, and a person in the business of charging an **advance fee** to
promote real estate through listing publications or referrals. The Legislature wrote the definition to
follow the money, not the business card.

Around that licensed core, the business offers occupations the licence does not govern, each touching
the transaction at a different point:

- **Lending and mortgage origination** — financing the purchase. Loan origination is regulated under
  finance law rather than under The Real Estate License Act, and it is a separate career path with its
  own licensing.
- **Title insurance and escrow** — searching, examining and insuring title, and closing the
  transaction. In Texas this industry is regulated under the Insurance Code; Module 09 introduces it.
- **Appraisal** — developing opinions of value under a separate licensing scheme. Note the careful
  carve-out in the broker definition itself: § 1101.002(1)(A)(xi) treats a *written analysis, opinion
  or conclusion relating to the estimated price of real property* as a broker act only when it is
  **not referred to as an appraisal**, is given in the ordinary course of business, and relates to the
  management, acquisition, disposition or encumbrance of real property. A licence holder may prepare a
  price opinion; calling it an appraisal is a different, separately licensed act.
- **Inspect

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: the twelve acts
chunks.excerpt:
ion** — examining improvements for condition. Texas inspectors are licensed under a
  companion chapter administered by the same Commission (Chapter 1102, named in § 1101.151).
- **Construction, development and land use** — creating the inventory the market trades.
- **Investment and asset management** — holding real estate for income and appreciation, the subject
  of two units in Module 05.

A sales agent's practice touches every one of these. The agent does not originate the loan, close the
sale, appraise the property or inspect the roof — but the agent coordinates with the people who do,
and the client experiences the agent as the guide to the whole process. That is why a principles
course spends its hours on property, ownership, title, finance and closing rather than only on selling.

**Where the licence itself fits.** Occupations Code § 1101.002(7) defines a **sales agent** as *a
person who is sponsored by a licensed broker for the purpose of performing an act described by
Subdivision (1)* — that is, the same acts, performable only through a broker. Section 1101.351
completes the structure: a person may not act as, or represent being, a broker or sales agent without
a licence; a business entity may not act as a broker without its own licence; and § 1101.351(c) states
the sponsorship rule in one sentence — *a licensed sales agent may not engage or attempt to engage in
real estate brokerage unless the sales agent is sponsored by a licensed broker and is acting for that
broker*. The two-tier structure — responsible broker, sponsored agent — is the organising fact of
Texas brokerage practice, and you will meet it again wherever supervision, advertising and
compensation appear in this program.

### Statute reading exercise: the twelve acts

chunks.heading: Unit: TREC Education Standards Advisory Committee
chunks.excerpt:
Open the quoted definition of "broker" in Occupations Code § 1101.002(1) as set out above and answer
in your notes: **(1)** Which listed act makes residential property management licensed activity?
**(2)** A person gives a written opinion of a home's likely sale price, calls it a "market analysis,"
and is paid for it as part of taking a listing. Which subparagraph makes this a broker act rather than
an appraisal, and what three conditions does it attach? **(3)** Why does an owner selling the owner's
own home fall outside the definition without needing any exemption? *(Answers: the rent-acceptance
item, § 1101.002(1)(A)(x); the price-opinion item, § 1101.002(1)(A)(xi), with the conditions that it
not be called an appraisal, be given in the ordinary course of business, and relate to actual or
potential management, acquisition, disposition or encumbrance; because the definition requires acting
"for another person," and an owner acts for the owner.)*

## Unit: TREC Education Standards Advisory Committee

The course you are taking exists in the form it does because Texas law places real estate education
under the Commission's control and gives the Commission a mechanism for keeping the standards current.

chunks.heading: Unit: TREC Education Standards Advisory Committee
chunks.excerpt:
**The Texas Real Estate Commission.** Occupations Code § 1101.051 establishes a nine-member
commission appointed by the governor with the advice and consent of the senate: six members who have
been engaged in the brokerage business as licensed brokers as their major occupation for the five
years preceding appointment, and three members who represent the public. The mixture is deliberate —
industry knowledge on one side, public accountability on the other. Under § 1101.151 the Commission
administers this chapter and Chapter 1102 (the inspector chapter), may adopt and enforce rules
necessary to administer them, and may establish standards of conduct and ethics for licence holders.

**Where course standards come from.** Section 1101.301 authorises the Commission, by rule, to
establish standards for the approval of qualifying educational programs and courses of study in real
estate conducted in this state — excluding programs offered by public high schools and accredited
colleges and universities — and to develop minimum education and experience requirements for
instructors. Section 1101.003 names the qualifying course subjects, *principles of real estate* among
them, and lets the Commission prescribe their content by rule. The course approval form this module is
built on — PRINS1-1, with its topics, units and suggested minutes — is that prescription at work.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Real Estate Market - Characteristics of Real Estate
chunks.excerpt:
**The advisory committee mechanism.** Section 1101.158 permits the Commission to appoint advisory
committees to perform the advisory functions the Commission assigns; members serve at the will of the
Commission and without compensation, and committee meetings are subject to the open-meetings law. The
Commission maintains an **Education Standards Advisory Committee** under this authority — a standing
committee through which education standards, course content requirements and course approval forms are
reviewed and recommendations are made to the Commission. For a student, the practical meaning is
this: the required topics you are studying are not a school's choices. They are the Commission's,
arrived at through a public advisory process, and a school's course is approved against them.

**Two statutory course-integrity rules worth knowing now**, because they govern your own study:
under § 1101.003(d), *a daily course segment for a qualifying course may not exceed 12 hours* — no
provider may credit you with more than twelve hours of qualifying coursework in a day; and under
§ 1101.003(e), the completion of a correspondence or alternative-delivery qualifying course may not
be reported to the Commission until the elapsed time from your registration exceeds **twice** the
number of credit hours claimed — for this 30-hour course, sixty hours must elapse between
registration and reported completion. Both rules exist to keep a qualifying course from being
consumed faster than anyone could learn from it.

## Unit: The Real Estate Market - Characteristics of Real Estate

chunks.heading: Unit: The Real Estate Market - Characteristics of Real Estate
chunks.excerpt:
Real estate markets behave unlike markets for shares, cars or groceries, and the differences follow
from physical and economic characteristics of the asset itself. This unit is economics rather than
law: no statute is cited because none governs it. What follows is the standard analytical vocabulary,
applied to Texas conditions.

**Physical characteristics.**

- **Immobility.** Land cannot be moved. Every parcel's value is therefore captured by its location,
  and markets are irreducibly local: a surplus of housing in one metropolitan area cannot ship to
  relieve a shortage in another. Immobility is also why real estate is governed and taxed where it
  sits, and why a licence to broker it is issued state by state.
- **Indestructibility.** Land endures. Improvements wear out; the land under them does not. This
  permanence is what makes land a durable store of value and makes long instruments — thirty-year
  loans, ninety-nine-year leases — sensible.
- **Uniqueness (heterogeneity).** No two parcels are identical, because no two occupy the same
  location. The law takes this seriously — you will see in Module 06 that Texas allows four years to
  sue for **specific performance** of a contract to convey real property, a remedy premised on the
  idea that money cannot fully substitute for a particular parcel — and valuation takes it seriously
  too, which is why appraisal compares and adjusts rather than looking up a price.

**Economic characteristics.**

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate Law
chunks.excerpt:
- **Scarcity.** Usable land in a given location is finite even where land in general is abundant —
  a truth vivid in Texas, where vast rural acreage coexists with intense competition for land in the
  growth corridors of the major metropolitan areas.
- **Improvements and modification.** Investment in a parcel changes its character and value, and the
  character of surrounding parcels; a subdivision, a highway or a reservoir re-prices its neighbours.
- **Permanence of investment.** Capital placed in land and improvements is long-lived and largely
  irreversible — the return arrives over decades, which ties real estate to credit markets and makes
  interest rates a dominant force in demand.
- **Location preference (situs).** People's preference for one location over another — commute,
  schools, flood risk, prestige — is the economic engine of value differences between physically
  similar properties.

**What these characteristics do to the market.** Because the asset is immobile and unique, buyers and
sellers cannot meet in a central exchange; they find each other through search, which is costly and
slow. Because transactions are infrequent, prices are discovered deal by deal rather than posted
continuously. Because supply responds slowly — construction takes years, and land in a location
cannot be increased at all — demand shifts move prices sharply before supply can answer. Economists
summarise all this by calling real estate markets **imperfect**: information is incomplete, products
are non-standard, entry is slow, and local conditions dominate. The brokerage business exists
precisely because the market is imperfect — the licence holder's stock in trade is local information,
search and negotiation in a market that lacks a ticker.

## Unit: Real Estate Law

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate Law
chunks.excerpt:
The remaining forty minutes of this topic introduce the legal frame that the rest of the course fills
in: what The Real Estate License Act is, whom it licenses, whom it exempts, and where it sits among
the other bodies of law a licence holder works inside.

**The Act.** Occupations Code § 1101.001 gives Chapter 1101 its citation name: *The Real Estate
License Act*. The chapter defines the licensed occupations (§ 1101.002), creates the Commission
(§ 1101.051) and arms it with rulemaking power (§ 1101.151), controls entry through education and
licensing (§§ 1101.003, 1101.301, 1101.351), and — in subchapters this course meets later in the
program — regulates conduct and provides sanctions.

**The licence requirement, in the statute's words.** Under § 1101.351(a), unless a person holds a
licence issued under this chapter, the person *may not act as or represent that the person is a broker
or sales agent*. Representation alone is enough: holding yourself out — a sign, a website, a business
card — is prohibited conduct for the unlicensed, whether or not a transaction ever happens. Under
§ 1101.351(a-1) a business entity may not act as a broker without an entity licence, and under
§ 1101.351(b) even a successful applicant may not act until the licence has actually issued. "Real
estate" for all these purposes is defined broadly by § 1101.002(5): *any interest in real property,
including a leasehold*, located in or outside this state — though not an interest held merely as
security for an obligation.

**Whom the Act does not reach.** Section 1101.005 lists the exemptions, and they reward careful
reading because each has edges:

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate Law
chunks.excerpt:
- **An attorney licensed in Texas** — exempt as such; but an attorney-in-fact under a power of
  attorney is exempt only for **not more than three** real estate transactions annually, a numbered
  limit that stops the power-of-attorney device from becoming an unlicensed brokerage.
- **A public official** engaged in official duties.
- **A licensed auctioneer** calling the auction of real estate — provided the auctioneer performs no
  other act of a broker; the exemption covers the gavel, not the marketing campaign.
- **A person acting under a court order or under the authority of a will or written trust
  instrument** — executors, administrators, guardians, trustees.
- **A builder's own sales employees**, for structures the owner erected in the course of the owner's
  business — the new-home sales office.
- **An on-site manager of an apartment complex** — on-site being the operative word; § 1101.002(1)
  still makes off-site single-family rent collection for others a broker act.
- **An owner, or the owner's employee, leasing the owner's own improved or unimproved real estate.**
- **Certain transaction types**: interests in minerals, mining and standing timber; cemetery lots;
  hotel and motel leasing; and — significant for Module 08 — *the sale of real property under a power
  of sale conferred by a deed of trust or other contract lien*: the foreclosure trustee conducting the
  sale is not thereby acting as a broker.
- **Internal transactions of limited partnerships and limited liability companies**, conducted by
  their general partners, managers or negotiating employees.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: exemptions with edges
chunks.excerpt:
The common thread is the one you met in the broker definition: the Act licenses those who broker
*for others, for compensation*, and leaves alone those who deal with their own property, act under
another licence or a court's supervision, or operate inside listed special markets.

**The wider legal frame.** The Act is one layer. A Texas transaction also moves through the
**Property Code** (conveyances, recording, liens, homestead — Modules 03, 07 and 08), the **Business
& Commerce Code** (the statute of frauds — Module 06), the **Tax Code** (property taxation and tax
liens — Module 03), the **Family Code** (community property — Module 05), the **Estates Code** (wills
and descent — Module 07), the **Insurance Code** (title insurance — Modules 07 and 09), and federal
law (settlement procedures and foreign-seller withholding — Modules 08 and 09). Principles I is the
map of that terrain; the later courses in the six-course program walk each region in depth.

### Statute reading exercise: exemptions with edges

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: which door into the business?
chunks.excerpt:
Re-read the § 1101.005 summary above. For each of the following, decide whether a licence is
required, and identify the exemption or definitional reason: **(1)** A ranch owner's full-time
employee negotiates leases of the owner's grazing land. **(2)** A friend holding a power of attorney
sells five houses this year for various acquaintances. **(3)** A trustee named in a recorded deed of
trust conducts the foreclosure auction of the secured property. **(4)** An off-site property manager
collects rent on twelve single-family homes for their various owners, for a monthly fee. *(Answers:
(1) exempt — owner's employee leasing the owner's real estate; (2) licence required — the
attorney-in-fact exemption stops at three transactions annually; (3) exempt — sale under a power of
sale conferred by a deed of trust; (4) licence required — § 1101.002(1)(A)(x) makes controlling the
acceptance or deposit of rent from single-family residents a broker act, and no § 1101.005 exemption
reaches an off-site manager acting for others.)*

### Applied exercise: which door into the business?

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
*A newly licensed sales agent is weighing three offers: (a) a residential brokerage team promising
listings support; (b) a property management firm managing 300 single-family rentals; (c) a builder's
on-site new-home sales office, which tells her she "won't even need her licence there."* **Task:**
for each offer, state which licensing rule or exemption governs the work, and identify what the agent
must verify before starting at each. **Model answer:** (a) ordinary brokerage under § 1101.002(1);
she may act only through a sponsoring broker per § 1101.351(c), so the team's broker must become her
sponsor. (b) single-family rent collection for others is a broker act under § 1101.002(1)(A)(x); the
firm must be operating under a broker licence and she must be sponsored by that broker — her licence
is fully engaged, not optional. (c) the builder's own sales employees are exempt under § 1101.005 for
the builder's structures; she could work there unlicensed as the builder's employee, but while doing
so she is outside brokerage — and if she wants to keep her licence active through a sponsor, or sell
anything other than the builder's own inventory, the exemption does not stretch to cover it.

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The Texas real estate business is a cluster of occupations around one asset; the licence reaches the
brokerage core, defined by twelve compensated acts done for others (§ 1101.002(1)). Sales agents act
only through sponsoring brokers (§§ 1101.002(7), 1101.351(c)); entities need their own licences; and
representation without a licence is itself unlawful (§ 1101.351). The nine-member Commission
(§ 1101.051) administers the Act with rulemaking power (§ 1101.151), prescribes qualifying education
(§§ 1101.003, 1101.301) with advisory committees under § 1101.158, and enforces two study-integrity
rules — the 12-hour daily cap and the elapsed-time rule — that govern this very course
(§ 1101.003(d), (e)). Real estate markets are local, slow and imperfect because the asset is immobile,
indestructible and unique; and the Act's exemptions (§ 1101.005) trace the same boundary as its
definitions — own property, other licences, listed special markets — leaving compensated dealing for
others as the licensed heartland.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 02

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 02

## TREC Topic: Real Property

**Prescribed time: 60 minutes.** Two units under the Commission's scope note *"Distinctions between
personal & real property"* — the boundary on which contracts, financing, taxation and closings all
depend.

**Learning objectives.** Distinguish land, real estate and real property as three layered concepts;
classify an item as real or personal by applying the fixture tests; explain why the classification
matters at sale, at loan and at death; and recognise the special case of fixtures financed under a
security agreement, where Texas commercial law and real property law meet.

## Unit: Land, Real Estate and Real Property

The three terms are often used interchangeably in conversation. In analysis they are layers, each
adding something to the one below.

**Land** is the physical layer: the surface of the earth within the parcel's boundaries, everything
beneath it to the centre of the earth, and the airspace above, together with what nature attached —
soil, minerals in place, native trees and standing water. Texas treats the severable natural
components as capable of separate ownership; mineral interests in particular are routinely severed
from the surface and traded on their own, which is why The Real Estate License Act's exemptions you
met in Module 01 carve mineral transactions out of ordinary brokerage.

**Real estate** is land plus **improvements**: everything humans have permanently attached —
buildings, fences, pavement, wells, irrigation works. The additions are called improvements whether
or not they improve value; the term marks permanence, not quality.

chunks.heading: Unit: Land, Real Estate and Real Property
chunks.excerpt:
**Real property** is the legal layer: real estate plus the **bundle of rights** ownership carries.
The classical bundle is possession (occupy the property), control (determine its lawful use),
enjoyment (use it without outside interference), exclusion (keep others out), and disposition (sell,
lease, mortgage, give or devise it). Every later module of this course is about some stick in that
bundle: estates measure how much of the bundle you hold and for how long; encumbrances are other
people's claims on particular sticks; leases transfer possession while ownership keeps the rest;
mortgages pledge the bundle as security.

Texas statute defines the trading unit of the licensed business in exactly these layered terms:
Occupations Code § 1101.002(5) defines **"real estate"** for licensing purposes as *any interest in
real property, including a leasehold, located in or outside this state* — but not an interest held
merely as security. Notice what that does: the licensed commodity is not dirt but *interests* — a
fee, a life estate, a leasehold, an easement are all "real estate" in a broker's hands, and Module 03
is a catalogue of those interests.

**Water deserves a Texas-specific note now**, ahead of its unit in Module 03: much of the water a
buyer sees is not part of the parcel at all. Water Code § 11.021 declares the water of the ordinary
flow, underflow and tides of every flowing river, natural stream and lake — and the storm and flood
water of every natural watercourse — to be **the property of the state**. A parcel bounded by a
creek includes land; the flowing water belongs to Texas.

chunks.heading: Unit: Personal Property
chunks.excerpt:
**Why the layers matter in practice.** A contract to sell "the property at 214 Brazos Lane" passes
the land, the improvements and the seller's bundle of rights — but only the sticks the seller holds.
If the minerals were severed by a prior owner, the buyer takes the surface without them; if a
recorded easement lets a neighbour cross, the buyer takes subject to it. The licence holder's job at
the contract stage is to know that "the property" is shorthand for a specific, possibly incomplete,
bundle — and that the documents, not the fence line, say what is actually being sold.

## Unit: Personal Property

Everything that is not real property is **personal property** (also *personalty* or *chattels*):
movable things — furniture, vehicles, equipment — and intangible rights. The classification sounds
academic until you watch it decide who owns the dishwasher.

**Crossing the line: annexation and severance.** Personal property becomes real property by
**annexation** — permanent attachment to land or improvements. A pile of lumber is personalty; the
deck built from it is part of the real estate. The reverse movement is **severance**: standing timber
is realty, felled logs are personalty; growing minerals in place are realty, produced oil in the tank
is personalty. Cultivated annual crops (**emblements**) are treated as personal property of the one
who planted them even before harvest — the classic accommodation to agriculture.

chunks.heading: Unit: Personal Property
chunks.excerpt:
**The fixture tests.** A **fixture** is an item that began as personal property and has become part
of the real estate. When a sale contract is silent, fixtures pass with the deed and personalty stays
with the seller — so the classification allocates real money. The common-law tests, applied by Texas
courts and taught in every serious course, ask three questions:

1. **Method of annexation.** How is it attached? Built-in, plumbed, wired or cemented items lean
   real; items resting by their own weight or plugged into an outlet lean personal. Damage on removal
   is strong evidence of annexation.
2. **Adaptation to the realty.** Was the item fitted to this property — custom cabinetry, a pool
   pump, a garage-door opener sized to this door? Adaptation leans real even where attachment is
   light.
3. **Intention of the parties.** The dominant test: would a reasonable person, viewing the
   attachment and adaptation, understand the item to have been made a permanent part of the property?
   Intention is judged objectively from the circumstances, not from a party's private plan.

**The practice answer is always the same: do not litigate the tests — draft around them.** A
well-made Texas contract lists what stays and what goes. The refrigerator, the mounted televisions,
the smart thermostat, the propane tank: name them, and the fixture tests never get called. Module 06
returns to this when it treats the promulgated contract forms.

chunks.heading: Unit: Personal Property
chunks.excerpt:
**Trade fixtures.** Items a commercial tenant attaches for the tenant's business — shelving, ovens,
salon chairs — are **trade fixtures**: as between landlord and tenant they remain the tenant's
personal property, removable at or before the end of the term, with the tenant responsible for the
damage removal causes. Left behind after the tenancy ends, they typically become the landlord's by
abandonment. The category exists so that renting space does not mean donating your equipment to the
building.

**Financed fixtures: where two bodies of law meet.** A dishwasher bought on credit is personal
property subject to a **security interest** under Article 9 of the Business & Commerce Code; built
into a kitchen it becomes a fixture in real estate that may itself be mortgaged. Which creditor wins?
Business & Commerce Code § 9.334 draws the lines: no Article 9 security interest exists at all in
*ordinary building materials incorporated into an improvement* — the lumber merges into the realty,
full stop — but for true fixtures, a **purchase-money security interest** perfected by a **fixture
filing** made before the goods become fixtures **or within 20 days after** takes priority even over
an earlier recorded real property encumbrancer, and readily removable office machines and replacement
domestic appliances get their own priority track. A licence holder does not practise secured-
transactions law; what the licence holder must recognise is the pattern — a financed water softener,
solar array or HVAC system may carry a lien that does not appear in the deed records' mortgage
chain — and the cure, which is asking, in every transaction, *is anything attached to this house
still being paid for?*

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: the state's water and the merchant's lumber
chunks.excerpt:
**Manufactured housing** is the classification question at its most consequential — a dwelling that
may be personal property (titled like a vehicle) or may have become real property depending on its
installation and the election made under the applicable titling law. This course flags the category;
the dedicated treatment belongs to later courses in the program. What Principles I asks of you is
only the reflex: *never assume a manufactured home is real estate; verify how it is held.*

### Statute reading exercise: the state's water and the merchant's lumber

Answer from the two provisions quoted or summarised above: **(1)** A rural listing's photographs
feature the creek that crosses the land. What does Water Code § 11.021 say about who owns the flowing
water, and what should the listing therefore not promise? **(2)** A supplier delivers brick to a
homesite on credit. After the brick is laid, can the supplier claim an Article 9 security interest in
the brick under Business & Commerce Code § 9.334? What different body of law — previewed in Module 03
— protects those who furnish materials that merge into an improvement? *(Answers: (1) the ordinary
flow of a natural stream is the property of the state; the listing may describe access and frontage
but not ownership of the watercourse; (2) no — § 9.334(a) says no security interest exists in
ordinary building materials incorporated into an improvement; the supplier's protection is the
mechanic's and materialman's lien of Property Code Chapter 53.)*

### Applied exercise: the contested farmhouse closing

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
*At the walk-through of a farm sale, the buyer finds the seller has removed: the antique dining
chandelier (replaced with a builder-grade light), the above-ground pool, the propane tank serving the
house (leased from a gas company), the corral panels (freestanding, pinned together), and the pump
from the irrigation well. The contract was silent on all five.* **Task:** classify each item using
the fixture tests and state who likely owns it. **Model answer:** chandelier — a fixture (wired,
adapted, objectively permanent); the seller's swap was improper unless the contract excluded it.
Above-ground pool — typically personalty (rests by weight, designed for disassembly); the seller may
take it. Leased propane tank — the gas company's personal property regardless of attachment; neither
party owns it, and the buyer contracts with the supplier. Freestanding corral panels — personalty by
method of annexation, though a close call on adaptation; seller likely keeps them. Irrigation pump —
plumbed and wired into the well and adapted to the land: a fixture that should have stayed. The
larger lesson: every one of these five arguments would have cost nothing if the contract had listed
them — which is the licence holder's actual job.

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Land is the physical parcel with what nature attached; real estate adds human improvements; real
property adds the bundle of rights — and the licensed commodity is *interests* in that bundle
(§ 1101.002(5)), down to leaseholds, while flowing water in natural watercourses belongs to the state
(Water Code § 11.021). Personal property crosses into realty by annexation and back by severance;
fixtures are judged by annexation, adaptation and, above all, objective intention; trade fixtures
stay with the commercial tenant who attached them; financed fixtures ride on § 9.334's fixture-filing
priority, and ordinary building materials merge into the realty beyond any security interest. The
professional habit the whole module teaches: classify early, and write the classification into the
contract so the tests are never needed.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 03

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate I — Module 03

## TREC Topic: Interests in Real Estate

**Prescribed time: 205 minutes.** Seven units under the Commission's scope note *"Deeds, encumbrances
and liens."* This is the course's first long module, and it is the conceptual spine of everything
after it: what kinds of interests exist in Texas land, and what claims other people can hold against
them.

**Learning objectives.** Trace how ownership concepts developed and why Texas terminology still
carries that history; identify the freehold and leasehold estates and state the Texas default rule
that makes every conveyance a fee simple unless limited; distinguish money encumbrances (liens) from
non-money encumbrances (easements, restrictions, encroachments); explain how and when the property
tax lien attaches and why it outranks nearly everything; catalogue the voluntary and involuntary
liens a title search reveals, including the constitutional strength of the Texas mechanic's lien
claimant's position; state who owns Texas water and what a buyer of waterfront land actually gets;
and apply the two distinct Texas homestead doctrines — protection from creditors and property-tax
exemption — to a family's principal residence.

## Unit: Historical Background

*This unit is history. It asserts no current legal rule, and no statute is cited for it.*

chunks.heading: Unit: Historical Background
chunks.excerpt:
The vocabulary of this module — estate, fee, tenement, tenure — is medieval English, and knowing the
story keeps the terms from being arbitrary. After the Norman Conquest, England organised land under
**feudal tenure**: all land was ultimately the Crown's, and everyone below the Crown *held of*
someone above in exchange for services — military service, labour, produce. What a person owned was
not the land itself but an **estate**: a bundle of rights in land, measured by duration. The word
**fee** (from *fief*) named an estate that could be inherited; **fee simple** was the fief with the
fewest strings — inheritable by anyone, alienable, enduring indefinitely.

Over centuries the services fell away, statutes made estates freely transferable and devisable, and
tenure hollowed out into a formality. The system that crossed the Atlantic was **allodial** in
substance: individuals own land outright, subject not to a lord's services but to the sovereign's
four residual powers — taxation, eminent domain, police power and escheat — which this course meets
in later units and modules. Texas adds its own layer of history: much of the state was originally
granted under Spanish and Mexican civil law, and the traces persist — surveying in **varas** (the
Spanish unit you will meet in Module 04), community property (Module 05), and generous homestead
protection (this module's final unit), all of them civil-law inheritances that distinguish Texas from
the purely English-derived states.

chunks.heading: Unit: Estates in Land
chunks.excerpt:
**The four residual powers, introduced.** The allodial owner's title is complete against every
private claimant but remains subject to four powers every sovereign keeps, and it is worth meeting
them here as a set because the rest of the course takes them up one at a time. **Taxation** — the
government's charge on ownership itself; this module's Tax Liens unit shows Texas securing it with
the strongest ordinary lien in the state. **Eminent domain** — the power to take private property
for public use on payment of compensation, exercised through condemnation; Module 07 places it among
the involuntary transfers. **Police power** — the power to regulate use without taking title:
zoning, building codes, subdivision platting (Module 04 shows the county version), environmental
rules. Regulation under the police power is not compensated; taking under eminent domain is — and
the line between them is one of the most litigated boundaries in American law, which is precisely
why a licence holder describes land-use restrictions and never opines on their validity.
**Escheat** — the state's taking of property left ownerless, the modern echo of land returning to
the lord when a tenant died without heirs; Module 07 meets it at the end of the intestacy ladder.
Four powers, four later landings: the frame built in this unit carries the whole course.

Why keep teaching the feudal frame at all? Because the *duration* idea survives intact. Modern law
still classifies interests by how long they last — forever, for a life, for a term of years — and
still uses the medieval names. When a Texas statute says a conveyed estate is a "fee simple," it is
speaking this language; the next unit shows Texas speaking it plainly.

## Unit: Estates in Land

chunks.heading: Unit: Estates in Land
chunks.excerpt:
An **estate** is an interest in real property that is or may become possessory, measured by duration.
Interests that never carry possession — easements, liens — are not estates; they are the subject of
the encumbrance units that follow.

**Freehold estates** last for an indefinite duration.

- **Fee simple absolute** — the greatest estate known to law: indefinite duration, fully inheritable,
  fully transferable, subject only to the sovereign powers and to whatever encumbrances its owner
  created or suffered. Texas states a powerful default in Property Code § 5.001: *an estate in land
  that is conveyed or devised is a fee simple unless the estate is limited by express words or unless
  a lesser estate is conveyed or devised by construction or operation of law* — and the ancient words
  of inheritance ("to A *and his heirs*") are expressly unnecessary. The practical meaning for every
  deed you will ever read: silence means fee simple; a lesser estate must be spelled out.
- **Defeasible fees** — fee estates that can end on a stated event: "to the school district so long
  as the land is used for a school." The holder has a fee that may last forever but is *defeasible* —
  capable of being defeated — with a future interest (a possibility of reverter or right of re-entry)
  waiting in the grantor or the grantor's successors. These appear in Texas practice mostly in old
  grants for schools, churches and railways, and they matter to a licence holder chiefly as a title
  finding that demands a lawyer, not a form.
- **Life estate** — an estate measured by a life: "to my mother for her life." The life tenant
  possesses and uses the property, and owes the future interest holder the duty not to commit
  **waste** — not to consume or degrade what must be handed on. At the meas

chunks.heading: Unit: Estates in Land
chunks.excerpt:
uring life's end the
  property passes to the **remainderman** (if the future interest was granted to a third person) or
  **reverts** to the grantor's successors (a *reversion*). Texas recognises the creation of future
  estates by ordinary deed: Property Code § 5.041 permits an inter vivos conveyance of a freehold
  estate *that commences in the future*, as freely as by will. Life estates arise in Texas both by
  deliberate estate planning and — as Module 07 shows — by operation of the intestacy statute, which
  gives a surviving spouse a life estate in one-third of certain land.

**Leasehold (non-freehold) estates** last for a definite or terminable period — the tenant's
possessory interest under a lease. The classical four:

- **Estate for years** — a fixed term with a stated end date, however short or long; no notice is
  needed to end it, because the calendar ends it.
- **Periodic tenancy** — repeating periods (month to month) that renew until notice.
- **Estate at will** — possession with the owner's consent, no fixed term, terminable by either
  party.
- **Tenancy at sufferance** — the holdover: a tenant who entered rightfully and stays after the
  right ends, possessing without consent but not (yet) a trespasser.

Two Texas anchors for leaseholds now, both already met: a leasehold is "real estate" in a licence
holder's hands (Occupations Code § 1101.002(5) includes leaseholds expressly), and a conveyance of an
estate *for more than one year* must satisfy the writing requirements of Property Code § 5.021 —
which is why the one-year line runs through leasing practice, and why Module 06 returns to it through
the statute of frauds.

chunks.heading: Unit: Estates in Land
chunks.excerpt:
**Reading an estate.** Every question about an estate is answered by three smaller questions: How
long does it last? What can end it early? Who takes when it ends? Run those three against any
granting language — "to A for life, then to B"; "to the church while used for worship"; "to T for
five years" — and the estate names fall out mechanically. The licence holder's discipline is humbler
and harder: *notice* when granting language is anything other than a plain fee, and route it to
counsel instead of improvising.

**The estate ladder, worked.** Classification is a skill, not a memory feat, and it is learned by
running the three questions against real granting language. Work each of the following before
reading its resolution.

1. *"To the City of Alpine, so long as the land is used as a public park."* — How long? Potentially
   forever. What ends it early? Non-park use. Who takes? The grantor's successors, holding the
   possibility of reverter. A defeasible fee; a title examiner will flag it, and no buyer should be
   told it is "basically a fee simple."
2. *"To my sister Carmen."* — No duration stated, no condition, no words of inheritance. Under
   Property Code § 5.001 the silence itself answers: fee simple absolute, because a conveyed estate
   is a fee simple *unless limited by express words*, and words of inheritance are unnecessary.
3. *"To Dr. Osei for her life, then to the county hospital district."* — A life estate in Dr. Osei,
   who possesses, pays the carrying costs, and must not commit waste; a remainder in the district,
   which waits. The district's interest is a present, transferable property interest even though
   possession is postponed — exactly the future-estate kind that Property Code § 5.041 lets a deed
   create as freely as a will.
4. *"Lease

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: what estate did the seller actually own?
chunks.excerpt:
commencing March 1 and ending the last day of February two years later."* — An estate for
   years: fixed term, ends by the calendar, no notice required. Being longer than one year, it lives
   under the writing requirement the statute of frauds materials in Module 06 develop.
5. *"Tenant may remain month to month after the initial term at the same rent."* — A periodic
   tenancy after the term ends: repeating periods renewing until proper notice.

The pattern to carry out of the drill: the deed's *granting and habendum language* controls, the
statutory default fills silence with fee simple, and every departure from a plain fee is a finding
to disclose and route — never to interpret away.

### Applied exercise: what estate did the seller actually own?

*Reviewing a rural listing's chain of title, you find a 1968 deed: "to the Brewster County School
District so long as the premises are used for school purposes, and if said use ceases, title shall
revert to the grantors, their heirs and assigns." The school closed in 2019; the district has been
renting the building to a feed store since. The district now wants to list the property.* **Task:**
name the estate the district received, name the interest the 1968 grantors kept, and state what the
2019 change of use may have done — then say what a licence holder does with a listing like this.
**Model answer:** the district took a defeasible fee (a fee simple determinable in classical terms:
"so long as" language with express reverter); the grantors kept a possibility of reverter passing to
their heirs and assigns. When school use ceased, the stated event occurred, and the grantors'
successors may now hold title — meaning the district may have nothing to sell. The licence holder
does not resolve this: the listing waits while the

chunks.heading: Unit: Encumbrances
chunks.excerpt:
district's counsel and a title company determine
ownership. Taking the listing and marketing "fee simple title" would market an estate the seller may
not own.

## Unit: Encumbrances

An **encumbrance** is any right or interest held by someone other than the owner that burdens the
