**Replacement cost** is the cost to construct an improvement of equivalent utility using current
materials, design and standards. Reproduction cost is the right measure for a historically significant
1910 Victorian in Galveston where the ornamental millwork is part of what the market is buying;
replacement cost is the right measure for ordinary properties, and is the one used far more often,
because no buyer wants a reproduced 1978 electrical panel.

Working the same Round Rock subject, with illustrative figures: replacement cost new of the dwelling at
$165 per square foot × 1,900 square feet = $313,500, plus site improvements (driveway, fencing,
landscaping) of $22,000, for total replacement cost new of **$335,500**.

Accrued depreciation, all three forms:

- *Physical deterioration*, by the age-life method: effective age 12 years against a total economic life
  of 60 years = 12 ÷ 60 = 20 percent. 0.20 × $335,500 = **$67,100**.
- *Functional obsolescence*: the original closed-off galley kitchen, which paired sales in the
  subdivision indicate the market discounts by **$8,000**.
- *External obsolescence*: the property backs to a six-lane arterial, which paired sales indicate costs
  **$12,000**.

chunks.heading: Unit: Three Approaches to Value
chunks.excerpt:
Total accrued depreciation $67,100 + $8,000 + $12,000 = **$87,100**. Depreciated cost of the
improvements: $335,500 − $87,100 = **$248,400**. Land value, developed by sales comparison of vacant
lots in the area: **$135,000**. Indicated value: $248,400 + $135,000 = **$383,400**.

The cost approach dominates for new construction, where there is essentially no depreciation to
estimate and cost data is current and reliable, and for special-purpose properties — a church, a school,
a fire station, a grain elevator — where sales of substitutes barely exist and there is no income stream
to capitalize. It weakens as buildings age, because estimating accrued depreciation on a
fifty-year-old improvement involves judgment that can swing the answer by six figures, and it is not
persuasive in a market where houses routinely sell for materially more or less than depreciated cost.

**The income approach.** Here the property is valued as an income-producing asset. Two techniques
matter at this level.

The **gross rent multiplier** is the simpler one, used for small residential rental property. The
multiplier is derived from sales of comparable rental properties: GRM = sale price ÷ monthly gross rent.
Suppose three rental comparables in the subject's own market:

| Rental comparable | Sale price | Monthly rent | GRM |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $360,000 | $2,400 | 150.0 |
| B | $378,000 | $2,475 | 152.7 |
| C | $345,000 | $2,300 | 150.0 |

chunks.heading: Unit: Three Approaches to Value
chunks.excerpt:
The indicated range is 150.0 to 152.7; the appraiser selects **151**. If the subject's market rent is
$2,550 per month, the indication is $2,550 × 151 = **$385,050**. The GRM is quick and crude: it uses
gross rent, so it ignores differences in vacancy, taxes, insurance and operating expense between the
subject and the comparables. It is evidence, not a substitute for analysis.

**Direct capitalization** is the serious technique, and it runs on the IRV relationship:

> **V = I ÷ R**, and therefore **R = I ÷ V** and **I = R × V**,

where **V** is value, **I** is net operating income, and **R** is the capitalization rate. The income
used is *net operating income* — income after vacancy and operating expenses, but before debt service
and before income taxes. Mortgage payments are a fact about the buyer's financing, not about the
property, and they never appear in NOI.

Take an illustrative six-unit retail strip center in Waco:

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Potential gross income (6 units × $2,100/month × 12) | $151,200 |
| Less vacancy and collection loss at 7% | −$10,584 |
| **Effective gross income** | **$140,616** |
| Property taxes | −$24,000 |
| Insurance | −$8,400 |
| Management at 5% of EGI | −$7,031 |
| Maintenance and reserves | −$12,500 |
| Utilities and common area | −$6,200 |
| **Total operating expenses** | **−$58,131** |
| **Net operating income** | **$82,485** |

Comparable sales of similar centers indicate an overall capitalization rate of 8.25 percent. Applying
IRV: V = $82,485 ÷ 0.0825 = **$999,818**, an indicated value of approximately **$1,000,000**.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Capitalization and the effect of rate movement
chunks.excerpt:
The other two forms of the formula are just as useful. If an investor pays $1,100,000 for this same
income stream, the rate that transaction establishes is R = $82,485 ÷ $1,100,000 = 0.0750, or **7.5
percent** — a lower rate, meaning the buyer paid more per dollar of income, which is what happens when
buyers perceive less risk or expect more growth. And if a market rate of 8.25 percent is applied to a
target value of $1,200,000, the income required is I = 0.0825 × $1,200,000 = **$99,000**. Hold onto the
inverse relationship: for a fixed income, value moves *opposite* to the capitalization rate. A rate
rising from 8.25 percent to 9.5 percent on the same $82,485 of NOI produces $82,485 ÷ 0.095 = $868,263 —
a loss of roughly $132,000 in value with no change whatsoever to the building or its tenants.

The income approach dominates wherever the property is bought for its income: apartments, office,
retail, industrial, self-storage. It is the approach commercial investors themselves use, which is the
real argument for it — an appraisal is most credible when it models the behavior of the actual buyers.
It is weak or inapplicable for owner-occupied single-family homes, because the buyers of those
properties are not pricing an income stream.

### Applied exercise: Capitalization and the effect of rate movement

Using the Waco strip center above:

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
1. One tenant vacates permanently and the owner cannot re-lease the space. Recompute potential gross
   income for five occupied units at the same rent, keep vacancy at 7 percent, keep every expense the
   same except management (still 5 percent of the new effective gross income), and find the new NOI.
2. Apply the same 8.25 percent capitalization rate to your new NOI. How much value did the loss of one
   tenant destroy?
3. A buyer offers $940,000 for the center at its original $82,485 NOI. What capitalization rate does
   that offer imply, and is the buyer treating the property as more or less risky than the market rate
   of 8.25 percent suggests?
4. Explain in one or two sentences why the owner's $6,300 monthly mortgage payment appears nowhere in
   any of these calculations.

## Unit: Pricing a Property

Everything to this point has been about the appraiser. This unit is about you, doing the closely related
thing that you are permitted to do, and about the line between the two — because the line is statutory,
and stepping over it is a criminal offense under § 1103.5545.

**The statutory boundary.** Occupations Code § 1101.002(1) defines a broker by listing the acts that
constitute brokerage. One of them, at § 1101.002(1)(A)(xi), is that the person

> provides a written analysis, opinion, or conclusion relating to the estimated price of real property
> if the analysis, opinion, or conclusion: (a) is not referred to as an appraisal; (b) is provided in
> the ordinary course of the person's business; and (c) is related to the actual or potential
> management, acquisition, disposition, or encumbrance of an interest in real property.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
Read that as the grant of authority it is. Producing a written price opinion is not merely tolerated for
a Texas license holder; it is one of the enumerated acts that *is* brokerage. Chapter 1103 confirms the
boundary from the other side. Section 1103.004(a) provides that the appraiser chapter "does not apply
to," among others, "(2) a real estate broker licensed under Chapter 1101 or a sales agent acting under
the authority of a sponsoring broker who provides to another person a written analysis, opinion, or
conclusion relating to the estimated price of real property if the analysis, opinion, or conclusion:
(A) is not referred to as an appraisal; (B) is given in the ordinary course of the broker's business;
and (C) is related to the actual or potential acquisition, disposition, encumbrance, or management of an
interest in real property."

Both provisions turn on the same three conditions, and all three must be satisfied.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
*It must not be referred to as an appraisal.* This is a rule about words, and it is absolute. Do not
call your work an appraisal. Do not call yourself an appraiser. Do not title the document "Appraisal,"
"Residential Appraisal," or "Appraised Value." Do not write "I appraised the property at $389,000."
Section 1103.201(b) separately forbids using the titles "certified real estate appraiser" or "licensed
real estate appraiser," or calling your product a "certified appraisal" or "licensed appraisal," without
the credential; § 1103.401 extends that to any "title, designation, initials, or other insignia or
identification that would mislead the public" about your credentials or competency. Section 1103.554
makes a knowing violation of § 1103.401 a Class B misdemeanor. Call your work what it is: a
**comparative market analysis** (CMA) or a **broker price opinion** (BPO).

*It must be given in the ordinary course of the brokerage business.* The exemption covers price
opinions that arise out of your brokerage practice — pricing a listing, advising a buyer on an offer,
advising an owner considering a sale or a refinance. It is not a general license to enter the valuation
business. A license holder who builds a separate line of business producing valuations for lenders and
litigants, unconnected to any brokerage relationship, is not obviously operating "in the ordinary course
of the broker's business," and the further that work drifts from brokerage the closer it comes to
§ 1103.201(a) and its penalties.

*It must relate to an actual or potential acquisition, disposition, encumbrance, or management of an
interest in real property.* There must be a real-world transactional purpose.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
One more thing that is *not* in the exemption: an appraisal for a lender in a federally related
transaction. Section 1103.003(6-a) defines a **federally related transaction** as a real estate-related
transaction that "requires the services of an appraiser" and "is engaged in, contracted for, or
regulated by a federal financial institution regulatory agency." Your CMA does not become an appraisal
merely because a lender looks at it, but you cannot supply the appraisal that such a transaction
requires. Note also § 1103.004(a)(6): the chapter does not apply to "the procurement or use of an
automated valuation model," and § 1103.003(4-b) defines an **automated valuation model** as an automated
system deriving value from public property records and analytic methodologies. That is why the
consumer-facing online estimates your sellers arrive with are lawful, and also why they are not
appraisals and not CMAs — they have never been inside the house.

**Building the CMA.** A defensible CMA borrows the appraiser's method, at a scope appropriate to the
assignment.

*Start with the subject.* Measure or verify GLA on the correct basis — finished, above-grade,
conditioned, measured to exterior walls. Confirm the room count, garage, lot size, and improvements with
dates. Walk the property. A CMA built from tax roll data on a property you have never entered is a
guess.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
*Select comparables.* Prefer closed sales in the subject's own subdivision, within the last three to six
months, similar in GLA, age, quality, condition and lot, and in the same school attendance zone. Three
to five closed sales is a normal working set. Exclude non-arm's-length transactions unless the market
itself is distressed. Add context: current *active* listings tell you the competition the seller will
face, and *pending* sales tell you what the market is accepting right now — but neither is evidence of
value, because an active listing proves only what one seller hopes for.

*Adjust.* Same rule as before: adjust the comparable, not the subject; superior comparable, subtract;
inferior comparable, add. Support your adjustment amounts with market evidence where you can, and be
honest with the seller where you cannot.

*Bracket the subject.* This is the single most important quality check available to you. Your set of
comparables should include at least one property superior to the subject and at least one inferior, so
that your conclusion falls *inside* a range the market has already demonstrated. Applying the Round Rock
grid from the previous unit: the unadjusted sales ran $371,000 to $402,000 and the conclusion landed at
$389,000 — bracketed on both sides. A CMA whose comparables are all inferior to the subject, so that
every adjustment is positive and the conclusion sits above every sale in the set, is extrapolation. It
is also the classic structure of an overpriced listing.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
*Reconcile and state a range.* You are not required to produce a single number, and in most cases you
should not. A recommended range with a suggested list price inside it — say, a supported range of
$383,000 to $393,000 with a recommended list price of $389,900 — communicates the real precision of the
work. Then add the market context the seller needs: **months of supply** (divide the number of active
listings by the average monthly closed sales — 63 actives against 21 closings per month is 3.0 months of
supply, a seller's market by most conventions), the median **days on market** for comparable sold
listings, and the **list-to-sale price ratio** in the neighborhood.

*Disclose what it is.* State on the document that it is a comparative market analysis prepared by a
license holder for the purpose of assisting the owner in pricing the property, that it is not an
appraisal, and that it was not prepared under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.
The statute requires a comparable disclaimer of appraisers themselves in the analogous situation:
§ 1103.405(c) requires an evaluation described by § 1103.004(4) or (5) to carry on its first page the
notice "This is not an appraisal performed in accordance with the Uniform Standards of Professional
Appraisal Practice." That specific notice provision governs those evaluations rather than your CMA, but
the plain-language principle it reflects — say what the document is not — is the right practice for your
CMA, and stating it is practice rather than a statutory requirement imposed on license holders.

**Overpricing and days on market.** Sellers overprice, and the pressure on you to help them do it is
constant. The mechanics of why it fails are worth being able to explain in a listing appointment.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
A property draws its most concentrated buyer attention in its first two to three weeks on market, when
every buyer already searching the price band sees it as new inventory. Price it above that band and
those buyers never see it — a house listed at $415,000 is invisible to the buyer whose search caps at
$400,000, even though that buyer would happily have paid $392,000. The seller then discovers the problem
slowly, through showings that do not come, and reduces in stages. By the time the price reaches the
supported range the listing has accumulated days on market, and buyers who do see it read the
accumulated days and the reduction history as evidence of a problem. Properties that arrive at the right
price late routinely sell for less than they would have brought if priced correctly at the start.

Illustratively: a house supported at $389,000 is listed at $415,000. It sits fourteen weeks with two
reductions and closes at $379,500. The seller's carrying costs — an illustrative $2,750 per month of
principal, interest, taxes and insurance — ran roughly $9,600 across the extra three and a half months.
Between the lower closing price and the carrying costs, the attempt to capture $26,000 of extra price
cost the seller nearly $19,100. There is nothing unlawful about a seller choosing to list high; the
price is the seller's decision, not yours. What you owe the seller is the analysis that makes the
decision informed.

chunks.heading: Unit: Pricing a Property
chunks.excerpt:
**Buying a listing.** The specific ethical failure that grows here has a name in the trade: **buying a
listing** — telling a seller the property is worth more than your own analysis supports, in order to win
the listing agreement over a competitor who told the truth, intending to work the price down later. It
is the pricing sin, and it is a discipline problem, not merely a bad look.

Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(5) authorizes the Commission to suspend or revoke the license of a holder
who, while engaged in real estate brokerage, "makes a false promise that is likely to influence a person
to enter into an agreement when the license holder is unable or does not intend to keep the promise."
A price assurance made to win a listing agreement the license holder does not believe and does not
intend to honor is squarely within that description. Section 1101.652(b)(1) reaches a license holder who
"acts negligently or incompetently," and (b)(2) one who "engages in conduct that is dishonest or in bad
faith or that demonstrates untrustworthiness." Section 1101.652(b)(6) reaches a license holder who
"pursues a continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation or makes false promises through an agent
or sales agent, through advertising, or otherwise." Read the whole subdivision: it takes a *course* of
conduct rather than a single misstatement, and it catches false promises made indirectly — through a
sales agent or through advertising — as readily as ones made face to face. And § 1101.652(a)(6) is
aimed directly at the sloppy end of the same problem: the Commission may discipline a license holder
who "fails to consider market conditions for the specific geographic area in which the license holder
is providing a service." That subdivision is a
statutory instruction to do the analys

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: The price opinion boundary
chunks.excerpt:
is — the specific geographic area, not the metro, not the county.

The professional answer is to bring the data and let it speak. Show the grid. Show the bracketing. Show
the months of supply and the list-to-sale ratio. Say plainly what the analysis supports and what it does
not. If the seller insists on a higher price, you may still take the listing at that price — that is the
seller's prerogative — but you should have documented your recommendation and the market evidence behind
it, and you should have agreed in advance on the review points at which you will revisit the price. As a
matter of practice rather than of any statutory requirement, keeping the CMA and your written pricing
recommendation in the transaction file is the license holder's best protection when a disappointed
seller later complains that the property was mispriced.

### Statute reading exercise: The price opinion boundary

Open Occupations Code § 1101.002(1)(A)(xi) and § 1103.004(a)(2), both quoted in this unit, and read them
side by side.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Pricing a listing in Round Rock
chunks.excerpt:
1. The two provisions state the same three conditions. Write them out and mark which is a rule about
   *what you call the document*, which is a rule about *the context in which you produce it*, and which
   is a rule about *its purpose*.
2. A license holder prepares a written valuation of a warehouse for a bank that is deciding whether to
   make a commercial loan, titles it "Broker Price Opinion," charges a flat fee, and has no listing or
   buyer relationship with anyone in the transaction. Which of the three conditions is most doubtful,
   and which section of Chapter 1103 would you look to next?
3. Section 1103.003(1) defines "appraisal" as an opinion of value or the process of developing one,
   "regardless of whether prepared for a federally related transaction." Given that definition, what
   exactly keeps a properly prepared CMA from being an appraisal under Chapter 1103?
4. Under § 1103.5545 and § 1103.5535, what are the two distinct exposures — one criminal, one civil —
   for a person who performs an appraisal without a credential and is paid $600 for it?

### Applied exercise: Pricing a listing in Round Rock

The owners of the Round Rock subject from the previous unit — 1,900 square feet, three bedrooms, two
baths, two-car garage, no pool, backing to a six-lane arterial — call you for a listing appointment. Your
grid produced an indicated value of $389,000 with a bracketed range of $369,108 to $393,120 in adjusted
sale prices. There are 63 active listings in the competing market area and closings have averaged 21 per
month over the trailing six months. The sellers open the meeting by saying that an online estimate shows
$427,000 and that another agent has told them $419,900.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. Compute the months of supply and state what it tells the sellers about negotiating leverage.
2. Your grid's three comparables all sit below $402,000 unadjusted. If you wanted to support $419,900,
   what would you have to do to the comparable set — and explain, using the bracketing principle, why
   that would make the analysis unreliable rather than merely optimistic.
3. The online estimate is an automated valuation model. Using § 1103.003(4-b) and § 1103.004(a)(6),
   explain to the sellers in two sentences what that estimate is, why it is lawful, and what your CMA
   has that it lacks. Then identify the one physical fact about this property that an AVM is least
   likely to have captured.
4. The sellers say they want to "start at $419,900 and come down." Draft the two-sentence response you
   would give, and identify which subdivision of § 1101.652 you would be at risk under if instead you
   simply agreed that $419,900 was what the property was worth.

### Module recap

This module moved from the regulator to the number on your listing presentation, and the through-line is
the difference between an appraisal and a price opinion.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
It began with Chapter 1103 of the Occupations Code, the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Act,
whose stated purpose under § 1103.002 is to conform Texas law to the federal Title XI framework and to
enforce appraisal standards. That federal origin explains the chapter's most distinctive feature: it
creates the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Board as an independent subdivision of TREC
(§ 1103.051), gives it authority to establish credential categories and issue credentials, and then
sends the substance — the hour counts, the categories, the passing score — to the Appraiser
Qualifications Board. Section 1103.202 states the three-legged qualification structure of education,
experience and examination without stating a single number, and the honest thing to say about the hours
is that Chapter 1103 does not contain them.

From regulation the module moved to vocabulary: cost is what you spend, price is what you get, value is
what it is worth; highest and best use must be legally permissible, physically possible, financially
feasible and maximally productive; value requires demand, utility, scarcity and transferability;
depreciation is physical, functional or external, and only the causes inside the fence line are within
the owner's power to cure. Then to method — the ordered process of defining the problem, setting scope,
collecting and verifying general and specific data, applying the approaches, reconciling without
averaging, and reporting — and to your part in it, which is to supply accurate data and access and never
a target number. Then to the economics that make markets move, and to the three approaches themselves,
each worked with arithmetic you should now be able to reproduce: a sales comparison grid adjusted and
bracketed to $389,000, a cost app

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
roach at $383,400, a gross rent multiplier at $385,050, and direct
capitalization solving V = I ÷ R to approximately $1,000,000.

Finally the module returned to you. Section 1101.002(1)(A)(xi) makes producing a written price opinion
one of the enumerated acts of brokerage, and § 1103.004(a)(2) carves that same work out of the appraiser
statute, on three conditions: it is not referred to as an appraisal, it is given in the ordinary course
of the brokerage business, and it relates to an actual or potential transaction in real property. You
should now be able to build a CMA the way an appraiser builds a grid, bracket your conclusion, state a
supported range, explain to a seller why overpricing costs money, and refuse to buy a listing — a refusal
that § 1101.652(a)(6) and (b)(1), (2), (5) and (6) turn from a matter of taste into a matter of your
license.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 04

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 04

## TREC Topic: Leases

**Prescribed time: 130 minutes.** This module carries the five units the Commission's PRINS2-1 course approval form places under *Leases*. The form gives this topic no scope note, so none is quoted here; the units below, and the minutes assigned to each, are the form's own.

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: distinguish the four leasehold estates and state how each is created and how each terminates; identify which acts in a lease transaction require a Texas real estate license and which fall inside a statutory exemption; explain the function of each common lease provision and identify the party each one protects; state the landlord's statutory repair duty, the tenant's notice obligations, the security deposit deadlines, and the penalties for bad faith under Texas Property Code chapter 92; and compute rent under a percentage lease and classify a lease as gross, net, ground, index, or sale-leaseback.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it.

## Unit: Leasehold Estates

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasehold Estates
chunks.excerpt:
A lease does two things at once. It is a **contract** — mutual promises about rent, repairs, conduct, and term — and it is a **conveyance**, transferring a possessory interest in land from the owner to the tenant for a period of time. Texas law recognizes the second half explicitly: Occupations Code § 1101.002(5) defines "real estate" for licensing purposes as "any interest in real property, **including a leasehold**, located in or outside this state." When a landlord signs a lease, the landlord has parted with something, not merely promised something.

What the landlord parts with is exclusive possession. What the landlord keeps is the **reversion** — the right to have possession come back at the end of the term. The tenant's interest is the **leasehold estate**; the landlord's remaining interest is the **reversionary estate**. Together they account for the whole of the ownership. A common error is to say the landlord *still owns the property and the tenant just rents it*, as though the tenant held nothing. During the term the tenant holds the present right to possess, and the landlord's right to enter is limited to whatever the lease and the statutes allow. Property Code § 92.001(5) shows how large that possessory interest can be: "premises" means "a tenant's rental unit, any area or facility the lease authorizes the tenant to use, and the appurtenances, grounds, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally."

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasehold Estates
chunks.excerpt:
Property law sorts leasehold estates into four categories. Those labels are general property-law doctrine rather than definitions written into the Texas Property Code; the Code supplies the operating rules — how notice is given, when a tenancy ends, what a landlord must do — that make the categories matter. Learn the four names, but hang the Texas rules on them.

**The tenancy for years** (also called an **estate for years**) is a leasehold with a fixed beginning and a fixed ending stated in advance. The name misleads: a tenancy for years can run six months, eighteen months, or ten years. What defines it is that the ending date is known when the lease is made. It is created by agreement, and Property Code § 92.001(3) tells you that for a residential dwelling that agreement can be oral, defining a **lease** as "any written or oral agreement between a landlord and tenant that establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules, or other provisions regarding the use and occupancy of a dwelling." Oral, however, does not mean enforceable at any length. Business & Commerce Code § 26.01 — Texas's statute of frauds — makes an agreement unenforceable "unless the promise or agreement, or a memorandum of it, is (1) in writing; and (2) signed by the person to be charged," and § 26.01(b)(5) applies that to "a lease of real estate for a term longer than one year." A fourteen-month oral lease is exposed in a way an eleven-month oral lease is not.

A tenancy for years terminates by the simple expiration of its stated term. Because the ending date was fixed at the start, no notice of termination is required to end it. That is the single most useful thing to remember about this estate.

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasehold Estates
chunks.excerpt: **The periodic tenancy** runs from period to period — month to month is the common Texas residential form, though week to week and year to year are also periodic — renewing automatically at the end of each period until one party gives notice. No ending date is fixed at the outset. Chapter 91, which supplies rules applicable to landlords and tenants generally, governs how a Texas month-to-month tenancy ends. Section 91.001(a): "A monthly tenancy or a tenancy from month to month may be terminated by the tenant or the landlord giving notice of termination to the other." Either side may end it; neither needs cause. Section 91.001(b) fixes the effective date: "If a notice of termination is given under Subsection (a) and if the rent-paying period is at least one month, the tenancy terminates on whichever of the following days is the later: (1) the day given in the notice for termination; or (2) one month after the day on which the notice is given." Where the rent-paying period is shorter than a month, § 91.001(c) substitutes a period equal in days to the rent-paying period.

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasehold Estates
chunks.excerpt:
Two refinements matter. Section 91.001(d) provides that if the tenancy ends on a day that does not line up with a rent-paying period, "the tenant is liable for rent only up to the date of termination" — no whole final month for occupying four days of it. And § 91.001(e) makes the scheme a default rather than a mandate: subsections (a) through (d) "do not apply if: (1) a landlord and a tenant have agreed in an instrument signed by both parties on a different period of notice to terminate the tenancy or that no notice is required; or (2) there is a breach of contract recognized by law." A lease requiring sixty days' written notice is enforceable on its own terms. Read the lease first, then fall back on § 91.001.

**The tenancy at will** exists when a person occupies with the owner's consent but with no fixed term and no agreed periodic term — possession continues at the will of both parties and may be ended by either. Lacking both a fixed end date and automatic renewal, it is the estate most likely to be created by accident: an owner lets a relative move in with no agreement about rent or duration, or a seller lets a buyer take possession informally before closing. The distinction matters, because chapter 92's protections attach to a "tenant," defined in § 92.001(6) as "a person who is authorized by a lease to occupy a dwelling to the exclusion of others and, for the purposes of Subchapters D, E, and F, who is obligated under the lease to pay rent." Read the whole definition: for the security-device, disclosure-of-ownership, and smoke-alarm subchapters, the occupant must also be obligated by the lease to pay rent, so an authorized occupant who owes no rent is not a "tenant" for those three subchapters even though he is one elsewhere in the chapter. And § 92.001(3) counts

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Which estate, and how does it end?
chunks.excerpt:
an oral understanding as a lease.

**The tenancy at sufferance** is the odd one out, because it is not consensual. It arises when a tenant who entered lawfully stays past the end of the right to possess — the classic **holdover**. The tenant is no longer a rightful possessor and is not a trespasser who entered wrongfully; the tenant is simply there, at the owner's sufferance, until the owner either evicts or accepts the situation and creates a new tenancy. Texas statutes assume the category without naming it: Property Code § 92.332(b) lists as "valid grounds for eviction or lease termination in any event" that "the tenant holds over after giving notice of termination or intent to vacate" (b)(4), and that "the tenant holds over after the landlord gives notice of termination at the end of the rental term" (b)(5).

Chapter 91 adds three rules cutting across all four estates. Section 91.005: "During the term of a lease, the tenant may not rent the leasehold to any other person without the prior consent of the landlord" — subletting is prohibited by statute unless the landlord consents, the opposite of what many students assume. Section 91.004 makes a landlord who "fails to comply in any respect with the lease agreement" liable to a non-defaulting tenant for the resulting damages, and gives that tenant a lien on the landlord's nonexempt property in the tenant's possession and on the rent due. And § 91.006(a): "A landlord has a duty to mitigate damages if a tenant abandons the leased premises in violation of the lease," a duty § 91.006(b) makes non-waivable. A landlord whose tenant walks out in month four of a twelve-month lease may not simply sit on the vacant unit and bill for the remaining eight months.

### Applied exercise: Which estate, and how does it end?

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasing Real Estate
chunks.excerpt:
A Fort Worth owner and a tenant sign a written lease for a duplex unit running September 1 through August 31, at $1,450 per month. The lease says nothing about what happens at the end. On August 31 the tenant does not move out; the tenant tenders $1,450 on September 1 and the owner deposits it.

1. What leasehold estate did the September 1–August 31 lease create, and what notice was required to end it on August 31?
2. On the morning of August 31, before any payment is tendered, how would you classify the tenant's status if the tenant stays? Which subdivision of § 92.332(b) treats that status as a valid ground for eviction?
3. If the owner instead agreed in writing to let the tenant continue month to month at the same rent, and in November the owner wanted the tenant out, what does § 91.001(b) require, and on what date could the tenancy terminate if notice were given on November 20?
4. The lease in this problem is silent on subletting. May the tenant sublet the unit? Cite the section that answers it.

## Unit: Leasing Real Estate

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasing Real Estate
chunks.excerpt:
Leasing is brokerage. That single sentence resolves most of the confusion license holders have about rental work. Occupations Code § 1101.002(1)(A) defines a "broker" as a person who, "in exchange for a commission or other valuable consideration or with the expectation of receiving a commission or other valuable consideration, performs for another person" any of a list of acts, and leasing appears throughout that list: one who "sells, exchanges, purchases, or **leases** real estate" (i); "negotiates or attempts to negotiate the listing, sale, exchange, purchase, or **lease** of real estate" (iii); "lists or offers, attempts, or agrees to list real estate for sale, **lease**, or exchange" (iv); "aids or offers or attempts to aid in locating or obtaining real estate for purchase or **lease**" (vii); or "procures or assists in procuring a prospect to effect the sale, exchange, or **lease** of real estate" (viii).

Subdivision (x) reaches further and catches people who never think of themselves as agents: a broker also means a person who "**controls the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a single-family residential real property unit**." That is a rent-collection act, not a marketing act. A person who, for compensation, takes in and banks the rent on someone else's rent house is performing a broker's act under § 1101.002(1)(A)(x) — even having never showed the house, advertised it, or negotiated a term.

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasing Real Estate
chunks.excerpt: Section 1101.004(a) ties the definition to conduct: a person is engaged in real estate brokerage by performing any act described by § 1101.002(1) for another with the expectation of valuable consideration, "as a part of a transaction or as an entire transaction." Note *as a part of a transaction* — doing one piece of a lease deal for pay is enough. Section 1101.351(a) closes the loop: unless a person holds a license, the person may not "(1) act as or represent that the person is a broker or sales agent; or (2) act as a residential rental locator." A **residential rental locator** is "a person who offers for consideration to locate a unit in an apartment complex for lease to a prospective tenant," excluding "an owner who offers to locate a unit in the owner's complex" (§ 1101.002(6)). Locating apartments for a fee is licensed activity in its own right. And under § 1101.351(c) a sales agent may not engage in brokerage "unless the sales agent is sponsored by a licensed broker and is acting for that broker." A sales agent's leasing work is the broker's work.

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasing Real Estate
chunks.excerpt:
Against that broad definition, § 1101.005 sets out who the chapter does not apply to. Four of its subdivisions matter constantly in leasing. Section 1101.005(8) exempts "**an owner or the owner's employee who leases the owner's improved or unimproved real estate**." An owner leasing her own duplex needs no license, and neither does the salaried employee who leases it for her. Section 1101.005(7) exempts "an on-site manager of an apartment complex" — the leasing office staff at a conventional apartment community are outside chapter 1101 by name. Section 1101.005(9)(C) exempts a transaction involving "the lease or management of a hotel or motel." And § 1101.005(10) and (11) exempt leases of real estate owned by a limited partnership or a limited liability company when handled by a general partner, manager, managing member, or an employee who negotiates the transaction in the course of employment.

Draw the boundary carefully, because the exemptions are about **whose property it is**, not about how modest the transaction is. The owner exemption is the owner's; it does not travel to an independent contractor the owner hires, and it does not cover leasing someone else's property. A person who manages four houses for four different owners is not "an owner or the owner's employee" as to any of them. A common error is to assume that a small lease, a short lease, or a lease of a single house is too minor to require a license. Nothing in § 1101.002(1) or § 1101.005 turns on size.

chunks.heading: Unit: Leasing Real Estate
chunks.excerpt: What the license holder actually does in a lease transaction tracks the sale side closely. On the landlord's side: analyzing the rental market, advising on asking rent and term, marketing and showing the unit, receiving and forwarding applications, coordinating the screening decision, preparing the lease on the form the parties have agreed to use, documenting move-in condition, and handling the money. On the tenant's side: identifying suitable properties, arranging showings, disclosing the representation relationship, assisting with the application, and negotiating terms. As a matter of practice, residential leasing compensation in Texas is commonly paid by the landlord out of the first month's rent or as a percentage of the term's rent, and commercial commissions are commonly a percentage of total rent over the term — market customs, not legal requirements, and nothing in the held sources sets a rate.

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
Handling money is where leasing work most often generates discipline. Occupations Code § 1101.652(b) lists grounds for suspension or revocation, and four are aimed squarely at funds: failing "within a reasonable time to properly account for or remit money that is received by the license holder and that belongs to another person" (b)(9); commingling, since (b)(10) reaches a license holder who "commingles money that belongs to another person with the license holder's own money"; failing "to deposit, within a reasonable time, money the license holder receives as escrow or trust funds in a real estate transaction... in trust with a title company authorized to do business in this state" or "in a custodial, trust, or escrow account maintained for that purpose in a banking institution authorized to do business in this state" (b)(30); and disbursing money from such an account "before the completion or termination of the real estate transaction" (b)(31). Application deposits, security deposits, and rent that come into a brokerage's hands belong to someone else. They go into a trust or escrow account, they are accounted for, and they are not spent.

Section 1101.652(b)(32) applies to leasing in terms: a license holder may not discriminate "against an owner, potential buyer, **landlord, or potential tenant** on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, or ancestry, including directing a prospective buyer or tenant interested in equivalent properties to a different area based on" any of those characteristics. Steering a rental prospect is a licensing violation as well as a fair housing violation.

## Unit: Common Lease Provisions

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
A lease is read clause by clause, and each clause is doing a job. For every provision, ask what risk it allocates and to whom.

**Parties.** The lease names the landlord and every tenant, and getting this right is not clerical. Property Code § 92.001(2) defines "landlord" as "the owner, lessor, or sublessor of a dwelling, but does not include a manager or agent of the landlord unless the manager or agent purports to be the owner, lessor, or sublessor in an oral or written lease" — a property manager who signs as though he were the owner has made himself the landlord for chapter 92 purposes. An occupant not named as a tenant is not a tenant and, under § 92.001(6), does not hold the tenant's statutory remedies. Where someone guarantees the lease, § 92.021(a) limits the exposure — but states the limit with its own exception attached: "A person other than a tenant who guarantees a lease is liable only for the original lease term except that a person may specify that the person agrees to guarantee a renewal of the lease as provided by Subsection (b)." The exception is part of the rule, not a footnote to it: a guarantor can be reached beyond the original term, but only on the statute's terms. A renewal guaranty is not effective merely because the guaranty form says so: under § 92.021(b) the original lease must state the last date, specified by the guarantor, on which a renewal will renew the guarantor's obligation; that the guarantor is liable under a renewal occurring on or before that date; and that the guarantor is liable only if the renewal involves the same parties as the original lease and "does not increase the guarantor's potential financial obligation for rent that existed under the original lease."

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
**Premises.** The clause identifies exactly what the tenant gets. Section 92.001(5) reaches "any area or facility the lease authorizes the tenant to use, and the appurtenances, grounds, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally," so a lease promising a garage bay, storage closet, or pool access has enlarged the premises and with it the area the landlord's duties cover.

**Term.** The term clause states the beginning and ending dates — what makes the lease a tenancy for years rather than a periodic tenancy — and usually what happens at expiration. Under Business & Commerce Code § 26.01(b)(5), a term longer than one year must be in a signed writing to be enforceable.

**Rent, and when it is due.** The clause fixes the amount, the due date, the place and method of payment, and whether partial payments are accepted. Method matters in Texas: under § 92.011(a) "a landlord shall accept a tenant's timely cash rental payment unless a written lease... requires the tenant to make rental payments by check, money order, or other traceable or negotiable instrument." A landlord who wants to refuse cash must say so in the written lease; one who takes cash must give a written receipt and record the payment (§ 92.011(b)).

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
**Late fees.** Section 92.019(a) permits a late fee only if "(1) notice of the fee is included in a written lease; (2) the fee is reasonable; and (3) any portion of the tenant's rent has remained unpaid two full days after the date the rent was originally due." Section 92.019(a-1) adds a safe harbor: a fee is reasonable if not more than 12 percent of the rental-period rent for a dwelling in a structure with not more than four units, or 10 percent for a structure with more than four; a larger fee is permitted only up to the landlord's uncertain damages from the late payment. An initial fee plus a daily fee count as one late fee. A landlord who violates the section owes "$100, three times the amount of the late fee collected in violation of this section, and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees" (§ 92.019(c)), and any waiver is void.

**Security deposit.** The clause states the amount, what it secures, and the conditions on its return. Its Texas rules are the next unit's subject; note here only that § 92.103(b) makes a lease requirement of advance notice of surrender "effective only if the requirement is underlined or is printed in conspicuous bold print in the lease." Formatting is substantive.

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
**Use and occupancy limits.** The use clause confines the premises to residential use; the occupancy clause names who may live there and how long a guest may stay. Texas caps occupancy by statute: under § 92.010(a) "the maximum number of adults that a landlord may allow to occupy a dwelling is three times the number of bedrooms in the dwelling," with "adult" meaning a person 18 or older and "bedroom" meaning "an area of a dwelling intended as sleeping quarters," excluding kitchens, dining rooms, bathrooms, living rooms, utility rooms, and closets. Section 92.010(b) requires a higher rate where a fair housing law requires one, and permits one for an adult "seeking temporary sanctuary from family violence" for up to one month.

**Maintenance and repair allocation.** This clause divides responsibility: landlord for systems and structure, tenant for cleanliness and for damage the tenant causes. The allocation is not fully negotiable in a Texas residential lease. Section 92.006(c) makes subchapter B's duties and remedies unwaivable "except as provided in Subsections (d), (e), and (f)." Subsection (f) permits an agreement making the tenant pay for repair of damage from wastewater stoppages caused by foreign or improper objects in lines exclusively serving the dwelling, damage to doors, windows, or screens, and damage from windows or doors left open — but only if the § 92.006(e)(4) formalities are met: a written lease; the repair agreement "either underlined or printed in boldface in the lease or in a separate written addendum"; "specific and clear"; and "made knowingly, voluntarily, and for consideration."

chunks.heading: Unit: Common Lease Provisions
chunks.excerpt:
**Alterations.** The clause bars painting, holes, fixtures, and installations without consent and states who owns improvements at the end. Section 92.163 intersects it: a security device installed, changed, or rekeyed under subchapter D "becomes a fixture of the dwelling," and, except for repair-and-deduct, a tenant "may not remove, change, rekey, replace, or alter a security device" without the landlord's permission.

**Entry and access.** The clause states when the landlord may enter and on what notice. Texas backstops the tenant's possession with two hard rules taken up in the next unit — § 92.008 on utility interruption and § 92.0081 on removing doors and locks and excluding the tenant.

**Assignment and subletting.** An **assignment** transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest; a **sublease** transfers something less, leaving the original tenant as sublessor with a reversion of his own. Section 91.005 supplies a restrictive Texas default: during the term "the tenant may not rent the leasehold to any other person without the prior consent of the landlord."

**Default and remedies.** The clause defines what counts as a breach and what the landlord may do. Section 91.006(a)'s non-waivable duty to mitigate means an abandonment clause cannot promise the landlord the whole remaining term without effort to re-let.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
**Holdover and renewal.** The holdover clause states the consequence of staying past the term, commonly a stated daily or monthly rate; § 92.332(b)(4) and (5) confirm that holding over after either party's notice is a valid eviction ground and not retaliation. The renewal clause states whether the lease renews automatically, converts to month to month — in which case § 91.001's notice rules take over — or simply ends. Finally, § 92.024(a) requires that "not later than the third business day after the date the lease is signed by each party to the lease, a landlord shall provide at least one complete copy of the lease to at least one tenant who is a party to the lease."

## Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes

Property Code chapter 92 is the core of Texas residential landlord-tenant law, and § 92.002 fixes its reach: "This chapter applies only to the relationship between landlords and tenants of residential rental property." Commercial leases are governed by their own terms and by chapter 91. Do not carry chapter 92's deadlines into a commercial deal.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
**Waiver.** Start with § 92.006, which tells you which rules can be bargained away. Section 92.006(a) is categorical: "A landlord's duty or a tenant's remedy concerning security deposits, security devices, the landlord's disclosure of ownership and management, or utility cutoffs, as provided by Subchapter C, D, E, or G, respectively, may not be waived." The same subsection bars waiver of the landlord's duty to install a smoke alarm under subchapter F and of the tenant's remedy for noninstallation, while allowing the smoke alarm inspection and repair duty to be waived by written agreement. Movement in the tenant's favor is allowed on a narrower list: under § 92.006(b) the duties and remedies concerning security devices, disclosure of ownership and management, or smoke alarms "may be enlarged only by specific written agreement." And § 92.006(h) bars waiver of the tenant's right to a jury trial. A lease clause contradicting these sections is not merely unwise; as to the covered duties it is ineffective.

**The duty to repair.** Section 92.052(a) states it: "A landlord shall make a diligent effort to repair or remedy a condition if: (1) the tenant specifies the condition in a notice to the person to whom or to the place where rent is normally paid; (2) the tenant is not delinquent in the payment of rent at the time notice is given; and (3) the condition: (A) materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant; or (B) arises from the landlord's failure to provide and maintain in good operating condition a device to supply hot water of a minimum temperature of 120 degrees Fahrenheit."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
Three things follow. The trigger is notice to the rent-payment address, not to whoever the tenant happens to reach — though § 92.060 makes a managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager the landlord's agent for notice. The tenant must be current in rent when the notice is given; a tenant who withholds rent first and complains second has forfeited the statute. And the standard is not "annoying" but a condition materially affecting health or safety, with the 120-degree hot water device named so no one has to argue about it. Section 92.052(b) removes the duty where the tenant, an occupant, a family member, or a guest caused the condition, "unless the condition was caused by normal wear and tear" — defined in § 92.001(4) as "deterioration that results from the intended use of a dwelling," excluding "deterioration that results from negligence, carelessness, accident, or abuse." Under § 92.052(d), the notice "must be in writing only if the tenant's lease is in writing and requires written notice."

**Notice mechanics and time for repair.** Section 92.056(b) sets six conditions for landlord liability, and rewards the tenant who sends notice trackably: notice to the rent-payment address; a condition materially affecting health or safety; "a subsequent written notice to repair or remedy the condition after a reasonable time to repair" **or** a first notice sent "by certified mail, return receipt requested, by registered mail, or by another form of mail that allows tracking of delivery"; a reasonable time elapsed; no "diligent effort" by the landlord; and a tenant "not delinquent in the payment of rent at the time any notice required by this subsection was given." The tracked-mail option is what lets a single notice do the work of two.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
How long is a reasonable time? Section 92.056(d): "there is a rebuttable presumption that seven days is a reasonable time. To rebut that presumption, the date on which the landlord received the tenant's notice, the severity and nature of the condition, and the reasonable availability of materials and labor and of utilities from a utility company must be considered." Note the last item: availability of utility service from the utility company is part of the calculation, not just materials and labor. Seven days is a presumption, not a deadline; a burst sewer line and a slow-closing window are not on the same clock. Section 92.053(b) adds pressure: if the landlord gives no written explanation for delay "on or before the fifth day after receiving from the tenant a written demand for an explanation," the landlord carries the burden of proving diligence.

**The tenant's remedies.** Under § 92.056(e) a tenant to whom the landlord is liable may terminate the lease, have the condition repaired under § 92.0561, deduct the repair cost from rent "without necessity of judicial action," and obtain judicial remedies under § 92.0563. A tenant who terminates gets a pro rata rent refund and the deposit back but gives up repair-and-deduct, and § 92.056(g) requires the lease to carry "language in underlined or bold print" informing the tenant of these remedies.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
Repair and deduct is capped: the deduction "may not exceed the amount of one month's rent under the lease or $500, whichever is greater" (§ 92.0561(b)), and repeated use is allowed so long as the monthly total stays within that cap. It reaches only the conditions listed in § 92.0561(d)(3) — failure to remedy "the backup or overflow of raw sewage inside the tenant's dwelling or the flooding from broken pipes or natural drainage inside the dwelling," a total cessation of potable water the landlord agreed to furnish, or inadequate heat or cooled air or another condition a local official has certified in writing to materially affect health or safety. Waiting periods under § 92.0561(e) then run: immediately for sewage or flooding; three days after notice of intent to repair for a water cessation or inadequate heat or cooling; seven days otherwise. Repairs must be made by "an independent company, contractor, or repairman," not by the tenant or the tenant's family or employees, and the bill and receipt go to the landlord with the rent balance. A landlord who is genuinely stuck may deliver a sworn **affidavit for delay** under § 92.0562, buying 15 days where parts cannot be obtained without the landlord's fault or 30 days after a natural disaster.

Judicial remedies under § 92.0563(a) include an order to repair, a rent reduction "in proportion to the reduced rental value," "a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500," actual damages, costs, and fees. The traffic runs both ways: under § 92.058(a), a tenant who withholds rent or deducts in bad-faith violation of the subchapter, after written warning, owes the landlord "a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: **Security deposits.** Section 92.101 sets the reach of subchapter C: "This subchapter applies to all residential leases." Section 92.102 defines the term: "A security deposit is any advance of money, other than a rental application deposit or an advance payment of rent, that is intended primarily to secure performance under a lease of a dwelling that has been entered into by a landlord and a tenant." The label on the money does not control; its function does. The deadline is § 92.103(a): except as provided by § 92.107, "the landlord shall refund a security deposit to the tenant **on or before the 30th day after the date the tenant surrenders the premises**." Section 92.107(a) is the exception: the landlord "is not obligated to return a tenant's security deposit or give the tenant a written description of damages and charges until the tenant gives the landlord a written statement of the tenant's forwarding address for the purpose of refunding the security deposit." That is a suspension of the duty, not a forfeiture of the money — § 92.107(b) provides that the tenant "does not forfeit the right to a refund of the security deposit or the right to receive a description of damages and charges merely for failing to give a forwarding address to the landlord." Under § 92.1041 the landlord is presumed to have complied if the refund or accounting is mailed and postmarked on or before the required date.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
Section 92.104 governs deductions. Subsection (a) permits deduction of "damages and charges for which the tenant is legally liable under the lease or as a result of breaching the lease," but subsection (b) is flat: "The landlord may not retain any portion of a security deposit to cover normal wear and tear." Subsection (c) requires the landlord who retains any part to give the tenant the balance "together with a written description and itemized list of all deductions," with one exception: no itemization is required if "(1) the tenant owes rent when he surrenders possession of the premises; and (2) there is no controversy concerning the amount of rent owed."

The consequences of getting this wrong are the most heavily tested figures in Texas residential law. Section 92.109(a): "A landlord who **in bad faith** retains a security deposit in violation of this subchapter is liable for an amount equal to the sum of $100, three times the portion of the deposit wrongfully withheld, and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees in a suit to recover the deposit." Section 92.109(b): a landlord who in bad faith fails to give the written description and itemized list "forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the security deposit or to bring suit against the tenant for damages to the premises" and owes the tenant's attorney's fees. Section 92.109(c) puts on the landlord the burden of proving retention "was reasonable." And § 92.109(d) makes the deadline bite: a landlord who fails either to refund or to itemize "on or before the 30th day after the date the tenant surrenders possession is presumed to have acted in bad faith."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
Tenants face a matching prohibition. Section 92.108(a): "The tenant may not withhold payment of any portion of the last month's rent on grounds that the security deposit is security for unpaid rent"; a tenant who does is presumed to act in bad faith and owes "three times the rent wrongfully withheld" plus the landlord's attorney's fees. Under § 92.105(a) a new owner taking title by sale, assignment, death, receivership, or bankruptcy "is liable for the return of security deposits... from the date title to the premises is acquired."

**Security devices.** Subchapter D requires hardware without the tenant having to ask. Under § 92.153(a) a dwelling must have a window latch on each exterior window; a doorknob lock or keyed dead bolt on each exterior door; a sliding door pin lock and either a handle latch or security bar on each exterior sliding glass door; and "a keyless bolting device and a door viewer on each exterior door." These "must be installed at the landlord's expense" (§ 92.153(c)). Section 92.154 requires a keyed dead bolt or keyless bolting device to sit "not lower than 36 inches from the floor" and no higher than 48 inches if installed on or after September 1, 1993, with a bolt throw of at least one inch.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: Rekeying runs on a clock: under § 92.156(a) a device operated by key, card, or combination "shall be rekeyed by the landlord at the landlord's expense **not later than the seventh day after each tenant turnover date**" — the date, per § 92.151(15), a tenant moves in "after all previous occupants have moved out." Further rekeying at the tenant's request is at the tenant's expense, with unlimited requests allowed. Section 92.158 requires the landlord to repair or replace an inoperable device on request, and § 92.161(a) presumes a reasonable compliance time of "not later than the seventh day after the date the request is received," shortened by § 92.161(c) to a presumed 72 hours where the tenant reports a recent unauthorized entry or attempt, or a crime of personal violence in the complex. Remedies under § 92.164(a) include install-and-deduct, unilateral termination without court proceedings after the statutory window, and suit for a court order, actual and punitive damages, "a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500," costs, and fees.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: **Disclosure of ownership and management.** Section 92.201(a) requires the landlord to disclose the name and street or post office box address of "the holder of record title, according to the deed records in the county clerk's office," and, where an off-site entity primarily manages the dwelling, the management company's name and street address. Section 92.201(b) gives three ways to make that disclosure: in writing "on or before the seventh day after the day the landlord receives the tenant's request for the information"; by continuously posting the information in a conspicuous place in the dwelling or at the on-site manager's office within the same seven-day period; or by including it in a copy of the lease or in written rules given to the tenant before the request. Remedies under § 92.205(a) include a disclosure order, the tenant's actual costs of discovering the information, "a judgment against the landlord for one month's rent plus $100," costs and fees, and "unilateral termination of the lease without a court proceeding."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt:
**Utility interruption and lockouts.** These are the two self-help temptations Texas forecloses. Under § 92.008(a) a landlord or landlord's agent "may not interrupt or cause the interruption of utility service paid for directly to the utility company by a tenant unless the interruption results from bona fide repairs, construction, or an emergency," and § 92.008(b) applies the same rule to service the landlord furnishes as an incident of the tenancy. The tenant may then "either recover possession of the premises or terminate the lease" and recover "actual damages, one month's rent plus $1,000, reasonable attorney's fees, and court costs, less any delinquent rents" (§ 92.008(f)); any waiver is void. A narrow exception in § 92.008(h) lets a landlord who submeters or allocates electricity interrupt service for an unpaid electric bill, but only under a written lease and with the specific notices the statute spells out. Separately, § 92.301 gives the tenant remedies when the *utility company* cuts off service the landlord agreed to furnish because the landlord did not pay the bill.

Section 92.0081(a) forbids removing "a door, window, or attic hatchway cover or a lock, latch, hinge, hinge pin, doorknob, or other mechanism connected to" one, or landlord-furnished furniture, fixtures, or appliances, "unless the landlord removes the item for a bona fide repair or replacement." Section 92.0081(b): "A landlord may not intentionally prevent a tenant from entering the leased premises **except by judicial process**" unless the exclusion results from bona fide repairs, construction, or an emergency; removing the contents of abandoned premises; or "changing the door locks on the door to the tenant's individual unit of a tenant who is delinquent in paying at least part of the rent."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: That last exception is narrow and conditional. Under § 92.0081(d) the lockout right must be in the lease, the tenant must be delinquent, and the landlord must have mailed notice "not later than the fifth calendar day before" the lockout or hand-delivered or posted it inside the main entry door "not later than the third calendar day before," stating the earliest proposed date, the amount that would prevent the lockout, where rent may be paid, and, "in underlined or bold print, the tenant's right to receive a key to the new lock at any hour, regardless of whether the tenant pays the delinquent rent." A notice on the front door at the time of the lockout must give a 24-hour on-site key location or a 24-hour phone number with a key delivered within two hours (§ 92.0081(c)), and § 92.0081(f) is unconditional: the landlord "must provide the tenant with a key to the changed lock... without regard to whether the tenant pays the delinquent rent." The landlord may not change locks "when the tenant or any other legal occupant is in the dwelling" or "more than once during a rental payment period," and may not lock the tenant out of common areas. Violation costs possession or termination at the tenant's election plus "a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees" (§ 92.0081(h)), with an additional month's rent for refusing the key. Section 92.009 gives the locked-out tenant a **writ of reentry** from the justice court on a sworn complaint; § 92.0091 gives an equivalent **writ of restoration of utility service**.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: **Retaliation.** Section 92.331(a) forbids retaliation because the tenant in good faith exercises a right or remedy "granted to the tenant by lease, municipal ordinance, or federal or state statute"; gives a notice to repair or exercises a chapter 92 remedy; complains in good faith to a code-enforcement body, public utility, or civic or nonprofit agency about a code violation or utility problem; or "establishes, attempts to establish, or participates in a tenant organization." Section 92.331(b) makes the window explicit: a landlord may not, "**within six months after the date of the tenant's action**," retaliate by filing an eviction proceeding except on the § 92.332 grounds, "depriving the tenant of the use of the premises, except for reasons authorized by law," "decreasing services to the tenant," "increasing the tenant's rent or terminating the tenant's lease," or "engaging, in bad faith, in a course of conduct that materially interferes with the tenant's rights under the tenant's lease."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Landlord & Tenant Statutes
chunks.excerpt: Section 92.332 preserves the landlord's legitimate grounds: raising rent "under an escalation clause in a written lease for utilities, taxes, or insurance" is not retaliation, nor is "increasing rent or reducing services as part of a pattern of rent increases or service reductions for an entire multidwelling project." Note what that second one requires: a *pattern* across the project, not a single targeted increase. Section 92.332(b) then provides that "[a]n eviction or lease termination based on the following circumstances, which are valid grounds for eviction or lease termination in any event, does not constitute retaliation": rent delinquency when the landlord gives notice to vacate or files an eviction action, intentional property damage or threats to personal safety, material breach other than holding over, and the holdover situations described earlier. The tenant's remedy under § 92.333 is "a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500, actual damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees," less delinquent rent; and under § 92.335, "in an eviction suit, retaliation by the landlord under Section 92.331 is a defense and a rent deduction lawfully made by the tenant under this chapter is a defense for nonpayment of the rent to the extent allowed by this chapter."

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Security deposits under Property Code §§ 92.103, 92.104, and 92.109
chunks.excerpt:
**Applications.** Subchapter I governs the front of the transaction. An **application deposit** is refundable if the applicant is rejected; an **application fee** is "a nonrefundable sum of money... given to the landlord to offset the costs of screening an applicant" (§ 92.351(1), (1-a)). Under § 92.352(a) an applicant "is deemed rejected by the landlord if the landlord does not give notice of acceptance... on or before the seventh day after" the completed application is submitted on the landlord's form, and bad-faith failure to refund costs "$100, three times the amount wrongfully retained, and the applicant's reasonable attorney's fees" (§ 92.354).

Finally, § 92.061 explains how this fits with older law: subchapter B's duties and remedies "are in lieu of existing common law and other statutory law warranties and duties of landlords for maintenance, repair, security, habitability, and nonretaliation." In Texas residential leasing, the statute is the field.

### Statute reading exercise: Security deposits under Property Code §§ 92.103, 92.104, and 92.109

Re-read the quoted text of Property Code § 92.103(a), § 92.104(a)–(c), and § 92.109(a)–(d) above. Then answer from that text alone.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A Houston security deposit dispute
chunks.excerpt:
1. From what event does the 30-day period in § 92.103(a) run — the last day of the lease term, the day the tenant gives a forwarding address, or the day the tenant surrenders the premises? Quote the words that decide it.
2. Under § 92.104(c), what are the two conditions that together excuse a landlord from giving a written description and itemized list of deductions?
3. Under § 92.109(d), what happens to a landlord who neither returns the deposit nor provides an itemization on or before the 30th day after surrender — and how does that presumption interact with the damages formula in § 92.109(a)?
4. Section 92.109(c) allocates a burden of proof. Whose is it, and what must that party prove?

### Applied exercise: A Houston security deposit dispute

A tenant leases a Houston apartment at $1,300 per month and pays an $800 security deposit. The tenant surrenders the premises on April 30 and hands the on-site manager a signed note with her new mailing address the same day. On June 4 the landlord mails a check for $200 with a note reading only "damages and cleaning." The carpet in the living room is worn in the traffic lane after the tenant's two-year tenancy; the landlord charged $400 to replace it. The tenant also owed no rent at move-out, and the landlord does not dispute that.

chunks.heading: Unit: Types of Leases
chunks.excerpt:
1. What was the landlord's deadline to refund or account under § 92.103(a), and was it met?
2. Does § 92.104(c)'s exception to the itemization requirement apply here? Why or why not?
3. May the $400 carpet charge stand? Apply § 92.104(b) and the definition of normal wear and tear in § 92.001(4).
4. Assume a court finds the landlord retained $400 of the deposit in bad faith. Using the formula in § 92.109(a), what is the landlord's exposure on the wrongfully withheld portion, before attorney's fees? Show the arithmetic. (Illustration only — the dollar amounts in this problem are invented for teaching; the multiplier and the $100 figure come from the statute.)

## Unit: Types of Leases

The four leasehold estates classify a lease by its **duration**. This unit classifies leases by their **rent structure** — who pays which of the property's operating costs, and how the rent is computed. These categories are commercial practice and market vocabulary rather than Texas statutory definitions; no held Texas source defines "triple net" or "percentage lease," and you should present them to a client as customary terms whose meaning comes from the lease document itself, never from a statute. That caution is not academic: two landlords in the same market can use "net lease" to mean two different cost splits. Always read the expense clauses.

chunks.heading: Unit: Types of Leases
chunks.excerpt:
**Gross lease.** The tenant pays a single stated rent and the landlord pays the operating expenses out of it — property taxes, hazard insurance, common area maintenance, and often some utilities. The tenant's cost is predictable; the landlord absorbs the risk that taxes or insurance rise mid-term. Most Texas residential leasing is effectively gross. A **modified gross** lease, common in office space, is a middle ground in which the tenant reimburses the landlord for increases in specified expenses over a base year while the landlord keeps paying the base amounts.

**Net lease.** The tenant pays a base rent plus some operating costs directly, and practice names the variants by counting the categories the tenant picks up. A **single net (N)** lease commonly adds property taxes; a **double net (NN)** lease adds taxes and insurance; a **triple net (NNN)** lease adds taxes, insurance, and maintenance, leaving the landlord structural and capital items and a nearly passive income stream. An **absolute net** or bondable lease pushes even structure and casualty risk onto the tenant. The economic logic is straightforward: the further along that scale, the lower the base rent a landlord can command, because the tenant is absorbing both the costs and the risk that they rise.

chunks.heading: Unit: Types of Leases
chunks.excerpt:
**Percentage lease.** Used in retail — shopping centers, malls, and pad sites — a percentage lease sets a base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above a stated **breakpoint**, aligning the landlord's return with the tenant's success. A **natural breakpoint** is the sales volume at which percentage rent alone would equal the base rent: base rent divided by the percentage rate. Parties may instead negotiate an **artificial breakpoint** at any number they choose. Percentage leases customarily also define "gross sales" in detail, require sales reporting, give the landlord audit rights, and often require continuous operation — all contract terms, not statutory rules.

Here is a worked computation. **The numbers below are an illustration invented for teaching; no Texas statute sets base rents, percentage rates, or breakpoints.**

> A retail tenant leases 2,400 square feet in a Texas shopping center. Base rent is $4,000 per month, or $48,000 per year. The lease calls for percentage rent of 6 percent of annual gross sales above a stated breakpoint of $800,000. In the lease year just ended, the tenant's gross sales were $1,150,000.
>
> Step 1 — Base rent for the year: $4,000 × 12 = **$48,000**.
> Step 2 — Sales above the breakpoint: $1,150,000 − $800,000 = **$350,000**.
> Step 3 — Percentage rent: $350,000 × 0.06 = **$21,000**.
> Step 4 — Total rent for the year: $48,000 + $21,000 = **$69,000**.
>
> Check the breakpoint against the base rent. The natural breakpoint at a 6 percent rate would be $48,000 ÷ 0.06 = $800,000. Here the stated breakpoint equals the natural breakpoint, so the tenant pays percentage rent only on sales beyond the point at which 6 percent of sales would have covered the base rent by itself. Had the parties instead set an artificial breakpoi

chunks.heading: Unit: Types of Leases
chunks.excerpt:
nt of $600,000, percentage rent would have been ($1,150,000 − $600,000) × 0.06 = $33,000, and total rent $81,000 — the same sales, $12,000 more rent, purely because of where the breakpoint was drawn.

A common error is to multiply the percentage rate by *total* sales rather than by sales *above* the breakpoint. In the illustration, 6 percent of $1,150,000 is $69,000, which would nearly double the percentage rent actually owed. Read the clause: overage rent is computed on the excess.

**Ground lease.** The tenant leases land only and builds the improvements at the tenant's expense, typically under a term long enough to amortize a building. Ground leases are usually net in structure. The central negotiating issue is what happens to the improvements at the end of the term: ordinarily they revert to the landowner with the land, which is why ground lease terms are long and why lenders financing leasehold improvements scrutinize the remaining term. Recall that the tenant's interest here is real estate under Occupations Code § 1101.002(5), which is why a leasehold can be mortgaged, assigned, and brokered.

chunks.heading: Unit: Types of Leases
chunks.excerpt:
**Index lease and escalation clauses.** An **index lease** adjusts rent periodically by reference to a published index, so rent moves with a measure of general price levels rather than by a flat negotiated step. An **escalation clause** more broadly is any provision raising rent on a stated trigger — a fixed annual step-up, an index adjustment, or a pass-through of increases in a defined expense.
