is a private disciplinary process under the association's own rules. It is not a TREC proceeding, it
cannot suspend or revoke a state license, and its outcome does not bind the Commission. Conversely, a
TREC order does not resolve an association ethics complaint. A member can face both, separately, for
the same conduct — and a private lawsuit besides, because § 1101.801 provides that discipline "does
not relieve the person from civil or criminal liability."

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
**Where to put your loyalty when the two systems disagree.** They usually do not, because association
codes generally aim higher than the statutory floor rather than in a different direction. But when a
private rule and the Act appear to conflict, the analysis is not a balancing test. The Act and the
Commission's rules define what you may lawfully do; a private association can ask more of its members
than the law requires, but it cannot authorize what the law forbids, and no association rule is a
defense to a § 1101.652 charge. Orient yourself by the statute first, then by your broker's policies,
then by any association obligations you have voluntarily assumed.

## Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value

This unit is economics, not law. Almost nothing in it is a legal rule, and where a legal rule does
appear it is cited; everything else is a description of how markets and businesses behave. Read it
that way. Its purpose is to give you a working theory of what you are actually paid for, because a
license holder who cannot articulate that will not survive the first slow quarter.

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
Start with the asset. Real estate is unusual among the things people buy. It is immobile, so its value
is bound to a location that cannot be changed. It is durable, so today's decision constrains uses for
decades. It is heterogeneous — no two parcels are identical, if only because they occupy different
ground — so there is no single quoted price the way there is for a share of stock. It is expensive
relative to household income, so nearly every residential purchase involves borrowed money and a
lender's independent judgment about value. It transacts infrequently, so most participants are
amateurs. And information about it is unevenly distributed: the seller knows the roof's history, the
buyer does not, and neither knows what the house two streets over actually closed for. Every one of
those characteristics is a reason the market needs intermediaries, and together they explain why the
brokerage business exists at all.

The Act's own definition tracks the breadth of the asset. Section 1101.002(5) defines **real estate**
as "any interest in real property, including a leasehold, located in or outside this state," excluding
"an interest given as security for the performance of an obligation." So the business is not only
selling houses. It includes leasing, which is the sale of a temporary interest; it includes options
and contract assignments, addressed by § 1101.0045; and it extends beyond Texas property, since the
definition covers interests "located in or outside this state."

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
**Where value comes from.** Value in real property is conventionally traced to four conditions
holding at once: someone must want the property (**demand**); it must be capable of satisfying that
want (**utility**); there must be a limited supply of comparable alternatives (**scarcity**); and the
property must be legally and physically capable of being conveyed (**transferability**). Remove any
one and value collapses. A remote parcel of desert with clear title has utility problems; a beautiful
house with an unresolved title defect has a transferability problem; an ordinary suburban lot in a
subdivision with two hundred identical lots for sale has a scarcity problem. This four-part framework
is a standard analytical convention in the field, not a statutory test, and no held source prescribes
it.

**Price, cost and value are three different numbers.** **Price** is what a specific buyer paid a
specific seller on a specific day — a historical fact. **Cost** is what it took to produce the
improvements: land, materials, labor, financing, entrepreneurial effort. **Value** is an opinion
about what the property should bring under stated conditions. A house can cost $400,000 to build,
appraise at $360,000, and sell for $375,000, all at the same moment, and none of those three numbers
is wrong; they are answers to three different questions. Those figures are illustrations chosen to
make the distinction visible, not market data.

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
The Act treats the difference between an opinion of value and a professional appraisal as a licensing
boundary, and it is worth seeing here in economic terms before you meet it again as law. Section
1101.002(1)(A)(xi) includes among the acts of a broker providing "a written analysis, opinion, or
conclusion relating to the estimated price of real property" where it "is not referred to as an
appraisal," "is provided in the ordinary course of the person's business," and "is related to the
actual or potential management, acquisition, disposition, or encumbrance of an interest in real
property." A license holder's price opinion is therefore squarely brokerage work — a service the
license authorizes.

**How value is captured: the economics of compensation.** The license holder's economic function is
to reduce the cost of a transaction that would otherwise be slow, risky and information-poor. That
function has four components worth separating. First, **search and matching** — connecting a
particular buyer to a particular property, out of thousands, at acceptable cost. Second,
**information production** — assembling comparable sales, condition information and market context so
that both sides negotiate against something more solid than hope. Third, **process management** —
carrying a transaction through financing, inspection, title and closing, where the number of ways to
fail is large and mostly invisible to a first-time buyer. Fourth, **risk absorption** — the license
holder and the sponsoring broker take on regulatory and civil exposure that the parties would
otherwise carry themselves, a point § 1101.803 makes concrete by holding the broker "liable to the
commission, the public, and the broker's clients" for conduct by a sponsored sales agent.

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
Compensation for that function is negotiated, not set. Two provisions of the Act say so directly.
Section 1101.155(c)(1) requires that a Commission-adopted listing form include "a provision informing
the parties to the contract that real estate commissions are negotiable." And § 1101.563(c)(2)
requires the written buyer agreement to "disclose in conspicuous language that broker compensation is
not set by law and is fully negotiable." Take those at face value: there is no standard rate, no
customary percentage you are entitled to, and no figure you should ever describe to a consumer as
what commissions "are." A license holder who says otherwise is not just making an economic error; a
statement likely to mislead the public is itself a disciplinary matter under § 1101.652(b)(23)(A).

Consider a simple illustration of how compensation actually reaches a new sales agent, using invented
figures purely to show the arithmetic. Suppose a Texas home sells for $400,000 and the seller has
agreed in the listing agreement to pay the listing brokerage a fee of 3 percent. That fee is
$400,000 × 0.03 = $12,000, payable to the *brokerage*, not to the individual. Suppose the sales agent
and the sponsoring broker have agreed on a 60/40 split in the agent's favor for this transaction: the
sales agent's gross share is $12,000 × 0.60 = $7,200 and the brokerage retains $4,800. Two legal
points ride on that arithmetic. First, the money must move through the broker: § 1101.651(b) forbids
a sales agent from accepting compensation for a real estate transaction "from a person other than the
broker that is sponsoring the sales agent or was sponsoring the sales agent when the sales agent
earned the compensation." The second half of that clause is the one agents forget: an agent who has
since moved to

chunks.heading: Unit: Real Estate - The Business of Value
chunks.excerpt:
a new brokerage may still be paid by the *former* sponsoring broker for a commission
earned while that broker sponsored them. Section 1101.651(c) forbids a sales agent from paying a
commission to a person "except through the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent at that time." Second, the $7,200 is gross, not income. Out of it
come self-employment taxes, license renewal and education costs, any association dues the agent has
voluntarily assumed, marketing, transportation and insurance. The 3 percent, the 60/40 split and the
$400,000 price are illustrations only; none is a required, standard or customary figure.

**Why the business is lumpy, and what that implies.** Because transactions are infrequent and large,
a license holder's income arrives in irregular blocks separated by months of unpaid work. That is a
structural feature, not a sign of failure, and no statute addresses it: work performed today is paid
for months from now, so cash reserves matter more than in salaried work, and the pipeline rather than
the current month's closings is the real measure of the business. It also means the temptation to push
a marginal transaction over the line is built into the incentive structure — which is precisely why
the Act attaches discipline to false promises likely to influence a person to contract
(§ 1101.652(b)(5)), guarantees of future resale profit (§ 1101.652(b)(17)), and inducing a party to
break an existing contract to substitute a new one (§ 1101.652(b)(21)). The prohibitions are aimed
exactly where the money pressure points.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
**The service business inside the asset business.** Finally, notice that a license holder sells two
different things at once. To the client, the license holder sells a *service*: representation,
judgment, and the management of a complicated process. To the market, the license holder presents an
*asset*: a specific property at a specific price with specific terms. Confusing the two produces the
most common failure mode in a new agent's practice — treating the property as the product and the
client as an obstacle to moving it. The property is the client's; the service is yours. The Act
encodes that priority in its own way, requiring a broker who represents a party to "at a minimum,
answer the party's questions and present any offer to or from the party" (§ 1101.557(b)(3)), and
making it a disciplinary ground to fail "to make clear to all parties to a real estate transaction the
party for whom the license holder is acting" (§ 1101.652(b)(7)). The economics and the law point the
same way: your value comes from whose side you are on and how well you serve it.

## Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do

A license is a permission with edges. This unit draws both — first the affirmative scope of what a
Texas real estate license authorizes, then the boundaries that mark where the authority stops and
another profession's or another statute's territory begins.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
**The affirmative scope.** A license authorizes you to perform, for another person and for
compensation or with the expectation of compensation, the acts listed in § 1101.002(1): to **sell,
exchange, purchase or lease** real estate for another and to **offer** to do so; to **negotiate** a
listing, sale, exchange, purchase or lease; to **list** real estate; to **auction** it; to **deal in
options**, including lease-purchase arrangements; to **aid a person in locating or obtaining** real
estate; to **procure a prospect** or **procure property** to effect a sale, exchange or lease; to
**control the acceptance or deposit of rent** from a resident of a single-family residential unit; to
provide a **written price opinion** meeting the three conditions of clause (xi); and to **advise an
owner about a short sale**. That is the positive content of the license, and it is broader than most
new license holders assume — it covers leasing and rent handling, not only sales.

**The core requirement.** Section 1101.351(a) provides that unless a person holds a license, the
person may not "act as or represent that the person is a broker or sales agent" or "act as a
residential rental locator." Two verbs there, not one: *acting* and *representing*. Telling people you
are an agent when you are not is itself the violation, even if you never touch a transaction.
Section 1101.351(a-1) applies the same rule to business entities, and § 1101.351(b) forbids an
applicant from acting before the license actually issues.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
**The sponsorship requirement, stated three ways.** Section 1101.351(c) provides that "[a] licensed
sales agent may not engage or attempt to engage in real estate brokerage unless the sales agent is
sponsored by a licensed broker and is acting for that broker." Section 1101.363(b) says the same
thing from the licensing side: the Commission may issue an inactive sales agent license to a person
who meets every requirement, but "[t]he person may not act as a sales agent unless the person is
sponsored by a licensed broker who has notified the commission." And the Commission's rule says it a
third time in 22 TAC § 535.55(c): "An inactive sales agent may not practice as a licensed sales agent
until sponsored by an active Texas licensed broker." Three sources, one rule. A sales agent acts
*through* a broker, not beside one. Section 1101.803 explains why the law insists: the broker is
"liable to the commission, the public, and the broker's clients" for the sales agent's conduct, so
the state will not let a sales agent operate outside a broker's supervision and liability.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
**Compensation boundaries.** A sales agent may not accept compensation for a real estate transaction
from anyone other than the sponsoring broker, or the broker who was sponsoring when the compensation
was earned (§ 1101.651(b)), and may not pay a commission to anyone except through the sponsoring
broker (§ 1101.651(c)). A broker may not compensate an unlicensed person for performing an act of a
broker, with the narrow exception for an out-of-state licensed broker who conducts none of the Texas
negotiations (§ 1101.651(a)). Dividing a fee with an unlicensed person is separately a disciplinary
ground under § 1101.652(b)(11). The recurring temptation this forecloses is the "referral fee" to a
friend who sent you a buyer: unless that friend holds a license, paying them for the referral is not
a gray area.

**Boundary one: the practice of law.** Section 1101.654(a) requires the Commission to suspend or
revoke the license of a non-attorney license holder who, for consideration or in connection with the
license holder's employment, agency or fiduciary relationship, "drafts an instrument, other than a
form described by Section 1101.155, that transfers or otherwise affects an interest in real property,"
or "advises a person regarding the validity or legal sufficiency of an instrument or the validity of
title to real property." Note the word "shall." This is not discretionary discipline. The protected
zone is defined by § 1101.654(b): completing a contract form for the sale, exchange, option or lease
of an interest in real property, incidental to acting as a broker, is not the unauthorized practice of
law if the form was adopted by the Commission for that type of transaction, prepared by a Texas
attorney and approved by that attorney for that type of transaction, or prepared by

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
the property owner
or by an attorney and required by the owner.

So, concretely: you **may** fill in the blanks of a promulgated Commission contract form, choose among
promulgated addenda, and complete an owner-required attorney-prepared form. You **may not** draft a
deed, write a custom special provision that changes legal rights, tell a client whether a title
commitment's exceptions are legally sufficient, or opine on whether a chain of title is good. When the
question is "is this legally valid," the answer is "ask your attorney" — and § 1101.555 requires you
to advise every buyer in writing to have the abstract examined by an attorney of the buyer's choosing
or to obtain a title policy anyway.

**Boundary two: appraisal.** A separate statute, chapter 1103 of the Occupations Code, is cited as the
Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Act (§ 1103.001). Section 1103.003(1) defines an
**appraisal**, "regardless of whether prepared for a federally related transaction," as "(A) an opinion
of value; or (B) the act or process of developing an opinion of value." Section 1103.201(a) provides
that "[a] person may not perform an appraisal of real estate unless the person is licensed or
certified as an appraiser under this chapter, registered as a temporary out-of-state appraiser under
this chapter, or acting as an appraiser trainee under the supervision of a supervisory appraiser," and
subsection (b) forbids an unlicensed person from using the titles "certified real estate appraiser" or
"licensed real estate appraiser" or calling their work a "certified appraisal" or "licensed
appraisal."

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
The carve-out that makes a broker's price opinion lawful is § 1103.004(a)(2), which provides that
chapter 1103 does not apply to "a real estate broker licensed under Chapter 1101 or a sales agent
acting under the authority of a sponsoring broker who provides to another person a written analysis,
opinion, or conclusion relating to the estimated price of real property if the analysis, opinion, or
conclusion: (A) is not referred to as an appraisal; (B) is given in the ordinary course of the
broker's business; and (C) is related to the actual or potential acquisition, disposition,
encumbrance, or management of an interest in real property." That mirrors § 1101.002(1)(A)(xi)
almost word for word, and the two provisions should be read as a matched pair: the same document is
brokerage under chapter 1101 and outside chapter 1103, but only if all three conditions hold.

The condition that trips people is the first. Call your price opinion an appraisal — in the document,
in an email, or out loud to a client — and you have characterized your own work as something you are
not licensed to perform. Do not use the word. Do not let a client's phrasing pull you into it. If a
lender, a court or a party needs an appraisal, they need an appraiser.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
**Boundary three: the § 1101.652 prohibitions.** The disciplinary list surveyed in unit 2 is also a
list of things a license holder may not do, and it helps to group the selection by the interest each
item protects. *Competence and candor*: you may not act negligently or incompetently ((b)(1)),
misrepresent a known significant defect or fail to disclose one ((b)(3), (b)(4)), make a false promise
likely to influence a person to contract when you cannot or do not intend to keep it ((b)(5)), or
publish a misleading advertisement or one omitting your broker's name ((b)(23)). *Clarity about whose
side you are on*: you may not leave any party unclear about whom you represent ((b)(7)), take
compensation from more than one party without everyone's full knowledge and consent ((b)(8)), act as
broker and undisclosed principal at once ((b)(16)), or take an undisclosed rebate or profit on an
expenditure made for a principal ((b)(13)). *Other people's money*: you must account for and promptly
remit it ((b)(9)), must not commingle it with your own ((b)(10)), must deposit escrow funds with a
title company or in a proper trust account ((b)(30)), and must not disburse them before the
transaction completes or terminates ((b)(31)). *The owner's control of the owner's property*: you may
not put up a sign without written consent ((b)(18)), offer property without the owner's knowledge and
consent ((b)(19)) or on unauthorized terms ((b)(20)), guarantee future resale profits ((b)(17)), or
sell by lottery ((b)(14)) or deceptive practice ((b)(15)). *Other brokers' contracts*: you may not
induce a party to break a contract to substitute a new one ((b)(21)) or negotiate with a party you
know is under another broker's exclusive written agreement ((b)(22)). And you may not discriminate
against an own

chunks.heading: Unit: The Purpose of Licensing Laws - What a License Holder Can and Cannot Do
chunks.excerpt:
er, potential buyer, landlord or potential tenant "on the basis of race, color,
religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, or ancestry, including directing a
prospective buyer or tenant interested in equivalent properties to a different area" on those bases
((b)(32)).

**What happens if you act without a license.** The consequences stack. Acting as a broker or sales
agent without a license is a Class A misdemeanor (§ 1101.758). The unlicensed person is liable to the
state for a civil penalty "of not less than the amount of money received or more than three times the
amount of money received" (§ 1101.753(a)), and liable to the aggrieved person for the same measure
(§ 1101.754(a)). The Commission may seek an injunction without proving the absence of an adequate
legal remedy (§ 1101.751) and may issue a cease and desist order after notice and hearing
(§ 1101.759). And the unlicensed person cannot sue to be paid: § 1101.806(b) bars an action to
collect compensation for a brokerage act performed in Texas unless the person proves they were a
license holder when the act commenced or an attorney licensed in any state. A licensed person who
knowingly helps that arrangement along is exposed too, under § 1101.652(b)(26) (associating with a
non-license holder expected to act as one) and (b)(27) (aiding, abetting or conspiring to circumvent
the chapter).

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Does this activity need a license?
chunks.excerpt:
**Where the license is not needed.** Balance the picture with § 1101.005 and § 1101.004(b), covered in
unit 1. An owner leasing the owner's own property, an on-site apartment manager, a licensed Texas
attorney, an executor selling under a will, a person building homes and selling what they built, a
trustee conducting a foreclosure sale under a power of sale in a deed of trust — none of these needs a
real estate license for that activity. Knowing the exemptions is not a loophole exercise; it is how
you answer the question a friend or a client will eventually ask you, and answering it wrongly in
either direction is a disservice.

### Applied exercise: Does this activity need a license?

For each of the following, state whether the person is performing an act that requires a Texas real
estate license, and cite the section that decides it. Reason only from this module. A sentence or two
each is plenty; there is no length requirement.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
1. Marisol owns a fourplex in Waco and shows the vacant unit to prospective tenants herself, signs the
   lease as landlord, and collects the rent.
2. Dev manages a single-family rental in Frisco for its out-of-state owner. He advertises the vacancy,
   screens applicants, and receives the tenant's monthly rent into an account he controls, for a
   monthly fee.
3. Ana, who holds no license, tells a coworker about a house for sale down the street and introduces
   the coworker to the seller. The seller later hands Ana $1,000 "for the help." Ana had not discussed
   payment beforehand but says she "figured something might come of it."
4. Tomás is a Texas-licensed attorney who negotiates the purchase of a commercial building for a
   client and is paid his hourly rate.
5. A Dallas sales agent prepares a written comparative price analysis for a homeowner considering
   selling, titles it "Comparative Market Analysis," delivers it in the ordinary course of her
   brokerage business, and does not call it an appraisal.
6. The same sales agent, at the homeowner's request, retitles the identical document "Appraisal of
   Fair Market Value" so the homeowner can send it to a lender.

## Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
**The Commission.** The **Texas Real Estate Commission** is defined in § 1101.002(3) simply as "the
Texas Real Estate Commission," and it is built by subchapter B. Section 1101.051(a) provides that it
"consists of nine members appointed by the governor with the advice and consent of the senate,"
comprising "six members who have been engaged in the brokerage business as licensed brokers as their
major occupation for the five years preceding appointment" and "three members who represent the
public." Members serve staggered six-year terms (§ 1101.055(a)) and are led by a presiding officer
whom the governor designates from among the members who are licensed brokers (§ 1101.056(a)).
Day-to-day operations belong to an executive director the Commission appoints, together with staff
including a general counsel, attorneys and investigators (§ 1101.101), under a policy that "clearly
separate[s]" policymaking from management (§ 1101.102).

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
**What the Commission can do.** Section 1101.151(a) requires the Commission to administer chapters
1101 and 1102, adopt rules on advertising by residential rental locators, maintain a registry of
certificate holders, and design and adopt a seal. Section 1101.151(b) permits it to "adopt and enforce
rules necessary to administer this chapter and Chapter 1102" and to "establish standards of conduct
and ethics for persons licensed under this chapter and Chapter 1102 to: (A) fulfill the purposes of
this chapter and Chapter 1102" and "(B) ensure compliance with this chapter and Chapter 1102." That
rulemaking power is why a
TREC rule is not advice: when § 535.55 tells you how many qualifying hours an initial sales agent
license requires, that rule carries the force the Legislature delegated in § 1101.151(b), and
§ 1101.652(a)(8) makes disregarding chapter 1101 a disciplinary ground while § 1101.656(a) reaches a
violation of "this chapter or a commission rule."

The Commission also sets fees by rule rather than by statute. Section 1101.152(a) directs it to adopt
rules charging fees "in amounts reasonable and necessary to cover the costs of administering this
chapter and the real estate recovery trust account," and lists the categories — original applications
and renewals for broker and sales agent licenses, examination applications, changes of sponsoring
broker or place of business, education program approval, fitness determinations, criminal history
checks and more. No dollar amount for any of those appears in the statute, and none is stated here;
look the current amounts up on the Commission's own materials before you quote one to anyone.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
**How a person becomes a Texas sales agent.** Four requirements, from § 1101.354, organize everything
else. At the time of application a person must "be at least 18 years of age" and "be a citizen of the
United States or a lawfully admitted alien"; must "satisfy the commission as to the applicant's
honesty, trustworthiness, and integrity"; must "demonstrate competence based on an examination under
Subchapter I"; and must "complete the required courses of study, including any required qualifying
real estate courses prescribed under this chapter."

**Education.** Section 1101.358(a) requires a sales agent applicant to show completion of "at least 12
semester hours, or equivalent classroom hours, of qualifying real estate courses required by
commission rule," and § 1101.003(a) supplies the list of eleven qualifying subjects from which such
courses are drawn. The Commission's rule fills in the detail. Rule 22 TAC § 535.55(a) requires "180
hours of qualifying real estate courses," specifically: "60 hours of Principles of Real Estate; 30
hours of Law of Agency; 30 hours of Law of Contracts; 30 hours of Promulgated Contracts Forms; and 30
hours of Real Estate Finance." The course you are reading now is one half of that 60-hour Principles
requirement. Section 535.55(b) then front-loads the next stage: a sales agent "must successfully
complete an additional 90 classroom hours in qualifying courses, including the 30 hour qualifying real
estate brokerage course, by the expiration date of the sales agent's initial licensing period." That
rule matches § 1101.454(a), which requires evidence of "at least 18 semester hours, or equivalent
classroom hours, of qualifying real estate courses" for the first renewal — and § 1101.454(d) adds
that the Commission "may not waive" it.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
Two delivery rules from § 1101.003 apply while you take those courses. A daily course segment for a
qualifying course "may not exceed 12 hours" (§ 1101.003(d)). And completion of an alternative delivery
or correspondence qualifying course may not be reported "until the elapsed time between the time the
applicant or license holder registers for the course and the time the completion of the course is
reported exceeds twice the number of hours for which credit is claimed" (§ 1101.003(e)). For a 60-hour
Principles course delivered online, that means more than 120 hours must elapse between registration
and the report of completion, no matter how quickly you read.

**Examination.** Section 1101.401(a) makes the examination the vehicle for the § 1101.354(3)
competency requirement, prepared or contracted for by the Commission and, under subsection (c), "of
sufficient scope in the judgment of the commission to determine whether a person is competent to act
as a broker or sales agent in a manner that will protect the public." The sales agent examination
"must be less exacting and less stringent than the broker examination" (§ 1101.401(d)). The Commission
must supply study material and references on which the examination is based (§ 1101.401(e)), and the
applicant "must satisfy the examination requirement not later than one year after the date the license
application is filed" (§ 1101.401(f)). The Commission may contract with a testing service so long as
it "retains the authority to establish the scope and type of the examination" (§ 1101.403(b)). Results
come not later than the 10th day after the examination, results are confidential, and a person who
fails may request a written analysis of their performance (§ 1101.404). A person who fails three
consecutive times "may not apply

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
for reexamination or submit a new license application unless the
applicant submits evidence satisfactory to the commission that the applicant has completed additional
education, as prescribed by the commission, since the date of the applicant's last examination"
(§ 1101.405(b)). No held source read for this module states a passing score, and none is given here.

**Fitness and background.** Section 1101.352(b) requires an applicant to disclose a guilty or nolo
contendere plea to a felony, or a felony conviction where the time for appeal has elapsed or the
conviction was affirmed, and subsection (c) requires the disclosure "even if an order has granted
community supervision suspending the imposition of the sentence." Section 1101.3521(a) requires a
complete and legible set of fingerprints for criminal history record information from the Texas
Department of Public Safety and the FBI, and subsection (b) requires the Commission to refuse to issue
or renew an active license for a person who does not comply. Anyone with a history that might raise a
question should know about § 1101.353: a person may request a **determination of fitness** before
applying, pay the required fee, and receive the Commission's determination with notice "not later than
the 30th day after the date the commission makes its determination." Section 1101.365 permits the
Commission to issue a probationary license on terms adopted by rule, and § 1101.364 entitles an
applicant who is denied to written notice and a hearing under § 1101.657.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Texas Real Estate Commission & Licensing Requirements
chunks.excerpt:
**Sponsorship — the last step, and the one that makes the license usable.** Satisfy the education and
examination requirements and the Commission may issue an **inactive** sales agent license
(§ 1101.363(b); 22 TAC § 535.55(c)). You are licensed. You may not practice. Section 1101.363(b)
provides that the person "may not act as a sales agent unless the person is sponsored by a licensed
broker who has notified the commission as required by Section 1101.367(b)," and § 1101.351(c) forbids
a sales agent from engaging or attempting to engage in brokerage without a sponsoring broker to act
for. Section 1101.367(b) supplies the mechanism: the Commission may return a sales agent license to
active status if, before the license's expiration date, "a licensed broker files a request with the
commission advising the commission that the broker assumes sponsorship of the sales agent, accompanied
by the appropriate fee." Section 1101.554 requires the Commission to deliver a copy of each sales
agent license to the sponsoring broker.

The relationship can end as easily as it began, and the notice duty runs both ways. Under
§ 1101.367(a), when the relationship terminates, "the terminating party shall immediately notify in
writing both the other party and the commission," and on receiving that notice the Commission "shall
place the sales agent license on inactive status." A sales agent between brokers is not unlicensed —
but is, for practical purposes, unable to work, which is why changing brokerages is something
practitioners plan rather than improvise.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Mapping a path to a sales agent license
chunks.excerpt:
**Keeping the license.** Section 1101.451(a) permits issuance or renewal "for a period of 24 months."
A first renewal requires the additional qualifying hours of § 1101.454(a) and § 535.55(b). Later
renewals require continuing education under § 1101.455 — at least 15 classroom hours prescribed by
rule, of which "at least eight" must cover the legal topics listed in subsection (e). Renewal also
requires the felony disclosure (§ 1101.452(b)) and compliance with the fingerprint and criminal history
requirements (§ 1101.4521). Miss the deadline and § 1101.451(e) applies a fee multiplier of 1-1/2
times for up to 90 days and two times for more than 90 days but less than six months; miss it by six
months or more and § 1101.451(f) forecloses renewal entirely — "[t]he person may obtain a new license
by complying with the requirements and procedures for obtaining an original license."

**And the step after that.** A broker license under § 1101.356(a) requires "at least four years of
active experience as a license holder during the 60 months preceding the date the application is
filed," the qualifying and related course hours required by rule "not to exceed 60 semester hours or
equivalent classroom hours," and attendance at the broker responsibility course approved under
§ 1101.458. The broker credential is not a longer version of the sales agent credential; it is a
supervisory office, which is why § 1101.803 makes the broker liable for the conduct of every sales
agent acting for the broker.

### Applied exercise: Mapping a path to a sales agent license

Priya is 19, a U.S. citizen living in Round Rock, and wants to be a Texas sales agent. Using only this
module, answer briefly — no minimum length.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. List, in order, the four § 1101.354 requirements Priya must satisfy, and name the source that tells
   her how many qualifying course hours the education requirement means in practice and how they are
   distributed among named courses.
2. Priya enrolls in a 30-hour online Law of Agency course on a Monday morning and finishes the reading
   Tuesday night. Can her provider report her completion on Wednesday? Cite the subsection and show
   the elapsed-time calculation.
3. Priya passes the examination and receives a license from the Commission, but has not yet found a
   brokerage. A neighbor asks her to list his house that weekend. What is her status, what may she do,
   and which three sources say so?
4. Priya was charged with a felony at 18; the case is still pending on appeal after a conviction. What
   must she disclose on her application, what background step does the Act require of every applicant,
   and what step could she have taken before spending money on 180 hours of coursework?
5. Two years later Priya's first renewal is due. What education must she have completed by then, and
   may the Commission waive it?

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
This module took a single statute — Occupations Code chapter 1101, The Real Estate License Act — and
worked it from the outside in. It began with what the Act *is*: a licensing and conduct statute whose
consumer-protection purpose shows in the competency standard of § 1101.401(c), the public-interest
forms authority of § 1101.155(a), the consumer-complaint priority of § 1101.204(h), and the recovery
trust account of § 1101.601. It established the vocabulary the rest of Texas real estate law assumes:
a **license holder** is a broker or sales agent (§ 1101.002(4)); a **sales agent** is by definition a
person sponsored by a broker (§ 1101.002(7)); **real estate** is any interest in real property,
including a leasehold (§ 1101.002(5)); and being a broker is a matter of performing any of the twelve
acts in § 1101.002(1)(A) for another, for compensation or the expectation of it.

The long middle unit walked all seventeen subchapters. You should now be able to hear a problem and
place it: a question about who sits on the Commission is subchapter B; about rulemaking or contract
forms, subchapter D; about complaint handling, subchapter E; about the schools, subchapter G; about
getting or holding a license, subchapter H; about the examination, subchapter I; about renewal and
continuing education, subchapter J; about what you may do in a transaction — disclosure, intermediary
status, the written buyer agreement — subchapter L; about a wronged consumer's last resort, subchapter
M; about prohibited conduct and discipline, subchapter N; about penalties, subchapters O and P; and
about who is liable to whom, subchapter Q.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Three unifying propositions run through everything. First, **authority follows the act, not the
title**: § 1101.002(1) and § 1101.351 make conduct the trigger for licensure, which is why the
exemptions in § 1101.005 and the boundaries in § 1101.654 and chapter 1103 matter as much as the
license itself. Second, **the broker is the load-bearing wall**: § 1101.351(c), § 1101.363(b),
§ 1101.651(b)–(c) and § 1101.803 all converge on the rule that a sales agent acts through a broker and
that the broker answers for it. Third, **law and private practice are different systems**: the state
issues a license, while trade associations, MLS participation and association ethics codes are
voluntary private arrangements that no held source makes a condition of practicing.

You should now be able to state what TRELA is and why it exists; navigate chapter 1101 by subchapter;
distinguish a license holder from a REALTOR®; explain in economic terms what a license holder is paid
for and why the Act insists that compensation is negotiable; say precisely what your license lets you
do and where it stops; and describe the education, examination, fitness and sponsorship path to a
Texas sales agent license — every one of those grounded in a section you have now read.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 07

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 07
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 07

## TREC Topic: Real Estate Brokerage and Law of Agency

**Prescribed time: 195 minutes.** This module carries the five units the Commission's PRINS2-1 course
approval form places under *Real Estate Brokerage and Law of Agency*. The form gives this topic no
scope note; none is stated here, and none has been invented to fill the space.

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: define agency and identify
the principal, agent, client and customer in a Texas transaction, distinguish express, implied,
ratified and estoppel-based agency, and distinguish actual from apparent authority; identify which
agency position a Texas license holder occupies in a given transaction — seller representation, buyer
representation, intermediary, or a non-representation showing — and state the written consent,
appointment, notice and written-agreement requirements that attach to each; explain how a Texas
brokerage is organized, how a sales agent's authority flows through a sponsoring broker, and how
compensation is earned, paid and disclosed; state each fiduciary duty and identify the subsection of
Occupations Code § 1101.652 that turns a breach of it into a ground for discipline; and apply the
Texas Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act to a real estate misrepresentation by
identifying whether the complainant is a "consumer," which enumerated practice is implicated, and
what the "knowingly" and "intentionally" findings do to the damages available.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it. This course is not
approved by the Texas Real Estate Commission and no Texas credit is offered for it.

## Unit: The Law of Agency

**Agency** is the legal relationship in which one person — the **agent** — is authorized to act for and
on behalf of another person — the **principal** — in dealings with third persons, and in which the
agent's authorized acts bind the principal as if the principal had acted personally. Every other idea in
this module rests on that sentence. A listing is an agency; a buyer representation agreement is an
agency; and the reason a license holder can lose a licence over a sentence said carelessly at a kitchen
table is that the license holder is not merely a helpful person in the room but someone else's legal
proxy.

Texas does not leave the existence of the relationship to inference. Occupations Code § 1101.557(a)
states it directly: "A broker who represents a party in a real estate transaction or who lists real
estate for sale under an exclusive agreement for a party is that party's agent." That confirms both that
representation creates agency and that taking an exclusive listing is agency in itself.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**The vocabulary, precisely.** The **principal** is the person the agent works for; in ordinary
brokerage speech the principal is the **client**. The person on the other side, whom the license holder
deals with but does not represent, is the **customer**. Neither word is defined in Chapter 1101, so do
not treat them as statutory terms. What Chapter 1101 does define, for the subchapter governing practice,
is **party**. Under § 1101.551(2), "'Party' means a prospective buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant or an
authorized representative of a buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant, including a trustee, guardian,
executor, administrator, receiver, or attorney-in-fact. The term does not include a license holder who
represents a party." That last clause matters: the license holder is never the party; the license holder
is the agent *of* a party.

**Who is the agent — the broker, not the sales agent.** This is the structural fact students most often
get backwards. Section 1101.002(7) defines a "sales agent" as "a person who is sponsored by a licensed
broker for the purpose of performing an act described by Subdivision (1)" — an act of brokerage. Section
1101.351(c) provides that "A licensed sales agent may not engage or attempt to engage in real estate
brokerage unless the sales agent is sponsored by a licensed broker and is acting for that broker." The
sales agent therefore has no independent brokerage authority. The agency runs between the *broker* and
the client, and the sales agent performs the broker's work. Section 1101.554 reflects this
administratively — the Commission delivers a copy of each sales agent licence to the sponsoring broker —
and § 1101.803 states the consequence: "A licensed broker is liable to the commission, the public, and
the broker's clients for any conduc

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
t engaged in under this chapter by the broker or by a sales agent
associated with or acting for the broker."

**What acts require the licence.** Section 1101.002(1) defines "broker" functionally: a person who, for
a commission or other valuable consideration or expecting one, performs for another person any of a
listed set of acts — selling, exchanging, purchasing or leasing real estate; offering to do so;
negotiating or attempting to negotiate a listing, sale, exchange, purchase or lease; listing or offering
to list; auctioning; dealing in options; aiding in locating or obtaining real estate; procuring a
prospect or procuring property to effect a transaction; controlling the acceptance or deposit of rent
from a resident of a single-family residential unit; and advising an owner about a short sale. Section
1101.004(a) restates that as a status, and § 1101.351(a) makes the licence a precondition: unless a
person holds a licence, the person may not act as or represent that the person is a broker or sales
agent, or act as a residential rental locator. Note what the definition turns on — acting *for another
person* with the *expectation of compensation*. Section 1101.004(b) draws the boundary from the other
side: constructing or repairing a building, participating as a principal in a real estate investment, or
entering into an obligation secured by an interest in real property is not, standing alone, brokerage.
Section 1101.005 lists persons to whom the chapter does not apply at all, including a Texas-licensed
attorney, an on-site manager of an apartment complex, and an owner or an owner's employee leasing the
owner's real estate.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**How an agency is created.** Agency law generally recognizes four routes, and it is worth being candid
about their source: Chapter 1101 does not enumerate them, so this module presents them as common-law
concepts rather than Texas statutory rules.

**Express agency** arises when the parties say so. A signed listing or buyer representation agreement is
express agency in writing; an oral appointment can be express too. That oral possibility is not
hypothetical here — § 1101.562(a)(1) permits a non-representation showing only where the broker "has not
agreed with the party, either orally or in writing, to represent the party," which tells you the
Legislature treats an oral agreement to represent as capable of creating the relationship. **Implied
agency** arises from conduct rather than words: the license holder advises on price, counsels on
strategy, behaves as the buyer's advocate, and the buyer reasonably understands the license holder to be
working for them, though nobody signed anything. That accident is what the 2026 amendments in the next
unit are built to prevent, and what § 1101.652(b)(7) punishes by making it a ground for discipline that a
license holder "fails to make clear to all parties to a real estate transaction the party for whom the
license holder is acting." **Ratification** occurs when a principal who did not authorize an act accepts
its benefit afterward with knowledge of the facts. **Agency by estoppel** arises when a principal's own
conduct leads a third person reasonably to believe someone is the principal's agent and that person
relies to their detriment. The last two are judicial doctrines; do not cite Chapter 1101 for them.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**Actual and apparent authority.** **Actual authority** is what the principal really gave the agent —
expressly in the words of the agreement, or by implication as reasonably necessary to carry the express
grant out. **Apparent authority** is what a third person is reasonably led by the principal's conduct to
believe the agent has, even where the agent in fact has less. Actual authority is the boundary the agent
must respect toward the principal; apparent authority is the boundary the principal may be held to toward
the outside world. These are common-law categories, but Texas has legislated at their edges in three ways
you must know.

On the **power to bind**: an ordinary Texas listing does not authorize the broker to sign the contract for
the seller. The broker markets, procures, communicates and negotiates; the party signs. Where a license
holder does hold power to bind, § 1101.557(c)(1) changes the license holder's status — "a license holder
who has the authority to bind a party to a lease or sale under a power of attorney or a property
management agreement is also a party to the lease or sale."

chunks.heading: Unit: The Law of Agency
chunks.excerpt:
On **liability for the agent's words**: at common law a principal can be exposed for an agent's
misrepresentations, and Texas has narrowed that by statute. Section 1101.805(b) provides that the section
"prevails over any other law, including common law." Under § 1101.805(d), a party is not liable for a
license holder's misrepresentation or concealment of a material fact unless the party "knew of the falsity"
and "failed to disclose the party's knowledge of the falsity"; subsection (e) runs the same protection the
other way for the license holder, and subsection (c) preserves the broker's responsibility for a sponsored
sales agent. Knowledge plus silence destroys the protection either way.

On the **outer limit of authority**: no agency authorizes practising law. Section 1101.654(a) requires the
Commission to suspend or revoke the licence of a non-attorney license holder who, for consideration, drafts
an instrument other than a form described by § 1101.155 that transfers or affects an interest in real
property, or who advises on the validity or legal sufficiency of an instrument or the validity of title.
Subsection (b) protects the ordinary work: completing a contract form incidental to acting as a broker is
not unauthorized practice if the form was adopted by the Commission for that type of transaction, prepared
and approved by a Texas attorney for that type of transaction, or prepared by the owner or an attorney and
required by the owner.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: what § 1101.557 actually declares
chunks.excerpt:
**How an agency ends.** Agency relationships end in the ordinary ways — performance of the object,
expiration of the term, mutual agreement, revocation or renunciation, or an event making performance
impossible. Those are general agency principles, not Chapter 1101 rules. What Texas legislates is the term.
Section 1101.652(b)(12) makes it a ground for discipline to fail to specify "a definite termination date
that is not subject to prior notice" in a contract — other than a property management contract — in which
the license holder agrees to perform services requiring a licence. An open-ended listing is not merely poor
drafting in Texas; it is a disciplinary exposure. Section 1101.563(c)(1)(B), effective January 1, 2026,
carries the same instinct to the buyer side, and § 1101.563(e)(2) caps a showing-only agreement at fourteen
days.

A common error is to assume that when the agreement ends, everything ends. Two obligations in particular
outlive the paperwork — what you may never say about the former client, and what you must do with the
former client's money. Unit 4 takes them up.

### Statute reading exercise: what § 1101.557 actually declares

Re-read the quoted text of Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) and (c)(1), § 1101.551(2) and § 1101.351(c) in
this unit. Then answer:

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
1. Under § 1101.557(a), what two circumstances make a broker a party's agent?
2. Under § 1101.551(2), can the license holder representing a seller also be a "party" for purposes of
   Subchapter L? Which sentence of the definition settles it?
3. Under § 1101.557(c)(1), what changes when a license holder holds authority to bind a party under a
   property management agreement?
4. A sales agent tells a buyer, "I don't work for a broker; I have my own book of business." Which
   subsection of § 1101.351 does that misdescribe, and what does it require?

## Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure

There is a small, closed set of positions a Texas license holder can occupy toward a person in a
transaction. Learn them as positions, not as feelings about whom you are helping. In every deal you must be
able to name yours in one sentence and prove it on paper.

**Position one: representing the seller or landlord.** The broker takes a listing and, under § 1101.557(a),
is that party's agent. Section 1101.557(b) sets a floor that cannot be bargained away: the broker "must
inform the party if the broker receives material information related to a transaction to list, buy, sell, or
lease the party's real estate, including the receipt of an offer by the broker," and "shall, at a minimum,
answer the party's questions and present any offer to or from the party." A listing broker who sits on an
offer because it looks weak is not exercising judgment but violating a statutory minimum.

**Position two: representing the buyer or tenant.** The mirror image, with the same statutory floor and the
fiduciary duties taken up in Unit 4. On the residential side, as of January 1, 2026, this position can no
longer drift into existence — see § 1101.563 below.

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
**Position three: intermediary.** **Texas does not use "dual agency" the way some other states do.** Do not
carry that phrase into Texas practice. Some states let a broker be the full agent of both buyer and seller at
once, owing each the complete set of fiduciary duties and holding two irreconcilable loyalties. Texas's
answer differs in name and in substance. Chapter 1101, Subchapter L, creates the **intermediary**, defined in
§ 1101.551(1): "'Intermediary' means a broker who is employed to negotiate a transaction between the parties
to a transaction and for that purpose may act as an agent of the parties." The intermediary is not two
agents. It is one broker in a defined, statutorily constrained middle position, and the constraints are the
point.

*Getting there requires written consent.* Section 1101.559(a) permits a broker to act as an intermediary
"if: (1) the broker obtains written consent from each party for the broker to act as an intermediary in the
transaction; and (2) the written consent of the parties states the source of any expected compensation to
the broker." Two requirements, both mandatory, neither satisfiable orally. Section 1101.559(b) says where
that consent normally lives: a written listing agreement or a written buyer or tenant representation
agreement "that authorizes a broker to act as an intermediary in a real estate transaction is sufficient to
establish written consent of the party to the transaction if the written agreement specifies in conspicuous
bold or underlined print the conduct that is prohibited under" § 1101.651(d). That is why Texas
listing and representation agreements carry a conspicuous intermediary paragraph — the consent is captured
at the front end, before anyone knows whether an in-house match will happen.

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
*How the intermediary must behave.* Section 1101.559(c) states the standard in five words — "An intermediary
shall act fairly and impartially" — and then answers the question students ask next: appointing an associated
license holder under § 1101.560 "to communicate with, carry out the instructions of, and provide opinions and
advice to the parties to whom that associated license holder is appointed is a fair and impartial act."

*Appointments.* Section 1101.560(a) provides that a broker who complies with § 1101.559's written consent
requirements "may appoint: (1) a license holder associated with the broker to communicate with and carry out
instructions of one party to a real estate transaction; and (2) another license holder associated with the
broker to communicate with and carry out instructions of any other party to the transaction." Section
1101.560(b) sets two conditions: the parties' written consent must authorize the appointment, and "the broker
provides written notice of the appointment to all parties involved in the real estate transaction." Then the
payoff, in § 1101.560(c): "A license holder appointed under this section may provide opinions and advice
during negotiations to the party to whom the license holder is appointed." Without appointments the brokerage
is limited to fair and impartial facilitation; with them, each side gets someone who may actually counsel them.

*What an intermediary may never do.* Section 1101.651(d) binds the broker and any broker or sales agent
appointed under § 1101.560. Such a person may not:

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
- "disclose to the buyer or tenant that the seller or landlord will accept a price less than the asking
  price, unless otherwise instructed in a separate writing by the seller or landlord";
- "disclose to the seller or landlord that the buyer or tenant will pay a price greater than the price
  submitted in a written offer to the seller or landlord, unless otherwise instructed in a separate writing
  by the buyer or tenant";
- "disclose any confidential information or any information a party specifically instructs the broker or
  sales agent in writing not to disclose," unless instructed otherwise in a separate writing by that party,
  unless disclosure is required by Chapter 1101 or a court order, or unless "the information materially
  relates to the condition of the property";
- "treat a party to a transaction dishonestly"; or
- "violate this chapter."

Notice the shape. Permission to disclose price flexibility runs only from the party whose flexibility it is,
and only in a *separate writing* — a clause buried in the listing will not do. And one carve-out runs the
other way: confidentiality never covers information that "materially relates to the condition of the
property." A buyer's confidence about how high they will go is protected; a seller's confidence about a
foundation problem is not.

*The intermediary is not optional once you hold both sides.* Section 1101.561(b): "A broker must agree to act
as an intermediary under this subchapter if the broker agrees to represent in a transaction: (1) a buyer or
tenant; and (2) a seller or landlord." And § 1101.561(a) resolves the conflict-of-laws problem: intermediary
duties "supersede the duties of a license holder established under any other law, including common law."

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
**Position four: showing property without representing anyone.** Effective January 1, 2026, § 1101.562(a)
permits a broker to "show real property available for sale or lease to a party without representing the party
if the broker: (1) has not agreed with the party, either orally or in writing, to represent the party; (2) is
not otherwise acting as the party's agent at the time of showing the real property; (3) does not provide to
the party opinions or advice regarding the real property or real estate transactions in general; and (4) does
not perform any other act of real estate brokerage for the party." Before such a showing, § 1101.562(b)
requires the broker to make the § 1101.558(b) disclosure if the broker represents the owner, or to provide the
written notice described by § 1101.558(b-1) if the broker does not. Section 1101.562(c) preserves one narrow
permission: "a broker showing real property under this section may confirm information to a party regarding
the size, price, and terms of the real property available for sale or lease." You may confirm the square
footage and the asking price. You may not tell them it is a good deal.

**The IABS written notice.** Section 1101.558 carries two distinct obligations that students routinely merge.
Subsection (b) is the *representation* disclosure: a license holder who represents a party "shall disclose,
orally or in writing, that representation at the time of the license holder's first contact with: (1) another
party to the transaction; or (2) another license holder who represents another party to the transaction."
Oral suffices; the trigger is first contact.

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
Subsection (b-1) is the *written notice* the business calls the Information About Brokerage Services form. "At
the time of a license holder's first substantive communication with a party relating to a proposed transaction
regarding specific real property, the license holder shall provide to the party written notice in at least a
10-point font that: (1) describes the ways in which a broker can represent a party to a real estate
transaction, including as an intermediary; (2) describes the basic duties and obligations a broker has to a
party to a real estate transaction that the broker represents; (3) describes the basic obligations a broker
has to a party to a real estate transaction that the broker does not represent; and (4) provides the name,
license number, and contact information for the license holder and the license holder's supervisor and broker,
if applicable." Under subsection (b-2) the Commission by rule prescribes the text required by (b-1)(1) and (2)
and the delivery methods, so exact wording and delivery are matters of Commission rule rather than of the
statute; TREC's article states that the changes effective January 1, 2026 to the IABS reflect the new notice
requirements.

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
Section 1101.558(c) excuses the (b-1) notice in three situations: "(1) the proposed transaction is for a
residential lease for less than one year and a sale is not being considered; (2) the license holder meets with
a party who the license holder knows is represented by another license holder; or (3) the communication occurs
at a property that is held open for any prospective buyer or tenant and the communication concerns that
property." The third is the open-house exception, and it is narrower than its reputation: it excuses the
*notice*, at that property, about that property, and nothing else — and after January 1, 2026 something else is
required.

**The § 1101.563 written agreement, effective January 1, 2026.** Section 1101.563(a) defines "residential real
property" as a single-family house; a duplex, triplex or quadraplex; or a unit in a multiunit residential
structure in which title to an individual unit is transferred to the unit owner under a condominium or
cooperative system. Subsection (b) states the rule: "A license holder who performs any act of real estate
brokerage for a prospective buyer of residential real property must enter into a written agreement with the
prospective buyer before: (1) showing any residential real property to the prospective buyer; or (2) if no
residential real property will be shown, presenting an offer to purchase residential real property on behalf of
the prospective buyer."

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
Subsection (c) prescribes the contents: the services to be provided; the termination date; whether the
agreement is exclusive or non-exclusive; as applicable, that the license holder either represents the
prospective buyer as the buyer's agent or does not represent the buyer if the only brokerage act is showing
property under § 1101.562; the amount or rate of compensation the broker will receive and how it will be
determined; and a disclosure "in conspicuous language that broker compensation is not set by law and is fully
negotiable." Subsection (d) requires a separate agreement if additional brokerage acts follow a showing-only
agreement. Subsection (e) caps the showing-only agreement twice over: it "may not: (1) be an exclusive
agreement with the license holder; or (2) state a termination date more than fourteen days from the date the
agreement is entered into."

Skipping it is not merely a lost deal. Section 1101.652(b)(34) makes it a ground for suspension or revocation
that a license holder "fails to enter into a written agreement with a prospective buyer as required by Section
1101.563."

chunks.heading: Unit: Agency Positions and Disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
**The open house, worked through.** TREC's article on the 2026 changes gives two scenarios showing how
§ 1101.558(c)(3), § 1101.562 and § 1101.563 interact. Where the agent hosting the open house is a member of the
listing broker's office, the article states the agent need not provide the IABS or enter into a written agreement
with prospective buyers, but must disclose that he or she represents the owner, orally or in writing, as
§ 1101.558(b) requires. Where the hosting agent is not a member of the listing broker's office and does not
represent the seller — a showing agent, for instance — the article states the agent must provide the IABS and
enter into a written agreement as described by § 1101.563(c) with prospective buyers, even when a prospective
buyer already has a written representation agreement with another broker. Both must happen before the showing,
so ideally the agreement is signed before the buyer enters the property. The article states the uncomfortable
consequence plainly: if a buyer refuses to sign, the agent cannot show the property, and license holders can face
disciplinary action for failing to enter into the agreement.

**Subagency, handled accurately.** TREC's article states that two references to subagency were removed from
TRELA, so the circumstances in which subagency could arise in practice are limited; it also states that subagency
has not been eliminated generally as a legal concept, and advises a license holder who thinks subagency may be
involved to contact the broker or an attorney. Both halves matter. Do not tell a Texas consumer that subagency
"no longer exists" — say that TRELA no longer references it, that its practical field has narrowed, and that
whether it arises in an unusual arrangement is a question for the broker and counsel.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: intermediary consent and appointment mechanics
chunks.excerpt:
**Two provisions police all of this.** Section 1101.652(b)(7) reaches a license holder who "fails to make clear
to all parties to a real estate transaction the party for whom the license holder is acting," and § 1101.652(b)(8)
one who "receives compensation from more than one party to a real estate transaction without the full knowledge
and consent of all parties to the transaction." Whom you serve and who pays you must both be on the table before the money moves.

### Statute reading exercise: intermediary consent and appointment mechanics

Using only the quoted text of Occupations Code §§ 1101.559, 1101.560, 1101.561 and 1101.651(d) in this unit,
answer:

1. Section 1101.559(a) sets two requirements for a broker to act as an intermediary. State both, and say which
   concerns money.
2. Under § 1101.560(b), what two things must be true before the broker may appoint associated license holders to
   the two sides? Which is a notice obligation, and who must receive the notice?
3. A seller told the listing agent orally, "I'd take $10,000 less if I had to." Under § 1101.651(d)(1), may the
   appointed license holder on the buyer's side be told? What exact form would the seller's permission take?
4. A buyer instructs the broker in writing not to disclose that the buyer is relocating on a deadline. The broker
   later learns the house has an active roof leak. Under § 1101.651(d)(3), which piece of information is protected
   and which is not — and what words in the statute decide it?

### Applied exercise: an in-house match in Round Rock

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
Sanchez Realty holds an exclusive listing on a house in Round Rock. The listing agreement contains a conspicuous
bold-print intermediary paragraph setting out the conduct prohibited by § 1101.651(d) and authorizing the broker
both to act as an intermediary and to make appointments. A buyer arrives through the brokerage's own website and,
after a first substantive communication about that specific house, signs a buyer representation agreement with
Sanchez Realty containing the same conspicuous paragraph and the same appointment authorization. The buyer now
wants to write an offer on the listing.

1. Is the broker permitted to proceed as an intermediary, and is the broker *required* to? Cite the subsections
   answering each half.
2. What must the broker do before the two associated license holders may advise their respective sides, and in
   what form?
3. The license holder appointed to the seller wants to tell the buyer's appointed license holder that the seller
   is motivated and will take less. What does § 1101.651(d)(1) require first?
4. If instead the buyer had signed nothing and simply asked to see the house, and the Sanchez Realty agent
   contacted does represent the owner, what does § 1101.562(b)(1) require before the showing, and what does
   § 1101.563(b) require in addition?

## Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business

A brokerage is a business built on a licence, and nearly everything distinctive about how it is organized traces
back to the fact that the licence — not the salesperson's reputation, not the office lease, not the sign — is
what the law regulates. This unit describes the legal architecture and the way the business actually runs, and
labels which is which.

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
**The broker is the licensed enterprise.** Section 1101.002(4) defines "license holder" as a broker or sales
agent licensed under Chapter 1101. A broker may be an individual or a business entity, and § 1101.351(a-1)
provides that unless a business entity holds a licence, the entity may not act as a broker. Section 1101.355(a)
adds two eligibility requirements for an entity: it must "designate one of its managing officers as its broker
for purposes of this chapter," and it must "provide proof that the entity maintains errors and omissions
insurance with a minimum annual limit of $1 million for each occurrence if the designated broker owns less than
10 percent of the business entity." Subsection (b) bars an entity from acting as a broker unless its designated
broker is a licensed individual broker in active status and good standing according to Commission records, and
(b-1) lets the Commission weigh disciplinary history and amounts owed in judging good standing.

Section 1101.355(c) requires a business entity that receives compensation on behalf of a license holder to be
licensed as a broker, but § 1101.355(d) and (e) create a narrow registration alternative for a wholly
compensation-receiving limited liability company or S corporation that performs no other acts of a broker,
registers with the Commission, and is at least 51 percent owned by the license holder whose pay it receives.

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
**Becoming a broker.** Section 1101.356(a) requires an applicant for a broker licence to show at least four years
of active experience as a license holder during the 60 months preceding the application, the qualifying and
related coursework required by Commission rule (not to exceed 60 semester hours or equivalent classroom hours),
and attendance at the broker responsibility course approved under § 1101.458. Subsection (b) exempts an applicant
already licensed as a broker in a state with comparable requirements; (b-1) leaves "active experience" to
Commission rule. That four-year requirement is why a Texas brokerage is not a flat organization of equals: the
person carrying the licence has, by statutory design, done the work longer.

**Where the brokerage sits.** Section 1101.552(a) requires a resident broker to maintain a fixed office in Texas,
with the address designated on the licence, and (b) requires an application designating a new location not later
than the tenth day after moving; (d) excuses a nonresident licensed broker from maintaining a Texas place of
business; (e) and (f) require every license holder to keep current contact information on file with the
Commission. Subsection (g) defines "associated broker" as "a broker who associates with and is paid through
another broker under a relationship that is intended to be a continuous relationship, including as an employee or
an ongoing independent contractor."

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
**Sponsorship: the spine of the organization.** Everything a sales agent does is done for the broker. Section
1101.351(c) forbids a sales agent from engaging or attempting to engage in brokerage unless sponsored by a
licensed broker and acting for that broker; § 1101.554 has the Commission deliver a copy of the sales agent
licence to the sponsoring broker; and § 1101.803 makes the broker liable to the Commission, the public and the
broker's clients for the conduct of the broker and of any sales agent associated with or acting for the broker.
Section 1101.652(b)(26) makes it a ground for discipline to establish "an association by employment or otherwise
with a person other than a license holder if the person is expected or required to act as a license holder" — the
provision that stops a brokerage from staffing production with unlicensed assistants quietly doing licensed work.

As a matter of business practice rather than law, most Texas sales agents are engaged as independent contractors
rather than employees, are paid by commission split rather than salary, and pay some combination of desk,
transaction or franchise fees. None of that is prescribed by Chapter 1101, and nothing is cited for it here. What
Chapter 1101 insists on is that whatever the internal economics, the *authority* is the broker's.

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
**Supervision.** Section 1101.458(a) provides that during the term of the current licence, a broker responsibility
course approved by the Commission must be attended by a licensed broker and by a sales agent "who supervises
another license holder." Subsection (b) has the Commission prescribe the course by rule and caps it at six
classroom hours; (c) lets those hours count toward the hours described by § 1101.455(f); (d) exempts a broker
exempt from continuing education under § 1101.456. Read with § 1101.803, the design is plain: the statute assigns
the liability to the broker and then requires the broker — and any supervising sales agent — to be trained in
carrying it.

**Listing and buyer representation agreements.** The business often calls these **employment contracts**: the
client engages the brokerage to perform services and agrees what it will be paid if it performs. That is a
teaching convention, not a statutory label, and it does not make the sales agent an employee of the client. What
the law adds is specific.

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
First, a **definite termination date** under § 1101.652(b)(12). Second, on the residential buyer side, the
**§ 1101.563 written agreement** described in the previous unit, with its required contents, its separate-agreement
rule in subsection (d), and its non-exclusivity and fourteen-day cap for showing-only agreements in subsection (e).
Third, the **writing requirement for suing over a commission**: § 1101.806(c) provides that "A person may not
maintain an action in this state to recover a commission for the sale or purchase of real estate unless the promise
or agreement on which the action is based, or a memorandum, is in writing and signed by the party against whom the
action is brought or by a person authorized by that party to sign the document." Section 1101.806(b) adds that no
one may maintain an action to collect compensation for a brokerage act performed in Texas without alleging and
proving that the person was a license holder when the act was commenced, or an attorney licensed in any state, and
subsection (a) carves out compensation-sharing agreements among license holders. Subsection (d) attaches a striking
forfeiture: a license holder who fails to advise a buyer as provided by § 1101.555 "may not receive payment of or
recover any commission agreed to be paid on the sale." Section 1101.555 requires that when an offer to purchase
Texas real estate is signed, the license holder advise each buyer in writing to have the abstract examined by an
attorney of the buyer's choosing or be provided with or obtain a title insurance policy — a failure independently
disciplinable under § 1101.652(b)(29).

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
**Compensation: how it flows, and what you must say about it.** Three rules control the flow. Under § 1101.651(a) a
licensed broker may not pay a commission to or otherwise compensate a person directly or indirectly for performing
an act of a broker unless the person is a license holder, or a broker licensed in another state who conducts none of
the negotiations in Texas. Under § 1101.651(b) a sales agent may not accept compensation for a real estate
transaction from anyone other than the sponsoring broker, or the broker who was sponsoring the agent when the
compensation was earned; under (c) a sales agent may not pay a commission to anyone except through the sponsoring
broker. Section 1101.652(b)(11) makes paying or dividing a fee with someone who is not a license holder or a broker
or sales agent licensed in another state a ground for discipline. The effect is a closed loop: a grateful buyer
cannot hand a cheque directly to the sales agent who found the house.
