chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
Now the sentence that must be said out loud. **Broker compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable.**
That is a statutory disclosure, not a slogan: § 1101.563(c)(2) requires the written agreement with a prospective
residential buyer to "disclose in conspicuous language that broker compensation is not set by law and is fully
negotiable," and § 1101.563(c)(1)(E) requires the agreement to state "the amount or rate of compensation the broker
will receive and how this amount will be determined." Chapter 1101 contains no commission rate and recognizes no
customary rate. Telling a consumer that a rate is standard or required is false, and if it misleads it is exposed
under § 1101.652(b)(23)(A) and under the DTPA in Unit 5. Related money duties: § 1101.652(b)(13) reaches accepting,
receiving or charging "an undisclosed commission, rebate, or direct profit on an expenditure made for a principal,"
and § 1101.652(b)(8) reaches compensation from more than one party without all parties' full knowledge and consent.

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
*Illustration, for arithmetic only.* Suppose a Texas seller and a listing broker negotiate a total fee of 5.5% on a
$400,000 sale, and the listing broker's written agreement with a cooperating broker allocates 2.5 percentage points
to the cooperating side. Total fee: $400,000 × 0.055 = $22,000. Cooperating side: $400,000 × 0.025 = $10,000.
Listing side: $22,000 − $10,000 = $12,000. If the listing brokerage's internal split with its sponsored sales agent
is 70/30 in the agent's favour, the agent's gross share is $12,000 × 0.70 = $8,400 and the brokerage retains $3,600
— and under § 1101.651(b) that $8,400 must reach the agent through the sponsoring broker, not from the title company
or the seller. Every number here is invented for the arithmetic; none is standard, customary or required.

**Advertising, names and teams.** Section 1101.652(b)(23) makes it a ground for discipline to publish or cause to be
published an advertisement that "(A) misleads or is likely to deceive the public; (B) tends to create a misleading
impression; (C) implies that a sales agent is responsible for the operation of the broker's real estate brokerage
business; or (D) fails to include the name of the broker for whom the license holder acts, which name may be the
licensed name, assumed name, or trade name of the broker as authorized by a law of this state and registered with
the commission." Subparagraphs (C) and (D) are the statutory basis for how Texas treats **team names**: a team may
market under a name, but the advertising must carry the broker's name and must not imply that the team or the sales
agent runs the brokerage. The registration requirements for assumed, alternate and team names are matters of
Commission rule; those rules are not among the sources read for this module, so nothing f

chunks.heading: Unit: Brokerage & Nature of the Brokerage Business
chunks.excerpt:
urther is stated here.

Section 1101.652(b)(18) forbids placing a sign offering property for sale or lease without the owner's or authorized
agent's written consent; (b)(19) and (b)(20) forbid offering to sell or lease property without the owner's knowledge
and consent or on unauthorized terms. Section 1101.804 protects anyone assembling market data: a license holder or
nonprofit real estate board or association that provides information about sales prices or terms of sale to
facilitate listing, selling, leasing, financing or appraisal "is not liable to another person for providing that
information unless the disclosure of that information is specifically prohibited by statute."

**Poaching and interference.** Section 1101.652(b)(22) makes it a ground for discipline to negotiate or attempt to
negotiate a sale, exchange or lease with an owner, landlord, buyer or tenant "with knowledge that that person is a
party to an outstanding written contract that grants exclusive agency to another broker in connection with the
transaction," and (b)(21) reaches inducing a party to break a contract to substitute a new one. Section
1101.557(b)(1) forbids instructing another broker to violate (b)(22). But § 1101.557(c)(3) creates a safe harbour:
sole delivery of an offer to a party does not violate (b)(22) if the party's broker consents, a copy is sent to that
broker unless a sealed-bid governmental process forbids it, and nothing else violating (b)(22) is done.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: setting up a new Texas brokerage
chunks.excerpt:
**Two structural cautions.** Section 1101.652(b)(16) makes it a ground for discipline to act "in a dual capacity as
broker and undisclosed principal in a real estate transaction," and § 1101.652(a-1)(1) reaches misrepresentation,
dishonesty or fraud when a license holder buys, sells, trades or leases property in the license holder's own name, a
spouse's name, or the name of a person related within the first degree by consanguinity. Buying for your own account
is lawful; doing it without saying so is not. And § 1101.801 removes any comfort from surviving a Commission
proceeding: "Disciplinary action taken against a person under Section 1101.652 does not relieve the person from civil
or criminal liability." The licence and the lawsuit are separate exposures.

### Applied exercise: setting up a new Texas brokerage

Dana holds a Texas sales agent licence and has been active for five of the past sixty months. She forms a Texas
limited liability company, "Hill Country Doors LLC," intending it to hold listings and receive commissions, and asks
a broker friend to serve as its designated broker while owning none of the company. She plans to advertise under the
team name "The Door Team," to hire an unlicensed assistant to hold open houses and answer buyers' questions about the
properties, and to pay a $500 referral bonus to a past client who sends her business.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
1. Under § 1101.351(a-1) and § 1101.355(a), what does the LLC need before it may act as a broker, and what additional
   proof does the designated broker's zero ownership trigger?
2. Under § 1101.356(a), is Dana presently eligible to apply for a broker licence? Which element is the obstacle?
3. Under § 1101.652(b)(26), what is wrong with the plan for the unlicensed assistant?
4. Under § 1101.651(a) and § 1101.652(b)(11), may the $500 referral bonus be paid to the past client?
5. Under § 1101.652(b)(23)(C) and (D), what must "The Door Team" advertising include, and what must it not imply?

## Unit: Fiduciary Duties

An agent occupies a position of trust, and the duties flowing from it are **fiduciary duties**. They require the agent
to subordinate the agent's own interest to the client's to a degree ordinary arm's-length dealing never demands. The
classical catalogue has six entries. Chapter 1101 does not set them out as a list under that heading, but nearly every
one has a Texas disciplinary provision behind it. This unit pairs each duty with that provision and is explicit where
no held source supplies one.

One Texas override first. Section 1101.561(a) provides that the duties of a license holder acting as an intermediary
under Subchapter L "supersede the duties of a license holder established under any other law, including common law."
When you are an intermediary, the governing description of your obligations is the Subchapter L framework from Unit 2
— written consent, fair and impartial conduct, the appointment mechanics, and the five prohibitions of § 1101.651(d) —
not the single-agency catalogue below.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
**Loyalty.** The agent acts in the client's interest, not the agent's own, and does not profit secretly from the
agency. Three provisions enforce it. Section 1101.652(b)(13) reaches accepting, receiving or charging "an undisclosed
commission, rebate, or direct profit on an expenditure made for a principal" — the repair invoice with a quiet markup,
the vendor kickback. Section 1101.652(b)(16) reaches acting "in a dual capacity as broker and undisclosed principal in
a real estate transaction" — buying the client's listing, directly or through a controlled entity, without saying the
buyer is you. Section 1101.652(b)(8) reaches receipt of "compensation from more than one party to a real estate
transaction without the full knowledge and consent of all parties to the transaction", which is also why
§ 1101.559(a)(2) requires intermediary consent to state the source of expected compensation. Notice what
each condemns: not the profit, not the second cheque, not the purchase — the *undisclosed* profit, the
*unconsented* second cheque, the *undisclosed* self-dealing. Disclosure converts a breach into a permissible arrangement.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
**Obedience to lawful instructions.** The agent follows the client's instructions within the scope of the agency —
lawful ones only. Sections 1101.652(b)(19) and (20) supply the enforcement: it is a ground for discipline to offer to
sell or lease property "without the knowledge and consent of the owner of the real property or the owner's authorized
agent," or "on terms other than those authorized by the owner." Section 1101.652(b)(18) adds the sign. The limiting
word is *lawful*. A seller's instruction not to present offers from buyers of a particular race is not one the agent
may obey: § 1101.652(b)(32) makes discrimination against an owner, potential buyer, landlord or potential tenant on
the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry — including steering
a prospect interested in equivalent properties to a different area on those bases — an independent ground for
discipline.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
**Disclosure.** The agent tells the client what the client needs to know. Section 1101.557(b)(2) requires a representing
broker to inform the party of "material information related to a transaction to list, buy, sell, or lease the party's
real estate, including the receipt of an offer by the broker," and (b)(3) requires the broker at a minimum to answer
the party's questions and present any offer to or from the party. Toward the other side of the table the duty is sharper
than students expect. Section 1101.652(b)(3) reaches "a material misrepresentation to a potential buyer concerning a
significant defect, including a latent structural defect, known to the license holder that would be a significant factor
to a reasonable and prudent buyer in making a decision to purchase real property," and (b)(4) reaches failing to
disclose such a known defect to a potential buyer. That duty runs to a *potential buyer* — a customer, not a client.
Representing the seller does not license you to conceal a known significant defect from the person across the table.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
Two boundaries deserve equal emphasis. Section 1101.556 provides that notwithstanding other law, a license holder is not
required to inquire about, disclose or release information relating to whether an occupant had or may have had AIDS, an
HIV-related illness or an HIV infection as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or whether "a death
occurred on a property by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the condition of the property"; § 1101.802
adds that a person is not civilly or criminally liable for failing to disclose the HIV/AIDS matters described. Running
the other way, § 1101.555 imposes the affirmative written advisory about an abstract examination or title policy, with
discipline under § 1101.652(b)(29) and loss of commission under § 1101.806(d) if it is skipped.

**Confidentiality.** The agent does not disclose the client's confidences, above all those that weaken the client's
bargaining position. In the intermediary setting the duty is statutory: § 1101.651(d)(1) and (2) forbid disclosing that
the seller will take less or that the buyer will pay more absent a separate written instruction from that party, and
(d)(3) forbids disclosing "any confidential information or any information a party specifically instructs the broker or
sales agent in writing not to disclose," subject to three exceptions — a separate written instruction, a requirement to
disclose under Chapter 1101 or a court order, and information that "materially relates to the condition of the property."
Outside the intermediary setting Chapter 1101 contains no general confidentiality section, and this module does not
pretend otherwise; in ordinary single agency the duty is a common-law fiduciary duty. But the property-condition
carve-out in (d)(3) shows how Texas res

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
olves the tension whenever it arises: negotiating posture is confidential,
defects in the house are not.

**Reasonable care and diligence.** Section 1101.652(b)(1) reaches a license holder who "acts negligently or
incompetently," and § 1101.652(a)(6) one who "fails to consider market conditions for the specific geographic area in
which the license holder is providing a service." Section 1101.652(b)(2) reaches conduct "that is dishonest or in bad
faith or that demonstrates untrustworthiness," and (b)(5) "a false promise that is likely to influence a person to enter
into an agreement when the license holder is unable or does not intend to keep the promise." Section 1101.652(b)(28)
requires providing, on request, a copy of a transaction document to a person who signed it, and § 1101.652(a)(5) reaches
failing to surrender a requested document to its owner without just cause. Care is also where competence has an edge:
§ 1101.654 draws the line at practising law, and the diligent answer to a legal question is a referral, not a guess.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
**Accounting.** Section 1101.652(b)(9) reaches failing "within a reasonable time to properly account for or remit money
that is received by the license holder and that belongs to another person," and (b)(10) reaches commingling another
person's money with the license holder's own. Section 1101.652(b)(30) requires depositing escrow or trust funds within a
reasonable time, either in trust with a title company authorized to do business in Texas or in a custodial, trust or
escrow account maintained for that purpose in a Texas-authorized banking institution, and (b)(31) forbids disbursing
from such an account "before the completion or termination of the real estate transaction." Section 1101.652(b)(24) adds
the paperwork: withholding from or inserting into a statement of account or invoice a statement the license holder knows
makes it materially inaccurate.

**Which duties survive termination.** The classical teaching is that the forward-looking duties end with the agency —
loyalty in future dealings, obedience, the duty to keep working — while two continue: **confidentiality**, because the
client's secrets do not become yours when the listing expires, and **accounting**, because money belonging to another
does not become yours when the relationship ends. Be precise about authority. No source read for this module states a
survival rule in so many words. What the text supports is this: the accounting provisions in § 1101.652(b)(9), (10),
(30) and (31) speak of money "that belongs to another person" and of the transaction's completion or termination, not of
a live agency, so an expired listing does not release the license holder from them; and the confidentiality prohibition
in § 1101.651(d)(3) contains no expiration and no exception for a concluded transaction. Beyond that te

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: the repair invoice and the expired listing
chunks.excerpt:
xtual
observation, the survival of confidentiality in ordinary single agency is a common-law proposition, identified here as
one rather than cited to a statute.

Finally, hold on to § 1101.801: "Disciplinary action taken against a person under Section 1101.652 does not relieve the
person from civil or criminal liability." A fiduciary breach in Texas can cost the licence and cost a judgment, and
neither proceeding substitutes for the other.

### Applied exercise: the repair invoice and the expired listing

A license holder representing a Bryan seller arranges pre-listing repairs. The contractor bills $4,200. The license
holder forwards the seller an invoice for $4,700, keeping the difference as "coordination time," and says nothing about
it. Separately, the seller told the license holder in confidence that a divorce is forcing a quick sale. The listing
expires unsold. Two months later the license holder, now representing a buyer, shows that same house — relisted with
another brokerage — and remarks, "They're divorcing; they'll take a lot less."

1. Which subsection of § 1101.652 does the invoice markup implicate, and what single act would have changed the analysis?
2. Was the seller's motivation the sort of information § 1101.651(d)(3) protects — and what does this module say about the
   authority for treating confidentiality as surviving the end of the agency?
3. If the license holder still holds $500 of the seller's unspent repair advance, which two subsections of § 1101.652
   govern what must happen to it, and does the listing's expiration change the answer?
4. Suppose the Commission takes no action. Under § 1101.801, is the license holder therefore safe from the seller?

## Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
Business & Commerce Code Chapter 17, Subchapter E — cited under its own short title in § 17.41 as the **Deceptive Trade
Practices-Consumer Protection Act** — is the statute that most often turns a careless sentence about a property into
personal liability for the person who said it. It is not a real estate statute. It is a general consumer statute, which
is precisely why it reaches so far into this business.

**How it is read.** Section 17.44(a) instructs that the subchapter "shall be liberally construed and applied to promote
its underlying purposes, which are to protect consumers against false, misleading, and deceptive business practices,
unconscionable actions, and breaches of warranty and to provide efficient and economical procedures to secure such
protection." Read the whole sentence: the liberal-construction command is tied to both halves of the purpose — consumer
protection *and* efficient, economical procedure. Section 17.44(b) provides that Chapter 27, Property Code, prevails over
the subchapter to the extent of any conflict. Section 17.43 makes the remedies cumulative rather than exclusive, while
cautioning that a violation of another law is not by itself a DTPA violation.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
**Waiver is presumptively void.** Section 17.42(a): "Any waiver by a consumer of the provisions of this subchapter is
contrary to public policy and is unenforceable and void" — valid only if it is in writing and signed by the consumer, the
consumer is not in a significantly disparate bargaining position, and the consumer is represented by legal counsel in
seeking or acquiring the goods or services. Section 17.42(b) voids it if that counsel was identified, suggested or
selected by a defendant, and § 17.42(c) requires the waiver to be conspicuous, in boldface type of at least 10 points and
headed "Waiver of Consumer Rights" or words of similar meaning. You cannot paper your way out of the DTPA with a clause in
your own agreement.

**Who is a "consumer."** This is the threshold question and the one students skip. Section 17.45(4): "'Consumer' means an
individual, partnership, corporation, this state, or a subdivision or agency of this state who seeks or acquires by
purchase or lease, any goods or services, except that the term does not include a business consumer that has assets of
$25 million or more, or that is owned or controlled by a corporation or entity with assets of $25 million or more." Two
elements: the person must *seek or acquire* — an actual or prospective purchaser or lessee, not a bystander — and what is
sought must be *goods or services*.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
Both terms reach real estate. Section 17.45(1): "'Goods' means tangible chattels or real property purchased or leased for
use." Section 17.45(2): "'Services' means work, labor, or service purchased or leased for use, including services
furnished in connection with the sale or repair of goods." Section 17.45(6) defines "trade" and "commerce" as "the
advertising, offering for sale, sale, lease, or distribution of any good or service, of any property, tangible or
intangible, real, personal, or mixed," including trade or commerce directly or indirectly affecting the people of Texas.
So a Texas buyer of a house is a consumer seeking goods, and a client engaging a brokerage is a consumer seeking services.
Section 17.45(10) defines "business consumer" — one seeking goods or services for commercial or business use — the
category the $25 million ceiling operates on, and § 17.45(12) defines "residence" as a single-family house, duplex,
triplex, quadruplex, or condominium or cooperative unit occupied or to be occupied as the consumer's residence, a
definition that matters for the exemptions below.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
**What is unlawful.** Section 17.46(a) declares that "False, misleading, or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of
any trade or commerce are hereby declared unlawful and are subject to action by the consumer protection division" under the
enforcement sections it names. Note how the subsection is built: the declaration of unlawfulness and public enforcement by
the consumer protection division of the attorney general's office arrive in the same breath, and a private consumer's route
to relief is § 17.50, not § 17.46(a). Section 17.46(b) then supplies the **laundry list**, introduced by
"includes, but is not limited to, the following acts." That open-ended phrase governs enforcement by the
attorney general; for a *private consumer suit* the list is closed, because § 17.46(d) provides that for
the relief authorized in § 17.50(a)(1) the term "is limited to the acts enumerated in specific
subdivisions of Subsection (b)." A private plaintiff must point at a numbered item.

The items a license holder is most likely to meet, in the statute's words:

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
- **§ 17.46(b)(5)** — "representing that goods or services have sponsorship, approval, characteristics, ingredients, uses,
  benefits, or quantities which they do not have or that a person has a sponsorship, approval, status, affiliation, or
  connection which the person does not." This is the workhorse. "The addition was permitted." "It's zoned for a duplex."
  "That's a new roof." Each is a representation about a characteristic, use or benefit.
- **§ 17.46(b)(7)** — "representing that goods or services are of a particular standard, quality, or grade, or that goods
  are of a particular style or model, if they are of another."
- **§ 17.46(b)(12)** — "representing that an agreement confers or involves rights, remedies, or obligations which it does
  not have or involve, or which are prohibited by law."
- **§ 17.46(b)(14)** — "misrepresenting the authority of a salesman, representative or agent to negotiate the final terms of
  a consumer transaction." Overstating your own authority to bind is itself an enumerated deceptive act.
- **§ 17.46(b)(20)** — "representing that a guaranty or warranty confers or involves rights or remedies which it does not
  have or involve."
- **§ 17.46(b)(24)** — "failing to disclose information concerning goods or services which was known at the time of the
  transaction if such failure to disclose such information was intended to induce the consumer into a transaction into which
  the consumer would not have entered had the information been disclosed." Read every element: the information must have been
  *known*, at the time, and the failure must have been *intended to induce*. Silence alone is not (b)(24); silence deployed to
  get the deal signed is.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
**The consumer's causes of action.** Section 17.50(a): "A consumer may maintain an action where any of the following
constitute a producing cause of economic damages or damages for mental anguish": (1) use of a false, misleading or deceptive
act "specifically enumerated in a subdivision of Subsection (b) of Section 17.46" *and* "relied on by a consumer to the
consumer's detriment"; (2) breach of an express or implied warranty; (3) "any unconscionable action or course of action by any
person"; or (4) an act in violation of Chapter 541, Insurance Code. Two features of (a)(1) matter: the standard is **producing
cause**, not proximate cause, and the laundry-list route requires **detrimental reliance**. "Unconscionable action or course of
action" is defined in § 17.45(5) as "an act or practice which, to a consumer's detriment, takes advantage of the lack of
knowledge, ability, experience, or capacity of the consumer to a grossly unfair degree" — a high bar, but a route that depends
on no numbered item.

**Damages, and what "knowingly" and "intentionally" do to them.** Section 17.50(b)(1) is worth knowing verbatim. A prevailing
consumer may obtain "the amount of economic damages found by the trier of fact. If the trier of fact finds that the conduct of
the defendant was committed knowingly, the consumer may also recover damages for mental anguish, as found by the trier of fact,
and the trier of fact may award not more than three times the amount of economic damages; or if the trier of fact finds the
conduct was committed intentionally, the consumer may recover damages for mental anguish, as found by the trier of fact, and
the trier of fact may award not more than three times the amount of damages for mental anguish and economic damages."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
Parse the tiers. **Knowingly** unlocks mental anguish damages plus additional damages of up to three times *economic* damages.
**Intentionally** unlocks mental anguish damages plus additional damages of up to three times the *combined* mental anguish and
economic damages. The base is defined in § 17.45(11): "'Economic damages' means compensatory damages for pecuniary loss,
including costs of repair and replacement," excluding exemplary damages and damages for physical pain and mental anguish.

The mental states are the practical heart of DTPA risk management. Section 17.45(9): "'Knowingly' means actual awareness, at the
time of the act or practice complained of, of the falsity, deception, or unfairness of the act or practice giving rise to the
consumer's claim... but actual awareness may be inferred where objective manifestations indicate that a person acted with actual
awareness." Section 17.45(13): "'Intentionally' means actual awareness of the falsity, deception, or unfairness of the act or
practice, or the condition, defect, or failure constituting a breach of warranty giving rise to the consumer's claim, coupled
with the specific intent that the consumer act in detrimental reliance on the falsity or deception or in detrimental ignorance
of the unfairness." Intention may be inferred from objective manifestations or "from facts showing that a defendant acted with
flagrant disregard of prudent and fair business practices to the extent that the defendant should be treated as having acted
intentionally." That closing measure matters: flagrant disregard is not itself intent, it is evidence from which intent may be
inferred, and only where it rises to the level at which the defendant should be treated as having acted intentionally. Neither
state requires a confession.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
Section 17.50(b) also authorizes injunctive relief, orders restoring money or property acquired in violation of the subchapter,
and other relief the court deems proper. Section 17.50(d) provides that "Each consumer who prevails shall be awarded court costs
and reasonable and necessary attorneys' fees" — mandatory, and often the largest number in a small case; § 17.50(c) balances it
by requiring an award of fees and costs to the defendant on a finding that the action was groundless in fact or law, brought in
bad faith, or brought for harassment. Section 17.50(e) excludes attorneys' fees, costs and prejudgment interest from the
computation of additional damages, and § 17.50(g) provides that Chapter 41, Civil Practice and Remedies Code, does not apply.

**Pre-suit notice and the settlement window.** Section 17.505(a) makes notice a prerequisite: a consumer "shall give written
notice to the person at least 60 days before filing the suit advising the person in reasonable detail of the consumer's specific
complaint and the amount of economic damages, damages for mental anguish, and expenses, including attorneys' fees, if any,
reasonably incurred by the consumer in asserting the claim." Section 17.505(b) excuses notice where 60 days is impracticable
because suit must be filed to prevent limitations from running, or where the claim is a counterclaim. Under § 17.505(c)–(e) a
defendant who received no notice may file a plea in abatement not later than the 30th day after its original answer, the suit
abates automatically on the 11th day after a verified, uncontroverted plea, and the abatement runs until the 60th day after
notice is properly served.

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
That period is an opportunity, not a formality. Section 17.5052(a) permits a person who receives § 17.505 notice to tender an
offer of settlement during the 60 days after receipt; under (d) the offer must separately state an amount settling the damages
claim and an amount for the consumer's attorneys' fees incurred to that date, and under (g) and (h), if the amount tendered proves
to be the same as, substantially the same as, or more than the damages the trier of fact finds, the consumer's recovery of damages
and fees is capped accordingly. A well-judged early tender therefore limits the exposure.

**Defenses.** Section 17.506(a) gives a defense to any damages or attorneys' fees on proof that "before consummation of the
transaction he gave reasonable and timely written notice to the plaintiff of the defendant's reliance on" written information
about the particular goods or service obtained from official government records or another source, or about a test required by a
government agency — in each case where the information was false or inaccurate and "the defendant did not know and could not
reasonably have known of the falsity or inaccuracy." Section 17.506(b) requires proof that the information was a producing cause
of the damage, and § 17.506(c) permits suit against the third party who supplied it, without privity. Section 17.506(d) supplies
a second, complete defense: a defendant who received the consumer's notice and, "within 30 days after the day on which the
defendant received the notice," tendered the damages claimed plus the consumer's reasonably incurred expenses including
attorneys' fees, has a defense to the cause of action. Section 17.565 sets the limitations period at two years after the act or
practice occurred, or two years after the consumer discovered

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
or should reasonably have discovered it, extendable by 180 days
where the delay was caused by the defendant knowingly acting to induce postponement.

**The exemptions — including one written for license holders.** Section 17.49(c) is the **professional services exemption**:
"Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a claim for damages based on the rendering of a professional service, the essence of
which is the providing of advice, judgment, opinion, or similar professional skill." It then removes five things from that
protection, among them an express misrepresentation of a material fact that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment or
opinion; a failure to disclose in violation of § 17.46(b)(24); and an unconscionable action or course of action that cannot be so
characterized.

Subsection (i) is written for this profession, and every Texas license holder should be able to recite its shape: "Nothing in this
subchapter shall apply to a claim against a person licensed as a broker or salesperson under Chapter 1101" of the Occupations Code
"arising from an act or omission by the person while acting as a broker or salesperson." The subsection then withdraws that
protection in three cases: "(1) an express misrepresentation of a material fact that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment,
or opinion"; (2) a failure to disclose information in violation of § 17.46(b)(24); or "(3) an unconscionable action or course of
action that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment, or opinion."

chunks.heading: Unit: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices - Consumer Protection Act
chunks.excerpt:
Understand what that gives you and what it does not. It protects the *advisory* part of the job — the market opinion, the pricing
judgment, the strategic counsel. It gives you nothing for a flat factual assertion. "I think this will appraise" is advice. "It
appraised at $412,000 last month" is an express misrepresentation of material fact if it did not. The exemption is drawn exactly
along the line between opinion and fact, and it is on the fact side that license holders get sued.

Two further exemptions turn on transaction size. Section 17.49(f) exempts a claim arising out of a written contract where the
transaction or set of related transactions involves total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000, the consumer was
represented in negotiating it by legal counsel not identified, suggested or selected by the defendant, and "the contract does not
involve the consumer's residence." Section 17.49(g) exempts a cause of action arising from a transaction or set of related
transactions involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, "other than a cause of action involving a
consumer's residence." Note the residence carve-out in both: the statute is most protective exactly where an individual's home is
concerned.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: working the § 17.46(b) laundry list
chunks.excerpt:
**The practical lesson.** Your Texas buyer or seller is almost certainly a "consumer" under § 17.45(4), because a house is "goods"
under § 17.45(1) and brokerage is "services" under § 17.45(2). The sentence that hurts you is the confident factual one: it lands
in § 17.46(b)(5) or (7), falls outside the § 17.49(i) exemption because it cannot be characterized as advice or opinion, and under
§ 17.50(a)(1) need only be a producing cause of economic damages and have been relied on. If the trier of fact concludes you had
actual awareness of its falsity — inferable under § 17.45(9) from objective manifestations — mental anguish damages and up to
treble economic damages come into play under § 17.50(b)(1), along with mandatory attorneys' fees under § 17.50(d). And § 1101.801
reminds you that none of this is instead of a Commission proceeding.

The defensive habits follow from the statute rather than from folklore. Attribute every fact to its source — the survey, the
appraisal district record, the inspection report, the seller's disclosure — in writing, which is also the posture § 17.506(a)
rewards. Say "I don't know; let's verify" instead of answering from memory. Disclose what you know about the property, especially
anything meeting the "known at the time" element of § 17.46(b)(24), remembering that § 1101.652(b)(3) and (4) independently
require disclosure of known significant defects. And when a demand letter arrives, read § 17.505 before responding: the 60-day
window is the cheapest moment the dispute will ever have.

### Statute reading exercise: working the § 17.46(b) laundry list

Using only the text quoted in this unit from Business & Commerce Code §§ 17.45, 17.46, 17.49 and 17.50, answer:

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: the flooded garage in Katy
chunks.excerpt:
1. Section 17.46(b) says the term "includes, but is not limited to" the listed acts. Why does § 17.46(d) mean a private consumer
   plaintiff must nevertheless identify a numbered subdivision?
2. A license holder tells a buyer the house has "a brand-new HVAC system" when the unit is nine years old. Which subdivision of
   § 17.46(b) fits most directly, and which alternative could also be argued?
3. Under § 17.46(b)(24), what two elements beyond mere silence must a plaintiff establish?
4. Under § 17.50(a)(1), what must the consumer show in addition to the enumerated act, and what is the required causal standard?
5. Under § 17.49(i), which is protected by the license holder exemption and which is not: (a) "In my view this street will hold
   its value well"; (b) "The seller replaced the sewer line in 2021"?

### Applied exercise: the flooded garage in Katy

A married couple buys a house in Katy for $365,000 as their residence. During a showing, the sales agent — who represents the
seller — is asked whether the garage has ever taken water. The agent, who two months earlier read an email from the seller
describing water in the garage after a storm, replies, "No, this place has never had any water intrusion." The buyers rely on the
answer, buy the house, and after the first heavy rain spend $18,000 on drainage and remediation. They also testify to sleeplessness
and distress. The agent was sponsored by a broker at all relevant times.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. Are the buyers "consumers" under § 17.45(4)? Identify the goods or services and confirm that no part of the definition's
   exclusion applies on these facts.
2. Which subdivision of § 17.46(b) does the statement most directly implicate, and could § 17.46(b)(24) also be in play? What
   element of (b)(24) would have to be proved?
3. Does the § 17.49(i) exemption protect the agent here? Identify the words of the exemption and of its exception that decide it.
4. Assume the trier of fact finds $18,000 of economic damages and finds the conduct was committed knowingly. Under § 17.50(b)(1),
   what becomes available that was not available without that finding, and what is the maximum multiple of economic damages the
   trier of fact may award? Now assume the finding is "intentionally" — what changes about the multiplier's base?
5. Under § 17.505(a), what must the buyers do at least 60 days before filing suit, and under § 17.5052 and § 17.506(d), what two
   responses are open to the agent and the broker during that period?
6. Under § 1101.652(b)(3) and (4) and § 1101.801, what exposure exists alongside the civil claim, and does resolving one dispose of
   the other?

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
This module traced one relationship from creation to consequences. It began with agency itself — the arrangement in which one
person acts for another and binds that other, declared for Texas brokerage by Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) and organized so that
the agency belongs to the broker while the sales agent works through the broker under § 1101.351(c) and § 1101.803. It
distinguished how an agency comes into being, and the difference between the authority the principal actually gave and the
authority a third person is reasonably led to perceive, marking where Texas has legislated over the common law: § 1101.805 on
liability for misrepresentation, § 1101.557(c)(1) on the power to bind, § 1101.654 on the boundary at the practice of law.

It then named the positions a Texas license holder may occupy. Seller and buyer representation are familiar. The two that make this
a Texas course are the **intermediary** — the mechanism Chapter 1101 supplies in place of the dual agency other states use,
requiring written consent under § 1101.559, permitting appointments under § 1101.560, and constrained by the five prohibitions of
§ 1101.651(d) — and the **non-representation showing** under § 1101.562, effective January 1, 2026, which arrives paired with the
written-agreement requirement of § 1101.563 and its fourteen-day, non-exclusive limits on showing-only agreements. Around both sits
the disclosure architecture of § 1101.558: an oral-or-written representation disclosure at first contact, a written notice at first
substantive communication about specific property, and three exceptions including the narrow open-house exception.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The brokerage unit set those positions inside a business — licensed entities and designated brokers under § 1101.355, sponsorship
and supervision under § 1101.351(c), § 1101.458 and § 1101.803, agreements with definite termination dates under § 1101.652(b)(12),
a closed compensation loop under § 1101.651(a)–(c), and the disclosure required by § 1101.563(c)(2) that broker compensation is not
set by law and is fully negotiable. The fiduciary unit gave the relationship its moral content, attaching each duty — loyalty,
obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, care, accounting — to the subsection of § 1101.652 that makes its breach a disciplinary
matter, while being candid about which propositions rest on common law rather than on a statute read for this course. The DTPA unit
then showed what happens when accurate speech fails: a consumer under § 17.45(4), an enumerated act under § 17.46(b), a claim under
§ 17.50 that the § 17.49(i) exemption will not cover because it was fact rather than opinion, and damages that escalate on findings
of knowing or intentional conduct.

You should now be able to name your position in any Texas transaction in one sentence, produce the writing that proves it, state
which duties you owe and what a breach costs under § 1101.652, and recognize before you speak the difference between an opinion the
law protects and a fact the law will hold you to.

lessons.title: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 08

chunks.heading: Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 08
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Principles of Real Estate II — Module 08

## TREC Topic: Fair Housing Laws

**Prescribed time: 170 minutes.** This module carries the five units the Commission's PRINS2-1 course
approval form places under *Fair Housing Laws*, a topic whose scope reaches federal, state and local
fair housing laws.

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: state the protected classes
listed in each subsection of 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and distinguish a reasonable accommodation from a
reasonable modification under § 3604(f)(3); apply the Fair Housing Act's own definitions of
"dwelling," "person," "handicap" and "familial status" in 42 U.S.C. § 3602; state the two exemptions
in § 3603(b), the conditions and limits on each, and explain why neither ever reaches § 3604(c);
identify housing for older persons under § 3607(b) and distinguish its 62-and-over structure from its
55-and-over structure; identify the protected classes, prohibited practices, exemptions and
enforcement path of the Texas Fair Housing Act, Property Code ch. 301, and name the agency that
administers it; define steering, blockbusting and discriminatory advertising and identify the
provision each violates, including the licence-discipline ground in Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(32); state what a "residential real estate-related transaction" is under 42 U.S.C.
§ 3605(b) and who § 3605(a) covers; state what 42 U.S.C. § 3606 reaches in the provision of brokerage
services and compare it with Property Code § 301.027; state what 42 U.S.C. § 3617 forbids and who it
protects; describe the administrative complaint route in 42 U.S.C. § 3610 — who may file, with whom,
within what period, and how conciliation and referral to a certified state or local agency work — and
set it beside the Texas Workforc

chunks.heading: TREC Topic: Fair Housing Laws
chunks.excerpt:
e Commission route in Property Code ch. 301; state the prohibited
bases and permitted inquiries under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1691(a) and (b), and
explain the adverse-action notification owed under § 1691(d); apply the Regulation B rules that
implement ECOA — the definitions in 12 C.F.R. § 1002.2, the general prohibition in § 1002.4, the
limits on requests for information in § 1002.5, and the notification requirements and timing in
§ 1002.9; and explain the congressional findings and purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act,
12 U.S.C. § 2901, describe the assessment and written-evaluation framework in 12 U.S.C. §§ 2902, 2903
and 2906 including the four statutory rating levels, and distinguish that affirmative community-credit
obligation from an individual anti-discrimination claim.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it. On the federal
fair housing side the sources held and read are 42 U.S.C. §§ 3601, 3602, 3603, 3604, 3605, 3606, 3607,
3610 and 3617, and this module teaches each of them from its own text. On the credit side the sources
held and read are 15 U.S.C. §§ 1691, 1691a and 1691c together with four sections of Regulation B, the
Bureau's implementing regulation — 12 C.F.R. §§ 1002.2, 1002.4, 1002.5 and 1002.9. On the community
reinvestment side the sources held and read are 12 U.S.C. §§ 2901, 2902, 2903, 2904, 2905 and 2906.
A few provisions this topic can touch are still **not** among the sources held: the Fair Housing Act's
remaining enforcement sections (42 U.S.C. §§ 3611–3614, which carry the federal election of forum, the
administrative hearing, judicial relief and the Attorney General's patt

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
ern-or-practice action); ECOA's
rulemaking, state-law and civil-liability sections (15 U.S.C. §§ 1691b, 1691d, 1691e and 1691f); the
remaining sections of Regulation B; and any HUD rule, Texas Workforce Commission rule or Texas
municipal ordinance. Where the module reaches those subjects it says so plainly, teaches the parallel
provision that *was* read, and tells you to read the text yourself rather than
paraphrasing text nobody opened. Texas Property Code ch. 301 is taught throughout alongside the
federal Act, not as a substitute for it: a Texas license holder is governed by both, and the places
where the two texts align and the places where they do not are worth knowing precisely. Every name,
address and dollar figure in the illustrations is invented to make a rule visible.

## Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing

Federal fair housing law begins with one sentence. 42 U.S.C. § 3601 says: "It is the policy of the
United States to provide, within constitutional limitations, for fair housing throughout the United
States." That is the whole section — an objective, with no prohibition, no penalty and no protected
class. Everything operative comes later, and a license holder who wants to know what is actually
forbidden must read § 3604. Still, the sentence tells you what kind of statute this is: it reaches
what private owners, landlords, brokers and lenders do with housing, and it does so nationally. A
rural Texas landlord with four units and a Houston management company with four thousand answer to
the same Act.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Where the Act came from, and when each class arrived.** The dates explain why the statute's own
lists are ragged. The source credit under § 3601 is Pub. L. 90–284, title VIII, § 801, Apr. 11, 1968,
and the statutory notes record that Pub. L. 90–284 "may be cited as the 'Civil Rights Act of 1968'"
and that its title VIII "may be cited as the 'Fair Housing Act.'" You will still hear practitioners
call fair housing matters "title VIII" cases. As enacted, § 3604 did not protect sex: the amendments
note under § 3604 records that in 1974 Pub. L. 93–383 "inserted ', sex' after 'religion' wherever
appearing in cls. (a) to (e)." The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, Pub. L. 100–430, then did
three separate things, each recorded in that same note under § 3604 — in § 3604(a) and (b) it
"inserted 'familial status,' after 'sex,'"; in § 3604(c) through (e) it
"inserted 'handicap, familial status,' after 'sex,'"; and § 6(a) "added subsec. (f)," the entire
disability regime, effective "on the 180th day beginning after" September 13, 1988. The § 3601 notes
also record that Pub. L. 104–76 (1995) "may be cited as the 'Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995'"
and amended § 3607.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
So **race, color, religion and national origin** are original 1968 classes, **sex** was added in 1974,
and **familial status** and **handicap** were added in 1988 by insertion rather than by rewriting the
section. That is why the lists differ from subsection to subsection, and why a student who memorizes
"the seven protected classes" as one uniform list will misread the statute. The seven bases § 3604
names somewhere in its text are race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin and
handicap. The federal statute says **handicap**, not "disability"; Texas says disability. Use each
statute's own word when you cite it.

**The words the Act defines for itself.** Section 3602 supplies the definitions used throughout the
subchapter, and several of them decide cases before any prohibition is reached.

**"Dwelling"** (§ 3602(b)) means "any building, structure, or portion thereof which is occupied as, or
designed or intended for occupancy as, a residence by one or more families, and any vacant land which
is offered for sale or lease for the construction or location thereon of any such building, structure,
or portion thereof." Two consequences. A *portion* of a building is a dwelling, so a single rented room
counts. And **vacant land offered for sale or lease for residential construction is a dwelling** — a
raw lot listed for a house is inside the Act, which matters in a state with as much lot inventory as
Texas. Property Code § 301.003(8) defines dwelling to the same effect, land included.

**"Family"** (§ 3602(c)) "includes a single individual," matching Property Code § 301.003(9). So a
statute written in terms of "families" is not a statute about households with children; do not confuse
this definition with familial status.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**"Person"** (§ 3602(d)) "includes one or more individuals, corporations, partnerships, associations,
labor organizations, legal representatives, mutual companies, joint-stock companies, trusts,
unincorporated organizations, trustees, trustees in cases under title 11, receivers, and fiduciaries."
The list opens with *individuals*. That single word is why a sales agent is personally a "person" who
may not do what § 3604 forbids — the brokerage's liability is not a shield, and Property Code
§ 301.003(12) makes the identical point on the Texas side.

**"To rent"** (§ 3602(e)) "includes to lease, to sublease, to let and otherwise to grant for a
consideration the right to occupy premises not owned by the occupant," so a sublease is inside the Act.

**"Handicap"** (§ 3602(h)) means, "with respect to a person— (1) a physical or mental impairment which
substantially limits one or more of such person's major life activities, (2) a record of having such an
impairment, or (3) being regarded as having such an impairment," and "such term does not include
current, illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance." Learn all three prongs. The third —
**regarded as** — means a landlord who acts on an impairment he wrongly believes the applicant has is
inside the definition, so being wrong about the facts is no defence. Texas Property Code § 301.003(6)
tracks the same three prongs and the same drug exclusion, then adds two exclusions the federal
definition does not contain, for sexual orientation and for a person who is a transvestite. On the
federal side the transvestism point is not in § 3602 at all; it appears in a statutory note printed
under the section, § 6(b)(3) of Pub. L. 100–430, which provides that "neither the term 'individual with
handicaps' nor the term 'handicap' shal

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
l apply to an individual solely because that individual is a
transvestite." Different placement, and worth noting when you are comparing the two texts.

**"Aggrieved person"** (§ 3602(i)) "includes any person who— (1) claims to have been injured by a
discriminatory housing practice; or (2) believes that such person will be injured by a discriminatory
housing practice that is about to occur." The second clause reaches an anticipated injury.

Finally, § 3602(f) defines a **"discriminatory housing practice"** as "an act that is unlawful under
section 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617 of this title" — the phrase that carries the substantive prohibitions
into the enforcement machinery. All four of those sections were held and read for this course.
Sections 3604 and 3605 are taught in this unit and in unit 4. The other two are taught in unit 3, and
it is worth knowing now what they are, because the definition you just read makes each of them a
"discriminatory housing practice" on the same footing as § 3604. **Section 3606** forbids denying a
person access to or membership or participation in "any multiple-listing service, real estate brokers'
organization or other service, organization, or facility relating to the business of selling or
renting dwellings" — the section that reaches your own trade organizations and your own MLS.
**Section 3617** makes it unlawful "to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any person" in
the exercise of, or on account of having exercised or having aided another in exercising, rights
granted or protected by §§ 3603, 3604, 3605 or 3606. Note what § 3602(f) does *not* list: § 3607, the
exemptions section, is not among the sections whose violation is a discriminatory housing practice,
because § 3607 creates no prohibition to violate. Familial stat

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
us, § 3602(k), is treated later in this
unit alongside § 3607.

**Read the opening clause first, then read 42 U.S.C. § 3603.** Section 3604 opens by subjecting
everything that follows to two cross-references: its prohibitions operate "[a]s made applicable by
section 3603 of this title and except as exempted by sections 3603(b) and 3607 of this title". Both
cross-referenced sections were read for this course, so we can follow the chain
rather than stopping at it. Section 3603(a) sets the reach. "Subject to the provisions of subsection
(b) and section 3607 of this title", the § 3604 prohibitions applied on enactment to four categories of
federally connected housing (§ 3603(a)(1)) — dwellings "owned or operated by the Federal Government";
dwellings aided by federal "loans, advances, grants, or contributions" under agreements entered into
after November 20, 1962; dwellings under § 3603(a)(1)(C) "provided in whole or in part by loans
insured, guaranteed, or otherwise secured by the
credit of the Federal Government" under such agreements; and dwellings provided by development or
redevelopment of property obtained from a public agency receiving federal slum-clearance or urban
renewal assistance. Then § 3603(a)(2): "After December 31, 1968, to all dwellings covered by paragraph
(1) and to all other dwellings except as exempted by subsection (b)."

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
That staged 1968–69 phase-in is spent history, and the only operative sentence today is the second one.
State it in the form you will use: **§ 3604 applies to all dwellings, except those § 3603(b) or § 3607
excepts.** The federally connected categories in § 3603(a)(1) are not a limit on the modern statute;
they are a record of which housing was covered first. The two exemptions are set out at the end of this
unit, and they are narrower than most people assume.

**§ 3604(a) — refusal to deal.** It is unlawful "[t]o refuse to sell or rent after the making of a
bona fide offer, or to refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of, or otherwise make unavailable or
deny, a dwelling to any person because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national
origin." Three wrongs: refusing after a bona fide offer, refusing to negotiate at all, and the
catch-all "otherwise make unavailable or deny." That catch-all is the workhorse — steering,
selectively applied screening criteria and never-returned calls all live there. *Illustration:* a Fort
Worth landlord tells one family the unit is spoken for and that afternoon accepts a materially
identical application from another. Nothing was said out loud about a protected class; if the reason
was one, the catch-all reaches it.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 3604(b) — terms, conditions, services.** It is unlawful "[t]o discriminate against any person in
the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling, or in the provision of services
or facilities in connection therewith," on the same six bases. Subsection (a) is about getting in the
door; (b) is about what happens after. *Illustration:* an El Paso community rents to all applicants
but charges one group a larger deposit, restricts their pool hours, and answers their maintenance
tickets in three weeks rather than three days.

**§ 3604(c) — advertising and statements.** It is unlawful "[t]o make, print, or publish, or cause to
be made, printed, or published any notice, statement, or advertisement, with respect to the sale or
rental of a dwelling that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race,
color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin, or an intention to make any such
preference, limitation, or discrimination." Here the list is seven bases — handicap is present. Note
the verbs (*make, print, publish,* or *cause to be*), which capture the agent who drafts copy and the
publisher who runs it; the objects ("any notice, statement, or advertisement," so a spoken remark at a
showing counts); and the test — the item must *indicate* a preference, limitation or discrimination,
or an intention to make one, and nobody need have been turned away. *Illustration:* a San Antonio
duplex advertised as *quiet building, perfect for a mature professional couple, not suited to
children* indicates a familial-status limitation on the face of the words.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 3604(d) — false unavailability.** It is unlawful "[t]o represent to any person because of race,
color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin that any dwelling is not available
for inspection, sale, or rental when such dwelling is in fact so available." This is the "sorry, it's
already leased" lie, given its own subsection because it is the usual way a refusal under (a) is
delivered.

**§ 3604(e) — blockbusting.** It is unlawful "[f]or profit, to induce or attempt to induce any person
to sell or rent any dwelling by representations regarding the entry or prospective entry into the
neighborhood of a person or persons of a particular race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial
status, or national origin." Three elements: **for profit**; **induce or attempt to induce**, so the
attempt alone completes the violation; and **representations regarding entry or prospective entry**,
so a prediction counts. Unit 3 works this practice in detail.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 3604(f) — handicap.** Paragraph (f)(1) makes it unlawful "[t]o discriminate in the sale or rental,
or to otherwise make unavailable or deny, a dwelling to any buyer or renter because of a handicap
of— (A) that buyer or renter," and it then reaches two further people: "(B) a person residing in or
intending to reside in that dwelling after it is so sold, rented, or made available; or (C) any person
associated with that buyer or renter."
Paragraph (f)(2) does the same for "the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental" and "the
provision of services or facilities," with the same three-part reach. So (f)(1) and (f)(2) are the
disability analogues of (a) and (b) — which is precisely why handicap is absent from those lists.
Notice how far the protection runs: a Plano seller who rejects an offer because the buyer's adult son
who will live in the home uses a wheelchair, or because the buyer's caregiver has a disability, is
inside (f)(1) even though the applicant is not the person with the handicap.

Paragraph (f)(3) says "discrimination includes" three things. Two of them are the pair students
confuse constantly, so learn them as a contrast.

A **reasonable modification**, (f)(3)(A): "a refusal to permit, at the expense of the handicapped
person, reasonable modifications of existing premises occupied or to be occupied by such person if
such modifications may be necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of the premises except that,
in the case of a rental, the landlord may where it is reasonable to do so condition permission for a
modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that
existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted."

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
A **reasonable accommodation**, (f)(3)(B): "a refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules,
policies, practices, or services, when such accommodations may be necessary to afford such person
equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling."

Four differences fall out of the words. **Object:** a modification changes the *premises*; an
accommodation changes *rules, policies, practices, or services*. **Expense:** modifications are "at
the expense of the handicapped person"; (B) says nothing about expense, because changing a rule
ordinarily costs nothing. **Standard:** "full enjoyment of the premises" versus "equal opportunity to
use and enjoy a dwelling." **Restoration:** only (A) has a restoration proviso, and it is narrow — a
*rental*, a landlord acting "where it is reasonable to do so," "the interior" only, "reasonable wear
and tear excepted."

A common error is to assume the landlord must pay for a ramp because "fair housing requires it."
Under (f)(3)(A) a ramp is a modification of the premises and the statute puts the expense on the
person with the handicap; the landlord's duty is not to *refuse permission* unreasonably. The
mirror-image error is to assume a tenant may be charged for waiving a rule. Waiving a no-pets policy
for an assistance animal, assigning a closer parking space, or accepting rent from a third-party payer
are changes to rules, policies, practices or services, and (B) attaches no expense to them. Memorize
the contrast: **modification = premises, occupant's expense, possible restoration; accommodation =
rules, no expense clause, no restoration clause.**

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
The third item, (f)(3)(C), is the **design and construction requirement**. For "covered multifamily
dwellings for first occupancy after the date that is 30 months after September 13, 1988," it is
discrimination to fail to design and construct them so that public and common use portions are
"readily accessible to and usable by handicapped persons"; doors are "sufficiently wide to allow
passage by handicapped persons in wheelchairs"; and all premises contain four "features of adaptive
design" — an accessible route through the dwelling, environmental controls in accessible locations,
"reinforcements in bathroom walls to allow later installation of grab bars," and kitchens and
bathrooms an individual in a wheelchair "can maneuver about." Paragraph (f)(7) defines **covered
multifamily dwellings** as "(A) buildings consisting of 4 or more units if such buildings have one or
more elevators; and (B) ground floor units in other buildings consisting of 4 or more units" — so a
walk-up fourplex is covered as to its ground-floor units. Compliance with "ANSI A117.1" satisfies the
adaptive-design features (f)(4), and (f)(8) preserves state or local law requiring "greater access
than is required by this subchapter." Finally, (f)(9): "Nothing in this
subsection requires that a dwelling be made available to an individual whose tenancy would constitute
a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals or whose tenancy would result in
substantial physical damage to the property of others" — a narrow, evidence-based provision about
*this* individual's tenancy, not a licence to act on assumptions about a category of people.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Familial status, defined.** Section 3602(k) defines **familial status** as "one or more individuals
(who have not attained the age of 18 years) being domiciled with— (1) a parent or another person having
legal custody of such individual or individuals; or (2) the designee of such parent or other person
having such custody, with the written permission of such parent or other person." A closing sentence
extends it: "The protections afforded against discrimination on the basis of familial status shall
apply to any person who is pregnant or is in the process of securing legal custody of any individual
who has not attained the age of 18 years."

Read that carefully, because the class is narrower and stranger than the phrase "families with
children" suggests. The trigger is **domicile with a person under 18** — not marriage, not household
size, not being a parent in the abstract. A grandmother raising a ten-year-old is protected; so is a
designee caring for a child with the custodial parent's *written* permission. And the closing sentence
protects two people who are not yet domiciled with any minor at all: a pregnant applicant, and a person
"in the process of securing legal custody." Property Code § 301.004 states the same three routes —
pregnant, domiciled with an individual younger than 18 as parent or legal custodian or with that
person's written permission, or in the process of obtaining legal custody. Federal and Texas familial
status are the same class described in the same terms.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Housing for older persons — § 3607(b).** This is where the familial-status class stops, and it is
the exemption a Texas license holder is most likely to meet in practice, because active-adult
communities are everywhere in this state. Section 3607(b)(1) does two things in two sentences: nothing
in the subchapter "limits the applicability of any reasonable local, State, or Federal restrictions
regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling," and "[n]or does any
provision in this subchapter regarding familial status apply with respect to housing for older
persons."

Note the width of that second sentence, and then note its limit. It removes **the familial-status
provisions and nothing else**. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin and handicap all continue to
apply in full inside a seniors community. A 55-and-over community that qualifies under § 3607(b) may
lawfully decline to rent to a household with a twelve-year-old; it may not decline to rent to a
62-year-old applicant on the basis of national origin, and it owes the same § 3604(f)(3) accommodations
and modifications as any other housing provider. "It's senior housing" answers exactly one question.

Section 3607(b)(2) defines **housing for older persons** as housing in any of three alternatives:

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
- **(A) Program housing** — housing "provided under any State or Federal program that the Secretary
  determines is specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons (as defined in the State
  or Federal program)." The Secretary is the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, per
  § 3602(a). Note that qualification here runs through a determination by the Secretary, not through
  the operator's own view of its program.
- **(B) 62-and-over** — housing "intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 years of age or
  older" (§ 3607(b)(2)(B)).
- **(C) 55-and-over** — housing, under § 3607(b)(2)(C), "intended and operated for occupancy by
  persons 55 years of age or
  older," *and* meeting three further requirements: "(i) at least 80 percent of the occupied units are
  occupied by at least one person who is 55 years of age or older"; "(ii) the housing facility or
  community publishes and adheres to policies and procedures that demonstrate the intent required
  under this subparagraph"; and "(iii) the housing facility or community complies with rules issued by
  the Secretary for verification of occupancy," which rules must "provide for verification by reliable
  surveys and affidavits" and "include examples of the types of policies and procedures relevant to a
  determination of compliance," with those surveys and affidavits "admissible in administrative and
  judicial proceedings for the purposes of such verification."

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Contrast (B) and (C) precisely; the difference is the whole point.** Sixty-two-and-over is a
*solely occupied* standard — every occupant meets the age, and the statute adds no conditions beyond
intent and sole occupancy. Fifty-five-and-over is a *threshold* standard with paperwork: only one
person aged 55 or older is needed in each qualifying unit, only 80 percent of the **occupied** units
must qualify (unoccupied units are excluded from the denominator by the word "occupied"), and the
community must additionally publish and adhere to age policies and comply with the Secretary's
occupancy-verification rules. A community that calls itself "55+" in its marketing, has never published
an age policy and cannot document its 80 percent is not, on this text, housing for older persons — and
every familial-status exclusion it has made is unprotected.

Two savings provisions follow, both practical, and each carries a proviso that is part of the
rule rather than a footnote to it. Under § 3607(b)(3), housing "shall not fail to
meet the requirements for housing for older persons" by reason of persons who were residing there as of
September 13, 1988 and do not meet the (B) or (C) ages, provided that "new occupants of such housing
meet the age requirements" of (B) or (C); or by reason of unoccupied units, provided that such units
are "reserved for occupancy by persons who meet the age requirements" of (B) or (C). So legacy
residents and vacant units do not break the exemption — so long as the community holds the line going
forward.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
Under § 3607(b)(5)(A), "[a] person shall not be held personally liable for monetary damages for a
violation of this subchapter if such person reasonably relied, in good faith, on the application of the
exemption under this subsection relating to housing for older persons." Subparagraph (B) then says how
that reliance may be shown — and the word to underline is *only*: "a person may only show good faith
reliance… by showing that— (i) such person has no actual knowledge that the facility or community is
not, or will not be, eligible for such exemption; and (ii) the facility or community has stated
formally, in writing, that the facility or community complies with the requirements for such
exemption." Both elements, and the second is documentary. This provision is aimed squarely at the
agent, manager or advertiser who takes a community's word for its status: **get the written statement
of compliance, or the good-faith defence is unavailable on the statute's own terms.** That is a
statutory point, not a practice tip.

Section 3607(b)(4) rounds out the section: "Nothing in this subchapter prohibits conduct against a
person because such person has been convicted by any court of competent jurisdiction of the illegal
manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance as defined in section 802 of title 21." Note how
narrow it is — *manufacture or distribution*, convictions only, and only of a controlled substance. It
is not a general permission to screen on criminal history.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Where Texas lands.** Property Code § 301.043 exempts from the Texas familial-status provisions the
same three categories: housing "intended for, and solely occupied by, individuals 62 years of age or
older"; housing "intended and operated for occupancy by at least one individual 55 years of age or
older for each unit as determined by commission rules"; and housing the commission determines is
designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a federal or state program. The structures
match, with one drafting difference worth knowing: **Texas routes the 55-and-over detail through
commission rules, while the federal 80 percent figure sits in the statute itself** at
§ 3607(b)(2)(C)(i). No Texas Workforce Commission rule was held for this course, so this module states
the federal percentage from § 3607 and does not state what the Texas rules require. Property Code
§ 301.062 requires the commission's substantive rules to impose obligations "the same as are provided
in federal fair housing regulations," which tells you the direction Texas points, but a rule you have
not read is not a rule you can quote to a client.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**The § 3603(b) exemptions, and the one thing they never cover.** Start with the opening words of
§ 3603(b), because everything turns on a five-word parenthesis: "**Nothing in section 3604 of this
title (other than subsection (c)) shall apply to**—". Read it twice. Section 3603(b) exempts qualifying
transactions from all of § 3604 *except subsection (c)*, and subsection (c) is the advertising and
statements prohibition. So a fully exempt owner may still refuse to sell for a discriminatory reason
without violating § 3604(a) — and may **not** make, print or publish a notice, statement or
advertisement indicating a preference, limitation or discrimination, or an intention to make one.
**There is no exemption from federal fair housing advertising law.** That is the single most useful
sentence in § 3603, it comes from the section's own first line, and it is the answer to the client who
says *I'm exempt, so I can put whatever I want in the ad.*

Two transactions are exempted.

**(1) A single-family house sold or rented by its owner** — § 3603(b)(1) exempts "any single-family
house sold or rented by an owner," subject to four provisos, each of which narrows it:

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
- **The three-house ceiling.** The exemption applies only where, in the statute's proviso, "such
  private individual owner does not own more than three such single-family houses at any one time".
- **The anti-evasion ceiling.** It applies further only if "such bona fide private individual owner does
  not own any interest in, nor is there owned or reserved on his behalf, under any express or voluntary
  agreement, title to or any right to all or a portion of the proceeds from the sale or rental of, more
  than three such single-family houses at any one time." This closes the obvious dodge of holding the
  fourth and fifth houses through an entity or a proceeds arrangement.
- **The one-sale-in-24-months limit for an absent owner.** "[I]n the case of the sale of any such
  single-family house by a private individual owner not residing in such house at the time of such sale
  or who was not the most recent resident of such house prior to such sale, the exemption granted by
  this subsection shall apply only with respect to one such sale within any twenty-four month period."
  Note who this catches: the owner who did not live in the house. An owner selling the home she has
  been living in is outside this limit.
- **The no-broker, no-advertisement condition.** "[A]fter December 31, 1969, the sale or rental of any
  such single-family house shall be excepted from the application of this subchapter only if such house
  is sold or rented (A) without the use in any manner of the sales or rental facilities or the sales or
  rental services of any real estate broker, agent, or salesman, or of such facilities or services of
  any person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or of any employee or agent of any such
  broker, agent, salesman, or person and (B) without the

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
publication, posting or mailing, after notice,
  of any advertisement or written notice in violation of section 3604(c) of this title." A closing
  clause preserves ordinary closing help: "nothing in this proviso shall prohibit the use of attorneys,
  escrow agents, abstractors, title companies, and other such professional assistance as necessary to
  perfect or transfer the title."

Clause (A) is the one that matters to you, and it is why this whole exemption is of limited practical
interest to a license holder. **The moment the owner uses your services, the exemption is gone.** The
statute does not say "unless the broker discriminates"; it says the sale is excepted *only if* it is
made without the use "in any manner" of a broker's, agent's or salesman's facilities or services. And
clause (B) makes the advertising point a second time, from the other direction: a § 3604(c) violation
does not merely go unexcused, it destroys the exemption for the transaction as a whole.

chunks.heading: Unit: Equal Opportunity in Housing
chunks.excerpt:
**(2) Rooms or units in an owner-occupied dwelling** — § 3603(b)(2) exempts "rooms or units in
dwellings containing living quarters occupied or intended to be occupied by no more than four families
living independently of each other, if the owner actually maintains and occupies one of such living
quarters as his residence." Four elements: living quarters for **no more than four** families; the
families living **independently of each other**; the **owner** occupying one of them; and occupying it
as the owner's **residence**, which the statute reinforces with "actually maintains and occupies." An
owner living in one unit of a fourplex and renting the other three is inside it. An owner who lives
elsewhere and rents all four is not. You will hear this called the "Mrs. Murphy" exemption in the
industry; the statute does not use that name and this module cites nothing for it.

**Who is "in the business of selling or renting dwellings."** Section 3603(b)(1)(A) denies the
exemption to an owner who uses the facilities or services of "any person in the business of selling or
renting dwellings," and § 3603(c) defines that phrase for the subsection. A person is in the business
