it first and regret it most, because it converts predictable small costs into unpredictable large
ones. **Corrective** maintenance repairs what has already failed — the ordinary work order, where the
§ 92.056 clock runs. **Emergency** maintenance cannot wait; § 92.0561(d)(3) and (e) single out sewage
and flooding inside the dwelling, cessation of potable water, and inadequate heating or cooling, with
the tenant's repair right arising immediately for sewage and flooding and after three days for water,
heat or cooling.

chunks.heading: Unit: Management Considerations
chunks.excerpt:
Security devices belong in the same plan. Section 92.153(a) requires, without any tenant request and
subject to stated exceptions, window latches, a doorknob lock or keyed dead bolt on each exterior
door, sliding-door pin locks and handle latches or security bars, and a keyless bolting device and
door viewer on each exterior door — installed "at the landlord's expense" under § 92.153(c) and
operable throughout the tenant's possession under § 92.153(h). Section 92.006(a) makes these duties
non-waivable, and § 92.152(b) reaches single-family houses, duplexes and units in apartment,
condominium and townhome projects. A make-ready checklist that skips them is not finished.

**Tenant selection.** This is where fair housing exposure is created or avoided, and the protection is
procedural: written criteria, applied the same way to every applicant, documented every time.

Texas Property Code § 301.021(a) provides that a person "may not refuse to sell or rent, after the
making of a bona fide offer, refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of, or in any other manner
make unavailable or deny a dwelling to another because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status,
or national origin," and § 301.021(b) extends that to the terms, conditions and privileges of a rental
and to services and facilities provided with it. Section 301.025(a) and (b) apply the same
prohibitions on the basis of disability — of the applicant, of a person who will reside in the
dwelling, or of anyone associated with the applicant — and § 301.025(c) provides that discrimination
includes refusing a reasonable modification at the disabled person's expense where necessary for full
enjoyment, and refusing "to make a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services
if the accommodation may be

chunks.heading: Unit: Management Considerations
chunks.excerpt:
necessary to afford the person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a
dwelling." The chapter's definition of **"to rent"** at § 301.003(11) includes "to lease, sublease, or
let, or to grant in any other manner, for a consideration, the right to occupy premises not owned by
the occupant" — the chapter is aimed at what a property manager does all day.

The federal provisions are parallel. Under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) it is unlawful "to refuse to sell or
rent after the making of a bona fide offer, or to refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of, or
otherwise make unavailable or deny, a dwelling to any person" on the same grounds; § 3604(b) covers
terms, conditions and privileges; § 3604(d) prohibits representing that a dwelling is unavailable when
it is in fact available; and § 3604(f)(1) through (3) address handicap, including the
reasonable-modification and reasonable-accommodation duties. Under § 3604(f)(9) nothing in that
subsection requires a dwelling to be made available to a person whose tenancy "would constitute a
direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals"; Property Code § 301.025(f) is to the same
effect.

chunks.heading: Unit: Management Considerations
chunks.excerpt:
Advertising is regulated separately and strictly. Property Code § 301.022 prohibits publishing "a
notice, statement, or advertisement that is about the sale or rental of a dwelling and that indicates
any preference, limitation, or discrimination or the intention to make a preference, limitation, or
discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national
origin," and 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) is the federal counterpart; Property Code § 301.024 and 42 U.S.C.
§ 3604(e) prohibit inducing a sale or rental for profit by representations about the entry of persons
of a protected characteristic into a neighborhood. Advertise the *property*, never the desired tenant.
Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(32) adds a licensing consequence: the Commission may discipline a
license holder who "discriminates against an owner, potential buyer, landlord, or potential tenant on
the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, or ancestry,
including directing a prospective buyer or tenant interested in equivalent properties to a different
area based on" those characteristics. Note that the TRELA list adds *ancestry*.

Within those constraints a manager may screen on legitimate, consistently applied criteria — income
relative to rent, verified rental history, creditworthiness. Write the standards down before the first
application is taken, and never take an owner's instruction to deviate from them; § 1101.652(b)(32)
makes the license holder responsible for the license holder's own act regardless of who suggested
it.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Build the operating statement
chunks.excerpt:
**Reporting to the owner.** Owner reporting closes the loop and prevents most disputes. A monthly
package showing income received, expenses paid with invoices, the operating account's cash position,
deposits held and for whom, occupancy and delinquency, and open and completed work orders leaves
little to argue about. Section 1101.652(b)(9) requires proper accounting and remittance within a
reasonable time and § 1101.652(b)(24) forbids materially inaccurate statements of account, so accuracy
here is not merely good service. Correct an error in writing in the next statement; concealment is
what converts a bookkeeping mistake into a disciplinary matter.

### Applied exercise: Build the operating statement

A Texas owner asks you to project the first year of a 12-unit property. Market rent is $1,100 per unit
per month. You estimate vacancy and collection loss at 8 percent. Your management fee is 8 percent of
effective gross income. Projected expenses are: property taxes $31,200; insurance $9,400; common-area
utilities $5,100; repairs and maintenance $14,300; landscaping and pest control $4,800; make-ready and
turnover $7,600; administrative and marketing $3,100. All figures are illustrative.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
1. Compute gross potential rent, vacancy and collection loss, and effective gross income, showing each
   step.
2. Compute the management fee, total operating expenses, and net operating income.
3. Compute the operating expense ratio. Would replacing the roof for $46,000 change it? Explain by
   reference to the definition of operating expenses given in this unit.
4. The owner's lender requires a mortgage payment of $9,300 per month. Does your net operating income
   figure tell you whether the property covers it? What would you have to add to the statement to
   answer that question?

## Unit: The Management Profession

Property management is a career, not a task, and it differs from brokerage in ways that suit some
people very well. Sales brokerage is transactional: episodic work, lumpy income, a client relationship
that ends at closing. Management is operational: recurring income, relationships that last years, and
a measure of good work that is simply that nothing dramatic happened.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
**The range of asset types.** The words "property manager" cover several occupations that share a
name. **Single-family and small residential** management handles detached houses, duplexes and small
multiplexes for individual owners; the properties are scattered and the economics turn on efficiency
per door. This is where the Texas licensing question bites hardest, because Occupations Code
§ 1101.002(1)(A)(x) reaches control of the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a
single-family residential real property unit, and because the on-site apartment manager exemption in
§ 1101.005(7) does not describe this work. **Multifamily** management runs apartment communities from
one address, staffed on site and measured on occupancy, delinquency, turnover cost and expense per
unit; careers run from leasing consultant to community manager to regional manager, and § 1101.005(7)
makes the on-site position available without a license, which is why multifamily is a common entry
point into the industry.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
**Commercial** management — office, retail and industrial — deals with business tenants, longer and
individually negotiated leases, and rent built from a base plus a share of operating costs, sometimes
plus a percentage of retail sales. It demands lease abstraction skills residential management does
not, and it operates outside Property Code ch. 92, which governs residential tenancies. Property Code
ch. 91 supplies rules applicable to landlords and tenants generally: § 91.001 on notice terminating a
month-to-month tenancy; § 91.005, under which "during the term of a lease, the tenant may not rent the
leasehold to any other person without the prior consent of the landlord"; § 91.004, making a landlord
who fails to comply with the lease liable to a non-defaulting tenant for resulting damages and giving
that tenant a lien on the landlord's nonexempt property in the tenant's possession and on rent due;
and § 91.006's non-waivable duty to mitigate damages when a tenant abandons the premises in violation
of the lease. **Community association** management handles common property and the governing documents
of a homeowners association or condominium regime, where the client is a volunteer board and the
"customers" are owner-members rather than tenants. Above all of these sits **asset management**,
concerned with the investment rather than operations, and property management is the usual path into
it.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
**Designations and trade organizations — practice, not law.** The industry supports national trade
associations and professional institutes serving apartment, commercial, single-family residential and
community association management, and these bodies confer designations earned through coursework,
documented experience and examination. State the legal position exactly, because students misremember
it constantly. **No Texas statute read for this course requires a property manager to hold any
professional designation or to belong to any trade organization.** Occupations Code § 1101.351
requires a *license* — a broker or sales agent license — of a person performing the acts of a broker,
and § 1101.002(4) defines a license holder as a broker or sales agent licensed under the chapter. That
is the legal credential. Designations are private and voluntary: conferred by private organizations
under their own rules and conferring no authority a license holder does not already have. This module
cites nothing for the value of any designation, because that is professional practice and not Texas
law, and it names no particular organization. Structured education does make managers better at a job
whose failures are expensive and often invisible until they are catastrophic. That is a good reason to
pursue a designation. "It is required" is not.

**Ethics: standing between the owner and the tenant.** The defining ethical feature of this work is
that the manager sits between two parties whose interests diverge daily and owes each of them
something different.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
To the owner, the manager owes the duties of an agent. Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) provides that a
broker who represents a party in a real estate transaction, or who lists real estate for sale under an
exclusive agreement for a party, is that party's agent, and § 1101.557(b) requires that broker to
inform the party of material information related to a transaction to list, buy, sell or lease the
party's real estate, including the receipt of an offer. Chapter 1101's disciplinary grounds reinforce
the point: § 1101.652(b)(1) reaches a license holder who "acts negligently or incompetently"; (b)(2)
conduct "that is dishonest or in bad faith or that demonstrates untrustworthiness"; (b)(7) a failure
"to make clear to all parties to a real estate transaction the party for whom the license holder is
acting"; (b)(8) receiving compensation from more than one party without the full knowledge and consent
of all; and (b)(9) and (10) the accounting and commingling failures examined in Unit 1. Together they
describe loyalty, disclosure, competence and honest accounting — the ordinary content of a fiduciary
relationship — enforced by license discipline rather than only by contract.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
To the tenant, the manager owes what the statute owes. The ch. 92 duties run against the landlord, and
§ 92.001(2) tells us the manager is not the landlord unless the manager purports to be the owner,
lessor or sublessor in a lease. But the manager is the person through whom those duties are performed
or breached: the manager receives the repair notice under § 92.052(a) at the place rent is paid, runs
the clock under § 92.056, holds and refunds the security deposit under § 92.103(a) "on or before the
30th day after the date the tenant surrenders the premises," prepares the "written description and
itemized list of all deductions" required by § 92.104(c), and honors or ignores § 92.104(b)'s rule
that no portion of a deposit may be retained "to cover normal wear and tear." Section 92.109(a) makes
a landlord who in bad faith retains a deposit liable for one hundred dollars, three times the portion
wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees, and § 92.109(d) presumes bad faith where the
landlord fails either to return the deposit or to provide the written itemization on or before the
thirtieth day after surrender. The penalties fall on the landlord, but they fall because of what the
manager did.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
Three ch. 92 provisions exist precisely because managers under pressure have been tempted to shorten
the process. Section 92.008(a) and (b) prohibit a landlord or a landlord's agent from interrupting
utility service, whether paid directly to the utility by the tenant or furnished by the landlord as an
incident of the tenancy, "unless the interruption results from bona fide repairs, construction, or an
emergency," subject to the narrow exception in § 92.008(h) for submetered or allocated electricity;
§ 92.008(f) gives the tenant possession or termination plus actual damages, one month's rent plus
$1,000, fees and costs. Section 92.0081(b) prohibits intentionally preventing a tenant from entering
the premises except by judicial process, subject to stated exceptions including a lock change for a
delinquent tenant under the notice requirements of § 92.0081(c) and (d); § 92.0081(f) requires that
the tenant be given a key "without regard to whether the tenant pays the delinquent rent," and
§ 92.0081(h) provides a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $1,000. Section 92.331 prohibits
retaliation — eviction, deprivation of the premises, decreased services, a rent increase, lease
termination, or a bad-faith course of conduct materially interfering with the tenant's rights — within
six months after the tenant exercises a right, gives a repair notice, complains in good faith to a
code authority, utility or civic agency, or participates in a tenant organization; § 92.332 preserves
ordinary grounds such as delinquency and material breach, and § 92.333 gives a civil penalty of one
month's rent plus $500 with damages, costs and fees.

chunks.heading: Unit: The Management Profession
chunks.excerpt:
So how does a competent manager honor both sets of obligations? By recognizing that they conflict less
often than they appear to. Loyalty to the owner is a duty to advance the owner's *lawful* interests,
and an owner's interests are never served by exposure to those penalties. When an owner asks for
something the law forbids, the loyal answer and the lawful answer are the same: explain the provision,
explain the exposure, and decline. Sections 1101.652(b)(1) and (2) both cut against a manager who
follows an unlawful instruction, and § 1101.803 places the broker on the hook for it. Where genuine
tension remains it is usually about candor rather than legality, and the discipline is to be honest
with everyone and keep no confidence about facts the other party is entitled to know. Section
1101.652(b)(7) is the starting point: a tenant who knows the manager works for the owner is not misled
by the manager advancing the owner's interests.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The instruction you should refuse
chunks.excerpt:
**Continuing competence.** Texas law speaks here too. Occupations Code § 1101.455(b) requires a
license holder not subject to the § 1101.454 education requirements to attend continuing education
courses approved by the Commission during the term of the current license, in a number of classroom
hours the Commission prescribes by rule, "which must be at least 15 classroom hours," and § 1101.455(e)
requires at least eight of those hours to cover listed legal topics — a list that reads like a
property manager's job description: commission rules; **fair housing laws**; **Property Code issues,
including landlord-tenant law**; agency law; disclosures to buyers, landlords, tenants and sellers;
and "the ethical requirements of engaging in real estate brokerage," among others. Beyond that
minimum, competence decays quickly for a specific reason: the Property Code chapters a manager lives
inside are amended regularly, and the amendments are usually procedural — a notice period, a fee cap,
a required disclosure — exactly the details a manager operates on autopilot. As a matter of practice
and not of legal requirement, managers who stay out of trouble re-read the operative chapters
periodically and keep lease forms and notice templates under review rather than treating them as
settled.

### Applied exercise: The instruction you should refuse

You manage a 60-unit property in Texas for an out-of-state owner. Three things happen in one week.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. A tenant delivers a written notice at the leasing office, where rent is paid, that raw sewage is
   backing up into her bathtub. She is current on rent. The owner tells you to wait until next month's
   budget cycle. Which provisions of §§ 92.052, 92.056 and 92.0561 do you cite to the owner, and what
   is the tenant entitled to do if you wait?
2. Another tenant is eleven days delinquent. The owner instructs you to shut off the water to that
   unit "until he pays." Identify the provision that answers this and the tenant's remedy.
3. A third tenant complained to the city code office about a stairwell railing three weeks ago. The
   owner now wants that tenant's lease terminated at the end of the term "because he's a
   troublemaker." Which subchapter applies, what is the time window, and what is the penalty?
4. For each instruction, state whether refusing it is disloyal to the owner. Support your answer from
   the ethics discussion in this unit.

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
This module built one argument in three steps. It began with the work — leasing, rent collection,
maintenance, accounting, reporting, tenant relations and compliance — and showed that the work itself
triggers regulation. Because a manager performs listed acts for another person for compensation,
Occupations Code § 1101.002(1)(A) makes leasing, negotiating leases, listing property for lease and
controlling the acceptance or deposit of single-family rent acts of a broker, and § 1101.351 forbids
performing them without a license. Section 1101.005 supplies the exemptions that decide most real
cases: the on-site apartment manager under subdivision (7), and the owner or the owner's employee
leasing the owner's own real estate under subdivision (8). Because a manager holds other people's
money, § 1101.652(b)(9), (10), (30) and (31) convert sloppy trust accounting into license discipline:
deposit promptly, never commingle, never disburse early, always account and remit within a reasonable
time.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The second unit took that licensed manager into the operating relationship. The management agreement
sets scope of authority, term — with § 1101.652(b)(12) carving property management contracts out of
the definite-termination-date requirement that governs listing agreements — compensation, owner
obligations, indemnification and accounting mechanics. The operating statement supplied the arithmetic
every owner conversation uses: gross potential rent less vacancy and collection loss yields effective
gross income, less operating expenses yields net operating income, with debt service and capital
expenditures excluded by definition. Maintenance is organized into routine, preventive, corrective and
emergency work because § 92.056(d)'s seven-day presumption sets the tempo, and tenant selection is
written and consistent because Property Code ch. 301, 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(32) all reach the same conduct.

The third unit placed the manager in a profession and an ethical position. Designations and trade
memberships are voluntary practice, required by no statute read for this course; the license is the
legal credential. The manager's agency duties run to the owner under § 1101.557 and the § 1101.652(b)
disciplinary grounds, while the ch. 92 duties protect the tenant and are performed or breached through
the manager's hands. Honoring both usually means recognizing that an owner's lawful interest and a
tenant's statutory right point the same way. You should now be able to decide whether a person needs a
Texas license to manage a given property, state the trust-money rules, build an operating statement
through to net operating income, and separate what the law requires from what the profession expects.

lessons.title: Texas Law of Agency — Module 01

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Agency — Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Agency — Module 01

## TREC Topic: Agency Concepts

**Prescribed time: 130 minutes.** This module carries the four units the Commission's LOA-1 course
approval form places under *Agency Concepts*, whose scope note is *"Disclosure of Agency;
relationship between principal & agent."*

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: explain what an agency
relationship is; identify the two bodies of Texas authority that govern it for a license holder —
The Real Estate License Act at Chapter 1101 of the Occupations Code and the Commission's rules at 22
TAC Chapters 531 and 535 — and state from § 1101.002(1) exactly which acts performed for another
person make a person a broker; say who must hold a licence, who is exempt, and where the line
between unlicensed and licensed activity runs under §§ 1101.004, 1101.0045, 1101.005 and 1101.351
and 22 TAC §§ 535.4 and 535.5; explain why the Legislature named agency law first among the
qualifying courses at § 1101.003(a)(1) and what a failure of agency practice costs; distinguish the
roles of principal, client, agent, sales agent, party, customer, intermediary and associated license
holder, and state what a Texas license holder owes to a person the license holder represents and
what the license holder owes to a person the license holder does not represent; and describe how a
principal–agent relationship is created under Texas law and why a friendly conversation is not an
agency agreement.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**Where the rest of this course goes.** This module teaches the vocabulary of the Act, the acts of
brokerage, who needs a licence, and the client/customer distinction. It does not teach the rest of
the course twice. Module 02 teaches basic agency relationships, the fiduciary Canons at 22 TAC
§§ 531.2–531.4 and 22 TAC § 535.156, and disclosure of representation under § 1101.558 and the IABS
rule at 22 TAC § 531.20. Module 03 teaches duties to third parties, Property Code § 5.008 and
§§ 1101.556, 1101.802, 1101.804 and 1101.805. Module 04 teaches seller agency, listing agreements,
§ 1101.806 and 22 TAC §§ 535.16 and 537.11. Module 05 teaches buyer agency and the 2026 changes at
§§ 1101.562 and 1101.563. Module 06 teaches intermediary brokerage at §§ 1101.559–1101.561 and
§ 1101.651(d). Module 07 teaches creation and termination, including § 1101.367. Module 08 teaches
brokerage disclosure policy. Module 09 teaches employment issues, broker responsibility and 22 TAC
§ 535.2 in full. Module 10 teaches ethics and § 1101.652 in full. Module 11 teaches the Deceptive
Trade Practices Act and the recovery trust account. Module 12 teaches implementation. Where this
module touches one of those authorities, it states the rule, cites it, and sends you to the module
that teaches it.

## Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
Start with the idea itself, before any statute. **Agency** is the legal relationship in which one
person is authorised to act for another, in dealings with third persons, in such a way that what the
first person does is treated by the law as though the second person had done it. The person who
authorises is the **principal**. The person who acts is the **agent**. The whole point of the
arrangement is substitution: the principal cannot be in two places at once, does not know the
market, does not want to negotiate, and so hands the job to somebody else and accepts the
consequences of that person's conduct.

That substitution is what creates the legal problem. If your acts bind me, then your judgment is
being exercised over my money, my property and my legal position, in circumstances where I usually
cannot watch you. Texas law responds by doing two things at once: it gives the agent power, and it
loads the agent with duties designed to make that power safe. When you hear that a Texas license
holder is a fiduciary, that is not a compliment about character. It is a description of a legal
position in which the law has decided that ordinary arm's-length behaviour is not good enough,
because the other side of the relationship cannot protect itself.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
Texas law does not begin its treatment of real estate agency with an abstract definition of that
kind. It begins with a licensing statute, and it approaches agency through the back door — by
describing the *acts* that, if you do them for somebody else and expect to be paid, make you a
broker and put you inside the statute. That is a very important structural point and most students
miss it. You will not find a section of Texas law headed *Definition of Agency*. What you will find
is a chapter of the Occupations Code that says: do these things for another person, and you are in
our world; and once you are in our world, here is what you owe. Understanding that the statute is
built around *acts* rather than around *titles* will save you from a whole family of errors later,
including the very common student belief that you are only an agent if somebody calls you one.

**The statute.** Chapter 1101 of the Texas Occupations Code opens at § 1101.001 with a short title:
"This chapter may be cited as The Real Estate License Act." That is the source of the abbreviation
you will see everywhere in Texas practice — **TRELA**. When a broker in Amarillo says *that is a
TRELA violation*, the broker means Chapter 1101 of the Occupations Code. It is an act of the Texas
Legislature. Nobody at the Commission wrote it; the Commission administers it.

**Who is a broker.** Section 1101.002(1) is the section on which the whole chapter balances. Under
subdivision (1)(A), "broker" means a person who, "in exchange for a commission or other valuable
consideration or with the expectation of receiving a commission or other valuable consideration,
performs for another person one of the following acts". Read that opening clause slowly, because
three of its elements are doing real work.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
First, **"for another person."** This is the agency hinge. Everything you are about to study in this
course flows from those three words. If you buy a duplex in Killeen for your own account, you are
acting for yourself, and you are outside § 1101.002(1) no matter how sophisticated the transaction
is. The moment you do the same work for somebody else, the statute engages.

Second, **"in exchange for a commission or other valuable consideration or with the expectation of
receiving a commission or other valuable consideration."** Note that the expectation is enough. You
do not have to be paid, and you do not have to have a signed fee agreement, for the statute to reach
you. A person who helps a neighbour list a house hoping that a commission or a referral fee will
follow is inside the definition; a person who genuinely does it for nothing is not. Students
routinely assume that *I never got paid* is a defence. Under the plain words of the definition, it
usually is not.

Third, **"one of the following acts."** The definition then enumerates twelve acts, and it takes
only one. Subparagraph (A)(i) reaches a person who "sells, exchanges, purchases, or leases real
estate"; (ii) reaches one who "offers to sell, exchange, purchase, or lease real estate"; (iii), one
who "negotiates or attempts to negotiate the listing, sale, exchange, purchase, or lease of real
estate"; (iv), one who "lists or offers, attempts, or agrees to list real estate for sale, lease, or
exchange"; and (v), one who "auctions or offers, attempts, or agrees to auction real estate." Notice
how much of that language is about *attempting* and *offering*. The statute is not waiting for a
closing. An attempted negotiation is an act of a broker.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
The list continues into activity that students often do not recognise as brokerage at all.
Subparagraph (A)(vi) covers a person who "deals in options on real estate, including a lease to
purchase or buying, selling, or offering to buy or sell options on real estate." Subparagraph
(A)(vii) covers one who "aids or offers or attempts to aid in locating or obtaining real estate for
purchase or lease" — that is the subparagraph that catches the friend who runs around Corpus Christi
finding rent houses for people and takes a small fee. Subparagraphs (A)(viii) and (A)(ix) are a
matched pair: one who "procures or assists in procuring a prospect to effect the sale, exchange, or
lease of real estate," and one who "procures or assists in procuring property to effect the sale,
exchange, or lease of real estate." Between them they cover finding the buyer and finding the house.
Subparagraph (A)(x) covers a person who "controls the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident
of a single-family residential real property unit" — property management, reached through the money
rather than through the leasing.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
Subparagraph (A)(xi) is the one that concerns your pricing work, and it is written with three
cumulative conditions. It covers a person who "provides a written analysis, opinion, or conclusion
relating to the estimated price of real property if the analysis, opinion, or conclusion" "(a) is
not referred to as an appraisal;" "(b) is provided in the ordinary course of the person's business;
and" "(c) is related to the actual or potential management, acquisition, disposition, or encumbrance
of an interest in real property". All three have to be true. That drafting is what makes a
comparative market analysis an act of a broker rather than an act of an appraiser. Finally,
subparagraph (A)(xii) covers a person who "advises or offers advice to an owner of real estate
concerning the negotiation or completion of a short sale."

Subdivision (1)(B) then adds two categories: a person who "is employed by or for an owner of real
estate to sell any portion of the real estate," and a person who "engages in the business of
charging an advance fee or contracting to collect a fee under a contract that requires the person
primarily to promote the sale of real estate by" listing it in a publication primarily used for
listing real estate or referring information about it to brokers.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**The other definitions you need immediately.** Section 1101.002(4) provides that a **license
holder** "means a broker or sales agent licensed under this chapter." That is the statute's own
umbrella term, and this course uses it rather than *agent* or *Realtor* because it is the term the
law uses. Section 1101.002(7) provides that a **sales agent** "means a person who is sponsored by a
licensed broker for the purpose of performing an act described by Subdivision (1)." Read that
definition again. A sales agent is *defined by sponsorship*. There is no such thing under Texas law
as a sales agent who is not sponsored by a broker and who is nonetheless out doing brokerage.
Section 1101.002(3) provides that the **Commission** "means the Texas Real Estate Commission" — that
is **TREC**, the nine-member state agency that administers this chapter. And § 1101.002(5) provides
that **real estate** "means any interest in real property, including a leasehold, located in or
outside this state. The term does not include an interest given as security for the performance of
an obligation." Two consequences: a lease is real estate for this chapter's purposes, and a lien or
deed of trust — an interest given as security — is not.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**Brokerage as an activity.** Section 1101.004(a) restates the same idea as a status: "A person is
engaged in real estate brokerage if the person, with the expectation of receiving valuable
consideration, directly or indirectly performs or offers, attempts, or agrees to perform for another
person any act described by Section 1101.002(1), as a part of a transaction or as an entire
transaction." The final clause matters. You cannot escape by doing only one slice of the work. If
you perform one enumerated act as part of somebody else's transaction, you are engaged in real
estate brokerage.

Subsection (b) then draws a boundary that keeps ordinary commerce out. A person is not engaged in
real estate brokerage, "regardless of whether the person is licensed under this chapter," based
solely on "constructing, remodeling, or repairing a home or other building"; "sponsoring, promoting,
or managing, or otherwise participating as a principal, partner, or financial manager of, an
investment in real estate"; or "entering into an obligation to pay another person that is secured by
an interest in real property." A general contractor in Lubbock does not become a broker by building
houses. An investor does not become a broker by putting money into a syndication. A borrower does
not become a broker by signing a note secured by a lien.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**The wholesaling section.** Section 1101.0045 deserves attention because it is where unlicensed
activity most often becomes licensed activity by accident. Subsection (a) allows a person to
"acquire an option or an interest in a contract to purchase real property and then sell or offer to
sell the option or assign or offer to assign the contract without holding a license issued under
this chapter" — but only if the person "does not use the option or contract to purchase to engage in
real estate brokerage" and "discloses in writing the nature of the equitable interest to any seller
or potential buyer." Subsection (b) supplies the consequence in one sentence: "A person selling or
offering to sell an option or assigning or offering to assign an interest in a contract to purchase
real property without disclosing the nature of that interest as provided by Subsection (a)(2) is
engaging in real estate brokerage." Notice the structure. The exemption is conditional, and the
condition is a written disclosure. Drop the disclosure and the same conduct is brokerage — which
means, for an unlicensed wholesaler, brokerage without a licence.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**Who is outside the chapter altogether.** Section 1101.005 lists the persons and transactions to
which the chapter "does not apply." Among them: "an attorney licensed in this state"; "an
attorney-in-fact authorized under a power of attorney to conduct not more than three real estate
transactions annually"; "a public official while engaged in official duties"; "an auctioneer
licensed under Chapter 1802 while conducting the sale of real estate by auction if the auctioneer
does not perform another act of a broker"; "a person conducting a real estate transaction under a
court order or the authority of a will or written trust instrument"; "a person employed by an owner
in the sale of structures and land on which structures are located if the structures are erected by
the owner in the course of the owner's business"; "an on-site manager of an apartment complex"; and
"an owner or the owner's employee who leases the owner's improved or unimproved real estate."

Read those exemptions the way a regulator reads them — narrowly, and with the qualifying clauses
attached. The attorney-in-fact exemption has a numerical cap of "not more than three real estate
transactions annually." The auctioneer exemption applies only "if the auctioneer does not perform
another act of a broker" — the auctioneer who starts negotiating terms has stepped outside it. The
builder's-employee exemption in subdivision (6) applies only where "the structures are erected by
the owner in the course of the owner's business." A new-home sales representative in a Georgetown
subdivision built by her employer is inside that exemption; the same person selling resale homes on
the side is not.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
The section also lists transactions rather than people. Subdivision (9) removes from the chapter a
transaction involving the sale, lease or transfer of a real property interest in "minerals, mining,
or a quarry," "standing timber," or "other energy sources"; the sale, lease or transfer of "a
cemetery lot"; "the lease or management of a hotel or motel"; and "the sale of real property under a
power of sale conferred by a deed of trust or other contract lien." Subdivisions (10) and (11) carve
out certain transfers involving limited partnerships and limited liability companies by their
general partners, managers, managing members, members and employees who negotiate in the course of
employment, and subdivision (12) covers "a person conducting a real estate transaction on behalf of
a commercial signage entity."

**The licence requirement.** Section 1101.351(a) provides that unless a person holds a license
issued under the chapter, the person may not "act as or represent that the person is a broker or
sales agent" or "act as a residential rental locator." Subsection (a-1) applies the same rule to
business entities: "Unless a business entity holds a license issued under this chapter, the business
entity may not act as a broker." Subsection (b) closes the gap between passing the exam and holding
the licence: "An applicant for a broker or sales agent license may not act as a broker or sales
agent until the person receives the license evidencing that authority."

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
Then comes the sentence that shapes your working life. Section 1101.351(c): "A licensed sales agent
may not engage or attempt to engage in real estate brokerage unless the sales agent is sponsored by
a licensed broker and is acting for that broker." Two conditions, both required, joined by "and."
You must be sponsored, *and* you must be acting for that broker. A sales agent is not a small
broker. A sales agent is a licence held inside somebody else's licence.

The statute follows that structure through to liability. Section 1101.803 makes a licensed broker
"liable to the commission, the public, and the broker's clients for any conduct engaged in under
this chapter by the broker or by a sales agent associated with or acting for the broker." Read what
that sentence does not do — it adds the broker; it does not subtract you. Your conduct is, by
statute, the broker's exposure. Module 09 teaches broker responsibility.

The Commission builds the operating system on top of that statute in 22 TAC § 535.2, which requires
a broker to notify each sponsored sales agent in writing of the scope of the sales agent's
authorised activities, makes the broker responsible for those authorised acts and for acts the
broker permits beyond that scope, and requires at subsection (f) that "Listings and other agreements
for real estate brokerage services must be solicited and accepted in a broker's name." That last
requirement tells you who the client's contract is actually with: when you take a listing in Plano,
the seller's agreement is with your broker, and you are the person through whom the broker performs.
Module 09 teaches § 535.2 in full.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**The rules, and why they bind you as hard as the statute.** New license holders often treat the
TREC rules as a kind of internal handbook, softer than *real law*. That is wrong, and it is an
expensive mistake. Section 1101.151(b) provides that the commission may "adopt and enforce rules
necessary to administer this chapter and Chapter 1102" and may "establish standards of conduct and
ethics for persons licensed under this chapter and Chapter 1102" to "fulfill the purposes of this
chapter and Chapter 1102" and "ensure compliance with this chapter and Chapter 1102." The
Legislature delegated; the Commission legislated within the delegation. The product of that
delegation is codified in Title 22 of the Texas Administrative Code — Chapter 531 (a short chapter
of conduct standards) and Chapter 535 (a long chapter of operational rules).

The enforcement provisions name the rules explicitly. Section 1101.701(a) allows the commission to
impose an administrative penalty on "a person who violates this chapter or a rule adopted or order
issued by the commission under this chapter"; § 1101.751(a) allows the commission to bring an action
to enjoin a violation of the chapter or a commission rule; and § 1101.759(a) authorises a cease and
desist order on the same footing. A rule violation is an enforceable violation. Learn both bodies of
authority, and learn which is which, because a well-trained license holder can say *the statute
requires X and the rule requires Y* and an untrained one says *TREC says* about everything and is
wrong half the time. Module 10 teaches the penalty and enforcement provisions.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
The rules also keep their own definitions, and they are not identical to the statute's. Rule 22 TAC
§ 531.1 defines only two terms for Chapter 531: "Commission–The Texas Real Estate Commission" and
"License Holder–A real estate broker or sales agent licensed under Chapter 1101, Texas Occupations
Code." Rule 22 TAC § 535.1 defines rather more for Chapter 535, including "Act–Chapter 1101, Texas
Occupations Code," and — importantly — a broader licence-holder definition: "License holder–A person
licensed or registered by the Commission under Chapter 1101 or 1102, Texas Occupations Code."
Chapter 1102 governs real estate inspectors. So when you read a Chapter 535 rule that speaks of a
"license holder," check whether the drafting reaches inspectors too. Section 535.1 also defines
"Compensation–A commission, fee, or other valuable consideration for real estate brokerage services
provided by a license holder under the Act" and "Place of business–A place where the license holder
meets with clients and customers to transact business." That last definition is the only place in
the sources read for this course where the words "clients" and "customers" appear side by side in a
definition — and note that it defines *the place*, not either kind of person. We will come back to
that in Unit 3.

chunks.heading: Unit: What is Agency? The License Act - Statute & Rules
chunks.excerpt:
**How far the Act reaches.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.4 answers the geography question that trips up
license holders working remotely: "The Act applies to any person acting as a real estate broker or
sales agent while physically within Texas, regardless of the location of the real estate involved or
the residence of the person's customers or clients. For the purposes of the Act, a person conducting
brokerage business from another state by mail, telephone, the Internet, email, or other medium is
acting within Texas if the real property concerned is located wholly or partly in Texas." Both
halves are traps in different directions. Sitting in El Paso brokering a New Mexico ranch, you are
within the Act because you are physically in Texas. Sitting in Santa Fe brokering an El Paso ranch,
you are within the Act because the property is in Texas.

The same rule tells you that showing is brokerage: "Unless otherwise exempted by the Act, a person
must be licensed as a broker or sales agent to show a property." And it defines showing broadly —
for purposes of that section, to show a property "includes causing or permitting the property to be
viewed by a prospective buyer or tenant, unlocking or providing access onto or into a property for a
prospective buyer or tenant, and hosting an open house at the property." Unlicensed assistants who
unlock doors are performing an act for which a licence is required. Section 535.4 further provides
that "A real estate license is required for a person to solicit listings or to negotiate in Texas
for listings," and that "A real estate license is required for a person to receive a fee or other
consideration for assisting another person to locate real property for sale, purchase, rent, or
lease, including the operation of a service which finds apartments

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Reading § 1101.002(1) as an enforcement lawyer would
chunks.excerpt:
or homes."

Rule 22 TAC § 535.5 supplies the mirror image. "Acting as a principal, a person may purchase, sell,
lease, or sublease real estate for profit without being licensed as a broker or sales agent." Owners
may deal for themselves. But the rule immediately narrows the point for co-owners: "A person who
owns property jointly may sell and convey title to his or her interest in the property, but to act
for compensation or with the expectation of compensation as an agent for the other owner, the person
must be licensed unless otherwise exempted by the Act." Selling your own half interest is not
brokerage; selling your co-owner's half for a fee is. Section 535.5 also provides that "An answering
service or clerical or administrative employees identified to callers as such to confirm information
concerning the size, price, and terms of property advertised are not required to be licensed under
the Act" — which tells your unlicensed assistant precisely where the line is, and it is a narrow
line: size, price, terms, and identification as clerical staff.

The common-law rules governing how agency relationships are created outside a licensing statute —
formation by ratification, by estoppel, by apparent authority — were not held for this course and
are not taught here. What you have, and what Texas will hold you to, is the statute and the rules.

### Statute reading exercise: Reading § 1101.002(1) as an enforcement lawyer would

Open Texas Occupations Code § 1101.002 and read subdivision (1) in full, then § 1101.004 and
§ 1101.005. Answer from the text only.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
1. Subdivision (1)(A) opens with a phrase about consideration before it reaches the list of acts.
   Write out that opening phrase and explain what it means for a person who performs one of the
   listed acts, is never paid, but hoped to be. Then find the phrase in § 1101.004(a) that carries
   the same idea and note how the wording differs.
2. Count the acts listed in § 1101.002(1)(A). How many must a person perform before the definition
   is satisfied? Quote the words in the opening clause that answer this.
3. Subparagraph (A)(xi) has three lettered conditions. Are they joined so that all three must be
   true, or so that any one will do? Identify the word in the text that settles it, and explain what
   changes if a license holder labels the document an appraisal.
4. Section 1101.005 exempts "an attorney-in-fact authorized under a power of attorney." Does the
   exemption have a limit? Quote it. Does § 1101.005 contain any similar numerical limit for the
   exemption covering an on-site manager of an apartment complex?
5. Section 1101.004(b) says certain activity is not brokerage "regardless of whether the person is
   licensed under this chapter." Why would the Legislature include that clause? What would change if
   it were deleted?

## Unit: Why Study Agency

There is a version of this question that deserves a blunt answer, so here it is. You are studying
agency because agency law is the subject on which Texas license holders most reliably lose their
licences, their commissions and their savings, and because the Texas Legislature thought it
important enough to name it first.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
Look at § 1101.003(a). The section defines "qualifying real estate courses" for purposes of the
chapter, and the list begins: "(1) agency law; (2) contract law; (3) principles of real estate; (4)
property management; (5) real estate appraisal;" and continues through brokerage, finance,
investment, law, marketing and mathematics. Agency law is subdivision (1). That ordering is not an
accident of alphabet — "agency" does precede "appraisal" and "contract" alphabetically, but the list
is not alphabetical after that point — and it is not decorative. The course you are taking exists
because a statute names it.

**Reason one: agency status determines what you owe, and to whom.** This is the practical core.
Almost every serious question a license holder faces in a live transaction resolves into a prior
question about relationship. May I tell this buyer that my seller is desperate? May I tell this
seller what the other buyer offered? Must I disclose that the roof leaks? Must I present this
lowball offer? May I take a fee from both sides? Every one of those answers changes depending on
whom you represent. If you do not know your own agency status in a transaction, you cannot know your
duties, and if you cannot know your duties you will breach one of them by accident.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
The Legislature made that failure a disciplinary ground in its own right. Section 1101.652(b)(7)
authorises disciplinary action against a license holder who, while engaged in real estate brokerage,
fails to make clear to all parties to a real estate transaction the party for whom the license
holder is acting. Read the elements: the obligation runs to all parties, not only to your own
client, and the standard is that the fact be made *clear* to the people in the transaction, not
merely known to you or recorded somewhere in a file. Module 10 teaches § 1101.652.

**Reason two: the disciplinary catalogue is dense with agency.** Section 1101.652(b) supplies
thirty-four grounds for disciplinary action against a license holder "while engaged in real estate
brokerage," and a large share of them are agency questions wearing other clothes — negligence and
incompetence, dishonesty and untrustworthiness, a known defect not disclosed to a buyer who is not
your client, compensation taken from more than one party, self-dealing on a principal's money, a
listing with no definite termination date, going around another broker's client, and, effective
January 1, 2026, failing to enter into the written buyer agreement § 1101.563 requires. Module 10
teaches that section subdivision by subdivision. What matters at this point in the course is the
shape of it: the grounds you are most likely to touch are the ones that turn on whom you represent.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**Reason three: what discipline actually costs.** Section 1101.701(a) allows the commission to
impose an administrative penalty on a person who violates the chapter, a rule, or a commission
order, and § 1101.702(a) sets the ceiling: the amount "may not exceed $5,000 for each violation,"
and "Each day a violation continues or occurs may be considered a separate violation for purposes of
imposing a penalty." Two numbers to hold: five thousand dollars, and per violation, with a per-day
multiplier available. Module 10 teaches the penalty provisions and the factors that set the amount.

Now the sentence that students most need and most often have never read. Section 1101.801:
"Disciplinary action taken against a person under Section 1101.652 does not relieve the person from
civil or criminal liability." A TREC order is not a settlement of the case. It is one of three
tracks, and the other two belong to the injured consumer and to the State.

The criminal track is real, if rarely travelled. Section 1101.756 provides that "A person commits an
offense if the person wilfully violates or fails to comply with this chapter or a commission order,"
and that "An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor." Section 1101.758 makes it a Class
A misdemeanor to act as a broker or sales agent without holding a licence.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
The money track is where unlicensed agency activity becomes catastrophic. Section 1101.753(a)
provides that in addition to injunctive relief, "a person who receives a commission or other
consideration as a result of acting as a broker or sales agent without holding a license or
certificate of registration under this chapter is liable to the state for a civil penalty of not
less than the amount of money received or more than three times the amount of money received."
Section 1101.754(a) gives the same range to the aggrieved person privately. Work the arithmetic once
and you will not forget it. An unlicensed person who collects a $9,000 fee for finding a buyer for a
house in Tyler faces a civil penalty to the State of not less than $9,000 and not more than $27,000
under § 1101.753(a), and a private penalty to the aggrieved person of not less than $9,000 and not
more than $27,000 under § 1101.754(a) — and the two provisions are separate, so the maximum exposure
from the two sections together on those facts is $54,000, on top of the $9,000 that was collected in
the first place.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**Reason four: you cannot sue for a commission you did not earn under a proper agency agreement.**
Section 1101.806(b) bars a person from maintaining an action to collect compensation for an act as a
broker or sales agent performed in this state unless the person alleges and proves that the person
was a license holder at the time the act was commenced or an attorney licensed in any state, and
subsection (c) bars an action to recover a commission unless the promise or agreement on which the
action is based, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party against whom the
action is brought. Module 04 teaches § 1101.806, including the commission forfeiture in subsection
(d) and the two matters subsection (a) keeps outside the section.

**Reason five: the broker's exposure and the allocation of misrepresentation risk.** We have already
read § 1101.803, which puts your conduct on your broker's licence. Section 1101.805 then allocates
responsibility for misstatements, and it does so with unusual force: a party is not liable for a
license holder's misrepresentation or concealment of a material fact, and a license holder is not
liable for a party's, unless the person both knew of the falsity and failed to disclose that
knowledge. Both tests are two-pronged and conjunctive, and knowing your seller has lied and staying
quiet is exactly the fact pattern the license holder's half of that allocation was written to reach.
Subsection (b) states that "This section prevails over any other law, including common law." Module
03 teaches § 1101.805; Module 09 teaches broker responsibility under § 1101.803.

chunks.heading: Unit: Why Study Agency
chunks.excerpt:
**Reason six: there is a fund, and it is not generous.** Subchapter M creates the real estate
recovery trust account, which the commission maintains "to reimburse aggrieved persons who suffer
actual damages caused by an act described by Section 1101.602" committed by a license holder, a
certificate holder, or an employee or agent of one. Recovery is capped and time-limited: an action
must be brought within two years of accrual under § 1101.605(a); payments arising out of a single
transaction "may not exceed a total of $125,000, regardless of the number of claimants" under
§ 1101.610(a), with a further per-license-holder cap of "$250,000 until the license or certificate
holder has reimbursed the trust account for all amounts paid" under § 1101.610(b); and § 1101.613(b)
removes the last comfort, providing that repaying the trust account "does not affect another
disciplinary proceeding brought under this chapter." Pay the fund back and you still face the
licence case. Module 11 teaches §§ 1101.601–1101.610.

**Reason seven: the conduct standards are written as competence obligations, and ignorance is itself
a violation.** Rule 22 TAC § 531.4 provides that "It is the obligation of a license holder to be
knowledgeable and competent as a real estate brokerage practitioner," and 22 TAC § 531.3 requires
"employment of prudence and caution so as to avoid misrepresentation, in any way, by acts of
commission or omission." Read together with the negligence and incompetence ground at
§ 1101.652(b)(1), those rules mean that not knowing the agency rules is not a defence to breaking
them. It is a second violation. Module 02 teaches the Canons at 22 TAC §§ 531.2–531.4.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The unlicensed finder in Tyler
chunks.excerpt:
That is why you study agency. Not to pass an examination — although you will need it for that — but
because the alternative is to spend a career making decisions about other people's money without
knowing whose side you are on.

### Applied exercise: The unlicensed finder in Tyler

Marcus is not licensed. He hears that a Tyler investor wants a small apartment building. Marcus
finds a twelve-unit property, introduces the parties, sits in on two negotiating sessions, and is
paid $9,000 when the sale closes at $1,150,000. The investor later sues, and TREC opens a file.

1. Identify by subparagraph at least three acts in § 1101.002(1)(A) that Marcus performed. Does the
   statute require more than one? Quote the language that answers this.
2. Under § 1101.753(a), state the minimum and maximum civil penalty the State may seek. Show the
   arithmetic.
3. Under § 1101.754(a), state the minimum and maximum penalty the aggrieved investor may recover.
   Combine the two figures with your answer to question 2 to state Marcus's total statutory penalty
   exposure from these two sections.
4. Under § 1101.806(b), may Marcus sue the investor for the $9,000 if the investor had refused to
   pay? Quote the two alternatives in the subdivision list and explain which, if either, Marcus
   satisfies.
5. Section 1101.758 makes acting as a broker without a licence an offence. What grade of offence,
   and does § 1101.801 allow the criminal case and the TREC case to proceed independently? Quote the
   sentence you rely on.

## Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
Here is a fact about Texas law that will orient everything else in this unit, and that most study
material never tells you: **The Real Estate License Act does not define "client" and does not define
"customer."** The word "customer" does not appear in Chapter 1101 at all. The word "clients" appears
in exactly two sections of the chapter — § 1101.553, which requires a residential rental locator to
display the licence "in a place accessible to clients and prospective clients," and § 1101.803,
which makes the broker "liable to the commission, the public, and the broker's clients." Neither
section defines the term. Among the Commission rules read for this course, the pair appears once, in
the 22 TAC § 535.1 definition of "Place of business–A place where the license holder meets with
clients and customers to transact business," which defines the place and not the people.

So where does the distinction come from? It comes from the concept of representation, which the
statute *does* address, and it is worth being honest about that: "client" and "customer" are the
vocabulary the industry uses to describe two positions the statute creates by other means. Learn the
statutory machinery and the vocabulary follows. Learn the vocabulary alone and you will be
confidently wrong the first time a fact pattern gets complicated.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
**The party.** Start with the statute's own word. Section 1101.551(2) provides that a **party**
"means a prospective buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant or an authorized representative of a buyer,
seller, landlord, or tenant, including a trustee, guardian, executor, administrator, receiver, or
attorney-in-fact. The term does not include a license holder who represents a party." Two things
follow. A party is one of the four transaction positions, or someone standing in that person's shoes
with legal authority. And a party is *not* the license holder. You are never a party to a
transaction merely by brokering it.

There is one place where that flips. Section 1101.557(c)(1) provides that for purposes of that
section, "a license holder who has the authority to bind a party to a lease or sale under a power of
attorney or a property management agreement is also a party to the lease or sale." A property
manager in San Antonio who can sign leases without the owner's further approval is, for § 1101.557
purposes, a party.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
**The principal, and the agent.** The principal is the person for whom the agent acts. The agent, in
Texas real estate, is the broker. Section 1101.557(a) states the rule with no wiggle room in it: "A
broker who represents a party in a real estate transaction or who lists real estate for sale under
an exclusive agreement for a party is that party's agent." Representing a party makes you that
party's agent; taking an exclusive listing makes you that party's agent; there is no third state in
which you have done one of those two things and are somehow not the agent. Subsection (b) then
attaches duties that a representation agreement may narrow but not go below — at a minimum,
answering the party's questions and presenting any offer to or from the party. Module 02 teaches
§ 1101.557 and the duties that follow from it.

**Where the sales agent sits.** The sales agent is not the client's agent in the client's contract;
the broker is. Section 1101.002(7) defines a sales agent as "a person who is sponsored by a licensed
broker for the purpose of performing an act described by Subdivision (1)," and § 1101.351(c)
requires the sales agent to be sponsored by a licensed broker *and* acting for that broker. Rule 22
TAC § 535.2(f) requires listings and other brokerage agreements to be "solicited and accepted in a
broker's name." When a Fort Worth seller says *you're my agent*, what is legally true is that the
broker is the seller's agent and you are the license holder through whom the broker acts. This is
not a technicality you can wave away — it is why your sponsoring broker gets to set the scope of
your authority, why § 1101.803 makes the broker liable for your conduct, and why your compensation
must flow through the broker.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
That compensation channel is statutory. Section 1101.651(b) forbids a sales agent to accept
compensation for a real estate transaction from a person other than the sponsoring broker, and
subsection (c) forbids the sales agent to pay a commission to a person except through that broker;
22 TAC § 535.3 states the same rule in terms of the sponsoring broker's written consent; and
§ 1101.651(a) closes the outer wall by forbidding a broker to compensate a person for performing an
act of a broker unless that person is a license holder or a broker licensed in another state who
conducts in Texas none of the negotiations for which the compensation is paid. Module 09 teaches § 1101.651(a)–(c) and the compensation
rules.

**Associated brokers, and the delegated supervisor.** Not every license holder under a broker's roof
is a sales agent. An **associated broker** is "a broker who associates with and is paid through
another broker under a relationship that is intended to be a continuous relationship, including as
an employee or an ongoing independent contractor" — the definition is at § 1101.552(g) and is
carried into the rules at 22 TAC § 535.1, and § 1101.552(e)(2) requires a license holder who is an
associated broker to give the commission "the name of the broker with whom the license holder is
associated." Separately, 22 TAC § 535.2(e) lets a broker delegate responsibility for assisting with
compliance without relinquishing overall responsibility for supervision, requires any license holder
who leads, supervises, directs or manages a team to be delegated as a supervisor, requires the
delegation to be in writing, and requires the broker to name each delegated supervisor to the
Commission "within 30 days of any such delegation that has lasted or is anticipated to last more
than th

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
ree consecutive months." If you join a team in Houston, somebody on that team is a delegated supervisor, and that
delegation is a written, reportable act. Module 09 teaches the supervision rule; Module 12 teaches
§ 1101.552.

**The customer.** A customer, in the working vocabulary of Texas practice, is a person you deal with
but do not represent — the unrepresented buyer who calls on your listing, the seller across the
table from your buyer. Because TRELA does not define the word, the useful question is not *what is a
customer* but *what does a Texas license holder owe a person the license holder does not represent?*
The held sources answer that clearly, and the answer is: quite a lot.

Rule 22 TAC § 531.2 makes the license holder's primary duty the representation of the client's
interests and then qualifies it in the same sentence, requiring that the license holder, "in
performing duties to the client, shall treat other parties to a transaction fairly." Rule 22 TAC
§ 535.156(b) says the same thing in the other order — the principal's interest above the license
holder's own, honest and fair dealing with all parties, fidelity owed to the principal only — and
subsection (d) adds a free-standing duty "to convey accurate information to members of the public
with whom the license holder deals." Module 02 teaches both rules.

Add to that the statutory defect duties in § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4), which run to a "potential
buyer," and the picture is complete: representation determines *advocacy*, not *honesty*. You may
advocate for one side only. You must be honest and fair with everyone. A student who leaves this
unit believing that a customer is owed nothing has learned the opposite of the rule.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
**Showing without representing, and the written buyer agreement.** Effective January 1, 2026 the
Legislature gave the customer relationship an express statutory form. Section 1101.562 permits a
broker to show real property available for sale or lease to a party without representing the party,
but only where the broker has not agreed with the party, orally or in writing, to represent the
party, is not otherwise acting as the party's agent at the time of showing, provides the party no
opinions or advice, and performs no other act of real estate brokerage for the party; subsection (c)
then lets the broker confirm information about "the size, price, and terms of the real property
available for sale or lease." Section 1101.563 requires a license holder who performs any act of
real estate brokerage for a prospective buyer of residential real property to enter into a written
agreement with the prospective buyer before showing residential real property or presenting an
offer, prescribes what that agreement must state, caps a showing-only agreement at fourteen days,
and forbids it from being exclusive. Module 05 teaches both sections, and the 2026 changes, in full.

Two things about those sections belong in a unit about roles rather than about paperwork. The first
two conditions in § 1101.562(a) are conditions of *fact*: an oral agreement to represent is enough
to defeat the non-representation posture, and the second condition asks what you were actually doing
at the time of the showing rather than what a form says. And the effect of the two sections together
is that Texas now has a statutory customer — a party defined by what the license holder does not do
for them — and a document that has to say which of the two positions the party occupies.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
**Disclosure of agency: § 1101.558.** This is the section the topic's scope note points at.
Subsection (b) requires a license holder who represents a party in a proposed real estate
transaction to disclose that representation, orally or in writing, at the time of the license
holder's first contact with another party to the transaction or with another license holder who
represents another party. Subsection (b-1) requires, at the time of a license holder's first
substantive communication with a party about specific real property, a written notice in at least a
10-point font describing the ways in which a broker can represent a party including as an
intermediary, the basic duties owed to a party the broker represents, the basic obligations owed to
a party the broker does not represent, and the name, license number and contact information for the
license holder and the license holder's supervisor and broker. Subsection (b-2) directs the
commission to prescribe the text of that notice, and the Commission has done so at 22 TAC § 531.20,
which adopts by reference the Information About Brokerage Services Notice, TREC No. IABS 1-2, sets
the permitted methods of delivery, and provides that a link to a completed notice "may not be in a
footnote or signature block in an email." Subsection (c) lists three situations in which the
subsection (b-1) written notice is not required; those exceptions do not touch the subsection (b)
disclosure, which stands alone. Module 02 teaches § 1101.558 and 22 TAC § 531.20 in full — T02U5 is
the form's own IABS unit.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
Two features of the held text belong here, because they bound what this course may say about the
section at all. Subsection (a) is shown as "Repealed by Acts 2015, 84th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1158 , Sec.
92, eff. January 1, 2016," and subsections (d) and (e) carry the identical repeal notation; the held
source does not preserve the text of any of the three, so this course does not state what they said.
And § 1101.558 carries a further amendment recorded as Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1172 (S.B.
1968), Sec. 9, eff. January 1, 2026. The held source gives that amendment at section level and does
not label which subsection each 2025 change touched, so this course states the section's current
operative text — subsections (b), (b-1), (b-2) and (c) — and does not assert which individual
subsection was added or reworded by that act.

**The intermediary.** Section 1101.551(1) defines the term: an **intermediary** "means a broker who
is employed to negotiate a transaction between the parties to a transaction and for that purpose may
act as an agent of the parties." An intermediary is a *broker*, not a sales agent, and the position
exists because one brokerage sometimes ends up with both sides.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
The machinery is §§ 1101.559 through 1101.561, and Module 06 teaches all of it. In outline:
§ 1101.559(a) lets a broker act as an intermediary only on written consent from each party that
states the source of any expected compensation, and subsection (c) requires that "An intermediary
shall act fairly and impartially"; § 1101.560 lets the broker, where the parties' written consent
authorises it and written notice goes to all parties, appoint an associated license holder to each
side, and only an appointed license holder may provide that party opinions and advice during
negotiations; § 1101.651(d) sets out what the intermediary and any appointed license holder may not
disclose, each prohibition carrying its own qualifier; and § 1101.561 makes those duties supersede
other law including common law and makes intermediary status mandatory where a broker agrees to
represent both a buyer or tenant and a seller or landlord. Nothing in this module should be relied
on to run an intermediary transaction.

chunks.heading: Unit: Roles People Play in Agency Relationships - Client or Customer?
chunks.excerpt:
**Subagency.** Students arrive with the word *subagent* in their vocabulary, so here is the accurate
position. The word *subagent* appears nowhere in Chapter 1101 as held for this course. Section
1101.002(8) is shown as "Repealed by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1172 (S.B. 1968), Sec. 13(1),
eff. January 1, 2026," and § 1101.805(f) is shown as repealed by section 13(2) of the same act,
effective the same date; the held source does not preserve the text of either repealed provision, so
this course does not state what they said. TREC's own explanatory article on the 2026 changes —
again, guidance rather than law — states that "Two references to subagency were removed from TRELA,"
that "This means the circumstances in which subagency could arise in your real estate practice are
limited," and that "However, subagency has not been eliminated generally as a legal concept." The
common-law doctrine of subagency was not held for this course and is not taught here. What you
should carry away is narrow and defensible: Texas statute no longer uses the term, the circumstances
in which it arises are limited, and if you think you are in one, that is a question for your broker
and a lawyer rather than for your own judgment.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: The words the Act defines, and the two it does not
chunks.excerpt:
**Putting the vocabulary together.** So: the **principal** or **client** is the party your broker
represents — the status § 1101.557(a) creates. The **agent** is the broker; you, as a **sales
agent**, act for and through that broker under § 1101.351(c). The **customer** is a party you deal
with but do not represent, a position the statute now gives express shape in § 1101.562, and to whom
you owe honesty, fairness, accurate information and defect disclosure under 22 TAC § 531.2, 22 TAC
§ 535.156(b) and (d), and § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4). A **party** is defined by § 1101.551(2) and
excludes a license holder who represents a party. An **intermediary** is a broker under
§ 1101.551(1) operating with written consent under § 1101.559. An **associated license holder** is a
license holder appointed under § 1101.560 to work with one side. And **subagency** is a term Texas
statute no longer uses.

### Statute reading exercise: The words the Act defines, and the two it does not

Open Texas Occupations Code § 1101.002 and § 1101.551, then 22 TAC § 535.1. Answer from the text
only.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The open house on Guadalupe Street
chunks.excerpt:
1. List the terms defined by § 1101.002(3), (4), (5) and (7). Quote the definition of "sales agent"
   and identify the single fact that definition makes essential to the role.
2. Section 1101.002(5) defines "real estate." Quote the sentence that excludes something from the
   term, and state whether a deed of trust lien and a ten-year ground lease are inside or outside
   the definition.
3. Search § 1101.002 and § 1101.551 for the words "client" and "customer." Which of the two appears
   anywhere in Chapter 1101, in which sections does it appear, and does any of those sections define
   it?
4. Read § 1101.551(2). Quote the sentence that removes a license holder from the definition of
   "party," and explain what that exclusion means for a sales agent negotiating a contract on a
   client's behalf. Then read § 1101.551(1): is an intermediary a broker, a sales agent, or either?
   Quote the words that settle it.
5. Open 22 TAC § 535.1 and find the definition of "Place of business." Which two words that Chapter
   1101 never defines appear in that definition, and what does the definition actually define — the
   people, or something else?

### Applied exercise: The open house on Guadalupe Street

Priya is a sales agent sponsored by Broker A. Broker A has the listing on a single-family house in
Austin. On Saturday, Priya hosts the open house. Three people arrive: Daniel, who is unrepresented
and has signed nothing; Sofia, who tells Priya she has a signed written representation agreement
with Broker B; and Wes, who is unrepresented and asks Priya to show him two other houses listed by
other brokerages the following week.

chunks.heading: Unit: Relationship between Principal & Agent
chunks.excerpt:
1. Under § 1101.558(b), what must Priya disclose to Daniel, in what form or forms, and at what
   moment? Quote the operative language.
2. Under § 1101.652(b)(22), what may Priya not do with respect to Sofia? Quote the subdivision and
   identify the element that must be satisfied about Priya's knowledge.
3. Wes wants Priya to show him the two other houses. Under § 1101.563(b), what must happen before
