deviation is that the Broker Contact Information section may be prefilled. You may not add your logo
into the body, reformat it to fit a page, trim a paragraph you find confusing, or otherwise tidy it
up. If your brokerage's template does any of that, it is out of compliance with § 531.20.

**A companion notice that is not the IABS.** 22 TAC § 531.18 adopts a different document by
reference, the Consumer Protection Notice, TREC No. CN 1-5, which carries a display-in-the-office
requirement the IABS rule does not, is not delivered at first substantive communication, and means
two links on your homepage rather than one. **Module 08 teaches § 531.18.** The Consumer Protection
Notice form itself was not held for this course.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Four conversations in Corpus Christi
chunks.excerpt:
**How the 2026 changes wire into all of this.** Section 1101.562(b), which you met in Unit 3, routes
a non-representation showing through this unit's two duties: before showing property without
representing the party, the broker must, as applicable, "disclose to the party as required by
Section 1101.558(b) if the broker represents the owner of the real property" or "provide to the
party the written notice described by Section 1101.558(b-1) if the broker does not represent the
owner of the real property." So the disclosure you owe depends on which side, if any, you are on.
Represent the owner: make the (b) representation disclosure, orally or in writing. Represent nobody
in the transaction: deliver the (b-1) written notice — the IABS.

**The habit to build.** Nothing in this unit is difficult. It fails in practice for one reason:
license holders treat the IABS as paperwork rather than as the first thing they do. Build the
sequence into muscle memory. Before you talk about a specific property with a party, deliver the
notice by one of the four permitted routes and keep the proof — and remember that 22 TAC § 535.2(h),
taught in Module 09, requires your broker to keep disclosures among the brokerage's records,
available to the Commission, for at least four years. If you cannot produce the IABS you say you
sent, your broker has a records problem as well as a disclosure problem.

### Applied exercise: Four conversations in Corpus Christi

You are a sales agent with Padre Coast Realty. Consider each situation separately and answer from §
1101.558 and 22 TAC § 531.20.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. You are hosting an open house at a Padre Coast listing on Ocean Drive. A visitor asks about the
   house's flood history and the neighbourhood. Is the (b-1) written notice required? Identify the
   subdivision of § 1101.558(c) you rely on and both of its elements. Separately, what does §
   1101.558(b) require of you here, and in what form or forms may you satisfy it?
2. That same visitor then asks you to help her lease out her own condo on Alameda Street for eight
   months. Does § 1101.558(c)(1) excuse the notice for that conversation? Work through both elements
   of the exception.
3. A prospective buyer emails you asking about a specific listing. You reply and attach the
   completed IABS Notice as a PDF; the body of your email reads only *Hi Marcus — here's the info
   you asked for, call me anytime.* Does that satisfy 22 TAC § 531.20? Quote the words in the rule
   that decide it.
4. Your team lead suggests putting the IABS link into everyone's email signature block so it goes
   out automatically. Quote the sentence in § 531.20 that answers her, and then state what the rule
   requires on the brokerage's homepage instead, including both permitted labels and their minimum
   font sizes.
5. Your brokerage's software prints an IABS with the paragraphs re-flowed into two columns and the
   office logo inserted in the middle of the page, with the Broker Contact Information already
   filled in. Identify which of those three alterations § 531.20 permits and which it does not,
   quoting the rule's language on reproduction.

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The through-line of this module is a single chain, and if you can draw it from memory you understand
the topic. A client authorises a broker; § 1101.557(a) makes that broker the client's agent — "A
broker who represents a party in a real estate transaction or who lists real estate for sale under
an exclusive agreement for a party is that party's agent." The broker authorises the sales agent in
writing and answers for the agent's acts; 22 TAC § 535.2(a) requires the written scope, requires any
limitation or revocation to be written too, and makes the broker responsible even for acts beyond
the explicit scope if the broker permits them. The sales agent may not act except for that broker; §
1101.351(c) says so, § 535.2(f) says listings are solicited and accepted in the broker's name, and §
1101.651(b) and (c) with 22 TAC § 535.3 keep compensation flowing through the broker — those last
three, and the rest of § 535.2, are Module 09's.

Agency in Texas can arise without a signature. Section 1101.562(a)(1) presupposes it by excluding a
party the broker has agreed to represent "either orally or in writing," and (a)(2) by excluding a
broker "otherwise acting as the party's agent." What follows the status is fiduciary: 22 TAC § 531.2
opens "A license holder, while acting as an agent for another, is a fiduciary"; § 535.156 opens "A
license holder's relationship with the license holder's principal is that of a fiduciary"; and §
531.2 carries the balancing clause you must never quote without — the license holder, in performing
duties to the client, "shall treat other parties to a transaction fairly."

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
On classification, remember that universal, general and special agency are classical vocabulary that
no held Texas source defines, and that a residential listing or buyer representation agreement is a
special agency because § 1101.557(c)(1) identifies only a power of attorney and a property
management agreement as instruments conferring authority to bind a party. Single agency is one
broker, one side. Dual agency is answered in Texas by the intermediary: § 1101.561(b) makes the
status mandatory where a broker agrees to represent both a buyer or tenant and a seller or landlord,
and everything else about it — consent under § 1101.559, appointments under § 1101.560, the
prohibitions in § 1101.651(d) — is Module 06's. Subagency's two references were repealed from TRELA
effective January 1, 2026 — § 1101.002(8) by Sec. 13(1) and § 1101.805(f) by Sec. 13(2) of Acts
2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1172 (S.B. 1968) — and the word appears nowhere in the chapter as held.
The no-representation showing is § 1101.562 and the residential buyer's written agreement is §
1101.563; both are Module 05's, and what you take from them here is the classification.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The number to retain from the duties unit is **two calendar days** under 22 TAC § 535.157 — "A
broker or sales agent must respond to his or her principal, a broker or sales agent representing
another party to a real estate transaction, or an unrepresented party to a real estate transaction
within two calendar days" — running to exactly those three categories and no others, in calendar and
not working days, with no stated form, no completeness requirement and no stated starting point. The
same two days run the other way, from a broker or delegated supervisor to sponsored sales agents,
under 22 TAC § 535.2(j), expressly in addition to § 535.157.

The six duties are a teaching frame, not a statute; no held Texas source enumerates six fiduciary
duties by name. Loyalty lives in § 531.2 ("place no personal interest above that of the client") and
§ 535.156 ("must put the interest of the license holder's principal above the license holder's own
interest"). Obedience lives in 22 TAC § 535.16(a) and stops at unlawful instructions. Disclosure
lives in § 535.156, whose offer-submission duty is switched off only "if the principal has agreed in
writing that offers are not to be submitted after the principal has entered into a contract to buy,
sell, rent, or lease a property," and in § 1101.557(b)(2) and (3), which oblige the broker to inform
the party of material information including the receipt of an offer and, at a minimum, to answer the
party's questions and present any offer to or from the party. Confidentiality's sharpest held
statement is § 1101.651(d)(3), Module 06's. Reasonable care lives in the Commission's canons, 22 TAC
§§ 531.3 and 531.4. The disciplinary consequences of breaching any of them sit in § 1101.652, which
is Module 10's.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: A second open-house fact pattern, as optional practice
chunks.excerpt:
Finally, the two disclosures, which are this module's to hold. Section 1101.558(b) is the
representation disclosure: made only if you represent a party, orally or in writing, at first
contact, to another party or to the license holder representing another party, with no exception
list of its own. Section 1101.558(b-1) is the IABS: a written notice in at least 10-point font, at
first substantive communication with a party relating to a proposed transaction regarding specific
real property, containing the four items in (b-1)(1)–(4), with the Commission prescribing the text
under (b-2) and the three exceptions in (c) — the under-one-year residential lease with no sale
being considered, the party you know is represented by another license holder, and the communication
at a property held open that concerns that property. 22 TAC § 531.20 adopts TREC No. IABS 1-2,
requires the labelled homepage link in one of two labels at 10-point or 12-point, permits four
delivery methods, forbids the link in an email footnote or signature block, and permits reproduction
only if the text "is copied verbatim and the spacing, borders and placement of text on the page must
appear to be identical to that in the published version of the IABS Notice, except that the Broker
Contact Information section may be prefilled." Keep the proof.

## Optional reference: A second open-house fact pattern, as optional practice

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it. It is here because the law it covers is real and a
license holder may need it, not because the course requires you to read it. You may skip it and go
straight to the next module; nothing later in this course depends on it.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: A second open-house fact pattern, as optional practice
chunks.excerpt:
**Optional practice — the Cedar Park open house.** This exercise is optional. It puts you on the
other side of the problem the required exercises test: not *what must I disclose*, but *when have I
begun representing someone without meaning to*. Its last two questions turn on a point no required
question in this module tests — that being paid nothing by a person does not answer whether you
represented that person, and that your broker's exposure follows yours.

Renata is a sales agent sponsored by Hill Country Realty, a brokerage that holds the listing on a
house on Little Elm Trail in Cedar Park. Renata is hosting the seller's open house on Saturday. A
couple, the Okonkwos, walk in. They are not represented by anyone. Over twenty minutes Renata
answers their questions about the neighbourhood, tells them the seller would probably take less,
suggests they offer $12,000 under list, and offers to write the offer for them that afternoon. She
is not paid anything by the Okonkwos and nothing is signed at the open house.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: A second open-house fact pattern, as optional practice
chunks.excerpt:
1. Under § 1101.557(a), whose agent is Hill Country Realty with respect to this property, and on
   which of the section's two triggers does that rest?
2. Renata told the Okonkwos that the seller would probably take less. Identify the subdivision of §
   1101.651(d) that makes that disclosure prohibited for a broker or appointed sales agent acting as
   an intermediary, and then explain why Renata's problem in this fact pattern is worse than an
   intermediary's would be, given § 531.2's statement about whose interests the license holder's
   primary duty is to represent.
3. Section 1101.562(a) lists four conditions a broker must satisfy to show property to a party
   without representing that party. Which of the four has Renata's conduct defeated, and quote the
   language that defeats it?
4. Nothing was signed and Renata was paid nothing by the Okonkwos. Explain, using § 1101.563(c)'s
   separate treatment of representation status and compensation, why the absence of payment does not
   answer the question of whom Renata was representing.
5. Section 1101.803 tells you who else now has exposure. State the provision's effect in your own
   words and name the person it reaches besides Renata.

lessons.title: Texas Law of Agency — Module 03

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Agency — Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Agency — Module 03

## TREC Topic: Duties and Disclosures to Third Parties

**Prescribed time: 125 minutes.** This module carries the six units the Commission's LOA-1 course
approval form places under *Duties and Disclosures to Third Parties*, whose scope note is
*"Fiduciary & other duties of an agent."*

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: separate the fiduciary
duties owed to a client from the non-fiduciary duties Texas law imposes toward everyone else, and
name the source of each; explain why fairness to the other side is not neutrality; apply the
definition of "party" in Occupations Code § 1101.551(2); compute the two-calendar-day response
deadline in 22 TAC § 535.157; distinguish a duty to disclose from a duty to investigate; apply
Occupations Code § 1101.805 with both conditions intact and in both directions; state what
§ 1101.804 protects and the qualifier it attaches; operate Property Code § 5.008 — who delivers the
notice, the subsection (f) deadline and remedy, what the subsection (e) exemptions do, and the
subsection (d) knowledge qualifier; and state exactly what Occupations Code § 1101.556 relieves you
of and what it leaves untouched.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it.

## Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties

chunks.heading: Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
Fiduciary duty — loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, accounting, disclosure of material information
— runs to the client, and Module 02 teaches it. Now look at the other people in the room: the buyer
on the other side of your listing, the seller across from your buyer, the unrepresented person who
walked into your open house in Round Rock asking about the foundation. You represent none of them
and owe none of them loyalty. Texas law is nonetheless not indifferent to how you treat them.

The label the Commission's course form uses is **non-fiduciary duties**, and the word does precise
work. A fiduciary duty arises out of a relationship of trust and confidence; a non-fiduciary duty
arises out of statute, out of Commission rule, out of the general law that forbids anyone in
commerce from lying to the people they deal with. It attaches because you hold a Texas licence and
are dealing with a member of the public.

**Texas states both duties in a single rule.** 22 TAC § 531.2 (Fidelity), taught in Module 02 and
read as an ethical whole in Module 10, states the primary duty and then attaches a proviso that
reaches everyone else: "that the primary duty of the license holder is to represent the interests of
the client, and the license holder's position, in this respect, should be clear to all parties
concerned in a real estate transaction; that, however, the license holder, in performing duties to
the client, shall treat other parties to a transaction fairly." Fairness to the other side sits
inside the definition of fidelity.

chunks.heading: Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
**The catalogue.** Here, in one place, is every non-fiduciary duty a Texas source actually imposes —
students believe the list is either much shorter than it is (nothing but "don't lie") or much longer
(a general duty to look after the other side, which no held source creates). Most of these
authorities are taught in full elsewhere; this module states the rule, cites it, names its home, and
shows how it operates toward someone who is not your client.

*Fair treatment and accurate information.* 22 TAC § 535.156 requires honest and fair dealing with
all parties and imposes a duty "to convey accurate information to members of the public with whom
the license holder deals." That second duty does not name a client; it names *members of the
public*. Module 02 teaches the rule; Unit 2 takes up what it demands toward the other side.

*Integrity, including by omission.* 22 TAC § 531.3 requires "prudence and caution so as to avoid
misrepresentation, in any way, by acts of commission or omission" — the phrase that makes silence
capable of being a violation. Module 02 teaches it as a fiduciary duty and Module 10 as a Canon.

*Disclosure of known significant defects to a potential buyer.* Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(4)
authorises discipline for failing to disclose to a potential buyer a significant defect described by
subdivision (b)(3) that is known to the license holder. Module 10 teaches § 1101.652 in full. What
matters here is the addressee: a *potential buyer* is not your client, so that duty runs across the
table.

chunks.heading: Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
*Disclosure of who you represent, and the IABS.* Occupations Code § 1101.558(b) requires disclosure
of your representation, orally or in writing, at first contact with another party or with that
party's license holder; § 1101.558(b-1) requires a written notice at first substantive
communication, and 22 TAC § 531.20 supplies its text by adopting the Information About Brokerage
Services Notice, TREC No. IABS 1-2. Module 02 owns the IABS, including the three exceptions in
§ 1101.558(c), which run to the written notice only and never to the § 1101.558(b) representation
disclosure. The notice belongs here because of one line of its required content: it must describe
"the basic obligations a broker has to a party to a real estate transaction that the broker does not
represent." *Before showing property to someone you do not represent.* Occupations Code
§ 1101.562(b) requires either the representation disclosure or the written notice, as applicable, and
§ 1101.563(b) requires a written agreement with a prospective buyer of residential real property
before showing any such property. Module 05 teaches both sections and the 2026 changes that produced
them.

*Timely response.* 22 TAC § 535.157 reaches "an unrepresented party to a real estate transaction."
Unit 3 below is that duty.

chunks.heading: Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
*The abstract-or-title-policy advice.* Occupations Code § 1101.555 requires a license holder, when
an offer to purchase real estate in this state is signed, to advise "each buyer, in writing," either
to have the abstract examined by an attorney of the buyer's choosing or to be provided with or
obtain a title insurance policy. *Each buyer*, not each client: if the buyer is unrepresented, that
written advice is yours to give, and failure is a ground for discipline under § 1101.652(b)(29).
Module 12 teaches § 1101.555.

*The Consumer Protection Notice.* 22 TAC § 531.18 requires each license holder to display TREC No.
CN 1-5 in a readily noticeable location in each place of business and to link to it from the
homepage of each business website. It tells strangers how to complain about you, so it is a duty
owed to the public at large. Module 08 teaches it.

*Non-discrimination.* 22 TAC § 531.19 forbids a license holder to inquire about, respond to or
facilitate inquiries about, or disclose information about an owner, previous or current occupant,
potential purchaser, lessor or potential lessee that indicates or is intended to indicate a
preference, limitation or discrimination on the bases the rule lists, and § 1101.652(b)(32) makes
discrimination against an owner, potential buyer, landlord or potential tenant a ground for
suspension or revocation. Both run to people who are not your clients; Module 10 teaches both.

chunks.heading: Unit: Non-Fiduciary Duties
chunks.excerpt:
*Disclosure when you are the principal.* 22 TAC § 535.144 obliges a license holder dealing on his or
her own behalf — or for a spouse, parent or child, a business entity in which the license holder is
more than a 10% owner, or a trust in the circumstances the rule describes — to disclose that
licensure in writing, and provides that such a license holder "shall not use the license holder's
expertise to the disadvantage of a person with whom the license holder deals." Again: *a person with
whom the license holder deals*, not a client. The companion obligation to furnish a broker price
opinion or comparative market analysis when you buy or list for your own account, 22 TAC § 535.16,
is taught in Module 04; Module 12 teaches § 535.144.

**What you do not owe.** The absences matter as much as the list. You do not owe a third party
loyalty, and you do not owe a third party confidentiality — that obligation runs the other way, to
your client. You do not owe a third party advocacy, negotiating help, advice about whether the deal
is good for them, or a duty to find problems you do not know about. **You owe the other side
truthfulness, fairness, accuracy, responsiveness, and the specific statutory disclosures — and
nothing that would require you to work against your own client.**

chunks.heading: Unit: General Duties of Honesty & Fairness
chunks.excerpt:
Texas now has a statutory category that makes this concrete. Occupations Code § 1101.562, effective
January 1, 2026 and taught in Module 05, permits a broker, on the four conjunctive conditions Module
05 sets out, to show real property "to a party without representing the party," forbids the broker
while doing so to "provide to the party opinions or advice regarding the real property or real
estate transactions in general," and permits the broker, in subsection (c), to "confirm information
to a party regarding the size, price, and terms of the real property available for sale or lease."
That is a legislative portrait of a non-fiduciary relationship. The license holder is in the house
with the buyer, is answering questions about size, price and terms, is bound to be accurate and fair
— and is expressly forbidden to give advice, because advice is what agents give clients.

**Do not read "non-fiduciary" as "no consequences."** Occupations Code § 1101.803, taught in Module
09, makes a licensed broker "liable to the commission, the public, and the broker's clients for any
conduct engaged in under this chapter by the broker or by a sales agent associated with or acting
for the broker" — the public before the clients. And § 1101.801: "[d]isciplinary action taken
against a person under Section 1101.652 does not relieve the person from civil or criminal
liability."

## Unit: General Duties of Honesty & Fairness

If you memorise one sentence out of this entire module, make it this one, from 22 TAC § 535.156, the
rule Module 02 teaches in full: "A license holder must deal honestly and fairly with all parties;
however, the license holder represents only the principal and owes a duty of fidelity to such
principal."

chunks.heading: Unit: General Duties of Honesty & Fairness
chunks.excerpt:
That sentence has two halves joined by a "however." Over-read the first and you become a mediator
who forgets who is paying for the advocacy; over-read the second and you become the kind of agent
who thinks representing a seller licenses you to mislead a buyer.

**Fairness is not neutrality.** This is the single most important conceptual point in the unit.
Being fair to the buyer does not mean giving the buyer the same service you give the seller, telling
the buyer the seller will take less, or warning the buyer that they are overpaying. Occupations Code
§ 1101.651(d), taught in Module 06, forbids even an intermediary to disclose that the seller or
landlord will accept less than the asking price, or that the buyer or tenant will pay more than the
price in a written offer, unless separately instructed in writing by that party. If that is
prohibited in the most balanced relationship Texas recognises, it is certainly not required in an
ordinary single-agency listing.

So what does fairness require? That the other side be able to rely on the accuracy of what you tell
them and on the regularity of the process you run. You may negotiate hard on price; you may not
misstate the terms of a competing offer. You may decline to volunteer your client's motivation; you
may not invent a deadline that does not exist. You may advocate for your seller's repair position;
you may not tell the buyer's agent the roof was replaced in 2021 when your seller told you it was
patched in 2013.

chunks.heading: Unit: General Duties of Honesty & Fairness
chunks.excerpt:
**The honesty standard in the Commission's own words.** 22 TAC § 531.3 is the broadest, requiring
"prudence and caution so as to avoid misrepresentation, in any way, by acts of commission or
omission" — "prudence and caution" imports a standard of care rather than a mere prohibition on
deliberate lying, so carelessness with facts is a violation, and "commission or omission" makes the
rule reach silence as well as speech. 22 TAC § 535.156 imposes the duty to convey accurate
information to members of the public. Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(2) reaches conduct that is
dishonest or in bad faith or that demonstrates untrustworthiness, none of which requires proof that
anyone lost money, and § 1101.652(b)(1) reaches negligence and incompetence. Every one of those
grounds is available to a complainant you never represented.

Two intermediary provisions bear on the same point and are taught in Module 06. Section
1101.651(d)(4) forbids an intermediary to treat a party to a transaction dishonestly, and
§ 1101.651(d)(3)'s bar on disclosing confidential information yields, among other exceptions, where
"the information materially relates to the condition of the property." Even the strictest
confidentiality obligation TRELA writes down yields to property condition: a client cannot gag you
about a defect.

chunks.heading: Unit: Define Third Party/Obligations to Third Party/Duty to Respond
chunks.excerpt:
**Where honesty problems actually arise.** Most Texas honesty complaints do not come from an agent
inventing a fact. The pattern that produces the most of them — repeating what a seller told you as
though you had verified it — is Unit 4's subject. The other is speaking outside your competence:
§ 1101.652(b)(1) reaches incompetence, and telling an unrepresented buyer in Bastrop County that the
property "is not in a flood zone" because you looked at a map on your phone generates both a
complaint and a claim.

## Unit: Define Third Party/Obligations to Third Party/Duty to Respond

**Start with the vocabulary problem.** TRELA does not define the phrase "third party." What it
defines, in Occupations Code § 1101.551(2), is *party*:

> "Party" means a prospective buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant or an authorized representative of
> a buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant, including a trustee, guardian, executor, administrator,
> receiver, or attorney-in-fact. The term does not include a license holder who represents a party.

That definition governs Subchapter L, and 22 TAC § 535.155 adopts a near-identical definition for
the advertising rule. Two features are load-bearing. It includes **prospective** buyers, sellers,
landlords and tenants — someone who has not signed anything and may never buy is still a party. And
its last sentence excludes a license holder who represents a party: your counterpart across the
table is not a "party"; the counterpart's client is.

chunks.heading: Unit: Define Third Party/Obligations to Third Party/Duty to Respond
chunks.excerpt:
So build the working definition from the statutory one. **In a Texas transaction, a third party is
any party to the transaction other than your own client, together with the people who serve the
transaction without being parties to it.** The first group is defined by § 1101.551(2): the buyer
when you list, the seller when you represent a buyer, the tenant, the landlord, the executor selling
the estate's house in Tyler, the attorney-in-fact signing under a power of attorney. The second —
inspectors, lenders, escrow officers, appraisers, surveyors, HOA managers, contractors, the other
brokerage's sales agent — are not "parties" under § 1101.551(2), but they are "members of the public
with whom the license holder deals" under 22 TAC § 535.156, and the duty to convey accurate
information reaches them.

That difference is not academic. Tell the appraiser that the seller's addition was permitted when
you know the seller told you it was not, and nobody hurt is a "party" to whom you owed a disclosure
under § 1101.652(b)(4), because an appraiser is not a potential buyer. But you have failed the
§ 535.156 duty to convey accurate information to a member of the public, violated § 531.3, and exposed
yourself under § 1101.652(b)(2). The vocabulary changes; the exposure does not.

**A word about the license holder on the other side.** The cooperating sales agent is not your
client and is not a "party," but is named in the two provisions that matter most in daily practice:
§ 1101.558(b)(2), the representation disclosure at first contact with "another license holder who
represents another party to the transaction," and 22 TAC § 535.157, the response rule.

chunks.heading: Unit: Define Third Party/Obligations to Third Party/Duty to Respond
chunks.excerpt:
**Obligations to a third party.** Unit 1 catalogued them by source and they are not restated here:
the representation disclosure at first contact and the IABS Notice at first substantive
communication, what is required before showing property to a person you do not represent, disclosure
of a known significant defect to a potential buyer, the written abstract-or-title-policy advice when
an offer is signed, and — throughout — accuracy, integrity, fairness, non-discrimination and honest
advertising. What this unit adds is the one obligation with a clock on it.

**The duty to respond.** Now to the provision that gives this unit its title. 22 TAC § 535.157
reads, in its entirety:

> A broker or sales agent must respond to his or her principal, a broker or sales agent representing
> another party to a real estate transaction, or an unrepresented party to a real estate transaction
> within two calendar days.

Module 02 dissects that rule. Two things about it belong to this unit. The first is its third
category — "an unrepresented party to a real estate transaction." A for-sale-by-owner in Killeen who
emails your listing brokerage about a buyer's offer is an unrepresented party; so is the
unrepresented buyer who toured your listing on Saturday and emailed a question about the survey on
Sunday. You owe each a response inside two calendar days although you represent neither.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Two calendar days in Kyle
chunks.excerpt:
The second is the unit of measure. The rule says **calendar** days and says nothing about business
days or holidays, so an unrepresented seller's 4:00 p.m. email on Friday, July 3 is answerable by
the end of Sunday, July 5. This is the most commonly misremembered number in the Commission's rules,
and the error always runs the same way: students convert it to business days and answer late.
Responding is also not resolving — an acknowledgement saying where the question has gone and when an
answer is expected satisfies it.

22 TAC § 535.2, taught in Module 09, adds two broker-side clocks that sit alongside § 535.157 rather
than replacing it: a sponsoring broker or delegated supervisor must respond to sponsored sales
agents within two calendar days, and must deliver Commission correspondence to them within three.

**What responding does not turn you into.** Answering an unrepresented buyer's questions promptly
and accurately does not make you their agent. Under Occupations Code § 1101.557(a), taught in Module
02, agency arises from representing a party or from listing under an exclusive agreement — not from
courtesy — and § 1101.562, set out in Unit 1, permits a broker to show property without representing
the party while forbidding opinions or advice about the property or about real estate transactions
in general. Facts, yes. Advice, no.

### Applied exercise: Two calendar days in Kyle

Priya is a sales agent sponsored by Hays Gateway Realty. She has an exclusive listing on a house on
Kohlers Crossing in Kyle. On **Friday, October 2**, three messages arrive:

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
- 9:15 a.m. — an email from Marcus, an unrepresented buyer who saw the house at Thursday's showing,
  asking whether the seller will consider a 45-day close and whether the fence on the south line
  belongs to the subject property.
- 2:40 p.m. — a voicemail from Dana, a sales agent at another brokerage who represents a different
  buyer, asking whether her offer was presented.
- 6:05 p.m. — a text from Priya's seller asking for an update on showings.

Priya is out of town at a family wedding through Sunday and returns Monday, October 5. She responds
to all three on Monday afternoon.

1. Under 22 TAC § 535.157, state the deadline for each of the three responses, by calendar date.
   Show the count.
2. Which of the three responses, if any, was late? Explain your reasoning using the rule's own
   words, and say specifically why the weekend does not help Priya.
3. Marcus asks a second question: "Should I offer full price, or do you think they'd take less?"
   Priya does not represent Marcus. Using § 1101.651(d) and § 1101.562(a)(3) and (c), identify which
   part of Marcus's question Priya may answer and which part she may not, and explain the
   difference.
4. Priya's broker, Renata, was copied on Dana's voicemail transcript on Friday and Priya emailed
   Renata that evening asking how to handle it. Renata replied the following Wednesday, October 7.
   Using 22 TAC § 535.2, state whether Renata met her own deadline and what that deadline was.
5. Suppose Marcus had instead been represented by a buyer's agent, and that agent sent the same 9:15
   a.m. email. Does § 535.157 still apply, and under which of its three named categories?

## Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
This is the longest unit in the module because it is where licences are lost. Almost every
disclosure complaint is a variation on one of four fact patterns: you said something untrue; you
stayed silent about something you knew; you repeated what someone else told you; or you gave an
opinion the listener heard as a fact.

**First: disclose versus investigate.** Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4), taught in
Module 10, make it a ground for discipline to make a material misrepresentation to a potential buyer
about, or to fail to disclose to a potential buyer, a "significant defect, including a latent
structural defect, known to the license holder that would be a significant factor to a reasonable
and prudent buyer in making a decision to purchase real property." Three qualifiers carry the rule
and none may be dropped. The defect must be **significant**; it must be one that **would be a
significant factor to a reasonable and prudent buyer** in deciding to purchase; and it must be
**known to the license holder**.

The third qualifier is where Texas draws the line between disclosure and investigation. The duty
attaches to what you know. **No source held for this course imposes on a Texas license holder an
affirmative duty to inspect the property, to test systems, to open the attic, or to research the
property's history in order to discover defects.** The Commission's disclosure architecture — the
seller's notice under Property Code § 5.008 and the buyer's right to obtain inspections — assumes
the physical investigation is done by the seller's disclosure and by a licensed inspector, not by
you.

Do not overcorrect. Three things narrow the comfort that offers.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
The first is 22 TAC § 531.3's "prudence and caution." A license holder who deliberately arranges not
to learn something — who tells a seller "don't tell me about the foundation, I'd have to disclose
it" — is not exercising prudence and caution to avoid misrepresentation by omission. Held Texas
sources do not use the phrase "wilful blindness," and this course does not attribute that doctrine
to Texas law; what the sources say is that a license holder must be prudent and cautious to avoid
misrepresentation by act of omission, and an arrangement designed to preserve ignorance is difficult
to square with that.

The second is § 1101.652(b)(1), negligence and incompetence: not knowing something a competent agent
in that market would have known is itself a ground for discipline, independent of any disclosure
duty, and § 1101.652(a)(6) points the same way, reaching a license holder who fails to consider
market conditions for the specific geographic area in which the license holder is providing a
service.

The third is that once you *do* know, the duty is immediate and does not depend on being asked.
Subdivision (b)(4) is a failure-to-disclose ground. Nobody has to ask you a question first.

**Second: puffing versus a statement of fact.** Every student arrives with a half-remembered idea
that agents are allowed to "puff." The common-law doctrine of puffery, as such, was not held for
this course, and this module does not state its elements. What Texas *does* hold, in statute, is a
line between opinion and fact that does the same work more precisely.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
Business & Commerce Code § 17.49(i) — the broker exemption, taught with the rest of the DTPA in
Module 11 — exempts from the Deceptive Trade Practices Act "a claim against a person licensed as a
broker or salesperson" under Chapter 1101, Occupations Code, "arising from an act or omission by the
person while acting as a broker or salesperson." Read only that far and you would think license
holders are immune. Read the rest of the subsection. The exemption "does not apply to" three things:
"an express misrepresentation of a material fact that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment,
or opinion"; "a failure to disclose information in violation of Section 17.46(b)(24)"; or "an
unconscionable action or course of action that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment, or
opinion."

That is your puffing rule, in statutory language. **A statement that can honestly be characterised
as advice, judgment or opinion sits inside the exemption. An express misrepresentation of a material
fact does not.** "This is a wonderful family home in a great school district" is opinion; "This home
is zoned for Bowie Elementary" is a fact, and if it is wrong the exemption does not protect you.
"You'll love the light in the mornings" is opinion; "The square footage is 2,410" is a fact.

Two warnings about the line. First, the exemption is from the DTPA. It is not an exemption from
TRELA discipline or from common-law claims; § 1101.652(b)(2) reaches dishonest conduct whether or
not the DTPA applies. Second, an opinion stated with the trappings of expertise starts to sound like
a fact, which is why 22 TAC § 535.17, taught in Module 12, requires a broker price opinion or
comparative market analysis to carry a disclaimer separating it from an appraisal.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Third: silence versus concealment.** Silence and concealment are not the same thing, and Texas
separates them.

Silence is the absence of a statement. Where no rule requires disclosure, silence is generally
permissible — that is the premise of § 1101.556, which we reach in Unit 6. Concealment is
affirmative conduct or a strategic omission that makes a false impression, and Texas reaches it in
several places at once. Section 531.3 forbids misrepresentation "by acts of commission or omission."
Section 1101.805 speaks of "a misrepresentation or a concealment of a material fact." And DTPA
§ 17.46(b)(24) makes it a false, misleading or deceptive act to fail "to disclose information
concerning goods or services which was known at the time of the transaction if such failure to
disclose such information was intended to induce the consumer into a transaction into which the
consumer would not have entered had the information been disclosed."

That subdivision is the DTPA provision most likely to be pleaded against a license holder, and
§ 17.49(i)(2) expressly preserves it against the broker exemption. Its elements are cumulative —
information concerning goods or services, known at the time of the transaction, a failure to
disclose, and an intent to induce the consumer into a transaction they would not otherwise have
entered — and that intent element separates ordinary silence from actionable concealment.

So the practical line is this. If you know a material fact about the property's condition and keep
quiet because disclosing it would cost your seller the deal, you are on the wrong side of
§ 17.46(b)(24) and § 1101.652(b)(4). If you have simply not volunteered your opinion of the
neighbourhood, you are fine.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Fourth: passing on the seller's word.** This is the fact pattern that produces the most confusion,
and the section that governs it is the one students most often misstate.

Occupations Code § 1101.805 is titled "LIABILITY FOR MISREPRESENTATION OR CONCEALMENT." Subsection
(a) adopts the § 1101.551 definition of "party"; subsection (b) provides that "[t]his section
prevails over any other law, including common law"; and subsection (c) provides that the section
"does not diminish a broker's responsibility for the acts or omissions of a sales agent associated
with or acting for the broker." Then come the two operative rules, mirror images of each other.

Subsection (d), protecting the *party* from the *license holder's* conduct:

> A party is not liable for a misrepresentation or a concealment of a material fact made by a
> license holder in a real estate transaction unless the party: (1) knew of the falsity of the
> misrepresentation or concealment; and (2) failed to disclose the party's knowledge of the falsity
> of the misrepresentation or concealment.

Subsection (e), protecting the *license holder* from the *party's* conduct:

> A license holder is not liable for a misrepresentation or a concealment of a material fact made by
> a party to a real estate transaction unless the license holder: (1) knew of the falsity of the
> misrepresentation or concealment; and (2) failed to disclose the license holder's knowledge of the
> falsity of the misrepresentation or concealment.

Now the misstatements to avoid.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
**Misstatement one: "Section 1101.805 means an agent is never liable for repeating what a seller
said."** It does not say that. It says the license holder is not liable for a misrepresentation
*made by a party* unless two things are both true. The shield covers the *party's*
misrepresentation. It does not convert the license holder's own independent assertion into the
party's statement.

**Misstatement two: "The agent is liable if the agent had reason to doubt the seller."** The
statute's word is **"knew."** Not "should have known," not "had reason to suspect," not "was
negligent in believing." The two conditions are conjunctive and both must be satisfied before the
shield drops: the license holder must have known of the falsity *and* have failed to disclose that
knowledge. A license holder who knew the statement was false and *did* disclose that knowledge to
the affected person has satisfied the second condition and remains protected by the section's terms.

**Misstatement three: "So if I don't actually know, I'm safe."** Safe from *this section*, on *this
claim*. Section 1101.805 addresses liability for the misrepresentation of another. It does not
address discipline under § 1101.652, and § 1101.652(b)(1) reaches negligence, § 531.3 reaches
carelessness, and 22 TAC § 535.156 imposes an affirmative duty to convey *accurate* information to
members of the public. A license holder who repeats a doubtful statement without qualification, and
the statement turns out to be false, has conveyed inaccurate information to a member of the public
regardless of what § 1101.805 does with the civil claim. The lesson is not "you are protected"; the
lesson is "the protection is narrower and more conditional than it looks, and it does not touch your
licence."

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
There is also a housekeeping point. Subsection (f) of § 1101.805 was repealed by Acts 2025, 89th
Leg., R.S., Ch. 1172 (S.B. 1968), Sec. 13(2), effective January 1, 2026. TREC's own article on the
2026 changes, held for this course as guidance rather than as law, explains that two references to
subagency were removed from TRELA and states that "subagency has not been eliminated generally as a
legal concept." That is a change to the statute's text, not to the underlying common law, which was
not held for this course.

**Fifth: what you are affirmatively protected for saying.** Section 1101.804 is short and useful: "A
license holder or nonprofit real estate board or association that provides information about real
property sales prices or the terms of a sale for the purpose of facilitating the listing, selling,
leasing, financing, or appraisal of real property is not liable to another person for providing that
information unless the disclosure of that information is specifically prohibited by statute."
Sharing comparable sales data for a legitimate transactional purpose is protected — subject to that
closing qualifier, which you must not truncate.

chunks.heading: Unit: Avoiding Disclosure and Misrepresentation Problems
chunks.excerpt:
**The practical protocol.** Four habits follow. *Attribute*: when the information came from the
seller, the appraisal district, an HOA or an inspection report, say so — attribution converts your
assertion into a report of someone else's, which is where § 1101.805(e) operates. *Refer out*: flood
risk to the flood map and the insurer, zoning to the city, structural questions to an engineer,
value to a licensed appraiser under Chapter 1103, because 22 TAC § 535.17 forbids you to supply an
opinion of value without that credential. *Deliver the statutory notices* on time and keep proof:
§ 1101.558(b) and (b-1), § 1101.555, and, for the seller side, the § 5.008 notice. *Correct the
record*: correction is the act that satisfies the second condition of § 1101.805(e) and most
reliably defuses a § 1101.652(b)(2) complaint.

**The DTPA, and where to find the rest.** Module 11 covers the Deceptive Trade Practices Act in
depth, including the § 17.46(b) laundry list; this module touches it only to frame your exposure to
a non-client, and the exercise below turns on three of its provisions. Section 17.50(b)(1) permits
recovery of economic damages, and if the trier of fact finds the conduct was committed
**knowingly**, mental anguish damages plus up to **three times** economic damages, and if committed
**intentionally**, mental anguish damages plus up to three times the sum of mental anguish and
economic damages. Section 17.45(9) defines "knowingly" as "actual awareness, at the time of the act
or practice complained of, of the falsity, deception, or unfairness of the act or practice," adding
that "actual awareness may be inferred where objective manifestations indicate that a person acted
with actual awareness." And § 17.565 requires suit within two years of the act or of discovery in

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The roof in Lubbock
chunks.excerpt:
the exercise of reasonable diligence, extendable by 180 days in the circumstances that section
describes.

### Applied exercise: The roof in Lubbock

Ivan is the listing agent for a 1,980-square-foot house on Slide Road in Lubbock. At the listing
appointment the seller, Georgia, tells him: "The roof's about eight years old, and we've never had a
leak." Ivan writes "roof approx. 8 yrs" in the MLS remarks without attribution. Two weeks later,
while retrieving a key from the garage, Ivan sees a stack of buckets under a stained ceiling panel
and a 2019 invoice on the workbench from a roofer for "temporary patch, north slope — recommend full
replacement." He says nothing.

Nadia, an unrepresented buyer, reads the MLS remarks, tours the house, and buys it for **$312,000**.
Four months after closing, the north slope fails in a storm. Replacement costs **$21,400**, and
interior repairs cost **$6,600**.

chunks.heading: Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)
chunks.excerpt:
1. Identify every statement or omission by Ivan that could be a ground for discipline, and cite the
   specific subdivision of Occupations Code § 1101.652(b) for each. Treat the MLS remark and the
   silence after the garage discovery separately.
2. Apply Occupations Code § 1101.805(e) to Ivan's position on Georgia's original statement about the
   roof's age. State both conditions in the statute and say whether each is satisfied, before and
   after the garage discovery.
3. Apply Business & Commerce Code § 17.49(i). Is "roof approx. 8 yrs" characterisable as advice,
   judgment or opinion? Which of the three carve-outs in § 17.49(i), if any, would let Nadia's DTPA
   claim proceed against Ivan?
4. Assume Nadia's economic damages are the sum of the two repair figures and that the trier of fact
   finds Ivan acted **knowingly** within the meaning of § 17.45(9). Using § 17.50(b)(1), compute the
   maximum economic-damages award (excluding mental anguish). Then compute it again assuming the
   trier of fact does **not** find the conduct knowing. Show the arithmetic.
5. Nadia closed on **March 14** and discovered the roof problem on **July 20** of the same year.
   Using § 17.565, state the last date on which she could ordinarily commence a DTPA action, and
   identify what fact would be required to extend it and by how long.

## Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)

Everything you have studied so far in this module imposes duties on *you*. Property Code § 5.008
does not: it imposes a duty on the **seller**. Your obligations around § 5.008 are real, but they
are obligations to get the seller's statutory duty performed correctly and on time, not to perform
it yourself and not to vouch for its contents.

chunks.heading: Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)
chunks.excerpt:
**Who it applies to.** Subsection (a): "A seller of residential real property comprising not more
than one dwelling unit located in this state shall give to the purchaser of the property a written
notice as prescribed by this section or a written notice substantially similar to the notice
prescribed by this section which contains, at a minimum, all of the items in the notice prescribed
by this section."

Parse the scope. **Residential** real property — not raw land, not a strip centre, not an office
condo. **Comprising not more than one dwelling unit** — a single-family house is inside; a duplex is
not, because a duplex comprises two dwelling units. **Located in this state.** And the notice goes
to "the purchaser," so the section speaks to sales rather than leases.

Also parse the form requirement. The statute lets the seller use either the notice it prescribes or
one "substantially similar" that contains, "at a minimum, all of the items in the notice prescribed
by this section." A shorter form is not compliance. A longer one can be.

**What the notice contains.** Subsection (b) provides that "[t]he notice must be executed and must,
at a minimum, read substantially similar to the following," and then sets out the form. Its caption
is the part a buyer's agent should be able to paraphrase from memory: "THIS NOTICE IS A DISCLOSURE
OF SELLER'S KNOWLEDGE OF THE CONDITION OF THE PROPERTY AS OF THE DATE SIGNED BY SELLER AND IS NOT A
SUBSTITUTE FOR ANY INSPECTIONS OR WARRANTIES THE PURCHASER MAY WISH TO OBTAIN. IT IS NOT A WARRANTY
OF ANY KIND BY SELLER OR SELLER'S AGENTS." The notice reports knowledge, not condition; it is dated
to the day of signature; and it is not a warranty, not by the seller and not by you.

chunks.heading: Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)
chunks.excerpt:
The body runs to eleven numbered items, and the optional reference at the end of this module walks
them one by one.

**The knowledge qualifier — subsection (d).** This is the qualifier students truncate most often, so
here it is whole:

> The notice shall be completed to the best of seller's belief and knowledge as of the date the
> notice is completed and signed by the seller. If the information required by the notice is unknown
> to the seller, the seller shall indicate that fact on the notice, and by that act is in compliance
> with this section.

Two consequences follow. First, the notice is a **knowledge document**: a seller who genuinely does
not know the age of the roof and writes "Unknown" has complied with § 5.008 — the statute says so in
terms. Second, the safe harbour operates only where the information genuinely *is* unknown.
"Unknown" written to avoid an answer the seller in fact has is a false statement on the notice, and
the kind that supports a fraud or DTPA claim later.

Do not tell a buyer that the § 5.008 notice is a warranty, and do not let a buyer treat it as an
inspection. The form's own caption forecloses both readings.

**The exemptions — subsection (e).** The section "does not apply to a transfer" in eleven listed
situations. Read them in the statute; what matters in practice is the pattern rather than the
recital.

chunks.heading: Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)
chunks.excerpt:
The exemptions cover transfers where the transferor has no meaningful personal knowledge of the
property — a court order or foreclosure sale, a trustee in bankruptcy, a mortgagee or deed-of-trust
beneficiary that took the property at foreclosure or by deed in lieu, a fiduciary administering a
decedent's estate, guardianship, conservatorship or trust, and a governmental entity — together with
transfers within a family or between co-owners, brand-new construction never occupied, and land
where the improvements are trivial relative to the whole, which is subdivision (11)'s five percent
test. Two come up constantly: subdivision (10) is why a builder selling a house nobody has lived in
delivers no notice, and subdivision (5) is why the executor selling grandmother's house in
Nacogdoches delivers none either. Note what does *not* change: the exemption is from § 5.008, not
from § 1101.652(b)(4). If you list that estate sale and you know the slab has moved, you still owe
the disclosure to a potential buyer under TRELA.

**The timing and the remedy — subsection (f).** The whole subsection:

> The notice shall be delivered by the seller to the purchaser on or before the effective date of an
> executory contract binding the purchaser to purchase the property. If a contract is entered
> without the seller providing the notice required by this section, the purchaser may terminate the
> contract for any reason within seven days after receiving the notice.

chunks.heading: Unit: Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code (Seller's Disclosure)
chunks.excerpt:
Take the deadline first. Delivery is due **on or before the effective date** of the binding contract
— not at closing, and not within some number of days after the offer. In practice the notice is
delivered during marketing and acknowledged by the buyer before or with the offer, which is why the
file should hold the executed notice long before an offer arrives.

Now the remedy, and read it exactly. If the contract is entered without the notice, "the purchaser
may terminate the contract for any reason within seven days after receiving the notice." Three
points students miss.

**The clock starts on receipt, not on the effective date.** A seller who delivers a late notice on
day twelve gives the buyer a seven-day termination right running from day twelve. A seller who never
delivers the notice at all never starts the clock, and the termination right does not expire on its
own under this subsection's terms.

**"[F]or any reason."** The buyer does not have to point to anything in the notice. The right is
unconditional once it exists. A buyer who receives a late notice, reads nothing objectionable in it,
and simply changes their mind about the neighbourhood may terminate within those seven days.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Working through § 5.008 subsection by subsection
chunks.excerpt:
**Section 5.008 states no damages remedy.** It gives a termination right, and it contains no clause
making that right exclusive. Compare Property Code § 5.012, the property owners' association notice,
which adds in subsection (e): "The purchaser's right to terminate the executory contract under
Subsection (d) is the purchaser's exclusive remedy for the seller's failure to provide the notice
required by this section." Section 5.008 contains no such sentence, and the other notice statutes in
the same subchapter anchor their counts differently again — read each one rather than assume they
run alike.

**Your role, precisely stated.** Section 5.008 imposes no duty on a license holder, but four things
are true about your position. You should get the notice completed and delivered on time, because a
seller who misses the subsection (f) deadline hands the buyer a free termination right — a practice
standard, not a statutory one, and this course cites no rule for it. You must not complete the
notice for the seller: it states the seller's knowledge and is dated as of the seller's signature
under subsection (d). You must keep it, because under 22 TAC § 535.2, taught in Module 09, a broker
must maintain "disclosures" among the records preserved "for at least four years from the date of
closing, termination of the contract, or end of a real estate transaction." And your own TRELA duty
stands independent of the seller's: if the notice says "No" to a question and you know the answer is
"Yes," § 1101.652(b)(4) requires you to disclose the defect to a potential buyer.

### Statute reading exercise: Working through § 5.008 subsection by subsection

Open Texas Property Code § 5.008 and answer from the text alone. Cite the subsection you relied on
for each answer.

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
1. A seller is transferring a duplex in San Marcos, both units occupied by tenants. Does § 5.008
   require a notice? Quote the words of subsection (a) that decide it.
2. Subsection (d) says a seller who indicates on the notice that information is unknown "by that act
   is in compliance with this section." List the conditions the subsection attaches to that
   sentence. Does the subsection say anything about the accuracy of an answer the seller *does*
   give?
3. Read subsection (e) in full and identify which subdivision exempts (i) a builder selling a newly
   constructed house that has never been lived in, (ii) a bank selling a house it took by deed in
   lieu of foreclosure, and (iii) a father conveying a house to his daughter.
4. Subsection (f) gives a purchaser a right to terminate. From what event does the seven-day period
   run? What happens to that period if the seller never delivers the notice at all? Does the
   subsection require the purchaser to give a reason?
5. Subsection (c) removes a duty from both the seller and the seller's agent. State the two
   categories it covers and write out the qualifier the statute attaches to the words "death by
   natural causes, suicide, or accident." Does subsection (c) mention murder?
6. Compare § 5.008 with Property Code § 5.012(e). Which of the two says that termination is the
   purchaser's exclusive remedy? What follows from the difference?

## Unit: Stigmatized Properties

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
A **stigmatized property** is one whose desirability is affected by something that happened in or
near it rather than by anything wrong with the bricks and the plumbing: a death in the house, a
prior occupant's illness, a crime, a rumour of a haunting. The physical condition is unimpaired; the
market reaction is not. Texas addresses part of this territory by statute, and the statute is
narrower than its reputation.

**The governing provision.** Occupations Code § 1101.556, in its entirety:

> Notwithstanding other law, a license holder is not required to inquire about, disclose, or release
> information relating to whether: (1) a previous or current occupant of real property had, may have
> had, has, or may have AIDS, an HIV-related illness, or an HIV infection as defined by the Centers
> for Disease Control and Prevention of the United States Public Health Service; or (2) a death
> occurred on a property by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the condition of the
> property.

Property Code § 5.008(c) says the same thing on the seller's side of the transaction: "A seller or
seller's agent shall have no duty to make a disclosure or release information related to whether a
death by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the condition of the property occurred on
the property or whether a previous occupant had, may have had, has, or may have AIDS, HIV related
illnesses, or HIV infection."

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
**What § 1101.556 gives you.** Three verbs: you are not required to **inquire about**, to
**disclose**, or to **release** the listed information. The relief from the duty to *inquire*
matters as much as the relief from the duty to disclose, because you are not obliged to interrogate
a seller about how a prior owner died. And the section opens with "Notwithstanding other law," so
the relief survives contrary rules found elsewhere.

**Now the qualifiers, which are where students go wrong.**

**Qualifier one: "unrelated to the condition of the property."** That phrase modifies the deaths in
subdivision (2). If a person died on the property *because of* the property's condition — a balcony
that gave way in a Corpus Christi condominium, carbon monoxide from a cracked heat exchanger, an
electrocution from faulty wiring — the death is not "unrelated to the condition of the property,"
and § 1101.556(2) does not relieve you of anything. Worse, the condition that caused it is very
likely a "significant defect … that would be a significant factor to a reasonable and prudent buyer"
under § 1101.652(b)(3), so if you know about it § 1101.652(b)(4) requires you to disclose it to a
potential buyer. The statute students remember as "you never have to disclose a death" turns, in the
case where the death matters most, into a duty to speak.

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
**Qualifier two: the enumeration.** Subdivision (2) lists three manners of death: **natural
causes**, **suicide**, and **accident** unrelated to the property's condition. It does not list
homicide, so a murder on the property is outside the words the Legislature chose. What Texas common
law requires or does not require about disclosing a homicide was not held for this course and is not
taught here; what can be said from the held text is that § 1101.556 does not supply relief for it,
and neither does § 5.008(c), whose list is identical.

**Qualifier three: what is not on the list at all.** Section 1101.556 covers occupant health status
in the specific AIDS/HIV terms of subdivision (1) and deaths in the specific terms of subdivision
(2). It says nothing about a prior methamphetamine laboratory — and the § 5.008 notice form itself
asks the seller about previous use of the premises for the manufacture of methamphetamine, so the
Legislature clearly regarded that as disclosable. It says nothing about registered sex offenders in
the neighbourhood; no source held for this course addresses a Texas disclosure duty regarding sex
offender registration, and none is taught here. It says nothing about hauntings, a neighbourhood's
reputation, a nearby landfill or a pending zoning change. Do not stretch a two-subdivision statute
across the whole field of stigma.

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
**Qualifier four — the most important one: relief from a duty to disclose is not permission to
lie.** Section 1101.556 says a license holder "is not required to … disclose." It does not say a
license holder may misstate. If an unrepresented buyer in Denton asks point blank, "Did anyone die
in this house?", you may decline to answer and explain that Texas law does not require you to
inquire about or disclose that information, or you may, with your seller's authorisation, answer
truthfully. What you may not do is say "No" when you know the answer is yes: § 1101.652(b)(2)
reaches conduct that is dishonest, 22 TAC § 535.156 requires accurate information to members of the
public with whom you deal, and § 531.3 forbids misrepresentation by acts of commission. The statute
removes a duty; it does not create a privilege to deceive.

**The AIDS and HIV provisions, and why they are drafted differently.** Two further sections work
with § 1101.556 on the health-status side, and the difference between them is real.

Occupations Code § 1101.802 provides that, notwithstanding § 1101.801, "a person is not civilly or
criminally liable because the person failed to inquire about, make a disclosure relating to, or
release information relating to whether a previous or current occupant of real property had, may
have had, has, or may have AIDS, an HIV-related illness, or HIV infection as defined by the Centers
for Disease Control and Prevention of the United States Public Health Service." Notice the
asymmetry: § 1101.556 relieves the *duty* for both categories, health status and qualifying deaths,
while § 1101.802 supplies an immunity from civil and criminal *liability* and only for the AIDS/HIV
category. No parallel liability-immunity section addresses deaths.

chunks.heading: Unit: Stigmatized Properties
chunks.excerpt:
And on the health-status side there is a duty pointing in the opposite direction. 22 TAC § 531.19,
taught in Module 10, forbids a license holder to inquire about, respond to or facilitate inquiries
about, or disclose information about an owner, previous or current occupant, potential purchaser,
lessor or potential lessee that indicates or is intended to indicate a preference, limitation or
discrimination on the bases the rule lists — and the rule adds: "For the purpose of this section,
disability includes AIDS, HIV-related illnesses, or HIV infection as defined by the Centers for
Disease Control of the United States Public Health Service." So for the AIDS/HIV category the two
rules stack into a bright line: § 1101.556 says you need not inquire or disclose, and § 531.19
independently prohibits inquiring, responding to inquiries, facilitating inquiries, or disclosing in
a way that indicates a preference or limitation based on disability.

**Handling the conversation.** Two positions, offered as practice rather than as law. Decide the
policy before the question arrives, with your broker and your seller: § 1101.556 removes a
requirement, not an authorisation, so a seller who wants a known suicide disclosed may instruct you
to disclose it. And answer the same way every time — answering some buyers and not others invites a
fair housing complaint and a claim that your silence with one buyer was strategic concealment under
DTPA § 17.46(b)(24).

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Separate the stigma from the condition. If a fire, a flood, a methamphetamine laboratory or a
structural failure produced the event, the *event* may be outside your disclosure duty while the
*damage* is squarely inside it; § 1101.652(b)(4) and, on the seller's side, items 3, 4 and 9 of the
§ 5.008 notice reach the physical consequence. A student who leaves this unit remembering only "you
never have to disclose a death in Texas" has learned the wrong sentence. The right sentence is:
*Texas relieves a license holder of the duty to inquire about or disclose a prior occupant's AIDS or
HIV status and a death by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the condition of the
property — and relieves nothing else.*

### Module recap

The through-line of this module is a single distinction: **fiduciary duties run to your client; a
different, statutory set of duties runs to everyone else, and the second set is real.** 22 TAC
§ 531.2 states both in one rule — the primary duty is to represent the interests of the client,
"that, however, the license holder, in performing duties to the client, shall treat other parties to
a transaction fairly." Fairness is not neutrality. You may negotiate hard; you may not mislead.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The non-fiduciary catalogue is worth carrying in your head as a list of section numbers, each with
the module that teaches it. Honest and fair dealing with all parties, and accurate information to
members of the public: 22 TAC § 535.156 (Module 02). Integrity, and no misrepresentation "by acts of
commission or omission": 22 TAC § 531.3 (Modules 02 and 10). Disclosure of a significant known
defect to a potential buyer, and discipline for misrepresenting one: Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4) (Module 10). Disclosure of your representation at first contact, and the
IABS Notice at first substantive communication: § 1101.558(b) and (b-1) with 22 TAC § 531.20 (Module
02) — and note that the notice must itself describe "the basic obligations a broker has to a party
to a real estate transaction that the broker does not represent." The written advice to each buyer
about an abstract or a title policy: § 1101.555, enforced by § 1101.652(b)(29) (Module 12).
Non-discrimination: 22 TAC § 531.19 and § 1101.652(b)(32) (Module 10). Disclosure and a CMA when you
are buying for your own account: 22 TAC §§ 535.144 and 535.16 (Modules 12 and 04). Broker liability
to "the commission, the public, and the broker's clients": § 1101.803 (Module 09). And § 1101.801:
discipline does not relieve civil or criminal liability.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
TRELA does not define "third party"; it defines "party" in § 1101.551(2) as "a prospective buyer,
seller, landlord, or tenant or an authorized representative," excluding "a license holder who
represents a party." Build your working definition from that: a third party is any party other than
your client, plus the inspectors, lenders, appraisers, title officers and cooperating agents who are
"members of the public with whom the license holder deals" under 22 TAC § 535.156. The response
clock is **two calendar days** under 22 TAC § 535.157, owed to your principal, to the license holder
representing another party, and to "an unrepresented party to a real estate transaction." Calendar,
not business.

On misrepresentation, the two liability sections are this module's own. Repeating a party's
statement is governed by § 1101.805(e): a license holder is not liable for a party's
misrepresentation or concealment "unless the license holder: (1) knew of the falsity … and (2)
failed to disclose the license holder's knowledge of the falsity." Both conditions, conjunctive; the
word is "knew," not "should have known"; and the shield covers the party's statement, not your own,
and does not touch your licence. Subsection (d) is the mirror image, protecting the party from the
license holder's misrepresentation on the same two conditions; subsection (b) makes the section
prevail over other law including common law; subsection (c) preserves broker responsibility for a
sales agent; and subsection (f) was repealed effective January 1, 2026. Section 1101.804 protects
you for supplying sales price and terms information for transactional purposes "unless the
disclosure of that information is specifically prohibited by statute." Around those two sections:
the duty to disclose is keyed to knowledge

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
, not to investigation — § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4) both
say "known to the license holder," and no held source imposes a duty to inspect, though
§ 1101.652(b)(1) reaches negligence and incompetence and § 531.3 requires "prudence and caution."
Puffing has a statutory boundary in Business & Commerce Code § 17.49(i), and silence becomes
concealment when § 17.46(b)(24)'s intent element is met. The DTPA itself belongs to Module 11.

Property Code § 5.008 is the **seller's** duty, not yours. It applies to "[a] seller of residential
real property comprising not more than one dwelling unit located in this state" — so not a duplex,
not commercial, not a lease. The notice is a knowledge document: subsection (d) requires completion
"to the best of seller's belief and knowledge as of the date the notice is completed and signed by
the seller" and provides that a seller who indicates that required information is unknown "by that
act is in compliance with this section." Subsection (e) exempts **eleven** transfers, and the
pattern is what to carry: transferors with no personal knowledge of the property — court order or
foreclosure sale, trustee in bankruptcy, mortgagee or deed-of-trust beneficiary, foreclosing
beneficiary or one taking a deed in lieu, fiduciary administering an estate, guardianship,
conservatorship or trust, and governmental entity — transfers within a family or between co-owners,
a never-occupied new residence of not more than one dwelling unit, and property where the value of
any dwelling does not exceed five percent of the value of the property. The timing rule is
**subsection (f)**, not subsection (d): it sets delivery "on or before the effective date of an
executory contract binding the purchaser to purchase the property," and gives the purchaser, if the
contract

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
is entered without the notice, the right to "terminate the contract for any reason within
seven days after receiving the notice" — seven days from **receipt**, so an undelivered notice never
starts the clock, and no reason need be given. Section 5.008 states no damages remedy and no
exclusivity clause; compare § 5.012(e), which makes termination the purchaser's exclusive remedy for
the property owners' association notice. Your own duty under § 1101.652(b)(4) survives every one of
the § 5.008 exemptions, because it never came from § 5.008.

Finally, stigma. Occupations Code § 1101.556 says that "[n]otwithstanding other law, a license
holder is not required to inquire about, disclose, or release information relating to whether" a
previous or current occupant had or may have AIDS, an HIV-related illness, or an HIV infection, or
"a death occurred on a property by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the condition
of the property." Property Code § 5.008(c) says the same for a seller or seller's agent. Say exactly
what that relieves: the duty to inquire, to disclose, and to release, for those two categories only.
Say exactly what it does not relieve: a death caused by the property's condition, because of the
qualifier "unrelated to the condition of the property"; a homicide, which is not among the three
manners of death the statute lists; the defect itself, which § 1101.652(b)(4) still requires you to
disclose to a potential buyer if you know of it; a false answer, because removing a duty to speak is
not a licence to lie; and, on the AIDS/HIV side, the prohibition in 22 TAC § 531.19 against
inquiring about, responding to, facilitating inquiries about, or disclosing information indicating a
preference or limitation based on disability, which that rule defines to

chunks.heading: Optional reference: The § 5.008 notice form item by item, and two optional practice exercises
chunks.excerpt:
include AIDS, HIV-related
illnesses, and HIV infection. Section 1101.802 adds an immunity from civil and criminal liability,
and it is drafted for the AIDS/HIV category alone.

## Optional reference: The § 5.008 notice form item by item, and two optional practice exercises

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it. It is here because the law it covers is real and a
license holder may need it, not because the course requires you to read it. You may skip it and go
straight to the next module.

**The § 5.008 notice form, item by item.** Unit 5 teaches what the notice is, who must deliver it,
when, on what knowledge standard, what the exemptions do and what the purchaser's remedy is. This is
the clause-by-clause tour of the form itself — useful the first time you sit at a kitchen table with
a seller who is filling one in, and useful when a buyer asks which line an answer belongs on.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: The § 5.008 notice form item by item, and two optional practice exercises
chunks.excerpt:
The body runs to eleven numbered items. Item 1 is the inventory of equipment and systems with
Yes/No/Unknown boxes, followed by the question whether the seller is aware of any of those items
"that are not in working condition, that have known defects, or that are in need of repair." Item 2
asks about working smoke detectors installed in accordance with Chapter 766, Health and Safety Code,
with a footnote explaining the buyer's right to require smoke detectors for the hearing impaired if
the buyer or a family member who will reside in the dwelling is hearing impaired, the buyer gives
written evidence of the impairment from a licensed physician, and "within 10 days after the
effective date, the buyer makes a written request for the seller to install smoke detectors for the
hearing impaired and specifies the locations for installation." Item 3 asks about known defects or
malfunctions in interior walls, ceilings, floors, exterior walls, doors, windows, roof, foundation
or slab, basement, walls and fences, driveways, sidewalks, plumbing, electrical, lighting fixtures
and other structural components. Item 4 lists conditions including active termites, previous
structural or roof repair, termite or wood rot damage needing repair, hazardous or toxic waste,
asbestos components, urea formaldehyde insulation, radon gas, improper drainage, lead based paint,
water damage not due to a flood event, aluminum wiring, previous fires, unplatted easements,
landfill or settling or soil movement or fault lines, subsurface structure or pits, a single
blockable main drain in a pool, hot tub or spa, and, in the form's two-column layout, previous use
