> employee with respect to the service for federal tax purposes.

The stray space inside the quotation marks around "broker" in paragraph (1)(A) is in the statute's
published text; it is reproduced here rather than silently corrected, because this course quotes
what the source says.

chunks.heading: Unit: Independent Contract Agreements
chunks.excerpt:
Fix the boundary before working through the conditions. Section 201.072 answers one question:
whether the service is "employment" for the purposes of the subtitle that contains it, the
unemployment compensation system administered by the Texas Workforce Commission. It does not
decide whether a sales agent is an employee for wage-and-hour purposes, for workers' compensation,
for discrimination law, for tort or vicarious liability, or at common law. The authorities that
would answer those questions **were not held** for this course; they are named at the end of this
unit.

Condition (A) ties the exclusion to the *work*: activity described by the definition of "broker"
in Occupations Code § 1101.002. It covers licensed brokerage activity, not everything a person
might do for a brokerage — a sales agent who also keeps the office books for an hourly wage is
not, in doing that, performing activity described by the definition. Condition (B) requires a
Texas Real Estate Commission licence; chapter 201 says "salesperson," the word the Legislature
used in 1993, and TRELA and the Commission's rules now say "sales agent," meaning the same
licence. An unlicensed or lapsed worker cannot use § 201.072, because condition (B) fails on its
face.

chunks.heading: Unit: Independent Contract Agreements
chunks.excerpt:
Condition (C) is the pay condition, and the one brokerages most often break by accident:
"[S]ubstantially all remuneration for the service, whether in cash or other form of payment, is
directly related to sales or other output, including the performance of the service, and not to
the number of hours worked." Commission on closings is output-based pay; an hourly rate for floor
duty or a guaranteed monthly salary is not, and a brokerage paying both has a mixed-remuneration
problem. The honest answer to it is that neither § 201.072 nor 26 U.S.C. § 3508 defines
"substantially all," and no Treasury regulation, Internal Revenue Service ruling, or Texas
Workforce Commission rule construing the phrase was held for this course. The threshold is not
taught here.

Condition (D) has two parts that must both be present: "the service is performed under a written
contract between the individual and the person for whom the service is performed," and — the
sentence people leave out — "the contract provides that the individual is not treated as an
employee with respect to the service for federal tax purposes." An agreement that calls the agent
an independent contractor, sets a split and allocates expenses but says nothing about federal tax
treatment does not satisfy condition (D): the statute asks not what the parties intended but
whether the contract *provides* it.

chunks.heading: Unit: Independent Contract Agreements
chunks.excerpt:
Paragraph (2) does the same for an instructor of a person licensed or seeking a licence as a
broker or salesperson, on two conditions: the individual "instructs in an educational program or
course approved by the Texas Real Estate Commission," and the written contract carries the same
federal-tax-purposes provision. It has no output-based pay condition, so an instructor may be paid
by the classroom hour and still fall outside "employment."

**What § 201.072 conspicuously does not require.** Nothing in the four conditions requires that
the agent be free from the broker's control, set their own hours, or be free to accept or reject
assignments. That absence is not an oversight: neighbouring exclusions in the same subchapter do
condition the exclusion on control. Section 201.070 requires, among other factors, that the
individual "determines the method of performing the service," and § 201.073 that the individual
"may accept or reject a job from the delivery service." The Legislature knew how to make freedom
from control a condition of an exclusion; in § 201.072 it chose not to. That resolves the tension you meet in Unit 5: a broker may supervise as closely as
the Commission's rules require without endangering the exclusion.

chunks.heading: Unit: Independent Contract Agreements
chunks.excerpt:
**The federal side.** For federal tax purposes the governing provision is 26 U.S.C. § 3508,
"Treatment of real estate agents and direct sellers." Subsection (a) states the general rule: "For
purposes of this title, in the case of services performed as a qualified real estate agent or as a
direct seller-" then "(1) the individual performing such services shall not be treated as an
employee, and (2) the person for whom such services are performed shall not be treated as an
employer." It cuts both ways, removing employer status from the brokerage and with it the federal
employment tax withholding and matching obligations. And its opening words are a limit: "For
purposes of this title" confines the section to Title 26, so § 3508 decides federal tax treatment
and nothing else — not your broker's supervision duty, not your status under Labor Code chapter
21, not anyone's liability to anyone.

Subsection (b)(1) supplies the definition the general rule turns on. "The term "qualified real
estate agent" means any individual who is a sales person if-" and then three conditions: "(A) such
individual is a licensed real estate agent," "(B) substantially all of the remuneration (whether
or not paid in cash) for the services performed by such individual as a real estate agent is
directly related to sales or other output (including the performance of services) rather than to
the number of hours worked, and" "(C) the services performed by the individual are performed
pursuant to a written contract between such individual and the person for whom the services are
performed and such contract provides that the individual will not be treated as an employee with
respect to such services for Federal tax purposes."

chunks.heading: Unit: Independent Contract Agreements
chunks.excerpt:
One well-drafted agreement satisfies both statutes, because they are one drafting pattern rather
than two regimes. Its statutory core is short: the parties by name; a statement that the
individual holds a Texas licence and will perform activity described by Occupations Code 
§ 1101.002; compensation measured by production rather than hours; and an express provision that the
individual will not be treated as an employee with respect to the services for federal tax
purposes.

**The non-interaction you must not get wrong.** Your status as an independent contractor for
unemployment compensation purposes under § 201.072, and for federal tax purposes under § 3508, has
**no effect whatever** on your broker's obligations under the licensing law. Those obligations
serve a different purpose — brokerage supervision and licensing responsibility — and are not
conditioned on employment. Rule 22 TAC § 535.2 says so in its closing sentence: "This section is
not meant to create or require an employer/employee relationship between a broker and a sponsored
sales agent." It does not make the broker's obligations lighter for a contractor; it says they
exist independently of employment status. Alongside it sits Occupations Code § 1101.803: "A
licensed broker is liable to the commission, the public, and the broker's clients for any conduct
engaged in under this chapter by the broker or by a sales agent associated with or acting for the
broker." The Legislature attached that liability to association, not to employment, so a clause in
your contractor agreement stating that the broker is not responsible for your acts is worth
nothing against § 1101.803.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Law
chunks.excerpt:
**Stated plainly: what was not held.** The Internal Revenue Service's administrative guidance and
the Treasury regulations under 26 U.S.C. § 3508, the Texas Workforce Commission's own rules and
audit practice under chapter 201, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Texas Payday Law, Texas
workers' compensation law, and Texas case law on common-law employment status and vicarious
liability were **not held** for this course. So where you have heard that the Internal Revenue
Service applies a twenty-factor control test, or that a brokerage must or must not carry workers'
compensation on its agents, this module states no position.

## Unit: Employment Law

Unit 1 established that a licensed Texas sales agent under a proper written agreement is, for
unemployment-tax and federal-tax purposes, not an employee. It does not follow that employment law
is irrelevant to a brokerage: brokerages hire receptionists, coordinators, bookkeepers, interns
and property management staff, and one subchapter of the state's employment discrimination statute
has a coverage threshold of a single employee. Note the change of subject. Section 201.072 serves
unemployment compensation and § 3508 federal tax; the statute in this unit serves **discrimination
law** and carries its own definitions of "employer" and "employee", and neither test from Unit 1
is imported into it.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Law
chunks.excerpt:
**The statute.** Texas Labor Code chapter 21 is the Texas Commission on Human Rights Act. Section
21.001 states its purposes, the first being to "provide for the execution of the policies of Title
VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its subsequent amendments (42 U.S.C. Section 2000e et
seq.)": the chapter is Texas's state-law counterpart to the federal employment discrimination
scheme, built to track it. The texts of Title VII and the ADA themselves were **not held** for
this course, so this module teaches the Texas chapter and does not state what the federal statutes
say. Section 21.0015 provides that "The powers and duties exercised by the Commission on Human
Rights under this chapter are transferred to the Texas Workforce Commission." Section 21.051
carries the core prohibition: an employer commits an unlawful employment practice if, because of
race, color, disability, religion, sex, national origin or age, it refuses to hire, discharges or
otherwise discriminates against an individual in compensation or the terms, conditions or
privileges of employment, or limits, segregates or classifies an employee or applicant so as to
deprive that person of an employment opportunity. Seven protected characteristics, two prohibited
modes. The chapter's remaining unlawful-practice provisions, its administrative process and its
damages caps are not taught in this course.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Law
chunks.excerpt:
**Who is an "employer," and who is an "employee."** Section 21.002(8) defines the term to include
"(A) a person who is engaged in an industry affecting commerce and who has 15 or more employees
for each working day in each of 20 or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar
year" and "(B) an agent of a person described by Paragraph (A)." Most Texas brokerages never reach
that threshold in *employees*: a Waco firm with eighty sponsored sales agents and three salaried
staff has three employees for this purpose, not eighty-three, provided the agents are genuine
independent contractors. Paragraph (B) also makes a supervisor who takes personnel decisions for a
covered firm an employer in their own right. Section 21.002(7) defines "Employee" as "an
individual employed by an employer" — circular on purpose, because chapter 21 supplies no test for
distinguishing an employee from an independent contractor.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Law
chunks.excerpt:
**The honest answer about sales agents.** A sales agent whose service is genuinely excluded from
"employment" under § 201.072 — output-based pay, written contract, the federal-tax clause — and
whose relationship with the broker is in substance a contractor relationship is not, on the face
of these definitions, an employee of the broker, and 22 TAC § 535.2 closes with the statement that
the section "is not meant to create or require an employer/employee relationship between a broker
and a sponsored sales agent." Notice the limits of what that establishes. Section 201.072 excludes
real estate service from "employment" **"In this subtitle"** — for unemployment compensation
purposes only — so it decides nothing under chapter 21, which sits in a different subtitle and
defines its own terms; and § 3508, confined to Title 26, decides nothing under Texas law at all.
Do not import either test into a chapter 21 question. Whether a Texas court applying chapter 21
would treat a particular sales agent as an employee turns on judicial decisions applying that
chapter's definitions to real facts, and **no case law was held** for this course. This module
therefore does not tell you that a sales agent can never bring a chapter 21 claim against a
broker, and it does not tell you that one always can.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Relationships between Brokers and Principals
chunks.excerpt:
**The one-employee subchapter.** Subchapter C-1, added in 2021, governs sexual harassment, and
§ 21.141 gives it its own definition: "'Employer' means a person who: (A) employs one or more
employees; or (B) acts directly in the interests of an employer in relation to an employee." One
employee. Section 21.142 makes an employer liable where sexual harassment of an employee occurs
and the employer or the employer's agents or supervisors "know or should have known that the
conduct constituting sexual harassment was occurring" and "fail to take immediate and appropriate
corrective action." A two-person brokerage is inside that subchapter the day it hires its first
assistant.

**What reaches you regardless of employment status.** Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(32) makes it
a disciplinary ground for a license holder engaged in real estate brokerage to discriminate
against an owner, potential buyer, landlord or potential tenant on the basis of race, color,
religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry, including steering a
prospect interested in equivalent properties to a different area on those bases. That ground
attaches to the licence whether you are an employee or a contractor; § 1101.652 and fair housing
law are taught in Module 10.

## Unit: Employment Relationships between Brokers and Principals

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Relationships between Brokers and Principals
chunks.excerpt:
This unit exists because of a word. Real estate law uses "employ" in a sense that predates labour
law: a principal *employs* an agent when the principal engages the agent to act on the principal's
behalf, which is what a listing agreement and a buyer representation agreement do. The seller
employs the broker. It is an engagement, and it has nothing to do with payroll, withholding,
unemployment tax or Labor Code chapter 21. The broker is employed by the client, and the sales
agent is not employed by anybody.

The Commission's rules use the labour-law sense where it matters: 22 TAC § 535.5(c) provides that
a real estate license is not required "for an employee employed by a business entity for the
purpose of buying, selling, or leasing real property for the entity," and § 535.5(d)(2) defines
that term: "An employee of a business entity means a person employed and directly compensated by
the business entity. An independent contractor is not an employee." Occupations Code
§ 1101.002(1)(B)(i), by contrast, uses the engagement sense, providing that "Broker" includes a
person who "is employed by or for an owner of real estate to sell any portion of the real estate."
Tell the senses apart from context.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment Relationships between Brokers and Principals
chunks.excerpt:
**Who the client's agent is.** Occupations Code § 1101.557(a) settles it: a broker who represents
a party in a real estate transaction, or who lists real estate for sale under an exclusive
agreement for a party, "is that party's agent." Not the sales agent. The broker. Section 1101.557
is taught in full in Module 02. Rule 22 TAC § 535.2 then provides that "Listings and other
agreements for real estate brokerage services must be solicited and accepted in a broker's name,"
and Occupations Code § 1101.351(c) puts the agent in position: "A licensed sales agent may not
engage or attempt to engage in real estate brokerage unless the sales agent is sponsored by a
licensed broker and is acting for that broker." Between them those provisions define the
architecture of Texas brokerage: the client contracts with the broker, the sales agent performs
the work as the person acting for the broker, and § 1101.803 supplies the answerability. A listing
therefore belongs to the broker and does not travel with you to a new firm, and what you are owed
on transactions worked before you left is governed by § 1101.651(b) in Unit 6.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants
chunks.excerpt:
**The trap at the boundary.** Section 1101.652(b)(26), taught in Module 10, makes it a
disciplinary ground to establish an association "by employment or otherwise" with a person other
than a license holder if that person is expected or required to act as a license holder. Those
four words are why the label does not matter: employee, contractor, partner or assistant, if the
person is expected to act as a license holder and is not one, the association itself is the
violation. The reverse trap is assuming that a broker "employed" by the seller owes a servant's
obedience. Rule 535.2 makes the duty the "highest fiduciary obligation" to the principal and pairs
it with a limit — "unless prohibited by other law" — so a seller's instruction to conceal a known
material defect is not authorised by the engagement.

## Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants

An assistant is the first hire most producing agents make, and it is where more licence trouble
starts than in any other staffing decision. What an unlicensed assistant may do is not a matter of
degree or of intention: 22 TAC § 535.4 lists the acts for which a licence is required and § 535.5
what does not, both taught in Module 01, and the assistant may do everything else and none of
those.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants
chunks.excerpt:
**Showing.** Section 535.4(c) provides that "[u]nless otherwise exempted by the Act, a person must
be licensed as a broker or sales agent to show a property," and the operative half is the
definition: "[f]or purposes of this section, to 'show' a property includes causing or permitting
the property to be viewed by a prospective buyer or tenant, unlocking or providing access onto or
into a property for a prospective buyer or tenant, and hosting an open house at the property."
That is broader than the word sounds: an unlicensed assistant cannot unlock a listing for a buyer,
and cannot sit an open house even under instructions to answer no questions. The rule reaches the
act of providing access, not the conversation that follows.

**Soliciting and negotiating.** Section 535.4(f) provides that "[a] real estate license is
required for a person to solicit listings or to negotiate in Texas for listings." The assistant
may do clerical work on a mailing campaign the broker designs and sends in the broker's name, but
may not call expired listings or for-sale-by-owner sellers to solicit.

**Supervising.** Section 535.4(e) provides that "[t]he employees, agents, or associates of a
licensed broker must be licensed as brokers or sales agents if they direct or supervise other
persons who perform acts for which a license is required." An unlicensed office administrator who
assigns leads, reviews contract work and directs how agents handle clients must be licensed.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants
chunks.excerpt:
**What the unlicensed assistant may do.** Section 535.5(g) is the clearest permission in the
rules: "An answering service or clerical or administrative employees identified to callers as such
to confirm information concerning the size, price, and terms of property advertised are not
required to be licensed under the Act." Every element is load-bearing: the person must be
*identified to callers* as such, the information must be *confirmation* of size, price and terms,
and the property must have been *advertised*. Confirming to such a caller that the Katy listing is
2,410 square feet at $389,000 with a 30-day close sits inside the rule; telling the caller the
seller will probably take $370,000 is negotiating and does not. Beyond § 535.5(g) the safe
territory is defined by subtraction: no held rule enumerates the tasks an assistant may perform,
so you start from § 535.4 and the § 1101.002 definition of broker and ask whether the task is on
the licensed side.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants
chunks.excerpt:
**Referrals: the trap with a dollar figure in it.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.20 provides that
"[r]eferring a prospective buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant to another person in connection with
a proposed real estate transaction is an act requiring the person making the referral to be
licensed if the referral is made with the expectation of receiving valuable consideration," and
then defines the term: "For the purposes of this section, the term 'valuable consideration'
includes but is not limited to: money; gifts of merchandise having a retail value greater than
$50; rent bonuses; and discounts." A $75 gift card to the neighbour who sent you a buyer is inside
that definition. Section 535.20(b) sets out a narrow exemption, and all four of its conditions
must be met: the person "is engaged in the business of selling goods or services to the public";
the person "sells goods or services to a real estate license holder who intends to offer the goods
or services as an inducement to potential buyers, sellers, landlords or tenants"; "[a]fter selling
the goods or services to the real estate license holder, the person refers the person's customers
to the real estate license holder"; and "[t]he payment to the person for the goods or services is
not contingent upon the consummation of a real estate transaction by the person's customers." The
moment the vendor's payment depends on whether the referred customer closes, the exemption is
gone.

chunks.heading: Unit: Employment and Compensation of Personal Assistants
chunks.excerpt:
**Who may pay the assistant.** Three provisions govern the money. Occupations Code § 1101.651(a)
constrains the broker: "A licensed broker may not pay a commission to or otherwise compensate a
person directly or indirectly for performing an act of a broker unless the person is: (1) a
license holder; or (2) a real estate broker licensed in another state who does not conduct in this
state any of the negotiations for which the commission or other compensation is paid." Note "or
otherwise compensate" and "directly or indirectly": the prohibition is not limited to commissions
and is not defeated by routing payment through someone else.

Rule 22 TAC § 535.147(a) restates it at rule level with its qualifier intact: "Except as otherwise
provided by the Act or Commission rules, a broker or sales agent may not share a commission or
fees with any person who engages in acts for which a license is required and is not actively
licensed as a broker or sales agent." Read the conjunction: the prohibited payee both engages in
acts for which a licence is required **and** is not actively licensed, which is why an assistant
doing only clerical work is not caught. Section 535.147(b) confirms it from the other side: "An
unlicensed person may share in the income earned by a business entity licensed as a broker or
exempted from the licensing requirements under the Act if the person engages in no acts for which
a license is required and does not lead the public to believe that the person is in the real
estate brokerage business."

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Staffing a team in Round Rock
chunks.excerpt:
Rule 22 TAC § 535.3 constrains the sales agent, and this is the provision agents forget when they
hire their own assistant. Its second sentence: "A sales agent may not pay a commission or other
valuable consideration to another person except with the written consent of the sales agent's
sponsoring broker." Note the breadth — "a commission or other valuable consideration," not merely
a commission. Occupations Code § 1101.651(c) is narrower: "A sales agent may not pay a commission
to a person except through the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent at that time." Whether an
hourly wage paid by a sales agent to a purely clerical assistant is "other valuable consideration"
within § 535.3 was not resolved in any source held for this course, and this module asserts no
answer. The safe course, a consequence of the rule's breadth rather than a legal conclusion, is to
obtain your broker's written consent before you pay anyone out of your own pocket in connection
with your practice.

### Applied exercise: Staffing a team in Round Rock

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Staffing a team in Round Rock
chunks.excerpt:
You are a sales agent sponsored by Hill Country Brokers. Your production has grown to the point
that you hire Marisol, who is not licensed, at $22 an hour, paid by you personally. Over one week
you ask her to do the following: (i) key your new listing into the MLS from the data sheet you
prepared; (ii) meet a buyer at your Round Rock listing and unlock the door so the buyer can walk
through while you finish a closing; (iii) answer your business line and, when a caller asks about
the advertised Georgetown listing, confirm the square footage, the list price and the seller's
requested closing date, after telling the caller she is your administrative assistant; (iv) call
the eleven expired listings in Hutto and ask the owners whether they would like to re-list; and
(v) accept a $100 restaurant gift card from your preferred lender for each buyer she refers to
him.

1. Take tasks (i) through (v) one at a time and state, with the specific rule subsection, whether
   each is an act for which a licence is required. Name the subsection of § 535.4 or § 535.5 that
   governs each.
2. You are paying Marisol yourself. Identify the sentence in 22 TAC § 535.3 that this implicates
   and state what you must obtain from Hill Country Brokers. Then state honestly what this course
   does and does not resolve about whether an hourly wage is caught by that sentence.
3. Suppose you had instead offered Marisol $500 for every transaction that closes from a lead she
   brings in. Apply § 535.147(a) and § 1101.651(a) and explain why this arrangement fails,
   identifying the two elements § 535.147(a) requires.
4. Marisol's lender gift card: apply § 535.20(a). Is a $100 gift card within the rule's definition
   of "valuable consideration"? Then test the arrangement against all four conditions of

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
§ 535.20(b) and state which one it fails.
5. Your broker suggests solving the problem by having the brokerage pay Marisol directly for the
   same five tasks. Does that change the answer to any of tasks (i) through (v)? Explain, using
   § 1101.651(a).

## Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)

Rule 22 TAC § 535.2 states what a Texas broker must do about the people the broker sponsors, and
it is the source of the apparent contradiction this module opened with: how can a broker be
responsible for a sales agent who is not the broker's employee? **A sales agent's independent
contractor status for federal tax or unemployment compensation purposes does not reduce the
broker's supervision duty by one line, and does not reduce the broker's responsibility for the
agent's authorized acts.** Section 1101.803 attaches liability to a sales agent "associated with
or acting for the broker"; § 201.072's exclusion carries no control condition, so supervision
cannot endanger it; and § 535.2 closes with the sentence "This section is not meant to create or
require an employer/employee relationship between a broker and a sponsored sales agent." Work
through the rule subsection by subsection.

**(a) The written scope notice.** "A broker is required to notify a sponsored sales agent in
writing of the scope of the sales agent's authorized activities under the Act. Unless such scope
is limited or revoked in writing, a broker is responsible for the authorized acts of the broker's
sales agents, but the broker is not required to supervise the sales agents directly. If a broker
permits a sponsored sales agent to conduct activities beyond the scope explicitly authorized by
the broker, those are acts for which the broker is responsible."

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
Three sentences, three rules. The notice must be *in writing* and must state the *scope*. The
broker is responsible for authorized acts unless scope is limited or revoked in writing, though
the broker "is not required to supervise the sales agents directly." And the trap is the third
sentence: a broker who writes a narrow scope and then knowingly lets an agent work outside it is
responsible for those acts anyway, so a written scope protects the broker only for as long as the
broker enforces it.

**(b) The fiduciary standard.** "A broker owes the highest fiduciary obligation to the principal
and is obliged to convey to the principal all information known to the agent which may affect the
principal's decision unless prohibited by other law." The trigger is information that "may affect
the principal's decision," not information the broker judges important, and the qualifier "unless
prohibited by other law" is part of the rule. The duty is the broker's but the knowledge is the
agent's, which is the whole reason this unit exists.

**(c) Trust funds.** "A broker is responsible for the proper handling of trust funds placed with
the broker and must comply with §535.146 of this chapter (relating to Maintaining Trust Money)."
Rule 535.146 is taught in Module 07; the two sentences of it that bear on this relationship are "A
sales agent shall not maintain a trust account. Any trust money received by a sales agent must be
immediately delivered to the sales agent's sponsoring broker."

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
**(d) Property management.** "A broker is responsible for any property management activity by the
broker's sponsored sales agent that requires a real estate license." Property management is where
sponsored agents most often operate semi-independently, and this subsection settles who owns the
consequences.

**(e) Delegation.** "A broker may delegate to another license holder the responsibility to assist
in administering compliance with the Act and Rules, but the broker may not relinquish overall
responsibility for the supervision of license holders sponsored by the broker. Any license holder
who leads, supervises, directs, or manages a team must be delegated as a supervisor. Any such
delegation must be in writing. A broker shall provide the name of each delegated supervisor to the
Commission using a process acceptable to the Commission within 30 days of any such delegation that
has lasted or is anticipated to last more than three consecutive months. The broker shall notify
the Commission in the same manner within 30 days after the delegation of a supervisor has ended.
In the event the delegated supervisor is a broker at the time of delegation or later becomes a
broker, that broker may, in lieu of the sponsoring broker, notify the Commission in writing when
the delegation ends."

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
Extract the operative facts. Delegation is only of the responsibility "to assist in administering
compliance"; overall responsibility can never be relinquished. Any license holder who "leads,
supervises, directs, or manages a team" must be delegated as a supervisor, in writing. The
Commission must be told the supervisor's name within **30 days** of a delegation that "has lasted
or is anticipated to last more than three consecutive months" — note both limbs — and within **30
days** after it ends.

**(f) Listings in the broker's name.** "Listings and other agreements for real estate brokerage
services must be solicited and accepted in a broker's name." It is a broker responsibility, not
merely an agent obligation, so the broker who tolerates listings taken in a team's name is the one
the Commission looks to.

**(g) Advertising.** "A broker is responsible to ensure that a sponsored sales agent's advertising
complies with §535.154 of this chapter (relating to Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and
Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements) and §535.155 of this chapter (relating to
Advertisements)." Those rules are taught in Module 12; what (g) adds is that a sponsored agent's
advertising is the broker's compliance problem.

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
**(h) Records: four years, eight categories.** "Except for records destroyed by an 'Act of God'
such as a natural disaster or fire not intentionally caused by the broker, the broker must, at a
minimum, maintain the following records in a format that is readily available to the Commission
for at least four years from the date of closing, termination of the contract, or end of a real
estate transaction." The eight categories are: "disclosures"; "commission agreements such as
listing agreements, buyer representation agreements, or other written agreements relied upon to
claim compensation"; "substantive communications with parties to the transaction"; "offers,
contracts, and related addenda"; "receipts and disbursements of compensation for services subject
to the Act"; "property management contracts"; "appraisals, broker price opinions, and comparative
market analyses"; and "sponsorship agreements between the broker and sponsored sales agents."

Three details students lose. The four years run from the triggers the rule names as they apply —
closing, termination of the contract, or end of the transaction — not from the date the file was
opened, so a listing that expires unsold in September 2026 starts its four years then.
"[S]ubstantive communications with parties to the transaction" includes texts and emails. And
the last category means the written agreement § 201.072(1)(D) demands is itself a record the
broker must keep for four years.

chunks.heading: Unit: Broker Responsibility (Relationships between Brokers and Agents, §535.2)
chunks.excerpt:
**(i) Written policies and procedures.** "A broker who sponsors sales agents or is a designated
broker for a business entity shall maintain, on a current basis, written policies and procedures
to ensure that" eight things are true. In order: that each sponsored sales agent "is advised of
the scope of the sales agent's authorized activities subject to the Act and is competent to
conduct such activities, including having competence in the geographic market area where the sales
agent represents clients"; that each agent "maintains their license in active status at all times
while they are engaging in activities subject to the Act"; that "[a]ny and all compensation paid
to a sponsored sales agent for acts or services subject to the Act is paid by, through, or with
the written consent of the sponsoring broker"; that each agent is given, "on a timely basis,
before the effective date of the change, notice of any change to the Act, Commission rules, or
Commission promulgated contract forms"; that beyond statutory minimum continuing education each
agent "receives such additional educational instruction the broker may deem necessary" to maintain
competency, with the specific floor that "when a sales agent performs a type of real estate
brokerage activity for the first three times, the broker must require that the sales agent receive
coaching and assistance from an experienced license holder competent for that activity"; that each
agent "complies with the Commission's advertising rules"; that all trust accounts "including but
not limited to property management trust accounts, and other funds received from consumers are
maintained by the broker with appropriate controls in compliance with §535.146"; and that
"[r]ecords are properly maintained pursuant to subsection (h) of this sect

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Auditing a brokerage against § 535.2
chunks.excerpt:
ion."

Two of those deserve a second look. Section 535.2(i) writes competence "in the geographic market
area where the sales agent represents clients" into the rule itself. And the first-three-times
requirement is the most concrete supervision obligation in it: not "encourage," not "make
available," but "the broker must require" coaching, for each *type* of activity — first three
listings, first three buyer representations, first three leases, counted separately.

**(j) and (k) The response clocks.** "In addition to the requirements of §535.157 of this chapter
(relating to Obligation to Respond Timely), a broker or supervisor delegated under subsection (e)
of this section must respond to sponsored sales agents within two calendar days." And: "A
sponsoring broker or supervisor delegated under subsection (e) of this section shall deliver mail
and other correspondence from the Commission to their sponsored sales agents within three calendar
days after receipt." Calendar days, not business days. Subsection (k) exists because under 22 TAC
§ 535.21(b), taught in Module 12, the Commission sends notices to an active sales agent at the
address of that agent's *sponsoring broker*.

**(l) and (m) Entities, and the closing sentence.** "When the broker is a business entity, the
designated broker is the person responsible for the broker responsibilities under this section."
The corporate form does not diffuse the responsibility; it rests on the human being Occupations
Code § 1101.355(a) requires a business entity to designate. And then the final subsection, which
this unit began with: "This section is not meant to create or require an employer/employee
relationship between a broker and a sponsored sales agent."

### Statute reading exercise: Auditing a brokerage against § 535.2

chunks.heading: Unit: Compensation Issues
chunks.excerpt:
Open 22 TAC § 535.2 and read every subsection.

1. Subsection (a) contains three sentences. State the rule each one lays down, and identify which
   sentence a broker is relying on when the broker says "I don't have to watch my agents every
   day."
2. Under subsection (e), a broker delegates supervision on 2 February expecting it to last six
   weeks, then extends it repeatedly until it ends on 30 November. Work out the date by which the
   broker had to provide the delegated supervisor's name to the Commission, and the date by which
   the broker had to notify the Commission that the delegation had ended. Show your reasoning from
   the rule's words.
3. Subsection (h) lists categories of records. Which category would a broker's own sponsorship and
   independent contractor agreements fall into? From what date does the four-year period run for a
   listing that expires without selling?
4. Subsection (i) contains a requirement expressed as a numerical floor about new activities.
   State it exactly. Does it apply once per agent, or once per type of activity?
5. Find the sentence in § 535.2 that addresses the employment relationship. Read it and then say
   what it does *not* do — specifically, whether it reduces any of the broker's obligations under
   the rest of the section.

## Unit: Compensation Issues

Everything in this module converges here, on one idea: **compensation for acts subject to the Act
flows through the broker.** Every violation in this area is a variation on someone trying to route
money around it.

**The core rule.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.3, "Compensation to or Paid by a Sales Agent," is two
sentences long and you should be able to recite both:

chunks.heading: Unit: Compensation Issues
chunks.excerpt:
> A sales agent may not receive a commission or other valuable consideration except with the
> written consent of the sales agent's sponsoring broker or the broker who sponsored the sales
> agent when the sales agent became entitled to the commission or other valuable consideration. A
> sales agent may not pay a commission or other valuable consideration to another person except
> with the written consent of the sales agent's sponsoring broker.

Both directions are covered, receiving and paying, and both require *written* consent. The
receiving sentence contemplates two possible consenting brokers, because the rule anticipates that
you may change brokers between earning and being paid.

**The statute behind it.** Occupations Code § 1101.651(b) is the provision to quote whole, because
the clause people drop is the one that solves the change-of-sponsorship problem:

> (b) A sales agent may not accept compensation for a real estate transaction from a person other
> than the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent or was sponsoring the sales agent when the
> sales agent earned the compensation.

Any version of § 1101.651(b) that stops after "the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent"
states a different and wrong rule, because it would make it impossible for an agent who changes
brokerages to be paid on a transaction earned at the old firm. Read it with its neighbours:
§ 1101.651(a) bars a broker from paying a commission to or otherwise compensating, directly or
indirectly, anyone who is not a license holder or an out-of-state broker who conducted none of the
Texas negotiations, and § 1101.651(c) provides that "A sales agent may not pay a commission to a
person except through the broker that is sponsoring the sales agent at that time."

chunks.heading: Unit: Compensation Issues
chunks.excerpt:
One supervision link belongs alongside those provisions: § 535.2(i) requires the broker's written
policies to ensure that each agent "maintains their license in active status at all times while
they are engaging in activities subject to the Act," which is why a gap between brokerages is not
merely administrative. Terminating a sponsorship under § 1101.367 is taught in Module 07.

**Receiving compensation through your own entity.** Occupations Code § 1101.355(c) states the
default: "A business entity that receives compensation on behalf of a license holder must be
licensed as a broker under this chapter." Subsection (d) supplies the exception, and every one of
its five conditions is required. The entity must receive "compensation on behalf of a broker or
sales agent licensed under this chapter that is earned by the license holder while engaged in real
estate brokerage"; it "performs no other acts of a broker"; it is "a limited liability company as
defined by Section 101.001, Business Organizations Code" or "an S corporation as defined by 26
U.S.C. Section 1361"; it "is registered with the commission"; and it "is at least 51 percent owned
by the license holder on whose behalf the entity receives compensation." Rule 22 TAC § 535.5(h)
states the same five conditions and points to § 535.35 for the registration process, and
§ 535.147(c) bars a license holder from sharing a commission or fees with an unlicensed entity
created to collect on the license holder's behalf unless it is exempt under § 535.5 and
§ 1101.355(d). So a general partnership will not do, a C corporation will not do, and a 50/50 LLC
with your spouse will not do.

chunks.heading: Unit: Compensation Issues
chunks.excerpt:
**Rebates to a party.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.147(d) permits a license holder to "rebate or pay a
portion of the license holder's fee or commission to a party in the transaction when the sales
agent has the written consent of the sales agent's sponsoring broker and the party represented by
the license holder." Three requirements must all be satisfied: that written consent from both the
sponsoring broker and the represented party; that the payment not be made "in a manner that
misleads a broker, lender, title company, or governmental agency regarding the real estate
transaction or the financial resources or obligations of the buyer"; and, where the rebate goes to
a party the license holder does not represent, the prior written consent of the party the license
holder does represent. The second ends careers: a rebate paid outside closing and left off the
settlement statement, on a loan whose cash-to-close was calculated without it, misleads a lender
about the buyer's financial resources or obligations.

**Undisclosed compensation.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.148 is taught in full in Module 05. Two
subsections bear on the flow of money here: (a) bars a license holder from receiving a commission,
rebate or fee from anyone other than the person the license holder represents without first
disclosing the intention to receive it and obtaining the client's consent — disclose first, then
consent; and (f) requires TREC No. RSC-4 for any payment received for services provided for or on
behalf of a residential service contract provider or administrator.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Following the money on a Denton closing
chunks.excerpt:
**Co-operation across state lines.** Section 1101.651(a)(2) permits a Texas broker to compensate
"a real estate broker licensed in another state who does not conduct in this state any of the
negotiations for which the commission or other compensation is paid." Rule 22 TAC § 535.131
elaborates: "A broker licensed in Texas may cooperate with a foreign broker and share earned
commissions with a foreign broker"; "Only Texas license holders may handle negotiations physically
conducted within Texas"; and a resident of a foreign country or territory that does not license
brokers "is considered to be licensed as a foreign broker for the purposes of §1101.651 of the
Act, if the person practices as a real estate broker in compliance with the law of the foreign
country or territory."

### Applied exercise: Following the money on a Denton closing

Priya is a sales agent sponsored by Redbud Realty. She represents a buyer on a $525,000 purchase
in Denton. The listing broker's offer of compensation to the buyer's broker is 2.75 percent.
Priya's split with Redbud is 65/35 in her favour. Along the way: the seller's home warranty
provider offers Priya $150 in marketing support because she recommended their product to the
buyer; Priya wants to rebate $2,000 of her share to her buyer at closing without showing it on the
settlement statement, because the buyer is short on cash to close; and Priya's newly formed LLC,
of which she owns 60 percent and her brother owns 40 percent, has asked Redbud to make the
commission cheque payable to the LLC. The LLC has not registered with the Commission.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
1. Compute the compensation to the buyer's broker and Priya's share under the 65/35 split. State
   which entity receives the funds at closing and cite the provision that requires it.
2. Apply 22 TAC § 535.148(a) and (f) to the $150 from the home warranty provider. What must Priya
   do before receiving it, and which TREC form does § 535.148(f) require?
3. Apply 22 TAC § 535.147(d) to the proposed $2,000 rebate. Identify each of the three
   requirements in that subsection and state precisely which one the plan to keep the rebate off
   the settlement statement violates, quoting the language that governs.
4. Test the LLC against all five conditions of Occupations Code § 1101.355(d). Which conditions
   does it satisfy and which does it fail? What is the consequence under § 1101.355(c) and 22 TAC
   § 535.147(c)?
5. Two weeks before closing, Priya moves to a different brokerage. Using § 1101.651(b) and 22 TAC
   § 535.3, state who may pay her, whose written consent she needs, and what § 1101.367(a)
   required to happen on the day she left Redbud.

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Start where the module started, with a single word used in two ways. In Labor Code chapters 201
and 21 the word "employment" carries tax and discrimination consequences. In the law of agency it
means an engagement: the seller employs the broker. Nothing about the first sense follows from the
second, and a student who keeps them separate will get every question in this topic right. The
corollary matters even more: each authority in this module serves one limited purpose. Section
201.072 serves unemployment compensation; 26 U.S.C. § 3508 serves federal tax treatment; Labor
Code chapter 21 serves discrimination law; 22 TAC § 535.2 and Occupations Code §§ 1101.351 and
1101.803 serve brokerage supervision and licensing responsibility; and 22 TAC §§ 535.3, 535.147
and 535.148 with Occupations Code § 1101.651 serve compensation. None of them decides a question
belonging to another.

For unemployment compensation, § 201.072 excludes real estate service from "employment" "In this
subtitle" on four conditions: activity within the § 1101.002 definition of broker; a Texas Real
Estate Commission licence; remuneration that is "substantially all … directly related to sales or
other output … and not to the number of hours worked"; and a written contract providing that the
individual "is not treated as an employee with respect to the service for federal tax purposes."
Paragraph (2) does the same for instructors of Commission-approved courses, without the
output-based pay condition. For federal tax, 26 U.S.C. § 3508(a) says a qualified real estate
agent "shall not be treated as an employee" and the person for whom the services are performed
"shall not be treated as an employer," and § 3508(b)(1) conditions that on a licence, output-based
remuneration, and a written contract with the same

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
federal-tax provision. Neither statute
conditions anything on freedom from control — compare § 201.070 and § 201.073, which are full of
control conditions — and neither defines "substantially all." Wage-and-hour law, workers'
compensation, common-law employment status and vicarious liability **were not held** for this
course, and this module states no position on them.

Chapter 21 is discrimination law with its own definitions. Section 21.051 prohibits an employer
from discriminating because of race, color, disability, religion, sex, national origin or age.
Section 21.002(8)(A) makes an employer a person "engaged in an industry affecting commerce" with
"15 or more employees for each working day in each of 20 or more calendar weeks in the current or
preceding calendar year," and § 21.002(7) defines an employee as "an individual employed by an
employer." Those definitions are the chapter's reach, and neither § 201.072's four conditions nor
§ 3508's three are imported into them; whether a genuine independent contractor sales agent can be
an "employee" under chapter 21 depends on case law that **was not held**. What the
fifteen-employee threshold does not limit is Subchapter C-1: § 21.141 defines "employer" there as
a person who "employs one or more employees," and § 21.142 makes an employer liable for sexual
harassment where the employer or its agents or supervisors knew or should have known and failed
"to take immediate and appropriate corrective action." Independently of employment status,
§ 1101.652(b)(32) makes discrimination in brokerage a licence matter; § 1101.652 is Module 10's.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The broker–principal relationship is the agency sense of employment. Section 1101.557(a) — Module
02 — says a broker who represents a party or lists under an exclusive agreement "is that party's
agent." Rule 535.2 states that the broker "owes the highest fiduciary obligation to the principal"
and must convey "all information known to the agent which may affect the principal's decision
unless prohibited by other law," and that listings "must be solicited and accepted in a broker's
name." Section 1101.351(c) puts the sales agent in position: sponsored, and "acting for that
broker." And § 1101.652(b)(26), taught in Module 10, catches an association "by employment or
otherwise" with a person who is expected to act as a license holder and is not one.

Personal assistants are a boundary problem with a clean method: start from 22 TAC § 535.4 and the
§ 1101.002 broker definition and ask whether the task is on the licensed side. Showing — which
§ 535.4(c) defines to include "unlocking or providing access onto or into a property for a
prospective buyer or tenant" and "hosting an open house at the property" — is licensed. Soliciting
or negotiating for listings under § 535.4(f) is licensed. Directing or supervising persons who
perform acts requiring a licence under § 535.4(e) is licensed. Confirming size, price and terms of
advertised property, by a person identified to callers as clerical or administrative staff, is
not, under § 535.5(g). Referring with the expectation of valuable consideration — including "gifts
of merchandise having a retail value greater than $50" — requires a licence under § 535.20(a),
subject only to the four-condition vendor exemption in § 535.20(b). Payment is governed by
§ 1101.651(a), § 535.147(a) and (b), and, when the agent pays out of pocket, the secon

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
d sentence
of § 535.3.

Broker responsibility under § 535.2 is the operational core, and it does not soften because the
agents are contractors: a written scope notice, with responsibility extending to acts the broker
permits beyond that scope; the highest fiduciary obligation; trust funds under § 535.146, which a
sales agent may never hold; property management activity; written delegation, with any team leader
delegated as a supervisor, the Commission notified within 30 days of a delegation lasting or
anticipated to last more than three consecutive months and within 30 days after it ends; listings
in the broker's name; advertising compliance under §§ 535.154 and 535.155; eight categories of
records kept at least four years from closing, contract termination or the end of the transaction;
eight written policies including mandatory coaching for a sales agent's first three times
performing a type of activity; a two-calendar-day response to sponsored agents and a
three-calendar-day forward of Commission correspondence; the designated broker personally
responsible when the broker is an entity; and the closing statement that the section "is not meant
to create or require an employer/employee relationship between a broker and a sponsored sales
agent."

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Compensation resolves into one sentence and its exceptions: money for acts subject to the Act
moves through the broker. Rule 535.3 requires written consent both to receive and to pay. Section
1101.651(b) permits a sales agent to accept compensation only from "the broker that is sponsoring
the sales agent or was sponsoring the sales agent when the sales agent earned the compensation" —
quote it whole, always. Section 1101.651(a) limits whom a broker may pay; § 1101.651(c) requires a
sales agent's payments to go through the sponsoring broker. An entity may receive an agent's
commission without a licence only on all five conditions of § 1101.355(d), including at least 51
percent ownership by the license holder and registration with the Commission under § 535.35.
Rebates require the sponsoring broker's and the represented party's written consent and must not
mislead a lender or title company about the buyer's financial resources or obligations, under
§ 535.147(d). Third-party compensation must be disclosed and consented to before receipt under
§ 535.148(a), with TREC No. RSC-4 required under § 535.148(f); the rest of § 535.148 is taught in
Module 05. And a Texas broker may share a commission with a foreign broker who conducts none of
the Texas negotiations, under § 1101.651(a)(2) and 22 TAC § 535.131.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: Reading § 201.072 against its neighbouring exclusions
chunks.excerpt:
Finally, the honest inventory. The Internal Revenue Service's administrative guidance and the
Treasury regulations under § 3508, the Texas Workforce Commission's rules and audit practice under
chapter 201, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Texas Payday Law, Texas workers' compensation law,
Texas case law on common-law employment status and vicarious liability, Title VII and the
Americans with Disabilities Act themselves, and judicial decisions applying Labor Code chapter 21
to real estate sales agents **were not held** for this course. Where those sources would have
settled a question, this module said so rather than guessing. That habit — knowing which of your
beliefs rests on an authority you have actually read — is the most valuable thing you can carry
out of a law of agency course into a career where other people's money is in your hands.

## Optional reference: Reading § 201.072 against its neighbouring exclusions

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it. It is here because the law it covers is real and a
license holder may need it, not because the course requires you to read it. Skipping it costs you
nothing: no later instruction depends on it, and Unit 1 is complete without it.

**Optional practice — reading § 201.072 against its neighbours.** This is document practice on the
primary sources rather than a brokerage fact pattern, and it is the only exercise in this module
that works directly with the Labor Code. Open Texas Labor Code § 201.072, then § 201.070 and
§ 201.073 in the same subchapter.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: Reading § 201.072 against its neighbouring exclusions
chunks.excerpt:
1. List the four conditions in § 201.072(1) in your own words. Which of them refers to an activity
   definition found in a different code entirely, and which code and section is it?
2. Sections 201.070 and 201.073 each condition their exclusion on a list of control factors.
   Identify three such factors from either section. Then state whether any equivalent factor
   appears in § 201.072, and explain what you conclude from the difference.
3. Section 201.072(2) covers real estate instructors. Which of the four conditions in paragraph
   (1) has no counterpart in paragraph (2)? Why would the Legislature have left it out for
   instructors?
4. A broker tells a new agent, "We don't need a written agreement, everyone here knows you're a
   contractor." Point to the specific language in § 201.072 that this defeats, and say what the
   consequence is under the section.
5. Section 201.072 opens with the phrase "In this subtitle." What does that phrase limit the
   exclusion to, and what does it therefore tell you about whether § 201.072 answers questions
   arising under Labor Code chapter 21?

lessons.title: Texas Law of Agency — Module 10

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Agency — Module 10
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Agency — Module 10

## TREC Topic: Agency, Ethics and the Law

**Prescribed time: 155 minutes.** This module carries the five units the Commission's LOA-1 course
approval form places under *Agency, Ethics and the Law*, whose scope note is *"An agent's duties,
including fiduciary duties."*

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: separate a legal duty
enforceable by the state from an ethical duty enforceable by a licensing agency or a private
association and from a moral conviction enforceable by nobody, and explain why a Texas license
holder can lose a license over conduct that is neither a crime nor a tort; state the protected
characteristics exactly as the federal Fair Housing Act, the Texas Fair Housing Act, and 22 TAC
§ 531.19 each state them, apply the reasonable-accommodation and reasonable-modification provisions
with their qualifying language intact, and identify which fair housing exemptions are destroyed the
moment a license holder touches the transaction; read the Canons of Professional Ethics and Client
Relations at 22 TAC §§ 531.1–531.20 as the ethical code that actually binds you, locate a given act
within the correct subsection of Occupations Code § 1101.652, and trace a consumer complaint from
filing through investigation under 22 TAC § 535.141 to a sanction authorized by § 1101.702 and
priced by 22 TAC § 535.191; describe what a trade association code of ethics is, how 22 TAC § 535.1
defines a Trade Association, why such a code binds by contract rather than by statute, and how a
private ethics complaint differs in forum, remedy and consequence from a complaint to the
Commission; and state the minimum ethical standard a Texas license holder must meet, drawing every
element of it back to a canon or a rule

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
you can cite.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it.

## Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals

The distinction this unit draws is not philosophical. It is jurisdictional. Three different
enforcement systems can reach your conduct in a Texas real estate transaction, each with its own
decision-maker, its own procedure, its own sanction, and its own vocabulary. If you cannot sort a
complaint into the right box, you will either panic over something that carries no consequence or
shrug at something that will cost you your license.

**Law is the set of rules the state itself enforces.** A criminal statute is enforced by a
prosecutor, in a court, against a defendant, with the state's coercive power at the end of it. A
civil statute or a common-law duty is enforced by a private party who sues, in a court, and collects
a judgment. Both are law. Their common feature is that the enforcer, ultimately, is a government
body with the power to take money, property or liberty. Texas fair housing law supplies an example
of a statute that reaches all three of those levels at once: Property Code § 301.171 makes
intimidating or interfering with a protected person by force or threat of force an offense, and
provides that "An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor"; § 301.151(a) lets an
aggrieved person file a civil action in district court; and § 301.112 lets a state agency assess
civil penalties administratively. One underlying prohibition, three enforcement machines.

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
**Ethics, in a licensed profession, is the set of rules a licensing body or a membership
organization enforces against people who have accepted its authority.** The word carries a soft
connotation in ordinary speech — a matter of conscience, or of taste. In Texas real estate it is
nothing of the kind. The Commission's Canons of Professional Ethics and Client Relations are
administrative rules published at 22 TAC Chapter 531, and they are enforceable. Occupations Code § 1101.656(a) provides that "In addition to any other
authority under this chapter, the commission may suspend or revoke a license, place on probation a
person whose license has been suspended, or reprimand a license holder if the license holder
violates this chapter or a commission rule." Section 1101.701(a) adds the money: "The commission may
impose an administrative penalty on a person who violates this chapter or a rule adopted or order
issued by the commission under this chapter." Read those two sentences together and the point is
unmistakable. The phrase "or a commission rule" and the phrase "or a rule adopted" are what convert
an ethical canon into an enforceable obligation with a license and a bank balance behind it. An
ethical breach in this field is not a matter of taste. It is a rule violation, and the state agency
that issued your license is the enforcer.

The second sort of ethics enforcement is private, and Unit 4 deals with it in detail. Hold on to the
structural difference for now: the Commission enforces against everyone who holds a license, whether
they like it or not; a trade association enforces only against its own members, and only because
they agreed to be bound when they joined and paid dues.

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
**Morals are the convictions a person holds about right conduct, enforced by nobody.** No procedure,
no sanction, no forum. That is not a criticism of morals — a license holder's private sense of
decency is usually the thing that keeps the other two systems from ever having to be invoked — but
it is a real limitation, and the limitation runs both directions. A moral conviction does not by
itself create a legal duty. It also does not excuse you from one.

Texas gives a sharp example of morals running against law. Suppose a buyer's agent in San Antonio
learns that a previous occupant of a listed house died of an AIDS-related illness. Many people's
moral intuition is that a buyer would want to know, and that concealing it is a species of lying.
The law says otherwise, in two places, and both were written deliberately. Occupations Code § 1101.802 provides that
"Notwithstanding Section 1101.801, a person is not civilly or criminally liable because the person
failed to inquire about, make a disclosure relating to, or release information relating to whether a
previous or current occupant of real property had, may have had, has, or may have AIDS, an
HIV-related illness, or HIV infection as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
of the United States Public Health Service." And 22 TAC § 531.19, the Commission's discriminatory
practices canon, closes with the sentence: "For the purpose of this section, disability includes
AIDS, HIV-related illnesses, or HIV infection as defined by the Centers for Disease Control of the
United States Public Health Service." Put those together and the agent who volunteers the
information has not merely done something the law did not require. The agent has made a disclosure
about a previous occupant's disability, which is exactly w

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
hat § 531.19 forbids. The moral intuition,
followed uncritically, walks you into a rule violation.

**Why a license holder can be disciplined for conduct that breaks no criminal law.** Discipline does
not require wrongdoing of the sort a jury would recognize — theft, fraud, a falsified document.
Title 22 TAC § 535.157 requires a broker or sales agent to respond
to a principal, to a license holder representing another party, or to an unrepresented party within
two calendar days; that rule is taught in Module 02. Failing to return a cooperating agent's call
for four days is not a crime, and very likely not a tort — the cooperating agent has no contract
with you and probably no damages. But it is a violation of a Commission rule, § 1101.656(a)
authorizes discipline for violating a commission rule, and 22 TAC § 535.191 places "22 TAC
§535.157" in the band for which "An administrative penalty range of $100 - $1,500 per violation per
day may be assessed." Per violation. Per day. That is the whole distance between ethics as a feeling
and ethics as an enforceable standard.

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
The three systems also run in parallel rather than in sequence, and TRELA says so expressly. Section
1101.801 provides: "Disciplinary action taken against a person under Section 1101.652 does not
relieve the person from civil or criminal liability." A single act — say, spending a buyer's earnest
money out of the operating account — can produce a criminal charge brought by a district attorney, a
civil suit brought by the buyer, and a Commission proceeding, and none of the three waits for the
others. Nor does winning one win the others. An acquittal in a criminal case does not bar the
Commission, whose burden and whose rules are different. A Commission order that assesses a penalty
does not compensate the buyer; § 1101.659(b) limits what a refund order may do, providing that the
amount "may not exceed the amount the consumer paid to the person for a service or accommodation
regulated by this commission" and that "The commission may not require payment of other damages or
estimate harm in a refund order." The Commission is a regulator, not a small-claims court. If the
consumer wants damages, the consumer sues.

chunks.heading: Unit: Distinctions between Law, Ethics, and Morals
chunks.excerpt:
It is worth noticing what forum the ethics system actually uses, because it is neither a court nor a
private tribunal. Under § 1101.657(a), "If the commission proposes to deny, suspend, or revoke a
person's license or certificate of registration, the person is entitled to a hearing conducted by
the State Office of Administrative Hearings," and subsection (e) provides that "A hearing under this
section is governed by the contested case procedures under Chapter 2001, Government Code." From
there, § 1101.658(a) gives "A person aggrieved by a ruling, order, or decision under this
subchapter" the right "to appeal to a district court in the county in which the administrative
hearing was held." So the ethics system does eventually touch the courts — but on review, and on an
administrative record, not as a fresh lawsuit. The record the Commission builds during its
investigation is the record you will argue from later.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Sorting three complaints in Lubbock
chunks.excerpt:
A last distinction that matters in daily practice. Law tends to be specific and bounded; ethics
rules in this field are frequently open-textured, and that is intentional. Compare Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(30), which tells you precisely where escrow money goes — "in trust with a title
company authorized to do business in this state" or "in a custodial, trust, or escrow account
maintained for that purpose in a banking institution authorized to do business in this state" — with
22 TAC § 531.3, which requires a license holder to exercise integrity "including employment of
prudence and caution so as to avoid misrepresentation, in any way, by acts of commission or
omission." The first is a rule you can comply with by following an instruction. The second is a
standard you comply with by exercising judgment, and it is written broadly precisely so that it can
reach conduct nobody anticipated. Your protection against an open-textured standard is not to hunt
for the loophole. It is to build habits that keep you well inside the line.

### Applied exercise: Sorting three complaints in Lubbock

Marisol is a sales agent in Lubbock sponsored by a broker whose office is on 19th Street. In the
same week, three things happen.

First, a cooperating agent in Amarillo emails Marisol an offer on Tuesday morning and calls twice.
Marisol is at a family funeral and does not respond until the following Monday. The offer is still
open and her seller accepts it; nobody loses money.

Second, Marisol tells a buyer that the seller *will definitely take $10,000 less* because she wants
the deal to close. The seller had told her no such thing. The buyer offers less, the seller is
offended, and the deal dies. The seller relists with another brokerage.

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
Third, Marisol privately believes that a landlord client is a dishonest man who overcharges his
tenants, though every lease he signs complies with its terms and no law restricts what he may
charge. She continues to represent him and says nothing to anyone.

1. For each of the three, identify which enforcement system — law, Commission-enforced ethics, or
   morals — can reach the conduct, and name the specific section that supports your answer for each
   system you say applies.
2. For the second incident, § 1101.652(b) contains more than one subdivision that could be charged.
   Identify at least two, quote the language you are relying on, and say which you think fits better
   and why.
3. The seller in the second incident wants money. Explain, using § 1101.659(b) and § 1101.801, what
   the Commission can and cannot do for that seller and what the seller must do to be made whole.
4. The first incident caused no harm to anyone. Explain why that fact does not dispose of it, citing
   the rule Marisol broke and the penalty band 22 TAC § 535.191 assigns to it.
5. Marisol's broker was never named in any complaint. Read 22 TAC § 535.141 and explain whether the
   broker is nonetheless drawn into the matter, and for what limited purposes.

## Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct

Fair housing is the body of law most likely to end a Texas real estate career, and it is the body of
law students most often learn wrong: a memorized list of *protected classes* that matches no
statute, held on the assumption that the federal Act, the Texas Act and the Commission's rule all
say the same thing. They do not, and the differences are the parts that matter. In this unit you
learn each list exactly as its own source states it.

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
**The federal Fair Housing Act.** The operative prohibitions live at 42 U.S.C. § 3604. Its opening
words matter: "As made applicable by section 3603 of this title and except as exempted by sections
3603(b) and 3607 of this title, it shall be unlawful—". Everything that follows is subject to those
two cross-references, which is why the exemptions discussed below are part of the statute rather
than an afterthought.

Subsection (a) makes it unlawful "To refuse to sell or rent after the making of a bona fide offer,
or to refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of, or otherwise make unavailable or deny, a
dwelling to any person because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin."
Subsection (b) makes it unlawful "To discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or
privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling, or in the provision of services or facilities in
connection therewith, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin."
Subsection (c) makes it unlawful "To make, print, or publish, or cause to be made, printed, or
published any notice, statement, or advertisement, with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling
that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex,
handicap, familial status, or national origin, or an intention to make any such preference,
limitation, or discrimination."

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
Read those three lists again, slowly. Subsections (a) and (b) name six characteristics: race, color,
religion, sex, familial status, national origin. Subsection (c) names seven: the same six plus
handicap. That is not a drafting slip. Disability protection was added to the federal Act later than
the original 1968 list, and Congress put the substantive disability prohibitions in their own
subsection, § 3604(f), rather than editing (a) and (b). So under federal law, refusing to rent
because of a disability is unlawful — but the provision you cite is § 3604(f)(1), not § 3604(a). Subsections (d) and (e), which deal with falsely
representing that a dwelling is unavailable for inspection, sale or rental and with inducing sales
for profit by representations about who is moving into a neighborhood, both include handicap in
their lists.

Section 3604(f)(1) makes it unlawful "To discriminate in the sale or rental, or to otherwise make
unavailable or deny, a dwelling to any buyer or renter because of a handicap of—" the buyer or
renter, a person residing in or intending to reside in that dwelling after it is so sold, rented, or
made available, or "any person associated with that buyer or renter." That last phrase is the
associational provision, and it catches a real and common error: refusing an applicant because the
applicant's adult child who will visit uses a wheelchair is a violation even though the applicant
has no disability.

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
Paragraph (f)(3) then defines what counts as discrimination in this context, and two of its three
branches are the provisions you will use most. Subparagraph (A) covers modifications: "a refusal to
permit, at the expense of the handicapped person, reasonable modifications of existing premises
occupied or to be occupied by such person if such modifications may be necessary to afford such
person full enjoyment of the premises except that, in the case of a rental, the landlord may where
it is reasonable to do so condition permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore
the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear
and tear excepted." Subparagraph (B) covers accommodations: "a refusal to make reasonable
accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services, when such accommodations may be necessary
to afford such person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling".

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
Notice four things in those two sentences that students routinely drop. First, a *modification* is a
physical change to the premises and it is made "at the expense of the handicapped person" — the
tenant pays. An *accommodation* is a change in "rules, policies, practices, or services," and the
statute does not put its cost on the tenant. Second, both are qualified by "may be necessary." The
statute does not say a modification or accommodation must be proven indispensable; it says it is
discrimination to refuse one that *may be necessary*. Truncating that qualifier — and it gets
truncated constantly, in brochures, in office training, and in courses — converts a broad protection
into a narrow one and gets people sued. Third, the modification provision has a landlord-side
qualifier of its own: on a rental, the landlord may, where reasonable, condition permission on the
renter agreeing to restore the interior, "reasonable wear and tear excepted." Fourth, the standards
differ: a modification must "may be necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of the premises,"
while an accommodation must "may be necessary to afford such person equal opportunity to use and
enjoy a dwelling." Full enjoyment; equal opportunity. Different words, deliberately.

Section 3604(f)(9) supplies the limit: "Nothing in this subsection requires that a dwelling be made
available to an individual whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to the health or safety of
other individuals or whose tenancy would result in substantial physical damage to the property of
others." That is a narrow safety valve about a specific individual's tenancy, not a general licence
to decide that a category of applicants is risky.

chunks.heading: Unit: Federal and State Law Relating to Conduct
chunks.excerpt:
The federal definitions are at 42 U.S.C. § 3602. "Handicap" means, with respect to a person, "a
physical or mental impairment which substantially limits one or more of such person's major life
