stay out of legal drafting under § 1101.654 and § 537.11; keep the file for four years under
§ 535.2; answer the Commission under § 1101.652(a)(4); and refuse, always, to inquire about, respond
to, facilitate or disclose the characteristics listed in § 531.19.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: The complete 22 TAC § 535.191 penalty schedule
chunks.excerpt:
Two closing cautions. First, this course is not TREC-approved and nothing in this module should be
read as a Commission publication; every proposition here is drawn from the statutes and rules named
beside it, and you should read those texts yourself. Second, the numbers in this module are the ones
that will be quoted back at you: $5,000 per violation per day under § 1101.702(a); the $100–$1,500,
$500–$3,000 and $1,000–$5,000 bands of § 535.191; four years for records under § 535.2 and four
years for complaints under § 1101.204(c); two calendar days under § 535.157; twenty days to accept
or contest under § 1101.704(a) and thirty days to pay or appeal under § 1101.707(a); and, in
§ 1101.652, eight grounds in subsection (a), three in (a-1), and thirty-four
in (b), with discrimination at (b)(32). Learn them as numbers attached to sections, not as numbers
floating free, because a number without its section is a number you cannot defend.

## Optional reference: The complete 22 TAC § 535.191 penalty schedule

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it, and nothing later in the course depends on it. You
may skip it entirely. It is here because the law it covers is real and a license holder may need it:
the penalty schedule is the first thing anyone looks up when the Commission prices a file, and the
bands that matter for the violations this module teaches are already in Unit 3, beside the
violations themselves.

chunks.heading: Optional practice: Pricing a Galveston enforcement file
chunks.excerpt:
**The bands, section by section.** That schedule is 22 TAC § 535.191, and it opens by confirming the
point: "The Commission may suspend or revoke a license or take other disciplinary action authorized
by the Act in addition to or instead of assessing the administrative penalties set forth in this
section." It then sets three bands. The lowest is "An administrative penalty range of $100 - $1,500
per violation per day," and it covers, among others, § 1101.652(a)(3), § 1101.652(a)(8),
§ 1101.652(b)(23), § 1101.652(b)(29), § 1101.652(b)(33), § 1101.652(b)(34), 22 TAC § 535.21, 22 TAC
§ 535.154, 22 TAC § 535.155 and 22 TAC § 535.157. The middle band is "An administrative penalty
range of $500 - $3,000 per violation per day," covering among others §§ 1101.652(a)(4) - (7),
§ 1101.652(b)(1), §§ 1101.652(b)(7) - (8), § 1101.652(b)(12), § 1101.652(b)(14), § 1101.652(b)(22),
§ 1101.654(a), 22 TAC § 531.18, 22 TAC § 531.20, 22 TAC § 535.2, 22 TAC § 535.16 and 22 TAC
§ 535.17. The top band is "An administrative penalty range of $1,000 - $5,000 per violation per
day," covering among others § 1101.651, § 1101.652(a)(2), §§ 1101.652(b)(2) - (6),
§§ 1101.652(b)(9) - (11), § 1101.652(b)(13), §§ 1101.652(b)(15) - (21), §§ 1101.652(b)(24) - (27),
§ 1101.652(b)(32), 22 TAC § 535.141(g), 22 TAC §§ 535.145 - 535.148 and 22 TAC § 535.156. And then
the multiplier: "The Commission may assess an additional administrative penalty of up to two times
that assessed under subsections (c), (d) and (e) of this section, subject to the maximum penalties
authorized under §1101.702(a) of the Act, if a person has a history of previous violations."

#### Optional practice: Pricing a Galveston enforcement file

chunks.heading: Optional practice: Pricing a Galveston enforcement file
chunks.excerpt:
Optional. This is arithmetic practice against the schedule above — no required exercise in this
module asks you to compute an exposure — and no assessment is drawn from it.

An agent sponsored by a Galveston brokerage takes a listing on a beach house. Over the course of the
file the Commission ultimately finds four things. (i) On eleven consecutive days, the agent failed
to respond to the buyer's agent, in violation of 22 TAC § 535.157. (ii) The agent never provided the
IABS notice to the unrepresented buyer at first substantive communication, in violation of 22 TAC
§ 531.20. (iii) The agent deposited the buyer's $9,000 earnest money into her personal checking
account for six days before moving it to the title company, implicating § 1101.652(b)(10). (iv) The
agent told the buyer the seller would *definitely* replace the seawall before closing, when the
seller had refused, implicating § 1101.652(b)(5). The agent has one prior Commission order against
her from three years ago.

1. Using 22 TAC § 535.191, state the penalty band that applies to each of the four findings, and
   quote the band language for each.
2. Compute the minimum and maximum administrative penalty for finding (i) alone, showing the
   arithmetic and stating the per-violation-per-day rule you relied on.
3. Compute the maximum administrative penalty for findings (ii), (iii) and (iv) treating each as a
   single violation on a single day, then apply the history-of-previous-violations provision in
   § 535.191 and recompute. State the ceiling that § 1101.702(a) places on your result and whether
   your figure hits it.

lessons.title: Texas Law of Agency — Module 11

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Agency — Module 11
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Agency — Module 11

## TREC Topic: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act

**Prescribed time: 140 minutes.** This module carries the five units the Commission's LOA-1 course
approval form places under *Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act*, whose scope note
is *"Deceptive trade practices."*

**Learning objectives.** After completing this module you will be able to: distinguish fraud,
negligent misrepresentation and innocent misrepresentation by the states of mind the Texas statutes
define; identify who qualifies as a "consumer" under Business & Commerce Code § 17.45(4), apply the
§ 17.46(b) subdivisions that realistically expose a Texas license holder, and recognise an
unconscionable action under § 17.45(5); compute a DTPA damages award under § 17.50(b), including the
multiplier for conduct committed knowingly and intentionally and the mandatory fees under
§ 17.50(d); assert the defenses the subchapter provides, including § 17.506(a), § 17.506(d), the
§ 17.49 exemptions with their exact dollar thresholds, the § 17.505 notice prerequisite and the
§ 17.565 limitations period; and connect civil exposure to the disciplinary grounds in Occupations
Code § 1101.652 and to the Real Estate Recovery Trust Account, stating its caps exactly.

**Every legal statement in this module comes from a source that was read for this course.** Where a
statement is practice rather than law, the module says so and cites nothing for it.

## Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
A buyer in Pflugerville asks a question you cannot answer. "Has this ever flooded?" "The seller said
the roof is four years old — is that right?" What you say next is the entire case, and its legal
character decides which body of law the buyer's lawyer reaches for and how much it costs you. Fraud,
misrepresentation and deception are not synonyms: they describe three levels of culpability, and
Texas law treats them very differently in who must prove what, what damages are available, and how
long the claimant has to sue.

**Start with what this course holds and what it does not.** The elements of common-law fraud in
Texas are stated in judicial opinions, not in a statute. No case reporter and no judicial opinion
were held for this course, and so **the common-law elements of fraud were not held and are not
stated here as law.** The same is true of the common-law elements of negligent misrepresentation and
of innocent misrepresentation: those formulations were not held. That is not a gap you should paper
over with something you half-remember from a study guide. It is the honest position, and it turns
out to matter very little in practice, for a reason you are about to see: the Texas Legislature has
written the distinction between these states of mind directly into the statutes that will actually
be used against you, and those statutes *were* held. Learn the statutory version. It is the one that
governs your license and your wallet.

**The statutory ladder of culpability.** Texas statutes describe at least four rungs of mental state
relevant to a false statement in a real estate transaction, each with a different consequence.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
The lowest rung is *no mental state at all* — a statement that is simply false, made by someone who
believed it was true and had no particular reason to doubt it. Under the Deceptive Trade
Practices-Consumer Protection Act, Business & Commerce Code § 17.46(b) declares a long list of acts
to be "false, misleading, or deceptive acts or practices," and most of the entries on that list
contain no scienter requirement whatever. Section 17.46(b)(5), to take the one you are most likely
to trip over, makes it a deceptive act to be "representing that goods or services have sponsorship,
approval, characteristics, ingredients, uses, benefits, or quantities which they do not have or that
a person has a sponsorship, approval, status, affiliation, or connection which the person does not."
Read that subdivision again and notice what is missing. It does not say "knowingly representing." It
does not say "falsely representing with intent to deceive." It says *representing*. If the
characteristics are not there, the representation violates the subdivision, and your sincerity is
irrelevant to liability. That is the single most important sentence in this module.

The next rung up is *negligence* — a statement made without the care a reasonable license holder
would use. Texas has not, in any source held for this course, defined negligent misrepresentation by
statute. Carelessness is nonetheless a disciplinary offence in its own right: Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(1) reaches a license holder who "acts negligently or incompetently." You need not have
lied; you need only have been sloppy.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
The third rung is *actual awareness*. The DTPA defines it at § 17.45(9): "Knowingly" means "actual
awareness, at the time of the act or practice complained of, of the falsity, deception, or
unfairness of the act or practice giving rise to the consumer's claim or, in an action brought under
Subdivision (2) of Subsection (a) of Section 17.50, actual awareness of the act, practice,
condition, defect, or failure constituting the breach of warranty, but actual awareness may be
inferred where objective manifestations indicate that a person acted with actual awareness." Two
things deserve your attention in that definition. The first is the time reference: awareness "at the
time of the act or practice complained of," not awareness acquired later. The second is the last
clause, which is the one defendants always wish were not there — "actual awareness may be inferred
where objective manifestations indicate that a person acted with actual awareness." You cannot
defeat a knowing finding simply by taking the stand and saying you did not know. A jury may infer
your awareness from what you did, what you had in your file, what you wrote in an e-mail, and what
any competent license holder in your position would have understood.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
The top rung is *intent*. Section 17.45(13) defines it, and this definition must be read whole,
because the last clause reverses the meaning of everything before it if you drop it. "Intentionally"
means "actual awareness of the falsity, deception, or unfairness of the act or practice, or the
condition, defect, or failure constituting a breach of warranty giving rise to the consumer's claim,
coupled with the specific intent that the consumer act in detrimental reliance on the falsity or
deception or in detrimental ignorance of the unfairness. Intention may be inferred from objective
manifestations that indicate that the person acted intentionally or from facts showing that a
defendant acted with flagrant disregard of prudent and fair business practices to the extent that
the defendant should be treated as having acted intentionally."

Sit with that last sentence. It says two separate things. First, intention may be inferred from
objective manifestations, the same evidentiary move the statute allows for knowledge. Second — and
this is the clause that catches license holders who thought "intentionally" meant a conscious plan
to cheat — intention may also be inferred "from facts showing that a defendant acted with flagrant
disregard of prudent and fair business practices to the extent that the defendant should be treated
as having acted intentionally." Flagrant disregard of prudent and fair business practices, if
flagrant enough, is treated as intent. A license holder who never formed a plan to deceive anyone,
but who behaved so far outside ordinary professional care that a jury describes the conduct as
flagrant, may be found to have acted intentionally. The words "to the extent that the defendant
should be treated as having acted intentionally" are not a limitation that sa

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
ves you; they are the
bridge that carries recklessness across into intent. Quote the definition without that final clause
and you will teach yourself the opposite of the law.

**Where the Occupations Code draws its own lines.** TRELA grades fault along the same ladder, and
Module 10 teaches those grounds in full: § 1101.652(b)(3), a material misrepresentation to a
potential buyer about a significant defect known to the license holder; (b)(4), a failure to disclose
such a defect; (b)(5), a false promise made when the license holder "is unable or does not intend to
keep the promise"; (b)(6), a continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation; and
§ 1101.652(a-1)(1), misrepresentation, dishonesty or fraud in the license holder's own name or a
close relative's.

The Commission rule that gives § 1101.652(b)(5) its reach is taught here in full. Rule 22 TAC
§ 535.145 provides that the term false promise "includes both oral and written promises." It
continues: "The fact that a written agreement between the parties to a real estate transaction does
not recite a promise made by a real estate license holder to one of the parties or that a person did
not detrimentally rely on the false promise will not prevent the Commission from determining that a
false promise was made." And it closes the last escape hatch: "In determining whether this section
has been violated, neither a written contractual provision disclaiming oral representations nor the
Texas Rules of Evidence Rule 1004, the parol evidence rule, shall prevent the Commission from
considering oral promises made by a license holder." What you said in the car on the way to the
property is evidence.

chunks.heading: Unit: Fraud versus Misrepresentation
chunks.excerpt:
**Who bears a misrepresentation, § 1101.805.** Module 03 teaches this section; subsection (e)
operates here. A license holder "is not liable for a misrepresentation or a concealment of a material
fact made by a party to a real estate transaction unless the license holder: (1) knew of the falsity
of the misrepresentation or concealment; and (2) failed to disclose the license holder's knowledge of
the falsity of the misrepresentation or concealment." Both conditions must be met, and the second is
in your hands.

**Why the DTPA swallows all of this in practice.** In the abstract those are three different lawsuits
with three different burdens; in a Texas residential transaction they collapse into one, and it is
the DTPA. First, liability does not turn on your state of mind: § 17.50(a)(1) makes a consumer's
action available where the defendant used "a false, misleading, or deceptive act or practice" that is
"specifically enumerated in a subdivision of Subsection (b) of Section 17.46 of this subchapter" and
"relied on by a consumer to the consumer's detriment," provided that act was "a producing cause of
economic damages or damages for mental anguish." Producing cause, not proximate cause; enumerated
act, not proven lie. Second, the DTPA pays the plaintiff's lawyer, in one unconditional sentence at
§ 17.50(d): "Each consumer who prevails shall be awarded court costs and reasonable and necessary
attorneys' fees." Not *may* — which is why a $9,000 repair dispute becomes a filed lawsuit. Third,
§ 17.50(b)(1) multiplies the award where the conduct was knowing or intentional. And fourth,
§ 17.44(a) directs that the subchapter "shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its
underlying purposes."

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: The two states of mind in § 17.45
chunks.excerpt:
**One place where the older causes of action still matter: time.** Civil Practice & Remedies Code
§ 16.004(a) provides that "[a] person must bring suit on the following actions not later than four
years after the day the cause of action accrues," and subdivision (4) of that list is "fraud."
Subdivision (5) is "breach of fiduciary duty." The DTPA carries its own two-year period at § 17.565,
so a claimant who sat on a claim for three years has lost the DTPA route and may still have a fraud
route. Chapter 16 does not name negligent misrepresentation anywhere in the sections read for this
course, and **which limitations period governs a negligent misrepresentation claim was not held.** Do
not guess at it, and do not advise a client about it; that is a question for their lawyer.

### Statute reading exercise: The two states of mind in § 17.45

Open Business & Commerce Code § 17.45 and read subdivisions (9) and (13) side by side, in full,
without skipping the final sentence of either.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
1. Both definitions permit a fact-finder to infer the defendant's state of mind. Write out the exact
   phrase each subdivision uses to authorise that inference, and explain what evidence a plaintiff's
   lawyer would gather to satisfy each one in a case about a license holder who advertised a house
   as having a "new roof."
2. Subdivision (13) permits intention to be inferred from a second, additional source that
   subdivision (9) does not mention. Quote that clause in full, including the words that follow
   "flagrant disregard of prudent and fair business practices." Explain, in your own words, what it
   means for a defendant to be "treated as having acted intentionally" when the defendant formed no
   plan to deceive anybody.
3. Subdivision (9) contains a time limitation on the awareness it requires. Identify it, and explain
   what it means for a license holder who genuinely did not know a fact at the time of a showing but
   learned it the following week.
4. Neither subdivision says anything about whether the consumer must prove the defendant's motive or
   profit. Confirm this by reading the text, and say why that silence matters to a defendant who
   argues "I gained nothing from the statement."
5. Read § 17.46(b)(5) and § 17.46(b)(13). One of them contains a scienter word and the other does
   not. Identify which is which and explain what a plaintiff must prove under each.

## Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection

Business & Commerce Code § 17.41 states the short title: "This subchapter may be cited as the
Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act." It runs from § 17.41 through § 17.63.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
**The interpretive instruction comes first, because it colours everything else.** Section 17.44(a)
directs that the subchapter "shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying
purposes, which are to protect consumers against false, misleading, and deceptive business
practices, unconscionable actions, and breaches of warranty and to provide efficient and economical
procedures to secure such protection." Where a court must choose between two readings, the statute
says which way to lean. Subsection (b) adds one cross-reference: "Chapter 27, Property Code, prevails
over this subchapter to the extent of any conflict." Chapter 27 is the residential construction
liability chapter. **Property Code Chapter 27 was not held for this course**, so this module states
nothing about its content; it says only that § 17.44(b) gives Chapter 27 priority, which makes a
construction-defect claim in a residence a matter for a lawyer.

**Who is a "consumer," and why you can be sued by someone who never paid you a dime.** Standing
under the DTPA runs through one definition. Section 17.45(4): "Consumer" means "an individual,
partnership, corporation, this state, or a subdivision or agency of this state who seeks or acquires
by purchase or lease, any goods or services, except that the term does not include a business
consumer that has assets of $25 million or more, or that is owned or controlled by a corporation or
entity with assets of $25 million or more."

Every clause does work.

*"Seeks or acquires."* No completed purchase is needed, so a buyer who walks away because of what you
said is still a consumer.

*"By purchase or lease."* Your leasing and property-management practice sits inside the Act.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
*"Any goods or services."* Section 17.45(1) defines "Goods" as "tangible chattels or real property
purchased or leased for use," so real property is expressly a good, and § 17.45(2) defines "Services"
as "work, labor, or service purchased or leased for use, including services furnished in connection
with the sale or repair of goods," so brokerage is a service.

*The $25 million exclusion.* A "business consumer," defined at § 17.45(10) as "an individual,
partnership, or corporation who seeks or acquires by purchase or lease, any goods or services for
commercial or business use," loses consumer status at $25 million in assets, or when "owned or
controlled by a corporation or entity with assets of $25 million or more." An asset test, not a
revenue test.

Now the point students most often miss. **Read the definition again and find the word "privity." It
is not there.** Section 17.45(4) asks who sought or acquired goods or services, not from whom, and it
does not require that the consumer bought anything from you, paid you, or had a contract with you.
That is why a buyer represented by a different brokerage, who never signed anything with you, can sue
*you*, the listing agent: the buyer sought to acquire real property, and you engaged in a practice
enumerated in § 17.46(b) that was a producing cause of the buyer's economic damages.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
**The four doors into a DTPA action.** Section 17.50(a) provides that "[a] consumer may maintain an
action where any of the following constitute a producing cause of economic damages or damages for
mental anguish," and then lists four. Subdivision (1) is the laundry-list door: "the use or
employment by any person of a false, misleading, or deceptive act or practice that is: (A)
specifically enumerated in a subdivision of Subsection (b) of Section 17.46 of this subchapter; and
(B) relied on by a consumer to the consumer's detriment." Subdivision (2) is breach of an express or
implied warranty. Subdivision (3) is "any unconscionable action or course of action by any person."
Subdivision (4) is a violation of Chapter 541 of the Insurance Code, which is not your subject.

Three features of subdivision (1) matter. It requires an act "specifically enumerated" in a
subdivision of § 17.46(b) — a general sense that you behaved badly is not enough. It requires
detrimental reliance. And it applies to the act of "any person," which § 17.45(3) defines as "an
individual, partnership, corporation, association, or other group, however organized." Section
17.46(d) locks exclusivity down from the other direction: the term false, misleading, or deceptive
acts or practices "is limited to the acts enumerated in specific subdivisions of Subsection (b) of
this section." For a private consumer suit the laundry list is a closed list.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
**The laundry list, applied to real estate.** Section 17.46(b) opens by providing that, "Except as
provided in Subsection (d) of this section," the term false, misleading, or deceptive acts or
practices "includes, but is not limited to, the following acts". Most of the thirty-four subdivisions
that follow — odometer tampering, kosher labelling, pyramid schemes — never touch your practice.
These will.

*§ 17.46(b)(5) — "representing that goods or services have sponsorship, approval, characteristics,
ingredients, uses, benefits, or quantities which they do not have or that a person has a
sponsorship, approval, status, affiliation, or connection which the person does not."* The workhorse
subdivision in Texas real estate litigation, and the one to memorise. "Characteristics" and
"quantities" are the operative words: a listing that states "2,860 sq. ft." when the measurement says
2,455, or "not in a flood zone" when the tract sits partly in a mapped floodplain. That you copied the
figure from the seller's old appraisal is no answer.

*§ 17.46(b)(7) — "representing that goods or services are of a particular standard, quality, or
grade, or that goods are of a particular style or model, if they are of another."* The listing
advertising a "new HVAC system" when only the compressor was replaced. Quality claims are checkable.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
*§ 17.46(b)(12) — "representing that an agreement confers or involves rights, remedies, or
obligations which it does not have or involve, or which are prohibited by law."* Tell a buyer that
the option period "lets you get out any time before closing," or a seller that a listing agreement
"can be cancelled by either side on a week's notice" when it cannot, and you have represented that an
agreement confers rights it does not involve — which is how careless explanations of contract forms
become a DTPA claim.

*§ 17.46(b)(13) — "knowingly making false or misleading statements of fact concerning the need for
parts, replacement, or repair service."* Note the "knowingly." A license holder who steers a seller
into an unnecessary $14,000 foundation job with a preferred contractor, knowing the statements about
the need are false, is inside this subdivision.

*§ 17.46(b)(14) — "misrepresenting the authority of a salesman, representative or agent to negotiate
the final terms of a consumer transaction."* Telling a buyer "I can accept that counter for the
seller right now" without that authority violates subdivision (14) — a distinctively agency-law
deceptive practice.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
*§ 17.46(b)(20) — "representing that a guaranty or warranty confers or involves rights or remedies
which it does not have or involve, provided, however, that nothing in this subchapter shall be
construed to expand the implied warranty of merchantability as defined in Sections 2.314 through
2.318 and Sections 2A.212 through 2A.216 to involve obligations in excess of those which are
appropriate to the goods."* "The warranty covers the whole HVAC system, so you don't need to worry
about the age" is a representation about what a residential service contract confers; if it excludes
pre-existing conditions or caps the payout, subdivision (20) is engaged.

*§ 17.46(b)(24) — "failing to disclose information concerning goods or services which was known at
the time of the transaction if such failure to disclose such information was intended to induce the
consumer into a transaction into which the consumer would not have entered had the information been
disclosed."* The silence subdivision, and the one to think about hardest: it is the only entry on the
list that makes *not speaking* actionable. Both express conditions must be met — the information must
have been "known at the time of the transaction," and the failure to disclose must have been
"intended to induce the consumer into a transaction into which the consumer would not have entered
had the information been disclosed" — so a fact you forgot, or never knew, is outside it. And
subdivision (24) is carved out of *both* statutory exemptions that would otherwise protect you.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
You list a house in Friendswood, and in the file from a prior listing sits an inspection report
noting active seepage at the north foundation wall. The seller's disclosure notice says no known
water penetration; it states the seller's knowledge and belief, so the seller's answer may be proper
as to the seller. That does not answer the question about you. If a fact-finder concludes you kept
quiet to get the deal closed, subdivision (24) is satisfied — and § 1101.652(b)(4) independently
makes that silence a disciplinary ground.

**Unconscionable action or course of action.** The second major door, § 17.50(a)(3), does not depend
on the laundry list at all. It reaches "any unconscionable action or course of action by any
person." Section 17.45(5) defines an unconscionable action or course of action as "an act or
practice which, to a consumer's detriment, takes advantage of the lack of knowledge, ability,
experience, or capacity of the consumer to a grossly unfair degree."

Every word is doing work. There must be harm — "to a consumer's detriment." The practice must "take
advantage of" one of four vulnerabilities: lack of knowledge, ability, experience or capacity. And it
must do so "to a grossly unfair degree," a bar ordinary sharp dealing does not clear. But notice what
the definition does *not* require: no false statement, no state of mind, no reliance. A course of
conduct can be unconscionable though no statement in it was false — the recently bereaved widow
persuaded to list her homestead well under market so the license holder's investor client can buy it,
with no comparative market analysis and no explanation of what a listing price means.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
**Waivers are void, with three narrow exceptions.** Section 17.42(a): "Any waiver by a consumer of
the provisions of this subchapter is contrary to public policy and is unenforceable and void;
provided, however, that a waiver is valid and enforceable if: (1) the waiver is in writing and is
signed by the consumer; (2) the consumer is not in a significantly disparate bargaining position;
and (3) the consumer is represented by legal counsel in seeking or acquiring the goods or services."
All three must be met, so a residential transaction where the buyer has no lawyer cannot produce a
valid waiver.

**The DTPA does not replace other law; it stacks on it.** Section 17.43 provides that "[t]he
provisions of this subchapter are not exclusive" and that its remedies "are in addition to any other
procedures or remedies provided for in any other law." It then draws a line students blur: "A
violation of a provision of law other than this subchapter is not in and of itself a violation of
this subchapter." Breaking a TREC rule is not automatically a DTPA violation — though the same
conduct can violate TRELA and the DTPA at once, and usually does, by two independent routes.

chunks.heading: Unit: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection
chunks.excerpt:
**The notice letter, and what you do the day it arrives.** Section 17.505(a) sets a condition
precedent: "As a prerequisite to filing a suit seeking damages under Subdivision (1) of Subsection
(b) of Section 17.50 of this subchapter against any person, a consumer shall give written notice to
the person at least 60 days before filing the suit advising the person in reasonable detail of the
consumer's specific complaint and the amount of economic damages, damages for mental anguish, and
expenses, including attorneys' fees, if any, reasonably incurred by the consumer in asserting the
claim against the defendant. During the 60-day period a written request to inspect, in a reasonable
manner and at a reasonable time and place, the goods that are the subject of the consumer's action
or claim may be presented to the consumer."

Sixty days, written, itemised. That letter starts the two clocks that matter, both running from
receipt: the sixty days in § 17.505(a) and the thirty-day tender window in § 17.506(d).

What you do the day it lands is practice, not law, and this course states no authority for it. Note
the date of receipt. Do not telephone the consumer, answer the allegations, or apologise; everything
you say now is evidence. Notify your sponsoring broker and your E&O carrier the same day, because
late notice can forfeit coverage. Preserve the whole file, alter nothing, and get the letter to
counsel within days.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The square footage in Round Rock
chunks.excerpt:
Two situations excuse the notice. Section 17.505(b): "If the giving of 60 days' written notice is
rendered impracticable by reason of the necessity of filing suit in order to prevent the expiration
of the statute of limitations or if the consumer's claim is asserted by way of counterclaim, the
notice provided for in Subsection (a) of this section is not required, but the tender provided for by
Subsection (d), Section 17.506 of this subchapter may be made within 60 days after service of the
suit or counterclaim." A consumer racing limitations, or one asserting a counterclaim, may skip the
letter — and you get sixty days from service to tender.

### Applied exercise: The square footage in Round Rock

You are the listing agent for a house in Round Rock. The seller told you the house was "about 2,900
square feet." The Williamson Central Appraisal District record shows 2,655. You entered 2,900 in the
MLS because the seller insisted. The buyers, represented by an agent from a different brokerage,
closed at $505,000, then had the house measured at 2,640 square feet. They have written to you and
to your broker.

chunks.heading: Unit: Damages
chunks.excerpt:
1. Identify by number and quote the § 17.46(b) subdivision that most directly fits the square
   footage entry, and explain which words in it the buyers will rely on. State whether that
   subdivision requires the buyers to prove you intended to mislead them.
2. The buyers never signed anything with you and paid you nothing. Using § 17.45(4), explain whether
   they are "consumers" who may sue you, and identify precisely which words of the definition give
   them standing. Then say what the definition does *not* require.
3. Under § 17.50(a)(1), name the two additional things the buyers must establish beyond the
   enumerated act itself, quoting the statutory language for each.
4. Suppose that instead of the seller's statement you had relied on a written measurement report
   from a third-party measuring service that turned out to be wrong. Read § 17.506(a)(2) and
   § 17.506(c), and state what you would have needed to do, and when, for that reliance to help you —
   and who the buyers could then sue.
5. The buyers' letter demands $22,000 and is dated the 3rd of the month; you received it on the 8th.
   Using § 17.505(a) and § 17.506(d), state the two deadlines that now exist and the date each one
   falls on if the month is March in a non-leap year.

## Unit: Damages

Much of what makes the DTPA frightening is arithmetic. The difference between an ordinary finding, a
"knowingly" finding and an "intentionally" finding is the difference between a claim your carrier
absorbs and one that ends a career.

chunks.heading: Unit: Damages
chunks.excerpt:
**Start with the base: economic damages.** Section 17.45(11) defines economic damages as
"compensatory damages for pecuniary loss, including costs of repair and replacement. The term does
not include exemplary damages or damages for physical pain and mental anguish, loss of consortium,
disfigurement, physical impairment, or loss of companionship and society." The item to notice in the
exclusive half is mental anguish: a separate category, available only as § 17.50(b)(1) allows.

**Section 17.50(b)(1) is the damages engine.** In a suit filed under the section,
"each consumer who prevails may obtain: (1) the amount of economic damages found by the trier of
fact. If the trier of fact finds that the conduct of the defendant was committed knowingly, the
consumer may also recover damages for mental anguish, as found by the trier of fact, and the trier
of fact may award not more than three times the amount of economic damages; or if the trier of fact
finds the conduct was committed intentionally, the consumer may recover damages for mental anguish,
as found by the trier of fact, and the trier of fact may award not more than three times the amount
of damages for mental anguish and economic damages".

Break that sentence into its three tiers.

*Tier one — an ordinary violation.* The consumer recovers "the amount of economic damages found by
the trier of fact." No mental anguish. No multiplier. Economic damages, full stop — plus the costs
and fees that § 17.50(d) makes mandatory.

chunks.heading: Unit: Damages
chunks.excerpt:
*Tier two — conduct committed knowingly*, as § 17.45(9) defines "knowingly." Two things unlock:
"the consumer may also recover damages for mental anguish, as found by the trier of fact," and "the
trier of fact may award not more than three times the amount of economic damages." At this tier the
multiplier's base is *economic damages only*, so mental anguish is recoverable but is not multiplied.
And "may award not more than" is a ceiling, not an automatic tripling.

*Tier three — conduct committed intentionally*, as § 17.45(13) defines "intentionally." Mental
anguish is again recoverable, and now the multiplier's base expands: "the trier of fact may award
not more than three times the amount of damages for mental anguish and economic damages." Mental
anguish joins the base. That is the entire difference between tier two and tier three, and in a case
with substantial mental anguish findings it is an enormous difference.

**Worked example one: the Round Rock square footage claim.** The buyers paid $505,000 for a house
advertised at 2,900 square feet that measures 2,640. Assume economic damages of $22,000, attorneys'
fees of $48,000 and court costs of $3,200.

At tier one, with no culpability finding, the judgment is economic damages of $22,000, plus $48,000
in fees and $3,200 in costs, for a total of **$73,200**. The fee award is nearly twice the damages.
That is not an anomaly; it is the ordinary shape of a DTPA judgment in a modest case, and it is why
these cases get filed.

chunks.heading: Unit: Damages
chunks.excerpt:
Now assume the jury also finds that you acted knowingly — you had the appraisal district record in
your file and entered 2,900 anyway. The jury finds mental anguish of $15,000. Tier two allows
economic damages of $22,000, mental anguish of $15,000, and additional damages of "not more than
three times the amount of economic damages." Three times $22,000 is $66,000. If the jury awards the
maximum, the damages total $22,000 + $15,000 + $66,000 = **$103,000**, and fees and costs of $51,200
are added on top, for **$154,200**.

Now assume instead a finding that the conduct was committed intentionally. Tier three allows
additional damages of "not more than three times the amount of damages for mental anguish and
economic damages." The base is now $22,000 + $15,000 = $37,000, and three times that is $111,000.
Maximum damages become $22,000 + $15,000 + $111,000 = **$148,000**, plus $51,200 in fees and costs,
for **$199,200**. The same false number in the same MLS field produced a $73,200 exposure, a
$154,200 exposure, or a $199,200 exposure, depending entirely on what a jury concluded about your
state of mind — and remember from Unit 1 that both § 17.45(9) and § 17.45(13) permit the jury to
infer that state of mind from objective manifestations.

**Do not include fees in the multiplier base.** Section 17.50(e) is explicit: "In computing
additional damages under Subsection (b), attorneys' fees, costs, and prejudgment interest may not be
considered." That is why the tier three base was $37,000 and not $37,000 plus $51,200. A student who
trebles the whole judgment has misread the statute.

chunks.heading: Unit: Damages
chunks.excerpt:
**Prejudgment interest.** Section 17.50(f): a court "may not award prejudgment interest applicable
to: (1) damages for future loss under this subchapter; or (2) additional damages under Subsection
(b)." Interest does not run on the multiplier.

**Attorneys' fees, in both directions.** Section 17.50(d) is unconditional for the consumer: "Each
consumer who prevails shall be awarded court costs and reasonable and necessary attorneys' fees."
But § 17.50(c) points the other way: "On a finding by the court that an action under this section
was groundless in fact or law or brought in bad faith, or brought for the purpose of harassment, the
court shall award to the defendant reasonable and necessary attorneys' fees and court costs." Also a
"shall," and it requires a finding by the court, not the jury.

**The other relief the statute authorises.** Section 17.50(b)(3) permits "orders necessary to
restore to any party to the suit any money or property, real or personal, which may have been
acquired in violation of this subchapter" — under which a commission you were paid can be ordered
returned. Section 17.50(b)(4) permits "any other relief which the court deems proper,
including the appointment of a receiver or the revocation of a license or certificate authorizing a
person to engage in business in this state if the judgment has not been satisfied within three
months of the date of the final judgment." Then the limitation: "The court
may not revoke or suspend a license to do business in this state or appoint a receiver to take over
the affairs of a person who has failed to satisfy a judgment if the person is a licensee of or
regulated by a state agency which has statutory authority to revoke or suspend a license or to
appoint a receiver or trustee." TREC holds revocation authorit

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: Computing the exposure in Mansfield
chunks.excerpt:
y over you, so the civil court will not
revoke your real estate license. TREC may still do so.

**Chapter 41 does not apply.** Section 17.50(g) states flatly: "Chapter 41, Civil Practice and
Remedies Code, does not apply to a cause of action brought under this subchapter." The general Texas
exemplary damages caps are unavailable to a DTPA defendant; the only ceiling is the one inside
§ 17.50(b)(1) itself.

**A limit on mental anguish that students miss.** Section 17.49(e): "Except as specifically provided
by Subsections (b) and (h), Section 17.50, nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a cause of
action for bodily injury or death or for the infliction of mental anguish." The DTPA is not a vehicle
for a stand-alone emotional distress claim.

### Applied exercise: Computing the exposure in Mansfield

A buyer purchases a home in Mansfield for $389,000 after the listing agent tells her, in writing,
that the home's foundation "was fully repaired in 2019 with a transferable lifetime warranty." The
repair was partial, and the warranty was never transferred. The buyer sues under § 17.50(a)(1). At
trial the jury finds economic damages of $31,500, and the court finds reasonable and necessary
attorneys' fees of $62,000 and court costs of $4,100.

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
1. Identify by number and quote the § 17.46(b) subdivision that the statement about the warranty
   most directly violates, and the separate subdivision that the statement about the repair most
   directly violates.
2. Compute the total judgment if the jury makes no culpability finding. Show economic damages, fees
   and costs separately, and cite the subsection that makes the fee award mandatory.
3. The jury instead finds the conduct was committed knowingly and finds mental anguish of $20,000.
   Compute the maximum damages the trier of fact may award under § 17.50(b)(1), showing the
   multiplier base you used and quoting the words of the statute that fix that base. Then state the
   maximum total judgment including fees and costs.
4. Now assume the jury finds the conduct was committed intentionally, with the same $20,000 mental
   anguish finding. Recompute the maximum damages, again showing the base and quoting the statutory
   words that expand it. State the dollar difference between the tier two and tier three maximums
   and explain in one sentence what factual finding produced that difference.
5. Opposing counsel argues the multiplier should be applied to the whole judgment including the
   $62,000 in fees. Cite the subsection that defeats that argument and quote it.

## Unit: Defenses

Take the defenses in the order a case unfolds: exemption, procedural prerequisite, limitations, then
the substantive defenses.

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
**The exemptions in § 17.49, beginning with the one written for you.** Section 17.49(i):
"Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a claim against a person licensed as a broker or
salesperson under Chapter 1101, Occupations Code, arising from an act or omission by the person
while acting as a broker or salesperson." Then, immediately: "This exemption does not apply to: (1)
an express misrepresentation of a material fact that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment, or
opinion; (2) a failure to disclose information in violation of Section 17.46(b)(24); or (3) an
unconscionable action or course of action that cannot be characterized as advice, judgment, or
opinion."

The general rule genuinely does exempt you. Note the wording: "broker or salesperson," the older term
TRELA has replaced with "sales agent," and the exemption is tied to an act done "while acting as"
one, so an act outside your brokerage capacity — flipping a house in your own name — is not within it
at all. The carve-outs are where every real case lives.

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
*Carve-out (1): "an express misrepresentation of a material fact that cannot be characterized as
advice, judgment, or opinion."* Four conditions in one clause: *express*, so a claim built on
implication is outside it; a *misrepresentation*, so a true statement is outside it; about a
*material fact*; and a statement that *cannot be characterized as advice, judgment, or opinion* —
which is why experienced license holders speak as they do. "In my opinion this neighbourhood has held
its value well" is opinion. "This house is 2,900 square feet" is a fact. "I think the roof looks to be
in good shape" is judgment. "The roof was replaced in 2021" is a fact. A court reads the substance,
so dressing a hard factual claim in the words "I think" will not convert it into an opinion.

*Carve-out (2): "a failure to disclose information in violation of Section 17.46(b)(24)."* Silence.
Every other subdivision must fight through carve-out (1) or (3); subdivision (24) is named by number
and walks straight through the exemption.

*Carve-out (3): "an unconscionable action or course of action that cannot be characterized as
advice, judgment, or opinion."* This is why § 17.45(5) matters so much: unconscionability requires no
false statement at all, and survives the exemption whenever the conduct cannot be recharacterised as
advice or opinion.

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
**The professional services exemption, § 17.49(c).** Alongside it sits a broader exemption for a
claim based on the rendering of a professional service "the essence of which is the providing of
advice, judgment, opinion, or similar professional skill." Its first three carve-outs match
§ 17.49(i) word for word; it adds two, for breach of an express warranty that cannot be characterised
as advice, judgment or opinion, and for a violation of § 17.46(b)(26).

**The two transaction-size exemptions, with their exact thresholds.** Section 17.49(f): "Nothing in
the subchapter shall apply to a claim arising out of a written contract if: (1) the contract relates
to a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions related to the same project involving total
consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) in negotiating the contract the consumer is
represented by legal counsel who is not directly or indirectly identified, suggested, or selected by
the defendant or an agent of the defendant; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's
residence."

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
All three conditions, joined by "and." More than $100,000 — not $100,000 or more. Section 17.45(12)
defines "Residence" as a building "(A) that is a single-family house, duplex, triplex, or quadruplex
or a unit in a multiunit residential structure in which title to the individual units is transferred
to the owners under a condominium or cooperative system; and (B) that is occupied or to be occupied
as the consumer's residence" — both the building type *and* the occupancy. A $640,000 house a family
will live in is over $100,000 but involves the consumer's residence, so condition (3) fails, and most
residential buyers have no lawyer, so condition (2) fails too. **The § 17.49(f) exemption almost
never protects a residential license holder.**

Section 17.49(g) is larger and simpler: "Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a cause of action
arising from a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions relating to the same project,
involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action
involving a consumer's residence." No written-contract or counsel requirement, but again the
residence exception: a $2.4 million industrial building sale is outside the DTPA; a $2.4 million
house the buyer will occupy is not. Commit both numbers exactly: **$100,000** at § 17.49(f),
**$500,000** at § 17.49(g).

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
**The notice prerequisite as a defensive tool, § 17.505.** What if the consumer gives no notice?
Section 17.505(c): "A person against whom a suit is pending who does not receive written notice, as
required by Subsection (a), may file a plea in abatement not later than the 30th day after the date
the person files an original answer in the court in which the suit is pending. This subsection does
not apply if Subsection (b) applies." Thirty days from your original answer — miss that window and
the tool is gone. Abatement is not dismissal, but it is real leverage and delay.

**The § 17.506(a) reliance-on-written-information defense.** This defense is aimed at what a license
holder does all day: repeating information gathered from records and other people. Section
17.506(a): "In an action brought under Section 17.50 of this subchapter, it is a
defense to the award of any damages or attorneys' fees if the defendant proves that before
consummation of the transaction he gave reasonable and timely written notice to the plaintiff of the
defendant's reliance on: (1) written information relating to the particular goods or service in
question obtained from official government records if the written information was false or
inaccurate and the defendant did not know and could not reasonably have known of the falsity or
inaccuracy of the information; (2) written information relating to the particular goods or service
in question obtained from another source if the information was false or inaccurate and the
defendant did not know and could not reasonably have known of the falsity or inaccuracy of the
information; or (3) written information concerning a test required or prescribed by a government
agency if the information from the test was false or inaccurate and the defendant did not k

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
now and
could not reasonably have known of the falsity or inaccuracy of the information."

Count the conditions, because students remember this as "I can rely on public records" and that is
not what it says. The information must have been **written**. You must have given **written notice of
your reliance before consummation of the transaction** — the condition that defeats almost every
license holder who invokes § 17.506(a) after the fact. The information must in fact have been **false
or inaccurate**. And you must prove you "did not know and could not reasonably have known" of the
falsity, an objective test as well as a subjective one.

Section 17.506(b) adds a causation requirement and a limitation on its effect: "In asserting a
defense under Subdivision (1), (2), or (3) of Subsection (a) of Section 17.506 above, the defendant
shall prove the written information was a producing cause of the alleged damage. A finding of one
producing cause does not bar recovery if other conduct of the defendant not the subject of a
defensive finding under Subdivision (1), (2), or (3) of Subsection (a) of Section 17.506 above was a
producing cause of damages of the plaintiff." The defense is claim-specific: defending the square
footage does not immunise you on the roof.

chunks.heading: Unit: Defenses
chunks.excerpt:
Section 17.506(c) opens the door to the real defendant: "In a suit where a defense is asserted
under Subdivision (2) of Subsection (a) of Section 17.506 above, suit may be asserted against the
third party supplying the written information without regard to privity where the third party knew
or should have reasonably foreseen that the information would be provided to a consumer; provided no
double recovery may result." The measuring service, the surveyor, the contractor who wrote the
report — each can be brought in, subject to the bar on double recovery.

**The § 17.506(d) tender defense — the cheapest exit in the statute.** Subsection (d) provides: "In
an action brought under Section 17.50 of this subchapter, it is a defense to a cause of action if
the defendant proves that he received notice from the consumer advising the defendant of the nature
of the consumer's specific complaint and of the amount of economic damages, damages for mental
anguish, and expenses, including attorneys' fees, if any, reasonably incurred by the consumer in
asserting the claim against the defendant, and that within 30 days after the day on which the
defendant received the notice the defendant tendered to the consumer: (1) the amount of economic
damages and damages for mental anguish claimed; and (2) the expenses, including attorneys' fees, if
any, reasonably incurred by the consumer in asserting the claim against the defendant."

Thirty days from receipt, and tender of the full amount claimed in both categories. Do that and you
have a defense to the cause of action itself: no mental anguish, no multiplier, no growing fee award
— a $22,000 demand tendered against a potential $199,200 judgment.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: The exemptions in § 17.49
chunks.excerpt:
**Limitations, § 17.565.** The section reads in full: "All actions brought under this subchapter
must be commenced within two years after the date on which the false, misleading, or deceptive act
or practice occurred or within two years after the consumer discovered or in the exercise of
reasonable diligence should have discovered the occurrence of the false, misleading, or deceptive
act or practice. The period of limitation provided in this section may be extended for a period of
180 days if the plaintiff proves that failure timely to commence the action was caused by the
defendant's knowingly engaging in conduct solely calculated to induce the plaintiff to refrain from
or postpone the commencement of the action."

Three components. The period is **two years**, running from the later of the date the act occurred or
the date the consumer "discovered or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered"
it. And there is a **180-day** extension, available only where the plaintiff proves the late filing
"was caused by the defendant's knowingly engaging in conduct solely calculated to induce the
plaintiff to refrain from or postpone the commencement of the action." Note "solely." Because
§ 16.004(a)(4) gives fraud four years, a claimant out of time under § 17.565 may still have a fraud
claim alive.

**And one defense that comes from TRELA, not the DTPA.** Occupations Code § 1101.805(e), quoted in
Unit 1, protects a license holder from a party's misrepresentation unless the license holder both knew
of the falsity and failed to disclose it. With § 17.506(a) it yields one posture: document in writing,
before consummation, the source of every fact you pass along.

### Statute reading exercise: The exemptions in § 17.49

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
Open Business & Commerce Code § 17.49 and read subsections (c), (f), (g) and (i) in full.

1. Write out subsection (i) and its three carve-outs verbatim. Then write out subsection (c) and its
   five carve-outs. Identify precisely which carve-outs appear in one subsection and not the other,
   and suggest why the Legislature might have given the broker exemption a shorter list.
2. Subsection (f) has three numbered conditions. State the exact dollar figure in condition (1) and
   say whether a transaction at exactly that figure qualifies. Then explain, using § 17.45(12), why
   condition (3) removes nearly every residential sale from the exemption's reach.
3. Subsection (g) states a different dollar figure with a different structure. State the figure
   exactly, identify the single exception written into the subsection, and explain how a $900,000
   commercial land sale and a $900,000 owner-occupied house are treated differently under it.
4. Neither subsection (f) nor subsection (g) says anything about the defendant's state of mind, and
   neither says anything about whether the consumer was harmed. Confirm this from the text and
   explain what kind of defense that makes them — one that defeats the claim, or one that reduces
   the damages.
5. Section 17.49(i) exempts a claim "arising from an act or omission by the person while acting as a
   broker or salesperson." Identify at least two activities a Texas license holder might undertake
   that would fall outside those words, and explain the consequence.

## Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
The first four units concerned money moving from you to a consumer through a courthouse. This unit
concerns the two tracks alongside it: the administrative track, where TREC can take the license, and
the fund the Legislature created for the consumer whose judgment cannot be collected.

**Two proceedings, two standards, one set of facts.** A DTPA judgment does not revoke your license:
§ 17.50(b)(4), under Damages above, bars a civil court from revoking the license of a judgment debtor
regulated by an agency that holds revocation authority, and TREC holds it. The civil court takes
money and TREC takes licenses, each on its own record. Settling a DTPA claim quietly for $18,000
resolves nothing with the Commission; a license holder whom TREC declines to discipline is not
thereby cleared in a civil suit.

**The disciplinary grounds that track DTPA exposure.** Occupations Code § 1101.652 is taught in
Module 10; what belongs here is the overlap. The grounds named in Unit 1 — (b)(1) negligence or
incompetence, (b)(3) and (b)(4) on known material defects, (b)(5) the false promise, (b)(6) a
continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation — reach the same conduct the DTPA reaches, on an
administrative record, with no consumer, no reliance and no dollar of loss required. Section
1101.652(b)(23) goes further, reaching an advertisement that "tends to create a misleading
impression."

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
One ground adopts the DTPA outright. Section 1101.652(b)(15) reaches a license holder who "solicits,
sells, or offers for sale real property by means of a deceptive practice," and the last sentence of
22 TAC § 535.149 supplies its content: deceptive practices "include, but are not limited to the acts
described in the Texas Business and Commerce Code §17.46, done in a manner defined in that section."
So a § 17.46(b)(5) misrepresentation about square footage is also, by rule, a "deceptive practice"
the Commission may suspend or revoke for. The two tracks are not merely parallel — they share their
definitions.

The same rule carries a second ground that catches licence holders through their marketing. Section
1101.652(b)(14) reaches a licence holder who conducts a lottery, and the first paragraph of 22 TAC
§ 535.149 supplies the elements: "the award or distribution of a prize or prizes by chance and the
payment of consideration for the opportunity to win the prize." Both elements are required, which is
why the rule's second paragraph can say that "[t]he giving of gifts as an inducement for prospective
clients does not violate this section or §1101.652(b)(14) of the Act" — a gift asks no consideration,
so there is nothing to win. The proviso that follows is the part to remember: licence holders "when
procuring prospects must otherwise comply with the provisions of §535.20 of this title," the referral
rule Module 09 teaches. A drawing that asks entrants to pay anything, or to buy anything, supplies the
consideration the definition wants and turns a marketing idea into a disciplinary ground.

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
**The rule that states the ethical duty directly.** Rule 22 TAC § 535.156, which Module 02 teaches,
resolves most DTPA questions before they become questions: "A license holder has a duty to convey
accurate information to members of the public with whom the license holder deals." Not to clients. To
members of the public. The buyer across the table, owed by you no fiduciary duty, is still owed
accurate information — § 17.45(4)'s privity-free consumer in another regulatory language.

**The Real Estate Recovery Trust Account: the consumer's backstop.** Suppose the consumer wins and
the license holder has nothing. Section 1101.601(a) provides
that "[t]he commission shall maintain a real estate recovery trust account to reimburse aggrieved
persons who suffer actual damages caused by an act described by Section 1101.602 committed by: (1) a
license holder; (2) a certificate holder; or (3) a person who does not hold a license or certificate
and who is an employee or agent of a license or certificate holder." Subsection (b) adds the timing
requirement: "The license or certificate holder must have held the license or certificate at the time
the act was committed."

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
Section 1101.602 defines the qualifying conduct: "An aggrieved person is entitled to reimbursement
from the trust account if a person described by Section 1101.601 engages in conduct that requires a
license or certificate of registration under this chapter and is described by Section
1101.652(a-1)(1) or (b), if the person is a license holder, or Section 1101.653(1), (2), (3), or
(4), if the person is a certificate holder." For a license holder that means § 1101.652(a-1)(1) — a
transaction in the holder's own name or a close relative's — or *any* ground in § 1101.652(b),
including negligence and incompetence at (b)(1).

**The deadline, and the order of events.** Section 1101.605(a): "An action for a judgment that may
result in an order for payment from the trust account may not be brought after the second anniversary
of the date the cause of action accrues." The account is not a first resort: § 1101.606(a) requires a
court judgment first and then, "after final judgment is entered, execution returned nulla bona, and a
judgment lien perfected, file a verified claim in the court that entered the judgment." *Nulla bona*
is the sheriff's return meaning no property was found to seize. And § 1101.607(2)(B) bars a license
holder seeking a commission in the transaction concerned: the fund is a consumer remedy, not a
fee-collection device.

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
**The caps, exactly.** Section 1101.610(a): "Payments from the trust account for claims,
including attorney's fees, interest, and court costs, arising out of a single transaction may not
exceed a total of $125,000, regardless of the number of claimants." Section 1101.610(b): "Payments
from the trust account for claims based on judgments against a single license or certificate holder
may not exceed a total of $250,000 until the license or certificate holder has reimbursed the trust
account for all amounts paid."

**$125,000 per transaction, regardless of the number of claimants. $250,000 per license holder**,
the second lifting only on full reimbursement. Both are inclusive of attorney's fees, interest and
court costs — the $125,000 is not damages plus fees, it is everything. Section
1101.610(c): "If the court finds that the total amount of claims against a license or certificate
holder exceeds the limitations in this section, the court shall proportionately reduce the amount
payable on each claim." And § 1101.610(e): "For purposes of this section, a business entity and the
broker who is the business entity's designated broker are considered a single license holder."

Return to the Round Rock arithmetic. A maximum tier-three judgment there came to $199,200. On a
single transaction, against a judgment-proof license holder, the trust account would pay at most
$125,000 of it, inclusive of fees and costs, leaving the consumer $74,200 short. The fund is a
backstop, not insurance.

chunks.heading: Unit: Ethical and Legal Concerns
chunks.excerpt:
**What happens to you afterwards.** Section 1101.612(a): "The commission is subrogated to all rights
of a judgment creditor to the extent of an amount paid from the trust account, and the judgment
creditor shall assign to the commission all right, title, and interest in the judgment up to that
amount." The debt does not disappear; it changes creditors, and the new creditor licenses you.
Section 1101.655(a) then makes the consequence automatic: the Commission "shall revoke a license,
approval, or registration" if it "makes a payment from the real estate recovery trust account under
Subchapter M on behalf of a license or registration holder" and the holder "does not repay the real
estate recovery trust account the full amount of a payment made on the license or registration
holder's behalf before the 31st day after the date the commission provides notice to the license or
registration holder." Thirty-one days. Section 1101.655(c): "A person is not eligible for a license
or certificate until the person has repaid in full the amount paid from the account for the person,
plus interest at the legal rate." Section 1101.655(d) applies the same machinery to "both the
business entity and designated broker."

Repaying the account does not settle the other track. Section 1101.613: "This subchapter does not
limit the commission's authority to take disciplinary action against a license or certificate holder
for a violation of this chapter or a commission rule," and "[a] license or certificate holder's
repayment of all amounts owed to the trust account does not affect another disciplinary proceeding
brought under this chapter."

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
One duty falls on you directly: § 1101.615(a) requires the Commission by rule to "prescribe a notice
regarding the availability of payment from the trust account for aggrieved persons and establish
methods by which each license and certificate holder shall provide the notice to consumers and
service recipients."

**The ethical proposition, stated plainly.** Neither track requires dishonesty before it bites, so
the practical ethic is not "do not lie." It is narrower and harder: **say only what you know, say
where you learned it, and correct it in writing the moment you learn it is wrong.** Every defense in
this module rewards that habit — § 17.506(a)'s written notice of reliance before consummation,
§ 1101.805(e)'s protection that fails only when you knew of a falsity and stayed silent, and the
§ 17.49(i) exemption that dies on express misrepresentations of material fact.

### Module recap

This module began with three words that students arrive confusing — fraud, misrepresentation,
deception — and ended with a fund the Legislature maintains because some license holders cause
damage they cannot pay for. The line running through it is a single proposition: in Texas, the legal
risk of what you say about a property is not calibrated to how honest you were. It is calibrated to
whether the statement was accurate, and your honesty enters the case only later, when the jury
decides what to multiply. Understand that inversion and the rest of the module follows.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The common-law elements of fraud, of negligent misrepresentation, and of innocent misrepresentation
come from judicial opinions, and no judicial opinion was held for this course, so those element
lists were not held and were not taught. What was held is the statutory ladder that replaces them in
practice. Business & Commerce Code § 17.45(9) defines "knowingly" as "actual awareness, at the time
of the act or practice complained of," of the falsity, deception, or unfairness — with the closing
clause that "actual awareness may be inferred where objective manifestations indicate that a person
acted with actual awareness." Section 17.45(13) defines "intentionally" as actual awareness "coupled
with the specific intent that the consumer act in detrimental reliance," and then adds that
intention may be inferred "from facts showing that a defendant acted with flagrant disregard of
prudent and fair business practices to the extent that the defendant should be treated as having
acted intentionally." That final clause is the whole point of the definition; drop it and you have
taught yourself the opposite of Texas law. Alongside those sit the Occupations Code's own grades of
fault: § 1101.652(b)(1) for negligence and incompetence, § 1101.652(b)(3) and (b)(4) for known
material defects spoken and unspoken, § 1101.652(b)(5) for a false promise made when the license
holder "is unable or does not intend to keep the promise," and 22 TAC § 535.145, which tells you
that oral promises count, that a merger clause and the parol evidence rule will not exclude them,
and that the Commission needs no proof of detrimental reliance.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The DTPA — Business & Commerce Code §§ 17.41 through 17.63, "the Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer
Protection Act" — is what a Texas consumer actually files. Section 17.44(a) tells courts to construe
it liberally. Section 17.45(4) defines "consumer" without any word about privity, excluding only a
business consumer with assets of $25 million or more or owned or controlled by an entity with assets
of $25 million or more, and § 17.45(1) makes real property a "good." Section 17.50(a) opens four
doors, of which two matter to you: subdivision (1), requiring an act "specifically enumerated in a
subdivision of Subsection (b) of Section 17.46" and "relied on by a consumer to the consumer's
detriment," and subdivision (3), "any unconscionable action or course of action by any person,"
defined at § 17.45(5) as conduct that "takes advantage of the lack of knowledge, ability,
experience, or capacity of the consumer to a grossly unfair degree." Section 17.46(d) makes the
laundry list a closed list for private suits. Within it, the subdivisions that bite in real estate
are (5) on characteristics and quantities, (7) on standard, quality and grade, (12) on the rights an
agreement confers, (13) on the need for repairs, (14) on misrepresenting an agent's authority to
negotiate final terms, (20) on warranties, and above all (24) on failing to disclose known
information where the silence "was intended to induce the consumer into a transaction into which the
consumer would not have entered had the information been disclosed."

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The numbers are the part you must carry exactly. Damages run from § 17.45(11)'s definition of
economic damages, which expressly excludes mental anguish. Section 17.50(b)(1) then sets three
tiers: economic damages alone; economic damages plus mental anguish plus "not more than three times
the amount of economic damages" where the conduct was committed knowingly; and economic damages plus
mental anguish plus "not more than three times the amount of damages for mental anguish and economic
damages" where it was committed intentionally. On $22,000 in economic damages and $15,000 in mental
anguish, that is a maximum of $22,000, then $103,000, then $148,000 in damages before fees — and
§ 17.50(d) makes "court costs and reasonable and necessary attorneys' fees" mandatory for a prevailing
consumer, while § 17.50(e) keeps fees, costs and prejudgment interest out of the multiplier base and
§ 17.50(g) removes the Chapter 41 caps entirely. Section 17.505(a) requires sixty days' written
notice as a prerequisite, and § 17.506(d) gives you thirty days from receipt of that notice to tender
the full amount claimed plus the consumer's reasonable fees and thereby obtain "a defense to a cause
of action".

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
The defenses have exact contours. Section 17.49(i) exempts a claim against a Chapter 1101 license
holder arising from an act or omission "while acting as a broker or salesperson," except for an
express misrepresentation of material fact that cannot be characterised as advice, judgment or
opinion, a § 17.46(b)(24) failure to disclose, and an unconscionable action or course of action that
cannot be so characterised. Section 17.49(c) does the same for professional services with five
carve-outs rather than three. Section 17.49(f) exempts written-contract claims where consideration
exceeds **$100,000**, the consumer was represented by independently chosen counsel, and the contract
"does not involve the consumer's residence" as § 17.45(12) defines that term; § 17.49(g) exempts
transactions of more than **$500,000** other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence.
Both are commercial exemptions and neither ordinarily saves a residential license holder. Section
17.506(a) gives a defense based on written information from official government records or another
source or a required test, but only where you gave "reasonable and timely written notice to the
plaintiff of the defendant's reliance" *before consummation of the transaction* and did not know and
could not reasonably have known of the falsity — and § 17.506(c) then lets the consumer sue the
information's source "without regard to privity." Section 17.505(c) supplies the plea in abatement,
filed within thirty days of your original answer. Section 17.565 gives two years, running from the
act or from when the consumer "discovered or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have
discovered" it, extendable by 180 days only on proof of conduct "solely calculated" to induce delay —
against a backdrop in which

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.004(a)(4) gives fraud four years.
Waivers are void under § 17.42 unless all three of its conditions are met.

The ethical track runs in parallel and shares the DTPA's definitions. Occupations Code
§ 1101.652(b)(15) makes it a ground to solicit, sell, or offer real property "by means of a deceptive
practice," and 22 TAC § 535.149 defines deceptive practices to "include, but are not limited to the
acts described in the Texas Business and Commerce Code §17.46, done in a manner defined in that
section." Section 1101.652(b)(23) reaches an advertisement that merely "tends to create a misleading
impression," with no consumer, no reliance and no loss required. Rule 22 TAC § 535.156 states the
affirmative duty in one sentence you should be able to recite: "A license holder has a duty to
convey accurate information to members of the public with whom the license holder deals."

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Behind all of it stands the Real Estate Recovery Trust Account. Section 1101.601 requires the
Commission to maintain it; § 1101.602 makes the qualifying conduct any ground under
§ 1101.652(a-1)(1) or (b); § 1101.605(a) bars an action for a qualifying judgment "after the second
anniversary of the date the cause of action accrues"; § 1101.606 requires a final judgment,
execution returned nulla bona, a perfected lien and a verified claim; and § 1101.607 bars a license
holder seeking a commission from the same transaction. The caps are **$125,000** for claims "arising
out of a single transaction ... regardless of the number of claimants," inclusive of attorney's
fees, interest and court costs, and **$250,000** for claims based on judgments against a single
license holder until that holder reimburses the account — with a business entity and its designated
broker treated as one license holder. Section 1101.612 subrogates the Commission to the judgment,
and § 1101.655 requires revocation if the license holder does not repay in full before the
thirty-first day after notice, with no new license until repayment "plus interest at the legal rate."

Two things were looked for and not found in the sources held for this course, and you should know
both. Property Code Chapter 27, which § 17.44(b) says "prevails over this subchapter to the extent
of any conflict," was not held, so this module states nothing about its content. And the limitations
period governing a negligent misrepresentation claim was not held; Chapter 16 names fraud expressly
at § 16.004(a)(4) but does not name negligent misrepresentation in any section read here. Where you
need either answer in practice, the answer comes from a lawyer, not from a course.

chunks.heading: Optional reference: The trust-account claim, worked end to end
chunks.excerpt:
## Optional reference: The trust-account claim, worked end to end

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it. It is here because a license holder may one day want
the practice, not because the course requires you to read it. Skip it and you have missed nothing
that the module, its exercises or its assessments depend on.

The practice below is optional and ungraded. It uses a fact pattern the two required exercises do not
— an insolvent judgment debtor, a second competing claimant, the statutory caps applied to an actual
judgment, and the subrogation and revocation that follow a payment. Every provision it relies on is
taught in the required prose of Unit 5, so nothing here is new law; it is only a chance to work the
trust-account arithmetic through by hand.

**Optional practice: the unpaid judgment in Waco.**

A buyer obtains a final judgment of $164,000 against a sales agent arising from a single transaction
