**The other considerations.** 22 TAC § 535.144 — the module's own rule and the one nobody else
teaches — requires written disclosure that you are a licensed broker or sales agent acting for your
own account, extends that to a spouse, parent or child, a business entity in which you are more than
a ten percent owner and certain trusts, and forbids using your expertise to the disadvantage of the
person you deal with. Compensation is confined by § 1101.651 and routed through the sponsoring
broker (Module 09); referrals for valuable consideration over fifty dollars require a licence under
22 TAC § 535.20 (Module 09); settlement-service referral fees are barred by 22 TAC § 535.148 (Module
05). Team, alternate and assumed names are registered before use under 22 TAC § 535.154, and the
office and contact-information duties are § 1101.552 and 22 TAC § 535.21 — again this module's.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
**Risk management.** Complaints must be signed and written, cannot be anonymous, and cannot reach
back beyond four years (§ 1101.204); they are triaged by 22 TAC § 535.141; a complaint against a
sales agent reaches the sponsoring broker; penalties, tiers and the disciplinary catalogue of
§ 1101.652 are Module 10's; the Recovery Trust Account and the DTPA are Module 11's; the allocation
of misrepresentation liability in § 1101.805 is Module 03's. What is yours is the day it happens:
tell your broker, correct the record in writing to everyone who relied on it, use the notice rules
that already exist if money is involved, add to the file and never subtract, answer the Commission,
and do not offer the injured person a legal conclusion about your own mistake.

**Where each topic lives.** Carry the course out as a map, not as twelve piles of citations. *Agency
Concepts* (Module 01) gives you the vocabulary of the Act and who needs a licence. *Basic Agency
Relationships, Disclosure and Duties to the Client* (Module 02) gives you the fiduciary Canons, the
timely-response and offer-conveyance rules, and the IABS. *Duties and Disclosures to Third Parties*
(Module 03) gives you the lesser but real duty of honesty to everyone, the seller's disclosure
notice, and the misrepresentation-liability allocation. *Seller Agency* (Module 04) gives you the
listing rules, the writing requirements behind your fee, and the CMA obligation. *Buyer Agency*
(Module 05) gives you the 2026 sections on written agreements and non-representation showings.
*Representing More Than One Party: Intermediary Brokerage* (Module 06) gives you the Texas answer to
conflict. *Creation and Termination of Agency* (Module 07) fixes when the relationship begins and
ends and what survives it. *Clarifying Agency Relatio

chunks.heading: Optional reference: A buyer-side sequence drill
chunks.excerpt:
nships* (Module 08) covers the consumer
information notice and brokerage disclosure policy. *Employment Issues* (Module 09) places you under
a sponsoring broker and sets the record, supervision and compensation rules. *Agency, Ethics and the
Law* (Module 10) supplies the standards, the disciplinary catalogue and the penalty scheme.
*Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act* (Module 11) supplies the consumer's own
weapon and the Recovery Trust Account. And this topic, *Implementation and Presentation*, is where
all of it becomes Tuesday morning.

If you retain nothing else from this module, retain the rules it owns, because they are the ones no
other module will teach you: 22 TAC § 535.17 for the price-opinion sentence you must reproduce
verbatim; 22 TAC §§ 535.154 and 535.155 for how you may present yourself and your team; 22 TAC
§ 537.11 for the practice-of-law line; 22 TAC § 535.144 for acting on your own account; § 1101.555
with § 1101.806(d) for the title advisory and the fee you forfeit without it; and § 1101.552 with 22
TAC § 535.21 for the office and the addresses at which the Commission will find you. For everything
else, retain the sequence and the module that holds the rule.

## Optional reference: A buyer-side sequence drill

This section is **optional**. Nothing in it is required to complete this topic, and no quiz,
scenario or examination item is drawn from it. You may skip it entirely; it is not required for
completion, and no later instruction depends on it. It is here because the 2026 buyer-side sequence
is the newest law in this course and the one most often got wrong in the first hour of a Saturday,
and a second run at it — on facts no required exercise in this module uses — is worth having if you
want the practice.

chunks.heading: Optional practice: A Saturday in Cedar Park
chunks.excerpt:
#### Optional practice: A Saturday in Cedar Park

At 9:40 on a Saturday morning a stranger calls your cell. She saw your sign at 2203 Silverstone
Drive in Cedar Park, a single-family house you have listed for the seller at 419,000 dollars. She
asks to see it at 11:00. She is not represented. At 11:00 she asks you three questions: how big is
the house, is 419,000 a fair price, and would the seller take 400,000.

1. Before you open the door, what must you deliver and what must you sign? Cite § 1101.558(b), §
1101.563(b) and, if you were not the listing agent, § 1101.558(b-1) and 22 TAC § 531.20, and say
which apply on these facts and which do not. 2. She does not want a representation agreement. May
you show the house under a showing-only agreement? State the two limits § 1101.563(e) places on such
an agreement. 3. Answer each of her three questions consistently with § 1101.562(c) and §
1101.562(a)(3). Which may you answer, which may you not, and what exactly does subsection (c) permit
you to do? 4. She decides to write an offer. You are the listing agent and your broker also intends
to represent her. State what § 1101.561(b) requires of the broker and what § 1101.559(a) requires
the written consent to contain. 5. She signs the offer at 4:15 that afternoon. State the written
advisory § 1101.555 requires, and state the consequence under § 1101.806(d) if you never give it.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 01

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 01

## Course Day 1 · Hours 1–4 · The market, the product, and what is being sold

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(1) Economy and social impact of real estate ·
(2) Real estate market and analysis · (3) Property rights
**Class hours:** 4 (a class hour is 50 minutes of instruction; 200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Separate the three words *land*, *real estate*, and *real property*, and say what each adds.
- Explain why the physical characteristics of land produce local markets, and predict what a
  demand shock does to price and vacancy when supply cannot move in the short run.
- Describe the four phases of a real estate cycle and identify which phase a set of indicators
  describes.
- Define a market area, select comparable properties, and state in plain words what a comparative
  market analysis is not.
- Apply a fixture test to a disputed item and explain which of the three factors decides it.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 01 — The real estate profession and its economic role
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | The real estate profession and its economic role | 1 | Section recorded as completed; engagement check answered |
| 2 | Supply, demand, and real estate cycles | 1 | Section recorded as completed; engagement check answered |
| 3 | Market data and comparative analysis | 1 | Section recorded as completed; engagement check answered |
| 4 | Real property, personal property, and fixtures | 1 | Section recorded as completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 5 |

---

## Hour 01 — The real estate profession and its economic role

## 1.1 Three words that are not synonyms

Almost every misunderstanding in the first week of a real estate course comes from treating three
words as interchangeable. They are not.

**Land** is the surface of the earth, the space above it, and the ground beneath it, to the extent
the law recognises rights in each. The classical formulation is that land runs from the centre of
the earth to the heavens; the modern formulation is narrower, because aviation law and mineral law
each cut into it. What matters at this stage is that land is a *physical* thing with a vertical
dimension, not a flat shape on a map.

**Real estate** is land plus everything permanently attached to it by nature or by people. A
stand of timber, a building, a well, a driveway, a fence — attach them and they stop being
separate objects and become part of the real estate. Detach them and they become something else
again. Hour 4 is entirely about the moment of attachment and detachment, because that is where
money is lost.

chunks.heading: 1.2 Why land behaves unlike other goods
chunks.excerpt:
**Real property** is real estate plus the legal interests a person may hold in it. This is the
concept the rest of the course actually operates on. When a licensee lists "a house", what is
being marketed is not the bricks; it is a set of legal rights in the bricks — the right to
possess, to use, to exclude others, to encumber, to transfer, and to do nothing at all. Those
rights can be divided among several people, limited by neighbours, limited by government, and
sold separately from one another.

The traditional shorthand for the set is the **bundle of rights**. It is a teaching image rather
than a legal doctrine, but it is a good one, because it makes visible the fact that a seller can
convey some sticks and keep others. A seller who conveys the surface and reserves the minerals has
sold real property and kept real property.

## 1.2 Why land behaves unlike other goods

Four physical characteristics explain most of what follows in the next 59 hours.

**Immobility.** A parcel cannot be moved. If demand rises in Richmond it cannot be met by shipping
in surplus houses from Roanoke. This single fact is why real estate markets are local, why
location dominates value, and why national statistics are close to useless for advising an
individual seller.

**Indestructibility, or more accurately durability.** The land itself survives. Improvements decay,
but slowly, and they are expensive to remove. The consequence is that the stock of housing in any
market at any moment is overwhelmingly made up of buildings built in the past, under past codes,
for past tastes.

chunks.heading: 1.3 The sectors and where a salesperson sits
chunks.excerpt:
**Uniqueness, sometimes called heterogeneity or non-homogeneity.** No two parcels occupy the same
space. Two identical houses on the same street are still not the same property, because one is
closer to the corner. This is why real estate cannot be traded like a commodity, why every
valuation is an estimate rather than a lookup, and why the doctrine of specific performance
applies to land contracts in a way it does not to contracts for ordinary goods.

**Scarcity.** Not "there is no land left" — there is a great deal — but that land in a particular
useful location is finite.

To these the economics texts add three economic characteristics: **improvements** change value in
ways that ripple to neighbours; **permanence of investment** means capital sunk into land
(sewers, roads, foundations) is not recoverable; and **area preference**, or situs, is the
observed human preference for a particular location, which is what people actually pay for.

## 1.3 The sectors and where a salesperson sits

Real estate as an industry is not one occupation. A student should be able to name the sectors
because a large part of a licensee's working life is knowing whom to hand a question to.

**Brokerage** connects the parties to a transaction. It is the sector this licence regulates.
**Lending** supplies capital and is regulated separately, largely federally. **Appraisal**
develops supported opinions of value and in Virginia is a separately licensed profession under a
different board. **Title and settlement** examine and insure title and conduct closings.
**Property management** operates income property. **Development and construction** create new
supply. **Land use planning** determines what may be built and where, through local government.

chunks.heading: 1.4 What licensure is actually for
chunks.excerpt:
A Virginia salesperson works inside brokerage and, critically, does not work alone. The licence
is not a licence to practise independently. Every salesperson is affiliated with a firm and
supervised by a supervising broker whose duties are set out at § 54.1-2110.1 of the Code of
Virginia. Hour 23 covers the structure in detail; the point to carry from Hour 1 is that a
salesperson's authority is derived, not original.

The other point to carry is the boundary of competence. The licence permits a person to provide
real estate brokerage services. It does not make that person a lawyer, an inspector, a surveyor,
an appraiser, a lender, or an accountant. A great deal of licensee discipline in every state
consists of people who forgot that.

## 1.4 What licensure is actually for

Licensing is a consumer-protection mechanism. Its logic is that a transaction which is infrequent,
expensive, legally complex, and information-asymmetric is a transaction in which an unqualified or
dishonest intermediary can do very great harm. Setting a minimum standard of competence and a
published standard of conduct, and attaching a disciplinary process to both, reduces that harm.

Notice what licensure does not do. It does not guarantee that any given licensee is good at the
job. It does not guarantee an investment result. It does not make the licensee an insurer of the
property's condition. And it does not displace the buyer's own responsibility to investigate —
which, as Hour 19 will show, Virginia takes further than most states.

### Hour 01 engagement check

**Question.** A seller conveys the surface of a parcel and expressly reserves the mineral rights.
Has the seller conveyed real estate, real property, or neither? Explain.

chunks.heading: Hour 02 — Supply, demand, and real estate cycles
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** Real property. The seller conveyed land and its improvements — real estate —
together with a defined subset of the legal interests in it, which is what makes the conveyance a
conveyance of real property. The reserved mineral rights are themselves real property that the
seller has retained. The bundle-of-rights image is the point: rights are separable, and separating
them does not turn either share into personal property.

---

## Hour 02 — Supply, demand, and real estate cycles

## 2.1 Demand, supply, and the lag that makes real estate different

In an ordinary market, a rise in demand raises price, the higher price draws out more supply, and
the price settles back. Real estate does the first two steps very slowly on the supply side.

**Demand** for housing in a market is driven by population and household formation, employment and
wages, the cost and availability of credit, expectations about future prices, and the price and
quality of substitutes such as rentals. A change in any of them shows up in the market within
weeks.

**Supply** is the existing stock plus whatever new construction can deliver. New construction
requires land assembly, entitlement, financing, permitting, and building. In most Virginia
localities that is a matter of years, not weeks. Meanwhile the existing stock changes only at the
margin, as owners decide whether to list.

chunks.heading: 2.2 The four phases
chunks.excerpt:
The consequence is the single most useful prediction in residential real estate: **in the short
run, supply is close to fixed, so a demand increase shows up almost entirely as price.** Days on
market fall, inventory falls, list-to-sale price ratios rise, and multiple-offer situations
appear. It is only later — sometimes years later — that new supply arrives, and by then demand may
have moved again. That mismatch is not a market failure. It is the structural reason real estate
cycles.

The same logic runs in reverse. When demand falls, supply cannot be withdrawn quickly. Sellers who
must sell still sell; builders finish what they started. Price falls further than an
instantaneous-adjustment model would predict, and vacancy rises.

## 2.2 The four phases

The conventional description of the cycle has four phases. They are descriptive, not predictive:
knowing the names does not tell anyone when the next turn comes.

**Expansion.** Demand is growing faster than supply. Vacancy falls below its long-run average,
rents and prices rise, days on market shorten, and construction begins to respond.

**Peak, then contraction — often called oversupply.** New construction started during expansion
completes. Supply catches up with, and then exceeds, demand. Vacancy rises, price growth
decelerates and then stops, concessions appear, and days on market lengthen.

**Recession.** Demand is below supply. Vacancy is above the long-run average, rents and prices
fall, construction stops, and distressed sales enter the market.

**Recovery.** Demand begins to absorb the surplus. Vacancy falls back toward its average, but
prices lag, because sellers and lenders remain cautious. Construction has not yet resumed.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Reading the indicators
chunks.excerpt:
The most common student error is to equate the cycle with interest rates. Rates are one input to
demand, not the cycle itself. Local employment is usually a stronger driver.

## 2.3 Reading the indicators

A licensee is expected to be able to look at a handful of local numbers and describe the market
honestly. The core set:

**Months of inventory** — active listings divided by the average monthly closed sales. It answers
"how long would it take to sell everything now on the market at the current pace?" A low figure
describes a seller's market and a high figure a buyer's market. The commonly quoted balance point
of around six months is a rule of thumb from national data, not a law of nature, and it varies by
market and price band.

**Absorption rate** — the pace at which available units are taken up, expressed in units per
period. Months of inventory is its reciprocal, scaled.

**Days on market** — median rather than mean, because a few very stale listings distort a mean
badly.

**List-to-sale price ratio** — closed price divided by the last list price, which measures
negotiating strength.

**Vacancy rate** — for rental property, the share of units unoccupied.

**New listings versus closed sales** — the flow into and out of inventory, which turns before the
stock does.

## 2.4 Honesty about what these numbers can do

Two constraints belong in the same hour as the indicators.

chunks.heading: Hour 02 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
First, **market statistics are historical**. Closed sales report decisions made 30 to 60 days
earlier. Nothing in the data set describes the future, and a licensee who presents an extrapolation
as a forecast is making a representation that may prove false. Under § 54.1-2131 A 4 the duty is
to exercise **ordinary care**; under 18VAC135-20-300 misrepresentation is a disciplinary matter.
The safe and accurate formulation is what the evidence shows, not what it predicts.

Second, **aggregates hide the property**. A median sale price for a county describes a mix of
properties, and a change in the median can be entirely a change in the mix. If more large houses
sold this quarter, the median rose without any individual property becoming more valuable.

### Hour 02 engagement check

**Question.** A large employer announces 3,000 new jobs in a locality where residential
construction takes about two years from entitlement to occupancy. Describe what happens to price
and to vacancy over the first six months, and explain why.

**Expected answer.** Demand rises quickly; supply is effectively fixed over six months, because
neither the existing stock nor new construction can respond in that time. Prices rise and vacancy
falls, and the adjustment is almost entirely in price rather than quantity. Days on market shorten
and the list-to-sale ratio rises. New supply arrives only after the construction lag, by which
time the price signal has already been given — which is the mechanism that produces the cycle.

---

## Hour 03 — Market data and comparative analysis

## 3.1 Defining the market area

chunks.heading: 3.2 Comparability
chunks.excerpt:
Before any comparison is possible, the analyst has to say what market the property is in. A market
area is the geographic area within which properties compete for the same buyers. It is bounded by
whatever actually changes buyer behaviour: school attendance zones, a river with few crossings,
an interstate, a jurisdictional line that changes the tax rate, the edge of a subdivision with its
own association.

The boundary is an evidentiary question, not an administrative one. A ZIP code is not a market
area; it is a mail-delivery convenience that frequently spans two school zones and two price
bands. A licensee who defines a market area by ZIP code because that is what the software offers
is starting the analysis with an error.

## 3.2 Comparability

A comparable property is one a buyer would have seriously considered instead of the subject. The
usual dimensions:

**Location** within the market area. **Physical characteristics** — living area, lot size, bedroom
and bath count, age, condition, garage, and functional layout. **Time** — how recently it sold,
because a sale from a different phase of the cycle describes a different market. **Terms of
sale** — cash, conventional, seller concessions, and whether the price reflects them. **Conditions
of sale** — an arm's-length transaction between unrelated parties acting without unusual pressure,
as distinct from a sale between family members, an estate sale, a foreclosure, or a relocation
company sale.

chunks.heading: 3.3 What a comparative market analysis is, and what it is not
chunks.excerpt:
**Closed sales are evidence. Active listings are not.** An active listing shows what a seller
hopes for; it is an offer to the market that has not been accepted. Pending sales are better
evidence than actives because a price has been agreed, but the price is usually not yet public and
the sale may not close. Expired and withdrawn listings are useful in a specific way: they show
prices the market **refused**, which brackets the top of the range.

## 3.3 What a comparative market analysis is, and what it is not

A comparative market analysis is a licensee's presentation of market evidence to help a client set
a list price or an offer price. It is a legitimate and expected part of brokerage.

It is **not an appraisal**. An appraisal is an opinion of value developed by a licensed or
certified appraiser under a professional standard, for an intended user and an intended use, with
a scope of work the appraiser must document. Virginia regulates appraisers under a separate board.
A licensee who presents a CMA as an appraisal, or who prepares something styled as an appraisal
for a lender, is on the wrong side of a line that exists for good reasons.

It is also **not an automated valuation**. An automated valuation model applies a statistical
model to recorded characteristics. It cannot see condition, it usually cannot see a renovation
that did not go through permitting, and it does not know that the subject backs onto a rail line.
Automated figures are a starting hypothesis at best.

The honest framing of a CMA to a client is: *here is what comparable properties in this market
area actually sold for, here is how the subject differs from each, and here is the range that
evidence supports.* Not: *your house is worth X.*

## 3.4 Building the analysis

chunks.heading: Hour 03 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
A workable sequence: define the market area and defend it; pull closed sales within a defensible
period, usually the most recent three to six months, extended only if data is thin; screen for
arm's-length conditions; select the three to five closest in physical characteristics; note every
material difference between each comparable and the subject; adjust in the direction that makes
the comparable resemble the subject; reconcile to a range rather than a point; and disclose the
limits — the number of sales, the age of the data, and anything the licensee could not verify.

Adjustment mechanics belong to Hour 43. The habit to build now is the discipline of writing down
*why* each comparable was included and each near-miss excluded. That written record is what makes
the analysis reviewable, and it is what protects the licensee if the price is later disputed.

### Hour 03 engagement check

**Question.** A subject property is a 1,900-square-foot three-bedroom house. Which is stronger
evidence of its value: a 1,950-square-foot house two streets away that sold four months ago
between unrelated parties, or an identical 1,900-square-foot house next door currently listed at a
price the seller chose last week? Explain.

**Expected answer.** The closed sale. It records a price a buyer actually paid and a seller
actually accepted, which is evidence of market behaviour. The active listing records only what one
seller is asking, which is an unaccepted offer and may be far from what the market will pay. The
active listing is still useful as competitive supply and as a bracket, but it is not a value
indicator.

---

## Hour 04 — Real property, personal property, and fixtures

## 4.1 The distinction and why it decides disputes

chunks.heading: 4.2 Fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
**Real property** is land, improvements, and the legal interests in them. **Personal property** —
also called chattels or personalty — is everything else: movable things, and intangible rights not
attached to land.

The distinction matters because the two transfer by different instruments. Real property is
conveyed by **deed**. Personal property is transferred by **bill of sale**, or simply by delivery.
A sales contract that conveys the house says nothing at all about the refrigerator unless someone
writes it in. Most fixture disputes are not legal puzzles; they are contracts that failed to say.

## 4.2 Fixtures

A **fixture** is an item that was personal property and has become real property by being attached
to the land or to an improvement. Once it is a fixture it passes with the deed automatically.

The classical test has three parts, and they are usually taught with the mnemonic **MARIA** —
Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of the parties, Intention, and Agreement — or in
the shorter three-factor form:

**Method of annexation.** How is it attached, and what happens if it is removed? An item bolted,
wired, plumbed, or built in is more likely a fixture. An item that would leave a hole, a scar, or
a non-functioning system is more likely a fixture. A picture hanging on a nail is not.

**Adaptation to the real estate.** Has it been fitted to this particular property? Custom-cut
shutters, a built-in bookcase sized to the alcove, a key to the front door, and a
custom-fabricated storm window are adapted, and adaptation makes an item a fixture even when the
physical attachment is slight. A key is the classic example: physically unattached, unquestionably
a fixture.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Trade fixtures
chunks.excerpt:
**Intention of the party who attached it.** Courts treat this as the controlling factor, and the
first two are largely evidence of it. Intention is judged objectively — by what a reasonable
person would infer from the circumstances, not by what the seller says afterwards.

The two supporting factors: **relationship of the parties** — the same item is treated differently
between landlord and tenant than between seller and buyer, and doubt is generally resolved in
favour of the party with the weaker position, historically the tenant and the buyer — and
**agreement**, which is decisive when it exists.

## 4.3 Trade fixtures

A **trade fixture** is an article installed by a *tenant* for use in the tenant's trade or business.
Trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease ends,
with the tenant responsible for repairing damage caused by removal. A restaurant tenant's walk-in
cooler, a salon's stations, a shop's display cases: attached, sometimes heavily, and still the
tenant's.

The trap is timing. Trade fixtures left behind after the lease term generally become the
landlord's by **accession**. The right to remove is real, and it expires.

## 4.4 In the other direction

Attachment is not one-way. **Severance** turns real property into personal property: standing
timber is real property, cut timber is personal property; a crop growing in a field is real
property, harvested grain is personal property; a hot-water heater in a box at the supply house is
personal property, and installed it is a fixture.

chunks.heading: 4.5 How a competent licensee prevents the dispute
chunks.excerpt:
**Emblements** are a distinct case worth knowing. Annual crops produced by a tenant's labour —
*fructus industriales* — are treated as the tenant's personal property, and a tenant whose tenancy
ends through no fault of their own generally retains the right to re-enter and harvest the crop
that was planted during the tenancy.

## 4.5 How a competent licensee prevents the dispute

The professional answer to fixture questions is almost never litigation. It is drafting.

At listing, walk the property and identify every item whose status a reasonable buyer might read
differently: mounted televisions and their brackets, mirrors, chandeliers and other light
fittings, appliances, window treatments and their hardware, shelving, playground equipment,
above-ground pools, generators, water-treatment equipment, security cameras, and anything the
seller intends to take. Record the seller's intention **before** marketing, and reflect it in the
listing information and in the contract. If a seller wants the dining-room chandelier, the time to
remove and replace it is before the first photograph — not after a buyer has seen it.

This is also a disclosure question. Under § 54.1-2131 A 6 the licensee owes the client disclosure
of material facts of which the licensee has actual knowledge; under 18VAC135-20-190 B 3 property
information in advertising must be consistent with the property's condition and contract status.
A photograph showing a chandelier the seller intends to remove is inconsistent property
information, and fixing it is not optional courtesy.

### Hour 04 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 01
chunks.excerpt:
**Question.** A seller installed a custom-fitted bookcase into a wall alcove, screwed to studs and
cut to the alcove's exact dimensions. The contract is silent. The seller wants to take it. What is
the outcome under the fixture test, and which factor decides it?

**Expected answer.** It is a fixture and passes to the buyer. Method of annexation points that way
— screwed to structure, removal would damage the wall — but the decisive factor is adaptation
combined with objective intention: an item cut to fit this specific alcove evidences an intention
to make it part of the property permanently. The seller's after-the-fact wish is not the test.
The correct professional response is that this should have been agreed in writing before listing.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 01

Hours 1 through 3 are national principles and are not derived from Virginia-specific authority.
Hour 4's disclosure and advertising statements rest on **§ 54.1-2131 A 6** of the Code of Virginia
and **18VAC135-20-190 B 3**, both read from law.lis.virginia.gov on 2026-08-20 and recorded in
`virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

Required-subject authority for the module is **18VAC135-20-400**, subdivisions 1, 2 and 3. The
regulation lists the 25 subjects and sets a floor of 60 class hours; **it allocates no hours among
them.** The four-hour allocation above is a StateCourse design decision, not a Board requirement,
and must be described that way in every submission document.

The six-month balance point cited in Hour 2.3 is a market convention drawn from national
inventory data, not a legal or regulatory standard, and is presented as a rule of thumb.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 02

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 02

## Course Day 2 · Hours 5–8 · Estates, ownership, private rights, and public control

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(3) Property rights · (9) Liens · (10) Home
ownership · (21) Planning subdivision developments and condominiums · (22) Regulatory statutes
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Classify an interest in land as freehold or leasehold and name the present and future interests
  in a life-estate arrangement.
- Distinguish severalty, tenancy in common, joint tenancy, and tenancy by the entirety, and state
  what happens on death and on transfer under each.
- Identify an easement by type and by how it was created, and distinguish it from a licence, an
  encroachment, and a restrictive covenant.
- State the four powers of government over land and match a fact pattern to the correct one.
- Explain how zoning, subdivision control, and the comprehensive plan relate to one another, and
  what a variance, a special use permit, and a nonconforming use each are.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 05 — Estates in land and future interests
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 5 | Estates in land and future interests | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 6 | Forms of ownership and home ownership | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 7 | Private rights, easements, and encumbrances | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 8 | Public controls, land use, and development | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 5 and again after Hour 10 |

---

## Hour 05 — Estates in land and future interests

## 5.1 What an estate is

An **estate** is the degree, quantity, nature, and extent of a person's interest in land. Two
questions define it: *what may the holder do?* and *for how long?* Everything in this hour is an
answer to the second question.

The primary division is between **freehold** estates, which are of indefinite duration and involve
ownership, and **leasehold** estates, which are of fixed or determinable duration and involve
possession without ownership. A tenant has an estate in land. It is simply not a freehold.

## 5.2 Fee simple

**Fee simple absolute** is the largest estate the law recognises. It is of potentially infinite
duration, freely transferable during life and at death, and subject only to the four government
powers and to any private restrictions the owner or a predecessor accepted. Unless a deed says
otherwise, a conveyance of land is presumed to convey a fee simple absolute.

**Defeasible fees** are fee estates that may end if a stated condition occurs. Two forms matter:

chunks.heading: 5.3 Life estates
chunks.excerpt:
A **fee simple determinable** ends automatically when the stated event occurs. The classic
language is durational — "so long as", "while", "during", "until". The grantor keeps a
**possibility of reverter**, and title returns without any action being taken.

A **fee simple subject to a condition subsequent** does not end automatically; it gives the
grantor the **right of re-entry**, which must be exercised. The classic language is conditional —
"but if", "provided that", "on condition that".

The practical significance for a licensee is that a defeasible fee is a title matter, it appears
in the record, and it belongs to the title examiner and the buyer's attorney. Discrimination-based
conditions in old instruments are unenforceable, and in Virginia § 36-96.3 A 6 makes it an
unlawful discriminatory housing practice to include such a covenant in a transfer or to honour or
attempt to honour one.

## 5.3 Life estates

A **life estate** is a freehold measured by someone's life. The holder — the **life tenant** — has
full use and possession, may lease or sell what they have, and takes the income. What they cannot
do is convey more than they own, and they may not commit **waste**: they must not damage the
property or allow it to deteriorate, and they must ordinarily pay the taxes and the interest on
existing debt.

When the measuring life ends, the estate ends and someone takes possession:

- If the property returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs, the grantor's retained interest
  is a **reversion**.
- If it passes to a named third party, that party holds a **remainder**.

chunks.heading: 5.4 Leasehold estates named
chunks.excerpt:
A **life estate pur autre vie** is measured by the life of someone other than the holder. It is the
one life estate that can be inherited — if the holder dies while the measuring life continues, the
remaining estate passes to the holder's heirs until the measuring life ends.

**Legal life estates** arise by operation of law rather than by grant. Virginia's marital property
regime has changed over time and the treatment of dower and curtesy is a matter of statute and
transitional law; a course document should not state a rule here without reading Title 64.2, and
this course does not. What a licensee needs to know is that a spouse may have an interest that
must be released at closing, and that determining it is a title and legal question, not a
brokerage one.

## 5.4 Leasehold estates named

Four, in decreasing order of definiteness:

**Estate for years** — a fixed term with a definite beginning and end. It expires on its own; no
notice is required. The name is misleading: a two-week lease is an estate for years.

**Periodic estate** — a term that renews automatically for successive periods until one party
gives notice. Month-to-month tenancies are the common case.

**Estate at will** — possession with the landlord's consent, for no fixed period, terminable by
either party. Statutes generally impose notice requirements.

**Estate at sufferance** — a tenant who came in lawfully and stayed past the term without consent.
This is the weakest interest recognised; it is distinguished from trespass only by the lawful
entry.

Virginia's residential landlord-tenant treatment is Hour 32. Leases as contracts are Hour 31.

### Hour 05 engagement check

chunks.heading: Hour 06 — Forms of ownership and home ownership
chunks.excerpt:
**Question.** A grants Blackacre "to B for life, then to C." A dies. Then B dies. Who owns
Blackacre at each stage, and what is C's interest called before B's death?

**Expected answer.** On the grant, B holds a life estate and C holds a vested remainder in fee
simple. A retains nothing, because the grant disposed of the entire estate; A's death changes
nothing. On B's death the life estate ends and C's remainder becomes possessory — C holds fee
simple. Had the grant said only "to B for life", A would have retained a reversion and A's heirs
would take on B's death.

---

## Hour 06 — Forms of ownership and home ownership

## 6.1 Ownership in severalty

**Severalty** means ownership by one person or one legal entity alone. The word misleads students
constantly — it comes from "severed", not "several". A sole owner may deal with the property
freely, and on death it passes by will or by intestate succession.

## 6.2 Concurrent ownership

**Tenancy in common** is the default when two or more people take title without specifying
otherwise. Each holds an **undivided fractional interest** — undivided meaning each has the right
to possess the whole, not a marked-off portion. Shares need not be equal. There is **no right of
survivorship**: on death an owner's share passes to that owner's heirs or devisees, who become
tenants in common with the survivors. Any co-tenant may transfer their share without the others'
consent, and any co-tenant may seek **partition**.

chunks.heading: 6.3 Entity and trust ownership
chunks.excerpt:
**Joint tenancy** adds the **right of survivorship**: on the death of a joint tenant, that
tenant's interest passes to the surviving joint tenants outside probate. The common-law
requirements are the four unities — **time, title, interest, possession** — acquired at the same
time, by the same instrument, in equal shares, with equal rights of possession. Survivorship is
not presumed; in Virginia it must be expressed in the instrument. A joint tenant who conveys their
interest destroys the joint tenancy as to that share, and the transferee takes as a tenant in
common.

**Tenancy by the entirety** is available only to spouses and treats them as a single owner. It
carries survivorship, and neither spouse may convey or encumber the property alone. Its practical
significance is creditor protection: a creditor of one spouse alone generally cannot reach
property held by the entirety. Virginia recognises this form, and it is a common way for married
couples to hold a home.

**Community property** is a marital-property system used in a minority of states. **Virginia is
not a community property state.** A student who learned the term from a national text should know
it does not describe Virginia title.

## 6.3 Entity and trust ownership

Property may be owned by a **corporation**, a **partnership**, a **limited liability company**, or
a **trust**. Two consequences for a licensee: first, the entity's authority to sign is a legal
question, evidenced by organisational documents and resolutions, and it is verified by the
settlement agent and counsel, not by the licensee. Second, an entity in a residential transaction
does not change the licensee's duties.

chunks.heading: 6.4 Common-interest ownership, introduced
chunks.excerpt:
**Trusts** separate legal and beneficial ownership: the trustee holds legal title and manages,
the beneficiary takes the benefit. A **living trust** is a common estate-planning vehicle for a
residence, and the trustee is the party who signs.

## 6.4 Common-interest ownership, introduced

Two forms will recur throughout the course and are covered fully in Hours 29 and 30.

A **condominium** divides a project into individually owned **units** and **common elements**
owned in undivided shares by all unit owners. **Limited common elements** — a balcony, an assigned
parking space — serve fewer than all units.

A **cooperative** is a corporation that owns the building; the resident owns shares in the
corporation and holds a proprietary lease of an apartment. The resident owns personal property,
not real property, which changes financing and title work entirely.

A property owners' association governs a subdivision of separately owned lots and enforces
covenants; it is not a condominium, and Virginia treats the two under separate statutory schemes.

## 6.5 Home ownership as a decision

Required subject 10 is **home ownership**, and it deserves to be taught honestly rather than as
advocacy.

The financial case for owning includes forced saving through amortisation, a hedge against rent
inflation, the possibility of appreciation, potential tax treatment, and control over the property.
The costs include the transaction costs of buying and selling, which are large and are paid twice;
property taxes and insurance; maintenance and capital replacement, which do not stop; the
illiquidity of the asset; the concentration of household wealth into one undiversified holding;
and the loss of mobility.

chunks.heading: Hour 06 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**Appreciation is not guaranteed.** A licensee who tells a client that a house is a sure
investment is making a representation about future value that no one can support, and 18VAC135-20-300
makes misrepresentation a disciplinary matter. The competent formulation is to identify the
factors and let the client, with their own advisers, decide.

Tax treatment is the clearest example of the boundary of the licence. Mortgage interest and
property-tax deductions, the exclusion of gain on a principal residence, and the interaction with
the standard deduction all depend on the individual's circumstances and on law that changes.
**Refer the client to a tax professional and say so in writing.**

### Hour 06 engagement check

**Question.** Two unmarried siblings take title as joint tenants with right of survivorship. One
sibling sells their interest to a third party. Describe the resulting ownership, and describe it
again if instead the selling sibling had died still owning the interest.

**Expected answer.** On sale, the unity of time and title is broken as to that share: the buyer
takes as a **tenant in common** with the remaining sibling, and there is no survivorship between
them. Had the sibling died still owning, the right of survivorship would have operated and the
surviving sibling would hold the whole in severalty, outside probate.

---

## Hour 07 — Private rights, easements, and encumbrances

## 7.1 Encumbrances

chunks.heading: 7.2 Easements
chunks.excerpt:
An **encumbrance** is any claim, right, or interest held by someone other than the owner that
affects title or limits use. Encumbrances do not prevent transfer; they travel with the land.
They fall into two families: those that affect **use** — easements, restrictive covenants,
encroachments — and those that affect **title as security for money**, which are **liens** and are
Hour 13.

## 7.2 Easements

An **easement** is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a stated purpose. It is an
interest in land, and it is created and transferred by written instrument or by operation of law.

An **easement appurtenant** benefits a parcel. The benefited parcel is the **dominant tenement**
and the burdened parcel is the **servient tenement**. It runs with the land: it passes to the next
owner automatically, whether or not anyone mentions it. This is the easement in most residential
transactions — shared driveways, access to a back lot, drainage.

An **easement in gross** benefits a *person or entity* rather than a parcel. Utility easements are
the everyday case, and commercial easements in gross are assignable.

**Creation.** By **express grant or reservation** in a deed. By **implication**, where a use was
apparent, continuous, and necessary at the time a parcel was divided. By **necessity**, the
landlocked-parcel case, which requires common ownership at the time of severance. By
**prescription**, from open, notorious, continuous, hostile use for the statutory period — this is
a legal determination, and the Virginia period must be read from statute before any document
states it, which this course does not do. By **condemnation**, when a public body takes an
easement rather than the fee.

chunks.heading: 7.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall
chunks.excerpt:
**Termination.** By merger, when one person acquires both tenements. By release from the dominant
owner. By abandonment, which requires conduct showing intent and not mere non-use. By the end of
the necessity, for an easement by necessity. By express terms.

## 7.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall

A **licence** is permission to do something on another's land that would otherwise be a trespass.
It is *personal, revocable, and not an interest in land*. Permission to park in a neighbour's
drive is a licence; if it were written, permanent, and running with the land it would be an
easement. The distinction decides whether the right survives a sale.

An **encroachment** is an unauthorised physical intrusion — a fence, a roof overhang, a driveway —
onto adjoining land. It is discovered by a survey, not by looking. It is both a title problem and
a potential dispute, and long-standing encroachments can mature into prescriptive rights. When one
is suspected, the professional answer is a survey and, if it exists, legal advice — not a licensee's
opinion about where the line is.

A **party wall** is a shared wall on a boundary, with each owner typically owning to the centre
and holding an easement of support in the other half.

## 7.4 Restrictive covenants

**Restrictive covenants** are private limits on use, imposed by a developer or by agreement, and
recorded so they bind successors. They regulate setbacks, minimum sizes, materials, outbuildings,
signage, use, and much else, and in a common-interest community they are enforced by the
association.

Three points a licensee must hold:

**They are private law, and they can be stricter than zoning.** Where zoning permits and a covenant
forbids, the covenant governs the owner as a matter of private obligation.

chunks.heading: 7.5 What the licensee actually does
chunks.excerpt:
**They are enforced privately** — by an association or a neighbour, by injunction or damages — not
by the locality.

**Discriminatory covenants are void and must not be honoured.** § 36-96.3 A 6 makes it an unlawful
discriminatory housing practice to include such a covenant in a transfer, sale, rental or lease, or
for any person to honour or exercise, or attempt to honour or exercise, such a covenant. Historic
racial covenants remain physically present in many recorded chains of title in Virginia; they are
unenforceable, and repeating them as though they operated would itself be a violation.

## 7.5 What the licensee actually does

The licensee is not the person who determines the existence, scope, or validity of an easement.
The licensee is the person who **notices** that a question exists and routes it correctly: to the
title examiner for what is recorded, to a surveyor for where things physically are, and to counsel
for what the instrument means. Under § 54.1-2131 A 6 the duty is to disclose material facts of
which the licensee has **actual knowledge** — a shared driveway the licensee knows about is a
material fact; the legal effect of the instrument creating it is not the licensee's to opine on.

### Hour 07 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer is told by a neighbour, "your seller has always let me cut across the back
corner to reach my dock." The arrangement is not in any recorded instrument. What is it most
likely to be, what is the risk to the buyer, and what should the licensee do?

chunks.heading: Hour 08 — Public controls, land use, and development
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** On these facts it is most likely a **licence** — personal and revocable —
because nothing was written and nothing was recorded. The risk is that long, open, continuous and
hostile use could have ripened into a **prescriptive easement**, which would bind the buyer, and
that is a legal determination on facts nobody in the conversation has established. The licensee
should disclose the conversation as a known material fact, and direct the buyer to the title
examiner and to counsel, and to a survey. The licensee must not tell the buyer whether the
neighbour has a right.

---

## Hour 08 — Public controls, land use, and development

## 8.1 The four government powers

Every limitation government places on land traces to one of four powers. The mnemonic is **PETE**.

**Police power** — the power to regulate for public health, safety, morals, and general welfare.
It is the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision regulation, and environmental controls.
No compensation is paid, because nothing is taken; use is regulated. In Virginia the power belongs
to the Commonwealth and is delegated to localities by enabling legislation in Title 15.2.

**Eminent domain** — the power to take private property for public use, with **just compensation**.
The taking is executed through a **condemnation** proceeding. A partial taking is common — a strip
for road widening — and compensation covers damage to the remainder.

**Taxation** — the power to levy against property to fund government, backed by a lien and
ultimately by sale. Hour 14.

**Escheat** — the reversion of property to the Commonwealth when an owner dies with no will and no
heirs. Rare, and the reason the list is four rather than three.

chunks.heading: 8.2 The comprehensive plan and zoning
chunks.excerpt:
The line between police power and eminent domain is where regulatory takings litigation lives.
That is a constitutional question and a matter for counsel.

## 8.2 The comprehensive plan and zoning

A **comprehensive plan** is a locality's long-range statement of intended growth, land use,
transportation, and public facilities. It is a policy document. **Zoning** is the ordinance that
implements it and has legal force.

Zoning divides a locality into districts and prescribes, for each, the permitted **uses** and the
**bulk** controls — height, lot area, lot coverage, setbacks, density, parking, and frequently
signage. Districts are conventionally residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, and mixed,
with numbered subdistricts of differing intensity.

Three release valves exist, and students confuse them:

A **variance** relieves a property owner from a **bulk or dimensional** requirement where strict
application would cause an unnecessary hardship arising from the property itself — an unusual
shape, topography, or size. A variance is granted by a board of zoning appeals. **A variance does
not authorise a use the district forbids**, and self-created hardship and mere financial
disadvantage are not grounds.

A **special use permit** — also called a conditional use permit — authorises a use the ordinance
lists as permissible in the district *subject to review and conditions*. It is not an exception to
the ordinance; it is the ordinance operating as written.

chunks.heading: 8.3 Subdivision and development
chunks.excerpt:
A **nonconforming use** is a use that was lawful when established and has since been made
non-compliant by a change in the ordinance. It is generally allowed to continue — "grandfathered"
— but typically may not be expanded, and may be lost if abandoned or destroyed. A licensee
marketing such a property should never assume the right survives a change of ownership or a
period of vacancy; that is a question for the zoning administrator in writing.

A **rezoning** is an amendment of the ordinance itself, granted by the governing body, and is a
legislative act.

## 8.3 Subdivision and development

Creating new lots from a parcel is **subdivision**, and it is regulated separately from zoning. A
typical sequence: concept plan; preliminary plat, reviewed against the subdivision ordinance;
engineering and public-improvement plans for streets, water, sewer, and stormwater; construction
of improvements, usually secured by a bond or letter of credit; final plat, which is recorded and
which legally creates the lots; and dedication of streets and utilities to public control.

**A lot does not exist until the plat is recorded.** Selling "lot 14" from an unrecorded
preliminary plan is selling something that has no legal description.

Development also passes through environmental review. In Virginia, the **Chesapeake Bay
Preservation Act** creates resource protection areas in localities that adopt implementing
ordinances, and § 55.1-703 expressly tells buyers to investigate whether such an ordinance affects
the property. Wetlands, floodplains, and stormwater requirements can each make a physically
buildable lot unbuildable.

## 8.4 The licensee's boundary, again

chunks.heading: Hour 08 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Everything in this hour is determined by a public body and recorded in a public office. The
licensee's job is to know that the questions exist, to know **who** answers each one — zoning
administrator, planning department, building official, health department for a well or septic,
VDOT for road access — and to send the client there in writing. Answering a zoning question from
memory is how licensees create liability, and under 18VAC135-20-300 an inaccurate statement of a
material fact is a disciplinary matter regardless of good intentions.

Note also the boundary § 54.1-2131 B draws: a listing licensee's disclosure duty covers material
adverse facts about the **physical condition of the property** actually known, and the statute
says that term does **not** include matters relating to governmental land use regulations, matters
outside the boundaries of the land, or matters relating to highways or public streets. That is not
a licence to conceal — it is a statement of what the physical-condition duty covers. Other duties,
including the duty of ordinary care and the client-side duty to disclose material facts under
§ 54.1-2131 A 6, operate independently.

### Hour 08 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer wants to run a small dog-grooming business from a house in a district that
permits only single-family dwellings and home occupations of a listed kind not including animal
care. The lot is unusually narrow. Which relief mechanism, if any, fits — variance, special use
permit, or rezoning — and why?

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** Not a variance: the narrow lot is a dimensional problem, and a variance
relieves bulk requirements, not use prohibitions. Not a special use permit either, on these facts,
because the ordinance does not list this use as permissible in the district subject to conditions.
The only route that reaches the desired use is a **rezoning or a text amendment to the ordinance**,
which is a legislative act of the governing body with no guarantee of success. The licensee's
correct action is to refer the buyer to the zoning administrator in writing before the buyer relies
on the intended use, and never to advise that the use "should be fine".

---

## Instructor source note for Module 02

Virginia-specific statements in this module rest on: **§ 36-96.3 A 6** (discriminatory covenants
may not be included, honoured, or exercised); **§ 54.1-2131 A 6 and B** (client disclosure of
material facts of actual knowledge; the physical-condition duty and the three matters the statute
excludes from it); **§ 55.1-703** (buyer due diligence, including Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act
resource protection areas); and **18VAC135-20-300** (misrepresentation or omission). All were read
from law.lis.virginia.gov on 2026-08-20 and are recorded in
`virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

Two rules are deliberately **not** stated in this module because the primary text has not been
read: the **prescriptive-easement period** in Virginia, and the current treatment of **legal life
estates and marital interests** under Title 64.2. Both are identified to the student as questions
for counsel rather than answered. They must be read before any instructor supplements this text
with a figure.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 02
chunks.excerpt:
Zoning and subdivision procedure varies by locality under the enabling legislation in **Title
15.2**; the sequence in Hour 8.3 is the general pattern and is taught as such, not as any
particular locality's ordinance.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 03

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 03

## Course Day 3 · Hours 9–12 · Describing land, conveying it, and proving title

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(3) Property rights · (5) Deeds · (11) Real property
and title insurance · (18) Search, examination, and registration of title
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Read a metes-and-bounds description well enough to detect an ambiguity, and explain why a street
  address is not a legal description.
- List the elements a deed must contain to be valid, and explain what delivery and acceptance add
  that signature does not.
- Distinguish a general warranty deed, a special warranty deed, and a quitclaim deed by what each
  promises.
- Explain actual, constructive, and inquiry notice, and why recording protects a buyer.
- Read a title commitment well enough to separate requirements, exceptions, and insured risks.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 9 | Legal descriptions, plats, and surveys | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 10 | Deeds and voluntary transfer | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 11 | Title search, chain of title, and notice | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 12 | Title defects and title insurance | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 10 |

---

## Hour 09 — Legal descriptions, plats, and surveys

## 9.1 Why the address will not do

chunks.heading: 9.2 Metes and bounds
chunks.excerpt:
A street address identifies a mailbox. It is assigned administratively, it can be changed by a
locality, it does not describe boundaries, and two different parcels can share one. A **legal
description** identifies a unique parcel of land in a way a surveyor could reproduce on the ground.
Deeds, deeds of trust, plats, and judgments use legal descriptions. Contracts should.

Three systems are in use in the United States. Virginia uses two of them.

## 9.2 Metes and bounds

**Metes and bounds** describes a boundary by walking it. *Metes* are distances and *bounds* are
directions and limits. A description begins at a **point of beginning** — a fixed, identifiable
starting point — and proceeds by a sequence of calls, each giving a direction and a distance,
until it **closes** back at the point of beginning. A description that does not close is defective.

A call reads, for example, *N 45° 30′ 00″ E, 210.50 feet to an iron pin*. The bearing is read as a
deviation from north or south, toward east or west: north forty-five degrees thirty minutes east.
Degrees, minutes, seconds — sixty minutes to a degree, sixty seconds to a minute.

**Monuments** are physical markers referenced in the calls: an iron pin, a concrete monument, a
stone, a tree, a road centreline, a watercourse. The traditional rule of construction is that
where a description conflicts internally, **monuments control over courses and distances**,
because a monument is what a person on the ground can actually find. A description calling for
"the centreline of Mill Creek" governs even if the stated distance no longer reaches it.

chunks.heading: 9.3 Lot and block
chunks.excerpt:
Metes and bounds is the dominant system in Virginia, as in the original thirteen colonies. It is
also the system with the most ways to go wrong: natural monuments that move or disappear, calls
that reference "the old Johnson fence", adjoining-owner references that changed hands a century
ago, and descriptions carried forward unchanged through generations of deeds while the physical
world moved.

## 9.3 Lot and block

The **lot and block** system — also called the recorded plat or subdivision system — describes a
parcel by reference to a **recorded plat**: *Lot 14, Block C, Fairview Estates, as recorded in Plat
Book 22, page 118, among the land records of the Circuit Court of ___ County, Virginia.*

The plat itself carries the metes and bounds of every lot, the streets, the easements, and the
surveyor's certification. Once recorded, the plat is incorporated into every deed that references
it. This is the system for essentially all modern subdivision property, and it is why Hour 8
insisted that a lot does not exist until the plat is recorded.

## 9.4 The rectangular survey system, and why Virginia does not use it

The **rectangular** or **government survey system** — principal meridians, base lines, townships
six miles square, thirty-six sections of one square mile each, sections of 640 acres divided by
quarters — governs most land west and north of the original colonies. **Virginia is not a public
land survey state.** A student who has studied a national text will meet township-and-range
questions on a national examination and should understand the arithmetic — a quarter of a quarter
section is 40 acres, a half of a quarter is 80 — but should not expect to see it in a Virginia
deed.

## 9.5 Surveys, and what they are for

chunks.heading: Hour 09 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
A **survey** is a licensed surveyor's determination of where the boundaries are on the ground.
A **plat of survey** shows the parcel, the improvements, and anything crossing a line.

A survey answers questions a title search cannot. The title record shows what *should* be true;
the survey shows what *is*. Encroachments, structures over setback lines, fences that do not follow
the boundary, driveways serving the neighbour, and a septic field on the wrong lot are found by
survey and by nothing else.

The licensee's role is to know when to recommend one — irregular parcels, older metes-and-bounds
descriptions, visible fences and structures near lines, planned construction, unimproved land, any
mention of a boundary dispute — and to route the question to the surveyor. Reading a plat and
opining on where the line is falls outside the licence.

Vertical descriptions matter too. Condominium units are described by reference to a recorded
condominium plat and by elevation, because the unit is a volume of space, not a footprint.

### Hour 09 engagement check

**Question.** A deed's description calls for a course of "S 12° 00′ 00″ W, 320 feet to a large oak
tree at the edge of the branch". A modern survey finds the oak stump 344 feet from the prior point.
Which controls, and why?

**Expected answer.** The **monument** — the oak at the edge of the branch — controls over the
stated distance, under the ordinary rule that monuments prevail over courses and distances. The
distance is treated as an approximation of a boundary the parties fixed by reference to a physical
object. The practical answer is nevertheless that the discrepancy is a title and survey matter, and
the licensee's job is to get it in front of the surveyor and the title examiner, not to resolve it.

---

chunks.heading: Hour 10 — Deeds and voluntary transfer
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 10 — Deeds and voluntary transfer

## 10.1 What a deed does

A **deed** is the written instrument by which an interest in real property is voluntarily
transferred from a **grantor** to a **grantee**. The deed is the operative act of transfer. It is
not the contract — the contract creates the obligation to convey, and the deed performs it.

A deed transfers title. **Recording** does not transfer title; it gives notice to the world. Title
passes on delivery and acceptance, whether or not the deed is ever recorded. Recording protects
the grantee against subsequent claims, which is why it is done immediately and why a gap of even
hours can matter.

## 10.2 The elements

For a deed to be valid it must have:

**A competent grantor.** Of legal age and legal capacity. A deed from a person adjudicated
incompetent is void; a deed from a person lacking capacity at the moment of signing is voidable.
Entities act through authorised signatories.

**A named grantee, identifiable with certainty.** A deed to a non-existent person or entity fails.

**A statement of consideration.** Something of value, though the deed need only recite it — the
common "for ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration" is sufficient recital, and deeds
of gift recite love and affection.

**Words of conveyance**, called the **granting clause** — "does grant and convey", or "grants,
bargains and sells". These words show present intent to transfer.

**An adequate legal description**, as Hour 9 required.

**The grantor's signature.** The grantee does not sign a deed. Where the property is held by the
entirety or a spouse has an interest, the spouse signs to release it.

chunks.heading: 10.3 Types of deed, ranked by what the grantor promises
chunks.excerpt:
**Delivery and acceptance.** The most misunderstood element. A signed deed sitting in a drawer
transfers nothing. Delivery requires the grantor's present intent to pass title; acceptance is
presumed where the conveyance benefits the grantee. This is why a deed handed over at closing with
instructions not to record until funds clear is a matter the settlement agent controls carefully.

**Acknowledgment** — the grantor's declaration before a notary or other authorised officer that the
signature is genuine and voluntary. Acknowledgment is generally not required for validity between
the parties, but it **is required to record**, and an unrecordable deed is a practical disaster.

Two things a deed does not require: the grantee's signature, and, at common law, witnesses in most
circumstances.

## 10.3 Types of deed, ranked by what the grantor promises

**General warranty deed.** The grantor warrants title against defects arising at any time,
including before the grantor owned the property. The traditional covenants are seisin, right to
convey, against encumbrances, quiet enjoyment, further assurance, and warranty forever. This is the
strongest deed and the norm in Virginia residential resale transactions.

**Special warranty deed.** The grantor warrants only against defects arising **during the
grantor's own ownership**. Anything from before is not warranted. Fiduciaries, corporations,
lenders selling foreclosed property, and relocation companies commonly use this form, and it is
usual in new construction from a builder.

chunks.heading: 10.4 Involuntary and testamentary transfer, briefly
chunks.excerpt:
**Quitclaim deed.** The grantor conveys whatever interest the grantor has — which may be nothing —
and warrants nothing at all. Quitclaims are curative instruments: clearing a possible interest,
correcting a name, releasing a spouse's interest, resolving a boundary. **A quitclaim is not a
lesser way to buy a house.** A buyer who accepts one is accepting the risk that the grantor owned
nothing.

**Special-purpose deeds** include the deed of trust — Virginia's security instrument, Hour 34 —
executor's, administrator's, trustee's, and commissioner's deeds, each carrying the authority
under which the fiduciary acts, and a deed in lieu of foreclosure.

Virginia deeds normally also carry a **deed of bargain and sale with English covenants of title**,
a formulation with a long local history. What matters for a student is to read what the covenants
say rather than to rely on the deed's label.

## 10.4 Involuntary and testamentary transfer, briefly

Not every transfer is by deed from a willing owner. Title passes by **will** — the testator is the
devisor and the recipient the devisee — or by **intestate succession** under Title 64.2 when there
is no will. It passes by **foreclosure sale**, by **tax sale**, by **eminent domain**, by
**adverse possession**, by **escheat**, and by **partition**. Each is a chapter of its own; the
point here is that the chain of title a searcher builds in Hour 11 will contain instruments that
are not ordinary deeds, and each carries its own questions about authority.

## 10.5 What the licensee does and does not do

chunks.heading: Hour 10 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 54.1-2101.1** of the Code of Virginia governs the preparation of real estate contracts by
licensees, and §§ 54.1-2131 A 2 b and 54.1-2132 A 3 b describe the licensee's role as *assisting in
the drafting and negotiating of offers and counteroffers, amendments, and addenda to the real
estate contract pursuant to § 54.1-2101.1*. That is the boundary. Assisting with contract forms in
the manner the statute permits is licensed activity. **Drafting or selecting a deed is not.** The
deed is prepared by an attorney, and choosing between a general warranty deed and a special
warranty deed is legal advice.

A licensee who is asked "which deed should we use?" has one correct answer: *that is a question for
your attorney or the settlement agent, and here is how to reach them.*

### Hour 10 engagement check

**Question.** A grantor signs and acknowledges a deed, puts it in a safe deposit box, and tells no
one. The grantor dies two years later and the deed is found. Did title pass? What element decides?

**Expected answer.** No. **Delivery** is missing. A deed takes effect on delivery with the present
intent to pass title, and a signed, acknowledged deed retained by the grantor and never handed over
evidences no such intent. Signature and acknowledgment make the instrument formally complete and
recordable; they do not transfer anything. The property passes instead under the grantor's will or
by intestate succession.

---

## Hour 11 — Title search, chain of title, and notice

## 11.1 The public records and what they hold

chunks.heading: 11.2 The chain of title
chunks.excerpt:
Land records in Virginia are maintained by the **clerk of the circuit court** of each city and
county. What is recorded there includes deeds, deeds of trust and their releases, plats,
easements, restrictive covenants, judgments, liens, wills and probate records, and lis pendens.

Recording is **constructive notice to the world**. That is the entire point of the system: it
allows a stranger to a transaction to discover, by searching a public office, what interests exist
in a parcel, without asking anyone.

## 11.2 The chain of title

A **chain of title** is the succession of recorded owners of a parcel over time, each conveyance
linking to the next. A searcher builds it by working **backward** from the current owner —
finding the deed by which the current owner took title, then the deed by which that grantor took
title, and so on — and then forward again, checking each owner's period for liens, judgments and
other adverse instruments.

Records are indexed by name, in **grantor and grantee indexes**. A search moves between the two:
the grantee index to find how someone acquired, the grantor index to find what they did with it.

Two defects a searcher looks for:

A **gap** is a break in the chain — a conveyance out from someone who never appears as a grantee,
or a period with no recorded transfer where one must have occurred. Gaps are often the result of
an unrecorded deed, a probate that was never recorded, or a name change.

A **cloud** is any recorded instrument or claim that casts doubt on the title without necessarily
defeating it: an unreleased deed of trust from 1988, an old judgment, an ambiguous easement, a
defective acknowledgment, or a deed from one of several heirs.

chunks.heading: 11.3 The three kinds of notice
chunks.excerpt:
**Marketable title** is title a reasonable, well-informed purchaser would accept — not perfect
title, but title free from reasonable doubt and from the threat of litigation. A sales contract
ordinarily requires the seller to convey marketable title, and it is the buyer's remedy when a
cloud will not clear.

A **quiet title** action is the judicial proceeding used to resolve a cloud that cannot be cleared
by curative instrument.

## 11.3 The three kinds of notice

This is the most examinable concept in the hour and the most commonly muddled.

**Actual notice** is what a person in fact knows. A buyer told about an easement has actual notice
of it.

**Constructive notice** is what the law charges a person with knowing whether or not they know it,
because it is recorded. Everyone is charged with notice of every properly recorded instrument in the
chain of title. This is why recording protects: a subsequent purchaser cannot claim ignorance.

**Inquiry notice** is what a person would have discovered by making the investigation the visible
facts demanded. Someone else in possession of the property is the classic trigger. A buyer who sees
a tenant living in the house, or a neighbour's driveway crossing the lot, is on notice to ask, and
is charged with what a reasonable inquiry would have revealed — even if nothing is recorded.

The practical lesson for a licensee: **possession is notice.** A property occupied by someone other
than the seller raises a question that must be answered in writing before closing.

## 11.4 Recording acts

chunks.heading: 11.5 The abstract and the opinion
chunks.excerpt:
States use one of three rules to decide priority between competing claimants. **Race** — first to
record wins. **Notice** — a subsequent purchaser for value without notice wins. **Race-notice** —
a subsequent purchaser for value without notice who records first wins.

Which rule Virginia applies, and its exact statutory formulation, is a question of Title 55.1 that
this course has not read from primary text and therefore does not state. What the student must
carry is the operating principle that follows under any of the three: **record immediately**, and
treat any delay as risk.

## 11.5 The abstract and the opinion

An **abstract of title** is a condensed history of everything recorded affecting the parcel. An
attorney's **title opinion** is a legal opinion on the state of title based on the abstract.
Together they were the traditional method, and title insurance largely supplanted them because an
opinion compensates only if the attorney was negligent, whereas a policy pays on the risk.

### Hour 11 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer walks a property twice and both times sees a family living in the detached
guest cottage. The seller says they are "just friends staying for a while", and no lease is
recorded. What kind of notice does the buyer have, and what must the licensee do?

chunks.heading: Hour 12 — Title defects and title insurance
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** **Inquiry notice.** Visible possession by someone other than the seller
obliges a reasonable purchaser to investigate, and the buyer will be charged with whatever a proper
inquiry would have revealed — including an unrecorded lease or claimed interest. The licensee's
duty is to disclose the observed occupancy as a material fact actually known and to insist the
question be put in writing to the seller and to the settlement agent before closing. The licensee
must not accept or relay the seller's characterisation as though it settled the question.

---

## Hour 12 — Title defects and title insurance

## 12.1 What title insurance is

Title insurance is an indemnity contract that protects against **loss from defects in title that
existed at the moment the policy was issued** and were not excepted from coverage. It looks
backward. Every other insurance product a buyer holds — hazard, flood, liability — looks forward
at events that may happen. That single difference explains most of what follows.

A **one-time premium** is paid at closing. There are no renewals.

## 12.2 The two policies

An **owner's policy** insures the buyer's interest, in the amount of the purchase price, for as
long as the insured or the insured's heirs hold an interest.

A **lender's policy**, also called a loan policy or mortgagee policy, insures the lender's security
