interest in the amount of the loan, and its coverage declines as the loan is paid down. Lenders
require it, and the buyer usually pays for it.

chunks.heading: 12.3 Reading a commitment
chunks.excerpt:
**A lender's policy does not protect the buyer.** This is the single most important consumer point
in the hour, and it is where buyers are most often left exposed. A buyer who pays for the lender's
policy and declines the owner's policy has purchased protection for someone else.

Virginia has a specific consumer protection here: the **Consumer Real Estate Settlement Protection
Act**, Chapter 10 of Title 55.1 (§ 55.1-1000 et seq.), governs settlement agents and is referenced
directly in the licensing statutes — § 54.1-2132 F and 18VAC135-20-155 A both point to it. The
detail belongs to Hour 40; the point here is that Virginia regulates the settlement side of this
transaction expressly.

## 12.3 Reading a commitment

Before the policy comes the **commitment**, sometimes called a binder or a preliminary report. It
is the insurer's statement of the terms on which it will insure, and it has parts a licensee should
be able to separate:

**Schedule A** — the facts: the proposed insured, the amount, the estate being insured, the current
record owner, and the legal description.

**Schedule B-I, Requirements** — what must be **done** before the policy issues. Pay off and
release the existing deed of trust. Obtain a death certificate. Obtain a signature from a spouse.
Record a corrective deed. These are action items with owners and deadlines, and they are the part
of the commitment most likely to derail a closing if nobody reads them early.

**Schedule B-II, Exceptions** — what the policy will **not** cover. Recorded easements, restrictive
covenants, mineral reservations, matters a survey would show, rights of parties in possession,
taxes not yet due. Exceptions are not defects; they are risks the insurer declines to carry, and
the buyer keeps.

chunks.heading: 12.4 What title insurance covers, and what it does not
chunks.excerpt:
**Exclusions** are different from exceptions: exclusions are printed in the policy form and remove
whole categories from coverage — governmental police power and zoning, eminent domain, defects the
insured created or agreed to, and matters first attaching after the policy date.

A **standard** owner's policy carries the general exceptions. **Extended coverage** removes some of
them, typically requiring a survey and an affidavit, and costs more. Recommending that a buyer
*ask the settlement agent about* extended coverage is proper; telling a buyer they do not need it
is not.

## 12.4 What title insurance covers, and what it does not

Covered, subject to the exceptions: forged deeds and signatures, undisclosed heirs, defective
acknowledgment, incapacity of a prior grantor, errors in the public records, improperly indexed
instruments, undisclosed liens, and clerical mistakes in the chain. Coverage includes the insurer's
duty to **defend** — which is frequently worth more than the indemnity.

Not covered: anything listed as an exception; the excluded categories; **and every problem with the
physical property.** A leaking roof, a failed septic system, radon, defective drywall, a boundary
the survey would have shown, and the neighbour's noise are not title defects. Buyers conflate the
two constantly, and a licensee who does not correct the confusion leaves a buyer believing they are
insured against something they are not.

## 12.5 Curative work

chunks.heading: Hour 12 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Most defects are cleared rather than claimed. A **release** or **certificate of satisfaction**
clears a paid-off deed of trust. A **corrective deed** or **scrivener's affidavit** fixes an error.
A **quitclaim** releases a possible interest. An **affidavit of heirship** or a probate proceeding
establishes succession. A **quiet title** action resolves what nothing else will. Each takes time,
and the deadline the contract sets for title objections is why Schedule B-I must be read the day it
arrives.

### Hour 12 engagement check

**Question.** A commitment lists, under Schedule B-II, "rights of parties in possession" and
"matters that an accurate survey would disclose". After closing the buyer discovers the neighbour's
garage sits three feet inside the boundary. Is the buyer covered? What should have happened?

**Expected answer.** Under a standard policy with those exceptions, **no** — an encroachment is
exactly the kind of matter an accurate survey would disclose, and it was excepted. The buyer should
have obtained a survey during the contract period and, on the strength of it, either resolved the
encroachment, negotiated, or sought extended coverage that removes the survey exception. The
licensee's part is to recognise the exception when the commitment arrives, tell the buyer in
writing what it means in plain terms, and route the buyer to the settlement agent and to counsel —
without opining on coverage, which is the insurer's contract to interpret.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 03

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 03
chunks.excerpt:
Virginia-specific statements rest on: **§ 54.1-2101.1** (preparation of real estate contracts by
licensees), **§§ 54.1-2131 A 2 b and 54.1-2132 A 3 b** (assisting in drafting and negotiating,
pursuant to § 54.1-2101.1), **§ 54.1-2132 F** and **18VAC135-20-155 A** (both referencing Chapter
10 of Title 55.1, the Consumer Real Estate Settlement Protection Act), and **§ 54.1-2131 A 6**
(disclosure of material facts of actual knowledge). All were read from law.lis.virginia.gov on
2026-08-20 and are recorded in `virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

Two matters are deliberately **left unstated** because the primary text has not been read: the
**Virginia recording act's priority rule** and its statutory location in Title 55.1, and the
**Virginia adverse possession period**. Hour 11.4 teaches the three recording-act models and the
operating consequence — record immediately — without asserting which Virginia applies. An
instructor supplementing this text with a rule must read Title 55.1 first.

That Virginia is **not a public land survey state** (Hour 9.4) is a matter of survey history, and
the rectangular system is taught only to the extent a national licensing examination requires it.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 04

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 04

## Course Day 4 · Hours 13–16 · Liens, taxes, and the law of contracts

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(4) Contracts · (9) Liens · (13) Taxes in real
estate · (18) Search, examination, and registration of title
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Classify a lien as voluntary or involuntary and as general or specific, and rank competing liens
  from stated recording facts.
- Explain ad valorem taxation from assessment through rate to bill, and calculate a tax estimate
  and a proration.
- State the four requirements of a valid contract and classify a contract as valid, void, voidable,
  or unenforceable.
- Trace an offer through revocation, rejection, counteroffer, and acceptance and say whether a
  contract formed and when.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 13 | Liens, priority, and release | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 14 | Taxes in real estate | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 15 | Contract foundations | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 16 | Offer, acceptance, and contract formation | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 15 |

---

## Hour 13 — Liens, priority, and release

## 13.1 What a lien is

chunks.heading: 13.2 Two classifications, used together
chunks.excerpt:
A **lien** is a charge against property that secures payment of a debt or performance of an
obligation. It is an encumbrance on title, and it gives the lienholder the right to force a sale of
the property if the obligation is not met.

Liens do not affect possession. An owner with three liens still lives in the house. What liens
affect is **title**, and therefore transferability: a lien must be satisfied or otherwise dealt
with before clear title passes, which is why they surface at closing rather than in daily life.

## 13.2 Two classifications, used together

**Voluntary or involuntary.** A **voluntary** lien is one the owner creates deliberately — in
Virginia, most commonly a **deed of trust** given to secure a loan. An **involuntary** lien arises
by operation of law without the owner's agreement: tax liens, judgment liens, mechanics' liens.

**Statutory or equitable.** A **statutory** lien is created by statute — the tax lien, the
mechanic's lien. An **equitable** lien arises from a court's application of fairness or from the
conduct of the parties.

**General or specific.** A **general** lien attaches to **all** of the debtor's property, real and
personal, within the jurisdiction: judgment liens, federal and state tax liens, estate liens for
death taxes. A **specific** lien attaches to **one identified parcel**: the deed of trust, the real
property tax lien, the mechanic's lien, the special assessment.

Every lien is describable in both dimensions. A judgment lien is involuntary, statutory, and
general. A deed of trust is voluntary and specific.

## 13.3 The particular liens

chunks.heading: 13.3 The particular liens
chunks.excerpt:
**Real property tax liens** secure ad valorem taxes. They are specific, involuntary, and — in most
states, and generally in Virginia — **superior to all other liens regardless of when other liens
were recorded**. That priority is not a matter of recording date; it is conferred by statute.

**Special assessment liens** secure the cost of a public improvement that benefits particular
properties — a sewer extension, sidewalks, street lighting. Specific, involuntary, usually payable
in instalments, and typically carrying a high priority.

**Deed of trust liens.** Virginia is a deed-of-trust jurisdiction rather than a mortgage
jurisdiction; the mechanics are Hour 34. As a lien, a deed of trust is voluntary and specific, and
its priority ordinarily runs from the date and time of recording.

**Judgment liens** arise when a court judgment is docketed and attach to the debtor's real property
in that jurisdiction. General, involuntary, and — importantly — they attach to property the debtor
acquires later as well as property owned at the time. A judgment against a seller shows up in the
title search and must be paid at closing.

chunks.heading: 13.4 Priority
chunks.excerpt:
**Mechanics' and materialmen's liens** secure payment for labour and materials furnished to improve
real property. They are the most dangerous lien for a buyer because of **relation back**: the
priority of a mechanic's lien is generally measured not from the date of filing but from an earlier
date tied to the commencement of work or the furnishing of materials, so a lien filed after closing
can outrank a deed of trust recorded before it. Virginia's mechanics' lien scheme is in Title 43,
with strict deadlines and formalities. **This course does not state those deadlines**, because
Title 43 has not been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee must know is the
warning sign: recent or ongoing construction on a property being sold is a question for the
settlement agent and counsel, every time, without exception.

**Federal tax liens** — from unpaid federal taxes — are general and involuntary. **Estate and
inheritance tax liens** attach on death.

**Association assessment liens** are created by the governing documents and by statute for
condominiums and property owners' associations, and are covered in Hours 29 and 30.

**Vendor's and vendee's liens** are equitable liens securing, respectively, an unpaid seller and a
buyer's deposit.

## 13.4 Priority

**Priority determines who is paid first from a forced sale, and whose lien survives it.** Liens
junior to the foreclosing lien are generally extinguished as to the property; senior liens survive
and the buyer takes subject to them.

The general rule is **first to record, first in right**. Three sets of exceptions:

**Statutory superpriority.** Real property tax liens and, in most schemes, special assessments come
first whenever recorded.

**Relation back.** Mechanics' liens, as above.

chunks.heading: 13.5 Release and the licensee's role
chunks.excerpt:
**Subordination.** A lienholder may agree in a recorded **subordination agreement** to take a lower
position than recording order would give. This is routine when an owner refinances a first deed of
trust while a home equity line remains: without subordination, the equity line would advance to
first position and the new lender would refuse to close.

## 13.5 Release and the licensee's role

A lien ends when the obligation is satisfied and a **release** — for a deed of trust, a
**certificate of satisfaction** — is recorded. Payment alone does not clear the record. Unreleased
paid-off deeds of trust are among the most common clouds a title search turns up, and clearing one
requires locating a lender that may have been acquired twice since.

Liens are found by title search, cleared by the settlement agent, and interpreted by counsel. The
licensee's contribution is timing and disclosure: get the title work ordered early, read Schedule
B-I when it arrives, escalate anything involving construction or a judgment immediately, and
disclose material facts actually known under § 54.1-2131 A 6 or § 54.1-2132 A 7.

### Hour 13 engagement check

**Question.** A property is sold at a foreclosure sale under a deed of trust recorded in 2019.
Also of record: unpaid real property taxes for the current year, a judgment docketed in 2021, and a
second deed of trust recorded in 2022. Rank the claims on the sale proceeds and say which liens
survive the sale.

chunks.heading: Hour 14 — Taxes in real estate
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** The **real property tax lien** is paid first by statutory priority regardless
of date. Then the **2019 first deed of trust**, the foreclosing lien. Then, from any surplus, the
**2021 judgment**, then the **2022 second deed of trust**, in recording order. The 2021 judgment and
the 2022 deed of trust are **junior** to the foreclosing lien and are extinguished as to the
property, whether or not they are paid; the debts themselves may survive against the debtor
personally. Nothing here is advice a licensee gives — this is why a buyer at a foreclosure sale
needs counsel.

---

## Hour 14 — Taxes in real estate

## 14.1 Ad valorem taxation

**Ad valorem** means "according to value". Real property tax is levied annually on the assessed
value of the property, by the locality — in Virginia, the city or county — and it funds schools,
public safety, roads, and local services.

The arithmetic has three moving parts:

**Assessed value** — the value the locality's assessor places on the property. It may equal market
value or a stated fraction of it, depending on the jurisdiction's practice, and it is set on an
assessment cycle rather than continuously.

**The rate** — set annually by the governing body. In Virginia it is conventionally expressed in
dollars per $100 of assessed value. A rate of $1.05 means $1.05 of tax for every $100 of assessed
value. Elsewhere rates are expressed in **mills** — thousandths of a dollar, so 10.5 mills is the
same as $10.50 per $1,000, or $1.05 per $100. Students should be able to move between the two.

chunks.heading: 14.2 Assessment, appeal, and what a licensee may say
chunks.excerpt:
**Exemptions and relief** — reductions available to particular owners or uses: religious and
charitable ownership, government property, land-use assessment for agricultural and forest land,
and relief programmes for the elderly, for people with disabilities, and for certain disabled
veterans. Eligibility is determined by the locality, not by the licensee.

**Worked example.** Assessed value $340,000; rate $1.05 per $100.
$340,000 ÷ 100 = 3,400 hundreds. 3,400 × $1.05 = **$3,570 annual tax.**

If instead the rate is expressed as 10.5 mills: $340,000 × 0.0105 = **$3,570.** Same answer.

## 14.2 Assessment, appeal, and what a licensee may say

An owner who believes an assessment is wrong has an administrative route — an appeal to the
assessor, then to a board of equalisation, then to court. The grounds are that the assessment
exceeds fair market value or is not uniform with comparable properties.

Two cautions belong here. First, **assessed value is not market value and must never be presented
to a client as evidence of it.** A buyer told that "the assessment is $340,000, so it's worth at
least that" has been misinformed. Second, an assessment can and often does change **after a sale**,
and a licensee who tells a buyer their taxes will stay at the seller's level is making a prediction
that will frequently prove false. The accurate statement is that the current tax is X, that
assessment practice is set by the locality, and that the buyer should confirm with the
commissioner of the revenue or assessor's office.

## 14.3 Other taxes touching real estate

chunks.heading: 14.4 The referral rule, stated plainly
chunks.excerpt:
**Recordation tax** is charged on recording deeds and deeds of trust; **grantor's tax** is charged
to the seller on conveyance. Rates and the allocation between the parties are set by statute and by
contract, and the settlement agent computes them. This course states no figure, because the
statutory rates in Title 58.1 have not been read from primary text for this project.

**Transfer of a principal residence and capital gain.** A homeowner selling a residence may be
eligible to exclude gain from federal income tax subject to ownership and use requirements and
dollar limits set by federal law. **Basis** is broadly the purchase price plus capital improvements
minus depreciation taken. Every element of this depends on the taxpayer's circumstances and on law
that changes.

**Income-property taxation** — depreciation, passive-activity treatment, deferred exchanges —
belongs to Hour 46 and to the client's tax professional.

**Property tax deduction and mortgage interest deduction** are federal matters subject to
limitations that change.

## 14.4 The referral rule, stated plainly

A real estate licensee is not licensed to give tax advice. The client's tax outcome depends on
facts the licensee does not have and on rules the licensee is not qualified to apply. Under
§ 54.1-2131 A 4 the duty is **ordinary care**, and telling a client something outside the
licensee's competence is not ordinary care. Under 18VAC135-20-300 a material misstatement is a
disciplinary matter.

The professional formulation: *here is the current annual tax on this property from the
locality's record; here is what the assessment cycle is; questions about what you will owe, and
about the tax consequences of buying or selling, go to your tax adviser, and I am putting that in
writing.*

chunks.heading: 14.5 Proration, introduced
chunks.excerpt:
## 14.5 Proration, introduced

**Proration** divides a shared expense between seller and buyer at closing according to the period
each owns the property. Taxes, association dues, rent, and prepaid fuel are commonly prorated. Full
mechanics are Hour 41; the concept is introduced here because it is a tax topic.

**Worked example.** Annual tax $3,570, paid in arrears, settlement on 15 September, using a
365-day year and charging the day of settlement to the buyer.
Daily rate: $3,570 ÷ 365 = **$9.7808** per day.
Seller's period: 1 January through 14 September = 257 days.
Seller's share: 257 × $9.7808 = **$2,513.67**, which appears as a **credit to the buyer and a debit
to the seller**, because the buyer will pay the whole bill when it comes due.

Change any convention — a 360-day year, a different settlement-day rule, taxes paid in advance —
and the number changes. **The convention comes from the contract, not from a habit.**

### Hour 14 engagement check

**Question.** A property is assessed at $412,000 in a locality with a rate of $0.89 per $100.
Compute the annual tax. Then state, in one sentence each, why the licensee may not tell the buyer
(a) that the property is worth at least $412,000 and (b) that the tax will remain at this level.

**Expected answer.** $412,000 ÷ 100 = 4,120; 4,120 × $0.89 = **$3,666.80**. (a) Assessed value is
an administrative figure produced on an assessment cycle for taxation and is not evidence of market
value; presenting it as such is a misrepresentation. (b) Assessment practice and rates are set by
the locality and commonly change after a sale, so a statement that the tax will stay level is a
prediction the licensee cannot support and the buyer must confirm with the locality.

---

## Hour 15 — Contract foundations

chunks.heading: 15.1 The four requirements
chunks.excerpt:
## 15.1 The four requirements

A **contract** is a legally enforceable agreement. Four elements are required:

**Mutual assent** — an offer and an acceptance, producing a meeting of the minds on the essential
terms. Assent must be genuine: fraud, misrepresentation, mistake, duress, and undue influence each
undermine it.

**Competent parties** — parties with legal capacity. Minors, persons adjudicated incompetent, and
persons lacking capacity at the moment of contracting are treated specially; a minor's contract is
generally **voidable by the minor**.

**Lawful objective** — the purpose must be legal. A contract to do something illegal is void and no
court will enforce it.

**Consideration** — something of legal value exchanged by each side. Courts examine whether
consideration exists, not whether it was adequate.

For contracts concerning land there is a fifth practical requirement: the **statute of frauds**
requires a contract for the sale of an interest in real property to be **in writing and signed by
the party to be charged**. An oral agreement to sell land is not enforceable, however clear the
evidence of it.

## 15.2 The four states of a contract

Students confuse these constantly, and examination questions exploit it.

**Valid** — meets all requirements and is binding on both parties.

**Void** — has no legal effect at all and never did. Nothing to enforce. An agreement with an
illegal objective, or a deed from a person adjudicated incompetent.

**Voidable** — valid and enforceable **unless** the party with the power to avoid it chooses to
disaffirm. A minor's contract; a contract induced by fraud, at the defrauded party's option. Until
disaffirmed, it operates.

chunks.heading: 15.3 Other classifications
chunks.excerpt:
**Unenforceable** — valid on its face but not enforceable in court. An oral land contract is the
standard example; so is a claim barred by the statute of limitations. The parties may perform it
voluntarily; no court will make them.

## 15.3 Other classifications

**Bilateral or unilateral.** In a **bilateral** contract each side makes a promise — a residential
sales contract is bilateral. In a **unilateral** contract only one party promises, and the other
accepts by performing; an open listing and a reward offer are the classic examples.

**Executory or executed.** **Executory** means something remains to be done — a ratified sales
contract before settlement is executory. **Executed** means fully performed. Note the trap: a
signed contract is often loosely called "executed" in the industry, meaning signed, while the legal
meaning is *performed*. Examinations use the legal meaning.

**Express or implied.** **Express** contracts are stated in words, written or spoken. **Implied**
contracts are inferred from conduct.

## 15.4 Discharge, breach, and remedies

A contract is discharged by **performance**, by **mutual agreement to rescind**, by **novation** —
substituting a new contract or a new party with the consent of all — by **operation of law**, or by
**breach**.

Remedies for breach in a real estate contract include:

**Damages** — money to put the injured party where performance would have. **Liquidated damages** —
a sum the parties fixed in advance, commonly the earnest money deposit. **Rescission** — unwinding
the contract and restoring the parties. **Specific performance** — a court order to convey, which
is available in land contracts precisely because every parcel is unique and money is treated as an
inadequate substitute.

chunks.heading: 15.5 The licensee's boundary
chunks.excerpt:
**Assignment** transfers a party's rights under a contract to another; **novation** replaces a
party entirely and, unlike assignment, releases the original party.

## 15.5 The licensee's boundary

**§ 54.1-2101.1** of the Code of Virginia governs preparation of real estate contracts by
licensees, and §§ 54.1-2131 A 2 b and 54.1-2132 A 3 b describe the duty as *assisting in the
drafting and negotiating of offers and counteroffers, amendments, and addenda to the real estate
contract pursuant to § 54.1-2101.1*.

Read those together and the shape is clear: filling in and assisting with contract forms in the
manner the statute permits is licensed activity. **Deciding what a clause means, drafting bespoke
language to solve a legal problem, or advising a client whether to declare a breach is not.** The
question "am I in default?" goes to an attorney every time.

### Hour 15 engagement check

**Question.** Classify each and give the one-line reason. (a) An oral agreement to buy a house,
fully agreed on all terms. (b) A sales contract signed by a 16-year-old buyer. (c) A contract to
buy a property for use as an unlicensed gambling operation. (d) A ratified sales contract awaiting
settlement in three weeks.

**Expected answer.** (a) **Unenforceable** — the statute of frauds requires a signed writing for a
contract concerning an interest in land. (b) **Voidable** at the minor's option — the minor lacks
full capacity, and the contract operates until disaffirmed. (c) **Void** — unlawful objective, no
legal effect from the outset. (d) **Valid and executory** — all elements are present and
performance remains outstanding.

---

## Hour 16 — Offer, acceptance, and contract formation

## 16.1 The offer

chunks.heading: 16.2 How an offer ends
chunks.excerpt:
An **offer** is a proposal that, if accepted, forms a contract. It must show present intent to be
bound, be communicated to the offeree, and state the essential terms with enough definiteness that
a court could enforce them — parties, property, price, and the material terms of the transaction.

An advertisement is generally **not** an offer; it is an invitation to make one. A listing is not an
offer to sell to whoever appears.

## 16.2 How an offer ends

An offer terminates on:

**Acceptance**, which forms the contract.

**Rejection.** Once rejected, an offer is dead. The offeree cannot change their mind and accept it.

**Counteroffer**, which is in law a rejection plus a new offer. This is the mechanic students most
often get wrong, and it has a practical consequence worth stating: **the moment a seller
counteroffers, the buyer's original offer no longer exists**, and if the buyer walks away the seller
cannot then accept the original.

**Revocation by the offeror**, effective when communicated to the offeree, at any time before
acceptance — unless the offeree has paid for an **option**, which is a separate contract holding the
offer open for a stated period.

**Lapse of time**, on the expiration stated in the offer, or after a reasonable time if none is
stated.

**Death or incapacity** of either party before acceptance.

**Destruction of the subject property** before acceptance.

## 16.3 Acceptance

Acceptance must be **unqualified** — the mirror image rule — and must be **communicated** in the
manner the offer requires or permits. Any change to terms is a counteroffer.

chunks.heading: 16.4 Multiple offers
chunks.excerpt:
The moment of formation matters because it starts every deadline in the contract. Two rules
compete. The traditional **mailbox rule** treats a mailed acceptance as effective on dispatch. Most
modern residential contracts displace it by requiring **delivery** of the signed acceptance, and
defining what delivery means. **Read the contract; do not assume the common-law rule.**

## 16.4 Multiple offers

The rules above resolve most multiple-offer confusion.

A seller may accept one offer, counter one, counter several, or reject all. Countering several
simultaneously creates a real risk: if two counteroffers are accepted, the seller may have two
contracts on one property. Sellers who wish to negotiate with several buyers at once need language
making acceptance subject to the seller's further written approval — and drafting that language is
a legal question.

The licensee's own duties in a multiple-offer situation are statutory and specific. Under
§ 54.1-2131 A 2 c a licensee engaged by a seller must **receive and present in a timely manner
written offers and counteroffers to and from the seller and purchasers, even when the property is
already subject to a contract of sale.** Under 18VAC135-20-300 3 it is misrepresentation or
omission to fail **to tender promptly to the client or unrepresented party every written offer,
every written counteroffer, and every written rejection**.

Two consequences follow that licensees get wrong: **every** written offer goes to the seller,
including one the licensee thinks is insulting; and an existing ratified contract does not stop the
obligation to present a later offer, though it does not entitle the seller to accept it either.

chunks.heading: 16.5 Amendments, addenda, assignment, and electronic signature
chunks.excerpt:
Whether to disclose the existence or terms of competing offers is a different question, controlled
by the client's instructions and by the confidentiality duty in § 54.1-2131 A 3. The client decides
what is disclosed about their own transaction; the licensee follows lawful instructions and does
not volunteer another client's confidences.

## 16.5 Amendments, addenda, assignment, and electronic signature

An **addendum** is attached at the time of contracting and forms part of the original agreement. An
**amendment** changes an existing contract and requires the assent of all parties. A **contingency**
is a condition that must be satisfied or waived for a duty to become absolute, and Hour 18 covers
their operation.

**Assignment** of a real estate contract transfers the assignor's rights to an assignee; whether it
is permitted depends on the contract's own terms, and many residential forms restrict it.

**Electronic records and signatures** are effective for real estate contracts under federal
E-SIGN and state adoptions of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, subject to the parties'
consent to transact electronically. The professional issues are practical rather than doctrinal:
verifying identity, preserving the record, controlling version drift when several counter-signed
copies circulate, and — the risk that actually causes losses — **wire fraud**, where an intercepted
email carries changed settlement instructions. Hour 50 is devoted to it.

### Hour 16 engagement check

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
**Question.** Buyer A offers $400,000. Seller counters at $415,000. While the counteroffer is
outstanding, Buyer B offers $412,000. Buyer A then says "we accept your counter" but has not yet
delivered a signed copy. The seller now wants Buyer B's offer. What is the position, and what must
the licensee do with Buyer B's offer?

**Expected answer.** Whether a contract with Buyer A has formed depends on the contract's own
delivery requirement: under most modern residential forms acceptance is effective on **delivery**
of the signed acceptance, not on an oral statement of intent, so on these facts a contract has
probably not yet formed and the seller may still revoke the counteroffer before delivery. That is
close enough to a legal question that the correct professional step is counsel, not a licensee's
ruling. What is not in doubt is the licensee's own duty: **Buyer B's written offer must be
presented to the seller promptly** under § 54.1-2131 A 2 c and 18VAC135-20-300 3, and it must be
presented even if the licensee believes a contract with Buyer A already exists.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 04

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 04
chunks.excerpt:
Virginia-specific statements rest on: **§ 54.1-2131 A 2 c** (receiving and presenting written offers
and counteroffers in a timely manner, even when the property is already under contract),
**§ 54.1-2131 A 3** (confidentiality), **§ 54.1-2131 A 4** (ordinary care), **§ 54.1-2131 A 6** and
**§ 54.1-2132 A 7** (disclosure of material facts of actual knowledge), **§ 54.1-2101.1** with
**§§ 54.1-2131 A 2 b and 54.1-2132 A 3 b** (contract preparation and the assisting-in-drafting
duty), and **18VAC135-20-300 3** (failure to tender promptly every written offer, counteroffer and
rejection). All read from law.lis.virginia.gov on 2026-08-20; recorded in
`virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`.

Three matters are deliberately **left unstated** for want of a primary reading: the deadlines and
formalities of the **Virginia mechanics' lien** scheme in **Title 43**; the **recordation and
grantor's tax rates** in **Title 58.1**; and the statutory formulation of **tax-lien priority**.
Each is identified to the student as a question for the settlement agent or counsel rather than
answered with a figure. An instructor supplementing this text must read the title first.

The proration in Hour 14.5 uses a 365-day year and charges the settlement day to the buyer. Both
are **conventions taken from the contract**, not rules of law, and the hour says so.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 05

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 05
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 05

## Course Day 5 · Hours 17–20 · The sales contract, disclosure, and the start of agency

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(4) Contracts · (15) Brokerage agreements and agency
contract responsibilities · (19) Title closing · (22) Regulatory statutes · (23) Housing
legislation
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Identify the standard components of a residential sales contract and say what risk each
  allocates.
- Distinguish satisfaction, waiver, and expiration of a contingency and build a deadline map from a
  ratification date.
- State what the Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act actually requires of an owner, and
  correct the common belief that Virginia is a condition-disclosure state.
- Apply the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement to a fact pattern.
- Distinguish client from customer, and state the two things § 54.1-2136 requires a licensee to say
  before any brokerage relationship begins.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 17 — Sales contract structure and risk allocation
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 17 | Sales contract structure and risk allocation | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 18 | Performance, breach, remedies, and contingencies | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 19 | Electronic transactions and property disclosures | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 20 | Brokerage agreements and agency fundamentals | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 20 |

---

## Hour 17 — Sales contract structure and risk allocation

## 17.1 A contract is a map of who bears which risk

A residential sales contract looks like a form to be filled in. It is better understood as a series
of decisions about **who carries which risk between now and settlement**. Every blank is a risk
allocation. A student who reads the form that way will never wonder why a clause exists.

## 17.2 The components

**Parties.** Full legal names, and the capacity in which each signs. A trust, an estate, or an LLC
signs through someone whose authority must be evidenced. Getting the party wrong is not a
typographical problem; it is a title problem discovered at closing.

**Property.** The legal description, and everything conveyed with it. This is where the fixture work
of Hour 4 lands: items included, items excluded, and personal property conveyed by bill of sale.

chunks.heading: 17.2 The components
chunks.excerpt:
**Price and deposit.** The purchase price, and the **earnest money deposit** — its amount, who holds
it, when it is delivered, and what happens to it in each way the contract can end. In Virginia,
deposit money held by a firm is escrow money subject to **18VAC135-20-181**, and the statutory
protections in **§§ 54.1-2108, 54.1-2108.1 and 54.1-2108.2** apply. The deposit is not the seller's
money and it is not the firm's; it is held.

**Financing terms.** Whether the purchase is cash or financed, the loan type and amount, and — the
operative part — the **financing contingency**: the period in which the buyer must obtain a
commitment, and what happens if they do not.

**Settlement and possession.** The settlement date, who conducts settlement, and when possession
transfers. **Settlement and possession are separate**, and any gap between them needs its own
written agreement.

**Title.** The quality of title the seller must convey, the buyer's right to examine and object,
the period for objection, and the seller's right and obligation to cure.

**Inspections and investigations.** Which investigations the buyer may make, in what period, at
whose cost, and what remedies follow an unsatisfactory result.

**Risk of loss.** Who bears a casualty loss between ratification and settlement, and what happens if
the property is materially damaged.

**Default and remedies.** What each party may do if the other fails to perform, and how the deposit
is treated.

**Notices.** How notice is given and when it is effective. This clause decides disputes about
whether a deadline was met.

**Time provisions.** Whether time is of the essence, how days are counted, and whether weekends and
holidays count.

chunks.heading: 17.3 Where the money sits
chunks.excerpt:
**Contingencies and addenda.** Everything conditional, and every attachment that forms part of the
agreement.

## 17.3 Where the money sits

A licensee should be able to explain the deposit's life cycle without hesitating: received;
delivered to the holder named in the contract within the time the contract and the regulations
require; deposited into a designated escrow account that is **in the firm's licensed name, labelled
escrow at the financial institution, and sufficient at all times to account for all funds held**
(18VAC135-20-181 A 1); disbursed only as the contract and the law permit; and accounted for in a
timely manner under § 54.1-2131 A 5.

The disputed-deposit situation is where licensees create liability. When buyer and seller both
claim the deposit, the firm may not simply pick a side. Virginia legislates this specifically at
**§ 54.1-2108.2**, which addresses protection of escrow funds on termination of a purchase
contract. The professional answer is to follow the contract, the statute, and the firm's written
policy — which § 54.1-2110.1 B 2 a requires the firm to have — and to escalate to the principal
broker immediately.

## 17.4 Issue-spotting without giving legal advice

A licensee reviewing a contract is looking for **incompleteness and inconsistency**, not for legal
meaning. Blanks not filled. Dates that contradict one another — a financing contingency expiring
after settlement, an inspection period ending before the contract was ratified. Parties named
inconsistently between page one and the signature block. Addenda referenced but not attached.
Initials missing where a change was made. A deposit whose delivery deadline has already passed.

chunks.heading: Hour 17 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Those are within the licensee's competence and are exactly what ordinary care under § 54.1-2131 A 4
requires. **What a clause means, and what a party should do about a breach, are not.**

### Hour 17 engagement check

**Question.** A ratified contract sets settlement for 30 October, a financing contingency expiring
15 November, and an inspection period of "ten days from ratification" where ratification occurred
on 2 October. Identify every problem a licensee should raise, and say what the licensee must not do.

**Expected answer.** The financing contingency expires **after** settlement, which is incoherent —
the buyer's protection would not resolve until after they were obliged to complete. The inspection
period ends 12 October, which is workable but tight and should be confirmed against the contract's
day-counting rule and its notice provision. The licensee should raise both, in writing, to their
client and to the other side immediately, and route them to the parties for correction by written
amendment. The licensee must **not** decide what the conflicting dates legally mean, must not tell
the client which date controls, and must not redraft the clause; that is counsel's work under the
limits of § 54.1-2101.1.

---

## Hour 18 — Performance, breach, remedies, and contingencies

## 18.1 What a contingency does

A **contingency** makes a party's duty to perform conditional on a stated event. Until the
condition is resolved, the contract exists and binds — but the conditioned duty is not yet absolute.

Three things can happen to a contingency:

**Satisfaction.** The event occurs. The buyer obtains the loan commitment; the inspection produces
an acceptable result. The condition drops away and the duty becomes absolute.

chunks.heading: 18.2 The common contingencies
chunks.excerpt:
**Waiver.** The party the contingency protects gives it up voluntarily, in writing. A buyer who
waives the financing contingency is now obliged to complete whether or not the loan arrives, and
their deposit is exposed.

**Failure with a stated consequence.** The event does not occur within the period, and the contract
says what follows — usually a right to terminate on written notice within a stated time, with the
deposit returned.

The fourth possibility is the dangerous one: **the period expires and nobody does anything.** Under
many forms a contingency not exercised in time is deemed satisfied or waived. A buyer who lets an
inspection period lapse without giving notice may have lost the protection entirely. That is why
deadline management is a core professional skill and not an administrative chore.

## 18.2 The common contingencies

**Financing.** The buyer must obtain a written commitment for a loan of a stated type and amount
within a stated period. Note what it does not do: a commitment is not funding, and a commitment can
be withdrawn if the buyer's circumstances change. The licensee's instruction to a buyer during the
contract period — do not change jobs, do not open credit accounts, do not move large sums — is not
folklore; it protects the commitment.

**Appraisal.** In practice usually tied to financing, sometimes separate. If the appraised value
comes in below the contract price, the lender lends against the lower figure and the gap must be
closed by the buyer, by the seller, or by termination.

chunks.heading: 18.3 Breach and remedies
chunks.excerpt:
**Inspection.** The buyer investigates the condition. Depending on the form, the buyer may have a
right to request repairs, a right to terminate outright, or both. **A home inspection is performed
by a home inspector**, defined for Virginia purposes in § 54.1-500, and it is not the licensee's
inspection and not the licensee's opinion.

**Title.** The buyer examines and objects; the seller cures or does not.

**Sale of the buyer's current home.** The most fragile contingency, and the one most often paired
with a kick-out clause allowing the seller to continue marketing.

**Association documents.** In a common-interest community, the buyer's right to receive and review
the governing documents and a resale certificate, with a statutory right to cancel within a period
set by Virginia's condominium and property owners' association statutes. Hours 29 and 30 develop
this.

## 18.3 Breach and remedies

A **material breach** is a failure that defeats the purpose of the contract. A trivial failure is
not a breach that permits termination, and calling one a breach is itself a breach.

Remedies, from Hour 15, applied here: **damages**; **liquidated damages**, usually the deposit;
**rescission**; and **specific performance**, which a buyer may seek because land is unique and a
seller may sometimes seek as well. Contracts frequently require **mitigation** — the injured party
must not sit still and let the loss grow.

chunks.heading: 18.4 Building a deadline map
chunks.excerpt:
The single most important sentence in this hour: **whether a party is in default, and what remedy
follows, are legal conclusions.** A licensee who tells a client "they've breached, keep the
deposit" has given legal advice and, if wrong, has caused a loss. Under § 54.1-2131 A 4 the duty is
ordinary care; the ordinary-care answer is *this needs your attorney, today, and here is the
deadline we are working against.*

## 18.4 Building a deadline map

A working method, and one a student should be able to reproduce:

Start from the **ratification date** — the date the last party signed and delivered, as the contract
defines delivery. Read the day-counting rule: are these calendar days or business days, is day zero
the ratification date or the day after, do weekends and holidays extend a deadline that falls on
one. Then list every deadline in date order: deposit delivery, inspection period end, notice
deadline following inspection, association document delivery and cancellation period, loan
application, appraisal, title examination and objection, seller cure period, loan commitment,
walk-through, settlement.

Against each, record **who acts, what document is required, and what happens if the date passes**.
Then work backward and set internal reminders several days ahead of each. A deadline discovered on
the day it falls is a deadline already partly lost.

### Hour 18 engagement check

**Question.** The inspection report identifies a failing HVAC system. The buyer's licensee is asked,
"can we just cancel and get our deposit back?" What does the licensee do, and what does the licensee
not do?

chunks.heading: Hour 19 — Electronic transactions and property disclosures
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** The licensee reads the contract's inspection contingency with the buyer and
identifies **what the contingency actually permits** — request repairs, terminate, or both — the
**deadline** for acting, and the **form of notice** the contract requires, and then makes sure the
buyer acts within that period. The licensee does **not** advise whether the buyer is entitled to the
deposit, does not characterise the seller's position as a breach, and does not tell the buyer the
inspection result is or is not serious. Whether termination is available and whether the deposit is
returnable are legal conclusions for counsel; the licensee's job is to protect the deadline and put
the question in front of the right person in time.

---

## Hour 19 — Electronic transactions and property disclosures

## 19.1 Electronic records and signatures

Electronic records and signatures are valid for real estate transactions under the federal
**Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act** and under state adoption of the
**Uniform Electronic Transactions Act**, provided the parties have agreed to transact
electronically. A contract is not less enforceable because it was signed on a screen.

The professional issues are practical. **Consent** must be obtained and recorded. **Identity** must
be established by the signing platform. **Integrity** of the record must be preserved, including
the audit trail showing who signed what and when. **Version control** matters more than people
expect: when three counter-signed copies circulate, the question of which document is the contract
becomes real. And **delivery** — the act that usually forms the contract — must be executed the way
the contract defines it, not the way habit suggests.

chunks.heading: 19.2 The Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act — what it actually says
chunks.excerpt:
## 19.2 The Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act — what it actually says

This is the section of the course most likely to be taught wrongly, because most national material
describes a different model.

In many states the seller completes a **condition disclosure form**: a checklist of the roof, the
plumbing, the electrical system, known defects, and so on. Virginia does not work that way.

**§ 55.1-703** is headed *Required disclosures for buyer to beware; buyer to exercise necessary due
diligence.* The owner of residential real property furnishes the purchaser a **residential property
disclosure statement**, and that statement is **provided by the Real Estate Board on its website**.
What the statement contains is a series of statements that **the owner makes no representations** —
about the condition of the property or its improvements, about covenants and restrictions, about
mineral rights conveyances, about current lot lines or the ability to expand or add structures,
about matters pertaining to adjacent parcels including their zoning and permitted uses, about
whether a historic district ordinance affects the property, and about whether the property contains
resource protection areas under a locality's Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act ordinance — each
coupled with advice that the purchaser **exercise whatever due diligence that purchaser deems
necessary**.

The statute names examples of that diligence: a **home inspection** as defined in § 54.1-500, a
**mold assessment** by a business following EPA guidance, a **residential building energy analysis**
as defined in § 54.1-1144, a **property survey**, and **contacting the locality** about zoning, lot
coverage, height and setback requirements.

chunks.heading: 19.3 What the licensee must disclose, which is a different question
chunks.excerpt:
So the correct statement of Virginia law is: **the seller's statutory instrument disclaims
representations and directs the buyer to investigate.** A licensee who tells a buyer "the seller's
disclosure will tell you about the roof" has described another state's law.

**Version warning.** The text read for this course carries the heading *(Effective until January 1,
2027)*. A successor version exists and has not been read. Every statement in this hour about the
statement's contents must be rechecked against the operative version before the course is delivered
on or after that date, under the legal-update control in `virginia/compliance/legal-update-sop.md`.

## 19.3 What the licensee must disclose, which is a different question

The Act governs the **owner**. The licensee's duties are separate and come from Chapter 21.

A licensee engaged by a **seller** must, under **§ 54.1-2131 B**, treat all prospective buyers
honestly, not knowingly give false information, and **disclose all material adverse facts pertaining
to the physical condition of the property that are actually known by the licensee**, in writing.
The statute then draws the boundary of that duty: "physical condition of the property" refers to the
land and the improvements on it and **does not** refer to (i) matters outside the boundaries of the
land or relating to adjacent or nearby properties, (ii) matters relating to governmental land use
regulations, or (iii) matters relating to highways or public streets.

chunks.heading: 19.4 Federal lead-based paint disclosure
chunks.excerpt:
Two consequences. First, this is an **actual knowledge** standard, not a duty to investigate — a
licensee is not required to discover defects. Second, it is narrower than students expect: a known
plan to widen the road in front of the house is a matter relating to highways or public streets and
sits outside the physical-condition duty, though other duties may still bear on it and the honest
professional answer is usually to say what you know and point the buyer to the locality.

**Defective drywall** is named specifically in both § 54.1-2131 B and § 54.1-2132 B: a licensee with
**actual knowledge** of defective drywall in a residential property, as defined in § 36-156.1, must
disclose it — the seller's licensee to the prospective buyer, the buyer's licensee to the buyer.

To the **client**, the duty is broader in subject and identical in standard: under § 54.1-2131 A 6
and § 54.1-2132 A 7 the licensee discloses material facts **related to the property or concerning
the transaction** of which the licensee has actual knowledge.

## 19.4 Federal lead-based paint disclosure

This is federal law and it applies in Virginia regardless of anything in state law.

For **target housing** — most residential housing built **before 1978**, excluding housing for the
elderly or persons with disabilities unless a child under six resides there, and zero-bedroom
dwellings — a seller or landlord must:

chunks.heading: Hour 19 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
- disclose known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards, and provide any available records
  and reports;
- give the purchaser or lessee the EPA-approved pamphlet;
- include the prescribed warning statement and acknowledgments in the contract or lease;
- and, **for sales**, give the purchaser a **ten-day** opportunity to conduct a risk assessment or
  inspection, unless the parties agree in writing to a different period.

The licensee's obligation is to ensure compliance and to retain the signed acknowledgment. This is
one of the few disclosure requirements where the licensee is personally exposed, and it is not
waivable by the seller's preference.

### Hour 19 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer asks, "the seller has to tell me about any problems with the house, right?"
Give the accurate Virginia answer in three sentences, and say what you would put in writing.

**Expected answer.** No — Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act is a **buyer-beware**
statute: the owner furnishes a Real Estate Board statement whose content is that the owner makes no
representations about the condition of the property, and which advises the purchaser to exercise
whatever due diligence the purchaser deems necessary. Separately, a **licensee** representing the
seller must disclose material adverse facts about the **physical condition** of the property that
the licensee **actually knows**, and any actual knowledge of defective drywall, in writing — but
that is an actual-knowledge duty, not a duty to investigate. In writing, I would confirm that the
buyer should obtain their own inspection, survey and any specialist assessments within the
contingency period, and name the deadline.

---

## Hour 20 — Brokerage agreements and agency fundamentals

chunks.heading: 20.1 The vocabulary, and why Virginia's differs
chunks.excerpt:
## 20.1 The vocabulary, and why Virginia's differs

Most national material teaches the **common law of agency**: principal, agent, fiduciary duties,
and a body of case law. Virginia has displaced it in this field. **§ 54.1-2144** is titled *Common
law abrogated*, and it provides that the common law of agency relative to brokerage relationships in
real estate transactions is **expressly abrogated to the extent inconsistent with the article**.

The practical instruction to a student is exact: **a Virginia brokerage-relationship question is
answered from §§ 54.1-2130 through 54.1-2146, not from general agency doctrine.** Where a national
text and the Code differ, the Code governs in Virginia.

Virginia's own vocabulary, from § 54.1-2130 and the sections that follow, distinguishes a
**standard agent**, a **limited service agent**, and an **independent contractor** representative,
and speaks of a licensee **engaged by** a client. The word "client" is the person the licensee
represents; a **customer** is a party to the transaction whom the licensee does not represent.

## 20.2 Client and customer

The distinction decides what is owed.

To a **client**, the licensee owes the full set of statutory duties in § 54.1-2131 (seller),
§ 54.1-2132 (buyer), § 54.1-2133 (landlord), § 54.1-2134 (tenant), or § 54.1-2135 (management) —
performance per the agreement, promotion of the client's interests, confidentiality, ordinary care,
timely accounting, disclosure of material facts actually known, and compliance with the article and
fair housing law.

chunks.heading: 20.3 What must be said before anything begins
chunks.excerpt:
To a **customer**, the licensee owes honesty, the statutory disclosures, and no knowing false
information — and, for a seller's licensee dealing with a prospective buyer, the written disclosure
of material adverse facts about the physical condition actually known.

**Ministerial acts** are the bridge. Under § 54.1-2131 C and § 54.1-2132 C a licensee may provide
assistance to the other side by performing ministerial acts, and doing so does **not** breach the
brokerage agreement and does **not** create a brokerage relationship with that party — provided the
acts are not inconsistent with the licensee's duties and are not prohibited by the agreement.
Opening a door, providing a form, transmitting a document: ministerial. Advising the other side on
price or strategy: not.

## 20.3 What must be said before anything begins

**§ 54.1-2136, Preconditions to brokerage relationship**, is short and absolute. Before entering
into any brokerage relationship, the licensee shall advise the prospective client of:

**(i) the type of brokerage relationship proposed by the broker**, and
**(ii) the broker's compensation and whether the broker will share such salary or compensation with
another broker who may have a brokerage relationship with another party to the transaction.**

Both, before the relationship begins. Not at the listing appointment's end, not at the contract.

## 20.4 The brokerage agreement itself

**§ 54.1-2137** governs. The relationship commences when the client engages the licensee, and
continues until performance is complete or the earlier of an agreed expiration date, mutual
termination, a default, or a termination under § 54.1-2139 G.

chunks.heading: 20.5 After it ends
chunks.excerpt:
**Except as otherwise provided, a licensee shall enter into a brokerage agreement with a prospective
client before providing brokerage services** — § 54.1-2137 B. Preparing property-specific materials
with the intent to obtain a relationship does not require an agreement first.

Brokerage agreements **shall be in writing** and shall:

1. **Have a definite termination date; if none is specified, the agreement terminates 90 days after
   its date.**
2. State the **amount of the brokerage fees and how and when they are to be paid**.
3. State the **services to be rendered**.
4. Include the other terms the client and licensee agreed.
5. Where entered in conjunction with consent to dual representation, carry the § 54.1-2139 A
   disclosures.

And under § 54.1-2110.1 B 6, brokerage agreements must **include the name and contact information
of the supervising broker**.

The buyer side carries an additional rule that surprises licensees from other states. **§ 54.1-2132
A 1: a licensee engaged by a buyer shall enter into a brokerage agreement with the prospective buyer
prior to showing property to such prospective buyer.** In Virginia, the agreement comes before the
showing.

## 20.5 After it ends

**§ 54.1-2137 D:** except as otherwise agreed in writing, after termination, expiration, or
completion the licensee owes **no further duties** except to (i) **account** for all money and
property relating to the relationship and (ii) **keep confidential** the client's personal and
financial information and anything else the client asked be kept confidential — unless the law
provides otherwise or the client consents in writing to release.

chunks.heading: 20.6 Compensation is not representation
chunks.excerpt:
Confidentiality does not expire with the listing. That is the duty licensees most often forget, and
it is the one most likely to surface years later.

## 20.6 Compensation is not representation

**§ 54.1-2140:** the payment or promise of payment of compensation to a real estate broker **does
not create a brokerage relationship** between any broker, seller, landlord, buyer or tenant.

A seller paying a cooperating broker's fee does not thereby become that broker's client. Who pays
and who is represented are separate questions, and § 54.1-2136 (ii) requires the compensation
arrangement to be explained up front precisely so that nobody confuses them.

Similarly, **§ 54.1-2141**: a brokerage relationship is not created by using a common source
information company.

### Hour 20 engagement check

**Question.** A licensee meets a prospective buyer at an open house. The buyer asks to see three
other properties that afternoon. List, in order, what the licensee must do before showing any of
them, and cite the source for each step.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 05
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** First, under **§ 54.1-2136**, advise the prospective client of (i) the type of
brokerage relationship proposed and (ii) the broker's compensation and whether it will be shared
with a broker representing another party. Second, under **§ 54.1-2132 A 1**, enter into a
**written brokerage agreement with the buyer before showing property** — Virginia requires the
agreement first. Third, that agreement must satisfy **§ 54.1-2137 C**: in writing, with a definite
termination date (or it ends in 90 days), stating the fees and how and when paid, stating the
services, and — under **§ 54.1-2110.1 B 6** — carrying the supervising broker's name and contact
information. Separately, if in the meantime the licensee has a substantive discussion about a
specific property with someone who is neither their client nor represented, **§ 54.1-2138 A**
requires written disclosure of any brokerage relationship with another party, no later than when
specific real estate assistance is first provided.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 05

chunks.excerpt:

B and C** (ordinary care, accounting, disclosure of material facts of actual knowledge, the

**§ 54.1-2138 A** (disclosure of brokerage relationship), **§ 54.1-2140** and **§ 54.1-2141**
(compensation and common source information companies do not create relationships), **§ 54.1-2144**
(common law abrogated), **§ 54.1-2110.1 B 2 a and B 6** (written escrow policy; supervising broker
named in brokerage agreements), **§§ 54.1-2108, 54.1-2108.1, 54.1-2108.2** (escrow protection),
**§ 55.1-703** (buyer-beware disclosure statement), **§ 54.1-500** (home inspector) and

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 06
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 06

## Course Day 6 · Hours 21–24 · Virginia brokerage relationships, licensing, and discipline

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(15) Brokerage agreements and agency contract
responsibilities · (22) Regulatory statutes · (25) Real Estate Board regulations
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Recite the statutory duties a licensee engaged by a seller and by a buyer owes, and identify the
  standard attached to each.
- Distinguish a standard agent, a limited service agent, a dual agent, and a designated agent, and
  state what document each requires and when.
- Describe the Board and DPOR, the licence categories, and the supervisory structure a salesperson
  works inside.
- Identify conduct that constitutes a prohibited act, a conflict of interest, or a misrepresentation
  under 18VAC135-20, and state the standard by which a broker is held responsible for a
  salesperson's act.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 21 — Virginia duties to sellers, buyers, landlords, and tenants
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 21 | Virginia duties to sellers, buyers, landlords, and tenants | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 22 | Virginia brokerage disclosures: dual, designated, limited service | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 23 | Virginia licensing structure and regulatory authority | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 24 | Virginia standards of conduct and discipline | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 25 |

---

## Hour 21 — Virginia duties to sellers, buyers, landlords, and tenants

## 21.1 Five duty sections, one architecture

The article assigns duties by **who engaged the licensee**:

- **§ 54.1-2131** — licensees engaged by sellers
- **§ 54.1-2132** — licensees engaged by buyers
- **§ 54.1-2133** — licensees engaged by landlords to lease property
- **§ 54.1-2134** — licensees engaged by tenants
- **§ 54.1-2135** — licensees engaged to manage real estate

The four transactional sections share an architecture. Learn § 54.1-2131 properly and the others
follow, with the differences noted below.

## 21.2 The seller's licensee — § 54.1-2131 A

Seven duties:

**1. Perform in accordance with the terms of the brokerage agreement.** The agreement is the first
source of duty, not an afterthought.

chunks.heading: 21.2 The seller's licensee — § 54.1-2131 A
chunks.excerpt:
**2. Promote the interests of the seller by** four named activities:
 (a) **conducting marketing activities** per the agreement, seeking a sale at the agreed price and
 terms or at a price and terms acceptable to the seller — and note the express carve-out: the
 licensee is **not obligated to seek additional offers while the property is subject to a contract
 of sale**, unless the brokerage agreement or the contract of sale so provides;
 (b) **assisting in the drafting and negotiating** of offers, counteroffers, amendments and addenda
 **pursuant to § 54.1-2101.1**, and establishing strategies for the seller's objectives;
 (c) **receiving and presenting in a timely manner** written offers and counteroffers to and from
 the seller and purchasers — **even when the property is already subject to a contract of sale**;
 (d) providing reasonable assistance to satisfy the seller's contract obligations and to facilitate
 settlement.

**3. Maintain confidentiality** of all personal and financial information received from the client
during the relationship, and any other information the client asked be kept confidential, unless
the law provides otherwise or the seller consents **in writing** to release.

**4. Exercise ordinary care.** Not "utmost care", not a fiduciary standard imported from the common
law — **ordinary care**, because § 54.1-2144 abrogated the common law to the extent inconsistent.

**5. Account in a timely manner** for all money and property received in which the seller has or may
have an interest.

**6. Disclose to the seller material facts related to the property or concerning the transaction of
which the licensee has actual knowledge.**

chunks.heading: 21.3 The seller's licensee toward the other side — § 54.1-2131 B
chunks.excerpt:
**7. Comply** with the article, with all fair housing statutes and regulations applicable to
residential transactions, and with all other applicable law not in conflict with the article.

## 21.3 The seller's licensee toward the other side — § 54.1-2131 B

Treat all prospective buyers **honestly**; do not **knowingly** give false information. Disclose
**all material adverse facts pertaining to the physical condition of the property that are actually
known** by the licensee, **in writing**. Disclose actual knowledge of **defective drywall** as
defined in § 36-156.1.

And the statutory boundary, which Hour 19 introduced and which must be memorised: "physical
condition of the property" refers to the physical condition of the land and any improvements on it,
and **does not** refer to (i) matters outside the boundaries of the land or relating to adjacent or
other nearby properties, (ii) matters relating to governmental land use regulations, or (iii)
matters relating to highways or public streets.

The section closes with two protections and one preservation: **no cause of action arises against a
licensee for revealing information as required** by the article or applicable law; the section does
not limit the **Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act**; and ministerial acts for a buyer,
under subsection C, neither breach the seller agreement nor create a relationship with the buyer.

Subsection D adds that a seller's licensee does **not** breach any duty by showing alternative
properties to prospective buyers.

## 21.4 The buyer's licensee — § 54.1-2132

The same architecture, with three Virginia-specific differences a student must be able to state:

chunks.heading: 21.5 Landlord, tenant, and management
chunks.excerpt:
**A 1 — enter into a brokerage agreement with the prospective buyer *prior to showing property* to
that prospective buyer.** Virginia puts the agreement before the showing. This is the single most
distinctive rule in the article.

**A 3 a — the licensee is not obligated to seek or show other properties while the buyer is a party
to a contract to purchase**, unless the relationship provides otherwise. The mirror of the seller
carve-out.

**B — in a residential transaction the buyer's licensee shall disclose to the seller whether or not
the buyer intends to occupy the property as a principal residence.** The buyer's expression of that
intent in the contract satisfies the requirement, and no cause of action arises from the
disclosure, from an inaccuracy in it, or from its absence.

The rest tracks § 54.1-2131: perform per the agreement; promote the buyer's interests by seeking
suitable property, assisting in drafting and negotiating under § 54.1-2101.1, presenting written
offers and counteroffers in a timely manner even when the buyer is already under contract, and
assisting to settlement; confidentiality; **ordinary care**; timely accounting; disclosure of
material facts of actual knowledge; compliance with the article and fair housing.

Subsection D confirms that a buyer's licensee does not breach any duty by showing properties the
buyer is interested in to other prospective buyers, by representing other buyers, or by representing
sellers as to other properties.

## 21.5 Landlord, tenant, and management

chunks.heading: 21.5 Landlord, tenant, and management
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 54.1-2133** and **§ 54.1-2134** carry the same duty architecture into leasing — perform per the
agreement, promote the client's interests, confidentiality, **ordinary care**, timely accounting,
disclosure of material facts of **actual knowledge**, compliance with the article and fair housing.
**But they are not identical, and the difference decides what a licensee does first.**

**§ 54.1-2134 A 1 requires a licensee engaged by a tenant to *enter into a brokerage agreement with
the prospective tenant prior to showing property to such prospective tenant*.** That is the same
requirement § 54.1-2132 A 1 imposes on buyer representation. **§ 54.1-2133 imposes no such
requirement on a licensee engaged by a landlord**, and neither does § 54.1-2135 on a licensee engaged
to manage. So the rule to carry out of this hour is: **on the tenant side and the buyer side the
agreement comes before the showing; on the landlord side and the owner side it does not.**

chunks.heading: 21.6 Reading the standards, not the vocabulary
chunks.excerpt:
One further leasing duty has no counterpart in the sale sections. **§ 54.1-2133 B** requires a
licensee engaged by a landlord to disclose to prospective tenants all material adverse facts about
the physical condition of the property **that are actually known**, and adds a specific item: *"if a
licensee has actual knowledge of the existence of **any pipe, pipe or plumbing fitting, fixture,
solder, or flux that does not meet the federal Safe Drinking Water Act definition of 'lead free'
pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 300g-6** in a residential property, the licensee shall disclose the same to
the prospective tenant."* **The disclosure must be in writing.** The same subsection carries the
three exclusions from "physical condition of the property" that Hour 21 has already met on the sale
side — matters outside the boundaries of the land or relating to adjacent properties, matters
relating to governmental land use regulations, and matters relating to highways or public streets —
and preserves the prospective tenant's own right to inspect.

**§ 54.1-2135** covers licensees engaged to manage real estate, where the accounting duty does the
heaviest work because the licensee handles other people's money continuously rather than once. Note
that its duty list is the **shortest** of the four: it contains **no "promote the interests of the
client" subdivision at all**, because the management relationship is defined by the management
agreement. **§ 54.1-2135 F** limits the section to residential — *"the provisions of this section
shall not apply to licensees engaged in commercial real estate transactions."* Hours 33 and 55
develop management practice.

## 21.6 Reading the standards, not the vocabulary

chunks.heading: Hour 21 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Four standards appear in these sections and a student should attach each to the right duty:

- **Ordinary care** — the general standard of performance.
- **Actual knowledge** — the trigger for both the client disclosure duty and the physical-condition
  duty toward the other side. There is no duty to investigate in these sections.
- **Timely** — accounting, presentation of offers, and disclosures.
- **In writing** — the physical-condition disclosure under § 54.1-2131 B, consent to release
  confidential information, and the brokerage agreement itself.

### Hour 21 engagement check

**Question.** A listing licensee learns from the seller that the county has approved a plan to widen
the road in front of the property, and separately observes active water staining on a bedroom
ceiling. What must the licensee disclose to a prospective unrepresented buyer, and on what basis?

**Expected answer.** The **water staining** is a material adverse fact pertaining to the physical
condition of the property, actually known, and must be disclosed **in writing** under
§ 54.1-2131 B. The **road widening** is a matter relating to highways or public streets, which the
statute expressly places outside the definition of "physical condition of the property", so the
§ 54.1-2131 B physical-condition duty does not reach it. That is not permission to mislead: the
licensee must still treat the buyer honestly and must not knowingly give false information, and the
professional course is to state what is known and direct the buyer to the locality and to VDOT.
Toward the **seller**, who is the client, the road plan is a material fact concerning the property
or the transaction of which the licensee has actual knowledge, and § 54.1-2131 A 6 requires it be
disclosed to the seller.

---

chunks.heading: Hour 22 — Virginia brokerage disclosures: dual, designated, limited service
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 22 — Virginia brokerage disclosures: dual, designated, limited service

## 22.1 Disclosure of brokerage relationship — § 54.1-2138

**The trigger** is a **substantive discussion about a specific property or properties** in a
residential transaction with an actual or prospective buyer or seller who is **not** the licensee's
client and **not** represented by another licensee. On that trigger, the licensee must disclose any
brokerage relationship the licensee has with another party to the transaction.

**The timing** is *in writing, at the earliest practical time, but in no event later than the time
when specific real estate assistance is first provided.*

**The form.** The disclosure may be combined with other disclosures or given with other information
— but if it is, it must be **conspicuous: printed in bold lettering, all capitals, underlined, or
within a separate box.** The statute prints a model form, and a disclosure complying substantially
in effect with it is deemed compliant.

**Leasing — subsection B.** For an actual or prospective landlord or tenant who is not the client
and not represented, the disclosure must be in writing and **included in all applications for lease
or in the lease itself, whichever occurs first**; if the lease terms do not provide for it, no later
than the signing of the lease. **It does not apply to lease terms of less than two months.**

**Change of relationship — subsection C.** If a licensee's relationship to a client or customer
changes, the licensee shall disclose that **in writing to all clients and customers already involved
in the specific contemplated transaction**.

chunks.heading: 22.2 Limited service agent — § 54.1-2138.1
chunks.excerpt:
**Retention — subsection D.** Copies of disclosures relating to **fully executed purchase contracts**
must be kept **three years**, whether or not the disclosure was acknowledged in writing.

The Board's regulation at **18VAC135-20-220 A** restates the requirement and adds the consent timing
for dual and designated relationships: written consent from all clients at the earliest practical
time, given to and obtained from the **buyer not later than the time an offer to purchase is
presented** to the licensee who will present it, and from the seller not later than the time the
offer is presented to the seller.

## 22.2 Limited service agent — § 54.1-2138.1

A licensee may act as a **limited service agent** in a residential transaction **only pursuant to a
written brokerage agreement** in which the licensee:

**(i)** discloses that the licensee is acting as a limited service agent;
**(ii)** provides a **list of the specific services** the licensee will provide to the client; and
**(iii)** provides a **list of the specific standard-agent duties** — from § 54.1-2131 A 2,
§ 54.1-2132 A 3, § 54.1-2133 A 2 or § 54.1-2134 A 3 as applicable — that the licensee **will not**
provide.

The disclosure must be **conspicuous and printed either in bold lettering or all capitals, and
underlined or in a separate box**. The statute prints consent language whose substance is that
**neither the other party nor any licensee representing the other party is under any legal
obligation to assist the client with duties the limited service agent is not performing.**

A limited service agent must still disclose dual agency under § 54.1-2139.

chunks.heading: 22.3 Dual agency and dual representation — § 54.1-2139
chunks.excerpt:
