**Subsection B** protects the licensee on the other side. A licensee engaged by one client who deals
with an unrepresented party, or with a party represented by a limited service agent, and who
**without additional compensation** gives that party information or helps them secure a contract or
meet its obligations, **does not incur liability except for gross negligence or wilful misconduct**,
and **does not create a brokerage relationship** by doing so. If that licensee instead charges a fee
for services or information, no brokerage relationship is created — but the licensee is held to the
**ordinary standard of care** in providing them.

**§ 54.1-2138.1 also reaches advertising**: 18VAC135-20-190 A requires advertising to comply with
the § 54.1-2138.1 disclosure when applicable.

## 22.3 Dual agency and dual representation — § 54.1-2139

A licensee acting for **both** clients in the same residential transaction is a **dual agent or dual
representative**, and Virginia permits it only **as disclosed dual agency with written consent**.
The subsection A disclosures must be given, and where a brokerage agreement is entered in
conjunction with consent to dual representation, **§ 54.1-2137 C 5** requires those disclosures to
be part of the brokerage agreement itself.

Subsection G provides for termination, and § 54.1-2137 A (ii)(d) makes a § 54.1-2139 G termination
one of the ways a brokerage relationship ends.

**§ 54.1-2139.01** authorises disclosed dual agency and dual representation in **commercial**
transactions on its own terms.

chunks.heading: 22.4 Designated agency — § 54.1-2139.1
chunks.excerpt:
The professional reality is worth stating plainly: a dual agent cannot advocate for either side on
price or terms, because advocating for one is acting against the other. What the dual agent can do
is facilitate — and clients frequently do not understand the difference until it matters. Explaining
it before consent is signed is the work.

## 22.4 Designated agency — § 54.1-2139.1

A principal or supervising broker may **assign different affiliated licensees** as designated agents
or representatives to represent different clients **in the same residential transaction**, to the
exclusion of all other licensees in the firm.

Two rules follow, and the second is the one licensees forget:

**Using designated agents is not dual agency** so long as no designated agent represents more than
one client in the transaction.

**The principal or supervising broker who is supervising the transaction is a dual agent or
representative.** The firm is on both sides; only the individual licensees are not.

Designated agents **may not disclose**, except to their own broker, personal or financial
information received from their client, or anything the client asked be kept confidential, unless
the law provides otherwise or the client consents in writing.

Disclosure is required, in the same conspicuous form, and the statute prints a model that names the
firm, identifies the clients, records the acknowledgment that the dual agent may not pass
confidences between the sides, and names each designated agent and the capacity in which they act —
**standard agent, limited service agent, or independent contractor**.

## 22.5 Two rules that prevent accidental relationships

**§ 54.1-2140** — the payment or promise of compensation **does not create a brokerage
relationship**.

chunks.heading: Hour 22 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 54.1-2141** — a brokerage relationship is **not created by using a common source information
company**.

And **§ 54.1-2138.2** requires a licensee to **disclose an ownership interest in specific real
property**. Buying or selling for one's own account is permitted; concealing it is not.

### Hour 22 engagement check

**Question.** A firm's supervising broker assigns Licensee A to the seller and Licensee B to the
buyer in the same residential transaction. The buyer asks Licensee B whether the seller would take
less. Licensee B does not know, but Licensee A does, and the supervising broker knows too. Who may
tell whom what, and what is the supervising broker's status?

**Expected answer.** This is **designated agency** under § 54.1-2139.1. Licensee A may not disclose
the seller's confidential information to Licensee B; designated agents may disclose client
confidences **only to their own broker**. The **supervising broker is a dual agent or
representative** in this transaction and therefore may not pass confidential information from one
side to the other, as the statutory disclosure form itself acknowledges. So the answer to the buyer
is that Licensee B does not know and cannot obtain it, and the required disclosures and written
consents from **both** clients must be in place — under 18VAC135-20-220 A 3, from the buyer no later
than when the offer is presented to the licensee who will present it, and from the seller no later
than when the offer is presented to the seller.

---

## Hour 23 — Virginia licensing structure and regulatory authority

## 23.1 The Board and the Department

chunks.heading: 23.2 Licence categories
chunks.excerpt:
The **Real Estate Board** is established under **§ 54.1-2104** and its general powers are at
**§ 54.1-2105**, which includes the power to promulgate regulations and to set educational and
experience requirements for licensure. **§ 54.1-2105.1** carries other powers and duties, and
**§ 54.1-2105.2** authorises cease and desist orders and civil penalties for unlicensed activity.

The Board sits within the **Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation**. In practice
the Board makes regulatory and disciplinary decisions and DPOR administers licensing, receives
complaints, and conducts investigations.

Board regulations are published at **18VAC135-20**, the *Virginia Real Estate Board Licensing
Regulations*, and **§ 54.1-2143** requires the Board's regulations to be consistent with the
brokerage-relationships article.

## 23.2 Licence categories

**§ 54.1-2106.1** requires licences. The categories a student must be able to distinguish:

**Salesperson** — an individual licensed to provide real estate brokerage services **on behalf of
and under the supervision of** a broker. A salesperson never holds a licence that stands alone.

**Broker** — an individual qualified to operate independently and to hold a firm licence.

**Firm** — the business entity licence. **18VAC135-20-20** sets its requirements.

**Principal broker** — the broker responsible for the firm, including responsibility for the firm's
escrow accounts, with signatory authority, under 18VAC135-20-181 A 1 b.

**Supervising broker** — the broker responsible for supervision of a place of business, a branch
office, **or a real estate team**, under § 54.1-2110.1 A.

**Branch office** — an additional place of business, each of which must be supervised.

chunks.heading: 23.3 Entry, activation, and renewal
chunks.excerpt:
**Real estate team** — expressly named in § 54.1-2110.1 A as requiring a supervising broker, and in
B 5 as something the supervising broker must ensure operates in accordance with the chapter and the
regulations. A team is not a firm and does not have its own independent existence.

**§ 54.1-2103** sets out exemptions from the chapter — the categories of person who may do things
that would otherwise require a licence.

## 23.3 Entry, activation, and renewal

**18VAC135-20-30 and -35** set the qualifications for individual licensure; **-45** covers a
salesperson or broker licence held as a business entity; **-50** concurrent licences; **-65**
universal licence recognition; **-70** activation or transfer of licence.

A licence must be **active** and held with a firm to be used. An inactive licensee may not provide
brokerage services.

**Post-licence education** is separately required. **§ 54.1-2105.01** requires educational
requirements for all salespersons **within one year of licensure**, and **18VAC135-20-95** carries
the post-licence education requirements. **§ 54.1-2105.03** and **18VAC135-20-101** govern
continuing education and qualification for renewal; **-110** the procedures for renewal;
**§ 54.1-2105.04** and **-140 through -150** reinstatement after failure to renew.

**This course does not state the hour counts, deadlines or fees** for pre-licence, post-licence or
continuing education, or the licence fees at 18VAC135-20-13 and -15, because those figures have not
been read from the primary text for this project and they change. A student's own obligations must
be read from the Board's current regulation and fee schedule.

## 23.4 Supervision — § 54.1-2110.1

chunks.heading: 23.4 Supervision — § 54.1-2110.1
chunks.excerpt:
Every place of business, branch office, and real estate team must be supervised by a supervising
broker, who must exercise **reasonable and adequate supervision**. The broker may designate another
broker to assist, **but the designation does not relieve the supervising broker of responsibility**.

Subsection B defines reasonable and adequate supervision, and a salesperson should know what their
broker is required to provide:

1. **Being available at reasonable times** to review and approve all documents — leases, contracts,
   brokerage agreements, and advertising — affecting the firm's clients and business.
2. Ensuring training opportunities and that the office has **written procedures and policies**
   giving clear guidance in eight areas: (a) escrow deposit handling; (b) federal and state fair
   housing compliance, if the firm does residential brokerage, leasing or management; (c)
   advertising and marketing of the firm and affiliated teams or entities; (d) negotiating and
   drafting contracts, leases and brokerage agreements; (e) oversight and limits on the use of
   unlicensed assistants; (f) creating agency or independent contractor relationships; (g)
   distributing information on new or amended laws and regulations; and (h) disclosing required
   information relating to the physical condition of real property.
3. Ensuring brokerage services are carried out competently and per the chapter.
4. Reasonable steps to ensure compliance by all licensees assigned to a branch office, **including
   ensuring licensees hold a current licence**.
5. Ensuring affiliated teams and business entities operate per the chapter and the regulations.
6. Ensuring **brokerage agreements include the supervising broker's name and contact information**.
7. **Maintaining these records for

chunks.heading: 23.5 Place of business and records
chunks.excerpt:
three years**, furnished to the Board's agent on request.

Subsection C adds that a supervising broker residing **more than 50 miles** from a supervised branch
office with licensees regularly conducting business there must certify supervision **in writing
quarterly**.

**18VAC135-20-165** adds four further duties: supervise brokerage services in a timely manner; take
reasonable steps to ensure only licensees undertake activities requiring a licence, per
18VAC135-20-335 A; provide adequate supervision over unlicensed individuals and entities, per
18VAC135-20-335 B; and act with reasonable diligence and promptness in responding to inquiries from
cooperating brokers.

**18VAC135-20-335** is the section that tells an unlicensed assistant what they may and may not do.
It is the everyday application of duties 2 and 3, and a salesperson working with an assistant should
read it directly.

## 23.5 Place of business and records

**§ 54.1-2110** requires a resident broker to maintain a place of business in Virginia;
**18VAC135-20-160** carries the regulation. **§ 54.1-2146** requires licensee maintenance of
records, and **18VAC135-20-185** sets out what the principal broker must keep. **18VAC135-20-225**
provides for audits. **§ 54.1-2109** deals with the death or disability of a broker;
**§ 54.1-2106.2** with certification of audit on renewal.

## 23.6 The Transaction Recovery Fund

chunks.heading: Hour 23 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**§§ 54.1-2112 through 54.1-2120** establish the **Virginia Real Estate Transaction Recovery Fund**:
a fund maintained by assessments on licensees from which a member of the public who obtains an
unsatisfied judgment against a licensee for improper or dishonest conduct may recover, subject to
limitations. **§ 54.1-2119** provides that a licensee's licence is **revoked** upon payment from the
fund on that licensee's account.

The Fund is a consumer-protection mechanism and, for the licensee, a reminder that the profession
collectively pays for individual misconduct.

### Hour 23 engagement check

**Question.** A newly licensed salesperson joins a firm whose supervising broker lives 70 miles from
the branch office where the salesperson works. The salesperson is given an unlicensed assistant and
asks the broker for the office's written policies. What is the broker required to do in each
respect, and where is each requirement found?

**Expected answer.** Because the supervising broker resides **more than 50 miles** from a branch
office with licensees regularly conducting business there, the broker must **certify supervision in
writing quarterly** — § 54.1-2110.1 C. The broker must have **written procedures and policies** in
the eight areas listed at § 54.1-2110.1 B 2, including oversight and limits on the use of unlicensed
assistants at B 2 e, and must provide adequate supervision over unlicensed individuals under
18VAC135-20-165 3 with reference to 18VAC135-20-335 B. The broker must also be available at
reasonable times to review and approve documents (B 1), ensure the salesperson holds a current
licence (B 4), and retain the supervision records for **three years** (B 7).

---

## Hour 24 — Virginia standards of conduct and discipline

chunks.heading: 24.1 Where the disciplinary power comes from
chunks.excerpt:
## 24.1 Where the disciplinary power comes from

**18VAC135-20-155 A** gives the Board power to impose a monetary penalty and to suspend or revoke a
licence or certificate where the licensee has violated, or cooperated with others in violating, any
provision of Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 21 of Title 54.1, **Chapter 10 of Title 55.1** — the Consumer Real
Estate Settlement Protection Act — or any Board regulation. It operates through the **Administrative
Process Act**, § 2.2-4000 et seq.

**Subsection B matters to conduct outside work.** A licensee failing to comply with Chapter 21 or
the Board's regulations in performing acts covered by § 54.1-2100 **may be charged with a violation
regardless of whether those acts are in the licensee's personal capacity or in the licensee's
capacity as a licensee.** Selling one's own house badly is within reach of the Board.

## 24.2 Prohibited acts — 18VAC135-20-260

chunks.heading: 24.3 Conflict of interest — 18VAC135-20-270
chunks.excerpt:
The section lists prohibited acts. Among them: obtaining or attempting to obtain a licence by false
or fraudulent representation; holding more than one broker or salesperson licence in Virginia except
as the chapter permits; signing an experience verification form without direct supervision or actual
knowledge of the applicant's activities, **or unreasonably refusing to sign one**; conviction or a
finding of guilt, however adjudicated, in any US jurisdiction of a misdemeanour involving fraudulent
or dishonest acts, a sexual offence, non-marijuana drug distribution, or battery, or **any** felony,
with review subject to § 54.1-204; **failing to inform the Board in writing within 30 days** of such
a conviction; having a professional or occupational licence suspended, revoked, or surrendered in
connection with a disciplinary action in any jurisdiction; and **failing to inform the Board in
writing within 30 days** of such a disciplinary action.

Two 30-day clocks. Both are self-reporting obligations, and both are frequently missed by licensees
who assume the Board will learn of the matter another way.

## 24.3 Conflict of interest — 18VAC135-20-270

Verbatim, the whole section:

> Actions constituting a conflict of interest include:
> 1. Being active with a real estate broker other than the licensee's principal broker, without the
> written consent of the principal broker; and
> 2. Acting for more than one client in a transaction governed by the provisions of §§ 54.1-2139,
> 54.1-2139.01, and 54.1-2139.1 of the Code of Virginia without first obtaining the written consent
> of all clients.

Subdivision 2 is the enforcement side of Hour 22: **dual and designated arrangements without written
consent from all clients are a conflict of interest**, not merely a paperwork lapse.

chunks.heading: 24.4 Misrepresentation or omission — 18VAC135-20-300
chunks.excerpt:
## 24.4 Misrepresentation or omission — 18VAC135-20-300

The section lists actions constituting misrepresentation or omission. The first five:

1. **Bait and switch** — advertising or offering property for sale or rent with the intent not to
   sell or rent at the advertised price or terms, unless the advertisement clearly states a specific
   limited quantity or period and the licensee in fact had that quantity at those terms at the time,
   including listing status and condition of property.
2. Failing, as a licensee representing a seller or landlord **as a standard agent**, to disclose in
   a timely manner to a prospective purchaser or tenant **all material adverse facts pertaining to
   the physical condition of the property that are actually known by the licensee**.
3. Failing **to tender promptly to the client or unrepresented party every written offer, every
   written counteroffer, and every written rejection** to purchase, option, or lease.
4. Failing to disclose in a timely manner **to the licensee's client all material facts related to
   the property or concerning the transaction** where the failure would be a failure to exercise
   ordinary care.
5. Failing to provide in a timely manner to all principals to the transaction the required written
   notices.

Subdivision 3 is worth stating twice, because it is the rule licensees most often break out of
misplaced judgment: **every** written offer goes to the client. Not the ones the licensee thinks are
worth presenting.

## 24.5 The other conduct sections

chunks.heading: 24.6 When is the broker responsible?
chunks.excerpt:
**18VAC135-20-280 — improper financial transactions and dealings.**
**18VAC135-20-310 — improper delivery of instruments.**
**18VAC135-20-240 — provision of information to the Board.**
**18VAC135-20-340 and -345 — the effect of disciplinary action on subordinate licensees and on
certificates, approvals and concurrent licences.** A firm licence problem does not stay inside the
firm.

## 24.6 When is the broker responsible?

**18VAC135-20-330**, which must be read exactly, because it is commonly taught backwards:

> Any unlawful act or violation ... by any real estate salesperson, employee, partner or affiliate
> of a principal broker, supervising broker, or both, **may not be cause for disciplinary action
> against the principal broker, supervising broker, or both, unless it appears to the satisfaction
> of the board that the principal broker, supervising broker, or both, knew or should have known of
> the unlawful act or violation and failed to take reasonable action under the circumstances to
> remedy the situation.**

This is a **knew-or-should-have-known** standard coupled with a **failure to remedy**. It is not
vicarious liability. A broker who did not know, could not reasonably have known, or who knew and
took reasonable action, is not disciplined for the salesperson's act.

Note what makes "should have known" bite: the supervision duties in § 54.1-2110.1 B. A broker
without written policies, without document review, and without oversight of unlicensed assistants
has a much harder time saying they could not reasonably have known.

## 24.7 The process, and what a licensee does when a complaint arrives

chunks.heading: Hour 24 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
A complaint is filed with DPOR; an investigation follows; the licensee is given notice and an
opportunity to respond; the matter may be resolved by consent order, by an informal fact-finding
conference, or by a formal hearing under the Administrative Process Act; and sanctions range from a
monetary penalty through suspension to revocation. **§ 54.1-2111.1** provides for a **voluntary
compliance program** for real estate brokers.

The professional response to a complaint is: tell the principal broker immediately; do not contact
the complainant to argue; preserve every record, and change nothing; respond within the time given;
and obtain counsel. **18VAC135-20-240** requires provision of information to the Board — failing to
respond is itself a violation.

### Hour 24 engagement check

**Question.** A salesperson receives three written offers and presents only two, believing the third
to be too low to be worth the seller's time. The supervising broker had written policies, reviewed
documents weekly, and learned of the third offer a month later. Identify the violation and state
whether the broker is subject to discipline.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 06
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** The salesperson violated **18VAC135-20-300 3** — failure to tender promptly to
the client every written offer — and, in substance, **§ 54.1-2131 A 2 c**, which requires receiving
and presenting written offers to and from the seller in a timely manner. As to the broker,
**18VAC135-20-330** applies: the broker is subject to discipline only if the broker **knew or should
have known** and **failed to take reasonable action to remedy**. On these facts the broker had
written policies and a document-review practice and learned only later, so the knew-or-should-have-known
element is not established on what is stated — and the answer turns on whether the broker took
reasonable action once they did learn.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 06

Every Virginia statement in this module is taken from text read directly from
law.lis.virginia.gov on 2026-08-20 and recorded verbatim or in substance in
`virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **§§ 54.1-2100, 54.1-2103, 54.1-2104, 54.1-2105,
54.1-2105.01, 54.1-2105.02, 54.1-2105.03, 54.1-2105.04, 54.1-2105.1, 54.1-2105.2, 54.1-2106.1,
54.1-2106.2, 54.1-2108–54.1-2110.1, 54.1-2111.1, 54.1-2112–54.1-2120, 54.1-2130–54.1-2146**, and
**18VAC135-20-20, -30, -35, -45, -50, -65, -70, -95, -101, -110, -140, -145, -150, -155, -160,
-165, -181, -185, -190, -220, -225, -240, -260, -270, -280, -300, -310, -330, -335, -340, -345**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 06
chunks.excerpt:
Sections quoted verbatim: **18VAC135-20-270** and **18VAC135-20-330** in full,
**18VAC135-20-165** in full, and the operative parts of **§ 54.1-2110.1 B and C**,
**§ 54.1-2131 A and B**, **§ 54.1-2132 A 1 and B**, **§ 54.1-2136**, **§ 54.1-2137 C and D**,
**§ 54.1-2138**, **§ 54.1-2138.1**, **§ 54.1-2139.1**, **§ 54.1-2140**, **§ 54.1-2144**,
**18VAC135-20-155 A and B**, **18VAC135-20-220 A**, and **18VAC135-20-260 1–7**.

**Deliberately not stated:** the pre-licence, post-licence and continuing-education **hour counts and
deadlines**, and the **fees** at 18VAC135-20-13 and -15. Those regulations were identified but their
figures were not read for this project, and they change. Hour 23.3 tells the student to read the
Board's current regulation and fee schedule rather than giving a number.

**A teaching correction is embedded in Hour 24.6 deliberately.** 18VAC135-20-330 is a
knew-or-should-have-known standard with a failure-to-remedy element; national material frequently
describes broker responsibility as vicarious. Any instructor supplement that states the broker is
"always responsible for the acts of the salesperson" contradicts the regulation and must be corrected.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 07

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 07
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 07

## Course Day 7 · Hours 25–28 · Escrow, records, advertising, and fair housing

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(16) Real estate marketing · (23) Housing legislation ·
(24) Fair housing statutes · (25) Real Estate Board regulations
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- State the escrow account requirements at 18VAC135-20-181 A 1 and the record retention periods at
  18VAC135-20-185 C 1 and § 54.1-2110.1 B 7.
- Audit an advertisement against 18VAC135-20-190 A and B.
- Recite Virginia's protected classes from § 36-96.3 and say which of them federal law does not
  cover.
- Explain why the § 36-96.2 owner exemption is unavailable to a licensee.
- Distinguish a reasonable accommodation from a reasonable modification, and state who pays for
  each.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 25 | Virginia escrow, records, advertising, and supervision | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 26 | Federal and Virginia fair housing | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 27 | Disability, accessibility, assistance animals, and housing legislation | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 28 | Real estate marketing and advertising compliance | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 25 |

---

## Hour 25 — Virginia escrow, records, advertising, and supervision

## 25.1 Escrow — the account itself

chunks.heading: 25.2 Escrow — the deposits
chunks.excerpt:
**18VAC135-20-181 A 1.** If money is to be held in escrow, each firm or sole proprietorship must
maintain one or more **federally insured** escrow accounts into which **all funds received in
connection with a real estate transaction must be deposited**. Then five requirements:

**a.** The account must be **in the name by which the firm or sole proprietorship is licensed.**
**b.** The **principal broker will be held responsible** for these accounts, **including having
signatory authority** on them.
**c.** The **supervising broker and any other licensee with signatory authority may be held
responsible.**
**d.** All such **accounts, checks and bank statements must be labelled "escrow"**, and the accounts
must be **designated as escrow accounts with the financial institution**.
**e.** The **balance must be sufficient at all times** to account for all funds designated to be
held by the firm.

Read (b) and (c) together: responsibility runs to the principal broker automatically and to anyone
else with signatory authority potentially. A salesperson given signing authority on an escrow
account has accepted exposure.

## 25.2 Escrow — the deposits

**18VAC135-20-181 A 2** requires that **all** of the following be deposited into escrow: down
payments, earnest money deposits, money received on final settlement, application deposits, rental
payments, rental security deposits, money advanced by a buyer or seller for the payment of expenses
in connection with closing, and money advanced by the broker's client or others.

chunks.heading: 25.3 Records
chunks.excerpt:
The statutory layer sits above it: **§ 54.1-2108** protects escrow funds held by a broker;
**§ 54.1-2108.1** addresses protection in the event of **foreclosure** of the real property; and
**§ 54.1-2108.2** addresses protection in the event of **termination of a real estate purchase
contract** — the disputed-deposit case.

**Commingling** — mixing escrow money with the firm's operating funds — and **conversion** — using
escrow money for any purpose other than the one it was entrusted for — are the two failures the
whole scheme exists to prevent. They are not accounting errors. A firm that pays its rent from the
escrow account has converted client funds.

**18VAC135-20-225** provides for **audits**, and **§ 54.1-2106.2** requires certification of audit on
renewal of a firm or sole proprietorship licence.

## 25.3 Records

**18VAC135-20-185 A.** The principal broker must maintain financial records for any transaction
under the authority of the broker's licence, **readily accessible from the broker's place of
business**, containing: from whom money was received; the date of receipt; the place of deposit; the
date of deposit; the final disposition of the funds; and anything else the chapter requires. Where
the principal broker's office is outside Virginia and the firm has a Virginia branch, **a copy must
be readily accessible in the Virginia office.**

**Subsection B** requires a bookkeeping or recordkeeping system that accurately and clearly
discloses full compliance, in sufficient detail to determine it.

chunks.heading: 25.4 Advertising — 18VAC135-20-190
chunks.excerpt:
**Subsection C 1** sets the retention period a licensee must know: **each brokerage agreement must
be retained for three years from the date of execution**, and **each disclosure and consent to dual
agency or dual representation, and to designated agency or designated representation, must be
retained for three years from the date of execution.**

Three other three-year periods sit alongside it and are easy to confuse — they are three separate
obligations that happen to share a number:

- **§ 54.1-2138 D** — copies of brokerage-relationship disclosures relating to **fully executed
  purchase contracts**, three years.
- **§ 54.1-2110.1 B 7** — the **supervising broker's supervision records**, three years, furnished
  to the Board's agent on request.
- **18VAC135-20-185 C 1** — brokerage agreements and dual/designated consents, three years from
  execution.

**§ 54.1-2146** is the statutory requirement of licensee maintenance of records.

## 25.4 Advertising — 18VAC135-20-190

**Subsection A**, in substance: **all advertising must be under the direct supervision of the
principal broker or supervising broker, in the name of the firm** and, where applicable, must comply
with the § 54.1-2138.1 limited-service-agent disclosure. **The firm's licensed name must be clearly
and legibly displayed on all advertising.**

**Subsection B 1:** all advertising by a firm or affiliated licensee must contain a **clear, legible
and conspicuous advertising disclosure** including **(i) the firm's name and (ii) the office contact
information**. And then the delegation students miss: **the office contact information and any
additional required information will be specified by the principal or supervising broker in the
firm's written policies.**

chunks.heading: 25.5 Place of business, and teams
chunks.excerpt:
That means the Board sets the requirement and the **firm** sets the format. A course cannot state a
required layout, and a licensee must read their own firm's written policy — which § 54.1-2110.1 B 2
c requires the firm to have for advertising and marketing.

**B 2:** all advertising by an affiliated licensee must be done under the policies of a principal or
supervising broker.

**B 3:** any property information provided by and in the licensee's control **must be consistent
with the property condition and the property's current contract status**. If a third party controls
the advertising, the licensee must make **a timely written request** for changes.

**B 4:** all advertising must be **updated in a timely manner** whenever there is a material change
to listing status or property description, with the same written-request rule where a third party
controls it.

Subsections B 3 and B 4 are why a sold listing left live with old photographs is a regulatory
problem and not merely untidy.

## 25.5 Place of business, and teams

**§ 54.1-2110** requires a resident broker to maintain a place of business in Virginia;
**18VAC135-20-160** carries the detail. **Real estate teams** must be supervised by a supervising
broker under § 54.1-2110.1 A, and the supervising broker must ensure affiliated teams operate per
the chapter and the regulations under B 5, and must have written policies covering **advertising and
marketing of the brokerage firm and any affiliated real estate teams or business entities** under
B 2 c. A team's branding is the firm's advertising.

### Hour 25 engagement check

chunks.heading: Hour 26 — Federal and Virginia fair housing
chunks.excerpt:
**Question.** A firm receives a $10,000 earnest money deposit on Friday. The office manager, who is
unlicensed, deposits it Monday into the firm's operating account "because the escrow account was
short this month", and the firm transfers it to escrow on Wednesday. Identify every failure and its
source.

**Expected answer.** Depositing an earnest money deposit into the operating account is
**commingling and conversion**: 18VAC135-20-181 A 1 requires all funds received in connection with a
real estate transaction to be deposited into a designated escrow account, and A 2 names earnest
money specifically. That the escrow account was "short" is itself a violation of **A 1 e**, which
requires the balance to be sufficient **at all times** to account for all funds held. The
**principal broker is responsible** for the accounts under A 1 b, and any licensee with signatory
authority may be under A 1 c. The supervising broker's failure engages § 54.1-2110.1 B 2 a, which
requires written policies giving clear guidance on handling escrow deposits in compliance with law
and regulation, and 18VAC135-20-165 3, which requires adequate supervision over unlicensed
individuals. Whether the broker is disciplined for the manager's act is decided by
**18VAC135-20-330** — knew or should have known, and failed to remedy.

---

## Hour 26 — Federal and Virginia fair housing

## 26.1 The federal floor

The **federal Fair Housing Act** — Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended in 1974
and 1988 — prohibits discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of dwellings on the basis of
**race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, and disability (handicap)**. Seven
classes. The 1974 amendment added sex; the 1988 amendment added familial status and disability.

chunks.heading: 26.2 Virginia goes further — § 36-96.3
chunks.excerpt:
**The Civil Rights Act of 1866** is older and narrower and, in one respect, stronger: it prohibits
**racial** discrimination in the sale or lease of all real and personal property, and — as the
Supreme Court held in *Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.* (1968) — **it carries no exemptions**. A
transaction exempt from the Fair Housing Act is not exempt from the 1866 Act if the discrimination
is racial.

**Prohibited practices** under federal law include refusing to sell or rent; discriminating in terms
or conditions; discriminatory advertising; representing that a dwelling is unavailable when it is
not; **blockbusting** — inducing sales by representations about the entry of protected-class persons
into a neighbourhood; **steering** — directing prospects toward or away from areas on a protected
basis; and **redlining** — denying loans or insurance based on the composition of an area rather
than the applicant or property.

**Enforcement** runs through HUD complaint, administrative proceedings, and federal civil actions,
with the Department of Justice bringing pattern-or-practice cases.

## 26.2 Virginia goes further — § 36-96.3

The **Virginia Fair Housing Law**, Chapter 5.1 of Title 36, is broader. Reading § 36-96.3 A 1, the
protected bases are:

**race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, elderliness, source of funds, familial status,
sexual orientation, gender identity, military status** — and **disability**, which appears throughout
subdivisions 3 through 9.

Five of those are not in the federal list. A licensee working from a national text will be working
from an incomplete list, and the five additions — **elderliness, source of funds, sexual orientation,
gender identity, military status** — are exactly the ones most likely to appear in a real complaint.

chunks.heading: 26.3 The nine unlawful practices, in the statute's own order
chunks.excerpt:
**Source of funds** deserves particular attention because it is the newest habit to break. Refusing
to consider a housing choice voucher, or advertising "no vouchers", is discrimination on the basis
of source of funds in Virginia.

## 26.3 The nine unlawful practices, in the statute's own order

§ 36-96.3 A makes it unlawful to:

1. **Refuse to sell or rent** after a bona fide offer, refuse to negotiate, or otherwise make
   unavailable or deny a dwelling, because of a protected basis.
2. **Discriminate in the terms, conditions, or privileges** of sale or rental, or in the provision of
   services or facilities.
3. **Make, print, or publish** any notice, statement, or advertisement indicating a preference,
   limitation, or discrimination, or an intention to make one. Two drafting rules live here:
   **the use of words or symbols associated with a particular religion, national origin, sex, or race
   is prima facie evidence of an illegal preference, and a general disclaimer does not overcome it**;
   but **reference alone to places of worship — churches, synagogues, temples, mosques — is not**
   prima facie evidence.
4. **Represent that a dwelling is not available** for inspection, sale or rental when it is.
5. **Deny access to or membership in** a multiple listing service, brokers' organisation, or similar
   facility, or discriminate in the terms of access.
6. **Include a discriminatory restrictive covenant** in any transfer, sale, rental or lease, **or
   honour or exercise, or attempt to honour or exercise, any such covenant.**
7. **Induce or attempt to induce a sale or rental by representations regarding the entry or
   prospective entry** into the neighbourhood of persons of a protected class — blockbusting, in the
   statute's own words.
8. **Refuse to sell or r

chunks.heading: 26.4 The exemption that does not help a licensee
chunks.excerpt:
ent, refuse to negotiate, or otherwise make unavailable or deny a dwelling
   because of a disability** of (i) the buyer or renter, (ii) a person residing or intending to
   reside there after the transaction, or (iii) **any person associated with the buyer or renter**.
9. **Discriminate in terms, conditions, privileges, services or facilities because of a disability**
   of the same three categories of person.

Subdivisions 8 and 9 reach **association**: discriminating against a buyer because of the disability
of someone associated with them is itself unlawful.

**Subsection C** extends the prohibition to **political jurisdictions**, their employees and
appointed commissions, in the application of local land use ordinances and in the permitting of
housing developments — including discrimination because a development contains affordable housing
units for households at or below 80 percent of area median income.

## 26.4 The exemption that does not help a licensee

**§ 36-96.2 A** exempts, in narrow circumstances, a single-family house sold or rented by a private
individual owner who owns no more than three at a time, subject to conditions — including that the
sale or rental occurs **without the use in any manner of the sales or rental services or facilities
of any real estate broker, agent or salesperson**, and without discriminatory advertising, which
remains prohibited by § 36-96.3 A 3 regardless.

Then the sentence every Virginia licensee must know:

> **This exemption shall not apply to or inure to the benefit of any licensee of the Real Estate
> Board or regulant of the Fair Housing Board, regardless of whether the licensee is acting in his
> personal or professional capacity.**

chunks.heading: 26.5 Practice rules that follow
chunks.excerpt:
A licensee cannot use the owner exemption. Not when helping an exempt owner — the exemption is lost
the moment a licensee is used — and **not when selling their own house**.

**§ 36-96.2 B** covers rooms or units in an owner-occupied dwelling with living quarters for no more
than four families. **§ 36-96.2 C** permits a religious organisation to limit or prefer as to
dwellings it owns and operates for a non-commercial purpose, unless membership is restricted on a
protected basis, and covers certain private membership clubs. **Advertising remains prohibited under
every one of these exemptions**, because each is expressed as an exception "except for subdivision
A 3 of § 36-96.3".

## 26.5 Practice rules that follow

**Use objective, uniform, written criteria** for qualification, and apply them to everyone.
**Never answer a "what kind of neighbourhood is it?" question with demographics** — answer with
objective sources the buyer can consult for themselves: school ratings, crime statistics published
by the locality, census data. **Show every buyer everything that meets their stated criteria**, and
let the buyer narrow. **Record what the client asked for in their own words.**

And under **§ 54.1-2131 A 7** and **§ 54.1-2132 A 8**, compliance with all fair housing statutes and
regulations applicable to residential transactions is itself a statutory duty owed to the client —
so a fair housing violation is simultaneously a Real Estate Board matter.

### Hour 26 engagement check

**Question.** A licensee is asked by a landlord client to "screen out the voucher people" and to
"keep the building quiet — no kids". A second client, selling their own home privately, asks the
licensee for informal help but says the licensee will not be paid. Address all three requests.

chunks.heading: Hour 27 — Disability, accessibility, assistance animals, and housing legislation
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** Refusing housing choice vouchers is discrimination on the basis of **source of
funds**, a Virginia protected class under § 36-96.3 A 1 and 2. Excluding children is discrimination
on the basis of **familial status**. The licensee must refuse both instructions and say so in
writing; § 54.1-2131 A 7 and § 54.1-2133 make fair housing compliance a duty owed to the client, and
a client's instruction cannot authorise a violation. As to the third request: the § 36-96.2 A owner
exemption **is lost as soon as a licensee's services are used in any manner**, and in any case the
exemption **does not inure to the benefit of any Real Estate Board licensee regardless of capacity**
— so the licensee has no exemption to rely on and must comply fully.

---

## Hour 27 — Disability, accessibility, assistance animals, and housing legislation

## 27.1 The two things a disabled person may ask for

**§ 36-96.3 B** defines discrimination to include a refusal in three situations, and the first two
are the ones a licensee meets constantly.

**Reasonable modification — B (i).** A refusal to permit, **at the expense of the disabled person**,
reasonable modifications of existing premises occupied or to be occupied, if the modifications may
be necessary to afford full enjoyment of the premises. In a **rental**, the landlord may, **where it
is reasonable to do so**, condition permission on the renter agreeing to **restore the interior** to
its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted.

**Reasonable accommodation — B (ii).** A refusal to make reasonable accommodations in **rules,
practices, policies, or services** when necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a
dwelling.

chunks.heading: 27.2 Design and construction — B (iii)
chunks.excerpt:
The distinction, in one line: **a modification is a physical change and the tenant pays; an
accommodation is a change to a rule and the housing provider bears the ordinary cost of making it.**
A grab bar is a modification. Waiving a no-pets rule for an assistance animal is an accommodation.
Assigning a parking space nearer the door is an accommodation.

## 27.2 Design and construction — B (iii)

For **covered multi-family dwellings** designed and constructed for first occupancy **after 13 March
1991**, failure to design and construct so that:

1. **public and common use areas are readily accessible** to and usable by disabled persons;
2. **all doors designed to allow passage into and within the premises are wide enough** for
   wheelchair passage; and
3. premises within covered units contain **an accessible route into and through the dwelling**;
   **light switches, electrical outlets, thermostats and other environmental controls in accessible
   locations**; **reinforcements in bathroom walls to allow later installation of grab bars**; and
   **usable kitchens and bathrooms** in which a person in a wheelchair can manoeuvre.

**"Covered multi-family dwellings"** means buildings of **four or more units** where the building has
**one or more elevators**, and **ground floor units** in other buildings of four or more units.

**§ 36-96.3 D** provides that compliance with **ANSI A117.1**, or with other standards adopted in
HUD regulations, is deemed to satisfy the design requirement.

## 27.3 Assistance animals

An assistance animal is not a pet, and the request to keep one is a **reasonable accommodation**
request under § 36-96.3 B (ii). The practical consequences a licensee must understand:

chunks.heading: 27.4 Familial status, elderliness, and housing for older persons
chunks.excerpt:
- A **no-pets policy does not defeat the request.**
- **Pet fees and pet deposits do not apply** to an assistance animal, because it is not a pet.
- The tenant remains responsible for **damage the animal causes** and for the animal's behaviour.
- A housing provider may seek **reliable information** confirming the disability-related need where
  the disability or the need is not readily apparent, but may not demand details of the diagnosis.

Virginia has enacted specific provisions on assistance animals in rental housing, and the
verification a provider may request is regulated. **This course does not state that procedure**,
because the relevant sections of Title 36 and Title 55.1 have not been read from primary text for
this project. A licensee handling such a request must read the current provisions or route the
question to counsel — and must not refuse the request in the meantime.

**Service animals under the Americans with Disabilities Act are a different question.** The ADA
governs places of public accommodation and commercial facilities; **housing is governed by fair
housing law**, not the ADA. A leasing office open to the public may be a place of public
accommodation, and the two regimes can apply to different parts of the same property. Do not import
ADA service-animal rules into a housing accommodation analysis.

## 27.4 Familial status, elderliness, and housing for older persons

**Familial status** protects households with children under 18, a person who is pregnant, and a
person in the process of securing legal custody. **Elderliness** is a separate Virginia protected
class.

chunks.heading: 27.5 Where fair housing meets the licensing statute
chunks.excerpt:
Federal law and Virginia law both permit qualified **housing for older persons** to operate as such
without violating the familial status prohibition, on conditions that must be met and documented.
**This course states no threshold**, because the qualifying conditions have not been read from
primary text for this project. A licensee marketing a community described as age-restricted must
obtain the community's own documentation of its qualification, in writing, and must not describe it
as exempt on the strength of its marketing.

## 27.5 Where fair housing meets the licensing statute

Two connections close the hour.

**18VAC135-20-330** names **Chapter 5.1 (§ 36-96.1 et seq.) of Title 36** alongside Chapter 21 as the
law whose violation by a salesperson can, on the knew-or-should-have-known standard, reach the
supervising broker. Fair housing is expressly inside the Board's supervisory scheme.

**§ 54.1-2110.1 B 2 b** requires a firm engaged in residential brokerage, leasing or management to
have **written procedures and policies giving clear guidance on complying with federal and state
fair housing laws and regulations.** A licensee should have read their firm's policy, and if the
firm does not have one, that is itself a supervision failure.

### Hour 27 engagement check

**Question.** A tenant with a mobility impairment asks a landlord for (a) permission to install a
ramp at the front entrance and grab bars in the bathroom, and (b) an assigned parking space nearer
the door in a lot with unassigned parking. The landlord asks who pays for what and whether the
tenant must undo anything.

chunks.heading: Hour 28 — Real estate marketing and advertising compliance
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** (a) is a **reasonable modification** under § 36-96.3 B (i): permission may not
be refused, and the modification is **at the tenant's expense**. Because this is a rental, the
landlord may — **where it is reasonable to do so** — condition permission on the tenant agreeing to
**restore the interior** to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted; the interior
grab bars are the natural candidate, and a front-entrance ramp is an exterior change to which the
restoration condition on its face does not extend. (b) is a **reasonable accommodation** under
§ 36-96.3 B (ii) — a change to a rule or practice — and the housing provider bears the ordinary cost
of making it; no fee may be charged for the accommodation itself.

---

## Hour 28 — Real estate marketing and advertising compliance

## 28.1 Marketing the property, not the people

The organising principle for compliant marketing is short: **describe the property, never the
occupants or the desired occupants.**

"Four bedrooms, two baths, fenced rear yard, walking distance to the elementary school" describes
the property. "Perfect for a young family" describes who should live there, and is an expression of
preference on the basis of familial status. "Quiet building, ideal for mature professionals"
expresses preference on elderliness and familial status. "Walk to St. Anne's" is, on § 36-96.3 A 3's
own terms, **reference alone to a place of worship and is not prima facie evidence** — but
"a wonderful Christian community" uses words associated with a particular religion and **is** prima
facie evidence of an illegal preference that a disclaimer will not cure.

The same rule applies to photographs, to the models used in imagery, and to the language of a
property's own website.

chunks.heading: 28.2 The Board's advertising rules, applied
chunks.excerpt:
## 28.2 The Board's advertising rules, applied

From Hour 25, applied to a real advertisement:

**Is it in the name of the firm, under the direct supervision of the principal or supervising
broker, with the firm's licensed name clearly and legibly displayed?** (18VAC135-20-190 A)

**Does it carry a clear, legible and conspicuous advertising disclosure with the firm's name and the
office contact information as the firm's written policy specifies?** (B 1)

**Is it done under the policies of a principal or supervising broker?** (B 2)

**Is the property information consistent with the property's condition and current contract
status?** (B 3)

**Has it been updated in a timely manner after any material change to listing status or property
description?** (B 4)

**Where a third party controls it, has a timely written request for changes been made?** (B 3 and
B 4)

**Where the licensee is a limited service agent, does it comply with the § 54.1-2138.1 disclosure?**
(A)

## 28.3 Digital, social, and third-party platforms

Everything above applies to a social post, a video, a syndicated listing feed, and a paid
advertisement, because the rules speak of "all advertising" without qualification.

Three digital-specific problems:

**Third-party control.** Syndication sends listing data to platforms the firm does not control.
18VAC135-20-190 B 3 and B 4 anticipate exactly this and prescribe the remedy: **a timely written
request for changes.** Keep the request; it is the evidence that the duty was met.

chunks.heading: 28.4 Teams, personal branding, and the firm's name
chunks.excerpt:
**Audience targeting.** Choosing who is shown a housing advertisement can itself make a statement of
preference. Restricting a housing ad's audience by age, by family composition, by ZIP code chosen
for its demography, or by proxies for a protected class implicates § 36-96.3 A 3 as surely as
printed words would. Platforms have built housing-specific advertising categories for this reason;
using them is not optional politeness.

**Persistence.** A post from last year advertising a property at a price that no longer applies is
still an advertisement, and B 4 requires timely updating.

## 28.4 Teams, personal branding, and the firm's name

A **real estate team** must be supervised by a supervising broker (§ 54.1-2110.1 A), and the
supervising broker must have written policies covering the advertising and marketing of the firm and
any affiliated teams or business entities (B 2 c) and must ensure teams operate per the chapter and
regulations (B 5). Combined with 18VAC135-20-190 A's requirement that all advertising be **in the
name of the firm** with the firm's licensed name clearly and legibly displayed, the rule for team
branding is: the team name may appear, but it may not displace or obscure the firm.

## 28.5 Truthfulness, and the specific trap of bait and switch

**18VAC135-20-300 1** makes it misrepresentation to advertise or offer property for sale or rent
**with the intent not to sell or rent at the price or terms advertised** — unless the advertisement
clearly states that the property is limited in specific quantity or to a specified time period **and
the licensee in fact had at least that quantity at those terms at the time of advertising**,
including as to listing status and condition.

chunks.heading: 28.6 Data, images, and consent
chunks.excerpt:
Two everyday versions: advertising a property already under contract in order to generate buyer
leads, and advertising a rent that is available only under conditions the advertisement does not
state.

## 28.6 Data, images, and consent

Photographs, floor plans, drone footage, and video are **copyrighted works**, usually owned by the
photographer unless the agreement says otherwise. A licensee who reuses another firm's listing
photographs after a listing changes hands is infringing, not economising. Written licences,
retained, are the answer.

Client data collected through a website is subject to privacy obligations and to the firm's own
policy; and lead information, once collected, is a record. Hour 50 covers data protection and wire
fraud, which is where a marketing website becomes a security question.

### Hour 28 engagement check

**Question.** Audit this social post and list every problem with its source: *"JUST LISTED by the
Carter Team! Charming 3BR in a quiet, established neighborhood — perfect for empty nesters. No
Section 8. Call Dana at 555-0100."* The property went under contract four days ago.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 07
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** **"Perfect for empty nesters"** expresses a preference on the basis of
**elderliness and familial status** — § 36-96.3 A 3. **"No Section 8"** is discrimination on the
basis of **source of funds**, a Virginia protected class — § 36-96.3 A 1, 2 and 3. **"JUST LISTED"**
on a property under contract for four days is property information inconsistent with the property's
current contract status — **18VAC135-20-190 B 3** — and a failure to update after a material change
to listing status — **B 4** — and, if the intent is to generate leads rather than sell at those
terms, bait and switch under **18VAC135-20-300 1**. The post carries **the team name and an
individual's phone number but not the firm's licensed name**, contrary to **18VAC135-20-190 A**, and
carries no **advertising disclosure with the firm's name and office contact information** as
required by **B 1** and specified in the firm's written policy under § 54.1-2110.1 B 2 c.

---

## Instructor source note for Module 07

Virginia statements rest on text read directly from law.lis.virginia.gov on 2026-08-20 and recorded
in `virginia/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **18VAC135-20-181 A 1 and A 2**, **-185 A, B and
C 1**, **-190 A and B 1–4**, **-160**, **-165**, **-225**, **-300 1–5**, **-330**; **§§ 54.1-2106.2,
54.1-2108, 54.1-2108.1, 54.1-2108.2, 54.1-2110, 54.1-2110.1 B and C, 54.1-2131 A 7, 54.1-2132 A 8,
54.1-2138 D, 54.1-2138.1, 54.1-2146**; and **§§ 36-96.2 A, B and C and 36-96.3 A 1–9, B, C and D**.

**§ 36-96.2 was read in its "(Effective until July 1, 2027)" version.** The legal-update control in
`virginia/compliance/legal-update-sop.md` must recheck it before any delivery on or after that date.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module 07
chunks.excerpt:
Federal statements — the seven Fair Housing Act classes, the 1866 Act and *Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer
Co.*, and the HUD enforcement route — are federal law and are stated at the level of the
well-settled requirement.

**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** the **verification procedure a Virginia
housing provider may use for an assistance animal request**, and the **qualifying conditions for
housing for older persons**. Hours 27.3 and 27.4 name each as a question to be read or referred, and
instruct the licensee not to refuse an accommodation request while the question is open. An
instructor supplementing this text with a procedure or a threshold must read Title 36 and Title 55.1
first.

The ADA/fair-housing boundary in Hour 27.3 is stated as a boundary, not as a summary of the ADA.

lessons.title: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 08

chunks.heading: Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 08
chunks.excerpt:
# Virginia Principles and Practices of Real Estate — Module 08

## Course Day 8 · Hours 29–32 · Common-interest communities and leasing

**Required subjects covered:** 18VAC135-20-400(8) Leases · (10) Home ownership · (21) Planning
subdivision developments and condominiums · (22) Regulatory statutes · (23) Housing legislation
**Class hours:** 4 (200 instructional minutes)
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Not approved. No Virginia pre-license credit is available for this course.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Distinguish a condominium, a property owners' association, and a cooperative, and name the
  Virginia chapter governing each.
- State what a contract for the resale of a unit in a common interest community must disclose under
  § 55.1-2308, and compute the purchaser's cancellation period under § 55.1-2312.
- Explain the consequences under § 55.1-2314 when a resale certificate is not properly provided.
- Classify a tenancy and distinguish an assignment from a sublease.
- Navigate Title 55.1 to the chapter governing a given tenancy question.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Class hours | Evidence of participation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 29 | Home ownership, associations, and common-interest communities | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 30 | Subdivisions, condominiums, and the Resale Disclosure Act | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 31 | Leasehold estates and lease agreements | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| 32 | The Virginia residential landlord-tenant framework | 1 | Section completed; engagement check answered |
| **Total** | | **4** | Unit quiz follows Hour 30 |

---

chunks.heading: Hour 29 — Home ownership, associations, and common-interest communities
chunks.excerpt:
## Hour 29 — Home ownership, associations, and common-interest communities

## 29.1 What a common interest community is

A **common interest community** is a development in which ownership of a unit or lot carries with it
mandatory membership in an association and an obligation to pay assessments for commonly held or
commonly maintained property. The obligation runs with the land: it is not a club a buyer joins, and
it cannot be resigned from.

Virginia governs the forms separately, in Title 55.1:

- **Chapter 18 — Property Owners' Association Act.** Subdivisions of separately owned lots.
- **Chapter 19 — Virginia Condominium Act.** Condominiums.
- **Chapter 20 — Horizontal Property Act.** The older condominium statute, still governing some
  older projects.
- **Chapter 21 — Virginia Real Estate Cooperative Act.** Cooperatives.
- **Chapter 22 — Virginia Real Estate Time-Share Act.** Time-shares.
- **Chapter 23.1 — Resale Disclosure Act.** The resale disclosure regime for all of them, and the
  subject of Hour 30.

There is also a separate regulator. The **Common Interest Community Board** licenses common interest
community managers and registers associations, under Title 54.1; § 55.1-2314 D gives it power to
assess monetary penalties and issue cease and desist orders for resale-certificate failures. A
licensee should know that the association side of a transaction has its own regulator.

## 29.2 Condominium

A condominium divides a project into:

**Units** — the individually owned volumes of space, described by reference to a recorded
condominium plat and, because a unit is a volume, by elevation as well as footprint.

chunks.heading: 29.3 Property owners' association
chunks.excerpt:
**Common elements** — everything else, owned by all unit owners as undivided interests: the land,
the structure, the roof, the corridors, the mechanical systems.

**Limited common elements** — common elements reserved for the use of fewer than all units. A
balcony serving one unit, an assigned parking space, a storage locker.

The unit owner's percentage interest in the common elements is fixed by the declaration and usually
determines both the voting power and the share of assessments.

The governing instruments are the **declaration**, which creates the condominium and defines the
units and common elements; the **bylaws**, which govern the association's operation; the recorded
**plats and plans**; and the **rules and regulations** adopted by the board.

## 29.3 Property owners' association

A POA governs a subdivision of **separately owned lots**. Each owner owns their lot in fee, and the
association owns or maintains the common areas — the entrance, the private streets if any, the
stormwater pond, the pool. The instruments are the **declaration of covenants, conditions and
restrictions**, the **articles and bylaws**, and the **rules**.

The critical difference from a condominium: in a POA the owner owns land and the structure on it,
and the association's authority comes from the recorded covenants rather than from a division of the
building itself.

## 29.4 Cooperative

In a cooperative, a **corporation owns the real property**. The resident buys **shares** in the
corporation and receives a **proprietary lease** of an apartment.

chunks.heading: 29.5 Assessments, budgets, and reserves
chunks.excerpt:
The consequence that changes everything: the resident owns **personal property**, not real property.
There is no deed. Financing is a share loan rather than a deed of trust. Title work, transfer taxes,
and the whole settlement mechanic differ. And the corporation's board generally has approval rights
over a transfer — subject, always, to fair housing law, which applies to a cooperative board's
decisions as it does to anyone else's.

## 29.5 Assessments, budgets, and reserves

**Regular assessments** fund the annual budget: insurance for what the association insures,
utilities for common areas, landscaping and maintenance, management, and a contribution to reserves.

**Special assessments** fund something the budget did not — a roof, a private road, litigation.
They are the single largest financial risk in common-interest ownership, and a buyer who has not
read the minutes and the reserve study has not investigated it.

**Reserves and the reserve study.** A reserve study estimates the remaining life and replacement
cost of major components and derives the annual funding required. A community with a large deferred
liability and a thin reserve is a community heading toward a special assessment, whatever the
current dues are.

**Assessment liens.** Unpaid assessments become a lien against the unit or lot under the governing
statute, and unpaid assessments are precisely what a resale certificate exists to reveal.

**Insurance.** The association's master policy covers what the declaration says it covers, and the
owner's policy — an HO-6 in a condominium — covers the rest. The boundary between them is set by
the declaration, and neither the licensee nor the buyer should assume it. Hour 49 develops this.

## 29.6 What the buyer must be told to investigate

chunks.heading: Hour 29 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
A buyer due-diligence list a licensee should be able to produce from memory: the declaration and
bylaws; the rules, including any restrictions on leasing, pets, parking, vehicles, signs and
exterior alterations; the current budget and dues; the reserve study and reserve balance; the last
two years of board and member minutes, where special assessments are first discussed; the status of
any litigation; any pending or threatened special assessment; the insurance summary and what the
owner must insure separately; and the association's approval or right-of-first-refusal provisions.

Leasing restrictions deserve their own mention. A buyer who intends to rent the unit and who
discovers after closing that the community caps rentals or imposes a waiting period has lost the
entire basis of their purchase. **Ask the question before the offer, and get the answer in writing.**

### Hour 29 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer is comparing a condominium unit and a house in a POA, and says "the dues are
$310 a month in one and $95 a quarter in the other, so the second is cheaper." What is wrong with
the comparison, and what would you tell the buyer to obtain?

chunks.heading: Hour 30 — Subdivisions, condominiums, and the Resale Disclosure Act
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** The comparison is between two different things. In a **condominium** the
association typically maintains and insures the building itself, so a large part of what an owner
would otherwise pay directly — roof, structure, exterior, often water and master insurance — is
inside the dues. In a **POA** the owner owns the lot and the structure and pays for its maintenance,
insurance and replacement personally, so a low assessment reflects a narrower scope, not a lower
cost of ownership. The buyer should obtain, for each: the declaration and bylaws, the current
budget, the **reserve study and reserve balance**, two years of minutes, any pending or threatened
**special assessment**, the insurance summary showing the boundary between master and owner
coverage, and the leasing, pet and alteration restrictions.

---

## Hour 30 — Subdivisions, condominiums, and the Resale Disclosure Act

## 30.1 Creating the community

Hour 8 covered subdivision procedure: concept plan, preliminary plat, public improvement plans,
construction secured by bond or letter of credit, and a **recorded final plat** that legally creates
the lots. A condominium is created by recording a **declaration** together with the plats and plans.

For a **new** unit or lot sold by the declarant, a **public offering statement** regime applies under
the Condominium Act and the Property Owners' Association Act, with its own delivery and cancellation
rules. **Resales** — every subsequent sale — are governed by Chapter 23.1, and that is what a
salesperson meets in practice.

## 30.2 The Resale Disclosure Act — Chapter 23.1

chunks.heading: 30.2 The Resale Disclosure Act — Chapter 23.1
chunks.excerpt:
This chapter is recent — enacted 2023 and amended in 2024 and 2025 — and it **replaced** the older,
separate resale-certificate provisions that sat inside the Condominium Act and the Property Owners'
Association Act. National course material and older Virginia material frequently still describe the
old regime. Read the chapter.

**§ 55.1-2308 — what the contract itself must disclose.** Unless exempt under § 55.1-2317, any
contract for the resale of a unit in a common interest community shall disclose:

**(i)** that the unit is **located in a common interest community**;
**(ii)** that the **seller or the seller's agent is required to obtain from the association a resale
certificate and provide it** to the purchaser or the purchaser's agent;
**(iii)** the **purchaser's right to cancel** the contract under § 55.1-2312;
**(iv)** that the purchaser or purchaser's agent **may request an updated resale certificate** under
§ 55.1-2311; and
**(v)** that the purchaser's right to receive the resale certificate and the right to cancel are
**waived conclusively if not exercised before settlement.**

And the remedy for a contract that omits them: **the purchaser's sole remedy is to cancel the
contract prior to settlement.**

**§ 55.1-2309 — delivery.** The **seller or the seller's agent shall obtain the resale certificate
from the association and provide it** to the purchaser or the purchaser's agent, and — the words
matter — **this requirement shall not be waived or changed by agreement.**

chunks.heading: 30.3 The cancellation right — § 55.1-2312
chunks.excerpt:
The association, its managing agent, or a third party preparing the certificate **shall deliver it
within 14 days after a written request** by the seller or the seller's agent. **If no certificate is
delivered within 14 days, the resale certificate is deemed unavailable.** The association **may not
require the purchaser's name** before preparing it. Delivery to the seller may be printed or in a
generally accepted electronic format as the seller requests. The information must be **current as of
a date specified on the certificate**.

**§ 55.1-2311** provides for an **updated resale certificate** and a financial update.
**§ 55.1-2310** prescribes the form and contents. **§ 55.1-2316** governs fees.

## 30.3 The cancellation right — § 55.1-2312

This is the section a licensee will use most, and its structure is a set of three timing rules.

**A — certificate or unavailability notice delivered *before* ratification.** The purchaser may
cancel within the period **agreed by all parties in the ratified contract**; if the contract
specifies no period, **three days from ratification**.

**B — delivered *after* ratification.** Cancel within the agreed period; if none is specified,
**three days from receipt** of the certificate or of the notice of unavailability.

**C — never delivered at all.** The purchaser **may cancel at any time prior to settlement.**

**D — the notice.** Written notice of cancellation must be given to the seller in accordance with the
contract's terms, and **the purchaser bears the burden of demonstrating delivery** of the notice.
That single sentence is why a purchaser's licensee sends cancellation by a method that produces
proof and retains it.

chunks.heading: 30.4 When the association gets it wrong — § 55.1-2314
chunks.excerpt:
**E — more than one association.** Where a unit is governed by more than one association, the
cancellation period runs **from the date of delivery of the last resale certificate.**
§ 55.1-2315 addresses properties subject to more than one declaration.

**F — the consequence.** Cancellation is **without penalty**, and the seller shall cause any deposit
or escrowed funds to be **returned promptly** to the purchaser.

## 30.4 When the association gets it wrong — § 55.1-2314

**A.** If the association, its managing agent, or a third party preparing the certificate fails to
comply with § 55.1-2310 or § 55.1-2311, the **purchaser is not required to pay delinquent
assessments or to remedy violations of the governing documents or rules existing as of the date of
the certificate or updated certificate.** The association may enforce a **previous owner's**
violation against the purchaser only if (i) the violation was **properly noted** in the certificate
or (ii) the **seller failed to provide** the certificate as § 55.1-2309 requires.

**B.** The purchaser must nonetheless abide by the governing documents and rules **as to matters
arising after acquiring the unit**, certificate or no certificate.

**C.** The **preparer is liable to the seller** for actual damages **not exceeding $1,000**.

**D.** The **Common Interest Community Board** may assess a monetary penalty against an association
under § 54.1-2351 or a common interest community manager under § 54.1-2349, and may issue a cease
and desist order under § 54.1-2349 or § 54.1-2352.

## 30.5 What this means for the licensee's practice

Four operating rules follow directly:

chunks.heading: Hour 30 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**Request the certificate in writing, immediately, and keep the request.** The 14-day clock in
§ 55.1-2309 B runs from a **written** request, and the deemed-unavailable consequence depends on it.

**Confirm the contract carries the § 55.1-2308 disclosures.** Their absence gives the purchaser a
right to cancel before settlement and gives the seller a problem.

**Diary the cancellation period the moment of delivery is known** — three days from ratification,
three days from receipt, or open until settlement, depending on which of § 55.1-2312 A, B or C
applies, and adjusted by any period the parties agreed.

**Never agree to waive the seller's obligation.** § 55.1-2309 A says it **shall not be waived or
changed by agreement**, and a licensee who drafts around it has drafted something ineffective.

### Hour 30 engagement check

**Question.** A contract for a condominium resale is ratified 3 June and specifies no cancellation
period. The seller's agent requests the resale certificate in writing on 5 June. Nothing arrives.
On 24 June the buyer, having heard about a pending roof assessment, wants out. What is the position?

chunks.heading: Hour 31 — Leasehold estates and lease agreements
chunks.excerpt:
**Expected answer.** The written request was made 5 June, so under **§ 55.1-2309 B** the 14 days ran
to 19 June; nothing having been delivered, the certificate is **deemed unavailable** — but the buyer
was never given the certificate *or* a notice of unavailability. That puts the buyer within
**§ 55.1-2312 C**: where neither the certificate nor a notice of unavailability has been delivered,
the purchaser **may cancel at any time prior to settlement**. Cancellation is **without penalty**
under subsection F and the deposit must be returned promptly. The buyer must give **written notice
in accordance with the contract's terms**, and under subsection D **bears the burden of proving
delivery** — so the notice goes by a method that produces proof, and the proof is retained.

---

## Hour 31 — Leasehold estates and lease agreements

## 31.1 What a lease is

A **lease** is simultaneously a **conveyance** — it transfers a leasehold estate and the right of
exclusive possession — and a **contract** — it creates mutual promises. Both characters matter:
the conveyance explains why a tenant may exclude even the landlord except as the lease and the law
allow; the contract explains why breach analysis works as it does.

The parties are the **lessor** (landlord), who retains a **reversion**, and the **lessee** (tenant),
who holds the leasehold.

## 31.2 The four leasehold estates, applied

From Hour 5: **estate for years** (fixed term, expires without notice), **periodic estate**
(automatically renewing until notice), **estate at will** (no fixed period, terminable by either),
and **estate at sufferance** (holdover after a lawful entry).

chunks.heading: 31.3 Essential terms
chunks.excerpt:
The everyday classification errors: calling a one-year lease a "periodic" tenancy because rent is
paid monthly — it is an estate for years, and the payment interval is not the term; and assuming a
holdover tenant is a trespasser — they are a tenant at sufferance, and removing them is a legal
process, not a self-help matter.

## 31.3 Essential terms

A residential lease should identify the parties; the premises; the term with definite start and end;
the rent, its amount, due date, place and method of payment, and any late fee; the security deposit
and its treatment; who pays which utilities; the permitted use and occupancy limits; maintenance
responsibilities on each side; the landlord's right of entry and the notice required; rules on pets,
smoking, parking and alterations; assignment and subletting; default and remedies; renewal or
termination; and the required disclosures.

The **statute of frauds** reaches leases: a lease for a term longer than the statutory period must
be in writing. The Virginia period is a matter of Title 55.1 that this course has not read from
primary text and therefore does not state; write every lease down regardless, which is the answer in
practice.

## 31.4 Security deposits

A security deposit secures the tenant's performance. Statutes typically regulate the maximum amount,
how it is held, the deadline for returning it, the itemisation required for deductions, and whether
interest is payable. Virginia regulates all of this in the **Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant
Act**, Chapter 12 of Title 55.1 — and **this course states no figure or deadline**, because Chapter
12 has not been read from primary text for this project. Hour 32 teaches the navigation.

chunks.heading: 31.5 Assignment and sublease
chunks.excerpt:
What is certain from the Board side: a deposit held by a firm is **escrow money**.
**18VAC135-20-181 A 2** lists rental security deposits among the funds that must go into the escrow
account, and § 54.1-2135 makes accounting a statutory duty for a licensee engaged to manage.

## 31.5 Assignment and sublease

**Assignment** transfers the tenant's **entire remaining interest** to another. The assignee comes
into direct relationship with the landlord. **Sublease** transfers **less than the entire remaining
interest** — a shorter period, or part of the premises — and the original tenant becomes a landlord
to the subtenant while remaining a tenant to the landlord.

The rule students must retain: **in neither case is the original tenant automatically released.**
Release requires the landlord's agreement, and that agreement is a **novation**. A tenant who
"assigned the lease and moved out" is still liable unless the landlord released them in writing.

Most leases restrict both, requiring the landlord's consent.

## 31.6 Termination, breach, and what a licensee must not do

A lease ends by expiration of its term, by mutual agreement, by proper notice in a periodic tenancy,
by surrender and acceptance, or by operation of law. It is not ended by a tenant leaving.

Landlord remedies for non-payment and other breaches run through a **statutory judicial process**.
**Self-help is prohibited**: changing the locks, removing the tenant's possessions, or shutting off
utilities to force a tenant out is unlawful. A licensee who advises a landlord client to do any of
those has advised a violation, and under § 54.1-2133 the licensee's duties include compliance with
applicable law.

chunks.heading: Hour 31 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Where a landlord asks what remedy to pursue, the answer is counsel and the statutory process — and
the licensee's contribution is documentation: the ledger, the notices actually given and how, the
condition record, and the correspondence.

### Hour 31 engagement check

**Question.** A tenant with eight months remaining transfers the apartment to a friend for the
