chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-04
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-04

## Hours 18–23 · Interests in real estate and legal descriptions

**Board topics covered:** REEB 25.033(5) Interests in real estate · REEB 25.033(6) Legal descriptions
**Clock hours:** 6 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Name the four government powers and match a fact pattern to the correct one.
- Classify freehold and leasehold estates and diagram present and future interests.
- Identify an encumbrance by type and say who enforces it.
- Explain riparian and littoral rights, the public trust doctrine, and where a water question goes.
- Distinguish the forms of co-ownership Wisconsin recognises, including its marital property regime.
- Read a rectangular survey description and compute the acreage of an aliquot part.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 18 | Government powers; estates in land | Section completed |
| 19 | Encumbrances: easements, covenants, encroachments | Section completed |
| 20 | Water rights and the public trust doctrine | Section completed |
| 21 | Forms of ownership; marital property; homestead; trusts; entities | Section completed |
| 22 | Cooperatives, condominiums, time-shares | Section completed |
| 23 | Legal descriptions: methods, land units, and measurements | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **6 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 18 — Government powers and estates in land

### 18.1 The four powers — REEB 25.033(5)(a)

Every public limitation on land traces to one of four. The mnemonic is **PETE**.

chunks.heading: 18.2 Fee simple — REEB 25.033(5)(b)
chunks.excerpt:
**Police power** — regulation for public health, safety, morals and general welfare. Zoning, building
codes, subdivision control, shoreland and floodplain regulation, and environmental controls all sit
here. **No compensation is paid**, because nothing is taken; use is regulated. In Wisconsin the power
belongs to the state and is delegated to counties, cities, villages and towns.

**Eminent domain** — the power to take private property for public use with **just compensation**,
executed through a **condemnation** proceeding. Partial takings are common — a strip for a highway
widening — and compensation covers damage to the remainder.

**Taxation** — the levy against property to fund government, backed by a lien and ultimately by sale.
Module WI-05 takes Wisconsin's provisions.

**Escheat** — property passing to the state where an owner dies with no will and no heirs. Rare, and
the reason the list is four.

### 18.2 Fee simple — REEB 25.033(5)(b)

**Fee simple absolute** is the largest estate: potentially infinite, freely transferable during life
and at death, subject only to the four powers and to private restrictions a predecessor accepted. A
conveyance is presumed to convey a fee simple absolute unless the instrument says otherwise.

**Defeasible fees** may end on a stated event.

A **fee simple determinable** ends **automatically** when the event occurs, and the grantor retains a
**possibility of reverter**. The language is durational — "so long as", "while", "until".

A **fee simple subject to a condition subsequent** gives the grantor a **right of re-entry** that must
be exercised. The language is conditional — "but if", "provided that", "on condition that".

Both appear in the record and belong to the title examiner and to counsel.

### 18.3 Life estates

chunks.heading: 18.4 Leasehold estates, named
chunks.excerpt:
A **life estate** is a freehold measured by a life. The **life tenant** has full use and possession,
takes the income, and may convey what they hold — but may not convey more than they own and may not
commit **waste**: they must not damage the property or let it deteriorate, and ordinarily must pay
taxes and interest on existing debt.

When the measuring life ends, either a **reversion** returns the property to the grantor or the
grantor's heirs, or a **remainder** passes it to a named third party.

A **life estate pur autre vie** is measured by another's life and is the one life estate that can be
inherited while the measuring life continues.

**The listing consequence is practical and immediate:** a life tenant alone cannot convey a fee. Every
holder of an interest must sign. Establishing that at listing rather than at closing is the licensee's
job.

### 18.4 Leasehold estates, named

**Estate for years** — a fixed term with a definite beginning and end; it expires without notice, and
its length is irrelevant to the name. **Periodic estate** — renews automatically until notice.
**Estate at will** — no fixed period, terminable by either party subject to statutory notice.
**Estate at sufferance** — a holdover after a lawful entry, distinguished from trespass only by that
lawful entry.

Module WI-11 takes leases, including **residential rental practices under ATCP 134.02, 134.06 and
134.09**.

---

## Hour 19 — Encumbrances

### 19.1 What an encumbrance is — REEB 25.033(5)(c)

An **encumbrance** is a claim, right or interest held by someone other than the owner that affects
title or limits use. Encumbrances travel with the land and do not prevent transfer.

chunks.heading: 19.2 Easements
chunks.excerpt:
They fall into two families: those affecting **use** — easements, restrictive covenants,
encroachments — and those affecting **title as security for money** — liens, which are Module WI-05.

### 19.2 Easements

An **easement** is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a stated purpose, and it is an
interest in land.

An **easement appurtenant** benefits a parcel: the benefited parcel is the **dominant tenement**, the
burdened one the **servient tenement**, and it **runs with the land**, passing automatically to the
next owner whether or not anyone mentions it. Shared driveways, access to a back lot, and drainage are
the everyday cases.

An **easement in gross** benefits a person or entity rather than a parcel — utility easements being
the common example, and commercial easements in gross being assignable.

**Creation.** By **express grant or reservation** in a deed. By **implication**, where a use was
apparent, continuous and necessary when a parcel was divided. By **necessity**, the landlocked-parcel
case, requiring common ownership at severance. By **prescription**, from open, notorious, continuous
and adverse use for the statutory period. By **condemnation**.

**Termination.** By merger, release, abandonment shown by conduct rather than mere non-use, the end of
the necessity, or the easement's own terms.

**This course states no Wisconsin prescriptive-easement or adverse-possession period**, because those
provisions have not been read from primary text for this project. Both are legal determinations in any
event.

chunks.heading: 19.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall
chunks.excerpt:
Two Wisconsin access questions recur and belong in every rural and waterfront intake: **access to
water**, which may be a deeded easement, a prescriptive right, an outlot, or mere tolerance; and
**private and town roads**, where whether the road is public, private, or a discontinued way — and
who plows it — decides whether a buyer can reach the house in February.

### 19.3 Licence, encroachment, party wall

A **licence** is revocable personal permission and is **not** an interest in land. The neighbour who
has "always" crossed the corner usually holds one — unless the use has ripened into a prescriptive
easement, which is a legal determination on facts nobody in the conversation has established.

An **encroachment** is an unauthorised physical intrusion across a boundary. It is found by
**survey**, not by looking, and long-standing encroachments can mature into rights.

A **party wall** is a shared wall on a boundary, each owner typically owning to the centre with an
easement of support in the other half.

### 19.4 Private land-use controls

**Restrictive covenants** are private limits on use, recorded so they bind successors. They regulate
setbacks, minimum sizes, materials, outbuildings, signage, and — increasingly — short-term rental.

Three points:

**They can be stricter than zoning**, and where zoning permits and a covenant forbids, the owner is
bound by both and must satisfy the stricter.

**They are enforced privately** — by an association or a neighbour — not by the municipality.

**Discriminatory covenants are void and must not be honoured.** Historic racial covenants remain
physically present in Wisconsin chains of title. Repeating one as though it operated is itself a fair
housing problem, and Module WI-10 takes **equal rights under s. 106.50**.

chunks.heading: Hour 20 — Water rights
chunks.excerpt:
**REEB 25.033(17)(e)** lists private land-use controls as a required topic in its own right, and
Module WI-12 develops them alongside the public controls.

---

## Hour 20 — Water rights

### 20.1 Why Wisconsin gives this its own paragraph

**REEB 25.033(5)(d)** lists **water rights** as a required topic. Wisconsin has more than fifteen
thousand inland lakes, two Great Lakes shorelines, and a public trust doctrine of constitutional
standing, and waterfront property is a substantial part of the state's market.

### 20.2 The vocabulary

**Riparian rights** attach to land abutting a **flowing** watercourse — a river or stream.
**Littoral rights** attach to land abutting a **lake** or other still water. Both are **appurtenant**:
they belong to the land, run with it, and are not owned separately by a person.

**Accretion** is the gradual deposit of soil by water, which the riparian owner gains. **Reliction**
is the gradual withdrawal of water exposing land, which the owner also gains. **Erosion** is gradual
loss. **Avulsion** is sudden change, which generally does **not** move the boundary.

**The ordinary high water mark** is the concept that separates private riparian ownership from the
public's rights on a navigable water. It is determined by physical evidence on the ground, not by a
map or a plat, and it is not a licensee's to identify.

### 20.3 The public trust doctrine

Wisconsin holds its **navigable waters in trust for the public**. The doctrine is the foundation of
the state's regulation of piers, dredging, bank alteration, boathouses, filling, and shoreland
development.

Two consequences for brokerage:

chunks.heading: 20.4 What a licensee does
chunks.excerpt:
**What a riparian owner may do at the water's edge is regulated.** A pier may need a permit or may sit
under an exemption; a boathouse may be a nonconforming structure that cannot be replaced; bank
alteration and dredging are permitted activities; and **shoreland zoning** administered by the county
governs setbacks, vegetation removal, impervious surface and nonconforming structures.

**Navigability is a legal determination**, and whether a water is navigable decides whether the
doctrine applies at all.

### 20.4 What a licensee does

Nothing but route. The questions and their offices:

**Is the water navigable, and where is the ordinary high water mark?** Department of Natural Resources,
and a surveyor.
**Is the existing pier, boathouse or shore structure permitted, and can it be replaced?** DNR and the
county zoning office, **in writing**.
**What does county shoreland zoning permit here — setback, vegetation, impervious surface?** County
zoning, in writing.
**Is any part of the parcel in a floodplain?** REEB 25.033(18)(f) — **s. 87.30 Stats. and ss. NR
116.01 and 116.06** — the municipality and the mapping.
**Are there wetlands?** REEB 25.033(18)(h) — **s. 23.32** — the DNR.
**Is there a private well, and what is the water quality?** A certified laboratory.

A licensee who tells a buyer they can build a pier, remove trees for a view, or replace the boathouse
has answered a question belonging to the DNR and the county — and has done it in the area where
Wisconsin enforcement is most active.

---

## Hour 21 — Forms of ownership

### 21.1 Severalty and co-ownership — REEB 25.033(5)(e)

**Severalty** is ownership by one person or one entity alone.

chunks.heading: 21.2 Wisconsin is a marital property state
chunks.excerpt:
**Tenancy in common** — each co-owner holds an **undivided fractional interest**, meaning each may
possess the whole rather than a marked-off part. Shares need not be equal. There is **no
survivorship**: on death an owner's share passes to their heirs or devisees. Any co-tenant may
transfer their share without the others' consent, and any may seek **partition**.

**Joint tenancy** adds the **right of survivorship**: on a joint tenant's death the interest passes to
the survivors outside probate. The common-law unities are **time, title, interest and possession**. A
joint tenant who conveys their interest severs the joint tenancy as to that share, and the transferee
holds as a tenant in common.

### 21.2 Wisconsin is a marital property state

This is the single most distinctive ownership fact in Wisconsin, and a licensee arriving from another
state must not carry that state's assumptions here.

**REEB 25.033(19)(f)** requires instruction on **property rights of married persons under ss. 766.31,
766.51, 766.60 and 766.63**, and **REEB 25.033(5)(k)** requires instruction on **homestead under ss.
706.01(7) and 766.605**.

**Wisconsin's Marital Property Act, ch. 766**, is a community-property-style regime. Its general
effect is that property acquired by spouses during marriage is presumptively **marital property** in
which each spouse holds an undivided one-half interest, subject to classification rules,
**individual property** categories, and any **marital property agreement** the spouses have made. It
also recognises **survivorship marital property**.

**Ch. 766 has not been read from primary text for this project, and this course states no rule from
it.** What it states is the **consequence for practice**, which is unavoidable and must be taught:

chunks.heading: 21.3 Trusts and business entities — REEB 25.033(5)(f) and (g)
chunks.excerpt:
**A spouse may hold an interest, and a spouse's signature may be required to convey or to encumber,
even where that spouse does not appear on the deed.** The **homestead** provisions make this
particularly acute for the residence.

**So the question is asked at listing, every time**: is the seller married; is the property the
homestead; is there a marital property agreement; and who must sign? And it is answered by the
**closing agent, the title company and counsel** — never by the licensee.

A licensee who takes a listing signed by one spouse alone, on a Wisconsin homestead, has taken a
listing that may not be performable.

### 21.3 Trusts and business entities — REEB 25.033(5)(f) and (g)

In a **trust**, the trustee holds legal title and manages; the beneficiary takes the benefit. **The
trustee signs.** A **revocable living trust** is a common way to hold a residence.

Property may also be owned by a **corporation**, a **partnership**, a **limited liability company**,
or another entity. Two consequences: the entity's **authority to sign** is a legal question evidenced
by organisational documents and resolutions and verified by the closing agent and counsel; and the
entity's involvement does not change the firm's § 452.133 duties.

Note **§ 452.133(3)(b)**: a licensee may not act in a transaction on behalf of **any organisation or
business entity in which the licensee has an interest** without the **prior written consent of all
parties, obtained in the transaction contract.**

---

## Hour 22 — Cooperatives, condominiums, and time-shares

### 22.1 Cooperatives — REEB 25.033(5)(h)

chunks.heading: 22.2 Condominiums — REEB 25.033(5)(j)
chunks.excerpt:
A corporation owns the real property. The resident owns **shares** and holds a **proprietary lease**.
The resident therefore owns **personal property**, not real property: no deed, financing by share loan
rather than mortgage, a different title and closing mechanic entirely, and a board that typically has
approval rights over a transfer — subject always to fair housing law.

### 22.2 Condominiums — REEB 25.033(5)(j)

Instruction is required **under ss. 703.08, 703.21 and 703.33**.

A condominium divides a project into individually owned **units** and **common elements** owned in
undivided shares by all unit owners, with **limited common elements** — a balcony, an assigned parking
stall, a storage locker — serving fewer than all units. The unit is a **volume of space**, described by
reference to a recorded condominium plat and by elevation.

The instruments are the **declaration**, the **bylaws**, the recorded **plat and plans**, and the
**rules**. The declaration fixes each unit's percentage interest, which usually determines both voting
power and assessment share.

**This course states no requirement from ch. 703**, which has not been read from primary text for this
project — including anything about the disclosure materials a Wisconsin condominium seller must
furnish or any cancellation right attached to them. **Read ch. 703 before stating one.**

What a licensee must do: obtain the declaration, bylaws and rules; the **budget** and current
assessments; the **reserve position**; **two years of minutes**, where a special assessment is
discussed long before it is levied; the assessment and litigation history; the **insurance summary**
and where the master policy stops; and the restrictions on **leasing**, pets, vehicles and
alterations — before the offer.

chunks.heading: 22.3 Time-shares — REEB 25.033(5)(i)
chunks.excerpt:
### 22.3 Time-shares — REEB 25.033(5)(i)

Instruction is required **under ss. 70.095, 707.02, 707.05, 707.40, 707.47 and 707.49**.

A time-share divides the right to occupy a property among many purchasers by period. Wisconsin
regulates time-share sales, disclosure and cancellation in **ch. 707**, and taxation of time-share
property is reached at **s. 70.095**.

**Ch. 707 has not been read from primary text for this project and no requirement from it is stated
here.** A licensee practising in time-share must read the chapter, and a licensee who meets a
time-share in a general residential practice should treat it as a specialty and route it.

---

## Hour 23 — Legal descriptions

### 23.1 Why an address will not do — REEB 25.033(6)(a)

A street address identifies a mailbox. A **legal description** identifies a unique parcel in a way a
surveyor could reproduce on the ground. Deeds, mortgages, plats and judgments use legal descriptions;
offers should.

### 23.2 The three methods

**Metes and bounds.** Describes a boundary by walking it: a **point of beginning**, then **calls** of
bearing and distance, closing back at the point of beginning. A call reads *N 42° 15′ 00″ E, 318.6
feet to an iron pin*. **Monuments control over courses and distances**, because a monument is what a
person on the ground can find.

**Rectangular or government survey.** **Wisconsin is a public land survey state**, and this system
governs most of its land. A student must be able to work it.

chunks.heading: 23.3 The rectangular survey system, worked — REEB 25.033(6)(b)
chunks.excerpt:
**Lot and block**, by reference to a **recorded plat**: *Lot 7, Block 3, Sunset Ridge, in the City of
___, ___ County, Wisconsin*, with the plat recorded in the register of deeds. The plat carries the
metes and bounds of each lot, the streets, the easements, and the surveyor's certification. **A lot
does not exist until the plat is recorded.**

Wisconsin also uses **certified survey maps** — CSMs — for smaller divisions, recorded and referenced
in the same way. Module WI-12 takes them with subdivision regulation.

### 23.3 The rectangular survey system, worked — REEB 25.033(6)(b)

**Principal meridians** run north–south; **base lines** run east–west. Wisconsin's land is surveyed
from the **Fourth Principal Meridian**.

**Township lines** run east–west, six miles apart, creating **tiers** numbered north or south of the
base line. **Range lines** run north–south, six miles apart, numbered east or west of the principal
meridian.

A **township** is the six-mile square where a tier and a range intersect — **36 square miles**.

A township contains **36 sections**, each **one mile square** and **640 acres**, numbered **1 through
36 in a boustrophedonic pattern**: section 1 in the north-east corner, running west to section 6,
then dropping south and running east to section 12, and so on, ending with section 36 in the
south-east corner.

**Aliquot parts.** A section divides into halves and quarters, and each of those divides again. The
arithmetic:

**A section** = 640 acres.
**A half section** = 320 acres.
**A quarter section** = 160 acres.
**A quarter of a quarter** = 40 acres.
**A half of a quarter of a quarter** = 20 acres.

**Read a description from right to left**, taking a fraction of what precedes.

chunks.heading: 23.4 Land units and measurements
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked:* **"The NE¼ of the SW¼ of Section 14"** — start with the section, 640 acres; take the SW
quarter, 160; take the NE quarter of that, **40 acres**.

*Worked:* **"The S½ of the NW¼ of the NE¼"** — 640 × ¼ (NE) = 160; × ¼ (NW) = 40; × ½ (S) = **20
acres**.

*Worked:* **"The W½ of the SE¼ and the NE¼ of the SE¼"** — SE quarter is 160; W half of it is 80; NE
quarter of the SE quarter is 40; total **120 acres**.

**Government lots** are the irregular parcels created where a section is cut by a lake, a river, or a
state boundary and cannot be divided into regular aliquot parts. **They are extremely common on
Wisconsin waterfront**, and their acreage is stated on the plat rather than computed — which is
exactly why a waterfront parcel's acreage cannot be derived from its description.

### 23.4 Land units and measurements

**1 acre = 43,560 square feet.** **1 mile = 5,280 feet.** **1 square mile = 640 acres.**
**1 rod = 16.5 feet.** **1 chain = 66 feet = 4 rods.** **80 chains = 1 mile.**

*Worked:* a lot measuring 264 feet by 330 feet. 264 × 330 = 87,120 square feet; ÷ 43,560 = **2 acres**.
*Worked:* 40 rods = 40 × 16.5 = **660 feet**, which is an eighth of a mile.

### 23.5 Survey and the licensee

A **survey** is a licensed surveyor's determination of where the boundaries are on the ground, and it
is the only thing that answers a boundary question. It finds what a title search cannot:
encroachments, structures over setback lines, fences that do not follow the line, and a septic field
on the wrong parcel.

When to recommend one: irregular parcels; older metes-and-bounds descriptions; government lots;
visible fences or structures near a line; planned construction; unimproved land; **waterfront**; and
any mention of a boundary dispute.

chunks.heading: Module WI-04 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
Reading a plat and telling a buyer where the line is falls outside the licence.

### Module WI-04 engagement check

**Question.** A seller wants to list forty acres described as "the SE¼ of the NW¼ of Section 9", with
a cabin near a lake at the north edge of the parcel and a driveway that crosses a neighbour's land.
The seller is married; his wife is not on the deed and "has nothing to do with it". What do you
establish before you take the listing?

**Expected answer.**

**The acreage checks out on its face**: 640 × ¼ (NW) × ¼ (SE) = **40 acres**. But if any part of the
parcel is cut by the lake it may in fact be a **government lot** rather than a regular aliquot part,
in which case the acreage is what the plat states and cannot be computed from the description. That
goes to the plat and to a surveyor.

**The wife's interest is not the seller's to characterise.** **Wisconsin is a marital property state**
under **ch. 766**, and **REEB 25.033(5)(k) and (19)(f)** require the homestead and marital property
provisions to be taught for exactly this reason: a spouse may hold an interest and a spouse's
signature may be required to convey or encumber **even where that spouse is not on the deed**. I do
not decide it — I raise it at listing and route it to the **title company, the closing agent and
counsel**, because a listing signed by one spouse alone may not be performable.

**The driveway** is a title and boundary question: it may be a recorded easement appurtenant running
with the land, a prescriptive easement, a revocable licence, or an encroachment — and which it is
decides whether the buyer has access. Register of deeds, a **survey**, and counsel.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-04
chunks.excerpt:
**The lake frontage** raises the **ordinary high water mark**, the **public trust doctrine**, **county
shoreland zoning**, and whether the cabin is a **nonconforming structure** that may or may not be
expanded or replaced. Those go to the **DNR** and the **county zoning office in writing**, before the
buyer relies on any plan for the property.

---

## Instructor source note for Module WI-04

Wisconsin statements rest on text read directly from `docs.legis.wisconsin.gov` on 2026-08-20 and
recorded in `wisconsin/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **REEB 25.033(5)(a) through (k)**,
**(6)(a) and (b)**, **(17)(e)**, **(18)(f)** and **(18)(h)**, **(19)(f)**; and **§ 452.133(3)(b)**.

**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** any rule from **ch. 766** (marital
property) or the **homestead** provisions at ss. 706.01(7) and 766.605; any requirement from **ch.
703** (condominiums) or **ch. 707** (time-shares), including any disclosure or cancellation right;
**s. 70.095**; Wisconsin's **prescriptive easement and adverse possession** periods; and the
**navigable waters, shoreland zoning and public trust** provisions administered by the DNR and the
counties.

**Hour 21.2 states Wisconsin's marital property regime as a practice consequence rather than as a
rule.** That a spouse may hold an interest and may need to sign even where not on the deed is the fact
a listing licensee must act on, and the hour routes the determination to the title company, the
closing agent and counsel. It states no classification rule, no presumption's operation, and no
exception. Any instructor supplementing this hour must read ch. 766 first and date the reading.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-04
chunks.excerpt:
**The public trust doctrine and the ordinary high water mark in Hour 20 are stated as concepts**, and
every specific question is routed. Wisconsin's navigable-waters regime has not been read from primary
text for this project, and no permit requirement, exemption, or setback is stated.

All rectangular-survey arithmetic in Hour 23 is worked in full so a reviewer can verify each figure.
That **Wisconsin is surveyed from the Fourth Principal Meridian** is a matter of survey history, and
**government lots** are described because Wisconsin waterfront parcels are commonly described that way.

lessons.title: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-05

chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-05
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-05

## Hours 24–27 · Taxes and other liens

**Board topic covered:** REEB 25.033(7) Taxes and other liens
**Clock hours:** 4 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Classify a lien as voluntary or involuntary and as general or specific.
- Rank competing liens from stated recording and statutory facts and say which survive a foreclosure.
- Explain Wisconsin's property tax cycle from assessment through equalization to the tax bill.
- Identify a construction lien risk at listing and route it.
- Say where the real estate transfer fee comes from and who computes it.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 24 | Liens: classification, priority, release | Section completed |
| 25 | Tax liens; assessment, equalization, and the Wisconsin tax bill | Section completed |
| 26 | Mortgage liens, construction liens, judgments | Section completed |
| 27 | Estate and inheritance tax liens; other liens; ss. 74.15, 74.47, 77.22, 77.27 | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **4 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 24 — Liens

### 24.1 What a lien is — REEB 25.033(7)(a)

A **lien** is a charge against property securing payment of a debt or performance of an obligation. It
is an encumbrance on **title**, and it gives the holder the right to force a sale if the obligation is
not met.

Liens do not affect **possession**. An owner with three liens still lives in the house. What they
affect is transferability, which is why they surface at closing rather than in daily life.

chunks.heading: 24.2 Two classifications, used together
chunks.excerpt:
### 24.2 Two classifications, used together

**Voluntary or involuntary.** A **voluntary** lien is created deliberately by the owner — in
Wisconsin, most commonly a **mortgage**. An **involuntary** lien arises by operation of law: tax
liens, judgment liens, construction liens.

**General or specific.** A **general** lien attaches to **all** of the debtor's property within the
jurisdiction — judgment liens, federal and state tax liens, estate tax liens. A **specific** lien
attaches to **one identified parcel** — the mortgage, the property tax lien, the construction lien,
the special assessment.

Every lien is describable in both dimensions. A judgment lien is involuntary and general; a mortgage
is voluntary and specific.

**Statutory or equitable** is a third axis: a statutory lien is created by statute — the tax lien, the
construction lien; an equitable lien arises from a court's application of fairness or from the parties'
conduct.

### 24.3 Priority

**Priority determines who is paid first from a forced sale, and whose lien survives it.** Liens junior
to the foreclosing lien are generally extinguished as to the property; senior liens survive and the
purchaser takes subject to them.

The general rule is **first to record, first in right**. Three sets of exceptions:

**Statutory superpriority.** Property tax liens come first, whenever recorded, because the statute
puts them there rather than because of their date.

**Relation back.** A **construction lien**'s priority is measured from a date tied to the commencement
of the work rather than from filing, so a lien filed after closing can outrank a mortgage recorded
before it. Hour 26.

chunks.heading: 24.4 Release
chunks.excerpt:
**Subordination.** A lienholder may agree in a recorded **subordination agreement** to take a lower
position than recording order would give — which is why refinancing a first mortgage while a home
equity line remains recorded requires one.

### 24.4 Release

A lien ends when the obligation is satisfied **and a release is recorded**. For a mortgage, that is a
**satisfaction of mortgage**. Payment alone does not clear the record, and an unreleased paid-off
mortgage is among the most common clouds a Wisconsin title search reveals.

The licensee's contribution is timing and disclosure: order title early, read the commitment's
requirements the day it arrives, escalate anything involving recent construction or a judgment
immediately, and disclose what § 452.133(1)(c) requires — in writing, to every party.

---

## Hour 25 — Tax liens and the Wisconsin property tax cycle

### 25.1 Tax liens — REEB 25.033(7)(b)

**Real property tax liens** secure the general property tax. They are **specific**, **involuntary**,
and hold **statutory priority** over other liens regardless of when those liens were recorded.

Unpaid taxes are enforced by the county through a statutory process on its own timetable, ending in
the county taking title. **This course states no delinquency period, interest rate, or redemption
period**, because those provisions have not been read from primary text for this project. They are
answered by the county treasurer.

### 25.2 Assessment, equalization, and the tax bill — REEB 25.033(7)(c)

The rule requires instruction on "general tax assessment, equalization, and tax bills", and Wisconsin's
cycle has features a licensee must be able to explain.

chunks.heading: 25.2 Assessment, equalization, and the tax bill — REEB 25.033(7)(c)
chunks.excerpt:
**Assessment** is performed by the **municipal assessor** — the city, village or town — who determines
the assessed value of each parcel. Wisconsin assessors are certified by the Department of Revenue.

**Assessed value is not market value.** Municipalities revalue on their own cycles, and between
revaluations assessed values drift away from the market. The **assessment ratio** — the relationship
between a municipality's total assessed value and its **equalized value** — is what measures the drift.

**Equalized value** is the Department of Revenue's estimate of the full market value of all taxable
property in a municipality. It exists because tax levies are shared across overlapping jurisdictions —
county, school district, technical college — whose boundaries do not match municipal boundaries. Without
equalization, a municipality that assessed at half of market would shoulder half its fair share of the
county levy. **Equalization apportions the levy fairly between municipalities; it does not change any
individual parcel's assessment.**

**The mill rate** is the levy divided by the assessed value base, conventionally expressed as dollars
per thousand of assessed value.

**The Wisconsin tax bill** is issued in **December** for the year just assessed, and it shows the
levies of each taxing jurisdiction, the state credits applied, and the net amount. Payment is made to
the **municipal treasurer** in the first instance, on the municipality's instalment schedule, with
later instalments and delinquent taxes going to the **county treasurer**.

chunks.heading: 25.3 What a licensee may and may not say
chunks.excerpt:
Two credits appear on a Wisconsin bill and a licensee should recognise them: the **school levy credit**
and **first dollar credit**, applied automatically; and the **lottery and gaming credit**, which
applies only to a property the owner used as a **primary residence** as of a stated date and **only if
claimed**. A buyer of a property that was not the seller's primary residence may not have the credit in
the first year.

### 25.3 What a licensee may and may not say

**May:** state the current annual tax from the municipality's or county's own record; explain the
assessment and equalization concepts; explain that the bill arrives in December; and direct a client to
the assessor, the treasurer, and the Department of Revenue.

**May not:** present assessed value as evidence of market value — that is a **misleading market values**
problem under **REEB 24.09** and inconsistent with **§ 452.133(1)(e)**'s duty to provide **accurate**
information about market conditions; or tell a buyer their taxes will stay at the seller's level, since
a sale frequently prompts a reassessment and credits may change.

**Proration** is Module WI-07's arithmetic, but the Wisconsin trap belongs here: **the tax year, the
billing date and the instalment schedule must be read from the actual bill and the municipality's own
schedule**, not assumed from another state's calendar.

---

## Hour 26 — Mortgage liens, construction liens, and judgments

### 26.1 Mortgage liens — REEB 25.033(7)(d)

Wisconsin uses a **mortgage**, not a deed of trust. Two parties: the **mortgagor**, who is the borrower
and gives the mortgage, and the **mortgagee**, the lender. The **note** is the debt and is not recorded;
the **mortgage** is the security and is recorded.

chunks.heading: 26.2 Construction liens — REEB 25.033(7)(e)
chunks.excerpt:
Priority ordinarily runs from the date and time of recording, subject to the exceptions in 24.3.
Wisconsin residential foreclosure is **judicial**, and Module WI-08 develops the instrument and the
process.

**Land contracts** — REEB 25.033(10)(e) — are a Wisconsin financing structure in their own right, and
Module WI-08 takes them. Their lien and title consequences are real: legal title remains with the
vendor while the vendee holds equitable title and possession.

### 26.2 Construction liens — REEB 25.033(7)(e)

**Wisconsin calls them construction liens**, not mechanics' liens, and they are governed by **ch. 779**.

They secure payment for labour, services, materials or plans furnished to improve real property, and
they are the most dangerous lien for a buyer of recently improved property because of **relation
back**: priority is measured from a date tied to the commencement of the work, so a lien **filed after
closing** can outrank a mortgage recorded before it.

Wisconsin's scheme also carries **notice requirements** — preliminary notices given by contractors and
subcontractors — with deadlines, and strict filing and enforcement periods.

**This course states none of ch. 779's notices, deadlines or periods**, because the chapter has not
been read from primary text for this project.

What a licensee must carry is the **warning sign and the routing**: **recent or ongoing construction,
a recent remodel, a new roof, a new well or septic, or an unpaid contractor dispute on a property
being sold is a question for the closing agent and counsel, every time.** A seller's assurance that
"everyone was paid" is not evidence, and a lien waiver is a document the closing agent obtains.

### 26.3 Judgments — REEB 25.033(7)(f)

chunks.heading: Hour 27 — The remaining liens, and the statutes the rule names
chunks.excerpt:
A **judgment lien** arises when a court judgment is docketed and attaches to the debtor's real
property in that county. It is **general** and **involuntary**, and — importantly — it attaches to
property the debtor acquires **later** as well as property owned at the time.

A judgment against a seller shows up in the title search and must be satisfied at closing. A judgment
against a **buyer** matters too: it attaches to the property the moment the buyer takes title, which
can defeat the lender's expected first position.

**Common-name searches** produce false positives, and clearing a judgment against a different person
with the same name is a routine title requirement that takes time — which is why title is ordered
early.

**Lis pendens** is not a lien but is recorded and gives notice of pending litigation affecting the
property, and it stops a transaction as effectively as a lien would.

---

## Hour 27 — The remaining liens, and the statutes the rule names

### 27.1 Estate and inheritance tax liens — REEB 25.033(7)(g)

Liens securing death taxes attach on death and are **general**. Whether any is in play depends on
federal law and on Wisconsin's own treatment, both of which change, and neither of which this course
states. Where a seller's title comes through an estate, the question belongs to the **title company and
counsel**, and it is one of several reasons an estate sale takes longer than a conventional one.

**Probate** is a listed topic at REEB 25.033(9)(d), and Module WI-07 takes it.

### 27.2 Other liens — REEB 25.033(7)(h)

chunks.heading: 27.3 The statutes REEB 25.033(7) names
chunks.excerpt:
**Special assessments** for public improvements benefiting particular properties — sewer, water,
sidewalks, street lighting. Specific, involuntary, frequently payable in instalments, and frequently
carrying a high priority. **A special assessment levied but not yet payable is a fact a buyer needs at
the offer**, and it is obtained from the municipality.

**Municipal utility charges** — water, sewer and refuse — which in Wisconsin can be placed on the tax
roll and become a lien if unpaid.

**Association assessment liens** in condominiums and planned communities, created by the governing
documents and by statute.

**Federal tax liens** from unpaid federal taxes — general and involuntary.

**State tax liens** — delinquent income, sales or withholding tax.

**Vendor's and vendee's liens** — equitable liens securing, respectively, an unpaid seller and a
buyer's deposit.

**Child support liens** and other statutory liens that attach by operation of law.

### 27.3 The statutes REEB 25.033(7) names

**Taxes under ss. 74.15 and 74.47(1) and (2)** — REEB 25.033(7)(i). **Ch. 74** governs property tax
collection, and the paragraphs named reach the mechanics of payment and of delinquency charges. **This
course states no figure from them**, because ch. 74 has not been read from primary text for this
project, and the county treasurer answers the question in any event.

**Taxation and transfer fees under ss. 77.22 and 77.27** — REEB 25.033(7)(j). Wisconsin imposes a
**real estate transfer fee** on conveyances, submitted with an **electronic real estate transfer
return** at recording. The fee is conventionally paid by the **seller** unless the parties agree
otherwise, and exemptions exist.

chunks.heading: 27.4 The licensee's part in all of it
chunks.excerpt:
**This course states no transfer fee rate and no exemption**, because ch. 77 has not been read from
primary text. The **closing agent computes the fee and prepares the return**, and a licensee who
quotes a rate from memory has answered a question they did not verify.

What a licensee should know: **the transfer return is filed at recording and the fee is a real closing
cost**; **exemptions exist** and a transaction that may qualify — a transfer between spouses, to or
from a trust, or on a divorce — goes to the closing agent early; and the return itself records the
conveyance's value, which is one reason Wisconsin closing figures are visible in the public record.

### 27.4 The licensee's part in all of it

Liens are found by **title search**, cleared by the **closing agent**, and interpreted by **counsel**.

The licensee's contribution is four things: **order title early**; **read the commitment's
requirements the day it arrives**; **escalate immediately** anything involving recent construction, a
judgment, an estate, a special assessment, or an unreleased mortgage; and **disclose in writing** what
**§ 452.133(1)(c)** requires — material adverse facts the firm knows that the party does not know and
cannot discover through reasonably vigilant observation.

### Module WI-05 engagement check

**Question.** A property sells at a Wisconsin foreclosure sale under a mortgage recorded in March 2019.
Also of record: unpaid current-year property taxes; a judgment docketed in 2021; a construction lien
filed in 2023 for a roof installed in **September 2018**; and a second mortgage recorded in 2022. Rank
them, and say which survive.

**Expected answer.**

**Property taxes are paid first** by statutory priority, regardless of when the other liens were
recorded.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-05
chunks.excerpt:
**The construction lien is the trap.** It was **filed** in 2023 but the work was performed in
**September 2018** — before the March 2019 mortgage was recorded. Wisconsin construction liens under
**ch. 779** **relate back** to a date tied to the commencement of the work, so on these facts the lien
may well be **senior** to the 2019 mortgage rather than junior to it. **Whether it does, and from what
date, is a ch. 779 question this course does not answer** — it goes to the closing agent and counsel,
and it is exactly why recent construction on a property being sold is escalated every time.

**Then the 2019 first mortgage**, the foreclosing lien. **Then, from any surplus, the 2021 judgment and
the 2022 second mortgage in recording order.**

**What survives:** the tax lien and anything senior to the foreclosing mortgage — which may include the
construction lien. The **2021 judgment and the 2022 second mortgage are junior** and are extinguished
as to the property, whether or not any surplus reaches them; the underlying debts may survive against
the debtor personally.

None of this is advice a licensee gives. It is why a buyer at a foreclosure sale needs a title search
and counsel before bidding.

---

## Instructor source note for Module WI-05

Wisconsin statements rest on text read directly from `docs.legis.wisconsin.gov` on 2026-08-20 and
recorded in `wisconsin/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **REEB 25.033(7)(a) through (j)**,
**(9)(d)**, **(10)(e)**, and **(13)(b)1.d**; and **§ 452.133(1)(c) and (1)(e)**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-05
chunks.excerpt:
**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** every provision of **ch. 779**
(construction liens), including its **notice requirements, filing deadlines, enforcement periods and
the date from which priority relates back**; every figure in **ch. 74**, including delinquency periods,
interest, and redemption; the **real estate transfer fee rate and every exemption** in **ch. 77**; and
the treatment of **estate and inheritance tax liens** under federal and Wisconsin law.

**The construction lien relation-back rule is taught as a warning sign rather than as a rule with a
date.** Hour 26.2 states that priority is measured from a date tied to the commencement of the work
rather than from filing, which is what makes the lien dangerous, and routes the determination to the
closing agent and counsel. The engagement check is written so that the correct student answer
identifies the risk and the referral — not a date.

**Wisconsin's equalization concept in Hour 25.2 is explained because it is a listed topic** at REEB
25.033(7)(c) and because licensees routinely misdescribe it. Equalization apportions a shared levy
between municipalities; it does not change an individual parcel's assessment. The **lottery and gaming
credit** is described as claimed by an owner using the property as a primary residence, without stating
any date or amount.

lessons.title: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-06

chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-06
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-06

## Hours 28–39 · Real estate contracts and the Board-approved forms

**Board topic covered:** REEB 25.033(8) Real estate contracts
**Clock hours:** 12 — the largest single allocation in the course.
**Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review; REEB 25.033 allocates no hours
among its nineteen topics.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- State the elements of a valid contract and classify a contract four ways.
- Trace an offer through revocation, rejection, counter-offer and acceptance and say whether and when
  a contract formed.
- Explain what a **binding acceptance** is in a Wisconsin offer and why every deadline runs from it.
- Distinguish a **counter-offer** from a **multiple counter-proposal** and say what each does.
- Name every Board-approved form REEB 25.033(8)(f) lists and say what each is for.
- Say precisely what a licensee may and may not do with an approved form.
- Manage a Wisconsin offer's deadlines from binding acceptance to closing.

## Timed sequence

chunks.heading: Hour 28 — Contract law and the elements of a valid contract
chunks.excerpt:
| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 28 | Contract law; elements of a valid contract | Section completed |
| 29 | Classifications; the statute of frauds; capacity and consent | Section completed |
| 30 | Offer, acceptance, counter-offer, and binding acceptance | Section completed |
| 31 | Performance, discharge, default and breach; remedies | Section completed |
| 32 | Ch. REEB 16 and the approved-form regime | Section completed |
| 33 | The offer to purchase: structure and the contingencies | Section completed |
| 34 | Counter-offers, multiple counter-proposals, amendments, notices | Section completed |
| 35 | Addenda; buyer agency agreements; listing contracts | Section completed |
| 36 | Disclosure forms: condition report, agency, buyer and seller disclosure | Section completed |
| 37 | Cancellation agreements and mutual releases; options; bills of sale; exchanges | Section completed |
| 38 | Understanding closing statements | Section completed |
| 39 | Arbitration under s. 788.015; the deadline map; file quality control | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **12 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 28 — Contract law and the elements of a valid contract

### 28.1 What a contract is — REEB 25.033(8)(a) and (b)

A **contract** is a legally enforceable agreement. Four elements are required, and a fifth practical
requirement attaches to contracts concerning land.

**Mutual assent** — an offer and an acceptance producing agreement on the essential terms. Assent must
be genuine, and it is undermined by **fraud**, **misrepresentation**, **mutual mistake**, **duress**
and **undue influence**.

chunks.heading: 28.2 Genuine assent, and where a licensee supplies the defect
chunks.excerpt:
**Competent parties** — legal age and legal capacity. A **minor's** contract is generally **voidable
by the minor**. A person adjudicated incompetent cannot contract; a person lacking capacity at the
moment of contracting produces a voidable contract. Entities act through authorised signatories,
trusts through the trustee, estates through the personal representative.

**Lawful objective** — a contract to do something illegal is **void** and no court will enforce it.

**Consideration** — something of legal value exchanged by each side. Courts examine whether it exists,
not whether it was adequate. In an offer to purchase the mutual promises are the consideration; the
**earnest money is evidence of good faith and ability to perform, not the consideration itself.**

**The statute of frauds** — a contract for the sale of an interest in real property must be **in
writing and signed by the party to be charged**. Wisconsin's conveyancing requirements sit in
**ch. 706**, and REEB 25.033(9)(a) requires instruction on the **requirements of a valid conveyance
under ss. 240.10, 706.02 and 706.03**. Module WI-07 takes them.

### 28.2 Genuine assent, and where a licensee supplies the defect

**Fraud** is a knowing misstatement of material fact relied on to the other party's detriment.
**Innocent misrepresentation** is the same statement made without knowledge of its falsity, and it can
still support rescission.

chunks.heading: 28.3 Capacity in a Wisconsin transaction
chunks.excerpt:
This is where the duties of Module WI-02 meet contract law. A firm that fails to disclose a material
adverse fact under **§ 452.133(1)(c)**, or repeats a seller's statement without qualification, has
supplied the element that makes the contract voidable — and **§ 452.139(2)(a)** does not protect the
client where "the firm or licensee is repeating a misrepresentation made by the client."

**REEB 25.033(14)(h)** lists **civil liability for misrepresentation** as a required topic in its own
right, and Module WI-10 takes it.

### 28.3 Capacity in a Wisconsin transaction

Three capacity questions recur and are established at listing rather than at closing:

**Marital property and homestead.** Wisconsin is a **marital property state** under ch. 766, and a
spouse may hold an interest and may need to sign to convey or encumber the homestead **even where not
on the deed**. Module WI-04 Hour 21.2. The question goes to the title company and counsel.

**Entities and trusts.** Authority is evidenced by organisational documents, resolutions, and trust
instruments, and is verified by the closing agent.

**Powers of attorney**, which must be in the correct form and recorded where the transaction requires
it. A power of attorney discovered at the closing table is a delayed closing.

---

## Hour 29 — Classifications, and the vocabulary examinations use

### 29.1 Four states of a contract

chunks.heading: 29.2 Bilateral or unilateral
chunks.excerpt:
**Valid** — all requirements met; binding on both parties.
**Void** — no legal effect at all, and never had any. An unlawful objective.
**Voidable** — valid and operative **unless** the party with the power to avoid it disaffirms. A
minor's contract; a contract induced by fraud.
**Unenforceable** — valid on its face but not enforceable in court. An oral land contract; a claim
barred by limitation. The parties may perform it voluntarily; no court will make them.

### 29.2 Bilateral or unilateral

**Bilateral** — a promise for a promise. An offer to purchase is bilateral.
**Unilateral** — a promise for an act; the offeree accepts by performing. An **open listing** and a
reward offer are the classic examples, and an **option** is unilateral until exercised.

### 29.3 Executory or executed

**Executory** — something remains to be done. A binding offer to purchase before closing is executory.
**Executed** — **fully performed**.

The trap: the industry says "executed" loosely to mean signed. **The legal meaning is performed**, and
examinations use the legal meaning.

### 29.4 Express or implied

**Express** — stated in words, written or spoken. **Implied** — inferred from conduct.

Note the Wisconsin overlay: an **agency** relationship arises from an **agency agreement**, and
**§ 452.135(2)(a)** requires the Disclosure to Clients not later than the time the firm enters into
it. The parties' conduct does not substitute for the agreement.

### 29.5 Assignment and novation

**Assignment** transfers a party's rights under a contract to an assignee. Whether it is permitted
depends on the contract's own terms, and Wisconsin's approved offer addresses it.

chunks.heading: Hour 30 — Offer, acceptance, and binding acceptance
chunks.excerpt:
**Novation** substitutes a new contract or a new party with the consent of all, and — unlike
assignment — **releases** the original party. A party who "assigned the contract" is not released
unless everyone agreed to a novation in writing.

---

## Hour 30 — Offer, acceptance, and binding acceptance

### 30.1 The offer

An **offer** shows present intent to be bound, is communicated to the offeree, and states the
essential terms definitely enough that a court could enforce them.

An advertisement is generally **not** an offer; it is an invitation to make one. A listing is not an
offer to sell to whoever appears.

### 30.2 How an offer ends

**Acceptance** — a contract forms.

**Rejection** — the offer is dead and cannot afterwards be accepted.

**Counter-offer** — in law a **rejection plus a new offer**. The moment a seller counters, **the
buyer's original offer no longer exists**, and if the buyer walks away the seller cannot then accept
it. This is the mechanic most often misunderstood and the one with the greatest practical consequence
in a multiple-offer week.

**Revocation by the offeror**, effective when communicated, at any time before acceptance — unless the
offeree has paid for an **option**, which is a separate contract holding the offer open.

**Lapse of time**, on the offer's own expiry or after a reasonable time if none is stated. A Wisconsin
offer states a **binding acceptance deadline**, and it is real.

**Death or incapacity** of either party before acceptance.

**Destruction of the property** before acceptance.

### 30.3 Binding acceptance — the Wisconsin concept every deadline runs from

chunks.heading: 30.4 Multiple offers
chunks.excerpt:
Wisconsin's approved offer to purchase uses **binding acceptance** as its reference point, and
essentially every deadline in the offer is expressed as a number of days from it.

**Binding acceptance occurs when a party accepts the offer or the counter-offer and delivers that
acceptance in the manner the offer requires.** Both halves matter: acceptance must be unqualified —
the mirror image rule — and it must be **delivered** as the form defines delivery.

Three consequences a salesperson must be able to state:

**An oral acceptance is not a binding acceptance.** "They said yes" starts no clock.

**The delivery method matters.** The approved offer defines what delivery means and how it may be
accomplished, and a licensee must read that provision rather than assume the common-law **mailbox
rule** that treats a mailed acceptance as effective on dispatch.

**The date of binding acceptance is the single most important date in the file**, because every
inspection, financing, appraisal, title and closing deadline is computed from it. Getting it wrong
mis-computes the entire deadline map.

### 30.4 Multiple offers

A seller may accept one offer, counter one, counter several, or reject all.

**Countering several simultaneously creates a real risk of two contracts on one property**, which is
exactly the problem Wisconsin's **multiple counter-proposal** form addresses — Hour 34.

chunks.heading: Hour 31 — Performance, discharge, breach, and remedies
chunks.excerpt:
The licensee's own duties in a multiple-offer situation come from Module WI-02 and do not bend:
**§ 452.133(1)(g)** requires proposals to be presented **objectively and without bias, with their
advantages and disadvantages disclosed**; **REEB 24.12 and 24.13** — listed at REEB 25.033(13)(b)3 —
require **fair presentation of offers**, **prompt delivery to buyer**, and **prompt notification**,
which Module WI-10 takes; and **§ 452.133(1)(d)** protects each party's confidences separately, so a
buyer's stated maximum is not the seller's to hear.

---

## Hour 31 — Performance, discharge, breach, and remedies

### 31.1 Performance and discharge — REEB 25.033(8)(c) and (d)

A contract is discharged by **performance**; by **mutual agreement to rescind**; by **novation**; by
**operation of law** — including bankruptcy, destruction of the subject matter, or the running of a
limitation period; or by **breach**.

**Substantial performance** is performance of everything essential with only trivial deviation, and it
generally entitles the performing party to enforce, subject to an allowance for the deficiency.

### 31.2 Default and breach — REEB 25.033(8)(e)

A **material breach** defeats the purpose of the contract. A trivial failure is not one, and calling a
trivial failure a breach is itself a breach.

**Time is of the essence** clauses make deadlines strict; where the clause applies, a day late is a
default.

**Remedies**: **damages**; **liquidated damages**, commonly the earnest money; **rescission**; and
**specific performance**, which is available on a land contract because every parcel is unique and
money is treated as an inadequate substitute. Contracts frequently require **mitigation**.

### 31.3 The earnest money, and the two questions about it

chunks.heading: 31.4 The sentence that governs the whole hour
chunks.excerpt:
**Where does it go?** Into the firm's **trust account** under **§ 452.133(1)(f)** and the rules under
**s. 452.13(5)** — Module WI-13 — or to another holder the offer names, in the time the offer and the
rules require.

**Who gets it when the deal fails?** That is a **legal** question. Wisconsin's approved offer contains
provisions governing disbursement of earnest money, including what happens when the parties disagree,
and a firm holding disputed funds follows those provisions and the trust-account rules.

**A licensee never picks a side.** The matter goes to the **supervising broker** and, where necessary,
to counsel. And a licensee who tells a client "you're entitled to the earnest money" has given legal
advice outside **§ 452.133(2)(am)**'s scope.

### 31.4 The sentence that governs the whole hour

**Whether a party is in default, and what remedy follows, are legal conclusions.** A licensee's job
when a deal is failing is to **know the deadline, put the facts in writing, and get the question in
front of the right person in time**. Under **§ 452.133(2)(am)** the duty to advise is limited to
matters within the scope of the knowledge, skills and training required under ch. 452, and default
analysis is outside it.

---

## Hour 32 — Ch. REEB 16 and the approved-form regime

### 32.1 Why Wisconsin has approved forms

**§ 452.05(1)(b)** empowers the Board to approve forms, and **ch. REEB 16** governs the forms used in
real estate transactions. REEB 25.033(8)(f) requires instruction on **"forms used in real estate under
ch. REEB 16"** and then lists fourteen of them.

chunks.heading: 32.2 What a licensee may do
chunks.excerpt:
This is a structural difference from most states, and it exists for a specific reason: **a licensee
completing a Board-approved form is not practising law.** The Board has approved the language; the
licensee supplies the facts the parties have agreed. Take the approved forms away and every completed
contract becomes a drafting question.

### 32.2 What a licensee may do

**Use the latest applicable approved form.** REEB 16.06(7) controls the version; 16.04 identifies when approved forms are required and its exceptions. Under 16.04(2), when no approved contractual form exists for the purpose, a licensee may use a party- or attorney-drafted form with the drafter identified. Under 16.04(3), a licensee acting as agent may negotiate an agreement and permit the parties or their attorney to prepare the agreement containing the negotiated terms.

**Complete the blanks and options to accomplish the party's contractual instructions.** Under 16.06(3), provisions may be crossed out if the deleted text remains legible. This is not the same as secretly deleting printed text from a reproduced standard form. Reproduction must comply with 16.06(1); the forms identified in 16.06(2) have a separate no-modification restriction.

**Use pre-prepared addenda only under the applicable rule.** An addendum covered by 16.06(4) must be prepared by an identified firm or attorney, properly incorporated, and relate to blanks or optional provisions. An addendum altering printed provisions under 16.06(5) must be prepared by an identified attorney, have no optional or multiple-choice provisions, and no blanks except the limited permitted items. Sections 16.06(6) and (9) allow the specified listing and buyer-agreement conversions.

chunks.heading: 32.3 What a licensee may not do
chunks.excerpt:
**Give a general explanation, not a legal ruling.** REEB 16.05(2) permits a general explanation of approved-form provisions at completion or delivery for acceptance. Paragraph (1) prohibits advice or opinions on legal rights, obligations, the effect of a specific contract or conveyance, or title. Paragraph (3) limits use to incidental real-estate practice; (4) prohibits a separate form-completion charge.

**Give the signer a copy promptly.** REEB 15.02(1) requires an exact and complete copy promptly when the person signs; do not wait automatically for closing.

**Do not conceal part of the parties' bargain from the lender.** If a licensee knows the entire agreement has not been disclosed to the financial institution or other lender financing the purchase, REEB 24.07(4) requires timely written disclosure of that fact to the lender.

### 32.3 What a licensee may not do

A licensee may not give the legal advice prohibited by REEB 16.05(1), disguise an altered reproduction as the unchanged approved form, make a separate form-completion charge, or ignore the addendum and version conditions. **A blanket ban on every alteration of printed provisions is incorrect:** legible crossing-out and the specific permitted conversions are addressed in 16.06.

The approved additional forms under 16.03 differ for brokers and salespersons. For example, the State Bar conveyance forms in 16.03(1)(a) are among the broker approvals and are not included in the additional forms granted to salespersons by (2). A salesperson must not infer deed-preparation authority from the broker provision. Consult the complete rule and supervising broker for the actual transaction.

### 32.4 The practical discipline

chunks.heading: Hour 33 — The offer to purchase
chunks.excerpt:
**Use the current version.** Approved forms are revised, and using a superseded version is an error a
reviewer will find.

**Complete every blank the transaction requires**, and do not leave a provision ambiguous because the
parties have not decided. An undecided term is a term to be decided, not a blank to be left.

**Attach every addendum the form references**, and reference every addendum that is attached.

**Initial and date every change**, by every party.

**Control the version.** Where several signed counterparts circulate by email, the question of which
document is the contract must never be genuinely open.

This course does not reproduce the Board-approved forms. The targeted current REEB 16 form-use rules were read on 2026-09-06; the actual current form must still be obtained for each transaction. A student is taught
the **structure and the discipline**; the forms in use are the Board's current versions, obtained from
the Board.
