chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-07
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-07

## Hours 40–44 · Title records and transfers of title

**Board topic covered:** REEB 25.033(9) Title records and transfers of title
**Clock hours:** 5 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- State what ch. 706 requires of a valid conveyance and where each requirement comes from.
- Distinguish the Wisconsin deed forms by what each warrants.
- Distinguish voluntary from involuntary alienation and name the Wisconsin routes of each.
- Explain probate's effect on a listing and on a closing.
- Explain recording, notice, and the difference between recording and transferring title.
- Read a title commitment well enough to separate requirements from exceptions.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 40 | Conveyance defined; requirements of a valid conveyance | Section completed |
| 41 | Types of deeds | Section completed |
| 42 | Involuntary alienation; probate; transfer by will | Section completed |
| 43 | Public records and recording; notice | Section completed |
| 44 | Evidence of title; title insurance; the commitment | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **5 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 40 — What a conveyance is and what makes one valid

### 40.1 Conveyance defined — REEB 25.033(9)(h)

chunks.heading: 40.2 Requirements of a valid conveyance — REEB 25.033(9)(a)
chunks.excerpt:
**§ 706.01** defines "conveyance" for the purposes of Wisconsin's conveyancing chapter, and the
definition matters because **ch. 706** is what governs the transaction's paper. The chapter reaches
deeds, land contracts, mortgages, leases of stated length, easements, and other instruments affecting
an interest in land.

**Ch. 706 has not been read from primary text for this project and this course states no definition,
exception or formal requirement from it.** What it states is the structure a licensee must recognise
and the routing.

### 40.2 Requirements of a valid conveyance — REEB 25.033(9)(a)

The rule requires instruction on the requirements **under ss. 240.10, 706.02 and 706.03**.

**§ 240.10** is Wisconsin's statute of frauds provision governing **real estate broker contracts** — it
is why a Wisconsin listing must be in writing and signed, and REEB 25.033(8)(f)1 cites it for listing
agreements.

**§ 706.02** sets out the formal requisites of a conveyance: broadly, a writing identifying the parties,
the land and the interest conveyed, signed by or on behalf of each of the grantors, with the formalities
the section prescribes — and Wisconsin's **marital property and homestead** provisions mean that
identifying "each of the grantors" is not always obvious from the deed.

**§ 706.03** addresses **agency and authority** — who may sign for whom, and the authority a signer must
have.

**Because the sections have not been read**, this course teaches the **consequences a licensee acts on**
rather than the elements:

chunks.heading: 40.3 Delivery and acceptance
chunks.excerpt:
**Everyone whose signature is required must sign**, and who that is includes co-owners, a life tenant
and the remaindermen, a trustee, a personal representative, an entity's authorised signatory, an
attorney-in-fact under a proper power, and — on a Wisconsin **homestead** — **a spouse who may not appear
on the deed at all**.

**Authority must be evidenced**, and it is verified by the **closing agent and the title company**.

**Both questions are established at listing**, because a signature problem discovered at closing is a
closing that does not happen.

### 40.3 Delivery and acceptance

A deed takes effect on **delivery** with the grantor's present intent to pass title, and on the
grantee's **acceptance**, which is presumed where the conveyance benefits them.

The consequence students most often get wrong: **recording does not transfer title.** A signed,
notarised deed locked in a drawer transfers nothing. Title passes on delivery; **recording gives notice
to the world**, and Hour 43 is why that matters enough to do immediately.

### 40.4 The licensee's boundary

**In Wisconsin the deed is prepared by an attorney or by the closing agent**, not by the licensee.
Selecting between deed forms is legal advice. A licensee asked "which deed should we use?" has one
correct answer: *that is a question for your attorney or the closing agent, and here is how to reach
them* — which is the sentence **§ 452.135**'s own printed disclosure supplies.

---

## Hour 41 — Types of deeds

### 41.1 The Wisconsin forms — REEB 25.033(9)(b)

Wisconsin deed forms are distinguished by **what the grantor warrants**.

chunks.heading: 41.2 The transfer return
chunks.excerpt:
**Warranty deed.** The grantor warrants title against all defects, whenever arising — including before
the grantor owned the property. The strongest deed and the norm in Wisconsin residential resale.

**Special warranty deed.** The grantor warrants only against defects arising **during the grantor's own
ownership**. Anything earlier is not warranted. Used by fiduciaries, entities, relocation companies, and
commonly by builders on new construction.

**Quit claim deed.** The grantor conveys whatever interest the grantor has — **which may be nothing** —
and warrants nothing at all. It is a **curative** instrument: clearing a possible interest, correcting a
name, releasing a spouse's or a former spouse's interest, resolving a boundary, or conveying between
family members. **A quit claim is not a lesser way to buy a house**, and a buyer accepting one is
accepting the risk that the grantor owned nothing.

**Trustee's deed**, **personal representative's deed**, **guardian's deed**, and **sheriff's deed** —
fiduciary and judicial deeds, each carrying the authority under which the signer acts, and each raising
the question whether that authority was properly obtained and exercised.

**Deed in lieu of foreclosure**, by which a borrower conveys to the lender voluntarily. Junior liens
generally survive it, which is why lenders often refuse it.

**Land contract** — REEB 25.033(10)(e) — is not a deed but is a Wisconsin conveyancing structure in
which legal title stays with the **vendor** until payment is complete while the **vendee** takes
possession and equitable title. Module WI-08 takes it, and a **deed** is delivered at the end.

### 41.2 The transfer return

chunks.heading: Hour 42 — Involuntary alienation, probate, and transfer by will
chunks.excerpt:
Every Wisconsin conveyance recorded carries an **electronic real estate transfer return** and, unless
exempt, the **real estate transfer fee** under **ss. 77.22 and 77.27** — Module WI-05 Hour 27.3. The
closing agent prepares the return and computes the fee.

---

## Hour 42 — Involuntary alienation, probate, and transfer by will

### 42.1 Involuntary alienation — REEB 25.033(9)(c)

Title passes without the owner's agreement in several ways, and each appears in a chain of title as
something other than an ordinary deed:

**Foreclosure**, which in Wisconsin is **judicial** for residential mortgages — a court action, a
judgment, a redemption period, and a sheriff's sale confirmed by the court.

**Tax delinquency**, ending in the county taking title.

**Eminent domain**, through condemnation.

**Adverse possession**, where possession that is open, notorious, continuous, exclusive and hostile for
the statutory period ripens into title. **This course states no Wisconsin period**, which has not been
read from primary text for this project, and adverse possession is a legal determination in any event.

**Partition**, where co-owners cannot agree and a court divides or orders a sale.

**Escheat**, where an owner dies with no will and no heirs.

**Bankruptcy**, where a trustee administers and may sell.

Each carries its own question about whether the process was completed correctly — which is why title
insurers examine such chains closely and why a transaction with one in it takes longer.

### 42.2 Probate — REEB 25.033(9)(d)

**Probate** is the court-supervised administration of a deceased person's estate. Its brokerage
consequences are practical and recurring.

chunks.heading: 42.3 Transfer by will — REEB 25.033(9)(e)
chunks.excerpt:
**Who may sign.** The **personal representative** appointed by the court, acting under **letters** whose
scope must be checked. A listing signed by a family member who has not been appointed is a listing that
cannot close.

**Whether court approval is required** for the sale, which depends on the form of administration and on
the will's terms.

**How long it takes.** Weeks at best, months commonly, and a purchase contract with a closing date that
ignores the estate's timetable is a contract that will need amendment.

**What deed the estate gives** — typically a **personal representative's deed** rather than a warranty
deed, which changes what the buyer is getting.

**Whether the estate is even in probate.** Wisconsin has mechanisms by which some property passes
without full administration — **transfer on death** designations for real property, marital property
agreements with survivorship features, and survivorship marital property — and which applies is a
**legal** question for the title company and counsel.

**This course states no Wisconsin probate procedure, threshold or period**, because ch. 851 to 879 have
not been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee does is **ask, at listing, whether an
owner has died**, and route the answer.

### 42.3 Transfer by will — REEB 25.033(9)(e)

A **testator** disposes of real property by **devise** to a **devisee**. A will is effective only on
death and only if admitted to probate, and until then the intended devisee owns nothing.

Where there is no will, **intestate succession** distributes the estate by statute, and Wisconsin's
**marital property** regime affects the result.

chunks.heading: Hour 43 — Public records, recording, and notice
chunks.excerpt:
The recurring problem in a Wisconsin chain of title is an **unprobated estate** — a deceased owner in
the chain whose estate was never administered. Title cannot be conveyed until it is, and the time that
takes is measured in months. It is discovered when the title commitment arrives, which is why title is
ordered early.

---

## Hour 43 — Public records, recording, and notice

### 43.1 The register of deeds — REEB 25.033(9)(f)

Wisconsin records land instruments in the **county register of deeds**. What is recorded there includes
deeds, mortgages and satisfactions, land contracts, easements, restrictive covenants, plats and
certified survey maps, judgments and liens, lis pendens, and probate documents affecting title.

**Recording is constructive notice to the world.** That is the point of the whole system: it allows a
stranger to a transaction to discover, by searching a public office, what interests exist in a parcel,
without asking anyone.

### 43.2 The three kinds of notice

**Actual notice** is what a person in fact knows.

**Constructive notice** is what the law charges a person with knowing whether they know it or not,
because it is recorded. Everyone is charged with notice of every properly recorded instrument in the
chain of title.

**Inquiry notice** is what a person would have discovered by making the investigation the visible facts
demanded. **Possession by someone other than the owner is the classic trigger.** A buyer who sees a
tenant in the house is on notice to ask, and is charged with what a reasonable inquiry would have
revealed — even if nothing is recorded.

The practical lesson: **possession is notice**, and a property occupied by anyone other than the seller
raises a question that must be answered in writing before closing.

chunks.heading: 43.3 Chain of title, gaps, and clouds
chunks.excerpt:
### 43.3 Chain of title, gaps, and clouds

A **chain of title** is the succession of recorded owners. A searcher works backward from the current
owner and forward again, checking each ownership period for liens and adverse instruments.

A **gap** is a break — a conveyance out from someone who never appears as a grantee. In Wisconsin the
usual causes are an **unprobated estate**, an unrecorded deed, or a name change.

A **cloud** is a recorded instrument or claim casting doubt on title without necessarily defeating it —
an unreleased mortgage, an old judgment, an ambiguous easement, a defective acknowledgment, a deed from
one of several heirs.

**Marketable title** is title a reasonable, well-informed purchaser would accept: not perfect title, but
title free from reasonable doubt and the threat of litigation. It is what the offer's title provisions
require the seller to convey.

**Quiet title** is the judicial proceeding used where nothing else will clear a cloud.

### 43.4 Record immediately

Wisconsin's recording act determines priority between competing claimants, and **this course does not
state which rule Wisconsin applies or where it sits**, because the provision has not been read from
primary text for this project.

What follows under any of the three models — race, notice, or race-notice — is the operating
instruction: **record immediately, and treat any delay as risk.** The closing agent records; the
licensee's contribution is to make sure nothing is holding it up.

---

## Hour 44 — Evidence of title

### 44.1 What "evidence of title" means — REEB 25.033(9)(g)

chunks.heading: 44.2 Title insurance
chunks.excerpt:
The seller must show the buyer that title is what the contract requires it to be. Historically that was
an **abstract of title** — a condensed history of everything recorded affecting the parcel — with an
attorney's **title opinion** on it. Wisconsin practice today uses **title insurance** in most
transactions, and the offer specifies what evidence the seller must furnish.

An opinion compensates only if the attorney was negligent. **A policy pays on the risk**, and it
includes a duty to **defend** — which is frequently worth more than the indemnity.

### 44.2 Title insurance

**Backward-looking indemnity** against defects in title **existing at the policy date** and not
excepted. One premium, paid at closing, no renewals.

An **owner's policy** insures the buyer's interest for the purchase price, for as long as the insured or
their heirs hold an interest. A **loan policy** insures the lender's security interest for the loan
amount, declining as it is repaid.

**A loan policy does not protect the buyer.** This is the most important consumer point in the hour: a
buyer who pays for the lender's policy and declines an owner's policy has purchased protection for
someone else.

### 44.3 Reading the commitment

**Schedule A** — the facts: the proposed insured, the amount, the estate insured, the current record
owner, and the legal description.

**Schedule B-I, Requirements** — what must be **done** before the policy issues. Pay off and satisfy the
existing mortgage. Obtain a death certificate. Complete a probate. Obtain a spouse's signature. Record a
corrective deed. Obtain a lien waiver from a contractor. **These are action items with owners and
deadlines, and they are the part of the commitment most likely to derail a closing if nobody reads them
early.**

chunks.heading: 44.4 What title insurance does not cover
chunks.excerpt:
**Schedule B-II, Exceptions** — what the policy will **not** cover: recorded easements, restrictive
covenants, mineral reservations, **matters an accurate survey would show**, **rights of parties in
possession**, and taxes not yet due. Exceptions are not defects; they are risks the insurer declines and
the buyer keeps.

**Exclusions** are different: printed in the policy form, removing whole categories — governmental
police power and zoning, eminent domain, defects the insured created or agreed to, and matters first
attaching after the policy date.

**Extended coverage** removes some standard exceptions, typically requiring a **survey** and an
affidavit, and costs more. Recommending that a buyer **ask the closing agent about** extended coverage
is proper; telling a buyer they do not need it is not.

### 44.4 What title insurance does not cover

Anything **excepted**. Anything **excluded**. And **every problem with the physical property** — a
leaking roof, a failed septic system, radon, a boundary a survey would have shown, the neighbour's
noise. Buyers conflate title and condition constantly, and a licensee who does not correct the confusion
leaves a buyer believing they are insured against something they are not.

### Module WI-07 engagement check

**Question.** Your seller's title commitment arrives with Schedule B-I requiring: (1) satisfaction of a
1998 mortgage; (2) completion of probate for a co-owner who died in 2019; and (3) the signature of the
seller's spouse, who is not on the deed. Schedule B-II excepts "rights of parties in possession" and
"matters an accurate survey would disclose". The seller says the spouse "has nothing to do with it" and
that the brother-in-law living in the basement "is just staying for a while". What do you do?

**Expected answer.**

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — title worked through
chunks.excerpt:
**All three requirements are action items with owners and deadlines, and I escalate them the day the
commitment arrives.** The **1998 mortgage** needs a recorded **satisfaction**, and locating a lender
acquired twice since takes time. The **2019 death** means an **unprobated estate** in the chain — title
cannot be conveyed until it is administered, that takes **months**, and the closing date in the contract
almost certainly needs amending.

**The spouse's signature is not the seller's to waive.** Wisconsin is a **marital property state**, and
**§ 706.02** requires the signature of each grantor while the **homestead** provisions may require a
spouse's signature **even where the spouse is not on the deed**. The title company has required it for a
reason. I route it to the **closing agent and counsel** and I do not accept the seller's
characterisation.

**The brother-in-law in the basement is inquiry notice**, and it lines up exactly with the Schedule B-II
exception for **rights of parties in possession**. A buyer who sees an occupant is charged with what a
reasonable inquiry would have revealed, and the exception means the policy will not cover whatever that
turns out to be. The occupancy is put in writing to the seller and the closing agent, and it is also a
fact I must consider under **§ 452.133(1)(c)** — a material adverse fact the firm knows that a buyer may
not be able to discover through reasonably vigilant observation.

**The survey exception** means the buyer should consider a **survey**, or ask the closing agent about
**extended coverage**. I recommend they ask; I do not tell them what they need.

---

## Extended treatment — title worked through

### E7.1 The deeds compared

chunks.heading: E7.2 A chain of title, read
chunks.excerpt:
| Deed | Warrants | Typical use | Buyer's risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warranty deed | Against **all** defects, whenever arising | Residential resale | Lowest |
| Special warranty | Only defects arising **during the grantor's ownership** | Fiduciaries, entities, builders | Pre-ownership defects uncovered |
| Quit claim | **Nothing** — conveys whatever the grantor has | Curative; family; releasing an interest | The grantor may have owned nothing |
| Personal representative's | The authority under which the signer acts | Estate sales | Whether the authority was properly obtained |
| Sheriff's | The judicial process behind it | Foreclosure sales | Whether the process was completed correctly |
| Deed in lieu | Voluntary conveyance to a lender | Avoiding foreclosure | **Junior liens generally survive** |

### E7.2 A chain of title, read

*The commitment shows: 1971 warranty deed to Harold and Ruth; 1998 quit claim from Ruth to Harold; 2004
warranty deed from Harold to the current seller; a 1999 mortgage marked unsatisfied; a 2016 judgment
against "H. Anderson"; and a 2021 easement to a utility.*

**The 1998 quit claim** is ordinary — a spouse releasing an interest, most likely on a divorce or an
estate plan — but a quit claim in a chain always raises the question of **what interest existed to
release**, and in Wisconsin the **marital property** question sits behind it.

**The 1999 mortgage marked unsatisfied** is a Schedule B-I requirement and probably the longest lead
item: locating a lender acquired twice since and obtaining a recorded **satisfaction** takes weeks.

chunks.heading: E7.3 Recording, notice, and the possession problem
chunks.excerpt:
**The 2016 judgment against "H. Anderson"** is a **common-name** problem. It may be the seller or it may
be a different person entirely, and clearing it requires an affidavit or a search the title company
directs. It is routine and it takes time.

**The 2021 utility easement** is a Schedule B-II **exception** — a risk the insurer declines and the
buyer keeps — and its location matters if the buyer intends to build.

**The licensee's part in all four:** read Schedule B-I the day it arrives, identify the owner and the
deadline for each requirement, escalate to the closing agent, and tell the client in writing what may
move the closing date.

### E7.3 Recording, notice, and the possession problem

**Recording gives constructive notice** and does not transfer title. **Title passes on delivery** with
present intent, and on acceptance.

**Possession is inquiry notice**, and it is the notice a licensee is most likely to encounter and least
likely to act on. A tenant, a relative, a former owner, a person storing equipment in an outbuilding —
each raises a question a reasonable purchaser must investigate, and the buyer is charged with what a
proper inquiry would have revealed even where nothing is recorded.

**And it lines up with the Schedule B-II exception for "rights of parties in possession"**, so the
policy will not cover whatever the inquiry would have found.

**What a licensee does:** disclose the occupancy in writing as a fact the firm knows —
**§ 452.133(1)(c)** — and insist the question go in writing to the seller and to the closing agent
before closing. **Never accept the seller's characterisation as settling it.**

### E7.4 Probate's effect on a timetable

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-07
chunks.excerpt:
| Step | Who | Typical effect on a closing date |
|---|---|---|
| Determining whether administration is required | Title company, counsel | Days |
| Appointment of a personal representative | Court | **Weeks** |
| Confirming the scope of the letters | Title company | Days |
| Court approval of a sale, where required | Court | **Weeks** |
| Executing a personal representative's deed | Personal representative | At closing |

**A purchase contract written on an estate property with an ordinary closing date is a contract that will
need amendment.** The licensee's contribution is to ask at listing whether an owner has died, route the
answer, and set a realistic date — not to discover it when the commitment arrives.

---

## Instructor source note for Module WI-07

Wisconsin statements rest on text read directly from `docs.legis.wisconsin.gov` on 2026-08-20 and
recorded in `wisconsin/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **REEB 25.033(9)(a) through (h)**,
**(7)(j)**, **(8)(f)1**, **(10)(e)**; and **§ 452.133(1)(c)** and **§ 452.135**.

**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** the definition of conveyance in **§ 706.01**
and the requisites in **§§ 706.02 and 706.03**, and **§ 240.10**, all of which the rule names and which
this module routes rather than states; Wisconsin's **recording act** and its priority rule; the
**adverse possession** period; Wisconsin **probate** procedure, thresholds and periods in chs. 851–879,
and the mechanisms by which real property may pass outside full administration; **ch. 766** marital
property and the **homestead** provisions; and the **transfer fee** in ch. 77.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-07
chunks.excerpt:
**Hour 40.2 teaches the consequences a licensee acts on rather than the elements of §§ 706.02 and
706.03**, and says so. That everyone whose signature is required must sign — including, on a Wisconsin
homestead, a spouse who may not appear on the deed — is stated as the practice consequence and routed to
the title company, the closing agent and counsel. An instructor supplementing this hour with the
statutory elements must read ch. 706 first and date the reading.

**Hour 43.4 deliberately declines to state Wisconsin's recording-act rule.** It teaches the three
models and the operating instruction that follows under any of them — record immediately.

lessons.title: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-08

chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-08
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-08

## Hours 45–51 · Real estate finance and basic math

**Board topic covered:** REEB 25.033(10) Real estate finance and basic math
**Clock hours:** 7 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- Describe buyer qualification and compute the ratios a lender uses.
- Distinguish the note from the mortgage and name the parties to a Wisconsin mortgage.
- Explain the clauses that decide outcomes and the effect of each.
- Explain a Wisconsin **land contract** and what the vendor and vendee each hold.
- Describe the payment plans a buyer will meet and what risk each carries.
- Explain the secondary mortgage market and why guidelines exist.
- Compute LTV, points, interest, a payment from a factor, prorations and cash to close.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 45 | Buyer qualification; credit; the consumer-protection frame | Section completed |
| 46 | Mortgage instruments: the note, the mortgage, the clauses | Section completed |
| 47 | Default, assignment, release, and "subject to"; foreclosure | Section completed |
| 48 | Land contracts | Section completed |
| 49 | Payment plans; programme categories | Section completed |
| 50 | The secondary mortgage market | Section completed |
| 51 | Basic math: LTV, points, interest, payments, prorations, cash to close | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **7 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 45 — Buyer qualification — REEB 25.033(10)(a)

### 45.1 What underwriting examines

chunks.heading: 45.2 The ratios
chunks.excerpt:
**Capacity** — income, its stability, and the ratios below. **Credit** — history and score, and the
explanation for anything derogatory. **Capital** — assets, reserves, and the **source** of funds; a
large undocumented deposit is a condition, and a gift needs a gift letter and a paper trail.
**Collateral** — the appraisal, and the property's condition and eligibility for the programme.

### 45.2 The ratios

**Front-end (housing) ratio** = monthly housing expense ÷ gross monthly income.
**Back-end (total debt) ratio** = total monthly obligations ÷ gross monthly income.

*Worked:* gross monthly income $7,800; PITI $2,180; other obligations $610.
Front-end 2,180 ÷ 7,800 = **27.9%**. Back-end 2,790 ÷ 7,800 = **35.8%**.

**PITI** is principal, interest, taxes and insurance, plus mortgage insurance and any association dues
the lender includes.

**The thresholds are the lender's and the programme's, and they change. This course states none.** A
licensee computes a ratio to help a buyer think; the lender decides.

### 45.3 Pre-qualification and pre-approval

A **pre-qualification** is an informal estimate from unverified information. A **pre-approval** rests on
a submitted application, verified documentation, and usually a conditional underwriting decision. A
seller evaluating offers is entitled to know which is in front of them, and a licensee who lets one be
presented as the other has misrepresented their buyer's position — a **§ 452.133(1)(a)** honesty problem
before it is anything else.

### 45.4 The consumer-protection frame

chunks.heading: 45.4 The consumer-protection frame
chunks.excerpt:
**TILA and Regulation Z** — disclosure of the cost of credit, principally the **annual percentage
rate**, and control of credit advertising through the **trigger terms**: the amount or percentage of a
down payment, the number of payments or the period of repayment, the amount of any payment, or the
amount of any finance charge. State one and the rest must follow. **"$1,850 a month!" in a property
advertisement is a credit advertisement.**

**RESPA and Regulation X** — the settlement process. **Section 8(a)**: no fee, kickback or thing of
value pursuant to an agreement or understanding for the **referral** of settlement service business.
**Section 8(b)**: no **unearned fees**. Affiliated business arrangements are permitted where disclosed
in the prescribed form, the referral is not required, and the only thing of value received is a return
on ownership interest.

Wisconsin has its own overlay: **§ 452.133(3)(a)** prohibits accepting any fee or compensation related
to the transaction from anyone other than the licensee's client or firm **without the prior written
consent of all parties**, and **§ 452.133(3)(c)** requires **written disclosure** of a referral interest.
A "marketing agreement" that is in substance payment for referrals engages both.

**TRID** — the **Loan Estimate** shortly after application and the **Closing Disclosure** received by
the borrower a defined period before consummation, with certain late changes **re-starting** that
period. **No period is stated here; the lender states it.**

chunks.heading: 45.5 What a licensee tells a buyer, and what they must not
chunks.excerpt:
**ECOA and Regulation B** — no discrimination in credit on the basis of race, colour, religion, national
origin, sex, marital status, age where the applicant has capacity to contract, receipt of public
assistance income, or the good faith exercise of consumer credit rights.

**HMDA**, **FCRA** and its adverse action notice, the **SAFE Act**, and **Dodd-Frank's ability-to-repay
and qualified mortgage** standards complete the frame. **REEB 25.033(19)(g)** separately requires
instruction on **mortgage banking under s. 224.71**, which Module WI-13 names.

### 45.5 What a licensee tells a buyer, and what they must not

**Tell them, in writing at binding acceptance:** do not change or leave a job; do not open credit
accounts or finance furniture, a vehicle or appliances; do not close accounts or pay off collections
without asking the loan officer; do not make undocumented large deposits; do not move money
unnecessarily; do not co-sign; do not miss a payment.

**Do not tell them:** that they will qualify, what rate they will get, or what a programme requires as
though it were settled. **§ 452.133(2)(am)** limits advice to matters within the scope of the knowledge,
skills and training required under ch. 452, and lending eligibility is outside it.

---

## Hour 46 — Mortgage instruments — REEB 25.033(10)(b)

### 46.1 Two documents, two jobs

**The promissory note** is the **debt** — the borrower's personal promise to repay, with the rate, the
payment, the term, late charges, prepayment terms, default and acceleration. It is a negotiable
instrument and can be sold. **It is not recorded.**

**The mortgage** is the **collateral** — it pledges the property as security and creates the lien. **It
is recorded**, in the county register of deeds.

chunks.heading: 46.2 Wisconsin uses a mortgage, not a deed of trust
chunks.excerpt:
Pay off the note and a **satisfaction of mortgage** must be recorded. A recorded but unsatisfied
mortgage is one of the most common clouds a Wisconsin title search reveals.

### 46.2 Wisconsin uses a mortgage, not a deed of trust

A **mortgage** has **two** parties: the **mortgagor**, the borrower who gives the mortgage, and the
**mortgagee**, the lender.

A **deed of trust** has three — borrower, trustee and lender — and the trustee conducts a sale under a
power of sale. **Wisconsin does not use it.** A student who learned "grantor, trustee, beneficiary" from
a national text, or from this project's Virginia course, must translate.

The consequence is procedural and large: **Wisconsin residential foreclosure is judicial.** Hour 47.

### 46.3 The clauses that decide outcomes

**Acceleration** — on default the lender may declare the entire balance immediately due. Without it a
lender could sue only for missed payments, and every foreclosure begins here.

**Alienation, or due-on-sale** — the lender may accelerate if the property is transferred without
consent. This makes most modern loans **non-assumable** and is why "taking over payments" is usually not
available.

**Prepayment** — whether the borrower may pay early and on what terms.

**Defeasance** — on full payment the mortgage is defeated and must be **satisfied** of record.

**Subordination** — an agreement to take a lower lien position than recording order would give.
Refinancing a first mortgage while a home equity line remains recorded requires one, or the equity line
would advance to first position.

chunks.heading: Hour 47 — Default, assignment, release, subject to — REEB 25.033(10)(d)
chunks.excerpt:
**Escrow or impound** — the lender collects taxes and insurance monthly and pays them when due,
protecting its own collateral against a tax lien or an uninsured loss. In Wisconsin, where the tax bill
issues in December, the escrow analysis a buyer receives in their first year is frequently the first
time they see the real annual figure.

---

## Hour 47 — Default, assignment, release, subject to — REEB 25.033(10)(d)

### 47.1 Default and acceleration

**Default** is failure to perform: missed payments most often, but also failure to pay taxes, maintain
insurance, or maintain the property. Federal servicing rules impose requirements on the servicer before
it may proceed, including loss-mitigation obligations.

### 47.2 Wisconsin foreclosure is judicial

The lender brings an **action in circuit court**. A judgment of foreclosure is entered, a **redemption
period** runs, and the property is sold at a **sheriff's sale** which the **court must confirm** before
title passes.

Wisconsin's scheme has features that matter to brokerage: the redemption period's length varies with
the type of property and with **whether the lender waives a deficiency judgment**; and the **confirmation
hearing** is a further step at which the court considers whether the sale price was fair.

**This course states no Wisconsin redemption period, no deficiency rule, and no confirmation standard**,
because ch. 846 has not been read from primary text for this project. What a licensee must know is the
**shape** — court action, judgment, redemption, sheriff's sale, confirmation — and that a distressed
borrower goes to **counsel and to a HUD-approved housing counselling agency**, not to a licensee, for
timing.

### 47.3 Assignment, release, and subject to

chunks.heading: 47.4 Alternatives to foreclosure
chunks.excerpt:
**Assignment of the mortgage** transfers the lender's interest, which is what happens on the secondary
market, and it is recorded.

**Assumption** — the buyer takes over the existing loan and becomes **personally liable**. The seller is
**released only by a written release from the lender**; without one the seller remains liable.

**Subject to** — the buyer takes title with the loan in place but **assumes no personal liability**. The
seller stays liable, the loan stays in the seller's name, and the **due-on-sale clause is very likely
triggered.** It is a structure clients hear about and should not enter without counsel.

**Release** — a partial release frees part of the security, used where a parcel is being split off, and
it is recorded.

**Satisfaction** — the full discharge on payoff, recorded.

### 47.4 Alternatives to foreclosure

**Reinstatement**; **modification**; **forbearance**; **repayment plan**; **short sale**, which requires
the lender's agreement and in which deficiency treatment must be addressed **in writing**; and **deed in
lieu**, which junior liens generally survive.

Each has credit and tax consequences the licensee is not qualified to explain. The professional response
is to identify them as options and route the borrower to the servicer's loss-mitigation department, a
HUD-approved counselling agency, and counsel — and never to advise a client to stop paying in order to
qualify for something.

---

## Hour 48 — Land contracts — REEB 25.033(10)(e)

### 48.1 What a land contract is

A **land contract** — the rule gives it its own paragraph, and Wisconsin uses them substantially more
than most states — is a financing structure in which the **seller** finances the purchase directly.

chunks.heading: 48.2 Why Wisconsin uses them
chunks.excerpt:
**The vendor (seller) retains legal title.** **The vendee (buyer) takes possession and equitable
title**, pays in instalments over the agreed term, and receives a **deed** when the contract is
performed.

It is a **conveyance** for the purposes of ch. 706 and it is **recorded**.

### 48.2 Why Wisconsin uses them

Land contracts appear where conventional financing is unavailable or impractical: **farmland and rural
acreage**; properties a secondary-market lender will not accept; **family transfers**; buyers with
credit or documentation problems; and transactions where the seller wants the income stream.

### 48.3 What the vendee must understand

**Equitable title is not legal title.** The vendee cannot convey a clear fee until the contract is
performed, and a purported sale by the vendee is a sale of a vendee's interest.

**Existing liens.** If the vendor has a mortgage, the land contract sits behind it, and the vendor's
default can put the vendee's interest at risk. **A due-on-sale clause in the vendor's mortgage may be
triggered by the land contract itself.**

**Taxes and insurance.** Who pays, and how the vendee verifies that they were paid, must be in the
contract. A vendee who has paid faithfully and discovers the vendor did not pay the property tax has a
serious problem.

**Default and its consequence.** Wisconsin provides remedies for a vendor on a vendee's default, and
the vendee's exposure — including the possibility of losing what has been paid — is real. **This course
states no remedy, notice period or cure right**, because the provisions have not been read from primary
text for this project.

**Recording.** The contract is recorded so that the vendee's interest is of record and third parties are
on notice.

chunks.heading: 48.4 What a licensee does
chunks.excerpt:
**And the deed at the end.** How and when the deed is delivered, and by what mechanism if the vendor has
died or become incapacitated, must be provided for.

### 48.4 What a licensee does

**Use the Board-approved land contract addendum or form** — REEB 25.033(8)(f)3 addenda, and ch. REEB 16.

**Get both parties to counsel before it is signed.** A land contract allocates risks that neither party
usually understands, and every one of the questions in 48.3 is legal.

**Disclose material adverse facts** as § 452.133(1)(c) requires, including anything the firm knows about
the vendor's existing financing.

**Do not advise on the structure.** § 452.133(2)(am) again: outside the scope of ch. 452.

---

## Hour 49 — Payment plans and programme categories — REEB 25.033(10)(c)

### 49.1 Payment plans

| Structure | Payment | Principal | Risk the borrower carries |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fully amortising fixed | Constant | Retired over the term | None from rate movement |
| Adjustable rate | Changes at each adjustment | Retired over the term | **Rate movement**, bounded by caps |
| Interest only | Constant during the period | **None** during the period | No equity from amortisation |
| Balloon | Constant, then the balance falls due | Partly retired | **Refinance or sale risk at maturity** |
| Graduated payment | Rises on a schedule | May negatively amortise early | Payment shock |
| Temporary buydown | Rises to the note rate | Normal | Increase at each step |
| Reverse | None required | Grows | Occupancy, tax, insurance and maintenance obligations continue |
| Land contract | As agreed | As agreed | **Legal title stays with the vendor** |

chunks.heading: 49.2 Programme categories
chunks.excerpt:
An **adjustable rate** moves with an **index** plus a fixed **margin**, bounded by an **initial cap**, a
**periodic cap**, and a **lifetime cap**. The question that matters is not the start rate but **the
payment at the caps**.

### 49.2 Programme categories

**The rule for this section:** programme guidelines change and eligibility depends on facts the licensee
does not have. **A licensee describes categories; a lender determines eligibility.**

**Conventional** — not insured or guaranteed by a government agency. **Conforming** loans meet the
purchase criteria of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac including an annually set maximum that varies by county;
**jumbo** loans exceed it. **Private mortgage insurance** is generally required below a 20 percent down
payment and **protects the lender**, not the borrower.

**FHA** — HUD **insures** loans made by approved lenders; low minimum down payment, more flexible credit
criteria, **mortgage insurance premiums** upfront and annual, county loan limits, **minimum property
standards**, and owner-occupancy.

**VA** — the Department of Veterans Affairs **guarantees** part of a loan to an eligible veteran or
service member; frequently no down payment, no monthly mortgage insurance, a **funding fee** that varies
and is sometimes waived, entitlement established by a **certificate of eligibility**, and occupancy
requirements.

**USDA Rural Development** — no down payment, **geographic eligibility** limited to designated rural
areas on maps that change, and **household income limits**. **Much of Wisconsin is within designated
rural areas**, which makes the programme more relevant here than in most states.

chunks.heading: Hour 50 — The secondary mortgage market — REEB 25.033(10)(f)
chunks.excerpt:
**WHEDA** — the **Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Authority** operates first-time homebuyer
and other programmes through participating lenders, with their own income and purchase-price limits.
**Name the programme; refer to a participating lender.**

**Local and portfolio lending.** Wisconsin community banks and credit unions frequently hold loans in
**portfolio**, set their own property standards, and will lend on property a secondary-market lender
will not — a farm, a large acreage parcel, a seasonal cottage, or a property with an unusual water
supply. Naming that category serves a client without advising on credit.

**No loan limit, mortgage insurance duration, funding fee, PMI cancellation threshold, income limit or
qualifying ratio is stated in this course.**

---

## Hour 50 — The secondary mortgage market — REEB 25.033(10)(f)

### 50.1 Primary and secondary

The **primary market** is where loans are **originated**: banks, savings institutions, credit unions,
mortgage bankers, and mortgage brokers.

The **secondary market** is where originated loans are **sold**. **Fannie Mae** and **Freddie Mac**
purchase conforming conventional loans; **Ginnie Mae** guarantees securities backed by government loans.

### 50.2 Why it exists and what it causes

Selling loans **returns capital** to the originator so it can lend again. Without it, a lender's capacity
would be limited to its deposits, and mortgage credit would be far scarcer and more local.

chunks.heading: 50.3 Servicing
chunks.excerpt:
The consequence a licensee must understand: **underwriting guidelines exist because the loan must be
sellable.** A loan that does not meet the purchaser's criteria cannot be sold, so the criteria govern
origination — which is why a lender's answer to "can you make an exception?" is usually no, and why a
**portfolio** lender can say yes where a secondary-market lender cannot.

### 50.3 Servicing

The loan's **servicing** — collecting payments, administering escrow, handling default — is frequently
sold or transferred, and the servicer is often not the originator. **Borrowers must be notified**, and
**the terms of the note do not change.** A buyer who receives a servicing transfer notice a month after
closing has not been sold to a different loan.

---

## Hour 51 — Basic math

### 51.1 Loan-to-value and down payment

**LTV = loan amount ÷ the lesser of sale price or appraised value.**

*Purchase $312,000, loan $249,600.* LTV = **80%**; down payment **$62,400**.

*Purchase $312,000, appraisal $298,000, lender lends 80% LTV.* The lender lends against the **lower**
figure: 0.80 × 298,000 = **$238,400**. The buyer must bring 312,000 − 238,400 = **$73,600** — the
$62,400 planned plus a **$13,600 appraisal gap.** This is the whole reason the appraisal contingency
exists.

### 51.2 Points and interest

**One point = 1% of the loan amount.** *Loan $249,600, 1.5 points:* 249,600 × 0.015 = **$3,744**.

**Simple interest: I = P × R × T.** *$249,600 at 6.375% for one month:* 249,600 × 0.06375 = $15,912 per
year; ÷ 12 = **$1,326.00**.

**Per diem at closing:** annual interest ÷ 365 × days. *Closing 12 September, first payment 1 November:*
19 days, 12–30 September. 15,912 ÷ 365 = $43.5945 per day; × 19 = **$828.30**.

### 51.3 Payment and amortisation

chunks.heading: 51.4 Area, commission, and tax
chunks.excerpt:
*Factor 6.24 per $1,000, loan $249,600:* 249.6 × 6.24 = **$1,557.50** monthly principal and interest.
First month's interest $1,326.00, so principal = 1,557.50 − 1,326.00 = **$231.50**, and the balance
after one payment is **$249,368.50**.

### 51.4 Area, commission, and tax

*A lot 264 ft by 330 ft:* 87,120 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = **2 acres**.
*Sale $312,000 at a 5.5% fee, split evenly between firms, salesperson at 65% of the firm's half:*
total 312,000 × 0.055 = **$17,160**; firm's half **$8,580**; salesperson 8,580 × 0.65 = **$5,577**.
*Assessed $268,000 at a mill rate of $19.40 per $1,000:* 268,000 ÷ 1,000 = 268; × 19.40 = **$5,199.20**.

### 51.5 Proration, on the Wisconsin basis

**The convention comes from the offer**, not from habit, and Wisconsin's December billing makes the
question live — Module WI-06 Hour 38.3.

*Worked, on a calendar-year basis with the closing day to the buyer, 365-day year.* Annual tax
$5,199.20; closing 12 September.
Daily: 5,199.20 ÷ 365 = **$14.2444**. Seller's days 1 January–11 September = **254**.
254 × 14.2444 = **$3,618.08 — a credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller**, because the buyer will
pay the whole bill when it issues in December.

### 51.6 Cash to close

= down payment + closing costs + prepaid items + escrow reserves − loan amount already counted − earnest
money − seller and lender credits − prorated items credited to the buyer.

*Worked:* purchase $312,000; down payment $62,400; closing costs $4,900; prepaid interest $828.30;
first-year insurance $1,410; escrow reserves $1,180; earnest money $4,000; seller credit $2,500; tax
proration credit to buyer $3,618.08.
62,400 + 4,900 + 828.30 + 1,410 + 1,180 = 70,718.30; less 4,000, 2,500 and 3,618.08 = **$60,600.22**.

chunks.heading: Module WI-08 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**This is an estimate.** The controlling figures are the lender's Closing Disclosure and the closing
agent's statement, and every estimate a licensee gives should say so in writing — which is what
**§ 452.133(1)(b)**, reasonable skill and care, requires.

### Module WI-08 engagement check

**Question.** A buyer wants a 60-acre parcel with a farmhouse, a private well, and an outbuilding. The
seller offers to sell on a **land contract** at a rate below what a bank would charge, and the buyer
asks whether that is a good idea and whether they should just do it instead of getting a mortgage.
Answer.

**Expected answer.**

**Whether it is a good idea is not mine to say**, and saying it would be advice outside
**§ 452.133(2)(am)**'s scope. What I can do is describe the structure and route it.

**In a land contract the vendor keeps legal title** and the vendee takes **possession and equitable
title**, receiving a deed only when the contract is performed. That is a materially different position
from owning subject to a mortgage, and the buyer must understand it before signing.

**The questions that must be answered before anything is signed**, all of them legal: is there an
existing mortgage on the property, and does the land contract **trigger its due-on-sale clause**; who
pays the **taxes and insurance** and how does the vendee **verify** they were paid; what happens on
**default**, and what does the vendee stand to lose; how and when is the **deed** delivered, and what
happens if the vendor dies or becomes incapacitated; and is the contract **recorded**.

chunks.heading: Extended treatment — finance developed
chunks.excerpt:
**So: both parties to counsel, before signing**, and the transaction on the **Board-approved form**
under ch. REEB 16. I also mention the alternative category rather than the alternative product — **a
Wisconsin community bank or credit union lending in portfolio** may finance a 60-acre parcel with a
farmhouse and a private well where a secondary-market lender would not, and that is worth a
conversation with a lender. And I disclose in writing anything I know about the property or the
seller's financing that **§ 452.133(1)(c)** reaches.

---

## Extended treatment — finance developed

### E8.1 An amortisation schedule, first four months

*Loan $249,600 at 6.375%, monthly payment $1,557.50.*

| Month | Opening balance | Interest | Principal | Closing balance |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $249,600.00 | $1,326.00 | $231.50 | $249,368.50 |
| 2 | $249,368.50 | $1,324.77 | $232.73 | $249,135.77 |
| 3 | $249,135.77 | $1,323.53 | $233.97 | $248,901.80 |
| 4 | $248,901.80 | $1,322.29 | $235.21 | $248,666.59 |

Four payments totalling $6,230.00 have retired **$933.41** of principal. That is what a buyer means when
they say the early years "all go to interest", and showing it beats asserting it — particularly to a
buyer weighing discount points against a short expected holding period.

**The break-even on points.** *1.5 points on $249,600 costs $3,744 and lowers the payment by $61 a
month.* 3,744 ÷ 61 = **61 months**, a little over five years. Whether that is worth doing depends on how
long the borrower holds the loan, which the borrower knows and the licensee does not.

### E8.2 The loan process, stage by stage, and what stops it

chunks.heading: E8.3 Managing the financing contingency
chunks.excerpt:
**Pre-qualification** — a conversation. **Pre-approval** — a submitted application with verified
documentation and usually a conditional underwriting decision.

**Application** — starts the TRID clock; the **Loan Estimate** follows.

**Processing** — documentation gathered: income, employment, assets, credit explanations, the accepted
offer and every amendment, and any condominium or association documents.

**Appraisal and title** — ordered by the lender and the closing agent. Both can stop a closing and both
are outside the buyer's control.

**Underwriting** — automated first in most cases, manual where the file requires it. The output is an
approval **with conditions**.

**Conditions** — prior-to-document conditions clear before the closing package issues; prior-to-funding
conditions before money moves. **This is the stage that most often breaks a closing date**, because a
condition raised on Tuesday for a Thursday closing cannot be met in time.

**Clear to close, Closing Disclosure, consummation, funding, recording.**

**Servicing** — frequently sold or transferred. The borrower is notified and **the terms of the note do
not change.**

### E8.3 Managing the financing contingency

Read the clause and extract four things: **the loan type and amount** it protects; **the deadline**;
**what notice** must be given and to whom; and **what happens** if the deadline passes without action.

Then work backwards from binding acceptance: application within the period; documentation to the lender
immediately; appraisal ordered early enough that a **reconsideration of value** is possible; conditions
chased **weekly, in writing**, with a record of each request and response; and escalation to the
supervising broker the moment a deadline is at risk.

chunks.heading: E8.4 The buyer behaviours that undo an approval
chunks.excerpt:
On a Wisconsin property with a **private well**, a **septic system**, an **outbuilding**, **acreage**, or
a **seasonal cottage**, add one more: find out early whether the lender's product has **property
standards** the property will not meet. Discovering an FHA minimum property standard problem two weeks
before closing is discovering it too late — and the answer is frequently a **portfolio lender**.

### E8.4 The buyer behaviours that undo an approval

Give this list in writing at binding acceptance, because every item on it happens:

Do not change or leave a job. Do not open credit accounts, and do not finance furniture, a vehicle, a
snowmobile or appliances. Do not close accounts or pay off collections without asking the loan officer —
either can move a score. Do not make large deposits that cannot be documented; a gift needs a **gift
letter and a paper trail**. Do not move money between accounts unnecessarily. Do not co-sign for anyone.
Do not miss a payment on anything.

Underwriting is frequently **re-verified immediately before closing**, so a purchase made a week before
closing can undo an approval given a month earlier.

### E8.5 A land contract compared with a mortgage

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-08
chunks.excerpt:
| | Mortgage | Land contract |
|---|---|---|
| Legal title | **Buyer**, subject to the lien | **Vendor**, until performance |
| Buyer holds | Fee, encumbered | **Possession and equitable title** |
| Instrument recorded | Mortgage | **The land contract** |
| Lender | A third party | **The seller** |
| Underwriting | The lender's | **The vendor's judgment** |
| Buyer's protection on vendor default | N/A | **Depends on recording and on the contract** |
| Effect of vendor's existing mortgage | N/A | **May trigger the due-on-sale clause** |
| Taxes and insurance | Usually escrowed | **Must be allocated and verified in the contract** |
| Remedy on buyer default | Judicial foreclosure | **Statutory remedies; the vendee's exposure is real** |
| Deed | Delivered at purchase | **Delivered at the end** |

Every row in the right column is a legal question, which is why Hour 48.4's instruction is that both
parties go to counsel before signing.

---

## Instructor source note for Module WI-08

Wisconsin statements rest on text read directly from `docs.legis.wisconsin.gov` on 2026-08-20 and
recorded in `wisconsin/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **REEB 25.033(10)(a) through (f)**,
**(8)(f)3**, **(19)(g)**; and **§ 452.133(1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(c), (2)(am), (3)(a) and (3)(c)**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-08
chunks.excerpt:
**Deliberately not stated, for want of a primary reading:** every Wisconsin **foreclosure** period,
redemption right, deficiency rule and confirmation standard in **ch. 846**; every **land contract**
remedy, notice period and cure right; **s. 224.71** on mortgage banking; and every federal programme
figure — conforming loan limits, FHA county limits and mortgage insurance duration, the VA funding fee,
PMI cancellation thresholds, USDA income and geographic limits, WHEDA limits, TRID waiting periods, and
qualifying-ratio thresholds.

**That Wisconsin is a mortgage state with judicial residential foreclosure** is stated as the structural
fact it is, and Hour 46.2 translates the deed-of-trust vocabulary a student may have met elsewhere.

**Land contracts are given a full hour** because **REEB 25.033(10)(e)** gives them their own paragraph
and because they are used substantially more in Wisconsin than in most states. Hour 48 teaches what the
parties hold and what must be answered before signing, and routes every one of those questions to
counsel.

All arithmetic in Hour 51 is worked in full. Prices, rates, factors and mill rates are illustrative
teaching figures and are not market data for any Wisconsin municipality.

chunks.heading: Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-09
chunks.excerpt:
# Wisconsin Salesperson Pre-License — Module WI-09

## Hours 52–55 · Appraisal and market analysis

**Board topic covered:** REEB 25.033(11) Appraisal and market analysis
**Clock hours:** 4 · **Hour allocation:** a StateCourse proposal for Board review.
**Course version:** 1.0 submission draft
**Regulatory status:** Development. Not approved. No Wisconsin pre-license credit is available.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module the student will be able to:

- State the principles of value and identify highest and best use.
- Adjust comparable sales in the correct direction and reconcile to a supported range.
- Compute value by the cost approach and classify depreciation by type.
- Compute NOI, value by direct capitalization, and value by gross rent multiplier.
- Reproduce the appraisal process in sequence.
- State the boundary between a licensee's market analysis and an appraisal, and the rule that draws it.

## Timed sequence

| Hour | Content | Evidence |
|---:|---|---|
| 52 | Basic principles of value; value, price and cost; highest and best use | Section completed |
| 53 | The direct market comparison approach | Section completed |
| 54 | The cost approach and the income approach | Section completed |
| 55 | The appraisal process; the licensee's market analysis and its boundary | Module engagement check |
| **Total** | **4 clock hours** | |

---

## Hour 52 — Principles of value — REEB 25.033(11)(a)

### 52.1 Value, price, and cost

**Value** is an opinion of what a property should bring under stated conditions. **Price** is what was
actually paid in a particular transaction, which may reflect unusual motivation or terms. **Cost** is
what it takes to create the improvements, which may be more or less than what they add to value.

chunks.heading: 52.2 The principles
chunks.excerpt:
**Market value** is the classic definition and its conditions do the work: the most probable price in a
competitive and open market, under conditions requisite to a fair sale, with buyer and seller each
acting prudently and knowledgeably, **neither under duress**, allowing a reasonable exposure time, with
payment in cash or its equivalent and terms typical of the market.

Strip out any one of those conditions — a distressed seller, a sale between family members, no market
exposure, a land contract at an off-market rate — and the observed price is not evidence of market value
without adjustment. That is the screen applied when comparables are selected.

Other values a Wisconsin licensee meets: **assessed value**, set by the municipal assessor for taxation
and drifting from the market between revaluations; **equalized value**, the Department of Revenue's
estimate used to apportion levies between municipalities; **insurable value**, a replacement-cost concept
that **excludes land**; **investment value**, value to a particular investor; and **liquidation value**,
which assumes an inadequate exposure period.

### 52.2 The principles

**Supply and demand** — value moves with the relationship between them, and real estate's supply is slow.

**Substitution** — a buyer will pay no more than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute.
This is the foundation of **all three approaches**: comparison, cost and income each ask what a
substitute would cost.

**Anticipation** — value reflects expected future benefits, not past cost.

**Contribution** — a component adds value equal to what it contributes to the whole, measured in the
market, which is frequently far less than it cost. The principle a seller most often needs explained.

chunks.heading: 52.3 Highest and best use
chunks.excerpt:
**Conformity, progression and regression** — value is maximised where a property conforms reasonably to
its surroundings; a lesser property gains from better neighbours and a superior property is dragged
toward the level of lesser ones.

**Increasing and diminishing returns** — additional investment adds value up to a point and then does
not.

**Competition** — excess profit invites competition, which erodes it.

**Change** — no condition is permanent, which is why every value opinion has an effective date.

**Plottage** is the increment from combining adjacent parcels under one ownership; **assemblage** is the
act of combining them.

**Externalities** — influences outside the property affect its value: the closed plant, the new bypass,
the neighbouring feedlot, the lake access that changed hands.

### 52.3 Highest and best use

The reasonably probable use that is **legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible,
and maximally productive** — all four, in that order.

Land is valued at its highest and best use **as though vacant**, which is why an obsolete building on a
well-located lot may sell for land value.

In Wisconsin the **legally permissible** test carries unusual weight, because a parcel's use can be
constrained simultaneously by county or municipal zoning, **shoreland zoning**, **floodplain**
regulation, **farmland preservation**, subdivision status, wastewater capacity, a conservation easement,
and private covenants. A highest-and-best-use conclusion that has not checked those is a guess.

### 52.4 The four forces

chunks.heading: Hour 53 — The direct market comparison approach — REEB 25.033(11)(b)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physical and environmental** — location, topography, soils, water, climate, improvements.
**Economic** — employment, income, credit, rents, construction costs.
**Governmental** — zoning, codes, taxation, public services.
**Social** — population, household formation, tastes.

---

## Hour 53 — The direct market comparison approach — REEB 25.033(11)(b)

### 53.1 The rule

**Adjust the comparable, never the subject.** The subject is the unknown; the comparables are the
evidence. Every adjustment answers: *what would this comparable have sold for if it had been like the
subject?*

**Comparable superior to the subject → adjust the comparable DOWN.**
**Comparable inferior to the subject → adjust the comparable UP.**

The memory hook: **comparable better, subtract.**

### 53.2 Selecting comparables

**Closed sales are evidence. Active listings are not** — an active listing is an unaccepted offer.
Pending sales are better evidence than actives. **Expired and withdrawn** listings are useful in one
specific way: they show prices the market **refused**, which brackets the top of the range.

Screen for **arm's-length conditions**: unrelated parties, adequate exposure, no unusual pressure, market
terms.

Then compare on **real property rights conveyed**; **financing terms**, including seller concessions and
land contracts at off-market rates; **conditions of sale**; **expenditures made immediately after
purchase**; **market conditions**, which is the time adjustment; **location**; **physical
characteristics**; and **economic characteristics, use and non-realty components** — the boat, the lift,
the equipment included in the price.

chunks.heading: 53.3 A worked grid
chunks.excerpt:
In Wisconsin three variables frequently dominate: **water frontage**, measured in feet and in quality —
lake versus river, sand versus muck, depth at the shore, exposure, and whether frontage is on a
recreational or a navigable-but-quiet water; **acreage with or without development potential**; and
**season**, because a February sale and a July sale in a recreational market are not evidence of the
same market.

### 53.3 A worked grid

*Subject: 1,880 sq ft, 3 bed, 2 bath, attached 2-car garage, 120 feet of lake frontage.*

| | Comp A | Comp B | Comp C |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sale price | $482,000 | $438,000 | $515,000 |
| Sold | 3 months ago | 8 months ago | 1 month ago |
| Market conditions +0.4%/month | +$5,784 | +$14,016 | +$2,060 |
| Frontage | 120 ft | 90 ft (−30) | 150 ft (+30) |
| Frontage adj. at $1,100/ft | $0 | +$33,000 | −$33,000 |
| Living area | 1,950 (+70) | 1,820 (−60) | 1,880 (same) |
| Area adj. at $85/sq ft | −$5,950 | +$5,100 | $0 |
| Garage | attached 2-car | detached 1-car | attached 2-car |
| Garage adj. | $0 | +$14,000 | $0 |
| **Net adjustment** | **−$166** | **+$66,116** | **−$30,940** |
| **Adjusted price** | **$481,834** | **$504,116** | **$484,060** |

Check the directions. Comp A is **larger** — superior — so the area adjustment is **negative**. Comp B
is **inferior** on frontage, area and garage, so all three adjustments are **positive**. Comp C has
**more frontage** — superior — so that adjustment is **negative**.

### 53.4 Reconciling

Indicated range **$481,834 to $504,116**, and reconciliation is **judgment, not averaging**. It weights
each comparable by reliability: how few adjustments it needed, how large the **gross adjustment** was,
how recent, how close.

chunks.heading: Hour 54 — The cost approach and the income approach
chunks.excerpt:
Comp B required **$66,116** of gross adjustment on a $438,000 sale — about 15 percent of the price — and
is the weakest evidence however tidy its arithmetic looks. Comps A and C are close together and are the
stronger indications, and a defensible conclusion sits near **$482,000 to $485,000**.

**Gross adjustment measures comparability; net adjustment does not.** A comparable whose large
adjustments happen to offset is not a good comparable; it is a lucky one.

---

## Hour 54 — The cost approach and the income approach

### 54.1 The cost approach — REEB 25.033(11)(c)

**Value = land value + cost new of the improvements − accrued depreciation.**

**Land value** is estimated separately, normally by sales comparison of vacant sites — which in
Wisconsin means comparing frontage, acreage, soils and wastewater capacity, access, and development
status rather than acreage alone.

**Cost new** is either **reproduction cost** — an exact replica including its obsolete features — or
**replacement cost** — a substitute of equivalent utility using current materials and methods.
Replacement cost is used more often, because nobody would rebuild the obsolete features.

**Depreciation** is loss in value from any cause, and it has three sources:

**Physical deterioration** — wear, tear and age. **Curable** where the cost to fix is recovered in
value; **incurable** where it is not.

**Functional obsolescence** — a defect in the design or utility of the improvement itself: one bathroom
for four bedrooms, a bedroom reachable only through another, a farmhouse layout in a market that wants
open plan. Curable or incurable.

chunks.heading: 54.2 The income approach — REEB 25.033(11)(d)
chunks.excerpt:
**External obsolescence** — loss caused by something **outside** the property: a closed employer, a new
highway, a changed neighbourhood, an adjoining use. **Always incurable**, because the owner cannot fix
it from inside the boundary.

*Worked:* land value $145,000; replacement cost new $296,000; physical deterioration $53,000; functional
obsolescence $11,000; external obsolescence $7,000.
145,000 + 296,000 − 53,000 − 11,000 − 7,000 = **$370,000**.

**Most reliable for new construction and special-purpose property**; least reliable for old improvements,
where the depreciation estimate carries most of the answer.

### 54.2 The income approach — REEB 25.033(11)(d)

**Potential Gross Income** — all income at full occupancy at market rent, plus other income.
**less Vacancy and Collection Loss**, supported by market evidence.
**= Effective Gross Income.**
**less Operating Expenses** — fixed, variable, and **replacement reserves**.
**= Net Operating Income.**

**Three items are excluded from operating expenses**, and the exclusion is the most examinable point:

**Debt service.** NOI measures the **property's** performance independent of financing. Including the
mortgage payment would give the same building a different NOI for every buyer.
**Depreciation.** An accounting and tax entry, not a cash expense.
**Capital expenditures.** A new roof is capital; the **replacement reserve** that spreads its
anticipated cost **is** an operating expense, but the outlay itself is not.

**Direct capitalization: Value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate**, written **V = I ÷ R**, with **I = V × R**
and **R = I ÷ V**.

chunks.heading: 54.3 The reserve line, and how a pro forma is dressed
chunks.excerpt:
*Worked:* 12 units at $1,150 per month plus $5,400 other annual income.
PGI = 12 × 1,150 × 12 + 5,400 = 165,600 + 5,400 = **$171,000**.
Vacancy and collection loss 7% = 11,970. **EGI = $159,030.**
Operating expenses $63,400, including a $6,000 replacement reserve.
**NOI = 159,030 − 63,400 = $95,630.**
At a market rate of 7.5%: **V = 95,630 ÷ 0.075 = $1,275,067**, say $1,275,000.

Two consequences. **The rate is derived from the market** — most defensibly by dividing comparable
sales' NOI by their prices — not chosen. And **a higher rate gives a lower value at the same NOI**: at
8.5% the same building indicates $1,125,059, about $150,000 less for one percentage point.

**Gross rent multiplier.** GRM = sale price ÷ **monthly** gross rent; value = GRM × the subject's monthly
gross rent. *Comparable GRMs of 11.8, 12.3 and 12.0; subject's monthly gross rent $14,250. At 12.0:*
**value = $171,000.**

**What the multiplier ignores is the point:** it uses **gross** rent, so it ignores vacancy and every
operating expense. Two buildings with identical gross rents and different expense structures look
identical to a GRM and are not.

### 54.3 The reserve line, and how a pro forma is dressed

The most common manipulation is **omitting the replacement reserve**. Remove the $6,000 above and NOI
appears to be $101,630; at 7.5% that indicates $1,355,067 rather than $1,275,067 — **$80,000 of apparent
value created by deleting one line.**

The second is presenting **market rent** as **contract rent**. A building with below-market leases is
worth what its leases produce until they roll.

---

## Hour 55 — The appraisal process and the licensee's boundary

### 55.1 The appraisal process — REEB 25.033(11)(e)

chunks.heading: 55.2 Which approach governs
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Define the problem** — client, intended user, intended use, type of value, effective date, property
   rights appraised, and any assumptions or limiting conditions.
2. **Determine the scope of work.**
3. **Collect data** — general data about the market, specific data about the subject and comparables.
4. **Analyse highest and best use**, as vacant and as improved.
5. **Estimate land value** separately.
6. **Apply the approaches** — comparison, cost, income.
7. **Reconcile** into an opinion or a range. Reconciliation weights; it does not average.
8. **Report** in the form the assignment requires.

Change the **intended use** — a mortgage loan, a divorce, an estate, a tax appeal, a relocation — and the
scope of work and sometimes the type of value change with it. That is why an appraisal prepared for one
purpose is not evidence for another.

### 55.2 Which approach governs

**Residential owner-occupied** — the **direct market comparison approach** governs; cost supports; income
is largely irrelevant.
**Income property** — the **income approach** governs; comparison supports.
**New construction and special purpose** — the **cost approach** carries more weight.

### 55.3 The licensee's market analysis, and the boundary

A licensee's **comparative market analysis** uses these methods to present market evidence to a client
for the purpose of setting a listing price or an offer price. That is ordinary brokerage, and
**§ 452.133(1)(e)** makes it a duty: the firm owes every party **accurate information about market
conditions** that affect the transaction, on request.

chunks.heading: 55.4 Common errors and their corrections
chunks.excerpt:
**It is not an appraisal.** Wisconsin licenses and certifies appraisers separately, under a different
regulatory scheme, and a licensee must not represent a market analysis as an appraisal or prepare one
for a lender in place of an appraisal.

**And Wisconsin has an ethics rule directly on the point.** **REEB 24.09 — misleading market values** —
is a listed topic at REEB 25.033(13)(b)1.d, and Module WI-10 takes it. A price presented to win a listing
rather than to describe the evidence is the conduct the rule addresses.

**The assembled method**, which a Wisconsin salesperson uses weekly:

Define the market area by what actually changes buyer behaviour — the lake, the school district, the
municipal line that changes the mill rate. Pull **closed** sales over a defensible period, extended
further only where thin data requires it and the extension is stated. **Screen for arm's-length
conditions** and write down every exclusion. Adjust toward the subject in the direction Hour 53 gave, and
record each adjustment's basis. **Reconcile to a range**, weighted by gross adjustment, recency and
location. **Disclose the limits** — how many sales, how old, what could not be verified. And **describe
the work accurately**: market evidence presented in the course of brokerage, not an appraisal.

### 55.4 Common errors and their corrections

chunks.heading: Module WI-09 engagement check
chunks.excerpt:
**Averaging the three approaches** — reconciliation weights.
**Using assessed or equalized value as evidence of market value** — assessed value is an administrative
figure for taxation, and equalized value apportions levies between municipalities.
**Adjusting the subject** — adjust the comparable, always.
**Treating net adjustment as a measure of comparability** — gross adjustment measures it.
**Using list prices as comparables** — they are unaccepted offers.
**Ignoring season in a Wisconsin recreational market.**
**Quoting a cap rate with no derivation.**
**Omitting the replacement reserve.**

### Module WI-09 engagement check

**Question.** A seller says: "The assessor has us at $412,000 and the neighbour listed at $469,000, so
list me at $469,000. And I put $60,000 into the kitchen last year, so add that." Respond, and name the
rules you are working under.

**Expected answer.**

**The assessment is not evidence of market value.** It is an administrative figure set by the municipal
assessor for taxation, on the municipality's revaluation cycle, and it drifts from the market between
revaluations — which is what the **assessment ratio** and **equalized value** measure. I would not use it
as a value indicator in either direction.

**The neighbour's listing is not evidence either.** An active listing is an **unaccepted offer** — it
tells us what one seller is asking, not what the market will pay. It is useful as **competitive supply**
and as a bracket, and if it later expires unsold it becomes evidence of a price the market **refused**.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-09
chunks.excerpt:
**The kitchen is the principle of contribution.** A component adds value equal to what it **contributes
to the whole, measured in the market**, which is frequently far less than it cost — and **regression**
and **conformity** explain why an improvement that lifts the house above its neighbourhood standard may
contribute less still. Whether the kitchen contributes $60,000, $25,000 or $10,000 is answered by
**paired comparable sales**, not by the invoice.

**What I will do** is present closed arm's-length comparables, adjusted toward this property, reconciled
to a **range**, with the basis of every adjustment and the limits of the data stated — and the seller
decides the list price.

**The rules:** **§ 452.133(1)(e)** requires the firm to provide **accurate** information about market
conditions; **§ 452.133(1)(b)** requires reasonable skill and care; and **REEB 24.09** addresses
**misleading market values**, which is exactly what a price adopted to win a listing would be.

---

## Instructor source note for Module WI-09

Wisconsin statements rest on text read directly from `docs.legis.wisconsin.gov` on 2026-08-20 and
recorded in `wisconsin/regulatory/primary-text-readings.md`: **REEB 25.033(11)(a) through (e)**,
**(7)(c)**, and **(13)(b)1.d**; and **§ 452.133(1)(b) and (1)(e)**.

**Appraisal method is taught because REEB 25.033(11) requires it** and because a Wisconsin licensee uses
the method to present market evidence, which **§ 452.133(1)(e)** makes a duty. **It is not taught as
appraisal practice.** Wisconsin licenses and certifies appraisers under a separate regulatory scheme
which has **not been read for this project**, and this course states no appraiser qualification,
standard or requirement.

chunks.heading: Instructor source note for Module WI-09
chunks.excerpt:
**REEB 24.09 is named and its subject stated — misleading market values — and its text is not quoted**,
because **ch. REEB 24 has not been read from primary text for this project.** Module WI-10 names each
cited REEB 24 section on the same basis.

All arithmetic is worked in full so a reviewer can verify each figure. **The prices, rates, adjustment
amounts, capitalization rates and multipliers are illustrative teaching figures and are not market data
for any Wisconsin market.** The $1,100 per foot of frontage in Hour 53.3 is a teaching number; real
frontage adjustments vary enormously by water body and shoreline character and are derived from paired
sales.
