[12 U.S.C. § 2607](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title12-section2607&num=0&edition=prelim) and [12 CFR § 1024.14](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/14/) require evaluation of the actual payment and services. A fee for bona fide services must be analyzed on its facts; a disguised payment for referral is not cured by an invoice label.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Debt, lien, and foreclosure
chunks.excerpt:
In a worked platform proposal, a mortgage company offers the brokerage $150 whenever a buyer submits an application through a link. The agent should not assume the link makes the fee permissible. The arrangement’s connection to settlement-service referrals, services actually performed, and applicable law require review before acceptance. The brokerage should preserve the proposal and obtain compliance advice rather than test the arrangement on a live buyer.

Data accuracy and security also matter operationally. A borrower should review information before submission, and the proper provider should handle sensitive financial documents through authorized channels. Do not alter income, debts, occupancy plans, or source-of-funds information to help approval. A mistaken application can delay financing and affect contractual performance; an intentional false statement can create serious legal exposure. Technology should improve the reliability of the record, not obscure who supplied or changed it.


### Statute reading exercise: Debt, lien, and foreclosure

Read Property Code §§ 51.0001, 51.002, and 51.003. Identify the parties, required state-law notice and sale framework, and the deficiency issue. Explain why that state-law reading alone does not authorize an agent to promise a foreclosure date when federal servicing rules, bankruptcy, or other protections may apply.

Feedback: The definitions identify the security and servicing roles; § 51.002 supplies the state sale framework; § 51.003 addresses deficiency and the statutory fair-market-value issue. Other controlling law and the actual documents must also be evaluated. A broker should obtain notices and refer legal advice, not run a sale from a classroom checklist.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Payment labels and referral law
chunks.excerpt:
### Statute reading exercise: Payment labels and referral law

Read 12 U.S.C. § 2607 and 12 CFR § 1024.14. Compare a payment for a referral, an unearned split of a settlement charge, and payment for actual documented services. State what facts are needed before concluding that a “technology fee” is lawful.

Feedback: The substance of the arrangement matters. Identify the referral agreement or understanding, thing of value, covered settlement service, actual work, and compensation basis. A label does not establish an exception or bona fide service. Obtain appropriate review before accepting payment.

### Applied exercise: The balloon behind the low payment

A seller offers a $150,000 loan amortized over 30 years but due in five. The buyer says the affordable monthly payment proves long-term affordability. Identify the separate maturity risk and the professionals and documents needed before agreement.

Feedback: Amortization and maturity differ. A substantial balance can remain at five years, requiring cash, sale, or refinancing that is not guaranteed. Review the note, security, lawful terms, buyer qualification, current disclosures, and legal requirements with appropriate professionals. Do not promise future refinancing.

### Applied exercise: One approval and two liens

The senior lender approves a short-sale payoff. A junior lienholder has not responded, and the seller believes all personal debt is forgiven. Identify the unresolved title and liability questions.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: The platform pays for every application
chunks.excerpt:
Feedback: The junior lien still needs proper treatment, and a discounted payoff approval does not automatically release personal deficiency liability. Obtain every required approval and release, read conditions and deadlines, and refer legal and tax consequences. Do not represent the file as ready to close based on one approval.

### Applied exercise: The platform pays for every application

A lender offers a brokerage a fixed payment for each borrower application through its website widget. No separate work is documented. Prepare a factual review request identifying the referral and origination concerns.

Feedback: State who receives the payment, what triggers it, what services are actually performed, whether the transaction is a covered settlement service, and what licensing or origination conduct occurs. The fixed payment and technology label do not resolve legality. Review the arrangement before use and avoid unsupported product rankings or rate claims.


### Module recap

Keep debt, security, personal liability, title, and servicing distinct. Read amortization and maturity separately. Owner financing and short sales require complete legal and financial documentation. Programs have current eligibility and underwriting rules; preliminary approval is not funding. Electronic systems do not remove origination boundaries, disclosure duties, or referral-fee restrictions.

lessons.title: Texas Law of Contracts — Module 09

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Contracts — Module 09
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Contracts — Module 09

## TREC Topic: Conveyance of Title

You will distinguish ownership from its evidence, identify voluntary and involuntary transfers, recognize estate and authority issues, and explain what recording and title insurance do within their actual limits.

This is student instruction aligned to the LOC-0 topic. Legal propositions identify primary authority; worked examples are hypothetical. A source labelled “Adapted teaching” is project-owned instruction revised for this course, with its exact origin recorded in the separate provenance manifest. References explicitly naming Principles I, Principles II, or Law of Agency identify the source discussion’s context, not a prerequisite or a Law of Contracts module number. The required instruction is presented here. The course does not establish regulatory approval or observed learner time.

## T09U1 — Title

Title is the legal ownership interest, not a single document that can be inspected without context. A deed is evidence and an instrument of conveyance; a chain of title records successive interests; a title commitment describes proposed insurance conditions; a policy insures according to its actual terms. The buyer needs to understand what estate will be conveyed and what outstanding interests or risks remain.
### Adapted teaching: The chain of title and the limits of an ownership assertion

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The chain of title and the limits of an ownership assertion
chunks.excerpt:
**Title** is the aggregate of rights that constitute ownership — and, in practice, the *provable
history* of those rights. Texas proves title through an unbroken **chain of title**: the sequence
of recorded conveyances and other instruments linking sovereign grant (Principles I Module 04's original
surveys) to the present owner. Breaks in the chain — a missing conveyance, a misspelled grantor, an
undischarged deed of trust, an heir who never signed — are **clouds** on title, curable by
corrective instruments, releases, affidavits or, at the limit, suit to quiet title.

**Warranties: what the deed promises about title.** Texas deeds are graded by the promises they
carry.

- **General warranty deed.** The grantor warrants title against defects arising at *any* time,
  under this grantor or any predecessor — the fullest assurance. Texas provides a statutory form:
  Property Code § 5.022 sets out the short-form general warranty deed ("…do grant, sell, and
  convey… and I do hereby bind myself… to warrant and forever defend all and singular the said
  premises…"), while § 5.022(b)–(c) adds two liberating rules: a covenant of warranty is **not
  required** in a conveyance, and parties may use any form not in contravention of law.
- **Special warranty deed.** The grantor warrants only against defects arising **by, through or
  under the grantor** — "I did nothing to impair title; for what came before me, look elsewhere."
  Common in commercial, foreclosure-related and estate transactions.
- **Deed without warranty.** A grant with no title covenants at all — it conveys whatever the
  grantor has, but a grant nonetheless, keeping the grantee inside the recording system's
  protections.
- **Quitclaim.** A release of whatever interest the maker may have, with no assertion of havin

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The chain of title and the limits of an ownership assertion
chunks.excerpt:
g
  any. Texas title practice treats quitclaims warily — recall from Principles I Module 07's adverse-possession
  unit below and Principles I Module 03's five-year statute that a quitclaim is expressly *excluded* as a "duly
  registered deed" for the five-year clock (CPRC § 16.025(b)) — and title companies commonly balk
  at chains that depend on them.

**The grades, priced by a hypothetical.** *In 2010, X forged a deed from the true owner and sold
to Y; in 2018 Y conveyed to Z; in 2025 the true owner surfaces and evicts Z.* What Z recovers
depends entirely on which deed Y signed. If Y gave a **general warranty deed**, Y warranted
against all defects whenever arising — the forgery predates Y, and Y must nonetheless make Z
whole. If Y gave a **special warranty deed**, Y promised only against defects arising by,
through or under Y — the forgery arose under X, and Y's warranty is not breached. If Y gave a
**quitclaim**, Y asserted nothing and released only what Y had (nothing), so Z holds the loss —
though Z's title insurance, if Z bought an owner's policy, answers where the warranty does not,
which is much of why Texas practice leans on policies over covenants. One clarification the
vocabulary invites: warranty grade never changes *what* passes — a special warranty deed conveys
the same estate a general warranty deed would; it changes only who pays when the estate proves
defective.

**Implied covenants ride along.** Even without express warranties, Property Code § 5.023 implies —
unless the conveyance provides otherwise — that the use of "grant" or "convey" promises that the
grantor has not previously conveyed the estate to another, and that the estate is free from
encumbrances; the implied covenant is independently actionable.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The chain of title and the limits of an ownership assertion
chunks.excerpt:
**Marketable title, the standard behind the vocabulary.** What all the curing serves is
**marketable title**: title a reasonably prudent buyer, properly advised, would accept — free of
reasonable doubt, not free of every recorded burden. The distinction matters daily: a parcel
subject to ordinary utility easements and subdivision covenants is perfectly marketable *with*
those burdens; a parcel whose chain depends on an unprobated will or a missing heir is not
marketable *at any price* until cured. Contracts promise marketable title implicitly or
expressly; commitments operationalise the promise as requirements; and the buyer's objection
window is where "unmarketable" gets said out loud, in writing, while it can still be fixed.

**Curing the cloud: the escalation ladder.** Clouds are cured along an escalating ladder practice
climbs only as far as necessary: a **release** for the paid-but-never-released deed of trust; a
**correction instrument** for the clerical error; a **new or corrective conveyance** where a
necessary party can still sign; **affidavits** (heirship, identity, non-production) where facts,
not signatures, are missing; and, at the top, the **suit to quiet title** or trespass-to-try-title
action — judicial determination, with time and cost to match. Each rung is someone's professional
work (title company, counsel), and the licence holder's contribution repeats this module's
refrain: find the cloud *early* — at intake, from the seller's own papers and one conversation
with the title company — because every rung climbs faster with weeks than with a closing date
three days out.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Ownership classification in the title review
chunks.excerpt:
**After-acquired title, in the practical sense:** warranties are also why the *form* of deed
matters downstream — a general warranty grantor who later acquires the title the deed purported to
convey is bound by the warranty to make it good, while a quitclaim maker walked away promising
nothing.

### Adapted teaching: Ownership classification in the title review

When an owner dies, the estate must pass through administration, and Texas's system is notably
efficient. The working concepts: **probate** is the judicial process proving a will and supervising
administration; the **executor** (named in a will) or **administrator** (court-appointed absent
one) collects assets, pays debts and distributes what remains; Texas's hallmark **independent
administration** lets most estates proceed with minimal court supervision once opened, which keeps
Texas probate faster and cheaper than the national reputation of "probate" suggests. Title to a
decedent's real property passes to devisees or heirs at death, subject to administration — so
during administration the personal representative may need to join in or make the conveyance, and
a buyer's title company will insist on the probate documents that authorise it.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Ownership classification in the title review
chunks.excerpt:
**Wills: the Texas formalities.** Estates Code § 251.001 grants will-making power to a person of
sound mind who is 18 or older, *or* is or has been married, *or* is a member of the armed forces.
Section 251.051 states the execution requirements: a will must be **in writing**, **signed** by
the testator (or by another at the testator's direction and in the testator's presence), and
**attested by two or more credible witnesses at least 14 years old** signing in the testator's
presence. Section 251.052 preserves the Texas exception every title examiner knows: a
**holographic will** — wholly in the testator's handwriting — needs no witnesses at all. A person
who dies **testate** distributes by these instruments; the vocabulary of gifts (devise of land,
devisee, legacy) attaches here.

**Reading probate paper in a chain.** Each probate document answers a specific chain-of-title
question, and the working set is short. **Letters testamentary** (or letters of administration)
are the court's certificate that this person is the estate's personal representative — the
signature authority a title company checks against every executor's deed. An **executor's or
administrator's deed** conveys estate property during administration. A **probated will**,
admitted to record, functions in the chain like a conveyance: it shows title's path from decedent
to devisee. An **affidavit of heirship** — Texas's workhorse where no administration was
opened — recites the family history on which intestate title rests; it is evidence, not
adjudication, which is why the blended-family affidavit in this module's closing exercise is a
flashing light: the facts it recites determine fractions under §§ 201.001–201.003, and an
omitted heir is an unsigned owner. The agent's discipline with all of it: collect w

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Ownership classification in the title review
chunks.excerpt:
hat exists at
intake, send it to the title company on day one, and calendar the estate's timeline as the
transaction's critical path — because it usually is.

**The formalities, tested on facts.** *A 17-year-old married rancher writes and signs a will* —
valid capacity: § 251.001 grants the power to a person who *is or has been married* regardless of
the 18-year floor, and if the instrument is wholly in his handwriting, § 251.052 excuses
witnesses entirely. *A typed will signed by the testator and one witness* — fails § 251.051's
two-witness demand, and being typed, cannot ride the holographic exception; the estate passes as
if unwritten, into the intestacy statutes of the next unit. *A will signed for a paralysed
testator by her nurse, at her direction and in her presence, then attested by two neighbours aged
16 and 19 signing in her presence* — valid: § 251.051 expressly allows signature *by another
person for the testator, in the testator's presence and under the testator's direction*, and the
witness floor is 14, not 18. The pattern for a licence holder is recognising that will validity
is exactly this technical — and that "Dad left a will" begins, never ends, the title inquiry.

**For the licence holder,** estate transactions carry three standing questions: *who* has authority
to sign (executor? all heirs? a court?), *what* documents prove it (letters testamentary, probate
orders, affidavits of heirship where administration was skipped), and *when* the sale can close —
all of them the title company's and probate counsel's to answer, and the agent's to raise on day
one rather than at the closing table.

chunks.heading: T09U2 — Voluntary Alienation
chunks.excerpt:
In a worked review, the seller’s deed names the seller, but a later recorded instrument grants a life estate to a relative. The earlier deed alone is not the complete present title picture. Obtain the chain and current evidence through the title process. The agent should communicate the discovered instrument and avoid promising a fee-simple conveyance until the necessary professionals evaluate it.

Marketability, insurability, and suitability for the buyer’s plan are related but separate. A title company may be willing to issue a policy with an exception for a recorded easement. The buyer may still object to the easement under the contract or find the intended use impractical. A policy commitment is not a zoning approval or guarantee that the buyer can build a particular structure. Identify the specific question rather than using “good title” as an all-purpose assurance.

## T09U2 — Voluntary Alienation

Voluntary alienation transfers an interest through the owner’s act, such as a sale, gift, or other conveyance. The instrument must identify the interest and parties and satisfy applicable legal requirements. A contract promising a transfer and a deed performing it are different instruments. A gift can still require a valid conveyance and can raise tax, family, creditor, or capacity issues beyond the agent’s role.
### Adapted teaching: Written conveyance, deed forms, and warranty distinctions

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Written conveyance, deed forms, and warranty distinctions
chunks.excerpt:
A **deed** is the instrument that conveys an interest in real property from **grantor** to
**grantee**. Its statutory skeleton is short. Property Code § 5.021 — the Texas conveyancing
statute you met in Principles I Module 06 — requires that a conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold,
or an estate for more than one year be **in writing**, **subscribed** (signed) by the conveyor or
the conveyor's authorised agent, and **delivered**. Around that core, Texas practice expects: a
competent, identifiable grantor whose name matches the record chain; an identifiable grantee; words
of grant (Texas needs no magic formula — recall § 5.001's rule that a conveyance passes fee simple
unless expressly limited, with no "and his heirs" required); an adequate legal description (Module
04); recital of consideration; and the grantor's acknowledgment before a notary — which, as the
recording unit shows, is what qualifies the deed for the public records rather than what makes it
valid between the parties.

**Delivery and acceptance** deserve their own sentence, because they are where deeds fail
invisibly: a deed conveys nothing until delivered with intent to pass title presently, and a signed
deed in the grantor's desk drawer conveys nothing at all. Delivery is ordinarily accomplished
through closing; oddities — deeds handed over "to take effect when I die," deeds recorded without
the grantor's knowledge — are attorney problems the licence holder routes, not solves.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Written conveyance, deed forms, and warranty distinctions
chunks.excerpt:
**The deed's anatomy, part by part.** Practice reads deeds in named pieces, and the vocabulary is
worth owning even though Texas law (as § 5.022(c) says expressly) prescribes no mandatory form.
The **premises** open the instrument: date, parties, recital of consideration. The **granting
clause** carries the operative words — "grant, sell and convey" in the statutory short form — and
with them, under § 5.023, the implied covenants unless the deed says otherwise. The **habendum**
("to have and to hold") states the estate granted, which is where a life estate or defeasible
limitation would appear and where silence, under § 5.001, means fee simple. The **warranty
clause**, if any, grades the deed as the previous discussion describes. **Reservations and
exceptions** subtract from the grant — a reserved mineral interest, an excepted easement — and
misreading them is how buyers come to own less than they celebrated. Then the **execution**
block: the grantor's signature (§ 5.021's "subscribed"), the acknowledgment that qualifies the
deed for recording (§ 12.001), and — from the newly met Property Code § 11.008 — the
confidentiality-rights notice that must ride at the top of instruments transferring an
individual's interest, telling natural persons they may strike their social security and
driver's licence numbers before filing. A licence holder never drafts any of these parts; a
licence holder who can *name* them can read a title company's draft against the contract and
catch the reserved minerals nobody negotiated.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The different routes by which an interest changes hands
chunks.excerpt:
**Correcting a deed that went wrong.** Names misspelled, descriptions mistyped, acknowledgments
botched — errors surface constantly in chains, and practice distinguishes the cures: a
**correction instrument** executed under the applicable statutory procedures for the error's
kind, versus a fresh conveyance where correction rules cannot reach the defect. Which cure fits
which error is precisely the kind of question this course keeps routing: the licence holder's
job is noticing the mismatch between contract, commitment and draft deed — counsel's job is
fixing it.

### Adapted teaching: The different routes by which an interest changes hands

Step back and see the whole map. Ownership moves by exactly four families of events, and every deed
chain is a braid of them:

1. **Voluntary alienation during life** — sale and gift, effected by deed: the ordinary commerce of
   the industry (its own unit, below).
2. **Transfer at death** — by will or by the intestacy statutes, administered through probate (two
   units below).
3. **Involuntary transfer** — by operation of law against the owner's will: foreclosure,
   condemnation, tax sale, adverse possession, escheat (final unit).
4. **Natural forces at the boundary** — accretion (gradual addition of soil to riparian land, which
   the owner keeps) versus avulsion (sudden change, which moves no boundary), and erosion — the
   water-edge doctrines that pair with Principles I Module 03's water unit.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: A deliberate transfer still requires the correct instrument and authority
chunks.excerpt:
**The water's edge, decided by speed.** The fourth family turns on one variable: how fast the
water moved. *Accretion* — the river deposits silt against a bank over decades — grows the
riparian parcel, and the owner keeps the gain; gradual loss to *erosion* shrinks it the same way.
*Avulsion* — the flood that cuts a new channel overnight — moves **no** boundary: the line stays
where the old channel ran, and an owner can end up with land on the far side of the water. On
rivers that shift, the deed's acreage and the ground's acreage drift apart, which is one more
reason rural transactions lean on current surveys (Principles I Module 04) rather than old descriptions — and
one more question ("has the river moved?") that belongs on a waterfront intake sheet.

The licence holder's use for the map is diagnostic: every unexplained name in a chain of title —
an executor's deed, a trustee's deed, a sheriff's deed, a decree — announces which family of event
occurred, and therefore which documents must exist to support it.

### Adapted teaching: A deliberate transfer still requires the correct instrument and authority

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: A deliberate transfer still requires the correct instrument and authority
chunks.excerpt:
**Alienation** — the transfer of title — is *voluntary* when the owner intends it: the sale
closing in a deed; the **gift** deed, valid without valuable consideration between the parties
(though recall § 13.001: a donee, giving no value, takes subject to prior unrecorded interests the
records would not have shown anyway — the recording system protects purchasers for value);
**dedication** of streets and parks to public use, met in Principles I Module 04's plats; and the owner's own
**will**, the voluntary transfer that waits. The unit's single doctrine is one already built:
writing, subscription and delivery (§ 5.021), acknowledgment for the records (§ 12.001), and
immediate recording (§ 13.001) — the voluntary transfer done *right*. Everything else in this
module is what happens when transfer is not voluntary, or not done right.

**Delivery, the quiet failure point, on facts.** Because gift deeds skip the closing table's
discipline, delivery problems cluster around them, and three scenarios teach the doctrine. *The
drawer deed*: mother signs a deed to daughter, tells no one, keeps it in her desk; at her death
the deed is found. Nothing was conveyed — no delivery with present intent during life — and the
land passes under her will or the intestacy statutes, not the deed. *The recorded surprise*:
father signs and records a deed to son without telling him. Recording supplies strong evidence of
delivery, and acceptance of a beneficial grant is presumed — the gift likely stands, though the
question is judicial, not conversational. *The conditional handoff*: "here's the deed, but it
only counts when I die." A deed cannot be a will: instruments taking effect at death must satisfy
the will formalities of this module's earlier unit, and a present deed with oral death
conditions

chunks.heading: T09U3 — Involuntary Alienation
chunks.excerpt:
is a litigation generator. The licence holder's translation for clients who ask about
"just deeding it over": gifts of land are real conveyances with real consequences — title,
homestead, the donee's creditors, the § 13.001 value problem — and an estate-planning wish
belongs with an estate-planning lawyer.


Consider a parent who wants to add an adult child to the deed to avoid future probate. The agent can recognize that a proposed conveyance is involved but should not choose the ownership form or draft the deed. The consequences for control, creditors, taxes, homestead, and later transfer need legal and tax advice. A downloadable quitclaim deed is not a universal estate-planning solution.

At a sales closing, compare the proposed conveyance with the accepted bargain. Confirm the legal description, estate, reservations, exceptions, and signing capacity through the title and legal process. If the deed differs materially, flag the discrepancy before execution. A signature should reflect an informed and authorized conveyance, not a last-minute assumption that all deeds say the same thing.

## T09U3 — Involuntary Alienation

An interest can change through legal events or proceedings without an ordinary negotiated sale by the owner. Foreclosure, condemnation, judicial sale, tax proceedings, adverse possession, and succession issues can involve different authority and procedures. The purchaser must evaluate the interest acquired and any surviving rights. A low auction price does not establish a clean or complete title.
### Adapted teaching: Foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, and statutory timing

Ownership also moves against the owner's will, and each mechanism has already earned a piece of
this course:

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, and statutory timing
chunks.excerpt:
- **Foreclosure** — the secured creditor's remedy: the § 51.0001 security instrument enforced by
  sale, previewed in Principles I Module 03 and given fully in Principles I Module 08.
- **Tax sale** — the Principles I Module 03 tax lien (§§ 32.01, 32.05) enforced to judgment and sale; the
  ultimate priority claim collecting itself.
- **Condemnation (eminent domain).** The sovereign's power to take private property for public
  use on payment of adequate compensation, exercised in Texas through a statutory procedure:
  Property Code § 21.012 requires the condemning entity, when it cannot agree with the owner on
  damages, to file a petition that describes the property, states *with specificity* the public
  use, names the owner, affirms the failure to agree — and affirms that the entity provided the
  owner the **landowner's bill of rights statement** and made a **bona fide offer** to buy
  voluntarily first. For a licence holder, a pending or threatened condemnation is a material fact
  in any transaction touching the corridor, and valuation in condemnation is specialist work.
  The § 21.012 petition requirements repay one more pass, because each element protects the
  owner: the petition must *describe the property* (Principles I Module 04's discipline, enforced against the
  government), state *with specificity* the public use (no vague "municipal purposes"), name the
  owner, and affirm both that the entity and the owner *could not agree on damages* and that the
  entity provided the **landowner's bill of rights statement** and made a **bona fide offer** —
  meaning the statute forces a real negotiation before the courthouse. For practice, three
  consequences: a corridor rumour is a disclosure conversation and a value question long before
  any petition is filed; a

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, and statutory timing
chunks.excerpt:
n owner approached by a condemnor has statutory protections and should
  have counsel *before* responding to the first offer; and a pending petition against a listing
  is a material fact the licence holder does not soften.
- **Adverse possession.** Long, hostile possession that ripens into title — Texas gives the
  doctrine three clocks, all read for this course in the Civil Practice & Remedies Code, all
  framed as limitation periods barring the record owner's suit:
  - **Three years** (§ 16.024) against a possessor claiming under *title or color of title* — a
    facially plausible but defective chain.
  - **Five years** (§ 16.025) against a possessor who *cultivates, uses or enjoys* the land,
    **pays the applicable taxes**, and claims under a **duly registered deed** — with quitclaim
    and forged deeds expressly disqualified.
  - **Ten years** (§ 16.026) against bare possession that cultivates, uses or enjoys — the
    "naked" claim — capped, absent a title instrument, at **160 acres** including improvements
    unless more is actually enclosed, and extended to instrument boundaries where a registered
    memorandum fixes them.
  The doctrine's elements — peaceable, adverse, continuous, hostile possession — reward the
  vigilant and punish the absent, which is the practice lesson: rural owners inspect their land,
  encroachments (Principles I Module 03) are addressed rather than tolerated, and "the neighbour has farmed
  that strip for years" is a sentence that should raise the hair on a licence holder's neck.
**Adverse possession, worked against the clocks.** The three statutes separate cleanly on facts.
*Fact set one*: a rancher fences and grazes a neighbouring strip for twelve years, no deed, no tax
payments. The three-year statute cannot run (no title or co

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, and statutory timing
chunks.excerpt:
lor of title); the five-year statute
cannot run (no registered deed, no taxes); the **ten-year** statute can — bare cultivation, use or
enjoyment is its whole demand, and twelve years exceeds it, within § 16.026's acreage frame.
*Fact set two*: a buyer takes a defective deed (void for a forged link upstream), records it,
pays taxes annually, and occupies for six years. The **five-year** statute fits — cultivation or
use, tax payment, and a duly registered deed — unless the deed is the *forged* one itself, which
§ 16.025(b) disqualifies along with quitclaims; against a facially regular but defective chain,
even the **three-year** statute may have run. *Fact set three*: a holdover relative lives in a
decedent's house "by everyone's kindness" for twenty years. No statute runs — possession with
permission is not hostile, and hostility is the element permission always defeats. The doctrine's
architecture, restated: the statutes bar the *record owner's suit* to recover the land; the
possessor's title ripens because the owner's remedy died. Which is why the practice advice runs
to owners, not squatters: inspect, post, paper every permission in writing (permission defeats
hostility), and act within the shortest plausible clock when an encroachment appears.

chunks.heading: T09U4 — Conveyance of Estates
chunks.excerpt:
Do not treat physical possession as proof of ownership. Adverse possession requires the applicable statutory and factual elements; mowing, occasional use, or a fence alone does not establish them automatically. [Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 16](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/CP/htm/CP.16.htm) contains the relevant real-property limitations provisions. The correct period and conditions depend on the asserted claim. A license holder should preserve facts and refer the title issue rather than pronounce ownership from a site visit.

In a worked auction file, a buyer asks whether a junior-lien foreclosure eliminates the first mortgage. The answer requires priority and the actual sale’s legal effect. The broker should obtain the lien and sale documents and recommend counsel or qualified title review before bidding. The phrase “foreclosure property” does not identify which interests survive or whether possession will be immediate.

Condemnation likewise requires the actual governmental authority, proceeding, property interest, and compensation record. A proposed road corridor is not the same as a completed taking. A buyer should know the stage and available information before deciding whether to proceed. The agent may explain the factual project status and refer legal consequences; the agent should not guarantee compensation or immunity from a future taking.

## T09U4 — Conveyance of Estates

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Death, probate, intestacy, and the evidence needed for a sale
chunks.excerpt:
The estate conveyed cannot be understood without the estate held and the authority of the conveyor. A life tenant, trustee, estate representative, co-owner, entity manager, and individual fee owner present different questions. A deed’s form does not expand the signer’s authority or eliminate another holder’s interest. Establish the title and capacity facts before promising delivery of the buyer’s expected estate.
### Adapted teaching: Death, probate, intestacy, and the evidence needed for a sale

When there is no valid will, the **intestacy statutes** write one, and the Texas version cannot be
understood without Principles I Module 05's community property system — the two bodies of law interlock.

**The community estate.** Estates Code § 201.003 governs the deceased spouse's share of community
property: it passes **entirely to the surviving spouse** if the decedent leaves no descendant, *or*
if all the decedent's surviving descendants are also descendants of the surviving spouse — the
intact-family rule. But if the decedent left a child of another relationship, the decedent's
one-half of the community passes to the decedent's descendants — and the surviving spouse keeps
only the spouse's own half. The blended-family house is the classic casualty: the surviving
stepparent discovers the stepchildren now co-own the home.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Death, probate, intestacy, and the evidence needed for a sale
chunks.excerpt:
**The separate estate.** Estates Code § 201.002 divides a married decedent's separate property:
with children, the spouse takes **one-third of personal property** and a **life estate in one-third
of the land** (Principles I Module 03's life estate arising by statute), with the rest to the children; with no
children, the spouse takes all personal property and **one-half of the land** outright, the other
half passing to the decedent's kin — and the spouse takes everything only if the decedent left no
surviving parent, sibling or their descendants.

**No spouse at all.** Estates Code § 201.001 runs the ladder: children and their descendants; then
parents and siblings by the stated splits; then the estate divides into two **moieties** for the
paternal and maternal kindred, ascending without end. Distribution among descendants follows
§ 201.101's **per capita with representation** rule: those in the nearest degree take equal
shares, and a deceased taker's share drops to that taker's own descendants.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Death, probate, intestacy, and the evidence needed for a sale
chunks.excerpt:
**The statutes, computed.** Intestacy is arithmetic once the estate is classified, so compute
three estates. *Estate one*: H dies intestate, survived by W and their two children; the home is
community. Under § 201.003's intact-family rule, H's half of the community passes entirely to W —
W owns the whole home. *Estate two*: same facts, but one of H's two surviving children is from a
prior marriage. Now H's one-half of the community passes to H's descendants — the two children
take H's half in equal shares (§ 201.101's nearest-degree rule), and W keeps only her own half:
the home is owned half by W, a quarter by each child. *Estate three*: W2 dies intestate owning
**separate-property** land, survived by husband H2 and her three children. Under § 201.002, H2
takes a life estate in one-third of the land, the children take the land subject to it — and if
one of the three children had predeceased W2 leaving two children of his own, § 201.101 drops the
deceased child's one-third to his two children, one-sixth each: per capita with representation
doing exactly what its name says. The discipline in all three: classify first (community or
separate — Principles I Module 05's Family Code rules), then apply the right section, then check every taker
against the family facts. Change one fact and the fractions change; that is why heirship is
proved, not assumed.


Death can create both ownership and administration questions. A will’s existence does not prove it has been admitted or that a particular person can convey. An affidavit of heirship has a particular evidentiary role and is not identical to a court order or warranty of ownership. A surviving family member’s belief about inheritance should be recorded as a claim requiring review, not accepted as a title conclusion.

chunks.heading: T09U5 — Public Records
chunks.excerpt:
In a worked inherited-property sale, three siblings agree to sell, but one deceased sibling’s children may hold an interest. The agent should not assume majority agreement is enough. Obtain the death, probate, marital, and title facts for counsel and the title company. The purchase contract should reflect the actual seller parties and a realistic path to conveyance. Do not use a relative’s informal power of attorney as if it survives the principal’s death without legal review.

The buyer’s intended estate also matters. A seller might offer only an undivided interest, a leasehold, or the surface estate. The buyer should not believe that paying the stated price acquires everything associated with the address. The authorized contract and deed process should identify the estate accurately, and legal interpretation should occur before execution if the arrangement is unusual.

Marital and homestead interests remain separate inquiries. A personal representative, surviving spouse, or trustee may need evidence beyond the vesting deed. The agent’s intake should ask factual questions and transmit relevant documents promptly. The role is to prevent a closing surprise, not to decide succession or signature law from a family tree drawn at the kitchen table.

## T09U5 — Public Records

Public recording supports notice and the orderly identification of interests. It does not mean the clerk has adjudicated validity. A document may be recordable yet contain an error, be forged, or require interpretation. Recording also differs from execution, acknowledgment, and delivery. Each act has its own role.
### Adapted teaching: Recordability, acknowledgment, and the consequences of recording

Texas maintains its land records county by county, and the system's logic is **notice**.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Recordability, acknowledgment, and the consequences of recording
chunks.excerpt:
**Getting in: acknowledgment.** Property Code § 12.001 provides that an instrument concerning real
property *may be recorded if it has been acknowledged, sworn to with a proper jurat, or proved
according to law* — and that a conveyance may not be recorded unless signed and acknowledged or
sworn to by the grantor before qualified witnesses or an authorised officer, with the recently
added requirement (in the text as held, amended effective December 4, 2025) that an individual
presenting a paper conveyance in person show photo identification to the county clerk. Section
12.0011 tightens the paper path: a paper document must bear an **original** signature, acknowledged
or sworn, to be recorded or to serve as notice — with electronic instruments under the
electronic-recording statutes accommodated separately. The acknowledgment, note well, is a
recording prerequisite: an unacknowledged deed can still convey between the parties; it simply
cannot enter the records and radiate notice.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Recordability, acknowledgment, and the consequences of recording
chunks.excerpt:
**Where, and by whom.** Two provisions of Property Code Chapter 11, read for this course, supply
the system's geography and its operator. Section 11.001 fixes the *where*: to be effectively
recorded, an instrument relating to real property must be recorded **in the county in which a
part of the property is located** — recording in the wrong county records nothing, and a tract
spanning a county line is recorded where a part lies, with careful practice filing in both. (The
statute even handles the county that did not exist yet: when a new county is created, a proper
prior recording keeps its validity and notice effect, and the new county obtains and indexes a
transcript.) Section 11.004 supplies the *who*: the **county clerk** must correctly record
qualifying instruments within a reasonable time after delivery, give a receipt, record
instruments relating to the same property **in the order filed** — the sentence undergirding
every priority race in this module — and maintain the indexes by which chains of title are
actually searched. The clerk records what qualifies; the clerk does not judge validity — which
is why forged and defective instruments can sit in the records looking official, and why
examination (the next unit) is a profession rather than a lookup.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Recordability, acknowledgment, and the consequences of recording
chunks.excerpt:
**What recording does: the notice statutes.** Property Code § 13.002 states the affirmative side —
a properly recorded instrument is *notice to all persons* of its existence and is open to public
inspection. This is **constructive notice**: the world is charged with knowing what the records
show, searched or not. Property Code § 13.001 states the punishing side: an *unrecorded*
conveyance, mortgage or deed of trust is **void as to a creditor or a subsequent purchaser for
valuable consideration without notice** — while remaining fully binding on the parties themselves,
their heirs, and any subsequent taker who paid nothing or who had notice. Texas is thus a
notice-race jurisdiction in effect for the honest purchaser: the buyer who pays value without
notice of a prior unrecorded deed takes free of it. The moral licences are built on: **record
immediately** — the grantee who delays recording is gambling the property on the grantor's honesty
— and **search always**, because the records bind you whether or not you looked.

**Kinds of notice, assembled.** Constructive notice from the records (§ 13.002); **actual notice**
from what a party in fact knows; and inquiry-type notice from facts demanding investigation — the
occupant who is not the record owner, the visible path across the land. A purchaser's protection
under § 13.001 evaporates with notice of any kind, which is why possession and inspection matter
alongside the record search.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Recordability, acknowledgment, and the consequences of recording
chunks.excerpt:
**The records are public — and that fact is managed.** Openness is the system's engine
(§ 13.002's "open to public inspection" is what makes constructive notice fair), and Texas
manages its cost in personal terms through Property Code § 11.008: instruments need no social
security number to record, preparers may not include one, and every instrument transferring an
individual's interest carries the boldfaced NOTICE OF CONFIDENTIALITY RIGHTS telling natural
persons they may strike social security and driver's licence numbers before filing. For the
licence holder the point is practical on both faces: everything recorded — price recitals,
liens, family circumstances an heirship affidavit narrates — is permanently public, a fact
sellers deserve to hear before unusual documents are drafted; and the identifying numbers the
system does not need should never be on the paper in the first place.


[Property Code Chapters 11–13](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/PR/htm/PR.13.htm) address public records and recording effects. Section 13.001’s protection for specified purchasers and creditors depends on its actual conditions, including value and notice. A slogan such as “first to record always wins” omits those conditions and can mislead. Counsel or a title professional should evaluate conflicting claims.

In a worked file, a buyer learns that the seller signed an earlier deed that was never recorded. The absence of that deed from an online index does not justify ignoring actual notice. The broker should preserve the information and notify the appropriate reviewers. Do not encourage a race to record as a substitute for legal analysis.

chunks.heading: T09U6 — Proof of Ownership
chunks.excerpt:
Online searches are practical tools with limits. Indexing variations, name changes, legal descriptions, document types, and recording delays can affect what a search returns. A broker’s casual search is not a title examination or title insurance. Use it to identify and communicate relevant facts, and obtain the professional title evidence the transaction requires.

Current recording mechanics also matter. [Property Code § 12.001(b)](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/PR/htm/PR.12.htm#12.001), amended effective December 4, 2025, includes a photo-identification requirement for an individual presenting a conveyance instrument in person to the county clerk. That requirement operates alongside the specified execution and acknowledgment or oath requirements; it does not replace them. Do not assume that a remembered pre-amendment checklist is complete. Distinguish an in-person presentation from an electronic-record submission, and confirm the requirements applicable to the actual submission method with the closing and recording professionals. A document’s formal eligibility for recording still does not settle every question about the parties’ rights or the signer’s substantive authority.

## T09U6 — Proof of Ownership

Proof of ownership is assembled from appropriate evidence. A deed, probate record, survey, title search, abstract, commitment, and policy can contribute different information. A utility bill or tax payment can show occupancy or payment without proving a complete ownership interest. The buyer needs the evidence appropriate to the interest and transaction.
### Adapted teaching: Abstracts, title commitments, owner and lender policies, and coverage limits

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Abstracts, title commitments, owner and lender policies, and coverage limits
chunks.excerpt:
How does a buyer *know* the seller owns what the contract promises? Four instruments of assurance,
in ascending order of modern use:

- **Abstract and attorney's opinion.** An **abstract of title** is a compiled history of every
  recorded instrument affecting the parcel; an attorney examines it and issues an opinion of title.
  Venerable, still met in rural Texas, and limited: the opinion is only as good as the abstract and
  the abstractor, and it insures nothing.
- **Attorney's certificate of title** — examination directly from the records, same limits.
- **Torrens-style registration** — title by government certificate; noted for completeness, not a
  feature of Texas practice.
- **Title insurance** — the Texas standard, and a regulated industry. Insurance Code § 2501.003
  defines **title insurance** as insurance that insures, guarantees or indemnifies an owner of real
  property or another interested party *against loss or damage resulting from a lien or encumbrance
  on or defect in the title, or the invalidity or impairment of a lien* — protection, unlike every
  other insurance, against the **past** rather than the future. Two structural facts distinguish
  Texas: the **premium is promulgated** — § 2501.003(8) defines premium as the rates promulgated by
  the state's insurance regulator, and expressly *includes* the charges for title examination and
  closing the transaction — so title policy pricing does not vary company to company; and the
  industry runs on **abstract plants**: § 2501.004 requires a plant that is geographically arranged
  (indexed by land, not just by names), covers a period beginning not later than January 1, 1979,
  and is kept current. In a transaction the machinery appears as the **commitment** (the insurer's
  offer to insure, listing re

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Abstracts, title commitments, owner and lender policies, and coverage limits
chunks.excerpt:
quirements to cure and exceptions it will not cover — the document the
  Principles I Module 03 applied exercise taught you to read), then the **owner's policy** protecting the buyer
  up to the price, and the **loan policy** protecting the lender's lien priority up to the debt.
  The escrow side of the same industry — § 2501.003's defined **escrow officer** — closes the
  transaction; Principles I Module 09 picks up there.

**What a policy actually does when title fails.** Assurance instruments are best compared at the
moment of loss. Under an abstract-and-opinion regime, the evicted buyer's recourse is a
professional-negligence claim against the examining attorney — only as good as the attorney's
error and solvency, and unavailable when the examination was flawless but the record lied (the
forged deed that looked perfect). A title policy answers differently: it is *indemnity*, not
opinion — the § 2501.003 definition insures against loss from defects, liens and encumbrances,
so the insurer pays covered losses and defends covered claims whether or not anyone erred. That
difference — negligence versus indemnity — is why the forged-deed hypothetical of the Title unit
lands on insurance, and why lenders will not fund without their own loan policy. The limits are
equally instructive: policies speak as of their date (new defects are the owner's problem),
exclude what their exceptions list, and pay up to stated amounts — the owner's policy at the
price, the loan policy at the debt. Insurance replaces neither examination nor curing; it prices
what examination and curing could not eliminate.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Abstracts, title commitments, owner and lender policies, and coverage limits
chunks.excerpt:
Under [Occupations Code § 1101.555](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/OC/htm/OC.1101.htm), when an offer is signed the license holder must advise each buyer in writing to have the abstract examined by an attorney chosen by the buyer or to obtain a title policy. This is an operational duty at the offer stage, not advice reserved for difficult title cases. Keep evidence of the required written advisory.

A lender’s policy protects the lender’s insured interest under its terms. It is not a substitute for the owner’s policy. Neither policy should be described as covering every possible loss or future event. Read the insured parties, amount, effective date, exclusions, exceptions, and conditions. Questions about policy coverage belong with the title insurer and counsel.

In a worked purchase, the commitment excludes a recorded utility easement crossing the proposed pool location. The buyer’s lender may accept the policy, but the buyer still needs to decide whether the easement is compatible with the intended improvement and whether a timely contractual objection or other action is available. Financing approval does not answer the buyer’s use question.

The agent should help the buyer receive and review evidence promptly. Forward the commitment, exception documents, survey, and relevant updates; identify missing material; track the contract’s delivery and objection provisions; and recommend appropriate professional review. Do not paraphrase an exception away or tell the buyer that title insurance makes document review unnecessary.

chunks.heading: Comparing evidence without overstating it
chunks.excerpt:
The final conveyance review asks whether the closing instruments deliver what the contract promised and whether the agreed insurance will issue on the expected terms. If a new exception or requirement appears, raise it before signing and funding. A complete record helps the client make an informed choice and allows the proper professionals to resolve the legal questions.

### Comparing evidence without overstating it

A buyer receives a deed copy, a tax-account printout, and a title commitment. Each answers a different question. The deed records the instrument’s stated conveyance and parties. The tax record identifies information used for assessment and administration. The commitment states the insurer’s proposed coverage subject to its requirements and exceptions. None should be treated as an all-purpose guarantee of ownership, boundaries, authority, and permissible use.

Suppose the tax account names a deceased owner, while a later recorded deed names a trust. The discrepancy is a reason to obtain and evaluate the title chain, not a reason for the agent to choose the more recent-looking screen. The relevant instruments and legal rules determine the ownership analysis. The title company and counsel may need probate, trust, or authority documents before accepting the proposed conveyance.

Suppose instead that the commitment identifies the expected seller, but an exception references an access easement. The buyer’s concern is whether the intended driveway is legally available. The short exception description is not enough. Obtain the referenced instrument and survey, identify the physical location, and have the appropriate professionals evaluate the right. A commitment can alert the buyer to a limitation without resolving whether the limitation suits the buyer’s plans.

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: Recording does not validate everything
chunks.excerpt:
Finally, distinguish evidence prepared before closing from the policy or instruments delivered after closing. A commitment is not the final issued policy. A proposed deed is not evidence that delivery and acceptance occurred. A release request is not the recorded release. Track the actual completed documents and remaining requirements. The agent’s status report should say what has been received and confirmed, while avoiding a legal certification of title the license holder is not authorized to provide.


### Statute reading exercise: Recording does not validate everything

Read Property Code §§ 12.001 and 13.001–13.002 and § 5.021. Distinguish signing, acknowledgment, delivery, recordability, and notice. Explain why a recorded forged instrument does not become valid merely because it appears in the index.

Feedback: These provisions address different steps and effects. Recordability and notice do not supply genuine execution or authority. A clerk’s acceptance is not adjudication of ownership. Conflicting or fraudulent instruments require title and legal review; the broker should preserve evidence and avoid a title opinion.

### Applied exercise: The commitment says “excepted”

A buyer receives a title commitment excepting an access easement. The lender accepts the proposed coverage. The buyer wants to build across the easement and assumes lender acceptance proves that is allowed. Identify the separate questions and the contract steps to track.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Feedback: Lender insurance acceptance, owner coverage, legal easement rights, intended construction, and contractual objections are separate. Obtain the easement instrument and survey, recommend legal and appropriate professional review, and track the actual objection deadline and response process. Do not promise that insurance authorizes construction or eliminates the easement.


### Module recap

Title is ownership; documents supply evidence and perform transfers. Identify the estate and authority, the transfer method, the public-record effect, and the actual insurance coverage. Recording is not validation, a lender’s policy is not an owner’s policy, and acceptance by a lender does not resolve the buyer’s intended use. Preserve the contractual opportunity to review and object.

lessons.title: Texas Law of Contracts — Module 10

chunks.heading: Texas Law of Contracts — Module 10
chunks.excerpt:
# Texas Law of Contracts — Module 10

## TREC Topic: Transaction Process and Closing

You will administer the accepted contract through closing, use a documented checklist without treating it as legal authority, coordinate financing, inspections and title, verify prorations, and distinguish signing from funding and possession.

This is student instruction aligned to the LOC-0 topic. Legal propositions identify primary authority; worked examples are hypothetical. A source labelled “Adapted teaching” is project-owned instruction revised for this course, with its exact origin recorded in the separate provenance manifest. References explicitly naming Principles I, Principles II, or Law of Agency identify the source discussion’s context, not a prerequisite or a Law of Contracts module number. The required instruction is presented here. The course does not establish regulatory approval or observed learner time.

## T10U1 — Transaction Process

The transaction process begins before the contract is accepted and continues after signatures at closing. Early work identifies the parties, representation, property, intended use, financing, disclosures, and required documents. Acceptance creates an operational calendar. Investigations and approvals inform decisions. Closing instruments and funds perform the core exchange. Post-closing obligations, possession, corrections, and record retention can remain.
### Adapted teaching: The sequence from accepted agreement to closing readiness

**Closing is a deadline system.** From effective date to closing date, the contract (Principles I Module 06)
schedules everything; the licence holder's professional contribution is running that calendar so
that no right lapses unnoticed. The standing critical path:

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The sequence from accepted agreement to closing readiness
chunks.excerpt:
- **Earnest money and option fees delivered** on the contract's clock, receipted by the escrow
  agent.
- **Title work.** The commitment issues; buyer and lender review; objections go out within the
  contract's window; cures are negotiated. Everything Principles I Module 03 taught about liens and Principles I Module 07
  taught about chains of title happens *here*, as tasks with dates: releases ordered, payoffs
  quoted, heirship documented, that pool contractor's lien resolved.
- **Survey** obtained or updated (Principles I Module 04's five-point pass), feeding both title objections and
  the lender's requirements.
- **Inspections and repairs** inside the option period; repair amendments negotiated in writing.
- **Financing.** Application, appraisal, underwriting, and the approach of the financing
  contingency's deadline — with the agent tracking conditions ("clear to close") rather than
  assuming them.
- **Seller's disclosure** delivered (Property Code § 5.008 — Principles I Module 07); **insurance** bound
  (the lender will not fund without it); utilities, HOA documents and resale certificates
  ordered where applicable.
- **The walk-through**: the buyer's final verification that the property's condition and the
  agreed repairs match the contract — the last, cheap moment to catch what would be expensive
  the day after funding.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The sequence from accepted agreement to closing readiness
chunks.excerpt:
**"Clear to close," tracked rather than assumed.** Financing is the critical path's longest pole,
and its milestones deserve the same calendar discipline as the contract's: application submitted
(with the § 1024.6 booklet obligations of this module's federal unit starting the clock on the
lender's side); appraisal ordered and received — with the contract's own machinery, not
improvisation, governing what happens if value comes in low; conditional approval, with the
conditions *listed and owned* (whose document, due when); and final underwriting clearance —
"clear to close" — before which no closing date is real, however confidently scheduled. The
licence holder's technique is unglamorous: a standing weekly status call pattern among agent,
lender and escrow officer, and a refusal to let "we're fine" substitute for a conditions list
with names on it.

**The association file, ordered early.** Where a property sits in a mandatory owners'
association, the contract's HOA machinery adds its own pre-closing thread: the association's
documents and account statement are ordered (associations bill for them, and turnaround times
are real), the buyer's review rights under the contract's terms run on their own clock, and
the association's transfer and statement fees take their place on the settlement statement as
the contract allocates them. The dues proration of the statements unit and Principles I Module 03's
assessment-lien discussion both land in this thread — one more place where the file's earliest
phone call prevents its latest crisis.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: The sequence from accepted agreement to closing readiness
chunks.excerpt:
**Funds at closing, and the fraud that hunts them.** The escrow officer will require the buyer's
cash to close in **collected funds** — a wire or the equivalent the instructions specify, not a
personal cheque that clears next week — and the amount comes from the settlement statement, not
from memory. Around that wire has grown the industry's most damaging crime: intercepted and
spoofed emails delivering altered wiring instructions days before closing. The professional
protocols are simple and non-negotiable, and a licence holder repeats them to every buyer:
wiring instructions come from the title company through a verified channel; any change to
wiring instructions is presumed fraudulent; and every wire is confirmed by a phone call to a
number *independently known*, never one taken from the email that asked for the money. Stating
these protocols is not legal advice; it is the standard of care in a market where a
misdirected down payment is usually unrecoverable.


Assign each step to the person who must perform it. The buyer supplies financial documents and makes decisions; the seller supplies required property information and performs agreed obligations; the lender underwrites; the title and escrow participants handle their authorized functions; inspectors and other professionals evaluate their subjects; the broker coordinates within its role. An agent’s reminder does not replace the party’s performance, but it can prevent a missed step.

chunks.heading: T10U2 — Sample Check List
chunks.excerpt:
The process should expose uncertainty early. A buyer depending on sale proceeds, a seller lacking authority documents, an unavailable survey, an insurance problem, or a repair requiring permits can affect the closing path. Record the issue, responsible participant, next action, due date, and source. Avoid a generic “pending” status that conceals which condition threatens performance.

In a worked file, the closing date is thirty days away, but the title company requests probate documents that are not yet available. The agent should notify the client and broker, identify the actual requirement, and coordinate with counsel. A promise that title will be ready because most transactions close in thirty days is not evidence. The parties may need a realistic negotiated amendment before the existing agreement reaches a crisis.

## T10U2 — Sample Check List

A checklist is an administrative aid. It should be derived from the accepted documents and applicable duties, not used as a substitute for them. An office checklist can omit a new addendum or assume a deadline that differs from the signed contract. Begin each file by reading the actual agreement and then customizing the factual task record within the broker’s procedures.

A useful row contains the task, source paragraph or authority, triggering event, responsible person, recipient, delivery method, due date or time, completion evidence, and unresolved issue. For example, “survey” is too vague. A better row identifies which party must furnish which survey-related documents, the date due, the recipient, and the evidence of delivery. A separate row tracks the buyer’s review or objection process under the contract.

chunks.heading: T10U2 — Sample Check List
chunks.excerpt:
At acceptance, confirm the complete signed agreement and addenda, communication of acceptance, effective date, party and notice information, escrow details, and money-delivery duties. Schedule inspections and other investigations while the relevant rights remain available. Request title documents and survey information. Confirm lender milestones without treating them as amendments of the contract. Track disclosures with their actual receipt dates.

Before a protection expires, confirm the client has the necessary information and understands the status. The checklist should not make the agent’s preferred decision for the client. It should identify available documents, unanswered questions, and the need for timely legal advice where appropriate. A client’s decision to proceed should be documented accurately, without a misleading statement that the agent guaranteed every risk was resolved.

At amendment, retain the signed change, update affected dates and amounts, and notify the appropriate participants. At closing readiness, compare the settlement figures with the contract, amendments, lender disclosures, payoffs, deposits, and invoices. Confirm identity and authority requirements, signing arrangements, funds, insurance, possession, and any final walkthrough. At completion, retain the final documents, confirmations, and remaining duties under the broker’s retention policy and rule.

A worked checklist defect is a row marked “financing complete” because a prequalification letter arrived. The evidence does not support the status. Replace the label with the actual stage: prequalification received; borrower approval pending; property conditions unresolved; funding not authorized. Separate entries give the client and broker a usable picture of what remains.

chunks.heading: A worked checklist that exposes dependencies
chunks.excerpt:
Another defect is a deadline calculated once and never updated after a signed amendment. The record should identify the original date, the amendment’s new date, and which dependent tasks changed. Do not delete the historical date; mark it superseded with the source. This preserves a reliable chronology if someone later asks why a notice was sent when it was.

### A worked checklist that exposes dependencies

Assume an accepted residential contract contains a third-party financing addendum, a negotiated termination option, an agreement to furnish an existing survey, and a seller temporary lease after closing. The office’s standard checklist contains generic rows for financing, inspection, title, and closing. Customize those rows by reading the actual documents. The purpose is to make dependencies visible before a delay in one workstream affects another.

For financing, record the lender contact, the buyer’s application and document status, the actual buyer-approval provision, property-approval issues, and the evidence needed for closing authorization. Do not place private financial details in a broadly shared checklist. The status can identify that income documentation remains outstanding without circulating the buyer’s tax return to every participant. Assign the next action to the person who controls it.

chunks.heading: A worked checklist that exposes dependencies
chunks.excerpt:
For inspection, record the buyer’s selected professionals, appointment dates, report delivery, review with the buyer, and any decision required before a contractual right expires. A report received the evening before a deadline creates a different risk from an appointment merely scheduled. The checklist should therefore distinguish scheduling, performance, report receipt, client review, and documented decision. None of those stages by itself means the seller agreed to repairs.

For survey, identify the exact documents promised, the delivery deadline, the actual receipt, and any issue affecting lender or title acceptance. An old drawing without the associated required information may not satisfy the contract. A newly constructed improvement may make the existing depiction inadequate for the buyer’s concern. The agent should coordinate the appropriate review and identify who bears any new-survey obligation under the signed terms.

For the temporary lease, record its signed version, commencement and termination terms, rent or deposit obligations, possession responsibilities, and insurance referrals. Do not let the main closing date overwrite the later possession date. A key-release row should identify the actual agreement and required confirmation. The buyer’s moving-company reservation is not the source of the seller’s surrender duty.

At each checkpoint, use a status supported by evidence: not requested, requested, received, under review, resolved, or superseded. The word complete should require the relevant completion test. If the title company requests an additional authority document after an earlier review, reopen the affected task and explain why. A checklist is useful because it reflects change accurately, not because every row stays green.

chunks.heading: T10U3 — Loan Approval
chunks.excerpt:
## T10U3 — Loan Approval

Loan approval is a process with defined conditions. Prequalification, preapproval, underwriting approval, satisfaction of conditions, closing authorization, and funding are not synonyms. The lender’s terminology should be clarified for the actual file. The agent should ask what conditions remain and what evidence will establish readiness, while the buyer remains responsible for truthful, timely documentation and decisions.

Borrower conditions can involve income, employment, credit, assets, debts, occupancy, source of funds, and other underwriting matters. Property conditions can involve appraisal, condition, insurance, title, and program standards. A change in either can affect approval. A buyer should not assume approval remains unconditional after taking new debt, changing employment, or receiving a property-related requirement.

The purchase contract has an independent calendar. The Third Party Financing Addendum’s buyer and property approval provisions must be read on their actual terms. A lender’s request for more time does not automatically extend a contractual right. If an extension is needed, the parties must agree through the proper process; if a right may be exercised, the notice and supporting requirements must be evaluated promptly.

chunks.heading: Coordinating the approval path without becoming the underwriter
chunks.excerpt:
The appraisal is an opinion prepared for its defined purpose and intended use. It does not replace a home inspection or guarantee future resale value. Current appraisal delivery requirements can change, including the 2026 UAD transition identified by Fannie Mae. The lender determines whether the submitted appraisal meets the applicable loan requirements. The agent can provide accurate property information and comparable-sale information through permitted channels without pressuring an appraiser to reach a desired value.

In a worked file, the loan is conditionally approved subject to proof that a debt was paid and a roof repair was completed. The buyer supplies proof of payment, but the repair is pending. It is inaccurate to tell the seller financing is fully complete. State which condition is resolved and which remains. Coordinate the repair evidence, lender review, and the contract’s deadlines rather than guessing that the remaining condition is a formality.

Finally, closing authorization and actual funding can be separate. A borrower may sign all documents while the lender still requires a final review or confirmation. The agent should obtain the appropriate closing and funding status from authorized participants before acting on possession or key-release instructions. Do not infer funding from the borrower’s signature completion.

### Coordinating the approval path without becoming the underwriter

chunks.heading: Coordinating the approval path without becoming the underwriter
chunks.excerpt:
A buyer’s loan file often contains several communications that sound final but are not equivalent. A preliminary letter may be based on unverified information. A conditional approval may depend on documents or property conditions. A closing authorization may still require final funding checks. Ask the lender to describe the present stage and outstanding conditions in terms the client can understand. Do not translate every positive update into an unconditional assurance.

Consider a buyer who has supplied income and asset records but plans to use a gift for part of the required funds. The lender may need documentation of the gift and transfer. The agent can remind the buyer to communicate accurately with the lender and avoid unexplained last-minute changes. The agent should not coach the buyer to describe borrowed money as a gift or conceal a repayment arrangement. Truthful information is essential to both underwriting and a reliable transaction.

Consider a property approval issue instead. The appraisal meets the price, but the lender requires evidence that a safety-related repair is complete. The price opinion alone has not satisfied that condition. Identify the required repair evidence, who will produce it, who will review it, and when review can occur. If the contract’s schedule is threatened, communicate early and use the proper amendment or legal-advice process. Do not assume that a lender’s verbal optimism extends the buyer’s contractual protections.

chunks.heading: T10U4 — Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
chunks.excerpt:
The buyer may also change lenders. A different lender can have different processing times, documentation needs, appraisal requirements, and conditions. The parties’ purchase agreement remains the governing contract unless properly changed. Review any applicable obligations concerning financing changes and promptly coordinate the consequences. A lower quoted rate is only one factor in whether the new lender can meet the actual transaction schedule.

Approval communication should be factual and limited. A useful update says that borrower documentation is complete, appraisal review is pending, and the lender expects to provide a further status on a specified day. An unhelpful update says the loan is guaranteed because the buyer has excellent credit. The lender makes the credit decision, and the buyer’s contractual rights still require their own analysis. This division of roles lets the agent coordinate effectively without claiming authority the agent does not possess.

## T10U4 — Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)

RESPA addresses specified residential settlement processes and prohibits particular referral and unearned-fee practices. Coverage and exemptions matter. Integrated mortgage disclosures also involve TILA and Regulation Z; a modern Closing Disclosure should not be described as simply the old HUD-1 with a new title. Identify the actual loan and disclosure regime.
### Adapted teaching: Settlement disclosures and the distinction between older and current forms

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Settlement disclosures and the distinction between older and current forms
chunks.excerpt:
**The federal frame.** The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act governs settlements involving
**federally related mortgage loans** — which, in practice, means most institutionally financed
one-to-four family residential transactions. Its declared purpose, from the text read for this
course (12 U.S.C. § 2601): reforms so that consumers are *"provided with greater and more timely
information on the nature and costs of the settlement process"* and are *"protected from
unnecessarily high settlement charges caused by certain abusive practices."* Two operative pillars
carry that purpose.

**Reading § 2601 as history.** The findings' vocabulary — "abusive practices," charges that
"unnecessarily inflate the costs" — records the pre-1974 settlement market Congress examined:
referral fees moving invisibly between settlement providers, borrowers meeting their costs for
the first time at the table with no ability to compare or refuse. Each pillar answers one
finding: itemised uniform disclosure answers the information failure; § 2607's prohibitions
answer the kickback economy. Knowing the history keeps the compliance from feeling arbitrary —
every disclosure this module walks exists because its absence was once somebody's business
model, and the licence holder's referral relationships are regulated precisely because
referrals are where the old abuses lived.

chunks.heading: Adapted teaching: Settlement disclosures and the distinction between older and current forms
chunks.excerpt:
**Coverage, read from the purpose.** Section 2601's findings name the market the Act polices —
