When a change occurs near closing, update the register instead of assuming the original scheduled date proves compliance. The agent can coordinate while the creditor determines its legal obligations.

### Applied exercise: A62 — Notice register

Create a notice register for application receipt, a completed application, appraisal completion, a scheduled consummation, and a later servicing transfer. Name the governing source to consult and the evidence to retain. Do not reuse “three business days” as a universal deadline.

Feedback: each event has its own rule and definition. An accurate register distinguishes delivery, mailing, receipt, and consummation where the applicable requirement does.

## T09U9 — Qualifying the Title

Title qualification asks whether the borrower can grant the estate and priority the lender requires. Review ownership, authority, legal description, existing liens, restrictions, easements, judgments, marital/homestead issues, and other exceptions. A title insurance commitment is a conditional promise to issue coverage when requirements are met; it is not an unconditional statement that no defect exists.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A63 — Ownership authority
chunks.excerpt:
An owner's title policy and a lender's policy protect different insured interests. The lender's policy does not automatically protect the buyer's equity. Insurance also contains exclusions, exceptions, conditions, and limits. A survey and other documents can reveal matters requiring title review; “the loan was approved” is not a reason to disregard a boundary or ownership issue.

A lender's title requirements also interact with the property description and intended use. A borrower may own the surface estate while mineral-related exceptions remain. A recorded access easement may be essential to lawful access yet contain maintenance obligations or use limits. An entity's manager may need evidence of authority beyond a business card. These matters call for review of the actual instruments and applicable law. Do not equate a title commitment with an abstract or legal opinion on every ownership question. The commitment specifies a proposed insurance contract, its conditions, and excluded risks.

### Applied exercise: A63 — Ownership authority

The seller died after signing the contract, and a relative offers to sign closing documents without estate authority. Identify the title and authority issues and explain why lender credit approval does not resolve them.

Add that the relative supplies a power of attorney signed by the seller before death and says it proves present authority. Prepare a factual referral packet containing the contract, death information, ownership record, offered authority document, and proposed signing names. Explain why title and counsel must determine actual authority rather than letting the agent choose a signature format. Identify the separate lender concern if the delay exceeds a rate-lock period.

chunks.heading: T09U10 — Review of the Title Commitment
chunks.excerpt:
Feedback: ownership succession, estate authority, required parties, and insurability need title/counsel review. Family relationship alone does not establish authority to convey.

Additional feedback: Possession of a document does not establish that it remains effective or authorizes the proposed act after the owner's death. The estate, title, and legal facts require qualified review. A lock extension is a separate lender/pricing question; neither a prior credit approval nor a lock resolves ownership succession.

## T09U10 — Review of the Title Commitment

Texas title commitments commonly organize transaction/coverage information in Schedule A, exceptions in Schedule B, requirements in Schedule C, and specified disclosures in Schedule D under the applicable promulgated form. Read the current form and every incorporated exception. A requirement to pay and release an existing lien is different from an exception that will remain in the policy.

Instructional commitment: A names the proposed insured lender and legal description; B lists a utility easement; C requires release of a $190,000 prior deed of trust and evidence of entity authority; D supplies required title-company disclosures. Paying the old loan addresses a C requirement. It does not erase the B easement. A proposed policy amount should match the intended coverage and transaction documents.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A64 — Commitment checklist
chunks.excerpt:
Read all schedules with the effective date and policy type in view. The commitment can identify requirements that must be resolved to the insurer's satisfaction, exceptions that remain unless changed, and conditions limiting the promise to issue a policy. A new matter arising after the effective date can require additional attention. Request the actual recorded documents underlying material exceptions, not just the short index description. The lender's willingness to accept an exception does not necessarily mean the buyer's intended improvement or use is unaffected. The buyer may need counsel, a surveyor, or other specialist even if financing can proceed.

### Applied exercise: A64 — Commitment checklist

Make a before-closing checklist from the specimen: obtain a payoff, arrange release, verify entity authority, review the easement's effect, and compare legal descriptions. State which items require satisfaction and which require understanding or acceptable treatment as exceptions.

Feedback: payoff/release and authority are requirements; the easement needs review and resolution or acceptance under the lender's standards. Never promise that title insurance removes the physical easement.

### Statute reading exercise: S24 — Read the Texas commitment itself

chunks.heading: T09U11 — Lender Closing Costs
chunks.excerpt:
Read TDI's currently linked [Form T-7, Commitment for Title Insurance](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form_t-07.pdf), including the information pages, conditions, and Schedules A–D. Confirm its presence in TDI's Basic Manual Section II rather than treating the form's older effective date as proof it is obsolete. Create a schedule map stating each schedule's purpose and the difference between an exception, exclusion, requirement, and condition. Apply it to a hypothetical prior deed of trust requiring release, an easement listed as an exception, a mismatch in proposed insured name, and an undisclosed new lien discovered before policy issuance. Identify what should be sent to the title professional and what may require counsel. Do not alter the promulgated form.

Feedback: the prior lien's required treatment is different from a continuing easement exception; proposed insured and estate information must be accurate; newly discovered matters need disclosure and review. The form explains that the commitment is a contract to issue a policy under its terms, not a general title opinion. A good map includes limitations as well as schedules. It does not promise that paying the premium removes a physical easement or insures every excluded risk.

## T09U11 — Lender Closing Costs

Distinguish charges for credit, third-party services, prepaid expenses, escrow reserves, government recording, and credits. A consumer can compare lender-controlled costs while also evaluating services and estimated future expenses. A “no closing cost” offer may use lender credits funded through pricing or finance costs into the loan; it does not mean every service is free.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A65 — Cost comparison
chunks.excerpt:
Check charges paid before closing and charges paid by another party. Avoid double counting and test whether credits meet program restrictions. A lower cash-to-close amount can result from a larger loan rather than lower costs. The Closing Disclosure should allow the consumer to see who pays and how cash is calculated.

### Applied exercise: A65 — Cost comparison

Offer A has $3,200 lender costs and no credit. Offer B has $3,700 lender costs and a $1,500 lender credit but a higher rate. Calculate net lender costs and identify the additional calculation needed to compare a planned five-year holding period.

For a simplified equal-balance comparison, assume Offer B's payment is $28 higher each month. Compute the extra payments over 24 and 60 months and offset them against B's $1,000 upfront saving. Draft a two-horizon explanation. Then remove the equal-balance assumption and name the loan details needed for a complete five-year comparison.

Feedback: A $3,200; B $2,200. Compare periodic payments, remaining balances, and expected exit over the same period. Upfront savings alone do not settle the decision.

Additional feedback: At 24 months the extra payments are $672, leaving B ahead by $328 under the assumptions. At 60 months they are $1,680, making B $680 more costly. Break-even is about 35.71 months. Actual amortization, financed fees, payoff costs, and the likelihood of the planned exit must be examined before making a recommendation.

## T09U12 — Case Study/Workshop

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A66 — Funding recommendation
chunks.excerpt:
Assemble a complete hypothetical file: price $380,000; appraised value $375,000; proposed first loan $300,000; subordinate assistance $15,000 with $0 periodic payment and repayment at sale; verified monthly income $8,000; first-loan P&I supplied as $1,896.20; taxes $500 monthly; insurance $200; association dues $80; other debt $680; closing costs $8,500; lender credit $1,000; seller credit $3,000; deposit $7,500. A $9,000 unexplained bank deposit appears shortly before closing. Title requires release of the seller's old lien.

First LTV on the lower value basis is 80%; combined outstanding-balance LTV is 84%. Price contribution is $65,000 after both loans. Net closing costs are $7,500 after the lender credit. Remaining cash to close is $62,000 after seller and deposit credits. Housing expense is $2,676.20 and DTI is $3,356.20 ÷ $8,000 ≈41.95%. Deferred assistance is still debt even with no periodic payment in this stipulated calculation.

### Applied exercise: A66 — Funding recommendation

Prepare a conditional-status memo with five parts: ratios, cash to close, source-of-funds exception, title requirement, and notice/delivery review. Then assume the $9,000 deposit is an undisclosed personal loan with a $250 monthly payment. Recalculate DTI and explain the required file corrections.

Feedback: corrected DTI is $3,606.20 ÷ $8,000 ≈45.08%. Disclose the debt, document the source, update application/underwriting, resolve title release, and verify disclosures before funding. The exercise does not authorize the agent to make the lender's final approval decision.

### Applied exercise: A81 — One file, reconciled sources and obligations

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A82 — Collateral and title decision packet
chunks.excerpt:
Analyze an original hypothetical file using the lender's supplied eligible-income amount of $7,650 monthly. Housing expense is $2,480. Known debt payments are auto $390 and revolving $125. The application omits a $210 monthly personal loan. The latest aligned account records show checking $18,000 and savings $42,000; an earlier savings statement showed $52,000 before a $10,000 transfer into checking. A documented earnest deposit of $6,000 has already left these current balances. Required remaining cash to close is $48,500. A separate $5,000 donor transfer has not yet arrived and its eligibility is unverified.

Calculate DTI before and after adding the omitted obligation. Reconcile current verified cash and reserves after closing without double counting the old statement, the transfer, or the earnest deposit. Calculate what reserves would be if the separate gift actually arrives and is accepted, labeling that as conditional. Write an exception memo assigning debt correction, source verification, updated underwriting, and cash-to-close confirmation to the responsible lender/settlement reviewers. Do not count the possible gift as monthly income.

Feedback: before correction, debt is $2,995 and DTI about 39.15%; after correction, debt is $3,205 and DTI about 41.90%. Current funds total $60,000, leaving $11,500 after the supplied remaining cash requirement. If the distinct $5,000 gift arrives and is eligible, reserves would be $16,500. Adding the old savings balance or subtracting earnest money a second time would distort the ledger. The memo must preserve the conditional status of the gift and require correction of the undisclosed loan.

### Applied exercise: A82 — Collateral and title decision packet

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
An original hypothetical purchase has a $410,000 price and a $400,000 appraisal made subject to completion of identified repairs. The lender's stipulated maximum loan is 85% of the lower price/value basis. Three comparable indications in the report are $398,000, $405,000, and $402,000; no mechanical averaging rule is supplied. The title commitment names the buyer correctly but describes Lot 42 while the contract and survey describe Lot 24. Schedule C requires release of a $220,000 seller loan; Schedule B contains an easement crossing the proposed garage location. The seller offers a receipt for repairs but no lender-accepted completion evidence.

Calculate the maximum loan and price contribution before costs. Prepare separate appraisal, repair, title-description, prior-lien, and intended-use exception entries. Explain why calculating the comparables' average would not resolve the title mismatch or automatically replace the appraiser's conclusion. Draft an evidence request and identify the lender, appraiser-review channel, title professional, surveyor, and counsel roles as appropriate. State the contract-deadline issue without assuming a right to extend or terminate.

Feedback: maximum loan is $340,000 and price contribution $70,000 before costs. The value opinion's repair condition requires lender-accepted resolution; a receipt alone may be insufficient. The lot mismatch, lien release, and easement effect are independent issues. Comparable indications require supported reconciliation, not an agent-directed target. A correct packet separates facts, missing evidence, decision makers, and time-sensitive contract questions rather than declaring “approved because appraisal exceeds the loan.”

### Module recap

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Deliver a concise exception report that separates supported facts, missing evidence, responsible decision makers, and deadlines. Complete T09's quiz.

Sources: [Regulation Z §1026.43](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/43/), [§1026.42](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/42/); [Regulation B §1002.9](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/), [§1002.14](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/14/); [Freddie Mac joint-GSE UAD transition](https://sf.freddiemac.com/faqs/uad-and-forms-redesign); [Freddie Mac joint-GSE URLA](https://sf.freddiemac.com/tools-learning/uniform-mortgage-data-program/ulad); [TDI T-7 commitment](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form_t-07.pdf).

lessons.title: Module 10: Defaults & Foreclosures

chunks.heading: Module 10: Defaults & Foreclosures
chunks.excerpt:
# Module 10: Defaults & Foreclosures

REF-0 topic T10 suggests 85 minutes. Default response depends on the contract, loan type, property, applicable federal protections, Texas law, and any court orders. An agent can recognize urgency, document facts, and make appropriate referrals; the agent should not improvise a foreclosure deadline or promise a debt release.

## T10U1 — Defaults

Default is failure to satisfy an obligation under the loan documents and law. Missed payments are common, but unpaid taxes, inadequate insurance, prohibited transfers, or other covenant breaches can matter. A late charge, default, acceleration, foreclosure notice, sale, and eviction are different events. A grace period for a late charge is not necessarily a right to delay payment without other consequences.

Review the payment history, notices, servicer identity, loan documents, and the borrower's circumstances. Contact the servicer promptly through a verified channel. Housing counseling and legal assistance can be important. Beware of rescue schemes asking for upfront money, deed transfers, or instructions to stop communicating with the servicer. A pending assistance request is not always an automatic cancellation of a sale.

For covered loans and servicers, Regulation X §1024.41 restricts the first foreclosure notice or filing before the borrower is more than 120 days delinquent, subject to specified exceptions. Loss-mitigation application timing and completeness can trigger additional protections. Do not apply this provision as though it covers every loan, every servicer, and every foreclosure step without examining scope and exceptions.

### Applied exercise: A67 — Default triage

chunks.heading: T10U2 — Adjustments & Modifications
chunks.excerpt:
A homeowner receives a notice and says a modification request was submitted but cannot locate acknowledgment. Prepare a triage checklist: notice date/type, sale date if any, loan/servicer coverage, payment history, application completeness, and urgent counsel/servicer contact. Explain why saying “your application automatically stops everything” is unsafe.

Organize the records into known facts, unverified assertions, and urgent missing items. The homeowner has a transmission receipt but no acknowledgment specifying completeness. Draft one inquiry asking the servicer for status and missing documents, and another requesting prompt legal review of the actual notice and scheduled event. Explain why the agent should preserve dates without announcing a legal stay or discarding notices while waiting.

Feedback: protections depend on the governing rule and facts, including completeness and timing. Obtain records and prompt qualified review; do not let a reassurance replace action on a deadline.

Additional feedback: A receipt can show transmission without proving a complete application or establishing every protection. The responsible reviewer needs the actual loan, servicer, history, notices, dates, and application contents. The client message should encourage prompt action and qualified assistance while avoiding either an unsupported protection promise or an unsupported claim that no protection exists.

## T10U2 — Adjustments & Modifications

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A68 — Workout comparison
chunks.excerpt:
Forbearance temporarily changes payment expectations; it does not ordinarily forgive the underlying debt. A repayment plan spreads arrears over specified payments. A deferral places eligible amounts at a later due date under its terms. A modification changes contractual loan terms. A refinance creates a new loan. A short sale requires approval to sell for less than amounts otherwise due, and a deed in lieu transfers property under an agreement. Each has different eligibility, credit, tax, lien, and personal-liability consequences.

Get the actual agreement. A trial payment plan may require successful completion and further conditions before a permanent modification. A reduced payment can result from term extension or deferred principal rather than debt forgiveness. A short-sale approval should be examined for release of the lien and treatment of any remaining personal obligation; the two are not automatically identical.

### Applied exercise: A68 — Workout comparison

A borrower owes $6,000 arrears. Plan A adds $500 to each of twelve payments; Plan B defers $6,000 to a later event without current additional installments under the stipulated agreement. Calculate the immediate payment effect and remaining deferred amount after twelve compliant months. Name the term that would establish forgiveness if it existed.

Feedback: A adds $500 monthly and cures $6,000 over the year; B adds no current installment but leaves $6,000 deferred. Forgiveness requires an actual cancellation/release provision, not the absence of a current bill.

## T10U3 — Types of Foreclosures

chunks.heading: Statute reading exercise: S08 — Texas sale requirements
chunks.excerpt:
Judicial foreclosure proceeds through a court action and order. A Texas nonjudicial sale under a contractual power of sale must comply with the instrument and Property Code §51.002 and other applicable law. Certain liens, including qualifying Texas home-equity liens, require court authorization even where a subsequent sale uses power-of-sale procedures. Tax foreclosure and other lien types have their own statutes; do not import an ordinary mortgage rule into every forced sale.

Section 51.002 generally provides public auction on the first Tuesday between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., with its January 1/July 4 exception and designated-location provisions. It generally requires at least 21 days' sale notice through the specified posting, filing, and certified-mail steps. For property used as the debtor's residence, subsection (d) requires at least 20 days to cure before sale notice is given. The statute specifies counting conventions and exceptions. Loan documents may provide additional rights, and federal law can impose additional restrictions.

Foreclosure is not the same as immediate lawful physical removal. Possession may require separate process. Bankruptcy can impose an automatic stay; military-service protections may require additional analysis. Junior interests, surviving liens, redemption rights for particular lien types, and title defects make auction purchases legally complex. Obtain qualified legal/title review rather than promising that every auction buyer receives a vacant property free of all liens.

### Statute reading exercise: S08 — Texas sale requirements

chunks.heading: T10U4 — Deficiency Judgments
chunks.excerpt:
Read Property Code §51.002(a)–(e), (g)–(i) and Regulation X §1024.41(f). Make separate columns for Texas sale mechanics, Texas residential cure notice, and covered federal pre-foreclosure restrictions. Explain why satisfying 21 days' sale notice alone does not prove the entire foreclosure is lawful.

Feedback: notice mechanics, cure opportunity, authority, contractual conditions, federal coverage, and court orders must all be considered. The statute's first-Tuesday rule has express exceptions; a generic calendar calculation should not be used as legal advice.

## T10U4 — Deficiency Judgments

A deficiency is an amount remaining after applying foreclosure proceeds and required credits to the debt, but a shortfall is not automatically an enforceable judgment. Texas Property Code §51.003 generally requires an action following a §51.002 sale within two years and permits the defendant to request a fair-market-value determination. The statutory offset considers value and surviving secured claims as specified. Applicable nonrecourse protections, defenses, agreements, and insurance credits can change the result.

For a simplified example, debt is $280,000, foreclosure price $220,000, court-determined fair market value $250,000, and no surviving lien or other adjustment applies. Initial shortfall is $60,000. The value above sale price is $30,000, yielding a $30,000 amount after the stated offset. This is a statutory-mechanics illustration, not a court judgment or a conclusion that every loan permits personal recovery.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A69 — Offset calculation
chunks.excerpt:
The fair-value offset is not the only statutory credit question. Property Code §51.003(d) addresses money the lender receives from a private mortgage guaranty insurer: the lender must credit that money to the borrower's account before bringing its own deficiency action. The provision also distinguishes the insurer's exercise of its own subrogation rights. A reviewer should identify the payment recipient, amount, ledger treatment, and claimant instead of assuming an insurance payment either belongs outside the accounting or releases every possible claim. Request the actual insurer and lender records and refer the legal effect to counsel. Do not subtract the same credit twice.

### Applied exercise: A69 — Offset calculation

Assume debt $310,000, sale price $245,000, court-determined fair market value $275,000, and no surviving liens or other adjustments. Calculate initial shortfall, offset, and remaining amount. List two legal facts needed before calling the result collectible.

Feedback: $65,000 shortfall, $30,000 offset, $35,000 remaining. Personal liability/recourse, timely action, applicable protections, competent value evidence, required credits, and defenses matter.

## T10U5 — Tax Impacts of Foreclosure

Foreclosure can involve both a disposition of property and cancellation-of-debt questions. Recourse and nonrecourse debt are treated differently for federal tax calculations. Adjusted basis, amount realized, debt discharged, fair market value, and applicable exclusions can all matter. A Form 1099-C or 1099-A is information to reconcile, not a self-contained determination of tax owed.

chunks.heading: Applied exercise: A70 — Tax referral packet
chunks.excerpt:
IRS Publication 4681 explains canceled debt, foreclosures, repossessions, and abandonment. The publication currently available during this review is labeled for 2025; a taxpayer's 2026 event requires current tax-year law. Do not promise that all principal-residence debt cancellation is tax-free or that a past temporary exclusion automatically continues. Bankruptcy and insolvency exclusions have their own requirements and possible tax-attribute consequences. Refer the homeowner to a qualified tax professional with the loan, sale, settlement, and basis records.

### Applied exercise: A70 — Tax referral packet

Create a document checklist for a homeowner after foreclosure: original purchase/basis records, improvement costs, loan history, recourse information, foreclosure sale/value documents, lender statements, cancellation forms, and facts relevant to any exclusion. Explain why the foreclosure sale price alone cannot establish all federal tax consequences.

Prepare two separate worksheet headings: disposition of the property and possible cancellation of debt. Under each, place the records that could affect the calculation. Then compare two borrowers with the same sale price but different adjusted bases and recourse status; explain why equal sale prices need not produce equal tax outcomes. Draft a referral note identifying the event year and any information form discrepancy without resolving an exclusion yourself.

Feedback: debt treatment and tax basis create separate calculations. A sale can produce a gain/loss analysis while cancellation can raise another issue; exclusions cannot be assumed from the property's former use alone.

chunks.heading: Module recap
chunks.excerpt:
Additional feedback: Basis, amount realized, debt treatment, and recourse facts can differ despite the same sale price. Form 1099-C is evidence to reconcile, not an automatic tax exemption or proof that the entire reported amount is taxable. The packet should identify the applicable tax year, retain source records, and ask the tax professional to apply current law to the actual facts.

### Module recap

Explain default versus acceleration, forbearance versus forgiveness, foreclosure versus possession, and shortfall versus judgment. Complete the T10 quiz and required course scenarios before the protected final examination process.

Sources: [Texas Property Code §§51.002–51.003](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/PR/htm/PR.51.htm); [Texas Constitution article XVI §50](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/CN/htm/CN.16.htm#16.50); [Regulation X §1024.41](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/41/); [IRS Publication 4681](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p4681). Current-source limitations are recorded separately for reviewer resolution.

lessons.title: Two application tests

chunks.heading: Learner reading
chunks.excerpt:
## Learner reading

The 2026 required federal topics begin with examination experience. The Multi-State Mortgage Committee selected ten subjects from multistate examinations completed during the fourth quarter of 2023 and first quarter of 2024. NMLS identifies them for continuing education delivered during calendar 2026; they are not interchangeable with another year's required list. [S1]

The committee includes ten appointed state-regulator members and one CSBS member. State regulators license and supervise relevant financial institutions, including mortgage lenders, and examine loan files and corporate records for compliance and risk controls. An examination is not merely a test of whether a company owns a written policy. Individual originators can also be held accountable for violations identified in examinations. [S1]

Reported examination responses included correcting disclosures, returning borrower money, additional audits, staff training and documented changes to internal controls. These are examples of possible consequences, not a fixed penalty schedule or a promise that training alone resolves a violation. The appropriate response depends on the facts and governing authority. [S1]

The course uses those findings to practice identifying the applicable rule, reconstructing what occurred and testing a correction. A required-topic list does not itself approve this provider or this course. [S1; provider-status limitation]

### Apply the idea to a new fictional file

At fictional Alder Crossing Lending, a reviewer finds that a disclosure process failed. A manager's response is: “Everyone attended a meeting, so the problem is closed.” No one has checked whether affected consumers received appropriate corrections or whether a later sample follows the revised process.

chunks.heading: Background source
chunks.excerpt:
Before moving on, identify one question about the affected files and one question about future performance. Useful questions include: “What evidence shows that the required corrective action was completed for each affected file?” and “What later sample would show whether the revised control actually works?” These are proposed review methods, not a regulator-prescribed sampling formula.

The next lesson applies this habit to application information, action notices and disclosure clocks. Do not assume that one definition or deadline governs every obligation in a mortgage file.

### Background source

S1 — [NMLS CE Required Topic List for Annual CE Year 2026, Background](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/nmlsEdFuncSpec/education/funcSpec/maps/topics/approvedCourseTopics/nmlsFS_approvedCETopics2026.html), version 2026.1, checked September 10, 2026. The published background requests two-to-three minutes; three is the proposed allocation, not measured duration.

## Purpose and boundaries

Experienced originators do not usually lose a file because they cannot name Regulation B or TRID. They lose control when information arrives by one channel, the decision happens in another, and the system of record is updated last. A customer receives a personal rejection while the CRM still says inquiry. A property address arrives by message, but the disclosure clock waits for a processor to create the loan. An incomplete-file queue quietly becomes a collection of unrecorded denials.

chunks.heading: Learning outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
This lesson uses ordinary consumer-purpose mortgage transactions subject to the Loan Estimate requirements in Regulation Z §1026.19(e). It does not extend TRID's six-item rule to every credit product, nor consumer-credit notice rules to all business credit. Assume the creditor received more than 150 applications during the preceding calendar year; the small-volume oral-notice exception is outside the case assumptions. Reverse mortgages, HELOCs, HMDA reporting classifications, and FCRA disclosures require their own coverage.

NMLS's 2026 required-topic list supplies the selection of subjects; the operative rules and official interpretations below supply the legal tests. This lesson addresses topic IDs 1-5: notifications, action tracking, specific reasons, records, and timely initial disclosures. See the [NMLS 2026 topic list](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/nmlsEdFuncSpec/education/funcSpec/maps/topics/approvedCourseTopics/nmlsFS_approvedCETopics2026.html).

### Learning outcomes

By the end, the learner should be able to:

1. Classify a consumer contact using the creditor's actual conduct, not the label assigned to it.
2. Apply the Regulation B and TRID application tests separately to the same facts.
3. Select an appropriate action or incompleteness notice and identify its trigger.
4. Trace adverse-action reasons to the actual decision, including decisions on incomplete files.
5. Assemble evidence that establishes what happened, when it happened, and what the consumer was told.
6. Propose a preventive control and a test capable of detecting its failure.

## 1. One customer, two application tests

chunks.heading: 1. One customer, two application tests
chunks.excerpt:
Regulation B asks whether there is an oral or written request for credit made under the creditor's procedures. Those procedures include what the creditor actually does, not only its manual. A completed application exists when the creditor has the information it regularly obtains and considers for that credit decision. The creditor must act with reasonable diligence to obtain needed information. That flexibility does not permit an endless queue of unworked files. [12 CFR §1002.2(f), comments 2(f)-1, -2, and -6](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/2/#f).

For the TRID transactions in this lesson, the application trigger uses six submitted items: name, income, Social Security number to obtain a credit report, property address, estimated property value, and mortgage loan amount sought. It is not a requirement to have a credit report, a signed purchase contract, verification documents, or a fully underwritten file. [12 CFR §1026.2(a)(3)(ii), comment 2(a)(3)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/#a-3-ii).

chunks.heading: Worked case: the missing address
chunks.excerpt:
| Decision to make | Legal test | Evidence an operations reviewer needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is this a Reg B application? | Request, actual procedures, and how the creditor responded | Conversation, request, decision, and communication records |
| Is it complete for the Reg B decision? | Information the creditor regularly obtains and considers | Required-item inventory, receipt dates, diligent follow-up |
| Has TRID's initial LE trigger occurred? | Receipt of the six specified items for a covered transaction | Earliest receipt time and source for each item |
| Has the company entered the file in its LOS? | Internal workflow fact, not a substitute legal trigger | System-created time separately from actual information receipt |

The table is an implementation aid, not a new legal definition.

### Worked case: the missing address

On Monday, Harbor Lending receives Maya's name, stated income, SSN, estimated price range, and requested loan amount. No property is identified. Maya asks for an explanation of possible terms. The originator describes general policies, explains that a later application and analysis will be necessary, and makes no credit decision.

On Tuesday, a different employee reviews Maya's credit information and tells her: “We reviewed your request and will not approve it because of the recent delinquent mortgage payments.”

chunks.heading: Primary source links
chunks.excerpt:
The company calls both contacts “prequalification.” That label does not settle the result. The Tuesday evaluation, decision to decline, and communication create the application/adverse-action issue identified in the official interpretation. The missing property address means the facts still do not establish all six TRID items. An ECOA notice obligation can therefore exist even though an LE has not been triggered. [Comments 2(f)-3 and -4](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/2/#Interp-2-f); [Reg B comment 9-5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#Interp-9).

Do not replace that analysis with “every credit pull is an application.” The official interpretation also describes prequalification activity that can remain an inquiry, depending on the response. A soft pull does not itself create an exemption, and a hard pull does not decide every classification. The compliance question is what the creditor did with the request and information.

**Decision pause.** What two records would distinguish Monday from Tuesday? Write your answer before reading on.

A useful answer identifies the actual communication and the decision record. A credit-bureau log proves a report was obtained, but does not prove whether the employee only explained terms, declined credit, or issued a commitment. A CRM status proves what someone labeled the interaction, not necessarily what happened.

lessons.title: The first Loan Estimate clock

chunks.heading: 2. The first LE clock cannot wait for verification
chunks.excerpt:
## 2. The first LE clock cannot wait for verification

Once the six-item TRID application is received, the initial LE ordinarily must be delivered or placed in the mail by the third business day after receipt. For this deadline, a business day uses the creditor's substantially-all-business-functions test. That differs from the more precise business-day definition applicable to other TRID waiting periods. [§1026.19(e)(1)(iii)(A) and comment 19(e)(1)(iii)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-1-iii); [§1026.2(a)(6)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/#a-6).

### Timeline exercise: late entry, not late application

Assume every Monday-Friday is a business day for Harbor, with no intervening holidays:

- Monday, September 14, 2026: an originator receives all six items by a recorded telephone application.
- Wednesday, September 16: a processor enters the information into the LOS.
- Friday, September 18: the customer uploads pay stubs and the signed purchase contract.
- The application remains pending, with no denial or withdrawal.

The LE must be delivered or mailed by Thursday, September 17. Wednesday's data entry cannot move that deadline to Monday. Friday's verification cannot start a new initial clock. The firm can request verification for underwriting, but cannot require the consumer to submit verification documents before providing the LE. [§1026.19(e)(2)(iii) and its official interpretation](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-2-iii).

chunks.heading: Two important limitations
chunks.excerpt:
A calendar calculation is only half the control. The record must preserve Monday's receipt event. If the LOS has only its creation timestamp, the organization has a detection blind spot: it can report every loan as timely while measuring from the wrong date.

**Operational recommendation, not a prescribed software feature:** create a six-item intake record across approved channels and an exception report comparing original receipt with LOS entry. The control should identify files where those dates differ and disclose whether the deadline was met.

### Two important limitations

First, an application denied or withdrawn within the initial three-business-day period may qualify for the LE exception described in comment 19(e)(1)(iii)-3. An internal plan to deny is not evidence that a permitted exception actually occurred. A later denial does not erase an earlier missed deadline. Regulation B duties must still be evaluated separately. [Official interpretation 19(e)(1)(iii)-3](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-1-iii).

Second, receiving an application through a mortgage broker does not allow the parties to leave the consumer without disclosures while they decide who owns the task. Either the creditor or broker may provide the LE under §1026.19(e)(1)(ii); the creditor must ensure compliance, and a broker that provides it must satisfy the relevant requirements. [§1026.19(e)(1)(ii)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-1-ii).

chunks.heading: Two important limitations
chunks.excerpt: This allocation is not identical to the Regulation B definition of creditor. A broker's actual participation in the credit decision matters under §1002.2(l). A referral-only person has specified nondiscrimination duties; do not assert that every broker has every creditor obligation in every file. [§1002.2(l) and comments 2(l)-1 and -2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/2/#l).

lessons.title: Incomplete applications and action notices

chunks.heading: 3. Incomplete does not mean unmanaged
chunks.excerpt:
## 3. Incomplete does not mean unmanaged

For information the applicant can provide, §1002.9(c) offers a structured path: within 30 days after receipt of the incomplete application, give an action notice or a written notice of incompleteness. The latter identifies what is needed, gives a reasonable response period, and explains that no further consideration follows failure to respond. An oral request does not dispense with the written notice if the application remains incomplete. [§1002.9(c)(1)-(3)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#c).

Scope exception: the requirement to provide a notice of incompleteness does not apply to preapprovals constituting applications under §1002.2(f). The incomplete-application examples in this section are not those preapprovals. Do not turn this exception into an exemption from all action-notice obligations. [Official interpretation 9(c)(1)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#Interp-9-c-1).

A proper notice is not merely a generic “documents outstanding” email. Equally, the regulation does not prescribe one universal number of days the applicant must receive to respond: the period must be reasonable in the circumstances.

### Worked case: three ways a file can go wrong

Harbor receives Luis's application on September 2. It lacks a required applicant-provided explanation of a deposit. The originator telephones him on September 5. The firm has insufficient information for a credit decision.

chunks.heading: Clock reference for ordinary consumer applications
chunks.excerpt:
- **Bad path A:** Leave the file pending indefinitely because a call was made.
- **Bad path B:** Mark it withdrawn on September 20 because Luis has not called back.
- **Available path:** Provide the notice required by §1002.9(c), or take and notify an appropriate action under the rule. If using a notice of incompleteness, identify the missing information, reasonable deadline, and consequence.

Change one fact: the decision-maker already has enough information to decline because of documented excessive obligations relative to income. The missing deposit explanation is not the principal reason for that decision. The notice must reflect the actual credit reason, not hide it behind “incomplete application.” [Comments 9(a)(1)-3 and -4](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#Interp-9-a-1).

Change another fact: Luis expressly asks the creditor to withdraw the application before a decision. Reg B's action-notice requirement does not apply to that expressly withdrawn application, but retention still does. Preserve the withdrawal evidence; do not manufacture it from silence. The separate, narrow approved-application provision in §1002.9(e) is not a general permission to classify unanswered files as withdrawn. [Comment 9-2 and §1002.9(e)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/).

### Clock reference for ordinary consumer applications

chunks.heading: Clock reference for ordinary consumer applications
chunks.excerpt:
| Event | Notice timing |
| --- | --- |
| Completed application | Within 30 days: approval, counteroffer, or adverse action |
| Adverse action on an incomplete application | Within 30 days of that action, subject to the rule's incompleteness alternative; this does not extend the separate §1002.9(c)(1) deadline for applicant-provided omissions |
| Incomplete regarding applicant-provided matters | Within 30 days after receipt: act/notify or provide compliant incompleteness notice |
| Counteroffer not expressly accepted or used | Adverse-action notice within 90 days after the counteroffer notification; a compliant combined notice can avoid a second notice |

Source: [§1002.9(a)(1), (c), and comment 9(a)(1)-6](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/). The counteroffer provision does not require holding an offer open for 90 days.

lessons.title: Actual adverse-action reasons

chunks.heading: 4. A reason is a fact about the decision, not an internal slogan
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. A reason is a fact about the decision, not an internal slogan

A written adverse-action notice must include the required action, creditor, ECOA, enforcement-agency, and reason/right-to-reasons components. If using the right-to-reasons alternative, the consumer has 60 days to request reasons; the creditor must provide them within 30 days of the request. Use a compliance-approved notice and the correct federal enforcement-agency information rather than copying another company's form. [§1002.9(a)(2), (b)(1), and Appendix A](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#a-2).

When reasons are supplied, they must identify the actual principal factors. “Does not meet our guidelines” does not explain the credit decision. Neither does a list of plausible factors that were not the reasons used. A credit report disclosure or a list of credit-score factors is not automatically a substitute for ECOA's actual decision reasons. [§1002.9(b)(2), comments 9(b)(2)-2 and -9](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/#b-2).

### File-repair exercise

Decision record:

- Verified monthly income: $7,500.
- Obligations included in the decision: $4,200 per month.
- The particular program used in this fictional case has a documented 45% maximum ratio.
- No exception was granted.
- The underwriter's actual principal reason was excessive obligations relative to income.

The calculated ratio is 56%. A draft notice says “Investor requirements,” and the originator wants to change it to “Insufficient credit score.”

chunks.heading: File-repair exercise
chunks.excerpt:
Neither proposed phrase accurately explains this record. A reason such as “Excessive obligations in relation to income” aligns with the stated decision. Do not add a credit-score reason absent evidence it was a principal factor. The 45% limit is a case assumption, not a universal legal or product limit.

**Further question:** If the lender's calculation accidentally counted the same debt twice, should the employee simply improve the notice wording?

No. A better description does not repair an incorrect underlying decision. Escalate for an authorized re-evaluation and an accurate notice/record. Keep both the original event and correction; never overwrite the audit history to imply the error did not occur. That workflow is a recommended control, not a claim that this lesson determines a particular applicant's eligibility.

lessons.title: Preserve and reconcile the record

chunks.heading: 5. Preserve the story an examiner must reconstruct
chunks.excerpt:
## 5. Preserve the story an examiner must reconstruct

For these consumer applications, Regulation B generally requires keeping the application, evaluation information, relevant notices and reason statements, and written complaints alleging violations for 25 months after notice of action or incompleteness. Certain applications without required notification use receipt of the application as the retention anchor. Investigation, enforcement, or litigation can extend retention. [§1002.12(b)(1), (3), and (4)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/12/#b).

The law permits accurate electronic retrieval; it does not mandate paper or one particular LOS. But a system that cannot reproduce the pertinent historical information is not made compliant by having a document-storage feature. TRID has separate retention periods, including special requirements for LE/CD evidence; do not use the ECOA 25-month period as the universal destruction schedule. [Comment 12(b)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/12/#Interp-12-b); [§1026.25(c)(1)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/25/#c-1).

### Evidence packet exercise

A supervisor finds a credit-bureau invoice showing 24 inquiries, but only 19 corresponding CRM records. There is not yet enough evidence to conclude that all five unmatched inquiries violated the notice rule.

Propose a defensible investigation:

chunks.heading: Consequences and prevention
chunks.excerpt:
1. Reconcile identity and timestamps without exporting unnecessary personal data.
2. Retrieve approved-channel communications and actual credit decision records.
3. Classify each contact under the relevant legal test, recording why.
4. Check applicable notice type, triggering event, deadline, and delivery evidence.
5. Preserve findings and escalate missing notices/records for correction and root-cause review.
6. Test the corrected workflow against a later independent sample.

The objective is not to make counts match by inventing records. Some inquiries may have been legitimate nonapplications; others may be missing applications, duplicate reports, or system-linking failures. A documented classification explains the difference.

### Consequences and prevention

Notification and retention violations can lead to enforcement, required remediation, or civil liability; the precise consequence depends on the governing law and facts. Regulation B addresses enforcement and liability, including actual damages and possible punitive damages, and distinguishes inadvertent errors from blanket immunity. This lesson does not quote inflation-adjusted penalty figures or promise that self-correction eliminates liability. [§1002.16](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/16/).

A credible corrective-action plan names an owner, an affected-file review, a fix, evidence of consumer remediation where warranted, and an independent re-test. “Everyone received training” is an action, not proof the control now works.

## 8. Transfer exercise: write the handoff, not just the rule

A colleague leaves you a file note: “Customer didn't qualify, never finished application, closed lead.” The only linked document is a credit report. Prepare a four-part internal request:

chunks.heading: 8. Transfer exercise: write the handoff, not just the rule
chunks.excerpt:
1. What facts and records are missing?
2. Which separate classifications and clocks must be tested?
3. Who should review the consumer communication and any overdue notice?
4. How will you preserve the original evidence and record any correction?

lessons.title: Begin with the charge, not the column label

chunks.heading: Purpose and learning outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
## Purpose and learning outcomes

An experienced originator may know that an appraisal fee is usually subject to zero tolerance and still approve an improper increase. The mistake often occurs one level deeper: the fee worksheet calls the provider “third party” without checking affiliation, the system uses the latest LE for every comparison, or an employee treats a closing-cost increase as its own changed circumstance.

This lesson teaches a file-based decision process. For a transaction covered by the TRID LE/CD provisions, ask:

1. Which rule applies to this charge, based on the actual service and relationships?
2. What is the legally usable comparison amount?
3. Did a permitted event actually change this charge?
4. Was the relevant revised disclosure provided on time and in the correct form?
5. What must be corrected if the consumer is charged too much?

By the end, the learner should be able to classify a charge from evidence; calculate an aggregate tolerance using the correct services and unrounded amounts; distinguish a current estimate from a valid revised baseline; document a permitted revision; apply LE/CD timing rules without mixing their business-day definitions; and identify a consumer refund/disclosure correction that requires escalation.

Scope: ordinary closed-end consumer mortgage transactions subject to §1026.19(e) and (f). Do not extend this treatment to HELOCs, reverse mortgages, or exempt transactions without a separate applicability analysis. Each case assumes a validly established consummation date; do not substitute funding or recording for consummation.

chunks.heading: 1. Begin with the charge, not the column label
chunks.excerpt:
The [NMLS 2026 required-topic list](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/nmlsEdFuncSpec/education/funcSpec/maps/topics/approvedCourseTopics/nmlsFS_approvedCETopics2026.html) identifies LE tolerance, zero-tolerance cost increases, and revised-disclosure reasons/timing as required subjects. The operative rules and official interpretations below control the legal explanations.

## 1. Begin with the charge, not the column label

The general good-faith rule compares the consumer's actual charge with the originally disclosed estimate. Exceptions permit particular variations or a properly supported revised estimate. A tolerance is not a markup allowance, and a fee does not become lawful merely because a worksheet turns green. [§1026.19(e)(3)(i)–(iv)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-3).

### A practical classification map

| Rule | Typical scope, subject to the stated conditions | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General/zero-tolerance rule | Creditor or mortgage-broker fees; affiliate fees; required third-party services the consumer cannot shop for; transfer taxes | Recipient/retention of the fee, affiliation, actual shopping permission, service identity |
| Ten-percent aggregate | Recording fees and qualifying unaffiliated required services for which the consumer could shop, including selection from the supplied list or no consumer selection | Valid shopping opportunity, written list, selected provider, affiliation, performed services |
| Permitted variations | Specified prepaid/escrow/insurance/tax charges and qualifying consumer-selected services outside the list or not required by the creditor | Best information reasonably available when estimated, bona fide charge, applicable selection and l

chunks.heading: Shopping is a real choice
chunks.excerpt:
ist facts |

Sources: [§1026.19(e)(3)(i), comments -1 through -4](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-i); [§1026.19(e)(3)(ii), comments -1 through -6](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-ii); [§1026.19(e)(3)(iii) and comments -1 through -4](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iii).

“Typical” matters. Paragraph (e)(3)(iii) expressly applies to its listed charges even when paid to the creditor or its affiliate, provided the charges are bona fide. Do not replace the actual rule with “anything involving an affiliate is always zero tolerance.” Conversely, a required settlement service does not escape the general rule just because an affiliate was one of several suggested providers.

“Paid to” also concerns who retains the fee, not simply whose account temporarily receives the money. A creditor collecting a county recording fee and passing it to the county does not turn that fee into creditor compensation. Investigate the service and ultimate retention, including reimbursement arrangements, before assigning the category. [Comment 19(e)(3)(i)-3](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-i).

### Shopping is a real choice

The written provider list is not a device for requiring the consumer to choose only from the lender's favorites. A creditor may impose reasonable qualifications, such as appropriate licensing, but requiring a selection exclusively from its list is not permission to shop under this rule.

chunks.heading: A permitted variation is not permission to lowball
chunks.excerpt:
Where shopping is permitted, the separate list must identify at least one available provider for each required shoppable service and state that the consumer may select a different provider. A business that no longer serves the property's area is not an available provider simply because its name remains in a template. [§1026.19(e)(1)(vi)(A)–(C), comments 19(e)(1)(vi)-1 through -5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-1-vi).

Consider three versions of the same required title service:

- The consumer can shop and selects an unaffiliated provider from the properly supplied list: ordinarily the ten-percent aggregate test applies.
- The consumer can shop and selects an unaffiliated provider outside that list: the permitted-variation rule may apply, but the initial estimate must still be reasonable on the information available.
- The consumer actually can shop, but the creditor fails to give the required list: the creditor has a list-compliance problem. Under the commentary, the unaffiliated service is evaluated under the ten-percent rule, not automatically under permitted variations. If the service provider is the creditor or its affiliate, the general rule applies.

This last situation is a useful precision test. “Missing list means zero tolerance in every case” is not the current commentary's rule. Neither is “the customer chose it, so there is no tolerance issue.” [Comments 19(e)(3)(ii)-3 and -6; 19(e)(3)(iii)-2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iii).

### A permitted variation is not permission to lowball

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Linden Mortgage estimates prepaid interest using a closing date it knows is unrealistic, solely to make the initial cash-to-close estimate smaller. An employee says prepaid interest has no percentage cap, so any number is acceptable.

That is incorrect. The estimate must use the best information reasonably available and be made through good-faith diligence. The same discipline applies to the specified property-insurance, escrow, property-tax, and other paragraph (iii) charges. A reasonable estimate that later changes is different from an unreasonably low estimate on facts already known. [Comments 19(e)(3)(iii)-1 through -4](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iii).

### Primary sources and authority boundaries

- [Current §1026.19, including official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/): (e)(1)(vi); (e)(3)(i)–(iv); (e)(4)(i)–(ii); (f)(1)(ii)–(iii); (f)(2)(i), (ii), and (v); (f)(3).
- [Current §1026.2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/): (a)(6) business-day definitions; use the specified definition for each event.
- [Current §1026.25](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/25/): mortgage-record evidence requirements.
- [NMLS 2026 annual topic list](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/nmlsEdFuncSpec/education/funcSpec/maps/topics/approvedCourseTopics/nmlsFS_approvedCETopics2026.html): topics 6–8 select the mandatory subject scope.

lessons.title: Ten percent applies to the qualifying aggregate

chunks.heading: 2. Ten percent applies to the qualifying aggregate
chunks.excerpt:
## 2. Ten percent applies to the qualifying aggregate

Do not calculate a refund simply because one qualifying fee rose by 11%, 20%, or 50%. Add the applicable estimated charges, add the corresponding actual charges, and compare the totals. Use unrounded amounts in the actual compliance calculation even when the forms display rounded dollars. [Comments 19(e)(3)(ii)-2 and 19(e)(3)(i)-7](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-ii).

For these examples, all displayed dollar figures are exact whole-dollar amounts. The baseline is valid, no permissible revision has occurred, all listed services are performed, and each service is correctly classified.

### Worked example A — a twenty-percent increase without an aggregate excess

| Qualifying charge | Valid estimate | Actual consumer charge |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unaffiliated settlement service, provider selected from list | $600 | $720 |
| Unaffiliated lender's title service, provider selected from list | $400 | $380 |
| Recording fees | $100 | $100 |
| **Aggregate** | **$1,100** | **$1,200** |

The settlement charge rose by $120, or 20%. But the permitted aggregate maximum is $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210. The actual $1,200 is below that maximum, so these charges do not produce a ten-percent aggregate excess. They still must satisfy other applicable rules, including the actual-charge rule.

The $20 decrease in one qualifying charge can offset an increase in another within this aggregate. Do not import that offset method into the separate zero-tolerance charges.

### Worked example B — a service never performed cannot pad the baseline

chunks.heading: Activity A — challenge the spreadsheet
chunks.excerpt:
Change the facts: the original LE also listed a $150 pest inspection in this bucket, but no pest inspection was obtained. The actual settlement fee is now $760; the other actual charges remain $380 and $100.

The printed original subtotal might suggest $1,250. That is not the proper comparison subtotal for these facts. Remove the $150 estimate for the service not performed:

- Applicable baseline: $1,250 − $150 = $1,100.
- Permitted maximum: $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210.
- Actual applicable charges: $760 + $380 + $100 = $1,240.
- Aggregate excess: $1,240 − $1,210 = $30.

Keeping the unused inspection in the estimate would create an artificial cushion and conceal the excess. This adjustment is specifically addressed in [comment 19(e)(3)(ii)-5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-ii).

The reverse mistake is treating an omitted individual qualifying charge as automatically subject to its own zero-dollar ceiling. The aggregate commentary accounts for an omitted individual charge when it genuinely belongs in this bucket. That does not excuse inaccurate disclosures generally or change a fee's correct category. [Comment 19(e)(3)(ii)-2.ii](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-ii).

### Activity A — challenge the spreadsheet

A reviewer sees a $30 aggregate excess in example B. The processor proposes to:

1. Leave the unused pest-inspection estimate in the baseline.
2. Move $30 of the actual settlement charge into prepaid interest.
3. Preserve the true categories and amounts and escalate the excess for correction.

Write two sentences identifying the defensible choice and why the other actions would obscure the facts. Do not use the answer section until you have responded.

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
### Primary sources and authority boundaries

- [Current §1026.19, including official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/): (e)(1)(vi); (e)(3)(i)–(iv); (e)(4)(i)–(ii); (f)(1)(ii)–(iii); (f)(2)(i), (ii), and (v); (f)(3).

lessons.title: Zero tolerance is not “net all the closing costs”

chunks.heading: 3. Zero tolerance is not “net all the closing costs”
chunks.excerpt:
## 3. Zero tolerance is not “net all the closing costs”

Suppose the following required charges fall under the general rule and no valid revised baseline or other exception applies:

| Charge | Valid estimate | Actual consumer charge | Increase requiring attention |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nonshoppable appraisal | $650 | $725 | $75 |
| Creditor processing charge | $800 | $780 | $0 |
| Transfer tax | $1,050 | $1,050 | $0 |

The appraisal has a $75 excess. The processing-charge reduction does not shrink that appraisal excess to $55. Compare each general-rule charge with its own valid estimate. The regulation's correction example adds the individual excesses; it does not pool all zero-tolerance costs into another aggregate. [§1026.19(e)(3)(i); comment 19(f)(2)(v)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#f-2-v).

The borrower paying the bill before closing does not make a nonshoppable appraisal immune from the LE good-faith analysis. The fee's timing of payment and its classification are different questions.

### Worked example C — the invoice is new, but the information was already available

Linden's current vendor schedule showed the $725 appraisal price before the initial LE. An employee accidentally used a superseded $650 schedule. The later invoice confirms $725, with no new service, property fact, consumer request, eligibility event, or other permitted revision reason.

chunks.heading: Worked example D — a valid revision changes one charge, not the whole file
chunks.excerpt:
Receiving the invoice is not a cure for the original estimating error. These facts do not establish a paragraph (e)(3)(iv)(A) changed circumstance. Calling the new invoice “new information” without considering what was already available would erase the good-faith requirement. The firm must deal with the $75 excess rather than reset the baseline merely by issuing another LE.

A genuine change can exist even when the appraisal is zero tolerance. But the file must show what changed, the information reasonably relied upon before the original estimate, and how the change actually affected this fee. [§1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(A), comments -1.i and -2; comment 19(e)(3)(iv)-5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-3-iv-A).

### Worked example D — a valid revision changes one charge, not the whole file

Before the original LE, the consumer's information reasonably indicated an ordinary one-unit property. The creditor used the then-applicable $650 appraisal estimate. Later verified information establishes a materially different property configuration that requires a more complex appraisal. The provider documents a $275 incremental cost caused by that fact. Assume due diligence, legal applicability, and all timing requirements are satisfied.

The revised appraisal baseline can be $925. The file contains:

- The original property description and basis for the $650 estimate.
- The later verified fact and the date sufficient information arrived.
- The provider's $275 explanation tied to the new complexity.
- The permitted reason for revision.
- The revised disclosure and evidence of timely provision/receipt.

chunks.heading: Lender credits can create an increase too
chunks.excerpt:
On the same revised LE, a processing fee rises from $800 to $875 because the firm wants to recover unrelated overhead. No separate permissible reason supports that change. Updating the displayed processing amount does not make $875 its valid tolerance baseline. The relevant baseline remains $800.

Under [comments 19(e)(3)(iv)-2, -3, and -5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iv), a revision can support only the increase actually attributable to its permitted reason. Updated disclosures still need current information, but an informational update is not a blanket baseline reset.

### Lender credits can create an increase too

Linden originally discloses a $900 lender credit. With no valid basis for revision, it provides only $750 at closing. The $150 reduction is an increased charge to the consumer for the good-faith analysis. A reviewer who checks only positive fee lines misses it.

Total lender credits include both general and specific credits as described in the commentary. Do not assume that shifting a credit from one display line to another changes the real amount provided, or that a lower fee automatically authorizes reducing a promised credit. [Comments 19(e)(3)(i)-5 and -6](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-i).

### Primary sources and authority boundaries

lessons.title: Separate the displayed estimate from the comparison baseline

chunks.heading: 4. Separate the displayed estimate from the comparison baseline
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. Separate the displayed estimate from the comparison baseline

A file may need current information on a revised disclosure without qualifying to use every updated number in the good-faith calculation. Maintain a distinct audit trail for:

- The original estimate.
- Each current disclosed amount.
- Each legally supported baseline adjustment.
- The reason, affected amount, and timing supporting that adjustment.

This is a recommended control design, not a regulator-mandated database schema.

### Permitted revision paths

| Provision | What must be established |
| --- | --- |
| §1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(A) | A qualifying changed circumstance affects settlement charges; for the aggregate bucket, the applicable increase exceeds 10% |
| (B) | A qualifying change in creditworthiness or collateral value makes the consumer ineligible for the previously estimated charge or terms, and the resulting service-cost increase exceeds the applicable tolerance; see comment 19(e)(3)(iv)(B)-1 |
| (C) | The consumer requests a revision to terms or settlement that causes a charge to increase |
| (D) | Rate-dependent charges change because the rate was not locked when the original LE was provided |
| (E) | Intent to proceed occurs after the applicable estimate-expiration period: more than ten business days or a longer period the creditor established |
| (F) | The specified new-construction/delayed-settlement conditions and required original disclosure statement are satisfied |

Source: [§1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(A)–(F) and their interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-3-iv). This table is not permission to use a generic “changed circumstance” code for all six provisions.

chunks.heading: Worked example E — a small changed circumstance does not reset the bucket
chunks.excerpt:
For path (A), qualifying changes include specified extraordinary/unexpected events, relied-upon consumer/transaction information that becomes inaccurate or changes, and qualifying newly discovered consumer/transaction information. Preserve evidence of what was reasonably available before the initial disclosure. Sending an LE before collecting one of TRID's six items does not let the creditor later treat receipt of that missing item as a qualifying changed circumstance. [Comment 19(e)(3)(iv)(A)-3](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iv-A).

For path (D), a subsequent rate lock ordinarily requires a revised LE within three business days with the rate-dependent terms. Once the CD has been provided, a corrected CD is required if the rate lock makes that CD inaccurate; the lock alone does not require correcting an unchanged, accurate CD. Unrelated charges do not become rate-dependent because they appear on the same document. [§1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(D), comments -1 and -2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-3-iv-D).

For path (E), do not restart an already timely intent to proceed merely because processing lasts longer than ten business days. The rule concerns when the consumer indicates intent relative to the applicable expiration period. A longer period communicated by the creditor matters. [Comments 19(e)(3)(iv)(E)-1 and -2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iv-E).

### Worked example E — a small changed circumstance does not reset the bucket

The original aggregate is $2,000. A documented qualifying settlement-cost change increases one charge by $120, with no other change. That is a 6% aggregate increase, below the $200 allowance.

chunks.heading: Activity B — an examiner asks for the reason
chunks.excerpt:
The creditor can give current information, but that particular path (A) event does not authorize changing the aggregate baseline from $2,000 to $2,120 for the good-faith test. The comparison remains anchored to $2,000. Otherwise, each small update could manufacture a new ten-percent cushion. [Comment 19(e)(3)(iv)(A)-1.ii](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-3-iv-A).

Now use a separate file with an original $2,000 aggregate. A documented qualifying change adds $80. Later another documented qualifying change adds $150. Together they increase the applicable estimated aggregate by $230, or 11.5%.

When sufficient information establishes the second change and the aggregate threshold is crossed, the revision clock starts. The first smaller documented change is not ignored merely because it occurred earlier. A timely permitted revision can reflect the supported cumulative increase. Do not reset the baseline for unrelated increases, and do not wait for the eventual closing statement before starting the clock. [Comment 19(e)(4)(i)-1.ii](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-4-i).

### Activity B — an examiner asks for the reason

An employee's sole explanation is “LE version 3 was sent.” Write the five missing facts that would establish whether the $275 appraisal increase in example D can be used in the tolerance comparison. A document number establishes sequence; it does not establish a permitted cause.

### Primary sources and authority boundaries

chunks.excerpt:
