lessons.title: Two disclosure forms, several clocks

chunks.heading: 5. Two disclosure forms, several clocks
chunks.excerpt:
## 5. Two disclosure forms, several clocks

For a revision used in the good-faith calculation, §1026.19(e)(4)(i) requires the applicable revised LE or CD reflecting the estimate within three business days after receiving information sufficient to establish the revision reason, subject to paragraph (ii). This is not automatically the day a committee approves the change or the day the LOS operator updates the fee.

A credible uncertainty can matter: the commentary describes a reasoned doubt about an appraisal followed by corroboration. But the creditor must preserve the basis for that doubt. Routine internal delay is not equivalent to lacking sufficient information. [§1026.19(e)(4)(i), comment -1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-4-i).

### Keep the clocks separate

| Clock | Business-day basis and key limitation |
| --- | --- |
| Three days to provide a supported revised disclosure under (e)(4)(i) | General creditor-business-functions definition |
| Receipt of revised LE at least four business days before consummation | All calendar days except Sundays and specified federal legal public holidays |
| Deemed receipt of a non-in-person revised LE | Three business days using that more precise definition; earlier actual receipt requires appropriate evidence |
| Initial CD receipt at least three business days before consummation | More precise definition, not merely days the lending office opens |
| Corrected CD | Apply (f)(2): some changes need a new three-business-day waiting period; others do not |

chunks.heading: Worked example F — provision, receipt, and consummation
chunks.excerpt:
Sources: [§1026.2(a)(6), including comments -1 and -2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/#a-6); [§1026.19(e)(4)(i)–(ii)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-4); [§1026.19(f)(1)(ii)–(iii) and (f)(2)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#f-1-ii).

Electronic delivery is not an automatic same-day receipt assumption. Apply the applicable electronic-disclosure requirements and retain valid receipt evidence; otherwise use the rule's deemed-receipt treatment. A portal “sent” event is not necessarily a consumer “received” event.

### Worked example F — provision, receipt, and consummation

Assume the creditor operates substantially all business functions Monday–Friday. There are no federal legal public holidays in the period.

- Monday, September 14, 2026: sufficient information establishes a permitted revision.
- Thursday, September 17: the creditor mails a compliant revised LE, before providing any CD.
- Friday, September 25: consummation is scheduled.

The provision deadline is Thursday, September 17: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday are the three general business days. For deemed receipt, count Friday the 18th, Saturday the 19th, and Monday the 21st. The consumer is considered to receive the revised LE on Monday the 21st.

There are four precise business days from that receipt to consummation: Tuesday the 22nd, Wednesday the 23rd, Thursday the 24th, and Friday the 25th. Both the provision and revised-LE receipt requirements are satisfied under these assumptions. The CD must independently satisfy its own delivery requirements.

chunks.heading: Once a CD is provided, do not issue another LE
chunks.excerpt:
If the revised LE is instead mailed Friday the 18th, deemed receipt is Tuesday the 22nd. Only three precise business days then remain to Friday's consummation, so the revised-LE receipt requirement is not met; the three-day provision deadline was also missed on these facts. A file reviewer must identify both defects rather than check only mailing or only closing.

### Once a CD is provided, do not issue another LE

The prohibition begins on the date the creditor **provides** the initial CD, not the later date of deemed receipt. No revised LE may be provided on that same date or afterward. A supported revision can instead be reflected on the CD or corrected CD under the current rule. [§1026.19(e)(4)(ii), comment -1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#e-4-ii).

Separate case: the creditor hand delivers the initial CD on Monday, September 21. The consumer requests a qualifying settlement change on Tuesday, September 22. Consummation is Friday, September 25. Assume the change does not make the APR inaccurate, does not change the disclosed loan product, and does not add a prepayment penalty.

The creditor must provide the applicable corrected CD so the consumer receives it at or before consummation. For this example, hand delivery on Friday also meets the three-general-business-day supported-revision deadline from Tuesday. A new LE is not permitted. [Comment 19(e)(4)(ii)-1.iii; §1026.19(f)(2)(i)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-e-4-ii).

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Three changes require a new CD waiting period: the APR becomes inaccurate under §1026.22, the disclosed loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. Not every APR movement is an inaccuracy under the rule; not every changed fee requires a new three-day wait. [§1026.19(f)(2)(ii), comments -1.i through -1.iii](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#f-2-ii).

A corrected CD is not a way to resurrect a missed revision deadline. It must reflect accurate information, but use of its increased charges as new baselines still requires the applicable permitted reason and timing.

### Primary sources and authority boundaries

- [Current §1026.19, including official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/): (e)(1)(vi); (e)(3)(i)–(iv); (e)(4)(i)–(ii); (f)(1)(ii)–(iii); (f)(2)(i), (ii), and (v); (f)(3).
- [Current §1026.2](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2/): (a)(6) business-day definitions; use the specified definition for each event.
- [Current §1026.25](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/25/): mortgage-record evidence requirements.
- [NMLS 2026 annual topic list](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/nmlsEdFuncSpec/education/funcSpec/maps/topics/approvedCourseTopics/nmlsFS_approvedCETopics2026.html): topics 6–8 select the mandatory subject scope.

lessons.title: Close the loop: correction, not cosmetic redisclosure

chunks.heading: 6. Close the loop: correction, not cosmetic redisclosure
chunks.excerpt:
## 6. Close the loop: correction, not cosmetic redisclosure

If a file has a $75 zero-tolerance excess and a $30 aggregate excess, the combined identified excess is $105. Do not subtract an unrelated fee decrease. Do not count a consumer payment, seller contribution, or existing promised lender credit as a new refund merely by changing its label.

Under §1026.19(f)(2)(v), the specified good-faith compliance treatment requires refunding the excess no later than 60 days after consummation; the corresponding corrected disclosure reflecting the refund must also be delivered or placed in the mail by that deadline. This does not excuse every other possible violation, or establish that planning to overcharge and refund later is acceptable business practice. [§1026.19(f)(2)(v), comment -1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#f-2-v).

Identify problems before consummation whenever possible. Preserve the calculation, approval, actual consumer benefit, delivery evidence, and any post-closing refund. The current §1026.25(c)(1) has mortgage-specific retention rules; a generic two-year TILA retention label does not cover the LE/CD file. [§1026.25(c)(1)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/25/#c-1).

Also keep two questions separate:

- Did the charge exceed the permissible estimate?
- Did the consumer pay more than the settlement provider actually received?

The second invokes §1026.19(f)(3), including its conditioned average-charge exception, and is developed in F03. A charge below a tolerance ceiling is not an authorization to retain an unsupported excess over the actual service charge. [§1026.19(f)(3)(i)–(ii)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#f-3).

chunks.heading: Consequences and a meaningful corrective control
chunks.excerpt:
### Consequences and a meaningful corrective control

The immediate file consequence can include recalculation, a corrected disclosure, consumer reimbursement, and delayed consummation where a waiting-period rule applies. Repeated errors also require review of affected files and the estimation/revision process. Penalties and broader liability depend on the governing provisions and facts; this lesson does not invent a fixed penalty amount.

A useful review samples original source information, actual recipients, provider lists, invoices, consumer requests, all disclosure versions, and delivery events. It then independently recalculates category membership and baselines. “The latest LE matches the CD” cannot detect an unsupported reset if both documents contain the same incorrect number.

Recommended review flags include an affiliate coded as an ordinary third party, an unused service in the baseline, a revised amount without a reason, an unrelated fee changed during a valid revision, a creditor-approval date substituted for sufficient-information receipt, and an LE issued after a CD. These are proposed controls, not mandatory software fields.

### Transfer task for human review

A closing officer receives an updated fee worksheet marked “all tolerances passed.” It compares every charge with the latest LE. One line is a required affiliated service, one is an unused inspection estimate, and one is an increased fee unrelated to the documented change.

Ask the learner to write a short hold/escalation note identifying:

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
1. Which source documents are needed before trusting the result.
2. Which classifications/baselines need re-examination.
3. Which original timestamps control disclosure timing.
4. How the correction would be documented without rewriting history.
5. Why a matching CD alone does not settle good faith.

### Primary sources and authority boundaries

- [Current §1026.19, including official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/): (e)(1)(vi); (e)(3)(i)–(iv); (e)(4)(i)–(ii); (f)(1)(ii)–(iii); (f)(2)(i), (ii), and (v); (f)(3).

- [Current §1026.25](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/25/): mortgage-record evidence requirements.

lessons.title: Required topic 9 — The estimate is not permission to keep the difference

chunks.heading: Scope and learning outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
## Scope and learning outcomes

This lesson addresses ordinary consumer-purpose, closed-end real-property mortgage transactions covered by Regulation Z's Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure requirements. Reverse mortgages, HELOCs, timeshares, exempt transactions, and a complete treatment of rescission are outside the cases. Whether a transaction is rescindable must be determined from its actual facts and applicable law; a refinance label alone does not decide that question.

The 2026 NMLS topic list determines the required subjects. The regulation and official interpretations determine the operative legal tests. **Topic 10's recipient is the person ultimately receiving payment for a settlement service. It does not mean the consumer receiving the CD.** This lesson teaches payee identification as the required topic, then separately addresses consumer delivery because a correctly completed form still has to reach the correct people. [S1, S3, S4]

By the end, the learner should be able to:

1. Reconcile a consumer charge with the service provider's actual receipt, not merely the last estimate.
2. Distinguish the actual-charge ceiling from Loan Estimate tolerance analysis.
3. Test a claimed average-charge program against every condition and exclusion.
4. Identify and substantiate the ultimate payee of a CD service line.
5. Distinguish a CD's service section from the facts governing tolerance classification.
6. Select required consumer recipients and calculate the ordinary CD receipt/waiting sequence.
7. Prepare a corrective-action record that preserves the original evidence and can be independently re-tested.

## 1. Required topic 9 — The estimate is not permission to keep the difference

chunks.heading: 1. Required topic 9 — The estimate is not permission to keep the difference
chunks.excerpt:
The annual examination finding describes an appraisal charge on a final CD exceeding the appraisal cost supported by the file. It directs attention to §1026.19(f)(3)(i). Although NMLS places this finding under a zero-tolerance heading, the operative issue here is a distinct actual-charge rule. Do not stop after comparing the CD with the LE. [S1, S2]

Under §1026.19(f)(3)(i), the amount imposed on the consumer for a settlement service cannot exceed what the settlement service provider actually receives for that service, unless the qualified average-charge exception applies. An invoice is important evidence of the service and amount due. The legal test is the amount actually received; reconciliation may also need the final disbursement record, adjustments, refunds, or other reliable payment evidence. An invoice marked paid is stronger evidence than an unverified draft quotation. [S2]

A practical review uses three different comparisons:

| Question | Compare | What a passing result does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Was the estimate in good faith? | Consumer's final charge against the applicable LE baseline and tolerance category | That the provider actually received that amount |
| Is this an excessive service charge? | Consumer's charge against the provider's actual receipt, subject to a lawful averaging program | That the LE tolerance or revision rules were satisfied |
| Is the CD accurately completed? | Service, amount, payee, payer, and payment timing against supporting records | That the disclosure reached the required consumers on time |

These are an operational review aid, not three interchangeable legal exemptions. The first test is principally §1026.19(e)(3)–(4); the second is §1026.19(f)(3); the third includes §1026.38. [S2, S3]

chunks.heading: Worked example: the fee passed the wrong test
chunks.excerpt:
### Worked example: the fee passed the wrong test

Maple Harbor Lending initially discloses a $690 appraisal fee. It does not permit shopping, and there is no permissible revision of the tolerance baseline. The final CD charges $690. The independent appraisal company's final invoice and payment record both establish $645 for the entire service. There is no average-charge program, no other appraisal-related service, and no additional provider payment.

The LE-to-CD comparison has no increase. Nevertheless, the consumer is being charged $45 more than the provider receives. Leaving the fee at $690 because “the borrower already accepted it” does not satisfy the actual-charge rule. If this is found before collection and consummation, correct the proposed charge and disclosure rather than deliberately collecting the overage. If discovered after collection, escalate for the applicable correction and reimbursement analysis with the original records preserved. Do not invent a universal cure deadline for every legal defect. [S2]

Now change the facts. The original LE is $620 and the provider actually receives $645. Charging the consumer $645 would meet the actual-charge ceiling, but the $25 increase still raises the separate zero-tolerance issue. An actual invoice does not itself supply a permissible reason to reset the LE baseline. F02's revision analysis remains necessary. [S2: §1026.19(e)(3)(i), (iv), and (e)(4)]

chunks.heading: The average-charge exception is a program, not an excuse
chunks.excerpt:
**Decision pause:** Which evidence would establish whether a $30 difference is an improper retained amount or payment for an additional real service? Identify the service order, final itemized invoice, payment evidence, and appropriate disclosure/tolerance treatment. Merely renaming the difference “handling” does not establish a service or make it lawful. This exercise does not approve a separate handling fee or decide every RESPA, compensation, or state-law issue.

### The average-charge exception is a program, not an excuse

Section 1026.19(f)(3)(ii) allows a creditor or settlement service provider to use an average charge when its conditions are satisfied. Consequently, a particular consumer's permitted average charge can exceed that transaction's individual service cost. That is not a license to keep an unexplained spread or choose averaging only on the files where it is profitable. [S2]

Test the proposed program in this order:

chunks.heading: The average-charge exception is a program, not an excuse
chunks.excerpt:
1. **Eligible service.** Averaging cannot be used for any type of insurance, any charge based on loan amount or property value, or where otherwise prohibited by law. A uniform title-insurance premium is not saved by a large sample. A percentage-based transfer tax does not become eligible merely because its average can be calculated. State and local restrictions still matter.
2. **Defined comparable class.** The class must use an appropriate period, geographic area, and loan type. The official interpretation permits a sampling period of at least 30 days and no more than six months, with a sample large enough for reasonable precision. A period within that range is necessary, not sufficient. Geographic area and loan type must not pool dissimilar populations.
3. **Supported average.** The charge cannot exceed the permitted average amount paid for the service across the class. Use supported service costs and the defined methodology, not a desired revenue figure. The interpretation generally relates the charge to the preceding defined period, with reasonable implementation lag permitted when subsequent periods are scheduled consistently.
4. **Uniform application.** Use the same average for the service throughout the defined class. Do not charge the average on inexpensive files and the higher actual amount on expensive files. Uniformity also does not permit charging for a service that is not required or is not obtained in the individual transaction.
5. **Continuing reconciliation.** Apply the retrospective-analysis requirements together with the specific deemed-compliance method described below. For other methods, reconciliation must address aggregate amounts collected above corresponding provider payments over time. The interpretation describes permissible methods, including

chunks.heading: Worked example: one average, two different costs
chunks.excerpt:
appropriate refunds or adjustment of future averages. The commentary deems its specified six-month period with rolling monthly reevaluation compliant even if collections exceed provider payments over time. A surplus alone therefore does not establish a violation when that method is satisfied. That method is available, not mandatory.
6. **Reconstructible evidence.** Retain the source records, class definition, calculation, receipts, ledger, and enough method documentation for an examiner to reproduce the result. Comment 19(f)(3)(ii)-9 specifies at least three years after any settlement for which the average was used. This is not permission to destroy CD-related records subject to the longer rule discussed below.

Authority: §1026.19(f)(3)(ii)(A)–(D), comments 19(f)(3)(ii)-1 through -9. These are source-based conditions; an employer's particular approval workflow is an implementation choice. [S2]

### Worked example: one average, two different costs

Assume a documented, otherwise lawful tax-certification averaging program for a properly defined comparable class. Its adequately supported prior-period cost is $4,800 for 48 services, producing a $100 average. Its methodology, exclusions, state-law review, uniform use, and retrospective controls all satisfy the rule. No other TRID tolerance issue is present.

chunks.heading: Consequences and prevention
chunks.excerpt:
In the next period, one eligible transaction's provider receives $84 and another's receives $118. Charging $100 for each is not automatically a violation simply because the first charge exceeds $84. That is the function of the qualified exception. Charging $100 on the first and $118 on the second would defeat uniform use. Charging $100 on a third file where that service is not required or obtained would not be justified by its membership in the class. [S2: comments -3 and -5]

Change one fact: the service is title insurance. Stop. The insurance exclusion applies before testing whether the arithmetic is accurate. Change another fact: the program has a properly calculated average but permits permanent retention of aggregate overcollections, using neither the specified deemed-compliance method nor another compliant retrospective reconciliation method. Stop again. A correct initial calculation does not excuse failure to reconcile the program over time. [S2: comments -5 and -7]

### Consequences and prevention

The immediate consumer harm is payment of an unsupported amount. Operational consequences can include correction, reimbursement analysis, broader file review, and findings that earlier controls failed. Do not teach a fixed penalty or assert that one refund extinguishes all possible liability. The annual list directs providers to discuss consequences; it does not supply a universal fine for this scenario. [S1]

chunks.heading: Averaging clarification source
chunks.excerpt:
**Recommended control:** require a fee-level reconciliation before release, followed by a check of actual disbursements. An averaging exception must point to the authorized program and eligible class, not free text reading “average.” An independent reviewer should sample both sides of the average and files with no service. A review that only samples transactions where the fee was below the average cannot test uniformity or detect all excess collections.

### Averaging clarification source

Reviewed September 11, 2026: [CFPB official comment 19(f)(3)(ii)-5](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/19/#Interp-19-f-3-ii). Read both the general retrospective requirement and the expressly deemed-compliant six-month/rolling-monthly method.

lessons.title: Required topic 10 — “To whom?” must have an answer

chunks.heading: 2. Required topic 10 — “To whom?” must have an answer
chunks.excerpt:
## 2. Required topic 10 — “To whom?” must have an answer

The 2026 finding identifies CDs that used placeholders for the ultimate recipients of mortgage-insurance and appraisal-completion payments. The controlling citation is §1026.38(f)(2), not the rule governing which borrower receives a disclosure. [S1, S3]

For services disclosed under **Services Borrower Did Not Shop For**, §1026.38(f)(2) calls for an itemized service and cost, the name of the person ultimately receiving each payment, the correct payment column, and the appropriate borrower-paid total. The scope is creditor-required settlement services supplied by persons other than the creditor or mortgage broker. Other CD sections have their own rules; do not put every fee into this section or assume this one provision decides every insurance entry. [S3]

### Worked example: the amount is right, but the destination is missing

A draft CD lists an appraisal-completion inspection at $165, borrower-paid at closing, with payee “TBD.” The lender required the service and did not permit shopping. A final invoice and verified payment instructions identify Granite Field Review LLC as the provider and ultimate recipient. The settlement agent will transmit the payment but will not retain it for its own service.

The amount and payment column may be correct; the payee field is not. Replace the placeholder with the supported ultimate recipient. Substituting the settlement agent's name only because the money first passes through its account does not identify the stated ultimate destination. Preserve the evidence linking the service, entity, amount, and disbursement. If records disagree, resolve the discrepancy rather than guess a payee. [S3]

chunks.heading: The section heading is not the tolerance category
chunks.excerpt:
This lesson's examples deliberately avoid complex appraisal-management-company, subcontractor, and split-title-premium arrangements. In a real multi-party arrangement, determine the actual service and payment structure before applying the disclosure rule; do not automatically substitute the individual who visited the property or the bank holding the wire account for the correct recipient.

### The section heading is not the tolerance category

Suppose a creditor permits shopping, provides the required written provider list, and a consumer selects a listed, unaffiliated provider for a required service. The charge was initially shown in the LE's services-you-can-shop-for section. On the CD, that service belongs under §1026.38(f)(2), **Services Borrower Did Not Shop For**, because the selected provider was on the written list. Assuming the other requirements are met, the charge can remain in the ten-percent aggregate tolerance category. The CD section name alone does not convert it into a zero-tolerance charge. [S3: §1026.38(f)(2)–(3); S2: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii)]

Conversely, §1026.38(f)(3) addresses the qualifying required service where the consumer shops and selects a provider outside that written list. It also requires the ultimate recipient's name. Moving a fee into a different section does not eliminate payee identification. [S3]

### What if information is not yet known?

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
The creditor must exercise due diligence and use the best information reasonably available when an actual term is unknown. A verified term sitting in the settlement agent's records is not unavailable merely because the originator has not requested it. Permitted estimation and later correction rules are not a blanket authorization to release a knowingly unresolved placeholder as the final answer. Obtain the actual information and provide corrections as required. The creditor remains responsible for ensuring compliant delivery even when the settlement agent provides the CD. [S2: comments 19(f)(1)(i)-2 and §1026.19(f)(1)(v)]

**Recommended release check:** flag empty payees and placeholder language, then have a reviewer compare nonempty entries with source documents. A field containing “Granite” passes a nonempty-string check even if the real payee is unrelated; therefore the automated check alone cannot establish accuracy. A changed recipient also merits payment-security verification under the firm's approved procedures. This is a recommendation for reliable implementation, not a claim that Regulation Z requires a particular software product.

lessons.title: Adjacent safeguard — The consumer receiving the CD

chunks.heading: 3. Adjacent safeguard — The consumer receiving the CD
chunks.excerpt:
## 3. Adjacent safeguard — The consumer receiving the CD

Keep the two meanings of recipient separate: the payee receives a service payment; the consumer receives the disclosure. A file can pass one test and fail the other.

### Multiple consumers

| Transaction facts | Federal CD delivery rule relevant here |
| --- | --- |
| Nonrescindable; two consumers each primarily liable | Delivery may be made to either primarily liable consumer |
| Nonrescindable; one principal debtor and a mere guarantor | Delivery to the guarantor alone does not satisfy delivery to a primarily liable consumer |
| Rescindable under §1026.23; more than one consumer has a right to rescind | Give the CD separately to each consumer who has that right |

Authority: §1026.17(d), comment 17(d)-2. A lender can adopt a more protective policy of delivery to all borrowers, but that policy should not be presented as the nonrescindable federal minimum. [S4]

A consumer with a right to rescind need not be a note signer. A natural person whose ownership interest in their principal dwelling is encumbered may have the right, subject to §1026.23's coverage and exemptions. Check title and occupancy as well as the note. Do not announce that all nonborrowing spouses have rescission rights or that every refinance is rescindable. [S5: §1026.23(a)(1), comment 23(a)(1)-2; S6: §1026.2(a)(11)]

### Receipt and the ordinary pre-consummation waiting period

chunks.heading: Receipt and the ordinary pre-consummation waiting period
chunks.excerpt:
For the covered ordinary transaction, the consumer must receive the initial CD at least three business days before consummation. Here business days are all calendar days except Sundays and the specified legal public holidays, whether or not the lender opens on Saturday. Consummation is when the consumer becomes contractually obligated on the credit transaction under applicable law, not automatically the funding or recording date. [S2: §1026.19(f)(1)(ii)(A); S6: §1026.2(a)(6), (13)]

If not given in person, receipt is presumed three business days after delivery or mailing; the creditor may instead rely on evidence of earlier actual receipt. Electronic delivery must satisfy the applicable E-Sign consent and other requirements. An email's sent timestamp alone is not evidence that the consumer received the disclosure that same day. [S2: §1026.19(f)(1)(iii), comments -1 and -2; S3: §1026.38(t)(3)(iii)]

Use two separate calendar calculations when relying on presumed receipt: first delivery-to-receipt; then receipt-to-consummation. Do not collapse them into “send three days before closing.”

**Calendar example — no intervening legal public holidays:**

chunks.heading: Corrections: not every change restarts three days
chunks.excerpt:
- In-person receipt Tuesday, September 22, 2026: Wednesday 23 is day one, Thursday 24 day two, and Friday 25 day three. The ordinary CD waiting rule permits consummation Friday 25, assuming every other condition is satisfied.
- Mailing Tuesday, September 22, with no evidence of earlier receipt: presumed receipt Friday 25. Saturday 26, Monday 28, and Tuesday 29 are the next three business days. The ordinary rule permits consummation Tuesday 29, not Friday 25.
- In a rescindable transaction requiring separate CDs, one required consumer receives a CD Tuesday 22 and the other Wednesday 23. The later consumer's ordinary waiting period reaches day three Saturday 26. Friday 25 is too early. Saturday being counted does not require a settlement office to open that day.

The pre-consummation CD waiting period is not the separate rescission period. For a rescindable transaction, the usual rescission period runs from the last applicable triggering event, including consummation, receipt of the required rescission notice, and receipt of material disclosures. This lesson does not authorize funding merely because the CD wait has elapsed. [S5: §1026.23(a)(3), (c)]

### Corrections: not every change restarts three days

chunks.heading: 4. Integrated capstone — The green dashboard, the red file
chunks.excerpt:
Before consummation, a new three-business-day waiting period is required when the APR becomes inaccurate under §1026.22, the disclosed loan product changes as specified in the rule, or a prepayment penalty is added. Other changes generally require corrected disclosures received at or before consummation, not an automatic new three-day wait. The consumer must also be allowed to inspect the known items during the business day immediately preceding consummation under §1026.19(f)(2)(i). For this inspection right, use the general creditor-business-function definition of business day; do not import the special CD receipt/waiting-period definition. [S2: §1026.19(f)(2)(i)–(ii); S6: §1026.2(a)(6)]

Do not teach “any APR change restarts the clock.” Accuracy must be evaluated under the applicable APR rule. Nor should a person assert that a fee change can never trigger a restart: its effect on APR or other specified terms must be evaluated. The exercises below expressly state whether a restart event exists instead of asking the learner to infer it from incomplete loan mathematics.

A waiver is not an ordinary scheduling tool. Section 1026.19(f)(1)(iv) requires a bona fide personal financial emergency, receipt of the disclosures first, and a dated written statement describing the emergency and specifically modifying or waiving the period, signed by all consumers primarily liable on the obligation. Printed forms for that purpose are prohibited. The required waiver signers are described by that provision; do not silently replace them with a different recipient test. No case here involves a waiver. [S2]

## 4. Integrated capstone — The green dashboard, the red file

chunks.heading: Evidence packet: Cedar Bridge Lending file CB-26-104
chunks.excerpt:
**Proposed 15-minute instructional exercise, not validated time.** Work from the fictional evidence, not the dashboard's green label. This is a pre-consummation review, with no fee yet collected. The exercise uses the ordinary rules and has no emergency waiver. All Monday–Friday dates below are business days for the initial-LE deadline; the precise calendar-day definition applies to CD timing. There are no intervening legal public holidays.

### Evidence packet: Cedar Bridge Lending file CB-26-104

1. On Monday, September 14, 2026, the originator receives all six TRID application items for Evelyn's covered consumer-purpose refinance in a recorded application. The application remains pending and is neither denied nor withdrawn. The initial LE is first delivered on Friday, September 18. The LOS was created Wednesday, September 16 and measures the initial deadline from that date. Any separate initial-LE pre-consummation waiting requirement is satisfied by the scheduled consummation date.
2. The applicable LE discloses $750 for a required appraisal from an unaffiliated provider. Shopping was not permitted. There is no valid revised baseline, no changed circumstance, and no average-charge program.
3. Clear Ridge Valuation LLC completes the entire appraisal service. Its final invoice and verified payment instructions establish a total of $710 to that company, with no additional service, split, or payment. The proposed consumer charge and pending disbursement must be brought into agreement before consummation, then actual receipt must be reconciled afterward.
4. The CD says appraisal $780, borrower-paid at closing, payee “TBD.” No part of that charge has yet been paid by the consumer. No other fee or credit changes are present in this exercise.
5. Evelyn signs the note. Noah d

chunks.heading: Learner tasks
chunks.excerpt:
oes not. Both own and occupy the principal dwelling, both ownership interests secure the credit, and the compliance determination establishes that this transaction is rescindable and both have a right to rescind. No exemption applies.
6. Evelyn receives her CD in person Tuesday, September 22. Noah has not received a CD. Staff plan consummation Friday, September 25. On Wednesday, September 23, the reviewer identifies the missing recipient and arranges in-person delivery of an accurate CD to Noah that day and the corrected CD to Evelyn. Assume the fee/payee correction leaves the APR accurate under §1026.22, does not change the loan product, and does not add a prepayment penalty.
7. The file contains the invoice but no linked review of receipt evidence, no support for “TBD,” and no record explaining the initial-LE trigger. The dashboard says “ready.”

### Learner tasks

1. Identify the initial-LE due date and the cause of the misleading green status. Can the later accurate CD erase that historical timing failure?
2. State the LE tolerance issue and the actual-charge issue separately. Determine the necessary reduction of the proposed $780 consumer charge on these facts. Explain why adding the two identified overages would double-count part of the correction.
3. Identify the proper payee and the supporting evidence. Does a “TBD” label become acceptable because the dollar amount is corrected?
4. Identify required consumer recipients. Calculate the earliest consummation allowed by the ordinary CD waiting rule after the stated Wednesday delivery. Explain whether the corrected fee alone creates a separate new wait for Evelyn.
5. Write a concise, factual explanation to the consumer without claiming the file was always compliant or pressuring a waiver.
6. Specify the retained evid

chunks.heading: Evidence retention
chunks.excerpt:
ence and one prevention test that can fail on this actual pattern.

### Evidence retention

For §1026.19(e)/(f) compliance evidence generally, §1026.25(c)(1)(i) specifies three years after the later of consummation, the required disclosure date, or the required action date. The more specific CD provision requires each completed required CD and all related documents for five years after consummation. When a creditor disposes of the loan and does not service it, copies must accompany the loan-file transfer to the owner or servicer, which retains them for the balance of that five-year period. The creditor's own five-year rule remains. Do not replace those requirements with F01's 25-month Regulation B period or apply the shortest period to the whole file. [S7]

Principal anchors: (e)(1)(iii); (e)(3)–(4); (f)(1)(i)–(v); (f)(2)(i)–(ii); (f)(3)(i)–(ii), including all nine average-charge comments. lessons.title: Why this belongs in annual ethics

chunks.heading: 1. Why this belongs in annual ethics
chunks.excerpt:
## 1. Why this belongs in annual ethics

The federal minimum for annual renewal education includes two hours of ethics covering fraud, consumer protection, and fair lending. NMLS also publishes a non-year-specific approved CE topic list covering ethics, fraud, and consumer protection. This provider-selected module emphasizes fair treatment; E02 supplies a distinct fraud/conflict/consumer-protection investigation. These particular titles, cases, and minute allocations are not mandates in the 2026 annual topic list. The mandatory 2026 Federal Law findings are addressed in F01–F03 and must not be counted again as additional Ethics time simply because this lesson mentions a shared rule. [S1, S2]

The practical question is not, “Can I recite a protected-class list?” It is, “Can another competent reviewer reconstruct why two applicants received the same or different help, information, documentation requirements, terms, and decisions?” A professional may sincerely believe that an extra condition protects a customer and still impose it because of an impermissible assumption. Conversely, consistent treatment does not require ignoring an actual difference in repayment evidence. The task is to distinguish a relevant credit fact from a prohibited shortcut and document that distinction without reconstructing a convenient story after a complaint.

By the end, the learner should be able to:

chunks.heading: Proposed learning sequence — not measured time
chunks.excerpt:
1. Identify less favorable treatment in an origination workflow, including before a final decision.
2. Apply the current Regulation B discouragement rule to a concrete communication, without substituting an outdated formulation.
3. Evaluate protected income individually and distinguish actual evidence from assumptions about age, family, or income source.
4. Distinguish lawful information collection, prohibited use, and voluntary reliance on support income.
5. Separate a joint application or necessary collateral signature from an impermissibly demanded spouse's credit obligation.
6. Compare matched files, identify a legitimate difference or an unsupported exception, and propose a correction that can be tested.
7. Communicate a concern factually without promising approval, erasing records, or declaring a legal violation from statistics alone.

### Proposed learning sequence — not measured time

| Block | Proposed minutes | Learner work |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Applicable rules and first-contact decisions | 8 | Distinguish legal coverage from policy and identify a discouraging statement |
| Income and family assumptions | 13 | Recalculate an income comparison; explain permissible evidence requests |
| Joint credit and signature scope | 9 | Separate liability from collateral requirements |
| Matched-file investigation | 12 | Produce a fact-based correction and comparison plan |
| Private formative practice and reflection | 8 | Apply the principles to new facts; review feedback |
| **Total proposed** | **50** | **Representative-learner timing remains outstanding** |

## 2. Establish the legal frame before judging a file

chunks.heading: 2. Establish the legal frame before judging a file
chunks.excerpt:
Regulation B prohibits discrimination on a prohibited basis in any aspect of a credit transaction. Its scope is wider than a final approve/deny decision: it reaches the information offered, application process, investigation, evaluation, terms, account administration, and collection. The official interpretation specifically addresses unequal product explanations, extra documentation, and exceptions applied differently to similarly situated applicants. A legitimate, nondiscriminatory factual reason matters; a convenient label that masks the real reason does not. [S3: §1002.4(a), comments 4(a)-1 and -2; S4: §1002.2(m)]

Regulation B's prohibited bases include race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age when the applicant has capacity to contract, receipt of public-assistance income, and good-faith exercise of protected credit-law rights identified by the rule. The rule also addresses associations with other people; it does not permit a lender to make a race-based decision by describing it as a judgment about the applicant's neighbors. Read the defined scope, not a shortened memory aid. [S4: §1002.2(z), comments 2(z)-1 through -3]

chunks.heading: Important September 2026 currency boundary
chunks.excerpt:
The Fair Housing Act separately prohibits discrimination in making available or setting terms of residential real-estate-related transactions because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability (the statute uses the term “handicap”). These lists are not identical: marital status is not familial status, and public-assistance receipt is not the same legal category as disability. Mortgage lending can implicate both statutes, and state or local protections may be broader. This lesson does not establish that an unlisted characteristic is lawful to use. [S8: 42 U.S.C. §3605(a)–(b); HUD fair-lending explanation]

For Regulation B's general discrimination and discouragement provisions, “creditor” includes certain regular referral and creditor-selection activities. An originator cannot safely reason that the final lender alone has obligations because “I only routed the customer.” The exact responsibility for another creditor's conduct depends on the definition and the actual involvement and knowledge; do not automatically attribute every participant's violation to everyone in the transaction. [S4: §1002.2(l), comments 2(l)-1 and -2]

### Important September 2026 currency boundary

chunks.heading: 3. First contact can change access to credit
chunks.excerpt:
The April 22, 2026 Regulation B final rule became effective July 21, 2026. It changed discouragement, disparate-impact provisions, and special-purpose credit program provisions. This manuscript uses the current §1002.4(b) and §1002.6(a), not a prior training deck. Current §1002.6(a) states that ECOA does not provide an effects test; its interpretation separately addresses prohibited intentional proxy use. Accordingly, an outcome disparity alone is not taught here as a completed ECOA violation. Investigate why it occurred and assess applicable law. This statement does not resolve Fair Housing Act theories, state-law claims, judicial challenges, or the validity of a particular special-purpose credit program. Those are separate legal-review matters. [S3, S5, S9]

The cases below test disparate treatment and explicit assumptions, not a disputed statistical-liability theory. Legal reviewers must recheck amendments, controlling court orders, and affected jurisdictions immediately before submission and release. “Current agency webpage” is evidence of published agency text, not a representation that every litigation issue has been researched.

## 3. First contact can change access to credit

### Worked case A — A retirement shortcut

Elliot calls Harborline Mortgage about a 30-year purchase loan. He says that he is 67 and retired. Before asking about income, assets, debts, or the requested loan, the originator replies: “At your age, a 30-year application is pointless. We won't approve someone who probably won't work again. Ask your daughter to apply instead.” The firm uses a judgmental underwriting process for this product. No incapacity issue exists.

chunks.heading: Worked case A — A retirement shortcut
chunks.excerpt:
The problem is not that the originator lacks a completed application or has yet to quote a rate. The statement is directed to a prospective applicant and expressly links likely denial to age and retirement rather than an individualized credit analysis. Current §1002.4(b) prohibits directed oral or written statements that the creditor knows or should know would cause a reasonable person to believe an application would be denied or receive less favorable terms because of a prohibited-basis characteristic. The current commentary itself includes a retirement-related example. [S3: §1002.4(b), comment 4(b)-1.i.A]

Age is not an absolute “never inquire, never consider” category. Regulation B contains limited rules for demonstrably and statistically sound scoring, pertinent elements of creditworthiness in judgmental systems, and favorable treatment of elderly applicants. Those exceptions do not authorize this blanket prediction. Pension and retirement income also cannot be discarded merely because they are retirement benefits. Amount and probable continuance may be considered under the applicable rule using the individual's facts. [S5: §1002.6(b)(2), (5), comments 6(b)(2)-1 through -6 and 6(b)(5)-1]

An appropriate response keeps access open without promising an outcome: “We can review the income and assets you want considered, your obligations, and the proposed transaction. Employment wages are not the only possible source of repayment. I cannot determine eligibility from age alone.” If a product has a legitimate eligibility restriction, staff must confirm its legal basis and applicability; they should not improvise one from a borrower's appearance or assume a relative should become the borrower.

chunks.heading: Discouragement is not a rule against all targeted encouragement
chunks.excerpt:
**Learner activity — change the evidence, not the person:** Rewrite the response if Elliot voluntarily reports that his only current benefit ends next month and he has no other income or assets he wishes to rely upon. Identify what can now be investigated. The changed fact permits examination of actual amount and continuance; it does not justify a blanket rule against retirees. The correct response still should not declare that the course has performed a complete underwriting decision.

### Discouragement is not a rule against all targeted encouragement

Current §1002.4(b) and its interpretation distinguish a discriminatory exclusionary message from encouragement directed at a group to apply. A workshop invitation encouraging first-time applicants is not automatically evidence that other people will be refused. This distinction does not create an exception for an advertised discriminatory loan policy or authorize an otherwise unlawful program. For this course, evaluate the actual statement, whom it addresses, the prohibited-basis link, and the reasonable interpretation; do not infer a violation solely because one audience was addressed. [S3: §1002.4(b), comment 4(b)-1]

**Operational recommendation:** Preserve the actual version of a script or message that produced the concern and have the authorized compliance reviewer correct it. Do not merely delete the troublesome sentence and report that the earlier interaction never occurred. Script versioning and a matched review of actual contacts are suggested controls, not a federal mandate to buy a particular software system.

lessons.title: Same total income does not justify different assumptions

chunks.heading: 4. Same total income does not justify different assumptions
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. Same total income does not justify different assumptions

### Worked case B — The unexplained income haircut

Assume these two otherwise matched applicants are applying for the same covered purchase program. The lender considers verified income, the stated amounts meet its lawful evidence and continuance requirements, and no other income, expense, adjustment, or eligibility issue distinguishes the files. The numerical exercise is a comparison tool, not the program's complete approval test.

| Item | Casey | Morgan |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Verified wage income per month | $6,400 | $4,600 |
| Verified retirement benefit per month | $0 | $1,800 |
| Total supported income | $6,400 | $6,400 |
| Stipulated total monthly debt used in comparison | $2,560 | $2,560 |
| Staff's proposed countable income | $6,400 | $4,600 |

The employee says, “We do not count pensions for customers in Morgan's age group; they are not paychecks.” Using the stated debt numerator, Casey's comparison ratio is $2,560 ÷ $6,400 = 40%. Morgan's correctly supported comparison is also 40%. Excluding the benefit solely for that reason gives $2,560 ÷ $4,600 ≈ 55.65%. The manufactured difference could change whether the applicant receives a full product explanation, is asked for another borrower, or is routed away before a fair review.

chunks.heading: Public assistance, part-time work, and support payments
chunks.excerpt:
Section 1002.6(b)(5) prohibits automatic discounting or exclusion because income is part-time, an annuity, a pension, another retirement benefit, or connected to a prohibited basis. The creditor may evaluate amount and probable continuance; it must assess the individual facts. The regulation does not require the use of unsupported income or guarantee approval. Here, however, sufficient evidence and continuance are expressly stipulated, so the staff member's categorical exclusion is not supported. [S5: §1002.6(b)(5), comments 6(b)(5)-1 and -3]

**Why the calculation matters:** A mathematical error can implement an ethical failure. A perfectly calculated 55.65% ratio would still be misleading if its denominator discarded income on an impermissible basis. An audit that checks only the spreadsheet formula would pass the wrong decision. Investigate source selection as well as arithmetic.

**Learner activity:** Write a three-part finding: the specific observed difference, the controlling rule, and the missing or contradicted justification. Then change the facts so that Morgan's benefit is verified to stop in two months without replacement. Explain why the earlier matched comparison no longer resolves treatment, and why an individualized continuance analysis is necessary. Do not change Morgan's age or demand that a family member join the loan as an automatic solution.

### Public assistance, part-time work, and support payments

chunks.heading: Family plans are not underwriting facts
chunks.excerpt:
Public-assistance income cannot be rejected merely because of its source. In an appropriate evaluation, actual eligibility duration and other pertinent factors may matter. Part-time work is not inherently unreliable; equally, the fact that a payment is protected does not make every stated amount verified or permanent. Keep two distinct questions visible: “What information is required and actually available?” and “Why is this amount being accepted, reduced, or excluded?” [S5: §1002.6(b)(2), (5)]

Suppose Arden chooses to rely on child support. Actual receipt history and whether payments are likely to be consistently made may be relevant; a belief that “support payments never last” is not an individualized analysis. A creditor asking whether income comes from alimony, child support, or separate maintenance must give the required disclosure that it need not be revealed if the applicant does not want it considered. Choosing not to disclose such income is not a reason to invent it, compel reliance upon it, or penalize the applicant for that choice. Income the applicant does not ask the creditor to consider need not be added to qualifying income; evaluate the other income and evidence actually relied upon. Necessary questions about obligations to pay support are a different inquiry. [S6: §1002.5(d)(2), comments -1 through -3; S5: §1002.6(b)(5), comment -2]

### Family plans are not underwriting facts

chunks.heading: National origin is not an immigration-status finding
chunks.excerpt:
Regulation B prohibits questions about birth-control practices, intentions concerning bearing or rearing children, or capacity to bear children. It allows appropriately neutral inquiries about dependents and dependent-related obligations or expenses. The distinction matters when an employee asks a pregnant applicant to sign a promise that she will return to work, without a factual income issue and without an equivalent process for others. The lender cannot assume that a category of people will have diminished or interrupted future income because they may bear or rear children. Actual, voluntarily supplied changes in income can require individual analysis; a categorical prediction cannot replace that evidence. [S6: §1002.5(d)(3); S5: §1002.6(b)(3)]

**Communication exercise:** Replace “Will you be having any more children during the loan term?” with a permissible inquiry addressing the loan's actual repayment facts. A useful answer describes current and reasonably supported future income and actual obligations without requesting family-planning information. The law does not prescribe this course's exact alternative wording.

### National origin is not an immigration-status finding

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
An accent or surname does not establish immigration status. Regulation B permits inquiry about permanent residency and immigration status and permits consideration of status and information needed to ascertain repayment rights and remedies. That permission is not a general authorization to use national origin or to infer legal status from appearance. Use the verified facts and the actually applicable rule; route uncertain eligibility, sanctions, or jurisdiction-specific questions to competent review. This lesson does not promise approval to every noncitizen or teach that every immigration-related eligibility distinction is automatically unlawful. [S6: §1002.5(e); S5: §1002.6(b)(7); S4: comment 2(z)-2]

lessons.title: A required signature needs a defined purpose

chunks.heading: 5. A required signature needs a defined purpose
chunks.excerpt:
## 5. A required signature needs a defined purpose

### Worked case C — “All married borrowers need a spouse on the note”

Jordan applies individually and independently qualifies for the requested amount and terms. Jordan's spouse, Taylor, owns an interest in the proposed collateral but is not a joint applicant. A documented state-law review establishes that Taylor must sign the security instrument to make the collateral available on default, but Taylor does not need to sign the note or incur personal liability. The employee's checklist nevertheless says “spouse: must co-borrow.”

The individual qualification finding is the starting point. Under §1002.7(d)(1), the creditor generally cannot require a qualifying individual applicant to obtain another person's signature on a credit instrument, subject to the specific exceptions. For secured credit, §1002.7(d)(4) permits signatures necessary, or reasonably believed necessary under applicable state law, to make the offered property available. Its interpretation distinguishes a needed lien signature from unnecessary personal liability. On the stated facts, Taylor's security signature has a legal purpose; the demanded note signature does not. [S7: §1002.7(d)(1), (4), comments 7(d)-1 and 7(d)(4)-1 through -3]

The corrective action is not “never ask a spouse to sign.” It is “identify which instrument, which legal purpose, and which support for necessity.” A state can have different property and signature rules. An integrated document combining note and security agreement requires particular care so that a needed lien signature does not silently create an unnecessary credit obligation. This fictional case stipulates the legal review; it is not a substitute for obtaining that review on an actual property.

chunks.heading: Joint application is a choice, not a retrospective label
chunks.excerpt:
### Joint application is a choice, not a retrospective label

A joint financial statement does not itself establish intent to apply jointly. Regulation B's interpretation requires evidence of joint intent at application and distinguishes it from a signature merely verifying information. A signature later placed on a promissory note cannot be used to establish the earlier joint application intent. Do not repair the file by changing Taylor's role to “joint applicant” after the fact solely because the software insists on a second borrower. [S7: §1002.7(d)(1), comments -2 and -3]

If Jordan did not qualify individually and another party's personal liability were needed under the lawful standards, the lender might request a qualified cosigner, guarantor, or similar party. It could not insist that this person be Jordan's spouse. A spouse may voluntarily serve, but marriage is not the prescribed remedy. [S7: §1002.7(d)(5), comments -1 and -2]

**Learner activity:** Prepare a signature-purpose log with four fields: requested signature, applicant's role/intent, the identified legal or credit purpose, and evidence supporting necessity. Complete it for Taylor's security instrument and proposed note. A passing answer permits the supported security signature and rejects the unsupported note requirement; it does not erase Taylor's property interest or fabricate joint intent.

lessons.title: Integrated matched-file investigation

chunks.heading: 6. Integrated matched-file investigation
chunks.excerpt:
## 6. Integrated matched-file investigation

### Evidence packet — Larkspur Mortgage review LM-26-208

Larkspur reviews two applicants, A and B. Both seek the same $320,000 purchase product on the same pricing day. The files stipulate identical relevant credit scores, supported income, debts, property type, loan-to-value ratio, lock period, documentation completeness, and authorized product eligibility. Both request the full set of options they qualify for. Their race differs and is known to the assigned employee. No special-purpose credit program applies.

The firm's lawful checklist requires one recent statement for the asset account shown. Both provide it. An audit trail shows:

1. A receives the full eligible product comparison and the ordinary checklist.
2. B receives only the highest-cost eligible option and a demand for three additional statements, despite no discrepancy or missing item in B's statement.
3. The employee writes privately: “People from B's group need extra proof; they usually don't understand the better option.”
4. When B asks why the conditions differ, the supervisor replies internally, “Delete that note and call it an investor requirement.” No such investor requirement exists.
5. No final credit decision has been made. The team can still correct the handling, but earlier records and contacts already exist.

### Learner work — complete before reviewing the guide

chunks.heading: A legitimate difference changes the analysis
chunks.excerpt:
1. Identify the exact adverse differences. State the evidence of their basis rather than concluding that any two different outcomes are discrimination.
2. Explain why “no final denial” does not resolve the concern.
3. Separate actions to correct B's present treatment from actions to preserve and investigate the earlier handling.
4. Draft a factual customer response that does not guarantee an approval, deny the concern without investigation, or falsely attribute the conditions to an investor.
5. Choose a comparison sample and an independently testable prevention control. Include both files that closed and those that stopped before underwriting.

### A legitimate difference changes the analysis

Change the evidence: B's statement contains a $35,000 deposit whose source is needed under the same lawful policy applied to everyone, while A's statement does not. A request proportionate to resolving that deposit can have a legitimate explanation. It does not authorize a racial remark, unnecessary unrelated conditions, or concealing eligible options. Record the actual difference, the policy's applicability, and the response. Neither automatic identical treatment nor automatic suspicion is the objective; supported, nondiscriminatory treatment is.

lessons.title: Practice: two events, two reasons

chunks.heading: Practice: two events, two reasons
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: two events, two reasons

This is a new fictional transfer case, not another reading of the earlier worked example. Cedar Point Lending applies a lawful policy requiring clarification of unusual deposits when those funds will be used at closing. At first contact, an employee withholds otherwise eligible product information from Morgan because of an explicitly recorded racial assumption. Two days later, Morgan supplies a statement showing an unexplained $28,000 deposit intended for closing. The same deposit policy applies to other applicants with comparable deposits. No loan decision has been made.

### Build the decision record

Make two rows in your own notes: **earlier treatment** and **present evidence request**. In each row identify the information available at that time, the reason actually used, the next investigative or corrective step, and what remains unknown. Do not move evidence received on the second day into the first day's record.

Test both possible overcorrections. If the later deposit is used to justify everything, which historical fact disappears? If every present condition is waived because of the earlier conduct, which real financial issue remains unresolved? Compare your reasoning with the feedback after answering. Your notes are for reflection; this system records your selected decision, not a reviewed written finding.

### Source and scope

[Regulation B §1002.4(a), comments 4(a)-1 and -2; directed first-contact statements: §1002.4(b)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/4/)

All names, statements and case facts are fictional. The workflow and note formats are instructional suggestions. This private practice does not issue NMLS credit or establish validated learning time.

chunks.heading: Practice: the document’s actual effect
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: the document’s actual effect

Avery qualifies individually for the requested loan. Spouse Cameron has an ownership interest in the collateral but did not apply jointly. A documented, applicable state-law review establishes that Cameron's signature is necessary only to make the collateral available, not to assume personal liability. The document system offers a combined note/security instrument whose current signature wording would make Cameron personally liable. A joint financial statement verifies household information but expresses no joint credit intent.

### Inspect purpose and effect separately

Prepare five entries in your notes: person, application role, supported legal purpose, effect of the offered document, and issue to route for correction. The case gives you the applicable legal review; do not invent another state's property rule. You are not being asked to draft or alter a legal instrument yourself.

Compare the supported collateral purpose with the additional obligation created by the current wording. Then test whether a signature affirming accurate financial information answers the different question of who wanted to apply for credit. A document-system limitation is a workflow fact, not a new legal permission. After answering, use the explanation to check both parts of your proposed routing decision.

### Source and scope

[Regulation B §1002.7(d)(1), (4); comments 7(d)(1)-2/-3 and 7(d)(4)-1 through -3](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/7/)

lessons.title: Practice: challenge a false pass

chunks.heading: Practice: challenge a false pass
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: challenge a false pass

After a substantiated first-contact problem, Cedar Point changes its written script. Its proposed monthly control checks only closed loans and verifies that each has a completed reason field. Intake records also contain contacts who stopped before submitting complete applications. Several contacts never reached the loan system. The control owner asks whether a green result would reliably show that the earlier type of problem stopped.

### Try to make the control fail

Name the affected population, the evidence to compare, one situation the proposed control could incorrectly pass, and what would trigger further investigation. Consider a staff member who enters a plausible reason but communicates something different to the customer. Would the current test see that difference?

Distinguish a completed field from an accurate record of conduct. Also distinguish a signal worth investigating from a conclusive legal finding. Select a stronger test, then compare your own proposed false-pass example with the explanation. No sample size, investigation outcome or particular software is mandated by this exercise.

lessons.title: The professional decision: protect the file without prejudging the person

chunks.heading: 1. The professional decision: protect the file without prejudging the person
chunks.excerpt:
## 1. The professional decision: protect the file without prejudging the person

Annual CE must include two hours of ethics encompassing fraud, consumer protection, and fair lending. That category requirement does not mean NMLS mandates this lesson title, these cases, or a particular fraud-detection system. This module applies current federal obligations to situations an experienced MLO can encounter; E01 supplies the complementary fair-lending treatment. [S1, S2]

Fraud resistance is not the ability to call a document fake quickly. It is the discipline to recognize an inconsistency, understand what decision depends on it, obtain appropriate verification, preserve a truthful record, and keep pressure from turning unresolved information into a convenient fact. There are two foreseeable failures. One is knowingly advancing unreliable information because a loan is close to closing. The other is treating every mismatch as proof of dishonesty and making an unsupported accusation against a customer who may be an identity-theft victim or the subject of a data-entry error.

Consumer protection also reaches conduct initiated inside the mortgage business. An accurate pay statement does not cure a referral kickback. A properly disclosed rate does not excuse prohibited steering. A signed borrower acknowledgment does not make coercion of an appraiser permissible. An ethical workflow examines the originator's incentives and conduct, not just the applicant's records.

### Learning objectives

By the end of the proposed instruction, a learner should be able to:

chunks.heading: Proposed learning sequence — not measured time
chunks.excerpt:
1. Separate an observed discrepancy, a supported finding, and an allegation of intentional fraud.
2. Apply the reasonably reliable third-party verification standard to income that a creditor relies on, without inventing a rule that borrower-delivered records are always unacceptable.
3. Preserve and escalate material evidence through a factual, proportionate process without using protected characteristics as substitutes for evidence.
4. Identify a thing of value, an agreement or understanding, and a settlement-service referral in a RESPA scenario, while recognizing actual-service and affiliated-business boundaries.
5. Distinguish a permissible request to correct valuation facts from prohibited pressure to reach a desired value.
6. Correct a misleading payment presentation and recognize compensation-driven steering without treating one disclosure as a universal safe harbor.
7. Write a defensible release-or-hold recommendation identifying the unresolved fact, responsible reviewer, and consumer communication, rather than manufacturing a clearance.

### Proposed learning sequence — not measured time

chunks.heading: 2. A red flag is a reason to investigate, not a verdict
chunks.excerpt:
| Segment | Proposed minutes | Learner work |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evidence, suspicion, and professional responsibility | 7 | Classify observations and claims |
| Income and identity discrepancies | 11 | Compare two source records and identify what verification can resolve |
| Referral conflicts and affiliated businesses | 9 | Trace benefits, services, referrals, and proposed exceptions |
| Valuation independence | 8 | Rewrite improper pressure into a factual request |
| Consumer information and integrated release decision | 8 | Reconcile a payment example and a conflict case |
| Formative retrieval and feedback | 7 | Complete original questions and review explanations |
| **Total proposed** | **50** | Representative-learner timing and instructional validation remain outstanding |

## 2. A red flag is a reason to investigate, not a verdict

Use this five-part working method: **observation → relevance → verification → decision → record**. This is a recommended operational method, not wording prescribed by a federal regulation.

chunks.heading: 2. A red flag is a reason to investigate, not a verdict
chunks.excerpt:
- **Observation:** identify exactly what differs. “Two payroll summaries for the same period show different gross base pay” is an observation. “Borrower is a fraudster” is a conclusion not established by that observation.
- **Relevance:** identify which pending representation or decision depends on it. Does the higher amount support repayment qualification? Does a name mismatch affect which consumer's credit report is being used? Is a payment actually compensation for a referral?
- **Verification:** identify a source capable of resolving the fact. Obtain authorized information through the institution's approved process. A manager's desire to close is not a source of income or identity evidence.
- **Decision:** the authorized reviewer evaluates the resolved facts under applicable law and program requirements. The MLO should not quietly substitute a preferred conclusion for that reviewer.
- **Record:** retain the original evidence, the explanation, the verification result, and the actual decision in the authorized record system. A correction should explain an earlier entry, not falsely suggest the earlier entry never existed.

This method is deliberately different from collecting more documentation from every applicant whose name, accent, neighborhood, family, or income source feels unfamiliar. Reg B prohibits treatment on a prohibited basis; E01 explains its current scope and exceptions. An actual mismatch may justify a proportionate inquiry, but a stereotype is not an identity-control exception. [S3]

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Do not assume an internal “fraud review” label pauses every disclosure, notice, or contractual deadline. Application status, adverse-action notices, and other obligations must be evaluated on their own rules. F01 addresses those clocks. This module does not award duplicate Federal Law time for repeating them. Likewise, reporting obligations, SAR decisions and confidentiality, criminal-law elements, breach notifications, and product-specific government or investor reporting require the appropriate specialist; this lesson does not invent a universal “report every discrepancy” rule.
