lessons.title: Worked case A — Two income records, one closing target

chunks.heading: 3. Worked case A — Two income records, one closing target
chunks.excerpt:
## 3. Worked case A — Two income records, one closing target

### Evidence packet: Harbor Lane file HL-26-411

Assume a closed-end consumer purchase loan secured by the consumer's dwelling is a covered transaction for the general ability-to-repay rule. No exemption, special refinance provision, or alternative compliance path is being invoked in this exercise. Creditor underwriting relies on Rowan's base salary, not collateral value, a hoped-for commission, or household averages.

The file contains:

| Record | What it says | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employer-issued monthly payroll summary A, uploaded Monday | Gross base salary: $7,400 for August 2026 | Whether an additional raise became effective later |
| Purported replacement payroll summary B, uploaded Tuesday | Gross base salary: $9,600 for the same August period | Why the same historical period changed |
| MLO note | “Need at least $9,500 base under this lender's stated conditions” | That the applicant actually earns that amount; the amount is a case-specific lender condition, not a federal threshold |
| Applicant message | “My recruiter said the new role pays more. I sent what I received” | Who created B, whether the change is approved, or whether the applicant intended deception |
| Supervisor message | “Use the new one, remove A, and mark salary verified; we cannot lose Friday” | Reliable verification or authority to falsify the review record |

The difference is $2,200 for the same monthly period. It is approximately 29.73% of the original $7,400: $2,200 ÷ $7,400 × 100. That percentage is a descriptive comparison, not a regulatory fraud threshold. It helps identify the material inconsistency. It proves neither which document is accurate nor who created the conflict.

chunks.heading: Learner activity: write the next four actions
chunks.excerpt:
For this covered transaction, the creditor must verify the income or assets it relies on using third-party records that provide reasonably reliable evidence. Individualized records matter: the employer's typical pay range or a website reporting average wages is not verification of Rowan's salary. The rule permits various sources, including payroll statements, financial-institution records, and records from the employer. A tax-return transcript is a possible source, not a universally mandated document. [S4: §1026.43(c)(3)–(4), comments 43(c)(3)-1 and -2, 43(c)(4)-1 and -3]

**The upload channel does not settle authenticity.** The official interpretation expressly permits obtaining third-party records directly from the consumer when they are reasonably reliable and specific to the individual. A borrower-uploaded employer statement is not automatically disqualified. Conversely, receipt through a familiar portal does not make contradictory information reliable. The question is the quality and substance of the evidence, not whether a preferred label appears beside the file. [S4: comment 43(c)(3)-2]

### Learner activity: write the next four actions

Before reading the guide, write four actions that address the inconsistency. For each, identify whether it is a legal verification requirement or a recommended method of satisfying and documenting that requirement. Also write one sentence that should **not** be sent to Rowan.

### Changed fact: a real raise, an inaccurate historical document

chunks.heading: A bank deposit is not automatically earnings
chunks.excerpt:
The approved verification process establishes that August base salary was $7,400. A signed employer record confirms a raise to $9,600 beginning October 1, subject to conditions stated in that record. This new evidence does not make B an accurate August payroll record. It changes the factual discussion: there is a verified historical amount and separate prospective employment information.

Whether and how the creditor can rely on the prospective amount is an underwriting and legal-applicability question, not permission to relabel future income as already earned. This ethics case does not prescribe a universal waiting period or a rule that every future raise must be ignored. Escalation must preserve both the actual verification and the remaining program question. A legitimate route forward can exist without a fabricated past.

### A bank deposit is not automatically earnings

Suppose the file also shows a new $12,000 bank deposit with no source description. “Money arrived” does not establish that it is income. The official interpretation gives an unidentified deposit as a case requiring a basis to conclude that funds are the consumer's income rather than, for example, loan proceeds. Do not turn an unexplained balance into qualifying salary merely because it fills the gap. [S4: comment 43(c)(4)-4]

## 4. Worked case B — An identity mismatch without a stereotype

The application identifies Cameron Vale III. A credit report displays Cameron Vale II with a different birth date. One uploaded document bears a shortened first name; that shortening alone might be ordinary. The birth-date and suffix differences could reflect a mixed file, entry error, family-member confusion, identity theft, or other facts not yet known.

chunks.heading: Learner activity: observation versus accusation
chunks.excerpt:
The proper initial statement is narrow: **the available records do not yet establish that the report belongs to the applicant**. It is not, “This name sounds foreign,” “This customer speaks with an accent,” or “People from this neighborhood often have problems.” Those are not identity evidence. [S3]

Apply the organization's approved identity-resolution and credit-report procedures, using appropriate access and authorization. Route the mismatch to the responsible specialist; confirm the factual identifiers through allowed channels and determine whether the report or application needs correction. This is a recommended process, not a claim that every MLO has the same federally mandated identity tool or must personally investigate a suspected crime. Avoid disclosing full identifiers in an unrestricted email chain or asking a customer to send sensitive records to an unapproved location.

For ability-to-repay purposes, the official interpretation recognizes that a creditor may know or have reason to know that a report is inaccurate, including information contradicting it or certain alerts or disputes. It discusses disregarding inaccurate or disputed information and does not impose an automatic requirement to obtain additional third-party records in every such case. That treatment is not permission to knowingly use somebody else's credit history to support the applicant's approval. Product rules, credit-report duties, identity controls, and notice obligations still require their own analysis. [S4: comment 43(c)(3)-3]

### Learner activity: observation versus accusation

Classify each statement as an observation, a reasonable issue to resolve, or an unsupported conclusion:

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
1. “The report birth date differs from the application birth date.”
2. “We need to establish whether the report is associated with this applicant before relying on it.”
3. “The customer has an unusual surname, so the documents must be false.”
4. “The applicant is definitely the person who altered the report.”

lessons.title: Worked case C — A “quality fee” that follows referrals

chunks.heading: 5. Worked case C — A “quality fee” that follows referrals
chunks.excerpt:
## 5. Worked case C — A “quality fee” that follows referrals

### Evidence packet: referral arrangement RL-26-52

Summit Quay Title pays MLO Jules, who is not its employee, $175 for every referred federally related mortgage loan that closes using Summit's settlement services. They agree to call the payment a “quality-review fee.” Jules does no review or other service for Summit. The ledger shows twelve closed referrals and a payment of $2,100. Borrowers pay Summit's ordinary price, with no separately identified surcharge for Jules's payment.

The title does not determine the legal analysis. Section 1024.14(b) prohibits giving or accepting a fee, kickback, or thing of value pursuant to an agreement or understanding that settlement-service business involving a federally related mortgage loan will be referred. A thing of value can extend beyond cash. An agreement need not be written; a practice or pattern can establish the understanding. A referral can be an action influencing selection of a settlement-service provider. [S5: §1024.14(b), (d), (e), (f)]

Apply the facts, not a generic slogan:

| Element | Evidence in this case |
| --- | --- |
| Thing of value | $175 per closed referred transaction; twelve × $175 = $2,100 |
| Agreement or understanding | Express agreement to pay when a referred loan closes with Summit |
| Referral of covered settlement-service business | Jules directs the borrower to Summit for the stipulated federally related mortgage transaction |
| Claimed services | No actual quality-review work; the invoice label is unsupported |

chunks.heading: What this does not mean
chunks.excerpt:
The actual-services provision does not protect a payment when the supposedly compensated services did not occur. The fact that the borrower did not pay an added charge does not convert the referral payment into a permitted one. The regulation also makes clear that a high price alone is not proof of a violation; the issue is not resolved simply by comparing consumer prices. [S5: §1024.14(g)(1)(iv), (g)(2)]

### What this does not mean

Not every payment involving a settlement-service business is a prohibited referral payment. The regulation recognizes specified payments and arrangements, including bona fide compensation for goods, facilities, or actual services, qualifying promotional or educational activities, and an employer's payment to its own employees for referral activities. Each has its own conditions. Jules is expressly not Summit's employee, and no real service exists in the stipulated case. Do not expand the own-employee provision to a payment from an outside title business merely because the MLO is somebody's employee. [S5: §1024.14(g)(1)]

For promotional or educational activities, “educational” is not sufficient by itself: the activity must not be conditioned on referrals and must not defray expenses that the person in a position to refer would otherwise incur. For actual-services arrangements, reasonable market value does not include the value of expected referrals. Where someone is paid for multiple services, the relevant services must be actual, necessary, and distinct from the person's primary services. [S5: §1024.14(g)(1)(vi), (g)(2)–(3)]

chunks.heading: Affiliated business: disclosure is one condition, not the whole exception
chunks.excerpt:
An agreement called a marketing-services agreement is therefore neither automatically unlawful nor automatically safe. The reviewer needs evidence of what is actually delivered, who receives value, how payment is determined, whether the work is real and distinct, and whether referrals are being purchased. A signed invoice stating “fair market value” is not independent proof of those facts.

This case concerns a referral payment under §1024.14(b). It does **not** teach that every disputed fee retained entirely by one provider automatically establishes a fee-splitting violation under RESPA section 8(b). That separate provision, its elements, and controlling judicial interpretation require a distinct analysis; do not collapse every pricing concern into the same violation.

### Affiliated business: disclosure is one condition, not the whole exception

Change the facts. Jules's employer owns an interest in a title business and refers consumers to it. The affiliated-business exception has multiple conditions, including the required relationship and estimated-charge disclosure at the applicable time, no required use except specified exceptions, and limits on things of value received, including permissible ownership returns. It is not a general permission to pay a per-file referral bonus when a disclosure has been signed. Returns labeled “dividends” are not protected merely by that label if they are really calculated on actual or expected referrals. [S6: §1024.15(b)(1)–(3), (c)]

chunks.heading: Learner activity: revise the recommendation
chunks.excerpt:
The default disclosure timing is no later than the referral; §1024.15(b)(1) specifies exceptions, including particular lender situations. This module does not replace those conditions with a universal “three days after application” instruction. Nor does it teach an absolute rule that no provider may ever be required: the regulation contains particular lender-related exceptions. Use the actual arrangement and controlling text before deciding whether the exception applies.

### Learner activity: revise the recommendation

Draft recommendation: “Approve the $175 payment because the borrower did not pay extra and the parties will sign an affiliated-business disclosure.”

Replace it with a recommendation grounded in the original facts.

lessons.title: Worked case D — Correcting a valuation versus buying the answer

chunks.heading: 6. Worked case D — Correcting a valuation versus buying the answer
chunks.excerpt:
## 6. Worked case D — Correcting a valuation versus buying the answer

### Evidence packet: valuation VI-26-79

For a consumer loan secured by the consumer's principal dwelling, an appraiser's written valuation is $398,000. The contract price is $420,000. The MLO writes: “Get this to $420,000 by tomorrow or you will not get another assignment. We will hold your fee until it closes.” Separately, a property record appears to identify a factual error in the reported lot size.

The $22,000 difference between contract price and appraised value is not itself evidence of appraiser misconduct. A contract price is not an instruction to deliver that value. The scope of §1026.42 matters: it addresses consumer credit secured by the principal dwelling and covered persons, including persons providing settlement services. Its valuation definition and commentary should be consulted for the actual service; do not assume every property-price opinion in every transaction has the same coverage. [S7: §1026.42(a)–(b)]

The regulation prohibits coercion and attempted coercion designed to make a valuation depend on something other than the valuer's independent judgment. Threatening future assignments, withholding payment to influence value, and conditioning compensation on consummation are among the expressly addressed forms of pressure. An attempt can be prohibited even if the appraiser refuses and leaves the number unchanged. [S7: §1026.42(c)(1), (c)(1)(i)(B)–(E); comments 42(c)(1)-2 and -4]

chunks.heading: A permissible request is factual and outcome-neutral
chunks.excerpt:
It also prohibits covered persons from falsifying a valuation and, subject to its terms, materially altering a valuation. The originator should not change the final value in the file to make a ratio work. A bona fide error is distinguished from misrepresentation; correcting a genuine fact through the proper process is not the same as manufacturing an outcome. [S7: §1026.42(c)(2)]

### A permissible request is factual and outcome-neutral

Section 1026.42(c)(3) permits requests to consider additional appropriate property information, provide further explanation, or correct errors. A rewritten request could say: “The attached property record appears to show a different lot size from page 2 of the report. Please review whether the reported fact is accurate and explain any resulting revision under your independent judgment.” The request supplies information and asks for analysis; it neither commands a target value nor links payment or future work to reaching one.

That correction request does not erase the earlier threat. If a creditor knows before consummation of a violation covered by §1026.42(e), it may not extend credit based on the valuation unless it documents reasonable diligence establishing that the valuation does not materially misstate or misrepresent the dwelling's value. Obtaining a second valuation is not automatically required in every case, and obtaining one does not retroactively make coercion proper. Route the incident to the responsible reviewer and preserve the evidence. [S7: §1026.42(e), comment 42(e)-1]

### Reporting threshold: do not punish independence

chunks.heading: Learner activity: classify the request
chunks.excerpt:
The reporting provision addresses a reasonable belief that an appraiser materially failed to comply with applicable USPAP or ethical/professional legal requirements. Under §1026.42(g)(1), the failure is material if it is likely to significantly affect the value assigned to the principal dwelling. The rule calls for reporting to the appraisal-certifying and licensing agency for the state where that dwelling is located, within a reasonable period after determining there is a reasonable basis for the report. It does not say “report an appraiser whenever a value is below contract” or impose a universal forty-eight-hour deadline. On the present facts, the appraiser's refusal to increase the value is not itself that material failure. [S7: §1026.42(g)(1)–(3)]

### Learner activity: classify the request

Classify each as a permitted type of request, prohibited pressure on these stipulated facts, or an issue requiring further evidence:

1. “Here is a recent comparable sale we believe may be relevant; please consider it independently.”
2. “Your next five assignments depend on reaching the contract price.”
3. “Please explain the treatment of the recorded easement.”
4. “The report has a one-digit typographical error; therefore the appraiser must immediately be reported for a material violation.”

lessons.title: Consumer protection: a correct number can still be an incomplete presentation

chunks.heading: 7. Consumer protection: a correct number can still be an incomplete presentation
chunks.excerpt:
## 7. Consumer protection: a correct number can still be an incomplete presentation

### Worked case E — The payment headline

A lender's ordinary website product page—not a banner linked to an application, a pop-up, television, radio, or an envelope—advertises a closed-end first-lien consumer mortgage secured by a dwelling as “Your entire monthly home payment: $1,850.” The $1,850 is principal and interest only. For the fictional example, taxes are estimated at $360 per month and homeowners insurance at $140 per month. There is no mortgage insurance or association charge in this exercise. The page provides no explanation that the advertised payment excludes taxes and insurance.

The known illustrative outlay is $1,850 + $360 + $140 = **$2,350**. The difference is **$500 per month**, or **$6,000 over twelve months** at those unchanged estimates. These figures do not guarantee future tax or insurance amounts and do not establish that every customer's costs are identical.

For an advertisement within §1026.24(f)'s scope that states a payment amount, the rule requires the applicable payment amounts and their periods. For a first-lien dwelling loan, it also requires disclosure, where applicable, that payments exclude taxes and insurance and that the actual payment obligation will be greater. The amounts and periods have an equal-prominence and close-proximity requirement; the tax-and-insurance statement must have prominence and close proximity. These are not identical wording requirements. A distant footnote is not the model supplied by the official interpretation. [S8: §1026.24(f)(1), (3), comment 24(f)-2]

chunks.heading: Worked case F — Steering for greater compensation
chunks.excerpt:
Do not fix the page solely by changing the headline to $2,350 and assume the advertisement is compliant. The example must accurately identify what its numbers include, what is estimated, applicable payment periods and other disclosures; an advertised payment also triggers the applicable additional-terms requirements in §1026.24(d). Interest-rate and APR presentations have separate rules. Any actual revised advertisement needs a complete review of its facts, medium, disclosures, and governing rules. This case isolates one failure rather than delivering preapproved advertising copy. [S8: §1026.24(c), (d), (f)]

### Worked case F — Steering for greater compensation

Two creditors with which a loan-originator organization regularly does business offer options for which the consumer is likely to qualify. The case stipulates that the options have identical loan amount, payment schedule, rate, fixed-rate period, prepayment provisions, service, and consumer-relevant features. Option A charges $750 less in upfront consumer costs. Option B produces greater creditor-paid compensation for the originator. There is no offsetting consumer benefit to B. The originator hides A, directs the consumer to B solely for the greater compensation, and the consumer consummates B.

chunks.heading: 8. Integrated release decision — The file is attractive, the evidence is not ready
chunks.excerpt:
For the transaction within §1026.36(e)'s scope, this is the conduct the steering prohibition addresses: directing a consumer to consummate a transaction because of greater creditor-paid compensation unless the consummated transaction is in the consumer's interest. The official interpretation states that this provision requires consummation for a violation. Do not describe an unconsummated suggestion as already satisfying every element of §1026.36(e)(1), although it warrants correction before harm and may raise other issues. [S9: §1026.36(e)(1), comments 36(e)(1)-1 through -3]

The rule is not a mandate to select the option paying the least compensation in every case, nor a command to search the entire mortgage market. Consumer interest can depend on actual costs and features, and the interpretation addresses creditors with which the originator regularly does business. What is impermissible in this stipulated case is suppressing the otherwise better available option for the compensation advantage without a consumer-interest justification. A signature saying “I selected B” does not establish that hidden A was fairly presented or that greater compensation was not the reason for steering.

This lesson is not the complete loan-originator compensation rule. Term-based compensation, dual compensation, product coverage, and the detailed non-steering safe-harbor conditions require their own review. Do not convert “showed three choices” into a universal safe harbor without satisfying the actual conditions.

## 8. Integrated release decision — The file is attractive, the evidence is not ready

chunks.heading: Learner assignment
chunks.excerpt:
The original Harbor Lane file returns for final preparation. Its status screen shows green checks for income, title selection, valuation, and consumer communication. The detailed record shows:

- Higher income was marked verified without resolving the two historical records.
- A title ledger contains the per-referral “quality fee” from case C.
- The valuation reviewer received the threat from case D, but nobody assessed its effect under §1026.42(e).
- The consumer's written comparison omits the lower-cost otherwise identical option from case F.
- A supervisor asks the MLO to delete the four supporting messages “because the summary is what the auditor reads.”

The green summary is evidence of a system status, not evidence that the underlying legal and factual conditions have been met. Each issue has a different legal basis. Do not combine them into a generic “fraud cleared” checkbox that conceals which fact was verified, which conduct occurred, and which legal review remains.

### Learner assignment

Prepare a short recommendation with five fields:

1. The specific unresolved fact or conduct.
2. The proposed release restriction and who can decide it.
3. The evidence that must be preserved or obtained.
4. The explanation to the consumer that is accurate without accusation or an unsupported promise.
5. The condition that would support the next decision, distinguishing a corrected fact from an earlier violation that still needs remediation.

lessons.title: Practice: preserve the income timeline

chunks.heading: Practice: preserve the income timeline
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: preserve the income timeline

Marlow's employer confirms September base pay of $6,800. A separate signed employer record describes a conditional increase to $7,600 beginning November 1. An earlier upload described September pay as $7,600; its author remains unknown. The lender relies on income for a covered general ability-to-repay transaction. The authorized reviewer has not decided whether the conditional future increase may be used.

### Sort the evidence before reaching a conclusion

Make three entries: verified historical fact, conditional future fact, and unresolved record or decision. Identify which document supports each entry and which inference you must not make about authorship. Do not treat an amount as belonging to the same period merely because the number appears in two documents.

Ask whether the employer's confirmation solves every issue or only a specific one. In particular, distinguish the amount paid in September from the underwriting decision about future income and from the origin of the inaccurate upload. Answer using only the supplied facts, then check your three entries against the explanation. This practice does not make a loan-approval decision.

### Source and scope

[Regulation Z §1026.43(c)(2)(i), (c)(3)–(4), including comment 43(c)(2)(i)-3](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/43/)

All names, statements and case facts are fictional. The workflow and note formats are instructional suggestions. This private practice does not issue NMLS credit or establish validated learning time.

lessons.title: Practice: follow the benefit

chunks.heading: Practice: follow the benefit
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: follow the benefit

Harbor Oak Title offers an outside mortgage originator a $900 credit toward the originator's office-software subscription after six referred federally related mortgage transactions close using Harbor Oak's settlement services. The arrangement expressly conditions the credit on those referrals. The originator is not Harbor Oak's employee and supplies it no goods or services. The parties call the credit technology support. Borrowers pay Harbor Oak's ordinary settlement price. No credit has yet been delivered.

### Evaluate the proposed arrangement

Build five entries: who benefits, what triggers the benefit, which business is referred, what work is actually performed for the payer, and what facts support any proposed exception. Separate an invoice label from evidence of work. The question asks whether to approve this arrangement as described, not whether every possible vendor relationship is prohibited.

Test three changes that alter appearance without necessarily changing the arrangement: paying the software vendor directly, charging the normal subscription price, and informing borrowers about the credit. For each, identify which original fact still needs analysis. Then select your recommendation and review why the other recommendations fail on these stipulated facts. Your written analysis is reflection, not a submitted legal opinion.

### Source and scope

[Regulation X §1024.14(b), (d)–(g): referral payments, things of value and specified exceptions](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/14/)

lessons.title: Practice: correction and conduct are different

chunks.heading: Practice: correction and conduct are different
chunks.excerpt:
## Practice: correction and conduct are different

In a covered consumer loan secured by the principal dwelling, an MLO threatens to withhold the appraiser's fee unless the valuation reaches the contract price. The appraiser refuses the demand. Later, the appraiser independently corrects a genuine garage-area error. Before consummation, the creditor learns of the coercion violation. Nobody has completed a documented reasonable-diligence determination about whether the valuation materially misstates or misrepresents the dwelling's value.

### Keep two tracks open

Write two headings: present reliance on the valuation and handling of earlier conduct. Under each, name the fact established, the decision still required, and the person or function that should receive the issue. Ask what the garage correction demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate.

Test whether a borrower acknowledgment or the mere ordering of another report answers the unresolved reliance question. Do not confuse ordering a report with choosing and lawfully relying on an unaffected valuation. Your decision must address the stated plan to extend credit based on the affected valuation. Compare both tracks with the explanation after answering.

### Source and scope

[Regulation Z §1026.42(c)(1), (c)(3), (e), and comment 42(e)-1](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/42/)

lessons.title: Start with three separate questions

chunks.heading: Scope and learning outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
## Scope and learning outcomes

The current NMLS CE approved-topic list, version 2026.1, places ARMs, negative-amortization loans, 15-year loans, Non-QM loans, and CSBS/AARMR nontraditional-product guidance within the two-hour Nontraditional category. That list is not specific to a single CE year and is broader than the narrow definition used in the 2006 banking guidance. The list supports this module's proposed category; it does not approve this course or validate its time. N01 develops product mechanics and consumer understanding. N02 separately develops underwriting evidence and repayment decisions; its time cannot be credited again for reading N01. [S1]

By the end, the learner should be able to distinguish interest-only from negative amortization; calculate principal-and-interest changes with explicit assumptions; separate interest-rate caps, payment caps, and balance caps; identify the correct current ATR payment rule; and explain material risks without treating disclosure or a signed acknowledgment as underwriting approval.

## 1. Start with three separate questions

A label such as “alternative loan” gives an originator almost none of the information needed for a competent conversation. Ask three different questions:

chunks.heading: 1. Start with three separate questions
chunks.excerpt:
1. **How does the obligation work?** Identify the interest-rate structure, required payments, principal deferral, possible balance growth, maturity, and any balloon. An adjustable rate describes how interest changes; it does not say whether the principal decreases.
2. **Which legal rules cover this transaction?** Consumer purpose, collateral, open-end versus closed-end structure, and any actual exemption matter. A consumer-purpose, dwelling-secured Non-QM loan is not excluded from the ability-to-repay rule merely because an investor calls it Non-QM. N02 develops the coverage analysis. [S3: §1026.43(a), comment 43(a)-1]
3. **Which approval or underwriting classification is being asserted?** Qualified Mortgage is a defined legal classification with multiple requirements. A lender's product name, a broker's preference, and NMLS approval of an education category are three different things.

An interest-only loan requires payments covering interest but no scheduled principal for a specified period. If all interest is paid, no fees are capitalized, and no new advances occur, the balance remains unchanged. It does **not** grow simply because principal is deferred. A payment-option ARM may permit a payment below accrued interest; if the unpaid interest is added to principal, the balance grows. A fully amortizing ARM can have changing payments while still paying principal down. A fixed-rate loan can nevertheless have a payment increase when an interest-only period ends. [S2: Appendix; S7: §1026.37(a)(10), comments 37(a)(10)-1 and -2]

chunks.heading: What the older guidance does—and does not—establish
chunks.excerpt:
Those distinctions prevent two opposite errors: describing every ARM as a negative-amortization product, and describing every fixed-rate product as having an unchanging total payment. Taxes and insurance can change even when scheduled principal and interest do not.

### What the older guidance does—and does not—establish

The 2006 interagency guidance addresses risks in institutions supervised by its issuing banking agencies. Its central examples are interest-only mortgages and payment-option ARMs. Its own footnote excludes fully amortizing residential products, reverse mortgages, and HELOCs except the simultaneous-second-lien discussion. NMLS's education-category list is broader; do not turn a difference in definitions into a contradiction. [S1; S2: introduction, footnote 1]

Supervisory guidance is not itself a statute or legislative regulation. The Federal Reserve expressly distinguishes it from law. The CSBS/AARMR framework is also listed by NMLS as an appropriate educational topic; this lesson does not establish whether or how a particular state adopted a binding requirement. Check the current state authority before asserting a state mandate. [S1; S8]

The older document is useful for understanding payment shock, risk layering, and balanced communication. It is **not** permission to apply its historical stated-income discussion instead of current verification requirements. Nor should its old qualifying-payment illustration replace the current Regulation Z interest-only rule: where §1026.43(c)(5)(ii)(B) applies, use the term **remaining at recast**, not a newly restarted original term. Current law, actual coverage, and the legal obligation control. [S2: Reduced Documentation and footnote 6; S3: §1026.43(c)(3)–(5)]

chunks.excerpt:

chunks.heading: 2. Interest-only does not remove the principal bill
chunks.excerpt:
## 2. Interest-only does not remove the principal bill

### Original case: Lena's five-year interest-only period

Lena considers a $360,000 loan with a 30-year total term, a fixed 6.00% annual note rate, monthly interest calculated as annual rate divided by 12, and interest-only payments for the first 60 months. Beginning with payment 61, principal and interest amortize over the remaining 300 months. There is no negative amortization, balloon, additional advance, capitalized fee, or voluntary principal payment. Ignore taxes, insurance, escrow, and fees in this calculation; they are added separately when evaluating the household obligation.

The interest-only payment is:

`$360,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $1,800.00 monthly interest.`

After 60 timely interest-only payments, the principal is still $360,000. The borrower has paid $108,000 of interest, not $108,000 of principal. The remaining time to repay principal is now 25 years, not 30.

For equal monthly principal-and-interest payments, use:

`Payment = Balance × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)^(-n)]`

Here `r` is the annual note rate divided by 12, expressed as a decimal, and `n` is the number of remaining monthly payments. This is a simplified monthly-accrual mortgage calculation, not an APR calculation.

`Payment = $360,000 × 0.005 ÷ [1 − (1.005)^(-300)] = $2,319.49.`

The increase is approximately $519.49 a month, or 28.86%, despite **no interest-rate increase**. The loan has not become more expensive because the lender secretly changed the rate. The required payment now retires the unchanged principal within a shorter remaining period. [S3: §1026.43(c)(5)(ii)(B), comment 43(c)(5)(ii)(B)-1; original arithmetic]

### Compare structure, not just the first payment

chunks.heading: Activity 1: separate structure shock from rate shock
chunks.excerpt:
These are separate hypothetical offers at the same 6.00% rate, solely to isolate structure. They are not market-rate quotes; actual products may have different rates and fees.

| Structure for $360,000 | Initial monthly P&I or interest | Scheduled principal treatment |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 30-year fixed, amortizing from the beginning | $2,158.38 | Principal begins decreasing with payment 1 |
| 30-year fixed, first five years interest-only | $1,800.00 | No principal reduction for 60 payments; then approximately $2,319.49 for 300 payments |
| 15-year fixed, amortizing from the beginning | $3,037.88 | Higher required payment retires the original principal over 180 payments |

The 15-year option is not automatically the appropriate recommendation: a payment that forces a household to consume essential reserves can create a different risk. The interest-only option is not automatically an improper product: it has a defined principal-deferral structure that must be evaluated lawfully and explained accurately. A professional comparison includes the borrower's objectives, verified repayment resources, payment transitions, total costs, and actual lender criteria—not simply the smallest number in the first-payment column.

### Activity 1: separate structure shock from rate shock

For a **different hypothetical adjustable-rate version** of Lena's loan, assume the rate becomes 8.00% exactly when amortization starts after the first 60 months, remains 8.00% thereafter, and the contract permits that reset. All other balance and term assumptions remain unchanged. Compute the 300-month payment before looking below.

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Worked result: $2,778.54 monthly P&I. This is about 54.36% above $1,800. The first scenario isolated principal deferral; the second adds a rate increase. Do not describe 8.00% as a forecast, the legal maximum, or the ATR qualifying rate; it is a deliberately stated sensitivity assumption. The contract and applicable regulation determine those other rates.

Now write two sentences for Lena: one explains why payment rises even at 6.00%; the other says what the 8.00% scenario does and does not predict. A sound answer does not promise that refinancing will prevent either transition.

chunks.heading: 3. A payment option can change the debt, not just the payment
chunks.excerpt:
## 3. A payment option can change the debt, not just the payment

### Original case: a minimum that leaves interest unpaid

This numerical extract illustrates 12 months of a hypothetical payment-option product. Opening balance: $180,000. During this entire illustration, the accrual rate remains 7.20% annually, or 0.60% monthly. The contractual minimum is $800 per month. All minimum payments are timely. Unpaid interest is added to principal monthly; no other fees, advances, or rounding adjustments affect the balance. Assume no balance cap or mandatory recast is reached during these 12 months. The extract is not a complete loan term sheet or a statement of product legality.

For each month:

`Interest = opening balance × 0.006`

`Closing balance = opening balance + interest − payment`

| Month | Opening balance | Accrued interest | Payment | Interest added to principal | Closing balance |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | $180,000.00 | $1,080.00 | $800.00 | $280.00 | $180,280.00 |
| 2 | $180,280.00 | $1,081.68 | $800.00 | $281.68 | $180,561.68 |

After 12 payments, the balance is approximately $183,473.13, using unrounded intermediate values. The consumer paid $9,600 during the year and owes about $3,473.13 more principal than at the beginning. Timely payment and growing principal are entirely compatible when the legal payment schedule permits negative amortization. [S2: Appendix; S3: §1026.43(b)(7); original arithmetic]

Compare three choices for **month 1 only**:

- $800 minimum: the balance increases to $180,280.
- $1,080 interest-only: all current interest is paid, and the balance remains $180,000.
- $1,100 payment, credited to interest and then principal: the balance declines to $179,980.

chunks.heading: Activity 2: challenge the apparent saving
chunks.excerpt:
The third payment reduces principal that month. Without the full contract and amortization period, it should not be labeled a sufficient fully amortizing payment for the whole loan. Also, the second month's interest-only amount changes with the opening balance and accrual rate; “interest-only” is not a permanently fixed dollar amount.

### Activity 2: challenge the apparent saving

A draft explanation says: “Choose $800 instead of $1,080 and save $280 every month.” Identify both defects.

First, the $280 is deferred interest added to debt, not a reduction in the interest charge. Second, the difference is not necessarily $280 every subsequent month: month 2 already has $281.68 of unpaid interest under the specified assumptions. Rewrite the explanation using the actual first-month comparison and the consequences for principal.

### Three different caps

An **interest-rate cap** limits a change in the accrual rate, as specified in the note. A **payment cap** limits certain scheduled payment increases. A **negative-amortization cap** establishes a balance-related trigger or limit under the contract. None should be substituted for another.

Suppose a contract permits a minimum payment to increase by no more than 5% at its next annual minimum-payment adjustment. An $800 minimum would become no more than $840 under that provision. That does not prove the accrual interest will rise only 5%, does not prove $840 covers accrued interest, and does not establish that the cap controls a mandatory recast. Read the provisions governing recast and their interaction with payment limits. Some structures stop permitting the low minimum when a stated time expires or a balance condition is triggered. [S2: Introductory Interest Rates, Appendix; S3: §1026.43(b)(7), (b)(11)]

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Do not multiply the initial principal by a stated balance-cap percentage and call that the exact regulatory maximum loan amount without modeling the contractual schedule. The permitted period, interest-rate path, payment adjustments, and cap trigger can produce a different amount. The current official commentary itself distinguishes the calculated maximum balance from a simple headline cap. [S3: comments 43(b)(7)-1 through -3]

The exit risk is not only a larger future payment. A larger debt can reduce equity, and selling involves transaction costs. A refinance requires a willing lender, a qualifying borrower and property, and acceptable terms at that later time. Those are not guaranteed by the current lender or the current appraisal.

lessons.title: A disclosed payment is not necessarily the underwriting payment

chunks.heading: 4. A disclosed payment is not necessarily the underwriting payment
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. A disclosed payment is not necessarily the underwriting payment

An originator should be able to show three separate outputs in a file:

| Output | What determines it | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contractual payment schedule | Executed legal obligation and actual rate/payment mechanics | Proof of affordability |
| Required disclosure | Applicable disclosure rules, including their stated projection assumptions | A prediction of future rates or automatically the ATR qualifying payment |
| ATR qualifying payment | Current applicable ability-to-repay rule and transaction facts | Necessarily the first advertised minimum or the largest payment disclosed anywhere |

For an ordinary covered transaction evaluated under §1026.43(c), the basic payment rule uses the **greater of the fully indexed rate and the introductory rate**, with substantially equal monthly fully amortizing payments. For interest-only and negative-amortization loans, apply their special rules rather than the general formula with the wrong balance or term. [S3: §1026.43(c)(5)]

The **fully indexed rate** uses the index or formula that will apply after recast, determined at consummation, and the maximum margin that can apply during the loan term. For an original simplified example, an applicable index of 3.25% plus an unchanging 2.50 percentage-point margin gives 5.75%. With an introductory rate of 4.50%, the greater-of-rate test uses 5.75%; if the introductory rate instead is 6.25%, it uses 6.25%. Assume no contractual lookback or lifetime-cap adjustment changes these example inputs. The result is not a prediction of the index several years later. [S3: §1026.43(b)(3); comments 43(b)(3)-1 through -2]

chunks.heading: 4. A disclosed payment is not necessarily the underwriting payment
chunks.excerpt:
For an actual file, apply the commentary's rules rather than grabbing an arbitrary online index quote. A contractual lookback can affect the eligible index value; a periodic adjustment cap does not reduce the fully indexed rate merely because that rate cannot be reached at the first adjustment. The commentary separately permits taking the lifetime maximum into account. For fixed- or step-rate obligations without an index, it identifies the maximum rate that may apply over the term. These distinctions are why the note and applicable calculation method must travel with a qualifying-payment number. [S3: comments 43(b)(3)-2 through -5]

- **Interest-only:** calculate P&I to retire the loan amount over the term remaining at recast, using the greater of the fully indexed and introductory rates. Lena's fixed 6.00% example therefore uses $360,000, 6.00%, and 300 months—not the $1,800 interest-only payment and not a new 360-month period.
- **Negative amortization:** first determine the maximum loan amount and recast timing under §1026.43(b)(7). Assume minimum payments for as long as permitted and the maximum interest rate reached as early as permitted, including periodic caps. Then calculate substantially equal monthly P&I on that maximum balance over the remaining term using the greater of fully indexed and introductory rates. The rate used to project balance growth and the rate used in the qualifying-payment formula need not be identical. [S3: §1026.43(c)(5)(ii)(C), comments -1 through -3]

These are the §1026.43(c) calculations. Other ATR/QM routes have their own requirements. Do not borrow a convenient piece of the General QM or special-refinancing rules while ignoring their eligibility conditions. N02 addresses why a Non-QM label does not eliminate current verification.

chunks.heading: Legal availability is a separate gate
chunks.excerpt:
### Legal availability is a separate gate

The arithmetic above does not authorize negative-amortization lending. For example, §1026.32(d)(2) prohibits a high-cost mortgage's regular payment schedule from increasing principal. The counseling requirement described next does not override that prohibition. State restrictions and other applicable federal requirements must also be checked before offering an actual product. [S5]

For covered negative-amortization counseling transactions, §1026.36(k) requires the creditor to receive documentation of qualifying HUD-certified or HUD-approved homeownership counseling before extending credit to a first-time borrower. The section applies to a closed-end, dwelling-secured transaction that may negatively amortize, with its stated reverse-mortgage and timeshare exceptions. “First-time borrower” here means a consumer who has not previously received a dwelling-secured closed-end loan **or open-end plan**—not simply someone who has never bought a home. The creditor may process the application before obtaining the documentation, but may not extend the covered credit without it; the creditor also may not steer the consumer to a particular counselor. A regular product explanation by the originator is not this counseling. [S6: §1026.36(k)(1)–(3), comments 36(k)(1)-1 through -4]

The required counseling must address the risks and consequences of negative amortization. Attendance at a generic homebuyer session without that content is not enough. [S6: comment 36(k)(1)-2]

chunks.heading: 5. Turn the product mechanics into an accurate conversation
chunks.excerpt:
## 5. Turn the product mechanics into an accurate conversation

For an applicable principal-dwelling variable-rate transaction with a term greater than one year, §1026.19(b) establishes early ARM booklet and program-disclosure requirements. Its timing depends on the application channel and the rule's exceptions. The basic timing is when the application form is provided or before a non-refundable fee, whichever occurs first, with a stated three-business-day mailing/delivery provision for telephone or intermediary/broker applications. Do not replace these requirements with “we will explain everything at closing.” This module is not an ARM notice-calendar exercise; the actual channel and full provision must be checked in the file. [S4: §1026.19(b), (b)(1)–(2)]

Where a Loan Estimate is required, the product description and Projected Payments table must reflect applicable features under §1026.37. An interest-only feature is not hidden by calling the rate fixed; where a payment feature permits negative amortization, the negative-amortization label has priority over interest-only under the prescribed hierarchy. Required disclosure projections follow their own assumptions, including rate caps and the special negative-amortization treatment. Do not populate a form by copying this lesson's one-rate illustration. [S7: §1026.37(a)(10)(ii)–(iv), (c); comments 37(a)(10)-2 and 37(c)(2)(i)-1 through -2]

chunks.heading: A usable explanation—not a waiver
chunks.excerpt:
The 2006 guidance's balanced-communication recommendation remains a useful practical discipline: describe the benefit and the material risk together, early enough to inform choice. It is a supervisory recommendation with its stated scope, not a newly invented universal disclosure form. Current applicable disclosure and consumer-protection law still controls. [S2: Consumer Protection Issues; S8]

### A usable explanation—not a waiver

For Lena's fixed-rate case, a precise explanation is:

“For the first five years your scheduled $1,800 monthly loan payment covers interest only. If you make only those payments, the $360,000 principal will still be due. With the same 6% rate, the following 25-year principal-and-interest payment is about $2,319.49. Taxes and insurance are separate from those figures. Refinancing before that change is not guaranteed.”

For the payment-option extract:

“At this month's balance and rate, $1,080 of interest accrues. Paying the permitted $800 minimum adds the unpaid $280 to your principal. Paying the minimum on time does not stop your debt from increasing. Later payment requirements depend on the contract's rate changes, balance trigger, and remaining repayment term.”

Ask the consumer to explain the consequence in their own words: “If you pay the minimum, what happens to principal?” and “What has to happen before the loan begins paying principal down?” A correct response is evidence of understanding, not a legal release of the creditor's responsibilities. If the explanation reveals confusion, resolve it; do not coach a consumer to repeat “I understand” solely to complete a checklist. [S3: comment 43(c)(1)-1.i; S2: Communications with Consumers]

### Activity 3: make the file handoff useful

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Write a short handoff for a loan that combines five-year principal deferral, an adjustable rate, a simultaneous second loan, limited liquid reserves, and variable self-employment cash flow. Separate: (a) confirmed contractual facts; (b) missing verification; (c) payment sensitivity; and (d) the decision requiring an authorized underwriter. Do not conclude that a high credit score cancels the other risks. N02 will show how to assemble the evidence rather than relying on that score or expected appreciation.

lessons.title: The first underwriting decision is which rules apply

chunks.heading: Scope and learning outcomes
chunks.excerpt:
## Scope and learning outcomes

NMLS's current CE approved-topic list, version 2026.1, includes Non-QM, collateral/portfolio lending, ARMs, and other products used to finance residential property in the Nontraditional category. This supports the proposed treatment of alternative-documentation residential underwriting here. It is not approval of this module. N01 covers payment mechanics; N02 uses distinct cases to evaluate evidence, coverage, and underwriting decisions. Do not count the same instruction toward both Federal Law and Nontraditional hours merely because a product lesson refers to Regulation Z. [S1]

Learning outcomes: distinguish credit purpose from product labels; explain the current ATR verification standard; reconcile business deposits to supported personal repayment resources; calculate the correct payment and combined monthly obligations; distinguish DTI rules from investor policies; and document an exception without allowing it to waive law.

## 1. The first underwriting decision is which rules apply

“Non-QM” is not another way to say “unregulated.” A loan outside a Qualified Mortgage definition can still be a covered transaction subject to the creditor's reasonable, good-faith ability-to-repay determination under §1026.43(c). A lender can offer a lawful non-QM product, but the label does not excuse required consideration or verification. Conversely, the fact that a property contains a house does not by itself make every loan consumer credit. [S2: §1026.43(a), (c)(1), (e); S3: §1026.3(a)]

chunks.heading: 1. The first underwriting decision is which rules apply
chunks.excerpt:
Before analyzing income, record the borrower, actual purpose, collateral, open- or closed-end structure, transaction type, and the exact coverage determination. “Broker says business purpose” is not a supported determination. Neither is “borrower is self-employed.” Someone who owns a business can obtain a consumer loan to buy their own home; someone employed on salary can borrow for a genuine business acquisition.

| Fictional transaction | Relevant initial scope conclusion | Boundary that remains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individual buys a one-unit principal residence with closed-end credit, for personal household use; no applicable exemption | Ordinarily covered by §1026.43; non-QM or bank-statement branding does not remove ATR | Apply the actual route's requirements and other applicable law |
| Individual borrows primarily to expand a business and pledges their residence | A qualifying business-purpose exemption can apply even though a residence secures it | Document actual purpose; this does not establish an exemption from every other federal or state law |
| Individual finances acquisition of a single-family rental and will not occupy it at all | Regulation Z's non-owner-occupied rental acquisition rule deems that credit business purpose | Evidence must support the facts; projected rent and lender eligibility still need assessment |
| Borrower seeks a HELOC | The HELOC is excluded from §1026.43 by (a)(1) | Other HELOC rules remain; a known simultaneous HELOC can still count in the first mortgage's ATR analysis |
| Consumer uses a trust for estate planning to hold their residence | Do not automatically treat the trust as exempt organizational credit | Comment 3(a)-10 treats specified consumer-purpose trusts as credit to a natural person |

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
The non-owner-occupied rental rule is specific. Under comment 3(a)-4, expected owner occupancy for more than 14 days in the coming year takes the property outside that special non-owner-occupied rule. Different owner-occupied rental rules and the actual primary-purpose analysis then matter; crossing that threshold does not automatically decide every transaction is consumer credit. Organizational credit also has a distinct exemption; genuine corporate borrowers and specified consumer trusts cannot be collapsed into one rule. [S3: comments 3(a)-1, -3 through -5, -9 through -10]

For this lesson's main repayment case, **assume a consumer-purpose, closed-end, dwelling-secured loan covered by §1026.43(c), with no special exemption or alternative QM compliance route**. It is not a reverse mortgage, HELOC, bridge loan, construction-phase loan, timeshare transaction, or special assistance-program loan. That assumption keeps the calculations tied to a defined rule rather than a shifting label.

lessons.title: Alternative documentation is still documentation

chunks.heading: 2. Alternative documentation is still documentation
chunks.excerpt:
## 2. Alternative documentation is still documentation

The general ATR framework asks the creditor to consider eight factors. It does not require every borrower to look like a full-time salaried employee, but it does require the creditor to support the information on which it relies. [S2: §1026.43(c)(2)]

| Factor | Evidence question for this module's file |
| --- | --- |
| Current or reasonably expected income or assets, excluding the dwelling securing the loan | What supported resources will actually be available for repayment? |
| Current employment status, if employment income is relied upon | Is the relied-on salaried or self-employment source current? |
| Payment on the covered loan | Was it calculated under the applicable §1026.43(c)(5) rule, not simply copied from the initial minimum? |
| Known or reasonably knowable simultaneous loan payment | Is another dwelling-secured loan financing part of this transaction? |
| Mortgage-related obligations | Have recurring property taxes, required insurance, association charges, and applicable other obligations been considered, whether or not escrowed? |
| Current debt obligations, alimony, and child support | What payment obligations must be included, including relevant obligations absent from the credit report? |
| Monthly DTI or residual income | Are the calculation and threshold supported under the applicable rule and underwriting method? |
| Credit history | Does the record support the assessment, rather than using the score as a substitute for the other factors? |

A complete matrix has an evidence location, an amount or conclusion, a calculation method, and unresolved questions. A box labeled “reviewed” without the actual source and reasoning is not a reproducible analysis.

chunks.heading: What the regulation actually requires
chunks.excerpt:
### What the regulation actually requires

Under §1026.43(c)(3)–(4), information relied upon generally must be verified through reasonably reliable third-party records, with the section's specific exceptions. Financial-institution records can be used; a W-2 is not the only lawful form of evidence. Records can be obtained directly from the consumer if they remain reasonably reliable and specific to that consumer. “Third-party record” refers to the evidence, not necessarily a rule that the creditor must receive every record directly from its issuer. [S2: §1026.43(c)(3)–(4), comments 43(c)(3)-1 through -2 and 43(c)(4)-1 through -3]

A bank statement establishes that a deposit occurred. It does not establish that the deposit is personal income. The official commentary specifically rejects treating an unidentified inflow as income without measures or a basis to confirm it. A borrowing, an account transfer, a refunded deposit, and a customer's payment can all appear as credits to the same account while having different economic meanings. [S2: comment 43(c)(4)-4]

chunks.heading: Joint applicants: income is not the same as obligations and history
chunks.excerpt:
Avoid making the opposite overstatement: current law does not require a separate independent verification for every obligation under every circumstance. A credit report is generally a reasonably reliable record of the obligations it reports; there are rules for inaccurate or disputed information. If the creditor relies on the report and the application states an additional current debt absent from it, §1026.43(c)(3)(iii) does not require independently verifying that stated obligation. The creditor still considers it; absence from the report is not permission to omit it. Employment status can be verified orally if a record is prepared. These narrow provisions are not general permission to accept unverified income. [S2: §1026.43(c)(3)(ii)–(iii), comments 43(c)(3)-3 and -6]

### Joint applicants: income is not the same as obligations and history

When joint applicants have primary liability on the obligation, the creditor need not use income or assets it does not need for a reasonable repayment determination. If one applicant's supported income is sufficient, the other applicant's unused income need not be considered or verified for this purpose. But the creditor must still consider the debt obligations and credit histories of all such joint applicants. Unused income does not turn a joint obligor into an invisible borrower. [S2: comments 43(c)(2)(i)-5, 43(c)(2)(vi)-2, 43(c)(2)(viii)-2 and 43(c)(4)-2]

### Different evidence without discriminatory assumptions

chunks.heading: 3. Original case: Mira's deposits are not her salary
chunks.excerpt:
Self-employment, part-time work, seasonal work, retirement benefits, and other documented sources may support repayment. The rule permits consideration of current or reasonably expected income and assets; expected income needs a reasonable, verified basis. A promise of a large future bonus without support is different from a documented expectation tied to reliable records. [S2: comments 43(c)(2)(i)-1 through -4 and 43(c)(2)(ii)-1]

Under Regulation B, a creditor may evaluate the amount and probable continuance of income but may not discount it because of a prohibited basis or merely because it is part-time income, an annuity, pension, or other retirement benefit. ATR does not authorize prohibited inquiries. A document request should address a material underwriting fact, not assumptions about age, family plans, national origin, or a borrower's preferred way of working. [S4: §1002.6(b)(5); S2: comment 43(c)(1)-3]

## 3. Original case: Mira's deposits are not her salary

Mira owns 100% of a small design business and is a joint applicant with salaried co-borrower Owen for a personal principal-residence loan. They are considering the interest-only Non-QM structure described in §4. For this educational exercise, the credit department has obtained reasonably reliable third-party financial records and corroborating business records supporting the following classification. This is a stipulated fact of the fictional exercise—not a claim that StateCourse verified a real business.

chunks.heading: 3. Original case: Mira's deposits are not her salary
chunks.excerpt:
| Twelve-month business-account credits | Amount | Evidence-supported treatment |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Total incoming credits | $360,000 | Starting point, not personal income |
| Transfer from Mira's separate savings | $36,000 | Remove from operating revenue; moving existing funds is not new revenue |
| Business equipment-loan proceeds | $24,000 | Remove from revenue; financing inflow, with the associated debt addressed separately |
| Return of a refundable lease deposit | $12,000 | Remove from recurring operating revenue under this exercise's facts |
| Customer operating receipts after those adjustments | $288,000 | Supported business revenue |
| Supported recurring business expenses | $180,000 | Deduct once under the stipulated cash-flow method |
| Supported annual income available to Mira before personal income taxes | $108,000 | $288,000−$180,000 |
| Monthly equivalent used in this exercise | $9,000 | $108,000÷12 |

Assume the expense figure includes all relevant recurring business costs and business debt service for the exercise; there are no additional retained working-capital requirements, ownership distributions to others, duplicated transactions, or unavailable funds in that stipulated $108,000. Those assumptions would require support in a real file. The property-related and household obligations used later are separate, and are not already deducted here.

chunks.heading: Why plausible shortcuts produce different answers
chunks.excerpt:
The point is not that every lender must use exactly 12 months or exactly this expense method. Section 1026.43(c) does not prescribe that universal method. It permits technical underwriting criteria consistent with a reasonable, good-faith determination; a particular product or investor may require a longer history, a different permitted calculation, or additional records. Such program conditions must be stated as program conditions, not as an invented federal formula. [S2: comment 43(c)(2)-1]

### Why plausible shortcuts produce different answers

Dividing all $360,000 of credits by 12 yields $30,000, more than three times the supported $9,000. Removing only transfers is insufficient because it still counts financing and other non-operating inflows, while ignoring expenses. Adding Mira's draws from the business to the $108,000 would also be wrong if the draws distribute the same earnings already counted. A payment from one account to another does not create another dollar of repayment capacity.

A blanket assumed expense factor is not made reliable merely by calling the product “bank statement.” If a lender's permitted method uses an expense factor, identify the actual policy, its conditions, and its reasonable application to the business facts. If the file already establishes materially higher expenses, ignoring that evidence to obtain a qualifying result is not justified by the label. [S2: §1026.43(c)(1), (c)(4); comments 43(c)(1)-1 and 43(c)(4)-4]

### Activity 1: identify what still needs reconciliation

The file receives three new items before the repayment decision:

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
1. A bank statement includes a $9,000 credit marked only “online transfer.”
2. Mira states that a customer responsible for one-third of annual revenue has ended its contract.
3. A reviewer suggests adding the business's $40,000 cash balance as a freely available personal asset, even though payroll and vendor bills are due from it.

Write the next evidence request for each item without accusing Mira of wrongdoing. The objective is to establish source, reasonable continuity, ownership, and availability. For item 1, obtain a basis to classify the credit; for item 2, assess current/reasonably expected income with corroborating evidence instead of relying mechanically on the old average; for item 3, establish whether funds can be withdrawn without undermining the business cash flow already supporting the loan. An unsupported answer remains unresolved; it is not converted to verified income by a checkbox.

The commentary distinguishes an unforeseeable post-consummation job loss from an income change evident before consummation. The creditor does not insure against every future event, but cannot disregard known evidence of a material repayment change in its determination. Do not manufacture a rule requiring prohibited personal inquiries in the name of predicting every change. [S2: comment 43(c)(1)-2 through -3]

lessons.title: Original case continued: use the payment the rule requires

chunks.heading: 4. Original case continued: use the payment the rule requires
chunks.excerpt:
## 4. Original case continued: use the payment the rule requires

For this step, return to the original supported $9,000 monthly Mira income; the three new uncertainties in Activity 1 are separate hypotheticals, not silently resolved facts. Owen has $3,200 of supported monthly gross salary. Assume both sources satisfy the fictional lender's documentation and continuity standards. Total monthly income used: **$12,200**.

The proposed covered loan has:

- $480,000 principal; 30-year total term.
- Fixed 6.50% annual rate; 60 interest-only monthly payments.
- No negative amortization, additional advance, capitalized fee, balloon, or extra principal payment.
- 300 monthly amortizing payments after the interest-only period.
- $950 of supported recurring monthly property taxes, insurance, and association charges in total; assume no other recurring mortgage-related obligations for this exercise.
- A simultaneous HELOC, secured by the same dwelling and known to the first creditor, with a required payment of $400 on the amount to be drawn at or before first-mortgage consummation. This figure has been calculated correctly from the plan's terms for the exercise.
- $700 in other current monthly debt obligations; no additional alimony or child-support obligation under the fictional facts.

Under §1026.43(c)(5)(ii)(B), the payment calculation uses $480,000 at 6.50% over the **remaining 300 months**, producing approximately **$3,240.99** of qualifying monthly P&I. The initial interest-only payment is $2,600, but that is not the qualifying P&I in this calculation. [S2: §1026.43(c)(5)(ii)(B), comment -1]

chunks.heading: The mistaken worksheet
chunks.excerpt:
| Included monthly obligation | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Covered loan's qualifying P&I | $3,240.99 |
| Recurring mortgage-related obligations | $950.00 |
| Known simultaneous HELOC payment | $400.00 |
| Other current monthly debts | $700.00 |
| Total monthly debt used | $5,290.99 |

`DTI = $5,290.994374... ÷ $12,200 × 100 = 43.37% approximately.`

`Monthly residual income under §1026.43(c)(7) = $12,200 − $5,290.994374... = $6,909.01 approximately.`

That regulatory residual-income calculation is **not** a statement that $6,909 is free discretionary cash after income taxes and all living expenses. The defined subtraction uses the specified income and debt inputs. A reasonable assessment may require attention to known recurring non-debt living expenses; the figure should not be misrepresented to the consumer as disposable income. [S2: §1026.43(c)(7); comment 43(c)(1)-1.ii.B.5]

### The mistaken worksheet

An originator uses $2,600 interest-only, adds $950 and $700, and omits the HELOC because it is absent from the credit report. The worksheet yields:

`($2,600+$950+$700) ÷ $12,200 = 34.84% approximately.`

That result understates the calculation by about 8.53 percentage points. Its two defects are independent: the wrong first-loan payment and the missing known simultaneous debt. Fixing only one leaves the other wrong. The first creditor's obligation to consider the known HELOC does not disappear because the HELOC itself is outside §1026.43. [S2: §1026.43(c)(2)(iv), (c)(5)(ii)(B), (c)(6)(ii); comments 43(c)(2)(iv)-1 through -2 and 43(c)(3)-4]

chunks.heading: Activity 2: can this loan be approved now?
chunks.excerpt:
For a simultaneous HELOC, the specific §1026.43(c)(6)(ii) calculation uses the plan's required periodic payment and the amount to be drawn at or before consummation. Do not say that this provision always requires the entire undrawn line limit, and do not assume zero when the transaction relies on a draw. A separate investor may impose a stricter stress test, but identify that as an additional program rule.

### Activity 2: can this loan be approved now?

Assume a fictional lender's written policy permits up to 45% DTI on this product, subject to all its other conditions and applicable law. At 43.37%, the example passes that **one policy screen**. It is not automatically approved. The authorized underwriter still needs the full current evidence, required considerations, documented exception decisions if any, and other applicable product/legal checks.

Now test a second version: Owen's supported qualifying salary is $2,400, not $3,200. Total income becomes $11,400. With unchanged obligations, DTI becomes approximately **46.41%**, and defined monthly residual becomes approximately **$6,109.01**. This version fails the fictional 45% policy screen absent a valid permitted policy exception. Federal law is not waived by a policy exception, and an originator should not edit income or omit obligations to get the ratio below 45%.

## 5. The obsolete 43% shortcut and the non-QM distinction

chunks.heading: 5. The obsolete 43% shortcut and the non-QM distinction
chunks.excerpt:
There is no universal maximum DTI in the general §1026.43(c) rule; the creditor determines an appropriate threshold in making its reasonable, good-faith decision. Nor should a 2026 course teach that the current General QM definition always caps DTI at 43%. The current official commentary explains that the General QM amendments removed that requirement and replaced it with pricing thresholds, among other revisions. The current General QM rule still requires consideration of income/assets, debts, and DTI or residual income, and verification under the specified provisions. [S2: comment 43(c)(7)-1; §1026.43(e)(2)(v)–(vi), comment 43(e)(2)-1]

General QM is not simply “DTI low enough” or “APR low enough.” Its requirements also concern regular payments and prohibited features, term, points and fees, qualifying-payment methodology, consideration and verification, and the applicable pricing test. Annual dollar thresholds and the relevant transaction characteristics must be checked in the operative rule. Special government, small-creditor, balloon, and other QM routes are distinct; this lesson does not qualify a file for them by implication. [S2: §1026.43(e)(2)–(7), (f)]

The main case's interest-only feature defers principal, so it does not satisfy the **General QM** payment-feature requirement in §1026.43(e)(2)(i). That is a feature-based conclusion, not a consequence of its DTI being 43.37%. A fully amortizing ARM is not disqualified from General QM solely because its rate adjusts; it still must meet the full applicable criteria. Non-QM is not a synonym for an illegal loan, bad credit, or no documentation. [S2: §1026.43(e)(2)(i), comment 43(e)(2)(i)-1 through -2]

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
Neither passing ATR nor qualifying as a QM is a universal statement that a product is the cheapest, the best personal choice, or free of every legal issue. Regulation Z's ATR standard should not be relabeled a universal “suitability” or fiduciary test with invented requirements. Applicable anti-steering, fair-lending, consumer-protection, state broker duties, and investor rules remain separate questions. A sound comparison explains options and costs without making a legal claim broader than the actual analysis supports.

lessons.title: Alternative repayment case: assets and access

chunks.heading: 6. Alternative repayment case: assets and access
chunks.excerpt:
## 6. Alternative repayment case: assets and access

Rafael has documented financial assets but limited current employment income. It is not inherently improper to evaluate supported assets other than the collateral dwelling. Section 1026.43(c)(2)(i) permits such assets; employment status needs verification under (c)(2)(ii) only if employment income is relied upon. The creditor still must make the full applicable repayment determination. [S2: comments 43(c)(2)(i)-1 and 43(c)(2)(ii)-1]

For this isolated worksheet, assume a **fictional educational policy** converts verified available financial assets into a monthly equivalent over 240 months. It excludes amounts earmarked for closing, pledged assets unavailable for withdrawal, and a separate protected reserve. This is not a federal asset-depletion formula or an actual StateCourse policy.

| Asset adjustment | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Verified account holdings before adjustments | $300,000 |
| Funds committed to closing | −$40,000 |
| Separate pledged portion unavailable for withdrawal | −$50,000 |
| Separate reserve excluded by this fictional policy | −$30,000 |
| Remaining amount permitted in this worksheet | $180,000 |
| Monthly equivalent under the stipulated 240-month method | $750 |

Assume the three deductions concern distinct portions and no further tax, withdrawal, valuation, or access adjustment is needed for this exercise. In an actual file, those issues require analysis. Dividing the entire $300,000 by 60 to claim $5,000 a month both ignores restrictions and invents a different depletion period. It is not an equivalent calculation.

chunks.heading: Activity 3: a source-and-availability note
chunks.excerpt:
A consumer's $700,000 collateral dwelling is different from the $180,000 available financial assets. The dwelling value cannot replace the income/assets considered under §1026.43(c)(2)(i). An appraisal may establish collateral value for a lender's separate credit decision, but it does not turn unavailable equity into monthly repayment resources under that factor. Do not count the same fund as both an asset being consumed and a perpetual income stream without a supported method addressing that interaction. [S2: §1026.43(c)(2)(i), (c)(4); comments 43(c)(2)(i)-1 and 43(c)(7)-3]

### Activity 3: a source-and-availability note

Draft three lines for Rafael: the issuer/date of the supporting asset record; the reason for each exclusion; and the authority for the conversion method. Mark the conversion method as lender policy, the asset-availability facts as verified or unresolved, and the ATR requirement as law. This separation lets another reviewer change a fact or policy without accidentally rewriting the rule.

## 7. Residential investment comparison: DSCR is not a universal escape hatch

For a distinct case, Serena seeks credit solely to acquire a single-family rental property she will not occupy at all. Assume the actual purpose and use are supported and the special non-owner-occupied rental acquisition rule applies. Regulation Z treats that credit as business purpose. A property-cash-flow calculation can be relevant to this residential-investment product; it is not evidence that every loan called “DSCR” receives this exemption. [S3: comment 3(a)-4; S1]

chunks.heading: Primary sources and authority boundaries
chunks.excerpt:
This exercise defines a fictional lender's debt-service coverage ratio as annual net operating income divided by annual debt service. No federal rule cited here requires this exact formula, vacancy allowance, threshold, or approval result.

| Input | Base case | Separate stress case |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Scheduled annual rent | $36,000 | $33,000 |
| Vacancy/collection allowance | −$3,000 | −$6,000 |
| Operating expenses, excluding the debt service below | −$10,000 | −$11,000 |
| Net operating income | $23,000 | $16,000 |
| Annual debt service | $20,000 | $20,000 |
| DSCR under this exercise's formula | 1.15 | 0.80 |

If the fictional base-case policy screen is 1.10, the base case passes that screen. The stress case shows a $4,000 annual cash-flow shortfall before any other uncovered costs. Neither result alone authorizes the loan. The reviewer evaluates reliable lease/rent evidence, realistic operating costs, reserves, collateral, product changes, and the actual lender criteria. Vacancy and variable debt-service risk are specifically discussed in the older supervisory guidance for non-owner-occupied nontraditional loans; that discussion is an institution-focused risk framework, not a nationwide law mandating this worksheet. [S5: Non-Owner-Occupied Investor Loans]

If Serena instead intends to use the loan for her personal principal residence, writing “DSCR” on the form does not let the lender replace a covered consumer ATR analysis with property rent assumptions. Escalate the changed facts and determine coverage correctly. Do not advise borrowers to misstate occupancy or purpose to fit a product.
